# Patrologia Latina, vol. 156

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

A complete, uniform, integral, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture and in what passages of their works. An edition of the greatest accuracy, and readily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, the smallness of the price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred volumes of the Latin edition cost 1,000 francs; the three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition, 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1104: Venerable Guibert, Abbot of Saint Mary of Novigento

[Col. 0009]

# The Works of Guibert

They now come to light for the first time, together with an appendix to Book Three of *On His Life*, namely, the three books of Hermann the monk *On the Miracles of Saint Mary*, or *On the Restoration of the Church of Laon*; *On the Deeds of Bartholomew, Bishop*; and *On the Origin and Growth of the Premonstratensian Order*. Also included are notes and observations, filled with ancient records, on certain books of Venerable Guibert.

To these are added supplements containing the *Lives of Saint Geremar, Blessed Simon Count of Crespy, and Saint Salaberga the Abbess*; likewise the three books of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, *On the Dogmas of the Christian Faith against the Heretics of His Time*; and the *Additions* of Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel together with the genuine *Appendix to Sigebert*.

All prepared through the study and labor of Dom Lucas d’Achery, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

(Paris, at the expense of Jean Billaine, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of Saint Augustine, 1651.)

# Preface

## To the Most Illustrious Lord Matthew Molé, First President of the Parliament of Paris

I freely confess, most illustrious First President, that I have not adequately understood with what intention this Guibert of ours desires once again to travel through the world. For many stretches of time Guibert’s book had slept among the dead in the quiet station of a library. Who has awakened it?

Certainly, he did not hate the light—he who, with the greatest labor and care, never ceased to drive from human minds, both openly and in writing, the pestilential darkness of so many errors and heresies of his age, and to carry a torch before the heralds of the divine word and theological truth. Just as he once shone upon his contemporaries by his speech, so now he shines upon posterity through his writing, like a wise abbot rising anew; mindful of the saying of the wisest king, or rather of uncreated Wisdom: “What advantage is there in hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure?” [Note: [Col. 0009] Ecclesiasticus 41:17.]

Yet this learned scribe remembers that the person who brings forth from his treasure things new and old [Note: [Col. 0009] Matthew 13] also knows that truth produces hatred, that in every age there are people who curse the day [Note: [Col. 0009] Job 3:8], and that those who flee the light, lest their private deeds be exposed, attack the works of others.

How, then, does he not fear bidding farewell to such a long repose? Why does he dare, in these times, to open not merely a shining but an accusatory truth? As far as I understand, most illustrious First President, he has decided now also to employ the same plan that he used while alive.

Whenever he had put the finishing hand to some work and wished to make it public, he considered nothing more important than winning the hearts of the great and securing patrons greater than his teaching—teaching which, although entirely in agreement with the writings of the holy Fathers, attacked errors clinging to deep roots, depraved conduct, and wicked customs, and would have been endangered had not a higher authority protected it as it emerged.

What wonder, then, if in our own age he hesitates to come into public except under the auspices of some most vigorous and wise defender? But whom, indeed, could the most diligent abbot desire more vigorous or wiser than you? In this storm of most serious times, when he observes the anxious cares of Your Eminence—cares through which you administer not only reciprocal legal disputes and the affairs of clients but also watch over the safety of the whole kingdom—he does not hang back from presenting himself at your threshold, nor does he fear troubling a man wearied by business. For he knows that, by the light of intellect with which you are endowed, you have emerged superior through the full exertion of both mind and strength. He knew that the unconquered Molé was refreshed by the weight of such great affairs, never crushed by it.

Having therefore found a most illustrious hero, a man seated upon—and indeed presiding over—the throne of Themis, Guibert returns more freely to life with the many offspring of his intellect, surviving under your protection. He greatly rejoices that light has been restored to himself and to his works under you as supreme judge.

In this matter Guibert is certainly not endowed with ordinary prudence: he considers himself safe only beneath the insignia of this most equitable president, under whose patronage he would place himself if he were alive. Rather, he is enlightened by singular wisdom, for, on account of the envy of certain people, he places his cause with Molé so that it may not fall. “For the causes of war stand ready” [Note: [Col. 0011] Virgil, *Aeneid* 7]—that is, he seeks to avert something from his cause before Molé.

For who would dare resist a supreme judge who is also most just? If you judge Guibert guilty of nothing, he will be innocent. If he is acceptable to your equity, the envy that rivals virtue will neither help nor harm him, since everyone will easily regard him as confirmed and complete in his own measure once the president of the most searching judgment has approved him as worthy of his assent and name.

Happy indeed is he to have found such a patron—one wholly devoted to royal and public affairs, who considers it the greatest happiness if he may offer and devote his whole self most willingly to defending learned men, and especially those who profess a more secluded life. Thus I raise to praise a dead prelate who desires to offer himself and his possessions to one who lives well and happily, sees the rights of all, and presides over the laws.

You see, therefore, most clear-sighted prince of the Senate, why the abbot of Novigento takes refuge in your bosom and in that of justice; why he presents himself uniquely to you; why he seeks honor in your purple; why he looks for authority in your wisdom; and why he asks that your name be placed at the front of his works.

Again, when he attempts to revive through his devotion before the whole world and to tear open his own burial and darkness [Note: [Col. 0011] Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 12], why should he not immediately turn toward the sun of the Gallic world? I call you the sun who watches over so many stars, the august crowns of senators [Note: [Col. 0011] Trebellius Pollio, *On Claudius*; Pliny, book 34], whom so many Fathers adorned with purple also admire:

“They know their own sun and their own stars” [Note: [Col. 0011] *Aeneid* 6];

and thus, with you judging and commanding, he rises like Lucifer, never destined to suffer eclipse, much less setting.

But if—although he has fully pleaded his cause in his writings—he should fear the judgment of the half-learned, among whom there is much malice and little wisdom [Note: [Col. 0011] Saint Bernard], is it any wonder if he appeals to you as the workshop of all the sciences, the end, perfection, and limit of human understanding [Note: [Col. 0011] Averroes, *On Aristotle’s On the Soul*, book 3], and, as the matter requires, as a judge who severely punishes the guilty?

These considerations seemed more than sufficient for Guibert’s votive offering, most illustrious First President, although many other and equally weighty motives moved him.

First, he was moved by your singular devotion to God, your remarkable justice, and your heavenly temperance.

Your devotion: by which, bound and linked to God, you worship and follow him with your inmost mind; and by which, as first president of the supreme court, you never cease, with exalted spirit, to render worship to him as the first principle of all things.

Your justice: by which, exercising the highest right over yourself, you refer yourself and all that is yours to the supreme Judge.

Your temperance: by which you lay down—and, more than that, submit—the dominion over which you hold power under the king to the supreme Lord of all things.

Therefore you owe not to me, nor to Guibert, but to your virtues the fact that the abbot devotes himself to you, since you have devoted yourself entirely to God. You owe it that the suppliant man of Novigento has recourse to the oracles of your justice, since you profess that everything is owed to the authority of the just Judge and that you exercise his office. You owe it that the dead comes to life again through you, since you long ago consecrated your soul to God, the author of life and death.

You were also moved by your outstanding devotion to the king and fatherland, which Tertullian called “the religion of the second majesty” [Note: [Col. 0011] *Apology*, ch. 35]. Thus it is true that nothing more excellent than this devotion of yours can be said or imagined. It was this devotion by which, amid so many dangers of destruction, you raised, supported, and strengthened the tottering condition of affairs. It was this by which, sustaining such a great burden of affairs upon your unbending shoulder, you made the kingdom of France immovable, firmly supported by the threefold fruit of this devotion of yours—faith, constancy, and prudence—as by the strongest pillars.

Hence it comes about that you admire not only your own prudence but also that of Louis the Just, whose memory is immortal: yours, when he chose you as first president of the Senate; his, when you managed everything with skill. The king made you as great as you are in the administration of justice; and you happily restored authority to the king and to his excellent son Louis, who reigns happily, after banishing savage danger.

Thus, through you, the king—who had never ceased to be king—was in a certain sense king more securely, when, after the metropolis of France had been reconciled to its prince from whom it had never truly fallen away, he appeared to have been more firmly established upon his throne.

On the other hand, if you cherish Guibert, if he shines at his birth, at your command, because he is ours, you will demonstrate not only the benevolence with which you regard this abbot but also your incredible humanity toward me and toward all the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

Indeed, no one is unaware of how clearly you demonstrated this long ago. We have learned what the beginnings of our family were in France; we observe its growth; we recognize both benefits that Your Eminence has continuously bestowed upon our congregation. Friends rejoice, and even those who are not favorable cannot deny, that both have flowed from your kindness as from a most abundant spring and continue to endure.

For when you were fulfilling the office of royal procurator, you received the congregation as it was being born with care. Then, when your virtue raised you to the highest tribunal of justice, you did not even then lay aside your role as its guardian. Rather, supporting it with greater authority, you helped the young institution by your protection, strengthened it by your efforts, and defended it by right.

Moreover, Your Eminence indicated to me, with your courtesy toward all, that you were extraordinarily pleased by the venerable learning of ancient writers. When I presented to you the letter of Saint Barnabas, elucidated by our Menard and dedicated to your name, your authority—which is supreme in my eyes—shone before me as I searched libraries, raised teachers of an earlier age from the dust, and restored them to their former brilliance.

You will therefore also be pleased with the little work that I have devoted, however modestly, to publishing these observations—not because I can bring light to Guibert, but because I am striving, in some measure, to moderate the excessive brilliance that might perhaps dazzle weak eyes.

You will be pleased with it, I say, because, having been sown and grown in the soil of your Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur, it is returned to you by full and solid right: surely the fruits follow the owner of the land.

Finally, you will be pleased not because I published it, but because you judged and commanded it. For God gave you supreme judgment over affairs, while the glory of obedience was left to me [Note: [Col. 0013] Tacitus, book 6, after the beginning]. It was also left to all the members of our congregation, as all their wishes convey and profess.

Most devoted to Your Eminence,

**Brother Lucas d’Achery**

[Col. 0013]

# To the Reader

[Col. 0013A]

Since I have attached to the observations many things that ought to have been said here in advance, there is no need, learned reader, for me to detain you with a lengthy preface. I shall merely give you these few preliminary remarks.

I was often and for a long time doubtful and uncertain whether I should devote study and labor to publishing the works of Venerable Guibert of Novigento. There were, after all, older works at hand. In the meantime, however, I met men distinguished in learning, wisdom, and piety. While conversing with them about ancient authors who had until then been wrapped in darkness, I happened upon the abbot mentioned above, a disciple of the great Anselm. After we had more than once exchanged discussions about his hidden learning, his doctrine, the beauty of his language, and his eloquence, they repeatedly urged me—and some even entreated me—to undertake, as a Benedictine, the task of committing the Benedictine works to the press.

Moved by their persuasion, I immediately and willingly set myself to the work. I examined the papers with the greatest diligence; met inquisitive investigators of antiquity; personally inspected, or arranged to have inspected, the shelves and cases of all the libraries to which access was available; and sought out everything that occurred to my mind that might illuminate this matter.

First, concerning the little book *How a Discourse Ought to Be Delivered*:

[Col. 0014A]

The Royal Library supplied the *Commentaries*, or ten books of the *Moral Reflections on Genesis*.

An extremely ancient copy of the *Tropologies on Hosea, Amos, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah*, formerly belonging to the monastery of Vaucelles of the Cistercian Congregation in the diocese of Cambrai, was supplied ten years ago by my brother Eustace d’Achery.

The treatise *On the Incarnation against the Jews*;

the book *On the Praise of Blessed Mary*;

and the little work *On Virginity* I extracted from a manuscript of the College of Paris of the Society of Jesus, on the indication of the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond.

As for the letter *On the Morsel Given to Judas*, I first had it copied from the library of the distinguished John Bigot, senator of the tax court at Rouen; then I collated it with two manuscripts, one belonging to the Royal Library and the other to the Paris College of the Society of Jesus.

[Col. 0014B]

The Royal Library lent three books *On the Relics of the Saints*.

For the rest, the manuscripts mentioned above from that library, as well as those of the Paris College, were formerly, if one may trust conjectures, the property of the monastery of Novigento and therefore of Guibert. The beginning of each volume indicates this, since the manuscripts preserve the age of Guibert himself.

The *History of Jerusalem*, or *The Deeds of God through the Franks*, was first published by Jacques Bongars in 1611, together with other writers of the same history. He gave that collection the title borrowed from Guibert, *The Deeds of God through the Franks*. In this repeated edition, however, we have divided the books into chapters.

A codex of Saint Remigius of Rheims, written in an exceptionally fine hand, supplied what was missing at the end of the ninth book in the edition published by another author. We also used another ancient manuscript of Corbie, by which we removed in many places blemishes that had perhaps crept in through the fault of copyists or the carelessness of printers. We arranged the verses in order according to poetic practice and adorned the margins here and there with various annotations.

[Col. 0015A]

Finally, I was able to find only a copy of our abbot’s books *On His Life*. It was written in a clear and more recent hand, but was filled with many errors: words were reversed, and sentences were sometimes altered or entirely omitted, so that several things had almost to be divined by me after closer examination. In other places, where words had escaped me, I supplied dots in their place or wrote other readings in the margin.

I had indeed heard, and had often been told, that the autograph was preserved in our own time among the ancient codices of the Church of Laon and had later been collated by an expert in antiquities, Monsieur Dey, a Doctor of Paris who has since died. I moved every stone to discover into whose hands it had subsequently passed, but in vain.

Since Guibert, in the third book *On His Life*, relates especially how the citizens of Laon raged like the most savage marauders, sparing neither sex, rank, nor any age, filling everything with slaughter and blood; how they put their shepherd to a most bitter death; how they burned the episcopal church; and how they committed other cruelties of that kind, I judged it highly appropriate to append, as it were, the three books of Hermann the monk *On the Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon*. They not only contain an extensive history of the restoration of both the city and the church of Laon, but also acknowledge Guibert as a contemporary writer.

Besides the works of Guibert listed above, he himself records in Book One of *On His Life*, chapter 16, that he published a little *Capitular Book on Various Sayings of the Gospels and Prophetic Books*. Yet it undoubtedly lies to this day somewhere covered in dust and neglect; or rather, I should say that it was suppressed by its own author, since one may infer from his words that it was far from polished:

“I postpone bringing this little book to an end until now, because, after completing what I presently possess, I intend, if God suggests it, to exercise myself several times in similar matters.”

For wherever I suspected that the little book might be hidden, I searched with useless effort.

I have illustrated certain minor works of the author with observations and notes—not so much of my own initiative as at the direction and command of those to whom I am bound by votive obedience and whom I consider it a religious duty not to disobey. I shall briefly explain what I have accomplished in them.

[Col. 0016A]

When I noticed that many monuments of antiquity were at hand, especially from the Middle Ages and from the age of our author—for I cite unpublished authors as testimony more often, and others much more rarely—I resolved, whenever the opportunity arose, to weave them into the work from time to time. My purpose was to satisfy, to some extent and until our own people prepare greater works, those who desire such materials.

In these matters I resolved to discuss everything and to examine everything with the greatest fidelity. Nevertheless, I know and fully recognize that no one is so fortunate as to be exempt from error, and that this belongs not to a madman but to a human being.

Therefore, benevolent reader, it will be the mark of your fairness if you correct gently and amicably whatever errors you find. If any documents, charters, or similar materials displease you, I ask that you not let them trouble you. For who could satisfy the wishes of all people?

[Col. 0016B]

When I observed that the volume would not grow to its usual size, I appended several additions to the observations intended to illuminate Guibert’s books *On His Life*: namely, the *Life of Saint Geremar the Abbot* from the monastery of Conches; the *Life of Blessed Simon, Count of Crespy*, which was sent to me from a manuscript of the monastery of Ourscamp; and the *Life of Saint Salaberga*, first abbess of Saint John of Laon.

The latter had indeed a model [or copy], but it was so full of errors that I would have entirely abandoned hope of publishing it, had not our Dom Placid Bertheau been available to correct and amend it with the help of the manuscript of Ourscamp. Its almost innumerable errors can be seen corrected in the margins.

You will find the reason for my decision to bring these lives into public circulation on pages 596, 602, and 652. [Note: [Col. 0015] The bold numbers inserted into our text represent the pages of the Acherian edition. Editor of the Patrology.]

Next comes the distinguished little work of Hugh of Rouen, divided into three books, *Against the Heretics of His Time*. Having until now struggled with mildew and moths, we copied it from a manuscript of Saint Martin of Paris and now make it public. You will see Hugh’s eulogies and letters on page 687 and following.

Moreover, there are the *Additions* of Robert of Torigni, commonly called Robert of Mont, that is, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount, or Mount Saint Michael in the Sea of Danger, together with the *Genuine Appendix to Sigebert*, and also the treatises *On the Changes of Monks*, *On the Abbots and Abbeys of the Normans*, and *On Their Builders*.

I was provided with two copies of the Appendix: one original copy from Saint Michael’s Mount, which I noted below on page 715, and another from the monastery of Jumièges. The latter is in some places shorter than the former. Matters absent from the copy from the Mount are indicated by italic type, an asterisk, and a marginal note.

It is worth your while, reader, to observe that at the beginning of the manuscript, as well as in the prologue and in the title of the Appendix itself under discussion, it is stated that Robert extended the Appendix to the year 1184. Yet in the prologue to that Appendix he professes to have composed it only as far as the year 1182.

[Col. 0017A]

From this one may somewhat doubt whether Robert, after completing the prologue, proceeded farther, or whether someone else composed the sequence of two years together with its continuation.

You ask what finally moved me to publish these works. You will learn this from the prefatory address placed there, on page 715.

As for those who assisted me, I have not omitted their names in their proper places, besides those praised in this preface—both to discharge my obligation of truthfulness and, above all, to commemorate with gratitude the labors and benefits of others.

Yet certain men must not be passed over, especially the most distinguished Putean brothers, famous for their varied learning. They lent whatever manuscripts were needed, both from the Royal Library and from their own, with their customary courtesy and from their naturally uncommon affection for learned men.

Francis Duchesne, well acquainted with historical matters, freely supplied, among other things, the *History of the Canon of Laon*, written in the hand of his own father, André Duchesne.

And our Philip de Romagny, learned in earnest and without ambition, undertook much work and labor, both in copying the various works contained in this volume and finally in annotating passages of Sacred Scripture.

These remarks concern the author’s works and additions. Farewell, reader, and love the man who helps—or at least wishes to help.

[Col. 0017]

# Summary of the Life of Venerable Guibert, Abbot

*(I have judged it useful to place briefly before your eyes, in advance, a summary of Guibert’s deeds while you read through the complete books of his* On His Life*.)*

[Col. 0017B]

Guibert, born in the town of Beauvais, set aside the splendor of his birth and donned the monastic habit at Flaviac, or the monastery of Saint Geremar, likewise in the diocese of Beauvais. There he was thoroughly educated both in piety and in letters.

He especially boasts, in Book One of *On His Life*, that he was instructed by Saint Anselm of Canterbury, then prior of the monastery of Bec—who frequently visited Guibert out of affection—in the manner in which the divine page ought to be understood and opened up.

When Guibert’s reputation for religious devotion, prudence, and learning had spread far and wide, he was finally elected by the monks of Blessed Mary of Novigento, situated in the territory of Laon near Coucy, as abbot in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1104.

For twenty years in this office he conducted himself admirably, wisely, and prudently. He devoted himself both to composing various works and to the salvation of souls through his sermons—he declares that whatever he interpreted from Sacred Scripture he interpreted for the benefit of preachers—as well as to refuting heretics, both publicly and in writing.

His writings everywhere testify that he was deeply devoted to the Mother of God. He died in the year 1124 of the restored salvation.

[Col. 0017]

# Testimonies Concerning Abbot Guibert

## Manasses, Bishop of Soissons

In the charter printed below, on page 625:

[Col. 0017C]

“Indeed, Dom Wibertus was in charge of that monastery, Novigento; by his wisdom and innocence he bound us very closely to himself.”

And shortly afterward:

“The same abbot, by the religious counsel in which he excelled,” and so forth.

## The Old Manuscript Martyrology of the Church of Laon

“This and many other matters pertaining to such an enormous crime were written with complete faith and truth by the aforesaid abbot, Guibert, who was present in those days,” and so forth.

See the observations on page 652.

## The Canon of Laon in a Manuscript Chronicle

Of this work we shall speak below, on page 646:

“This Galdricus, when he had once returned from the dedication of the church,” and so forth, “saying in the vernacular that Abbot Wibertus had thus explained it poetically,” and so forth.

## John Halgrin, Cardinal, Called of Abbeville

In the manuscript *Summa* preserved in the library of Saint Michael’s Mount, he cites Guibert in various places in the following manner:

[Col. 0017D]

“Guibert in the *Moral Reflections on Genesis*,” and so forth.

## Jacques Bongars in His Preface

“Guibert, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Novigento, which is situated beneath the castle of Coucy in the district of Laon” [Col. 0018C]—as appears from the title of the work itself and the end of the preface.

He lived in the very age whose history he partly describes. He wrote during the reign of Baldwin, brother of Godfrey: Book Two, chapter 12, and Book Seven, chapter 21.

He wrote of Bohemond, husband of Constance, daughter of the king of the Franks, at the end of Book One.

He wrote two years after the death of Manasses, Archbishop of Rheims, at the end of Book Six.

He completed his writing after Bohemond had already died: the last book, chapter 38.

He wrote in the year after the martyrdom of Gervase, an excellent knight: the same book, chapter 40.

He professes himself an interpreter of another person’s history: Book Two, chapters 10 and 13.

The same appears in the letter to Lisiard and in the preface that follows it: the same undertaking had been carried out on the same subject by Robert the monk and by Baldric, as stated above.

Like them, he supplied what was lacking from the reports of those who had seen the events: Book Two, chapter 3; Book Three, chapter 13; Book Seven, chapter 24; and the last book, and so forth.

He followed an obscure manner of writing, avoiding, as he himself says, crude and inelegant expressions: at the beginning of Book Five. He calls it “careful elegance of language” at the end of the letter to Lisiard.

[Col. 0018D]

That he was born of noble stock appears from Book Four, the final chapter, where he tells of a military man distinguished by knightly office who had held the benefices of his parents and owed them homage.

In Book Five, chapter 15, he refrains from expressing the municipal surname of the brothers William and Alberic, out of respect for their modesty, being bound to their family by a friendly kinship. Yet he gives the name that Baldric suppresses, calling William “of Grantmesnil,” on page 114, line 28:

“For we ought not,” he says, “to spare the infamy of those who, excessively fearful for themselves, did not spare their own reputation.”

He was also known to the Greeks: in Anna Comnena’s *Alexiad* he is **γελίελμος ὁ σραντεμανη**, “William of Grantmesnil.” [The transmitted Greek is uncertain.]

Tyre, in Book Six, chapter 5, calls him an illustrious man from Apulia who had the sister of Bohemond as his wife. The French translators give a fuller account: “a great man born in Normandy, who held many places in Apulia.”

More on these matters may be found in the indexes, if God grants that I complete them.

He criticizes the history of Fulcher of Chartres, which he had not read, on the basis of hearsay: the last book, chapters 29, 30, 31, 38, and 39.

At the end of his work he excuses himself if anything has been explained less carefully by him, because he is occupied with another profession and has described things he did not see with excessive timidity. Yet he himself testifies that he wrote other works, at the beginning of Book Five and in the letter to Lisiard.

He mentions expositions of Genesis and other treatises.

The title that Guibert gave his work—otherwise a genuinely scholastic title—we have assigned to this collection: *The Deeds of God through the Franks*. No other title could be imagined that is either more suitable or truer.

Just as we say that God is in heaven, not because he is not elsewhere, since he is everywhere, so we call these events the deeds of God, not because God does not move, govern, and direct all other things, great and small, but because in these events he appears to have been present so manifestly as he is seated upon heaven and the stars, and so forth.

We call them deeds performed through the Franks because the plan for this expedition was conceived in the kingdom of the Franks, and because by far the greater part of the princes and soldiers came from the kingdom of the Franks. Thus either the valor or the number of the Franks was preeminent, and so forth.

But Guibert begins his history with the successes in the East of the rising Muslim unbelief and with the aid requested from the Christian princes of the West by a letter of the emperor of Constantinople to Robert, Count of Flanders. This preceded the Council of Clermont. He continues the account to the reign of Baldwin I, and so forth.

## Aubert Miraeus in the *Supplement to Ecclesiastical Writers*

Guibert, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Novigento, situated near the castle of Coucy, or Coucy, in the district of Laon, lived in the very age whose history he partly described, and so forth.

He reports the same matters as Bongars above, but more briefly.

## Note of Jean de Launoy, Doctor of Paris

Prefixed to Guibert’s books *On the Relics of the Saints*, which are preserved in manuscript in the Royal Library:

“Guibert, abbot of Novigento,” page 129. He calls himself the minister and servant of the Mother of God, page 1.

He began to govern in 1104, when his predecessor Godfrey was consecrated bishop of Amiens, page 29.

He was a contemporary of Radulph, Bishop of Rheims, and Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, who are otherwise known to have risen to the summit of ecclesiastical dignity in 1114.

He indicates that he was writing to Louis VI, son of Philip I, who died on 1 August 1138.

## Gerard John Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, Book Three, p. 705

“Guibert, a noble Gaul, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Novigento, situated in the district of Laon beneath Coucy, flourished in the year 1110 and left a work entitled *The Deeds of God through the Franks*, and so forth.

“He also says that Guibert commented on Genesis, though in a simpler style than the one he employs here, and so forth.”

[Col. 0019]

# [Moral Reflections on Genesis]

## Prologue to the Commentaries on Genesis by the Venerable Guibert, Monk of Saint Geremar of Flaviac, Later Abbot of Blessed Mary of Novigento

[Col. 0019C]

### 1. To Bartholomew, Father and Lord, Bishop of the Holy Church of Laon

Guibert prays that what the bishop’s name signifies may be accomplished.

While I consider to whose name I ought to dedicate this little work, I conclude that nowhere can it be more fittingly attached than to you. For to one whose lineage is wholly ancient, illustrious and not without proximity to royal blood; whose name everywhere is recognized by an innate generosity; to one upon whom God, together with the sacrament of the pontificate, has bestowed the glory of the purest celibacy, and, not without profound humility, an abundant impulse toward devotion—to one, I confess, to whom I am altogether bound by the great familiarity granted me with you—I have resolved to dedicate whatever worthy work I may be able to produce, so that, through your magnanimity, what gives less satisfaction because of my own slender resources may attain distinction.

God has placed upon your head two eyes brighter than stars: on your right you have Anselm, acclaimed as the teacher of the whole Latin world. His rigor in asserting Scripture and the faith is so sincere that, by his instruction, he is proved to have made more people true Catholics than any heretic of our age could have established as erroneous ones. On the other side stands Radulphus: just as the liveliness of his intellect and learning does not differ from that of the brother mentioned above, so his integrity emulates him in every form of goodness.

If, therefore, you graciously authorize an unworthy author, I beg you to appoint these men above all others as judges of this page after yourself. I shall submit to their judgments with all the greater confidence because I have found that they will limp toward neither side.

There have been those who objected that I had not first called this work an Exameron, or given it some such title for the books that follow. They should have understood that I rightly refrained, fearing the reputation of madness that would attach to me if I wove either discordant or equivalent things beside the blessed Augustine. And how could I have attained to the history of such majesty, when I rarely understand the explanations—or rather, the opinions—of that aforementioned teacher?

I therefore turned to morals. In reasoning about them, I was permitted to diverge with all the greater safety, since this subtlety, drawn forth from an inward model through contemplation, could comment without incurring treachery or falsehood.

Moreover, I would have added a good deal under allegorical meanings, had I not feared exceeding the limits of the work. Indeed, at the request of a certain friend, I had first published a little book on this subject, because he had asked for material from which to make a sermon. Accordingly I treated it in a more diffuse style than the rest and prefixed a few points about how a sermon should be made; for the remainder, I ventured on the basis of the experience of what I had begun, relying only on divine hope.

## 2. THE BOOK BEGINS: IN WHAT ORDER A SERMON OUGHT TO BE MADE

[Col. 0021]

It is extremely dangerous for a person whose duty is to preach to cease from teaching. For just as it is blameworthy to display examples of wickedness, so it is evidently close to condemnation for one who does not wish to heal sinners through instruction.

There are, however, various attitudes among people concerning this matter. Some refuse to do it because they are overcome by pride, others by disgust, and others by envy. I say that they reject preaching out of pride, and they disdain the very thing that many eagerly desire to do, and do merely for vainglory. They do not want to be called preachers, because that class of people is accustomed to be infamous: they speak for the sake of their belly. Hence Gregory of Nazianzus calls them “belly-speakers” (*ventriloqui*) (*Apologetic Oration* 1); from excessive pride, they disdain this type.

If a comparison is made among such people, the one who vaingloriously preaches, though harmful only to himself, and supplies others with teachings from which they may be instructed, is found to be far more useful than the man who arrogantly conceals what he understands to be useful. The latter is good neither for himself nor for others.

Some are held back from sacred preaching by envy in two ways. Envious of the good morals of others, they do not wish to say anything by which those people might become better. They also pretend not to possess the knowledge of Scripture that they do possess, and do not take care to expound it to eager and understanding hearers, fearing that through their teaching the hearers may progress so far in learning as to become their equals, or perhaps surpass them.

There is also a third form of envy. When someone begins to envy others who devote themselves earnestly to preaching, he kindles himself more ardently to speak, disentangles obscure passages of Scripture, expounds various unusual matters, and strives to paint weighty judgments in carefully composed language—not to build up his hearers for good action, but, being eager for a little glory, to demonstrate that he knows more than others. Yet although he dispenses good things badly and loses himself in seeking distinction over others, we must rejoice whenever Christ is proclaimed (*Phil.* 1:18), and no one who deals with the word of faith should simply be rejected, since the hired laborer is useful in many respects.

There are also those who disdain speaking of good things. Since their hands cease from every pious action, it is no wonder if their tongue grows sluggish in the pursuit of holy speech. For one who proposes to do nothing good—how, I ask, can he long keep good things turning over in his mind?

Nevertheless, there are people who live well and continually, but because they do not hold a pastoral office in the Church, they think that they ought not to speak the word of sacred preaching to their brothers. This is highly absurd. For if God wished to rebuke a prophet’s foolishness through a mute beast of burden—that is, through a she-ass, according to blessed Peter (*2 Pet.* 2:16)—how much more worthy, and almost beyond comparison, is human nature for teaching and imparting discipline to those who are its equals?

Let us therefore speak, all of us who have acquired knowledge of the sacred page, as from God—that is, having God as the source of our entire discourse—and seeking, before God, to please no one from our composition of words except God alone. For if everything pertaining to the exhortation of souls ought to sound only of God, and ought to proceed from nowhere but him, as from its own source, what sacrilege does the person commit who presumes to seek his own praise in divine matters, where only God’s praise should be sought? If theft is the most shameful offense in human affairs, what crime should we think it to be when someone takes away what belongs to God and claims it for himself?

Let us also flee from being counted among those two most evil and utterly disordered—if I may put it so—orders whom we do not have in the Church as brothers, but tolerate as enemies: one consists of those who do evil, the other of those who refuse to do good.

These are represented by Judah’s two sons, Er and Onan. The first, wicked in the sight of the Lord and struck down by him, represents the life of the wicked who are punished by God for their crimes. The second, who refused to raise up seed in his brother’s name and deserved to be killed by divine judgment, signifies those who refuse to produce, through the seed of God’s word planted in the hearts of the faithful, the fruit of good works to Christ’s honor. They are no less overcome by condemnation than those who actually do evil.

For if, according to blessed Ambrose (*On the Duties*, book I, chapter 36), one who does not ward off an injury from his companion when he can is as much at fault as the person who inflicted it, what prevents us from saying that one incurs precisely the same guilt if he sees someone sinning and refuses to correct him? According to the Apostle, not only those who do such things, but also those who approve of those who do them, are said to deserve death (*Rom.* 1:32).

[Col. 0023A]

Even if he is not a bishop or an abbot, or does not excel through any authority, let him nevertheless act, according to blessed Augustine, in accordance with the person he bears. He is a Christian; if he wishes to live as a Christian, let him glorify the Christian name in others just as in himself.

In Deuteronomy we also read (*Deut.* 23:3): “Moabites and Ammonites shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, even after the tenth generation, forever.” And when he supplies the reasons for each, he says of the Moabite that he did not meet the Israelites with bread and water when they came out of Egypt; and of the Ammonite, that he hired the diviner Balaam to curse them (*ibid.*, verse 4).

What are the Moabite and the Ammonite except the two kinds of people mentioned above: those who refuse to be useful and those who do evil? Where it says that he did not meet them with bread and water, he is blamed because he refused to be of use. Where it says that he hired Balaam against Israel, he is accused because he did harm.

These people do not enter the Church of God, because they are never joined to the body of Christ, which is the Church—not only those who are occupied with evil works, but also those who are too lazy to nourish others with spiritual food and drink.

Far be it that in so great a body there should be—not to speak of a dead member—even the smallest claw that is useless or idle. Although they have reached the tenth generation—that is, although in baptism they have promised to possess faith in the Trinity—and have received the gift of the sevenfold Spirit under the bishop’s right hand, it is certain that, because of the wickedness of their minds, they cannot belong to the Lord’s body.

The number ten consists of three and seven, and therefore signifies the Trinity together with the seven gifts. Thus, although they receive the ecclesiastical sacraments along with true believers, because of their uselessness they nevertheless lie outside the company of the faithful like dead members. They would not harm the Israelites if they did not hire Balaam, for they would not trouble their brothers unless they first gave themselves to the devil and afterward, having become united with him, joined battle against the good.

In this connection it must plainly be noted that whatever is done mystically in the Church is, according to its dispensation, shared no less by the reprobate than by the elect. Baptism, the Eucharist, and the giving of the Spirit are not administered more effectively, as regards the benefit of those who receive them, by the good than they are given by the reprobate.

For although the Holy Spirit is said to flee from deceit (*Wis.* 1:5), it must be noted that this statement is qualified by “discipline.” He flees, as regards their own salvation, from those who live unworthily; yet he is present insofar as, through those who are filthy with every misery, he generously distributes the gifts of his grace to others. A channel receives water only in order to transmit it elsewhere; so these people likewise have it for another, but not for themselves.

They do not have the Spirit of discipline, because they do not share in the labor of human beings and do not deserve to be scourged with them (*Ps.* 72:5). Since they are outside discipline, according to the Apostle they are illegitimate children and not sons (*Heb.* 12:8).

[Col. 0024A]

This is the Spirit who, although good, teaches us goodness. He establishes us in a good and simple disposition, and then teaches us discipline, so that we are not wearied when we are rebuked by God. For when we are judged by him, the correction is given so that we may not be condemned with the world. Through this we acquire much knowledge and discernment, so that we learn that temporal glories are followed by eternal griefs, and that momentary scourges are compensated by everlasting goods.

Herod and Antiochus did not have the Spirit of discipline. He did not touch them with any spiritual love amid their scourges, nor did he cause them to learn anything of God—for *discipline* is so called from learning. Rather, he left them in their obstinacy, to be crushed by a double contrition, here and in the future.

We have said these things at length in order to show the difference between the good and the wicked solely in their disposition of mind. That disposition is nothing other than good will, a devout feeling, and a clear conscience. Christian authors have taught that nothing is happier than this (*Ambrose, On Psalm 28*, verse 1; *On Duties*, book II, chapter 1). In this, if we wish, we are separated from the perverse; by this particular quality we are distinguished from their lot.

This is the wedding garment: whoever is not clothed in it is cast out from participation in the sacred table.

All the other things that are displayed outwardly are given and received by the good and the wicked alike. They are initiated into the same sacraments and initiate others into them; they perform the same miracles. Let us therefore be members of the holy Church—not dead members, but members rendering an appropriate service to the Lord’s body—so that, just as outwardly we resemble the good in the performance of the sacred mysteries, so inwardly also, in feeling and action, we may be their equals in complete piety.

Let our book, from which the text of our speech proceeds, be a pure conscience, so that while our tongue announces good things to others, the memory of sin may not gnaw at us within and impede the force of our speech through hidden shame. Let prayer precede the sermon, so that a mind burning with divine love may fervently express what it feels about God. Thus, just as it burns inwardly within itself, it may inflame the hearts of its hearers.

For a sermon delivered lukewarmly and languidly, when it does not please even the person who delivers it, would hardly be expected to please anyone else. Nor could words spoken by a broken-down and prostrate speaker raise others up. We have certainly learned by experience that such speech does not calm the minds of its hearers, but usually burdens them with disgust and gravely provokes them to anger.

When, therefore, we feel that the keenness of reason is weak within us, that our speech is blunted, that we lack an abundance of things to say, and that the mind, confined within narrow limits, suffers from deficiency, then, as I judge, the sermon is extended from that point for no one’s benefit.

For even when an abundance of words overflows and the tongue proceeds according to the desire of the heart, a sermon ought not to become excessively long—still less when memory does not supply what ought to be said, speech is impeded, and the mind is sluggish. Blessed Ambrose writes (*On Duties*, book I, chapter 22) that a tedious speech provokes anger. When the same things are repeated too often, or different matters are stretched beyond measure, the result is usually that those overcome by weariness lose everything alike—the beginning, the middle, and the end—and the few things that might have been useful, poured out excessively and without discrimination, are turned into disgust and almost into hatred.

For just as food taken moderately remains in the body for its nourishment, while food devoured without measure becomes harmful and provokes vomiting; and just as a man who joins himself to his wife with legitimate seed, emitted sparingly and modestly, produces offspring, whereas one who spills his seed accomplishes nothing useful but defiles the flesh—so the person who speaks excessively takes away what had been planted in the hearts of his hearers and might have prospered.

When, therefore, great fervor of spirit is present in the preacher, and abundant material for treatment is not lacking in his memory, and the possibility and adornment of eloquence exceed what necessity requires, let him consider the weak powers of those who listen silently. Let him judge that it is better for a few things to be received pleasantly than for countless things to be heard without any being retained. He should not delay bringing the sermon to an end, so that when he is going to speak again he may find his hearers eager rather than wearied.

Moreover, another point must be impressed upon us: while preaching light and straightforward things to the unlearned, the preacher should also strive to mingle some higher matters suited to the learned. While he offers each person what pleases that person’s capacity, he should explain it—if I may put it so—by grinding it down with the millstone of circumlocution, so that what previously seemed hard and difficult even to the educated becomes so clear and open that what is said can be understood by the ignorant and simple.

Just as milk is familiar and very necessary nourishment for little children, so that infants are thought unable to live without it, yet milk is not used by children alone, and softened pieces of bread provide food even for the very old, so simple teaching is generally offered to the common people, while something is inserted there for the more understanding, in which their intellects may be exercised. In this way it usually nourishes the dull, while the addition of more solid food—that is, an interjected weightier judgment—also delights the wise.

When passages from the Old Testament are introduced into explanations of the Gospels, they commonly make hearers more attentive. For when something new sounds in their ears, it renews their minds, as it were, through a certain pleasing resonance. This usually happens to those who gladly seek out the secrets of Scripture and are always eager to learn.

We have also found that some people enjoy introducing simple stories and the deeds of the ancients into a sermon, adorning it all, as it were, with a picture made from different colors.

We must also say what kind of treatment a teacher ought especially to maintain. There are four rules of Scripture, by which the whole sacred page is, as it were, turned on wheels: history, which recounts things that happened; allegory, in which one thing is understood from another; tropology, that is, moral discourse, in which the formation and ordering of conduct are discussed; and anagogy, namely spiritual understanding, through which, when we are about to discuss what is highest and heavenly, we are led upward.

[Col. 0026A]

For example, according to history, Jerusalem is a certain city; according to allegory, it signifies the holy Church; according to tropology, that is, morality, it signifies the faithful soul of any person who longs for the vision of eternal peace; according to anagogy, it signifies the life of the heavenly citizens who see the God of gods in Zion with his face revealed.

Thus, although every treatment can be made according to these four modes, or at least according to each of them individually, nevertheless, if what is more useful for the care of the inner person is considered, morality seems more suitable and intelligible for exposition.

Allegory, when it is sought in prophetic and apostolic books, builds almost nothing other than faith. For when we attentively read that God once spoke through the prophets in many ways and by many means, we undoubtedly discover there the sacraments of the Christian age foretold in advance.

By God’s grace, faith is now known to everyone’s heart. Although it is proper to impress and review it frequently with hearers, it is nevertheless appropriate to speak no less—and indeed much more frequently—about those things that can shape their conduct. We can discuss the nature of virtues more easily and safely than we can debate the sacraments of the faith, about which one must speak to some people with great moderation. For error can arise among those who understand little from preaching that is too profound; from moral instruction, however, the benefit of discernment is especially acquired.

Although allegorical meaning, when it is occasionally mingled with a sermon, is usually very welcome, and although things that instruct us in faith and in the understanding of sacred Scripture should sometimes truly be said, nevertheless all the vigilance of our speech should be directed toward the movements of the inner person—that is, toward thoughts. Their experience is so common to everyone that, as I believe, such a treatment can be obscure to no one, especially since each person observes within himself, as though written in a book, whatever the preacher’s tongue recounts about various temptations.

Instruction should be given no less about the origin and preservation of virtues than about the interconnection and avoidance of vices. When the teacher carefully and distinctly explains which vices are natural and which are contrary to nature, which are generated from others, and how harmful they are both in themselves and through what they propagate, he provides a benefit of immeasurable usefulness.

When the hidden things of Scripture are explained to the simple and ignorant, they quickly slip from their memories. For those accustomed only to bodily things, it is no wonder if they lack strength of memory for spiritual matters, which they do not see, since they often lack it even for bodily matters, which they can perceive and see. Some people are so dominated by the animal part of themselves that they scarcely understand anything except material things, including those visible even to beasts. They do not understand at all the movements and vices of their own bodies and souls, which they constantly suffer within themselves, until they hear about them from others. When they have heard, would that they might retain them through firm repetition.

I have spoken the truth, and I have spoken it plainly: it is no less beneficial sometimes to treat the nature of vices than to treat the nature of virtues. For if I do not recognize vice, how shall I love the sincerity of virtue? And how shall I flee vice unless I know something good, sound, and whole, for the sake of attaining and enjoying which vice ought to be avoided?

There are vegetables, and there is also hemlock. One is beneficial, the other deadly. If, therefore, there were someone who gladly ate vegetables but, not knowing the difference between vegetables and hemlock, believed that hemlock too should be eaten like vegetables, what benefit would it be that he had used vegetables for a while, if afterward, through his negligence, by eating hemlock he came to madness and death?

The origin of each vice must therefore be carefully examined. Once the nature of vice is clearly recognized, its opposite, virtue, may be distinguished more clearly, like grain separated from chaff. Life, which is virtue, will then be loved with greater devotion in proportion as vice, which is death, is avoided with greater caution.

No preaching seems more salutary to me than that which shows a person to himself, restores him—scattered outwardly beyond himself—to his interior, that is, to his mind, and, while reproving him, sets him, so to speak, depicted before his own face.

Someone may perhaps ask how he can know these matters, about which he ought to treat according to the inner person. I answer that, apart from blessed Gregory’s *Morals* and the book written by a certain Cassian—also called John—entitled *On the Institutes and Conferences of the Fathers*, whose reading provides immense benefit to diligent readers, and apart from the other holy authors who instruct us in such matters, I consider the following especially useful for all who guard themselves and resist vices, both for knowing and discerning vices: they should diligently gird themselves against the shifting desires of their thoughts and actions.

If they fight faithfully in these struggles, there is nowhere they can learn so much about the qualities of conduct. For one who seeks to be instructed in these matters solely through reading any number of books forgets all the more quickly because he does not reread within himself, through experience, what he has read or heard.

Experience is more useful to the human mind than anything else. As the mind perseveres earnestly in its struggle, it sometimes rejoices in the happiness of its victory. Then, when the condition of the mind changes again, it grows weary in the face of temptations of the heart or flesh. The person who had rejoiced that his heart was impenetrable to perverse desires, once that firmness has softened, loses confidence in his ability to endure the heat of vices. While his wavering mind vacillates between hope and fear, God supplies occasions for him to rise again. After being carried around for a long time in that unstable pool, where he was borne blindly and almost drunkenly, he finally returns to a solid way of thinking.

God provides occasions for rising again while we are engaged in the struggle of temptation or are sunk in mental torpor. Sometimes he suggests to our reason the spirit of compunction, making us consider the misery of our will. At other times, by God’s own arrangement, we hear ourselves praised by someone, or we are compelled to deliver a sermon of exhortation to others. Through these means we are brought back to see ourselves as we are and where we lie, and we groan.

Or else we are roused from the languor of the mind by the living eloquence of another person’s sermon, or by reading the divine page; or in countless other and wholly unexpected ways we are recalled to good action.

We must therefore give thanks to the Lord, especially those who go down to the sea—that is, humble themselves in the storm of temptation—yet are in ships, that is, in the direction of a pious intention. Although they are tossed, they are not drowned. They conduct their work upon the waters (*Ps.* 106:23), that is, amid the clashes and collisions produced by the fiercest carnal and spiritual impulses against one another.

They serve good action in this respect: they do not abandon the effort to resist, nor, oppressed by evils, do they fall into the pit of despair. Instead, with the insight of reason, they cast themselves upon God, who is able to rescue them.

These people have seen—or rather, have experienced—the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep (*ibid.*, verse 24): in the abasement of the mind, in the darkness of uncertainty, and in the fear of sinning. Those who have been magnificently tempted have been rescued even more magnificently, and they owe magnificent thanks.

When they reflect upon the dangers they have escaped, they can understand how they deserved to fall from the good condition in which they had been placed: through excessive security, by which they thought they could preserve their religion intact without great fear or caution; through foolish joy, by which they rejoiced more than was right in their own good qualities and in the perseverance of the good; or through contempt, by which, because of their sluggish life, they became indignant at others lying far beneath them, as they supposed.

They can also understand how they fell into temptation, or into idleness and torpor, and how they escaped the furnace of their passions—that is, their desires—sometimes by succumbing to them and sometimes by overcoming them. In these contrary experiences, anyone who endures them can grasp many remarkable and exceedingly useful things. They instruct the understanding mind powerfully, even without letters or a book.

Anyone charged with the duty of teaching can, if he wishes to be instructed subtly in these and similar matters, begin with himself. What the experience of his inner battles has taught him, he can afterward use to instruct others much more abundantly than we are able to say, according to the advantages and disadvantages of his experiences that he has impressed upon his memory for retention.

Any idler, even one who has never begun to practice the military life, can say much about wars because he has seen combatants or heard wars recounted. But very differently does the man recount wars who fought in war and was attacked, who performed military actions and endured them.

So it happens in spiritual matters. We hear some people eloquently recounting what they have read in books or heard from others. But the person who speaks about spiritual combat with entirely different authority, displaying what he says as though with his finger, is the one whose conscience stands as witness to the things he utters with his mouth.

It greatly benefits the learned when the things they themselves know are eloquently said to them. But if they are said less accurately, they produce disgust and contempt in them. Therefore, when we address learned and unlearned people gathered together, we ought to offer both groups some less customary yet intelligible material, by which we can remove the weariness of those who already know well what we are saying.

This happens when, in explaining readings from the holy Gospel, we introduce something moral in a way different from customary explanations, and, as it were, by applying a new coating over an old wall, make it new.

There are certainly some Gospel passages treated by the Fathers only allegorically and expounded as referring to the persons of the Jews and the nations. Yet if an acute and diligent student of Scripture wishes to investigate them according to the other rules of interpretation, scarcely—or perhaps never—will an interpretation be lacking somewhere. Wherever the spirit and will of the reader goes, there too the wheel—that is, sacred Scripture—will be present.

Nevertheless, although this kind of exercise can be extremely valuable to those who possess a strong knowledge of the sacred page, no one should presume to undertake it unless, through long practice, he has fully learned how allegories are customarily composed through various modes of expression and diverse meanings under one and the same subject.

No one, I say, should presume to do so unless he has been shrewdly steeped in letters and, under the same things and names, has been thoroughly trained to perceive multiple meanings. For example, rock, foundation, water and heaven, grass and wood, sun and moon, and countless other things have many meanings in Scripture.

When someone is working through an obscure passage and encounters one of these names, he should consider in how many ways it is customarily understood in Scripture. For example, gold signifies divinity, gold signifies wisdom, and gold signifies the splendor of life. After considering all these possibilities, he may confidently assign the meaning that seems most suitable to the passage he is discussing.

Thus, gradually acquiring confidence day by day, when he sees through his knowledge of meanings that sacred Scripture responds favorably to him, he progresses to greater things. Encouraged by the hope of still better discoveries, he undertakes matters that he once would never have dared to attempt. The testimony of sacred speech, presenting itself to him in great numbers, gives him no small encouragement in penetrating these matters.

This is usually accomplished in two ways: by example and by reasoning. By the example of preceding passages of Scripture, as I have said; and by reasoning, namely when examples are less available and, through consideration of the nature of the thing under discussion, something suitable to allegory or morality is found.

This is the case with precious stones, birds, and beasts. Whatever is said figuratively about them is expressed only because of the meanings conveyed by their natures. Even if no passage of Scripture sometimes bears witness to a given interpretation, it may nevertheless be legitimately conjectured through examination of nature.

Gregory of Nazianzus, a man of wonderfully extensive learning, testifies in one of his books that it was his custom to allegorize whatever he saw for the instruction of his mind. If someone becomes accustomed to doing this through intellectual acuity, he will find not only in the divine books but also in almost everything placed before his eyes abundant comparisons suitable as examples and useful significations of those things that, through constant use, we regard as worthless.

These things are all the more usefully considered the more generously they are spoken of, and they are all the more pleasing the less customary they are to their hearers.

Much could also be said about what is discovered through reasoning. But I fear that if I began to speak on this subject I would extend my words beyond measure, and I do not know whether I could explain it as clearly as I would wish.

The sincere intention of the speaker, free from every desire for praise, also usually benefits hearers greatly, when it is understood that the only things sought are their instruction in divine matters and their salvation; when a desire for personal glory through great eloquence does not turn them away, and no affectation can be detected.

Nothing is more accustomed to offend a hearer than knowing, or supposing, that the preacher is disputing for the sake of money or display.

A preacher recognized as such provokes irritation rather than preaching. The more attractively he strives to adorn his words with eloquence, the more sharply he drives the hearts of those standing before him—alas!—to despise even the good things he says, and most of all he torments them with disgust toward himself. Yet however proudly such things might be uttered, they ought to be received with a submissive spirit as divine words.

This is how, according to my poverty, I have said that you ought to treat these matters, most beloved man. From this point onward I shall begin, with God’s help, to speak about the subjects from which you may sometimes take material for speaking.

For anyone submerged in the confusion of vices, it is certainly very useful to declare how dreadful the punishments of hell are and to describe how infinite they are together with that ineffable horror. Just as those placed in the heavenly kingdom will lack nothing of blessedness, so, conversely, those condemned forever will lack nothing of misery or of anything pertaining to punishment.

Although they are tormented without any remedy, even for a moment, one thing in particular torments the minds of the lost incomprehensibly: they have no hope of escaping their torments even after a thousand thousand years. They know that they will suffer immortal death throughout the ages of ages.

Hope—even sometimes false hope—restores minds placed in adversity. But there neither true nor false hope will exist that could console them.

Yet a carnal person, that is, one who lives like a beast and whose senses cling entirely to the things he sees bodily, does not grasp the things of God. The habit of earthly pleasure blinds him so completely that nothing said to him about the future age can deter him. Even if it sometimes deters him, because he does not yet feel what is being said, the warning quickly slips from his mind.

The torments and fears that he now suffers while doing evil or on account of doing evil must therefore be set before him, together with the fact that he gains from it nothing except labor and the most shameful pain.

For example, someone is accustomed to theft. Overcome by desire for whatever object it may be, he proceeds to steal—not, I say, frightened by the fear of the night, which I would fear greatly, nor even terrified by the loss of his limbs or by hanging itself, from which he knows he will not escape if he is caught. He is certainly afraid and shaken by grim trembling, but the force of his desire overcomes him.

When such a thief is convicted, he is hung upon the gallows.

I shall also speak of incest, but I shall do so more suitably in the words of that noble man Boethius:

“What shall I say of pleasures, whose desire is indeed full of anxiety, but whose satiety is full of repentance?” (*Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, prose 7.)

What could be truer than this saying? A man placed in the desire for a criminal act is tormented; he burns as he considers how to bring his perverse desire to an even worse deed. While he fears that what he is doing will become known, he is consumed by dreadful and intolerable anguish. While, unable to endure the heat of his desire, he tries to rid himself of it, whether he wishes to or not, he is overcome by the force of his own habit.

While he burns with desire, he bitterly complains against himself about the battle he is enduring and declares himself most wretched, so that he becomes disgusted with himself and weary of living. Once he has completed what he desired, what tortures, what groans, what belated repentance follow that unhappy man!

Concerning this I would undoubtedly say that if, after the perpetration of sin, he had as much genuine sorrow and fruitful repentance as he has after the fulfillment of lust or some other crime—and even during the very conception of the act, before he commits it, first anxiety as to how he might accomplish it, and then the grief which, from satiety with sin, he customarily suffers for a time, until, that is, his accustomed fervor returns—he would offer God the greatest fruit of his contrition, worthy of every acceptance. But it is altogether true that “the children of this world are wiser and, so to speak, more vigorous than the children of light in their own generation” (Luke 16:8). For it is said to the apostles—surely you see how Judas does not sleep—not because Judas’s vigilance was better than the apostles’ sleep, but because his skill in evil ought to have been present in the apostles for good. And Paul, speaking in human terms (Rom. 6:19), because of the weakness of our flesh, wishes us to present our members for serving holiness at least as readily as we presented them for serving iniquity, if not more so.

He knew the keenness and ingenuity of the human mind for evil: if such people were equally zealous for good things, they would be worthy of great praise. Let such persons therefore be confronted with the torments and stings under which they pass their miserable pleasures; let them be confronted with the disgraceful reputation [8] by which alone, whether their crimes are open or concealed, their honor is polluted. If, then, they do not yet deign to fear future evils because they do not have them before their eyes or at their sides, let them at least fear being driven by such savage torments for so trifling a pleasure, from which they gain nothing except the peril and destruction of their honor. That pleasure, as the aforesaid author says, resembles a bee (Boethius, cited above, meter 7): it carries honey in its mouth—that is, in the very suggestion of the little delight—but a sting in its tail, because afterward it repays whatever low sweetness it has drawn up with the bitterness of savage suspicion.

Saint Gregory says (Morals on Job, book XII, chapter 21): “Nothing is happier than a simple mind.” Against this someone says that “a mind guilty in itself is always driven by its own goads; while desiring to do evil, or fearing the evil it has done, it is very often burned by inward fires.” If, therefore, he takes counsel for eternal destruction, let him take counsel also [or “but” for “and”] for present shame; and, turning toward his heart, let him learn to resist evil habits, carefully inquiring what difference there is between flesh and spirit—indeed, what flesh and spirit are. For a soldier is armed in vain unless he has a keen spirit with which to resist his enemies. And what benefit is there in recognizing virtues opposed to fleshly wantonness, if reason, sluggish and torpid, is unwilling to rise up to attack them?

Let us therefore take something from a true history as an example; while examining its hidden meanings, we shall open for ourselves many instruments of instruction. Let no one suppose that we are devising novelties in this matter, knowing that, if it was permitted the poet,

> Always it was permitted, and always it will be permitted,

to bring forth a name marked by a present stigma, much more is it permitted to all who are learned in sacred Scripture, without violating the faith and according to the rules of the ancient interpreters, to investigate the abundance of the Scriptures through their various meanings. Let us therefore speak.

**[Col. 0031] THE PROEM ENDS.**

**THE FIRST BOOK OF THE MORALS ON GENESIS BEGINS.**

**[9] CHAPTER ONE.**

**[Col. 0031C]**

**VERSE 1. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”** At the beginning of our conversion we are divided within ourselves into two things, greatly opposed to one another, which, I think, cannot possess even a momentary peace between them in anyone who lives well. They are flesh and spirit. Here, and often elsewhere when it is used for the vices of the flesh, “flesh” is understood in an evil sense.

For man was so fashioned by God, free from every superfluous and disordered movement of his mind and flesh, and was created with such harmony between these two parts, that he suffered absolutely no trouble within himself until, obeying the serpent, he transgressed the divine command. In this way he immediately felt the flesh opposed to the dominion of the mind. And it was just that, so long as he himself obediently submitted to God, he should suffer no opposition of himself against himself; nor was it less just that, when he was unwilling to submit to God, he should no longer possess himself under his own authority. Hence, when they had eaten from the forbidden tree, both are said to have made themselves *perizomata* (Gen. 3:7), that is, coverings wrapped around them, because those who previously had seen nothing by desiring anything now felt, by an equitable judgment, that they were shamefully provoked against one another.

From that time, therefore, disobedience arising from desire reigns in us; it also invites us, unwilling though we are, to disgraceful movements. Thus, in those who avoid the chaos of vices and have made a good beginning of conversion through goodwill, God creates heaven and earth, because he distinguishes and raises up the Spirit—that is, reason—and earth—that is, carnal affection—which previously were carried confusedly mixed together in the heart of the faithful. He establishes heaven above and grants it a certain dignity of principate, so that earth, with all that belongs to it, may hope for direction from its command.

For just as light is poured down from heaven, and rains are supplied everywhere on earth through the movement of the clouds, and the earth is fanned by the four winds of heaven, so from reason, which is the highest part of us, proceeds the clarity of understanding, right intention, and discernment. In it the heavenly things of the ancient Fathers are cleared of clouds, preserved, and made into teachings to be handed on. When others have been drenched by these, it also irrigates the earth of their own body—that is, all the parts of their senses—with this fullness of spiritual knowledge, so that it may bear fruit in good works; and by the four spiritual and principal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—it wipes away and dries whatever there is of vicious moisture, as though by the forceful impulse of a certain breeze.

For, if you attend carefully, the earth is almost nothing unless it receives from heaven whatever good it produces. Thus our body remains barren of every good and foul with the misery of sin unless it is governed by reason. Reason is nothing other than understanding, through which we are made like God and the angels, through which we comprehend the things that are God’s, and through which alone in this life we differ from beasts. By this understanding we must govern and order our animality—that is, our carnality—which we share in common with beasts.

We therefore have heaven within us, by which we sigh for heavenly things; and, conversely, we have earth, by which we are dragged down to desire lowly things like cattle. These, according to the Apostle, oppose one another, so that we are often unable to do the good things we desire (Gal. 5:17). When, therefore, we turn to God, we raise up reason, which had been lying beneath carnal affection like a maidservant, in an inverted and very perverse order; and we resolve to wage perpetual battle against him who, with servile boldness, had risen up against his mistress. Then heaven and earth are first created in us, when the understanding of these two things and their ordered distinction according to justice begins to be held in the mind. But let us see in what way the following text explains the earth itself.

**VERSE 2. “But the earth was formless and empty.”** By “earth,” as I said, we should here understand either our body or our carnal affection.
