Carnal affection is rightly called “formless,” because, insofar as it depends on itself, it possesses nothing solid, stable, or constant. Just as flesh collapses entirely when its bones are removed, unable to stand by itself, so the lower part of us—namely, our animality—unless reason is present to govern it, knows how to do nothing weighty or useful, but everything vain, shameful, and harmful.

This formlessness pertains especially to the inner man, namely to the worse part of his affection, when his thought and care are occupied far from God, and what he meditates is either completely idle or harmful. Since, therefore, there is formlessness in the wandering desire of the heart and, so to speak, pitiable sterility apart from the divine seed, it necessarily follows that there is emptiness in the production of good works. For it would be very strange if a tree had lost its vital sap from its roots and, with its inner leaves dried up, still produced leaves and fruit.

The earth, therefore, is first formless inwardly and empty outwardly of usefulness. “He who is of the earth,” it says, “is of the earth and speaks of the earth” (John 3:31), because if a man were to examine what he possesses from himself, he would find absolutely nothing except what benefits an ass in the absence of God. For what is man—not, I say, without reason, but without God, who illumines reason—except an animal? For reason, unless joined to divine love, should be called worldly and diabolical cleverness rather than prudence capable of achieving anything good.

When this reason, under God’s inspiration, knows and embraces the law as spiritual, according to the Apostle, it nevertheless suffers carnal affection, being unwillingly subjected to vanity (1 Cor. 7:15). Hence it does not understand what it does—that is, it does not approve or love it. For through the spirit, that is, reason, which agrees with God and sees from God and with God, it considers the good that ought to be done and desires to do it; but the flesh resists and the man is “sold”—that is, alienated from his own power through the habit of sinning. What he would not wish to do through the spirit, he does through his affection; and precisely because he does unwillingly what he does, by that very fact he consents to the law of God, since it is good.

And, to establish more clearly this formlessness of the earth, the Apostle adds in the same place. For after saying, “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:17)—that is, it does not proceed from my rational will that I do evil, but from the necessity of a perverse habit—he adds: “For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (ibid. 18).

Every creature without God, insofar as true being is concerned, is nothing; and, if it is deprived of the highest good, it is never good by itself. Every nature, however, because it is made by God, is good. The devil, therefore, in this respect is good, but from his own will he is exceedingly evil. Hence it is true that the earth, insofar as it has anything from itself, is formless, thinking of nothing useful; it is empty, producing nothing suitable for use. Formless, therefore, inwardly, and empty outwardly.

Our authorities say that in the ancient translation it does not say “formless and empty” (Gen. 1:2), but “invisible and unformed.” This agrees exceedingly well with the moral interpretation. For the mind of a man established in the depth of sin, when through the habit of sinning it reaches a reprobate sense, is so weighed down by love of the vices to which it is accustomed that it cannot attend to itself at all and does not see in what dishonor of body and destruction of soul it lies.

Such is the reprobate sense that it blinds the minds of the perishing to such a degree that, although they are placed amid stench and misery and the contempt and horror of all who see them, they dare to consider themselves alone blessed and truly worthy of honor from others because of their prosperity and good outcomes, by which they boast that they will be happier than others. These are the people of whom Solomon says: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). This is especially characteristic of the reprobate sense.

Before God, therefore, as we said above, distinguishes heaven and earth, the earth was invisible. Before he gave anyone guilty the grace of discernment in his heart, how sordid and how detestable carnal affection was was completely invisible—not to God, from whom nothing is hidden, but to the person who suffers from it. For just as a drunkard does not know what he is suffering, so one full of vices cannot distinguish what is honorable from what is dishonorable.

Just as, if a living and a dead person are placed somewhere, the living can see the dead, but the dead cannot see the living, so a person whose mind is rationally awake can see how detestable vices are; but one who has already entered into the depth of evils and now despises and despairs does not consider what virtue is, what moderation is, or what the other good things are. For “their fury is like that of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp that stops its ears” (Ps. 57:5).

The reprobate sense is a frenzy that forces those turned into madness to live irrationally and, so to speak, like pigs. It is “like a serpent,” namely an asp, because when an asp senses an enchanter, it presses one of its ears against the ground and blocks the other with its tail, so that it may not hear the enchanter’s song. So these people, when they hear the words of sacred eloquence or of any preacher speaking about contempt for pleasures, immediately recall their former delights; with these, as though with a tail, they cover the ear of their heart, and they attend at the same time to the present things with which they burn and for which they yearn. By dragging their whole understanding down toward earthly things, they close themselves against God who calls them.

**[11]** These are the invisible earth, because they do not know how to weigh the plague in which they themselves are. “Filled with iniquities, they are darkened in the houses of the earth” (Ps. 73:20); that is, bent toward their own lusts, they seek to know nothing except what is sweet to the flesh, and they have lost the eyes of their mind for seeing divine things.

And because they are not yet able even to look upon themselves, rightly the earth, which is first called invisible, is followed by “unformed.” For unless someone loses the gaze of inward self-examination, he never proceeds to outwardly evil, unformed, and disordered works. Just as a blind person does not know how to arrange neatly and decently the things attached to his body—his clothing and the rest—or to avoid the dirt adhering to them, so one who has incurred blindness of mind through vices is wholly unable to moderate inwardly the shameful and unworthy acts in which he ardently takes pleasure.

It is written in Solomon: “An apostate man, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth” (Prov. 6:12). Unless he had first apostatized inwardly from God, he would not have come to the incongruous and reprobate gestures of the outward man. Let the beginning of blindness therefore be guarded against, lest the outpouring of obscene deeds follow.

**[Col. 0036B]** But divine discourse carefully reveals from where these things arise: “And darkness was over the face of the abyss.”

Literally, this can be understood in two ways: “Darkness was over the face of the abyss,” that is, over the depth of the waters properly called the abyss; or “over the face of the abyss,” that is, more than in the abyss.

Allegorically, the human mind is called the abyss. Every person knows how great and how incomprehensible its depth is if he has had occasion to experience the inscrutable height, the instability of its waves, and the disturbance of his heart. It also happens in the hearts of the good, when the flesh fights against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17), that the mind is in such density of thought that it can scarcely detect in itself what state it is in—whether it follows the impulse of the flesh or the impulse of the spirit.

Whoever wishes to know this more fully should read blessed Augustine’s treatise on “Abyss calls to abyss” (Ps. 42:8). And if we suppose that there is a chasm in the hearts of the wicked, what immensity of darkness must there be there, if so much obscurity exists even in the minds of the elect?

If, according to the prophet, thorns of worldly cares and brambles of carnal desires grow up over the soil of God’s people, how much more over the house of the joy of the rejoicing city? (Isa. 23:13.) What does this mean? If those who have nothing more precious in this world than to weep over their pilgrimage away from the Lord, to weep over the hardship of the present age, suffer troubles, tumults, and clouds of mind, how much more do those suffer who thirst for crimes with all their inmost being, pant after avarice, are befouled by lusts, waste away with envy, and swell with pride?

From these darknesses, therefore, arise the invisibility and formlessness of which we spoke above. Yet there are some who, although through many crimes they have fallen into this Babylon—that is, into confusion of mind—nevertheless retain something of reason, like a spark from a great fire, by which they are able to contemplate the exceedingly fearful abyss of that misery in which they are submerged.

Although there are some who are utterly extinguished, who, as it is said in the psalm, “sleep in the tombs” (Ps. 87:5)—that is, are weighed down by an evil habit—and of whom “God remembers no more” (Ps. 87:6), whom he never again visits by recalling them to the light of self-knowledge, there are nevertheless those whom we have mentioned, whose eye, though greatly troubled, is not completely blinded. Raising their head from the abyss, they are accustomed to cry: “Out of the depths I have cried to you” (Ps. 129:1), and so forth. What follows is fitting for them.

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” In sacred Scripture, waters sometimes signify the pleasures of the flesh. Hence in the Gospel the spirit that has gone out from a man is said to pass through waterless places (Luke 11:24).

Therefore, when minds are established in the flood of many waters (Ps. 31:6)—that is, in the flow of many carnal desires—the Spirit of God is borne over them, because, while the spark of discernment is still alive, the unhappy mind considers the miseries it suffers.

And just as it is read concerning the king of Babylon, that he killed the sons of King Zedekiah of Judah before Zedekiah’s eyes (Jer. 52:10), so, when a person observes that his good works are being killed and destroyed by the devil through the injection of vices, it cannot be said with what groaning he sees this. He sees himself utterly perishing, grieves, and would prefer to die; yet he is in no way able to resist the desires and habits implanted in his very marrow.

The prophet Jeremiah deplores many such things under their persona in his lamentations. Some delight in pots of meat in Egypt and willingly engage in works of clay and brick. But there are others who, compelled and grieving, are driven by taskmasters to filthy and fragile works, signified by clay and brick, and serve Pharaoh—that is, the devil—against their will. They cry out with the Psalmist to God: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:7).

Hearing their inward groaning, God “leads out the prisoners” (Ps. 67:7), bound by the cords of their crimes, so that they may possess strength to resist their evil movements. Likewise he raises up those who provoke him (ibid.), so that, with David, they may hear: “I have found a man according to my heart” (Acts 13:22). He makes the memory of their iniquity perish amid the sound of the blasphemies with which they used to clamor against God. He turns the wicked, and they are wicked no longer; and to those dwelling in the tombs of forgetfulness he cries: “Lazarus, come out!” (John 11:42).

That is: dispel that pestilential intoxication of sin by the fiercest heat of repentance, and sleep it off; and you who lay enclosed in the abyss of vices as though dead, senseless, and speechless, come—that is, approach him who calls you inwardly through lamentation for sin—so that you may come out, that is, emerge into the open through the performance of good works.

For he himself sees the affliction of his people and descends—that is, he has compassion in order to show mercy to them—and he says to them:

**VERSE 3. “Let there be light, and there was light.”** What, then, should we understand by “light” except that first good which is given to those who turn toward the heart (Ps. 84:9)? What is the first good except the fear of God, which is called the beginning of wisdom? (Ps. 110:9.)

We observe in many places of Scripture, not just one, that wisdom is called light. If wisdom itself is light, and its beginning is the fear of God, then fear, since it is a part of wisdom, is also the whole in this respect: it is light.

The wise man says: “I resolved to have her for light” (Wis. 7:10). Another says: “Have mercy on us, God of all, and look upon us, and show us the light of your mercies” (Sir. 36:1). And, explaining what light he means, he adds: “And,” that is, “send your fear upon the nations that have not sought you” (ibid. 2)—that is, upon our vices, which do not allow us to seek you. “So that they may know” (ibid.)—that is, so that they may make us know, once they have been conquered and subdued by us with your help—“that there is no God but you” (ibid.).

But when we have said above that those oppressed by vices are driven by fear of their own destruction, we must see how this fear differs from the better fear that we call light.

Some fear being discovered in their crimes; such fear encourages them to do evil more than it restrains them. As the poet says of such people:

> The more the hidden fire is covered, the more fiercely the covered fire burns.

We too can say, in the same sense, that the more secretly a sin is committed, the more vehemently the desire of the one committing it is aroused. For what is done secretly, and what is forbidden to be done, is perpetrated more eagerly.

“I did not know desire,” says the Apostle—that is, I had not experienced it as so serious—“unless the law had said: You shall not desire” (Rom. 7:7). A certain wise man also says: “Fear is nothing but an aid to presumption” (Wis. 17:11), because when a person burns inwardly with fear, that burning, which consists entirely of servile fear, provokes him to the accomplishment of crime more than it restrains him. It is “the betrayal of the resources of thought”—that is, it shows that fear itself assists those perverse thoughts panting after evil, namely, that it supplies them with strength.

Some fear being discovered; some even fear the betrayal of their own intentions. But because such fear does not arise from the grace of God and does not consist in love, it does not overcome the ardor of vices. The children of Israel feared the punishments threatened by the law, but neither fear of punishment nor the reward promised for carnal things could keep them from transgressing the law, because they applied their minds to doing good through no love of God. They did everything under compulsion, slavishly, not in the spirit of adoption.

The fear we call light, therefore, is that which both scatters the darkness of obscene thought and kindles us toward the love of virtue.

**[Col. 0038D]** The one who first grieved over his torpor without fruit, from which he could not shake himself because heavenly grace was absent without light, now grieves, but his grief is not empty, because the anointing of the Holy Spirit—which teaches him about everything and strengthens him—is present.

In ancient times, when men trained for the wrestling ground, they customarily anointed themselves, plainly so that, because their naked bodies were made slippery by the oil, the wrestler might be held less firmly by the hands of the one wrestling with him. Naked—that is, impeded by love for worldly things [perhaps *expediti*, “freed”]—and anointed—that is, smeared with the sweet delight of divine love—we are commanded to declare single combat against the devil. His steadfastness in fighting is proportionately weaker and more fragile as the grace of compunction in the penitent’s heart is more fervent.

**VERSE 4. “When the light had been made, God saw that it was good.”** What is “God saw” except “he caused it to be seen”? It is also said of the centurion: “When Jesus heard this, he marveled” (Luke 7:9). How could he marvel, through whom every marvelous thing was created and apart from whom nothing is marvelous, except that he wished to show us something marvelous, something spoken by a faithful man for the common example?

God therefore saw that the light was good—that is, he caused it to be seen how good it is to dedicate the mind to divine fear and love. Those brought up amid delights and pleasures do not know what misery is; those nourished amid squalor and filth do not know what delights and happiness are. “Illness shows what good health possesses,” someone says; we learn what we had after we cease to have it.

When, therefore, after countless crimes we return to God and change vices into virtues, then for the first time we notice in what abyss of pestilence we had lain. And the more intensely we blush for the crime committed, the more abundantly we burn to cover our former life with the novelty of good works.

It is not merely fear lest we be discovered in our vices; even if it were permitted to sin with impunity, we would no longer wish to sin because of our love for justice, once tasted. This justice now rewards us so greatly that, even after the fear of destruction has been cast aside, it grants us the security of attaining glory.

It follows:

“And he divided between the light and the darkness” [another reading: “And he divided the light from the darkness”]. What does “he divided” mean except that he taught us to have discernment between vices and virtues? For the more closely we persist in guarding the virtues, the more keenly we recognize whatever things are opposed to them.

But there is another very important discernment, namely, that we must sharply and unceasingly attend to what we have from ourselves and what we have from God (2 Cor. 3:5). Divine mercy often impresses this upon us with wondrous skill.

At the beginning of our conversion, God often grants us such abundance of tears and such persistence in prayer that we already seem to ourselves to have gone beyond human nature and, through contemplation, to imitate the angelic. When this continues with us for some time, we presume inwardly to rejoice in our progress more than is right.

But God, by a marvelous dispensation, restrains our pride. After his grace has brought us back—we who had wandered in the wilderness, that is, lived irrationally and like beasts without God—to the road by which the city is sought, whose builder is God (Heb. 11:10), he says: “You do not have [another reading, according to the Vulgate: ‘we do not have’] a lasting city here; seek the one to come [another reading: ‘we seek’]” (Heb. 13:14).

After allowing us to taste something of heavenly sweetness, he is accustomed to withdraw the abundance of grace, to make us hunger and thirst with inward thirst and hunger, and to permit us to waste away amid evils—all for our instruction, so that he may show us what he himself says: “For without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Yet he does not utterly abandon us (Ps. 118:8). When he sees us intent and watchful in seeking him, as the bride in the Song of Songs is said to seek her beloved through the nights on her bed (Song 3:1), he finally satisfies souls empty and hungry with good things, and by the fire of his returning Spirit he dissolves the bonds of temptations that customarily rush upon us when God withdraws for a time.

What of the fact that our soul sometimes so detests all the nourishment of sacred reading, from which it used to draw the strength of compunction, that it seems to approach the gates of death (Ps. 106:18)—that is, the vices by which one goes to death? But he who tests us—not to destroy us, nor to know, but to make us know whether we love him—sends the word, that is, the taste of his word, into us, and heals us and rescues us from destruction (Ps. 106:20).

God does these things in us so that we may know that we have good things from him and evil things from ourselves, and thus divide between the light and the darkness.

**VERSE 5. “And he called the light day, and the darkness night.”** There is a certain highest light that enlightens every person (John 1:9), namely, by giving reason to each. He therefore calls—or, that is, chooses—the light, namely the reason of each person, making it day.

How day? As someone says: “Day is the sun above the earth; the sun beneath the earth is night.” If our reason wishes to be light, as it ought, let it place the sun above itself—that is, let it suppress earthly desires through love and imitation of Christ—so that it may also be called day. The wicked would not be night unless they placed Christ and their own reason beneath their lowest desires.

In Scripture, “to call,” understood as “to summon,” can be taken in two ways. In a good sense: “I have called Bezalel by name” (Exod. 31:2). In an evil sense: “He summoned famine upon the earth” (Ps. 104:21), and similarly elsewhere.

He calls darkness “night” when he hands over those who live perversely and sin voluntarily to night, that is, to a reprobate sense (Rom. 1:28). He calls it so insofar as he permits it to come about, as in: “Do not lead us into temptation.” The proper order of life, however, is that the movements of the flesh should be subjected to reason, while reason itself should first be subjected to God.

“And evening was made [*factus*, masculine; another reading, according to the Vulgate: *factumque*, ‘and it was made’], and morning, one day.” What is evening except adversity? What is morning except prosperity? “You will make the going forth of the morning into evening, and the evening into morning a delight” [another reading, according to the Vulgate: “The going forth of the morning and the evening you will make a delight”] (Ps. 64:8)—that is, you will make them delightful, because for those who love God the Spirit works all things together for good, whether in adversity or prosperity.

Evening and morning therefore make one day, because whether the saints are pressed by evils or heaped with honors, they are the same, and the same divine splendor always remains in them.

It can also be said in another way: “Evening was made and morning, one day.” We have evening in the present, because although we strive to live well, we do not yet possess perfect clarity. “We know in part and prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9). In some things we are darkened by human ignorance and the violence of temptations; in others we are suffused, as if by a certain light, with divine knowledge and the use of experience.

We therefore have evening now and morning in the future. Thus, although the order is inappropriate according to the literal sense, it is excellent according to the meaning that evening is placed first and morning afterward, because through the exercise of the body, which weighs down the soul because it is corruptible (Wis. 9:15), we arrive at the morning brightness of heavenly understanding.

For it is said to God: “Will you add days upon the days of the king?” (Ps. 60:7.) The days are now ours in the evening of this age, in which we serve God; but other days are added to them, in which, renewed by unfailing light, we shall serve God our king himself. Yet these are one day, because they form one whole and render one service to God.

Again, that same one day can be understood as fear. Since, as we said above, it is the beginning of wisdom (Sir. 1:16) and arises from love, it always enlightens us in adversity and prosperity alike, and is recognized as the first step by which one reaches wisdom. It is called one because it is first.

**VERSE 6. “And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.”** In sacred writings, waters often signify kinds of knowledge, as in: “You who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55:1)—this in a good sense—and: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17)—this in an evil sense.

For it is sufficiently clear that there are two kinds of knowledge: one divine and the other worldly. The Apostle James defines worldly knowledge as earthly (James 3:15), that is, yearning for earthly things; animal, that is, seeking only what irrational animals desire; and demonic (ibid.), because it is occupied solely with this: it counts it as triumph and glory if it can deceive others, make its profits from the losses of others, amass wealth from the tears of the poor, inflict harm cautiously on another in revenge for itself, and—what is worse—commit evil gratuitously and boldly exult in having committed it.

In Scripture this is called by the name of wisdom in a highly abusive sense, just as law and judgment are called so: although these ought always to be good, sometimes “evil law” and “perverse judgment” are spoken of.

But “the wisdom that is from above” (James 3:17), as the same Apostle says first, is “pure” (ibid.), because, in its own beauty, it desires to please no one but God alone, rather than to please another by adulterous love—a vice with which all human wisdom, or, more correctly, cunning or craft, is allied.

Then it is “peaceable” (ibid.), because it does not persist in the clamor of words or disputes; rather, governing itself tranquilly, it benevolently joins the hearts of others to itself. It is also “moderate” (ibid.), because it permits us to do nothing indiscreetly. It is likewise “persuadable” (ibid.), because it entirely avoids obstinacy and, readily obeying reason, does not reject anything that ought to be believed. Its power is so great that without it no one can accomplish anything virtuous.

We understand wisdom in two ways. We call Christ the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24), who says through a certain wise man: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24:5). We also call wisdom the rational and intellectual capacity created by God in angels and human beings, which says: “From the beginning and before the ages I was created” (ibid., 14). This wisdom, proceeding from the mouth of God, creates that capacity in us; joined to our mind, it supplies strength for knowing the truth and doing what is honorable [Col. 0042A], and, making virtue effective in our weakness, it strengthens and confirms whatever in us is fragile and old. Our mind, then, joined to this wisdom and taking from it an inward richness and an outward abundance, becomes reason. Reason is named from *ratum*, that is, “firm,” because nothing is firmer than what is done with reason. Yet reason, unless supported by that heavenly wisdom, is wholly changeable, harmful, and perverse, and cannot even properly be called reason. It therefore becomes a firmament whenever it joins itself to divine prudence, because from it it receives the strength by which it may sustain the waters above through thirst and place those below under the dominion of reason.

For we possess the mysteries of spiritual knowledge above, not so much locally as, so to speak, mentally. We ought to yearn to drink them—indeed, to draw them in with all our desires—because they instruct us through heavenly teaching, build up our conduct, quell our vices, increase our disciplines, oppose our weariness, invite us with rewards, suggest punishments, and lead us through the sharpness of contemplation into the height of all truth. “Above,” I say, not in location but in dignity. Hence the Apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, and set your minds on them” (Col. 3:1).

Beneath us we have the cunning of secular life, which teaches and urges us to seek bodily goods, neglect the soul, love frauds and quarrels, and desire and hold whatever is contrary to salvation. Between these two runs reason, which, armed from above against what is below, strives so faithfully to cling to what rules it and from which it receives the sufficiency of its steadfastness that it wants to keep subject to its own authority the animal nature—that is, its body—and whatever the prudence of the flesh, which the Apostle calls “death” (Rom. 8:6), demands from it.

Through this firmament, therefore, the waters above the heavens—that is, so to speak, the waters above reason—and those below, which roll us down toward the depths, are divided. For the mind’s power, strengthened by the love of God, as it subjects itself to heavenly understanding, as is fitting, aspires upward; and, by placing itself above unworthy desires, it exercises over them the authority proper to a master. Its vigor and integrity must be such that whatever pertains to divine wisdom, whether in word or deed, is done for no hope of temporal advantage. And if anything is done either for the body’s mere necessity—or even without necessity, but from perverse desire—the blind judge of himself must not imagine that he is doing it appropriately and sincerely out of devotion to divine service.

This, then, is how the firmament seems to me both to stand and to be able to stand between the waters. Yet this same firmament is called “heaven” by God. Heaven contains many mysteries, and not undeservedly is likened to our mind, in which whatever is suited to the soul’s salvation, healing, and consolation is guarded, as in a treasury, until the proper time when circumstances require it to be brought forth. We discussed this more fully above, when we were treating of heaven and earth.

## VERSE 8.—“And it was evening, and it was morning, the second day.”

According to blessed Gregory, our beginnings are mixed with evils. Although morning illumines us with devout dedication to God [Col. 0043A], very often the darkness of our former—indeed, natural—habit still envelops us. The mind grows dark through the fault of its earthly burden, lest we become proud because of grace, God ordering this for our benefit; but then it is illumined again by the ardor of contrition, lest it sink into the abyss of despair or crime. Thus, while we are led alternately upward to the heavens and downward to the abysses, with the heavenly hand serving as our oar, we come through these changes to the point where we may exist without danger and without fear even of danger—that is, to the celibate life.

This is the second day because, after fear, which is the first degree, piety is the second. Piety pertains to the worship of God, as in the Apostle’s words: “Let us live soberly, justly, and piously” (Tit. 2:1). This is explained as follows: soberly within ourselves, justly toward our neighbor, and piously toward God. Hence the impious are properly called those who are alien from faith. What greater piety, what greater affection toward God, can there be for any of us than to recline the whole intention of our mind in the bosom of divine wisdom, and to make ourselves weak and foolish in the affairs of this world, in which certain people boast that they are especially capable and wise? After the fear of God, this is a very suitable and appropriate degree.

But a serious question arises here: why, whereas on the preceding day and on the following days it is said, “God saw that it was good,” is this omitted today? We know that it is said of the devil that “he did not stand in the truth.” As long as he clung to the highest Truth, he himself was truth insofar as he was joined to it. For “whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Of him it is written in Job: “Let them dwell in his tabernacle”—namely, his impious companions—“who is not” (Job 18:15). Who is the one “who is not” except the devil, who, insofar as he fell away from true being, ceased even to be? For how can one be who is so wretchedly alive—or rather, who is eternally in death without dying?

We understand the same to be true of ourselves, because we fell from the vision of God in our first parents, passed from truth into vanity, and truly lost our being, except that we believe we are restored by God’s grace alone, though through our own most arduous toil and struggle. Thus, while we labor with great sighs to swallow the saliva of our head—that is, to taste beforehand the wisdom of our Creator—we find ourselves placed in strong opposition to ourselves, and in the work of salvation we suffer no nearer or more hostile enemy than ourselves. Hence the Psalmist complains: “You have shown me many tribulations, many and grievous” (Ps. 70:22). Elsewhere, under the hope of future good, he rejoices: “For the days in which he was humbled, the years in which he saw”—that is, experienced—“evil” (Ps. 89:17).

Since, therefore, the days are evil (Eph. 5:16), and the world lies in the evil one (1 John 5:19), and since we endure this conflict of the lower waters—where pride contends against the higher waters, in which humility and holiness are established—in the valley of tears, in the lake of misery, that is, in the present age; since prophetic and apostolic speech declares this to be not life and homeland but exile and death, how can God “see”—that is, make it appear—that what he wishes us to avoid and recognize as deceptive evil is good? The Apostle cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). Should we call good the torments we endure, the struggle of the flesh against the spirit and of the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17)?

And if we do some good, since we are always amid turmoil and in danger of sin, let us sigh for Noah—that is, Christ—to make us rest, like Noah’s dove, because here we have no rest. It is rightly called the second day, because we do not see that it is good. After losing in our first parent the glory we possessed in the first day, in paradise, and being cast down to this place, we find pains, not goods. This is aptly signified by the tract traditionally sung after the Alleluia on Holy Saturday, which teaches that after the joy of paradise we have fallen into the labor of this age.

## VERSE 9.—“And God said: Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.”

The waters under heaven are secular cunning, skilled chiefly in worldly business and especially in deception, yet restrained beneath the yoke of our understanding. They are gathered into one place because all our anxieties—which previously flowed about, wandering and unstable—are compelled, whether they wish it or not, to serve God, who is our place, in whom we live, move, and are (Acts 17:28).

In Scripture, faithful people are often called God’s places, or even God’s place; but God himself is much more properly called our place, outside whom neither we nor anything else exists. Because he gives life to those whom he receives, he is rightly called one.

All the prudence we possess from the world is then fully converted to God when secular people gird themselves for managing ecclesiastical affairs and external concerns, which learned men ordinarily know less about, out of zeal and love to serve those who devote themselves to contemplation, so that they may have more freedom to attend to God. Such people no longer use their skill to deceive the poor. Rather, they devoutly spend the gold and silver they brought out of Egypt on building God’s tabernacle in the wilderness—that is, outside the crowds of vices.

These are the haircloths of God’s house, who endure the dust of secular cares so that the hyacinth and purple of holy minds may bear no external disturbance but may persist continually in their chosen purpose. “And let the dry land appear,” he says. For by the fact that a formerly fluid conscience is restrained toward God, the earth of our heart, dried out from the flooding of superfluous thoughts, now appears ready to bear the fruits of good works.

## VERSE 10.—“And God called the dry land earth, and the gathering of the waters he called seas.”

The earth, smoothed by the moisture of carnal wantonness and greed, is indeed fit for divine cultivation and fruitfulness. But the gatherings of the waters, not voluntarily restraining themselves under the rule of reason, stir up in us the bitterest waves of temptations. Hence they are very appropriately called “seas,” for *maria* means “bitterness.”

From these arise storms of fierce anger, lust, and other movements. When they are restrained by the command of the mind, they are like the seething, bubbling heat of a strait attempting to leap forth. But God’s mercy does not leave the exercises of this struggle unrewarded. He sees—or makes us see—how good and health-giving are the things we do, and from contemplating them, with his inspiration, the mind grows ardent to do better things. Hence by his invisible nod he speaks—that is, he attributes prosperous accomplishment to good dispositions.

## VERSE 11.—“Let the earth,” he said, “bring forth green grass and produce seed.”

The earth brings forth grass when the heart of each believer, made clear of all the world’s wantonness, sends forth through the seed of God’s word the beginnings of a way of life. It is green grass because it lives by the sap of eternal hope. Whatever is done for human approval is withered and sterile [Col. 0045B].

“And producing seed,” he says. Whoever effectively carries out in action the religious purpose he undertakes produces seed. Or, certainly, the green grass produces seed when someone does not cease proclaiming to others, out of goodwill and so that they may imitate him, the good he has begun to do within himself.

“And the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind.” What is meant by the fruit-bearing tree except an arduous way of life progressing from devout beginnings to holier things? But what does holiness accomplish if its goodness is of no use to others? When, in the tenderness of our beginnings, we willingly offer to others the good things we have begun to taste, then, by God’s gracious generosity, we become worthy of being advanced to better things. Hence it is said: “Producing fruit according to its kind” [Col. 0045C]—that is, gaining one’s neighbor for God.

Our kind is human nature. We therefore bear fruit according to our kind when, by teaching and praying, we make our neighbors participants in the gift that exists within us. It is said in Job: “And visiting your dwelling, you shall not sin” (Job 5:24), which is the same as if he said: “You shall produce fruit according to your kind.” It continues:

“Whose seed is in itself upon the earth.” Our seed is our works, which we perform here for the fruit of the heavenly prize. We are commanded to have this seed within ourselves, lest, while doing good and being anointed by the tales of flatterers, we be carried away like straw by the wind of praise toward something found outside us. Let our virtue therefore be grain; let it not leave the granary of the heart.

But our fruit must not be so hidden within that it is not brought forth as an example to our neighbor: “Let it be upon the earth,” that is, let it come into the visibility of bodily work. It is possible both to do good and to despise praise when it is offered. What follows is a repetition of what preceded.

## VERSE 13.—“And it was evening, and it was morning, the third day.”

What is this third day except knowledge, the third degree for those who, after fear and piety, strive toward wisdom? Nothing is more appropriate to spiritual knowledge than restraining worldly cunning and, when one has acted well, calling others to pursue holiness.

According to blessed Gregory, knowledge pertains to teaching, while wisdom pertains to life. Evening and morning suitably correspond to knowledge, because scarcely anyone is able to possess everywhere the light of understanding in Scripture. The sacred words have a body, like evening, in the covering of the letter; and they have a soul, like morning, in the splendor of morality and allegory.

## VERSE 14.—“And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day and the night.”

It is sufficiently appropriate to interpret these two lights as Christ and the Church, according to the passage: “Day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. 18:2), and so forth. We call Christ the model set before the strong for imitation; and we rightly understand the Church to be set forth in its ordinary members as a model for the young and the less capable.

It is certainly more tolerable for weak eyes to look at a lamp beneath a lantern than to see the sun’s radiance in the power of its own sphere. God gives the sun authority over the day when he bestows the gifts of contemplation upon men endowed with intellectual understanding.

We plainly see some people of either sex who, having professed virginity, prefer the poverty of Christ to the possession of worldly things and devote themselves to God. There are others, however, who can neither abandon the world, nor live celibately, nor devote themselves wholly to God. Therefore he gives the moon and the stars authority over the night.

For those of us who do not dare to presume upon the highest things, and who cannot imitate Noah—that is, rulers—or Daniel—that is, celibates—he grants that we may follow Job, who did good works and devoted himself to mercy. Those who do not hope to reach the golden reclining place—that is, blessed rest—by the purple ascent, namely martyrdom, may at least reach it by the middle way, spread with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem.

Whoever, therefore, does not dare to follow wherever he goes the Lamb shining forth from the eternal mountains (Rev. 14:5), should attend to the mountains illumined by him. Even if he cannot follow them in everything, he should strive to follow them in something, so that he may be reckoned as a member of the Church. When these things come to pass—that is, when some choose the difficult and perfect things while others propose the easier ones—day and night are divided, because the quality of one’s life is revealed by the pursuits each person chooses.

“Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years, and let them illumine the earth.”

The phrase “for signs and seasons” means no more than if he had said, “for signs of the seasons,” as in the expression, “He poured libations from bowls and with gold,” meaning “from golden bowls” [Col. 0046D].

Christ and the Church are signs of the seasons, because whatever has been or is being done appears one way in reality and signifies another thing. Christ and those who belong to him, while they live in the present, endure the reproaches and hardships of the world. If glory is sought from those who are fed by the world, why do they endure these things? “Because,” they say, “our time has not yet come, but your time is always ready” (John 7:6).

The time of the saints’ glorification is not yet present, because they do not have here a lasting city (Heb. 13:14). Rather, they have a place in which those who have chosen to be gold are melted and in which they are crushed by afflictions, so that they may be built into the temple of the King without axe or hammer (1 Kings 6:7).

The time of the perverse, while they live here, is always at hand, because neither does opportunity lack for them to be honored temporarily if fortune smiles, nor do they themselves lack honors. The word “time” is used both for evil and for good; common speech even says to those to whom evil things are destined: “You will have your time.” Hence in the psalm: “And their time shall be for ever” (Ps. 80:16). Here they will have the time of glory; there, the time of misery.

There is no time after the end of this age, according to the passage in the Apocalypse: “And time shall be no more” (Rev. 10:6). But “time” and “age” are customarily used in the same sense for what constitutes life. Hence the Apostle says: “You once walked according to the age of this world” (Eph. 2:2). The psalm likewise says: “You have placed our age in the light of your countenance” (Ps. 89:8), that is, our life. We also commonly say of someone: “That man is living through an evil age.”

Since Christ, therefore, in the days of his flesh sought reproaches rather than honors, and since the Church still willingly endures poverty and labors, this is a sign that they did not wish to fasten their minds upon these temporal goods. Rather, its members extend themselves toward future things, “forgetting what lies behind” (Phil. 3:13), and they delight and strive to become heirs of those things, since they are eternal.

“And days, and years.” Days are the individual virtues given through the manifestation of the Spirit for the common benefit—not merely kinds of tongues or interpretation of speech, but, more beneficially, patience, kindness, mercy, charity, and chastity [Col. 0047C]. Whoever attains any one of these has a day. Whoever possesses the perfection of them all—which we do not doubt existed among the apostolic men—has, or rather is, a year, so long as the present age endures. Although such people are exceedingly rare, we hope that some will not be lacking.

Just as a year is composed of many days, so each person is recognized as perfect through the varied light of the virtues. The daughter of Job is appropriately called “Day,” and Job himself is said to have died “full of days.”

## VERSE 16.—“And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.”

God therefore makes the greater light, which illumines the lesser, because the Word made flesh illumines the Church through knowledge of himself, and the Church illumines the earth—that is, the conscience of those who love earthly things—through its example and teaching. “And the stars.”

## VERSES 17 AND 18.—“And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, to rule the day and the night.”

Not only Christ but also the harmony of the universal Church, in which its members belong to one another, must be impressed upon the firmament of heaven—that is, the strength of the mind. We must attend not only to the holiness of the whole Church but also to the simplicity of individuals, who are represented by the stars. They rule the day and the night because they protect us in the keeping of the virtues and instruct us, through consideration of their teaching and practice, in avoiding vices [Col. 0048A]. “For we are not of the night or of darkness, but of the day and of light” (1 Thess. 5:5).

## VERSE 19.—“And it was evening, and it was morning, the fourth day.”

Although we have said many things about the statement repeatedly given beforehand, “God saw that it was good,” we must especially note this: when God grants increase to his gifts within us, and, conversely, we perceive from how little he has made us and what he has made us, the greatest depth of humility is generated in our minds.

God sees that it is good when he makes us humbly consider what we once were and what we are now. From contemplating the good we have begun, he kindles our mind toward better things. Hence he compels us, with the Apostle, to say: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

The fourth day is the fourth degree, namely the strength of spiritual graces [Col. 0048B]. What strengthens the mind more, and from what is strength more greatly nourished, than when we consider God himself and his chosen ones despising prosperity and nowhere fearing the adversities of the world? If we are outside discipline and refuse to be scourged with others, we are adulterers and not sons.

Let strength therefore spring up in evening and morning, in adversity and in joy, from such examples; and let every darkness of weariness yield to the vigor of our minds, powerfully aroused by these things.

The greater light may also be understood as reason, the lesser light as the will, and the earth as carnal affection. For just as the moon is illumined by the sun and the earth by the moon, so our will is entirely comparable to the moon, because it never remains in the same condition and often wanes. Unless it is ruled by reason with a strong restraint, it is very frequently led to consent to carnal desire, which always thirsts for filth.

But just as a son is restrained by his father from the company of parasites, so the will is compelled to obey the spirit; and consequently it itself compels the movement of the flesh to serve it. When these things have been ordered in the manner we described—when the will has been made an appendage of reason and carnal affection has been placed under the command of a just will—they must necessarily be fixed, together with the stars, that is, with the brightness of all our virtues [Col. 0048D], in the firmament of heaven—namely, in him by whose Word, or rather through whom, the heavens themselves were made and established, and all their strength is by the Spirit of his mouth (Ps. 32:6).

## VERSE 20.—“And God said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature with a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth, beneath the firmament of heaven.”

What is meant by the creeping creature except the subtle alertness of minds for understanding and penetrating the obscurities of the divine books? Water is the abundance of divine knowledge: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who cover yourself with waters” (Ps. 103:3), and so forth. The following can also be understood positively: “The fish of the sea that pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8:9).

The waters bring forth creeping creatures when the use of sacred Scripture makes our hearts keen in discovering the most subtle things and swift in explaining them. In these things we are, as it were, generated and transformed into their nature, to such an extent that without them we cannot live or think anything agreeable apart from them. For what is more unworthy, what more burdensome to a living soul—to speak according to the text, and to say nothing here of the dead whom secular things nourish—than to abstain from divine reading and pass a day without the fruit of study?

These, then, are the living creeping creatures who immerse their breasts in this holy knowledge as in the purest waves. Knowledge concerns morals and the proper conduct of human affairs: it treats how these should honorably be done and teaches the same to one’s neighbors.

By the flying creature above the earth we understand those who study wisdom and, through the excellence of contemplation, rise above all earthly things. We define wisdom as knowledge of eternal things and understanding of God. Contemplation, however, we understand in two ways: first, when we examine keenly the distinction between true and false, virtues and vices, useful and useless things; and second, in the contemplation of the divine majesty and the glory of the heavenly citizens.

Those who devote themselves to contemplation and wisdom, like those we mentioned earlier who seek knowledge, take their origin from the waters—that is, from Scripture—because, nourished by it, they learn how they ought to exercise themselves in seeking spiritual meanings.

But although they raise themselves on the wings of holy thought above earthly things, they must nevertheless lower themselves beneath the firmament. Here the firmament may be understood as the angelic nature, which, while others fall, remains with perpetual stability in the seat of blessedness. Although the angels always behold the face of the Father, according to the Gospel (Matt. 18:10), yet, because they are creatures, they cannot in any way comprehend the majesty of their Creator.

Although they have not even the slightest desire to sin or the burden of flesh by which they might be weighed down and prevented from contemplating God, they are permitted to see him to some extent but never to see through him completely. What can a sinful human being, weighed down by corruptible matter, see in a place where even spiritual nature is partly obscured?

For that nature itself, in comparison with God, is corporeal, because it can be circumscribed whereas God cannot; and because it is not identical with God, it cannot comprehend what God is. Let us therefore consider whether anyone could be so holy that, through a mirror and an enigma, he might sparkle toward that supreme light, and how far below the angelic dignity he still lies, since the angelic nature, although most pure, is nevertheless created and therefore sees God less fully [Col. 0049D].

Let us therefore fly beneath the firmament. Even if we discuss divine things, we must consider in all our contemplation that we are far removed from the angels’ acuity and cannot presume in this life to attain either their likeness or, still less, their equality.

By the firmament we may also understand the humility of the Savior, which, through the resurrection, has become immortal and impassible and has already, as it were, been made firm. It is much more probable and safer to direct the mind imaginatively beneath this humility and to sigh toward it with the devout heat of desire than to direct an eye, even a bleary one, to a place where something unfitting concerning God might be imagined, and from which an intellect unaccustomed to spiritual things, presumptuously raising itself toward what is too lofty, might fall into fantastical thought.

God is not seen through the coarseness of imagination but entirely through spiritual acuity. For God is Spirit. Let us therefore contemplate the Word made flesh, through loving whom we may be raised above earthly things.

## VERSE 21.—“God created the great whales, and every living and moving creature, which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every flying creature according to its kind.”

What are the great whales except the most illustrious teachers, whose extraordinarily capacious minds we admire above all? What were Augustine, Jerome, and finally Gregory, if not enormous wonders to their own age and to ours? To say it briefly: I do not mean merely that so many and such great things could be found and retained by them, but—more wonderfully—that they were able to write such innumerable works that we can scarcely grasp even half of them, or even simply read them.

Who could read through the sayings of the glorious Origen in five thousand books? Who could worthily understand the mysteries of Dionysius the Areopagite? We pass over these divine spectacles, which should more rightly be pondered by the reader’s mind, rather than say little—or indeed nothing—about them in proportion to what the matter itself deserves.

God makes such remarkable creatures, but he also makes the living soul—that is, those who live by faith. Even if they do not perform works, their faith, according to the Apostle, is counted as righteousness (Rom. 4:22). He also makes the moving creature, namely those who know how to give lively movements not only toward believing but also toward doing good.

There are indeed those who are saved by the sacrament of faith alone, such as infants, for whom the faith of others comes to their aid, and those whom the necessity of death compels to receive Christianity [Col. 0050C]. There are also others whom pure willingness and desire for an eternal reward urge toward the pursuit of right living. The former are living creatures; the latter, moving creatures.

Yet all originate from the waters, because from the preaching of sacred Scripture they conceive the inclination to think well and bring to completion what they have conceived well. These creeping creatures also have their kinds, and the flying creatures their genus, because those who believe well, live justly, and contemplate subtly each possess varied charismatic gifts according to their measure, and these diverse gifts produce a common purpose in a single intention.

## VERSE 22.—“And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.”

It is as though God, observing our exercises by which we burn to earn better things through good merits, were plainly saying: “Increase in understanding, and multiply by instructing one another in the sacred words; fill the waters of the sea”—that is, the fullness of Scripture—with allegorical and moral interpretations; and let those whom the wing of contemplation raises up, in discernment of spirits and contemplation of heavenly mysteries, burn with spiritual love upon the earth—that is, let them be drawn away from the allurements of earthly desire.

The waters of the sea are not inappropriately compared with sacred Scripture, because it is Scripture that makes the belly of John bitter in the Apocalypse (Rev. 10:10), and that increases the thirst of the one who drinks the more it is drunk. Hence Isaiah cries out to the thirsty to come to the waters (Isa. 55:1). God also sees that it is good, because through delight in the gifts received he arouses our gaze toward the desire for better things.

## VERSE 23.—“And it was evening, and it was morning, the fifth day.”

The fifth degree of divine grace is counsel. What task is counsel more appropriate to than investigating the questions of sacred Scripture? For nowhere does one err more dangerously than by departing from the rules and interpretations of the ancient Fathers.

Let their judgment therefore be maintained everywhere—those who wrote how the obscurities of sacred speech should be investigated—and let inquiry be made of those from whom the answers are sought with the same ardor of the Spirit by which those who discovered the answers are known to have sought them.

In all our affairs let us have them beside us, as it were, to protect us by their counsels: lest we hurl down a definite judgment on doubtful matters; lest, when understanding is lacking, we wish to accuse the authors of excessive obscurity or rusticity, which would be a dreadful crime.

In such discussions, even if we sometimes suffer the evening of failure or darkness, through constant meditation, accompanied by the heat of divine love, we shall be able to attain the morning of intelligible light. A person scarcely ever reaches anything supreme in a languid state of mind—or never, as I have learned from myself. What I thought, when lukewarm, no one could accomplish, I easily broke into when more spirited than usual.

## VERSE 24.—“And God said: Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind: cattle, and creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.”

In many places, and especially the mind of each believer, and generally the whole Church, is called “earth,” on account of its fertility and cultivability, because it is cultivated by the mattocks of the divine commandment and is recognized as fruitful in good works.

The Church produces a living soul at God’s command, because that true Solomon, although he has sixty queens, nevertheless has eighty concubines, and there is no number of young women (Song 6:7). In the people of God, although not all leave everything behind, and although they cannot be virgins, God has nevertheless established a middle place for his people, from which, if one lives rightly, the desired salvation may be attained. Therefore there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house (John 14:2); therefore star differs from star in glory (1 Cor. 15:41), because in this valley of pilgrimage there are very diverse orders of life among us.

There are certain souls who possess a spark—not necessarily of ardor for acting energetically, but at least for willing what is good—and who willingly give alms, devoutly attend ecclesiastical services, and, performing other moderate good works with devotion, restrain themselves as far as they can from the pollution of capital sins. Thus they live insofar as love of God or faith is concerned. They are cattle insofar as they offer help to anyone through good consolation or kindness.

But it must be noted that he says “according to its kind,” because “we have gifts differing according to the grace” (Rom. 12:6): one in this way, another in that. The Apostle repeatedly unfolds these gifts in many places and in various ways. Hence he says that although our members have different functions in the body (ibid., 4), they nevertheless preserve unity through the harmony of their functions and mutual assistance. What he calls “members” there is called here “kind” or “kinds.”

Animals suited to service are called cattle. They appropriately signify the life of certain secular people who, although inclined toward some earthly occupations, are nevertheless greatly restrained from their own freedom insofar as they strive to serve the needs of others. This interpretation is supported by the fact that such animals are largely dependent upon the earth.

The Church also has creeping things, because it contains certain people who cling so closely to worldly cares and pleasures [Col. 0052B] that they are separated from temporal things by no interval of virtue. Nevertheless, they live—and this by faith alone. With its help, although they have no foot of works, they slide across the earth through the activity of a lively understanding. They know that they do wrong and cling to transitory things; yet, groaning within themselves in hope of obtaining mercy, they are accustomed to make leaps over the things to which they cling.

The authorities report that creeping things—which in this passage we understand as serpents—possess their vital soul chiefly in the head, so that even if the rest of the body is entirely cut off, provided that at least a measure of a palm remains attached to the head, they cannot die because of the vitality that remains in the head.

This closely resembles what the teachings of our faith maintain: a sinner entangled in any error, even if he repents with a groan at the very moment of death, will, as he dies, belong to the company of those who are to be saved. For it is written: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:12). They are saved by faith, as the Apostle says: “To the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Rom. 4:45).

They do not have the body—that is, works—but, living by the head—that is, by faith—they work for themselves from that one thing by which they always live. This is supported by the fact that serpents customarily expose their entire body to danger in order to protect only their head.

So these people, often despising the temporal things they possess through fear of God, and sometimes at the moment of their death or amid whatever dangers, save the head for themselves—that is, Christ or faith in Christ—by becoming monks or by living well in some other way.

Among the beasts of the earth are figured certain people within the Church distinguished by a savage disposition and cruelty. Although, through the secular power they exercise, they commit many evils, yet when they return to their senses they often fear God’s judgment greatly and consequently bestow many benefits. If they perform these humbly, do not take confidence from the good work as a license to sin, and cannot be entirely freed from worldly concerns, I dare not say that such people are to be despaired of. Who was worse than Nebuchadnezzar, to whom the prophet says: “Redeem your sins by mercies toward the poor” (Dan. IV, 24)? And if Daniel did not neglect to preach repentance to an idolater and a pagan, and another prophet preached the same to the people of Nineveh, not only overwhelmed by countless crimes but wholly ignorant of the true God, it is sufficiently astonishing that repentance was announced to those who had no knowledge of the faith. If it was announced to these, how much more will it profit Christians? And who would despair of the faithful, if so great a hope is given even to the impious?

God has established each of these within the Church according to the degree of his own life, to make clear to us that, if one is not able to strive toward the highest discipleship of God, that is, toward imitation of him, one should at least know that there is an intermediate place for those who have lesser ability. For the same one who, when praising virginity under the name of eunuchs, said, “Let him receive it who is able to receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12), also said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess” (ibid. 21), and so forth. He did not say, “Unless you sell it, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” For what he said—“Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33)—means the same as if he had said: “He cannot imitate me perfectly if it is established that he desires earthly riches.” Whoever decides to profess himself someone’s disciple does so with this intention: that, in the one from whom he wishes to have a teacher, he desires to become like him. And although there may be a teacher who goes about teaching many people, they are not ordinarily called his disciples unless they walk specially at his side, solely for the purpose of learning.

Thus the water that produces flying creatures from the fullness of saving wisdom and knowledge has men of distinction, with the wing of contemplation. The earth—that is, the humanity of Christ—has the minds of simple people as though they were beasts of burden, creeping things, and beasts. If they cannot fix their eyes upon the light of the Word, nevertheless they steadily attend, through the gaze of faith and hope, to Christ incarnate for the redemption of sinners. Since uttering the Word belongs to the day, “night to night consequently declares knowledge” (Ps. XVIII, 2), the Church contains within itself these conditions of the living, who rightly deserve to be called cattle in comparison with those who conduct themselves rationally. Or they are called this with reference to piety, because they serve the needs of human beings—that is, of those who live rightly and wisely—as domestic animals. For there is nothing among living creatures, or even among inanimate things, that is not useful to human beings in some respect. Under this figure, while God waters the mountains from his heights, through them he provides drink for beasts and wild asses, and from them once again carries hay and grass for human service (Ps. CXLVI, 8). The mountains in which hay is produced are called by the same name because of their height, while in the same passage the beasts are so called because of their ferocity.

Even the faithful soul, although it has risen to the highest stages of life, indeed suffers these movements within itself most bitterly. Beasts of burden are present not only in us, who scarcely possess the beginnings of conversion, but also in holy and most intelligent people—namely, in the apostle Paul and those like him. They are the dullnesses of this burden-bearing mortality of ours, by which the alacrity of the inner person is blunted and frequently weighed down, when he sees “another law in his members warring against the law of his reason” (Rom. VII, 23). Because of this, the entire spiritual Church cries out with things that can be felt more readily than spoken by anyone: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII, 24.)

Creeping things are present too: the lowest and wholly carnal desires, which habitually incline us. With these we creep on our belly—that is, we cling through affection to earthly pleasures—and, through the frequent stimulation of tickling sensations, we become slippery and soft like a snake, our spirit’s firmness having been thinned. For when we believe that we have reached the heights of virtue, lest the abundance of grace should lift us up, by God’s favorable judgment “a thorn in the flesh” is sent to us “by an angel of Satan to buffet us” (II Cor. XII, 7). Thus, when we fall from supercelestial reflection to meditate on things, so to speak, lower than earthly, we perceive what we are in ourselves without God’s work.

Nor are beasts absent—namely, beastly habits, insolence, anger, and resentments. Although they cannot drive holy men into perpetual discord, they nevertheless generate great disturbances in their hearts for a time. While they prevent the ferocity of the inner murmur from emerging in speech, they make them endure within themselves the most burning heats of thoughts that hurl themselves against one another and return insults with great uproar. Vices, however, scarcely ever—or never—attack anyone all at once; they assail us in turn. When the stimulus of pleasure has been put to sleep, anger rages; when anger has rested for a time, lust boils up; and when these have again been subdued, empty glory or pride creeps in.

These three things that we have presented under the figures of beasts of burden, creeping things, and beasts are also suitably indicated in another figure in the psalm: “We offer you fattened burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I will offer you oxen with goats” (Ps. LXV, 15). We offer burnt offerings when we consume everything that we are in the love of God. They are fattened when, without the inner fatness of charity, the bones of our virtues are not bare; for the branch of good action is dry if it has no sap of divine and mutual charity. We offer them with incense—that is, with burning and consumption of all stubbornness—which we know is signified above by the beasts and here by the ram.

We must offer burnt offerings because, if the devil is “king over all the sons of pride” (Job. XLI, 25), and if the son of so great a monster and the devil’s servant brings gifts to God, what could appear more ungrateful, more shameful, or more unworthy to God himself? Nevertheless, I say this so long as he has decided to lie in the very depth of death.

We offer oxen when we change every burden, and the sin that surrounds and weighs us down, which makes us animal-like and dull in the things of God, through fervor, the sharpness of reason, and spiritual vitality; and in changing it we consume it as far as nature permits. These are signified above by the beasts of burden.

We burn goats in reconciliation to God when, in our flesh and in the innermost affections of the soul, we scatter the fluid excesses of wantonness. These goats—or rather, those things figured by goats—are the creeping things we have brought forward. Everything has been named according to the nature of each animal: the ram is a proud and warlike animal; the ox is heavy and dull, whence Solomon says of the fool, “She follows him as an ox led to the slaughter” (Prov. VII, 22); the goat is wanton and lascivious, whence Ovid says of Galatea:

> More wanton than a tender kid  
> (Met. XIII, 790).

When these and similar things are trampled beneath the foot of great authority by those who possess the days of virtue described above—whether they do not know how to turn to the right or to the left, that is, whether they neither know how to be lifted up by the increase of virtues, which is the right, nor to be cast down by the assaults of vices, which is the left—God, who rejoices in our progress, continually increases the gifts of grace and finally perfects in us that toward which all our struggle and desire are directed.

Whatever good we undertake, we plainly do it—or rather, ought to do it—for no other reason than that we may be restored to conformity with the divine image that we have lost. Therefore God, who anticipates those whom he wishes to act well by the gift of grace, and assists those who follow grace with pious efforts in accomplishing what they had desired, raises them to the highest fellowship of his likeness, saying, so to speak:

## Verse 26

“Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Although some believe “image” and “likeness” to be the same, at times they differ greatly. An image properly means something painted or sculpted in order to represent the memory of something, even if it is not like the thing for which it is fashioned. “Likeness,” however, is used indiscriminately of all things that are similar to one another in any way, even if one was not made on account of the other.

I could be called an image of my father even if I did not resemble him in appearance, because my father was the cause of my existence. Hence, in this way, both image and likeness can be spoken of one thing, if they were made on account of the same thing and are alike.

Virgil, however, introducing Andromache speaking about Ascanius, says:

> O you, the sole surviving image of my Astyanax!  
> (Aeneid III, 489).

In reality, he used “image” for “likeness,” and perhaps still called him an image because, although he was not that man’s son, he derived his form from his relationship to him.

Adam possessed the image of God in his soul, in that part by which it is eternal, since God is eternal by nature whereas the soul is eternal by gift. They define the image in terms of eternity and likeness in terms of moral character.

We can plainly say that we possess the image of God in this respect: just as God, filling the whole world, is present generally to all things while nevertheless being perceived as wholly present in his own way to each individual thing, so our soul, incorporated into the body, fills the body, makes it move and live, and governs it with perfect order. And just as it cannot be discerned of God whether he is considered more present to heaven than to earth, so the soul is in no way felt more in the head than in the smallest toe. Whoever is injured in either place suffers in the same way; for the soul is found wholly in each and every member. You know how grievously you suffer when a nail is injured. The body has spirit everywhere, just as the world has God everywhere.

God is the universal reason by which the whole structure of things is governed in a marvelous and incomprehensible order, in which nothing seems extraordinary, nothing without cause, and nothing unsuitable to those who think rightly. The same gift is clearly granted to human beings, since they can arrange their external person through the intellectual power of the inner person, so that nothing inept or shameful may be found in the presentation of their works.

God lives and understands. He has placed in the fleshly mass a soul that is alive through itself and life-giving, which renders its bodily burden vigorous outwardly, while inwardly it possesses foresight through participation in heavenly light.

We are therefore the image of God; we were made for his glory and honor, not for the sake of our own merit or usefulness—for he had no need of us, but made us so that we might enjoy him blessedly. The cause of our existence, as of all created things, was that he might be glorified through us—not that he should gain anything from our glorification, but that, by glorifying him both in considering him and in considering the marvelous ordering of the whole world on our account, man might become more glorious.

We, therefore, must be conformed to the order by which he governs us and the world, [lacuna], namely, existing as our own masters, ruling over our vices, and conducting all that is ours with virtue, so that we may be made like the heavenly image.

We said above that likeness must be considered in moral character, because just as God is love, justice, piety, purity, and whatever good can be spoken or conceived, so he made the human soul capable of every grace and holiness. Hence John says of our highest good—namely, what it is fitting for us to possess: “As he is,” he says, “so are we in this world” (John IV, 17).

God is naturally pious. In the fullness of his divinity he deals with us and denies the bowels of mercy to no one, so that he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. V, 45). Indeed, he grants his gifts, though bodily ones, no less—rather, much more generously—to the impious than to those who are known to live justly.

Therefore, just as God is, so are we in this world: just as he withdraws the generosity of his beneficence from no one, even one wholly hostile to him, so we must have charity toward those who hate us. There are many further and sufficiently difficult matters that could be discussed concerning this image of God, but, since we are hastening toward other subjects, we think these things sufficient for ordinary readers.

“And let him rule,” he says, “over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the beasts, and the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.”

When God raises those who have deserved well of him to conformity with himself, who is nothing other than virtue, this is done so that, through the heavenly illumination by which each person has received subtlety of understanding, he may learn to exercise judgment in the Scriptures—which is signified by the fish of the sea—and may know how to rule the birds of the sky. That is, he must most cautiously balance the sharpness of contemplation in divine matters, knowing and thinking nothing imaginary or sensual about God.

And when, after great revelations, the bitterness of temptations follows—as almost always happens—one mindful of rational dominion must at once impose servitude upon the body against the beasts of anger, pride, and earthly movements, that is, desires, and the creeping things of lust. Vindicating the dignity of his freedom, he must exercise authority over these things.

Understand the sea as Scripture, salted with the salt of wisdom, which arouses us to spiritual thirst and stirs up the sound of great agitation in the hearts of the penitent, making their minds bitter, where the fearful sinner seethes amid tears as though amid heaps of threats. The fish of this sea is the natural faculty that investigates its hidden things.

## Verse 27

“Therefore God created man: in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.”

It is rightly said first that man was created in the singular, and afterward that male and female were created, because before the transgression the human being was one in himself and nowhere divided. He devoted himself to his one Creator; he thought nothing foreign either to himself or to God. But afterward, when he despised the yoke of his Maker and wished to be his own master, he lost the vision of God by which he had often been refreshed and did not possess himself, because afterward he could never fully rule his own impulses, even if he wished to.

For although he did not entirely lose the spirit—which is the male—in order to think or act bravely, Eve, nevertheless, a rebellious and untamed animal, never willingly yields to the will of the spirit. She always resists the pursuit of virtue with stubbornness. Eve is our flesh, which, at the devil’s suggestion, seduces reason and bends it toward consent to dishonorable desire. For Adam, as the Apostle says, was not deceived, but Eve, and she also deceived the man (I Tim. II, 14).

At first there was a certain unity in man, but afterward division arose as a punishment for sin, so that humanity was divided into two.

## Verse 28

“And he blessed them and said: Increase and multiply and fill the earth.”

We increase and multiply when we fill the earth—that is, when, by the performance of good works, we do not allow our outer person to remain empty anywhere.
