Or we increase when, through the growth of holy action, we stretch toward heavenly things with better hope. We multiply when we are strengthened by the abundance of virtues. Thus the earth is filled when the whole range of our senses is occupied with pious exercises, each according to what is appropriate to it. [23]

“And subdue it.”

We subdue the earth when we compel Eve to obey our rule, so that the servant—namely, the flesh—does not, in reversed order, precede her mistress, reason.

“And rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky, and over all living creatures that move upon the earth.”

The fish may likewise be understood as worldly cunning, by which human ingenuity is skilled in tracking out the paths of the sea—that is, the affairs of the world. Birds may also be understood as the exalted thoughts of the proud, by which each person flies higher in proportion as, inflated by empty successes, he thinks more glorious things about himself.

What are living creatures except impulses, thousands of which habitually creep into human hearts? This accords with the fact that *animus*, from which *animositas* is derived, has a Greek etymology and comes from the word meaning “wind.” And what should the impulses that we endure, so many, so varied, and so foolish, more fittingly be called than “windinesses”? By making us desire empty things, they inflate us to the point of bursting and produce nothing except sin.

“These move upon the earth”—that is, in the earth. For *super* is frequently used in the Old Testament in place of *in*, as in: “If I remembered you upon my bed” (Ps. LXII, 7), meaning “in my bed.” Living creatures move in the earth when foolish thoughts entice our bodies toward illicit movements. They can indeed move upon the earth—that is, precede our flesh—and, among the things adjacent to them, plunder as thieves; but may they never be able to subjugate the imperious king, namely, reason.

## Verse 29

“Behold, I have given you every plant bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees that have within themselves the seed of their own kind, that they may be food for you, and for all the living creatures of the earth, and for every bird of the sky, and for everything that moves upon the earth in which there is a living soul, so that they may have food.”

First, a literal point must be inserted: altogether, before the Flood, the eating of flesh was not practiced in that first period.

Symbolically, however, although these things can be understood according to what we said in the treatise on the third day, and according to what has been explained concerning the other days—namely, that they are said to be given as food to the one who is already a new creation, that is, for the imitation of the intellectual things described there, by whose examples he ought to be sustained as by nourishment—we may perhaps explain them in another way if we make the effort.

Since grass is short and close at hand, we may understand by it any bodily good, such as fasting, receiving a guest into one’s home, giving alms, teaching the ignorant, and the other things that human kindness provides for the needy. These are certainly good, but without the assistance of certain spiritual virtues they are nothing. They can be done with either a good or a bad intention. Therefore, if they are done well—that is, not for love of praise or through envy, so that another’s good may be obscured—these and similar works are highly useful.

Nevertheless, they ought to bear seed, since they provide nourishment of good example for the spiritual creature. Even when grass dies, its seed usually remains, from which the species may be restored. What is grass except a good work? What is the seed of grass except the reward of a good work, by consideration of which others are especially moved to act well?

A good work may sometimes appear good but lack a reward in God’s eyes, because although the agent’s intention is not for praise or through envy, as we have said, he nevertheless does not perform the good he does out of desire for an eternal reward, but so that God may more abundantly increase prosperity for him in the present age. Hence it is said: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII, 6)—that is, let him pray only for temporal things. And there: “He will praise you when you have done good to him” (Ps. XLVIII, 19). Likewise, the carnal Jews are promised nothing in the Law except temporal things.

For this grass to have seed, the intention must be changed, so that others may be raised up through it. The intentions of some people are often disclosed even in the present life, by God’s just judgment, either through open crimes or through some apostasy; and therefore no fruit comes from them. For scarcely anyone is moved by the example of one whose end is rejected.

Fruit-bearing trees signify spiritual virtues, which are performed only with a good intention and cannot be shared by the wicked: charity, humility, patience, and others. They possess within themselves both great strength of perseverance, the glory of excellence, and the usefulness of fruit through imitation. Each of these must nevertheless contain its own seed, so that the good being done is performed not for external things but for the eternal salvation of the one who does it.

Thus they are given as food to the birds—that is, to those endowed with the excellence of holiness—and to all living creatures, namely, those who live by faith and have movements toward good action, in the earth—that is, in bodily manifestation—so that they may strengthen their conduct and their spirit by the pious examples of such people.

Grass, being a light thing, may also signify the active life, which is open to all God’s people. Trees, however, signify the highest contemplative life, in which few among the learned—and I do not know whether anyone among the unlearned—can set the foot of the mind.

This is understood in Deuteronomy through the command that, when anyone takes eggs or chicks from a nest, whether they are in a tree or on the ground, he must not take the mother sitting upon them at the same time, so that they may live for a long time (Deut. XXII, 6). The meaning is this: When our mind either fosters the eggs of good thought and purpose or nourishes the chicks of good but still tender action until they reach the appropriate strength of perfection, whoever observes this through experience can imitate both the pious intention and the religious work. But if he wishes to live happily forever, he must not remove or discourage the mother—that is, the conscience of the one acting—from the good undertaking.

By the earth, then, the active life is understood; by the tree, the contemplative life. This is what we said was figured there by grass and tree.

## Verse 31

“And God saw all that he had made, and they were very good.”

As we said above, and as happens frequently, when God sees, he causes us to see. Our seeing is like his approving, because when we attain the summit of virtue, love of the good is transformed into our nature, so that even if it were permitted to sin with impunity, the mind would never turn a step away from the course of what is right.

We therefore see the good things that God has placed in us—that is, we understand them. Hence the sixth day appears, and at the same time, corresponding to it, the sixth grace, the Spirit of understanding, shines forth.

When God had set the human being, formed according to his image, as a kind of intellectual judge among the fish and birds and, again, the creeping things, and had commanded him to possess the rights of judgment, so that he might know which things he ought to use temporarily and which he ought to enjoy eternally, and might recognize what he should seize within himself, by what he should shape himself, what he ought to subject to himself, and over what he ought to rule—what more eminent gift could he give him than to make him in some way equal to the angels?

If we say that we surpass beasts in this respect, that we can speak, I reply that this is true in part. But if we pay attention, we certainly find that we scarcely communicate anything to one another more clearly by speaking than they communicate, in their own manner, by gesture and voice. This difference, therefore, is not greatly worthy of praise. Rather, the difference to be praised above all is that by understanding God we are united with the angels in goodness.

This is what the Apostle calls “the discernment of spirits” (I Cor. XII, 10), by which, with the intellectual palate, we taste what comes to us from God, what the evil spirit suggests, and what the wantonness of the flesh naturally produces from itself.

Nothing, therefore, is more appropriate to the work of this day, when man is placed over the ordering of created things, than that the brightest light of discernment should also be present.

# Chapter II

## Verse 1

“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment.”

The heavens are completed when the minds of the faithful apply all the powers of reason to divine wisdom. The earth is completed when, with all perverse movements put to sleep, the flesh is subjected to the will of reason.

But who, placed in mortal flesh, could fulfill these things perfectly? No one is better than Paul, who sees another law in his members warring against the law of his mind (Rom. VII, 23), who follows if he may comprehend, and who does not consider that he has comprehended (Phil. III, 12). And who would be so negligent as to detract from Paul’s perfection? For he is conscious of nothing against himself, yet “he is not justified by this” (I Cor. IV, 4).

We call holy men perfect insofar as bodily weakness permits. As long as they remain in it, they cannot attain the peace of soul and flesh that either the angels possess or the saints will possess after the resurrection.

Their adornment is whatever is indicated, through the works of these days, as pertaining to virtue of soul or bodily uprightness, or whatever is found elsewhere through reading.

## Verse 2

“And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.”

When we accomplish something, we say that we completed the work on the very day on which we finish it, rather than on the following day. What does it mean, then, that God does not complete his works on the sixth day but on the seventh, except that he brings to an end the holy practices of the present life that he effects through us—not in this age, which is called the sixth age, but in the seventh, in which the Sabbath-rest of souls remains for God’s people, when he has bestowed the reward?

For as long as we live in this world, we cannot and must not rest from doing good. In the seventh age of the world we are released from labor, according to what is said in Job: “In the seventh, evil will not touch us” (Job. V, 19). There the month—that is, the perfection of blessedness—will be the month of perfected labor, and the Sabbath of eternal rest will be ours, since we have rested from perverse work.

In this life, therefore, it is time to struggle; there eternity remains for us to be crowned. Before that final morning, when with the Psalmist we shall hear God’s mercy, when God will illuminate the hidden things of our hearts (Ps. CXLII, 3), it ought to seem vain to us to rise—that is, to be lifted up—into any security concerning our good action.

But after we have sat in this valley of tears, which is the place of the gold of Arabia—that is, of the humble elect—in which they are melted down and, according to Daniel, made white (Dan. XI, 35), then we must rise—that is, aspire to glory. We dwell in these forty years in the desert of Idumea, concerning which David cries: “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn” (Ps. LXII, 2). We delight in the nourishment of spiritual manna, namely, the Holy Scriptures, yet we eat the bread of sorrow (Ps. CXXVI, 2), because our whole bed is occupied by our weakness.

And the bread for which the reprobate, according to Jeremiah, “gave their precious things” (Lam. I, 11)—selling their own salvation or souls to spend it on temporal pleasure—becomes abhorrent to us in our life. Alas, we cry out, “Our sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 20), thinking worldly pleasure a madness and pressures and sorrows the cause of the crown.

When, therefore, we reach this seventh day—that is, the most perfect light—we shall place the foot of the soul upon the highest degree, which is wisdom, because, illumined without end and without any interruption of spiritual evening, we shall know God. Amen.

*The first book of the Moral Works is completed.*

# The Second Book of the Moral Works on Genesis Begins

In the preceding commentary, after God had separated heaven and earth, the discussion concerned what he had done on each of the days and what had proceeded from heaven and earth. The mystical narrative therefore follows, saying:

## Verse 4

“These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when God made heaven and earth.”

“On the day,” he says—that is, in that illumination of the mind by which heaven, which is reason, is raised up from the darkness of the confusion of vices and separated from the earth, namely, the carnal affection. In the inner person these things begin to be generated which can be brought about through seven days, that is, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“When they were created”—that is, when the seeds of these good things were planted in the mind to be renewed through the conception of a good will.

## Verse 5

“And every shrub of the field before it rose upon the earth, and every plant of the region before it sprouted.”

God makes the shrub—that is, strong works of virtue—before they rise upon the earth, that is, before they are displayed through the manifest exercises of the body, when the faithful soul is inspired to act well upon the earth but, because the affection or practice of the old person still hinders it, the mind does not prevail in works. They are therefore first formed in purpose. Hence the Apostle says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it” (Rom. VII, 18).

He also makes every plant of the region before it sprouts when, with God giving life, we conceive lesser and weaker goods, which nevertheless we cannot perform as we desire.

The green growth of desire for heavenly things may also be understood by the plant. In it we live here through pious actions in hope, until in the land of the living it brings forth the shoots of complete vision in reality.

By the shrub we may also understand contemplative or spiritual pursuits, because of their strength and height. Now they are cultivated by us with great labor, before they arise in that land which the meek will possess, in eternal and incorruptible stability, spontaneously and never ceasing.

“For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth.”

When a pious will is first implanted in us, the abundance of the grace of our reason—that is, spiritual rain—is not poured in so greatly that the hardness of earthly affection is entirely dissolved within us for the accomplishment of good. Our beginnings are mixed with evils.

Hence it is rightly added: “And there was no man to work it.”

Because God delays the fullness of his infusion, the weakness of our works signifies that there is no man who subjects and cultivates the body by the authority of reason. For one who has not learned to live with complete reason is not worthy of the name “man.”

## Verse 6

“But a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

Each person must consider with remarkable subtlety whether the things he judges himself to possess as good are truly good. For if something is done for worldly respectability but is not good in God’s sight, who could call it good?

God rightly had not rained, and there was no man to work the earth, because the spring of human cleverness, gushing from a low intention, watered the appearance of the outer person—that is, the whole surface of the earth.

This is worldly respectability, by which people, while concealing themselves as though prudently beneath the appearance of great religion, accomplish nothing. Hence it is said: “The children of Hagar are those who seek the knowledge that is from the earth” (Baruch III, 23).

The Gospel passage about the six water jars (John II, 6) fits this interpretation very well in a moral sense. Since the spring was from the earth, it watered not the interior but the surface of the earth. There are indeed many good things that are discerned as belonging to God by intention alone, such as piety, generosity, chastity, and many others.

## Verse 7

“Then the Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life.”

Since human knowledge, by arranging itself outwardly in good conduct without the contemplation of God, accomplishes nothing, the merciful Creator, when he is about to form the whole human being, must soften the earth of our breast by pouring in the water of grace. For man, who bears the image of God, truly consists of such clay and no other.

But this clay must possess the face that the Lord commands us to wash by looking upon it, and which the Bridegroom asks to be shown to him: “Show me your face,” he says, “for your face is beautiful” (Song II, 14).

The breath of life is applied to it, so that through his spirit he may become poor in spirit, by which poverty he may become blessed; may be filled with the one who leads him into a straight land; may open his mouth to cleanse his conscience through confession, so that he may receive the spirit of discipline, which shuns hypocrisy; and finally may strive to open his mouth wide for teaching good things, so that the heavenly breath, pleasantly entering, may fill it.

By breathing in we draw in and release the spirit. Hence it is said: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII, 13).

“And man became a living soul.”

Just as a body cannot live without a soul, so the soul, if it lacks God dwelling within it, lies overthrown by a worse death. When the clay had been made and the breath given to his face, the whole man was already fully alive.

The sincerity of that face by which we know God and by which we are known by God is the reason that, when certain less sincere people cry out, “Lord, open to us,” he says, “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12). There is pallor of failing life in one who carries within himself the pledges of the life-giving spirit.

## Verse 8

“Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed.”

The paradise of pleasure is the serenity of holy conduct. When shoots of virtue rise everywhere in it and the grasses of unfading hope grow green, the north wind arises and southern mildness approaches.

For *paradise* is Greek; in Latin it is called a garden.

If a secure mind, which no shameful fault bites, is, according to Solomon (Prov. XV, 15), like a continual feast—whereas the mind conscious of evil is always disturbed by its own goads—what is more glorious or delightful than the testimony of a simple soul?

But this paradise is said to exist from the beginning. From what beginning, unless from the example of our first creation itself? Let us consider in what great rest of mind man stood before he sinned, and let us understand that this is the intellectual paradise, better than the earthly one, in which God wishes to place us, if we are willing.

### Verse 9

“And God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to look upon and pleasant to eat.”

Thus, once man has been established in that solidity, every tree is brought forth: the strength and excellence of every upright work. It is beautiful to look upon when our light shines before men, “so that they may see” (Matt. 5:16), that is, may be instructed; it is pleasant to eat when, through imitation of works, they are nourished by the glorification of God. For whoever is strengthened toward right action by considering you feeds upon your fruit.

But how is it pleasant when the way that leads to life is narrow (Matt. 7:14), and every discipline in the present is sorrowful? (Heb. 12:11.) In truth, it is narrow for the imperfect and untrained, but afterward it will yield the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those exercised in it. “For my yoke is easy” (Matt. 11:30), and so forth.

Let us consider, however, from what earth these things arise. “Earth” is understood to mean “humble.” Let humility, therefore, be regarded as earth, and it is sufficiently clear that the things we have mentioned cannot be believed to occur without this virtue. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Therefore the righteous man is like a tree planted beside streams of water, while the wicked are like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:3–4).

There is also “the tree of life in the middle of paradise.” The tree of life is wisdom. Wisdom, however, is spoken of in three ways: the wisdom of this world, which is also craftiness; creative Wisdom, which is the Son of God; and the reason divinely illumined in angels and holy men.

The Apostle briefly touches upon the first two: “The world did not know in the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:21)—by “wisdom,” understand the wisdom of the world, and by “God” God himself. Wisdom is also called that reason which is divinely illuminated in angels and holy men. This is the wisdom that says, “In Jerusalem is my power” (Ecclus. 24:15), and so forth.

This wisdom supplies its own life with nourishment through strength, fruit, and shade, provided that it stands in the middle of paradise. The carnal affect must not tyrannically drive it from the royal seat from which it orders the army surrounding it; rather, running through the interior like marrow in the bones, it must impart vital juices.

There is also “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” This is our will. The will is the movement of the soul, compelled by no one, toward doing or desiring something. If someone is compelled, he is not led by his will. The devil, however, compels no one by suggestion; rather, he places before a person what is to be desired and, without distress or force, draws the willing mind along.

Therefore, in this sense, we sin by the will alone, not by necessity, and we surrender ourselves, though free, to slavery. Since the will can be turned toward good or evil, here and in what follows it is understood in the evil sense. For knowledge—that is, experience—of good and evil is especially effective in evil. It is one thing to know that fornication is a sin, and another to experience its character through deeds.

Moreover, through the experience of evil one recognizes far more clearly how good the good that one possessed was than one can discern any evil through observing the good. What health is, after all, is learned better with illness as one’s teacher.

The tree’s strength is stupidity, its fruit corruption, and its shade blindness. Therefore, to misuse the will is to touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

### Verse 10

“And a river went out from the place of delight to water the paradise.”

This river is the abundant knowledge of sacred discourse and the profound understanding of moral matters.[^c0006-27] It waters paradise because, through the daily instruction of teachings, it supplies pious souls with strength for right action.

For if it belongs to the pursuit of wisdom to treat of God and heavenly things, and, insofar as is humanly possible, to transcend the condition of this life, it belongs properly to knowledge to arrange with just moderation the matters conducted among us, to distinguish vices and virtues, and faithfully to explain each to those concerned.

Hence it is added: “which is divided from there into four heads.” The place of our delight is God—not a place in the local sense, but God himself. All things dwell in him generally, but those who delight in him alone dwell in him much more specially, insofar as they are spiritual. From this very place the force of the river flows forth. It casts down spiritual wickedness and is divided into four heads, which are the four principal virtues, from which all the others take their beginnings.

### Verse 11

“The name of the one is Phison; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Evilath.”

Phison is interpreted as “the mouth of the pupil.” With the mouth we speak, and with the pupil we see. This signifies prudence, which is itself so called because it sees ahead. True prudence is that by which we carefully infer to what outcomes various things may lead.

Thus the nose of the Church is compared to a tower (Song 7:4), since impending evil is avoided by foresight, and the pursuit of virtue loves its own success on account of its merit. Its fruitfulness is fully demonstrated when we not only foresee well but also strive to communicate what we foresee to others, performing the office both of the pupil and of the mouth.

Evilath is interpreted as “grieving” or “giving birth.” The person grieves who bears with difficulty the hardships and exile of the present age; when he has become poor and poured out his prayer before God, he says, “I have been struck down like grass” (Ps. 101:5), and what follows.

The person gives birth who, although crowned with twelve stars, having the moon beneath her feet and clothed with the sun (Rev. 12:1), nevertheless cries out amid her anguish, “What I do I do not understand” (Rom. 7:15), that is, “I do not approve.” “For I see another law in my members” (ibid. 7:23), and so forth. Elsewhere: “Every creature groans and is in labor until now” (Rom. 8:22), that is, it performs good works with pain.

Phison encircles—that is, fortifies—not the dust that the wind of pride casts from the face of the earth, that is, of Christ, but the earth: those who are stable and solid, who grieve that they do not have here a lasting city and who, giving birth, cry out for the child who is to be caught up to God and to his throne.

In this earth, enclosed by this fortification, the gold of holy souls is born, and it is the finest gold; for if holy simplicity is good, how much more excellent is learned holiness? Thus it is said: “where gold is born” (Gen. 2:11).

### Verse 12

“And the gold of that land is excellent.”

For it is a great thing not to labor only for oneself but to strive to benefit everyone. Gold has both splendor and value: its value comes from religion, and its splendor from learning.

“There is bdellium there, and the onyx stone.”

According to some, bdellium is an aromatic tree, black in color and the size of an olive tree, with a leaf like that of the bramble and fruit resembling that of the wild fig.

There are some who are Phison, that is, prudent; some are Evilath, strong in doing good amid obstacles; and some are earth, steadfastly immovable. The fragrances of these flow from a pious reputation; and although they are lofty like palms, they are nevertheless black like a raven, either through the pursuit of humility or through remembrance of their former manner of life. They strive to seek out those who excel in acts of charity and mercy, signified by the olive, and who, together with the Apostle Paul, by the bramble leaf—that is, the word of the Lord’s Passion, accomplished for sinners—also urge others toward the grace they have attained.

The onyx stone receives its name from its resemblance to a fingernail. I observe a fingernail where it grows out: at first it is suffused with a kind of arched whiteness, while in the middle I see redness mixed with white; above, where it extends beyond the flesh, it shines with clear brightness.

Our first whiteness comes from baptism. Yet it is restrained, as by a yoke, by the arch of divine Scripture and divine judgment. Later it is mixed with red, troubled by the assault of passions that must be overcome, until, released from the prison of the flesh, it enjoys the free light of heaven.

Its fruit, however, resembles that of the wild fig, which is black when it has fully ripened. For when holy men have attained perfection in charity and mortify their vices, they complete their life, if opportunity is given, by shedding their blood; for spilled blood commonly becomes black.

### Verse 13

“And the name of the second river [or: ‘of the second river’] is Gehon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Ethiopia.”

Gehon is interpreted as “breast” or “precipice.” By “breast” may be understood fortitude, which is frightened by none of the things that prudence has foreseen and does not yield to adversity. For what we cannot accomplish with our arms, we usually push or draw with our chests.

Hence some animals have greater strength there; and under this figure the pallium rests upon archbishops at that place, so that, by going before others, they may draw them forward with strength.

“Precipice” is not said without reason. For if you desire to be strong in adversity, you must first break away the things that flatter you temporally before your eyes.

By Ethiopia, which has black peoples, contrary things are represented, just as prosperous things were signified by whiteness both now and among the ancients. Thus Gehon encircles it because it surrounds and binds under the authority of its seed whatever external trouble invades and whatever Ethiopian earthliness intrudes; with the abundant flow of counsel it circles around and washes it away.

### Verse 14

“And the name of the third river is Tigris; it flows toward the Assyrians.”

Tigris is interpreted as “arrow.” By the arrow, temperance is understood in a fitting way; temperance is directed against the pleasures of the flesh.

If the bow—that is, the stupidity of the body—is bent by inner virtue and directs the arrow of temperance against the clouds of desire, it must see what it strikes; it must not lack the feather of the virtues, must excel in the inward direction of its intention, and, with the sharpness of subtle understanding as though with iron, must divide what needs regulating, lest, while it sees soundly beforehand and endures more healthily, it should, trusting itself too little soundly, over-arrange its actions by excessive discrimination.

Pleasure must be cut away when it is foolish, but necessity must not be entirely removed. Nor should anyone, while believing himself strong, despise the minds of others as weak.

This temperance—which is also discernment—must fly ahead like an arrow from a bow, so that nothing may come upon us and strike us unprepared.

This river of God, filled with waters, does not encircle the Assyrians; it goes against them like an enemy. For it is rightly said that Phison encircles Evilath and Gehon encircles Ethiopia, when the one fortifies, the other subjects to our authority, closes in adversities, and specifically attacks and excludes pleasure completely.

For it is said, “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18), which is to say, “Flee the opportunity for falling.” This vice lies deep within us, and therefore must be pursued with greater caution.

This is Assur, which is interpreted as “court.” Since a court is the house of kings or powerful men, it signifies the pleasure of the world—and not without reason. For in courts we see the dens of every kind of obscenity.

Hence the saying: “Those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11:8), that is, those who embrace what is loose and luxurious are household members of demons. These are the Assyrians, that is, the courtiers, whose examples must be pursued no less than the vices themselves within us. For vices are often restrained by shame, whereas a wicked example arouses and nourishes them more fiercely.

The fourth river is the Euphrates. It too is interpreted as “fruitful.” By this is understood justice, by which God is loved above all and one does not deny one’s neighbor what is his according to the rule.

This is the source, this is the fruitful branch among the three virtues already mentioned and all the others, both spiritual and otherwise, like sap and marrow in trees. It is defined as a disposition of the soul that, while preserving the common good, assigns to each person his proper dignity.

There is something perfect in the sound of this: to conduct oneself fruitfully toward each person in such a way that the common welfare is not abandoned. This is nothing other than honoring each person according to what he is and what he deserves, lest, through the contempt or excessive honoring of one or a few, scandal be generated for everyone.

Thus the Euphrates bears the fruit of life, because “the righteous person will live in his righteousness, which he has practiced.”

### Verse 15

“So the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it.”

God takes the man when he removes him from his own will. He places him in the paradise of delight when, inspiring him to do his will, he makes known that to know God is to live, and to serve him is to reign.

We work the paradise when, through the zeal of good works, we do violence to the kingdom of heaven; we seek God himself; and we guard his righteousness by closing the entrance to empty glory while acting well.

### Verse 16

“And God commanded him, saying: ‘You may eat from every tree of paradise, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.’”

We eat from every tree of paradise when we pass our life filled with every virtue. We do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil when we do not misuse our will by entering into the experience of sin, through which the good we possessed is recognized more fully.

But enough has already been said about these matters above.

### Verse 17

“For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death.”

We eat when we consent to receive the taste of wicked delight even without an external act. But since the power of sin is death—that is, it is recognized as delight—we die the death when we are cast down from the state of pious intention by exclusion from the divine desire.

But why does it say “on the day,” when night signifies sin? “Day” is sometimes taken for any prosperity, as in: “If only you had known on this day what makes for peace” (Luke 19:42). For the person wishing to sin, when opportunity smiles prosperously, a certain day shines forth, destined to return to darkness.

“Day” is also commonly understood as knowledge, just as “night” signifies ignorance. Some sin while fully understanding the measure of their crime; of them it is said, “They descend alive into the underworld” (Ps. 113:17). Others do not know how to measure it and rush blindly; of them it is said, “They are placed like sheep in the underworld” (Ps. 48:15).

Therefore, a person dies to the same extent that he is shown to have understood what he commits.

### Verse 18

“And the Lord God also said: ‘It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself.’”

Here we understand “man” to mean the person who rules the movements of his flesh by the authority of reason and does not wander like an animal.

Accordingly, above the psalm is written, “A song of Moses, the man of God.” Although the spirit, and both good and evil human beings, belong to God, this man is so called on account of his integrity. Likewise: “On that day a man will nourish a cow of the herd” (Isa. 7:21).

Yet if this purity of man remains in him continually, or even for some time, it can become his greatest danger, as Paul testifies, to whom a thorn was given (1 Cor. 12:7) lest he be exalted by revelations.

For although the saints are called heaven, scarcely half an hour of silence is granted in heaven. The man would therefore be alone if he possessed this rest of silence. But it is not good that he should be so, lest he produce in himself a form of arrogance.

Finally, God makes for him a helper like himself, when the one who is himself originally fragile is recalled to knowledge of himself through the continual immersion in natural frailties, which is inflicted as the punishment of sin. Since he has a body subject to suffering, lest he grow proud of some condition of mind, he suffers the burdens of passion in his mind. Thus he has near him a reminder that, through fragility similar to his own, he should help himself.

God does this when, by a just judgment, he permits it to happen.

### Verse 19

“Therefore, when the Lord God had formed from the earth all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them.”

The Lord forms the birds of heaven and the animals of the earth from the earth when, through the humility of temptations and knowledge of ourselves, he restores within us more distinctly the good of contemplation and active life according to the heavenly model, and forms within us the image of his own condition and that of the angels.

He brings them to Adam when he subjects these things, to be ordered and cared for, to the authority of our reason.

“He might see”—that is, Adam himself, meaning that he might discern—“what he would call them,” that is, by what distributions of qualities he would distinguish each virtue.

“For whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.” Names are ordinarily assigned to substances according to their quality, and also to other things that are not substances. “Name” is often used for opinion or estimation, as in: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22:1).

Thus Adam calls living souls—that is, he carefully distinguishes the vital pursuits of virtue through subtle investigation for the sake of understanding.

There are also souls that do not live, because they are works that outwardly bear the name of life but are inwardly dead through vainglory. This is how we moderns think about the knowledge of the virtues, as we have received it from those fathers who were true Adams.

But we must observe how subtly the name Adam itself is introduced here. According to what is read in the following passages, “man” and “woman” were called by God, and Adam is interpreted as “man.” The one who clings to the Lord is, according to the Apostle, “one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Our animal nature, fully supported by understanding, is truly already man, having been refined by the softening of fragility.

Therefore, rightly, after God begins to make virtue in our weakness, after he has called by their Adamic names the birds of heaven—that is, spiritual graces—and the animals of earth, namely the forms of knowledge by which human action is illuminated with the beauty of holiness, and after he has learned by varied investigations to discern the craftiness or ferocity of demons or vices, then Adam is first rightly introduced: this Adam of ours, perfected in knowledge and work.

But in these bestowals of grace there is no helper who places before his eyes the humility of his own humanity. With the abundance of virtues overflowing on every side according to his desire, the mind seems almost more than human to itself.

Therefore, lest this condition drive him into a fall, divine providence gives him a helper like himself, through whose frequent stimulation he may be reminded to pay attention to his own condition.

Hence it is said: “But for Adam no helper like himself was found.” And thereafter:

### Verses 21–22

“So the Lord God cast a sleep upon Adam, and took one of his ribs, and built the rib into a woman.”

Sleep is cast upon Adam when, by God’s ordering, his great heat is allowed to cool and grow lukewarm for a while.

His rib is taken from his side when the onset of a providential temptation, like an unexpected thief, tears away some virtue whose firmness he had trusted.

God does this in the sense that he permits it to happen. We are less cautious at our side because we see less there; therefore we understand the rib as that good which a person fears less to lose.

We also commonly call those who help or protect us our “sides,” as in “the sides of the north” (Ps. 47:3) and “I will sit on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14:13), in the Psalm and in Isaiah.

The enemy therefore attacks most strongly the place where he sees us most fortified and where he observes us to be least watchful. Hence, under the excellent figure of an unwary mind, Peter’s side is struck by an angel in prison.

While Adam sleeps—that is, while he is established in excessive security—the rib is taken away, because the unwary person is deserted by virtue.

But we must note what is added: “He filled it with flesh for it.” By flesh, which is soft, remission is understood. For whenever our enemy sees us begin something arduous, he commonly suggests, as though reasoning:

“If you devote yourself so intensely to this undertaking, you will surely be overcome by weariness or weakness and will not be able to persist in it. Therefore set a limit to your work, indulging in intervals of pious recreation and relaxation, so that after a time you may return to it more willingly and energetically.”

The phrase “for it” agrees with this interpretation. For he pretends to say this as though offering some assistance for the preservation of religious devotion. While the poisonous counsel is gratefully received, remission—the cause of ruin—is not rejected, as though it were a remedy for weariness. Thus flesh is recognized as filling the place of virtue.

Finally, the rib that the Lord had taken from Adam is built into a woman, because from the occasion of a virtue temporarily lost there arises in the mind an immense mass of temptation. Whatever benefit was previously perceived in the habit of virtue is considered insignificant, because the impulse of inward weakness has now exceeded the strength of all reason.

Thus God builds—that is, permits to be built—from the rib a woman, because from our good the devil obtains material for temptation. Drawing it outward from the foundations of imagination into words and finally into the full execution of deeds, he raises in the wavering mind a structure of shameful softness.

God, who does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Cor. 10:13), brings this woman to us because, under the authority of our renewed power of reason, he reduces every wavering of the mind, like a fugitive slave, under subjection.

But let us hear what our more cautious Adam, now recalled from this state, thinks of it.

### Verse 23

“This now is bone from my bones,” he said, “and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called virago [a strong woman], because [or, according to the Vulgate, ‘because’] she was taken from man.”

This is to say: this is what has returned from feminine inconstancy to proper order.

“Now bone”—that is, the strength of virtue, which he has received from the bones, meaning from the fellowship of the virtues. And she is also “flesh from my flesh,” because, when the flow of desire transfers the strength of the soul into a carnal condition, from the flesh of sin “which weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15) there has arisen flesh—that is, the weakness and softness of the evil appetite that tempts us. What previously had been the firmness of bone becomes, through the sudden movement of the heart, the weakness of carnal affect.

Therefore she is rightly called woman, because from man—that is, from understanding—our weakness receives strength by which to act steadfastly; yet, unless it is watched, through feminine sluggishness it overturns the manly condition.

Let her therefore be called virago from the better part, so that she may not misuse the strength of reason in a womanly manner; and although she sometimes arises from the occasion of virtue, let the man not perversely follow her, but let her, once subjected without resistance, follow him.

### Verse 24

“Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh.”

“For this reason,” he says, the one who has been separated from bestial life will leave his father, the devil, and his mother, desire. He will cling to his wife—that is, to his will, which must be governed rationally.

“And the two will be one flesh”: understanding and will will be one flesh, that is, one affect. For our affect, since it never remains fixed in the same condition while yearning for worldly things, as soon as it begins to devote itself to God is brought to rest upon one thing, willingly or unwillingly.

Thus the two are one flesh when these two establish for themselves, as it were, the seat of a kingdom in a third thing, and the two proceed harmoniously toward the same goal, their affection being set in agreement.

### Verse 25

“Now both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.”

When the will is in agreement with the spirit in holy men, it strips itself with the spirit of external things, casting off the garments of desire and, above all, relieving itself of the very pursuit of praise.

But when they despise these things and desire to appear as nothing in the world, the most contemptible people often look down upon them. Yet they are not ashamed, because the more truly they rejoice that they have been made poor, the more readily they accept being despised for that reason by anyone wicked.

## Chapter III

### Verse 1

“But the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made.”

This should be connected as follows. The statement “they were naked” appears to have been placed abruptly. They were not only despised outwardly on account of their nakedness, but the serpent—who, while the spirit and will remain in the good, slips away through earthly things—namely, carnal affect, habitually surrounds those two more cunningly than the other passions of earthly movements, signified by the animals of the earth, are able to do by themselves.

For the nearer and more inward something is, the more effective it is at creeping in and deceiving. This is the one who creeps in our members so that they may oppose the law of the mind, although willingness lies beside it (Rom. 7:18) and it delights in the law of God according to the inner man (ibid. 7:22), yet, while this other force resists, it cannot find a way to accomplish what it wishes.

But many do not think that will and affect differ in any way. Let them therefore hear the Psalm: “My soul desired to desire your justifications” (Ps. 118:20). This is as if it said: “My soul wished to affect your justifications.” For when the Apostle said, “The will lies beside me,” and added, “I do not find how to accomplish it” (Rom. 7:18), it is the same as if he had said, “I do not find the affect.” For it creeps here and there.

A sick person wishes to eat but does not feel the desire; a sober person feels too strong a desire to eat but does not wish to do so. The same distinction can easily be demonstrated in many cases.

The will, therefore, like a daughter in relation to her mother, is all the more a follower—that is, more worthy of being called affect—the nearer it is to reason.

Although it is slippery and more prone to fall, it is held under the authority of its mother. The text is defective here: “[perhaps: he has more frequently found this one, rather than the younger, more susceptible to seduction, and therefore tries to tear her away from behind her reasoning mother].” For this reason he first attacks the woman, namely the will itself.

### Verse 2

“Why,” he said, “did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?”

It is customary for persons wholly obscured to examine every lofty matter insolently and arrogantly. Thus this serpent, the first of all created beings to name God, imputes to God what he never said.

God did not forbid human beings every tree of paradise, but only one. Yet the serpent expresses the matter as though it were everything, with astonishing rage:

“Why,” he says, “did God, since he is God and, by the dignity of divinity, neither wishes nor is able to sin, impose upon us earthly creatures, subject to suffering in both body and soul, so many commands, impossible for mortal nature to bear? By depriving us of the experience of evil, he has at the same time taken away all the trees of life—that is, the virtues—that we might use. For if I do not know what evil is, how shall I love the good that opposes it? Through the experience of illness, surely, the integrity of health is guarded more eagerly.”

Therefore, to command someone not to know evil but to do good is the same as ordering a blind person to beware of arrows while someone else sees and is safe. The affect follows this carnal reasoning with the sufficiently lukewarm response of the will, by which it claims that only consent to evil—that is, touching it—and eating—that is, the act, because it introduces the taste of the thing sensed—have been forbidden.

### Verse 3

“He commanded us,” she said, “not to eat from it and not to touch it.”

Certainly, when the law prohibits touching and eating carrion, it keeps us away from favoring and carrying out dead works. But that seducer, introducing this softness of figurative womanliness, softened it still further with an even stronger wave.

### Verses 4–5

“Certainly you will not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

“When,” he says, “for the sake of gaining any experience—an experience intended merely to acquire caution and skill—you admit the stain of guilt, ‘on whatever day’ signifies that, in whatever manner prudence is gained, the light of understanding will mark us very greatly. The eyes of your discernment will be opened for future precaution, so that at last, possessing complete knowledge of good through the acquisition of evil, you will be like gods.

You will certainly not die the eternal death, which is properly called death, through the loss of God, since, remembering the malignity experienced in sinning, you will no longer wish to sin and, with a certain divine power infused into you, will no longer even be able to do so.”

### Verses 6–7

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to look upon; and she took of its fruit and ate. She also gave it to her husband, who ate. And the eyes of both were opened.”

But lest I seem to have passed over the point, the serpent says, “God knows”—that is, approves—“that on whatever day,” that is, in acquiring whatever understanding, you undergo vice not solely for the sake of vice, you will deserve nothing mortal but will become more perceptive for the sake of caution.

A delight slowly received approves the suggestion of the affect through the consent of the will. The woman “saw”—that is, desired, indeed coveted—the foolish pleasure of the tree, which had grown hard through thought arising from consent, as good—that is, already offering flavors to the palate of the miserable mind for accomplishment; outwardly beautiful to the eyes, delightful according to the appearance of the imagination.

She “took”—that is, assumed the boldness—to taste with the mouth of execution the fruit of action, nourished by the long heat of delights. After the act of sin, what has been tasted remains flavorful for a long time in memory and is ground by the teeth of external performance, so that a shameful satiety is brought upon the perishing soul.

The woman ate first because the will first bends toward consent in wickedness in response to the affect’s suggestion. She offers the same to the man when, through persistent instigation, she makes reason participate in the same poisonous sweetness.

The eyes of both are opened when they recognize from where they have fallen and to what they have come. They are also opened when they carry before their eyes, written and clearly expressed, what they had barely touched, so to speak, in dreaming. Whether they wish it or not, what they once gladly swallowed they repeatedly reconsider, often in a much worse condition than before and against their will.

By a just judgment it comes about that those who fell of their own accord, when they could easily have stood, cannot free themselves from this state even when they wish to do so.

“And when they had recognized that they were naked, they sewed together fig leaves and made themselves loincloths.”

They discover that they are naked because they recognize that they have been deprived of works of righteousness and of heavenly protection, and they see themselves exposed to the wind of the evil spirit.

They sew together fig leaves because they cloak their collection of wickedness with religious words. But since fig leaves are not round like most leaves, but are winding, gaping with openings, as though possessing tongues, and rough, we may understand by their roughness an old continence that they preserve outwardly after the fall; by the thinness of the leaf, the subtlety of hypocrisy, which nevertheless cannot entirely conceal grave vices, because the leaves themselves possess tongues:

> Impiety, long covered over and unwilling to remain hidden, sometimes violates the modesty laid on by art;  
> as bright light passes through glass, so it penetrates the face.

### Verse 8

“And when the Lord God was walking in the paradise toward the evening breeze, Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God among the trees of paradise, when they heard his voice.”

The voice of the Lord walking in paradise is a rebuke, or the memory of former righteousness that no longer stands. After sin has been committed in the mind, righteousness is nothing other than God in us, because the fallen reason itself complains about itself.

This occurs “toward the evening breeze,” when the heat of temptation has already begun to cool through its effect, and when the spirit of man, in accordance with the sense of God, surveys each place of the heart because of its own failure. Yet his spirit was not faithful with God: “His spirit was not faithful with God” (Ps. 77:8).

“For Adam and his wife hid themselves among the trees of paradise.” The tree of paradise is the affect of the soul. Whoever is buried in the middle of it, in its evil habit, so that the freedom of emerging in every direction is denied and he cannot breathe toward knowledge of God, is hidden there. The Apostle calls this “sin” (Rom. 7:17), because he does not find good in his flesh.

But “Adam” here does not mean the whole man who once was Adam. It means Adam insofar as the name is interpreted as “earthly,” or “red earth”: one who savors earthly things and is addicted to the passions of the body. And his wife means the will,[^c0006-29] which was once joined to him in an indivisible embrace, through the grace of God binding them together, but now has been separated by so great a division of the soul through the mediation of the devil. It is joined in closer consent not to its husband, heavenly reason, but to earthly craft in the love of temporal goods.

They obey the divine voice admonishing them from behind, but hide themselves through the hardening of mind that we have described.

If we take the singular “tree” as standing for the plural “trees,” just as sacred Scripture uses *coenomyam* and *ranam* for “gnats” and “frogs” (Ps. 77:45), then whoever, while acting badly, cloaks himself with the fellowship of holy men hides himself naked in the middle of the trees of paradise.

Hence certain people say to them: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matt. 25:8). That is: “Because we grow dark through our own works, grant us the benefit of your companionship, so that, if we cannot shine by our own light, we may at least shine by yours.”

### Verses 9–10

“And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: ‘Adam, where are you?’ He said: ‘I heard your voice, Lord, in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.’”

The Lord calls Adam when, after the fall, he summons a person’s reason within him and calls it to repentance.

“Where are you?” he says. “Pay attention to the place in which you lie. What other place is it than pride? You who had once learned to stand humbly—where are you now?”

“I heard your voice, Lord, in paradise,” he says. “I hear what you command: namely, to resume pious pursuits and mourn the losses of the paradise of former virtues. But I fear the austerity of repentance and this poverty of nakedness. I have decided, therefore, for the moment to conceal my shame by an outward display of appearance and conduct.”

### Verse 11

“For who told you that you were naked, unless it was that you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?”

This is as though God were saying to man:

“How do you know that you have been abandoned by my protection, unless you know that you have offended me through the guilt of your transgression? For even the guilty commonly fear a Lord who is absent and unaware. But what human stubbornness says to the spirit that thinks with God must now be heard.”

### Verse 12

“The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.”

“The fragile and changeable will,” he says, “which you placed in human reason, gave this instruction and brought this about. You, who imposed so many unbearable commands upon man, ought to have provided that the condition of the will should be inflexible toward the passions that would assail the mind.”

**VERSE 13, 14.**—And God said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” The will is confronted by the same author, but humanly transfers the offenses to the affections. “You, O God,” she says, “why did you give the will so unstable an affection, which not only does not help those who stray from the good, but even entices and causes those perfected in divine conduct to deviate? How can it be restrained by what is wicked, when it cannot be fully held in check even by what is wholly good?” The whole answer is: “The serpent deceived me.”

But God, with corrected understanding, turns the complaints foolishly poured out against himself toward consideration of, and responsibility for, not himself but the perverse affection. Thus God speaks, by the impulse of reason, to the serpent concerning earthly things: “Because you have done this, you are accursed among all the animals and the beasts of the earth.” “Because,” he says, “you lie in wait for the seduction of the faithful, you must be accursed among the living pursuits of the virtues, which are signified by the animals and beasts of the earth—namely, the fierceness of the flesh, that is, vices. You scatter good things; you incite crimes.”

“You shall walk upon your breast.” We have the heart in the breast, and reason in the heart. Affection therefore walks upon the breast when it usurps for itself the authority of reason. Hence the left hand is commanded not to know what the right hand does (Matt. VI, 3). It also proceeds upon the breast when it naturally presses desire downward toward lower things.

In another sense, in sacred Scripture blessing is used for multiplication, and cursing for decline. Therefore, among all the animals—that is, among the gentler vices of the flesh, such as excess in food, drink, and sleep—and among the beasts, namely the cruel and dreadful vices, let this affection, which is their source, have the outcome of eternal decline.

“You shall eat earth all the days of your life”—that is, in every appearance of prosperity, which is signified by day, you shall feed upon earthly things, by which you live chiefly against the life of the faithful. Whoever eats earth, however much he may have eaten, has more left to eat than he has been able to consume. So it is with those who desire: however much they obtain, more things remain to be desired.

[Col. 0075A]

**VERSE 15.**—“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” This happens whenever our will relies upon divine reason. Then the appetite of the flesh finds no regard with that will, because the seed of the Holy Spirit, by which it is made fruitful, is wholly hostile to diabolical suggestion and creates an infinite disagreement between the two.

“She shall crush your head.” The head—that is, the beginning—of the wicked appetite was the desire, after abandoning the common good, namely God, to will certain things as one’s own. Hence the Lord, declaring that he will not cast out the one who comes to him, adds the reason: that he has not come to do his own will (John VI, 37–38).

A right will crushes this head when, insofar as it prevails, it leaves nothing shamefully as its own. For when something private is sought from the first man, he is cast down from the serenity of paradise; but the followers of the second Adam, wholly submitting themselves to God’s pleasure, are admitted into heaven.

“And you shall lie in wait for his heel.” By the heel, which is the body’s final part, we understand intention, which is the end of all actions. Therefore, when we subordinate our will to God’s will and renounce both secret and open vices, he places snares especially in the intention of our good deeds, so that those whom he cannot entangle in disgrace may at least have their moral perversity stained by some regard for popular favor.

But now the will itself must hear from divine reason, its teacher, what it ought also to think about itself. It is said to it:

**VERSE 16.**—“I will multiply your troubles and your conceptions.” He suffers multiplied troubles who sees the good that ought to be done and wishes to do it, but, subject to vanity, is unable, whether he wishes it or not, to accomplish what he desires because he is hemmed in by mortal limitation. Hence one man says: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 24.) This is better said through experience than through speech.

Conceptions are multiplied, but sons are brought forth in pain, when we do not propose even these very small goods without great conflict of thought and, having been deprived of the impulses of the flesh, restore them with labor. Yet even if we begin with some small spiritual delight, who can say with what pain and crying we give birth?

But if she wishes these things to suffice for childbirth and the first conception, she must necessarily be under the authority of a husband—that is, of reason—as one needing discipline. Through its loss, a certain youthful wantonness of the will can be restrained. Yet, lest the mind’s own governing power, which ought to resist the excesses of desire, go away unpunished, Adam is reproved under its figure.

[Col. 0075D]

**VERSE 17, 18.**—“Because,” he says, “you listened to the voice of your wife”—that is, because the wicked appetite that ought to have been subject to you has sounded in your heart, and has passed over my laws by admitting sin—“the earth is cursed in your work,” because the stability of your mind, which according to the Apostle is God’s cultivation (1 Cor. III, 9), is hindered by being subjected to decline and instability instead of the zeal for doing good. Earth is used to signify stability because it is a more solid element than the others.

“In labors you shall eat it all the days of your life.” We eat earth with labor when, with the mind restrained for a time from its mobility, we are made firm by some inspiration of God to perceive a little light. For just as we are nourished in that state, so, as pilgrims, we fail from it; by using husks, we bring nothing upon ourselves but a burden. We do this with labor because, with Job (chapter III, 24), before we eat, we sigh. And we do this all the days of our life—that is, whenever we understand our one life to be Christ. For we have said above that days signify understanding. We understand him when we single-mindedly hunger for him with inward savor.

“With labor,” I say, “you shall eat”; for nothing remains without labor even for mortals in earthly things. “For it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” You will cultivate your own mind, but while it is being cultivated, corrupted by the original and actual corruption of decay, it will produce more abundantly the thorns of greed and the thistles of lust.

For just as thistles bristle with denser spines than thorns, so the luxury of many minds is pricked more frequently—indeed, more naturally—than by greed. “And you shall eat the herbs of the earth,” because you will gladly receive soft and wanton thoughts and the desires of your flesh, fostering yourself with them as though with fodder.

[Col. 0076C]

**VERSE 19.**—“In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” The pores are struck open, and sweat flows from within. The face is named from the will, because the will of the one thinking appears especially in the face. Therefore, we eat bread in the sweat of the face when, emptied of all the softness of desire from the hidden places of the soul and washed by that process, we feed inwardly upon the bread that descended from heaven, so that we may see God face to face.

“Until you return to the earth from which you were taken.” We devote ourselves to eating that bread until we return to the earth—that is, to that heavenly stability and freedom from suffering—from which we were taken by the devil’s deceit to undergo misery.

Bread may also be understood in another way, as a form of perfection. Wheat dust, which is called flour, is moistened with water and, by much kneading, brought to the hardness of dough; then, when heat is applied, the moist mass is completely made into bread. So once we were like dust, yielding to every breath of the demon; we were infused with the water of the divine Spirit. But because our beginnings are tender and fluid, we have been hardened through repeated revolutions of temptation. Finally, through the threshings of suffering that bake our hearts to purity, we are made worthy of the faithful’s eating—that is, we are ultimately made into an example. With sweat, therefore, we attain this bread.

“You are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Since we are naturally changeable, like dust, if we strive to return to this bread of consummation, or to the earth of substance, we must return to dust—that is, confess that we are sinners. “You will take away their spirit,” says the Psalm, “and they will return to their dust” (Ps. CIII, 29). Therefore, after our will has been made to sweat out the moisture of every vice, we are led, as by the sweat of the face, to the taste or existence of this bread. For the sevenfold Spirit enters watery places.

[Col. 0077A]

**VERSE 20.**—“And Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all the living.” Once our conduct has been corrected to this state, our Adam now names his wife Eve—that is, with firm discernment, life: namely, the will subjected to right reason and already made fruitful by the fruit of good works through that very subjection. For without a good will none of the good things we do possesses life.

She provides the beginning for our vital pursuits and, so to speak, their soul. Eve is interpreted as “life.” If she is well governed by reason, supported first by reason in God, she is indeed the spirit of life for all the actions that follow.

**34. VERSE 21.**—“The Lord God also made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” When, therefore, in the disposition of the inner person, we follow the order we have set forth through vigorous exercise of holiness, we not only recover the rank of our former grace but also merit a garment of skin—that is, a garment bearing the suffering-memory of sin after the fall. Once the experience of sin has occurred, nothing usually troubles the mind more than its memory. But if this has happened without the suffering of desire, it not only does no harm but also greatly advances compunction and caution.

A skin tunic ordinarily contains both hide and wool. In the hide, therefore, the memory of a dead work is understood; in the wool, which is insensible, the virtue of freedom from suffering is understood. By these, the intellect is fortified, according to the merit of perseverance, together with a favorable will.

[Col. 0077B]

**VERSE 22.**—“And he said: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.’” “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit,” according to the Apostle (1 Cor. VI, 17). Although, therefore, we ought not to allow ourselves to fall into evil, God says of those who have fallen but have steadfastly repented: “Behold, Adam has become like”—that is, truly one of those who specially cling to me and are united to me—“one who has reached true knowledge of good through experience of evil,” so that, in a certain sense, insofar as it lies within a human being, he neither wishes to sin nor is able to do so.

We commonly say of something we strongly do not wish to do: “I cannot do this.” There are also abundant examples of some having been stronger after their fall than they had been before it.

**VERSE 23.**—“Therefore, lest he perhaps take from the tree of life and live forever, the Lord sent him out of the paradise of delight, to work the earth from which he had been taken.” Here we understand the tree of life, placed in an evil sense, as the folly of worldly remembrance. Some who wish to be celebrated in time desire to do things worthy of being recorded; they ennoble themselves through military service, poetry, and other arts, by which they may live for a long time in the memories of mortals.

This also steals upon religious people, so that they build reputations for themselves in posterity through almsgiving, novel benefactions, and the construction of churches. Therefore, so that they may not presume upon this kind of stupidity, which is not unfittingly signified by the tree, God sends them out from that special and delightful flourishing of the mind which suffers the bite of no sin. Thus, through the memory of their former contagion, which continually pricks them, they return by the strenuous practice of good works to the earth—that is, to that state of freedom from suffering—from which they were taken, having been dragged away by the devil.

[Col. 0078A]

**VERSE 24.**—“And he cast out Adam, and placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and the flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.”

When Adam has been cast out from that innocent sincerity of mind, the cherubim is placed before paradise—that is, before consideration of conscience. The name is interpreted through a vermilion painting, or as “many,” or as “a multitude of knowledge.” Vermilion is red by nature and makes anything red. A painting, however, is a sign, not the reality.

Through vermilion, which is blood-colored, sin can be represented, by which we have been infected and have infected others. The Prophet agrees: “Though your sins be red like vermilion, they shall be white like wool” (Isa. I, 18).

Through the painting, the representation of sins is understood—something that ought to be present in us by memory, not in reality. This means that the imaginings, or rather recollections, of all the evils we have committed ought always to be present to us through humble consideration.

And although it is “of many,” indeed “many,” we must not nevertheless think that we truly are so—namely, that we belong to those who have been multiplied beyond number. Thus we may hope, yet not be without fear. The painting is therefore placed, and is called “as if,” so that neither may exist without the other: we should hope while fearing, and fear while hoping.

Hence there follows, appropriately, this multitude of knowledge—that is, discernment—so that through the virtues we may distinguish ourselves from vices. The passage is connected in this way: always mindful of the crimes we have committed and by which we have corrupted others, we must fear lest we not belong to the number of the elect, which is “as many”; and for this reason we must be watchful in distinguishing ourselves from evil actions. Hence we must also hold the flaming and turning sword.

When a sword is rightly held for striking, it has an edge on both sides: against the one who strikes and against the one who is struck. By this is understood care for ourselves and for our neighbor, so that while we strive to care for what belongs to another, we may strike our own faults sharply.

But in all our action we must flee obstinacy, because the sword must be turning—that is, flexible and relaxed if reason demands it. It is flaming so that a sincere affection may govern what we do for ourselves and for our neighbor. Fire is recognized by nature as purer than all the elements.

When, therefore, we have carefully considered what we once were, and have taken no less care concerning whether we shall be among the elect in the future; when, finally, through moderation in our works, we have obtained a multitude of knowledge; when we devote as much care to ourselves as to our neighbors and display this with a pure conscience—when, I say, we have established these things before the paradise of our mind, we shall block every entrance to the way of the tree of life, that is, to the thought of worldly fame by which we delight in living superstitiously in human memories.

**35. CHAPTER FOUR**

[Col. 0079]

**VERSES 1, 2.**—“And Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying: ‘I have acquired a man through God.’ And again she bore his brother Abel. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer.”

If, when the Apostle says, “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. XV, 54), he calls carnal desire death, why should Eve, whose name means “life,” not be called the good will? When Adam knows her well—that is, loves her ardently, since love itself, as someone has said, is knowledge—he supplies her with the seed of God’s word, that she may conceive and bear Cain, that is, possession.

The possession of our rational will is our outer person, and she is set over him to govern and cultivate him. Hence Eve continues: “I have acquired a man,” not by my own strength but through God. When the will of the soul has been subdued, not by human effort but by God’s help—“no human being can tame the tongue” (Jas. III, 8); and if he cannot tame a part, how can he tame the whole—Abel is born. His name means “mourning” or “vanity,” because already then the present life begins to wither. It is wholly vanity to the mind that is separated from God’s joy.

Abel is also said to mean “vapor” or “wretched.” We call Abel the virtue of the inner person, just as we understand Cain as the outer person. The inner person mourns that he is subject to vanity; although he is constrained by bodily misery, he emits toward God a manifold vapor of virtues.

A little column of smoke arises from aromatic substances; and it is certainly easier for anyone to practise fasting, vigils, and the distribution of possessions than to attain inwardly patience, humility, and charity. Human favor often lifts up the former things, but the latter, which are performed with God alone as witness, are more arduous. Therefore Cain is not unfittingly born before Abel.

“Diligently cultivate your field,” says Solomon, “so that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. XXIV, 27). Abel is a shepherd of sheep because he is the author and nourisher of the inner person’s charity and simplicity of conduct, which shine clearly in the qualities of sheep. The sheep is a gentle animal and fruitful in wool.

Cain is a farmer, which clearly signifies bodily exercises. Bodily exercise, according to the Apostle, is useful for little (1 Tim. IV, 8).

[Col. 0079D]

**VERSES 3, 4, 5.**—“After many days Cain brought an offering to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel also brought from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat portions; and the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings. But upon Cain and his offerings he did not look.”

“After many days”—that is, proceeding with tireless ardor of mind through those eternal days which we rightly pursue by despising these brief days, which are regarded as a watch in the night—we offer sacrifices of praise to God from the fruits of the earth, that is, by wearing down the flesh externally and making it good.

But God does not regard these outward deeds, infected as they commonly are by human favor, because he does not touch the heart of the one offering them with the grace he ordinarily gives, nor does that heart trust that any of these good things are pleasing either to God or to the judgment of good people.

“Make your face shine upon your servant,” says the Psalm (Ps. CXVIII, 135). Show that you hold a cheerful affection toward what I do, so that these deeds may be seen and you may be glorified. Ignorant people also commonly suppose that deeds displeasing to God have been foolishly performed.

Abel offers from the firstborn of his flock when the inner person gives forth the fragrance of primal virtues. The first human being was created by God full of spiritual goods, without any bodily mortification. Hence, although bodily labor later became necessary for restraining the fault of the flesh, if patience, humility, and simplicity are placed after it, everything is immediately regarded as backward and is stolen away by popular praise.

In a flock of sheep, gentleness, innocence, and piety are understood through the giving of wool. These are the firstborn, which principally imprint the image of God upon the human mind. When they are offered, they are recognized and regarded by God as belonging to his own likeness.

But Abel is regarded first, and afterward his offerings, because God first weighs the intention of the one acting and afterward his actions.

Our mind, however, for which bodily things are more readily accomplished than spiritual things—because they are nearer to praise—while it recognizes that inward things are better and more acceptable to God and to all good people, nevertheless considers them more difficult for itself than outward things. It becomes angry, that is, disturbed by carnal will, and its face falls, because the good will that inwardly desires to act is overwhelmed by the appetite for outward approval. It considers bodily things more advantageous to itself because they please for a time and to the eye.

[Col. 0080B]

**VERSE [number not supplied].**—“Why,” says the Lord—that is, rationally suggesting this to us—“are you angry?” In other words, why have you been driven to the fury of despair as though spiritual things were impossible? “And why has your face fallen?” That is, why have you been cast down in the disposition of your mind?

“Is it not so that, if you do well”—namely, in secret—“you will receive in the future,” even if no human praise follows your works in this age? “But if you do evil, sin will immediately be at the door.” That is, if you pervert the intention for the sake of reputation, the opportunity for sin will immediately appear at the first suggestion of the mind, with the devil providing it.

But so that you may not excuse yourself by accusing the devil of imposed violence, “his desire will be under you, and you will rule over him.” Yet because reason is not illumined by God and Cain—that is, our bodily endeavor—is empty, it draws Abel, whatever spiritual richness there is within, into the sacrilege of vainglory. For Abel’s sacrifice consists of fat portions—that is, of inward grace—so that nothing in a human work may remain except what can please the eyes of the flesh and be praised.

**VERSE 8.**—“Let us go out,” Cain says—that is, outside.
