Since it is exceedingly difficult to persist in attaining so many and such great spiritual things, which no one fully achieves, let us at least set these aside for a while and exercise outwardly those things that may meanwhile benefit our honor and advantage.

When they were in the field—that is, in outward activity—with the gaze of the heart already withdrawn from inward consideration and the mind’s rigor softened by habitual favor, the entire simplicity of inward things is overcome by Cain—that is, by the outer person—on the surface of external works.

When God complains, in the voice of reason, about the inward death, human wickedness replies:

**VERSE 9.**—“I do not know.” We commonly answer that we do not know about things for which we do not care, even when we truly do know.

**VERSE 10.**—“Am I my brother’s keeper?” That is, “Have I alone undertaken to guard spiritual things, which no one is capable of observing in their entirety?” The murderous mind, crushed beneath the millstone of carnal glory, gives this answer.

But reason, although it is not believed because it thinks with God, complains of the immensity of the apostasy. “Consider,” it says, “how criminally you have acted. The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.”

The voice commonly precedes the word, as a shadow precedes the reality. Therefore, let us understand “voice” as that grief which arises from sin in someone’s heart, but which is not followed by the truth of the word—that is, by any effective repentance. This voice before God is more a provocation than a peace offering.

It cries from the earth because the person, richly nourished by the knowledge and fruits of reason, which is firmly rooted like earth, sees how perverse are the things he commits. For even when reason is twisted toward a wicked affection, it does not entirely lose the eye by which it distinguishes good and evil. “For the one who knows the good and does not do it, for him it is sin” (Jas. IV, 17).

It cries because what is horrible sounds in God’s ears: outwardly he displays divine and holy works, while inwardly he knowingly and deliberately dedicates himself as a shrine of the devil. There is a cry wherever all impurity is carried out knowingly, deliberately, and without reproof.

This is the voice of the brother’s blood, that is, of the inward good once begotten from the same will. Blood, however, is sin. The voice of blood cries out, therefore, when, despising the complaint of sin through the arrogance of the mind, it sharply disturbs God’s patience.

[Col. 0081B]

**VERSE 11.**—“Now therefore you shall be accursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.”

Therefore, relying upon earthly things and upon works performed hypocritically on the surface alone, you shall be accursed—that is, once the fiction of your vanity has been recognized, you shall be held worthy of execration.

The earth receives blood from your hand with open mouth because the earthly affection, having opened itself wide through its own greed, eagerly receives from the hand—that is, from the glory of external works—the death of the inner person, namely its blood.

**VERSE 12.**—“When you work it”—that is, when you wear down the body with fasting, vigils, and other practices—“it shall not give you its fruits,” namely the earthly praise you seek, “because you will be a wanderer upon the earth.”

This means that, unstable under every impulse of temptation, even in the evident performance of your works, you will fall from one vice into another.

You will also be a fugitive, since the guilt of a foul conscience demands that you be subject to fear at every movement. For flight of the mind is fear. Moreover, the one who flees commonly runs ahead of the one pursuing and drives himself into flight.

Our pursuer is the devil, who attacks us in three ways: either when he tempts us, or when he supplies opportunities for enticement to our desires, or when he adds up rewards by endorsing the iniquities we have committed.

He is often falsely accused of being the instigator, because the wicked invention of the one thinking precedes the devil’s pressure. Hence it is said to someone: “I will throw you like a ball upon a broad land” (Isa. XXII, 18), because when a ball is thrown it sometimes travels farther than the one who throws it wishes. Elsewhere it is said: “The fool flees when no one pursues” (Prov. XXVIII, 1); and again: “They departed without strength before the face of the pursuer” (Lam. I, 6).

In this way every hypocrite becomes a fugitive, either yielding to the tempter or anticipating the tempter.

When the mind, as though God were speaking within it, foresees these things through reasoning, or gradually perceives them through experience, it does not receive the anointing of the Spirit. It therefore sets a wall of despair between itself and God.

[Col. 0082A]

**VERSE 13.**—“My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon.” “The interweaving of my vices,” he says, “is so great that no accumulation of good works can disentangle me from it.”

**VERSE 14.**—“Behold, you cast me out today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.”

In vain, surely, would I strive. For you cast me from the face of the earth—that is, from knowledge of myself—depriving me of your grace, so that, having fallen into a rejected mind, I may confess myself to be earth, that is, a sinner. For it was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19).

I do not see my sins, and this “today”—that is, as long as I enjoy the understanding of discernment. It is as though he were saying: “When, by blinding me, you make me alien from yourself and from myself, it may seem very unjust that, while I still grieve over my errors, you also cause me to be hidden from your face—that is, to be taken away as an impious person from seeing your glory in the future—by allowing me to become a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, unstable through vices and a fugitive from every good thing through my evident works.”

“Everyone who finds me will kill me.” He finds me who discovers my being—that is, my life—by searching for it; and he kills me if, terrified by the magnitude of my crimes, he takes away from me the hope of pardon.

But we must note how a human being turns his wickedness against God. “You,” he says, “cast me from the face of the earth”—that is, “you take away your care of me from me”—and you do this “so that I may be hidden from your face,” which is to be excluded from seeing you. Therefore, I am now declared by human beings to be utterly without hope.

[Col. 0082C]

**VERSE 15.**—“Not so,” says the Lord; “but whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

Not “whoever kills you,” but “whoever kills Cain.” Insofar as you are your own possession, insofar as you chastise yourself and reduce your body to servitude, because, not knowing with what intention you do this, you have been condemned by the guilt of hypocrisy, whoever kills you will be punished sevenfold. He will be held guilty for the destruction of your outward and inward works.

The number seven is divided into four and three. The body consists of the four elements; the soul consists of three principal movements: understanding, memory, and will.

Therefore, whoever condemns a human being—although he may be a hypocrite or vicious, yet the condemner has not established with certainty that he is a hypocrite or truly vicious—binds himself to homicide insofar as it concerns him, even if that person’s bodily and spiritual goods are nonexistent. The same person would indeed readily inflict this wrong upon any genuinely good person if he indiscreetly reviled one unknown to him.

“And the Lord placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.” The Lord places a mark on Cain when he does not allow the marked—that is, concealed—wickedness of human beings to be judged in this age by anyone as deserving eternal death. For if we judged abruptly, we would often hand over to death one who was worthy of life.

[Col. 0082D]

**VERSE 16.**—“And Cain went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land, toward the eastern region of Eden.”

Because Cain’s conscience is temporarily hidden within him, he goes out secure from the face of the Lord—that is, scattered among human favors, he does not consider that God knows the evils he secretly commits, or that God knowingly conceals them and mercifully forgives them.

He dwells as a fugitive in the land, fixing his mind upon earthly things and not seeking that city whose architect is God (Heb. XI, 10). Clinging to what is lowest, but fleeing everywhere through vices wherever his affection sows itself, he dwells toward the eastern region of Eden, whose name means “delights.”

He is not in the east, as though he belonged to those of the East—among whom Job was great—and were illumined by the light of the true East. Rather, he is toward the eastern region: that is, toward the simulation of the intention of those whose conduct is in heaven (Phil. III, 10) and for whom to live is Christ (Phil. I, 21).

The delights of the saints are the sacred writings. Hypocrites especially display themselves as delighting in them and treating them willingly; thus, through the spiritual words of Scripture, they seem to illumine themselves with a kind of eastern light.

In these delights, the bride is called most beloved in the Song of Songs (Song VII, 6). Hence, although such people wholly desire earthly things and works of complete darkness, they habitually cloak their inner selves by speaking subtly about seeing God and contemplating heavenly things, as though surrounded by the glory of some delightful brightness. They prefer to present in words what cannot at all be understood by their dark minds through actual savor.

[Col. 0083A]

**VERSE 17.**—“Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch.”

Although Cain appears to dwell in the eastern region of delights, he nevertheless has a wife—namely, that woman who, through her own opportunity, commonly turns away those invited to God’s supper.

“I have married a wife,” he says, “and therefore I cannot come” (Luke XIV, 20). This wife is pleasure, in which he is entangled through transitory possession and praise, although he pretends otherwise and appears to pursue more sincere things.

A little later, in the genealogy of this same Cain, Noema, a woman, is added at the end. Her name means “pleasure,” and in her the final intention of the reprobate is signified.

Everyone knows her who, for the sweetness of present things, postpones the blessedness of the future. Miserably indeed does the one know her who declares that, if the present age could last forever, he would never want another age.

From this she conceives and bears Enoch—that is, “dedication”—because such a great and pestilential love of the world produces obstinacy in the mind. We make a dedication when we display the firmness of our mind in persevering love for the delights of the age.

“And he built a city, and called its name after the name of his son Enoch.” A city is built when a wicked person gathers a meeting-place of people like himself. He calls it by the son’s name when an impenitent heart urges its followers toward the same determination of the worst purpose.

I would say much about these matters and certain things that follow, if I did not know that blessed Augustine and some of the Fathers had treated them. Here also, as elsewhere, I have avoided a heap of Hebrew names.

**THE SECOND BOOK OF THE MORALS ENDS.**

**THE THIRD BOOK OF THE MORALS ON GENESIS BEGINS.**

[Col. 0083]

**CHAPTER FIVE**

[Col. 0083C]

**38. VERSE 31.**—“When Noah was five hundred years old, he begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth.”

Noah was the son of Lamech. Lamech is said to mean “discipline”; Noah, “rest.” From discipline, therefore, rest arises. Although in the present it is a matter of sorrow, it will nevertheless render the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those exercised in it (Heb. XII, 11).

For this intellectual Lamech, when he begets Noah, says: “This one will comfort us from our works and from the labors of our hands on the earth which the Lord has cursed” (Gen. V, 29).

When, through the exercise of struggle, one arrives even in this age at the rest of a limited freedom from suffering, then truly Noah—whom we have begotten through the embrace of discipline—comforts us from the labors we have endured. We are no longer striking the air; we have reached some measure of mastery or rest, and through the abundance of grace we have grown above the earth’s curses—that is, above bodily declines.

But this rest has certain degrees. Lamech, when written with *ch*, is said in Hebrew to mean “struck” or “striking”; it means “discipline” only when the letter is used as an element and the word is finally written with *d*.

The rational mind is struck when, in Job and in the Psalms, it complains of arrows fixed in it through susceptibility and is pierced by the darts of temptation (Job VI, 4; Ps. XXXVII, 3). It also strikes when, by resisting, it courageously withstands the troubles that assail it. It begets Noah, which means “rest,” when it reaches the tranquility of victory.

This rest, I say, has degrees. First we cease outwardly from evil action; afterward, though with much greater difficulty, we cease from perverse thought. Hence Noah is said to be five hundred years old.

By the number five, outwardness is understood because of the five senses; by one hundred, perfection is signified. This means ceasing from wicked pursuits through the fullness of outward good works. The years are the lights of divine things and the gladness of duties by which this state of mind is filled—the state called “the flower-filled bed of the Church” in the Song of Songs (Song I, 15).

In this Sabbath, therefore, Shem, Ham, and Japheth are begotten. Shem is interpreted as “named,” and in him faith is understood: the name which is to be blessed upon the earth, and in which alone we receive that we must be saved (Acts 4:12). This is the honorable name before him of those redeemed from usury and iniquity (Ps. 71:14). For if those who are in Christ will rise first (1 Thess. 4:15), plainly on account of the dignity of the Christian name, why should it be considered doubtful that they themselves should obtain some more powerful reward in heaven, distinguished as they are by participation in so great a name? Hence in baptism each believer receives a name, by which he subscribes to the carrying out of Christ’s signs through his profession of spiritual warfare.

But to one who is thus named while fleeing from Babylon’s disgrace, Ham must be added by the bond of brotherhood. Ham is interpreted as “hot,” in which hope is not inappropriately signified. For if heat is derived from the nature of fire, and fire by its origin progresses toward heavenly things, hope is therefore rightly understood through heat: hope eagerly strains toward God through the fervor of charity. To him Japheth is joined, whose name is said to mean “breadth”; by this charity is clearly understood, since it extends no less through enemies than through friends. These three, then—breadth, length, and height—which are mentioned by the Apostle (Eph. 3:12), begin to appear in us when we have become true Noah, that is, when through the exhibition of good works we have rested from what is useless. For to take a holiday from evil and yet not undertake the good is itself evil. Then they truly emerge, because faith does not stand without good works, nor hope without faith, nor charity without both.

## CHAPTER VI

### Verses 1–2

“And when human beings began to multiply upon the earth and had begotten sons, the sons of God, seeing the daughters of human beings, that they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all those whom they had chosen.”

As the pursuit of the virtues grows, human beings are multiplied not merely on the earth but above the earth, because very dense swarms of human movements are borne into the human soul—not such as are easily subdued by the power of reason, but such as can subject the earth, that is, the firmness of the mind, to vices. For virtue is not proved except when the enemy is near.

These same human beings beget daughters when they frequently set the softness of fragile thoughts before their inward vision. The sons of God see these daughters when the excellence of intellectual perceptions, at the introduction of suggestions, lowers the eye of contemplation toward something like prostitution, toward the appearance of pandering. For what are the pleasures of imagination but certain beautiful faces that entice us? King Pharaoh wishes to cherish these daughters when he orders the males to be killed (Exod. 1:17).

From all these women whom the sons of God choose, they take wives for themselves, because, according as they incline toward their own mixture or lust, they recklessly fasten upon the mind corresponding pleasures as rational movements; from these an infamous offspring emerges, namely, obscene actions. For avarice is more readily at hand for some, pride for others, and lust for very many.

### Verse 3

“And God said: ‘My spirit will not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh.’”

When the conflict of vices disturbs our rest—which we thought we had obtained by sword and bow, that is, by our discernment and foresight—God speaks inwardly to us through experience as mediator, declaring that his spirit will not remain in human beings forever: that is, the power of reason will not persevere in the human heart. Nor would this be expedient, because human beings are flesh, that is, fragile, and by their innate mutability beget ruin for themselves from their own condition.

For a person becomes proud if he seems to himself to have accomplished something properly, just as a poor man would if he suddenly came into wealth that he had not labored to acquire. This abandonment by the spirit is therefore necessary, provided that it is not total, in accordance with David’s prayer in the psalm that he not be utterly abandoned (Ps. 118:8).

“And their days will be one hundred and twenty years.”

We said above that the number one hundred signifies fullness; through the number twenty, duplicity is signified, as in: “Whether he can meet the one who comes against him with ten thousand, while he comes against him with twenty thousand” (Luke 14:31). And in the Apocalypse: “Twenty thousand ten-thousands” (Rev. 9:16).

Here I do not understand duplicity as hypocrisy, but as that violent impurity contracted through the necessity of sinning, by the admixture of evils rushing upon us. In accordance with this, the Church will not have a blemish or wrinkle in the future (Eph. 5:27)—not because she has a wrinkle of hypocrisy in the present, for hypocrisy is entirely banished from her, but because now, through the occupation of temptations and the flesh, she appears more constricted and less free toward God.

We therefore have one hundred for the integrity of good will, and twenty for that impurity of action mentioned above, while, according to the Apostle, “we do the evil that we do not want” (Rom. 7:19). Or we have twenty on account of the transgression of the divine law, when we do what we do not approve, while the law of our members resists the law of the mind (Rom. 7:19–23).

Alternatively: eight times fifteen make one hundred and twenty. Through the number eight, temporality is understood; through five, corporeality; through ten, spirituality. Therefore, as long as we live temporally, our spiritual striving is weighed down by external sensuality, as though ten were overcome by five, so that what “day” means—that is, human virtue—may be recognized by human beings. Because of the brevity of its glory, the height of day is called this in the psalm (Ps. 55:4).

### Verse 4

“Now there were giants upon the earth in those days.”

In these exercises of the virtues, which we understand through the days, giants—that is, proud movements of the soul walking above themselves in marvelous ways—were upon the earth. For good works are displayed on the surface of the body, and they bring upon a mind vainly elated a semblance of pride through gratification in its praises.

“For after the sons of God had gone in to the daughters of human beings, and they had borne children, these were the mighty men of old, men of renown.”

The sons of God go in to the daughters of human beings when our intellectual movements—which Job calls “strong in power” (Job 36:19), and which are generated in us by God—immerse themselves in order to experience the fluctuations of carnal desires.

But these are “the mighty men of old,” because after they have slipped into the abyss of every impurity, worldly devotion reigns with greatest power in their hearts, so that no people in the world appear more hopeless than those who once seemed scarcely to have lived for God. For they involve themselves in worse vices in proportion as, from a stricter resolution, they rush more greedily into the luxuries of the world.

“These are men of renown,” because, surpassing human wickedness and imitating diabolical wickedness, and deriving boldness from crime—whence they are also called giants—after they have fallen into a reprobate mind, they are spread abroad with the stench of a corrupt reputation, worse than other wicked people.

### Verses 5–7

“And God, seeing that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was directed toward evil at all times, repented that he had made human beings upon the earth.”

Established in this most desperate Babylon, God sees—that is, he makes them see—how wickedly they devote themselves outwardly to the effects of carnal works, and how continually they propose worse things inwardly. God therefore sees, that is, discerns, and at last God repents.

For if repentance is a good thing, and this good comes not from us but from God, then it is rightly said: “It repented him that he had made human beings upon the earth.” The one who recovered his senses repented, because, having applied his interior self to his exterior self—which is the whole human being—and to those things that are visible only on the surface, he groaned after returning from the exterior to the interior, that is, to the spirit.

Struck inwardly by grief of heart and taking precautions for the future, he says: “I will wipe out the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from human beings to the birds of heaven” [another reading: “to living creatures”], “from reptiles to living creatures” [another reading: “the birds of heaven”].

To be touched by grief, to take precautions for the future, and the other expressions of this kind are not passions of God but actions of God in us. The one who repented is therefore touched inwardly by grief of heart, so that the pain of compunction may not be momentary or merely apparent, but may penetrate the marrow of the soul—namely, the hidden places of intention—and may guard against future entanglements, lest he repeat the words of prayer. For if someone weeps but does not correct what he wept over, he shows that he is playing a game rather than grieving inwardly.

To use “human being” for “carnality” is customary in Scripture. He therefore wipes out the human being who, obliterating the carnal affection engraved upon him through imaginings like inscribed tablets, wipes away the one whom he created—that is, whom he aroused from the movements of the flesh for the strengthening and fulfillment of passions.

For *creas* (Greek *kreas*) means “flesh”; from it *creare* (“to create”) is derived, and *artocreae* and *creagrae* are so called. But here the human being is to be wiped out “from the face of the earth,” that is, from attention to and love of earthly things; “from human beings,” that is, from those movements of the soul which are, as it were, endowed with reason, such as honesty and moderation when possessed not for God but in a worldly manner; “to living creatures,” that is, to the eradication of desire, which is indeed inclined toward the earth but is excused on the grounds of necessity and, as it were, suspended; and “from reptiles,” immersed in the stench of the mire of shameful acts, “to the birds of heaven,” that is, the vainglorious display of hypocrisy, which are carried along by vanity. All these are to be brought to ruin. In their total extinction it is proved that the following statement is true: “For I repent that I have made them.”

### Verse 8

“But Noah found favor before God.”

When these evils cease, the rest of the mind that has begun, removed from its former disturbances, is drenched with spiritual serenity before the Lord—that is, in the innermost places where God alone sees. For where does the Spirit of God rest except upon one who is quiet, whose mind has not been deafened by the clamor of vices, and upon one who is humble and does not grow proud over their defeat? (Isa. 66:2.)

### Verses 9–11

“These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just and perfect man among his generations. And he begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.”

Our generations are thoughts, intentions, and actions, together with whatever arises within. The just person is one who, according to human knowledge, so arranges what must be done toward himself and his neighbor that he remembers the things belonging to knowing and observing God; the habit of wisdom corresponds to these.

The perfect person is one who, even if he cannot fulfill everything completely, nevertheless has a heart fully disposed by goodwill to undertake them, mutilated in no respect. He walks with God who in no way disagrees with what reason, illumined by God, suggests must be done.

Then he finally generates three sons, when, free from external labor, he is at leisure for God through faith, hope, and charity.

“But the earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with iniquity.”

### Verses 12–13

“And when God had seen that the earth was corrupt—for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth—he said to Noah: ‘The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity from their face, and I will destroy them along with the earth.’”

From human beings to living creatures, from reptiles to the birds of heaven, the earth is corrupted; that is, the mind, drawn away from its proper stability, falls prostituted into the abysses of every kind of wickedness.

For all flesh had corrupted its way, because the softness of carnal appetite had scattered and infected the way toward which it ought to be directed, and which is the true way of proceeding rightly—namely, reason. And this happened “upon the earth,” that is, not only within the hidden places of the mind, but even as far as the manifest examples of depravity carried out through the body, our earth.

When God had seen these things—that is, when he had set before the blind sinner the evils in which he was involved, so that they might be seen—he suggests through the prompting of inward inspiration what must be done if he wished to become intellectual Noah.

“For the end of all flesh has come before me.” The consummation of every kind of bodily pleasure takes place if one comes “before me,” that is, into my good pleasure. For whatever is established in my mind, I wish to have before me and before my eyes. In contrast, Scripture says: “For you will set them as their back” (Ps. 20:13).

When one comes to God’s good pleasure, therefore, whatever the luxury of the flesh demands is immediately rejected.

“From their face”—namely, from that of living creatures, human beings, and reptiles—that is, from the intention of desires and lusts. For by the face we both direct our attention and are the objects of attention.

“The earth is filled with iniquity,” because, while the inner human being rests upon shameful desires, the outer human being—that is, the earth—is indiscriminately exposed to the production of wicked deeds.

“And I will destroy them along with the earth,” when he removes the inhabitant, namely the soul, and the body, unquestionably its earthly dwelling, from earthly affairs insofar as this is relevant to both.

### Verse 14

“Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood; you shall make compartments in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and outside.”

“Ark” is derived from *arcere* (“to restrain”), as is *arx, arcis* (“citadel”). We therefore make an ark when we prepare such a conscience that it restrains impure desires from itself and retains the mystery of pious intention or action under the sign of faith.

It is constructed from smoothed wood when the conscience is supported by virtues stripped of the burden of earthly praise and of the weight of carnal affection.

We make compartments in the ark when we establish the purposes of various holy professions. When, for example, we prepare patience against adversity and chastity against lust, we thus find within ourselves, for each matter, a separate house that shelters us as we flee.

It should also be noted that *mansiunculae* (“little dwellings”) derives from *manere* (“to remain”) and is expressed diminutively. In “remaining,” therefore, stable and certain perseverance is understood; in the diminutive form, humility. In these there are distinct refuges against every danger that assails us.

It is coated with pitch inside and outside because, although the grace of charity bestows benefits outwardly upon our neighbors, the soul of the holy is not thereby emptied inwardly of the same gift. Beneficence is outward, according to the Apostle, while inwardly, as far as unanimity is concerned, they do not forget to share with one another (Heb. 13:16). For either one without the other is little or nothing.

Pitch is of a very adhesive nature and is insoluble in water. Service produces friends and binds them to itself; and although charity makes the minds of the holy terrible, like an ordered battle line, they are not breached by any assault or flood of vices. Since pitch is also made from mud, it signifies the grace of humility, by which all good deeds are seasoned.

### Verse 15

“The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.”

Through the number three, the Trinity; through one hundred, integrity; through the cubit, firmness of work; through length, the extension of intention is understood.

Let us therefore not hope for God’s mercy while doing evil, but let us extend the intention of the mind toward God, who is Trinity, founded upon firm and complete works.

The three hundred cubits may also be understood as the three chief and perfect stages that the Lord names: “Ask, seek, knock” (Matt. 7:7)—ask, namely, by praying; seek, by reading; knock, by acting. When we carry these out with continual effectiveness, our hope is rightly directed toward the one for whom this is done.

The number fifty, being composed of seven times seven plus one, is nevertheless customarily used by itself to signify rest, as in the Jubilee, and also in the distribution of fifty among the eating of the seven loaves.

By breadth we understand contemplation, through which we range, however slightly, in the vision of God. “For every creature is narrow to one who sees the Creator” (Gregory, *Dialogues* II.35).

But if we desire to reach this state, we must rest from wicked work and subject the seven—that is, our body and soul—to the sevenfold grace. For, as we have said elsewhere, the body consists of four elements and the soul of three principal movements; together these make seven.

When we have therefore subjected ourselves inwardly and outwardly to spiritual grace, only then shall we come, with great breadth of heart, to contemplate that One with all our love—namely, God.

After we have labored in the knowledge of God, it is necessary also to measure the thirty cubits of height by consideration of ourselves. Five times six makes thirty. Through the number six, perfection is understood, because God perfected his works in six days; and by this same number the human being can be signified, since the human being was made on the sixth day.

Through five, external understanding is understood on account of knowledge through the five senses; and ten is contained three times in thirty.

The whole meaning is that we ought to turn the knowledge of our outer human being toward contemplation of our first origin and dignity, and to order thought, speech, and action according to the precepts of divine law, which are called ten.

This height, therefore, is the sum of our condition, toward which we ought frequently to direct our attention: how perfectly it was made by God.

### Verse 16

“You shall make a window in the ark, and you shall finish it with a cubit at its summit.”

A window usually admits and excludes light from houses. Through it discernment can reasonably be understood, by which through reasoning we repel evil and receive good through worthy choice.

By this discernment we restrain not only darkness but also light when it becomes harmful. For when inept joy or confidence arises in us from remembering the good things we have done, the memory of former sins is rightly recalled to the mind like a kind of shadow.

“Place,” says Isaiah, “your shadow as night” (Isa. 16:3).

God also creates a cloud over the whole place of Mount Zion by day. The summit of all these things is finished with a cubit, because in eternal rest the summit—that is, the end—of a laboriously perfected conscience is commanded to be hoped for. For from *cubitus* (“elbow, cubit”) we derive *accubitare* (“to recline”).

Hence in the Song of Songs there is a golden couch (Song 3:10), and in the Gospel it is said that he will make them recline at table (Luke 12:37). There what is practiced here will be perfected without labor; in Jerusalem the vow will be fulfilled.

“But you shall place the door of the ark in its side below; you shall make upper rooms and three stories in it.”

We should understand the door of the ark as our mouth, through which the secrets of the conscience are opened. The door is so called from *ostendere* (“to show”); hence it is commanded that the lamp not be placed under a bushel (Matt. 5:15), so that those who enter—those, namely, who are admitted through conversation to knowledge of us—may see, that is, may be taught.

This is the meaning of: “Do not bring every person into your house” (Sir. 11:31): do not disclose your mind to everyone.

We place this door in the side when, watchful against creeping deceptions, we look carefully in every direction to determine what we ought to keep silent about and what we ought to say. We place it below when we either refuse to scrutinize matters too lofty or express what must be said with fitting humility of mind and tongue.

We make upper rooms when we suspend all our desires from earthly pleasure.

The third story appears to be named from the three states. There are truly three states of our being:

1. The first is in bodily vision.
2. The second is in the memory of imaginings.
3. The third is in intellectual prudence.

Each of these also has its own triads, which it would take too long to pursue. When a person has carefully weighed their qualities, let him subordinate the first two for their usefulness and, with the Apostle Paul, spring upward to the third heaven, namely, the intellectual mystery (2 Cor. 12:2).

It is said by many that human beings dwelt in the third chamber, and not without reason. For we have visions and imaginings of bodies in common with beasts, but we share with God and the angels the glory of reason.

It is also said that the first station was a dung-place, where the dung of the animals and human beings dwelling there was deposited; the second was a storeroom, where things suitable for food for both were kept; the third was a dwelling-place, where only human beings lived.

Our first state, likewise, in vocation is confession of sin; the second, in justification, is the performance of life-giving works; the third, in glorification, is when we shall be in the kingdom as the elect alone.

### Verse 17

“Behold, I will bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, to destroy every flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven; everything that is upon the earth shall be consumed.”

The water of the heavenly flood is knowledge of the sacrament, by which every obscenity of sin is washed away upon the earth, that is, in our body.

“I will pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed” (Ezek. 36:25).

This water—that is, wisdom—is brought upon the earth when spiritual dignity surpasses the flesh through the standard of justice.

“Every flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven” is killed when our members, which are upon the earth and still live and flourish in us, are put to death (Col. 3:5), so that we may say with the Apostle Paul: “I live, yet no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

They are put to death only to this extent—not so that they are utterly destroyed, but so that they are said to reign in nothing.

The spirit lives “under heaven” when, although pressed by the rule of reason—which is called heaven because of the divine mysteries that it contains—the blasts of temptation drive us.

Through this savor of wisdom, therefore, everything that is upon the earth is consumed, while the worldly heat of the affections is quenched by the wave of heavenly love, insofar as the spirit is permitted to prevail over the flesh.

### Verse 18

“And I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall enter the ark—you and your sons, your wife and the wives of your sons with you.”

He establishes his covenant with us when, after worldly pleasure has been extinguished, he teaches us inwardly to taste and see that it is good to cling to him (Ps. 72:28). Through the power of this covenant, such constancy arises in the hearts of certain holy people that, even if there were no punishments of hell, they would nevertheless never wish to abandon the justice they had accepted.

Our Noah enters the ark, together with his sons, when the mind, free from the disturbance of vices and content with the inward testimony of its virtues, hides itself within the secrets of conscience.

To this wonderfully corresponds the account of Mary coming to the tomb in the morning with two disciples (John 20:1–3).

Our wife is our will, which, faithfully joined to reason, is made fruitful by works of piety. The wives of the sons are those wills subject to the purposes of each individual profession.

The Church is one, although many are spoken of on account of their location. In the same way, many wills are spoken of, although there is one on account of the distinction among the things we will.

Noah and his sons are distinguished separately, as are the wife and the wives of the sons, because our spirit and its works, and then its principal will toward God and the swarms of miscellaneous wills, must be distinguished with the utmost subtlety. For there are people in whom everything is confused.

All these, therefore—the wills of actions and the actions of wills—are stored within the now peaceful mind, which does not scatter itself uselessly outward but glories inwardly in the Lord.

### Verse 19

“And of every living creature of all flesh you shall bring two of each into the ark, so that they may live with you, male and female.”

From every kind of desire, born from whatever fragile affection, we bring two into the ark, in which there is a female and a male. We bring near to the mind, willingly or unwillingly, the fluid and almost feminine movements of the flesh arising from the necessity of sinning; nevertheless, we immediately subject them to the authority of the male, namely reason, by whose power they are constrained according to a rule, so that they may live with us—that is, so that they may be compelled not to pour the poison of vice into us, but to perceive and perform with us the things belonging to life.

Thus Adam and Eve are joined together.

### Verse 20

“Of the birds according to their kind”—that is, of the movements of pride, whether pride is displayed in a worldly manner or under the guise of religion—“of the beasts according to their kind,” that is, of desires, whatever the object of desire may be; “and of every reptile of the earth according to its kind,” that is, of every kind of shameful act by which one sins through the desires of the flesh.

Two of everything enter with us, so that they may live. Whatever is suited to luxury and guilt, once admitted within us through thought, is immediately brought under the yoke of the manly mind, so that, while we use temptation well, it may benefit us for life.

The Apostle John also mentions these three kinds of sin, as though asserting that the material of all crimes—everything that is in the world—is either “the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

### Verses 21–22

“Therefore you shall take with you from all the foods that can be eaten, and you shall store them with you; and they shall be food for you and for them.”

We store up among us all the foods that can be eaten when we gather, in many forms and in many ways, the words and deeds spoken and performed by the Fathers for the example and formation of life. We nourish ourselves with them as with fodder, restrain the incentives of depravity that press upon us, and, as it were, feed these incentives when we answer their suggestions with the life-giving words and deeds of the saints.

Thus Noah did everything that God had commanded him.

## CHAPTER VII

### Verse 1

“And the Lord said to him: ‘Enter, you and all your household, into the ark; for I have seen you to be just before me in this generation.’”

After we have dug out a treasure with much toil, we rejoice, in accordance with Job’s words, to find a grave (Job 3:22). For when we have exposed our bodies to every kind of suffering for God’s service, we think that in this world we can obtain nothing greater from God than to reach some degree of impassibility of mind: namely, that when we have fulfilled what God commands to be done, we may be hidden within the rest of the mind, free from external conflict, together with all our spiritual wealth.

In this spiritual generation of sons, by which the Apostle also says that the woman will be saved (1 Tim. 2:15), God does not see—that is, approve—our justice solely in the mortification of the body.

### Verse 2

“From all clean animals take seven and seven, male and female; but from the unclean animals, two and two, male and female.”

Seven and seven make fourteen. Seven is customarily used for spiritual grace or for the whole human being, namely the inner and outer human being.

Our works, therefore, with the body subjected and the soul subjected to the divine spirit through observance of the Decalogue, attain the heights of the Gospel and become clean animals. Yet it is necessary that there be a male and a female, so that, insofar as the animals are living creatures and have feminine softness for embracing temporal things, there may be present something like an authority of reason, which may restrain them manfully.

Our good deeds, however they are performed, scarcely shine with complete purity. What wonder, then, if unclean animals require this masculine governance all the more? They are two because the things we desire in this world divide us from the unity of God and from human beings; or they are two and two, that is, four, because through love of temporal things our desires flow into carnal, unclean animals unless the reins of understanding turn them back to the line of purity, namely God.

### Verse 3

“And likewise of the birds of heaven, seven and seven, male and female, so that seed may be preserved upon the face of the whole earth.”

If actual-life goods are signified by the living creatures, and illicit movements that have been healthfully corrected by reason by the unclean animals, contemplative excellence is not inappropriately signified by the birds of heaven. Having conquered the wantonness of the body by grace, this excellence is balanced above the ether by tasting God.

But the reason why these are subjected to intellectual dominion is added: “so that seed may be preserved upon the face of the whole earth.” For unless it rules, the will—which is the seed and origin of a good work—immediately perishes and produces no commendable fruit on the surface of the earth, that is, in the outer human being.

The preservation of the seed, therefore, comes from the command of reason.

### Verse 4

“For after seven more days I will rain upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every substance that I have made from the face of the earth.”

Seven is understood as fullness. Forty, because it is made from four and ten, signifies the temporal course, which consists of four variations, in which the soul exercises itself under God’s law. It is called the Decalogue on account of the ten principal commandments.

After the previously mentioned bestowals of virtues, therefore, God promises that after seven days—that is, after the fullness of spiritual graces—he will still rain upon the earth for forty days and nights. In this life, namely, in which obedience is given to God’s commands amid adversity and prosperity, signified by days and nights, he will soften the hardness of our carnal affection through divine infusion.

In this way he wipes out every substance that he made from the surface of the earth, when he obliterates the will of the soul, which rests upon carnal desires as upon certain accidents, insofar as it is fluid and capable of such things, from the face of the earth—that is, from the thought of the mind already made firm.

He made this substance because, on account of our deserving evil, he permitted it to be made.

### Verses 5–7

“So Noah did everything that God had commanded him.”

After the present age has become so worthless that its light is like its darkness (Ps. 138:11), then our Noah begins fully to attain what God commanded. For it rained forty days and forty nights.

“And he was six hundred years old when the waters of the flood inundated the earth.”

Sacred history corresponds to our states when it recounts the heats of temptation that this Noah suffered after five hundred years, and the good things with which he flourished, already perfected in complete rest, no less inwardly than he appeared outwardly. This is signified by the six hundredth year.

Even if at some time we rest from evil work, nevertheless we endure severe battles in the mind. But the perfect person, sufficiently established by six and one hundred, is full of the virtues signified by the collection of years.

He is illuminated by the waters of the flood because wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subjected to sins (Wis. 1:4). Scripture says: “You have desired wisdom” (Sir. 1:33), that is, excellence of contemplation? Keep the commandments. For the beast that touches the mountain is commanded to be crushed (Exod. 19:13).

Therefore, so that the just person may still be justified, water of purification is poured in, so that he may reach, to some degree, the height of divine vision, and the carnal earth of affection may sink down before the spirit.

“And Noah entered, and his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons with him into the ark, because of the waters of the flood.”

If we beget sons—that is, good works—we must see to it that we have wives, that is, that we do not lack the will to do good. Otherwise, when we have sown much, we may bring in little; that is, when we have labored greatly for God, we may obtain little reward because we acted not from love but servilely, through fear.

By willing as we work and working as we will, let us cover ourselves within the conscience, where we may rest from useless noise and drink the waters of wisdom, by which we are also washed.

### Verses 8–10

“Of clean and unclean animals, and of birds and of everything that moves upon the earth, two and two entered into the ark with Noah, male and female, as the Lord had commanded Noah. And after seven days the waters of the flood inundated the earth.”

All this has been treated above, except for the statement “of everything that moves upon the earth.” In an evil sense, this is understood to mean our carnal movements, which wish to advance above the earth—that is, beyond the state of reason. Of these it is said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you may not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

Or it may be understood in a good sense, as our spiritual alacrity, by which we advance above the earth—that is, beyond our animal nature. Since these movements are felt to be less than complete before God, they are corrected according to the rule of understanding and preserved with God, hidden within the ark of the heart.

Thus, after the full grace of the divine gifts has been granted, we come to the glory of contemplation.

### CHAPTER VII

**VERSES 11, 12.** [Cols. 0095C–0096A] — In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, all the fountains of the great abyss burst open, and the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rains fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.[45]

Three degrees are set down here, not without purpose: days, months, and years. Let us therefore begin with the day. The number ten refers to the commandments; the number seven, because the age of the world revolves through seven days, pertains to temporal things. We have the seventeenth day when, holding the commandments of God more desirable than gold (Ps. 18:11), we transcend all worldly things through them and strive toward better things on the day of good will.

The first month is an evident profession of religion; the second is its attainment, and is displayed in the inward disposition of virtue; the number six, as we have said, refers to humanity, for man was made on the sixth day; the number one hundred, which passes over to the right hand, pertains to contemplation. Unless we pass beyond humanity, we do not reach the subtlety of divine contemplation.

Thus from day one comes to month, and from month to year, because after the beginning of conversion we advance toward an increase of virtues; and from the gathering of these we in turn undertake to behold God, the end of all things. When it happens that we reach this, the fountains of the great abyss burst open, because the hidden recesses of human conduct are opened clearly through the gift of knowledge. A person who was previously unknown to himself, when he receives the power of discernment, finds within himself, as it were, a manifold fountain from the deepest abyss, since he learns prudently to distinguish and perceive the hidden natures of passions and human dispositions. For “deep calls to deep” (Ps. 42:8), according to the Psalm, and Scripture often uses this image to signify the human heart.

The fountain of that great abyss is therefore broken open for the person to whom knowledge of himself is opened through understanding. The floodgates—that is, the windows—of heaven are opened for the person whose intellectual eyes are sharpened to receive the light of spiritual grace. From these fountains, that is, the sources of knowledge, and from the floodgates of heaven—the luminous fissures, so to speak, of inward wisdom—rain is poured upon the earth, namely, an abundance of heavenly graces. Through these, reaching from the ten of the Law to the four of the Gospel, we regard the days of prosperity as darkness and consider the nights of adversity as light.

**VERSES 13–16.** [Col. 0096B] — On that very day Noah entered, up to the point where it says, “as God had commanded him.”

“On that very day,” that is, in the subtle guardianship of a good will tested and nourished from ancient times, Noah, the cultivator of inward tranquility, enters the conscience with the three principal virtues, together with his wife and the wives of his sons—that is, with his own desire and that of all his works to advance. For a son without a wife is one whose zeal is neither directed nor eager toward better things.

The animals, cattle, and birds have been explained both in the first treatise and in this one. “And the Lord shut him in from outside,” that is, he confines us on every side by the words of Scripture, lest, because of certain things we may perhaps have done well, we should be carried outside ourselves by the wind of some vanity. He shut him in “from outside” because he restrains us from desiring all those things that are materially subject to the eyes.

**VERSES 17, 18.** [Cols. 0096B–0096C] — The flood came upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and the waters multiplied and lifted the ark high above the earth; they increased greatly and covered everything upon the surface of the earth.

When our mind is so washed by the flowing stream of wisdom that the following is fulfilled in us:

> Drive away joys.

> [Drive away fear; let there be no grief,  
> and put hope to flight.]

As we have often said, this is signified by the forty days and nights. The waters, both lower and higher, through which we know and understand, are multiplied; and they lift the soul, advanced from knowledge of itself toward the vision of divine things, as though on two wings—namely, fear of itself and love of God—to seek eternal things, leaving all earthly concerns behind. They overflow so greatly through the practice of thought and love that whatever we say, and whatever we finally accomplish upon the surface of the earth—that is, in the realm of the senses—exhales nothing other than that life-giving sap of spiritual prudence whose love makes us fragrant.

**VERSE 19.** [Cols. 0096D–0097A] — The ark was carried upon the waters. The waters prevailed exceedingly over the earth, and all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered.

The ark is carried above the waters when the mind, relying upon wisdom as its foundation, directs its works according to its prompting as according to a rule. The waters prevail over the earth because, at the command of their inspiration, they govern and restrain the mother of works, as a disciple, and subject the conscience to themselves.

“All the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered,” because when we are permitted, even briefly, to flash within that light of lights, the God of virtues, whatever height in virtues we thought we possessed is immediately covered by the sight of such glory, like a lamp in the sun. And why speak of the vision of majesty when the text says “under the whole heaven”? The mountains beneath heaven are covered when the things beneath God, who is heaven, are considered; and in view of them whatever we are or can be appears worthless. For, to say nothing of other things, who would not find himself foul in his own eyes when contemplating even the least of the angels?

But we should note that when it says “under heaven,” it adds “the whole.” For although we may be said to possess certain likenesses of God, nevertheless the whole heaven itself so far surpasses comparison with creation that, in these very things, *super quibus* (“over which”), [f.: *quibus super*, the same meaning], we seem to bear his image, when his particular attributes are considered, we are believed not merely to possess nothing, but altogether to be nothing.

**VERSE 20.** [Col. 0097B] — The waters rose fifteen cubits above the mountains that they had covered.

Fifteen is composed of seven and eight. Let seven refer to spirituality, that is, wisdom; and eight to temporality, that is, knowledge, which is necessary for temporal affairs. Whatever subtlety, discernment, and understanding we seemed to have developed by human effort is utterly overwhelmed when God pours in the grace of contemplation. We discover that we possess neither knowledge for administering temporal matters nor wisdom for discerning heavenly things.

By fifteen cubits the water rises above the mountains: the majesty of contemplation, extended by the cubit of intention directed toward God, rises above the virtues that can be exercised in knowing and understanding. For by the arm, to which the cubit is attached, we work, and by that same arm we extend ourselves for measuring.

**VERSES 21–24.** [Cols. 0097C–0098A] — Every living creature that moved upon the earth perished: birds, animals, beasts, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth; all human beings; and everything on the earth in which there was the breath of life died. He destroyed every substance that was upon the earth, from man to cattle, both creeping things and the birds of heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth.

When God illuminates our inward parts with the rays of his vision, the flesh that moves upon the earth—that is, carnal movements, which made the stability of the earth, namely of reason, fluctuate—is consumed. So are the birds of pride, the animals of desire, the fierceness and rage of beasts, and the reptiles of lust, which secretly creep into our hearts; and human beings, that is, those things performed as though rationally for the sake of worldly respectability alone. So too are all things that try to produce within us the breath of earthly desire, and every perverse will that supports itself like a foundation for foolish thoughts and stands unworthily upon reason, which is called earth because of its firmness.

From those things that are rationally defended, so to speak, down to those that are so bestial that they cannot be defended—from lust that creeps through the mire to the rage of hypocrisy striving toward heaven—all lose their former seats, namely, our breasts as their dwelling places, through the sudden inpouring of heavenly water. This does not mean that they perish utterly, but that, when God visits us for a time, they become still.

“But Noah alone remained, and those who were with him in the ark.” The waters of the flood prevailed over the earth for one hundred and fifty days.

After these things had been extinguished, our Noah remains peaceful in a kind of blessed solitude, with his hundredfold virtues. For he has opened the latch for his beloved (Song 5:6), and he dines with him (Rev. 3:20).

The waters of the flood possess the earth when our members, which are upon the earth (Col. 3:5), or the very faculties of our senses, are ruled by wisdom. We have said that perfection is signified by the number one hundred, and rest by the number fifty. Thus the day reaches one hundred and fifty when, to someone imbued with heavenly perceptions, rest of mind—though only briefly—is granted in perfection. One hundred and fifty is also three times fifty; and we never truly rest until we come to the vision of the Trinity.[46] While we taste it somewhat in the present age, we cannot reach it without at least a passing rest of the heart.

### CHAPTER VIII

**VERSES 1, 2.** [Cols. 0098B–0098C] — God remembered Noah and all the animals and all the cattle that were with him in the ark, and he brought a wind over the earth, and the waters diminished. The fountains of the abyss and the floodgates of heaven were closed, and the rains from heaven were restrained.

When we were explaining that “it is not good for man to be alone,” we said that there is no small danger to the soul if it attains the excellence of tranquility and contemplation according to its own desire. God therefore remembers us when, in his providential ordering, he withdraws from us the grace of his gift—which would truly harm us if it remained with us for too long.

He remembers the animals and cattle when he withdraws from us, for the salutary remembrance of humility, the efficacy of the spiritual goods implanted in our soul and of the benefits that we display bodily. We call the external and, as it were, coarser works “cattle,” for cattle are customarily used to represent bodies, as in: “He shut up their cattle in death” (Ps. 78:50). But “animals,” because they are so called from the soul, signify inward goods, such as charity and the rest.

God brings a wind, namely, the movement of temptation. But when the earth—that is, the flesh—or our mind is shaken by an unexpected blast, the floodgates, that is, the subtle vision of the divine majesty, are closed as the waters of heavenly influx diminish. Through them, something had been touched of that immense heaven of which it is said, “His going forth is from the end of heaven” (Ps. 19:6). Even the fountain of the great abyss is stopped when the contemplation and knowledge of ourselves fail within us; and when the tranquility of the mind is disturbed, it can neither contain itself nor grasp the mysteries of God, since the calm trickle of the divine dew is turned aside by the assault of the passions.

**VERSE 3.** [Cols. 0098C–0099A] — The waters returned from the earth, going and returning, and began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days.

The waters return from the earth when, from a heart now occupied not with heavenly things but with earthly ones, the sources of intellectual thoughts, having been raised up, are rolled back to their former state. For just as ice, when it freezes and melts for various reasons, is nevertheless always water by nature, so our thought, although by accident it is called contemplation, is always thought.

The waters therefore return to themselves from the earth—that is, because of immersion in an earthly affection—when thoughts that had been contemplative slide back to what they ordinarily are in human beings. Having fallen back into the customary use of mortality, and continually going and returning for the worse through the attacks of temptations, they nevertheless groan more often when the taste of the sweetness and contemplation once experienced is recalled. Hence it is said to someone, “Remember from where you have fallen” (Rev. 2:5).

They begin to diminish after one hundred and fifty days because, unless either the silences of contemplation granted for an hour have passed away or the perfection of tranquility has fallen away through the assault of some trouble, temptation will not be able to find a place in which to immerse itself and diminish our prudence.

**VERSE 4.** [Cols. 0099A–0099C] — The ark rested in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia.

When, after the providential withdrawal of the waters, they return and pour into us the spirit of recollection and correction, the seventh month is observed. The memory of the divine illuminations in which we once kept Sabbath—and in which, while remembering them, we keep Sabbath for a little while—is recalled to the heart. For a month is a collection of days, and the seventh is the Sabbath.

But if the seventh month sounds something good, the twenty-seventh day of the month disturbs whatever good we had foretold. Through twenty, duplicity is expressed; through seven, again, rest; through the day, good will. Thus a good will for keeping Sabbath is available when we recall how good it is to have a secure conscience. But when we look toward the appetite of the flesh, we are immediately proved not to desire this sincerely, and indeed to desire it doubly. “The sluggard wills and does not will,” says Solomon (Prov. 13:4): he would carry out the good if it could be done without any restraint of the flesh, whereas in this very respect it is clear that he does not will it at all.

The ark rests upon the mountains of Armenia because the conscience of such sluggish people turns back to the examples of the saints, who are truly called mountains because of their excellence and steadfastness, and especially to the examples of those who attained some holiness after falling.

In another translation, “upon the mountains of Ararat” is read. *Ararat* is called Armenia in Hebrew, and the same word is interpreted as “a plucked-up mountain.” A plucked-up mountain is holiness that has been abandoned. When the mind of some religious person is tempted, the uprooted mountains come before it—namely, the falls of the saints, who nevertheless strove to return, with their strength restored, so that they might be called mountains. The ark remains among these because it delights to consider their falls and subsequent risings as possibilities that can be imitated.

**VERSE 5.** [Cols. 0099D–0100B] — But the waters continued and diminished until the tenth month.

The waters go and diminish when thoughts of spiritual prudence withdraw from us. But because we are a “passing spirit” (Ps. 78:39) that goes forth by itself, yet does not return by itself (ibid.), they fail as they tend toward the tenth month.

Although this interpretation of the tenth month is less customary, it can reasonably be understood as referring to the order of human condition.[47] The tenth order was created after the nine created orders of angels. When carnal enticements press upon the mind, a person not only admits as an example for embracing depravity those who, through Adam’s transgression and the consequent necessity of sinning, have committed some serious offense; he also considers Adam and Eve themselves, the founders of our race, who enjoyed God’s converse and suffered no incentives from their flesh. He observes how easily they fell and presents these losses as deserving excuse on account of natural weakness.

“If they,” he says, “did this or that, with what strength could I, a mere little human being, resist?” When they consider the month—that is, the number, as it were, of days—in that tenth sinner, namely Adam, they think that they may sin with excuse under such authorities, since those authorities too sinned.

For in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the summits of the mountains appeared. In that first state itself, which we have called the tenth month, on the first day—that is, at the very entrance of happiness—the summits of the mountains appeared: the proud arrogance of the founders of our race. Some customarily speak in this way: “If they sinned through pride and greed, which are not natural vices, why should we be surprised that we sin through food, drink, and bodily pleasure, which are implanted in the marrow of our being from the beginning?” Thus they observe the mountain summits when they defend themselves by appealing to the vices of those ancestors.

**VERSES 6, 7.** [Cols. 0100B–0100C] — When forty days had passed, Noah opened the window of the ark and sent out a raven. It went out and did not return until the waters had dried up upon the earth.

The forty days pass when, as the night of wickedness comes upon us, we are deprived of the understanding through which we had shone by observing the Decalogue and the Gospel. Noah then opens the window of the ark when the mind, with a most pernicious freedom, opens the windows of bodily sensuality to drink in every pleasure.

He sends out the raven when he allows the appetite to go uncontrolled toward every shameful thing. It goes out—that is, it wanders in desiring external things—and does not return until the waters dry up; that is, it never returns, if it is permitted to follow its own will, until whatever piety and grace exists within, the divine moisture in us, is completely dried up in the earth—that is, in our minds.

**VERSES 8, 9.** [Cols. 0100C–0101A] — He also sent out a dove after it, to see whether the waters had now ceased from the face of the earth. When it found no place where its foot might rest, it returned to Noah in the ark.

Although carnal affection easily slips here and there, reason nevertheless follows and weighs it with groaning. Though it is badly entangled and unable to resist, it considers by what means its affection is dragged through the rolling places of vices and how much the face of the heart has hardened, as though the earth were without rain.

But while the memory of religion still burns and the barrier of human shame resists, the dove’s foot—that is, the affection of reason—does not find within the ark of conscience an opportunity for sin, a place where it might rest. As though repentant of desire, it withdraws into itself. Hence it follows:

“For the waters were upon the whole earth. And he stretched out his hand, and took her and brought her into the ark.”

The weight of spiritual prudence ordinarily restrains the soul’s foolish movements for a considerable time. Thus the waters still hang over the earth, preventing a person, through reverence for himself, from going out toward unlawful things.

He stretches out his hand: he brings forth the strength of works and pushes into the ark—that is, into himself—reason corrected by a certain renewal of the spirit, so that it may care only for inward things. For when the mind is ashamed of its wandering on several occasions, it angrily establishes for itself a stricter plan of life. This is what is meant by his taking hold of the dove.

**VERSES 10, 11.** [Cols. 0101A–0101D] — After waiting another seven days, he again sent the dove out from the ark. At evening it came to him, carrying in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves. Noah therefore understood that the waters had ceased from the earth.

Human shame is not the extinction of sin but its postponement. For even if boldness seems to contract for a time, the intention nevertheless waits for, indeed looks beyond itself toward, opportunities for sinning.

The present age passes away through seven days, by which we can understand the flow of the mind. Seven days are awaited, namely, days of decline, and different from the forty through which conduct is instructed by both the New and the Old Testament. For times are provided for a more negligent conscience when the memory of heavenly things has grown cold, so that no fear of God may oppose the committing of crimes.

The dove, therefore—that is, reason, which truly has no gall of wickedness, if it is reason—is sent out from the ark when one passes irrationally into the affection of the heart. The first sending forth is pleasure, the second consent, and the third the accomplishment of sin. For as long as the mind wavers in thought, it beats back its evil movements by some retreat of reason, either through fear of God or through human shame, until it yields, enticed by the charms of its imaginings.

It returns, therefore, not to correct its errors, but at evening, so that it may willingly fail of the warmth and light of God, and bring back an olive branch in its mouth—that is, it promises upon the surface of thought, the mouth, but not with the desire of its intention, a pronouncement of divine mercy: that God rejoices more over penitents than over ninety-nine righteous persons (Luke 15:7).

The leaves of this branch are green because these words appear alive to the perceptions of the heart, vibrant with heavenly richness: to those who fall and return, greater grace is promised than to the righteous. God also permits some to fall in order that, through the example of many, he may make their rising more glorious.[48]

The dove therefore returns from its wandering so that, when these things have been considered, it may answer the mind and bend it toward crimes under the hope of pardon. The wretched mind therefore understands that the spiritual waters within it have dried up, yet it lends an infected ear to counsel that it does not doubt is evil.

**VERSE 12.** [Cols. 0101D–0102A] — Nevertheless he waited another seven days and sent out the dove, which did not return to him again.

We referred the preceding seven days to the mind’s decline. It is not absurd to understand these seven days once more as the time itself—that is, the opportunity of time—in which the conceived crime is carried out.

Noah awaits both this and the former event when he either, unwilling to endure his inward decline, nevertheless tolerates it and does not try to resist, or considers a suitable time for carrying out what he has desired.

But the dove, following the raven, does not return, because reason, perversely taking affection as its guide, after rushing into the deed of crime, has plunged the heart down so deeply that it will no longer return by itself to those things with which it was once willingly imbued and which it has come to love.

**VERSES 13, 14.** [Cols. 0102A–0102D] — In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters had diminished from the earth. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.

The year, which is a kind of totality of time, signifies the common conduct of worldly people. The month expresses the condition and manner of life of each person. The first day, in which the ruling concern of the world chiefly consists, signifies bodily pleasure.

When someone therefore falls from the six hundredth year—from the intention of a perfected work—into sin, he first descends into the year, that is, to the former manner of conduct and association that he previously possessed, by which it was once permitted to sin lawfully. Finally, he falls into the first month, that is, into the former manner and custom of life from which he had once departed. He reaches the day when he directs himself to doing the will of the flesh rather than that of God.

The waters diminish from the earth because the more the insolence of the flesh increases, the less a person, now made carnal, apprehends the things that belong to God. Nevertheless, the waters do not cease altogether, although they diminish, because through the impulse of the spirit they sometimes rebuke the negligence of the person who acts wickedly.

“And Noah opened the covering of the ark, and looked, and saw that the surface of the earth was dry.”

Noah opens the covering of the ark when someone reveals, through an evident work of wickedness, what evil he carries within. He looks and sees that the surface of the earth is dry when he openly displays for inspection that no divine sweetness remains—not only in his intention but even in the surface of his thought, which belongs to reason.

If the first month signifies our former manner of life in the world, let the second month be understood as the state after we have returned through apostasy to that condition: the impenitence and hardness of heart. Let seven refer to grace, twenty to the duplicity of hypocrisy, and the day to diligence.

When we have fallen into the dullness of obstinacy, and know that we are acting as enemies of God, yet deliberately pretend under the cover of hypocrisy to live according to his grace, then we should know that we have incurred a reprobate mind. When we adorn filthiness with a pious appearance, without being summoned to repentance by any shame concerning ourselves, we no longer possess either lower or upper irrigation. The earth has been completely dried up.

But if anyone is surprised that we have assigned day, month, and year to a negative interpretation, let him recognize that in Scripture day is often used for harmful knowledge or prosperity. If day can be used in this way, why should not a collection of such days—or even their total, which is a month and a year—be used likewise? Very many examples could be supplied concerning these matters.

**VERSES 15–19.** [Cols. 0103A–0103D] — God spoke to Noah, saying: “Go out from the ark, you and your wife, your sons and the wives of your sons with you. Bring out with you every living creature that is with you, of every kind of flesh, both birds and beasts and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth. Go out with them upon the earth; increase and multiply upon it.”

“He brings out the bound in strength, and those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs” (Ps. 68:7). However we may sin, his compassionate inner being always overflows with mercy. He therefore visits a fallen and already despairing heart with inward speech and urges it to return to him, as though saying:

“You who lie hidden in the consciousness of sin within yourself, come out after confession and reveal your way to me. For the things that are reproved are made manifest by those who become lights” (Eph. 5:13).

“You,” he says, “and your wife”—not the good will that accompanies those entering the ark, but desire, fertilized by the devil through what had been instilled, bore sins for you.

“You and your wife,” that is, first remove yourself from the stage of vices, and then confess the desire to which you were subjected. For many readily confess their sins, but they themselves do not depart from their evil habit.

Thus bring forth your sons, that is, your wicked works, so that you allow nothing to remain in you of the pleasure of repeating those same works. “You,” he says, “and your wife, your sons and their wives.” For as someone approaches the dawn of confession, the cloud of former desire intrudes, together with the habit of every harmful work, like some unwelcome spouse.

“Every living creature,” that is, the desires of the appetites that lie hidden within you, generated from every kind of affection, whether in the winged exaltation of worldly pride and empty religion,[49] or in the bestial savagery of anger and rage, or in lust, which, although it ought to be subject, is a creeping thing over the heart.

“Bring them out with you,” so that confession of sins may not take place without our correction, nor our correction unless confession of evils precedes it.

“And go out upon the earth,” namely, you and your pursuits, now wholly changed into righteousness. After you have stripped off your foul conscience, you must enter into the inward things that you had cast away, as is written, in your life, so that your only concern may be the inward joys. This is in order that you may now be firmly established upon the earth, taking reason as your foundation, and not be carried about by every temptation (Eph. 4:14).

“Increase” upon this foundation, rooted in contemplation, restoring in yourself the height that you lost; “and multiply” toward your neighbor through the breadth of charity.

Thus the living creatures are sent out from the ark—that is, the desires by which we are stirred toward harmful things, for the soul is naturally desirous; and the cattle, namely, the sensualities that assist the soul’s movements toward evil with a kind of goad; and the thoughts that, like serpents, creep slippery and indiscriminately through the inward parts; and the rest, as has been explained above.

**VERSES 20–22.** [Cols. 0104A–0105C] — Noah built an altar to the Lord. He took some of all the clean cattle and of all the clean birds and offered burnt offerings upon the altar. The Lord smelled the pleasing fragrance.

I see nothing more fitting for that altar than humility. For just as no victim is effective except upon an altar, so no virtue pleases God unless it is accompanied by humility.

We build humility when we proceed from the foundation of intention to the walls of thought and then to the display of the work, as though to the summit of the structure.

He did not take all the cattle, but took some from all the cattle. The cattle seem to me to signify our active works, which we exercise in brotherly love. We do not carry out all of them as we ought, but we take something from every kind of piety, because we possess the desire to fulfill all of them as commanded, if the opportunity were available.
