By the birds is expressed whatever spiritual subtlety there is in examining divine and human affairs. These are clean when the former are performed without the breath of human favor and the latter are sought without the stain of error.

Nor is it surprising that they are clean, since they are burnt offerings, cooked by the fire of sincere prayer and compunction. For in the fervor of the spirit we fully discern whether what we do is pure and right. There we set them on fire—that is, we make them worthy of approval.

Hence the Lord is said to have smelled, because the virtue of discernment and foresight comes to us from the Lord. For we distinguish odors with the nose and perceive beforehand, by smell, things that are placed before us. Thus in Terence someone is said to have “smelled out” what he had foreseen by conjecture.

Both of the virtues mentioned above are therefore understood from smelling. It is said that the Lord did this because he himself does the same within us: when, having fallen into vice through arrogance and security, we are now returning to God, we raise within ourselves the altar of humility and burn with the fire of fear whatever is hard and whatever is wrongly moist in our minds. Who could declare what discernment, prudence, and holy sweetness we draw inward from the sweetness of virtues? There we taste how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 34:8).

And he said to him: “I will never again curse the earth because of human beings, for the sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from its youth. Nor will I again strike every living creature, as I have done. For all the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day shall not cease.”

We have said that a curse is customarily used for defect, and the meaning is clear, as though he were saying: “I will never again curse; I will certainly no longer permit the earth—that is, the state of the human heart—to fail because of human beings,” namely, because of the examples of any of the saints, who are called human beings because they govern themselves rationally. Thus it is written: “He will look upon human beings and say, ‘I have sinned’” (Job 33:17).

While the ark rests upon the mountains of Ararat, the dove of suggestive wandering is sent out through the raven into an excursion of pleasure and consent to the deed. When God therefore speaks to us inwardly through inspiration, after a fall we sense, through a certain inward skill, that from the experience of ruin we can now strongly avoid a similar failure. From the fall of another—even of David or Solomon—we recognize that it is the height of madness to make another’s loss our own.[50]

There is a kind of childhood in those who have recently come to conversion. In their beginnings God keeps them from the battles of vices, just as, when the children of Israel had come out of Egypt, he did not immediately wish to impose the hardships of warfare upon them, for according to this interpretation their minds were still childish.

But when we have reached some strength of virtue and begin to be troubled by the heat of temptations, we enter the period of spiritual adolescence. Hence it is said: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2:1).

We therefore guard against failure and against the example of failure. Through the struggle with vices that attack us, we suppress the rising pattern of vice as though it were adolescence arising from virtue, while we continually perceive that the outward sense and the imagination of thoughts are inclined toward evil unless restrained by reason. And while the soul is kept suspicious through fear of its own weakness, it is never brought to such ruin that all the living creatures within it—that is, its vital pursuits—are utterly destroyed.

Throughout all the days of the earth—that is, through every understanding of our earthliness and weakness, when we attend to it carefully—seedtime, the beginnings of our conversion, and harvest, the sum of perfection, are found never to be free from the disturbance of temptations. Whether we lie idle in the cold of torpor and negligence; whether, according to Job, we go “from the waters of snow to heat” (Job 24:19), that is, to an excessive fervor of religion; whether we possess a little serenity of mind like summer; whether, blinded by the cloudy sickness of the soul, we resemble winter; whether pressed by the night of adversities or scattered abroad in the day of prosperity—in whatever condition we live, so long as the spirit governs these limbs, we cannot be without the malicious tickling of temptation. Thus we never rejoice in freedom from sin in such a way that we wish to repeat our sins.

### CHAPTER IX

**VERSES 1–3.** [Cols. 0105D–0106A] — God blessed Noah and his sons, saying: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth. Let your terror and dread be upon every animal of the earth and upon every bird of heaven, together with everything that moves upon the earth. All the fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand. Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you.”

To obtain inward tranquility for Noah—that is, for our spirit—and for his sons, namely, his works, a counsel of blessing, that is, of abundance, is given. “Increase,” he says, in hope. But lest you do this fruitlessly, “multiply” first in good works, and “fill the earth”—that is, occupy your sensuality with spiritual duties.

“Let your terror and dread be upon every animal of the earth,” that is, upon the vices that arise from animality. This does not mean that the vices themselves have substance, so that they can be terrified and tremble, but that, before the authority of the spirit, the conscience ought to be terrified by vice, even to the trembling of the body.

“And upon every bird of heaven,” that is, upon all the pride of demons, together with everything that moves shamefully and carnally within your body.

“All the fish that traverse the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8:9)—that is, every keenness of intellect capable of discerning the various cunning devices of the mind—are joined to your hand, namely, to your work, as helpers who suggest what ought to be done.

Everything that has the movement of a pious work and lives by faith is set before you for imitation.

“As green herbs I have given you everything.”

### VERSES 4, 5, 6, 7

“Except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood. For I shall require your blood, the blood of your lives, from the hand of every beast, and from the hand of man. From the hand of man and of his brother I shall require the life of man. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed. For man was made in the image of God.”

“Green plants,” that is, raw things, are not suitable for eating among us. Thus, as green plants, all the things mentioned above are handed over to us by God when they are not performed for the sake of worldly respectability or knowledge, nor dissolved by the water of human pleasure and the fire of ambition, as though cooked, but are retained solely for the greenness of inner hope.

Thus it should be understood allegorically. We do not eat flesh with its blood if we do not take the fault of any carnal person as a model for the establishment of our life. For blood is sin. You ought not, I say, to imitate perverse things, since it is established that punishment is exacted from me for the hand of all the beasts—that is, for the work of all the demons who impelled you to sin—and punishment is exacted from the man who committed those deeds. The blood of souls is their death; their death, however, is the consent of their pleasures.

From the hand of the man—that is, of the pastor, who ought to possess a manly spirit for restraining the feminine softness of his subjects—the life of man is required. Hence the bishop wears a ring, because he has a bride, so that he may not fail, either in bodily or spiritual necessities, the one whom he has presently consented to govern, as though he were to render an account with him concerning them. The life of a brother is sought from his hand if we do not extend to the man placed beside us the care that is owed to our neighbor. For if he perishes through our negligence, it is rightly demanded from us.

He sheds human blood who compels someone wavering in the conception of sin, by his persuasions, to carry it out. This happens not only by persuasion but also by providing examples. Let the seducer therefore weigh what punishment from God he owes in retribution, since he has destroyed in a human being the image of God.

Alternatively: he sheds human blood who exposes another person’s hidden vice by slander. Whoever has done either of these things should therefore know that his own blood must be shed, because whoever has either led another astray or brought someone’s crime to light suffers, by the infliction of the same thing, what he inflicted upon another—and not unjustly. For he is deserving of danger who arrogates to himself God’s judgment and dishonorably defames the dignity of the divine image, and who imposes upon that image the blemish of corruption. For man was made in the image of God.

But you, free from these pestilential evils, grow in pious works, multiply in understanding, enter into the sight of God, lest you be soothed by the favor of the crowd upon the earth; that is, be established firmly in Christ, and fill it—that is, nourish him with holy deeds, for he hungers for your salvation.

### VERSES 8, 9, 10, 11

“God also said this to Noah and to his sons with him: Behold, I shall establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living soul that is with you, both among the birds and among the cattle and all the beasts of the earth that came out of the ark, and with all the beasts of the earth. I shall establish my covenant with you, and there shall never again be destruction by the waters of the flood, nor shall there henceforth be a flood destroying the earth.”

“When,” he says, “you have applied yourselves to such duties, behold, without delay I shall establish my covenant with you. I shall bind you to myself in a particular love, and after you”—that is, after you have departed through bodily death—“I shall establish with your offspring,” namely, your good work, “a covenant of blessed perpetuity.” Hence the Psalm says: “And their children shall sit upon your throne forever” (Psalm 131:12). We have children as works, and children of children as the rewards of works.

Noah, therefore—that is, our spirit—receives the divine covenant when it more closely subjects itself to the divine will. He establishes the covenant with our works after us when, through the grace of reward, he shows that those works have pleased him in the future.

A covenant is made with every living soul, namely, with the birds, cattle, beasts, and animals, when, through their coming out of the ark—that is, through the confession of sin—they are brought to usefulness. For Lazarus is told: “Come out” (John 11:43). Those things that had been proud, greedy, lustful, and savage, when brought under the rule of modesty, become useful. For the corruption of what is good becomes vice [perhaps: “a vice”]. These things, washed through confession, again become virtue, and conceive heavenly covenants. Those covenants remain unbroken, with the memory of the former fall continually weighing down the soul, so that not all flesh may be destroyed by the water of the flood—that is, so that there may not be such an excellence of contemplation as completely to overthrow all the struggles of the flesh. Thus, while the mind is continually pressed by repeated impulses, the devout mind may always flee, humbler than itself, beneath the wings of God’s mercy.

For a flood destroying the earth is the virtue of speculation destroying in the mind the regard for humility. Lest the greatness of revelations exalt Paul, a thorn is given to him (2 Corinthians 12:7).

### VERSES 12, 13, 14, 15

“This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you, and every living soul that is with you, for everlasting generations. I shall set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign between me and the earth. When I cover the sky with clouds, my bow will appear in the clouds, and I shall remember my covenant with you and with every soul that gives life to flesh; and the waters of the flood shall never again be present to destroy all flesh.”

The bow is recognized as consisting at once of a red and a green color. The bow is Sacred Scripture, from which God makes his arrows burning (Psalm 7:14). Through the fiery color is understood fear, which torments us; through the greenness, hope, which longs for heavenly pasture. When these two, proceeding from God’s bow, continually occupy our hearts, the sign of the covenant is made in the clouds—that is, the indication of divine love in our thoughts—by which we rightly come to agreement between ourselves and God, advancing through generations of virtues that raise us to blessed eternities.

For when one fears in such a way that one does not despair, there is no place in the soul where pride or sluggishness may gather. Thus, when the sky—that is, the mind—is covered with clouds, namely, the mists of thoughts, this bow, by which hearts are wounded with charity, is introduced, appearing like the morning star shining in the darkness.

### VERSES 16, 17

“And I shall remember,” he says, “my covenant with you,” that is, “I shall make you remember the pledge by which you offered yourselves to me to serve me in return for forgiveness of your sins and the reward of eternal life.”

This covenant is also made with every soul—not with the soul borne by the flesh, but with the soul that rules carnality and carries the pallet with the paralytic. And while hope is tempered by the foresight of fear, if at some time an abundance of heavenly inspiration should be available, it will not be so great that swelling arises from it, because, by God’s dispensation, the memory of carnal deeds is in no way erased from the soul.

“There shall be a bow in the clouds,” because our heart is the place of sacred speech. “And I shall see it,” that is, through continual meditation I shall expound it so that it may be clearly seen. “And I shall remember the covenant,” that is, “I shall make them remember the spiritual sweetness by which they are attached to me”—the sweetness, I say, of the everlasting covenant, which meanwhile, while we live, binds us and God together, but in the future unites us in a special way.

This covenant is made with all flesh—that is, with humanity—which is upon the earth, that is, which rises above itself.

### VERSE 18

“Therefore the sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Moreover, Ham himself was the father of Canaan. These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole human race was spread over all the earth.”

From our spirit, faith, hope, and charity are spiritually begotten, as was explained above under the persons of the three sons. They come out of the ark when they compel us to come out of a stinking conscience through confession. Such expressions abound in Scripture, as in: “He purchased a field with the wages of iniquity” (Acts 1:18), that is, “he caused it to be purchased.”

Moreover, Ham himself is the father and author of Canaan, which is interpreted as “their movement.” For when we often consider how arduous is the execution of our purpose, and attend to the perseverance necessary for the good things begun, movement and change arise from laziness and despair—namely, movement and change of works. For when faith is exercised through the duties of charity, and hope strives to take delight in invisible goods, that hope is drawn away from contemplation of them by the allurements of visible things, which are more readily available, having been overcome by weariness of work.

Ham, therefore, is the father of Canaan, because hope, through its own weakness—not because it disbelieves in eternal goods, but because, in view of the burden of labor, it despairs of attaining them—chiefly moves and changes the pursuits of the mind. For Canaan means “changed.”

From these three, our spiritual sons, the whole human race—that is, every kind of rationality—is infused over the earth of human condition.

### VERSES 20, 21, 22

“Noah, a husbandman, began to cultivate the earth, and he planted a vineyard. Drinking wine, he became drunk and lay naked in his tent. When Ham, the father of Canaan, saw that his father’s nakedness had been exposed, he told his two brothers outside.”

Our spirit, a lover of inner rest, is a husbandman when it exerts the powers of its intelligence to seek the fruits of the field of sacred Scripture, namely, the spiritual field. It cultivates the earth when it presses upon the body through the exactions of labor. It plants a vineyard when, attending to bodily exercise in itself as useful only to a limited degree, it establishes piety—namely, spiritual goods—in the love of God, from which it pours forth the shoots of inner virtue.

It drinks wine when it tastes heavenly desire. According to Zechariah, this wine produces virgins (Zechariah 9:17). It becomes drunk when, forgetting earthly things, it stretches itself toward the contemplation of heavenly joys alone. But when it is extended toward tasting heavenly things, then, for the first time and more fully, it recognizes the misery of human mortality.

He therefore strips himself naked in the tent who considers himself stripped of the robe of impassibility and immortality even in the body itself, which in Scripture is ordinarily called a tent. According to Paul: “For while we are in this tent, we groan, being burdened” (2 Corinthians 5:4). Alternatively, he does so when, from the very taste of glory, he considers how lacking in virtue the mind is.

But when the frailty that often arises amid bodily labors and difficult things for the expiation of sins comes before the mind, and hope, made weaker by its remission in this respect, is called a brother, it presents for contemplation the nakedness of the soul—that is, of its father. By placing before faith and charity the difficulty, indeed the impossibility, of repentance in view of these naked things, namely, sins, faith and charity whose reasoning sometimes wanders outside us, it announces this as though to two brothers placed outside. And, as if mocking the father who has formed the purpose, it compels them to desist from that purpose by means of sluggishness.

### VERSE 23

“But Shem and Japheth took a cloak, placed it upon their shoulders, and, walking backward, covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s nakedness.”

Shem and Japheth place a cloak upon their shoulders when faith and charity, reviving through their own reasoning, do not wholly reject the excess of shame—which is the mother of despair—but place it behind the mind. Hence it is said: “Walking backward,” because, although they reject shame insofar as it is excessive, they nevertheless walk backward through the memory of their former life.

The shame of sin must not be abolished but moderated. Their faces are turned away when, having been tested by despair, the intellectual eyes are directed toward what lies ahead—namely, the hope of eternal things promised to the penitent.

They therefore cover their father’s nakedness, which is not to be viewed with indiscriminate shame, when faith and charity, having already taken hope to themselves and using their own powers, cover it with fruits worthy of repentance.

It should be noted, however, that the father of Canaan is here called simply Ham, when he suggests the guilt of a perverse movement.

### VERSES 24, 25, 26, 27

“When Noah awoke from his wine, and learned what his younger son had done, he said: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of servants to his brothers. Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem; let Canaan be his servant.”

Noah awakens from wine—that is, from the gift of grace—when the mind, having discovered the deceit of the suggestion, rouses itself to resist its temptations.

The younger son is rightly called younger because faith slips only with difficulty in some matter. Faith, however, very quickly freezes through excuses based on impossibility, and through it charity likewise grows cold unless reason is present. I say that it freezes, for this is the evangelical egg, which is warmed by the maternal heat of charity. Hence Ham is also called “hot,” and the scorpion’s poison opposes him.

We have already often said that “cursed” is customarily used to indicate defect. Let Canaan therefore fail—that is, let the movement of instability cease. The servants of the brothers are reason, will, and affection, which obey faith, hope, and charity, or whatever good works are done inwardly or outwardly.

One who had been enlisted as a supplementary soldier alongside these troops said: “I say to this one, ‘Go to perform an actual duty,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come to the study of spirituality,’ and he comes; and to the servant”—that is, to wandering affection—“‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matthew 8:9).

This demonstrative word, “this,” is customarily said of a present thing. Do this, therefore—that is, do those things by which you are present to yourself, that is, to your soul. And because “this” is a demonstrative pronoun, he says: do those things that reason shows you must do—not outside yourself, but within yourself.

If these are servants, who will be more worthily their servant than Canaan—that is, mutability and movement—so that it may neither command nor resist in anything, but serve the virtues unto the crown?

### VERSE 26

“Blessed be the God of Shem.” In faith, which is understood through Shem, let God’s blessing—that is, the increase of divine knowledge—shine forth, and let the movement of perverse mutability be subjected to it.

### VERSE 27

“May God enlarge Japheth.” That is, if charity reaches friends, may it spread, through God’s enlargement, even to enemies themselves.

The tents of soldiers and travelers properly belong to those who fight and journey. But since faith is meanwhile the substance of things hoped for, when we arrive at those things it will entirely cease. Shem therefore fights and journeys—faith, namely, in the present. But its warfare is judged useless if it is deprived of the companionship of charity.

If, therefore, we do not wish faith to die, let Japheth dwell in the tents of Shem. Let us adorn belief with the work of love, and let the movement of hope, which must never be shaken, be subject to us.

### VERSE 29

“Noah lived after the flood three hundred and fifty years. All the days of his life were nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.”

Through years is expressed holy conduct, which is composed from the collection of virtues, as from the collection of days. Through three hundred is understood the perfection of faith, hope, and charity, of which we have just spoken. Through fifty is understood rest, in which, through the exercise of these virtues, one ceases from wicked pursuits as though in a jubilee of remission.

Yet everything we do, however brightly we may shine with the light of religion, is done imperfectly by us. This is understood through the nine hundred years, which lack one ten, because “in your sight no living person shall be justified” (Psalm 142:2), even if he appears justified by human judgment.

Perhaps this is why some author—I do not know who—repeats nine times in the offertory verse: “that I may see good things,” seeking that ten, the supreme good, perfect goodness, which is given to those laboring in the vineyard. This is also understood here through the fifty, no longer as temporal duration but as eternal rest.

“And he died,” insofar as concerns the vices of this world.

### THE THIRD BOOK ENDS

### THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE MORALS ON GENESIS BEGINS

[Col. 0111]

## CHAPTER XII

### VERSE 1

“The Lord said to Abram: Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you. I shall bless you and magnify your name.”

To the exalted father—Abram is interpreted as “exalted father”—that is, to the spirit that will govern the mind with paternal authority and raise it from earthly baseness, God suggests these things through an inspiriting word:

“Go out from your land,” that is, shake off your earthliness; or, you who are submerged in sin within yourself, come out by confessing from your sinful conscience. And go out “from your kindred,” from the imagination, thoughts, and carnal pleasures that arise from that same earth.

“And from your father’s house,” namely, from that outward conduct in the world which our former father, the devil, possessed, presiding over his court like a strong armed man. For the mobility of the inner person cannot be restrained unless one flees outside the world’s companionship.

“Come, therefore, into the land that I shall show you,” namely, into that solidity of body and mind that I shall reveal to you either through inner suggestion or through reading Sacred Scripture. “And I shall make you into a great nation”: I shall equip you with a multitude of virtues. There you will be blessed with an abundance of spiritual grace and magnified in name—that is, in eminent reputation—to the praise of the heavenly Father.

### VERSE 3

“I shall bless those who bless you.” I shall certainly multiply those who assist your growth by preaching and by providing examples. “And the kindreds of the earth”—not of that earth from which you are commanded to go out, but of those spiritual offspring of the heart that are intellectually revealed to you by me—“shall be blessed in you,” not merely by popular reputation, but in the truth of your inner disposition and work.

This kindred is a gradation formed by a certain chain of virtues proceeding from one another.

“I shall curse those who curse you,” he says. Those vices of your flesh that inflict the injury of defect upon you I shall reduce to defect.

### VERSE 4

“Abram therefore went out, as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him.”

With Abram going out, as has been explained, Lot goes with him, because it is right that carnal affection, which often declines from what is right within us, bound by the habit of natural vice, should follow the authority of reason. For Lot is interpreted as “declining” or “bound.”

“Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran.”

Haran is interpreted as “a thing with an ark.” Through the ark is signified the capacity of desire; through the thing are represented those things that can be desired. Some people, when they are converted, renounce possessions, but do not renounce the desire to possess—that is, the ark. Whoever rejects desire and whatever can be desired goes out from Haran.

He is seventy-five years old when he goes out, when, through the sevenfold grace fulfilling the Decalogue of the Law, he presides over the five bodily senses with the integrity of virtues, as though through a collection of years.

### VERSE 5

“Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot the son of his brother, and all the substance that they possessed, and the souls that they had made in Haran. And they went out to go into the land of Canaan.”

Sarai means “my princess” and signifies the will. United in the manner of a wife to Abram—that is, to the husband, the spirit—and to Lot, the son of his brother, namely, to affection, which is born from bodily seed, with which the soul possesses a certain natural kinship, she is led in proper order when these things have thus been established.

With these, our Abram takes all the substance that they jointly possessed, when we have in our power everything that rightly serves our understanding as earthly things. We do not allow ourselves to be servilely ruled by them; rather, we rule them as a paralytic rules his pallet (John 5:9).

Hence Job says: “For their good is not in their hand; let the counsel of the wicked be far from me” (Job 21:16). For whatever reason possesses by condemning it will immediately be subject to the command of both will and affection.

Souls are made in Haran when vital and spiritual goods are performed through a complete renunciation of the world. They go out toward the land of Canaan when they attain the solid transformation of conduct that they have professed. For Canaan means “changed.”

### VERSE 6

“When they had come into it, Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem and as far as the illustrious valley.”

When we attain the efficacy of conversion, our spirit passes through the burden of an earthly dwelling, which weighs it down, and comes to the place of Shechem—that is, to the stability of persevering obedience. Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder,” and we also carry with the shoulder. Thus we rightly understand obedience, under whose command we are humbly bent as we bear it.

We call the place the immobility of the soul. But if we obey, we must come to the illustrious valley—that is, to the nobility of humility—so that we may offer willing service not only to superiors but also to inferiors, seeking to serve spontaneously.

### VERSE 7

“Now the Canaanite was then in the land. And the Lord appeared to Abram and said to him: To your offspring I shall give this land. And he built there an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him.”

The more illustrious we are in relation to God and the world, the more humble we ought to be. But the Canaanite is in the land because the spirit of vainglory and the type of foolish shame rage in earthly affection.

Canaanite is interpreted as “merchant,” which signifies the commerce of empty glory. This inserts itself especially into good works, since a person may even become proud through his very humility.

Canaanite is also said to mean “one who is ashamed,” namely, human shame, which strikes the mind with regard to more humble commands.

These were then in the land when they were seething beneath the conscience in our innermost good qualities. The Lord therefore appears to Abram when he teaches reason through evident illumination that, although it is exalted, it nevertheless regards humble things, and strengthens with the hope of victory one who distrusts his own strength in resisting such things.

He says: “To your offspring”—that is, to the merit of your work—“if you persevere, I shall subject the movement of earthly affection that you acknowledge.”

We build an altar there when, together with the appearance of overcoming this, we also construct hope—not in empty praise but in heavenly reward—adding it as the material of the remaining virtues. For none of our good is good if it is not founded upon divine hope, just as there is no sacrifice without an altar.

### VERSE 8

“From there he moved on to the mountain that was opposite Bethel, and he stretched out his tent, with Bethel on the west and Hai on the east.”

Bethel means “house of God.” We advance from the place of the altar to the mountain when we do not despair merely of victory over vices, but also desire excellence in every virtue.

This mountain is situated toward the east of the house of God because whatever virtue we possess longs for conformity to Christ and desires to be illumined by the vision of Christ, here and in the future. He is the true East of the house of God—that is, the minister of light to the minds of the faithful, in whom God dwells.

We stretch out our tent there when we advance the desire of the spirit toward serving God.

We have Bethel on the west when we oppose to our defect, which sometimes creeps in, or even to our despair, the heavenly beauty of the house of God or the purity of past action.

We have Hai on the east—or Gai, according to another translation—when, amid the luxuriant success of virtues, as though from an excessive glory of light, we introduce into the mind consideration of the confusion of hell or of whatever sins have been or may be within us. For Hai means “question,” and Gai means “confusion.”

The whole meaning is: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils, and in the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclesiastes 11:27).

Here also Abram builds an altar when, watchful amid victories, our spirit is already firmly rooted in charity, after the course of hope, so that God may be invoked in the lodging of his mind.

“For these are your altars, Lord of hosts, in which the turtledove found a nest and the sparrow a house” (Psalm 83:4). Hence it follows:

### VERSE 9

“Abram journeyed onward, going and advancing farther toward the south.”

We go toward the south when we strive to attain the complete fervor of devotion. We go when we exercise the purpose of the mind in work. We advance farther when we burn with the scope of pious desire to undertake greater things than our frailty allows us to accomplish.

### VERSE 10

“There was a famine in the land. Abram descended into Egypt to sojourn there.”

After such an abundance of grace, temptation must follow, lest an excess of glory descend into pride. Thus famine occurs in the land when there is a lack of divine taste in the mind.

He descends into Egypt when our spirit humbly contemplates the harm of tribulation constricting it. For Egypt is interpreted as “constricting tribulation.”

He sojourns there when, in the heat of temptation—which, according to the Apostle, occurs for testing (1 Peter 4:12)—the mind, temporarily estranged from itself, wanders. And not unjustly: famine had prevailed in the land, that is, the poverty of divine counsel ruled in the conscience.

### VERSES 11, 12, 13

“When he was near entering Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: I know that you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife,’ and they will kill me but preserve you. Say, therefore, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me on your account and my soul may live because of you.”

After we have reached the darkness of the mind—for Egypt, which is said to mean “darkness,” has that meaning—amid the very uncertainty of temptation we say to Sarai, namely, to our will, which has not yet been separated from the command of its husband, reason:

“It is certain that you desire good things, and that you do not lack the appearance of goodness, as though possessing a certain beauty of character, although you cannot carry it out in action. But if the Egyptians—that is, the carnal impulses that darken you—direct the edge of their attack against you because you will things contrary to them, they will judge you to be my wife, led by love of me, your reason. They will press upon me, the spirit, more fiercely, overwhelm me with temptations, and seize you for themselves, so that you will now desire nothing but carnal things.

“I am therefore unable to resist the assaults of so many evils. Let me yield. Thus I beg you to say that you are my sister—that is, that you think the same as I do—so that, with the authority of the husband overwhelmed, carnal will and reason may think alike. Thus it may go well with me with regard to the storms of the mind, which I shall escape by consenting to the suggestion, and my soul may live—that is, my life may experience how much sweetness there is in serving the world according to the pleasure of its own will.”

### VERSES 14, 15

“When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was exceedingly beautiful. And they reported her to Pharaoh, praised her before him, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.”

We enter Egypt when, having lost the light of good intention, we fall into the darkness of the mind.

The Egyptians see that the woman is beautiful when bodily impulses—which sometimes arise naturally and spontaneously even without thought—envy the beauty of pious will and press upon it by their solicitation. For although we often go astray, nevertheless we are altogether grieved that we go astray, because, according to the Apostle: “The evil that we do not wish, that we do” (Romans 7:19).

The princes report to Pharaoh when our external senses, to whom it is said, “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Psalm 23:7), complain to our carnal affection about the remnant of pious desire and make it known.

Pharaoh rightly signifies carnal affection. His name is interpreted as “dissipating” or “uncovering,” for he destroys the spirit inwardly and strips it of the garment of virtues.

They praise her when, by flattering suggestion, they proclaim the intelligence and bodily disposition as suitable for pursuing the advantages of the world.

The woman is transferred into Pharaoh’s house when a soft and enervated will is brought into a lasting association with carnal affection. For by “house” is understood the duration of a dwelling.

### VERSE 16

“Abram was treated well on her account, and he had sheep, cattle, asses, servants, maidservants, female asses, and camels.”

Sheep signify foolishness; cattle, the weightiness of wickedness; asses, wantonness; servants, arrogance; maidservants, a conscience easily led astray and timid only before human eyes; female asses, thought made fruitful by continual pollution; and camels, a perverse and distorted desire inclined toward every movement of perversity. For “camel” is named from a Greek derivation referring to curvature.

Pharaoh uses Abram well outwardly, not inwardly, when reason is softened by affection for a corrupt will—not by true goods, but by imaginary, that is, temporal goods.

### VERSES 17, 18, 19

“But the Lord struck Pharaoh and his house with very great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife. Pharaoh called Abram and said to him: What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Now, then, behold your wife; take her and go.”

The Lord strikes Pharaoh when God sometimes terrifies affection, numb from the effect of its desires, by consideration of present and future evils.

He strikes his house when, through fear of temporal punishment or eternal judgment, he destroys the desire to persevere in the evil he had planned. This happens because of Abram’s wife, Sarai—that is, until the will is restored to reason as to its proper husband.

Pharaoh calls Abram when affection, now humbled, applies itself to reason.

“Why,” he says, “O intellectual judgment, did you not restrain the wantonness of the will, which was rightly subject to you, and allow it to be so lightly drawn away from you through the deception of my foolish affection?”

When all the assaults of my irritation have been calmed, “take her”—that is, restrain her from now on with strong continence, joined to you—but afterward go as quickly as possible: that is, strive to advance toward better things. “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27).

### VERSE 20; CHAPTER 13, VERSE 1

“Pharaoh commanded his men concerning Abram, and they led him away, with his wife and all that he had.”

“And Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, toward the southern region.”

Pharaoh commands his men concerning Abram when carnal desire, pierced by fear of God, joins the authority of its own assistance to the manly senses of reason.

They lead him away, together with his wife and all that he has, when the mind displays all its powers for expediting understanding, for joining the will to understanding, and for preserving the remaining goodness of the soul.

Abram ascends with his wife and Lot from Egypt when our spirit departs from the desire of this world, and, with its will and affection corrected from their former deviation, proceeds toward the southern region—that is, toward the fervor of spiritual life.

“Rise up, O north wind, and come, O south wind” (Song of Songs 4:16).

### VERSE 2

“He was very rich in possession of silver and gold.”

After we rise from the sluggishness of sin to the disciplines of more ardent devotion, we are enriched with the silver of knowledge. For we understand the discernment of spirits, the natures of vices, and the various conditions of human conduct more deeply because, having once suffered these things, we now rejoice that, with God’s help, we have escaped them.

We are enriched with the gold of wisdom when we are already satisfied with the contemplation of God and are illumined by the understanding of virtues or of any mysteries.

Wisdom may also be understood as referring to excellence in religion, while knowledge may be understood according to the discernment taught by ecclesiastical instruction.

### VERSES 3, 4

“He returned by the way by which he had come, from the south to Bethel, as far as the place where he had first pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai, at the place of the altar that he had previously made; and there he invoked the name of the Lord.”

We come from the south to Bethel when, from the warmth of faith that is active in good works, we reach the beauty of the house of God, which is Bethel, in order to love and seek it.

The house of God may mean either our mind or that house in which there are said to be many dwellings (John 14:2).

Moreover, we return from Egypt by the same way by which we came when, through the same exercises of virtue by which we declined into guilt, we return to grace—namely, as far as the place where we had pitched our tent: the stability of sincere humility, which is the dwelling place of holy minds in the present, just as pride is the dwelling place of perverse minds.

There we promised that we would conduct spiritual warfare while the spirit governs these limbs.

At the place of the altar that we previously made between Bethel and Hai—that is, in the faith of Christ—we do everything, and in it, as in a foundation, we have firmly placed the hope of our rewards for good things, without which we do not offer sacrifice, as though without an altar.

On one side we rejoice through contemplation of Bethel—that is, the heavenly house of God. On the other, we moderate our joys through contemplation of Hai—that is, Tartarean confusion. Thus we invoke for ourselves the name of the Lord, which is Jesus, that is, Savior.

### Verses 5–7

“But Lot, who was with Abram, had flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and tents. The land could not contain them, so that they might dwell together. For their possessions were many, and they could not live together. Hence strife arose between the herdsmen of Abram’s flocks and those of Lot.”

Lot—that is, our affection—so long as it clings to reason, represented by Abram, has flocks of sheep: namely, a multitude of simple thoughts directed toward oneself and beneficial thoughts directed toward others. Sheep bear fleeces not only for themselves but also for others. There are herds of cattle as well, namely, strong works of virtue. Finally, there are tents, since, knowing that here we have no abiding city (Heb. 13:14), he considers himself to be living in this world as though in the military service of a camp. Tents, after all, belong to soldiers or to travelers.

Yet the land cannot contain them so that they may dwell together, because earthly-mindedness, which weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), does not allow the carnal appetite to consent immovably and indivisibly to intellectual understanding, so long as we live in this flesh: “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). For the substance—that is, the discord of the lowest movements that cling to the mind—does not permit body and spirit always to share a common desire in what pleases God. Hence unceasing strife arises between the herdsmen of the two flocks, while rational thought desires to be fed either on the pursuits of virtue or on the sayings of sacred Scripture, whereas the carnal element is fattened on temporal glory. Bodily tears and every kind of frivolous amusement feed rational movements: “My tears have been my bread” (Ps. 41:4).

### Verses 8–9

“At that time the Canaanite and the Perizzite were dwelling in that land. Therefore Abram said to Lot: ‘I ask you, let there be no quarrel between me and you, nor between my herdsmen and yours; for we are brothers. Behold, the whole land is before you. If you go to the left, I will hold to the right; if you choose the right, I will go to the left.’”

At the time when the quarrels of the herdsmen within us—that is, of the heavenly and earthly elements—are being waged, the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwell in our earthly affection. Canaanite is interpreted as “he has returned”; Perizzite as “surpassing,” or “scattered.” For when our appetite, after a momentary peace, returns as if to its accustomed battles, the seeds of thoughts and pleasures are scattered over the soul, by which it is often overcome.

Let Abram therefore speak to Lot: “Do not,” he says, “strive to exercise and admonish reason against affection in matters opposed to honesty, since, proceeding from one mind, a kindred bond of nature in some way binds us to one another. When there is such unity of nature, what madness is it to envy one another or to set traps for one another’s ruin?”

“Behold, the whole land is before you”—that is, the appetite for every kind of earthly-mindedness lies open. If you proceed leftward along the slopes of crimes, know that I, representing virtue—which is the right hand, as the saying goes—will defend myself with beak and claws. But if, in the very guardianship of the right hand, namely of virtue, you choose to attack me through an assault of arrogance, I, proceeding leftward by the contemplation of sins once committed by me, will blow back the swelling thoughts I have conceived with the goad of discernment.

### Verse 10

“Lot, lifting up his eyes, saw the whole region around the Jordan, which was everywhere watered, before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, like the paradise of the Lord and like Egypt as one approaches Segor.”

Lot raises his eyes when the carnal appetite grows proud through its eager contemplation of worldly things. He sees not the Jordan—that is, their descent, namely the descent of the wicked, by which through love of visible things they slide into invisible destruction—but the whole region around it, that is, the entire setting of sin, namely the pleasure of this world. The descent itself is sin; the region around the descent is temporal glory.

This whole region is watered like God’s paradise, because deceitful desire of the mind fabricates for itself the belief that, in using transitory goods without incurring any crime, it possesses the grace of moral goodness, and that the mind and its use ought lawfully to be directed toward those things which, because of their excessive beauty, are like a kind of paradise planted by God’s hand. This confidence in one’s own goodness is that fountain which, at the beginning of this book, is said to have watered the whole surface of the earth.

We water the region, therefore, as though it were God’s paradise, because we promise that we can possess the world religiously and chastely, since it was so beautifully planted by the word of God. But the paradise that we falsely boast of becomes, in the course of time, Egypt—that is, darkness and hardening of the heart—not, however, for anyone except those who are coming into Segor, that is, who through the soul’s downward flow are slipping into wantonness. Segor is said to mean “heifer” or “southern.” By these meanings are understood the mind’s perverse heat and wantonness. While we trust in a good that does not exist, we fall into the real evils that are within us.

### Verses 11–13

“Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan and departed from the east; and they separated from one another, brother from brother. Abram, however, dwelt in the land of Canaan. Lot lived in the towns that were near the Jordan, and he dwelt in Sodom. Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked before the Lord.”

All these foolish presumptions of the mind that we have just outlined arise before God overturns Gomorrah in us—that is, the sedition of the people, which is nothing other than the turbulence of vices—and Sodom, namely the blindness arising from vices. Once both have been overthrown, all the things of the world immediately become displeasing to us.

Lot departs from the east when, after the quiet of a brief peace—which at the beginning of our conversion we sometimes experience—our affection, while God mercifully permits battles to rise up against us, recoils from the light of reason to which it had previously consented. He chooses the region of the Jordan because, through the continual movements of his desires, he looks toward the glory from which he is to be deprived. They are divided from one another because the flesh always seeks what is contrary to the spirit.

Abram dwells in the land of Canaan when reason, in agreement with God, always desires the change of conduct that it has professed. Canaan is interpreted as “changed.” Lot lives in the towns around the Jordan because, while he trusts in the virtue of his own moral goodness, the semblance of his purpose gradually flows away, as though from certain clay towns, and he comes to dwell in Sodom—that is, to conform himself to secular life.

Sodom is plainly said to mean “their likeness,” namely, the likeness of evil things. Its inhabitants are “exceedingly wicked before the Lord,” that is, their disposition dwells in the inner person, although in the eyes of human beings their conduct may be judged to possess some degree of uprightness.

### Verse 14

“And the Lord said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him: ‘Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and toward the south, toward the east and toward the west. All the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed forever, and I will make your seed like the dust of the earth.’”

To our spirit, which resists the allurements of vice, God’s inward address grants the hope of deserving better things. “Lift up your eyes,” he says: remove the attentiveness of your thoughts from the lower desires of visible things. “And look from the place”—that is, from the condition of mind in which you now act—toward the north of temptations, which make the mind sluggish; toward the south of spiritual grace, which produces in us, through worthy works, the warmth of faith; toward the east of divine contemplation, which brings the rays of subtle understanding into the recesses of your mind; and toward the west of active administration, which, as the east receives the rising sun, so receives its setting—that is, the end and perfection of charity, which begins from divine love and is exercised in kindness toward human beings.

Once you have gained possession of the north, you will immediately possess the three regions that follow, and likewise the whole land—that is, the earthly-mindedness of which you remain suspicious, lest you fall into it. “I will give it to you”—or rather, to your seed. That is: when I subject vices to you, do not attribute this privilege to your nature, but to my grace and to the merit of the good action that you have attained through my grace. This is “your seed.” For good works are our seeds, as it is written: “The seed of his servants shall possess it” (Ps. 68:37).

### Verses 16–17

“And I will make your seed like the dust of the earth.”

Although dust comes from the earth, it is lifted from the earth without damage to the earth. So our good works, though movable in every wind of temptation, neither injure nor benefit Christ, who is our earth, from whom we are fed and sustained, and to whom we cling or from whom we fall away.

He therefore makes this seed like dust when he shows us the lightness of all our good unless it is moistened with spiritual moisture. And because we are commanded to labor not for the sake of the works themselves but for our own sake, we are instructed according to the Gospel to say, when we have done good: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10).

Someone may count this seed, even though it is dust, but cannot count it completely. For although he fully measures the instability that it suffers, he does not at all know whether, because of those same works, he is considered worthy before God of hatred or love (Eccl. 11:1), since he does not know at what value God weighs them.

Rise, therefore, from every form of idleness. Survey the land of your conscience and your body, and traverse it by bringing it low, according to the length of perseverance and the breadth of charity. Thus, with God’s gift, what was once the domain of vice will become wholly ours, here and in the future.

### Verse 18

“Therefore Abram moved his tent and came and dwelt in the valley of Mambre, which is in Hebron; and there he built an altar to the Lord.”

He moves his tent when our spirit, stationed in battle array against vices, advances toward the exercise of the military service appointed by God. He then dwells in the valley of Mambre—that is, he lowers himself into the lowliness of humility, through which he may flourish anew in clarity of understanding and in the discernment of good and evil things.

Mambre signifies “divisions” and “clarity.” Not without reason: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), and “the spirit rests upon the humble and quiet” (Isa. 66:2).

This valley of divisions is in Hebron, which is said to mean “participation in sorrow” or “eternal increase.” None of the things we have mentioned can be obtained except through rejection of every earthly joy and desire for eternal increase in the seeking of the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

Hebron is also said to mean “eternal vision.” By this is understood divine contemplation, which begins here but will be perfected in the future. There the altar of our mind will be firmly established, filled with spiritual victims; and all the parts of the sacred arts will come together like a building and extend upward to the understanding of divinity.

## Chapter XIV

### Verses 1–3

“It came to pass at that time that Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Pontus, Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, and Tidal, king of the nations, waged war against Bera, king of Sodom, and against Birsha, king of Gomorrah, and against Shinab, king of Admah, and Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and against the king of Bela, which is Segor. All these assembled in the wooded valley, which is now the Salt Sea.”

Through these four who waged war against five kings, we understand four principal evils: pleasure, consent, action, and habit. These struggle with great force against the external appetite, which is rightly signified by the number five. This happens at the time when Lot has turned aside to the towns of Sodom.

By the number five, I say, those things that are close to sensuality are represented. For our appetite, having naturally been made desirous of good things, seeks corruptibly what is external while neglecting what is inward. By the kings mentioned above it is compelled from the practice of repairing necessity to the fulfillment of the excessive pleasure of lust.

Five also consists of four and one, as though with a superior ruler represented by the one. Hence our affection ought to place above temporal glory—which is represented by four—the authority of its principal majesty.

The first, therefore, is Amraphel, whose name is interpreted as “he said that he might fall.” This chiefly pertains to pleasure, as to a deliberation about falling.

The second is Arioch, who is called “drunk” or “bringing into solitude.” In him is understood the madness of consent, deprived of counsel, which, having rejected the worship of God, leaves the human being to himself alone.

The third is Chedorlaomer, whose very name seems to signify “a beautiful sheaf.” A sheaf is the fruit of work, while the fruit of evil work is the very sweetness of pleasures. It is therefore not truly a beautiful sheaf, but something apparently beautiful, because in such actions there is not genuine beauty but a deceptive and imaginary sweetness.

The fourth is the king of the nations, because a reprobate mind arises from the habit of crimes. Just as a king gathers an army, so that mind gathers for itself an assembly of every kind of wickedness, like a host of many nations.

These kings begin war against our carnal affection, as though they were applying wind to flames and drawing it under their own authority.

The first movement of our defection is therefore, as it were, a king who does not rule but crushes, and it is in Sodom. Sodom is said to mean “mute.” Our mind is mute when it gives no response worthy of reason to the mockeries of pleasure.

Gomorrah means “sedition of the people.” By it is signified the tumultuous lack of restraint of wicked thoughts within the city of the mind.

Admah is interpreted as “bloodshed.” In Latin usage blood is called *cruor* when it is seen to flow from the body. Thus bloodshed signifies sins that proceed from inward sedition into evil action.

Zeboiim means “goat,” or “doe,” or “its station in the sea.” By this is understood our affection itself. When it has been mute as Sodom, seditious as Gomorrah, and finally transgressive as Admah, it is raised upward by empty hope like a goat, which desires steep places; then, after the manner of a doe, a timid animal that fears losing what it possesses, it descends through fear to the lower regions. Thus its station becomes in the sea, since it never ceases to fluctuate from a proper state of mind under the unending impulse of its movements.

Then follows Bela, which is interpreted as “he swallowed” or “he cast down.” For when the soul has been cast down by these miseries to the abandonment of life, it is swallowed up in a certain abyss of forgetfulness, so that it scarcely wishes any longer to remember amid what sea of storms it has been placed.

All these are kings because the movements of the flesh gather hosts of thoughts to themselves. Four kings rise against five when the aforesaid defections of the mind either bring about other relaxations and wickednesses in our affection, or intensify and inflame those same ones.

Hence it follows: “All these assembled in the wooded valley,” that is, every host of negligence came together in a mind that was humble but had been cast down from the excellence of holiness and covered with the forest-like horror of sin, manifold darkness, and carelessness.

From this comes the Salt Sea—that is, from this there arises in the soul a rejection of God’s wisdom, namely, the wisdom of the flesh. Salt, since it is here said of the sea, signifies cunning. The sea can appropriately signify both the world and the flesh, which always seethes with desires. The wisdom of the flesh, which the Apostle calls death (Rom. 8:6), glories only in exercising and pursuing pleasures.

### Verse 4

“They served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they withdrew from him.”

Through Chedorlaomer, whom we said is called something like “a beautiful sheaf,” we understand pleasure, which is the fruit of all wickedness and, as it were, its beauty. Three multiplied by four makes twelve. We serve him for twelve years when we subject the trinity of the mind—namely, reason, will, and memory—to pleasure, which holds precedence in the kingdoms of vices, as though under the quaternary of this temporal existence.

We also serve him for twelve years when we subject the trinity of the mind, as we have said, and the bodily dimension to the same pleasure in a certain annual perfection. But we withdraw from him in the thirteenth year when we establish God, who is unity, as our ruler and governor in body and soul.

### Verses 5–7

“In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, together with the kings who were with him, and they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, and the Zuzim with them, the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in the mountains of Seir, as far as the plains of Paran, which is in the wilderness. They struck the whole region of the Amalekites and the Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar. Then they returned to the spring of Mishpat, which is Kadesh.”

After Abram fixes his tent in the valley of Mambre, we had rejected pleasure, the most wicked king. It surpasses the other kings because nothing rules over human hearts more tenaciously than pleasure.

But when the state of the mind again grows lukewarm, as often happens, and subjects the denarius of divine law to the quaternary of temporality, the memory of pleasure, equipped with the support of former pleasure, consent, and habit, strikes the Rephaim at Ashteroth.

That is, through its defenseless tenderness, by which it resists no movements, it arouses and stirs up giants—the meaning of Rephaim—to test the mind that is about to fall. Ashteroth is said to mean “they make explorers.”

This striking is not a killing but an agitation of the soul that is secure and excessively confident in itself. Vessels are commonly struck so that flies or bees quietly settled within them may be stirred up; hence Peter’s side is said to have been struck in prison.

After the testing of the weak mind, which grows warm toward vices at every recollection, it is struck—that is, moved—by Carnaim, which means “horns.” By these is signified confidence in resisting the suggestion of memory. Some people confidently take pleasure in their thoughts, relying on their own strength and thinking that they can resist evil action.

The horns are therefore struck when deceptive resistance is allowed to achieve the poison of pleasure sweetly drawn into the act of crime. Animals defend themselves with horns. But the Zuzim—also called Zomzommim elsewhere—are aroused together with them.

Since our nature is vicious, it carries within itself the seeds of vices, yet does not know that it suffers from them until the force of temptation awakens them. *Zomzommim* is the complete form of the word, whereas *Zuzim* is formed by abbreviation. *Zomzommim* is interpreted as “What is this water?” or “those prepared for battle.”

For when the mind deceitfully raises its horns—that is, its strength to resist evil actions—and lightly carries off the softness of its first pleasure, suddenly, as the winds of thoughts and bodily movements gather, it melts like a certain hardness of ice when fire is applied. Then, having fallen back from that great strength, it is forced to say within itself: “What is this water? Where have so many desires, so fluid and unexpected, come from?” For although it had thought that it possessed its own movements under its own authority, it suddenly perceives them arrayed in battle against it.

The Emim are also stirred up at Shaveh, when the captive mind begins to propose not only dreadful things but also natural evils. Shaveh is interpreted as “captive” or “thorns.” The thorns signify the multitude of carnal desires that wound us.

In more carefully corrected texts it is not *Sabe* but *Save*, or even *Savhe*, which is rightly interpreted as “elevation,” signifying that the soul deservedly suffers these assaults because of its arrogance. Horrible wickedness is stirred up not only among the thorns—that is, bodily movements—but also at Kiriathaim, which means “city of forests.” By this is signified a mind that is uncultivated and besieged by wickedness.

The Horites are also aroused in the mountains of Seir by this struggle, because the external senses, which the Horites signify, are gloriously lifted up to the heights of pride by the excesses of the lusts they have committed. The Horites are interpreted as “from the holes,” and our body is permeated by the touch of external things through its senses, as through openings or holes.

Seir is said to mean “he-goat,” in which the stench of lust is understood. The same kings proceed as far as the plains of Paran, which is in the wilderness, because the madness of their swelling pride, by which they glory in their evil deeds, is thrown back beneath the renewed ferocity of every kind of crime and is scattered in the manner of a plain. Whatever had remained in the mind of divine memory returns to the horror of the wilderness.

Everyone who lives without God as an inhabitant is plainly in the wilderness. Paran is interpreted as “their ferocity,” unquestionably the ferocity of vices, which drives the defenses of minds into the weakness of a plain.

They return to the spring of Mishpat, which means contemplation. From it we draw the dew of all divine and human reason. Our spring, to which we return and from which we water our sensuality, which is failing toward carnal things, as though it were a withering field, is reason. Mishpat signifies contemplation or judgment. Reason judges all things because it is spirit, and it is judged by no one.

After the members of the outer person have been corrupted by every kind of wickedness, they seek to extinguish reason, which alone often survives, sees its misery, and groans, lest it suffer by weighing the evils that are within it. When the sons are killed, Zedekiah’s eyes are put out.

Reason itself is also Kadesh. Kadesh is interpreted as “holy” or “changed.” What had been holy, by resisting carnal appetite and separating itself from Lot, is changed when the light of true clarity—that is, of contemplation—is taken away from it, and it temporarily submits to the will of the most wicked kings who return after the revolution of crimes to besiege it.

They strike the whole land of the Amalekites because they incite and inflame affection, will, understanding, and sensuality—according to the Psalmist, the land of those who “lick up” the enemies of God (Ps. 71:9)—not only to desire the advantages of this world but also to lick them through flattery. Amalek is said to mean “licking people,” signifying those who seize by hypocrisy and the blandishments of the tongue what they cannot seize by force.

The Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar is also struck. That is, empty glory is aroused, unquestionably embittering God, because it pretends through persistent enjoyment of victory to possess continually the defenses of every kind of vice.

Amorite is said to mean “embittering.” Hazazon-tamar means “city of palms,” and victories are also represented by palms. When the mind deceitfully arrogates to itself the honor due to God for victory over sin, it makes God bitter through a kind of profanation of idolatry and sacrilege. And when it pretends to be free from certain vices by which it is for a time less troubled, it glories in a kind of civic fortification of itself and in victory over sin, and, like a king, dwells within itself.

For not all vices attack us at once. When we are bound by a principal evil, we seem meanwhile to be victorious over the others, because they leave us alone; yet, when the occasion returns, we promptly submit to them by our own will.

All these things, therefore, although they do not enter the mind of the one being tempted all at once, nevertheless customarily break forth little by little during the delays of temptation: through taking pleasure, consenting, acting, and revisiting.

Five kings therefore go forth and draw up a battle line against four in the wooded valley, when our affection—which ought to direct itself toward eternal things—is hemmed in by the movements of its quaternary, that is, of temporality. It wishes to take pleasure in thinking about and seeing these things, yet, as though to resist the act of sin itself, it prepares the battle line of reason, while also softening the pleasure of bodily things for itself under the name of necessity. It loves them, however, not so much for use as for lust.

The four rise against the five when what seemed to be loved religiously under the appearance of God’s creature is shown to be enjoyed by the human being in the most filthy manner. From this it happens that he slips into consent to wickedness and that affection rolls into habit. Thus, little by little, affection, together with the torpor of the mind by which it is governed, is inclined through the aforesaid stages of emerging evils.

### Verse 10

“Now the wooded valley had many pits of bitumen.”

The valley is nothing other than the mind’s sinking into the depths. The wooded character is the carelessness of thought. When the mind has fallen into the depth of crimes, it will find bitumen: an inextricable bondage. For “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).

We are a spirit that goes forth by itself but does not return by itself. From ourselves we have the power to fall; from God alone we rise again.

“Therefore the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah turned their backs, and they fell there; those who remained fled to the mountain.”

The king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah turn their backs when conscience, defenseless and mute before the suggestion of sin, and filled with the sedition of the wicked movements of its own carnality, like one province governed by two kings, turns its back on the battle line of rationality that it had proposed. At the vices’ cry, “Bend down so that we may pass,” it bends the whole firmness of uprightness and falls into the pits of bitumen.

Those who remain flee to the mountain because, when our thoughts perceive the danger of their fall, corrected by their earlier fall they flee from the things in which they may fall thereafter toward the desires of virtue.

### Verses 11–12

“They took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah and all the provisions for food, and they departed. They also took Lot and his possessions, Abram’s brother’s son, who was dwelling in Sodom.”

The possessions of the soul that is speechless like an animal—for this is what Sodom means—and established according to the meaning of Gomorrah, in the turbulence of sin, are taken away when, after the fall, even the foundation of good will and the affection of repentance are removed.

Everything that pertains to food is taken away when all the counsels of sacred Scripture, by which we are refreshed, are removed from the mind. After they have done these things, they depart, because, once the unhappy soul has been completely subjected to them, the demons cease their attack, as though against something obedient to them.

How can any substance for repentance remain in Sodom when Lot—that is, our affection—has been torn away by turning aside from good things and has no good will upon which to lean, which might support it like a little boat in which it could find refuge? Hence the voice of one who has fallen says: “I am stuck in the deep mire, and there is no foothold” (Ps. 68:3).

The brother whose son Lot is represents our body. It is joined to our spirit, namely Abram, by a remarkable kinship, and by impressing carnal affection upon the soul from outside it gives birth to that affection. It dwells in Sodom because, if permitted, it persists in negligence.

### Verse 13

“And behold, one who had escaped came and reported to Abram the Hebrew, who was dwelling in the valley of Mambre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; for these had made a covenant with Abram.”

One who escapes reports to Abram the Hebrew because the memory of the crime committed—which alone, for the moment, was unable to act, but thrusts itself upon reason with biting harshness and sets before it the evil deeds—urges him to cross over. That is, by withdrawing from vices, he fulfills the name of the Hebrew, which means “one who crosses over.”

He had once been accustomed to dwell in the valley of Mambre—that is, in the humility of discernment, which is the mother of clarity. This valley of Mambre belongs to the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner, because humility, which makes us discern clearly between good and evil, must now be related to bitterness and repentance.

The movement of repentance draws to itself, by a kind of natural kinship, a fiery purity of soul. From this, as though through another relationship, the bodily affection—namely, the brother—immediately becomes a lamp.

Amorite means “embittering”; Eshcol means “wood” or “all wood”; Aner means “lamp.” From the bitterness of repentance one arrives at the complete fervor and purity of the soul, which is obtained when the appetite is restrained under the leadership of enlightened reason.

With these states of a holy mind we had once made a covenant at the beginning of our conversion, when we professed the rule of religious observance amid the waters of baptism. There we received the lamp and the mystery of the white garment.

### Verses 14–16

“When Abram heard that his brother Lot had been taken captive, he counted the three hundred and eighteen trained servants born in his household, and pursued them as far as Dan. Dividing his forces, he fell upon them by night, struck them, and pursued them as far as Soba [or Hoba], which is on the left of Damascus, and as far as Phoenicia. He brought back all the possessions, and Lot his brother with his possessions, as well as the women and the people.”

Abram hears that his brother Lot has been taken captive when our spirit understands that affection, entangled in many allurements of evil, is being dragged captive into the abysses of filth.

By the three hundred, through the combination of three and the perfect hundred, we understand the love of the Trinity. By the ten, the keeping of God’s commandments. By the eight, the hope of the reward of the blessed resurrection, which strengthens us to do good.

With these supports, as with the native servants of our soul, freed from every debt of vice, we pursue the sins to which we were once subject, as far as Dan—that is, judgment, namely, as far as the fruit worthy of repentance by which we avenge our sins. For the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:13).

We divide our companions and fall upon them by night when, just as we rightly offer the good things we do, so we rightly divide them. We have them as though they were our fellow-soldiers, and we fall upon the vices that oppressed us, so that they may be crushed through confession of sin, as though through acknowledgment of our night.

We strike them when, by weakening their power to reign over us, we take away their strength. We pursue them as far as Soba when, even in our good actions, we cut away from ourselves the hope of temporal praise. Soba is said to mean “cutting,” from *secare*, “to cut.”

No one abstains from evils unless, when it has emerged, he also cuts away the appearance of that very abstinence. This is Soba on the left of Damascus. For although the life of some people is removed from the favor of the saints, there are nevertheless many whose eye is blood—that is, whose intention is toward sin—and who regard the pious on the left, that is, who press them through adversities.

Damascus is said to mean “eye of blood.” Let the cutting away therefore be from the desire for favor. For when holy men begin to be praised, wicked people thereupon burn with envy. Let there also be a cutting away from every stealthy intrusion of resentment toward such people.

Soba is also interpreted as “commandment.” Soba is therefore on the left of Damascus when the chief commandment of charity extends even to loving those who inflict adversities. This is how far vices must be pursued.

After this, action must continue as far as Phoenicia—that is, as far as the subjugation of all the passions that arise from the corruption of the flesh.

Through Phoenicia, which produces red peoples and receives its name from redness, we understand the desires of the body that arise from blood. Hence that blood-colored hue called scarlet is commonly called Phoenician.

Thus Lot is brought back—that is, our affection—together with its spiritual possessions. The people, namely the thoughts, and the women, namely the fluid desires, are also brought back under the authority of reason.

### Verse 17

“The king of Sodom went out to meet him after he had returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, in the valley of Shaveh, which is the King’s Valley.”

After we have conquered Chedorlaomer—that is, the movement of pleasure—together with his accomplices, who arise from flesh and spirit, when we have returned from battle to the gate of our examination, the king of Sodom comes to meet us.

He is a certain animal-like silence, namely a suggestion of security after victory over vices. He urges us to be less strict in fasting, vigils, and custody of the mind, as though we were already victorious, and to live once more in the animal-like muteness of conscience against the quarrel of sin.

Sodom is said to mean “a silent animal.” He does all this in order to hold us in the mind’s dejection, which is signified by the valley. It is the king’s valley because this most evil and foul humility of the mind is especially devoted to the ruling devil.

The valley of Shaveh, which means “elevation,” can also be understood as pride. When it is abandoned to itself, it belongs to the king, because the devil rules over the children of pride.

VERS. 18, 19, 20.—But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine—for he was priest of God Most High—blessed him and said:

“Blessed is Abram by the Most High God, who created heaven and earth; and blessed is the Most High God, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands.”

And he gave him tithes of everything.

Melchizedek himself is our intellect, which, because it rules us justly, is called—by interpretation—“king of righteousness,” in accordance with what is said to the Samaritan woman: “Call your husband” (John 4:16). But because nothing lukewarm pleases God, “Salem,” which means “perfect” and “complete,” is added, so that, since he is the king of righteousness, he may strive to adhere to righteousness perfectly.

When the king of Sodom is remiss and languid in his urging, this intellect brings forth the bread of divine eloquence, which strengthens the human heart, and the wine of spiritual grace, which makes us perpetually drunk with forgetfulness of worldly business. Such is the priesthood of the intellect, that whatever is brought forth without it is frivolous. It brings forth bread and wine through the presentation of devout works. It blesses Abram—that is, it obtains for him, by his own merit, the grace of prosperous results. Through Melchizedek one comes to Abram, although they converge into one, because through the kingdom of righteousness one comes to excellence of life.

“May rationality,” he says, “advance toward contemplating the divine height, which created in itself the heaven of contemplative wisdom and the earth of practical knowledge; and may the manifold sublimity of God’s power be praised, for he has subjected to the law of reason, to be broken down, the vices that had hostilely ruled over it.” These things are said not so much in words as in reality.

He gives Abram tithes to Melchizedek from everything when the intellect itself acquires for itself the fullness of its reward, acting in no respect lukewarmly in any of the things it has overcome. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that we have wished to understand the same person through Melchizedek as through Abram, since many such instances are found in Scripture—especially since the etymology of the names suits the passage, and since, in the case of the king of Sodom mentioned above, it is evident that the same thing is likewise represented through the angels in Revelation.
