In one passage they signify the same thing, while elsewhere they signify something different, as in: “The saints will reign with Christ for a thousand years.” And immediately, in another sense: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released” (Rev. 20:6).

VERS. 21, 22, 23.—Then the king of Sodom said to Abraham: “Give me the persons, and take the rest for yourself.” He answered him:

“I lift up my hand”—referring my works to God—not for temporal things, but in order to attain him on high, for he possesses inwardly the heaven of my rationality and the earth of my affectivity. These we bind and make firm so that our works may not flow away, “from a thread of the warp,” [63] as it were.

(VERS. 24.) “Do not say,” he says, “I enriched Abram”—that is, do not rejoice that, through the admission of some hypocrisy, by which intention is especially corrupted, you have brought about for me the wealth of the spirit, namely pride in the victory over sin.

The things that the young men eat are excepted, because one must fear that, outside the hope of reward, the ticklings of presumption—or of joy secretly stealing in because of a good result—may at times seize something for themselves. “Youth” is commonly taken to signify pride and folly.

Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, who come with us, have a share, because among the good things we have received from God we mix in certain improper things from our own side. They therefore receive a portion of us when our devout minds punish their own additions within themselves. Although good things come from God, we receive portions bearing the admixture of human involvement, purified by fire and divine light—that is, we restrain them by strong self-control. For whatever comes from our own side is sin.

EXPLICIT LIBER QUARTUS

THE FOURTH BOOK ENDS

INCIPIT LIBER QUINTUS MORALIUM IN GENESIM

THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE MORAL INTERPRETATIONS OF GENESIS BEGINS

[Col. 0129]

[Col. 0129A] I know that some do not look with equal eyes upon the things we set forth, and, having been reproved for devising novelties, attack us—though secretly—with biting whispers, twisting toward vice the things we piously undertake. What we forge is plainly new, yet in no respect discordant with the ancients, either in faith or in meaning, because we act according to the charity of the new commandment. And if we are gnawed by some, we patiently allow ourselves to be gnawed along with those whom they call old and ancient.

They endured the same in their own times. Therefore, knowing, according to the Apostle (2 Cor. 1:6), that the same endurance of sufferings is to be brought about by God in our brotherhood, we pursue what we have begun with greater security.

CHAPTER XV

VERS. 1.—The word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: “Do not fear, Abram; I am your protector, and your reward is exceedingly great.”

After each person has begun, in a fatherly manner, to govern his inward household—namely, his thoughts—without servile fear, he is rightly called “exalted,” since he is led to do good not by earthly loss or advantage, nor even by Gehenna, but by a heavenly reward.

After such a person has struck down the temporal things signified by the four kings, which wage war against our five senses—namely, the other kings—and has attributed the tithes, that is, the perfection of victory, not to himself but to Melchizedek, the king of peace, then God inspires this truly exalted father through a vision—that is, with an awakened heart, while his body is lulled to sleep amid worldly cares. For Abram means “exalted father.”

“Do not fear,” he says, “because I will be your protector in every temptation, so that you do not fall; and a great reward is stored up for you in the bestowal of recompense.”

(VERS. 2.) And Abram said: “Lord God, what will you give me? What reward do you promise me, when you deny me the causes of rewards—namely, good works?” The more holy men attend to themselves, the more they disparage themselves in their actions.

“I shall go childless”—that is, my mind rests in no stability of lordship, but wanders about in servile roving. It does not beget free children for the liberty of righteousness or of the kingdom; rather, it propagates works, which are its children, to serve the yoke of the devil and of the world.

VERS. 3.—“The son of the steward of my house, this Damascus Eliezer, will be my heir; my household servant. But you have not given me offspring.”

A steward is so called because he “cares for what is outside” (*porro curet*), whereas it belongs to the Lord to care inwardly for all great things. Thus the appetite of the flesh, which manages external matters, is the steward, and its work is its son; this work carries away our inheritance, namely the rewards we deserve.

Its riches had been acquired through the steward’s son—that is, through the works of the appetite—concerning which it was said: “You received your good things during your life” (Luke 16:25). For Damascus is said to mean “drinking blood,” or “the eye of blood.” This is the one whom the Lord calls “the left hand” (Matt. 6:3), from whom the right hand is commanded to beware; he drinks iniquity, that is, blood, as though it were water, and has an eye—that is, an intention—inclined toward sins.

Eliezer, however, means “God my helper”—not because Damascus dwells in the help of the Most High so as to be saved in soul, but because he supplicates God as helper only in bodily matters. Hence: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108), that is, let him pray only for temporal things. And: “He will confess to you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19).

He is a household servant because he does not seek a lasting home, but only some small temporal reward; he loves not the Lord but the Lord’s little gift. “But you have not given me offspring,” because, while my carnal appetite licks the earth, I find in myself no action worthy of eternal reward.

VERS. 4, 5.—“This one,” said the Lord, “will not be your heir, but the one who will come forth from your womb will be your heir.” And he brought him outside and said to him: “Receive the sky and count the stars, if you can. So will your offspring be.”

By the womb, which is the more secret part of our inward person, we should understand rationality. David urges it: “All my inward parts, bless the Lord” (Ps. 102:1); and elsewhere: “In his life he exposed his inmost parts” (Sir. 10:10).

Therefore, the act that is emitted intellectually not from wandering sensuality but from our inward and higher essence is our heir, if we so will; for, since its origin is the one to whom it belongs, the recompense of good belongs in some manner to the good act, provided it is done chastely. This is the fruit that remains after death.

God brings us outside when, through contemplation, he makes us surpass the narrow confines of the flesh. We receive the sky when, although we do not see through it completely, we nevertheless sparkle toward God for a little while. We attend to the stars when we weigh the rewards of the innumerable saints, which have been placed in him.

That God is called “heaven” is a frequent usage in the Psalms, as in: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 112:16). In this, then, our rewards are fixed. Although they seem to us, lying far away, to be perhaps small—just as they are thought to be tiny—they are in fact great stars, whose excellence cannot be counted or comprehended.

“So will your offspring be,” that is: Although you may see fully how much you labor, you will in no way be able in the present to see what you will receive in the future.

And so that you may hold these things with certainty, remember that—

(VERS. 7.) “I am the Lord who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land and that you might possess it.”

Ur means “fire”; the Chaldeans are understood as “breasts,” “wild men,” or “demons.” God therefore draws us out of the fire—that is, the heat of lusts—with which the king of Babylon was boiling our strength against him: first bringing upon us the breasts, as it were, of suggestion; then the wildness of pleasure; and finally, as it were—indeed truly—the demonic fury of action and habit.

He assigned us the earth, namely the earthly will, to cultivate with the evangelical plough, and commanded us also to hope that in the future we might possess it, impassible, with the meek.

VERS. 8.—But he said: “Lord God, how may I know that I shall possess it?” This means: “From where can I now have hope that in the future I shall possess the land with the meek?”

(VERS. 9, 10.) And the Lord said: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram; also a turtledove and a pigeon.” Taking all these, he divided them through the middle and placed the two parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds.

By the heifer, which is a heavy animal, is understood sensuality, which, once weighed down, is never—or scarcely—lifted from low things.

By the she-goat, which is eager for steep places, perceptive, and hot by nature, is understood intellectuality, insofar as this belongs to the learned according to physical theory.

By the ram, which is a stiff-necked animal, is understood carnal imagination, because with the horns of pride it resists the spirit.

The ram may also signify reason, which is our leader and guide; and the heifer may signify the will, which, placed between reason and the appetite of the flesh, is extremely susceptible to deception unless it is restrained by reason.

By the she-goat, an obscene animal, is understood the evil appetite. These things can be directed both toward good and toward evil, because spiritual reason is divided against human reason, and appetite and will are directed against evils for the sake of good.

What distinction there is between will and affect, we explained in the second treatise.

They are commanded to be three years old so that they may be imbued with love of the Trinity; or so that, through prayer and action, and through reading—which is the third thing that instructs the other two—they may be perfectly strengthened.

By the turtledove, which is more excellent, is understood love of God, which makes contemplatives.

By the pigeon, which is gregarious, is understood love of one’s neighbor, which also nourishes active people.

Our nature, therefore, corrupted by the necessity of sinning, is necessarily divided against itself in the three things mentioned above. These virtues, however, are naturally the same in themselves and also unite us. For “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). But the Spirit of God, which is love, is undivided in itself and subjects us to itself.

VERS. 11.—And birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.

The demons, because they move aloft in pride, are called birds. They are thrown into confusion by our mortification, which is never better accomplished than by that division. Nevertheless, they do not cease to provoke us; but when Abram drives them away, they flee.

In the preceding words, notice that it says: “Take for me.” Whoever is lax and fluid in his own movements, whether external or internal, must take these things—that is, hold corrected movements within his power—but not for the favor of the crowd; rather, for God, that is, for the honor of God.

(VERS. 12.) And when the sun was setting, sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark terror seized him.

The sun sets when, by God’s dispensation, the fervor of righteousness temporarily grows lukewarm in the heart of the saints.

Sleep falls upon them when unexpected sluggishness suddenly closes the eyes of the mind for a little while to watchfulness over itself.

A great and dark terror seizes them when the insolence of temptation, accompanying inertia, shakes the condition of the heart and almost extinguishes the light of counsel with a certain darkness, because the person cannot find where he should turn. And it is said to him:

VERS. 13, 14.—“Know with foreknowledge that your offspring will be foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and they will subject them to servitude for four hundred years. Nevertheless, I will judge the nation whose servants they will be, and afterward they will go out with great substance.”

The spark of reason illuminated from heaven therefore suggests that their good works will suffer something strange and very foreign amid the troubles of struggles, while the heart of one approaching the service of God must be prepared for temptation (Eccl. 2:1), and that their reward will be deferred in the future.

For an iron gate led Peter to the city (Acts 12:10). Let them therefore endure in a land that is not theirs, so that in their own land they may possess double.

Here we are subjected to servitude when, willingly or unwillingly, we are tributaries to our body and are constrained by the necessity of sinning. We are afflicted for four hundred years—that is, throughout the entire course of the present age, which is constituted for us by four groups of four. For there are in human beings four winds, four regions of the world, four elements, and also four movements, about which we often speak.

Nevertheless, God judges the nation whose yoke weighs us down—that is, the vices—when by powerful reason he discerns and regulates them within us. But when for a time we endure patiently and with equanimity, we emerge, as though with great resources of patience, like gold from the furnace, destined for a crown.

VERS. 15, 16.—“But you will go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they will return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time.”

Before we go out, we go to our fathers when we compare ourselves in merit with those whose remarkable examples we admire as having gone before us. Already established in the peace from vices, and having laid aside youthful presumption, we humbly confess our old age and are buried: that is, we are withdrawn from the turmoil of worldly affairs and concealed within the chambers of the mind.

We go out through the death of the body to our rewards, but we return here—that is, to the land promised for possession—in the fourth generation, which is the final resurrection. First we are generated from the flesh; second, from baptism; third, by passage to the soul’s rest; fourth, by the resurrection of the body.

But if the second robe is delayed for souls already possessing the first, let them endure patiently, knowing that the iniquities of the Amorites—those who embitter God by their wickedness—are not yet complete. These people are necessary for the good whose number is awaited, just as fire is necessary for gold; and, once the righteous have been fully purified through them, they will be reserved for judgment to be punished.

VERS. 18, 19, 20, 21.—On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: “To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”

When, therefore, the sun of divine compunction, as we said, was absent for a time, a smoking furnace appeared—that is, the interior heat of temptation clouding the edge of the mind—and a passing lamp of fire, namely a ray of divine reason that illuminates only in passing, subtly teaching the distinction between light and darkness, and healthfully revealing to a person, by abandoning him for a time, what he is of himself.

On this day, in this light of the lamp, God makes a covenant with us, promising us, through the perseverance of his love, the hope of victory in the conflict by inspiring it within us.

He promises to give this land to our offspring, not to us who are barren: namely, these earthly movements that we endure. That is, on account of our good works, he promises to subject them to us. They begin from the river of Egypt, which is knowledge—the knowledge by which we know how to examine Egyptian things, namely worldly things—and he leads them to the great river Euphrates, namely wisdom, through which we contemplate divine things. Euphrates is interpreted as “increasing,” because through contemplation one advances into action.

Ten movements are inserted here, representing through this number the totality of the vices.

When the Kenites are said to mean “possessors,” this pertains to avarice, the head of evils.

The Kenizzites mean “jealous,” and this pertains to its daughter, envy.

“Cedmon” means ancient sadness. These are the two things that first inflicted sorrow upon our first parents: through avarice, they fell into the envy of the devil.

The Hittites mean “stunned,” for the dullness of the reprobate sense follows.

The Perizzites mean “surpassing,” or “scattered”—namely, shameful and illicit movements now disseminated everywhere.

The Rephaim mean “giants.” This is pride, when the audacity of sinners grows from what seem to be successful outcomes of crimes.

The Amorites mean “embittering,” for God is embittered by such people.

The Canaanites mean “those who blush,” or “merchants.” Those imbued with these things blush to think about repentance, since the devil is known to deny them leisure for practicing vices. For it is called “business” (*negotium*) because it denies leisure (*otium*).

The Girgashites mean “those who drive out the settler”—first driving themselves out, and therefore driving others out as well from the heavenly dwelling in which they were called to live.

Finally, the Jebusites are called “those who are trampled,” in that lake which, according to Revelation, will be trampled outside the city (Rev. 14:20), where they will suffer the pressure of eternal condemnation.

CHAPTER XVI

VERS. 1, 2.—Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children. But she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, and she said to her husband: “Behold, the Lord has closed me off, so that I may not give birth. Go in to my maidservant; perhaps I shall receive children from her.”

We know by experience that there are two wills in a human being: one carnal and the other spiritual. Sarai means “my princess,” and our will, when it rests upon reason as upon a queen, becomes its princess.

When joined to Abram—that is, to the spirit—and made fertile by heavenly seed, it begets children worthy of freedom, since truth has made them free.

But when the soul, in the fervor of temptations, wanders in its affect away from the sweetness of the heavenly, the sluggish will, seeing that divine things are not supplied to its desire, speaks in some such way to its reason:

“God has withdrawn from me the gift of grace for doing good. Since I am not able to attain spiritual things, what reason is there that I should also cease from some honest worldly action? If, therefore, you cannot accomplish inward things because God does not will it, at least manage something useful outwardly, by which your neighbor may be helped, lest you be found entirely empty of fruit.”

This is the Egyptian maidservant, worldly care, who is called Hagar—that is, “a foreigner.” She is not native to holy minds but adventitious, thrusting herself forward impudently and not received graciously.

VERS. 3.—When he consented to her entreaty, Hagar the Egyptian maidservant was taken, after ten years from the time they had begun to dwell in the land of Canaan, and given as a wife to her husband. He went in to her, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised her mistress.

Many people, with the woman mentioned above, promising themselves with eager satisfaction that they will be trained in divine duties, promise themselves this while carrying on worldly affairs.

Hagar is therefore received after ten years because, after they had vowed to dwell in the land of Canaan—that is, in the stability of a changed way of life—in violation of the command of divine law, all the powers of reason are weakened by the entry of the maidservant, that is, by experience of worldly desire.

Canaan means “changed,” and it is clear that “land,” because it is a stable element, is used for stability. She is therefore taken as a wife when she is firmly joined to the mind. But once she becomes pregnant with some desire—for both things cannot happen, serving God and devoting oneself to the world—the spiritual will is first despised by the carnal will.

VERS. 5, 6.—“You act unjustly against me,” said Sarai to Abram. “I gave my maidservant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, she holds me in contempt. Let the Lord judge between me and you.”

Abram answered her: “Behold, your maidservant is in your hands; use her as you please.”

When Sarai afflicted her, she fled.

It is as though the devout will, fearful of its own fall, were to bring this accusation to reason:

“You must be charged with injustice. You took the maidservant, who was subject to my authority, as something to be brought beneath your bosom, to be embraced and restrained under you, so that you might care for external matters in such a way that you would not diminish inwardly. Now you endure, not without your own disgrace, that she holds me in contempt.

‘Let the Lord judge,’ that is, let him distinguish—let him make you distinguish—that it was more fitting for you to adhere to me than to her.

“And if the maidservant was yours, as you assert, you should not have forced her upon me. Therefore subject her to your service; and if you wish to exercise the authority of reason, use her herself as a maidservant.”

Sarai therefore afflicts her. She is called “my princess” because every vigor of reason takes its beginning from her. Through frequent restraints and the presentation of the fear of God, she narrows and constrains the maidservant. But the maidservant flees because, fearing the authority of so powerful a mistress, she withdraws from wantonness under her governance.

VERS. 7, 8, 9.—When the angel of the Lord found her beside a spring of water in the wilderness, which is in the desert on the road to Shur, he said to her: “Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, from where have you come, and where are you going?”

She answered: “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.”

He said: “Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand.”

The angel of the Lord is either divine inspiration or the admonition of divine eloquence. These find us when they discover us in our wickedness, even though we do not seek them.

We are beside the spring of water when we desire to cling to the one in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. This spring is found in the wilderness because the depth of divine understanding is attained only by those who have returned from external wandering to the heart.

But the wilderness is located in the desert because this rest and unity of mind are perfectly perceived only when the desires of the world have been entirely deserted. And this happens on the road of Shur.

Shur is interpreted as “blackness,” “anguish,” or “strength.” Through blackness comes knowledge of sin, for the bride’s hair is black like a raven (Song 5:11). Through anguish comes repentance for sins, and afterward strength follows against the troubles of adversity.

He therefore says to Hagar, whose name you now interpret as “converted,” and whom you now recognize as Sarai’s—that is, the princess’s—maidservant:

“Consider how great the difference is between the place from which you come, namely worldly wandering, and that toward which you now strive, the refuge of divine protection. ‘From the face’ means from the consideration of the spiritual will that presides over me and sets the divine judgments before me; I am afraid.

“Return to her”—that is, to the one from whom you flee while your fear is still premature. Turn back to carry out and love her commands, and humbly obey her works, submitting to them as though to her hand and grumbling at nothing.”

VERS. 10, 11, 12.—“Multiplying, I will multiply your offspring, and they will not be numbered because of their multitude. You have conceived and will give birth to a son; you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your affliction. He will be a wild man; his hand will be against all, and everyone’s hand against him; and he will pitch his tents opposite all his brothers.”

If, by my permission, your hardships and conceptions are multiplied, as was said to Eve, do not be afraid. For when people approach God, innumerable movements of temptation arise, which are the seeds of the flesh.

“You have conceived the hope of every kind of desire; but through confession you must give birth to it. The name of this son—the first discernment of good, namely repentance—is called Ishmael, that is, ‘the hearing of God,’ because God has heard, that is, has caused your affliction to be heard or understood: the terror of heavenly indignation inflicted upon you by the spiritual will.

“This first state of your conversion will indeed be a human being because of the constant assaults of carnal temptations, but it will be wild because those temptations are repelled with manly force, not with feminine sluggishness but with a certain royal authority.

“His hand”—that is, his power—will be against all the assaults of mind or flesh, and the attack of all those assaults will in turn be directed against him.

“He will pitch his tents opposite his brothers,” namely the animal movements generated with him from the same level of the mind, which is called appetite. For through this appetite we desire both good and evil.

“He will pitch them,” that is, with a fixed command he will establish them, so that, just as the desire of the body wars against the spirit, the spirit will strive to mount and ride over that same desire.

[Col. 0136B] VERS. 13, 14.—Hagar called the name of the Lord who spoke to her: “You are the God who saw me.” For she said: “Certainly here I have seen the back of him who sees me.”

Therefore she called that well “The Well of the Living One who Sees Me.” It is between Kadesh and Barad.

To call upon the name of God is, according to what he says to us inwardly by giving us discernment, to acknowledge with fitting thanksgiving his goodness by which he sees us. For he reveals to us the error in which we were.

The “front” of God is the vision of his glory. “In your remnants,” says the Psalm, “you will prepare their faces” (Ps. 20:13). The “back” is eternal condemnation: “He struck his enemies on their backs” (Ps. 77:66).

Here, then—that is, in knowledge of ourselves—we see, meaning we understand, how sad it is for anyone to be made a back, namely to lose the face of God, since it is so evil for anyone to live without regard for God and for himself, according to his perverse mind.

The well is the depth of the consideration of our life, both present and past, from which an inundation of the sweetest compunction is very often drawn. We therefore call it a well when, by paying attention and distinguishing, we recognize a certain origin of vital understanding, by which we know both ourselves and the one by whom we are known. For this is eternal life: “that they may know you,” he says (John 17:3).

Kadesh is interpreted as “changed” or “holy”; Barad means “blessing.” While on the one side we are exercised toward the change of our former conduct, through which we may attain holiness, and on the other we are stretched toward attaining the blessing of the heavenly kingdom, we are placed, as it were, in a certain middle space, pulled this way and that, and do not yet perfectly grasp either one.

From this well we draw strength by which we may strive toward both.

Barad is also more accurately translated as “hail.” This suggests the shaking of conscience, because the mind is indeed defended on one side through change and holiness, but, accused by the frequent incursions of sins and humanity, is harassed, as though by a hailstorm of thoughts accusing or even defending it on either side, according to the Apostle (Rom. 2:15).

VERS. 16.—Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

The number eight, consisting of fours, refers to temporal things, whose appetite we suffer at our beginnings. The number six refers to progress in the good works we desire to perform. For although we seem to act well outwardly, we are nevertheless often inwardly pierced severely by the goads of desire.

We give birth to Ishmael when, through God hearing us—that is, making us understand the foolishness of our conduct—we bring the fluidity of carnal affect to confession of sin.

CHAPTER XVII

The Whole Chapter Is Explained in a General Way

What follows has also been treated tropologically by many teachers, and some passages are sufficiently clear in themselves. Therefore the less evident portions, scattered here and there, must be examined more briefly up to the place where it says: “The Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre.”

VERS. 1.—He had begun to be ninety-nine years old when God changed his name, because the inward person had not yet reached the hundred of divine contemplation, which is transferred to the right hand, although he seemed to himself to be Abram, “exalted father,” on account of certain external forms of self-restraint that he had attained.

“Walk before me and be perfect,” he is told, so that you may strive to advance and be perfected not so much before human beings as inwardly, that is, before God.

At this Abram falls on his face, because the one who thought he possessed the height of merit, immediately reproved for his inward unworthiness, blushes at his own foulness. This is what Scripture means by falling on one’s face.

(VERS. 4.) “I am,” he says—that is, essentially unchangeable—“and therefore my covenant is with you, if you are strong and substantial against inward vices.”

Therefore do not now boast vainly that you are exalted, but know that you have unquestionably been established as the father of many nations, so that by a father’s administration you may know how to govern the people of inward insolence.

“I will set you among nations,” because the more you advance, the greater the uproars you will endure. But from you will arise kings—that is, powerful movements of reason—to suppress these things and contain them.

“I will be God of your offspring after you,” namely the provider and rewarder of your work, when you have ceased to exist temporally.

VERS. 12.—“A male child eight days old shall be circumcised among you.”

The person who, composed of the four elements, has overcome his own body, and has changed these temporal things—distinguished by an equal number of names of virtues—as though by the light of days, will be cleansed everywhere from the assaults of corrupt admixtures.

Note the Apostle’s distinction (Phil. 3:2) between “mutilation” and “circumcision.” Nor should it escape notice that Pharaoh commanded the females to be preserved and the males killed, whereas here the females are passed over and the males circumcised.

And the one who is not of our stock is commanded to be circumcised, because there are virtues, so to speak, that are more than natural, such as virginity and voluntary poverty. The first of these excels so greatly that to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is rightly called angelic.

In these, the foreskins of superfluities are cut away all around. For Isaiah says: “All our righteousness is like a menstrual cloth in your sight” (Isa. 64:6).

In our flesh this covenant is eternal, because in our carnal affect—which above is called the land of our pilgrimage, and Canaan, since through it we wander from the right state and are subjected to mutability—the discipline of continence by which we are joined to God must necessarily be observed.

VERS. 14.—“The male whose flesh has not been circumcised shall perish from his people.”

This means: A strong spirit, not degenerate through feminine softness, which has not cut away carnal affects, will perish through the excessive vulgarity of emerging desires and through its own animal nature.

You will not call Sarai—that is, the will joined to the spirit as a wife to her husband—specifically “my princess,” referring to your external action by which you seem exalted and which you perform for the sake of worldly respectability. Rather, you will call her simply and absolutely “princess,” the leader of all devout action, more inward than outward.

For whoever seems to restrain himself while doing good not for God but for some personal honor is truly ruling himself.

From this marriage of spirit and will Isaac is born, namely hope of heavenly joy, and through the descent of heavenly multiplication he is blessed.

(VERS. 17.) Abraham laughs in his heart and falls on his face, because the more he is imbued spiritually, the more he rejoices in his inward instruction; and in rejoicing he is humbled.

“Do you think,” he says, “that a son will be born to a hundred-year-old man, and that Sarah, who is ninety, will give birth?”

This is to say in proper order: “Can I hope that the will, although it is still placed in the number ninety and lacks the perfection of ten—for ‘to will lies close at hand, but to accomplish it he does not find’ (Rom. 7)—will reach the fulfillment of desire, as though arriving at childbirth, while the spirit has already attained the summit of contemplation?”

## Verse 18

“Would that Ishmael might live before you.” But why do I speak of the excellence of virtues, when I still fear that Ishmael—that is, the carnal affection which wishes to obey itself rather than God—may die amid vices?

## Verse 19

“Sarah,” God said, “shall bear you a son, and I shall establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant.” Ishmael will not merely fail to die by assenting to his desires; rather, Sarah—that is, the will itself, now ruling inwardly and outwardly—will conceive, from the purity of conscience, the fruit of joyful hope, from which the mind itself will receive the firmness of eternal love. [Col. 0138D]

## Verse 20

“Concerning Ishmael also, whom you tremble may be overwhelmed by the masses of temptations, I have heard you: he shall generate twelve leaders”—that is, he shall produce, through the efficacy of his inward leadership, faith in the Trinity together with the observance of evangelical teaching. For four times three, and three times four, make twelve; and faith in the ternary number is dead without works—that is, without the quaternary of the Gospels, or of the four chief virtues. He generates twelve leaders if affection conceives and earnestly desires apostolic teaching from the depths of the heart.

## Verse 21

“My covenant shall be with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear for you at this time in the following year.” The covenant is established with Isaac when God promises eternal rewards to our hope as an incentive to love. [Col. 0139A] Sarah bears him at this time in the following year when the will, in this very disposition of the soul—namely, when God speaks with it through the illumination of reason—pursues hope to the manifestation and effective accomplishment of a worthy and suitable work, not merely in this year, in which the struggle against vices is still being waged through the fullness of enlightened action, but in the other, in which, once the disturbances have been quieted, the yearly solemnity of contemplating the eternal blessednesses hoped for is not brought to completion, even when the disturbances have been quieted. Hope cannot properly be called hope if no living act commends it through actual execution.

## Verse 22

“When he had finished speaking, God went up from Abraham,” when at times, by withdrawing himself in a providential manner, he shows the human spirit that the grace of divine inspiration is by no means subject to its own control, but must be sought from above, from the Father of lights. [Col. 0139B]

## Verses 24–25

Abraham, therefore, is circumcised when he is ninety-nine years old, while the eye of the spirit is cleansed for the right hand of the divine vision and also for the glory to be tasted beforehand in the present—the foretaste that is a kind of anticipation of the future denarius. For, as has been said, the hundred passes into the right hand, which we sometimes attain when the God who is the summit of our blessedness beholds us. Ishmael is said to have been circumcised at fourteen years of age because carnal affection is brought to the virtue of purity through observance of the Decalogue and the keeping of the Gospels.

## Verses 26–27

On that same day all the males of his household are circumcised, because everything inward that is virtuous requires the same inspiration by which God speaks rationally to the mind—just as a fruit-bearing branch needs diligent cleansing in order to bear more fruit. The foreigners and those who are not of our lineage are explained by the same interpretation, as we indicated above; we shall treat the remaining matters below.

# Chapter XVIII

## Verses 1–2

Now the Lord appeared to Abraham as he sat in the valley of Mamre, at the entrance of his tent, in the very heat of the day. When he raised his eyes, three men appeared to him standing near him.

After Abraham—that is, “the father seeing the people”—had circumcised Ishmael, that is, affection which obeys itself rather than God, distinguishing the crowds of thoughts; for Ishmael means “obeying himself”; after examining the household servants, namely, the innate goods naturally belonging to him, and the purchased servants, namely, those acquired through any kind of labor, and after completely cutting off the foreigners, namely, vices [69] attached from every direction, the Lord appears to him in the valley of Mamre. A valley is humility; Mamre means “divisions” or “clear-sightedness.” For those established in humility divide—or rather, discern—clearly both what we are and what we ought to do.

The tent is the service in which we serve as soldiers for God. It has an entrance because within it there is hope of going forth from this life to rest. We sit in it because in this hope we rest perseveringly; for “he sleeps among the middle heaps” (Psalm 67:14), and to sit means to persevere, as in: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Psalm 1:1). “In the very heat of the day” means in the same spiritual understanding of the mind in which the circumcision mentioned above was carried out. He raises his eyes when he lifts the gaze of his heart, shut off from every lowly imagination, to contemplate intellectual realities alone.

Three men appear to him standing when sensuality, imagination, and intellectuality, for a moment while the mind is stretched toward divine things, remain at rest; and, for our sake—that is, near us—they cease from external wandering and lower themselves while God is perceived by the humble mind.

## Verses 3–4

When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the entrance of his tent and bowed to the ground. He said, “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant; but let me bring a little water, and wash your feet, and rest beneath the tree.”

When we perceive that our animal dispositions are supporting the grace that comes upon us, we run to meet them, preparing the activity of our free will to receive what flows into us. We do this from the entrance of the tent—that is, from the hope with which the mind longs for heavenly things, from the service of our warfare. He therefore bows to the ground, humbling himself after recognizing the lowliness of his condition.

“If,” he says—that is, if you deem me worthy through the grace of your spiritual gifts—“do not touch me only momentarily, as you sometimes do, but remain present so that you may stay and console me for a while. I shall bring a little water”: that is, I shall labor at something suited to compunction and grace, so that your feet, O sensuality, imagination, and intellectuality, may be washed—cleansed of the mobility by which you slip through earthly sins. At least while the opportunity is available, rest beneath the tree; that is, breathe through the virtue of the Holy Spirit, which protects you from the heat of vices and nourishes you. [Col. 0140C]

## Verse 5

“I shall set out a morsel of bread, and strengthen your hearts; afterward you shall go on your way. For this is why you have turned aside to your servant.” They replied, “Do as you have said.”

We set out a morsel of bread when we offer the mind something from Sacred Scripture to be chewed over, something by which it may become more fervent, so that reason, strengthened by it, may devote itself to God with greater vitality.

“Afterward you shall go on your way”: when you have satisfied the desire of the heart, you will be able for a time, as is customary, to withdraw what has been offered. For this reason you turned aside to your servant, because God, bending your severity, turned you aside. We are servants of all our impulses, since we serve them by attending to them so diligently. Thus they assent to divine reason. [Col. 0140D]

## Verses 6–7

Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah and said to her, “Hurry; knead three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.” He himself ran to the herd, took from it a tender and choice calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried and cooked it.

When opportunity and a disposition of soul favorable to supplication before God smile upon us, let Abraham hurry—he whom we have said is interpreted as “the father seeing the people,” because by paternal piety and legitimate authority he sees, that is, provides for, the people. Let this spiritual Abraham hurry into the tent to Sarah, who here is interpreted as virtue, joined to him as an acquired good will, without which whatever we do is not virtue. Let him undertake the divine warfare and speak to her according to the actual achievement of things:

“Three measures of fine flour,” he says—namely, a pure outward human being, a pure memory of the inward person, and, finally, the pure subtlety of contemplation—“mix together for one intention pleasing to God, and make loaves”: establish bright and disciplined ways of life. Yet press them down against the rising form of pride with the ashes of an old but extinguished fire—that is, the memory of sin that once ruled in you.

The herds of God are the proposed forms of every strong virtue. Herds are so called from arms, because in ancient times weapons, cuirasses, helmets, and shields were made from them. To this herd every spiritual Abraham runs with the speed of devotion and seizes a new calf—yet mature through the gravity of its intention—having cast off secular oldness, and tender through the absence of stubbornness, and excellent without the voluntary admission of carnality or negligence. He seizes the established form of any principal virtue. For although the saints may appear to flourish in all virtues, they nevertheless rely upon certain special graces: “There are divisions of graces, according as the Spirit grants to each” (1 Corinthians 12:4).

We give this calf to the servant when we submit our good, as though for examination, to the example of that new human being, Christ, as to a true rule. He cooks it quickly when whatever hardness arises in us from ourselves is softened more rapidly by the swift flame of his spirit.

## Verses 8–10

He also took butter and milk, and the calf that he had cooked, and set them before them. He himself stood beside them under the tree. When they had eaten, they said to him, “Where is Sarah your wife?” He replied, “Look, she is in the tent.” He said to him, “Returning, I shall come to you at this same time, life accompanying me, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.” When Sarah heard this, she laughed behind the entrance of the tent.

We take butter when we undertake to bestow upon others the benefits of charity. We take milk when we live innocently within ourselves. There are people who live harmlessly for themselves but show no piety toward others. Butter is not only pleasant as food, but also fattens other things; hence it signifies the service of charity. We understand the same thing in the prophet, where it is written: “He shall eat butter and honey” (Isaiah 7:15), and so forth.

When, therefore, we are good in ourselves and bestow goodness upon our neighbors, then we rightly bring forward a calf of some holy profession, cooked in the fire of purity. We set it before them—that is, before our understanding, memory, and senses—so that these may be nourished by it as by food and refreshed from within. They eat, therefore, and the more sharply they complain about the humility of their condition:

“Where,” they say, “is Sarah your wife?” It is as though they said: “If you have now begun to sense, to some degree, that God has shone upon you, consider where Sarah is situated—that is, what firmness belongs to your recently illuminated will. For the more deeply we are refreshed, the more closely we contemplate what we are.”

“Look,” he says, “she is in the tent,” because this is the reply of a conscience beginning to advance: it is fighting against the examinations of vices. The will itself introduces the matter and itself reports it. “And he said to him…”

It should be noted that although it was said earlier that they ate and said, “Where is Sarah?”, it is now said that one of them spoke individually. We may therefore understand, without absurdity, that in a moral sense we have received one meaning from the Lord appearing and another from the three men standing.

The Lord therefore said:

The first appearance of God to a human being occurs in conversion. Yet, without abandoning us, he withdraws wholly from us while educating us through our experience and our victory over sin. Then he returns to us with a more abundant glory.

Let the inner person not therefore question his own weakness if life accompanies him—that is, if he perseveres in the purpose of his life—and if the same time, that is, the same disposition and condition of soul, remains. For the Lord appeared to speak in the heat of the day after the unity of his way of life had been maintained amid the temptations of his conduct.

A son is given to Sarah because hope—no longer timid as before, but delightful, full of certainty, and illuminated by heavenly reason—is promised to a will that is no longer inexperienced, but labors manfully and with a certain courage against vices.

Sarah laughed at this because, although our will strives toward good things, nevertheless, considering its own weakness, it distrusts, as though mocking, what has been assigned to it by hope. Hence she is also said to have laughed behind the entrance of the tent, so that it might be understood that distrust in her labor had fallen away from hope for a little while. We customarily call our children our hopes, because of their posterity.

Sarah therefore has no son as long as the mind, darkened by the clouds of passions, fears the lower things all the more, loves the higher things all the less, and therefore hopes all the less, still wavering and clinging to itself. But when the Lord visits us after the triumph over temptations, and complete gladness is poured into the heart, Sarah certainly receives a son.

[Col. 0142C]

## Verses 11–12

Now both were old and advanced in age, and Sarah’s menstrual periods had ceased. She laughed secretly, saying, “After I have grown old, and my lord is aged, shall I give myself to pleasure?”

It is as though the will were saying: “I have grown old among all my enemies in a foreign land” (Psalm 6:8; Baruch 3:11), and my husband—the spiritual understanding—now knows only what belongs to the old human being. In vain would I labor to acquire the pleasure of divine contemplation, since the grace of compunction is lacking at the beginning.

“Womanly functions” means the monthly periods of women. When these cease, women cease to bear children. What, then, are the menstrual periods except the emptying, through confession, of the inner filth of the soul?

When the will does not see perfection residing in itself, but only the beginnings of conversion in the confession of guilt, and when, according to the humility of self-examination, it has been advanced within the conscience into the sluggishness typified by old age, it has nothing from itself and finds nothing around itself from which it could presume that the joys of sincere and fearless hope—promised through the intimate inspiration of God—would be born to it.

For one who deserves nothing, if commanded to hope for rewards, unless he looks to grace, rejoices less in the promise than he fears being mocked because he has not deserved it.

But the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying:

## Verses 13–14

“Why did Sarah your wife laugh, saying, ‘Shall I truly bear a child, old as I am?’ Is anything difficult for God? At the appointed time I shall return to you, life accompanying me, at this same time, and Sarah shall have a son.”

It is as though God were saying openly:

“If you, a human being, doubt because of your weak will—when the will to do good is not even available to you, and you find yourself unable, I do not say to accomplish it, but even to begin—why do you mock the omnipotence of God in despair, when you have before your eyes so many of his mercies in every kind of sin?

Let the life that I have breathed into you by inspiration accompany you with the greatest perseverance in the display of every good work. Persevere in this same time—that is, in this very fervor of your inner person—so that with the help of these things you may always strive to subject the rebellious movements of carnal will to reason. Then, when I return to you to reward your triumphs, let the offspring of the brightest hope arise for you.

First apply the medicine by which you may be free from fevers; afterward I shall provide you with the dishes of virtue by which you may recover from the weakness contracted through those fevers. If you do for your salvation what I have appointed—and it is easy to do—then it is not difficult for me to supply you with the growth of which you seem to despair.”

The will, conquered by appropriate reasoning, pretends as though it had not despaired. Now inflamed by the majesty of the promises to undertake better things, it is ashamed to repeat in thought what it had felt. Yet the understanding, a true witness, accuses it reproachfully in order to summon it to repentance for its foolish despair. Hence, when it says:

## Verse 15

“I did not laugh,” he says, “you did laugh.”

## Verse 16

When the men had risen from there, they directed their eyes toward Sodom, and Abraham went with them, accompanying them.

Since the sweetness of the heavenly banquet is tasted only by humble people, by senses contracted through divine fear, and, in a certain sense, by those who are sitting, they are rightly said to have risen when they are directed toward external pursuits with an anxious firmness of mind.

They direct their eyes toward Sodom when they fix their intentions upon the likeness and conformity of carnal impulses or of carnal people. Sodom is interpreted as “their likeness,” or “blindness,” or “a silent beast.” After conformity to vice or to worldly people, we fall into blindness of heart; and when sensuality, together with the imagination, has been drawn into lust, we come to bestial silence, when no encounter with reason takes place against the assault of the flesh, but a destructive peace is maintained under the dominion of some sin.

For in the usage of Sacred Scripture “let it be silent” is worn smooth in the sense of “let it rest” and “not resist,” as in: “Let all the earth be silent before the face of the Lord” (Habakkuk 2:20).

Abraham accompanies them and walks with them when reason, driven on by sight and by fantastic thought, is led toward the slopes of wrongdoing. It knows its error but does not resist because of weakness. This usually happens: one knows one’s own falls and groans over them before complete blindness is born in the mind.

## Verse 17

The Lord said, “Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?”

Therefore the Lord declares that he cannot hide from Abraham what he is about to do. Abraham is destined to become a great and powerful nation (Genesis 12:2), because to our own spirit, violently driven by vices, there is often infused some foreknowledge of its future ruin and resurrection. When it sees itself scattered through crimes, it nevertheless receives hope, by God’s provision, that it will return to its former exercises of doing good.

For Abraham’s sake the Lord brings forward everything he has said, just as, for the sake of the inward mind’s groaning over the perversity it observes in itself but cannot overcome, he supplies assistance for victory—like Israel crying out in Egyptian slavery. For “the Lord raises up the son of the widow,” having had mercy on the mother’s affection (1 Kings 17:22).

## Verses 20–21

The Lord therefore said, “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I shall go down and see whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Gomorrah is said to mean “rebellion of a people” or “fear.” In the mind of a people that has been overturned, there is the rebellion of carnal disturbances, and, arising from the reproach of an evil conscience, fear—not of God, but of human beings.

From Sodom and Gomorrah, therefore—that is, from blindness of heart and the rebellion of crimes—an outcry arises when, with shame cast aside, whatever is wicked and indecent is practiced within the mind or even outwardly. This outcry becomes heavier in many ways when it is hardened through the long duration of habit.

God speaks these things to Abraham when the enormity of our sin is disclosed to us by him. Hence he also “goes down”: that is, he makes us descend from the arrogance of our pride. And he sees: that is, he makes us see whether we have completely fulfilled our desires in action. They themselves are the outcry in God’s ears, so that he may say, “that I may know”—that is, “that I may make known into what abandonment the wretched mind has fallen, what it has desired, and what it has also done after desiring it.”

[Col. 0144C]

## Verse 22

They turned from there and went toward Sodom, while Abraham still stood before the Lord.

When our outer person now desires, through perverse thought, to be conformed to the world, it must turn away from that place—that is, from the humble self-examination which it first conceived when God was speaking to our Abraham—and turn away from God himself, so that, by directing its attention toward a bestial life, that is, toward Sodom, it may become blind.

But Abraham still stands before the Lord because the understanding, divinely perceiving, considers within itself, with groaning, the evils toward which it is hastening. This person approaches the Lord when, examining every state of mind according to the Scriptures, he strives to investigate within himself what God thinks about each one.

## Verse 23

“Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked?”

It is as though he were saying:

“Even if, because of the weakness of the flesh, I struggle toward vice, will I—the spirit that delights in the law of God and prefers to live according to the inner person—also be condemned to blindness, so that I may not see, or, seeing, desire to carry out, what is just?”

## Verse 24

“If there are fifty righteous in the city, will they perish together?”

By the number fifty repentance is understood, as is plainly proved by the fiftieth psalm. Fifty righteous are therefore in the city when worthy movements of repentance are active in the mind.

## Verse 26

“If I find fifty righteous in the midst of the city,” he says, “I shall spare every place for their sake.”

The righteous are found in the midst of the city when movements of compunction arise in the very center of the heart—not for an hour or from the side, as usually happens, but perseveringly and with an undivided resolve to correct vices. Every place is spared when the mind, gathered from its dispersion and now made wholly concentrated, is shown mercy so that it does not fall into worse things.

## Verses 27–28

“I shall speak,” he says, “to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes. What if there are five fewer than fifty righteous?” The Lord said, “I shall not destroy it if I find forty-five.”

We speak to the Lord when we complain to him in prayer about our perversity. We confess that we are dust when we recognize either that we are sinners or that we are unstable in every condition of temptation; for it was said to the sinner: “You are dust” (Genesis 3:19).

Ash is the sign of fire that has been consumed. It signifies the memory of past sins, which, like ash tending and rekindling a fire, nourishes and revives the heat of every vice. We are therefore ashes whenever we nourish our former evils through pleasurable recollection.

Yet we are not destroyed if we are found to have five fewer than fifty righteous, because although we repent of what we have committed, and the weakness of the inner person cannot fully restrain the five senses of the flesh, divine clemency will not reject so small a desire for repentance. Nor does it destroy the remaining good will within, when the mind restrains sensuality less than it ought, not through boldness but through weakness.

Forty-five are found in us when, through the grace of the Gospel, signified by the quaternary, and through the guidance of the Decalogue, signified by the denary, inward sensuality—that is, imagination—is fully governed. For unless these bodily senses were much more closely inserted into the soul, the pleasures that arise from what we have heard, touched, or smelled would never so deeply immerse themselves in the memory.

## Verse 29

“But what if forty are found?” He said, “I shall not strike because of the forty.”

We are in the number forty when we either subject our body, which subsists from the four elements, to the ten of the law, or—because ten consists of seven and three, while seven consists of four and three—we bring our body, figured by the quaternary, and our soul, figured by the ternary, to the knowledge of the Trinity through the observance of the four Gospels or the four chief virtues. We mean nothing else by this except diligence in observing God with body and soul.

The degrees of the states in which the virtue of self-restraint advances from repentance should be noted numerically; nor is a pious intention shaken when the merit of a perverse act demands it.

## Verse 30

“What,” he said, “if you find thirty there?” He replied, “I shall not destroy it because of the thirty.”

Thirty consists of six times five. Since God completed his works in six days, six is taken for perfection. Five refers not only to the outward and inward senses but also to actions themselves. For the division of bodily things is fivefold: the person who does something, the matter from which he does it, the motion by which he does it, the occasion for which he does it, and the effect that he produces.

When, therefore, as far as human ability allows, we bring sensuality, imagination, and the order of our actions to perfection, we set the foot of the mind in the number thirty. In this state, therefore, there is a place not for destruction but for salvation.

## Verse 31

The number twenty follows, in which the city still does not perish. Twenty consists of two sevens and a six. By one seven, therefore, temporal things are understood, which revolve through seven days; by the other, our body and soul; and by the six, the grace of spiritual creation, to which, as to a teacher, we submit ourselves in order to restrain ourselves and the various desires of the world. For the human being was made on the sixth day. When we have placed ourselves and our outward things beneath this grace, we arrive at the first rule of charity, namely unity, in which we cannot perish.

## Verse 32

“I beg you,” he said, “do not be angry, Lord, if I speak once more. What if ten are found there?”

It should be observed that he recalls having begun to speak to the Lord only once. In the Scriptures we find “once” used for something established unchangeably. Whoever persistently seeks from God, through prayers and the zeal of his works, the pattern of a more perfect life begins, therefore, to speak to the Lord unchangeably.

The number ten is placed last; it is promised to those who labor in the vineyard (Matthew 20:2). This is the universal perfection, namely the eternal vision of God, which is now pursued through labor so that it may be seen in the future. It is the source of all complete happiness, just as ten constitutes a certain perfection of number, without which there is no gathering of the numbers that follow.

## Verse 33

The Lord departed after he had ceased speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.

After this illumination of conscience, through which we vigilantly attend to what must be done by us in the various states of life, as though God were speaking to us through the touch of reason, the Lord departs. He leaves us, after showing us the path of life, the gift of free will, and, withdrawing for a time, as though in a providential manner, allows us to do what we wish by putting us to the test.

While God presides over our mind, we are above ourselves. When he withdraws in this providential way, we return to our place, because we immediately relapse into that torpid condition of soul which we possess from our merely human nature. For if we consider what we are from ourselves, we perceive in ourselves only the lie of word and deed.

# Chapter XIX

## Verses 1–2

Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gates of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them, bowed face down to the ground, and said, “I beg you, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant and stay there. Wash your feet, and in the morning you shall go on your way.”

The two angels signify sensuality and imagination. They are rightly called angels—that is, messengers—because the outer sense announces to the vision of thought what it has sensed outside, and imagination in turn reports to intellectuality what sensuality has impressed upon it from without.

These two come to Sodom when they rush into the blindness of worldly cares, and in the evening, when the warmth of divine hope begins to fail.

Lot sits at the gates of the city because our mind, already turning aside from the line of justice, bound by the nets of pleasures and breathing out the flames of greedy desire, grows sluggish and weak at the entrances of suggestions. We must stand against these things—that is, we must struggle. For when the Apostle said, “Stand firm in the faith,” he immediately explained that standing by saying, “Act manfully” (1 Corinthians 16:13).

The one who earlier was called Abraham because of the understanding of discernment enlightened by God is called Lot after he returns to his own place. As explained above, Lot means “turning aside,” “bound,” or “would that.” The word “would that” appropriately expresses what is read: “Every idle person is in his desires” (Proverbs 21:25), for “would that” is the word of one wishing. To sit is also the act of one judging.

Lot therefore sits at the gates of the city when human reason, although turning aside from what is right and dragged by the bond of desire, examines the entrance to its own pleasure according to worldly respectability.

When we see our senses and thoughts slipping into bestial silence, and producing no living sound of any good action in the ears of God, we often restrain the flow of our wantonness because we fear human shame. We rise—that is, we lift up our sluggish mind to repress these things—and we bow face down to the ground, humbling our proud affection lest it overflow, by considering the lowliness of our condition.

“I beg you, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant”: that is, restrain yourselves from outward wandering within the secret place of conscience, and allow the service of reason to be offered to you. “Stay there”: restrain yourselves with persevering insistence under this discipline. “Wash your feet”: cleanse through repentance the filth of wickedness which you contracted by desiring earthly things. “In the morning you shall go on your way”: when the ray of divine charity shines upon your senses, you shall approach Christ, who is the way for those advancing toward him, with the steps of holy desire.

They said, “No, but we shall remain in the street.”

## Verse 3

He pressed them strongly to turn aside to him. When they had entered his house, he made a banquet for them, baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

They wish to remain in the street because the movements of our senses and thoughts avoid the narrow and constricted way by which one advances toward life. They love the broad place for dwelling when they do not fear leaving the gates of mind and body open to every kind of triviality, and when they do not assent to the reason that teaches, according to the law, that every vessel without a cover is unclean.

We are driven strongly when, fearing humanly that we may gradually grow lukewarm and fall, before the eyes of men, into some serious crime, we restrain the impulse of the flesh. Or, by setting before ourselves the fear of divine judgment, we finally turn aside from the public place of negligence into the asylum of reason.

To those who protect themselves with this fortification of conscience there is then offered a banquet of prayer, reading, and contemplation. Once the leaven of wickedness has been purged away, the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:7) is baked in the holy fire of the spirit to purity. By the pleasure of this nourishment, sensuality, wandering both inwardly and outwardly, is held in check.

## Verses 4–5

Before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded his house, from the child to the old man—all the people together. They called Lot and said to him, “Where are the men who entered your house at night? Bring them out here, so that we may know them.”

We go to bed when the noise of external business begins to rest within us. Before the mind is lulled to sleep by these things, however, the men of the city—namely, the fierce movements of the body—surround the house, that is, constrict knowledge.

By the old men we may understand original sins; by the children, the actual sins that we add and devise. For example, although lust is naturally present in us—to say nothing of other matters—we daily marvel at new forms of lust, contrived beyond the established rule of intercourse, and in our amazement we grieve.

Children arise daily from old men because from innate corruption a new stench of vice continually emerges. There are also certain crimes that are not natural, without which, it is handed down, the times before the Flood existed in part: greed, vainglory, and pride in outward forms of worship. Discovered—or rather produced—much later, these now burn with more furious madness. The old men, meanwhile, are gluttony, anger, sadness, and lust.

These, together with the whole people of carnal thoughts, call Lot out because they set before reason the sweetness of past pleasures and the loves of things presently possessed, and compel it to draw nourishment from outward goods.

“Where,” they ask, “are the men who entered your house at night?” That is: “Consider the state of that once tender sensuality of yours, both inward and outward, which you have now constrained under manly strength: whether it is possible for you to persevere in it. They entered you at night—that is, unexpectedly—when they forced their way from the outward concerns proper to them into spiritual matters, which are not their office and cannot be borne by them.”

“Bring them out here”: bring forth your senses to carry out the order and use of temporal things, for the enjoyment of which they were made, “so that we may know them”—so that, through constant experience of pleasure, we may add knowledge of them to ourselves.

### VERSES 6, 7, 8

Lot went out to them, and, shutting the door behind him, said: “Do not, my brothers, do this evil. I have two daughters who have not yet known a man; I will bring them out to you, and abuse them as you please, provided that you do nothing evil to these men, for they have entered under the shelter of my roof.”

Lot goes in to them when the power of reason is brought to bear on examining the character of the vices by which he is challenged. He shuts the door behind him when he bars the entrance of the mind to things that are behind—namely, temporal things—while seeking what is before, that is, eternal things; and in the very examination of sin he fortifies himself lest pleasure secretly steal upon him.

Our brothers are the bodily impulses themselves, begotten from the same mind from which virtues also proceed. For the same earth that produces grain likewise produces thorns and thistles. “Do not,” he says, “do this evil”: that is, provoke me to an obvious crime.

The two daughters seem to signify two things that produce great tenderness in good minds: the desire to possess and the love of reputation, that is, vainglory. For scarcely anyone engaged in spiritual progress is free from the temptation to possess something; scarcely is any just person empty of the impulse toward vainglory, even when he is more just. These, then, are what weaken the strength of reason. Hence they are called daughters who have not known a man, because they do not experience the dominion of reason. For it is said to someone: “Call your husband” (John 4:16), that is, your understanding.

There are countless people who are accustomed to fear bodily vices and those commonly regarded as disgraceful—such as gluttony and extraordinary lust—more than spiritual vices, such as avarice and pride, which they shudder to confront. These daughters are brought out when they are prostituted to demonic will by that still excessively worldly-wise reason, which longs for earthly things, and that will abuses them through the very same crimes.

He promises to do this when he says that no evil will be done to the men—that is, to the senses acting manfully—namely, no scandal, because they have entered under the shelter of his roof. From the heat of carnal desires they have withdrawn to reason, to me, in order to have there the protection of the Holy Spirit, who is the covering for my head in the day of battle.

### VERSE 9

But they said: “Go away from there!” And again they said: “You came in as a stranger; are you now acting as a judge? We will afflict you more than them.” And they pressed violently upon Lot.

This is altogether as if the appetite of the flesh, under the appearance of vices, were ironically saying to reason: “Go away, then, from the use of temporal goods, to which you could lawfully cling, and proceed to the height of intellectual understanding in which you cannot persevere. And there, while the senses of the body ridiculously refrain too much from their own duty, do you think you can conceal yourself?

“I confess that reason was given to man, and that it ought to be free for God without any desire for external things. This is native and, so to speak, indigenous to man. But you, as something adventitious, enter the entrance of conscience like a handmaid, deceitfully imitating mastery. You pursue spiritual vices while rejecting bodily ones merely out of human shame. Consider with what strength of soul you will be able to maintain the seat of judgment against us.

“We do not therefore raise the engines of temptation so much against your senses as against the new extravagances of your inflated pride that must be blown away.” Thus the whirlwind of an inward storm is heaped upon this typological Lot.

### VERSES 10, 11

They were now close to breaking down the doors. And behold, the men stretched out their hands, brought Lot in to themselves, and shut the door. But they struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door.

The doors are broken down when the commandments of God—or the virtue of the soul by which God is admitted and the enemy excluded—are damaged in us while the devil knocks. But they stretch out the hand and bring Lot in to themselves when, rejecting both forms of sensuality with their natural softness, they bring forth manly strength, seize reason for themselves by the hand of divine assistance, and seek the inner regions. They shut the door—that is, the windows of the body through which death enters—and thus, by despising them, abandon all temporal things that provoke us, from the least to the greatest. They show them as blinded, with no light of prosperity shining upon them—namely, no light by which anything worthy of desire could be sought by anyone of sound judgment.

When these things have been judged unworthy, for the time being—that is, during the period of temptation—of every regard of the heart, there is no longer in the conscience a door through which flattering things may steal in.

### VERSES 12, 13

They said to Lot: “Do you have anyone here who belongs to you—a son-in-law, or sons, or daughters? Bring out of this place all who belong to you. For we are going to destroy this place, because their cry has grown great before the Lord, who sent us to destroy them.”

When our senses fear being seduced by the flattering attractions of the earthly glory that lies before our eyes, by their very passion they teach reason that all the affections of the world must be cut away from them. The sons-in-law are wicked men who, by their examples, advice, or companionship, cast our daughters—that is, our still-weak desires not yet wholly inclined toward God—down before earthly things.

The sons also signify our hope, which is to be transferred into the future: either secular power or the strong works of the world. Hence Job says that he chose death for his bones (Job 7:15), and bones are commonly represented by the person of males. All these are commanded to be expelled from the conscience.

They see that it is impossible to nourish inwardly the fire of desires without allowing the straw placed near the fire of pleasures to be carried away. Let desire be extinguished, and the opportunity for sin will do no harm.

We bring out of the city all who belong to us when we separate the insignia of rationality from the desires of the flesh, as grain from straw. The Apostle says: “Let us go out to Jesus outside the camp” (Heb. 11:34). The senses destroy the place when, as far as they can, they obliterate from themselves the imaginations of worldly things and foreign visions.[^c0014-75]

Our place is this world, in which gold is refined, according to Job (Job 28:1), and which is the valley of tears established by God. They have been sent to destroy it because they were created—or sent forth—from bodily pleasure, in order to exterminate within themselves the appetite for the world. For the howling of an evil desire rises from there to God.

### VERSE 14

And so Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters, and said: “Rise and go out from this place, because the Lord will destroy this city.” But he seemed to them to be speaking in jest.

The sons-in-law may be understood more deeply. We said that the two daughters are avarice and vainglory, because when some people begin to advance in the performance of a good work, they aspire to the ambition of honor, money, or human favor.

These daughters, then, are the fluid conceptions of a fluid mind; their husbands—or rather, the men who violate them—are the acquisition of the desired thing or of external praise. For when we obtain what we desire, we rejoice as though in the fulfillment of lust. The sons-in-law who are going to take the daughters are therefore the fruits of avarice and empty glory, which are expected to come.

We dissuade them from Sodom when we warn them to hope for nothing in the world and not to be disfigured by its likeness. We say that they should rise by casting off sluggishness, and that they should go out by putting away their habits, because in this way the Lord will destroy the love of the world in our affections.

Yet he seems to them to be speaking in jest because the discernment of reason not fully illuminated by God is unable to persuade the movements of the flesh of anything serious, stable, or certain. For the spirit has not been touched by the oil.

Lot goes out to speak these things to them because the spirit, while treating the enticements of the flesh in advance through thought, passes beyond them, even if not through action.

### VERSE 15

When morning came, the angels urged him, saying: “Rise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, lest you too perish in the crime of the city.”

As long as we endure the crowd of the soul’s disturbances while being tempted, it is night for us, and we remain in Sodom—that is, in a certain blindness of mind. But when God’s illumination shines into the breast of the heart, morning comes, and at once we are ashamed of our former thought.

For now we are compelled by the angels themselves—namely, by our senses, which earlier were compelled by the authority of Lot, that is, of reason. They are compelled by the angels when they themselves announce to reason their own necessity: that the senses cannot be restrained from desire while in Sodom, that is, while dwelling amid secular conduct. For no one can fail to burn in the flames.

“Rise, then,” they say, “you leading reason: raise yourself to resist vices. Take your wife—that is, your will—which until now did not allow itself to be held by the yoke of its husband, which is understanding, but was scattered among adulterous loves. Take her, that is, the one who had borne you wrongly, just as the paralytic is told: ‘Take up’ (Luke 5:24). Learn now to govern her.

“And take the two daughters with her, so that you may now desire not earthly things in Sodom but heavenly things in the divine realm, and pursue purity rather than empty external glory, lest you too perish together with the silent beast.”

### VERSES 16, 17

While he hesitated, they seized his hand, the hand of his wife, and the hands of his two daughters, because the Lord spared him. And they brought him outside the city [another reading: “There they spoke to him”], where the Lord had spoken to him.

“Save your life; do not look back, and do not stand anywhere in the surrounding region, but save yourself on the mountain.”

We hesitate when we postpone the good that our senses and imaginings announce ought to be done for our spirit, even though it is troublesome. They seize the hands of him, his wife, and his daughters when the weakness of doubtful thought and sensuality strongly relies upon the help of reason, good will, and a pious eagerness for holy works, together with hope not of vanity but of eternity. Thus they are placed outside the city, and thus they are alienated from the desires of the world.

“Save,” the Lord says to reason, indicating what must be done, “your life. Do not look behind you”—that is, do not return to the things to which, by despising them, you turned your back [possibly: “to which you yielded”]. Do not be in contact with the matter of the vices you rejected. For example, do not be related to women, because through them you relapse into something worse.
