But move to the mountain—that is, strive upward into whatever height of virtue you are able to reach—lest, from proximity to evil, an opportunity contrary to your salvation arise.

### VERSES 18, 19, 20, 21

“I cannot,” he said, “be saved on the mountain, lest evil perhaps seize me and I die. Here is a city nearby to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not little, and will my life live?”

“Behold,” said the Lord, “I have also received your request in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken.”

“I cannot be saved on the mountain,” that is, in an excessively arduous work of holiness, lest the evil of pride or apostasy seize me. While I attempt to take a burden upon myself, may I not be driven backward and find a fall.

“There is a city nearby”: a humble steadfastness of repentance lies ready within the power of choice. Although it is small and not excessively austere for my capacity, there I shall grasp salutary refuges. “Is it not little?” As if he were saying: “If the origin of the first destruction proceeded from pride, will it not be possible to be saved through the lowliness and moderation of humility?”

“Let my life live,” he says: let my life persevere in the condition of some good work.

“I have received,” says the Lord, “your request in this matter”: although it might seem just, if God intended to judge strictly, that one who neglects the good he is able to do should also lose what he does do, nevertheless you avoid such an arduous way of life and pursue what is small—that is, what is moderate.

For the very inclination to repent would rightly be overthrown in a person who does not exercise the other virtues he is able to practice. Since God therefore condescends to our condition, even when it is lukewarm, he clearly indicates that, when he bestows upon us the grace of compunction, he does not reject the little that we accomplish. Thus he does not overthrow the city we choose, even though it is small.[^c0014-76]

### VERSE 22

“Hurry and save yourself there.”

That is: if you choose what is small, at least be diligent and active in carrying it out, hastening to secure the place in which you may be saved.

“I cannot do anything until you enter there.”

For as long as we delight in yielding to vices and in keeping bestial silence in Sodom, God cannot accomplish any work of virtue in us. For, as it is said to the sons of Zebedee, “to sit at the right or the left” (Matt. 20:23) is not his to give to us in our pride.

First, as he says elsewhere, he casts out demons, and only then completes healings; and this could in no way happen unless the demons had been expelled. There is no hearing unless deafness is first excluded.

Let us therefore enter the refuge of holy moderation, so that, once the obstinacy of sin has been renounced, God—who cannot do anything unjust—may be able to apply to us the medicine of virtues. For it would be unjust if God were to dwell together with a person whom the devil possessed. In this respect, therefore, God is wholly unable to act.

That is why the name of that city was called Segor: “The sun went out over the earth, and Lot entered Segor.” Segor is interpreted as “southern” or “small”: small on account of humility, southern because of the shade it provides amid the heat of vices. For the virtue of the Most High, which overshadows us, descends only upon the humble and the quiet. This spiritual fortification to which we flee is rightly marked by that name.

### VERSE 23

The sun—that is, the fervor of temptation arising from the corruption implanted in the body—goes out over the earth, that is, toward the activity of bodily impulses, whether we wish it or not. But Lot, namely our reason, enters beneath a kind of shelter, Segor—that is, humility.

### VERSES 24, 25, 26

Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven. And he overthrew those cities, the entire surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and everything green upon the earth. But his wife, looking behind her, was turned into a pillar of salt.

The Lord rains upon Sodom and Gomorrah when, through the instillation of heavenly admonition, he shows us that the stench signified by sulfur and the torment signified by fire are present in the blindness and rebellion of vices.

The good that is in us, insofar as it is good, is as God dwelling within us. Therefore the Lord—that is, the goodness dwelling in us—draws from the Lord and rains upon us from heaven, namely, through reason touched by God, in order to overthrow the demons who inhabit the cities, that is, our senses.

“Every surrounding region” signifies the world’s affinity; “everything green upon the earth” signifies every delight of earthly hope. Through this infusion of knowledge God extinguishes them and clearly shows how foul and tormenting are the cares of crimes.

Lot’s wife looks behind her when the good will that had formerly rested upon reason from the depths grows lukewarm in its desire for the pleasures of the world that it had rejected. She looks behind her when, falling away from the state she had begun, she desires something beneath her.

But she is turned into a pillar of salt when salutary wisdom, observing this dullness of apostasy, rebukes it within her. For to recognize fully one’s own stupidity, which the pillar signifies, is the greatest part of knowledge, and this is indicated by salt.

### VERSES 27, 28

Abraham rose early in the morning at the place where he had previously stood with the Lord. He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole land of that region, and he saw the smoke rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace.

Abraham rises in the morning when, with God illuminating him, the mind lifts itself to contemplate higher things, returning to the same state in which, concerning the disposition of good minds, it had contended with the Lord through the degrees of numbers. Hence the mind now receives again the name Abraham, “father of the seeing people.” Until now it had been called Lot, from the time when, bound to integrity, it had begun to decline.

He stands with the Lord when, through uprightness of soul, he does not dissent from him. He looks upon Sodom and Gomorrah and the land of the region when, divinely illuminated, he perceives the turbulence of crimes, the blindness of a reprobate sense, and the surrounding matter of both.

He sees the smoke rising from the earth when he now understands that the compunction of repentance rising from the innermost conscience is necessary to him: it is, as it were—or rather truly—the smoke of a furnace, a sign of ardor and inward torment.

“Touch the mountains,” it says, “and they will smoke” (Ps. 143:5), that is, they will release the pain of the heart through tears.

### VERSE 29

When, therefore, God overthrew the cities of that region—that is, when he demolished the strongholds of the devil’s vices dwelling in man—he remembered Abraham. He caused reason to remember its dignity, and he graciously rescued Lot, namely the humanly fallen part, lest it be overturned into a reprobate mind through the vices to which it had been subjected.

### VERSE 30

Lot went up from Segor, and his two daughters with him, for he had been afraid to remain in Segor. He himself and his two daughters remained in a cave.

Lot goes up from Segor when the human intellect, fearing human shame—lest its human fall be publicly exposed as a disgrace—fears remaining in the way of life that is less demanding, and is promoted to a more excellent institution of conduct, as to a mountain.

This unworthy inclination, which we have preferred, is marked by the destructive cohabitation of the two daughters whom we have explained. For the reasons already stated, he passes from the lukewarm way of life, remaining in it as though fearful, that is, from Segor, to the mountain. Yet there he is destined to live in a cave, which is the dwelling of wild beasts and robbers, because cruel desires never leave one to whom such daughters offer their companionship.

### VERSE 31

The elder said to the younger: “Our father is old, and no man remains in the land who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole earth.”[^c0014-77]

The elder is rightly understood altogether as vainglory. When it performs some good work, it does not do so so that God may be glorified, but, as if through a kind of idolatry and sacrilege, so that a human being may be honored perversely.

Vainglory therefore speaks to desire when it suggests that what cannot be seized by force can be acquired through the simulation of holiness.

“Our father”—that is, the mind, which in its own ruin begot such daughters through carnal affection—“is old”: he is inclined toward ancient and temporal things. “And no man remains”—no fully intellectual impulse, that is, none of the impulses that govern our affective softness—“in the land,” namely in the once-fruitful and cultivated conscience, “who can come in to us,” breaking into the obstinacy of the eager heart in order to overturn us, “according to the custom of the whole earth,” that is, insofar as, or according to what, the former custom of the whole conscience would need to be restored.

Reason could indeed enter to rebuke anyone’s mind, but it does not easily enter to renew the way of life.

### VERSE 32

“Come,” she said—“listen, you desire, since you cannot use force to obtain the things you want; come, then, use my services secretly. Let us make him drunk with wine,” that is, let us fill the mind with the joy of temporal pleasure; “and let us sleep with him,” that is, let us overwhelm his foresight with the sleep of complete forgetfulness and negligence, “so that we may preserve offspring from our father,” that is, so that we may draw from his mind inclined toward the affections of such offspring the fruit of some temporal advantage, or the pleasure of some sin to be repeatedly produced through frequent propagation, after the manner of a woman.

### VERSE 33

And so they gave their father wine to drink that night.

This night is the affection of conceived wickedness. The elder enters and sleeps with her father when empty glory, having drawn the whole assent of reason to itself, abuses the mind, which has entirely forgotten itself.

Hence it is said that he did not perceive his own guilt with distress when he lay down, that is, when he bent his heart toward wickedness; nor when he rose, that is, when he raised himself to boldness in the accomplishment of the crime.

The elder—vainglory—also impels the younger, clearly desire, to sleep with the father. For after some wretched person has seen himself prospering through hypocrisy, he begins, under a concealed pretense, to grow unrestrained toward the madness of open desire; and with a blinded heart he allows himself to be entangled by it.

The second night is the obstinacy of a reprobate sense arising from an ingrained will to sin. For from the image of feigned holiness one very quickly descends to the disgrace of open perversity. Wine, by feigning that temporal glory smiles upon it, drives the soul into the fury of public recklessness, so that it does not perceive the daughters lying with it or rising, and does not grieve with any discernment over the filth that defiles it, nor restrain the minds that rejoice in the same pollution.

The daughters of Lot therefore conceive from their father when the vices implanted in us foster a hope of admitting any form of depravity, after having received that hope from an already wavering mind.

The elder bears a son when vainglory brings what it has wrongly begun to a worse result, and calls him Moab, which means “from the father”—not merely “from her father,” but absolutely “from the father,” that is, from the devil, the author of all iniquity, who chiefly perished and deceived mankind through the type of empty glory.

Moab is also said to mean “outlaw,” because the hypocrite, although he appears to act according to the law, lives alienated from the divine law within himself, and is all the more wicked because, as far as human judgments are concerned, he cannot meanwhile be condemned by any law.

The younger, who is desire, gives birth to Ammon, that is, “son of my people,” namely of the one concerning whom it is said: “Forget your people” (Ps. 44:11), in whom you have certainly accumulated the tumult of vices.

In sons we chiefly place the hope of propagation. But avarice is the propagator of all wickedness, as it were of an infinite people, since it is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10).

Yet how avarice or vainglory can give birth to itself may seem absurd if mothers and sons are taken as referring to the same thing. The explanation, then, is this: the daughters who give birth to males are at first the tender, wavering affections of the mind. These emit acts of great presumption and audacity, and gather around themselves peoples of imitators through the authority of their examples, just as those women produced the Moabites and Ammonites.

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155C] My weariness from the labor is relieved by the fact that I observe my work to be approved by benevolent and learned people. It is no less supported by the knowledge that, if it were possible, its purpose would benefit the whole Christian community. Moreover, whether what I have said proves useful or appears useless, I shall, relying on God’s help, continue what I have begun, judging that I have said nothing contrary to faith or moral honesty.

## CHAPTER XX

### VERSES 1, 2

Abraham departed from there into the southern land, dwelt between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar. And he said of Sarah his wife: “She is my sister.” Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and took her.

It is certain, as we read, that proud minds cast away their innermost things in life to the same degree that they are known to flow away through the shifting movements of external things.

Our Abraham therefore goes out from the valley of Mamre—from the lowliness of humility, in which, dwelling within himself, he enjoyed the light of discernment—now forgetful of his own divine power. He moves into the southern land, to be dried out by the suns of desires, so that he may taste the earth and, saturated there with the waters of avarice and lust, thirst for them again, in accordance with what the Lord says to the Samaritan woman.

He dwells between Kadesh and Shur when, on one side, thought devastates understanding, like a moth moving him away from a devout state, while, on the other, the memory of the past strength he displayed against vices constricts him. For Kadesh is said to mean “the disturbance of a moth,” while Shur means “strength” or “anguish.”

The south may also signify the lukewarmness of the soul, from which a great fervor toward worldly pursuits commonly rises. Hence in Job: “Consider,” he says, “the paths of Teman, the journeys of Sheba” (Job 6:19).

Finally, Abraham sojourns in Gerar when our spirit, growing sluggish in its heavenly desire, wanders amid proud impulses. Gerar is said in Latin to mean “expelling the colonist”; it chiefly signifies pride, through which both angelic and human nature are cast down from their proper region.

Thus Sarah, who is subject—that is, the will properly attached to reason—is admitted as a sister when, with dominion despised, she is summoned into a destructive equality. Nor is it surprising if the will rejects dominion, when reason itself, in its decline, has renounced its own rule.

Abimelech is interpreted as “my father is king,” but he is the king of Gerar. He who is king is himself the father of the pride that casts man out from God: the devil, who is also called the father of lies (John 8:44). “My” refers to those who, through pride and falsehood, belong to him in the worst kind of sonship.

Abimelech therefore sends for her and takes her when, after a modest effort toward religion, the devil suggests to the human will the desire for a kind of precedence now supposedly owed to him.

It is therefore appropriate to note the difference between the two captivities: our spiritual will, like Sarah, is first drawn away by Pharaoh, at the beginning of conversion, into the Egypt of its former worldliness; afterward, by Abimelech, king of Gerar, it is not so much overcome as disturbed and assailed for a time. Hence it is declared untouched by the latter, while the former is not so described.

For the memory of an old habit, recently abandoned, brutally provokes us toward vices. But when people have advanced through ecclesiastical usefulness, desires—arising, as it were, from the side—insert themselves into us under the pretext of acquiring the advancement of others’ benefit, or of pastoral office. There is therefore a great difference between the two.

Sarah is finally taken when the intention of the will is carried away toward this kind of ambition with the favor of reason.

### VERSES 3, 4

But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: “Behold, you will die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” But Abimelech had not touched her.

God comes to Abimelech in a dream when we withdraw our minds from concern for corruptible and external things and are held only by the contemplation of invisible things. In this reflection, with God present, what Gerar is, what the king is, and what that fatherhood is become apparent.

It takes place at night when, in the very light by which he desires to be enlightened, the darkness of pride is perceived intellectually.

“You will die,” he says, “because of the woman whom you have taken”: you will deserve to be condemned to the punishment of death unless you cease giving birth to the offspring of the pride you have conceived, since you have taken the will subject by right to reason’s authority, O proud vanity, to be toyed with in meretricious prostitution.

But Sarah is not touched by the king when the proud appetite does not achieve its desired effect. For the end of knowing is touching; those who attain by whatever means the heights of honor they covet are touched by the king.

### VERSE 5

And he said: “Lord, will you kill a people that is ignorant and just? Did he not say himself, ‘She is my sister,’ and did she herself not say, ‘He is my brother’?”

Touched by divine fear, our stiff-neckedness gathers itself together, bent back upon itself. It gathers itself, I say, when, from the wisdom of the world—which seeks nothing except praise or profit and was scattered outside itself—it is restricted to the happy confession of ignorance that it attains.

“When,” he says, “with you inspiring me, I have blown back whatever I formerly thought arrogantly, and, according to the Apostle, wish to become a fool for God’s sake (1 Cor. 4:10), so that through the cultivation of this ignorance—which nevertheless concerns secular things—I may share in heavenly wisdom, which is the summit of justice: when I have done these things, have I, ignorant in this way and therefore just, deserved to be killed by you, who are justice?

“For if I have sinned, I do not deny the fault. It happened to me through the confusion of the soul, where neither understanding presided nor the will obeyed. Rather, the will had made itself equal to reason by a kinship that was not merely unworthy, and reason itself was excessively and perversely subject to it.

“In the simplicity of my heart and the purity of my hands I have done this.”

“Simplicity” is commonly used for foolishness. “Although,” he says, “I fell into error through dullness of heart—that is, of reason—I nevertheless kept my hand clean, since you preserved me from running into a wicked action.”

### VERSES 6, 7

And the Lord said to him: “I know that you did this with a simple heart, and therefore I guarded you lest you sin against me, and I did not allow you to touch her. Now therefore restore the wife to her husband, because he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. But if you are unwilling to restore her, know that you will die the death, you and all that is yours.”

“Because,” he says, “you sinned through the weakness of the flesh and human foolishness, I guarded you lest you go beyond it into action. For to those who sin knowingly, the pit of ruin lies open through pride. But make the wandering will submit its neck to its husband, understanding, because he is a prophet—that is, the chief provider for inward and outward welfare.

“When, freed from carnal affection, he has sharpened his intellectual power to provide for himself, whatever he does and whatever he considers will be worthy of prayer and of the reward of life. But if you delay, you will fall into the insensibility of obstinacy and impenitence, which is the death of the soul, and if any good has remained with you, you will lose that as well.”

### VERSE 8

Abimelech rose immediately in the night, called all his servants, and spoke all these words in their hearing. And all the men were greatly afraid.

Abimelech rises in the night when the movement of pride, which truly comes from the devil as father, lifts itself from the darkness of conceived avarice, which blinds prudent minds. He summons his servants—that is, the thoughts that serve him in suggesting vanities—to think rationally, and he tells them intellectually what God has made known to him by inspiration, so that he may instill divine fear in them.

### VERSE 9

He also called Abraham and said to him: “What have you done to us? How have we sinned against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin? You have done to us things that you ought not to have done.”

Abraham calls when he sharpens all the powers of understanding in order to illuminate himself.

“Consider,” he says, “what you have done. Since it is your responsibility, by the natural liveliness of your intelligence, to restrain animal and bodily disturbances, we have not sinned against you by exceeding humanly in these movements as much as you have sinned against us. By the authority of your free choice you ought to have ruled us.”

As if he were saying: “If you ought not to have admitted me—that is, the movement of pride—for a time, why did you admit its kingdom of condemnation? Therefore a great sin has fallen upon you, not so much because you received me as because, through the long duration of your counsel, you received the kingdom of pride.”

### VERSE 10

“What did you see,” he said, “that you did this?” That is: what account do you offer for this wrongful consent of yours?

### VERSES 11, 12

Abraham said: “I thought within myself, saying: Perhaps there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife. Yet in another respect she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father and not the daughter of my mother, and I took her as my wife.”

The place that has no fear of God is our heart, withered by lukewarmness. It dares neither to rule nor to defend the marriage of the will, because it fears being killed by the force of temptations.

Yet he says: “I do not deny that she is, in a certain sense, my sister,” because, through propagation from the devil as father, like Belial—that is, “without a yoke”—I allow the will to go free. But she is not the daughter of my mother, eternal wisdom, from whom I took a wife. The original teachings of that wisdom instruct me that I ought to have her not as an equal or a mistress, but as a wife, with marital severity.

### VERSE 13

But after God led me out from my father’s house, I said to her: “You will show me this kindness: in every place into which we enter, say that I am your brother.”

We are led out of our father’s house when we depart through confession from a conscience conformed to the devil as father.

We say to our will that it should show us kindness when, as if reasoning with it, we suggest that it should not seize an excessively arduous rule of life. Hence it is said that it enters a place: when a languid mind begins to undertake the purpose of some humble way of life, without any desire for improvement, it wants to remain within that very thing as if within a fixed place, and from there it often happens to relapse shamefully because it is unwilling to progress.

The will shows kindness when it favors a relaxed reason.

### VERSES 14, 15

Therefore Abimelech took sheep and oxen, servants and maidservants, and gave them to Abraham. And he restored his wife Sarah to him and said: “The land is before you; dwell wherever it pleases you.”

Abimelech takes when the devil, the kindler of pride, or pride itself, does not resist the reason that is taking. Hence it is said: “He did not open the prison to his captives” (Isa. 14:17), which means that he shut it.

Reason takes sheep when it entirely withdraws from the intention of attaining honor the benefits of charity, which “covers a multitude of sins” (James 5:20), aptly signified by wool-bearing flocks.

We call oxen the exercise of preaching. Servants and maidservants signify strong and weak concerns of thought inclined toward the world. For one thing we can handle through force, another by serving fragile flattery.

He gives these to Abraham when he no longer opposes the spirit that wishes to possess them. He restores the wife when he ceases from irritating that very will.

“The land,” he says, “is before you”: the freedom of conscience is available to your choices. Live in whatever purpose of holiness pleases you, and dwell there.

### Verses 16–18

But he said to Sarah: “Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother. Let this be for you a covering of the eyes before all who are with you, and wherever you go, remember that you have been exposed.” When Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his slave women, and they gave birth. For God had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.

Abimelech says this to Sarah when, ceasing from his own assault, he allowed her to see what lay beneath the events through their evident effects: “Listen, you,” he says, “will, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother”—that is, while ceasing from every suggestion of covetousness, I have not refused you, who are joined by kinship to the intellect, the opportunity to reject the whole of earthly wealth. This renunciation will be a protection not so much of possessions as of desires, a defense for your eyes—that is, for your intentions—so that they are not burdened by the rheum of cares; and so that all who are with you, namely, the rational movements of your soul, or the pursuits of virtue that are present with us as though they were familiar companions, may be covered by this refuge of immunity. Whatever purposes of piety you pursue, and even if you should at some time reach a lofty height of holiness, nevertheless, separating yourself from my region, which you once experienced, remember that you have continually rushed into the chasms of pride.

We take “a thousand pieces of silver” as signifying the fullness of all earthly substance, as in: “A man brings a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit” (Song 8:11). Abimelech gives them when he does not disturb [the soul].

Abraham, moreover, prays for Abimelech, and the Lord heals him, his wife, and his slave women, when our spirit, on account of the assault of pride that it has suffered, entreats God. God heals its movement, together with the desire that was shamefully and fruitlessly laid beneath it, and the enslaved and sordid wantonness, when he calls the animal appetites and lusts together to take greater delight in himself; and they give birth when they conceive a love of doing good. For as long as the will is distracted by adulterous desires, the womb of the household—that is, the entrance of the conscience—is closed against receiving the power of the divine seed.

## CHAPTER XXI

### Verses 1–5

God visited Sarah as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold to her. Abraham called the name of his son, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, when he was one hundred years old; for Isaac was born to his father at this age.

At last, therefore, after these things, God visits the will when it has overcome the impulses of vices from every direction—he who had promised to the one who conquers that he would give him to eat from the tree of life (Rev. 2:7). The will gives birth to a son conceived through spiritual desire when, from an excessive fervor of mind, it recovers a sure hope. We commonly call our hopes “children,” both because of their posterity and because they sustain us when we grow old.

The blessed Antony had already experienced this sure hope, without any further scruple of sin, when he said: “I no longer fear God, but love him.” He gives birth to this hope in old age—that is, after every youthful presumption has been exhausted—and in the fullness of days, namely, in the manifold light of virtues, and at the time God had foretold: that is, when, through contemplation of God, he had assumed the hope of attaining perfection.

This hope is called Isaac by Abraham—that is, by rational insight itself—and is understood discerningly as Isaac, which means “laughter” and “joy.” Through the gift of hope, this is already understood here in pledge, from which it is demonstrated to us that we shall receive the same thing, though far more ineffably, in reality.

Finally, we circumcise him on the eighth day because intellectually we understand that we shall be stripped of all the miseries of passibility only in the resurrection. We do this at the age of one hundred years when, released from the left hand of the present age, we strive to fly forward toward love and hope of the future; this is the transfer of the number to the right. At this age Abraham gives birth to the intellectual substance of spiritual joy; age itself means nothing other than advancement in holiness.

### Verses 6–7

“God,” Sarah said, “has made laughter for me; whoever hears it will laugh with me.” And again she said: “Who would have believed Abraham that Sarah would nurse a son whom she bore to him when he was already old?”

“Rightly,” she says, “shall I call him this,” since in this Egypt—the place of sorrow and distress—God has now made me taste beforehand the eternal joys that are to come. Whoever hears—that is, whoever tastes the same thing with the palate of the heart—will certainly not be unwilling to share in my genuine joys.

“Who,” she says, “could have supposed that reason, once prostituted in the mockery of sin, could have come to taste heavenly things so deeply; and that the will, which was accustomed to serve the mind the poison of every lust from the breasts of sensuality, would now desire to nourish, as though with the purest milk, a longing conceived through the brightness of Scripture—that longing which it has now brought forth for its own spirit by willing only what is pious and holy, having become barren of every conception of earthly frivolity?”

### Verse 8

The child grew and was weaned; and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.

There are two poisonous breasts by which the perversity of our affection is nourished: sensuality, inclined toward the sight of bodily things, and the imagination of that sight, much worse than the open sight of the present object. There are also two other breasts by which the beginnings of the inner person are advanced toward maturity: either the two Testaments, or the twofold commandments of love. Through their use, while spiritual Isaac grows in holy infancy, he is advanced toward tasting the sweetness of the very bread of angels, once the inertia of his original childishness has been removed.

The day of weaning is the illumination of divine contemplation, where that ineffable banquet takes place—not now with the simplicity of milk, but with the provision of eternal solidity. For then the Lord sups with us, and we with him.

### Verses 9–11

When Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with Isaac, she said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” Abraham took this very hard because of his son.

During the times of our spiritual infancy, as long as we need milk, Hagar the Egyptian—that is, worldly affection—appears before us. She has a son because she is not without some worldly hope; we have often said that hope is received through children. He plays with Isaac because he turns the glory of our spiritual desire toward empty and frivolous things.

But the freedom of the holy will, unwilling that the joy of the spirit should be destroyed, commands that affection for the world, together with its hope, be excluded by the authority of reason, which is Abraham. Reason nevertheless takes this hard, because although the will is inclined toward it, it finds no power to cast away what it has begotten. For it is often drawn along by hope, even false hope. Yet the son of the slave woman is rightly cast out, because the reward of the heavenly kingdom is diminished to the degree that servile hope has withdrawn from love of it.

According to the Apostle, therefore, he must be crucified to the world (Gal. 6:14); but first the world itself must be crucified to him.

### Verses 12–13

“Let it not seem grievous to you,” God said, “because of the boy and because of your slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for in Isaac shall your seed be called. But I will also make the son of the slave woman into a great nation, because he is your seed.”

Even if, he says, you are dragged along by the chain of affection and are troubled by empty hope, do not take it bitterly that all this must be cut away. Carry out the force of the spiritual will as it has admonished you, knowing that, from the desire of eternity, the fruit of unfailing joy is called forth from Isaac and nowhere else.

The son of the slave woman, although still uncultivated, may aspire to what lies outside; but once he has become your seed—that is, once he has shown himself capable of everlasting fruit and has ceased wanting to sow carnal things—he will become, through thought, speech, and action, a great nation of honorable pursuits.

It should be noted, however, that hope of producing fruit is also commonly both seed and fruit.

### Verse 14

Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin of water, and placed them on her shoulder. He handed over the boy and dismissed her. When she had departed, she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.

Abraham rises early when our spirit, from the divine light, is raised from its own torpor to restrain the mind’s fluctuations. He places bread and a skin of water on her shoulder when the mind depresses the harshness of worldly affection, as though beneath a yoke, with the nourishment of divine love and the moderation of saving knowledge.

The skin is not inappropriately taken as a sign of temperance. Hence God is said, as though in a skin, to have established the waters of baptism; according to the condition of those who receive it, he both pours out and retains its grace. Water commonly signifies knowledge, and bread, love.

He hands over the boy and dismisses her when he rejects every hope, together with all his depraved affections. As she departs from us, she wanders in the wilderness because, once the mind has become solitary and withdrawn from occupations, carnal appetite totters, having no seat in the heart where it may rest locally.

Thus the spirit expelled from a person is said to walk through waterless places, through the strong dispositions of the mind in every virtue (Luke 11:24). Beersheba is interpreted as “well of fullness,” for once the well—that is, the depth of desires—has reached the fullness of satiety and the mind has recoiled from it, then the mind can become solitary within itself and be free for God.

### Verses 15–16

When the water in the skin had been consumed, she cast the boy under one of the trees that was there. Then she went and sat opposite him at a distance, as far as a bowshot.

The water in the skin is consumed when the power of knowledge and discernment in the mind is weakened. A certain movement resembling despair, and a failing arising from that despair, commonly emerges in the soul after worldly affection—Hagar, namely, together with her son—has begun to be rejected. For it observes the difficulty of pursuing heavenly things and gravely fears the scarcity of earthly things.

She therefore casts the boy under one tree when she places her hope by relying on the person of some powerful individual—or, to follow the historical sense, casts him down through apostasy from her first good will, as though, raging and falling away from God, she submits herself to some human being as though he might better help her.

A tree, taken singly, signifies a person. Hence in the Apocalypse the four angels are restrained so that the wind should not blow upon any tree (Rev. 7:3). It is therefore appropriately said of the tree that it was there, since things that are nearby, that can be held in the present, and that can immediately be brought to bear upon our affairs, are more readily loved than eternal things.

She departs, then, from the beginning of her good purpose and sits opposite, at a distance, when the condition of the conscience is bent in expectation of temporal gain. It becomes “as far as a bowshot” because, although she sits in a transient state and gazes greedily, she nevertheless restrains herself from the appetite by which she is drawn, checking herself through reason out of fear of God, as far as the judgment of reason can determine by expression. Reason is signified by the bow because it sends forth what it senses as though it were an arrow toward a definite target.

### Verse 17

For she said: “I shall not see the boy die.” And sitting opposite, she raised her voice and wept. God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of the Lord called Hagar from heaven.

The boy dies when hope directed entirely toward worldly things is utterly destroyed. She therefore does not wish to see the boy dying when carnal affection, not ignorant of divine fear, cannot endure to pursue the world with total hope for its own destruction, while heavenly things are despised.

The voice is carnal appetite, the desire for worldly gain. She raises this voice when she exalts her desire from temporal to eternal things. Yet she sits opposite because, although according to human weakness she sees herself bent down by an unworthy sitting toward the depths, where she ought to have stood in battle, nevertheless, according to the will of reason, she cries out against them.

She weeps when, through the continual anguish of the soul, she pours out from herself the waters of her inward fluctuations.

It should be noted that God is said to have heard not the mother’s voice but the boy’s, because God habitually hears not the appetite moved by the flesh, but the hope that is intent upon the poverty of the spirit and is already being deprived of the joy of the present age.

For when the poor person is anxious and pours out his prayer before God, according to the title of the psalm—“The prayer of the poor man, when he is troubled and pours out his supplication before the Lord” (Ps. 101)—it reaches God as a cry (ibid., v. 2).

Hence the angel of the Lord calls Hagar from heaven, because the divine word, announcing all that is good, resonates from the sublime mystery of sacred Scripture with the things taking place within us and questions us about our condition. This heaven is stretched out like a skin (Ps. 103:3).

“What are you doing, Hagar?” he says. “Do not be afraid.” It is as though he were saying: Consider that God will be a helper to those who place their hope in him, and therefore do not fall away from him through any movement of want. Continue, then, what you are doing.

“For the Lord has heard the voice of the boy from the place where he is.” It is heard when the desire of our will, wishing to raise hope from the depths, is kindly received by God from the position of good intention—which is our place and ought to be our place. While we stand there, we move toward true being.

### Verse 18

“Rise,” he says, “take the boy and hold his hand, for I will make him into a great nation.”

Rise from the distrust of hesitation; lift hope from the depths to the heights. Let perseverance be in the hand of that higher hope—that is, in the strength of self-restraint—for by such actions it must be extended into the branches of holy works.

### Verses 19–21

God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the skin, and gave the boy a drink. God was with him; he grew, remained in the wilderness, and became a young archer. He dwelt in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

God opens her eyes to see the well of water when he uncovers the veil of the mind so that it may perceive and taste Christ, who is the fountain of living water and the source of wisdom and knowledge, and who wished us to learn nothing from him except that he is gentle and humble in heart.

Approaching him with the full reach of her desires, she fills the skin—that is, she restores the powers of knowledge within the mind, which has now become temperate. She gives the boy drink when, affection having been turned toward God, the same gift of grace is bestowed upon the desires of our hope that burn with longing.

God is with him because, when affection turns solely toward the love of piety, devotion immediately accompanies hope inseparably. For what you despair of being able to attain, I am surprised if you can long for very long. Hope grows from transitory things toward eternal things, and it remains in the wilderness when it removes from itself the noise of conscience so that it may extend itself toward God alone.

From this he becomes a young archer when, through experience of such events, the intellect of our hope becomes subtle and articulate in discerning spirits. For when the wood of the body is bent by the string of reason, the power of spirituality is sharpened and directed like an arrow toward a definite judgment.

Nevertheless, although it now desires the quiet of solitude, it sometimes dwells in the wilderness of Paran and endures the exceedingly troublesome horror of the ferocity of vices. For his mother, his desire—the desire that once gave birth to him in sins—took for him a wife from the land of Egypt, namely the flesh, by whose blandishments the rigor of the mind may be softened; she brought it close, oppressed by every tribulation because of the weight of its earthly nature. She brings it close, certainly, because she drives it toward evil with unceasing goads.

Paran is interpreted as “their ferocity”; Egypt, as “tribulation that constricts.”

### Verses 22–23

At that same time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham: “God is with you in everything that you do. Therefore swear to me by God that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my stock, but that, according to the mercy that I have shown you, you will deal with me and with the land in which you have lived as a resident alien.”

The glory of victory is always closely allied to pride. When the breeze of reputation has begun to circulate, the power of vainglory attacks the mind. At that same time, therefore—that is, in the very condition of the victorious soul, when it has boldly raised itself against the evils mentioned above—Abimelech and Phicol speak to Abraham, namely pride and vainglory, through spiritual suggestion.

“God,” they say, “whether prosperity or adversity comes upon you, works together for your good. You should know that no assault of vice can bring upon you a ruinous or hopeless danger, since you have been granted victory by God amid so many attacks upon the mind.”

“Swear by the Lord,” which is to say: Since you experience such clemency from God toward you, receive the glory of your reputation confidently, since it flies through everyone’s mouth, as one who can know for certain that you are praised not without God’s will.

Therefore, “by the Lord”—that is, by the confidence through which you rely upon God—“promise me,” says Abimelech, who is pride, that you will harm neither me, by destroying me in your works, nor my descendants, namely praise, which follows works, by casting it away, nor my stock, namely intention, which is the root of works, by extinguishing it.

Abimelech is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father,” which is pride, over which the devil reigns. Hence it is said: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25).

Phicol means “mouth of all”; by this is understood empty glory, which seeks to celebrate itself through everyone’s mouth. Glory is also commonly defined as frequent report about someone accompanied by praise.

Abimelech acts mercifully toward us when he suggests an abundance of temporal glory. We minister the same thing to him when, with perverse delight, we favor the swallowing of honors.

We show mercy to the land in which we have lived as resident aliens when we indulge care for our body, in which, during the times of our abstinence, we once behaved not as members of the household but as though we were strangers and resident aliens.

Abraham, therefore—our intellectual faculty—is bent by these suggestions, however simply they are made, and promises that he will act according to them.

### Verses 24–26

“I will swear,” he said. Yet Abraham reproached Abimelech because of the well of water that his servants had seized by force. Abimelech said: “I did not know who had done this. Moreover, you did not tell me, and I did not hear of it until today.”

The well of water is the depth of discernment and understanding. The servants of the king seize it when the wicked works of pride, which serve pride as though it were their king, introduce the blindness of a condemned sense into us.

But when we oppose this proud thought to its suggestion, as though reproving it, it replies that it does not know who has done this, because it does not permit the matter to be attributed to its own guilt. It also declares that it cannot be proved by those arguments that the clarity of the mind has been obscured through it.

It says that it did not hear of it until today because it claims to know and understand nothing except “today”—that is, the light of the false testimony by which divine glorification in its works and the preservation of propriety are alleged, while it is in fact proud and vainglorious.

It hears “today” because it asserts that it understands and does everything simply, wholly, and clearly within itself, without any knowledge of a condemned sense that could be convicted by any evidence.

### Verses 27–28

Abraham took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant. Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs of the flock.

Abraham gives sheep and cattle to Abimelech when our intellect, having admitted the kingdom of pride into itself, delivers to pride for consumption rather than lending it the simplicity of the soul and the benefit of love—both of which are understood in the sheep because of their gentle nature and their provision of wool—and also the labor of preaching, which is signified in the cattle.

The two make a covenant when reason and pride, with the world’s glory smiling upon them, agree irrevocably.

It should be noted that although Abimelech and Phicol are two vices, they are so closely joined that pride can never be separated from vainglory. This is shown especially by the fact that Phicol is called Abimelech’s commander.

Vainglory is recognized as possessing all the forces of pride within itself, since it strives to exalt itself through the pretense of holiness all the more fiercely the more humbly it behaves in human eyes. One who acts falsely acquires more of this evil sickness than one who is openly proud.

By the seven ewe lambs we understand the universal graces of the Holy Spirit. We set them apart when, while the mind is pouring itself out elsewhere, we judge with discernment that these graces must be preserved amid pride and vainglory.

But Abimelech wonders what this separation of the ewe lambs means, because it is clear that the type of pride always suffers indignantly from the companionship of good intention.

### Verses 29–32

“What do these ewe lambs mean,” he said, “which you have set apart?”

He replied: “You will receive seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that they may be a testimony for me that I dug this well.”

Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath. They made a covenant over the well of the oath.

It is as though he were saying: As long as it pleases me to serve your trifles, you will not wrest from my hand—that is, from my spontaneous deliberation—the purpose of my holy and spiritual intention. Rather, you will receive it as a deposit belonging to another, to be preserved and not consumed.

For we knowingly admit certain evils into ourselves, yet do not abandon the intention of a good will. Thus, he says, this pious affection may be a testimony for me, because once I cleansed the fountain of discernment and knowledge for myself, as though it were a neglected pool filled with the debris of carnal things.

That place is therefore called Beersheba, “the well of the oath,” because there the two swore an oath: some evils are deliberately received into the bosom of the mind, yet are rejected in part lest they force it to fall into a condemned sense. The vice promises the conscience that it will in no way advance beyond the rule; the conscience replies that access must not be denied to the arrival of temporal glory, as to something honorable, yet without any guilt of infamy.

But one ought to pay attention to the fact that “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. 5:9). We commonly observe certain people in whom some evils are evident while they nevertheless retain some good things, and we do not consider that it is one thing for them to sin through weakness or ignorance, another for us to sin through proud deliberation, one thing to be harmed by natural vices, another to submit voluntarily to vices that are not natural—namely, pride and vainglory.

“Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4), although through wisdom itself repentance is inspired in the sinner.

The place is therefore called Beersheba while miserable reason strives to establish, as though it were a local condition, this wicked participation of God and the devil within a single soul. But light has no participation with darkness; light plainly flees the darkness of sin.

They make a covenant over the well of the oath when certain people, unwilling to be without vices yet fearing to fall into crimes not because of fear of God but rather because of the world’s disgrace, establish within themselves that these conditions will never remain stable, so that the well of knowledge may not be buried. For this reason both the mind and the vice soon swear oaths to one another that will prove empty.

### From verse 33

But Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, rise and return to the land of the Philistines, because the beginning of sin, once admitted, always rises more powerful through itself, seizing authority over the already captive mind and forcing us to return to the earthiness of the Philistines—that is, to the “drinking of those who fall,” namely those who, intoxicated by the wine of worldly glory, deviate from sound judgment and fall into the deadly perils of evils.

### Verse 33

Abraham planted a grove in Beersheba, called there upon the name of the eternal God, and lived as a resident alien in the land of the Philistines for many days.

Abraham plants a grove when the mind, already fixed in deliberation, gives birth to pleasures belonging to the world’s course—uncultivated thoughts, entangled in inextricable error, and blind thoughts.

Yet he calls there upon the name of God because, returning frequently to his heart, he complains before God about the ruin to which he is now subject against his will. Hence “eternal” is beautifully added, because, although the loosening of this condition seems difficult to him because of the magnitude of his wickedness, he nevertheless remembers the eternal God, who in ancient times performed wonders in such circumstances and does not cease to do so in our own times.

Thus it is said: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8); he will be able to release those bound in this way. Their voice is: “Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. 129:1), and so forth.

He becomes a resident alien in the land of the Philistines for many days because, the more the intellect of divine illumination for knowing God grows within him, the more grievously the mind’s sadness about its prolonged dwelling among vices is revealed.

“I have grown old,” someone says, “among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8). And: “My sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5). “I am a man,” says another, “who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3:1).

## CHAPTER XXII

### Verses 1–2

After these things had happened, God tested Abraham and said to him: “Abraham.” He answered: “Here I am.” He said: “Take your only-begotten son Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of vision; offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall show you.”

From this sequence of events we come to the point at which God tests Abraham. It is well known that here “testing” is understood as nothing other than examination. He therefore tests when, by putting our spirit to the proof amid all these things, he educates and examines it.

It is said in one place that “the righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24:16). According to Jerome, this is understood as meaning that the righteous fall under various assaults of temptation, yet, through the affection of good intention, always rise again to the state of repentance and therefore do not lose the name of righteousness, because they do not cease to guard against sins; through these, once instructed, they subsequently learn to stand firmly.

Therefore no one should wonder, while in these little works we investigate the inner meaning of moral interpretations, that after setting forth the glory of whatever virtues we append the opposition of vices, since the very subject matter of the text seems to smile upon our opinion. No one, I say, should wonder; rather, let him consider the misery of the present life, so that almost nothing of virtue in a human being is left untouched by some weakening of sin at some time.

God therefore tests when he calls Abraham by name. It is as though he were saying: If you desire to advance toward the merit of testing through your own exertion, father of many nations—that is, shepherd of the many thoughts that are the origins of actions—you must first strive to excel.

“Here I am,” he says—that is, I shall not be lacking in carrying out what you command.

“Take,” he says, “the hope which it is fitting for you to pursue with undivided affection, hope that, leaving the depths, will cleave to Isaac—that is, to eternal laughter—and go with the steps of desire into the land”—namely, the solid certainty of vision, that is, divine contemplation.

Although visions ordinarily occur through images of bodies, nevertheless, in prophetic activity, even if they were perhaps—or indeed truly were—displayed through bodily likenesses, as far as those who saw them are concerned, the very images that were shown to others were, for the seers themselves, open contemplations, since through the images they understood fully what was signified.

Hence it is said: “Then you spoke in a vision to your holy ones” (Ps. 88:20). In this vision, which is the understanding of contemplation, we find the land of a firm kind of knowledge, because when we approach its warmth, we immediately become certain about what, while lukewarm, we doubt.

We offer the son as a burnt offering when, smelting hope away from worldly dross in the fire of heavenly desire, we present it pure to God alone by seeking him in our vows and actions.

The one mountain shown to us by God—that is, the singular mountain—is understood as humility. Without it, the land of vision is emptied and the whole devotion of the burnt offering is annulled. Nor is it inappropriate to understand the mountain as humility, since Truth declares that the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Matt. 18:4).

He indicates this mountain to us when he specifically commands the apostles concerning it: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Whoever therefore makes a proper offering should establish the hope that rises from good works upon the excellence of humility as upon a stable foundation.

### Verse 3

Abraham rose during the night, saddled his donkey, and took with him two young men and his son Isaac. When he had cut the wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place that God had commanded him.

Abraham rises during the night when our spirit skillfully extricates itself from the perplexity, darkness, and negligence of its thoughts, which were signified above by the grove.

He saddles the donkey when he continually restrains the wantonness of the body; if allowed to live according to itself, the body would live as a donkey.

He takes two young men with him together with his son Isaac when reason joins will and affection to itself. Unless these two are restrained by the gravity of reason, nothing in a human being is lighter than they; hence Scripture rightly expresses them under the name of young men.

He likewise brings hope—that is, Isaac—with him through the same desire. We cut wood for the burnt offering when we select examples from Scripture by which we may kindle more sharply the desire of the soul.

We go to the place that God commanded when, advancing day by day, we reach the summit of humility.

### Verses 4–5

On the third day, Abraham raised his eyes and saw the place from a distance. He said to his young men: “Wait here with the donkey. I and the boy will hurry there; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

The first day of those who return to their heart is the will to do good. The second is the determination of a fixed purpose, under which profession they are to live. For various wanderings commonly present themselves to such people: the desert, or solitude, or monastic life, or an undertaking involving pilgrimage.

The third day is when, having fixed their purpose, they commit what they have determined to action. On this third day divine grace is especially accustomed to shine upon the minds of converts. On this day the wedding takes place at Cana of Galilee, where, in a marvelous moral sense, water is changed into wine (John 2:9).

On this day, I say, when the piety of desire has broken forth into the fruit of worthy action, the eyes of the heart are lifted from the depths toward the contemplation of higher things, freed from the dross of the world. The place is seen from a distance because, after the waves and present instabilities of misery, the firmest station—God—is perceived through a certain inward taste.

God is the universal place, but especially the place of those who cling to him. He is first seen through faith—that is, believed—and afterward known through contemplation. He is viewed from a distance because whatever is perceived of what God is through human thought is far removed from what God is.

The young men to whom Abraham speaks are our sensuality and imagination. They behave and understand as children and scarcely ever withdraw from consideration of bodily things; hence they are ordered to wait there with the donkey. Because of their excessive weight, they never approach the swiftness of contemplation.

Reason, however, possessing the power to rise to lofty things by a natural wing, hurries there with the boy—that is, with holy hope—through continual growth, while it desires in hope the heavenly goods that it understands.

For the progress of the soul is desire itself. Hope is also so called, as though it were *pes* (“foot”), by which we advance toward God. It is rightly signified by the boy, because just as we hope that a child will grow through the care of nourishment, so no one is unaware that hope advances through good works toward the perfect security of attaining glory.

“After we have worshiped, we shall return to you”—that is, when, having attained something of divine knowledge, we have humbly contracted into ourselves whatever we are, because of its supreme incomprehensibility, we shall return again to understand and handle human things.

### Verse 6

Abraham also took the wood of the burnt offering and placed it upon his son Isaac; but he himself carried in his hands the fire and the sword.

We take the wood of the burnt offering when we gladly receive the words of sacred Scripture, by which, as though with the fuel of true fire, we increase the flames of our devotion.

We place it upon our son Isaac when, to urge our hope toward heavenly joys, we pour the words of sacred discourse concerning heavenly blessedness upon it like oil upon flames.

Abraham carries fire in his hands when our reason wisely displays the fervor of its inward desire through the performance of pious works.

He carries the sword when, even in the administration of virtues, he does not exceed the rule of discernment. For if you offer correctly but do not divide correctly, you have sinned.

### Verses 7–8

As the two continued on together, Isaac said to his father, “My father?” He answered, “What is it, my son?” “Behold,” he said, “the fire and the wood; where is the victim for the holocaust?” “God,” he replied, “will provide for himself a victim for the holocaust, my son.”

The two proceed together when we both hope rationally and reason in accordance with hope, and when, seeking one and the same thing, they act as one. The father of hope is not improperly called the intellect, because we infer from reason the source from which hope proceeds, and, when the breast of charity is offered to it, hope advances from the nature of the spirit. Hope calls upon the intellect when, moved by carnal desires toward despair of heavenly things, it summons the intellect to its aid. The intellect calls hope its son when, by teaching, it determines that hope ought to adhere to it through a kind of natural union, as the condition of uprightness.

[Col. 0169D]

“Behold,” he says, “the fire and the wood,” as if he were saying: “Behold, the fervor of good action lies before me, and the promise of the Scriptures, with testimonies flowing together from every side, shines forth as something great if I persevere. But, with the frost of so many bodily desires rushing upon me, where can that complete consumption of worldly affection be found, and where the heat that kindles the Holy Spirit?”

[Col. 0170A]

The mind itself is the victim, and it is a holocaust when it leaves no vice unconsumed. But when reason lifts up hope, and hope repeatedly takes counsel, and while taking counsel strives to rouse reason, both must necessarily be referred to God, the provider of the victims. For by our free will we both plant and water what has been planted, but nothing that we do among ourselves exists unless God gives the growth by grace (1 Cor. 3:6).

### Verse 9

They proceeded together, then, and came to the place that God had shown him. There he built an altar and arranged the wood upon it.

[Col. 0170B]

They proceed together when, with one and the same intention, they seek heavenly things and God—when the spirit is neither without rational hope nor hope without spiritual uprightness. We come to the place God shows us when, in the vision of God, we pause for a moment, as though in a place, withdrawing from our own wavering. Yet we attain this only when preceded by his illumination.

There we build an altar and arrange wood upon it when, with the gathering of the other virtues lending support, we raise up the devotion of our conscience, and collect sayings of sacred eloquence from every side, piling them upon the altar of the heart so as to kindle it ever more intensely.

When Isaac his son had been bound, he placed him upon the pile of wood.

### Verse 10

[Col. 0170C]

He stretched out his hand and seized the sword in order to sacrifice his son.

We bind Isaac when we fasten hope, placed in heavenly joys, to God alone with steadfast charity. We place him on the altar, upon the pile of wood, when we lay beneath him the foundation of a devout will and the authority of Scripture, more sacred than any altar. For what could give better strength than reliance upon the purity of the mind and divine truth?

We say *extendere*—“to stretch out”—in the sense of stretching beyond. Thus whoever, delighted by heavenly aspiration, attempts the exercise of contemplation beyond his own powers stretches out his hand.

We seize the sword in order to sacrifice the son when we embrace the divine word with such firmness of spirit that we wish, as far as possible, to destroy entirely our use of the present world in the meantime. For although it is said, “Be still, and know that I am” (Ps. 45:11), only harmful things must be discerned and abandoned; this does not mean abandoning care for useful and natural affairs, but rather the sinful passions that must be mortified in the very members upon the earth.

[Col. 0170D]

That little abbot John, who tried to live as an angel, stretched out his hand when he wished entirely to strip himself of human life. He would indeed have sacrificed his son if, by contemplating God alone inflexibly, he had directed the gaze of hope toward God. Hope can be utterly removed from the world, but the contemplation of our hope cannot always be maintained. In this sense, surely, the living creatures return when they move forward.

### Verses 11–12

And behold, the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, saying, “Abraham, Abraham.” He answered, “Here I am.” And he said, “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, and do not do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, and that you have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake.”

[Col. 0171A]

The angel of the Lord calls from heaven when the voice of sacred eloquence, announcing good things to us, resounds from the mystery of Scripture as though from heaven. Sacred Scripture is called heaven because of the divine secrets that it conceals, as in the words, “He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth” (Ps. 146:8).

Here Abraham is called twice, although shortly before he was named only once. This is rightly believed to have a meaning. There he is called once during the testing, so that he may be turned away from the pride he had conceived; here his name is doubled, so that it may be understood not merely that the holy soul has been turned from its torpor, but that it has also attained the glory of justification through a rich devotion to piety. Thus he responds to the one calling him, “Here I am,” showing that he offers the service of due obedience to the words of the sacred page.

[Col. 0171B]

“Do not stretch out your hand against the boy”—that is, do not extend the effort of your contemplation beyond the capacity of your strength toward the weak things signified by the boy. “And do not do anything to him”: when we stretch out our hand against him, namely against the boy, we do something to him; that is, we believe that we can add something from ourselves and from our own virtue to our human weakness, although without God we can do nothing except vice.

Therefore, do not stretch out your hand: that is, do not take upon yourself the burden referred to in the saying of the wise man, “You shall not lift it upon yourself” (Deut. 12:18), lest you soon arrogate something proudly to yourself while seeming to do nothing from yourself.

[Col. 0171C]

“Now I know”—that is, “I have made known to you”—that you fear God, since you were unwilling to spare your only-begotten son; that is, since you have shown that nothing of worldly hope remains within you, but have made hope itself your only-begotten son, wishing to direct it toward no one other than God alone. For we spare our hope when we allow something worldly to remain in it through human weakness.

### Verses 13–14

Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw a ram caught by its horns among the thorns. Taking it, he offered it as a holocaust in place of his son. And he called the name of that place, “The Lord sees.” Hence, even to this day, it is said, “On the mountain the Lord will see.”

[Col. 0171D]

Abraham lifts up his eyes when our spirit raises the acuity of its understanding from its own excessive purpose toward the admonitions of Scripture as it thunders.

He sees a ram caught by its horns among the thorns when, with sacred eloquence prompting him, he subtly understands the stiff-neckedness of pride held fast among the thorns of desires by the horns of assumed power, secretly arising in the mind. Pride commonly steals upon those who wish to contemplate with excessive subtlety—almost from behind, where they pay less attention to themselves. It clings to the desire for honors or praise like a ram entangled in the thorns, hanging by the horns of the desire for power or for worldly mire. Power is customarily signified by horns.

Thus intellectual Abraham scarcely distinguishes this unless he turns back to himself and raises his eyes, weighing what is creeping into him from the very contemplation of God that he longs to contemplate.

[Col. 0172A]

Contemplation, as we have often said, is understood not only as the vision of divine things, but also as consideration of spiritual matters and every examination of truth. In this, when the mind seems to excel itself, it is often pierced, out of a kind of reverence for its knowledge, by pride and the thought of seeking precedence.

We must therefore slaughter this ram of swelling pride and boastfulness in place of the son, while we do not permit the gaze of our hope—as far as active life is concerned—to be extinguished, but consume the vice of pride together with its ambition in a complete burning. Thus we must hope for understanding from God in contemplation without cutting off our concern for active life.

The son would indeed be killed if our hope, directed solely toward heavenly things, failed in the useful affairs of active life. The Lord sees this place—that is, this condition of the heart—and approves it when he slays whatever arrogance arises. Hence those who possess knowledge of divine things today understand with certain discernment that the Lord sees on the mountain, because he exalts with the glory of the future age those established on the summit of humility.

[Col. 0172B]

He sees his own here by approving them through continual assistance; he will see them by crowning them with eternal splendor. Hence it is said: “But I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

### Verses 15–17

The angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son, I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.”

[Col. 0172C]

After the angel’s first call from heaven, which took place after the testing, when, having entered upon conversion, we advanced through the divine words toward justification, we are roused a second time by the same heavenly admonitions of Scripture to the hope of glorification.

God swears by himself when, through the constancy of truth, he establishes in us justice and uprightness. “I am,” he says, “the way and the truth” (John 14:6). Whoever restrains himself from the deceit of sin holds to the truth. Every good has its being in the supreme good; sin, however, has no essence, because “without him nothing was made”—that is, sin was made as nothing, and when human beings sin, they become nothing with respect to true being.

[Col. 0172D]

Because, then, you spared your carnal will in no respect, so as to allow it to rejoice in the hope of worldly good, but directed it toward one God alone, in the manner of a one-horned creature, according to the Psalm (Ps. 91:11); because you performed a deed—that is, you cultivated not the usefulness of the body but of the spirit—in order to produce the fruit of undivided hope, signified by the only-begotten son: “I will bless you,” that is, I will advance you through the effect of every virtue; “and I will multiply your offspring,” namely, I will increase the merits of your works, which here, according to the Psalmist, are sown in tears, with a hundredfold reward (Ps. 125:5), so that you who have been faithful over a few things may be set over many things (Matt. 25:21, 23).

[Col. 0173A]

By the stars of heaven we understand the virtues of the soul. Just as the stars are never separated from heaven in eternal blessedness, so they will not be separable from the minds of the saints.

By the sand of the seashore we understand the body’s freedom from suffering, which will exist after the resurrection. Then, established upon the shore of security and freed from the swell of disturbances, we shall believe that, just as we know salt is made from sand, the entire heaviness and corruptibility of the flesh will be seasoned by the wisdom dwelling within us.

“Your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies.” (Verse 18.) “And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.”

The offspring possesses the gates of its enemies when virtues rule over the vices beneath them. These vices are called gates because through them one enters into association with demons, who are called “enemies” by antonomasia.

All nations are blessed in the offspring when our good works are increased by charity, which is the chief of all seeds. For charity “covers a multitude of sins” (James 5:20), and it is called “the bond of perfection” (Col. 3:14).

### Verse 19

Abraham returned to his young men; and they went together to Beersheba, and he lived there.

[Col. 0173B]

After the subtlety of divine contemplation, we fall back, through a certain unavoidable weakness, into the use of human will and feeling, which infuse us with the lightness of childhood.

Beersheba is said to mean “the seventh well.” We go to the seventh well when we return to the habitual use of the inner and outer senses. From this chasm we frequently draw out the waters of desires arising within us, yet, so long as the creature is subjected unwillingly to vanity (Rom. 8:20), it is never drained completely.

The number seven consists of four, which signify the body, and three, which signify the soul. Through these, with the addition of the well, is understood a depth as unfathomable as an abyss, namely, the inward and outward sensuality.

[Col. 0173C]

We dwell there when we move about in the depths of diverse desires and yet, like masters in a house, suppress their servile tumult by ruling over it. In Scripture, “to dwell” is often used for “to rule.” This is not inappropriate, since *habitare* (“to dwell”) is a frequentative derivative turned from *habere* (“to have”); and we say that we rule those things that we possess. Thus, by dwelling in Beersheba, the seventh well of the familiar senses of flesh and mind, we rule them, restraining their wandering and carrying away for a time our fluid desires, like waters, from the lowest depths.

## Chapter XXIII

### Verses 1–2

Sarah lived for one hundred and twenty-seven years. And she died in the city of Arba, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan.

[Col. 0173D]

Through Sarah, whose name is interpreted as “princess,” the will previously understood by me is recognized, because, imbued with the counsel of reason, it is found to be the beginning of every good action.

One hundred and twenty-seven years express the perfection of knowledge and action. In the hundred, perfection is signified; in the twenty, where the form of the Decalogue is doubled, the teaching and execution of divine law are expressed. The perfection of both is led to the number seven, which is a figure of spiritual gifts, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is known to have descended upon the one hundred and twenty believers (Acts 1:15). For the Spirit rests upon the humble and the one who trembles at the words of God (Isa. 66:2). The Spirit dwells in those who know and do these things, and avoids what is feigned.

[Col. 0174A]

Accordingly, Sarah lives in keeping with what these numbers suggest, because our will rightly exercises rule when it possesses such a condition. But after she returns to Beersheba and is joined to the young men, she descends to die in the city of Arba.

The city is the soul; Arba is said to mean “four.” From animality—that is, from the lowest part of ourselves—we endure the miseries of four passions: fear, desire, joy, and sorrow. When we are occupied with these in a worldly manner, we are wholly distracted from the care of divine worship.

Hebron, or Chebron, is interpreted as “enchanter.” This mournful fourfold power performs the office of an enchanter when it persuades the soul to pursue the thought of any one of these desires. All this takes place in the land of Canaan, because, by stirring up the business of continual restlessness in the earthly mind, these things do not fear to prepare it for perpetual condemnation. Canaan is indeed said to mean “merchant” or “prepared for humiliation.”

[Col. 0174B]

And Abraham came to mourn and weep for her.

Abraham comes when our reason returns from its dispersion to care for itself. He weeps when he sends forth, as though they were waters, the fluid softness within him through the eyes of his intentions. He mourns when, in his outward bearing, he exhibits as though through his voice the anxiety of his heart, by which he sincerely repents inwardly. Many are ashamed to do this openly.

### Verses 3–4

When he had risen from the duty of mourning, he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying: “I am a stranger and sojourner among you. Give me the right to a burial place with you, so that I may bury my dead.”

[Col. 0174C]

We rise from the duty of mourning when, after displaying repentance, we are raised up in the hope of pardon.

Heth is interpreted as “fear” or “stupor.” We speak to the sons of Heth when, with our thoughts—which are, as it were, certain offspring of our mind—we consider the inner benefit of our salvation after those thoughts have been touched inwardly by divine fear and, because they fear being the land of Canaan—that is, being prepared for external and useless humiliation—have been carried by this fear even to bodily stupor.

“ I am a stranger among you,” he says. We are strangers because we have only recently returned to the heart. We are sojourners because we have not yet settled within the bosom of conscience. A sojourner (*peregrinus*) is so called from *peragrare*, “to travel through.”

[Col. 0174D]

We demand from them the right to a burial place when we seek within ourselves the rest owed to us from the natural turbulence of these very thoughts. According to Job, those who dig for treasure rejoice when they find a grave (Job 3:21–22). In accordance with this figure, Mary weeps outside at the tomb (John 20:11).

We bury the dead when we confine within the walls of reason the mind that hopes for nothing in this world and has already been crucified.

### Verses 5–6
