The sons of Heth answered Abraham: “Hear us, my lord. You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs, and no one among us will be able to prevent you from burying your dead in his tomb.”

The sons of Heth answer Abraham when fearful thoughts rejoice together with the counsel of reason.

[Col. 0175A]

“Hear us, my lord,” they say—that is, discern us intellectually. For you exercise the authority of God in our interior life. Hence, in the Apocalypse, you are permitted to sit with God upon the throne—that is, with judicial power—by conquering (Rev. 3:21), when you divide what is useful from what is harmful.

The chosen tombs in which we bury the dead are the secret place of the active and contemplative life, although any virtue by which a person hides from the tumult of vices may be called a tomb.

“If,” they say, “you wish to rule legitimately among us, in agreement with God, no movement of the flesh will be able to prevent you. Once the diseased thoughts have been put to sleep, there will necessarily be no longer any troublesome perverse action that hinders the placing of the dead in the tomb—that is, restraining within the memory, for the incitement of repentance and not for the renewal of wickedness, the license of sin.”

A tomb (*monumentum*) is so called from *monere*, “to admonish,” as though it were *monimentum*. We call sin dead because we have ceased to commit it.

### Verses 7–9

[Col. 0175B]

Abraham rose and bowed before the people of the land, namely, the sons of Heth, and said to them: “If it is pleasing to your souls that I bury my dead, hear me and intercede with Ephron son of Seor, so that he may give me the double cave that he has at the end of his field. I will give him money worthy of it; let him transfer it to me [alternatively, “let him transfer it to me for a worthy sum”] before you, as a possession for a burial place.”

Abraham rises when, from the assent of his thoughts, the intellect raises itself in hope of attaining holiness.

He bows before the people of the land when, with humble devotion, he receives the obedience of a thought that has now become firm.

[Col. 0175C]

“If it is pleasing to your soul,” he says—that is, to this pious courage of yours by which you have aspired to the desire for holy conduct—“that I may shelter my mind from external pressures, hear me,” obey my command, “and intercede with Ephron.” That is, deal with your feeling, which, like useless dust, is cast from the face of the earth by the wind of pride, so that he may give me the double cave: namely, permit me to possess the twofold cavern of sensuality and imagination, which, with a kind of savage greed, longs for bodily things and is incapable of spiritual knowledge.

Ephron is interpreted as “useless dust,” in which is found unstable feeling. He is at the end of the field, namely, among those things that lie externally beside the body.

The field is the body, which must be cultivated by the knife of understanding.

[Col. 0175D]

“I will give him money worthy of it”—namely, that wine of which it is said in the Song of Songs, “Sweet for the beloved’s lips to chew, and for his throat of flavors” (Song 7:9): that is, I will supply him with knowledge of Scripture worthy of every diligence and meditation.

It is always appropriate and salutary for our feeling to attend to this knowledge, rejecting worldly cares, expanding through the many expenditures of interior affairs, and increasing by giving rather than by holding itself back.

“Let him transfer it to me before you as a possession for a burial place”—that is, when the feeling has received the money of the sacred page from me to care for and handle, so that, once it has begun to abstain from outward things, it may devote itself to interior gains. Then that former carnal appetite will transfer it to me—the one who wishes to possess the double cave—and will in no way contradict me, with the whole movement of thought consenting before you to its becoming a possession for a burial place. Thus it may be permitted to preserve safely within the enclosure of conscience the condition of a mind already crucified to the world.

### Verses 10–11

Ephron was dwelling in the midst of the sons of Heth. Ephron answered Abraham in the hearing of all who entered the gate of his city, saying: “By no means, my lord; rather, listen to what I say. I will give you the field, and the cave that is in it; in the presence of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead.”

[Col. 0176A]

Ephron dwells among the sons of Heth when our feeling—which is rightly called useless dust—binds and solidifies itself, through a kind of spiritual moisture, to the judgment of thoughts crushed by divine fear.

[Col. 0176B]

That thoughts may be called “sons” we gather from the word of the wise man, who compares the thoughts of fools to generations of vipers: “They devour the mind, their mother,” he says.

Ephron dwells in the midst because our feeling, relying upon reason, now usefully fortifies and compacts itself with those same thoughts, as a leader with his soldiers.

Ephron answers Abraham when the feeling gratefully accepts the admonitions of reason.

Those who enter the gate of the city hear him when all our animal impulses—which experience the fear of God, the gate to God and to the city of the heart, as they return—obey the purpose of religion.

[Col. 0176C]

“By no means, my lord,” he says. “Do not insist too strenuously that the knowledge of Scripture be commended to me. For even if there were no one to admonish me, I could not in any way be found lukewarm in carrying out the will of God.”

We think such things when, for a time, we are inflamed affectively by spiritual desire. Hence it is added: “Listen to what I say,” because at times he proposes much greater things. When affection burns with novelty for the moment, it proposes more than the spirit, which moderates this excessive alacrity, wishes to undertake.

[Col. 0176D]

“I will give you the field,” he says: “I will subject the body irreversibly to your right; I will grant you the twofold capacity of sensuality and imagination, namely, the double cave, in the presence of the sons”—that is, of the thoughts—“no longer wandering away from their inward care, but standing by and devoted to their pious duty.”

### Verses 12–15

Abraham bowed before the people of the land and spoke to Ephron in the presence of the people: “Please hear me. I will give you money for the field; accept it from me, and then I will bury my dead there.”

Ephron answered: “My lord, hear me. The land you request is worth four hundred shekels of silver. What is that between me and you? Bury your dead.”

[Col. 0177A]

Abraham bows before the people of the land when, with the crowd of thoughts returned from its dispersion, gathered into one, and in a sense brought into his own presence, reason humbles itself before God.

Hence they are called the people of the land when the mobility of our thoughts is stabilized for a time like the earth. This people surrounds him while Abraham speaks to Ephron, because thought, established in the fervor of its devotion, stands round about, guarding its inmost parts on every side and not separating itself from the oracle of reason. It also stands ready to obey the spirit and struggle at every assault of the vices. For “to stand” is, as it were, the proper posture of one who fights.

“Please,” he says, “do not trust too much in your present heat; I beg you, hear me”—that is, do not refuse to learn, be quick to hear, and believe that you can do nothing without the testimony of Scripture. Accept this, then, for the field, so that you may rejoice not in the uncultivated and barren cultivation of the body, but in advancement through spiritual money.

[Col. 0177B]

According to what is written, a shekel contains twenty obols. An obol is named from its resemblance to an obelus, which is an arrow. A shekel, therefore, containing twenty obols, is sacred Scripture, which sets before us the Decalogue of knowledge and the denarius, that is, the perfection of good action. By these arrows the vices of the soul are struck, and by them the mind is again touched so as to be wounded by charity. The number twenty contains twice ten.

Since four hundred contains four times one hundred, and the four Gospels teach renunciation of the world, which is perfection, those who possess the denarii—that is, the perfections—of complete knowledge and integral action through the instruction of the legal Scripture attain the hundredfold of perfection through the sayings of the four Gospels, by denying themselves.

To the young man who had observed the law from his earliest years the Lord says that, if he wishes to be perfect, he should sell what he possesses (Matt. 19:21). He had attended to the Decalogue of external observance, and therefore the arrow of the intellectual Decalogue does not wound him.

[Col. 0177C]

The land of our body is therefore worth four hundred shekels, because it has nothing stable, constant, or strong in itself unless it is redeemed from the dominion of vices by the expenditures of the sacred Scriptures. This is the price between reason and feeling, because whenever the wantonness of carnal feelings bursts forth and improperly seizes the field of the body for its lusts, our spirit has nothing more suitable at hand to set against the appetite of the flesh than the instruction of Scripture.

“But what is that?”—as if he were saying: “Although the testimonies of Scripture may seem to you to abound in some measure against the assault of the body, still, when the appetite has been brought into agreement with the judgment of reason, it is nothing great.”

“Bury your dead,” then: cover the corruptible body with good works, lest, through the relaxation of life, it break forth into the stench of crimes.

### Verse 16

[Col. 0177D]

Abraham heard this when his feeling, in agreement with God, gratefully accepted its goodwill.

He weighed out the money Ephron had requested in the hearing of the sons of Heth, because the intellect proposes to feeling the justice of divine Scripture, by which it ought to direct its life and which, through the obedience of the sons of Heth—namely, our thoughts touched by divine fear—it resolves to follow.

This money is public and approved, because the institutions of the sacred page are questioned by no one except a madman. “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. 18:10).

[Col. 0178A]

The divine law is a kind of currency in which God established everything by measure, number, and weight: number signifies the totality of counsels; measure, the proportion of each thing individually and of all individuals together; and weight—named from weighing—signifies contemplation of that truth which is the end of all things.

“Upon this,” the Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40). It is public because the sincerity of justice can naturally be recognized by the inexperienced and by minds, as it were, belonging to the common people. It is approved because, without external arguments, the purity of sacred Scripture shines forth and stands preeminent by itself.

### Verses 17–19

Thus the field formerly belonging to Ephron was confirmed—the field in which was the double cave facing Mamre, both the field itself and the cave, together with all its trees within all its boundaries on every side—as Abraham’s possession, in the sight of the sons of Heth and of all who entered the gate of his city.

And so Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the double cave of the field facing Mamre. This is Hebron in the land of Canaan.

[Col. 0178B]

The field formerly belonging to Ephron—that is, the body once subjected to the appetite of the flesh—in which the double cave of sensuality and imagination burns with snares of avarice and rapacity, is confirmed as Abraham’s possession when what was observed with difficulty at the beginning of conversion passes into delight through the continual persistence of unremitting devotion.

We appropriately understand the cave as the senses and images, because just as a lion and a robber have learned to hide in caves, so feeling that longs for bodily things occupies the two aforementioned places, within and without, as though they were hollows. It knows nothing except bodily things. From these it emerges to lust; through these bodily desire enters into it to make its suggestion.

[Col. 0178C]

After the weakness of the body has been strengthened by the power of the mind, it faces Mamre, which is interpreted as “divisions” or “clarity.” For once the mind restrains itself from the flow of vices, it attains clarity of division—that is, discernment.

Thus the field itself and the cave, as we have said, are strengthened by inward vigor. The trees also within all the boundaries are made firm: namely, all thoughts that send forth the fruit of pious action and the leaves of holy speech, established in all their intention, which is recognized as a kind of provision for the end in everything we do.

[Col. 0178D]

The sons of Heth see when no movement of thought envies such activities. All who enter the gate of the city—namely, all rational, imaginative, and sensual impulses that gather themselves into the city of God through the gate of divine fear, “for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” and through confession of sins—favor these transactions.

Hence it is said: “His people and sheep, enter his gates with confession” (Ps. 99:4).

[Col. 0179A]

Abraham therefore buries his wife in the cave of the field that faces Mamre when, under the direction of the intellect, sensuality and imagination, tending toward the virtue of discernment and contained beneath the field of spiritual exercise, restrain themselves from the pleasure of visible things and also cherish the will of the inner person, guarding it as though within two enclosures.

“This is Hebron in the land of Canaan.” Hebron is interpreted as “eternal increase” or is said to mean “eternal vision”; Canaan, however, signifies “change.”

Mamre, therefore—that is, the clarity of discernment—reaches toward this end, so that it may become eternal vision and increase forever, when the subtlety of discerning spirits advances all the way to the contemplation of God. This begins here, but rises from a riddle and a mirror toward the increase of eternity, which will be completed when we begin to see face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

This takes place in the land of Canaan, where true change into eternal stability occurs, since nothing mutable is any longer permitted to remain in us in the land of the living.

### Verse 20

[Col. 0180A]

“And the field,” he says—that is, the body, already made firm by long vigilance against the passions under the dominion of Abraham, namely, of reason—“was confirmed,” and the cave of conscience, in no way murmuring against the rule of justice, was established as a possession by right of a tomb. Thus they may continually admonish the memory of the mind concerning the profession it made of its own mortification of the flesh and may recall its purpose. For a tomb both covers the dead and takes its name from admonishing.

## The Sixth Book Ends

## The Seventh Book of the Morals on Genesis Begins

[Col. 0179]

[Col. 0179B]

### 92

As I undertake, with God’s help, the seventh treatise in Genesis, I beg the presence of the Holy Spirit. I also humbly ask my reader that, if he should notice anything set forth less clearly than it ought to be, supported by fewer examples from Scripture than he might wish, or compressed with excessive brevity, he graciously forgive my inexperience. In this first little work of mine I wished rather to discover what I might be able to do, and I undertook these things solely for my own benefit—or rather, I did not wish to forge them, but to touch upon them in summary so that, when I reread them, I might restore them to memory.

I could plainly have strengthened many things with testimonies, but, impatient of delay, I was unwilling to do so. Let us therefore gird ourselves with the sevenfold Spirit for what remains.

## Chapter XXIV
[Col. 0179C] **VERSES 1, 2, 3, 4.**—“Now Abraham was old and advanced in many days, and the Lord had blessed him in all things. And he said to the elder servant of his household, who was in charge of everything he possessed: ‘Place your hand beneath my thigh, so that I may bind you by the God of heaven and earth, that you may not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell; but that you may go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac.’”

After Sarah has been buried in the manner we noted, our intellectual Abraham grows old through the gravity of his conduct and becomes white with the days of many virtues; and the Lord pours into him every blessing, namely, an increase of spiritual gifts. If, then, Abraham is understood according to the meaning inferred from his name, what is better expressed by the elder of the household, who is in charge of all his own, than the desire to do good? Once this desire has been joined by diligent service to the maturity of reason, it is found to be, as it were, the guide and teacher of all that we do piously.

By Abraham’s thigh we understand the propagation of spiritual understanding, which is enlarged in the mind through divine readings and the experience of a long way of life. “Place,” he says, “your hand beneath my thigh”—that is, press down the power of your good eagerness, by which you long for holy actions, beneath the understanding of my intelligence, because you must expect the force of your activity from the origin of rational knowledge, so that no presumption of empty alacrity may steal upon you. The thigh, indeed, is recognized in some way as the source of propagation; through it the seat of understanding itself—not unfittingly called truth—is received by us. Therefore our desire is adjured by the God of heaven and earth, because through the humble lowering by which it bends itself toward supreme truth it establishes law and rectitude, through knowledge of him “who gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. CXVIII, 130). He is the God of heaven, that is, of our intellectual nature, illuminating it by his own radiance; and through that heaven he supplies the rains of sacred instruction to the earth, namely, to the pious desire itself.

He adjures it not to take a wife for his son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom he dwells—that is, not to mingle a fickle will, according to the desires of worldly people destined for eternal condemnation, with humility prepared for them and with hope once fixed in heavenly joy, as though joining it to his son Isaac, so that it might turn its eyes from the daughters of Jerusalem toward the Canaanite women. A son has a wife when hope of heavenly things lifts the will above earthly things, so that it wills by deed, not by word, what it hopes for. But he joins a Canaanite daughter to himself when heavenly alacrity lowers itself to the softness and wantonness of the world.

We go to the land to take a wife from Abraham’s kindred when, striving toward the soul’s impassibility insofar as possible—which is true stability, for this is what “land” signifies—we desire spiritually to live in conformity with our mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, with whom our outward human self, while living rightly, possesses a kindred relationship. Hence we pray that God’s will be done “in heaven as on earth” (Matt. VI, 12). We take a wife from that kindred when, moved by the desire to live blessedly, we embrace the grace of a pious will above all else.

**VERSES 5, 6.**—“The servant answered: ‘If the woman is unwilling to come with me to this land, must I bring your son back to the place from which you departed?’ Abraham said: ‘Beware that you never bring my son back there.’”

Abraham speaks to the servant when reason instructs the desire about whatever must be done. The servant of Abraham answers here when, in response to what the spirit suggests should be undertaken, he objects with the obstacles he expects, believing that the desired results cannot be supplied to his will. The woman is unwilling to come with him to the land when soft and shifting thought chooses rather to be carried about by the whirlwind of worldly affairs than, with the fluctuation of the passions stilled, to be stabilized in the likeness of land.

The son is brought back to the place from which he departed when our hope, because of some breath of temptation, falls back from heavenly things through despair into its former condition of worldly desire, from which it once departed at the time of conversion. Why we understand “son” as hope, we have explained above: we place hope in both propagation and consolation, and therefore in common usage we also call those who are hoped for “sons.” Hence the Psalm: “And may you see the sons of your sons” (Ps. CXXVII, 6), that is, the fruits of your hopes.

“Do not,” he says, “turn the gaze of my hope back toward the whirlpools of former pleasures, because”—**VERSE 7**—“the Lord God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore, saying, ‘To your offspring I will give this land,’ he himself will send his angel before you, and you will take a wife for my son from there.”

It is as though he said: God, who builds me up by intellectual light, who took me from the consciousness of sin in which the devil’s authority dwelt while I conformed myself to him as to a father—or from worldly conduct; for “the prince of the world” is said to guard his own court (Luke XI, 21)—and from the earthliness in which and toward which we were born from that same devil as father; he who spoke inwardly to me through the bestowal of hope, and swore—that is, established me by right within Christianity, promising by an inward pledge to my offspring, namely, to the merit of your good action, which you have sown in hope of eternal fruit: “I will submit the weight of this earthly body of yours, so that it may experience the grace of spiritual alacrity.”

God, he says, who has done these things and promised that he would do them, will himself send before you the angel of his divine utterance, who announces what must be done. That is, he will make him your guide; and from there, from his instruction, you will see which will you ought to choose, of the body or of the soul, to be joined, as it were, to your hope.

**VERSE 8.**—“But if the woman is unwilling to follow you, you will not be bound by the oath”—that is, if seductive and wanton thought refuses to be corrected according to the desire for the justice you possess, and exceeds the law and rule of truth, you will no longer be bound to it; rather, unbridled and wandering, you will slip through every vice. “Only do not bring my son back there.” This means: Even if you refuse to be held by the reins of divine law, at least do not cast hope down entirely from heaven and plunge it into the labyrinth of the world.

**VERSE 9.**—“Therefore the servant placed his hand beneath the thigh of Abraham his lord and swore to him concerning this matter.”

The servant places his hand beneath his lord’s thigh when the pious desire, under the protection of truth—which is the dwelling-place of all divine seed—joins the strength of its good activity to it in due service. He swears concerning this matter when the weakness of our desire directs and conforms itself according to the judgment of understanding.

**VERSE 10.**—“And he took ten camels from his lord’s herds and departed, carrying with him some of all his goods. He set out and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.”

By the camel, which chews the cud but does not divide the hoof, and which received its name from its bent posture, like a furnace and a chamber, we understand a life distinguished in great part by observance of divine law, yet still distant from perfection because of its lack of discernment, since it does not yet fully divide between vices and virtues; and for this reason it bends itself with fitting humility through consideration of its own unworthiness.

Thus by the ten camels is understood love and frequent recollection of the divine law, whose summary is the Decalogue. When this law is tasted by the eager mouth of the mind, the strength of the soul is raised by faithful rumination and the desire of the flesh is weakened. When the mind considers that it cannot be perfected to the very point, as it desires, because of the obstacle of the flesh, it immediately reforms itself through the humility arising from its inability to accomplish in deed what it cannot master.

The Lord’s herds, from which we take the ten, are the multitudes of the other commandments. From them we receive what is more perfect when we choose to preserve love of God and neighbor, on which “the whole law and the prophets depend.” Hence he is also said to have departed carrying some of all his lord’s goods: whoever possesses the virtue of love carries, insofar as he is able, something from all goods, even if not all are present, when through the duty of charity—which is the material of all goods—he subjugates the will of the body. He departs when he continually extends his desire toward better things.

Mesopotamia means in Greek “between the rivers”; in Hebrew it is interpreted as “an elevated calling.” One is first called to faith, but the calling is raised up through renunciation of the world, where, amid the waves of the storms of mind and of the age, it is necessary to dwell in spirit as one poor. Through this Mesopotamia we proceed to the city of Nahor, which is interpreted as “rest of light,” when through sufferings we advance toward the perfection of charity. Charity is light, according to the apostle John (I John II, 10), and through it we truly rest; or we proceed toward the heavenly city, where, resting more truly in light, we may behold light.

[Col. 0182D] **VERSES 11, 12.**—“And when he had made the camels kneel outside the town, beside the well of water, in the evening, at the time when women customarily go out to draw water, he said: ‘Lord God,’ etc.”

The town is the world, over which the strong armed man presides and reigns (Luke XI, 21). Hence it is said to the apostles: “Go into the village that is opposite you” (Matt. XXI, 2), and rightly “opposite,” because “in the world you will have tribulation” (John XVI, 33).

We make the camels kneel outside the town when we separate our good works, by which we conform to divine law, from both the carnal and spiritual fellowship of the world, while we reject its vices and praises. We kneel beside the well of water in the evening when, as the heat of vices within us cools, we find rest through the expectation of holy hope in Christ, as though at the fountain of living water, of which whoever drinks “will not thirst forever” (John VI, 35). For whoever drinks the water of the town will thirst again.

“While the impious man exalts himself, the poor man is set on fire” (Ps. IX, 23). The women go out to draw water when fragile hearts, like women, come forth from their wicked and hidden conception into manifest evils, so that they may draw not the waters of Christ but those of the town—that is, fulfill their desires in evil rather than in good. At that time, when they abuse the period granted them for repentance by turning it to pride, all the saints labor to perform their works outside the town.

**VERSE 12.**—“‘Lord,’ he said, ‘God of my lord Abraham, meet me, I pray, today, and show mercy to my lord Abraham.’”

This means: Lord, who rule over my reason, which under your protection I desire today to inhabit—namely, the dwelling of your light—you who are everywhere present and always the day, grant me the encounter with your aid, and glorify the reason that presides over me, not according to merit but according to mercy.

**VERSE 13.**—“‘Behold, I stand beside the fountain of water, and the daughters of the inhabitants of this city will come out to draw water.’”

He stands beside the fountain when our desire, strengthened by a draught from the eternal fountain, now fights manfully against the assault of the devil and the flesh. The camels kneel and the servant stands because the pursuits of virtue rest in hope of their reward, although the pious desire exercises itself by fighting in defense of religion. Each person fights by standing.

The inhabitants of the city are our rational impulses, to whom the governance of the mind belongs. They have daughters when those impulses, or virtues, generate from their successful outcome the wantonness of empty thoughts. These daughters go out of the city to draw water when they leave the inward care of the soul for a time and go forth to seek the temporary joys of praise.

**VERSE 14.**—“‘Therefore let the girl to whom I say, “Bend your jar so that I may drink,” and who answers, “Drink, and I will also give your camels a drink,” be the one whom you have prepared for your servant Isaac; and by this I shall know that you have shown mercy to my lord Isaac.’”

By the girl we understand purity and the brightness of a new conscience. We tell her to bend the jar for drinking when we rationally urge her to humble within herself the pride of worldly desires, so that we may drink it—that is, consume it completely within us. In this way the Israelites drank the calf after it had been crushed, and the dragon is given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia (Ps. LXXIII, 14).

She answers, “Drink,” when cheerful goodwill obeys the reason that offers good instruction, in order to chastise the conscience within itself. She promises drink to the camels when she restores strength to the virtues from the wandering of her own desire.

“When,” he says, “a mind friendly to purity smiles upon me in this manner, I shall undoubtedly know and discern that this will, which deserves to be joined to Isaac—to everlasting laughter—is being prepared in me not by my own exertion but by the gift of your grace. Isaac now laughs in hope, yet he serves by campaigning in your duties, Lord.”

[Col. 0184A] **VERSES 15, 16.**—“Before he had finished speaking inwardly, behold, Rebecca was coming out, the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother; she had a jar on her shoulder. The girl was exceedingly beautiful, a most beautiful virgin, and unknown to man.”

We often use the word *verba*—“words”—in an absolute sense for any empty utterances that possess nothing but sound. Hence the saying: “Every love gives words” (Ovid.).

Before we finish the words, behold, Rebecca goes out, because before we have fully expelled the clouds of frivolity from the heart, Rebecca—that is, patience, for this is how her name is interpreted—suddenly attempts to depart by failing under the excessive labor of repulsion, as weariness arises. “Blessed is the one who endures temptation” (Jas. I, 12).

Bethuel is called “the virgin of God,” in whom the state of incorrupt faith is expressed. Rebecca is born from him because, while we believe those things that are held by faith alone, patience is begotten in us amid present evils for the sake of eternal hopes.

Hence Bethuel is called the son of Milcah, that is, of “the queen” or “the one who will reign,” because what is now endured in faith amid trials arises from the perfect glory that we believe in: the heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, which already reigns in part and will reign fully after the day of judgment.

Milcah is the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, because she who already reigns is the bride of him who is the true light, in whom all who rest in true peace find rest. Nahor himself is Abraham’s brother because the light that illuminates the world, when it became flesh, became the brother of all who imitate Abraham’s name and works through faith.

She carries a jar on her shoulder because she reluctantly bears the weight of desires, signified by the talent of lead in Zechariah (Zech. V, 7), which force themselves upon her. The jar signifies desire; the water signifies pleasure. She is therefore burdened by the desire for pleasures: beautiful in her desire, without the corruption of favor; most beautiful in her effect; unknown to man, since she wishes in no way to lie open to the devil’s boldness.

We do not say that she already possesses all these qualities, but that she strives to become such, just as the Apostle calls the Church “without wrinkle or spot” (Eph. V, 27).

**VERSES 17, 18.**—“She had gone down to the fountain and filled her jar, and was returning. The servant ran to meet her and said: ‘Give me a little water from your jar to drink.’ She replied: ‘Drink, my lord,’ and quickly lowered the jar onto her arm and gave him a drink.”

The conscience goes down to the fountain when it turns away from heavenly desire toward the fleeting things of this world. It fills the jar when it seeks to satisfy avarice with the lowest glory of the world. After this it returns, because, once any desire has been fulfilled, the repentant mind often returns to itself.

The servant meets her on her return when the desire for virtue plays upon the conscience as it comes to its senses. He asks for a little water to drink whenever the intellectual desire wishes to empty the breast of the mind of the streams of desire. Quickly obeying, she lowers the jar onto her arm when she refuses, through an unjust patience, to bend her shoulder downward under the mass of carnal things, but undertakes with the arm of due strength to govern the wantonness of pleasures and offers it to be consumed by the mouth of reason.

**VERSES 19, 20.**—“And when he had drunk, she added: ‘I will also draw water for your camels, until they have all drunk.’ She poured out the jar into the troughs and ran back to the well to draw water, and gave what she had drawn to all the camels.”

A mind touched by God rejoices not only when the power of rationality consumes desire in some single matter, but also promises to draw water for all the camels—that is, to provide a place of refreshment for the humble pursuits of the virtues—and to drain away every harmful softness.

Virtue has nowhere to remain unless the spirit turns the moisture of vice into the sweat of fire. We pour water into the troughs when through humility of thought we empty out the excess of worldly concerns. The trough, because of its concavity, signifies the humility of the mind. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like royal purple bound in channels” (Song VII, 6).

We run back to the well to draw water and give what we have drawn to the camels when we bring the mind’s gaze back to consider the whole mass of our desire, so that we may thrust it out from our breasts and nourish the troops of the various virtues through the consumption of lusts.

**VERSES 21, 22.**—“The man, meanwhile, observed her silently, wishing to know whether the Lord had made his journey prosperous or not. When the camels had drunk, the man brought out two golden earrings weighing two shekels and two bracelets weighing ten shekels.”

We contemplate the virgin silently when, with our minds quieted from external noise, we examine within ourselves how glorious it is to possess a conscience free from the bite of sin. In delight at her beauty we receive a kind of indication of whether the Lord is making the course of our desire prosperous. For when we devote ourselves solely to seeking the beauty of divine things, there, as though reading in a book, we foresee to some extent what good or evil we shall pursue and what we shall receive now and in the future.

When the camels have drunk—when, that is, whatever vice is within us has been consumed by the virtue of humility—the man brings forth what is signified by the earrings: the intellect, with feminine softness now excluded, offers to God and to human beings a double obedience, so that when it strives to obey both God and those who preside over it as fathers and are present as brothers, the ear may not refuse the ornament of obedient service. For we must submit not only to fathers but “to every human creature for God’s sake” (I Pet. II, 13).

Obedience, moreover, according to the poet, “produces friends” (Terence, *Andria*). Therefore an equal number of bracelets is placed on the girl’s hands. By the bracelets, which stand out upon the hands like a crown, the fruit of good work is understood: peace first with God, then with one’s neighbor. Peace is the reward of completed war; peace is the culmination of labors. The hands signify works, by which we obey God and offer examples to our neighbor.

The reward of works, even in the present, is our love for God, which adorns and protects us like the encircling bracelets; God’s love toward us in return; and, arising from pious work, our neighbor’s love toward us and our love toward our neighbor.

The earrings weigh two shekels because true obedience cannot be offered without humility and patience. They are golden when the commands of obedience are carried out for God alone. The bracelets weigh ten shekels when our body, which subsists from four elements, and our soul, which consists of three principal gifts—understanding, memory, and will—hang and incline toward the desire for the one Trinity.

For *pondus* (“weight”) and *pondo* (“by weight”) are said from *pendere*, “to hang”; and what hangs tends toward something. Hence lovers too are said to hang.

**VERSES 23, 24, 25.**—“And he said to her: ‘Whose daughter are you? Is there room in your father’s house for us to stay?’ She answered: ‘I am the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him. We have a great quantity of straw and hay, and ample room for staying.’”

When we fervently attend to the rigor of our conduct, we often carefully examine the origin and cause of our conversion, or even of our intention. We investigate whose daughter such a shining conscience is—whether it has been produced by God or propagated by the devil—when we cautiously consider whether we have begun what is good, as usually happens, from a wicked intention.

The house of the devil is here called the world. But this father’s house, namely God’s house, is nothing other than the mind itself, which is directed spiritually when he inhabits it. And just as we are scattered under the devil, so under God, the true Father, we remain within ourselves, as household members, in the care of the inner person.

The dwelling-place of the faithful is charity—not a temporary charity but, so to speak, one that provides a permanent habitation. Hence the Holy Spirit descended on Pentecost upon those who remained in the same place.

“I am,” she says, “the daughter of Bethuel.” Bethuel is called “the virgin of God”; and nothing is more appropriately understood as a virgin than truth, which, because it is from God, has nothing purer than itself. The pious mind, therefore, is Bethuel’s daughter because, born from the chastity of truth, it receives nothing except the teachings of sincerity. “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice” (John XVIII, 37).

Bethuel is the son of Milcah because truth arises in us only through reason. Reason is rightly called Milcah, “queen,” because, divinely illuminated, it rules our senses with complete propriety. Hence Nahor is said to have begotten him; Nahor is called “rest of light,” because whatever true knowledge is generated within us through Milcah, that is, through reason, is referred to God the creator, in whom we rest sweetly in true light, away from the work—that is, sin—of one “walking in darkness” (Ps. IX, 8) of folly.

By straw, which is beaten away from grain, we understand the things that are superfluous in us, namely our faults. By hay human frailty is understood. Therefore whoever never ceases to consider both faults and the continual weakness of his own flesh has much straw and hay.

But there is also ample room for staying in the house, because although we suffer the weight of the body and the sin that surrounds us, we nevertheless preserve among ourselves the broad commandment of charity, which even embraces the enemy and covers a multitude of sins. Hence it is said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. XXX, 9).

It is “for staying,” that is, for persevering, so that we may love not in word and tongue but “in deed and in truth” (I John III, 18)—that is, with a sure immutability of our state. For what is changed is not in truth.

[Col. 0187A] **VERSES 26, 27.**—“The man bowed and worshiped God, saying: ‘Blessed is the Lord, the God of my lord Abraham, who has not withdrawn his mercy and his truth from my lord, and has led me by a straight path to the house of my lord’s brother.’”

Whenever we feel that our will to do good responds to our desire as we wish, we must humble before God the rigor of our humanity and bless him, the ruler of our intellectual nature, who mercifully grants us faith together with works and, fulfilling his promises by the generosity of reward, will display truth at the end. Through the path of his teachings he will lead us into the heavenly house of Christ Jesus, who is the brother of all who live rationally and according to the conduct of faithful Abraham.

He is called “lord” because reason rules the desire; and Christ is called the brother of this lord because he is joined by complete kinship especially to those who rule over their own corrupt impulses.

**VERSES 28, 29, 30.**—“The girl ran and reported to her mother’s house everything she had heard. Rebecca had a brother named Laban, who hurried out to the man at the fountain. When he saw the earrings and bracelets on his sister’s hands and heard all the words she reported—‘This is what the man said to me’—he came to the man who was standing beside the camels and near the fountain of water.”

The mother’s house is that virtue of reason which protects us. Running to it, the girl reports what she has heard when the purity of the conscience returns with complete diligence in all its desires to the judgment of reason and arranges itself under that judgment.

Rebecca means “patience,” while Laban is interpreted as “brightness.” A patient conscience is therefore joined by kinship to eternal brightness; for unless hope lifted it toward heavenly radiance, endurance would immediately grow weary like a woman amid pressures.

He hurries out to the man at the fountain because this expresses the attentive gaze of thought: intellectually, before our human desires that threaten worldly cravings, it considers what the glory of that light is which no defect can harm. For Laban’s going out to the man means nothing other than the expression of a reasoning spirit, according to the judgment of heavenly brightness, against the movement of humanity.

He sees the earrings and bracelets on his sister’s hands when he sets before the patient soul the exercise of the obedience owed doubly to God and to human beings, and the fruit of a twofold activity, which must likewise be offered to divine honor and to fraternal edification. From this he urges us to discern what crown is owed to one who endures the loss of so many labors.

That earrings signify obedience is attested by Job, when earrings were given to him in his restoration (Job XLII, 11). He hears the girl reporting her words when he causes the soul intelligently to heed the provision of its good desire, which brings it to earn the light of heavenly glory.

Laban comes to the man who stands beside the camels near the fountain when heavenly desire approaches the affection already fighting manfully in defense of humble virtues against the world’s flux—that is, against the threatening well.

Someone reproved me for taking “fountain” in a bad sense; but let him remember that the name “fountain” is taken in an evil sense where and from which the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman. We have explained above how the camels are to be understood.

**VERSES 31, 32, 33.**—“‘Enter, blessed of the Lord; why do you stand outside? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.’ And he brought the man into the lodging, unsaddled the camels, and gave them straw and hay, and water for washing the feet of the camels and of the men who had come with him. And bread was placed before him.”

Our desire is blessed by the Lord when it is directed toward an increase of religion. It is urged to enter when it is drawn away from external noise into the quiet of the mind through the brightness of inward joy.

For this intellectual Laban prepares a house and a place for the camels when he both removes sin from the house of the conscience and establishes in that same house the seat of every virtue, namely, a good will. He brings the man into the lodging when, during the time of this pilgrimage, he does not cease to conceal works of piety within the secret of the mind, because of the intrusion of passing praise.

The camels are unsaddled when any coverings of holiness with which we had faithfully girded ourselves to receive God dwelling in us are loosened by our humble estimation of ourselves and are considered worthless for purchasing the brightness of future blessedness. Alternatively, Laban unsaddled them when heavenly love lifted the pursuits of virtue from every weight of sin and empty thoughts.

He gives them straw and hay when he presents to pious exercises both the misery of rejection and the glory of divine election, so that his heart may rejoice in the hope of election while fearing the divine name because of the fall of rejection.

We shall provide examples showing that the reprobate are called “straw” and the elect “hay.” The Gospel says that he will burn the straw “with unquenchable fire” (Luke III, 17); and in Job, Behemoth eats hay like an ox (Job XL, 10).

Water is then supplied for washing the feet of the camels because, from hope and fear, heavenly irrigation—“the upper irrigation and the lower irrigation” (Josh. V, 19)—is poured upon the excess desires of our virtues, to cleanse them.

These camels are also guided by men because our intellectual impulses, which Job calls strong in power (Job XXXVI, 19), direct the works of virtue within us.

Bread is therefore placed before him because, for our desire, now quieted from its activities, the delight of the contemplation of God alone is recognized as present; hence bread is said to have been placed before him.

It should be noted that the feet of the camels and the men are washed first, and afterward bread is placed before him, because unless the mind and virtue are completely washed from their excesses by the grace of compunction, the mind is never refreshed by divine contemplation, which is tasted only by the pure in heart.

“Before I eat, I sigh,” says someone (Job III, 24). But when this bread has been placed before him, the servant refuses to eat until he has completed his words, because he considers himself incapable of eating the bread that feeds the angels unless our desire fulfills the affection of devotion conceived within it through the effect of pious action.

This bread—or rather, because of the unity of the Trinity, this one bread—the friend returning from a journey urgently requests from his friend (Luke XI, 6).

Laban gives permission for him to speak because heavenly desire chiefly helps us to bring into effect what has been rightly conceived. It is beyond doubt that “words” are often used for “things” in sacred Scripture, especially in the Old Testament.

**VERSES 34, 35.**—“‘I am Abraham’s servant,’ he said, ‘and the Lord has greatly blessed my lord.’”

This means: insofar as I am desire, I submit myself to reason, whose dominion God enriches with an increase of progress. He has been made great by attaining the summit of virtue. He has sheep, signifying benevolence toward his neighbor and simplicity in himself; oxen, maturity of conduct and the grace of preaching; silver, knowledge and eloquence; gold, wisdom or sacred religion; male servants, by subjecting bodily obstinacy to its lawful rule; female servants, by restraining inward wantonness with the severity of chastity; camels, by refining heaviness toward activity; and asses, by sharpening stupidity and ineptitude toward divine subtlety.

What follows up to the passage where he says, “If you will show mercy and truth toward my lord, tell me,” has already been sufficiently explained above and should not be repeated, since so much remains to be examined.

There is, however, one point that, although it may seem to have been discussed, could trouble someone: namely, the statement, “Today I came to the fountain of water.” If the fountain of water, according to the interpretation we have followed almost everywhere in this passage, is understood as a figure of desire, it seems contradictory that “today” is added. Yet “today”—that is, through the illumination of grace—we come to the fountain, namely to that well of blind desire, when, with God illuminating us, we recognize its abyss of confusion. Hence the servant is said to have been placed beside the well, standing—that is, fighting vigilantly.

Even if we prefer to understand the name “fountain” differently, taking it in a good sense, we come to the fountain today because we reach the fountain of divine knowledge, wisdom, and life only through the day. For God himself must be sought through himself: “I am the way,” he says (John XIV, 6).

It is said to Bethuel and Laban—that is, to the grace of God, than which nothing is chaster or more entire—from which the brightness of heavenly desire is born in us: “Will you show mercy and truth toward our lord?” From grace we receive mercy, the forgiveness of sins; from truth we receive the promises of heavenly brightness toward which our desires sigh. Therefore, insofar as we feel both the power of grace and the fervor of heavenly desire within us, let us know that our future mercy and truth are being worked out in us.

[Col. 0189D] **VERSES 49, 50.**—“‘But if you have another preference, tell me this also, so that I may go either to the right or to the left.’ Laban and Bethuel answered: ‘The word has proceeded from the Lord; we cannot speak anything else to you beyond his pleasure.’”

This means: If, because my sins deserve it, it does not please God, working through you, to grant me forgiveness and the fulfillment of promised blessedness—which is grace and truth—make this known also by divine inspiration, so that, turning toward the right, I may exercise myself with greater zeal in virtue, or, entrusting myself to the left, may be pierced by repentance for my past lapses. For we have the left from contrition for sin, and the right from progress in good.

To this, the grace of God together with what it has begotten—heavenly desire, namely Laban and Bethuel—respond intellectually: “The word has proceeded from the Lord.” From the judgment of the hidden decree, as an arrow from a quiver, the sentence of God has flashed forth through the gift of your evident inspiration. From it you can gather that the anointing by which you are taught inwardly must be held by you as a kind of heavenly oracle, certifying your future progress—or rather, your perfection.

For we cannot suggest anything uncertain to you except what he himself wills, since we are unquestionably from him.

Verses 51–52–53.—[Col. 0190B] “Behold, Rebecca is before you; take her and depart, and let her be the wife of my lord’s son, as the Lord has spoken.” When Abraham’s servant heard this, he worshiped the Lord upon the ground. Then, bringing out vessels of silver and gold and garments, he gave them to Rebecca as a gift, and presented gifts to her brothers and mother.

“If,” they say, “you choose the right hand of virtue, behold Rebecca—that is, recognize that patience must be held before the eyes of your mind. For it is necessary to prepare yourself for temptation and to enter the kingdom of God through tribulations (Acts XIV, 21). If, therefore, you wish to depart, that is, to advance by good works, take her up from a lowly intention, raising it aloft, so that you may not think the trouble must be endured for the sake of a present reward, but join her to the son of your lord—that is, to divine hope begotten from the intellect as its teacher. From him, amid afflictions [Col. 0190C], she may receive the kiss of heavenly consolation. The Lord speaks these things when he teaches those who suffer persecution everywhere to hope for heavenly things alone.

“The servant hears these things—that is, the affection serving reason understands them—and prays to the exalted God on the ground, that is, upon the firmness of humility, without which there is no patience, praying to him all the nearer because he prays more humbly. The silver vessels are the capacity of sacred speech and knowledge. The golden vessels are the fruitfulness of charity, so that knowledge may not puff up. The garments are works of holiness, with which we cover the members that must be put to death upon the earth. We bring these things forth when we make them useful to our neighbors. We give them to Rebecca as a gift when, from these things, we provide some consolation for the one laboring in patience. To her brothers—that is, to the virtues of the soul and to the spirit striving manfully in support of them—and to the mother, charity, which loves [Col. 0190D] what it endures, we likewise offer gifts of consolation.”

(Verse 54.) “When the meal had been prepared, they remained there, eating and drinking together.” After our affection, having conceived human fear, breathes patience and humility anew through love, it begins a banquet with all those mentioned above, when it embraces and desires what at the beginning of its conversion it had endured with difficulty—namely, the adversities of the world, drawn solely by the sweetness of virtue. We eat when we wear down with the tooth of reason whatever harsh and harmful thing presents itself to the mind, and, converting it to use, are spiritually strengthened. We drink when, drawing the cup of the sevenfold grace, we digest what has been eaten. We remain together when we allow ourselves in no way to be separated from the religion we have undertaken or from the things we have set forth above. [Col. 0191A] “There,” because it is a local word, signifies the state of good will, without which no one can dwell together with these things.

Verses 55–56.—“But when he arose in the morning, the servant said: ‘Release me, so that I may go to my lord.’ Her brothers and mother answered: ‘Let the girl remain with us at least ten days, and afterward she shall depart.’ He said: ‘Do not hold me back, because the Lord has directed my way.’”

The servant rises in the morning when effective affection, with due diligence, bursts forth from the infancy of the mind into the manly strength of virtue. That “morning” is used for diligence is attested by the psalm: “In the morning my prayer shall anticipate you” (Psalm LXXXVII, 14); and: “My chastisement was in the mornings” (Psalm LXXII, 14).

“Release me,” he says, “so that I may go to the Lord”—that is, enlarge my narrowness through the abundance of your instruction, [Col. 0191B] so that I may be joined to reason, the mistress of all things. But the effect of the mother, charity, and of the other good things answers by asking that the girl remain with them for ten days: throughout the totality of this time, which is accomplished in seven days, she is to exercise patience amid the three things that chiefly trouble her—namely, thought, speech, and action—so that, when she has broken these through the law of religion, she may depart to Isaac, the jubilation of eternal joy. The number ten, moreover, consists of seven and three.

“Why,” he says, “am I restrained by your frugality, when by contemplating I already taste beforehand the glory of my future direction?”

[Col. 0191C] Verses 57–60.—“They said: ‘Let us call the girl and ask her will.’ When she had been called and had come, they questioned her, saying: ‘Do you wish to go with this man?’ She replied: ‘I will go.’ So they sent her away, together with her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his companions, invoking prosperity upon their sister and saying: ‘You are our sister; may you increase to thousands upon thousands, and may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.’”

We call the girl when, with the counsel inspired by the mother and brothers according to what has been said, we inquire of our conscience whether it wishes to persevere in the pursuit of holiness. She comes when, by the judgment of reason speaking publicly, she stands there in her entirety.

Thus, responding fully to the heavenly desires, to the grace of God, and to the affection of charity—to her brother Laban, to Bethuel, and to her mother—she follows the servant, [99] that is, the appetite of piety. She is expanded and opened out in the breadth of contemplation, together with her nurse, that is, providence, which must ensure [Col. 0191D] that nothing be done to excess and must restrain excess; and together with Abraham’s servant, namely the appetite everywhere subjected to the intellect, she rejoices to proceed freely with the spiritual company of virtues, invoking prosperity—that is, causing the soul itself to invoke for itself the pursuit of better things, now joined to it in true kinship.

“You are our sister,” as though they said: “Through communion with the divine offspring, you possess with us the nature of virtue. For patience, unless it is exercised for God, is foolishness. You shall be ennobled by the fruitfulness of virtues. May you increase to thousands upon thousands”—that is, may you advance to complete perfection. For this is what that multitude of numbers signifies. And may your offspring, that is, your good works, possess and subjugate the gates of their enemies—namely, the vices through which one enters into fellowship with demons, who are commonly and antonomastically designated by the name “enemies.” [Col. 0192A] These same vices are called in the Psalms “the gates of death” (Psalm CVI, 18) and in the Gospel “the gates of hell” (Matthew XVI, 18).

Verse 61.—“Then Rebecca and her girls mounted the camels and followed the man. He was returning hastily to his lord.”

Rebecca has girls as companions because the thoughts of neither humble modesty nor simple temperance are absent from patience. They mount camels and follow the man when they likewise lean upon the height of humble virtues and follow the appetite for heavenly good as their leader and husband, by whom they may always be made fruitful. He hastens back to his lord because, by the nature of virtue, as fire rises to lofty places, the appetite turns toward him from whom it is given, with insatiable love.

[Col. 0192B] Verses 62–63.—“At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is ‘Living and Seeing.’ For he dwelt in the southern land, and he had gone out to meditate in the field when the day was already declining. When he had raised his eyes, he saw camels coming from afar.”

In this state of the soul, with vows burning everywhere, Isaac walks along the road that leads to the well, when the hope of heavenly joy advances by walking through him who is the way for those journeying toward him, toward the knowledge of that very one who is himself also the well—that is, the depth of the entire treasury of wisdom and knowledge. Its name is “Living,” since it possesses both its own life and the life of all in general; and it also has the name “Seeing,” because it sees itself, which is life, and makes others see.

He dwelt in the southern land—that is, in the grace of spiritual fervor and firmness. [Col. 0192C] For the south wind is hot, and the bridegroom summons it in the Song of Songs to blow upon his spices (Song IV, 16). But after the excellence of spiritual understanding, the height of the intellect had gone out to meditate in the field, when it is necessarily brought down to the examination of the body’s passions, which must be cultivated for us after the manner of a field.

He goes out into the field to meditate—or, according to certain copies, “to reap”—when the mind, imbued with heavenly joys, is compelled from the chamber of inward contemplation to meditate upon the care of active affairs, or to set boundaries for itself, and the mind is forced by the sudden distress of temptation to impose limits upon the body’s restraint. This happens when the day is already declining—that is, when the light of divine contemplation has been withdrawn for a little while.

But Isaac raises his eyes and sees [Col. 0192D] camels from afar when he is again lifted from awareness of his own frailty to the height of divine vision, where he beholds the strength of virtue, revived and already returning. We call the camels virtues, both because they ruminate and because they are named from curvature—that is, from humility. Although they do not indeed divide the hoof, they nevertheless display a sign of discernment through the division of their hump.

Verses 64–66.—“Rebecca also, seeing Isaac, descended from the camel and said to the servant: ‘Who is that man who is coming through the field to meet us?’ He answered: ‘It is my lord.’ Then she quickly took her veil and covered herself. The servant recounted to Isaac everything that he had done.”

Rebecca, seeing Isaac, descends from the camel when patience, weighing inwardly what she sees above, lays down by her own judgment every height of virtue [Col. 0193A] in herself, judging that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us (Romans VIII, 18). Wondering, therefore, she addresses her own affection.

“Who,” she says, “is this movement of such humanity in God? With what profound gaze of the mind must he be attended, who, through the field—that is, through spiritual exercise—always comes by gratuitous aid to meet us as we journey toward him!”

God is also customarily called human according to his very divinity; the spirit likewise is called human and stable, since our words must necessarily be transferred to divine realities. By “man,” therefore, is meant humanity, that is, piety. “The kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared” (Titus III, 4).

“This is,” says the affection, “my lord. Not undeservedly have I preferred him to every dominion: he is so greatly compassionate that he both makes us his own cultivation and, when we resist and turn away proudly, comes to meet us, ready [Col. 0193B] to entreat us to return.”

Then Rebecca quickly takes up her veil and covers herself, because although patience may seem to itself to suffer many things for God, it assumes the adornment of modesty: it considers nothing that it does to be of value and is ashamed of what lies behind it. Thus, through this very humility, it notably covers itself before the eyes of God.

The veil, which is broader below and narrower above, may also signify the active and contemplative life: the one is broad in its care for one’s neighbor, while the other is sharpened toward the vision of God. Our affection recounts what Isaac has done when it brings back whatever it seems to accomplish through action or contemplation, in order to earn the grace of heavenly joy.

Verse 67.—“He brought her into the tent of [Col. 0193C] Sarah, his mother, and took her as his wife. He loved her so greatly that he tempered the grief that had arisen from his mother’s death.”

Isaac brings Rebecca into his mother’s tent when the desire for heavenly joy receives patience as its fellow soldier within the bounds of pious will—which is the mother of every good thing—and receives it to be made fruitful by holy works. He rejoices to suffer for God to such an extent that the grief of penitence, which had once arisen from the failure of that same good will, is now entirely softened by the progress of love and by the sure hope of pardon.

# Chapter XXV

Verse 1.—“Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.”

Keturah is interpreted as “offering incense” or “joined.”

After Sarah—that is, the will, which is [Col. 0193D] the chief element of Abraham, namely of reason, not because it rules over reason, but because from its fellowship comes the beginning of all goodness—after this will, I say, has died to the world, she becomes Keturah, when she is so consumed by the whole ardor of desire that the life of a human being, joined to God through an inward and indivisible covenant of love, is carried toward God, furnished with every fragrance of holiness.

(Verse 5.) Abraham gives everything that he possesses to Isaac, because whatever the intellect earns as spiritual substance is all contributed toward multiplying the profits of heavenly joy.

(Verses 6.) He bestows gifts upon the sons of his concubines when he assigns the rewards of temporal, not eternal, prosperity to works begun rationally but completed with the less legitimate admixture of human affection. “And he separated them,” it says, “from Isaac his son,” while he himself was still living, toward the eastern region. [Col. 0194A]

For while we live, we must separate them from Isaac toward the eastern region, because, while we are flooded with the living light of the true East, we must carefully discern lest works performed in a human manner be mixed with the intention of heavenly reward. We call the sons of the concubines the works of bodily affections, and Isaac, the son, the hope of heavenly joy. The order is: “While he was living, toward the eastern region, he separated them.”

Verses 7–8.—“The years of his life were one hundred and seventy-five years. And failing, he died in a good old age, advanced in years and full of days.”

Through the number five our outer man is understood, on account of his five senses. The number seventy more clearly presents seven and ten. [Col. 0194B] In the seven, which is a spiritual number and consists of four and three, our spirit may be understood: it surpasses the four principal virtues, reason, will, and affection, and alone is suited to receive the sevenfold grace. We add the ten to the seven when we imbue the mind with the teaching of the sacred law.

From there, when it passes to one hundred, we are carried to the right hand—that is, we ascend to the contemplation of God, which is already the beginning of eternal blessedness. In this way Abraham could intellectually live in the world as far as one hundred, but, having been established at this point, he died, failing in the desires and business of those desires. He was “full of days”—that is, filled with the manifold light of sacred knowledge—and “advanced in years,” having been promoted through the lofty steps of holiness in old age, not the old age in which one grows stale [Col. 0194C] among enemies in a foreign land (Psalm VI, 8; Baruch III, 11), but that in which one has fully ripened through the long duration of a good religious way of life.

Verse 9.—“He was gathered to his people, and Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the double cave situated in the field of Ephron,” and so forth.

Isaac and Ishmael, Abraham’s sons, bury him in a double cave when both the hope of heavenly joy and the affection already obedient to God cover the principle of inward rest with grace, so that they neither expose to God the spirit intent upon him in the cave of sensuality nor in the imaginational faculty itself, which is usually more troublesome; rather, by sparing it the affairs of cares and cherishing it, they consent to its service. The remaining matters may be sought in what was treated above.

[Col. 0194D] But before he is buried, it is said with sufficient order that he was “gathered to his people.” Unless the intellect gathers itself from its dispersion to unite with the multitude of thoughts, as with a people, it will never reach that tomb of the mind’s rest.

(Verses 11.) “After his death God blessed Isaac his son, who dwelt beside the well of the Living and Seeing.”

God blesses Isaac, his son, after Abraham’s death when he multiplies the abundance of the spiritual joy of our hope, after our intellect has entirely failed in its desire for worldly glory. He dwells beside the well of the Living and Seeing when the glorying of the inner man, by careful observance, frequently attends upon him in whom is the source of every good thing and from whom we draw the streams of all spirituality and vitality. [Col. 0195A] We customarily sit beside the thing that we wish to guard and enjoy; thus he dwells beside the well.

Verses 17–18.—“The years of Ishmael’s life were one hundred and thirty-seven. Failing, he died and was gathered to his people. He dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which looks toward Egypt for those entering Assyria; he died in the presence of all his brothers.”

The number seven signifies temporality, which unfolds through seven days. Thirty pertains to love of the Trinity; it is completed through the performance of pious works, since six times five makes thirty. God performed his works in six days, and on the sixth he also created humanity. The six of works therefore suggests perfection, which restrains the disorder of the five external senses. One hundred, because it is on the right, signifies the contemplation of God.

Whatever temporality is in us, [Col. 0195B] therefore, let our true affection, Ishmael, expend upon the love of God—not in word, but in complete action—if it wishes to perfect the human being and reach the blessedness of the vision of God. That number is the fullness of years, namely the brightness of virtues. Hence it is appropriately said afterward that he was “gathered to his people,” when, after so many splendors of holiness, having abandoned the inhabitants of Kedar, he now desires to be joined only to the people of his true, heavenly homeland—to his fellow citizens—and is later to be joined to them in reality.

“He dwelt from Havilah to Shur,” that is, he ruled his movements from the beginning of his conversion, in which “the whole creation groans and is in labor until now” (Romans VIII, 22), to Shur—that is, to the strength of spiritual fortitude against all disturbances. Yet that fortitude [Col. 0195C] “looks toward Egypt,” that is, toward the darkness of constricting tribulation, for those entering Assyria through the affections of the flesh—that is, those wishing to imitate courtiers devoted to pleasure. For we know that the halls of all pleasures are places of rolling and filth. Those who are clothed in soft garments are in royal houses (Luke VII, 25).

Havilah is interpreted as “the one giving birth” or “suffering”; Shur as “fortitude”; Egypt as “constricting tribulation” or “darkness.” In Scripture, “to dwell” is used in the sense of “to rule.”

When we perform any difficult deeds and are tempted by the pleasure of the world as though entering a royal hall, we must attend to Egypt, the place of sorrow and darkness, which is the whole world. Assyria is called a hall.

He dies in the presence of all his brothers when, with all the pious [Col. 0195D] movements of the soul having returned from their wandering and standing ready to secure him, he happily dies to worldly distraction and business. Hence, above, he is first said to have failed and afterward to have died. Unless Ishmael fails completely in earthly affection, how can he fully die to the effects of sin?

The matters that follow (verses 18–22) have already been treated elsewhere, except that Isaac, being forty years old, took Rebecca—by fulfilling the Decalogue, reaching the sum of the Gospel, which is marked by the number four, and attaining the embrace of patience, which is the height of perfection.

“Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife because she was barren; and he heard him and granted Rebecca conception, but the children struggled in her womb. She said: ‘If this was to happen to me, why was it [Col. 0196A] necessary for me to conceive?’ And she went to consult the Lord.”

After we embrace the laws of patience at the beginning of our conversion, we find it barren, because although it tolerates adversaries, it nevertheless considers it exceedingly difficult to serve them kindly. It is therefore necessary that we pray the Lord to grant Rebecca conception. We are heard, and now conceive twins: namely, that we admit those whom we tolerate into grace without any scruple, and that, once we have loved them, we take care to do good to them and serve them even when they persist in evil.

But the children struggle in the womb because an immense conflict arises within the conscience of the mind attempting to do these things. For when the mind sees service received ungratefully by an enemy, it is indignant with itself, asking why it should love such a person. To love and not [Col. 0196B] be loved, to offer service and yet be despised—at both it is gravely indignant with itself, while unreceived service disturbs inward love, and love itself suffers greatly from the offering of service.

“What,” it says, “will it profit me to have conceived the affection for this good action, when it leads to so sad an effect upon the conscience?” But the oracle of intellectual understanding must be sought, where we may consult the Lord.

Verses 23–25.—“For two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be divided from your belly; one people will overcome the other, and the greater will serve the lesser. The one who came out first was red and entirely hairy like a skin. His name was called Esau. Immediately the other came out, holding his brother’s heel with his hand; therefore he called his name Jacob.”

[Col. 0196C] Two nations are in the womb of the patient soul, within the womb of the conscience: namely, the thoughts of the flesh and the spiritual movements of reason. From the belly—that is, from human frailty—two kinds of mutually hostile desires will arise, while the condition of corruptibility impedes the state of unity. Yet one people overcomes the other, and the greater serves the lesser, when the animal nature, which first rules in every human being—for, according to the Apostle, comes first what is animal and afterward what is spiritual (1 Corinthians XV, 46)—is subjected to spirituality as worthy of dominion.

“Do not,” he says, “be troubled within yourself if you wish to be crowned with the reward of patience.”

The one who comes out first is red because the movement that first appears in us, coming from the passion of desires, is as though from the origin of flesh and [Col. 0196D] blood, inflamed with concupiscence. That color resembles both fire and blood, and therefore signifies the heat of carnal desire.

He is hairy like a skin when he is always bristling with the roughness of invading and superfluous thoughts [and] movements. By the skin we may understand memory, which is a representation of an animal already dead. Our memory, therefore, is filled with as many assaults of suggestions as any skin has density of hairs.

Esau is said to mean “a heap of stones.” Our carnality is therefore called a heap of stones when the weight and hardness of spiritual and bodily evils are continually heaped upon it, so that it is scarcely lifted toward the pursuit of heavenly things.

But immediately the other comes out, holding his brother’s heel with his hand, when spiritual zeal follows [Col. 0197A] and overturns with the strength of reason the heel—that is, the intention of the perverse desire, which is both the end of a thought and of a deed.

Jacob, therefore, that is, “supplanter,” is the name the mother gives to patience, which indeed removes whatever we await with an evil intention. This is what is written: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians V, 17).

The time of birth, which had passed us by above, when the twins are found in the womb, I consider most suitably to mean the very troubles of temptation. These produce twins when they first tickle us in a carnal manner and afterward, for the overthrow of wickedness, awaken the spirit as a champion of virtue. The womb itself is the invisibility of the conscience in which these things take place.

[Col. 0197B] Verses 26–28.—“Isaac was sixty years old when the children were born to him. When they had grown up, Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a farmer, while Jacob, a simple man, dwelt in tents.

“Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunts, and Rebecca loved Jacob.”

Children are born to us when, having been fully exercised in the battles against vices, the carnal and spiritual elements alike become manifest to our discernment. They are born to Isaac at the age of sixty when, through the complete works of the perfected human being, signified by sixty, these dispositions arise usefully for the glory of testing in our hope already intent upon heavenly joys.

The children grow when the sluggishness of suggestion bursts forth into the heat of excessive attack. Yet if carnality burns, the spiritual impulse must necessarily [Col. 0197C] burn still more ardently and never cease to burn against it.

One child is good and the other evil, but both are good if we so wish. Thus Esau, although a man skilled in hunting and also a farmer, is nevertheless loved by Isaac because Isaac ate of his hunts. A hunter, by all his activity, seeks nothing other than flesh. A farmer, though he works the earth, nevertheless demands fruit.

Esau, therefore—that is, the affection of the flesh—seeks only bodily desires. Yet, like a farmer, when he works the soil of the flesh with many labors, he provides our reason, which looks toward heavenly things and fights for them, with great tastes of fullness from the outcomes of victories.

Jacob, a simple man, dwells at home. Rebecca—or rather she herself—loves him because the mind, devoted to simplicity, that is, to the unity [Col. 0197D] of the mind, attends solely to one thing and rejoices to contemplate one thing. Dwelling at home, that is, ruling the conscience, he is loved by patience in a womanly fashion, which rejoices as though in its own rest, while Jacob, established in simplicity, is driven inwardly by no storm and does not sufficiently consider what benefit might arise from temptation.

Verses 29–31.—“Jacob cooked a stew. When Esau came from the field, tired, he said to him: ‘Give me some of this red stew, for I am very tired.’ For this reason his name was called Edom. Jacob said: ‘Sell me your birthright.’ Esau replied: ‘Behold, I am dying; what good will the birthright do me?’”

Jacob cooks the stew when some spiritual vigor of knowledge and the fire of divine charity soften whatever carnal hardness [Col. 0198A] he perceives within himself.

Esau comes tired from the field when our animal nature, wearied by earthly affairs, gathers itself toward the conscience seeking spiritual things. The cooking is red: it is the fiery restraint of the passions of flesh and blood. Redness signifies blood, carnal heat, or sin.

“Give me,” he says, “some of the red stew”—that is, cook my greedy desires for me, and, since I am exhausted by my cravings, fill me by dispelling the destructive hunger itself. For this reason our affection is called Edom, because it is continually constricted by earthly passions. Edom is interpreted as “earthly” or “bloody.”

“Sell me,” he says, “your birthright,” so that you may no longer usurp primacy for yourself in any of my habits by private authority, but, yielding to the command of royal majesty, [Col. 0198B] may profess that you will follow the footsteps of spirituality.

“What,” says the carnal affection, “will it profit me to plot wicked and unworthy dominions against reason, when I gain nothing from this except the losses of eternal death?”
