(Verses 33–34.) “Jacob said: ‘Swear to me.’ Esau swore to him and sold his birthright. Then, having received bread and a dish of lentils, he ate and drank and departed, thinking little of having sold his birthright.”

Esau swears while selling his birthright when the appetite of the flesh turns toward justice and right order, accepting the price of spiritual freedom and subjecting itself to the rule of reason.

He then receives bread and a dish of lentils when, after the hunger of avarice, he is refreshed by the bread of charity and nourished by consuming the carnal passions signified by the redness of lentils. He eats—that is, with the strong tooth of discernment [Col. 0198C] he wears down whatever is harmfully hard within him. He drinks, namely from the cup of spiritual grace. He departs, that is, he advances in virtue and places the primacy of wickedness beneath spiritual service.

103

# Chapter XXVI

Verses 1–2.—“A famine arose in the land, after the barrenness that had occurred in the days of Abraham, and he went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerara. The Lord appeared to him and said: ‘Do not go down into Egypt.’”

A famine arises in the land after the barrenness that occurred in Abraham’s days when the taste of divine sweetness is withdrawn from the mind in order to suppress the pride of our earthly nature, swollen by victory over its vices. This follows the barrenness by which Abraham—that is, the intellect—first became privately [Col. 0198D] unfruitful and tasteless before the shaking of the conscience. For reason first grows sluggish from the taste of God’s word; afterward, because of that very starvation, the conscience languishes severely. “Days” means the understandings of Abraham—that is, of reason, which during this night are wasting away.

Isaac goes to Abimelech, the king, in Gerara because the mind, intent upon heavenly joy, goes beyond itself toward the kingdom of its father, which is the world. There, when it strives to rejoice, it encounters the devil, who is the father of the lovers of the world, as king of those who are strangers—that is, of those who love the pilgrimage of this age as their homeland and thereby draw near to him.

Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father”; Gerara is interpreted as “an approaching stranger.”

The Lord appears to him when the intellect reveals the soul’s error [Col. 0199A] to its eyes. It says that he must not descend into Egypt—that is, must not flow downward into conformity with worldly people—but must remain in the land that it will show him.

(Verses 3.) “And dwell as a stranger in it.” Lower yourself and grow quiet from the labor and burden of worldly business upon the firm ground of humility. Do not have here a lasting city, but, as a stranger, seek the one that is to come (Hebrews XIII). I call those burdened and laboring to rest and to learn that I am meek and humble of heart (Matthew XI, 29).

“For to you and to your seed I will give all these regions”—that is, on account of the merit of your good will and the work that you sow here in hope of eternal fruit, I will give you all the senses of your body to possess and to restrain by the law of reason. These are the cities attributed in the Gospel to those who lend out their money well (Luke XIX, 17, 19), and in the Psalm are called the sides [Col. 0199B] of the house (Psalm CXXVII, 3)—namely, all the parts of our body.

Verse 4.—“Fulfilling the oath that I swore to your father Abraham. And I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven.”

That is, I will perfect whatever knowledge and uprightness serves with complete certainty the knowledge of intellectual understanding that protects you, and your works—or certainly the inward grace from which those works spring as from seed—like stars, that is, like virtues. They will shine both upon the heaven of your mind and upon the earth, giving the light of example to sinners.

“And I will give your descendants all these regions,” that is, to your imperishability and incorruptibility, which will be born for you after what now exists [Col. 0199C] in regeneration, I will give all the distinctions of body and soul to possess in blessedness.

“And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed,” that is, through the spiritual grace with which you are inwardly anointed, all bodily actions directed toward the worship of piety will be multiplied as though from true seed.

(Verses 5.) “Because Abraham obeyed my voice”—that is, your spirit obeyed my voice, meaning the inward suggestion—and kept my ceremonies and laws, having plainly reached the observance of good things through abstinence from evil.

Ceremonies are called *caerimoniae*, as though from *carere* (“to lack” or “to abstain”), because we patiently abstain from unlawful things in order to keep God’s laws.

### Verses 6, 7, 8, 9

So Isaac remained in Gerar. When the men of that place questioned him about his wife, he replied, “She is my sister.” For he had been afraid to confess that she was his wife, lest they kill him on account of her beauty. When many days had passed and he was still living there, Abimelech, looking through the window, saw him playing with his wife Rebekah. Calling for him, he said: “It is obvious that she is your wife. Why did you say that she was your sister?” He replied: “I was afraid that I might die because of her.”

If Abimelech signifies the kingdom of my father—that is, of the devil—for all lovers of the world are his subjects, and if the name Gerar itself means “expelling the sojourner,” because the conformity of such people expels a person from the worship of his own mind into the error of negligence, Isaac remains there when the mind, previously intent upon heavenly things, lies torpid amid the contemplation of worldly joy.

He is questioned by the men of that place about his wife when he is examined by whatever virtues, or even by the very movements of reason, which still courageously claim a place for themselves within the same conscience, concerning the condition of his will. Yet he replies that she is his sister, since he declares by his actions rather than by his words that he exercises this will not under intellectual judgment, as though under marital authority, but according to the discretion of free power. He fears being overwhelmed by the weight of temptations if he undertakes to resist any wrongful license. Thus some become weary of preserving the appearance of the mind amid its troubles.

Many days pass while he remains there, when, for anyone growing lukewarm, the reasonings of many understandings, and memories of virtues, as though certain successive days, bring themselves forward one after another like flashes of light.

Abimelech looks through a window when some worldly person belonging to the kingdom of the father—that is, the devil—examines the condition of a spiritual person through a window—that is, through the outward disposition of the senses. He sees him playing with his wife Rebekah when he sees the will subject to reason as to a wife’s rightful authority, not desiring to revel in worldly pleasures but eagerly willing to rejoice amid adversities in order to practice patience.

Perhaps that worldly person attacks him while he is attempting such things and complains about the restraint of his own will in divine matters: “If,” he says, “you had decided to rule your fluctuating impulses rationally, why did you display yourself as though unbridled and free through the evident slackness of your actions?” He replies: “I was afraid that I might be destroyed by the troubles of assaults if I attempted to resist the crowd of thoughts.” Let it therefore be regarded as human that he was afraid; but let it now be divine that he has regained strength against the world’s vanity.

### Verse 10

“Why,” Abimelech said, “have you imposed this upon us? Someone from the people might have lain with your wife, and you would have brought great guilt upon us.”

There are worldly people—and almost all are such—who, whenever they have detected religious men wavering for a little while through any signs, reproach them with great severity. “You,” they say, “who ought to have been a mirror of holiness for us, why did you impose occasions of offense upon those who wished to do well? You allowed your will, which ought to have been subject like a wife, to depart without a yoke, loosening its reins. Through the example of your laxity, some inexperienced and ignorant person could fall into the same pit of lust and error into which your shameless will has now rushed, and the whole mass of sin could fall upon us through you.”

And he commanded all the people:

### Verse 11

“Whoever touches this man’s wife shall surely be put to death.”

After the sinner appears to have corrected the just man, as though out of love for justice, he will attempt, if he can, to spread the same account everywhere among the nations under the same figure, so that by this means his own wickedness may be concealed. It is as though he were saying: “This man is celebrated among you as an image of holiness; but know that whoever allies himself with his ill will incurs the greatest crime.”

### Verses 12, 13, 14

Isaac sowed in that land and obtained a hundredfold in that same year. And the Lord blessed him. The man became rich, and advanced and increased continually, until he became exceedingly great. He also possessed flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and a very large household.

Isaac sowed in that earthly condition of his when the soul, recovering from the worldly state toward heavenly joy, covered humanity’s fall with the seed of good works.

A year signifies the perfection of some good thing. For just as a year shines through its days, so each virtue shines through the efforts of pious thoughts, words, and deeds. In this fullness of virtues, therefore, he obtained a hundredfold, when with foreseeing mind he faithfully gathers the sum of eternal reward, already awaited.

Thus he is blessed—that is, increased by spiritual substance—and enriched; yet, so that he may always remember his own frailty, he is called a man. Advancing, therefore, in virtue and increasing in hope, he proceeds—that is, he is drawn by desire—toward the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. 3:14), until he conquers his lowest desires through the greatness of holiness.

He possesses flocks of sheep and herds of cattle when he obtains an abundance both of active and contemplative goods without the participation of human praise. Since sheep are wool-bearing and simple, we understand them to signify the humble act of beneficence. Herds signify the strong works of religion, which also raise contemplative men to see divine things. The household is so called from serving; therefore he has a very large household who, however high a summit of virtues he has attained, nevertheless endures a crowd of thoughts, even though they serve reason whether they wish to or not.

### Verses 15, 16, 17

Because of this, the Philistines, out of envy, stopped up all the wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug at that time, filling them with earth, so that Abimelech himself said to Isaac: “Depart from us, for you have become much more powerful than we.”

So he departed from there and went toward the torrent of Gerar, where he settled.

The Philistines—also called Palaestinians—who are understood to signify demons falling through drinking, that is, through an excessive draught of pride, envy us because of the abundance of divine grace given to us. They bury under the earth of earthly thought the wells of capacity and understanding which the memory, will, affection, and the other interior movements of the soul—servants indeed of reason—had prepared after the rubbish of inertia had been removed. They block with the weight of cares the opening through which the depth of living waters is reached, namely, the subtlety of the intellect.

The demons’ envy burns so fiercely that through Abimelech—that is, through some wicked person belonging to the kingdom of the father of evils—they openly say to a religious person: “Depart from us, because you have become much more powerful than we.” This means: “If the excellence of your life surpasses us, do not appear among us, who still serve the world; live far away from us and conspicuously, as though you were merely pretending.”

The torrent of Gerar signifies the changeability and rush of human life, namely, of the stranger who approaches the end of his pilgrimage. The more, therefore, a pious person is troubled by those greedy for worldly glory, the more he is driven to consider earthly transience, and in this contemplation he fixes the state of his mind.

### Verses 18, 19

Isaac dug again the other wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug and which the Philistines had stopped up long ago after Abraham’s death. He called them by the same names by which his father had formerly called them. They dug in the torrent and found living water.

Abraham dies when understanding is separated from God. The other wells, which Isaac digs after they have been stopped up, signify knowledge of God and the knowledge of each virtue, from which we draw a life-giving stream. Through the failure of reason, these are filled by demons with an obstruction of earthly things. But when the soul breathes again toward heavenly joys, they are emptied through spiritual pursuits that serve reason—namely, the true Abraham—by the diligent care of discernment.

He calls them by the same names by which his father had called them when he so distinguishes himself by his reputation for holiness before God and human beings that the subtlety of reason itself dictates that he ought to do so.

We dig in the torrent when we examine the transience of this temporal condition. There we find living water, because, measuring the course of the world, we see that the fountain of water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:14) is sufficient for us to attain glory once the transience of present things has been despised.

### Verses 20, 21, 22

But there was also a quarrel there between the shepherds of Gerar and the shepherds of Isaac. They said: “The water is ours.” Therefore he called the name of the well, because of what had happened, “Calumny.” They dug another well, and they quarreled over that one also; so he called it “Hostilities.” Departing from there, he dug another well, over which they did not contend.

By the shepherds of Gerar we understand the senses of our flesh, which nourish us with little draughts of worldly wantonness. The shepherds of Isaac are the contemplative movements, which restore the soul’s failings with spiritual food.

Carnal things therefore quarrel against spiritual things and say, “The water is ours,” when they persuade us that worldly knowledge is altogether superior to spiritual knowledge, whose glory is readily apparent.

He calls the well “Calumny” because of the event, when from that understanding which is gathered by examining the torrent an illustrious and perpetual calumny against the shepherds of Gerar is stirred within the inner person.

The other well that is dug signifies the virtue of sacred preaching. Drawing strength from the excavation of the torrent and from drinking the life-giving water, it offers drink to others all the more purely the nearer it stands to the spring. They quarrel over this well also, because whenever those who speak well are found to have any weakness in their own conduct, it is immediately brought against them.

He calls it “Hostilities,” and not incongruously, because, according to the poet, “truth produces hatred at this time” (Ter. *Andr.* 1.41).

It is therefore necessary to depart from there—that is, to advance toward a better state of life—and to dig a well. After the earthly affections have been removed from the soul, one must seek the purest fountain of life not on the surface of thought, imagination, or outward vision, but in the deepest interior of understanding.

For the order of our action proceeds from the inner vein of our intention; from it examples of instruction flow out to others. First, therefore, the well of doctrine is dug; afterward, the well of righteous action is dug. The latter is altogether free from contention, because such people generally receive the greatest reverence from those who can bring no charge against them.

First, I say, the soul of one who labors, according to Solomon, labors for itself, because “his mouth has compelled him” (Prov. 16:26). Indeed, on account of the duty of preaching, lest the preacher be found reprobate, the exercise of pious action is usually greatly extended.

And conversely: “The sluggard,” he says, “hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it back to his mouth” (Prov. 19:24).

Therefore he also called its name “Broad Place,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and caused us to increase upon the earth.”

If charity is called breadth, charity is certainly greatest when one labors in speech for the salvation of one’s neighbor and wisely orders one’s life so that it may accord with one’s speech and benefit others by example.

Alternatively: In the Gospel, God is accustomed, by wondrous grace, to enlarge the understanding of those who labor the more earnestly, so that they may recognize and eloquently clarify the mysteries of sacred speech. He does not say, “The Lord has enlarged me,” but “us,” in the plural, because whatever a pious person attains either in doctrine or in the pursuit of virtue, he considers to have been given by God not so much for his own benefit as for that of his neighbor.

God causes us to increase upon the earth when he makes us excel in spirit over the desires of the body, or when he makes us rise above the earth—that is, above Christ, who nourishes all who are founded upon him—through virtues.

### Verses 23, 24

Isaac went up from that place to Beersheba, where the Lord appeared to him that very night, saying: “I am the God of your father. Do not be afraid, because I am with you.”

Beersheba is said to mean “the well of satiety,” or “the fifth well.” The well of satiety is the fullness of contemplative refreshment. It is called “fifth” because it surpasses the fourfold dignity of all temporality.

Some also say—and this is true—that it is not the fifth well but the seventh. This accords well with the meaning, because wisdom concerning spiritual gifts is the seventh degree, where there is fullness of life and glory, since God is wisdom.

From that place, therefore—from the breadth of charity mentioned above—we ascend to Beersheba, that is, to a draught of the divine vision, for only in that breadth can one stand rightly.

There, amid the obscurity of the mirror and the riddle, God warns us not to fear. He is the one who has already filled our Abraham—that is, our understanding—with his knowledge. He will be present with us in the multiplication of the seed—that is, of grace—so that we may behold him not dimly but openly.

### Verse 25

So he built an altar there, invoked the name of the Lord, spread his tent there, and commanded his servants to dig a well.

We build an altar there when, the more we know God, the more eagerly we establish an ever stronger and better will to do good. Without this, every virtue is narrow. By bringing together virtues from every side, we raise this will to God.

Hence it is also said that, after invoking the name of God, he spread his tent, since by the effects of his works he extends the desire of his good will toward carrying out service to God—not for his own reputation but for the praise of God alone.

This is what the tent signifies. He commands his servants to dig a well when he orders his interior and exterior movements to investigate how great it may be to taste God face to face, if it is so great to contemplate him in the mirror and riddle.

### Verses 26, 27, 28

When Abimelech, Ochozath his friend, and Phicol, the commander of his army, came to him from Gerar, Isaac said to them: “Why have you come to me, a man whom you hate and whom you expelled from your midst?”

They replied: “We have seen that the Lord is with you.”

Gerar is said to mean “their horned one,” by which is understood the desire to harm, unquestionably that of demons.

From there, therefore—from the impulse of their own malice—they come to the altar, which is the principal place. Abimelech, whose name means “my father is king,” or “the kingdom of my father,” signifies pride, which the devil chiefly commands, since he is king over all the sons of pride (Job 41:25).

Ochozath—we do not know who he was, yet we do not doubt that he was his accomplice—may reasonably be understood to signify envy, the daughter of pride. Hence his name is interpreted as “holding” or “comprehending,” because he holds the heart which he has seized so tightly that it is difficult for it to resist.

In another translation Abimelech is called his “bridegroom’s companion,” because when pride luxuriates in carnal pleasures, its envy follows its excesses like a kind of bridesmaid—that is, an accompaniment of wickedness.

Phicol, the commander of the army, signifies empty glory, the support of every perversity. His name is interpreted as “the mouth of all,” because he takes particular delight in the breath of human praise.

These three—pride, envy, and empty glory—intrude upon a person who rejects earthly things and loves heavenly things with a special persecution, and all the more perniciously because they come under the name of friends with an appearance of devotion, as though to give counsel.

Isaac nevertheless answers them and anticipates their words, as though saying: “What fellowship do I have with you, when I have found in you nothing but a deadly poison for my soul, and when your very detestability, by its horror, has driven me away from the ambition of the world?”

“We have seen,” they say, “by the very evidence of your works, that God is with you. Since you excel spiritually, you are worthy of every temporal honor, as you see many obtaining it undeservedly, because the favor of your religion is spread everywhere.

“Consider, therefore, that we desire to benefit you. Do not refuse to lend your ears to those who give good counsel. Consider that we have never harmed you or diminished your prosperity; rather, we have allowed you, strong in manifold praise, to flourish until now.

“Do not reject our covenant, since you perceive yourself increasing as God multiplies you, if you heed our warnings.”

These words, expressed in equivalent form, accord with their meaning.

### Verses 30, 31, 32, 33

So he made them a banquet. After they had eaten and drunk, they rose in the morning and swore an oath to one another. Isaac dismissed them peacefully to their own place.

And behold, on that very day Isaac’s servants came and announced to him concerning the well which they had dug, saying: “We have found water.” Therefore he called it “Abundance.”

Isaac makes a banquet for these three when he increases and nourishes these very flatteries of the vices by means of certain reasonings.

They rise after food and drink when, after the dishes of temporal glory—which are watered by the drinks of human rational counsel—they are lifted up in hope of fulfilling their ambition.

They swear to one another in the morning when, in the very smile of prosperity, the faithful soul and vice enter into an alliance with one another.

Morning, or dawn, and even day are used of favorable circumstances, as in Job: “If the dawn should suddenly appear, they consider it the shadow of death” (Job 24:17).

He dismisses them peacefully to their own place when he permits them to wander through the affections of vanity without any rebuke from the spirit. But on that very day, the movements of pious thought that serve reason suggest to the inner person that they have found water, that they have tasted some knowledge of God.

Therefore he calls it “Abundance,” because it recalls him from the desire for temporal things to the overflowing abundance of divine eternity.

And the name was given to the city, Beersheba, even to the present day.

This city is the multitude of the heavenly Church, which is nourished by the fountain of life, where “light is seen in light, and day from day” (Ps. 35:10).

The name Beersheba is imposed upon it because the thirst of avarice or of any vice, burning in this world, is extinguished through contemplation of this fountain by eternal satiety. In the future, the whole portion of the saved will be made blessed by its sole infusion.

For that well—namely, the knowledge of God—reaches even to that unfailing day, seen in the present, which is “better in his courts than thousands of days” (Ps. 83:11).

### Verses 34, 35

Esau, now forty years old, took as wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon, a man of the same place. Both of them offended Isaac and Rebekah.

Esau, whose name is interpreted as “in vain,” signifies the lower part of us, namely, the carnal affection intent upon vanity.

Being forty years old—that is, devoted to temporality, which is signified by the number four—he took wives representing wantonness and worldly desire.

Judith means “praising” or “confessing”; Beeri, “of the well”; and Hittite, “stunned.” Confession and praise offered to God solely on account of worldly prosperity are the daughter of what is fleeting, accomplishing nothing worthy of virtue, and the daughter of wells—that is, of carnal desires—because they emerge from the darkest pleasure.

For he confesses not out of any love for eternity, but because you have benefited him in the present. Such confession, while people imagine themselves devoted to God, casts them into a reprobate mind and into bewilderment, so that they freely imagine themselves able to practice every stench of vice.

Basemath is interpreted, in the names, either as “delinquent” or “deposed.” By this pride is understood, for pride greatly exults in the celebration of names. In Scripture a name is commonly used for reputation. When pride sins by exalting itself vainly, it moves toward the fall of eternal deposition.

Elon is said to mean either “a level region” or “an oak.” A level region suggests the breadth of worldly life; a plain displays the mind’s lack of cultivation. An oak, whose fruit feeds swine, signifies workers of wickedness, in whom demons rejoice.

The daughter of such parents, therefore—pride, born from the worst of parents—is joined to Esau, that is, to affection. She is also said to be of the same place: the breadth of perversity according to its errors, the rustic and ill-disciplined work of the sinner, perverse and loved by demons.

When this affection freely flows through these things among worldly people, it irritates Isaac—that is, the soul thinking upon heavenly joy—when reason bends itself toward such things even for a little while, and it greatly troubles Rebekah—that is, patience—which attempts most fiercely to resist these movements.

## Chapter 27

### Verses 1, 2, 3

Isaac grew old, and his eyes became dim, so that he could not see. He called Esau, his elder son, and said to him: “My son.” He replied: “Here I am.” His father said to him: “You see that I have grown old and do not know the day of my death. Now take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out into the open country.”

Isaac’s old age is the soul’s decline from spiritual strength. His eyes grow dim when wicked desires strike back the sharpness of his mind from God.

After the intellect ceases from interior vision, it must immediately pass into the affection of the heart, according to the Psalm (Ps. 72:7). Therefore he calls his son “elder,” not because of dignity but because of a certain priority in temporal use—that is, he calls the affection itself: “My son.”

It is as though he were saying: “Since you naturally proceed from me, it is not absurd if you serve my desires. You see that I have fallen away from heavenly love, and I do not know the day—that is, the understanding—of this decline inflicted upon me by God.

“Take, therefore, the quiver of counsel, in which you may heap up an abundance of arrows—that is, of judgments—and the bow of cunning and deceitful action, with which you may discharge the deceits you have conceived. Armed with these, go out: neglecting interior things, exercise outward cares.”

Accordingly the sinners say in the Psalms: “They have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver” (Ps. 10:2), so that wicked movements may kill rightly directed reasonings.

And when you have caught something in the hunt:

### Verse 4

“Prepare me a dish from it, as you know that I desire, and bring it to me so that I may eat, and my soul may bless you before I die.”

The soul goes hunting and catches something when, seeking carnal goods, it binds some suitable desire in the nets of its longing.

It prepares a dish from it when, cooking the same thing in the fire of desire, it draws it wholly into the softness of pleasure. For whatever is pursued in the world, whether laboriously or pleasantly, has some pleasure as the end of its intention.

“Bring it,” he says, “as you know that I desire, so that I may eat”—that is, just as you infer that the human affection takes delight in each thing, so bring me that by which I ought to nourish my appetite, so that my soul may bless you before I die: that is, so that my animal nature may persist in increasing you in many ways before it is destroyed by some worldly grief over glory.

### Verses 5, 6

When Rebekah heard this, and he had gone into the field to fulfill his father’s command, she said to her son Jacob:

When reason has been bent toward a worldly affection—namely, when Rebekah, patience, is terrified by the loss of labors already expended—she recalls the spiritual appetite, which, now wandering toward earthly gain, may supplant the vice of desire.

“I have understood,” she says, “the intellect that ought to have supported you acting together with affection in the exchange of carnal things. But do not refuse to devote your desire and zeal to the hope of heavenly things.”

### Verse 7

“Go to the flock and bring me two excellent young goats, so that I may prepare from them food for your father, which he gladly eats.”

We go to the flock when we devote ourselves to the multiplicity of virtues.

We offer two excellent young goats when we mourn before God with great devotion the evils both of ourselves and of those whom we have caused to sin, and confess them with the same due humility. For a young goat signifies a sinner.

I do not know whether I have said elsewhere in this work what a prudent reader may judge appropriate here: that the saying of Isaiah spoken by the Lord applies to this passage: “Though your sins be as scarlet, and again, as crimson” (Isa. 1:18); and that snow corresponds to scarlet and wool to crimson, under the excellent significance of these two.

From them Rebekah prepares food which the father gladly eats when patience, from the material of repentance, prepares other virtues, with which, as with seasonings, she changes and obtains the support of reason for herself.

### Verse 10

“When you bring them to him,” she says, “he will bless you before he dies.”

That is: when he has recovered strength from virtue, before he falls again into some failure, he will anticipate you by acquiring the grace of divine increase.

### Verses 11, 12, 13, 14

“You know that Esau my brother is a hairy man, while I am smooth. If my father touches me and feels me, I fear that he will think that I wished to mock him and bring a curse upon myself instead of a blessing.”

But she said: “Let that curse be upon me, my son. Only listen to my voice: Go and bring me what I have said.”

He went, brought them, and gave them to his mother.

Esau—that is, the carnal affection—is bristling and rough with the hairs of so many bodily passions. He is called my brother because we proceed from the same mind. I, resting upon divine tranquility, am naturally smooth and peaceful.

If the intellect whom I follow as my father, and upon whom the care of doing good rests, perceives the roughness of so many passions arising, I fear that he will attribute to mockery and frivolity the desire to undertake such difficult things, and that all this may incline me toward a worse failure rather than toward any progress in life.

For despair concerning a good undertaking is accustomed always to fall back into something worse.

“I,” says the mother Patience, “will bear the troubles and weariness of the curse—that is, of this failure, if there is one. Only proceed by undertaking the pursuit of piety, and bring what you have done wrong by confessing it—or rather, cleanse it by the offering of confession.”

He departed, advancing from lower things to higher. He brought the works of repentance, which the mother, that is, patience, receives for preparation with the seasoning of other virtues, and which she anxiously brings to birth.

### Verses 15, 16, 17

She prepared the food just as she knew his father desired. She clothed him in Esau’s very fine garments, which she had in the house with her, and wrapped the skins of the young goats around his hands and covered the naked parts of his neck. She gave him the dish and handed him the bread which she had baked.

Rebekah prepares food according to the father’s desire when patience, according to what has been implanted in it by the intellect, composes and orders the refreshment of virtues through endurance of passions. For there is no virtue that the endurance of temptations does not commend.

We have Esau’s very fine garments at home with us when we possess, naturally implanted as though in the house of the mind, the adornments of pious desire, without which we preserve no good things; and when, with all carnality excluded and its affection removed, we clothe the mind that supplants vice—namely, Jacob—in these garments.

She wraps the hands in young goats’ skins when she protects future action from a similar fall by the memories of sins committed.

She covers the naked parts of the neck when she protects the unguarded parts of one’s own speech and thought with continual humility and remembrance of former error. For we produce through the neck the words that we think, and therefore we use it for both.

She gives the dish when she softens and dries the mind with the fire of spiritual desire, removing all moisture and hardness of blood—that is, of sin.

Afterward she hands over the bread which she had baked when she proposes the weakness of conversion to the mind for observance, through the ardor of divine charity, as flour transformed into the strength of bread, so that it may attain the solidity of holy conduct.

Patience does all these things when, amid the murmuring of carnal movements, she persists in the zeal of religion. When these things have been brought to the father, reason must provide for them in a fatherly manner.

When he has obeyed and extended his affection as though toward his children, Jacob—that is, the spiritual appetite—says:

### Verse 19

“I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you commanded me.”

That is: “If you ask whom I profess to be, I declare that I have lived according to affection and the senses of the body, which is the human being’s first life. I do not deny my carnality, just as I know that you teach me.

“Rise, therefore, to defend my tenderness; sit for the display of judicial discretion; eat from my hunt—that is, be refreshed by the complete consumption of carnal things—so that your soul may bless me, that is, so that your life may attribute spiritual increase to me.”

The soul is plainly accustomed to stand for life, as in the saying: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it” (John 12:25). But by “life” we mean the quality of life.

### Verse 20

“How,” Isaac said, “were you able to find it so quickly?”

The will replied: “It was God’s will that what I wanted should quickly meet me.”

Sometimes reason marvels that, so suddenly, a spirit of compunction should be infused into it from such great hardness. Yet through the appetite for piety it attributes everything to the grace of God.

### Verses 21, 23, 23

“Come here,” he said, “so that I may touch you, my son, and test whether you are my son Esau or not.”

He came to his father, and after touching him Isaac said: “The voice is indeed Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.” He did not recognize him, because his hairy hands reproduced the appearance of his elder brother.

Isaac touches Jacob as he approaches in order to test whether he is his son Esau, when the soul, now longing for heavenly joys, attempts with certainty to experience whether the pious affection now fitting for it truly repents of the affection of carnality to which it once devoted itself—that is, whether it recognizes itself as Esau.

Touch is recognized as the end of knowing. Just as a son proceeds from a father, so a pious or worldly affection receives from reason—whether humanly or divinely inspired—an occasion, so to speak, of coming into being: for example, empty glory arises from virtue, or the vice of complacency just as a worm arises from manna.

After the true confession of the supplanter has been tested, therefore, he affirms that the voice is Jacob’s but the hands are Esau’s. Although he abhors and condemns the works of his former carnality, he nevertheless praises the voice of the penitent—indeed, of the just person who, while supplanting vices, accuses himself of them at the outset.

To the extent that he lived carnally, he is now no longer recognized—that is, he is not approved—because the hairy hands, namely, the imagined forms of dreadful works, whether he wishes it or not, bring a worldly affection upon him.

Understand that he is called “elder” because the animal nature is the first to be active in a human being.

### Verse 24

“You are my son Esau?” he said.

“You confess that you exercised a bestial affection within my soul.”

“I confess,” he replied.

And he said:

### Verse 25

“Offer [or: bring] me food from your hunt, my son.”

That is: “If, then, you confess that you have gone astray according to affection and that you repent of the desire for carnal gain, which you have turned into food—that is, into the seasonings of virtue—offer it to me for my refreshment.”

When he had eaten what was offered, he also gave him wine.

He ate what was offered when he turned whatever carnality was in him to the use of virtue.

He also gives wine when he composes and orders all these things through the gift of spiritual grace. For this makes not only human beings glad, as it is written (Ps. 103:15), but God himself also.

### Verse 26

After he had drunk it, he approached and kissed him, because, with his mind made fruitful through the spirit, Jacob approaches Isaac by the movement of thought. As he truly repents of his dreadful works, he reaches Isaac’s kiss—that is, a taste of heavenly joy.

### Verse 27

As soon as he perceived the fragrance of his garments, he blessed him and said:

“See, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed.”

The fragrance of the garments is perceived when the faithful soul, in its desire, experiences through foreknowledge the preparation of pious actions and the sweetness of its holy purpose, as though through its sense of smell.

While blessing, that is, multiplying these things with every kind of discernment, he declares the fragrance of the son to be like the fragrance of a full field. For just as a conscience cultivated through discipline and abundantly filled with the fruits of virtues gives off a heavenly scent, so the appetite itself, immediately imbued with the same flavor, gives off nothing other than what makes the mind itself smile.

God blesses the person whom he causes to advance.

### Verse 28

“May God give you of the dew of heaven”—that is, spiritual abundance—“and of the richness of the earth”—namely, the affections which are the lower part of you, made strong to receive the dew of heaven—“an abundance of grain,” meaning knowledge; “of wine,” meaning wisdom, that is, divine knowledge, which makes us forget the evils of this life; “and of oil,” meaning fraternal charity, which restrains the knowledge acquired through worldly disciplines of prudence, so that we may not become puffed up.

### Verse 29

“May peoples serve your victory, and may they adore you.”

That is: may those spiritual realities which are called “tribes” from their Trinity—faith, hope, and charity—piously urge you outwardly toward the love of divinity.

We say *adorare*—“to adore”—as though from *ad* and *orare*, “to pray alongside”; for *ad* in compounds commonly expresses proximity. Nothing is more “alongside” than what is within the mind. They therefore pray alongside it when they admonish the mind.

“Be lord of your brothers,” namely, of the movements generated from the same mind.

“And let the sons of your mother bow before you”: let your strong works, which have been produced from charity—the charity that gave birth to you for God—be humbled in your consideration.

“Let whoever curses you be cursed”: whatever wages war against your failure—that is, the vices—will fail within you.

“And let whoever blesses you be filled with blessings”: whatever contributes to your progress—without doubt, the pursuits of virtue—let it always increase.

With these matters treated as the Holy Spirit prospers them, let the conclusion now come to our seventh work on Genesis.

**The seventh book ends.**

## The eighth book of the *Moralia on Genesis* begins.

From the book of Daniel we learn that “many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4). We attribute this multiplicity of knowledge to ourselves in no way; rather, filling the smallness of our little basket with fragments of the Lord’s things, and setting them before minds neither weighty nor superior but equal and comparable, we continue what we have begun through the midst of the ranks of those who protest.

## Chapter 27 follows.

### VERSES 30, 31

Isaac had scarcely finished speaking, and, as Jacob went out, Esau came. He brought his father cooked food from the hunt, saying, “Rise, my father, and eat,” and so forth.

Isaac had scarcely finished speaking—scarcely, indeed, had he begun to carry into effect what had just been said with devout affection—and Jacob went out: that is, worldly desire had plainly been supplanted and overthrown, and a devout affection proceeding from the innermost purpose went forth to the open display of holy works. Then Esau came. Esau is the carnal will. While the faithful soul establishes a good will for itself outwardly, the carnal will secretly hunts after carnal desires; but while spiritual things are being considered by that soul, the carnal will, overcome by the devotion of its pious desire, comes to the same conclusion. What it had sought carnally, it cooks through the fervor of the spirit and, reduced to spiritual tenderness, places before the mind hungering for righteousness. What follows has already been treated above.

### VERSE 32

“Who are you?” he said.

We know that there are two wills in a human being: one bodily and the other spiritual. The former lies hidden in the heart while the mind is occupied with spiritual things, so deeply concealed that it is thought completely extinguished unless an opportunity arises to reveal it. When, therefore, the earthly will suddenly presents itself to one who is at leisure for heavenly things, it is as though someone asks who an unknown person is.

“I am,” he says, “that carnal affection of yours to which, as your firstborn—that is, as what is natural and originally implanted in you—you ought chiefly to have clung.”

### VERSE 33

The mind is seized with overwhelming astonishment. A short while earlier it had seemed heavenly to itself; now, moved by some base material, it meditates on something more than earthly. Having recently cooked food, it now does not hesitate to grow raw again into the hardness of flesh. It marvels on both sides at who he is and who he has been. It had ascended as far as the heavens, but now it descends as far as the abyss.

“Who, then, is he who brought me the game that he had just caught?”

It is as though he were saying: “If you are the carnal will, as you truly are, and thrust yourself upon me so openly, who—or whence—was he who recently came upon me: that spiritual affection which, after the carnal desire had, as I thought, been thoroughly cooked away, restored me almost entirely with heavenly desire? Because of his worth, his usefulness, and the need to increase him within me, I judged that I should multiply him and, if I could, enlarge him further with perpetual growth.”

This is what follows: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”

### VERSE 34

When Esau heard his father’s words, he roared with a great cry and, dismayed, said:

When the animal will hears—that is, understands—the admonitions and firmness of reason, it rages with bestial agitation within the conscience. Roaring belongs to wild beasts; yet, when the mind’s judgment remains firm, that fury is consumed within itself like a flame and becomes quiet.

Hence it is that the demon, when it is driven out by the Lord, almost kills the boy as it departs (Luke 9:42). Thus, when animality has already been turned toward religion and devoted to the spirit, it wishes and asks to be blessed—that is, to grow through divine gifts.

### VERSES 35, 36

“Your brother came deceitfully,” Isaac said, “and took away your blessing.”

Esau added: “His name was rightly called Jacob; for he has supplanted me these two times.”

He comes deceitfully as a brother when, at the time of conversion, the devout will surrounds and deceives the flow of affection by many evasions of reasoning. He takes away his blessing when the desire for earthly advancement is changed into the gains of heavenly benefit. We have often said that “blessing” signifies multiplication.

“He is rightly called a supplanter,” Esau says, “who first overturned me at the beginning of my conversion and then, when the storm of temptations arose, overthrew me through victory over all perversity.”

For there are two stages. The first is conversion, which is the exodus from Egypt. The second is the overcoming of temptation, which consists in the battles fought before the promised land is possessed. The third is not under discussion here.

“He has taken away my birthright, and now a second time he has stolen my blessing.”

This means: “He first removed from himself me, to whom it principally belonged—indeed, to whom it belonged naturally—to rejoice in the movements of the body. Then, when I wished to make some progress in this world, in what would have been sufficiently lawful, he took away from me the hope of all worldly advancement. But since I cannot oppose the spiritual appetite fighting with the strength of the spirit, tell me,” he says, “whether, when I finally return to my heart, you will grant me hope of spiritual advancement.”

### VERSE 37

“I have made him your lord,” Isaac said—that is, I have decreed that you should obey the dominion of the devout will, and that all the movements of the mind that dissent from its unity—movements called “brothers” because they are generated in some way from the same mind—should be subjected to it.

“I have established him with the grain of the word of God and the wine of the sevenfold grace. And what can I do for you now, my son?”

The whole meaning is: “If you refuse to obey the just appetite honored with divine gifts, what remedy can I specifically bring you?”

### VERSE 38

“Have you only one blessing? Bless me also, I beg you.”

He is saying: “Are you so inclined to care only for the good will that you refuse to take care of the things that you desire perversely and humanly? Say something by which I may make progress.”

### VERSES 39, 40

When Esau wept with a great lament, Isaac was moved and said:

“Your blessing shall be in the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above. You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother. The time will come when you will shake off and loosen his yoke from your neck.”

Esau no longer roars like a wild beast but laments like a human being. Grieving over his vanity through the impulse of a devout will, he stirs within the spirit itself a movement of piety and devotion.

“You can be blessed,” he says, “in the fatness of the earth”—that is, if you confess that you are earth, a sinner, then, once wicked affections have been put to sleep, grow fat with the dew of heaven: with grace and the infusion of understanding. This understanding, as though it were heaven above you, must give you light and the rains of instruction, making you fertile for the fruit of good works.

“You shall live by the sword”: you will obtain life through the discernment of good and evil. You will serve your brother—that is, the devout affection which proceeds from the same reason as you, as from a mother—but only for a time. For after you have reached the perfect warmth of divine love, you will no longer be subject to the good will or even to reason. Rather, you will be transformed into what the good will or reason is; you will feel what it feels and be what it is.

### VERSE 41

Esau therefore always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. He said in his heart:

“The days of mourning for my father will come, and then I shall kill my brother Jacob.”

Although the perverse will is for a time harmonized with the devout affection, can lasting harmony exist if it is able to remain? For “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5:17).

To the extent, therefore, that Esau recognizes that he agrees with his father—that is, with reason—he hates Jacob. Esau’s heart is the evil intention of the affections. Thus, so that faithful understanding—Isaac—may find material for mourning, the perverse affection thinks that it can destroy the good will through love of temporal things.

But he speaks of “days” that are to come: the brightnesses of false prosperity, by which he may overwhelm Isaac—that is, the heavenly joys within the soul.

### VERSE 42

These things were reported to Rebekah. She sent for her son Jacob and said to him:

“Behold, your brother Esau threatens to kill you. Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice; rise and flee to Laban, my brother, in Haran, and dwell with him a few days, until your brother’s fury subsides,” and so forth.

These things are reported to Rebekah when, amid the conflicts of such quarrels, weariness is inflicted upon patience as it struggles on. Yet, fearing the losses of past endurance, she sends the heavenly reward as a messenger; through it she draws the devout appetite toward herself and fortifies it against the ferocity of the approaching carnality.

“Obey,” she says, “the heavenly things that promise endurance. Rising from the lowest desires, flee worldly things, advancing toward brightness—indeed, toward the white-robed army of the heavenly Church. Under God the Father, it is our brother; while you live, you should imitate him by acting in holiness and election, as though dwelling in Haran. You shall dwell with him: you shall rule your foolish movements after his example. For this is what the shortness of the days of this world demands: that the fury of the perverse affection be restrained and that, intoxicated by the grace of reason, it forget the wantonness of its earlier life, from which it has been deprived.”

Laban is called “white”; Haran means “chosen,” or also “being angry.” This perhaps suggests that you cannot become chosen unless you are always found angry with bodily allurements: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5).

### VERSE 45

“Afterward I shall send for you and bring you back here.”

Jacob is brought back from there after Esau’s fury has been put to sleep when, from victory over the passions—as from Haran—and from contemplation of heavenly glory—as from Laban—we return to consideration of ourselves and of what we once were.

Rebekah sends for Jacob to bring him back when, with the messenger of reason going before, good patience indicates that the good will must return to itself lest it think too highly of itself.

“Why should I be deprived of both my sons in one day?”

She is saying: “Why should I spend myself on momentary joys, joys lasting as though for a single day, and on brief allurements of fleeting desire, and meanwhile kill what remains to me of the good will?”

### VERSE 46

“I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth,” Rebekah said to Isaac.

Patience, relying upon heavenly joys, complains with them—as though with her own Isaac—of the difficulty and weariness caused by vices. We have already sufficiently explained that the daughters signify fluid desires, while Heth signifies stupor, that is, a reprobate sense.

“If Jacob takes a wife from the stock of this land, I do not wish to live.”

If the devout will clings to earthly desires, I show through evident signs that I choose eternal death.

She too is weary of her life when, under the onrushing pressure of evils, the practice of piety—which is truly life—begins through human weakness to weary patience.

## CHAPTER 28

### VERSES 1, 2

Isaac therefore called Jacob and blessed him. He commanded him, saying:

“Do not take a wife from the race of Canaan. But go and depart to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s brother, and take a wife for yourself there from the daughters of Laban, your maternal uncle.”

Isaac calls Jacob when the faithful soul, sighing for heavenly joy, stirs the good will toward itself. He blesses him when he strives to add virtue to his virtue.

The sense of his words is this: “Do not cling to the allurements of pleasures from the race of Canaan”—that is, of merchants—for you will certainly become like those who expend faith and good works in carrying out their carnality. Rather, strive to advance so that you may resemble those souls who, through the brightness of purity and not through the flow of lust, are daughters of eternal whiteness, toward whose kinship I sigh through endurance.

“Go therefore to Mesopotamia of Syria”—that is, undertake a vocation lifted up from the lowest desires, which is renunciation of the world, so that through contemplation you may rise and stand exalted. Mesopotamia means “elevated vocation”; Syria means “sublime.”

Mesopotamia is also so called in Greek because it is “between the rivers.” This is highly appropriate to the soul struggling amid the dangers of temptations. Yet these very things raise us up to Syria—that is, to sublime realities.

In these sublime places is the house of Bethuel, that is, of the virgin of God: plainly the super-heavenly Church, which no longer has wrinkle or blemish (Ephesians 5:27), than which nothing is now more pure.

Bethuel is the brother of our mother because that heavenly people is joined by kindred affinity to the Church, our mother, which is on earth.

### VERSES 3, 4

“May the Lord multiply you,” he said, “so that you may become a multitude of peoples, and may he give you the blessings of Abraham, and to your seed after you, so that you may possess the land of your pilgrimage which he promised to your grandfather.”

This means: “May God strengthen you with such power of mind that you may exist—that is, stand firmly—amid the turbulence of vices. May he enlarge for Abraham—that is, for understanding—the gift of knowledge, and repay your seed—that is, your merit—after death with the gifts of true blessing, so that you may possess the land of the body in which you have lived as a pilgrim, rising again in happiness.

“He promised this through the prophets to Christ, the father and author of the universal mother, the Church, and thus to your grandfather, Christ himself, the ancestor of you who are children of that same Church.”

### VERSE 5

When Isaac had sent him away, he departed and went to Mesopotamia, and so forth. What has been treated above may suffice. Nevertheless, Isaac’s sending him away means nothing other than directing the effect of the good will from the intention of heavenly joy.

### VERSES 6–9

Esau saw that his father had blessed Jacob and sent him to Mesopotamia of Syria to take a wife from there, and that after the blessing he had commanded him, saying, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.” The whole of this is clear from what we discussed above; let us now proceed.

When Esau perceived that his father did not look favorably upon the daughters of Canaan, the carnal affection—shaken by the growth of the good will and by the practice of virtue—burns more fiercely against the spirit that longs for heavenly things. It repeatedly thrusts upon the spirit those desires of the world from which reason recoils more strongly.

Hence he also goes to Ishmael: he advances toward the desires of the world, by which each person obeys not God but himself. Ishmael means “obedient to himself.”

In addition to these wives—that is, worldly cares and necessities by which he was bound—he embraces the daughter of Ishmael, the wantonness of bodily pleasure.

It should be noted, however, that Ishmael is called the son of Abraham because, from the great strength of reason, there sometimes arises a great movement of desire or vainglory, as well as of carnal lust, and an even fiercer movement—a certain wicked and degenerate son.

The daughter herself, the fluid will, is called Meleth [variant: Maheleth], which is interpreted as “chorus.” Although “chorus” is usually used in a good sense for harmony, here, because it is recognized as belonging to dancing women, it signifies that inner harmony of lust in the heart which introduces Sirens to us, sweet even unto destruction, and surrounds us by its seductive arts.

She is the sister of Nabajoth, whose name means “prophesying,” because carnal desire rejoices in a prophecy that clings to it as a kind of sister: when, in old age, the concern of youth has cooled, it promises itself the practices of penitence and celibacy.

### VERSES 10–13

Jacob therefore departed from Beersheba and went toward Haran. When he came to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, he took one of the stones that lay there, placed it beneath his head, and slept in that place. He saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, its top touching heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder.

Jacob departs from Beersheba—that is, from “the seventh well,” or “the well of fullness”: plainly from the abyss of worldly lust, which revolves through seven days and which, under the influence of heavenly joy, is beginning to become full—that is, to become wearisome.

Jacob, the good will, goes forth and travels toward Haran, which is interpreted as “a matter with an ark,” so that he may possess both the ark of conscience and, since “ark” derives from *arcere*, “to restrain,” restrain from it whatever is harmful. In it there should also be a “matter,” that is, truth, so that everything contained within may be recognized as customary and substantial, rather than wandering about through empty things.

The certain place to which he comes is the place in which the universality of the whole creation, and especially of all goodness, exists and subsists. When someone approaches it through desire and merits, he rests there only after sunset—that is, after the heat of bodily passions has been quieted.

Even then, he must first take as an example one of the stones that lie there: the holy ones, who are firm like stones and conduct themselves humbly. They are rolled upon the earth, according to Zechariah (Zechariah 9:16). He must place such a stone beneath his head—that is, beneath his mind—as support, so that in the place which is always the same, plainly God, he may be lulled to sleep away from worldly noise.

He sees the ladder in a dream while he closes the mind’s gaze to love of present things. This is the ladder of humility, which does not totter but stands firmly upon the earth—plainly Christ, humble and nourishing us with his fruit. He sees it because no one intent upon earthly things knows what humility is.

That Christ is called “earth” is attested by the Apocalypse: “The earth helped the woman” (Revelation 12:16).

This ladder has many steps, consisting of nothing other than advancement through contempt for visible things. The summit of its perfect humility touches the heaven of divine contemplation, because God reveals to the little ones what he conceals from the wise (Matthew 11:25).

If we live angelically, we descend by this ladder to knowledge of ourselves and ascend by it to the vision of God. The Lord leans upon this ladder because this virtue is principally and especially strengthened by his authority and command:

“Learn from me,” he says—not vigils or fasts, but “because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Modern and ancient writers have said many subtle things about its steps.

“I am,” he says, “the God of Abraham your father”—that is, of the reason by which you are governed in a fatherly manner—“and the God of Isaac,” who inspires in you the joy of heavenly glory.

“I will give you the land in which you sleep”—that is, Christ, in whose likeness you rest from the labor of the world—to you and to your seed, that is, to your imitators, to cherish. The seed of the work will be like dust, dry from the moisture of all carnal wantonness—not dust that the wind blows away, but dust that clings to the earth, that is, to eternal stability.

“You will spread out” toward recognizing the setting of your own defect, toward tasting beforehand the rising of inward light, toward guarding against the north of sloth and torpor, and toward drawing in the south of the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 14

“And in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.”

In your faith and in the works of faith—or through the inward grace that is the seed of good works—all the trinities of the conscience will be multiplied: understanding, will, and memory; or your beginning, progress, and end; also faith, hope, and charity; or thought, speech, and action.

### VERSE 15

“And I shall be your guardian wherever you go”—wherever, plainly, you direct your mind, I shall guard your action.

“And I shall bring you back to this land”—if ever you wander in a human manner, I shall bring you back to this state of mind, in which you are now made solid like earth.

“And I shall not leave you until I have fulfilled everything that I have said.” I shall not cease to cooperate with you until, by the bestowal of the future reward, I fulfill what I have said.

### VERSES 16, 17

When Jacob awoke from sleep, he said:

“Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.”

And, afraid, he said:

“How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

Jacob awakens from sleep when the mind is briefly withdrawn from its repose, and is without divine sweetness. Then he truly declares that the Lord is in the place when he proves that something divine is present in that small measure of stability of mind—indeed, that it can occur only through a divine inpouring.

Yet while we possess these things, we do not know how lofty and divine they are. But when we are delivered over to our former sluggishness, we experience that they are brought about by God and not by ourselves.

He is also afraid and marvels at the terror of the place when he considers both the renewal of his thoughts within himself and the terror of the devil, by which he is shaken because of the spatial condition of our mind—that is, its stable truth.

The place is called “terrible” because of the aerial spirits, “like an army set in battle array” (Song of Songs 6:3, 9).

That mind is also said to be nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven: it is governed by God dwelling within it, and opened by God so that spiritual and heavenly things may be contemplated.

### VERSES 18, 19

Jacob rose in the morning, took the stone that he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil over it. He called the name of the city Bethel, which had previously been called Luz.

He rises in the morning when he lifts himself toward the divine light.

He takes up the stone that he had placed beneath his head when he grasps Christ—the unique firmness of his own people, whom he had placed beneath his heart as a foundation—with his hand, that is, through imitation in action.

He raises it as a pillar when he attends to Christ as though to the proposed model of all holiness.

He pours oil over it when, by following the more excellent way of charity and mercy according to the Apostle, he anoints Christ with devout works (1 Corinthians 12:31).

He calls the city Bethel when he proves by evident signs that the soul, fortified by the vigilant wall of protection, is marked as the dwelling place of divine glory.

Bethel means “house of God.” Luz, however, is called *Boia*, which we call “a fetter.” Therefore the place that is now the house of God was formerly called Boia, because it was both constricted within itself by the misery of vices and attempted to fetter others with the same allure.

He therefore makes a vow, saying:

### VERSES 20, 21

“If God is with me and guards me on the way in which I walk”—that is, in the action I have undertaken, by which I desire to advance toward better things—“and gives me bread to eat that has descended from heaven, and clothing of charity and innocence to put on, and if I return to the house of my super-heavenly father, the Lord shall be my God.”

He, plainly, whom I have begun to serve under a certain measure of fear shall be my God, to be loved as a father, since he is the author of my whole being.

### VERSE 22

“And this stone, Christ, whom I have set before myself as a sign, whom, when I placed him beneath my head, I put on, shall be called the house of God.”

Since he himself is the inhabitant, he is also the dwelling place, because the likeness of him that he has made in us will itself be inhabited.

“And of all that you give me I shall offer you tithes”: I shall attribute to you the perfections of the good things I accomplish with your favor. In the perfection—or, according to another reading, the imperfection—of the number nine, I shall ascribe the tenth of wholeness to you.

## CHAPTER 29

### VERSES 1, 2

Jacob therefore departed and came to the land of the east. He saw a well in a field and three flocks of sheep lying beside it. For animals were watered from it, and its mouth was closed with a large stone.

He departs when he extends himself with greatness of spirit.

Jacob comes to the land of the east when the faithful soul reaches the solidity of heavenly illumination. Here and often elsewhere we use “land” for firmness, because earth is a solid element. For, according to Ecclesiastes, “the earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4).

He sees a well in the field when he attends to the fountain of prudence and discernment in spiritual practice.

Three flocks of sheep lie beside it because there are three orders of the Church. In the Old Testament they are signified under the figures of Noah, Daniel, and Job, and in the New Testament under the figures of those who cultivate, those who grind, and those who rest in bed. At times, resting from the labor of the world, they are refreshed by a saving draught and by nearness to the well.

From this the animals are watered. For the water of saving wisdom softens our dullness and our animal ignorance.

But its mouth is closed with a large stone because the entrance and exit of the wisdom and knowledge given to us by God must be guarded, lest anything indecent enter or leave, by thinking and speaking with the great weight of humility.

Such stones are placed by Joshua at the mouth of the cave in which the five kings had hidden, so that the window of the bodily senses may be pressed down with a great weight appropriate to each person.

### VERSE 3

It was customary that, when all the sheep had been gathered, they would roll away the stone; and when the flocks had been refreshed, they would place it again over the mouth of the well.

The sheep are customarily gathered when all the simple movements of the mind are collected to draw in the counsel of reason.

The stone is rolled away when the judgment of discernment is opened by the hand of great authority so that it may give answers to inward complaints.

There are some among whom no stone—the weight of a judgment that must be delivered—is examined with difficulty; rather, it is hurled down more lightly than any chaff.

When the flocks have again been watered, the stone is placed over the mouth of the well when, after the mind—whether its own or another’s—has been refreshed through counsel, it is not moved by vanity concerning its own clarity of understanding, but is again pressed down by the same majesty of gravity.

### VERSE 4

He said to the shepherds:

“Brothers, where are you from?”

They said:

“From Haran.”

After the vision of the well, Jacob asks the shepherds where they are from. This occurs when, after understanding discernment, the mind—the supplanter of vice—inquires from what source the spiritual movements or virtues that govern themselves arise; that is, from what intention they emerge.

They do not breathe anything from the appetite for praise or the desire for gain. Rather, with the full brightness of their affection, they answer that they proceed from Haran—that is, from the devotion of attaining election. For Haran signifies “chosen.”

### VERSES 5–7

“Do you know,” he said, “Laban, the son of Nahor?”

They said:

“We know him.”

“Is he well?” he said.

“He is well,” they replied.

“And behold, Rachel his daughter is coming with her flock.”

Jacob said:

“There is still much of the day remaining.”

“Do you know,” he asks, through experience, the brightness of heavenly life that is born from God, which is known to be the repose of light?

They answer that they have learned this also through devout affection. Laban’s health signifies the integrity of heavenly desire. The shepherds therefore declare that he is well when they proclaim that no testimonies of the virtues arise in the mind except from above.

But in this very state and vigor of mind Rachel arrives with her flock, because that glorious and virginal purity of divine contemplation enters at the proper time with a generous gift of the other graces.

She is called Laban’s daughter because she proceeds from love of the heavenly brightness.

Rachel is interpreted as “principle of vision”—namely, that which says, “I am the principle, and therefore I speak to you” (John 8:25).

“There is still much of the day remaining.”

This means: “Although I attain some spark of divine contemplation, the excellence of that divine light incomparably surpasses me, and no keenness of mine can penetrate it.”

Or otherwise: when the mind begins to understand something divine above itself, it thinks that it has reached the summit of every virtue. But intelligently it tells itself that much of the day remains for it—that is, much labor remains for one working in the vineyard—and that it is not yet time for the flocks to be led back to the folds: that is, for virtues still imperfect to be granted eternal rest.

“Give the sheep drink first”: provide the infusion of spiritual grace for the virtues established amid the great heat of temptations, and gather them, refreshed by inward dew, toward the nourishment of sacred Scripture, bringing them eagerly from the drink to the pasture.

For if the mind is not inwardly infused, the whole usefulness of reading is nullified.

The faithful soul speaks these things to its own thoughts—indeed, to its own understandings, as though they were shepherds.

### VERSE 8

“We cannot,” they said, “until all the animals have been gathered.”

That is: “We cannot offer them spiritual refreshment until we restrain the crowds of thoughts from their wandering and remove the stone—the hardness of torpor and negligence—which blocks the mouth of the well, that is, which kills the eye of inward discernment. Only then can we provide refreshment from saving water to the flocks of virtues.”

### VERSE 9

While they were still speaking, Rachel came with the sheep of her father.

Often, while the life to be established is still being discussed with the perceptions of the inner person, the virtue of contemplation suddenly enters with the soul’s complete simplicity. Yet all these things are given to it by the Father of lights.

For contemplation itself nourished the flock of all devout thought and action with spiritual nourishment.

### VERSES 10, 11

When Jacob saw her and knew that she was his cousin and that the sheep belonged to Laban, his maternal uncle, he moved away the stone with which the well was closed. After watering the flock, he kissed her.

Jacob sees her and recognizes her as his cousin when, understanding the glory of contemplation, he recognizes that he has a natural kinship with it. For he perceives that he was made by God himself in order to see and enjoy God.

He sees the sheep of Laban, his uncle, when the faithful soul devoutly imitates the virtues of those who display brightness and who, through their kinship of life and conduct, are brothers of the super-heavenly Church, their mother. They are called sheep because of their simplicity and usefulness.

Jacob removes the stone with which the well is closed when the discerning spirit shakes off the weight of inertia by which knowledge of the truth is obstructed.

After watering the flock of thoughts or virtues with the wave of heavenly sweetness, he kisses her when he binds himself harmoniously to the sweetness of the eternal Word and of the Spirit of wisdom.

In this kiss we discern both the mouth of divine speech through its inward savor and are imbued with the breath of the sevenfold grace; through it we are anointed with the saliva of wisdom.

### VERSE 12

He raised his voice and wept, and told her that he was her father’s brother and Rebekah’s son.

He raises his voice when he increases the desire for piety. He weeps when he cleanses the mind, as though it were the head, of every harmful fluid of vice.

Through these things he shows that he is her brother when he indicates by devout actions that he clings to God by kinship. And because he is Rebekah’s—that is, Patience’s—son, such affection has proceeded from her as from its principal mother.

She hurried and announced this to her father.

The contemplation represented by Jacob hastens to announce his presence to the father when, through the evident effect of grace, it indicates to God—from whom every perfect gift comes (James 1:17)—the earnestness of the soul preparing to obey, showing that it has been received and accepted without any spiritual delay in its growth.

### VERSE 13

When he heard that Jacob, the son of his sister, had come, he ran to meet him.

In sacred Scripture, “to hear” means “to understand,” as in: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Psalm 44:11).

Laban therefore hears—that is, understands. Indeed, he causes our mind to understand the true Jacob, who labors to supplant vices and who, solely through God’s action, has come into his presence.

Laban runs to meet him because the desire for heavenly glory spontaneously brings to the mind, as it were, an encounter with the abundance of heavenly grace.

He embraced him, rushed into kisses, and brought him into his house.

Laban embraces Jacob when heavenly devotion is uniquely joined to the mind.

He rushes into kisses when, having renounced the loves of the world, he binds himself to the beauty that must be sought in an indivisible covenant.

He truly rushes when he pours himself wholly into it.

He brings him into his house when he advances him until the conduct of the heart is transferred into heaven.

### VERSE 14

When he had heard the reasons for his journey, he answered:

“You are my bone and my flesh.”

He hears the reasons for the journey when he makes us understand the intentions of all our action through heavenly splendor—namely, our spiritual perfection by which we strive toward God. Thus he responds to our good will in effect, not in word.

“You are my bone”: you possess the strength of understanding that you have from me.

“And you are my flesh”: you are able to govern the weakness of the flesh by reason, just as flesh is governed by bones, because flesh exists only so long as it is held together by bones.

### VERSE 15

After a month had been completed, he said to him:

“Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing? Tell me what your wages shall be.”

The days of one month are completed when the brightnesses of the virtues, together with the will to do better things, are brought to perfection through the wholeness of a month.

“Because,” he says, “you are joined to me by the kinship of good devotion, will you serve me without any hope of your own advancement? Tell me, then, what you will receive.”

### VERSES 16, 17

He had two daughters. The name of the elder was Leah; the younger was called Rachel. Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel had a beautiful face and an attractive appearance.

According to what our elders have said, we understand these two daughters as the active life, which suffers greatly from weak sight amid the troubles of the world, and Rachel as the contemplative life, which, with a face made wholly clean and with the blessedness of a pure heart, directs a clear eye toward seeing God.

We may also understand Leah as knowledge, which concerns only those things that are carried on among us—for example, human conduct and the nature of every passion.

Rachel may signify wisdom, which shines chiefly through knowledge of God and through the keenest discernment between truth and falsehood.

Because knowledge is exercised in lower things, it is evidently involved in much darkness.

Leah means “laborious.” Rachel means “sheep,” or “seeing the principle.” Each meaning corresponds well to the interpretations given above.

For in the sheep, simplicity accords with contemplation and with wisdom intent upon God alone. Laboriousness accords with the active life, the moral life, and every kind of knowledge.

Rachel can also signify love of God; Leah can signify love of neighbor. Both of these dualities, as though they were the two daughters of Laban, are begotten by love of eternal brightness.

Leah is called the elder because she must first be practiced, so that one may come to the form of what follows.

### Verses 18–19

Rachel, therefore, loved Jacob and said: “I will serve you for Rachel for seven years.” Laban replied: “It is better that I give her to you than to another man.”

Rachel loves Jacob when the mind more eagerly desires contemplation, in which one lives more peacefully. He serves seven years for her when he expends the whole body—which consists of the four elements—and the soul, which is pre-eminent in its three faculties, namely intellect, memory, and will, in order to obtain inward vision. He serves for seven years who devotes the sevenfold number of body and soul, as we have said, to years—that is, to the fullnesses of virtues as though of days.

“It is better,” says the effect of heavenly desire, “that I grant you the beauty of divine contemplation, since you labor to hold fast to unity, than to another man”—that is, than to one accustomed to alternate now toward the world, now toward God. “Remain with me,” that is, persevere in the pursuit of heavenly life.

### Verse 20
