Jacob therefore served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him only a few days because of the greatness of his love. That is, the whole splendor of human righteousness seems small and slight to one who diligently considers and intelligently loves the beauty of heavenly blessedness.

### Verse 21

Jacob then said to Laban: “Give me my wife, for my time is completed, so that I may go in to her.”

I understand Jacob’s words to Laban as nothing other than the appetite of inward desire directed toward the whiteness of eternal glory: “Give me my wife,” because the pleasure of divine contemplation, with its power, may now be granted to me. For I have already fulfilled the measure of my body and soul’s expenditure, so that I may be admitted to her embrace and delights.

### Verses 22–24

Laban gathered many groups of friends for a banquet and made a wedding. In the evening he brought his daughter Leah to him, giving her a maidservant named Zilpah.

The groups of friends are nothing other than companies of useful thoughts, words, and actions, which constitute the soul’s true faithfulness and friendship. Laban calls them to a banquet and makes a wedding when the love of eternal whiteness gathers them together for a draught of heavenly sweetness and offers the embrace of divine delight.

But in the evening—that is, when the mind’s brightness has grown faint—his daughter Leah is brought to him, because every holy mind falls back into the labor of the active life when inward repose is dispersed.

Zilpah means “a walking mouth.” Leah therefore has as her maidservant one who is called “a walking mouth”: active human praise, which advances through the mouths of flattering attendants, runs about, and is softened by services; for it operates openly.

### Verses 25–26

When Jacob had gone in to her according to custom, morning came and he saw Leah. He said to his father-in-law: “Was it not for Rachel that I served you? Why have you given me Leah?”

Laban replied: “It is not customary in our place to give the younger before the elder in marriage.”

Jacob goes in according to custom to the woman joined to him when the faithful soul, in order to consider the rule of its purpose, returns to the heart for the sake of discernment. But when morning comes through divine illumination, and the labor of conscience is found to have been brought about by concern for one’s neighbors, he complains against the grace of inward repose that he had desired, as though against Laban:

“I was seeking the inner beauty of contemplation; why am I being swept back into the labor of so many affairs?”

The reasoning of inward light replies: “It is not customary among those who have decided to live locally and steadfastly according to our laws to give the younger before the elder”—that is, no one is joined to virtues until he has attempted to overcome the battles of vices. These are called “younger” not because they are inferior in dignity, but because, after the triumphs over temptations, they are considered lighter in their entire exercise and more pleasing through a certain ineffable novelty of their own.

Nothing is sweeter than a simple mind. In this respect contemplation is the younger: it does not concern itself with labors or cares, and one must advance from active struggle to the rest of contemplation.

### Verse 27

“Complete the week of days of this union, and I will give you this one also for the work by which you will serve me for another seven years.”

The week of days of the union is completed when someone is bound to the love of the Creator through the full execution of good works. Then the other one is given for the work of seven additional years, when contemplation is added as a kind of reward of our inward peace, in which we rest from vices.

The first seven years are spent in inward and outward struggle; the final seven are peaceful and tranquil in both respects—in body and soul—after the victory over sin. Thus the Sabbath is observed on both sides through the number seven: first outwardly in action, afterward inwardly in thought.

Understand Laban’s words as nothing other than the judgment of illuminated reason.

### Verses 28–29

Jacob agreed; but Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, was added to her. Bilhah is interpreted as “the ancient one.” This antiquity seems to me to mean nothing other than the imagination of bodily things, which is always perceived as hostile to contemplation of spiritual realities.

The novelty of contemplation therefore grows old when it is assailed by images of corruptible things, although it is subjected in the manner of a maidservant.

### Verse 30

When Jacob had obtained these marriages, he preferred the love of the one who followed—that is, of the contemplative woman—to that of the first—that is, of the active woman.

### Verse 31

When God saw that Leah was despised, he opened her womb, while her sister remained barren.

The Lord sees—or, more precisely, makes us see—that we do not properly esteem Leah, that is, the active life, when we think it safer to attend only to ourselves than to labor under the care of our neighbor. He opens her womb, that is, he shows her usefulness and fruitfulness, because the common good ought to be preferred to the private good, while her sister remains barren: that is, while from the fruitfulness of active life only its individual usefulness is considered and no attention is given to the advancement of one’s neighbors.

### Verse 32

The actual life conceived and brought forth a son, that is, it manifested in general the practice of pious work, and called his name Reuben. It judged, as it were, within itself the sum of that work which is worthy to be named before God.

Reuben means “see in the midst,” which signifies not providing for oneself alone, but rather for the common good. Reuben is interpreted as “see in the midst,” and “midst” is used for “common.”

“God has seen my humiliation,” she said—that is, he makes me attend to my need, in which I often experience the humility of my neighbor and am compelled to repay the kindness that I have experienced from others.

“Now my husband will love me.” The intellect, to whom belongs the governance of the inner person, says that, once its disgust with labors has been driven away, it will breathe freely in the very love of love. It will do this even now—that is, in the present world—by singing:

> “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity!”  
> *(Psalm 132:1)*

### Verse 33

Again she conceived, bore a son, and said: “Because the Lord heard that I was held in contempt, he has given me this one also.” And she called his name Simeon.

She conceives when she forms an inward purpose; she bears when she administers it outwardly.

“Hears” is used for “understands.” Thus the Apostle, when he said, “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” *(1 Corinthians 2:14)*, added: “For neither does he hear”—that is, understand. The Lord hears when he makes us understand.

Therefore, when, by God’s inspiration, we understand that we are held in contempt if we bestow the gift of beneficence upon our neighbor merely for the sake of receiving it back, God gives us this son also, whose name is Simeon. Simeon is interpreted as “the Lord has heard” or “hearing sorrow,” because in everything we do, it is divine rather than human hearing that must be considered. We must think not about what human beings report, but about what pleases God.

And hearing—that is, the perception of sorrow—must not be absent even when we perform great deeds, because “we do not know whether we are worthy of love or hatred” *(Ecclesiastes 9:1)*. As it is written: “The heart knows the bitterness of its own soul, and no stranger will share in its joy” *(Proverbs 14:10)*.

### Verse 34

She conceived a third time and bore another son, saying: “Now my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore she called his name Levi.

Levi is interpreted as “added.” After Reuben, in whom provision is made for the common benefit of all, and Simeon, in whom divine hearing is sought more than human hearing, a third is rightly added, signifying the Trinity. For whoever acts with attention directed solely toward God is undoubtedly added to the lot of the elect, which is the vision of God.

Then she bears three sons. After a good action and a pious intention in one’s deeds, as though after two sons, we produce the reward of good action by laboring to bring forth the third. The true intellect—the husband who impregnates the soul with divine seed, mindful of the reward awaiting it—then applies itself more vigorously to pious action.

### Verse 35

A fourth time she conceived and bore a son, saying: “Now I will confess to the Lord.” Therefore she called his name Judah, and she ceased bearing.

When we have come to eternal glory, we shall then be placed in the fourfold number, signified by the fourth son—that is, established in unshaken solidity. Then we shall conceive Judah, eternal glorification, in our heart and bear him through an endless effect.

Judah means either “confessing” or “glorifying.” “Now,” she says—that is, in this eternity, which is suitably signified by the present time—“I will confess,” meaning, “I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to the Lord” *(Psalm 49:14)*.

She then ceases bearing when she ceases, as she now does with groaning, to produce the fruit of good work.

## Chapter 30

### Verse 1

Rachel, seeing that she was barren, envied her sister and said to her husband: “Give me children, or else I shall die.”

Rachel envies her sister because she is barren when the mind of contemplative persons, observing the effectiveness of active persons, sometimes imitates their works and marvels at the abundance of their praise.

“You,” she says, “O intellect, rejoice in contemplation, but through it you do not stand out in any conspicuous work. Thus you offer no examples of holiness as evidence of your reputation.”

### Verse 2

He said: “Am I acting in the place of God for you, who has deprived you of the fruit of your womb?”

The reasoning replies: “Am I acting in God’s place for you? God has deprived you of the fruit of your womb”—that is, he has not granted you the skill for bodily activity, which, insofar as it concerns the breezes of fame, is fragile like a womb—“so that my care may give you what God himself denies?”

There are people whose abilities suit contemplation, but whose bodies are not suited to conducting affairs. Contemplation, therefore, is disturbed when it is driven by the desire for fame.

### Verse 3

She said: “I have my maidservant Bilhah. Go in to her,” that is, “I possess knowledge of secular matters. Although it submits to the yoke of the wisdom you desire, nevertheless enter into it by mingling yourself with it, and descend to this wisdom called worldly wisdom, so that she may bear upon my knees”—that is, so that, bending the uprightness of her position, she may bring me certain fruits of temporal joy.

Through Bilhah, whose name signifies antiquity, we understand secular matters, which are called old in Scripture *(Colossians 3:9)*.

### Verses 4–5

The intellect therefore entered into the inner chambers of knowledge and secular intention, as though into the service of a maidservant; it conceived and bore a son—that is, it formed a proposal and produced an unsuitable work.

### Verse 6

Rachel said: “God has judged for me and has heard my voice, giving me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan.

Understand Rachel’s statement as the distorted thought of a certain contemplative person:

“God has judged for me,” that is, “God has shown favor toward my work, since I am publicly praised as I deserve.”

He has “heard my voice” when he has fulfilled my desire to benefit others through my works, as though by producing children through example and attaching fame to them.

Dan, therefore, whose name means “judgment,” is called a son because, insofar as his works are praised according to secular estimation, he thinks that they are accepted by God just as they are approved by human beings according to their judgment, and that God himself speaks through human mouths.

### Verses 7–8

Bilhah conceived again and bore another son. Rachel said of him: “God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed.”

It should be noted that conception is placed before nearly every birth, because the sin committed without deliberation and through mere haste is very small. We conceive when we make a plan.

Bilhah bears another son, and Rachel calls him Naphtali when worldly wisdom adulterously confuses itself with God’s wisdom, seeking to expand itself through praise and to be compared with the praised. It does all this not from true affection, but under the false name of Rachel, that is, of contemplation.

Naphtali means “he has enlarged me” or “he has compared me.” Those who live in solitude often come forward to preach publicly and thereafter seek little glories. Thus, having been compared with those publicly acclaimed in active life, she says that she has prevailed, displaying openly and effectively what she can and what she is capable of doing.

### Verses 9–11

When Leah perceived that she had ceased bearing, she gave her maidservant Zilpah to her husband. After she had conceived and brought forth a child, she said: “Fortunate!” And she called his name Gad.

Through both women it is shown what takes place in both lives.

The active life, Leah, ceases to bear when the good intention—which is like the power of conception—fails in the mind. When it ceases, Zilpah, that is, empty glory, is introduced. For, as was said above, she is interpreted as “a walking mouth,” and the freedom of the spirit is defiled by servile association.

The conceived wickedness produces a perverse work, namely, the outcome of passing prosperity. She says “fortunate” when an abundance of honors smiles upon her, but she cannot say it sincerely, because she seeks only the decay of the world.

Gad means “fortune,” and everyone knows that fortune is always uncertain and unstable. Whoever therefore devotes himself to producing and nourishing a son of fortune fluctuates upon an endless sea.

### Verses 12–13

Zilpah bore another son under Leah’s name, and she called him Asher. This occurs when the desire for human praise, under the covering of active life, obtains an effect of glory as though a son, and proclaims it with the honor of blessedness.

Here is understood that kind of glory which is arranged after death for remembrance: the distinction of buildings, the magnificence of pyramids, the renown of books, and poems, which commonly serve as memorials of the dead.

These things are Asher—that is, the greatest blessedness among the foolish. Asher indeed means “blessed.” Thus Leah rejoices that she is called blessed—not truly, but imaginatively—not by men, but by women, because she is animated by the favor of light-minded and undiscerning people.

### Verse 14

Reuben went out during the wheat harvest into the field and found mandrakes, which he brought to his mother Leah.

Reuben is called from the fact that he “sees in the midst,” that is, provides for the common good. He goes out into the field during the wheat harvest when, through the exercise of conscience, he is snatched forward in spirit toward the end of the world.

The wheat harvest signifies the gathering of the saints into the heavenly granary *(Matthew 13:39)*. Hence in Revelation the angel is urged to send the sickle when the harvest has ripened *(Revelation 14:15)*.

The field is the mind, which we never cultivate better than when we remember our final lot. We go out into it when, freed from wicked affairs, we return to its care.

There Reuben—that is, prudent concern—finds the mandrakes and brings them to his mother Leah when he transfers to the effectiveness of holy active life, the mother of all piety, the fragrance drawn from within through divine inspiration.

A mandrake is a fragrant plant. Rachel said: “Give me some of the mandrakes of your son.”

It is as though the renewed power of contemplation, divinely touched, brings itself to action: “Share with me the impulse toward pious work that you have received, so that you may bring to the exercise of contemplation the affection of devotion that you possess.”

She answered:

### Verse 15

“Is it not enough for you that you have taken my husband from me, unless you also take my son’s mandrakes?”

This means: “You have removed from active duty the intellect by which I am governed, for the sake of contemplation and excellent living. Is the thing that most supports and lies nearest to me so little in your estimation that you must also draw this momentary visitation of heavenly fragrance into the exercise of thought alone?”

“Let him sleep with you tonight,” she said, “in exchange for your son’s mandrakes”—that is, “Let him rest with you amid this turmoil of affairs, which is hostile to the active life, only so that I may breathe again toward inward sweetness and taste how sweet God is.”

### Verse 16

Jacob returned from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him. She said: “You will come in to me, for I have hired you with the mandrakes of my son.”

Leah goes out to meet Jacob when, as the heat of empty glory cools, the opportunity for holy labor meets the spirit returning from inward exercise to attention toward God, after having been tripped up by vices. She offers an open entrance into conscience because, for the sake of worthy activity, she has provided Rachel—that is, contemplation—with the pure perfumes of love which the devout concern of active life, her pious offspring, has brought forth, so that love itself may overflow all the way to the vision of God.

That night he slept with her.

### Verses 17–18

God heard her prayers. She conceived and bore a fifth son, saying: “God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband.” And she called his name Issachar.

Jacob sleeps with Leah at night when our spirit rests in the labor of good work even amid the darknesses of temptation. In this way God especially hears the prayers of his people.

She conceived through affection and bore through work a son—not the fourth, which is dispersed through temporal things, for there are four seasons—but the fifth, that is, a spirit which transcends all these things with singular authority. The number five consists of four together with the one that presides over them.

Issachar means “reward.” He is so called because she subjected to her husband—that is, to the intellect—the maidservant who bore offspring of every kind of filth, so that he might restrain her.

When we submit ourselves to God, God then subjects vices to us as though in repayment of a debt.

### Verses 19–20

Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son, saying: “God has endowed me with a good dowry this time also. Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him six sons.” Therefore she called his name Zebulun.

Leah bears a sixth son when she fully and perfectly attains the degree of activity. On the sixth day God completed his works *(Genesis 2:2)*.

She says that she has been endowed with a good dowry, not only at conversion, when she arrives at fear of God, but especially when she is carried into a love that cannot be separated either by death or by life.

“When I have reached the perfection possible for a human being,” she says—that is, after I have brought forth the sixth offspring—“my husband, the intellect, will necessarily be joined to me, because I have completely emptied myself of carnal affection.”

Zebulun means “the flow of night” or “the dwelling of strength.” Thus, while we live now as impassible persons, night flows away from us: the ignorance of worldly affairs and the decline caused by adversities, which takes place in the mind. The inner person, restored, begins to be a dwelling of strength against every danger.

### Verse 21

After him she bore a daughter named Dinah.

Although the soul is God’s dwelling and although it powerfully withstands every assault, it must always finally bear Dinah, a female, so that after the virtues it may place its own fragility before itself and not become swollen with pride.

Dinah means “this judgment” or “cause.” This judgment—that is, discernment—must be maintained among the best things, specifically as a safeguard against an unsuitable intrusion.

### Verses 22–24

The Lord also remembered Rachel, heard her, and opened her womb. She conceived and bore a son. She said: “God has taken away my reproach.” And she called his name Joseph.

God remembers Rachel when, through God’s inspiration, the mind of a contemplative person is brought back to knowledge of itself. He hears her when he shows himself ready to bring effect to her affection. He opens her womb when, through the expansion of love, he makes room in the mind for divine seed.

She therefore bears a son and says that her reproach has been taken away, because, once she has attained the office of divine contemplation—that is, once she has finally brought forth the son of her desired hope—God removes the reproach of the adultery of servitude that lay upon her.

Therefore she calls his name Joseph, meaning “increase,” because the beginning of contemplation by which we still taste God temporally and according to our ability awaits an increase into eternal vision.

“May God add another son to me,” she says—that is, may he grant and increase for me, who see in a mirror and in an enigma, the fruit of true and open knowledge.

### Verse 25

When Joseph had been born, Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Send me away, so that I may return to my homeland and to my land,” and so forth.

After the increase of the hope of perpetual vision of God has been born in the mind, Jacob—that is, the intellect—speaks to Laban, that is, to eternal whiteness, over which the true light presides.

Laban is called his father-in-law because he is father to two daughters, namely the active and the contemplative life, which are formed in the womb of the earthly Church according to the pattern of that heavenly whiteness.

“Send me away, so that I may return to my homeland and my land”—that is, accept me as free and released from bodily chains, wishing to return to the homeland from which I have fallen and to the land where I may obtain a state of immobility.

### Verse 26

“Give me my wives and my children, for whom I served you, so that I may depart.”

That is: “Do not prolong for me the active life, in which day and night I have no rest, according to Revelation, while praising God” *(Revelation 14:11)*, “nor the contemplative life, in which I think of nothing but God. I have truly served your glory for these fruits of my works, which are kings and free persons in heaven, not for earthly things. Let me depart, and I shall no longer be in distress.”

“You know the service with which I served you.” It is as though he were saying: “You, heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, know the carnal and worldly temptations through which I have served in order to obtain your glory, since you too have endured these things.”

### Verses 27–28

Laban said to him: “If I have found favor in your sight, I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you. Set your wages, and I shall give them to you.”

Laban speaks to Jacob when the candidate of the heavenly army, with the intellect as interpreter, seems to say even to the intellect itself:

“If your present labor is prolonged for a little while, great favor toward me will be found before your inward eye when you come to the enjoyment of blessedness. Experience has made it certain that God grants an increase of glory and joy to blessed spirits whenever someone approaches the heavenly kingdom to be glorified.”

For the great Origen says *(on Leviticus, chapter 10, homily 1, section 7, before the middle)* that the saints do not possess perfect joy as long as they see the sorrow of their brothers under temporal tribulation. Hence it is clear that their triumph and glory are greatly increased by the rescue of their companions.

“Tell me,” that is, “consider carefully and provide for the reward that you ask me to give you.”

We do such things with the holy spirits whenever we seek their protection in order to obtain glory, and as intelligent persons we hear this from them intellectually.

### Verse 29

Jacob said: “You know with what hardship of mind and body I have served you in order to win you, and how great a possession of yours has been in my hands.”

That is: “O company of the blessed, it has been evident how highly I have valued your possession—which is God—in the exercise of my hands, that is, of my works.”

### Verse 30

“You had little before I came to you.”

Your heavenly number was diminished before human nature was joined to your glory. Now, O blessed army of the saved, you have become rich through my fellowship. The Lord has blessed you—that is, he has multiplied you—at my entrance.

“It is therefore right that I should at some point provide for my own household.”

The whole meaning is this: You rejoice in secure happiness, and you ought—and do—ask the same for those established in misery. Obtain for me, therefore, what is just: just as you provided for yourselves while you lived, so may I provide for myself a dwelling in the Father’s house, where there are many rooms *(John 14:2)*.

And certainly one provides for a household when one strives to ensure that there are people by whom the household may be honored.

### Verses 31–32

“What shall I give you?”

Jacob replied: “I want nothing. But if you will do what I ask, I will again feed and guard your flocks.”

The reasoning says: “O holy city, I seek no earthly profit from you. But if you will turn all your flocks around”—that is, if, through another circuit of discernment, you will enable me to see the whole usefulness of virtue by means of your favor—“and separate all the sheep that are variegated, and those with fleeces of mixed color”—

that is, if you will grant me to distinguish, within the virtues themselves, the admixture of every vice and deed through the breezes of favor, as though through the scattering of fleece by which the limbs are covered on the earth—

“whatever is reddish,” whether through the passion of desire or through knowledge of sin—for this is what that color signifies—“whatever is spotted” through the incursion of wrongdoing, and variegated through insinuating hypocrisy, let this be reckoned to me as a great gift.

Nothing is more useful to me than knowledge of myself. For it is said: “You performed judgment and then justice in Jacob” *(Psalm 98:4)*.

If you, heavenly mother and pious interpreter, obtain this for me, then I, who until now have fed in fear on the heavenly food appropriate to the inner person, will from now on feed and guard again—that is, I will provide nourishment for life and entrust care of the living pursuits to guardianship.

He says that his wages are in the sheep and goats because he believes that the beginning of his reward is present in active benefits, signified by sheep because they are useful through offspring, fruit, and fleece, and in contemplative persons, signified by goats because they feed in high places.

### Verse 33

“My righteousness will answer me tomorrow, when the appointed time comes before you.”

That is, my righteousness will meet me and correspond with me in a worthy reward—the righteousness by which I shall at first be my own accuser—when, God rewarding me, my life is proved before the saints to have pleased him.

### Verse 34

Laban said: “I accept what you ask.”

For nothing is more pleasing to blessed spirits than what is accomplished through the grace of eternal salvation.

When we do these things intellectually within ourselves, we both speak them and feel as though they are answered to us from heaven.

### Verse 35

On that day he separated the goats and sheep, the he-goats and rams, the variegated and spotted animals. That is, in the spiritual light in which he considered these things, he caused Jacob—that is, reason—to distinguish between contemplative and active things, between wanton and animal impulses, and the rams of rational faculties, which provide us with guidance. In all these things he considered what is sinned through the variegation of hypocrisy and what through natural ugliness.

But he placed the entire one-colored flock—that is, those with white and black fleece—in the hands of his sons.

### Verse 36

He set a distance of a three-days’ journey between himself and his son-in-law, who was feeding the remainder of his flocks.

That is, he entrusted to the hands of his sons—that is, to the power of the saints, who already possess a definite divine sonship—the whole multitude of virtues which, through innocence, shines white in one color, while also retaining the blackness of the memory of sins, not passively but in order to proclaim more ardently and laudably the God who rescued them from those sins.

He “set”—that is, he judged—there to be a distinction between the advancing human intellect and the heavenly senate, between the active and contemplative teacher, the father of two spiritual wives, and the most perfect knowledge of God, in which there is the mystery of the Trinity, as though of three days.

The intellect itself feeds the remaining flocks of Laban because it nourishes the virtues that are less perfect in this world.

### Verse 37

Jacob then took green rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree and partly stripped them of their bark. When the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in the places that had been stripped. But those that remained intact stayed green, and in this way the color became variegated.

Through the almond, which alone among these three bears fruit, we understand intelligence. In it, as a kernel beneath bark and shell, lies the knowledge of God amid all the bitterness of the passions of the flesh and the harshness of humanity.

Through the poplar and plane tree are signified imagination and sensation. When intelligence governs them as the middle faculty, each, though barren by itself, is seasoned by the flavor of its neighbor.

The green rods are the uprightnesses of inward charity, moistened by its sap. The man who overthrows sin—this same Jacob—takes the ordered dispositions of these three, drawn as though according to a rule, and cuts away part of their surface bark, that is, of their outward appearance. Immediately the whiteness of inward grace appears.

Because imagination and sensation cannot be entirely stripped of the vanity of visible things, the green of good intention remains in those parts that cannot be stripped away. For “to will is present with me” *(Romans 7:18)*. Thus the color becomes variegated when the spirit begins to divide itself against the flesh.

Where this variegation is absent, the old person is wholly pleased with himself.

### Verse 38

He placed the rods in the channels where the water was poured out.

He places them in the channels when he pours out and somehow establishes whatever is upright in humility, lowering the senses of the inner and outer person. There the heavenly wave of grace habitually flows down from above.

Thus, whenever the flocks came to drink, they would have the rods before their eyes. That is, whenever crowds of thoughts and other movements approached the counsel of spirituality, they would have before the gaze of the heart the rules of the direction set before them, and they would conceive better pursuits and graces through that sight.

A good person is kindled toward better things by contemplating his own good qualities.

### Verse 39

It happened that, in the heat of mating, the sheep looked at the rods and bore spotted and variegated offspring, sprinkled with different colors.

The heat of mating occurs when our sluggish animal nature, represented by the sheep, is joined to the spirit like a male’s ardor.

In this heat the sheep look at the rods when our simple and dull thoughts attentively apply themselves to the sentences of right understanding. They bear offspring sprinkled with different colors because the more subtly they inspect their innermost parts through divine inspiration, the more they discover the variety of their own instability and of their vanity, which opposes the truth.

### Verse 40

Jacob divided the flock and placed the rods before the eyes of the rams.

The rams signify the intellects of thoughts and are leaders of the flocks. When they strive to impregnate the mystical sheep, they must not turn away from considering the direction given by the rods.

Everything that was white and black belonged to Laban; the rest belonged to Jacob, with the flocks separated from one another.

This was stated somewhat above, and I shall not repeat it.

### Verse 41

Whenever the sheep were ascending for the first mating, Jacob placed the rods before the eyes of the rams, and so forth.

The first ascent, like the first resurrection, occurs when spirituality subdues animal nature so that it may bear offspring through good works.

Therefore, in the channels of the lowered and, as it were, excavated senses, where the waves of faithful waters may flow, the rods of governance must be placed before the consideration of the intellects.

Observe the sounds and correspondences of the individual words: humility is in the channels; in the water is the Holy Spirit, who pours himself especially into the humble. From this comes the rod, namely the power of all direction and righteousness, which is set before the rams—that is, before the intellects.

### Verse 42

But when the late mating took place, and the final conception, he did not place them there.

The late mating signifies the reception of the heavenly kingdom at the end, when God is admitted into the hearts of all, not partially as here, but so as to fill all things completely and to be all in all *(Ephesians 1:23)*.

There is the final conception: the unfailing purpose of praising God, to which the affection for no other thing succeeds. When this has occurred, a person will no longer need to set down judgments by which to direct his own mind, since he will possess within himself the God who governs all things.

The things of the first time belong to Jacob—that is, they concern the overthrow of sin. The things of the late time, which remain at the end of the world and shine according to the sincerity of heavenly brightness, belong to Laban.

### Verse 43

The man became exceedingly rich and possessed many flocks, maidservants, servants, camels, and asses.

A man becomes excessively rich when excessive righteousness is turned into the vice of indiscretion. Hence he has many flocks, because through excessive confidence in himself he falls into many divisions of the soul.

He has maidservants and servants—that is, impulses which are wanton in a servile and filthy manner, and which rebel against the spirit with servile boldness.

He has camels as well, burdened by desire and, like humped animals, inclined toward earthly things; and asses, namely those made stupid by inertia and sluggishness.

## Chapter 31

### Verse 1

Afterward he heard the words of Laban’s sons, who said: “Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and from his wealth he has become famous.”

When the inner person deviates from what is right, he perceives the complaints of thoughts that rejoice in being sons of heavenly brightness.

“He has arrogated to himself,” they say, “everything that he ought to have attributed to God the heavenly Father, and from the inward wealth he has sought to be considered famous outwardly.”

The word “famous” is formed from *clio*, which in Greek means “fame.”

## VERSE 2

Jacob noticed Laban’s face—that is, the grace of the heavenly light—was not toward him as it had been “yesterday and the day before yesterday,” that is, in the manner in which, when he regarded the present glory as something passing and dissipating, he despised it as “yesterday,” since that is already past. *Nudius* is formed from *nunc* (“now”) and *dies* (“day”). Laban was not toward him as “the day before yesterday,” that is, as when, with his heart present to the divine light, he walked in contemplation of the Trinity.

**VERSE 3.** The Lord spoke to him especially through the mouths of Scripture: “Return to your land,” that is, to that stability of mind in which your heavenly-citizen fathers, whom you have proposed to imitate, are known to have stood; and return “to your kindred,” namely, to the righteous, which will be blessed. “And while you are doing this, I shall be with you.”

## VERSES 4–5

He sent and summoned Rachel and Leah to the field where he was pasturing the flocks, and said: “I see your father’s face, that he is not toward me.”

He sends forth desire and summons it through the reward of contemplation and the practice of action, so that they may return to the field of spiritual discipline, where the true Jacob feeds the flocks of thoughts that are wasting from inward hunger. “I understand,” he says, “that the favor of the divine serenity has turned away from me. But the God of my father was with me, and I recall the gifts of his grace.”

**VERSE 6.** “You yourselves know that I served your father with all my strength”—namely, him who is the author of the life of both: God. “I am certain that I did these things.”

**VERSE 7.** “But your father deceived me,” that is, at the beginning of the conversion he offered, he enticed me with flatteries and changed my reward ten times. This means that, when through long labor I had earned the soul’s repose—the fivefold number belonging to the external senses, and likewise the fivefold number of sensuality, which is also more vividly present in the mind through imagination—he changed both of these, understood as ten occasions, against me. For, naturally, since it attacks reason, he changed them not into peace for me but into wars. Yet God did not permit him to harm me: since God is essentially God, and since it belongs properly to God to be merciful, his own natural grace did not allow him to permit the approaching battle of temptation to be turned into my destruction.

## VERSE 8

“When he said, ‘Your wages shall be varied,’ all the animals bore varied offspring. But when, on the contrary, he said, ‘You shall take all the white ones as your wage,’ all the flocks bore white offspring.”

This means that his original clemency truly restrained him from doing harm. For if, at some time, intellectually, within myself and through myself, he said that I should devote myself to recognizing the instability of my variation, and I considered this to have been given to me as a reward, he thus fulfilled my desires. Whenever, at his direction, I sought the whiteness of virtue, my thoughts and inward movements, with his assistance, conceived blessed and joyful pursuits.

## VERSE 9

“God took away your father’s substance and gave it to me.” That is, God took from the rationality of my father, which once served him, the intellect, memory, and will—these unquestionably being the substance of your father, who is God himself—and gave them to me so that I might use them properly and beneficially.

**VERSE 10.** “After the time of the sheep’s conception had come, I lifted up my eyes and saw in a dream males mounting females, varied, spotted, and of different colors.”

That is, when I had advanced to the point at which the barrenness of foolish thoughts ought to bring forth something fruitful, I raised my intentions from what was lowest. Sleeping with respect to outward senses and waking inwardly, I saw—that is, I understood—the powers of rationality, presiding over gentle desires as males over females, and indicating the varieties of carnal miseries and spiritual stains.

## VERSE 11

“The angel of God”—that is, either reason or the word of Scripture—“said to me in a dream,” with the gaze of the heart certainly closed to visible things: “Jacob!” As though he were saying: “Remember your name, and supplant your vices.”

And he said: “Here I am,” that is, “I am present for inward care.”

**VERSE 12.** “Lift up your eyes.” This has been explained above. The sense is: What I had seen through inward vision, as though in a dream, I learned through the message of Scripture concerning the lifting of the eyes and the mounting of the males, and I hold it as certain.

“For he saw everything that Laban did to you,” that is, “I made you understand what adversities you have endured for the sake of the glory of eternal brightness.” Laban is said to have done those things whose cause brought them about. You ought not, therefore, to grow weary because of what you have been made to endure.

**VERSE 13.** “I am the God of Bethel,” that is, “of the house of God”—namely, the God who can make you my house—“where you anointed the stone.” That is, where, through me as the indweller, who am oil—that is, love—you made the weight and harshness of the undertaking begun under fear gentler and milder; and where you vowed a vow to me, namely, to persevere within that same rigor of discipline.

“Now therefore arise”—that is, while you still have the present time—and, in accordance with the Apostle, “while it is called Today” (Heb. 3:13), shake yourself free from inactivity, for you are uncertain about the future. “And go out” in your conduct from your earthliness, returning to your land—that is, to the true solidity and region of the living—which belongs to you by birth, that is, is owed to you originally.

## VERSE 14

Rachel and Leah said, together with whom the whole activity of life and this intellectual interpretation speak:

“Do we still have any share in the possessions and inheritance of our father’s house?”

That is: We, whose wages he changed ten times, upon whom he imposed so many difficulties, what hope can we hope to have remaining for ourselves in the kingdom and glory of God?

**VERSE 15.** “Does he not regard us as foreigners, as though we were evildoers whom he burdens with investigations of danger? He sells us, when, by permitting us to be inserted into temptations, he withdraws us from our freedom. He demands the price of the sale when he seeks from us thanksgiving and every joy whenever we fall into various temptations” (Jas. 1:2). He himself eats this price, because our patience feeds him above all.

**VERSE 16.** “But God took away our father’s wealth and gave it to us and to our sons.”

That is, God took away from the service of the devil the goodness naturally implanted by him in our substance, and made it beneficial both to our present life and to our sons—that is, to the fruit of our reward.

It is said, “God took away our father’s wealth,” as though it said, “his own wealth,” just as in the passage, “The Lord rained from the Lord,” that is, from himself. Such expressions abound in the prophets.

Therefore do everything that he has commanded you, understanding that even in every adversity he cooperates with you.

## VERSES 17–18

Jacob therefore arose, and, having placed his children and wives upon camels, departed. He took all his substance, his flocks, and everything he had acquired in Mesopotamia, and went to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.

He rises when the mind raises itself against itself. He places wives and children upon camels when he sets both kinds of life, and the works born from them for the sake of heavenly freedom alone, above the weight of the flesh, and as though he presses the flesh down beneath them.

“Everything he possessed” means natural gifts. “Flocks” means the frequent multitude of thoughts. “Mesopotamia”—that is, “the elevated calling”—means the heavenly favor. When we come to conversion, we acquire these things; and thus we go to the father, in whom are the joys of eternal laughter, into the true land, namely, stability. We proceed to Canaan, whose name means “change,” where we shall truly be changed from corruption into incorruption (Ps. 101:28). Hence the Psalm says: “For those who shall be changed” (Ps. 44:1).

## VERSES 19–20

At that time Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s idols. Jacob did not wish to tell his father-in-law that he was fleeing.

“At that time,” that is, in that disposition of mind by which one tends toward God, Laban—which means the desire for inward brightness—had gone, or rather had made us go, “to shear the sheep,” namely, to strip thoughts of their superfluities.

Yet we often strive in vain to cut these things away, because Rachel, thinking that by seeing she adheres to the source of all things, secretly acquires idols—that is, imaginary forms—in her mind in place of God himself. For she slips back toward herself through her humanity.

Jacob does not wish to confess to his father-in-law that he is fleeing because, although a person may see what he ought to avoid, he does not wish, drawn back by love of the flesh, to express his flight from sin through the performance of works, even though through the rationality of his mind he flees from sin.

The father-in-law, however, is God, to whose daughters—action and contemplation—we are joined, and to whom we confess chiefly through our work.

## VERSES 21–22

When he and everything that belonged to him had departed, and he was journeying after crossing the river toward the heap of testimony—for this is how Gilead is interpreted—it was reported to Laban on the third day that Jacob was fleeing.

After the intellect and everything that ought to be subjected to it have already gone forth through pious desire, and have crossed the waves of worldly cares, the true Jacob proceeds toward the heap which below is widened through love of neighbor and above is sharpened in love of God. There he finds death, by which he turns away from the cloudy valley of this world.

“On the third day,” that is, through understanding of the Trinity, which is God, we announce to the chosen army of the saints knowledge of our flight, by which we avoid sins. For our continence is known by the holy spirits in proportion as we are illumined by a greater knowledge of God.

## VERSE 23

He took his brothers with him—that is, the angelic spirits, summoned through the prayers of the true Laban as brothers under God the Father to help us—and pursued him for seven days, that is, throughout the span of the whole life, following him with divine assistance. Angels come to those who are to inherit salvation (Heb. 1:14).

Alternatively, he pursues Jacob’s vices after obtaining for him the gifts of the sevenfold grace. He catches him on Mount Gilead, namely, in the excellence of love of neighbor and of God, which is the distinctive testimony of our Christianity. There the delight of heavenly brightness fully seizes us.

The heap, as I said, spreads out below and narrows above; within it are both love of neighbor and contemplation of God.

**VERSE 24.** God appeared in a dream, saying to him: “Beware that you speak nothing harsh against Jacob.”

Laban—that is, that shining city—already sunk in sleep within divine repose, sees, that is, understands, God inspiring him not to be moved by any harshness against human beings who share his nature, but to have compassion on them in remembrance of his own former frailty.

## VERSE 25

Jacob had already spread his tent on the mountain when Laban overtook him with his brothers.

Jacob spreads his tent when any faithful person enlarges and extends the practice of divine warfare. Laban overtakes him with his brothers when he is fortified by the assistance of angels and strengthened by the aid of prayers.

On the same Mount Gilead Laban fixed his tent, because, while he still lived in the flesh, he once established himself in the discipline and excellence of both kinds of life: that happy city, the desire of intention. For *intentio* (“intention”) and *tentorium* (“tent”) are both said to derive from *tendere*, “to stretch.”

## VERSES 26–27

He said to Jacob:

“Why did you act in this way, secretly driving away my daughters as captives by the sword? Why did you wish to flee without my knowledge and not tell me, so that I might send you away with joy, songs, tambourines, and lyres?”

As though he were saying: Since you now see yourself established at the summit of love, from which you have chosen—without consulting my examples—to drive away from yourself the devotions of both kinds of life, although you prove that you reign through victory over evils, why did you choose to drive them away secretly from me as captives by the sword—that is, carried off through the mortal sin of desertion and apostasy?

Why, I ask, did you wish to flee from the undertaking you had begun without my knowledge—that is, without discussion with me, as was stated above—when fleeing in mind means being afraid? Why did you not inform me, after reconsidering the counsels of my triumphs, so that, through the vigor conceived from them, I might at once bring you the joys of my comparison, dispel weariness with an inward song of gladness, and bring near the tambourine of divine contemplation, more enduring than every bronze instrument? Here it begins and in the future never ends. I might make the sweet wonder resound in the mysteries of God, and bring near the lyre by which fitting love toward neighbors, great and small, is offered like the sound of the heart.

For while you are enriched beyond measure, while you complain about deception and the alteration of your reward, you have begun to act as though I were unaware.

## VERSE 28

“You did not permit me to kiss my daughters,” that is, you did not permit me, through the mouth and spirit of my counsels and intentions—which you see in my actions—to imbue your lives, which I call my daughters because of their conformity to me as to a mother.

“You have acted foolishly.”

**VERSE 29.** “And now my hand is able to repay you evil.”

That is: God, who is my hand—that is, my strength—is able to repay you evil now, namely in eternal things, where nothing passes away and nothing is future, but everything is always present.

“But the God of your father”—that is, your Father—“said to me yesterday.” That is, through the memory of my former passion, which I experienced while living in a human being, he made known to me that I should not disdain to have compassion on human beings, even though I was already held in glory.

## VERSE 30

“Let it be so,” he said, as though saying: Let us now grant that you certainly desire to return to your own citizens, namely the heavenly ones, and to your father’s superheavenly house. But how will you defend the fact that you stole my gods—that is, that, while you considered yourself rich beyond measure and subtle in contemplation, you improperly fashioned a god for yourself through innumerable images and fantasies?

For what is done secretly is not done rightly. Therefore he steals gods who privately devises how to attribute forms to God.

**VERSE 31.** But Jacob—that is, our spirit, as though reasoning—replied:

“Because I departed without your knowledge”—namely, because I rashly attempted to depart somewhat from conformity to you—“I was afraid that you would violently take away your daughters,” that is, that the excess of the undertaking I had begun would cause me to fall away from both kinds of life.

## VERSE 32

“Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live; before his own brothers (*suis*) let him be put to death”—or, according to another reading, “before our brothers” (*nostris*).

That is: If you accuse me of false belief, then, in whatever sense of the mind you find something fictitious concerning God, let it be destroyed by the judgment of other understandings belonging to the same mind.

“Search out whatever of yours you find with me and take it away.”

That is: Teach me to search, and whatever of yours—that is, whatever spiritual things are more properly yours—you see being corrupted in me, namely in my sensual imagination, remove by example and prayer.

These words are ordinarily both inferred and referred intellectually from contemplation of the brightness of the saints.

While saying this, he did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols. There are indeed people who think they have contemplated something great if they attribute certain glorious forms to God. They do not know that Rachel, who ought to be wholly intellectual, commits theft if she invents anything imaginary about God according to her own will.

## VERSE 33

Laban entered Jacob’s tent and Leah’s tent and the tents of both maidservants, but he did not find them.

Jacob’s and Leah’s tent signifies the exercise of reason and action. The two maidservants signify every kind of virtue subordinate to both kinds of life.

Laban did not find idols in any of these, because in those things administered according to human knowledge, the spirituality of heavenly brightness, when the subject is not God, does not find formulas concerning God.

## VERSE 34

When he had entered Rachel’s tent, she hurriedly hid the idols beneath the camel’s bedding and sat on top of them.

Laban enters Rachel’s tent when the spiritual splendor examines the contemplation by which she stretches herself toward God. “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:15).

Therefore, when the spirit illumines the mind, Rachel—that is, inward discernment—quickly hides whatever bodily thing she had imagined about God, placing over it the virtues of the mind, which are the camel’s bedding: the defenses and adornments of sluggish flesh. In examining these, one can move about with much greater freedom than when contemplating God without an image.

She sits on top of them when, established upon virtue and supported by it, she presides over foolish movements of fantasies, pressing them down.

When Laban searched the tent and found nothing, she said:

**VERSE 35.** “Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for what is customary among women has happened to me now.”

As though she were saying: Do not be indignant, lord—for whatever is subject to the Lord is subject to the one to whom he wishes to give it—that I cannot rise before you, namely, in the inward person, and rise toward you in order to contemplate you as you are, because I am suffering according to the custom of human softness.

Thus the diligence of the one searching is deceived. The diligence of the one searching is deceived when, because God’s grace anticipates us, what ought to be punished is not found within the grasp of our own discernment.

## VERSES 36–37

Jacob, swelling with indignation, said with reproach:

“For what fault of mine and for what sin have you become so inflamed against me and searched through all my possessions? What have you found of all the substance of your house? Set it here before my brothers and yours, and let them judge between me and you.”

When the human mind considers that conscience ought to be examined with such strictness, it often endures great disgust within itself. Hence, swelling and seeming almost inwardly enraged, it cries out:

“What excess of guilt demands that you pursue me with such zeal, O spiritual diligence, and probe and gather up all the recesses of my mind? What have you found with me of substance—that is, of all those earthly things which properly ought to stand beneath and be subject to your house, that is, to the conscience of your own people? Let it be placed in the judgment of your divine reason and my human reason, and surely it will be found in favor of my freedom from sin.”

## VERSE 38

“For twenty years I was with you”—that is, I served the tenfold fullness of the Law in the mind and the tenfold number of virtues, namely, the years of perfection.

“I served Laban, the heavenly brightness, in my work. The sheep of simple benefits and the goats of contemplation were not barren through hypocrisy. I did not consume the rams—that is, rational movements, the leaders of the flocks of thoughts—within myself by admitting vices.”

**VERSE 39.** “Nor did I make a show to any of the saints of anything taken by a beast”—that is, of an inward good plundered by the devil.

Hence the Psalm says: “Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be put to shame because of me” (Ps. 68:8).

“I returned every loss,” namely, compensating for sins through labors. “Whatever was lost by theft”—that is, through the devil’s stealth—you demanded from me, with the understood meaning, “that I restore it.”

**VERSE 40.** “By day I was consumed by the things I understood; by night, by the things I did not understand.”

That is: In good things and in evil things, I was burned by the heat of vainglory in good things, and from that very torpor of mine I was, as it were, cooked by frost in evil things. The sleep of negligence fled from my intentions, which is to say, from my eyes.

We know, however, that understanding pertains only to good things, because nothing is known unless it is true. If what is false is known, it is known insofar as it is known to be false; but whatever is true is proved to be good insofar as it is true.

## VERSE 41

“For fourteen years I served you for your daughters, and six years for your flocks.”

By the number four we understand the Gospels, and by the number ten, the Law. When we have fulfilled first the Law and then the Gospel, we shall approach the daughters of the heavenly mother, the Church—namely, the active and contemplative lives.

The number six, since it pertains to fullness—for God made all things in six days—signifies years wholly complete in the brightness of virtues, which we demand from ourselves in full measure so that we may rule over the flocks of thoughts, after the likeness of the heavenly city, which already possesses these in utterly unshaken peace.

“You also changed my wages ten times.”

He complains that his wages were changed ten times when, through the weight of carnal storms, the soul—which is signified by the number three, while the body is signified by four because of the elements—is turned even from hope of reward to fear of punishment, though it hopes for impassibility among its chief goods and seeks to know God, who is the Trinity, from the depths.

## VERSE 42

“Unless the God of my father Abraham”—that is, the God who presides over my reason—“had restrained me.”

Abraham is said to mean “father seeing the people,” and it is properly understood to pertain to the intellect to provide fatherly care for the common multitude of thoughts.

“And the fear of Isaac”—that is, fear of the loss of eternal joy. Isaac is said to mean “laughter,” perhaps because of all the difficulties.

“O Laban”—that is, heavenly brightness—which, the more earnestly it is sought by me, the more it is delayed: “you would have sent me away utterly naked and powerless in righteousness into the lusts by which the body is afflicted.”

“God looked upon my affliction and the labor of my hands”—that is, of my works—under which, amid the threshing of evils, I perform these very small good deeds. “And yesterday he rebuked you,” that is, through evident proofs he showed you, by the example of past humanity, what clemency you ought to show toward those who are in danger while you enjoy the haven of salvation.

“Yesterday” is used for the past. Thus Isaiah says: “Topheth has been prepared from yesterday” (Isa. 30:33).

These things take place especially in the conscience when we ardently desire the saints and feel that they are slow to help us.

## VERSE 43

Laban said:

“The daughters and sons, your flocks, and everything that you see are mine.”

It is as though the heavenly Jerusalem were speaking:

The weak and the strong souls in the Church, whether rulers or the movements that are to be ruled in the conscience, and the mass of thoughts forced down into the depths—even if you have directed toward yourself whatever things are good—you have them from my examples and teachings.

“What can I do for my daughters and grandchildren?”

That is: How could I harm those whom I have begotten for faith or works, or those who have been begotten for the same purpose through those whom I have begotten?

Therefore do not grow arrogant and do not provoke quarrels. Rather:

**VERSE 44.** “Come to my conformity,” and through this we shall enter into a covenant of the love that is owed, so that love itself may be a testimony that you are not torn away from my transformation.

## VERSE 45

Jacob therefore took a stone. The intellect seized for itself the solidity of the mind, so that thereafter it would not fly away into vanity. He raised it as a monument, because whenever any movements within or outside him are stirred up, he returns to it as to a conspicuous refuge.

Solidity is sincere humility itself.

**VERSE 46.** He said to his brothers—whether these are the stronger movements of the soul or virtues, as though children born from the same mind:

“Bring stones,” that is, set forth solid and humble affections in every action of yours.

They gathered them and made a mound. That is, striving toward unity, they expanded themselves in proper order through love below, so that above they might become subtle in contemplation.

Upon it they eat, when, rooted and founded in love and in the divine sweetness that is readily available to those who love (Eph. 3:17), they refresh themselves.

## VERSE 47

Laban called it “the Mound of the Witness,” and Jacob “the Heap of Testimony,” each according to the character of his own language.

Laban thinks and speaks one way, Jacob another, because the understanding of those who already live above is one thing, and their efficacy another; while the understanding of those who dwell in the flesh is another, and their desires are different.

A mound is customarily called a mound of the dead. And a witness is more than testimony, because testimony needs a witness more than a witness needs testimony.

Laban, therefore, is that shining senate which has already undergone death and, through an explicit testimony of faith and work, has already become an established and experienced witness.

Jacob, however, is present fragility, which gathers a heap with much sweat while bearing the testimonies of its profession.

**VERSE 48.** The mound is a witness between Laban and Jacob when Jacob longs for the lot of those already saved, while those already saved stoop down to assist the suffering of those who are to be saved.

For when we remember the example of the saints, we look back, as it were, toward the mound. They themselves look back toward the mound—that is, toward the memory of what they once were—when they take pity on us, who are still swimming in the same sea.

## VERSES 49–50

“May the Lord look upon us and judge between us when we have departed from one another, whether you afflict my daughters and bring other wives in addition to them.”

No one is a witness to our speech except God, who looks on while present.

Laban departs from Jacob when any of the saints, even though they have left examples behind, nevertheless leave us to our own judgment.

We afflict the daughters and bring other wives over them when, having removed the fellowship of both kinds of life, we bring adulterous wills to our own lust. It is certain that God is the overseer of these things and the discerning witness of what is inward, for he alone sees consciences.

## VERSE 52

“If I pass beyond this point while going toward you, or if you pass beyond this point while thinking evil against me”—that is, if, while I profess that I am going toward you, I pass beyond that testimony by sinning, or if you pass beyond it—which cannot happen—thinking only of yourself and rejoicing in your own glory, so that you cease to pray for me who am laboring, then this will certainly be evil for me.

**VERSE 53.** “God shall be the discerner and judge of these things—the God of Abraham,” that is, of your intellectual nature, O Jacob, “and likewise the God of Nahor,” that is, the repose of light, which is Laban, the eternal brightness, who is the God of the father, their God—namely, the God of Christ according to the person of the servant.

For he rules the heavens in such a way that he also rules the earth.

Jacob swears by the fear of his father Isaac. He confines himself within the laws of divine law, fearing that by transgressing he may deprive himself of the eternal vision of his father’s joy.

## VERSE 54

After sacrifices of all vices, truly pleasing to God, had been offered on the mountain—that is, in the eminence of virtue—Jacob, that is, the intellect, calls his brothers, the sons of the same mind, namely every rational movement, so that, now that every crime has been slaughtered, they may eat the bread of angels, which is Christ.

They eat and remain there. For, tasting Christ as bread, they are incorporated into him with perseverance.

**VERSE 55.** Laban, rising by night—that is, causing the true Jacob to rise from the torpor of sin—kissed his sons and daughters. He strengthened with heavenly bread and sweetness the strong and weak dispositions of mind whom he had begotten for heavenly hope. He blessed them—that is, increased them by his example—and returned, or caused him to return, to his own place: Christ, who, although he belongs to all, is nevertheless the special place of those who love him.

# CHAPTER XXXII

## VERSE 1

Jacob also went on the journey he had begun, and the angels of God met him.

The intellect continues the undertaking begun through Laban’s covenant, and words of divine speech meet his pious intention like angels, announcing the good things that must be done.

**VERSE 2.** When he saw them—that is, understood them—he said:

“These are the camps of God.”

Camps properly belong to those engaged in warfare. “These,” he says, “proclaim nothing other than the exercises and restraint of divine warfare.” For *castra* (“camps”) is derived from *coercere* (“to restrain”).

They keep the enemy away from themselves and restrain themselves through discipline.

He called the name of that place *Mahanaim*, that is, “camps,” because he regards Christ—or Scripture itself, in which we ought to be stationed—as his fortification and restraint.

## VERSES 3–4

Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to Esau his brother, into the land of Seir, the region of Edom, and commanded them, saying:

“I have lived as a stranger with Laban until the present day.”

The messengers who go before Jacob to Esau are movements of compunction and desires of piety. These often send the intellect to soften the affection that once ruled it wickedly.

He is called a brother because he is begotten from the same mind from which reason is also born.

This Esau dwells in the land of Seir, which is interpreted as “hairy,” because affection, rejoicing in lying among earthly things, is covered by continual superfluity. For it is often willingly devoted to vanity.

And he dwells in the region of Edom, that is, of sin, which is situated around sin, and in it he moves with complete eagerness. Edom means “blood,” and blood signifies sin.

“With Laban,” he says—that is, by longing for heavenly brightness—“I have lived, extending myself toward him who neither passes away nor is future, but is present with the constancy of eternity.”

For he himself says: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14), and: “He who is has sent me” (ibid., 15).

## VERSE 5

“I have oxen,” signifying maturity and prudence in examining earthly things; “donkeys,” signifying non-resistance and simplicity; “sheep,” signifying generous usefulness; “servants,” signifying the boldnesses of the soul; and “maidservants,” signifying wantonness and the ticklings of the flesh.

“I have these so that they may rule, and those so that they may be subject. Now I send an embassy”—without doubt, the devotion of the soul—“to the Lord,” namely to you, who until now have usurped power over me, “so that I may find favor in your sight,” that is, so that you may permit the grace of God, rather than luxury or avarice, to be found in your intention.

## VERSE 6

The messengers returned to Jacob.

The messengers return to Jacob when intellectual desires are scourged by carnal affection.

“We came,” they say, “through the offering of a pious will, to the effect; and behold, he is hurrying to meet you with four hundred men”—namely, with the whole mass of temporal pride—“stirring up against you the troubles of adversities.”

Through “men,” as also through “males,” foolish audacity is understood; through the number one hundred, universality; and through four, temporality.

## VERSES 7–8

Jacob, greatly afraid, divided the people who were with him, as well as the flocks, sheep, camels, and oxen, into two companies.

When we sense the assault of the flesh approaching, we separate from the sheep, oxen, and camels—that is, from pious generosity, holy seriousness, and humility—and also from the flocks, namely the true and useful substance of thoughts acting in a flock and according to discipline.

We divide the people clamoring with the common wantonness of the flesh into one company and another, so that “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17).

“If Esau strikes one,” he says—that is, if affection raises a rebellion in bodily things—the part that has acted more remotely from them will be saved in spiritual things.

But in so great a conflict the inner person must turn to God.

**VERSE 9.** “God of my father Abraham and God of Isaac”—that is, God who, through reason, serves as my light and as the protector of my hope of eternal joy—“Lord, who said to me that I should return to my land,” that is, to the cultivation of a fruitful mind, “and through it to the place of my birth,” namely, to the state of immutability originally owed to me, “so that it might go well with me for eternal life.”

**VERSE 10.** “I am less than all the mercies”—that is, all the merciful gifts—“and than all the truth that you have bestowed and will bestow upon me without merit.” For grace surpasses service, and I am less than the truth in which you have fulfilled and will fulfill your promises.

“With my staff I crossed this Jordan,” relying on these temporal goods as on the support of a staff, until I had been completely stripped of its desires.

I crossed the Jordan of the present age, which is called the descent of those who traverse the valley of tears; and now I return with two companies, that is, with a strong division of the spirit against the flesh, to him who always now possesses power—perhaps, according to another reading, “to power”—of deity. No longer inclined toward any worldly thing, I return as though without a staff.

## VERSE 11

“You, Lord, deliver me from the hand of my brother,” namely, from the power of carnal affection, “for I greatly fear that, when he comes to the inner chambers of reason, he will strike the mother, love, together with her children,” that is, her effects.

**VERSE 12.** “You said that you would enlarge my seed,” namely, my pious intention, from which good fruits proceed, “like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude.”

That is: Just as salt is made from sand and food is seasoned with salt, so my intention and action would be seasoned with divine wisdom. My intention would be made wise, and from that very savor my action would be seasoned.

Sand, moreover, since it is very heavy, also signifies the maturity of humility. Salt is made from it because God gives understanding to the little ones (Ps. 118:130). This sand is not counted because the fruits of humility and understanding are comprehended by no one.

## VERSE 13

When he had slept there that night, he separated from what he possessed gifts for Esau his brother.

He sleeps by night when the spirit, intent upon inward things, rests from the desire for visible things amid the terror of temptation.

He separates gifts for Esau from what he possesses when, from his abundance of virtue, he gathers within himself what can reasonably restrain the gaping affection.

That he slept there signifies that he slept within the same intention, expressed under the figure of seed.

**VERSE 14.** Two hundred she-goats signify the perfection of a twofold contemplation, namely divine and moral, which is especially called the virtue of discernment. For goats seek high places.

Twenty he-goats. The number twenty consists of two tens; the ten consists of seven and three. Through three, faith is understood; through seven, the giving of the Spirit. Through these two the Christian is made complete.

We give she-goats when we oppose the power of prudent contemplation to the desire of the flesh.

We give twenty he-goats when we moderate the stench of carnality through the invisible sacraments of faith and the Spirit that we have received: one ten through the sacrament itself, and another through the inward efficacy of the same sacrament, as though through the number twenty.

Two hundred sheep. Sheep signify simplicity in themselves and, because of the gift of wool, the extension of benefit toward others.

Two hundred sheep are therefore given when the perfection of piety is brought not only to ourselves but also to our neighbors, whereby the perversity of the heart is restrained.

Rams symbolize stiffness of neck. They are given through the doubled ten because through the inward and outward fulfillment of the Decalogue wicked desires are pressed down by the neck.

### Verse 15

**“Pregnant camels.”** The camel, named from its bent posture, signifies endurance, which is “pregnant” when it loves those whom it supports. We give these in groups of thirty when we act solely for love of the Trinity.

**“Forty cows.”** Cows are given by the number forty when worldly wantonness is restrained through the four Gospels and the Decalogue.

**“Bulls,”** whose flesh is suitable for eating but whose blood is deadly, signify an outwardly good action but a corrupt intention. They are brought in through a doubled denarius, composed of seven and three, so that by faith and grace the desires of an evil intention may be changed.

We understand **“she-asses”** as sluggishness and dullness; to these we assign a denarius for the visible and invisible efficacy of the sacraments, as above. But the she-asses, roused from torpor by the vigor of faith and the Spirit, have ten colts—that is, works or affections according to the Decalogue.

**Verse 16.** “And he sent each of these by the hands of his servants,” while he strives to display them through the functions of the members that serve the mind.

And he said to the boys: **“Go on ahead of me, and let there be space between flock and flock.”** The boys go ahead when humble desires precede the effects of works. There is space between flock and flock when a definite distinction is established between the movements of reason and the affections of the flesh.

### Verses 17–19

“And he commanded the first, saying: ‘If Esau my brother meets you and asks you, “Where are you going, and whose are you, and whose are these things that follow you?” you shall say: “Your servant Jacob’s; he has sent gifts to my lord Esau.”’”

The first, second, third, and the others who follow the flock seem to me to represent different dispositions of the mind, which confront and resist the first suggestion, the second pleasure, the third consent, and the remaining stages of evil. From these we obtain the number corresponding to the things with which they deal.

**“If,”** he says, **“a carnal will assails you, examines where you are directing your intention, whom you serve as Lord, and to whom the usefulness of what you are undertaking belongs, you shall say: ‘I have brought the spirit of my mind to God alone. I have resolved to obey him, overthrowing vices, not for his benefit but for mine. I have devoted to him the whole pursuit that I am following, and to you, O affection, who once abused my service, I have sent by reasoning whatever may satisfy your bestial ferocity.’”**

**Verse 20.** “And you shall add: ‘Your servant Jacob himself, who once served you—that is, the intellect—also follows our journey, strongly fortifying the devotion of our desire.’”

For he said: **“I will appease him with the gifts that go before; afterward I shall see him—perhaps he will be gracious to me.”** This means that he supposes he can soften him by the affections and effects of the pious acts already offered. Afterward he will “see” him—that is, he will cause him to see, which means to understand him—and once he has understood, he will act more leniently.

**Verse 21.** The gifts go ahead, but Jacob remains in the camp that night, because although reason has already performed the highest good deeds, as long as it is night—that is, as long as temptation or the world remains—and it does not know whether it is worthy of love or hatred (Eccles. 9:1), it withdraws within the camp of self-restraint and fear.

### Verse 22

“And when he had risen early, he took his two wives and as many maidservants, with his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of Jacob.”

Jacob is called either “wrestling” or “arena”; in him the conflict and the place of conflict are understood as the world and its temptation. But because the same arena is called a ford, the outcome that will come from God together with the temptation is indicated.

He rises early when he raises himself from the lightness of thought by the hand of seriousness. He takes the wives and maidservants with the eleven sons when, as far as he can, he lifts contemplation and action above temporal things, together with the vices subject to them in the manner of maidservants and with works that have not yet reached the apostolic perfection of the number twelve. He crosses the ford according to the measure in which the most turbulent sea is so for many weak people, treating it with contempt as he crosses over with Jedithun.

### Verses 23–24

“And when he had brought across all that belonged to him, he remained alone; and behold, a man wrestled with him until morning.”

He brings across everything that belongs to him when he establishes the spirit and the fruit of all his virtue beyond the ford in the heavenly harbor. He remains alone because, whether he wishes it or not, he is held by the body in temporal things.

A man wrestles with him until morning when heavenly virtue, while he wishes to ascend to its summit, resists him by a providential arrangement, in order to kindle more strongly the desire of reason.

**“I sought him,”** she says in the Song of Songs, **“and I did not find him; I called, and he did not answer”** (Song 5:6). Yet the morning of divine illumination, which awakens hope in the struggle, is not long delayed.

### Verse 25

“When he saw”—plainly, God saw—that by delaying he could not overcome his desires, **“he touched the sinew of his thigh,”** that is, he tamed the obstinacy of his bodily wantonness, and immediately it withered from the excessive moisture of relaxation.

**Verse 26.** “Let me go,” he said, “for the dawn has risen already.” As though he were saying: “You now have the morning for which you were waiting; you may now cease from pursuing me.”

**“I will not let you go,”** he said, **“unless you bless me”**—unless, that is, you lead me to certainty regarding eternal blessedness.

**Verse 27.** “What is your name?” That is: “Recall the profession of your purpose.”

He answered: **“Jacob.”** “I have resolved,” he says, “to live for the overthrow of vices.”
