**Verse 28.** He does not say: “From now on the concern of overthrowing vices will rest upon you.” That is, you will not be called Jacob, but Israel—“a prince with God,” or “beloved of God”—so that now, through a certain shared divinity, you may hold the principate with God within yourself; and when the noise of the passions has been lulled to sleep, you may direct yourself from God to God. With all these things pacified, devote yourself to the One. For if you are strong enough to seek and embrace God anxiously with perseverance, how much more will you prevail against human beings—that is, against the temptations of humanity?

**Verse 29.** And Jacob said: **“Tell me by what name you are called.”** That is: “Reveal how I may estimate the excellence of your dignity.”

He said: **“Why do you ask my name, which you can neither hear nor, if you could hear it, comprehend?”** And he blessed him in that same place—that is, he enriched him with a multiplicity of virtues, as he persevered in charity, which makes hearts one and the same, in a truly solid and stable place.

**“You have set my feet,”** he says, **“in a spacious place”** (Ps. 30:10).

**Verse 30.** He called the name of that place **Phanuel**, which means “the face of God,” because in the chief form of love there is knowledge of God, and whoever possesses this is known by God, according to the Epistle of John. For in the face there is recognition, and God himself is love (1 John 3:16).

**“I have seen the Lord [alternatively: God] face to face, and my soul has been saved.”** This means: “I have understood the Lord, my recognition being illumined by the understanding of his knowledge; and because, through knowing him, I do not doubt that I am known by him—that is, chosen by him—I hold the spirit of my soul’s salvation with certainty.”

### Verse 31

“And immediately the sun rose after he had passed beyond Phanuel.”

That is, the light and warmth of righteousness immediately grew hot in the mind after reason had attained the knowledge of God.

Phanuel can also mean “transgression,” apart from the general knowledge of God, namely, contemplation of God himself. The intellect itself, without doubt, **limped in its foot**, because it had lost the power of a corrupt affection.

**Verse 32.** For this reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew—that is, they do not admit the vice of obstinacy, which has withered in the desires of the intellect—in order that the intellect, truly liberated, might everywhere reach God, who is the day present everywhere. This is because God had softened the hardness of its lustful habits and it had become numb—that is, even in this life it had already attained the grace of impassibility.

The children of Israel are those who exercise the role of God by ruling as princes within themselves.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### Verses 1–2

“Lifting his eyes, he saw Esau coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children of Leah and Rachel and of both maidservants, and placed the two maidservants and their children first; Leah and her children in the second place.”

He raises the mind’s intention from earthly things and perceives the affection of the flesh threatening him, together with the presumption of all worldliness. We have spoken more fully above about the four hundred. He distinguishes between the works of pious activity and the works of Bilhah and Zilpah—that is, of antiquity and empty glory—and exposes every vice arising from vices in the open through confession, because “the righteous man is his own first accuser” (Prov. 18:17).

Leah, that is, the active life, with her children—that is, with her pursuits—is placed in the second position, so that they may serve the neighbor below while carrying their intention above, to God. But Rachel and Joseph he places last, because he knows that contemplation of God belongs to sincere and perfect minds, which always look toward the son Joseph—that is, the fruit of eternal increase.

**Verse 3.** “And he himself went forward and bowed prostrate to the ground seven times, until his brother came near.” He too advances toward the same contemplation and toward the increase of perfect vision. Seven times means that he is humbled prostrate in both body and soul, considering only his own lowliness, as long as earthly pride threatens him through these affections. We have often said that the fourfold number pertains to the body and the threefold number to the soul; together they are seven.

### Verse 4

“So Esau ran to meet his brother, embraced him, clasped his neck, kissed him, and wept.”

The carnal will offers reverence to the divine fervor when it meets it—that is, to obedience. It embraces when it presents to the judgment of the intellect both the right hand of prosperity and the left hand of adversity. It clasps the neck when it gladly gathers his counsels to itself. The voice is emitted through the neck. It kisses when that same wise affection allows itself to be moistened by the saliva of wisdom and is imbued with the sweetness of the spirit. It weeps when it is dried by that same spirit, as by a torrent, of harmful moisture.

**Verse 5.** “And lifting his eyes, he saw the women and their children. ‘Who are these?’ he said. ‘Do they belong to you?’”

He now lifts the eyes of his mind from the depths and sees that he no longer envies the fruitfulness of pious purposes. He investigates their still-tender effects: what they wish to obtain for themselves through these pursuits, and whether they pertain to some fruit of understanding. For the flesh is accustomed, especially amid labors, to seek its reward.

He said: **“They are the children whom God has given your servant.”** That is: “They are the beginnings of the virtues, although still weak, which God has given me, so that here I may obtain honor for you, and in the future may gain rewards worthy of service.”

### Verses 6–7

“The maidservants and their children drew near and bowed; Leah and her children likewise bowed; and last of all Rachel and Joseph bowed.”

The vices, with their effects, approach the light of confession from the recesses of their hiding places and are bent beneath the yoke of reason. Leah likewise worships with her children, because the active virtue and its works arrange themselves under the instruction of reason after the suppression of vice. Rachel and Joseph, the last, worship because the contemplation of God, together with the increase of perfect vision for which it waits, humbles itself as the highest of sanctities before supreme reason.

**Verse 8.** The affection says: **“What are these companies which I encountered?”** That is: “What are these heaps of virtues which I had against me? What cause led you to do this?”

The intellect answers: **“So that I might find”—that is, might cause to be found in the presence, in the field of your consideration—not avarice but grace.**

**Verse 9.** “I have plenty, my brother; let what is yours be yours.” As though he were saying: “You strive in vain so greatly, since I possess many honorable things in my will, sufficient for life, and I have no need of so many new things being thrust upon me, which I see you have with you. Do not, intellect, fail so far from what you have begun.”

**Verse 10.** “But if I have now once found grace in your eyes”—that is, in your intention—“accept this little gift from my hands,” which means, “accept it from the exercise of my works.”

“For when you first began to favor the intellect, I saw”—that is, I accepted—“your face,” namely, your knowledge, by which you had begun to be known, that is, approved, by God, “as though I had seen the face of God,” so that I might truly and plainly understand the will of God to have entered into you. Or “your face” may mean that I recognized you as having feared the severity of God.

### Verses 11–12

“Accept, therefore, not what you think a loss, but a blessing,” that is, an increase through multiplication.

Only with difficulty does he accept when his brother presses him—that is, only with difficulty does he favor reason. He says, for it is the habit of the human will to become readily enough animated toward something spiritual and just as readily to fail:

**“Let us travel together; let us strive together, and I shall be your companion from now on.”**

To desire something is, in a certain sense, to go toward it. But reason must restrain an excessively hasty impulse.

### Verses 13–14

**Verse 13.** “You know, my lord, that I have tender children, and sheep and cattle with me that are giving birth; if I make them labor by walking, all the flocks will die in one day.”

This means: “You know, from my very recent conversion, that I possess beginnings which are weak, and sheep of simplicity, and cattle of discernment—for cattle break up the earth—which are now first giving birth through the mere desire to do good. If I force them to act beyond their strength, they will die in one day from weariness and failure: at the very beginning of their illumination, the entire heap of pious thoughts will perish.”

**Verse 14.** “Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, and I shall follow little by little in his footsteps, as I see my children are able, until I come to my lord at Seir.”

“Your part,” he says, “is to go ahead of all the movements of the mind in willing, and I shall follow the footsteps of a good intention through the practice of seriousness, acting as I know my tenderness can endure, until I come to you, who ought to lead the mind as Lord by going before its holy desires and ought to be its guide, at Seir—that is, until I am joined to you in one mind in the confession of the harshness of your sins.”

### Verse 15

Esau says to him: **“I ask you to leave with me at least some of the people who are with me as companions for your journey.”**

“For,” he says, “you suggest that I trust you; if you wish me to obey you, at least mix with your purpose some practices of less harmful thoughts and some worldly works, whether for the sake of a little relaxation or remission.”

Reason answers: **“It is not necessary.”** That is: “This is how our weariness is more effectively relieved. I need only one thing, so that I may find in your presence”—that is, in your grace—“divine provision.”

### Verses 16–17

“So Esau returned that day by the way he had come to Seir. And Jacob came to Succoth, where, after building a house and pitching tents, he called the name of the place Succoth,” that is, “tabernacles.”

The carnal appetite, already bright with the light from above, returns by the same steps of devotion by which it had agreed with reason, remembering penitentially each sin as it had been committed, until it is slain by consideration of its own excess, harshness, and stench. For Seir means “hairy” or “goat.”

There it dwells perseveringly, as though in a house; it pitches tents and takes root, stretched out in charity. It calls the condition of the place “tabernacles,” because in the immobility of charity there is much labor and much warfare.

### Verse 18

“From there he crossed over to Salem, which is interpreted as ‘perfect,’ the city of Shechem,” which means “shoulder.” In this obedience is understood, for the shoulder is placed beneath the burdens of the commandments—plainly, patience itself. The city is regarded as a threefold fortification in Canaan, that is, in the land of change, in which the complete transformation of conduct is understood. For Canaan means “changed.”

The whole passage means this: He progressed as far as Salem, the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, plainly to the perfection of humility and obedience, which alone is the stronghold and support of every other virtue and the foundation of the change made in one’s conduct.

After Jacob returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, he dwelt beside the town—that is, where by a lofty calling, a divine one, he is raised from the depths, and our spirit returns to itself and dwells, as it were, beside the town in the help of the Most High, who truly gives us aid (Ps. 90:1).

**Verse 19.** “And he bought a portion of the field”—that is, a portion of the mind, which is an area worthy of cultivation—namely, the carnal affection itself, which is the lower part of the mind and in which he had already fixed the tents of spiritual warfare inwardly.

He bought it, I say, from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs, having paid out the full price of all pleasures. He drove it away from the works of the flesh, which produced nothing in us except labor, as from the sons of Hamor—which means “ass”—the father of Shechem—which means “labor”—so that he might use it according to God, although previously he had used it according to the world. The whole was bought for a hundred lambs, that is, through perfect humility and simplicity.

**Verse 20.** There he raises an altar, because he elevates faith through the support of righteous action. He invokes upon it the strongest God of Israel, when, leaning upon it as upon a foundation, he calls the strongest God into himself—not only in these matters but also in others—when efficacy is granted by him to rule with God over vices. For Israel is said to mean “a prince with God.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### Verse 1

“Dina, the daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region.”

Dina is interpreted as “this judgment.” In it, or in her, we understand discernment, which itself is often called judgment. Since “this” is demonstrative, it signifies a present matter, and nothing ought to be more readily at hand than discernment, which is always necessary.

She goes out when she is led to examine the weak actions of others. She is called the daughter of Leah because through her the active life is found to be rightly fruitful. For where nothing is discerned, there is certainly nothing being done. The women of the region are seen when the lukewarm practitioners of our own religion are indicated.

### Verse 2

“Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite saw her.”

He sees her when the affection claims her for itself—an affection in which envy is wholly at work: truly the son of the worst of asses, begotten from the worst fervor of carnal desires. For Hamor means “ass”; Hivite means “worst” or “wild”; Shechem means “labor.”

From the wildness of bodily desire, signified by the ass, arises labor against others in the form of envy, which certainly enjoys no rest. Of it the following is said:

> Nothing is more just than envy,  
> which first gnaws and torments  
> its own author.

We long to know the condition of others for this reason: when we discover blemishes of vice in them, we think that honor has increased for us because we see them below us.

Hamor is prince of the land of the Hivites, because asinine and foolish desire rules altogether over earthly things in their wildness. Those who desire undoubtedly envy others for possessing what they themselves desire.

Shechem loves Dina because the labor of envy seeks to tear discernment away from the mind. He rapes her when it becomes sweet to him to examine the lives of others. He sleeps with her when, overpowering the virgin by force, he mingles with her by removing the sincerity of her intention. He loves her through receiving the suggestion, rapes her through consent, and sleeps with her through the imposition of action. For this is the syllogism he uses.

**Verse 3.** “His soul clung to her.” The very intention of envy—that is, advancement of oneself through the disgrace of others, which is as it were the soul of envy—adheres deeply to our discernment.

He soothes the grieving woman with flatteries when he consoles and anoints one who at times regrets the vice begun, with the praise born from another person’s disgrace.

**Verse 4.** “He asked his father Hamor to obtain her for him as a wife.” This happens when the lusts of desire are brought forward so that, by enticement, they may bind the wretched soul to themselves.

### Verse 5

“When Jacob heard this, while his sons were absent and occupied in feeding the cattle, he kept silent until they returned.”

Our reason understands this corruption of itself through works, through empty glories, which are a kind of feeding of external senses. For through these we are like cattle, scattered everywhere; but when silence has been made from the clamor of desires, they return.

### Verses 6–7

“Hamor the father of Shechem went out to speak with Jacob, and behold, his sons were coming from the field. When they heard what had happened, they were exceedingly angry, because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel and had committed an unlawful deed by violating Jacob’s daughter.”

Hamor goes out to speak with Jacob after silence has been made because, when the crowd of the mind has been lulled to sleep, carnal desire, unable to endure quiet for long, does not permit itself to remain silent. It wishes to attack reason and is offended by the return and restraint of wandering works.

They hear what has happened and become angry when reason, mindful of former labors, is taught through the very works how much it loses of the merit of works through the inner violation of chastity and how much it ought to grieve when the daughter of rational discernment is corrupted by the leprosy of the whole race.

### Verses 8–9

Hamor speaks to them: **“Shechem my son’s soul has clung to your daughter. Give her to him as a wife, and let us join our marriages with one another.”**

Hamor speaks to the sons when the flow of desires presses toward overthrowing our actions. “Worldly envy,” he says, “has subtly—and, so to speak, intentionally—clung to your discernment.”

This is signified by the fact that it is not the body but the soul that is said to have clung. It has entered so deeply that it cannot be torn away from the mind. Therefore nothing remains except that the union of both should be made by mutual consent, so that you may gladly receive the envy from which you cannot be free and experience its supposedly useful prudence.

“Your daughters”—that is, whatever in you is unstable and fragile—“give to us to be nourished as livestock; and accept our daughters,” that is, whatever softness is brought from us.

**Verse 10.** “Dwell with us in an unbreakable alliance. The land”—that is, your body—“is in the power of your free choice. Exercise it toward pleasures; trade in uncertainty, giving spiritual things for visible ones; possess it at will and use it as you please.”

**Verse 11.** Shechem—that is, envy—also has words: **“Let me find favor in your sight, and whatever you determine I shall give.”** That is: “I shall not be unwelcome to you, because I shall be able to provide you with much more than any patience could provide.”

**Verse 12.** **“Increase the bride-price.”** That is: “Ask what gifts you wish to obtain as the advantage of admitting me; declare what you want to secure in worldly fashion. It is better for me to give these things to you than for you to obtain them through the negligence of religion.”

### Verses 13–14

“The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father deceitfully, being enraged because of the violation of their sister: ‘We cannot do what you ask, nor give our sister to an uncircumcised man, for this is unlawful and wicked among us.’”

Reason gathers strength from the memory of former virtues; hence Scripture says that the sons acted—that is, that they signify works. They answer deceitfully because inwardly they propose to do much more against vice than they display outwardly through works.

“We consider it wicked,” they say, “to betray our discernment, devoted to sincerity, to the incontinence of envy.”

**Verse 15.** “But in this we shall be able to make a covenant with you: if you are willing to become like our frugality, so that every male”—that is, everything proud, through which envy is especially begotten—“is cut off from you.”

In this there is a faithful deceit, because if boldness is driven from desire and envy from pride, neither can stand. Yet this cannot happen, because just as heat cannot be separated from fire if it is to remain fire, so the accustomed presumption cannot be separated from desire, pride, and envy without ceasing to be the vice itself.

### Verses 16–19

“Then,” he says, “we shall be able to be joined in due unanimity when we perceive that you are intent upon purity. Otherwise, with our discernment separated from your contagion, we shall be divided.”

The offer pleases the father and son, and he is immediately circumcised, because it is customary for vices, for a time, deceitfully to submit themselves to virtue.

“For he loved the girl exceedingly, and he was himself renowned throughout his father’s entire household.”

He loves the girl exceedingly because the devil, through envy, especially desires to defile the beauty of discernment by immersing himself in it. This movement of envy is renowned—that is, it is known in advance among all vices—even in his father’s household: namely, in the household whose daughter the king desired and which he is commanded, together with his people, to forget (Ps. 44:11–12). For among ordinary people the father of the devil is held in great abhorrence.

### Verses 20–23

“They entered the gate of the city and spoke to the people: ‘These men are peaceful,’” continuing to the point where it says, **“we shall become one people”** [alternatively: “let us make one people”].

They enter the gate of the city when they allow the vices to be brought to the examination of conscience and, as though calmly, endure them for a moment. The gate signifies judgment, because in ancient times doubtful matters were debated at the gates. There are sufficient examples of this.

They speak to the people because, for the time being and deceitfully, they appear to favor the establishment of peace and the calming of the mind’s tumult.

“Viril and honorable and peaceful,” they say, “is this restraint. Let it dwell with us in the land of the body; let it seek the profits of its business and activity. The body itself, pursuing spacious and broad things, needs cultivation by which these may be cut back. We shall place your daughters”—that is, their unstable desires—“before us, and we shall inject into the rational movements of the mind every wantonness and softness belonging to our parts.

“One good alone is being deferred for us: that we should circumcise the males for the present—that is, restrain our rash impulses for a little while, though not for long—while pretending to imitate their rites and institutions of mind. Thus it will happen that, gradually entering into their minds, we shall claim for our own power their intention, which is as it were their substance because it lies beneath them like a foundation, together with the cattle—that is, the works of pious guardianship—and all their other vices, or the body itself, which their own rational faculties appear to possess.”

### Verse 24

“All agreed, and every male was circumcised.”

For a time the vices are silent, while the movements of open presumption are lulled to sleep.

### Verses 25–26

“On the third day, when the pain of the wounds was most severe, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dina’s brothers, took swords and entered the city boldly. They killed every male, and together they killed Hamor and Shechem, taking Dina their sister from Shechem’s house.”

The first day is called suggestion, the second pleasure, and the third consent. They are called days when they are distinguished through understanding.

After vice has begun gradually to break out, when it is detected as already wishing to advance toward consent, we receive the swords of inner and outer discernment through hearing sorrow—for Simeon is interpreted as “hearing”—and through assuming inner virtue. Unless we are rightly saddened against vices, we shall never be assumed by the Spirit of God.

Levi, moreover, means “assumed.” Without hearing sorrow—that is, without knowledge of one’s own misery—there is no assumption of righteousness, which we do not so much assume as are assumed by it, that is, firmly held by it. These two are joined to Dina, our discernment, by a kind of brotherhood and are altogether necessary to it.

They enter the city of conscience and, after consuming the movements of the boldness that has already arisen, kill desire and envy together—Hamor and Shechem—and rescue discernment from the wicked union.

### Verse 27

“After they had gone out, the other sons of Jacob fell upon the slain,” by the permission of the power granted them by God.

That is, the remaining virtues of the mind spoil the conquered vices by victorious action. They desolate the city of conscience of its customary tumult and compensate for the losses caused by corruption.

### Verse 28

“They took the sheep of improvidence and foolishness, the herds of dullness or curiosity, the asses of lust, and everything that was in the houses and fields”—that is, in the minds and external activities. “With these, as though with weapons, we cover our vices from ourselves.”

### Verse 29

“They took captive the little ones and the wives”—that is, the works already begun and the pleasures of those works—“after the power of ruling in the mortal body had been taken away.”

### Verse 30

“After these things had been boldly accomplished, Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: ‘You have troubled me.’”

Where sins are vigorously resisted, Jacob—that is, reason acting according to human conditions—reproves itself for having begun both the hearing of sorrow and the assumption of grace, as though it could not persevere in them.

“You have troubled me,” that is, “You have stirred up a crowd against the vices and made me hateful to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the inhabitants of the land.” For I have almost never been free from the affairs of the mind’s earthly desire, and I have put an end to the flesh’s stupor and constant inclination toward evil.

“You,” I say, “the spiritual movements, are the authors of this hatred.”

For a Canaanite means “merchant,” while a Perizzite means “stunned” or “stupefied.” A business proceeding through darkness, and the stupor of a reprobate sense or of bodily heaviness, yearn for the earth.

**“We are few.”** For the number of virtues is small in comparison with the number of vices.

“Therefore, when they gather together what you have begun to conquer, they will strike me and I shall be destroyed, and my household also. This very little good that I possessed outwardly will be destroyed, and the house of conscience will be laid waste.”

### Verse 31

But the virtue of rational faculties, raised up by God, says: **“Should they have treated our sister as a prostitute?”**

That is: “Should our discernment, born from the mother who brought us forth as an excellent offspring through reason, be prostituted to the filth of any sinner?”

## CHAPTER XXXV

### Verse 1

Meanwhile, while the struggles of the mind were making Jacob foolish, God addresses him inwardly:

**“Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there, and make an altar to God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau.”**

This means: “Rise from your lowest thoughts and advance through the virtues until you become the house of God,” which is what Bethel means. “Make an altar of good will to God, who shone upon you so that you might flee the carnal affection in which you sacrifice the offerings of pious actions.”

### Verse 2

“Jacob summoned his entire household and said: ‘Cast away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments.’”

After the erection of the altar he had proposed, he summons his household because he restrains the dispersions of conduct and of the whole mind.

“Cast away,” he says, “the things that you served as though they were images: the vices that were among you”—that is, that held the throne of dominion in your mind—“and purify yourselves in conscience, and change the coverings of your works.”

### Verses 3–4

“Rise; let us go up to Bethel,” as stated above.

“They gave him the foreign gods that they had”—that is, they offered their vices to reason to be consumed. For it says that they gave them, not that they resisted. That crimes are called gods is attested by the psalm: **“If you had listened to me, there would be no new god in you”** (Ps. 80:10).

“The earrings of the gods” are obedience, by which obedience was given to sins.

“But he buried them beneath the terebinth that is behind the city of Shechem.”

After we have set aside Shechem—that is, the labor of envy—we hide the gods, that is, the crimes, together with their earrings, namely their obediences, beneath the breadth and fragrance of charity. For the terebinth is a broad and fragrant tree.

### Verse 5

“When they had departed, the terror of God fell upon all the cities round about, and they did not dare pursue those who were leaving.”

When we advance toward God, the outward senses, in which envy and desire have been implanted and which are also placed around us like certain cities, are weighed down by the fear of God. They do not dare to inflict violence when their desires are rejected.

### Verse 6

“Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, also called Bethel, he and all the people with him.”

Luza means “almond”; Bethel means “house of God”; Canaan means “changed.”

Jacob comes to the almond when our spirit, through bodily passions and bitterness, reaches through something like a shell to the kernel of inner sweetness. Yet this occurs in the land—that is, in a mind already cultivable and changed—changed, namely, for the purpose of becoming the house of God.

And all the people of his thoughts are now not against him but with him, in his support.

### Verse 7

“There he built an altar, and he called the place ‘the house of God,’ because there God had appeared to him when he was fleeing from his brother.”

He builds an altar there because he establishes the state of holy will upon the purpose of that very transformation. He calls it the house of God because he judges that only a pious affection is suitable for God to inhabit. For there—that is, through this affection—God shone upon him when he feared the carnal affection.

### Verse 8

“At that time Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel beneath an oak; and the name of the place was called ‘Oak of Weeping.’”

In this same temperance of pious intention, the carnal stimulus dies. It presents sweetness in the manner of suggestion, but at the end, through the effect of sin, it has the greatest bitterness.

For Deborah means “bee.” Hence Boethius (*The Consolation of Philosophy*, book 3, meter 7):

> Every pleasure has this:  
> it drives the frenzied on with goads;  
> and like a swarm of flying bees,  
> when it has poured out its welcome honey,  
> it flees and wounds hearts  
> with its excessively clinging bite.

This stimulus nourishes Rebekah—that is, patience—because she grows strong through being exercised by such things.

It is buried at the foot of Bethel because it is hidden away under divine fear, which is the root of the house of God, so that it may be made firm. It is placed beneath the oak when it is depressed by perpetual negligence and by a certain rustic contemptibility. Such a tree is sought nowhere except by pigs.

But because only the pain of repentance ought to visit it, it was rightly called the Oak of Weeping.

VERS. 9, 10.—God appeared again to Jacob, [Col. 0252C] after he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and he blessed him, saying: “You shall no longer be called Jacob,” and he called him Israel. From Mesopotamia of Syria—that is, from the calling which lifts us from the depths and brings us to exalted things—our spirit has its return from the boundaries of envy. There God appears to it again through the increase of grace and the illumination of contemplation, so that in the first appearance it may be corrected, and in the second the grace that had been lost may be restored. “You shall no longer,” he says, “be tossed about in struggles with vices,” which is expressed by the name Jacob; rather, “Israel shall be your name,” that is, you shall rule as a prince with God through the power of the virtues.

(VERS. 11.) “I am God Almighty,” and so forth. This is as if he were saying: If you believe me to be almighty, do not doubt that nations and peoples of the nations will come forth from you. “Nations,” namely, of vices, and “peoples” spontaneously arising in the mind; yet because I am believed by you to be almighty, you will overcome them. Therefore, grow in the height of hope, but first multiply in good works. For kings of rational movements will go forth from your loins—that is, proceeding from the implanted origin of your desires, they will surpass carnality (VERS. 12); and your earthly nature, just as Abraham and Isaac—that is, reason and the hope of eternal things—must be subjected, I shall subject to you and to your seed, namely, to those who will imitate you.

(VERS. 13.) And he departed from him, leaving him, that is, to his own free choice.

VERS. 14, 15.—But he erected a stone monument in the place where God had spoken to him, pouring libations over it and pouring oil upon it, and he called the name of that place Bethel. A stone monument is erected in the place where God appeared when the light of humility—than which nothing is firmer—is established in the mind, upon which God is accustomed to shine as upon his own special place. Here we pour libations and oil when upon such a foundation we lay our prayers and, by the merit of humility itself, obtain that the oil of divine grace be poured into us. 134 Hence we judge that to live in this way is truly to be the house of God.

(VERS. 16.) And departing from there, he came in the springtime to the land that leads to Ephratha. We depart in the springtime when, through the warmth of the divine Spirit infused into us, we go beyond the boundaries of the desires of the flesh. We come to the land that leads to Ephratha when we reach that region of steadfastness of mind through which one comes to the fruitfulness of divine knowledge. While Rachel was giving birth there (VERS. 17), she began to be in danger because of the difficulty of the delivery. Rachel gives birth when the virtue of contemplation, longing for the true fruit—which is God—desires to attain the reality of inward vision with great difficulty and sometimes even with the dangerous exhaustion of the mind.

But the midwife who is accustomed to stand against our dangers—namely, reason—encourages the mind not to fear. For she consoles it, provided that it perseveres and does not withdraw from what it has begun, with the prospect of possessing the eternal fruit, as though it were a future son.

VERS. 18.—As her soul was departing because of the pain, and death was already imminent, she called the name of her son Benoni, that is, “son of my pain.” When devotion to contemplating God presses upon us, the soul departs in pain, because the mind is unable to reach the bread of life. For it is necessary that the animal sense be stripped away from the heart and, as far as it can, die to the desires of the world. [Col. 0253C] Therefore, by the mother herself—namely, charity, which, among the virtues over which she labors, still groans and gives birth in travail (Rom. VIII, 22)—the offspring produced by such great burden is called “the son of pain.” But the divine understanding, by whose sincere seed charity is impregnated as by that of a true father, calls him the “son of the right hand,” because whatever is accomplished under him through charity serves the right hand of the eternal kingdom.

(VERS. 19.) Rachel died and was buried on the road that leads to Ephratha. Because, as far as the sphere of the world is concerned, it is necessary for the soul intent upon the vision of its Creator to die and to be buried—that is, to be hidden from public commotion—in Christ, who is the way. For those buried with him are granted the pastures of the fruitful region, namely, of his divinity. The traces of his likeness lead to this region, where Bethel is properly found, truly the house of God.

(VERS. 20.) And Jacob erected a stone monument over her grave: “This is the monument of Rachel to the present day.” Jacob erects a monument over Rachel’s grave when, as the virtue of contemplation dies to the world, that which it possesses inwardly also displays outwardly the brightness of humility. The monument is said to derive its name from a Greek word, *titan*, that is, “sun.” This monument continues to the present day because this humility deserves everlasting remembrance; it stands in that unfailing day which is God, whose presence no one escapes. It is called “stone” so that its firmness, durability, and weight may be signified.

(VERS. 21.) Departing from there, he pitched his tent beyond the Tower of the Flock. The Tower of the Flock is the excellence of an undivided and unanimous thought directed toward God. We depart from there when, after overcoming the difficulty of the passions of the body, like the difficulty of childbirth, we advance beyond the tower to pitch the tent of the flock—that is, beyond every imaginary and, as it were, gregarious power, we extend the gaze of the spiritual mind toward God himself.

VERS. 22.—While he was dwelling in that region, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine; and this did not escape him. Reuben is said to mean “seeing in the midst”; Bilhah, “grown old.” When we linger in that noble region of heavenly vision, our upright understanding—which neither deviates to the right nor to the left but holds and observes the middle, and which is signified by Reuben—withdraws from holy contemplation and grows sluggish in some pleasure of ancient things, that is, temporal things. She is called his father’s concubine because the authority of that understanding—which is our king and father—is excessively and adulterously inclined toward her. Yet this intrusion does not escape the Father, because the foulness of its flux is clearer than light to the spirit, although he remains silent, withholding the punishment it deserves.

(VERS. 27.) Jacob also came to his father Isaac at Mamre, the city of Arbe, which is Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned. Our spirit comes to Mamre, the city of Arbe, when it approaches the division—that is, the discernment—of this temporality, which is signified by the number four and which truly is a city of the greatest fortification. It understands that whatever is transitory is a certain misery. For Mamre means “divisions”; Arbe, “four”; and Hebron is said to mean “participation in sorrow.” Abraham and Isaac therefore sojourn in Hebron, because the understanding itself and the hope of inward joy that we possess, while it recalls the anguish of its own sojourn, as long as it is occupied in the body, never fails to dwell in participation in sorrow.

VERS. 28, 29.—And the days of Isaac were completed: one hundred and eighty years. Consumed by age, he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. By one hundred years the fullness of virtue is expressed; by eighty, which contains fours, temporality is understood—the temporality found in those who long for heavenly joy. Isaac is surpassed by the perfection of the hundredfold, as by a perfection of lights. Isaac is consumed by age and dies when, after the joy of the flesh has been entirely demolished, all our hope, insofar as it concerns the world, is extinguished. He is gathered to his people, full of days, when a mind full of the lights of the virtues is conformed in a special way to the heavenly people who belong to it.

And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him—that is, the understanding and the affection, which are generated from a mind intent upon heavenly rejoicing. After they have learned to take delight in knowing nothing except God and in being moved by nothing else, they protect and conceal within themselves from the troubles of the world the very mind from which they proceed.

[Col. 0253] THE EIGHTH BOOK ENDS.

135 THE NINTH BOOK OF THE MORALS ON GENESIS BEGINS.

[Col. 0255]

[Col. 0255A] I do not profess to be an author in the investigation of the Scriptures; yet, following the rules of the saints with devout faith, if I happen to find anything useful there, I intend to discuss what follows, offering my thoughts according to God to the devout desires of the humble and of those who wish to learn. For I owe this to my neighbors. Let whoever wishes hiss at this and laugh, and insult it as though it were something novel, like Saul prophesying; provided only that we sing something that may benefit at least one person. Therefore, let us proceed.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Chapter 36 is omitted.] CHAPTER XXXVII.

VERS. 2.—When Joseph was sixteen years old, he was pasturing the flock with his brothers while still a boy, with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. Joseph, whose name is interpreted as “increasing,” signifies our spirit, which is always intent upon spiritual growth. He is sixteen years old when he subjects the outward and inward human being—for on the sixth day humanity was made into a living soul (Gen. I, 27; II, 7)—to the tenfold number of the divine law, in order to attain the fullness of mystical years.

He pastures the flock with his brothers while still a boy when, still situated among his first advances, he nourishes a thought constrained under divine fear with the pasture of heavenly aspiration and the divine word, together with the other virtues begotten from the same mind—or with his brothers, namely, the carnal movements that arise from Bilhah and Zilpah, that is, from worldly antiquity and the impulse of empty glory. We have said enough about both of these above. For worldly pleasure and vainglory are especially hostile to those who are making progress. Both have abused our father—that is, the understanding—in a legitimate marriage, though not legitimately. Hence they too are called wives, just as the Samaritan woman’s five men are called husbands.

And he accused his brothers before his father of a very serious crime. For it belongs properly to that same understanding to accuse before the intellectual faculty the carnal movements begotten from the same mind of being criminal. It brings before itself the charges of the subjected flesh. Indeed, it is the throne—that is, the judge—which presides over the throne. What is especially evil is that it knowingly opposes God.

VERS. 3.—Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he had begotten him in his old age; and he made him a many-colored tunic. Our spirit, insofar as it rules as a prince with God—for Israel is interpreted as “prince with God”—loves Joseph, that is, the desire for eternal growth, more than all its sons, namely, its works. For where there is no desire for progress, any good movements that may be present are easily stirred.

He is begotten in old age, because such eagerness is acquired when the heat of desires and the rigidity of youthful presumption have cooled. He made him a many-colored tunic because the spirit itself fashioned for itself a life established in diverse kinds of virtues. We may also understand Joseph as the religious affection that always strives toward progress.

(VERS. 4.) When his brothers saw that he was loved by his father more than all his sons, they hated him and could not speak anything peaceful to him. The more our spirit devotes itself to the desire for holiness and to worship, the more frequently the carnal elements rise up against it as though in hatred. They speak nothing peaceful because they are always driven against the tranquility of the inner person.

VERS. 5.—It also happened that he reported a dream he had seen to his brothers; and this became the cause and seed of greater hatred. He reports the dream to his brothers when he sets against the movements arising from his corruptible nature those things that he spiritually perceives concerning external matters while asleep and concerning inward things while awake. Thus he inflames them with greater fury, the more tightly he restrains them.

(VERS. 7.) “I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as though rising up, stood, while your sheaves, standing around, worshiped my sheaf.” It is as if he were saying: You unjustly claim dominion over yourselves. But I thought—and this is also true—that together we ought to restrain the fruits of our works under the discipline of the fear of God. Nevertheless, I thought that the dignity of reason should surpass the disgrace of my condition, that I should contend on behalf of you who lie everywhere amid pleasures, that I ought to rise first for the same battle, and that you ought to rise up after me and bow the necks of your stubbornness to me.

(VERS. 8.) “Will you perhaps be our king,” they said, “or shall we be subject to your authority?” That is: How can it happen that, after so many desires of bodily necessity have been extinguished, you alone will rule?

VERS. 9.—He saw another dream also, and, when he related it to his brothers, he said: “I saw in a dream, as it were, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars worshiping me.” 136 If, as we have already indicated, we understand Joseph as the desire to do good—for it is proper to him to breathe toward growth—we call the sun the understanding and the moon the will, because, just as the moon is illumined by the sun, so the will is illumined by reason.

By the eleven stars we understand the inward and outward movements. Since eleven consists of six and five, we assign six to the perfection of good will and five to the mobility of the bodily senses. For six stands solid in all its parts, while five does not. Thus, through their inequality, the two together produce eleven, which signifies transgression. “To will lies near at hand” (Rom. VII, 18), but the members of the outward person impede it.

All these things worship the affection of holiness, because reason, will, the inner person, and even the outward person—whether he wishes it or not—specifically desires its growth and awaits the increase of holy desire through prayers offered to God. Or, because “to worship” is said in relation to “to pray,” the person who prays according to Joseph—that is, according to growth—asks for nothing from God except an increase in holiness.

Will and affection, when they are holy, although they may appear to be one, are not one. We are well-disposed toward many things, but we withdraw from them by the will that is more closely joined to reason. For we examine the place and the time and attend to all the other circumstances.

(VERS. 10.) When he had related this to his father and brothers, his father rebuked him, and so forth. His father rebukes him because the agility of holy affection is held back by the timid gravity of an understanding fearful of frailty, lest it undertake something too hastily.

“Shall I and your mother and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” He says, as it were: Shall I, from whom the divine seed is introduced into your mother—that is, into the good will, without which what is begotten is rejected—and your mother herself, who gives birth to you insofar as you truly are, be subjected to you, together with the inward and outward movements, to such an extent that you are upon the earth, seeking no eminence except that of the heavenly life?

(VERS. 11.) Therefore his brothers—that is, the thorns and thistles that arise from the soil of the heart together with the good grain—were envious; but his father, the understanding, inwardly and outwardly considered the matter in silence amid his activities, while remaining intent upon the purpose.

VERS. 12.—When his brothers were staying in Shechem to pasture their father’s flocks, and so forth. These brothers do not pasture one flock but flocks of discord and division—that is, they nourish thoughts by repeatedly discovering occasions for avarice, pride, and envy. [Col. 0257C] They are also called their father’s flocks because the dispersions of thoughts are known to reach even to the vexation of the understanding.

Shechem is said to mean “shoulder” or “labor.” They therefore dwell in Shechem when, placing the shoulders, so to speak, beneath the burdens of cares and unjust endurance, they rest under deadly labor.

(VERS. 13.) His father therefore said: “Come, I shall send you to them.” Return, he says, from your dispersion, so that you may be directed against the vices of your thoughts, and let the desire for holiness not delay its own presence.

(VERS. 14.) “Go,” he said, “and see whether all is well with your brothers and the flocks, and report to me what is happening.” Go through the direction of intention, and afterward you will see, through the gaze of discernment, whether your animal impulses, while they grasp the goods of the world, can enjoy any inward prosperity.

There is this difference between brothers and flocks: some vices defend themselves as though by reason, while others are altogether bestial. He reports what the brothers are doing when the heat of holy desire brings its gains or losses to the examination of the understanding.

Sent from the valley of Hebron, he came to Shechem. Hebron is said to mean “eternal growth” or “eternal vision.” Joseph, therefore—that is, the desire for growth—is sent from the humility of the mind, through which he hopes for perpetual growth, and from the vision of God, which through faith and love he already enjoys here under the hope of eternity, to examine those activities in which the flesh willingly engages.

But he comes to Shechem because, by lingering among the things he ought merely to discern and reject once discerned, he is sometimes detained in them by a certain sluggishness; and, placing his shoulder beneath them, he suffers the same misery of labor.

[Col. 0258A] VERS. 15.—He found him wandering in the field and asked what he was seeking. The man is the understanding itself, which questions the affection about its wandering through the field—that is, through worldly things.

(VERS. 16.) “I am seeking my brothers,” he said; “tell me where they are pasturing their flocks.” It is as if he were saying: While I examine the excesses of my carnality, I see that I myself have also gone beyond proper bounds. Therefore, if you possess the wisdom of a man, show me the foulness of this senseless and disordered pasturing.

(VERS. 17.) “They have departed from this place,” he said. “But I heard them saying: ‘Let us go to Dothaim.’” Dothaim is said to mean “their green place,” “their pasture,” or “sufficient failure.” After we have devoted ourselves to spiritual vices, we prefer, withdrawing from their labor, to descend into the more agreeable pleasure of the flesh. This is signified by the pleasantness of greenness, which is their pasture, though not refreshment, but the sufficiency of complete inward failure.

VERS. 18.—He went after his brothers and found them in Dothaim when, pursuing them solely through consideration, he discovered them failing amid earthly desires.

(VERS. 18, 19, 20.) When they had seen him, before he approached them, they planned to kill him. They spoke to one another: “Behold, the dreamer is coming. Come, let us kill him and throw him into this old cistern, and we shall say: ‘An evil beast has devoured him.’”

Joseph’s brothers see him when the animal movements plainly envy the holy affection. Before he approaches, they plan to kill him because, before he consents to error through an actual deed, they arrange through an evil affection to overthrow him. 137 “Behold,” they say, “the one who rejects visible things and extends the gaze of his mind toward invisible things, and who lives, as it were, in a dream. O mass of carnal pleasures, come, claim him for yourselves, throw him into the ancient chaos—that is, the reprobate sense, the old cistern lacking the waters of divine understanding—in which he once behaved shamefully before his conversion; and say that he has been consumed and overcome by some evil beast, that is, by a sudden and unforeseen temptation. Or declare that he has been overcome by the devil’s violence.”

For sinners themselves are accustomed to put forward such excuses “to excuse their excuses in sins” (Ps. CXL, 4). Then it will become clear what their dreams accomplish for them—that is, what folly it is to abandon visible things for invisible things and certainties for uncertainties. For a dream is to attend, while sleeping, to things that are not seen by the eyes. “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V, 2).

VERS. 21, 22.—When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue him from their hands. “Let us not kill his soul,” he said, “nor shed blood; but throw him into this cistern, which is in the wilderness, and keep your hands innocent.” He said this because he wished to rescue him from their hands and restore him to his father.

Reuben, whose name is said to mean “seeing in the midst,” is the power of discernment, intent upon the midpoint of an unbending direction. When it perceives the danger to holy affection, it strives to rescue it from the power of carnal desires.

“Let not the soul,” he says, “be destroyed by some capital crime”—which is to shed blood, that is, to release the flow of carnality. Instead, lead it only to the cistern, namely, the pit of its former worldly life, which suffers solitude because God, its inhabitant, is absent. Follow the soul’s sluggishness, but do not let it fall into the actual guilt of some shameful crime. It is certainly easier to rise from sluggishness of mind than to emerge from the ruin of an accomplished fault. Thus crafty discernment seeks to avoid a greater destruction through a lesser one, until he is restored to his father, that is, to his own understanding in its fullness.

VERS. 23, 24.—Therefore, as soon as he came to his brothers, they stripped him of his long and many-colored tunic and threw him into the cistern, which had no water. He comes to his brothers when he inserts himself into the effect of carnal stimulation. They strip him of his long and many-colored tunic when they deprive him of the variety of virtues in which he had resolved to persevere—for the long tunic signifies this. They throw him into a waterless cistern when they confine him in his former life, in which there is no knowledge of spirituality.

(VERS. 25.) And sitting down to eat bread, they saw Ishmaelite travelers coming from Gilead, with their camels carrying spices, resin, and stacte to Egypt. They sit to eat bread because, having lost their upright position, they act carelessly in order to refresh themselves with temporal pleasure. For bread signifies this, as it is written: “His soul makes bread abominable to him in his life” (Job XXXIII, 20).

We interpret Ishmaelites as those who obey themselves. They are called travelers because they appear to walk along the way, which is Christ, yet they obey themselves, since in these acts they seek not the praise of God but their own.

They see them coming from Gilead because they judge them, in appearance at least, to descend through the imitation of examples from the heap of testimony—that is, from the multitude of saints who testify by their works that they belong to the elect. Their camels carry these things into Egypt when bodies—which are called camels because of their weight, since they “weigh down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15)—outwardly display various goods that do not give off their fragrance for the honor of God but merely for worldly ostentation. Egypt signifies the world, as it is written: “You shall not abhor the Egyptian” (Deut. XXIII, 7); the spices signify outward virtues.

VERS. 26, 27.—Then Judah said to his brothers: “What profit is there for us if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites and that our hands not be defiled; for he is our brother and our flesh.” Judah is interpreted as “confession.”

The necessity of confession after sin itself is often a great obstacle to those who wish to sin. For one is ashamed to commit what it is even more shameful to confess. “What fruit,” he says, “did you have then from the things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI, 21.) Reverence for confession therefore restrains perverse movements.

“What benefit,” he says, “will there be in falling away from the good will and bringing a deadly crime upon the mind, which, once committed, the mind itself will not be able to conceal if it wishes to care for its own salvation? Let him be sold to the Ishmaelites—that is, handed over to the examples of hypocrites—and let our outward action not be defiled by the stain of a conspicuous fault. For the affection itself, if it is disgraced by shameful works, is joined to us with such intimacy that through it our flesh, that is, our entire outward nature, is corrupted.”

VERS. 28.—His brothers agreed to his words. [Col. 0260A] And when the Midianite merchants passed by, they drew him out of the cistern and sold him for twenty pieces of silver. The brothers agree when the carnal movements yield to shame, though it is human and nevertheless useful. For they choose rather to be subjected to spiritual things, which are less apparent, than to bodily things.

They draw him out of the cistern when they remove their ways from worldly life and turn to those who appear, for the sake of business, to live well. Yet these men, who are Midianites—that is, who are to be judged justly—draw them away when they turn to their examples. For Midian is said to derive its name from judgment.

They sell him for twenty pieces of silver when, by imitating them, they subject themselves to them, distributing themselves according to the number of duplicity. For the number twenty signifies duplicity, according to the saying: “Whether he can meet the one who comes against him with twenty thousand, while he himself has ten thousand” (Luke XIV, 31). Silver, because it is a resonant metal, signifies the tinkling of such a small reputation; and the words of those who praise are like certain fragments of coins.

They brought him into Egypt because, moved by the allurements of their imitation, they drag the desire for progress into the sphere of mere worldliness.

VERS. 29, 30.—Reuben returned to the cistern and did not find the boy. Tearing his garments, he went to his brothers and said: “The boy is not here; and I, where shall I go?” Reuben returns to the cistern and does not find the boy when our discernment is led by reflection to the condition of the former life, but the affection—once it has relapsed into carnal things, as commonly happens—is not found there, because it has become entangled in the snares of vainglory, from which it is scarcely recalled to simplicity, and in a much worse condition.

He tears his garments and goes to his brothers when he disperses through the mouths and eyes of human beings, in a spirit of seeking favor, the holy works that ought to be joined to God. As he laments, he is driven to correct the perverse movements of the inner person: “Woe to him who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclus. II, 14). “The affection,” he says, “has slipped away irrecoverably through empty glories. What will my discernment now accomplish in it, where there is no sense of holiness?”

VERS. 31, 32.—They took his tunic, dipped it in the blood of a kid whom they had killed, and sent someone to carry it to their father and say: “We found this; see whether it is your son’s tunic or not.” His tunic is the habit of his inward affection. They dip it in the blood of the kid whom they had killed when they pollute the condition of the conscience with the desire for carnal sin, which flows like blood.

The kid whom they had killed is the outrage they had committed. For the type of empty glory is accustomed to be inflated through the effect of carnal guilt. They send someone to carry it to the father when, through the cunning of their thoughts, they attack reason.

“Consider,” they say, “into what condition the affection that you seemed to have brought forth well for God has fallen. Or, if you do not acknowledge such an affection as yours, see from what source you have emerged in such a condition of conscience. Certainly, if you could not persevere in this condition, you ought never to have desired the pursuit of virtue.”

VERS. 33.—“It is my son’s tunic. An evil beast has eaten him; a beast has devoured Joseph.” “This,” he says, “is truly the habit of my affection, but it has been corrupted by the cruelty of the devil and the savage violence of carnal pleasures.” Human reason is accustomed to excuse willingly committed wickedness as though it had been done through the violence of demons and of the flesh.

Joseph has been devoured by these things because the entire desire for holiness and progress is believed to have been consumed by them.

(VERS. 34.) Tearing his garments, he put on sackcloth and mourned for his son for a long time. He tears his garments when, having lost the unity of his intention, he scatters through empty things his proper work, by which he ought to cover his members upon the earth. He puts on sackcloth when he is surrounded by the goads of pleasures. He mourns his son for a long time when he continually displays his affection as worthy of mourning.

(VERS. 35.) When all his children had gathered together to soothe their father’s grief, he refused to accept consolation and said: “I shall go down to my son mourning into the underworld.” The children gather together when the powers of reason, which recall us from the service of sin to the freedom of life, are temporarily assembled under the fear of God.

They soothe and wish to console the father’s grief when they strive to temper the misery of sin through the remedy of conversion and repentance. But, refusing this through his conduct and not believing the spirit that feels with God, he permits himself, after the affection of wicked pleasure—that is, after his son—to descend through grief into the abyss of despair.

VERS. 36.—While he persisted in weeping, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and captain of the army. While our spirit persistently performs works worthy of weeping, Joseph—that is, our good desire—is handed over to Egyptian blindness through the example of those who belong to judgment and to punishment.

Potiphar is interpreted as “a mouth inclined to cutting apart.” The mouth signifies an evil desire, which is always inclined to destroy. He is a eunuch and captain of the army because he is sterile of every good and leader of the entire army of vices. At the price of temporal pleasures, he draws away from himself the affection for progress.

CHAPTER XXXVIII.

VERS. 1.—At that time Judah, departing from his brothers, turned aside to a man of Odollam, whose name was Hiram. Judah means “confession”; Hiram is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” When the mind is thus divided from itself, the memory of holy confession—which above warned the tender boy, that is, the purpose, to spare him—descends from the pride of the brothers, namely, bodily desires, and turns away from worldly commotion toward the vision of him who is truly the one brother, Jesus Christ.

He is called a man because in him nothing but the height of virtue is seen. Odollamite means “testimony in water.” In the water of baptism we put on Christ himself (Gal. III, 27). When by our conduct we contradict him, we find in this water a testimony against us; yet when we give attention to him as to a brother, we discover him by seeing him.

VERS. 2.—He saw there the daughter of a Canaanite man, whose name was Shua, and, taking her as his wife, he went in to her. If Christ is a man, he is surely called a Canaanite, just as he is called a Samaritan, because he himself is the true transformation of his own people. For Canaanite, as has often been said, means “changed.”

He has a daughter, namely reason itself, which is called Shua—that is, “speaking” or “song”—because, while others bark at us, she alone speaks intelligibly to us. Through the gentleness or harmony of the spirit, she produces in us not the goads of stimulation but complete serenity. She is a daughter because she resembles him who is supreme reason.

Judah sees her as belonging to himself because the humility of true confession judges her alone useful for him to follow. He joins her to himself as wife because, through contempt for the world, he makes her fruitful in the knowledge of sin for the performance of good works.

(VERS. 3.) She conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er, which is interpreted as “resurrection,” “vigils,” or “leathern.” When we approach rational living, it is first necessary that we rise again and then keep watch over ourselves, because after conversion we often labor under the memory of dead works, which the skin signifies.

VERS. 4.—Again conceiving and bearing a son, she called his name Onan, which is said to mean “their sorrow,” referring to weariness. From the difficulty of overcoming the passions that arises from remembering the pleasures of the world, great weariness is often generated in the purpose once begun. Hence the Psalm says: “Their soul abhorred every kind of food” (Ps. CVI, 18), and so forth. For the saints are tortured by the heats of thought up to the gates of death—that is, up to the abandonment of religion.

(VERS. 5.) She bore a third son also, whom she called Shelah, which is interpreted as “his shadow,” referring to the protection of the Holy Spirit. For he himself brings about progress, so that when we are tested we can endure.

In the first two we cry out as women in labor; in the third a male is born, who is brought to the throne of God to rule with an iron rod (Ps. II, 9), with a kind of victory belonging to long-established impassibility. After he was born, she ceased to give birth, because once the mind has reached perfect charity, it no longer bears children in pain; whatever it does now rises as though by natural ease.

VERS. 6.—Judah gave his firstborn son Er a wife named Tamar, which is interpreted as “bitterness.” This means discipline. For we ought to set the bitterness of discipline against the allurements of temptations: it is indeed bitterness in the present, but it will produce a most peaceful fruit in those who are exercised by it (Heb. XII, 11).

VERS. 7.—Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and he was killed by him. God kills Er, who is wicked in his sight, when he destroys in the soul—which alone is visible to him—the incitements of lust, both spiritual and bodily, which God especially condemns, through the strength of established reason.

(VERS. 8.) Judah said to his son Onan: “Go in to your brother’s wife and join yourself to her, so that you may raise up offspring for your brother.” Judah speaks to Onan when the humility of confession and repentance shapes the sadness of spiritual sloth. He is called a son because that failure itself was born from the occasion of his action.

“Join yourself,” he says, “to holy bitterness; enter it intelligently, as though penetrating within, and unite yourself to the tribulation of the present world, as to a wife destined to bear eternal fruits for you, so that you may raise up offspring for your brother—that is, for the bodily movement—namely, a posterity of heavenly reward. For the body is dead because of sin (Rom. VIII, 10); therefore, raise it up through an act of righteousness.”

[Col. 0263A] **VERSE 9.**—But he, knowing that children would not be born for him, went in to his brother’s wife and spilled his seed upon the ground, lest children should be born in his brother’s name. He goes in to his brother’s wife when, by reflection, he perceives the gravity of discipline. He knows that children are not born for him because he recognizes the soul’s sluggishness in producing worthy fruits of repentance. He spills his seed upon the ground when he turns the good that he does toward earthly glory.

**VERSE 10.**—God strikes him because he acts detestably: either He judicially punishes him, or corrects him by reproving him in some manner, when He shows him the horror of his own wickedness.

**VERSE 11.**—For this reason Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar: “Remain a widow in your father’s house until Shelah, my son, grows up”; for he was afraid that he too might die, like his brothers. And she went away and lived in her father’s house. The humility of confession, turning toward Tamar—that is, toward the keeping of discipline—says: “Recognize your bridegroom, Christ, who died for you; therefore await, within your conscience, which is the house of your heavenly Father, the increase of grace that may overshadow you. May you have the Holy Spirit as your Paraclete in place of your bridegroom; cling to Him as to a son to be nourished by the sustenance of the divine Word, whom nevertheless you have conceived through the freedom of the will.” For it fears, while the mind thus renews itself through memorials, lest it again be endangered by temptation as before and fall. Thus she acts.

**VERSE 12.**—When many days had passed, Shuah, Judah’s wife, died. After he had received consolation following the mourning, he went up to the shearers of his sheep, he and Hira the Odollamite shepherd of the flock, to Timnah. The days pass when, through the soul’s gradual tepidity, the virtues decline. Shuah, Judah’s wife, dies when reason—which kindles in us the spirit of gentleness and which the piety of confession makes fruitful—is abandoned. After this reason had received the consolation of pardon following the mourning for sin, it ascends by the progress of the mind to the examples of the saints, through whom the superfluous cares of the world are cut away from its simple thoughts. “It ascends,” I say, “to Timnah.” *Timnah* is interpreted as “those who fail,” or “numbers,” or “the faithful.” It is therefore advanced to this end: first, that it may fail in itself and advance in God, and thus reach the number of the faithful. Accordingly, he and Hira—whom we have said signifies Christ—go together, because his own conduct does not divide him from Him. [Col. 0263C–D]

A shepherd is called a hired man. I would call Christ a hired man in the sense in which He testifies that we are His sheep (John X, 15), given to Him by the Father, and that, in return for the suffering He endured, He received them as wages. “When He gives sleep to His beloved, behold, the Lord’s inheritance: children, the reward, the fruit of the womb” (Psalm CXXVI, 2). And: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” etc. (Psalm II, 8).

**VERSES 13, 14.**—And Tamar was told that her father-in-law was going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. She removed the garments of her widowhood, took a *teristrum*, changed her clothing, and sat at the fork in the road that leads to Timnah, because Shelah had grown up and she had not received him as her husband. Tamar is told that her father-in-law has gone up to shear the sheep when the fervor and zeal of holy conduct—which at first is bitter and narrow, but afterward is pursued with a joyful and expansive heart—is touched by the message of the divine Word or of the Holy Spirit and is kindled to follow the true confessor, who directs his mind toward cutting away the superfluities of his thoughts (St. Benedict, *Prologue to the Rule*, near the end). [Col. 0264A]

She removes the garments of widowhood when she humbles the virtues through love of the bridegroom who died for her. She takes the *teristrum*, which according to some is either a kind of summer covering or a type of veil, when she receives purity or simplicity of soul—which is called the head—or the brightness of works. She changes her clothing when she renews the state of her mind. She sits at the fork of the road that leads to Timnah—not at the fork of which it is said, “Woe to him who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclesiasticus II, 14), but at that by which one advances toward God through love and turns toward love of one’s neighbor; by this road one truly travels toward fellowship with the faithful. To sit means to persevere. She does this because Shelah—that is, the spiritual love that overshadows us—does indeed grow inwardly, but not so continuously and indivisibly that it always clings like a husband. [Col. 0264B]

**VERSE 15.**—When Judah saw her, he thought that she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face so that she would not be recognized. Judah suspects that she is a prostitute when he looks upon her because, after more frequently considering the beginning of his action, he fears that penitential humility is being urged to act well not for the sake of the eternal reward, which is God, but for some empty advantage. Thus the will of intention—which is the face—is covered by clouds of thoughts, so that it can scarcely be discerned what is being done and with what state of mind. [Col. 0264C]

**VERSE 16.**—Going in to her, he said: “Allow me to have intercourse with you.” For he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. He goes in to her when, by reasoning, he examines the inner aspects of his purpose. “Permit,” he says, “the love of holy confession to mingle with you and rest continually upon you.” For he does not know—that is, he has not yet experienced—that Shelah, the shadow of spiritual love, is protected as though by the authority of a husband. It is as though he said: “Since I do not yet feel the fervor of the spirit, at least let me enjoy the lament of repentance.”

“What will you give me,” she says, “so that you may enjoy intercourse with me?”

**VERSE 17.**—He said: “I will send you a kid from the flock.” If you desire to join yourself to me in the manner of one who repents and fears, since you do not yet love fervently, tell me what you will contribute. “I will send you,” he says, “a kid from the flock”—that is, from your sin, by which you stink before God—“removed from the throngs and divisions of thoughts,” or “snatched from the flocks,” that is, from the assaults of demons, who are called flocks because of the diversity of their pursuits and because they are strangers to unity. [Col. 0264D]

**VERSE 18.**—She said: “I will accept what you wish, if you give me a pledge until you send what you promise.” Judah said: “What pledge shall I give you?” She answered: “Your ring, your bracelet, and the staff that you hold in your hand.”

If the finger in Scripture sometimes signifies intention, according to the passage in which God teaches our fingers for war (Psalm CXLIII, 1), then a ring on the finger is the brightness of holiness in the resolve of one’s intention. A bracelet on the arm is the virtue of continence from attractions, displayed in the practice of good works. The spiritual staff by which we are supported is the consolation of grace amid these things. [Col. 0265A]

These are given to us as a pledge until Judah sends the kid he promises, because, before the persistence of repentance and confession fully discloses the stench of our original and actual misery, it is first necessary that his labor attribute these three things to our discipline. Without their light, no one can know himself perfectly.

Thus the woman conceived from the single intercourse.

**VERSE 19.**—Then she arose and went away; and, removing the clothing she had taken, she put on the garments of her widowhood. At the simple entry of the divine infusion, her softened and fruitful soul proposes to do good; rising in the hope of pardon, it eagerly presses toward the inner things, that is, the heavenly things. By the grace of humility she lays aside the glory of her inward clothing; she remembers the mercy of her husband Jesus, who died for her, and thus, in her own presence, lowers herself as a widow because of so great a debt. [Col. 0265B]

**VERSES 20, 21.**—Judah sent the kid by his Odollamite shepherd in order to recover the pledge he had given the woman. When he did not find her, he asked the men of that place: “Where is the woman who was sitting at the fork in the road?”

Through Christ, who is our special shepherd and daily exhorts us to do good, the humility of confession sends us knowledge of ourselves. For the more we follow the fragrance of Christ’s ointments (Song of Songs I, 3), the more we understand the stench of our fragile condition.

Judah therefore recovers the pledge he had given the woman because, the more clearly we discern ourselves, the more we attribute to Him rather than to our own powers whatever virtue has been implanted in us through the practice of repentance, according to the Lord’s command of humility. [Col. 0265C]

We call the woman the purpose of the discipline that has been begun, because of the affection and fruitfulness of pious works. But the true shepherd does not find her in the clothing of a prostitute, since her intention is directed solely toward pleasing God. The woman may also be said to sit at the fork in the road when she is thought to be doing something good for God while actually doing it for the world.

**VERSE 22.**—The men of that place signify rational movements, which the Odollamite shepherd honored by granting them a settled status. They deny that the prostitute sat there—that is, that the evil of some spiritual adultery persevered. Sitting pertains to the practice of sin, as in: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Psalm I, 1). Their denial consists in showing clearly by its effect that this is not what occurs among them. [Col. 0265D]

**VERSE 23.**—Judah said: “Let her keep it for herself; surely she cannot accuse us of falsehood. I sent the kid that I had promised, and you did not find her.”

“I,” he says, “had promised that, from the pledge of holy intention, careful action, and divine consolation amid adversity, the kid of self-knowledge would come. I say that the usefulness of pious confession brought about what I promised, but you, eternal shepherd, did not allow her to be found sitting at the fork of the road of good conduct and empty glory—that is, acquiescing in herself. Therefore let the discipline of our life possess, as the pledge of eternal reward, your gifts, since your truth—which promised progress to those who repent in righteousness—cannot be accused of falsehood.” [Col. 0266A]

**VERSE 24.**—But after three months they told Judah: “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has committed fornication, and it appears that her womb is swelling.”

The three months seem to me to signify the three plenitudes of actions: namely, conversion, progress, and perfection—which is the integrity of charity. After these three, complaints arise against our humble confession, from which no summit of virtues should be separated, because of the tickling of the spirit of pride; they accuse us of swelling in the womb, that is, in the conscience, and proclaim that we have fallen away from the marriage of Shelah—that is, of the Holy Spirit—through the fornication of arrogance.

But true confession, which always comes into the light, commands that she be brought out. “Whatever is reproved,” according to the Apostle, “is manifested by the light” (Ephesians V, 13). This is also done so that she may be burned and purified by the conflagration of the divine fire. [Col. 0266B]

**VERSE 25.**—When she was being led out through confession to the punishment of repentance, she sent to her father-in-law.
