That is, she returned to the beginnings of her former confession and repentance, which, through humility, had generated for her a husband of the spirit, as it were Shelah, whose name is interpreted “shadow.” She declared that she had not conceived hypocrisy from worldly desire, but from the impulse of humble confession, which had bestowed upon her the mystical ring, bracelet, and staff—the affection of persevering devotion.

**VERSE 26.**—When he recognized the gifts, he said: “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.”

He recognizes the gifts because he knows that both the beginnings of his conversion and the growth of his advancement are present in him through God. “She is more righteous than I,” he says, as though saying: “By her perseverance she has led me to a more righteous state; in a certain way she herself has made me more righteous. And because I could not soon overshadow the beginnings of her love with the charity of the Holy Spirit, she preferred to be made fruitful under the fear of repentance—by me, that is, by the grace of confession—for the production of good fruits.” [Col. 0266C]

Nevertheless, he did not know her again; that is, he who previously seemed to have grown swollen by excessive attention to his own good deeds, having forgotten his former humble confession, now refrains from examining the urgency of his purpose, lest he be vainly exalted.

**VERSE 27.**—When the time of birth arrived, twins appeared in the womb; and, during the very delivery of the infants, one put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it. Labor is at hand when the fulfillment of the purpose approaches the pious affection. Twins appear in the womb when two affections are understood to flow from the conscience as streams from a single source. During the delivery of the infants, one puts out his hand when the first effect of the love of God emerges through compunction of the inner person, as the breadth of the soul approaches the manifestation of the work.

The midwife ties scarlet around that hand when reason—which withstands every mishap of the soul—conspicuously preserves in its work the mortification of carnal desires. [Col. 0266D]

**VERSE 28.**—“This one,” he said, “will come out first”—that is, the love of God that has been conceived will leap forward even to the effectiveness of divine contemplation. For such is often the fervor of beginners: while they do not know themselves, they claim for themselves the height of virtue. But when, by God’s dispensation, the inward strength of love is diminished somewhat through a defect in action, the other comes forth—namely, the service of fraternal love. Although this is inferior in dignity, it nevertheless comes first by the necessity of duty. For the visible neighbor must first be loved, so that through this the invisibility of the deity may be reached. This is signified by the two gifts of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0267A]

**VERSE 29.**—The woman said: “Why has the wall been divided because of you?” Therefore she called his name Perez.

The woman is so called from the softness of the soul and signifies reason that is still wise in part according to human judgment. Hence her very words seem to sound in a human manner. “Why,” she says, “has the union of thoughts, like stones, been divided into many changes of care?” For our mind is held together as one by the cement of divine love; it is divided when, in doing good to our neighbors, it is troubled by concern for many things, according to the Gospel (Luke X, 41). Thus Perez is called “division,” because, through fraternal care, divine contemplation is inwardly dispersed for a time. [Col. 0267B]

**VERSE 30.**—Afterward his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread; and she called his name Zerah. *Coccus*, from which *coccinum* (“scarlet”) derives, is said according to its Greek etymology to come from fire, and it also displays the redness of blood. God, however, who is called “a consuming fire” (Hebrews XII, 29), must first boil away by His own fervor the passions of sins that arise from flesh and blood, so that, once the inward and outward work has been purified, the face may be made pleasing through the antimony of charity, for beholding the East of eternal light. Zerah is interpreted as “east”—namely, the very love of God, which is the fullness of the whole law, like a universal light (Romans XIII, 10), and the place and origin in which the vision of God is said chiefly to exist. [Col. 0267C]

# CHAPTER XXXIX

**VERSE 1.**—Therefore Joseph was taken down to Egypt, and Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh, commander of the army, an Egyptian man, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites, by whom he had been brought there. This has been explained above, and it is tedious to repeat it. But we must note how God was with him while he was placed amid so many evils and prospered all that he did.

It is certain that God allows many to fall, not in order finally to abandon them, but in order to correct them through their fall. He seems not to be with them while they sin; yet He is with them so that they may progress from sin. This is sufficiently demonstrated both in the children of Israel and in the Apostle Peter, who in their very falls are visited by God rather than rejected. Since, therefore, they are not abandoned by Him even amid their crimes, every adversity of sin is turned for them toward prosperity.

**VERSE 2.**—Because the Lord was with him, he was now marked by the name of “man”—that is, one who acts manfully against vices. And he lived in the house of his master.

**VERSE 3.**—His master knew very well that the Lord was with him and that everything he did was directed by Him. “To live” is used here as a frequentative form derived from *to have*, in place of *to rule*. Thus, in the house—that is, in the conscience—in which wicked desire had formerly ruled, the affection for progressing toward God now rules; and desire learns by experience that God accompanies its pious progress, since He directs all its power in the execution of its works. [Col. 0267D–0268A]

**VERSE 4.**—Joseph found favor in the sight of his master and ministered to him. He appointed him over everything, and Joseph governed the house entrusted to him and all that had been committed to him. Joseph finds favor before his master when the desire for sacred growth, over which wicked affection had previously ruled, finds, at the arrival of carnal temptation, as it were before the very assault, the protection of divine grace.

He ministers to him when, turning away from his foulness and suggestions, he applies and supplies to him every duty of uprightness. He is appointed over everything by him because, providing from the material of inward struggle an opportunity for overcoming, he—that is, affection—sets us above our impulses while he strives to subdue them. We govern the entrusted house and all that has been handed over to us when we wisely rule the conscience committed to us by God and the other goods of the soul. [Col. 0268B]

**VERSES 5, 6.**—The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph and multiplied all his substance, both in the houses and in the fields; and he knew nothing else except the bread that he ate. The Egyptian’s house is blessed because of Joseph when a conscience formerly oppressed by the darkness of blindness and ignorance is raised through the desire to progress well by divine gifts. Both in the houses of inward virtues and in the fields—that is, in bodily exercises—all the substance of his rationality, which underlies the structures of works like a strong foundation, is increased. Once the practice of former disgraces has been removed, the bread of eternal life alone is recognized.

Now Joseph was beautiful in face and handsome in appearance—that is, with the face which the Lord commands to be washed, by whose singular beauty God is then seen. [Col. 0268C]

**VERSE 7.**—After many days, his mistress cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: “Sleep with me.” After many illuminations of the virtues, concupiscence, having been silent for a time, rises again, remembering its former dominion; and what had seemed to have turned away gathers its eyes—that is, its intentions for testing—upon the good will.

“Sleep,” she says, “with me”—that is, consent to receive the sleep of the offered pleasure.

**VERSES 8, 9.**—But refusing to consent to the wicked deed, he said to her: “Behold, with everything entrusted to me, my master does not know what he has in his house; nor is there anything that is not in my power or that he has not entrusted to me, except you, who are his wife. How then can I do this great evil and sin against my God?” [Col. 0268D]

He says: “He who ruled me has subjected all his follies to my authority, and in his former house—that is, in the conscience—he does not know what can be marked as his own; everything obeys the judgment of reason except you, concupiscence, who are the ill-begotten wife of a perverse affection. Since you do not cease suggesting evil, you cannot be completely subdued. How, then, can I do this evil and sin against my God?”

This means: “Since my desire, which once ruled me, has at some time surrendered itself to me—that is, has allowed itself to be handed over irrevocably to my authority—how can my continence conform to the fulfillment of your desires?”

[Col. 0269A] **VERSE 10.**—With words of this kind the woman harassed the young man day after day, but he refused the outrage. Through each illumination of the virtues, the mind, continually reaching the manly strength of youth, is opposed to the softness of affectivity, as though feminine; but it refuses the lusts imposed upon it.

**VERSES 11, 12.**—It happened one day that Joseph entered the house to do some work without witnesses. She seized the hem of his garment and said: “Sleep with me.” Joseph enters the house on a certain day when, with the uncertain understanding of rationality—that is, with the will, which is light—our pious affection examines every recess of the conscience, as though the light available for doing good were less than full, like a doubtful light.

For the word “a certain” is used in the sense of something uncertain. Hence he is said to have done something without witnesses, because, placed in a tepid state, he does not possess the full power of discernment. The inward witnesses are, in fact, examining movements.

When the conscience is less fervent, concupiscence easily tends to steal in. During the examination itself, a certain torpor creeps in because of the difficulty of weariness. Hence she seizes the hem—that is, the intention which, through perseverance, is directed toward God and gathers the cloak of our inward disposition into the unity of a good will—and draws it toward herself. For from a hem (*lacinia*) all things made of strips are called *laciniosa*, that is, long; and nothing is more extended than what stretches all the way to God.

She asks him to sleep with her when she invites him to fall together into the labyrinth of forgetfulness and negligence. He leaves the cloak in her hand and flees outside. We leave the cloak in the woman’s hand when we choose to expose our inner person more to the strength of temptation than to yield pleasantly to its lust. Job was handed over into this hand, yet his soul was preserved (Job II, 6). We flee and go outside when we are seized by fear—which is the flight of the soul—and go outside ourselves through the confession of our thoughts. [Col. 0269B–C]

**VERSES 13, 14, 15.**—When the woman saw that the garment was in her hands and that she had been despised, she called the men of her household and said to them: “Look, he has brought us a Hebrew man to mock us. He entered to me in order to have intercourse with me. When I cried out and he heard my voice, he left the cloak that I was holding and fled outside.”

The woman sees the garment in her hands and sees herself despised when concupiscence observes that power and opportunity have been granted to it for attacking, but laments that it has no ability to overcome. The garment in her hands is the inward condition of one under the weight of temptation.

She calls the men of her household when she arouses the carnal movements of the conscience. “Look,” she says, “he has brought in”—there is no doubt that this means the weakness of carnal affection, a temporary and momentary religion, a transitory manliness, which is signified by the name “Hebrew.” For a Hebrew is called one who passes over: he strives to undertake the path of holiness, but does not persevere in advancing toward any growth.

“He entered to me”: the desire for holiness entered under the appearance of piety, not to amend but to defile, so that it might be said: “This man began to build, and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV, 30). When I had cried out rationally that it is better not to vow than not to fulfill one’s vows (Ecclesiastes V, 4), and he had understood the force of the voice, he left the cloak—the covering of inward reverence—for me to abuse at will, and now began to go outside into a shameful effect.

A sluggish mind often claims such things for itself when it is so disturbed that it cannot discern whether it has conquered or been conquered. [Col. 0269D–0270A]

**VERSES 16, 17, 18.**—Therefore, as evidence of her accusation, she displayed the cloak she had retained to her husband when he returned home, and said: “The Hebrew servant whom you brought to us entered to me to mock me. When he saw me cry out, he left his cloak and fled outside.”

The husband of the soul is the intellect. He returns to the house when he returns from dispersion to the heart. The cloak is displayed to him as evidence when a mental disposition infected with wickedness is brought forward as proof of transgression.

“He entered to me,” she says: “a certain servile movement, not of love but of fear—not one that would remain forever in the house, but Hebrew, that is, transitory. Your husband, the intellect, brought him in only at the beginning of affection, with no progress toward advancement, as a kind of prelude. When he perceived me crying out—for whoever answers before hearing demonstrates that he is foolish—he fled, because I did not know that I was being called inwardly and, impatient under the inward impulse, refused to rise to things too arduous; that is, he fled by returning to the remedy of a pleasurable act.” [Col. 0270B]

**VERSES 19, 20.**—When his master heard these words and, excessively credulous toward his wife’s statements, became very angry, he handed Joseph over to the prison where the king’s prisoners were kept, and he was confined there.

The master hears—that is, understands—the wicked desire that had formerly ruled, after being admonished by its concupiscence and inflamed by its incentives. Having turned with complete delight toward what it desired as toward a wife, it rages against the desire for intellectual progress and hands Joseph over to prison. This happens when it thrusts the heart that longs for pious growth into temptation that constricts it on every side.

There the king’s prisoners were kept because those who, pressed by the bonds of the body, desire to be released and to be with Christ (Philippians I, 23), when they are attacked by diverse assaults, are guarded from the vanity of exaltation. He is also confined there because the mind is so often fenced in by its own revolt that no avenue appears by which the present misery might be escaped. [Col. 0270C–D]

**VERSES 21, 22, 23.**—But the Lord was with Joseph and, having mercy on him, gave him favor in the sight of the prison governor. He placed in his hand all the prisoners who were held in custody, and everything that was done was under his authority. He knew nothing of all that had been entrusted to him, for the Lord was with him and directed all his works.

The prison governor signifies the intellect, which presides over the narrowness of temptation. He places in Joseph’s hand those prisoners who are held in custody when he brings under the power of the good desire all the enticements of thoughts by which the soul’s strength is hindered.

Everything that is done is under him because whatever is administered outwardly is under the providence of reason. And when he entrusts all his innermost things to the pursuit of progress, he knows nothing, certainly, except the increase of virtue. For the Lord is with him, creating strength in weakness and directing works through temptations, as though sowing seeds amid the torpor of winter. [Col. 0271A]

# CHAPTER XL

**VERSES 1, 2.**—After these things had happened, it came to pass that two eunuchs, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the baker, sinned against their master. Pharaoh, angry with them—for one was over the cupbearers and the other over the bakers—sent them to the prison of the commander of the soldiers, in which Joseph was bound.

After the soul has thus been strengthened amid temptations, then the guilt of those two eunuchs who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God is recognized. By the baker is understood the power of reason, which knows how to pound every doubtful matter with the hand of discernment; by the cupbearer, good will, which is accustomed to receive the cup of spiritual love. Therefore, after grace is found in the sight of the governor of the prison, its fruit is disclosed through the recognition of the fault of reason and will. [Col. 0271B]

Both are said to belong to the king of Egypt, because before conversion both our reason and our will are known to have served the devil, the prince of the world. Moreover, they sin when they do not conceal their sins. Hence those who falsely justify themselves are called righteous: “I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous” (Matthew IX, 13). But they sin against their master, because everything that they confess in repentance to have sinned is done to provoke and increase the devil’s power.

Although there are many forms of reasoning and many wills according to their causes, nevertheless one divinely inspired will and reason, as it were the cupbearer and baker, has precedence. Pharaoh, when angry, sends them to the prison of the commander of the soldiers when, under pressure from the devil, reason itself together with will is brought under the laws of reason, which holds first place in our inward warfare. For reason is subjected to itself when, seeking something by human subtlety, it is brought back by divine moderation. And if the will is good, it is nothing other than reason. Yet this is not without the greatest regard for discernment; thus they are distinguished both by names and by realities. Hence in the Apocalypse thrones, living creatures, angels, and elders are spoken of (Revelation V, 6): they signify the same things, yet are different in another respect. [Col. 0271C–D]

Of this imprisonment the Apocalypse says: “Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, and you will have tribulation for ten days” (Revelation II, 10). Joseph is held bound in this prison when the very desire for inward growth is impeded by a devilish storm.

**VERSE 4.**—But the baker and the cupbearer are entrusted to Joseph by the keeper of the prison when reason and will are compelled, by the divine intellect which presides over them and which alone is sufficient to guard them amid afflictions, toward the desire for heavenly growth as though toward a singular refuge. Good will, however, is one thing and the desire for growth in goodness another, even though it is itself good will; for some have a good affection toward their neighbors but are unwilling to advance to higher things. Joseph ministers to them, because the desire to pursue better things alone refreshes and renews their deficiencies. [Col. 0272A]

**VERSE 5.**—Some time had passed, and they were held in custody. Both saw a dream in one night, each according to an interpretation suited to himself. Some time passes when the craving for temporal things is in part withdrawn from the soul. Yet, while held in custody, they see a dream in one night because, though they are not yet free of bodily distress, they are for a time lulled from outward affairs and keep vigil in heart, so that, by the mind’s sleeping vision in a clearer light, they consider matters useful and suited to their life, in order that they may come forth from custody to confess the name of God.

**VERSES 6, 7.**—When Joseph entered to them in the morning and saw them sad, he asked, saying: “Why is your countenance today sadder than usual?” Joseph enters to them in the morning when, as the illumination of divine visitation penetrates the affection, every recess of the conscience—what it understands and whatever it wills according to God—is examined; and then they are seen to be sad, because intellect and will are afflicted all the more as they are more subtly entered by the examination of the higher light. “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes I, 18).

Yet the affection of piety tempers and consoles this sorrow; and it asks why they bear the countenance of the heart, by which God is to be seen, more turned away than usual from the inward joy of that very unfailing light in which it has been established today. For useful sadness, unless cautiously moderated, often turns into the disease of acedia. [Col. 0272B]

**VERSE 8.**—They said: “We have seen a dream, and there is no one to interpret it for us.” And Joseph said: “Does not interpretation belong to God? Tell me what you have seen.” “We have seen a dream, but there is no one to interpret it,” because in contemplating we intellectually grasp many things concerning the state of a right life, but we do not yet have the means to set forth what we have understood in fitting effects. But Joseph—that is, the desire for holy growth, which conquers all the bitterness of weariness—says that interpretation belongs to God, because what our mortality is hindered from accomplishing is accomplished by God’s help. “Tell me what you have seen,” that is, refer to God the maker what you purpose. [Col. 0272C]

**VERSES 9, 10, 11.**—The chief cupbearer first related his dream: “I saw before me a vine, on which were three branches; it gradually put forth buds, and after the flowers the grapes ripened. Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. So I took the grapes, pressed them into the cup which I held, and gave the cup to Pharaoh.”

The chief cupbearer is the affection of good will, which, because it rests upon God’s will, rules over all other wills. He relates his dream first, because unless it takes the lead, reason speculates and thinks in vain. He sees a vine before him when he sets before himself, as something to be loved, good will itself, the source of spiritual wine—that is, of charity. For we desire to have before our eyes what we love.

There are three branches upon it because there are three principal members of charity: the first directed toward God, the second pertaining to oneself, and the third looking from the example of oneself toward love of one’s neighbor. For it is as though it said: “You shall love yourself and your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XIX, 19). The buds gradually grow when the juices of inward devout thought fashion definite purposes of holiness. And rightly “gradually,” because these things come about with great difficulty. After the flowers the grapes ripen when, after the display of works which diffuse everywhere the fragrance of holy reputations, the living powers of conscience fully advance in the sweetness of holy love. [Col. 0273A]

Pharaoh’s cup is in his hand when every passion of perverse desire, sent in by the devil, is restrained under the power of rational will. Thus he takes the grapes in order to press them into the cup he holds, when he mingles the divine sweetness hidden within with the passions that he often bears with difficulty. For we press when, with the hand of discernment, we examine the future glory that will be revealed in us (Romans VIII, 18), so that we may season the bitterness of this present time. The Gospel testifies that passion is signified by the name of a cup: “Can you,” he says, “drink the cup?” (Matthew XX, 22; Mark X, 38), etc.

Then we give the cup to Pharaoh when we repay him the recompense which he has rendered to us (Psalm CXXXVI, 8). “In the cup,” it says, “in which she mixed for you, mix double for her” (Revelation XVIII, 6). By Pharaoh, whose name means “destroyer,” we understand the devil. [Col. 0273B]

**VERSES 12, 13.**—Joseph replied: “This is the interpretation of the dream: The three branches are three more days, after which Pharaoh will remember your service and restore you to your former position, and you will place the cup in his hand according to your office, as you were accustomed to do before.”

“For doing good,” he says, “your condition hinders you from the holy eagerness to advance in God; but you will be released to do those things which you rightly perceive ought to be done.” The three branches are three days, because God’s love first illumines us; then knowledge and care of ourselves enlighten us, so that the light of our love and our examples may reach our neighbor. After this Pharaoh remembers our service and restores us to our former position, when he makes us remember the pleasure of our former life, by which we served the devil to our destruction. Thus, through the countless invasions of temptations, we seem to have been carried away by him to the condition in which we formerly lived as worldly people. But we give him the cup according to our office, as we were accustomed to do before, when, returning forcefully to our heart, we boldly bring forward, as befits the dignity of our rationality and as we have been accustomed to receive from the time of our conversion, the cup of combat, insofar as we can.”

**VERSES 14, 15.**—“Only remember me when it goes well with you, and show me mercy, by suggesting to Pharaoh that he bring me out of this prison, because I was stolen away from the land of the Hebrews, and here, though innocent, I was thrown into the pit.”

“Only,” he says, “do not set aside the continual intention of progress when you have taken up the strength to carry the cup against Pharaoh. Press him with so many blows of virtue that, overcome, he may bring you out—or, whether he wishes it or not, allow you to be brought out—from the war he has waged, or release the siege or the chains. For by a secret suggestion I was taken from the land of the Hebrews—that is, from the solidity of thoughts already passing from the depths to higher things—and yet I was thrown innocent of the desire to sin into the pit of fluctuation.” In seeking these advances, our affection asks them insistently from the good will that cooperates with it.

**VERSES 16, 17.**—When the chief of the bakers saw that he had wisely explained the dream, he said: “I too saw a dream: I had three baskets of flour upon my head; and in one basket, which was higher, I carried all the foods made by the baker’s art, and birds were eating from it.”

Our governing faculty—namely, reason illumined by God, and therefore mistress of all human reasoning—understands that the desire for progress had thoroughly imbued benevolence, which goes before it, with things invisible. For this desire gives the name “dream” to its own effects and introduces it itself.

He says that he has three baskets of flour upon his head, when he recognizes in his mind three principal offices of thought: understanding, will, and memory. It is clear that in Scripture “head” is usually used for “mind.” Flour, because of its fineness, is rightly taken for thought. Hence: “Take the millstone, grind flour” (Isa. 47:2). The one basket that is higher than the others is reason itself, which stands altogether above will and memory. In it we carry all the foods made by the baker’s art, because there we retain all that is vital, which diligent discernment can examine. [Col. 0274C]

Birds eat from it when demons, lifted up through the vice of pride, consume us in our very exaltation, insofar as the good things we prudently take hold of are concerned.

**VERSES 18, 19.**—Joseph said: “The three baskets are three more days, after which Pharaoh will take away your head and hang you on a cross, and birds will tear the flesh from you.”

Understanding, memory, and will, although they are, so to speak, the mind’s daily lights, are nevertheless baskets: fragile, like reeds, because of their condition as flesh. But Pharaoh takes away the head after these days when, after the illumination of the inner senses, pride slips in and the capital virtue, humility, separated from the members of the virtues, disappears.

Pharaoh hangs him on a cross when, after governing humility has been removed, the mind, condemned and rendered powerless and empty, is deprived of the body of all good works. All these things are done by the devil, represented by Pharaoh. Birds eat the flesh when proud demons refresh themselves on the carnal works that follow from us.

Our affection, therefore—that is, Joseph, now desiring spiritual growth—resolves these two mysteries, as though they were two dreams, through divine wisdom. In them are understood two things: charity, namely benevolence itself, signified by the chief cupbearer, and knowledge, represented by the chief baker.

Charity that is not tested by temptation is not charity; but charity itself brings back the cup of recompense from Pharaoh with strength and courage. Thus a simple will makes progress after passing through sufferings. For charity, because it is naturally humble, builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). Knowledge, however, because it often puffs up (ibid.), feeds demons.

Hence the three baskets are said to have been upon his head, because knowledge cannot be complete without three things: talent, practice, and memory. In these the flour is handled—that is, the subtlety of thought is worked through. By the reed, from which the baskets are called what they are, superfluity of speech and eloquence is signified. The sense is that some people progress through simple benevolence without knowledge or letters, by patience; while others, through pride arising from the arrogance of wisdom, provide nourishment for demons.

**VERSE 20.**—“Then the third day was Pharaoh’s birthday.”

On the third day Pharaoh is born, when, after an inept kind of joy that first arises within as though it were a light, then the boastfulness of words, and finally an open and confident assurance—as though it arose from the clear day of his knowledge—the wicked desire, Pharaoh, that is, the dissipator of holiness, rises in the soul. These deadly illuminations commonly succeed one another in us.

He who made a great banquet for his servants remembered, amid the feast, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.

**VERSES 21, 22.**—“He restored one to his place, so that he might present the cup to the king; the other he hanged on the gallows.”

Pharaoh, conceived in the heart, is raised to the strength of obstinacy through the three days we mentioned; then, with the nourishment of the worst kinds of glory, he inflates childish thoughts, thoughts carried about by every wind of doctrine.

He remembers the chief cupbearer and the chief baker amid the feast when, after or amid the gulping down of various kinds of pomp as though they were delicacies, he makes us remember, under the very weight of our pride, on the one hand the chief of our good things, namely the piety of the will, which is consigned to the prison; and on the other the teacher of the subtleties of reason, who is likewise drawn into the symbol.

Pharaoh therefore restored one to his place, so that he might present the cup to the king; he hanged the other on the gallows. For when, from contemplating our folly and pride, we begin to grow weary, our will, through his own instigation—though the devil is unwilling to provide the opportunity—receives the occasion of restoration and seeks again the place of pious intention, which properly belongs to us. Thus we return to Pharaoh, as though by a cup, the recompense that he returned to us: “the daughter of Babylon,” that is, the flow of temptation by which we are confounded (Ps. 136:8). And we fasten—or rather hang—the understanding of all kinds of knowledge, as the chief of the baker’s art, upon the gallows of divine fear; for by this understanding we examine each thing as though kneading it, lest we be lifted up in pride. To hang it means to raise it up from the lowest desire.

Pharaoh does these things because, while the devil tempts us, or a wicked desire forces us to them by necessity, he unites and constrains the mind toward God and toward itself. The truth of the interpreter is therefore proved by this: the desire for holy progress is judged by its effects to be truthful and to contain equity in distinguishing eternal things from temporal ones.

**VERSE 23.**—When prosperity followed, the chief cupbearer forgot his interpreter. For although inner troubles are overcome with difficulty, once even a little peace has followed, the desire for progress is easily drawn away from the soul.

**CHAPTER XLI**

**VERSE 1.**—After two years Pharaoh saw a dream.

The first year is understood as divine thought; the second as the execution of a good work. Concerning these the Psalm says: “I will give you understanding and instruct you” (Ps. 31:8), so that you may cooperate with your understanding. For just as a year shines through its days, so both shine through pious actions and perceptions.

The third year, in which the dream is seen, is the intention of perseverance; hence what follows there: “I will fix my eyes upon you” (ibid.), namely, so that I may direct them according to your progress. After the year, therefore—that is, after the illumination of heavenly knowledge—and likewise after the year of action, namely when the establishment of pious perseverance is proposed with firmness, the wickedness of our desire, which is rightly designated by the name of the dissipator, Pharaoh, or the devil himself, by means of a certain subtle knowledge of his own, known only to himself like a dream, foretells and anticipates within himself the dangers that will come after the experience of grace.

**VERSES 7, 8.**—Pharaoh awoke after his sleep, and, when morning came, he was terrified by fear. He sent for the interpreters of Egypt and all its wise men; and, when they had been summoned, he told them the dream, and there was no one who could interpret it.

Pharaoh’s sleep is the cunning by which he delays for a time the trouble of his attack. He awakens when he assails the soul through a crowd of temptations. He is terrified by fear when morning comes, when, during the temptation, his mind, divinely illumined, is disturbed by sudden repulsion.

He sends for the interpreters of Egypt and all its wise men when he endeavors, through calculations of worldly cunning, to surround the spiritual thought and investigate its intentions. He tells the dream after they have been summoned when, amid the accumulated multitude of inner movements, the devil disputes about the uncertainty of invisible things.

There is no one to interpret it because the spiritual soul, judging all things, is not circumscribed by carnality.

**VERSE 9.**—Then at last the chief cupbearer, remembering, said: “I confess my sin,” and so forth.

The chief cupbearer remembers and confesses his sin when the good will that offers the heart, against Pharaoh, the drink of salutary counsel, accuses itself of negligence because, when a little rest smiled upon it, it interrupted the soul’s desire to grow—that is, it forgot the interpreter.

Joseph, whose name signifies “increase,” is called the interpreter for this reason: the mind can never be capable of the divine secret unless it is always desiring heavenly growth.

**VERSE 10.**—“The king, angry with his servants, ordered me and the chief baker to be confined in the prison of the captain of the guard.”

The king—that is, the devil, who rules over the sons of pride (Job 41:25)—is angry with his servants, not with those who are his servants now, but with those who once were and have already been freed by the truth. Against them he rages more fiercely. He confines the will—that is, free choice—and the governing understanding, which examines and kneads things, in the prison of the captain of the guard. For he compels and restrains it within the prison of that same Satan, who is the prince of those vices that wage war against the soul (1 Pet. 2:11).

Understand the remainder as it was explained above.

What he says—**VERSE 12:** “There was there a Hebrew boy, servant of the same leader”—means that the same leader, who once followed the devil himself, had returned to the newness and innocence of childhood. For he had become a *transitor*, which is what “Hebrew” means, in the prison. Concerning this it is written in the Apocalypse: “Behold,” he says, “the devil is about to cast some of you into prison” (Rev. 2:10), and so forth.

**VERSE 14.**—Immediately, at the king’s command, they brought Joseph out of prison; they shaved him and, after changing his clothing, presented him to Pharaoh.

At the king’s command Joseph is brought out of prison—not because the devil’s command is able to free our pious desire, except insofar as God alone permits it, but because, according to the perversity of some, the meaning is believed to be relaxed when, at God’s command, it ceases from its attacks. Thus in Daniel Nebuchadnezzar is said to strike, humble, and kill whomever he wished (Dan. 5:19), although his heart was in God’s hand alone.

Joseph is shaved when he is deprived of the superfluity that had grown during the temptations by the sharp blade of ready discernment and the double shears of charity. His clothing is changed when the habit of the mind is renewed. He is presented to Pharaoh by those from whom he was shaved when, through the support of spiritual movements, he is advanced so that he may resist the devil.

For *offerre*—composed from *ob* and *fero*, *fers*—properly means “to carry against.” Hence, in the comic poet, it is aptly said that a vice was “offered” to a maiden, clearly signifying violence (Ter. *Ad.* 3.1.9).

**VERSE 15.**—“I saw dreams,” he says, “and there is no one who can explain them.”

The enemy deliberately, and as though at his own command, rests from oppressing us, as we have said, so that, against the quiet and secure, he may introduce through a round of questions what he could not introduce by attacking. The sense is therefore this: “I saw”—that is, I understood—the uncertainty of the invisible things you desire, because he has mocked you with certain dreams; and there is no strength of reason capable of explaining what you are thinking. I heard that you interpret them most wisely—that is, I discovered that you do not reach them through knowledge but estimate them through conjectures.

Notice that he claims to have heard the reputation of the interpreter, although he says that he saw dreams. Seeing is more certain than hearing. “I know for certain,” he says, “that those things are like dreams which I take in as though from hearsay: that you most wisely—that is, more providently than necessary—wish to conjecture.”

**VERSE 16.**—Joseph replied: “Without me, God will answer favorably for Pharaoh.”

This means: “Not by my estimates, but by divine inspirations, useful and fitting answers will be given to you, devil, and to your suggestions.”

**VERSES 17, 18.**—Pharaoh therefore said: “I thought that I was standing upon the bank of the river, and seven cows were rising from the river, exceedingly beautiful and fat in flesh; they were cropping green plants in the marsh as they grazed.”

The bank of the river on which Pharaoh stands is the renunciation of this world. While we are safe from the waves of the world, we are nevertheless subjected to the devil’s footprint under other forms, namely spiritual vices. For some kind of harbor of the sea is contempt for worldly care.

He thinks that he is standing upon the bank and above it, over the river, because he not only subjects the river of worldliness to himself, but also trusts that the Jordans—that is, those who descend from the haughtinesses of the world—flow into the mouth of his power.

The seven cows seem to me to signify the seven spiritual virtues that the prophet mentions resting upon the flower (Isa. 11:1–2), by which he indicates the fullness of all good things; for this number signifies totality. It can also signify the four principal virtues mingled with our three natural faculties—understanding, reason, and imagination—which, like cows, break up and examine the earth of our sensuality.

They are exceedingly beautiful and fat in flesh because, when possessed, nothing is happier in every respect than they, and nothing is purer except God. They are spoken of in the feminine gender because they are the mothers and substance of all religion.

They ascend from the river when they tear themselves away from conformity to the world. They crop the green plants in the marsh as they graze when, in the present life—which is a marsh and an enticement—they refresh themselves piecemeal, through the loveliness of the hope of immortality, seeing as through a mirror and in a riddle.

**VERSES 19, 20, 21.**—“And behold, seven other cows followed them, so deformed and gaunt that I had never seen such in the land of Egypt. After they had devoured and consumed the first ones, they gave no sign of satiety; but they remained sluggish in the same gauntness and squalor.”

By the seven other cows either temporality, which runs its course through seven days, or the whole of humanity is represented. Humanity consists in the body of four elements, while in the soul it is distinguished by talent, will, and feeling. When these are possessed without the love of God, they are deformed, away from the richness of spiritual good and from the image of God.

They follow and devour the first cows because it has happened to many, after the height of holiness, to fall shamefully into the laziness of humanity and the luxury of temporality. Thus, through the misery of a reprobate mind, they surpass the filthiness of the Egyptians—that is, of worldly people, who have never proposed anything good. They do not grieve over the fall of their former life, nor, because they have consumed it, finally demand any remnant of tears from its memory by which they might be refreshed; instead, they waste away in the same squalor of sin with which they were once imbued.

**VERSES 22, 23, 24.**—“Awaking and then again being weighed down by sleep, I saw a dream: Seven ears were sprouting on one stalk, full and very beautiful. Seven other ears, thin and scorched by blight, were growing from the stubble; they devoured the beauty of the first ones.”

While the symbolic Pharaoh speaks these things in our thoughts, threatening the ruin of the holiness we have undertaken, he awakens because, through the reconsideration of such fortunes in the mind of one who is meditating, he arouses great unrest. Yet he is again weighed down because the fear of this invasion is sometimes lulled to sleep.

“I saw another dream,” so that what he has already thrust upon us through suggestions he may make more dangerously intimate through consent, namely the spirit of invisible good things, resembling dreams. Hence even today, among certain grammarians, there is a serious controversy concerning predestination, to the ruin of the unlearned.

The seven ears are the fullness of the virtues; hence they are called full and beautiful. Their coverings of chaff and the bristling of awns signify the outspread superfluities of thoughts and the anxious concerns of wicked affections standing erect in the already aroused mind.

They sprout on one stalk because, since there is one faith, one baptism, and one God (Eph. 4:5), they must necessarily arise from this unity. The stalk may also signify the mind itself, marked by its instability. With its fruits, the seven other stalks—sterile stubble of temporality and animality, scorched by the winds of empty glories—overthrow it and, once overthrown, consume it through the complete forgetfulness of pious action.

For this reason he calls those cows “bearing” or “pregnant,” not because of their fertility, but because the neighborhood of an effeminated will weakens and frustrates manly work.

“I told the interpreters of dreams, and there is no one who can explain it.”

This means: “I presented these things, which I suggested to your prudence, to many others endowed with talent; I brought them before those who skillfully examine invisible things, but I received from them nothing certain or worthy of belief.”

**VERSE 25.**—Joseph said: “The king’s dream is one. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.”

As though he were saying: “You wish to set present things before me as future things and, moreover, to frighten me with the troubles of temptations. But I know that the tales you bring forward, threatening ruin after the pursuit of holiness, signify one thing: namely, that you may turn me away from doing good. Although you see everything as exalted and are king over all the sons of pride (Job 41:25), God shows you how he humbles the hearts of the just through temptations; and, having preserved them through humility, crowns them forever, while you and yours are condemned, according to your name, to dissipation.”

The same force of the dream is therefore contained in the seven beautiful cows and the seven full ears (**VERSE 26**), because although you are burdened by our advancement, you speak of our very progress for the purpose of turning us away from it, while you threaten coming misfortunes.

These dreams, therefore—that is, as far as you are concerned, vain and empty things, since you foresee nothing for us except what is wicked—we shall recognize as possessing the force of manifest truth when, while vigilantly foreseeing adversities, we do not fail because of them but stand firm.

The seven years of abundance signify for us, as a type, the fullness of spiritual lights and the abundance of heavenly sweetness. Yet from the river which, according to the Psalmist, must be crossed (Ps. 65:6), they rise through the foot of humility—that is, from the course of the present age—like a hideous image of lustful cows, lacking heavenly sap. This image consumes whatever, insofar as it is concerned with the estimation of the one who suffers, exists inwardly as virtue. Hence it is said: “The righteous man falls seven times,” according to the humbling of the spirit, “and rises again,” according to the return of virtues and hope (Prov. 24:16). We refer the sevenfold famine to the movement of the world, in that respect in which we abound in poverty.

What you saw a second time, pertaining to the same matter, is an indication of the firmness of everything, because the word of God is spoken and is fulfilled more quickly. “You saw,” he says—that is, “you made me experience something in a singular way.” To those who are hostile to us we are accustomed to say, “You saw me alone.”

You therefore made me experience the same matter of your, not my, determination first through suggestion and second through delight; this is an indication of the firmness of all my spiritual vows, since they have persisted amid your provocations. It is so because the word of God is fulfilled—namely, “If the spirit of one who rules rises against you, do not leave your place”—and is fulfilled more quickly, so that the delight that has slipped in may not be carried into effect.

**VERSES 33, 34, 35, 36.**—“Now therefore let the king provide a wise and diligent man, and set him over the land of Egypt. Let him appoint overseers throughout the regions and gather a fifth part of the produce during the seven years of fertility that are now about to come; let all the grain be stored under Pharaoh’s authority and kept in the cities for the future famine of seven years.”

As though he were saying: “While you direct deceptive threats against me as I seek heavenly growth, you ought, by God’s grace, to have provided me with an understanding capable, through strength and diligence, of refuting such things. While you try to subject me to the desires of this earthly body—which truly is the land of Egypt, namely, a place of distress and darkness—you introduce causes for exercising authority as you press me.

Thus the understanding, solicited in this way, establishes powerful movements of reason throughout the several regions of the outward senses for inward protection. It will store up and preserve, in the granary of the conscience, the frugality of those same five senses for the time of necessity, as long as heavenly fullness overflows inwardly, and will increase it.

I mean the time when you have received the power of tempting for the dissipation of the soul. In the cities of the guardianship of the several inner virtues—or of the temperance of the senses themselves—the abundance of all that fertility ‘with which the valleys abound in grain’ (Ps. 64:14), namely, heavenly wisdom, is to be prepared, by careful distribution, for tasting the word of God during the famine brought upon the mind by God’s humbling action.

This famine oppresses Egypt because it shakes and covers the mind, narrowed by repeated tribulations, with a certain darkness arising from want of counsel, as though adding to its evil. Yet when this has happened, the land will not be consumed by famine: for, with the seed of pious intention preserved through the summer’s serenity, the fruitfulness of our heart, like cultivated soil in the manner of an ant’s storehouse, can endure the winter of temptation.”

**VERSES 37, 38.**—The counsel pleased Pharaoh and all his servants. He said to them: “Can we find such a man, who is full of the spirit of God?”

For Pharaoh to be pleased means nothing other than to yield, as it were, to evident reason, or to be subjected and submit to the wicked effect—which is itself also Pharaoh.

His servants are the movements of our animal nature. “Can we,” those desires say with their goads, “find anything, so to speak, more virtuous and more in accord with the spirit of God than the understanding that alone can resist so many disadvantages?”

**VERSE 39.**—“Since God has shown you all that you have spoken”—that is, because you excel in the foresight given to you by God; and because you cling to God, you are one spirit.

**VERSE 40.**—“You shall be over my house”—that is, “I shall set you above the world, once my house.” If I wish to be the daughter of the King, I am commanded to forget that house (Ps. 44:11–12), because it is the house of my ancient father, the devil, and not only his house but also his desires.

“And at the command of your mouth all the people shall obey.” This is the people that the Psalm commands to be consigned to forgetfulness together with the aforesaid father’s house (Ps. 136:5). Yet although the multitude of vices obeys the command of the mouth—that is, of reason—it is preceded by the one throne of carnal desire, because it is wholly overcome by no mortal, even in the smallest matters.

**VERSE 41.**—“Behold,” he said, “I have appointed you over the whole land of Egypt.”

If the house and the people are subjected to you, then all the earthliness of worldliness will immediately be compelled to obey you. These words, spoken under the appearance of Pharaoh, are so applied to the devil that they signify not benevolence but necessity—the necessity by which he is not allowed to harm us in our life. Thus they suit the wicked desire, so that they may agree more clearly and correctly with that desire once it has been corrected.

**VERSE 42.**—He took the ring from his hand and gave it into Joseph’s hand. He clothed him in a linen robe and placed a golden chain around his neck.

The ring in Pharaoh’s hand is the mystery of iniquity in the practice of action. It is given by him to Joseph when the affection is transferred from the perversity of desires to the desire for holiness. Things that must be concealed are marked by the ring, through which a covering for wickedness is received.

The linen robe is the hope of incorruptibility already becoming glory, or purity of conscience. He clothes us in it when he does not hinder us from putting it on. Recall the Gospel concerning the prodigal—but repentant—son, and the gifts he received from his father when he returned (Luke 15:22).

We emit our voice through the neck, and through it we also admit food; by it we receive the force of counsel, which we expend upon ourselves and others. A golden chain is placed around it when, by the instruction of heavenly truth—than which nothing is more precious—our speech is both fortified, with nothing obstructing it, and the virtue of our discernment is illumined.

**VERSE 43.**—He also caused him to ascend upon his second chariot, while a herald proclaimed that all should kneel before him.

Pharaoh’s chariot is the force of ambition. The second chariot is no longer the desire for material things, but the desire for human praise, which especially attacks holy men who are voluntarily poor. The bitterness of what follows is greater than that of what came before.

He causes Joseph to ascend upon this chariot when he permits the course of avarice to be subdued by heavenly desire. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses” (Ps. 19:8): that is, some in desires and others in pride.

The herald cries out when the voice of sacred Scripture or of divine fear, near to the heart and ears, repeatedly announces that every rigidity of bodily insolence should bend whatever stubbornness it possesses toward the pursuit of eternal things.

**VERSE 44.**—“I am Pharaoh,” he says. “Without your command no one shall move hand or foot throughout the whole land of Egypt.”

Although I am naturally light-minded and desirous of evil, from now on, at your command, I shall move neither the foot of affection nor the hand of action in the land of Egypt—that is, in the corruptible body “which weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15)—except in accordance with your will.

**VERSE 45.**—He changed his name and called him in the Egyptian language “Savior of the world.”

He changed it—that is, he caused to be changed what, according to its former condition, was called wicked desire; now it is called an affection of piety.

The Egyptian language calls him “Savior of the world” when, through the experience of the tribulation that constricts itself—for this is what “Egypt” signifies—the flesh and the worldliness, through a judgment changed by repentance from its former vanity, confess the heavenly desire to be the author of their own salvation.

He gave him Aseneth as a wife, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis.

*Aseneth* is interpreted as “ruin”; *Potiphera* as “mouth inclining to cut apart”; and *Heliopolis* as “city of the sun.” The daughter of our wicked desire, which always inclines the mouth—that is, the entrance of the conscience—so that it may cut apart and separate what has been united to the Spirit of God, is the ruin of sin. For “when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin” (James 1:15).

Pharaoh is said to mean “dissipating” or “uncovering him.” This wife is given to Joseph by Pharaoh when, from that wicked desire itself, she is joined to the desire for heavenly growth like a wife: first because of the dissipation caused by vices, and afterward because of the foul uncovering that exposes everything to disgrace. Thus, when the ruin of the evils committed is considered, and the fruit of those same iniquities—signified by the names of Pharaoh and Potiphera—is observed, the offspring of pious action may be propagated more earnestly.

Potiphera is a priest of Heliopolis because the sacred—that is, accursed—leader of the way by which one goes to the city is the wickedness of desire: not to the city of the true sun, whose maker and founder is God (Heb. 11:10), but to the city that it builds where the fires of manifold temptation burn.

**VERSE 46.**—Joseph went out into the land of Egypt. He was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, the king, and he traveled throughout all the regions of Egypt.

He is said to go out into the land of Egypt and then to travel through the regions of Egypt because, unless we surpass the earthliness of the world by the majesty of the mind, we cannot, with due authority, look down upon all the parts of our sensuality as though they were the sides of Egypt.

Although we are established in the body, we must go out beyond its desires, as though beyond the camp, to him who suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13:12). For just as someone accustomed to foul smells does not recognize the misery of the stench he suffers until he moves out into the purity of free and clean air, so one submerged in the confusion of vices does not perceive the cruelty of the evils by which he is besieged until he surpasses those very plagues after first tasting the fragrance of moral goodness.

Hence in the Apocalypse the lovers of Babylon are said to stand far away (Rev. 18:15), so that, separated from it, they may be able to weigh its destruction.

The number three pertains to the Trinity; ten pertains to the execution of the commandment. When these two are present in us as desire, it is already sufficiently fitting that we stand before Pharaoh—that is, before the present violence of the demon. This standing means contending against his assaults.

**VERSES 47, 48.**—The fertility of the seven years came, and the crops were gathered into bundles and stored in the granaries of Egypt. Every abundance of grain was also stored in each city.

In the time of abundance the crops are gathered into bundles when, as the prosperity of divine sweetness smiles upon us, our good things and all our actions are bound together under judgment, as though by a bond of heavenly love. This is to have oil in one’s vessels.

They are gathered into the granaries of Egypt because we have this treasure in earthen vessels. The abundance of grain is gathered in each city when the complete virtue of self-restraint is established—or rather stored—in each of the senses. This is understood to signify vigilant concealment.

**VERSE 49.**—There was so great a quantity of wheat that it equaled the sand of the sea, and its abundance exceeded measure.

The quantity of wheat equals the sand of the sea when the overflowing of virtue, the serenity of the mind, and its lightness come together and are joined. For sand is soft and pleasant in its level surface. Abundance exceeds measure when the capacity for doing good is often supplied beyond the practice customary among human beings.

**VERSE 50.**—Two sons were born to Joseph before the famine came; Aseneth bore them to him, and so forth.

His sons are born to the soul eager for heavenly growth when, after the good of repentance has gone before, the work of holiness follows. She is the daughter of the desire that cuts apart and that had as its guide the one leading toward the noonday of crimes. They are born because, where sin abounded, grace was poured out more abundantly, according to the Apostle (Rom. 5:20).

That the name “sun” signifies the heat of temptation is proved by the passage saying that, when the sun rose, people were scorched (Matt. 13:6), as the Lord says.

**VERSE 51.**—The firstborn was called Manasseh, a name said to mean “forgetting,” because, he says, “God has made me forget all my labors and my father’s house.”

True repentance exists when, forgetting the old and former things in which we labored and were burdened, and blocking the entrance to the house of our devilish fatherhood, we extend ourselves toward future newness.

**VERSE 52.**—The second was called Ephraim, which is said to mean “fruitful”: “God has made me grow,” he says, “in the land of my poverty.”

By this are understood the exercises of piety, which are living fruits now emerging in the body that was formerly the poverty within, providing the soil in which, with the order reversed, we now receive increase.

Verses 53–54.—After the seven years of abundance that had occurred in Egypt had passed, the seven years of want that Joseph had foretold began to come, and famine prevailed throughout the whole world. When the fullness of divine outpouring has been exhausted, deprivation of inward nourishment follows, because unless grace withdraws for a time, temptation finds no place into which it may enter; and throughout the whole world—that is, in the perfection of everything—the misery of inner languor, which had formerly been present, settles in. “The world” is used for what is perfect because of its roundness, as in: “Hear, you who inhabit the world” (Psalm 48:2). In the entire land of Egypt there was no bread.

Verse 55.—When it was hungry, the people cried out to Pharaoh, asking for food. There is no bread in the whole land of Egypt because, amid every worldly desire, there is no nourishment for the mind. “I do not find,” says the Apostle, “what is good in my flesh” (Romans 7:18). When the bread of grace has been consumed, Egypt—that is, darkness—and distress, which constricts it, having nothing with which to fill the emptiness of its belly, and finding nothing substantial even in the husks, rightly grows hungry. It cries out to Pharaoh because, in accordance with the Gospel, it seeks the ruler of the region; but since it does not satisfy its hunger with the food of swine (Luke 15:15–16), it repeats its request as though in response to the ruler or Pharaoh, and is compelled to desire the bread of hired servants. “Go,” he says, “to Joseph; seek heavenly increase, and whatever he commands you, do.” For just as desire is the teacher of evils, so pious affection is the teacher of all good things.

Verse 56.—The famine grew daily in every land because, as the disease of bodily impulses increased, the impoverished conscience had nothing to offer or suggest to its own deficiency. Therefore, three loaves must be sought from the friend Joseph, to be set before the Egypt that has returned from the road (Luke 2:5). Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold to the Egyptians, for famine had oppressed them also.

Verse 57.—All the provinces came to Egypt to buy provisions and moderate the evil of want. Joseph opens all the storehouses when the hunger for inner progress, rising up, displays the resources of the whole rational faculty, in accordance with what is appropriate to each matter. He sells to the Egyptians when he receives from them, through confession, what belongs to their being Egyptians—that is, what they have devoted to worldliness—and afterward distributes the wages of fitting consolation. Famine oppresses them because these bodily impulses chiefly endure this sickness. All the provinces come to Egypt to buy provisions when all the dispersions of our outward nature approach the narrowness of tribulation, as well as the miseries of grief and their own darkness, there to demand for themselves some remedy of refreshment at the cost of pain. “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 42:4). The name Egypt signifies both tribulation and the other things we have mentioned above.

[Column 283]  
THE NINTH BOOK OF THE MORALS ON GENESIS ENDS.

THE TENTH BOOK OF THE MORALS ON GENESIS BEGINS.

[Column 285]

[Column 285A] With God’s help we undertake the tenth little book on Genesis, which we also suppose to be the last—the book that is a ten for those laboring on their own behalf—and we ask that he who has granted us the course thus far may bestow an honorable end. For in this little work we wish to serve both his honor and the salvation of his servants. The sacred history therefore follows.

CHAPTER 42

Verses 1–2.—When Jacob heard that provisions were being sold in Egypt, he said to his sons: “Why are you neglecting this? [152] I have heard that grain is being sold in Egypt. Go down and buy what we need, so that we may live and not be consumed by want.”

The true supplanter of sin—that is, our understanding—perceives this, for this is what its hearing means: that spiritual nourishment is acquired in Egypt, that is, in the confession of one’s own misery. “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Psalm 119:131). It rebukes, as sons, the thoughts born from the seed of knowledge for their negligence. “Go down,” he says—that is, humble yourselves—and offer the price of pious repentance, so that you may obtain the help necessary for life.

Verses 3–4.—So Joseph’s ten brothers went down to Egypt to buy grain, while Jacob kept Benjamin at home. He had said to his brothers: “Lest he suffer any harm on the journey.”

The ten brothers of Joseph—either the whole of virtue established according to the Decalogue, or body and soul resting upon the love of the Trinity and joined by a kindred bond to heavenly increase—bend themselves toward seeking inner nourishment. But Benjamin, who is called “son of the right hand,” that is, love of the heavenly life, is kept at home by Jacob, because the spirit must always be bound indivisibly within the conscience, lest, if it goes forth outwardly, it be detained by some harm amid the breezes of empty praises.

Verse 5.—They entered the land of Egypt with the others who were going to buy provisions.

They enter the land of Egypt when the gathered powers of the inner person strive to break through and overcome the darkness and narrowness of earthly affection. Thus they imitate the others who pursued, or are pursuing, the same holy commerce.

There was a famine in the land of Canaan. Canaan is said to mean “prepared for humility.” It signifies a mind cast down by the earthly affection represented through Egypt, as though by a certain wicked humility, and awaiting the destruction of its inward hunger unless Joseph, set over Egypt, comes to its aid by generously supplying life-giving grain.

Verses 6–7.—When his brothers had bowed down to him and he had recognized them, he spoke harshly to them as though they were strangers, asking them: “Where have you come from?”

“From the land of Canaan,” they said, “to buy provisions for food.”

They bow down when they hold him in reverence; they are recognized when our rational impulses experience and love his sweetness. Heavenly desire speaks harshly, as though to strangers, when by divine dispensation it often pleases the mind less than the mind itself would wish.

“From where,” he says, “will you be able to hope for heavenly things, you who do not depart from worldly love?”

“We have left,” they say, “the earthliness to which we offered the back of our wicked humility for demons to cross over, when they commanded us to bow down. We seek the nourishment of eternal vitality at the cost of present things.”

Verse 8.—Although he himself recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him.

He recognizes the brothers when he makes us recognize the conduct of complete holiness. But he is not recognized by them because, even if he is partly seen and known through some form of love, spiritual increase is never grasped to perfection in this life.

Verse 9.—He remembered the dreams that he had once seen and said to them: “You are spies; you have come to see the weaker places of the land.”

He remembers the dreams when he continually sets before himself the providence concerning future things with which he has been imbued.

“It is not as you say,” he declares, “that you have rejected Canaan. But your intentions are striving to investigate not only the weak things that pertain to humanity, but also the things weaker still by which earthly minds are stained—that is, vices.”

Verse 10.—“No, my lord,” they said, “it is not so. Your servants, mindful of the duties of heaven, desire these things as though they were food, to be refreshed by them, and expend every pleasure as their price.”

Verse 11.—“We are all sons of one man.”

That is, of the one whom seven women seize because of his unity (Isaiah 4:1). And because he is both a man and one, we have now come in peace before God and human beings.

“When we strive to please God and our neighbors for God’s sake, what evil do you suppose we are plotting?”

Verse 12.—“You have come,” he said, “to observe the unfortified places of this land.”

That is, you are still watching for opportunities to sin, and, paying attention not to the powers of the mind but to the fragile body, you are acting foolishly.

Verse 13.—“We, your servants, are twelve brothers.”

Because, through love of the Trinity, we pursue with equal kindred devotion the perfections of the four Gospels or of the four principal virtues. And when we were in the land of Canaan, we were called to be sons of that one man already mentioned.

“The youngest” is so called not because of unworthiness but because of the subtlety of spirituality. It is our hope, which is with the heavenly Father; in this respect also we dwell apart. “Another is no more”: the worldly desire that once rode over us is now beneath us through our longing for heavenly things.

Verse 14.—“This is what I said,” he declared: “You are spies” [Note: [Column 287D] Something seems to be missing here.].

Tharsis is said to mean “the exploration of joy”; yet “God shatters the ships of Tharsis with a mighty wind” (Psalm 48:8). Now I shall test whether you are still pursuing worldly joys.

Verse 15.—“By the health of Pharaoh, you shall not leave this place until your youngest brother comes.”

The health of Pharaoh is not that by which Pharaoh is saved, but rather that by which we are saved from the assault of the typological Pharaoh.

“Thus,” he says, “may I be saved from the dissipator of all good things: you may not depart from here—that is, from the desire for heavenly increase—toward earthly things until the fruit of eternal hope, which is hidden in heaven with the Father, comes.”

He is also called the youngest because the youngest are usually loved and cared for more. All this pertains to hope.

[Column 287B] Verse 16.—“Send one of your number, and let him bring him; but you shall remain in bonds until what [153] you have said has been proved, whether it is true or false.”

Send the one who is principal, as though he were a pledge of love, so that what you contemplate in hope may be shown to you in reality. But meanwhile, know that you must be restrained from worldly looseness by the bonds of discipline, so that under my accusations it may be proved that a defense has been made of your devotion and perseverance.

Verses 17–18.—Therefore he placed them in custody for three days. On the third day, after bringing them out of prison, he said: “Do what I have said, and you shall live, for I fear God.”

The first day is conversion; the second, advancement in virtue; the third, heavenly reward. Thus, under the call of conversion, under the justification of advancement, and under the glorification that is still held by hope of reward, we are confined in the custody of reason. But when, on the third day of fear, we are brought out of prison, he now more gently urges us to purchase life by fulfilling the commandments.

“For I fear God,” he says—not now in a punitive sense, but partly from the desire of fatherhood.

Verse 19.—“If, then, you have begun to have peace with me from vices, let your one brother be bound. Let that love, now suspecting nothing concerning punishment, mourn the prison in which it is detained from the kingdom. But you go away from the concern with outward things and turn toward the separate paths of the virtues of divine savor. Carry grain.”

Verse 20.—“May the youngest brother—that is, hope enlarged for me—come to me, and may the profession of your claim become more truthful and evident for the reward of life.”

Verse 21.—They did as he had said and said to one another: “We rightly suffer these things because we sinned against our brother. We saw the anguish of his soul when he entreated us, and we did not listen. That is why this tribulation has come upon us.”

After we yield in our actions to heavenly desire and consider the heaviness of the change of life, we discuss these things within ourselves:

“We rightly suffer these evils of difficulty because we sinned against the inner person. Although he was consenting to God’s law, because it is good, he was unwillingly dragged amid the narrowness of temptation toward guilt, as though being led there by argument, and we did not listen.

“Therefore, in the matter into which we fell freely and without compulsion, we justly lie beneath an unceasing scourge of evils.”

“For the sake of this brother, lest he be scandalized, the Apostle does not eat meat forever” (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Verse 22.—One of them, Reuben, answered: “Did I not tell you: ‘Do not sin against the boy’? But you did not listen to me. Behold, his blood is being demanded.”

Let the inner impulses complain against themselves in this manner. Reuben, whose name is said to mean “seeing in the midst”—that is, reason, which judges both bodily and spiritual matters together—rebukes them, recalling his admonition: he had forbidden them to sin against one still dull within himself and tender for the labors of conflict, but they had not listened. God inflicted punishments upon those who despised the sin, which is blood.

Verses 23–25.—They did not know that Joseph understood, because he spoke to them through an interpreter. He turned away from them for a while and wept; then he returned and spoke to them. He took Simeon and bound him before their eyes.

While the inner senses thus groan over the sicknesses of the soul, they often do not know that this very understanding is infused into them by the mystical Joseph. For unless they strove after spiritual increase, bodily vices would never weary them, since a complaint of thought runs between the two. Yet the very thing that is touched by distaste for present matters, and about which it argues with itself, is infused by the same one who desires them to be increased in better things.

He therefore turns away for a while and weeps when he removes transitory things from the heart and openly expels from himself whatever harmful moisture exists in the affections. This is done “for a while” because such authority over itself is not granted to the mind for long. Thus he returns and speaks to them, because willingly or unwillingly he is quickly recalled to the arguments mentioned above.

Simeon, whose name is said to mean “hearing sorrow,” is the spirit that is always saddened by its own instability. He is taken away when he is lifted up from low things; he is bound before their eyes because, when the external and internal senses are drawn together for this very purpose, he is fastened by the nails of divine fear.

Simeon may also be understood as carnal affection, which experiences the repeated sorrows of temptations.

He ordered his servants to fill their sacks with grain and to put each man’s money back in his sack, supplying provisions for the journey above it; and they did so.

The servants are thoughts. They are ordered to fill the sacks with grain—that is, to strive to console the troubles of bodily passions with the nourishment of the divine word—so that they may sing with the Psalmist: “You have torn my sackcloth and wrapped me in gladness” (Psalm 30:12). Through these servants, whatever has been drawn in from outside is suggested for reason to examine.

They put each man’s money back in his sack when they store in their memories judgments suitable for strengthening each sense. They supply provisions as well when, along the course of this age, they faithfully minister the appropriate refreshments of heavenly grace by obeying the desires of understanding.

Verse 26.—They carried the grain on their donkeys and departed—that is, in bodies, which, insofar as they are considered in themselves, are something crude in the manner of donkeys. By carefully governing and restraining them, they proceed toward their purposes while carrying the treasures of divine wisdom.

Verses 27–28.—When one of them opened his sack to give his animal fodder at the lodging place, he saw the money at the mouth of the sack and said to his brothers: “My money has been returned to me. Behold, it is in the sack.”

One opens the sack when any sense of the mind, through experience, reveals to itself the nature of any passion. From there he gives fodder to the animal at the lodging place because, from the very occasion [154] of the assault, he is compelled to seek heavenly food to set before bodily desire in the remote places of the conscience.

The mouth of the sack is the entrance to sin, where the money of the divine judgment ought to be found for refuting it. He announces to his brothers that the money has been returned when, at the proper time—that is, during temptation—he communicates to the movements of the same mind the memory of a testimony from Scripture that has been offered to him, and strengthens them for that very purpose with thanksgiving.

The money is in the sack when the force of the divine commandment is inserted into carnal desire, lest perhaps we drift away.

They were stunned and troubled and said to one another: “What is this that God has done to us?”

It is truly very astonishing to human senses when they see themselves bound by the restraints of God’s commandments—those who once could scarcely be frightened away from crimes even by swords hanging over them.

Verses 29–30.—They came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened to them. “The lord of the land,” they said, “spoke harshly to us,” and so forth.

They come into the land of Canaan when the kindred powers of rationality break into the earthliness of affection, which is shamefully lowering itself toward the desires of sin, until they approach the eminence of understanding, which supplants the whole of vice.

Understanding is called the contemplative knowledge of God, and for that reason it surpasses every mode of reason. They report to it what has happened to them because everything adverse or favorable that has overwhelmed them is referred to it for examination.

“The lord of the land spoke harshly to us”—that is, the desire for spiritual increase, which rises above all earthly glory, presented to us, who were proposing the beginnings of good living, the difficulties of the trouble that was to come. The remaining matters that follow have been treated above and, in my opinion, do not need to be repeated.

Verses 35–36.—When they had said these things, as they poured out the grain, each found his money tied at the mouth of his sack. When they were all terrified, their father Jacob said: “You have made me childless. Joseph is no more; Simeon is held in bonds; and you will take Benjamin away. All these evils have fallen upon me.”

After everything has been weighed on the scales of understanding, each pours out the grain when they sprinkle the inner senses with the supports of divine counsel. They find the money tied at the mouth of the sacks when, in the very suggestion of the flesh, they preserve the judgments of salutary teaching, inserted into the passions, which they have acquired through the habit of resisting them.

They are all terrified together when the vigilance of the inner person is carefully armed against bodily allurements according to the decrees of Scripture.

But when understanding is disturbed by the harassment of so many guardians, it declares that it has been broken and made childless through weariness—that is, without the fruits of good works—while striving toward everything and seeing, as it were, that it has accomplished nothing.
