“Joseph,” he says—that is, the care of heavenly increase—“does not surpass the love of visible things,” as is customary. The affection that on account of its pious groaning was once rightly called Simeon is bound by the chains of carnality.

You wish to take away Benjamin, who is understood as the hope of election, signified by the right hand, because you presumptuously undertake everything. When it happens that you are worn away by them, you will compel me also to despair of salvation.

Intellectuality, falling back upon itself in a human manner, commonly says these things:

“All this excellence of holiness will fall upon my evils.”

Verse 37.—Then Reuben, whose name is said to mean “seeing the son”—that is, intellectuality itself, now beginning to be corrected as it becomes more subtle and attending to the fruit of the work it has begun, because whatever is good is brought forth not without pain—answered:

“Put my two sons to death if I do not bring him back to you. Place him in my hand, and I will restore him to you.”

As though he were saying:

“Put to death within yourself the two principal affections of love, namely, love of God and love of neighbor, which I cherish while they attain the strength of future perfection, if you entrust him to my hand. That is, if you direct hope according to the operation and teaching of rationality, I will present it back to you through the achievement of blessedness, making in reality true what you believe or hope.”

Verse 48.—“My son shall not go down with you,” he said.

Divine and human reason commonly alternate in the mind: the former gives lofty admonition and counsel, while the latter recommends lukewarmness under the name of discernment.

“You, relying excessively on your own powers, presume upon high things. But the exercise of my life, which is the son of the right hand—that is, hope of obtaining election—does not proceed with us toward difficult things. Rather, as it is written: ‘You shall not lift a burden upon yourself’ (4 Kings 9:25). It will move toward its purpose with measure, because such an ascent would be nothing other than a descent to the lowest things.

“His brother—the understanding that has died according to the authority of majesty due to it—has perished; only this one remains, namely hope of future things. If anything happens to him in the land—that is, while you are struggling against earthliness and striving to obtain it—you will bring my gray hairs, that is, my decline and old age, down to the underworld of final despair.

“For who in the underworld will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6).

CHAPTER 43

Verses 1–2.—Meanwhile, famine was pressing hard upon the whole land. When they had consumed the provisions they had brought from Egypt, Jacob said to his sons: “Return and buy a little food.”

When the mind is struck too forcefully by temptation, it dissolves into [155] laziness and, under the guise of moderation, utters the things that have been mentioned above. Yet the fruit that had arisen from the first confession—humility and compunction—is entirely consumed, and the provisions brought from Egypt perish, as it were, when the usefulness of repentance for sins is abolished and the mind is meanwhile worn down by lack of counsel.

But understanding, seeing itself conquered and languishing, admonishes its sons—that is, pious movements of thought—to return to the knowledge of themselves by confessing again, so that when they have returned to the heart, even a little food of inner savor may lift them up.

Verses 3–5.—But Judah said: “That man solemnly charged us, swearing: ‘You shall not see my face unless your youngest brother is with you.’ If you are willing, send him with us, and we shall go; and we shall buy what is necessary for our use. But if you are unwilling, we shall not go.”

Judah and Reuben—namely, confession and the experience of grace, which is the vision of the son—address our Jacob, our understanding, in a particular way. They do so lest the labor of confession and repentance already performed perish, and lest what it has already experienced and tasted of divine mercy and sweetness collapse. They especially seize and renew the gray hairs of the reflective intelligence, which, according to the prophet, had already covered it, but had not recognized it—that is, they seize and renew its old age and decline.

The man who places earthly things after heavenly increase virilely denounces those made effeminate. Under the testimony of Scripture and the assertion of truth itself, he declares that no one pleases him in the innermost thought unless he brings with him the hope that, because of its subtle vitality, is established with God.

This hope is nothing, or wholly childish and lowly, unless a brother—that is, the fellowship of merits—surrounds it. Without this, then, we cannot go, because it is foolish to seek if we hope for what has not been sought. For we read that it was said to us: “Hope in the Lord and do good” (Psalm 31:3).

Verse 6.—“You have brought this misery upon me by telling him that you had another brother.”

These are the words of one who is weary, who would have preferred not even to undertake the beginnings of good. To begin them is to have shown hope of heavenly things to desire; to have fallen away from them is misery anew.

Verse 7.—“The man,” they said, “asked us carefully about our family: whether our father was alive and whether we had a brother. We answered him accordingly, in keeping with what he had asked. Could we have known that he would say: ‘Bring your brother with you’?”

The man asks carefully about our family when the rational desire, intent upon inner increase, examines the modes and degrees of our conduct and conversion.

Its order is this: whether the father and ruler of the mental household, understanding, is strong; whether the kindred of good sons—that is, of works—namely, our hope, which gazes upon divine things, remains indivisibly attached to us. In regard to these matters, the whole power and rationality of the mind must answer, not in words but through the affection of its efforts, that it does not lack them, since without them the spiritual increase we seek cannot be obtained.

Before we asked for the grace of conversion, could we have known what the devotion of religious profession would demand from us?

Verses 8–10.—“Send the boy with me,” Judah said, “so that we may set out and live, lest we die, both we and our little ones. I will take responsibility for the boy; require him from my hand. Unless I bring him back and set him before you, I shall be guilty of sin against you forever. If delay had not intervened, we would already have returned a second time.”

Judah asks that the boy be sent so that they may set out when confession, fearing a relapse into former defilements, admonishes hope to be directed toward God, so that they may advance to the pursuit of virtue, obtain life inwardly, and so that the very powers of the mind may not perish together with the first display of pious actions.

For this reason accept the boy as hope, because hope must always become newer in itself through the appearance of good works.

“I will take responsibility for the boy,” he says, when under hope of forgiveness he accepts the burden of repentance. If he should perish, I judge that his destruction ought to be attributed to my inactive work, if I do not show hope to you through reality and do not hand over to you for enjoyment, face to face, what you hope for. Throughout all ages I shall suffer the punishments of guilt against you, whose advancement I ceased to desire.

If the delay caused by a humanly stirred dispute had not intervened, a second confession would already have been made for this very sluggishness that we endure. This means entering Egypt to investigate oneself and returning again to carry out the works of holiness.

Verse 11.—Then Israel, their father, said to them: “If it must be so, do what you wish. Take in your vessels some of the best fruits of the land and carry gifts to the man: a little resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth, and almonds.”

He who above was perhaps called Jacob because of his supplanting of himself is now called Israel—“upright with God”—when he is restrained from human reproach. Therefore he is also called the father of those things that have been rightly understood.

“If it must be so,” he says—if it is not permitted for hope to exist without the accompaniment of good and rational efforts, so that neither can have value without the other—“do what you have proposed. In the receptacles of your conscience take some of the best things of the land, that is, examples and virtues of Christ, by whose fruitfulness, like that of the land, we are nourished. And because ‘the rivers return to the place from which they flow’ (Ecclesiastes 1:7), attribute to Joseph, namely, your spiritual desire, the very things you have received from him, so that he may be carried from good works to better ones; offer them to him.”

By resin, which gives off some fragrance, understand a good [156] reputation among one’s neighbors; in honey, understand kindness of character; through the remaining items, understand the fragrance of virtues and their fruits—that is, the usefulness of action.

These things seem worthy to be offered and suggested to our desire, which virilely governs the unstable flow of earthly things and eagerly pursues pious advancement.

[Column 292D] Verse 12.—“Carry double money with you, so that in this way you may teach others outwardly, insofar as you first nourish yourselves inwardly through the same teachings. Let your springs flow out, yet drink from them alone, without strangers. And take back with you the money that you found, lest it perhaps have happened through error.”

If you think that you possess some discernment concerning the insolence of carnal passions, by whose harshness we are surrounded, refer it to the examination of heavenly wisdom, lest you deceive yourselves by some human reasoning.

For we refer Joseph himself, whom we call increase, to the understanding of heavenly things, by which alone it is good to be increased. It is easy to prove that no one is increased by earthly things.

Verse 13.—“To this man,” he says, “when we have brought back the brother—that is, hope born from the same heavenly-illumined reason—from the lowest desire, we proceed by continual advances, while we perceive things ever nearer to God and salvation.”

Verse 14.—“May my God make him favorable to you, and may he send back with you your brother whom he holds, and Benjamin also.”

Joseph becomes favorable to us when, once worldly impulses have been quieted, the majesty of spiritual increase is not difficult for us. The brother whom he holds is sent back when affection, wandering whether we wish it or not, yet restrained by that majesty as by a law of the mind, is eventually released in obedience to the inner person without any further force.

Benjamin is sent back when the fruit of our hope is shown to us, established at the right hand in the kingdom.

“But I,” he says, “shall be bereft and without children.”

He considers himself bereft for the time being when the mind, placed amid conflict, reckons itself to be nothing and to accomplish nothing, as though situated in a kind of darkness.

Verse 15.—So they went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.

They humble themselves in considering Egyptian tribulation, and the more deeply they bend toward contemplation of it, the more eagerly they rise before Joseph—that is, in the desire for advancement—to understand heavenly things.

Verse 16.—When he saw them, and Benjamin with them, he ordered the steward of his house: “Bring the men into the house, prepare a feast, and slaughter victims, because they shall dine with me at noon.”

Joseph sees them with Benjamin when understanding no longer envies itself the movements of reason or the advances of hope in undertaking heavenly increase.

The steward of the house is our spirit. It is commanded by heavenly love to bring these manly states into the conscience. The victims of sin and of the flesh must be slaughtered so that afterward an inner feast with God may be prepared, so that he may dine with us at the noon of fervent love. According to the Apocalypse, he himself may be refreshed with us and we with him (Revelation 3:20).

Verses 17–18.—He did as he had been commanded, because a spirit touched by God brings commands to rapid fulfillment.

There they were terrified and said to one another: “We have been brought in because of the money that we previously returned in our sacks, so that he may bring an accusation against us, subject us and our donkeys to slavery.”

They are terrified when brought in because, when the mind begins to be examined spiritually, whatever virtue is in us is immediately disturbed by fear.

They tremble because of the money they had returned, fearing that they may have put the teachings of holy knowledge into the sacks of their carnality in a way less adequate than required.

They fear that accusation will be brought against them and that both they and their donkeys will be subjected to slavery, fearing that the indignation of divine judgment is pressing upon them, that by their own deserts they may fall under the rule of sluggish vices, and that both the powers of the mind and the movements of the flesh may succumb in foolishness.

Verses 19–20.—Therefore, approaching the steward at the very doors, they said: “We beg you, lord, to listen to us. We came down previously to buy provisions,” and so forth.

The doors are dispositions of fear, through which there is a kind of entrance into the inner chambers of love. The Psalmist urges us to enter these gates with confessions (Psalm 100:4).

Established in these, we approach the steward when, restrained by divine fear, we now more freely undertake that ordinary reasoning.

“We came down previously,” they say, “through confession of guilt, so that we might be lifted up by divine banquets.”

Verse 21.—“When we had obtained these provisions and had opened our sacks to examine the various bags of desire in our consciences, we remember, with our conscience as witness, that we set the judgments of divine speech before the very suggestions of evil movements. We bring back to your judgment that mystical money, laden with the same weight of heavenly love, so that, with you as judge, it may become clear whether we have done anything unworthily.

Verse 22.—“But we have also brought other silver in abundance, the knowledge that reaches the effect of good action, so that we may purchase God, who is necessary to us above all things, with the expenditure of our entire work.

“It is not in our conscience that we know who put it into our pouches—that is, we do not claim this knowledge for ourselves or attribute it to any human being. We give thanks to him alone for this knowledge of God, which we keep inserted in the little compartments of our memory.”

Verse 23.—“Peace be with you,” he said. “If the peace of reconciliation and concord is present, there is no place for fear.

“Your God and the God of your father—the one who performed wonders with your fathers and is glorified in your times—he himself gave you the money in your sacks, namely, discriminating [157] knowledge, as though it were legitimate coin for distinguishing your temptations.

“Hence what follows: ‘As for the money that you gave,’ that is, the power of prudence that you brought to my examination, ‘I accept it as having been rationally tested.’”

And he brought Simeon out to them.

Simeon is brought out to them when affection that had previously been bound carnally is released for the consent of rational movements.

Verse 24.—Having brought them into the house, he brought water, and they washed their feet; and he gave fodder to their donkeys.

When they have returned whole to the house of the heart, the inner steward suggests a wave of compunction by which the traces of affection are cleansed. Sound counsels then arise, by which the bodily impulses are met as though with fodder.

Verse 25.—They prepared gifts until Joseph entered at noon, for they had heard that they were going to dine there.

The gifts that are prepared are pious incentives to compunction, by which compunction is kindled more intensely and our Joseph advances in the heat of sacred desire.

Verse 26.—Joseph entered his house, and they offered him gifts, holding them in their hands; and they bowed down, prostrate on the ground.

Joseph enters his house when the care of heavenly increase approaches the inner chambers of the mind.

They hold the gifts that they offer in their hands when they carry out in works the holy things that they propose inwardly.

They bow down prostrate on the ground when, while entreating God, they consider the weakness of their own carnality.

Verse 27.—After he had courteously returned their greeting, he asked them: “Is your elderly father well, of whom you told me? Is he still alive?”

He courteously returns their greeting when the effect of devotion does not differ from the affection.

He asks whether the elderly father is safe and alive when, having attained advancement, he considers with reason whether the condition of weakness into which he had nearly fallen before can come to life again.

According to the understanding that is presently being experienced, hope is given concerning his welfare.

Verse 28.—“Your servant is well,” they said.

He is truly a servant—the one over whom the desire for eternal things rules.

Again they bowed and worshiped him because those who had first descended in mind finally express, through the evidence of their works, the fruit of the humility they had conceived.

To worship him is to offer reverence to one’s purpose through acts of service. Hence the Apostle says that Jacob “worshiped the top of Joseph’s staff” (Hebrews 11:21).

**VERSE 29.**—Joseph, lifting up his eyes, saw Benjamin, his uterine brother, and said: “Is this your youngest brother, of whom you told me?” He lifts his eyes when he raises his intentions from the lowest depths toward things above. He sees his uterine brother because he is sufficiently perceptive to attend to the fruit of eternal hope, begotten with him from the womb of the heavenly Church, which is truly a mother—namely, the son of the right hand. “This,” he says, “is the subtlety of holy hope, which until now I have touched only with the ear, but now, when it has first been presented, I have deserved to discover what it tastes like. May God, with whom such things have power, have mercy on you. Since you have proceeded from my understanding, you occupy with me the place and position of a son, and are worthy to be marked not by feminine sluggishness but by masculine alacrity.”

**VERSE 30.**—And he hastened, because his inner parts had been stirred over his brother, and tears burst forth; and entering his chamber, he wept. He hastens when he moves quickly toward the things above that he has once tasted. His inner parts are moved over his brother, and the zeal for inner growth is stimulated by the brotherhood of those who are already passing to heavenly things, when they rejoice with God while he remains placed amid miseries. Tears burst forth when, as the inner grace with which we are infused overflows, inward purposes come forth into visible acts, as though by force. He enters the chamber and weeps when, in the hidden place of conscience, the course of desire burns.

**VERSES 31–32.**—Then, having washed his face again, he went out, restrained himself, and said: “Set out the bread.” When these had been placed before them, Joseph was served separately, and his brothers separately; the Egyptians who were eating were also served separately—for it is unlawful for Egyptians to eat with Hebrews. He washes his face again when, after the cleansing of compunction, the power of understanding purifies itself from every desire for praise. He goes out and restrains himself when, proceeding to action, he keeps the flow of vain thought away from the favor of others. The rational faculty that dispenses the mysteries is now commanded to set out the bread, because when the mind has been completely restrained, the breads of grace and life are then placed before it to be tasted on account of their merit.

Joseph is served separately because spiritual gifts are grasped far more profoundly by understanding—hence Joseph, as a type of it, is interpreted as “increasing”—than by the movements of reason, since the brothers are begotten from the same soul. Understanding properly concerns divine things, whereas reason concerns human things. The Egyptians, that is, the disposition of secular knowledge, are entirely separate, because they know neither how to handle anything divinely nor how to discern human conduct properly. Therefore, with the Hebrews—that is, with those who pass through the world—there can be no place for an inner refreshment shared with the Egyptians. They regard such a feast as profane, for they greatly dread becoming fools in this world on account of Christ.

**VERSES 33–34.**—So they sat before him, the firstborn according to his firstborn status, and the youngest according to his age. And they were exceedingly astonished, having received portions from him; but Benjamin’s portion was greater, so that it exceeded the others by five portions. They sit before him when, while Joseph—truly “the one who has increased”—understands whatever strengths of goodness adhere to the mind, they necessarily humble themselves as he feeds them spiritually. To sit signifies to be humbled.

The firstborn adheres to his firstborn status when the inner man, who was perfectly created first in the image of God, sits beside spiritual goods, which are themselves known as primordial. For it was not bodily mortification that was enjoined upon the first man, but a spiritual matter, namely obedience. The youngest sits according to his age when the outer man fulfills the abstinence due to the body because of its still slippery condition. Its age, however, is corruption itself, which assigns limits to his sitting.

They are therefore exceedingly astonished because those who previously possessed extraordinary things both within and without are struck dumb by the miracle of this new ordering. Having received the portions that they had received from him, Benjamin’s portion was greater, because among all the things by which we temporally increase in virtue, the right hand of election is far greater than what we desire. For there is the gift of divine sonship. It exceeds by five portions whatever can be grasped by the five bodily senses. It is indeed that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Cor. 2:9), and so forth.

And they drank and were intoxicated before him: that wine, certainly, “which gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15), makes it serene through forgetfulness of evils—and this before him, in that spectacle of blessed intellectuality and eternal increase.

## CHAPTER XLIV

**VERSES 1–2.**—Joseph commanded his steward, saying: “Fill their sacks with grain, as much as they can hold, and put each man’s money at the top of his sack. But put my silver cup, and the price that he paid, at the mouth of the youngest man’s sack.” Our reason, which is also called spirit and which dispenses inner and outer things, is commanded to fill the sacks of this rough carnality with the divine grain of counsel, insofar as human nature can be supported by divine laws. It is also commanded to place at the very opening of each sack, as though at its summit, the sacred sayings of Scripture suited to each temptation, lest, when it is permitted to expand somewhat in divine things, it should forget itself and become excessively confident because of the evil movements that usually follow immediately.

Joseph’s silver cup is the intellectual and anagogical sense of sacred speech. It is placed at the mouth of the youngest man’s sack when it is inserted at the beginning of the rising despair that greatly threatens the progress of hope—namely, our more subtle and therefore more beloved son. For we embrace the youngest more dearly, and we love more what we hope for. We also call our hopes “sons.” The price that he paid is likewise placed at the mouth of the sack because the hope of present things, which confidence in future things has laid aside, is itself justly brought forward at the beginning of a false inference, as is the renunciation of the world that he made.

**VERSES 3–4.**—And it was done so. When morning came, they were sent away with their asses. They had already gone out of the city and had proceeded a little way. Morning arises when the mind is renewed by light against vices. They are sent away with their asses by divine inspiration because the inner movements, now taught from heaven, are left to act according to free choice against the absurdities of carnality, lest they become inflated by the glory of lasting peace.

They had already gone out of the city because they had stripped themselves of the circuit of this world. They had proceeded a little way because they had already drawn near to thinking about and seeking heavenly things. Then, having summoned his steward, Joseph said: “Rise and pursue the men, and when you have caught them say: ‘Why have you repaid evil for good?’”

**VERSE 5.**—“The cup that you stole is the very one from which my master drinks and in which he is accustomed to practice divination.” Understanding commands reason to rise—that is, to raise itself for the suppression of inner swelling—and to pursue the men: whatever possesses a robust condition, it must continually scrutinize through indivisible investigation. Let it say to those whom it has caught why they have repaid evil for good; let it accuse their restricted and restrained flows of arrogance, so that it may show how they have attributed to themselves anything of what was given them by God. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

“Why,” it says, “do you claim for yourselves the knowledge of intellectuality?” The silver cup is the receptacle of transparent capacity. “My master drinks from it” because from it he draws what enables him to water every recess of the mind—he to whom it is fitting to rule, even over all the powers of my reason. “In it he is accustomed to practice divination” when, relying upon heavenly prudence, he is able to be transformed with regard to the future states of eternal blessedness.

**VERSES 6–8.**—“You have done a very wicked thing, claiming for yourselves what belongs to God.” He did as he had been commanded. And having caught them one after another, he spoke to them: “Why does our lord speak in this way, as though your servants had committed so great a crime? The money that we found at the mouth of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan; how, then, could it follow that we should have stolen gold or silver from the house of your lord?”

The spirit of intellectuality obeys the command because it receives from it whatever just discernment it possesses, as from a heavenly spring. Thus the apprehension—that is, the gathering together of the excursions of thought—issues commands through the successive orders of the individual intentions. But minds that are less perceptive do not detect in themselves what the highest heights of understanding gather together.

“We,” they say, “who faithfully serve rationality and submit ourselves with you to the rule of sacred understanding: from the land of Canaan—that is, from the earthly affection in which we were humbled by vices—we take care to bring back for your examination the money of divine speech, which we recognized as something to be set against the entrance of sin as a defense. How, then, could it follow that we should wish to take for ourselves what we bring back to you?”

For it is certain that what we give to you we take away from ourselves. Therefore we have stolen neither the gold of wisdom nor the silver of knowledge from God, who is the house and dwelling place of every pious intellectuality.

**VERSE 9.**—“With whomever of your servants it is found, let him die, and we shall be servants of our lord.” If, in any movement of your inner faculties that obey you, a type of arrogance appears, let it be extinguished; thereafter we shall bend ourselves to penetrating toward divine things through a profession of perpetual humility. For such things are “hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones” (Matt. 11:25; Luke 10:21).

**VERSE 10.**—He said: “Let it be according to your word: with whomever it is found, let him be my servant; but you shall be innocent.” “In whatever disposition of mind,” he says, “this sacrilegious obstinacy appears, let that disposition be assigned to the service of reason; let the remaining innocent parties be judged free from guilt.”

**VERSE 11.**—And so, quickly putting their sacks down on the ground, each of them opened his sack. To put the sacks quickly down upon the ground is to ascribe to ourselves, with humble diligence, all the lowliness of the temptations we suffer, since we still understand ourselves to be earth. Each opens his sack when each examines the movements of his mind.

**VERSE 12.**—Having searched them, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest, he found the cup in Benjamin’s sack. He searches from the eldest to the youngest when reason examines the whole structure of its work, from visible things—which, as though by their grossness, are more prominent—to invisible and spiritual things, which are more subtly present.

The cup is found in Benjamin’s sack when excessive arrogance in knowledge and speech tends to arise in the very right hand, which is the confidence of election and glory. Such people are accustomed, as though for their security, to appropriate authorities and teaching offices for themselves.

But they, having torn their garments and loaded their asses again, returned to the town. When the vices of the spirit of the mind are subtly detected by God, the seemingly inextricable work of virtue is accused and frequently abandoned. Their garments are therefore torn when their works are severed through disgust. The asses are loaded again when the foolish movements of the flesh rejoice that they are at times weighed down by wicked anxieties. They return to the town when they take pleasure in returning to the world, which assists the devil. Of this it is said to two men: “Go into the village that is opposite you” (Matt. 21:2; Mark 11:2).

**VERSE 14.**—Judah entered first with his brothers to Joseph—for he had not yet departed from the place—and they all fell to the ground before him. When their feet are almost moving, and the steps of their nearly troubled affections are poured forth, Judah—that is, confession—first approaches the understanding, restraining within itself the associated movements of the mind. The understanding had not yet moved from the intention of God, which is its proper place; Judah therefore complains to it about his change. They all fall together before him when they humbly confess that they have acted unworthily, submitting themselves to his intellectual judgment.

**VERSE 15.**—He said: “Why did you wish to act in this way? Do you not know that there is no one like me in the knowledge of divination?” “Why,” he asks, “do you defend what you have done, even secretly, when you know that I carefully pursue each of your states of mind and judge them individually from the hidden recesses of your intentions?”

**VERSE 16.**—Judah said to him: “What shall we answer our lord, or what just thing can we put forward? God has found the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are all our lord’s servants, both we and the one with whom the cup was found.” It is as though he says: Since our life on earth is a fall and a temptation, what sentence could we offer God in our defense? Since God, through his universal presence, sees everything throughout, he also clearly investigates every wickedness of the mind through reason illumined toward him.

“Now enslave both us and the one guilty of arrogance to the fear that stands before your intellectuality, lest the state of the mind fall altogether through a repeated crime.”

**VERSE 17.**—Joseph replied: “Far be it from me to act in this way! The one who stole the cup shall be my servant; but you, go up freely to your father.” “It is not just,” he says, “that every innocent affection of the mind in any virtue should be punished. Rather, the one to whom the foulness of pride has clung must be punished by the yoke of due humility. You, therefore, free from guilt, follow the traces of the rationality that has begun to protect you.”

**VERSE 18.**—Judah came closer and said confidently: “I beg you, my lord, let your servant speak a word in your ears, and do not be angry with your servant.” Judah comes closer when the power of the mind strives to enter, through confession, the very joints and marrow of thoughts and intentions that are to be revealed. Acting more confidently from that purity, he approaches the summit of intellectuality not so much by words as by deeds.

“Since,” he says, “you rightly rule over all inner movements by the special capacity of heavenly things, let the affection of piety, which serves your offices, speak that word—not elemental, not spiritual, but intellectual, in which falsehood has no place—in the inner chambers of your understanding. Thus may its desire be fulfilled: may it perceive through the continual influx of sweetness that you are favorable toward it, so that it may rejoice to become your servant.”

**VERSE 19.**—“For you are my lord after Pharaoh.” After I abandoned the devil—or the dissipating desire for the good—I placed myself under your rule.

**VERSE 20.**—“You previously asked your servants: ‘Do you have a father or a brother?’ And we replied to you, my lord: ‘We have an old father, and a little boy who was born in his old age.’”

When we were proposing to act well, you, with reason as interpreter, asked us about the one whom we would judge to be granted to us by inner fatherhood. We replied that we wished to receive reason, although old and inclined toward weakness; because it grows old and appears to be approaching destruction unless it comes to life again through you, it is compelled, on account of its own condition, to retain a still tender and feeble hope.

“His uterine brother is dead, and his mother alone has him.” The uterine brother dies when, in the mind that is the mother of two hopes, the inner affection of worldly hope is entirely extinguished. His mother alone has him when the mind—or rather the good will of the mind—cherishes exclusively the worship of heavenly hope.

“But his father loves him alone” because our spirit, which, as its author, has begotten it through its processes of reasoning, awaits and directs itself toward the fruit of divine hope alone.

**VERSE 21.**—“You said to your servants: ‘Bring him to me, and I will set my eyes upon him.’” He says that he should be brought to him when understanding commands hope to be advanced through the processes of thought toward the sense of highest contemplation. He sets his eyes upon him when, through intellectual intentions, he protects the desire of hope itself.

**VERSE 22.**—“We suggested to my lord: ‘The boy cannot leave his father; for if he leaves him, he will die.’” The movements of inner tenderness, conscious of the soul, declare that hope cannot leave reason—which still moves among human things—since, because of its youth, it lacks the strength to use the solid food of contemplation. For if it abandons what is moderate and raises itself too high, it rises up as though dead and without substance.

**VERSE 23.**—“He said: ‘If your youngest brother does not come with you, you shall not see my face again.’” That is: Unless you take hope as your companion in contemplation—the hope that must be your subtle means of walking toward God—you will never attain knowledge of me, which is signified by the face, that is, experience of inward beauty, according to the more advanced condition of those who make progress.

**VERSE 24.**—“When we had gone up to your servant our father, we told him everything that my lord had said.” They go up to the father when thoughts, intending to consult her about each matter, seek their own higher reason. They tell him everything that that lord says when they examine, together with reason, whether the things they grasp from intellectuality, in view of their own mediocrity, ought to be undertaken. Understanding is lord of reason insofar as the former discusses heavenly things while the latter discusses human things.

**VERSE 25.**—“Our father said: ‘Return and buy a little grain for us.’” The father commands them to return in order to buy grain when they are recalled from the effort to undertake higher things by an excessively human discernment, as though to moderation, so that at least at the price of faith in divine inspiration they may obtain nourishment—and only a little, so that they may attain the degree of tepid moderation that they prefer.

**VERSE 26.**—“We said to him: ‘We cannot go unless our youngest brother descends with us. We shall depart together; otherwise, if he is absent, we do not dare to see the face of the man.’” They reply that they cannot go unless the youngest brother descends with them because, gathering the inner movements from the same reason, they declare that they cannot inwardly desire to be fully refreshed—for *proficisci* signifies to desire or strive—unless the support of divine hope, which must be raised from this place energetically toward higher things, descends from every earthly ambition.

They depart together when one lives rationally and hopes only for what is fitting to blessed eternity. They do not dare to see the face of the man in his absence because, for those who lack confidence in hoped-for blessedness, aspiring to knowledge through contemplation is exceedingly presumptuous.

**VERSES 27–29.**—He replied: “You know that my wife bore me two sons. One went out, and you said: ‘A beast devoured him’; and he has not appeared to this day. If you take this one also from me, and something happens to him on the way, you will bring my gray hairs down to the underworld in sorrow.”

“Do not,” he says, “undertake greater things for yourselves. For you know that two desires are present in the will that has been joined to me, reason, by the right of marriage. It is called a wife because, being subject to it, the spirit is made fertile by its seed.

“One goes out when the worldly desire, unable to endure the charity of duality, is carried outward to seek external things alone. You said that he had been devoured by a beast when you attributed to the devil’s ferocity, for your own excuse, what you had done through the human inclination toward evil, so to speak. For it is clear that the devil is signified in Scripture by the name ‘beast’ because of his savagery.

“He has not appeared to this day because he does not rise above the earthly things into which he is immersed. If, then, you carry away this small portion of hope, which I have obtained either by rising again from these things or through certain good works, by lifting it up toward what is unbearable, you will bring my gray hairs—my changeability, frailty, and proximity to ruin—down to the underworld of despair. I grieve insofar as rationality still glimmers but cannot resist.

“These are the words of a spirit that prefers to grow lukewarm in a human manner rather than burn in a divine one.”

**VERSES 30–31.**—“Therefore, if I enter your servant my father and the boy is absent—for his life depends upon the life of this one—and he sees that he is not with us, he will die.” Judah enters the father when the power of the mind returns to the inner chambers of the spirit, which ought to serve the offices of supreme understanding, through repentance and confession. “If,” he says, “I bring confession and repentance over what has been wrongly thought before reason, whose movement I am as though its son, and offer no fruit of hope in return for so great a labor—since the life of reason depends upon living hope—and if, when it sees the emptiness of despair among us who are the effects of its own character, it is itself deprived of life by the warmth of living love, it will die.”

**VERSES 32–33.**—“I myself shall properly be your servant, for I received this one into my keeping and pledged myself, saying: ‘Unless I bring him back, I shall be guilty of sin against my father forever.’ Therefore I shall remain your servant, in the service of my lord, and let the boy go up with his brothers.”

“I,” he says, “shall be specially subjected, beyond the other movements of the mind, to your service of perpetual fear, always confessing my error. Because of the hope of obtaining pardon and grace, I accepted the faith of confession and promised that, unless I held that hope steadfastly until the manifestation of actual truth, I should be judged guilty of sin and disobedience before that reason which urges good conduct.

“I shall therefore remain in your penitential service, so that the mystical boy may rise from his lowest tenderness by the elevation of inner virtue, together with the other powers of the inner man, toward the summit of tasting your intellectuality.”

**VERSE 34.**—“For I cannot return to my father without the boy, lest I stand as a witness to the calamity that will overwhelm my father.” A return to the father without the boy is the gathering of thoughts into the spirit, which is the father of inner things, lifelessly, amid weak works and without any gain of good hope. There the witness of the father’s calamity stands when he sees himself miserably subject to spiritual sickness and does not resist.

## CHAPTER XLV

**VERSE 1.**—Joseph could no longer restrain himself before all those standing nearby. Therefore he commanded everyone to go outside, and that no outsider should be present at their mutual recognition. Let us understand the words spoken above by Judah to his father in this way—not that any power of confession exists without reason as its parent, but that the spirit itself, which is also called reason, either divinely arouses itself within itself in its different states through an impulse of the mind, or buries itself humanly through the enticement of the flesh.

Joseph could not restrain himself while many stood before him because the intellectual power, through a certain pious vehemence of divine inspiration, was rising up against its own lukewarmness, while many forces of virtue came forward ready to meet it. He commands everyone to go outside when he strives to eliminate from the heart everything that obstructs it. Otherwise, an outsider would be present at the mutual recognition if he allowed any part of the opposing power to remain in the conscience as it hastened toward recognition of the truth.

**VERSES 2–3.**—And he raised his voice with weeping. The Egyptians heard it, and the entire household of Pharaoh. And he said to his brothers: “I am Joseph. Is our father still alive?” His brothers could not answer, shaken by exceedingly great terror.

He raises his voice with weeping when he commends the cry of inner desire—which alone, according to the title of the psalm, sounds in the ears of God from the anxiety of the poor (Ps. 101:1)—through the grace of outward beneficence. For weeping descends from the head to the face, and when the wine that “gladdens God and human beings” (Judg. 9:13) has made the human heart radiant, it flows even toward the brightening of the outer man’s face through oil (Ps. 103:15), that is, through the sweetness of inward grace. The pious qualities of minds are accustomed to shine most graciously in faces.

He raises his voice who exalts desire from the depths. The Egyptians and the entire household of Pharaoh hear it when, after the heavenly desire has been stirred within us, they obey patiently, whether they wish to or not, together with the worldly desires and all the other vices of the world. For the world is the house of Pharaoh.

Then he testifies that he is Joseph because, once the disturbances have been silenced and intellectuality has been joined to rationality, the fullness of heavenly increase is revealed. “Does your father,” he says, “the spirit of your interiority, truly live after it has reached the power of intellectuality?” The brothers cannot answer, terrified, because the inner movements, stunned by so sudden a change, fear to report anything certain about the present condition of their own state, being ignorant of future outcomes.

**VERSE 4.**—He said to them kindly: “Come closer to me.” When they had come near, he said: “I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold in Egypt.” “Cast away,” he says, “your distrust of the future state, and draw near to heavenly wisdom’s kindness. When you have approached it with an inward approach of devotion, then you will understand that I am not alien to you, since it belongs to you and to human nature to know heavenly things and to desire to be increased by them—things that once you were not ashamed to hand over to worldly forgetfulness and negligence.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Do not be afraid, and do not let it seem harsh to you that you sold me in these regions; for God sent me before you for your salvation into Egypt.” You should not fall into the evil of despair because, for the sake of an outward desire, you once ceased to desire inward things. It happened for your salvation that you first experienced darkness and Egyptian tribulation, so that at last you might know more fervently how to seek the way of true freedom and light.

**VERSES 6–7.**—“For two years there has been famine in the land, and five years still remain in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved upon the earth and might have food to live.”

The famine of two years occurs when the poverty of the earthly heart consumes whatever there is of light and integrity in intention and thought. Five years still remain in which there is neither plowing nor harvest when the works administered outwardly through the five senses so flow away that neither good is practiced nor any care taken for the harvest of eternal recompense.

God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved upon the earth, placing me before the gaze of your heart so that, ruling over the earth of the body, you might be preserved against every temptation and might be raised up vitally by the divine food of consolation.

**VERSE 8.**—“It was not by your plan but by God’s will that I was sent. He made me as a father to Pharaoh, lord of his entire household, and ruler throughout all the land of Egypt.” It did not happen through your foresight but through God’s dispensation, so that my being brought into Egypt might become a means of salvation and my fall an occasion of restoration. He established me as father—not in effect but in authority and excellence—over the dissipating desire or the devil, so that it might be subject to me; he made me ruler over the earthly body in which we are confined and lord over the entire desire of this world.

The word “father” is used for “author” and “teacher,” as the present book itself bears witness, where at the beginning Jubal is called “the father of those who play the flute and the organ” (Gen. 4:21).

**VERSE 9.**—“Hurry and go up to my father, and say to him: ‘Thus says your son Joseph: God has made me lord of the whole land of Egypt.’”

The father of intellectuality is our reason, or our spirit, because understanding is recognized as proceeding from reason, although it is specially illumined by the light of intellectuality—just as reason itself proceeds from the soul, although the soul is wholly bright with the sole honor of reason.

They hurry upward to him when, through each successive degree of inner advancement, they raise themselves from every irrationality. They announce, by Joseph’s command, that he rules over all Egypt when the movements of the inner senses, inspired intelligibly, are urged to confer joyfully with reason itself and with the reason set over them, concerning how, through the unexpected gift of God, they may direct the whole of Egypt—that is, the works of darkness.

**VERSES 10–11.**—“Descend to me; do not delay. You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me—you, your sons, and your sons’ sons, your sheep and your herds, and everything that you possess. There I shall feed you. For five years of famine still remain, lest you perish.”

If you desire to reach knowledge of me, humble yourself and do not wish to postpone your descent from day to day.

> Whoever is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow.  
> —*Ov. R. am.* 94

Goshen is interpreted as “approaching the touching of them.” Therefore whoever governs and orders his body, as though it were his land, so that he may strive through discernment to approach the touching—that is, the temptation—of carnal impulses, dwells in the land of Goshen.

According to the usage of divine Scripture, the word “dwells” is often used for “rules,” as in: “Dwell in the land, and you shall be fed by its riches” (Ps. 36:3).

Therefore you, reason, together with the examination of the thoughts and intentions subject to you, and of the other dispositions of the mind as though they were sons—and the hopes of reward for works, which are the sons of sons—together with your sheep, namely weak things, and your herds, namely the strong works of virtues, and whatever is worthy of reason’s possession, will be nourished by closeness to me and fed by my influx.

For the weakness of hunger still remains in thought. Therefore provide for your danger, lest the integrity of all continence and good purpose be led, with an equal failure, all the way to the gates of the outer man, where it will openly perish. For thus the house of conscience is extinguished, and the gains of virtue possessed within or without are lost.

**VERSE 12.**—“Behold, your eyes and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see that my mouth is speaking with you.” With the intention of your rational senses now directed and with the contemplation of my brother, the son of the right hand—that is, of future blessedness, to which the virtue of intellectuality is inwardly and naturally related—you see, that is, you believe, that I am speaking these things to you through the mouth of the whole of rationality.

**VERSE 13.**—“Tell my father of all my glory and of everything that you have seen in Egypt. Hurry and bring him to me.” “You,” he says, “shoots of the inner heart, make known to the spirit of intellectuality my glory. And, so that it may receive it more gratefully, set before it the misery of Egypt, and avoid sluggishness in repeatedly suggesting these things.”

**VERSES 14–15.**—When he had embraced Benjamin and fallen upon his neck, he wept; and Benjamin likewise wept upon his neck. He kissed all his brothers and wept over each one. After this they dared to speak with him.

He embraces Benjamin when the fervor of understanding expands the human being as far as the power of action. Since an embrace is made with the arms and binds lovingly, it indicates that charity is to be understood together with good works.

In the neck, steadfastness of counsel is signified. Food is admitted through the neck, the voice is sent forth through it; it is also offered to others, and through it what is offered is suggested by the one who offers it. He therefore returns to Benjamin’s neck when the love of understanding is continually bent toward the counsel of heavenly hope.

He weeps there, and Benjamin likewise weeps upon his neck, when understanding is moved by the expectation of hope and hope is pierced by consultation with intellectuality. He kisses his brothers and weeps over each of them when, through the spirit of wisdom, he joins the inner movements of the mind to himself and, attaching them to the progress of each, burns with an affection of piety.

For those whom we kiss are often imbued with our spirit and moistened with our saliva. Since they themselves taste spiritually, they make the intellectual understanding itself into a taste through the saliva of wisdom.

**VERSE 16.**—The report was heard and spread abroad through the royal court: “Joseph’s brothers have come.” And Pharaoh and all his household rejoiced.

It is heard in the royal court when this change in the affection of the carnal mind resounds heavily and is mockingly celebrated as something that is soon to be overthrown. It is called a court because the devil chiefly dwells there and walks about like a king.

His joy, and that of the vices that become his followers, seems to arise from this: the more fervent the state of the mind that generally precedes, the more rabid the desire and the greater the opportunity for sinning that subsequently follows.

[Note: The word is derived from *assecla*, which is sometimes also written *assecula*.]

**VERSES 17–18.**—Pharaoh said to Joseph that he should command his brothers: “Load your beasts and go into the land of Canaan; take your father and your kindred from there and come to me. I shall give you all the good things of Egypt, so that you may eat the marrow of the land.”

Pharaoh speaks to Joseph and through him attempts to command the brothers when affectivity undertakes, through its enticements, to dissipate intellectuality and tries through it to subjugate the lower states of thought.

“Load your beasts”: occupy your bodies with the cares and anxieties of the world. That “beasts” signifies bodies is attested by the Psalm: “He did not spare their souls from death, but enclosed their beasts in death” (Ps. 77:50).

“Go into the land of Canaan”: attend to the business of profit that will be useful to you; for Canaan is interpreted as “merchant.” “Take your father from there”: care for worldly things with the body alone, while allowing reason to remain free for God. “Take your kindred also and come to me”: raise the growth of your virtues from the world, and, now secure concerning your former way of life, turn your hearts confidently toward undertaking certain things according to me—that is, according to worldly affection. When you have used the world with such moderation, then, with an abundance of every good thing, you will taste on the innermost palate the marrow of all earthly usefulness—which is pleasure—and discover what sweetness it contains within.

### Verses 19–20

“Command also that they take wagons from the land of Egypt for transporting their little ones and their wives, and say: ‘Take your father and hurry, coming as quickly as possible. Do not leave anything of your household goods, because all the wealth of Egypt shall be yours.’”

Wagons are taken from Egypt when the revolving movements of worldly cycles are cherished; these are compared in the Gospel to millstones turned by an ass (Matt. XVIII, 16). Wives and little ones are transported in them because fragile wills, together with weak works, are conveyed by these means into mystical Egypt. He commands them to go with their father and all their household goods, since he does not permit any purpose or pursuit of virtue to be retained by the seduced reason through which it might be redeemed from Egypt. “In this way,” he says, “worldly things will be available to you, so that you will not grieve over having lost spiritual things.”

[Col. 0306A]

### Verses 21–22

“The sons of Israel did as they had been commanded. Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharaoh’s command, and provisions for the journey. To each he ordered two garments to be brought; but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver together with five finest garments.”

The rational movements that were formerly directed with God—for this is what “Israel” is interpreted to mean—obey the command of the corrupted intellect. He gives wagons when he supplies the materials of external circling, according as either affection or the devil commands. He provides provisions for the journey when he brings the consolations of emerging fortunes, so as to entice the person more strongly into the excursion of desire.

He brings two garments to each when he promises each state, amid worldly activities, sacred restraints both of thought and of action. He gives Benjamin three hundred pieces of silver when he boasts that he will give his understanding, memory, and practice—without which, in these numbers, the silver of divine knowledge certainly does not shine—as a support for hope or election. He also gives five finest garments when he falsely promises himself freedom from passion and purity in the external senses.

[Col. 0306B]

### Verse 23

“Sending his father the same amount of money and clothing, he added ten asses to him, which were to carry some of all the wealth of Egypt, and as many she-asses, bearing wheat and loaves of bread for the journey.”

He sends his father the same amount because he promises the spirit no less discrimination and knowledge, as well as holiness, than he had given to the wretched certainty of hope and future blessedness. He adds ten asses to him when, under a false love of the Trinity, he supplies that same spirit with the body, which consists of four elements, and the soul, which is distinguished by three things—understanding, will, and affection. Thus he does not so much give the ass to the spirit as deceitfully add it to him.

These animals carry not the wealth of Jerusalem but the wealth of Egypt, because whatever goods are proposed are contractions of darkness. As many she-asses carry wheat for the journey and loaves of bread when the wanton movements of body and soul, under the feigned love of God who is Trinity, carry the word of God—superficially, as if on a journey—by which they feed others while remaining themselves hungry; and when they hypocritically display loaves of graces and divine gifts useful not to themselves but to others.

[Col. 0306C]

### Verse 24

“So he dismissed his brothers, and as they departed he said to them: ‘Do not become angry on the way.’”

He dismisses his brothers when he abandons the inner gatherings to their own judgment, without any opposition from reason or intellectuality. He prohibits those departing from becoming angry on the way because he warns those who have gone out from the right intention not to fail, amid their pursuit of avarice, through any opposition of sadness to their appetite for present joys.

### Verse 25

“Those who went up from Egypt came into the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. And they announced to him, saying: ‘Joseph lives, and he rules over all the land of Egypt.’”

They go up from Egypt when, turning away from contemplation of inner distress or tribulation, they move into earthly transactions. Or rather, this may be understood as follows: After receiving the counsel of evil relaxation, one goes up from an Egyptian thought to reason in the land of Canaan—where he now yearns for the world—when the entire inner company is led to examine the condition of the already-failing soul.

“Joseph,” they say, “has been increased through understanding and lives vitally in himself; hence it is necessary that the earthliness of Egyptian blindness be subject to him.” It is as though they add: “Why then are you still entangled in what you left earlier?”

### Verse 27

“When Jacob heard this, he awoke as if from a deep sleep, yet he did not believe them. But they, for their part, reported the whole sequence of events.”

He hears when he understands the thoughts that are reasoning. He awakens from a deep sleep when he rouses himself from the excessive torpor already conceived. Yet he does not believe them because, after these dissipations of the will, our spirit loses confidence in the life of intellectuality. They, for their part, report the sequence of events when, accusing on one side and excusing on the other, they lay bare the condition of the mind amid temptations.

### Verse 28

“When he had seen the wagons and all that he had sent, his spirit revived, and he said: ‘It is enough for me if my son Joseph still lives; I shall go and see him before I die.’”

He sees the wagons and the other things that are sent when, with deep examination of the heart, he reviews how falsely the revolutions of glory and the imitations of restraint are being introduced. His spirit therefore revives from this, because he gathers hope of inner life from subtly discerning whatever in himself ought to be reproved.

“‘It is enough for me,’ he says, ‘as an incentive to rise again, if the keenness of understanding remains vigorous. Therefore I shall go forth from the purpose of inertness to be sharpened in the light of intelligibility, before I am extinguished by the deadly postponement of change.’”

## Chapter XLVI

[Col. 0307C]

### Verses 1–2

“Israel set out with all that he had and came to the Well of the Oath. There he sacrificed victims to the God of his father Isaac, and heard him calling him in a vision by night.”

Israel sets out with all that he had when spirituality, tending toward the desire for progress, is directed with God—for Israel means “directed by God”—and when all the exercises of piety are represented together with it.

He comes to the Well of the Oath when, relying on the examination of good pursuits, our spirit reaches that hidden fountain of divine wisdom where the laws of the whole religion are established. Hence he sacrifices victims to the God of his father Isaac because, having tasted the savor of inner sweetness—or rather, of the living well—he offers God victories over vices: the God of the supercelestial citizens, who are his fathers and forerunners toward the laughter of eternal joy.

Then he hears God calling him in a vision when, through the comparison of graces, he understands his election, by which he is called to glory. The vision itself is mystical, and is also hearing. The one calling therefore says: “Jacob, Jacob.” The repetition of the call—which also signifies “supplanter”—changes the spirit, first toward the overthrow of the vices in which we formerly grew old, and then toward the overthrow of the deadly security that we conceived as though it were virtue. To this call he must reply without delay, “Behold, here I am,” by obeying it.

[Col. 0308A]

### Verses 3–4

“God said to him: ‘I am the mighty God of your father. Do not fear; go down into Egypt, because there I shall make you into a great nation. I shall go down with you there, and I shall bring you back when you return. Joseph also will place his hand upon your eyes.’”

Why, you ask, do you fear the overthrow of every harmful thing, when you know that the strong God can also strengthen and fortify the powers of your reason? You believe him to be the company of your former fathers, the heavenly one who has already triumphed over these things with the greatest strength, and whom you imitate as Father.

“Humble yourself in the valley of sorrow, which is Egypt, because such a descent will produce for you a great kind of virtue. I shall descend with you,” for I am joined to the humble through the gift of grace. “And from there I shall bring you back when you return”; from the tribulations that confine you—that is, from Egypt—I shall raise you to the glory of freedom from passion.

Joseph—that is, the increase of intellectuality—while you dwell in Egypt, will protect and guard the eyes of your intentions with the hand of his authority and power, under the proper guise of honor.

[Col. 0308B]

### Verses 5–7

“Jacob arose from the Well of the Oath, and his sons carried him, together with the little ones and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry the old man. They also carried everything that he had possessed in the land of Canaan. He came into Egypt with all his offspring: his sons and grandsons, his daughters, and the whole progeny together.”

He rises from the Well of the Oath when our spirit grows from the innermost fountains of divine thought, through which alone the purposes of holiness are strengthened.

But when he rises, his sons carry him in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent, because the thoughts and works that proceed from us at the beginning of conversion are governed not so much by us as by the fluctuating condition of the former life, introduced by the devil. They govern the old, unstable, and downward-inclined spirit by means of the wives of wantonness and desire, or the little ones of weak execution.

Everything that he had possessed in the land of Canaan accompanies him because, willingly or unwillingly, we carry with us whatever lightness we had in worldly conduct. We come into Egypt with all our offspring when, descending into Egypt—that is, into the confession of knowledge of ourselves—we bring forth everything generated from our carnality.

“Offspring” may also mean the will itself, which we have made entire, since we are not without goodwill toward any good things whatsoever. Sons are our works; grandsons—the sons, that is, of sons—are the fruits and rewards of works, though still held in hope. Daughters are whatever is done with feminine softness, together with the entire mixed progeny of administration, namely, of good and evil things.

[Col. 0308C]

### Verse 27

“All the souls of the house of Jacob that entered Egypt were seventy.”

Everyone can see that seven times ten makes seventy. The soul, however, is understood as nothing other than animality. The denary pertains to the Decalogue; the septenary pertains to the course of the present world.

Thus, with animality placed between these two things opposed to it—God’s law and the world—the spirit, bearing a heavy burden of itself, approaches Egypt, that is, the still-dark hiding places of the mind. For “the spirit is willing and consents to the law, but the flesh is weak and resists” (Matt. XXVI, 41).

### Verse 8

“Jacob sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph, to announce him; and Joseph met him in Gessen.”

If we wish, through the supplanting of sin, to reach the summit of understanding by means of confession—for this is what the name Judah signifies—we must anticipate his knowledge through confession. We therefore rightly send this intermediary ahead, and soon perceive it to be present nearby, after we have cleansed our consciences by confessing.

For Gessen is said to mean “nearness.” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

[Col. 0309B]

### Verse 29

“When he had arrived there, Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to meet his father at the same place.”

We have already said above that Gessen is also interpreted as “approaching their touch.” The spirit, no longer weak, comes near through the subtlety of examination to the suggestions by which the allurements of vices touch us. Joseph harnesses his chariot and goes up to meet his father because, through fear of God, the intellectuality of all his wisdom, gathered into a single force, rises to bring aid to the spirit—that is, to reason, whose offspring is noble—for the overthrow of the devil’s kingdoms.

“And when he saw him, he fell upon his neck and wept in his embrace.”

### Verse 30

“His father said to Joseph: ‘Now I shall die happy, because I have seen your face and leave you alive.’”

He sees him when the intellect itself displays to him the usefulness and excellence of reason illumined by God. He falls upon his neck when he gratefully applauds the counsel of his spiritual voice. He weeps in his embrace when he manifests, through the evidence of works of piety, the ardor of his inner desire by which he is bound to God and to the spiritual realm. For tears flow to the face from an inner movement.

“‘Now I shall die happy,’” he says, “because, having experienced the sweetness of heaven, the spirit now gladly desires to be completely extinguished with respect to worldly glory.” For the spirit rejoices that it has reached the face—that is, that most radiant appearance of understanding—and does not grieve because it has died to the world, since through that death it sees the inner person rising more vigorously above all else.

[Col. 0309C]

### Verses 31–32

“He spoke to his brothers and to all his father’s household: ‘I shall go up and announce to Pharaoh, and I shall say to him: My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. They are shepherds of sheep and take care to feed flocks. They have brought with them their sheep and cattle and everything they have been able to possess.’”

He speaks to his brothers and to his father’s household when the intellect reasons with the strong dispositions of the soul and with the mind itself, which is the house of the spirit.

He goes up and announces to Pharaoh the arrival of his father and brothers when our innermost self, bringing everything we have mentioned up from the depths, challenges the devil with great effectiveness, through the mighty determination of its vows, as though by means of a messenger.

Canaan is said to mean “being ashamed.” “They are ashamed,” he says, “to have pursued earthly things, since they see that they have obtained no fruit whatsoever from their pursuit. From now on they wish to live intelligently, and manfully to perform and nourish sheep—that is, works of simplicity. They do not pursue the divisions of desire and envy or the scandals of pride, but exercises of virtue that cohere peaceably and as a flock in humility, and are therefore worthy to be nourished and tended.”

They permit no remnant of carnal license to remain in them. They have brought their sheep and cattle—their weak and strong deeds, and whatever of their own could be corrected according to the rule—under the power of heavenly knowledge.

[Col. 0310A]

### Verses 33–34

“When he calls you and says: ‘What is your occupation?’ you shall answer: ‘We, your servants, are shepherds, from our childhood until the present, both we and our fathers.’ You shall say this so that you may dwell in the land of Gessen, because all shepherds of sheep are detestable to the Egyptians.”

Pharaoh calls us and asks about our occupation when he strikes us with temptations, and the devil himself cunningly investigates the reasons for our works and the works themselves.

But we must answer manfully concerning the shepherding of simplicity. Although, through the dullness of an infantile spirit, we have served him by panting after the present and neglecting the future—namely, through our principal movements and the whole paternity of the spirit—we must nevertheless strive with all our strength so that the land of inner cultivation, by which we stand against the touch of vices, may remain freely available for us to inhabit and govern; and this all the more diligently because worldly people everywhere abhor pursuits of innocence and purity.

The matters that follow have already been explained; let us set forth what has not been explained.

166 **CHAPTER XLVII**

[Col. 0310C]

### Verses 2–3

“He also placed five of his brothers, the last ones, before the king. The king asked them: ‘What is your occupation?’”

It should nevertheless be noted that Joseph is not said here to have gone up, but to have entered Pharaoh’s presence. For when we have ascended from the sluggishness of vice to the step of virtue, we enter, as it were, into Pharaoh’s presence, when, faithfully breaking into his inner chambers through the powers of understanding, we appropriate for ourselves those things which he had cruelly and tyrannically held within us.

The five men, the last of Joseph’s brothers, are five final virtues—virtues of great manliness, acquired, so to speak, only through the labors of the utmost degree, and which come to the aid of the intellect with a certain fraternal assistance. They are final because scarcely anyone either wishes or is able to reach them.

The first is diligence in reading; the second, the care of discussing what has been less understood with more learned people; the third, vigilant memory for retaining what has been heard; the fourth, humble reverence toward every teacher; the fifth, complete contempt for worldly glory.

When we have truly placed these men before the dispenser, we shall certainly besiege all his cunning through their unanimity. Yet he asks what occupation they have when, at times, discouraging them from the study of Sacred Scripture, he rebukes them by reproaching, in a certain way, their pious concern: why do they persist so earnestly in acquiring knowledge?

“‘We are shepherds of sheep,’” they say, “‘both we and our fathers.’” This means: “We have undertaken to nourish fruitful and simple pursuits, because our fathers and authors in both understanding and spirit, the truest of all, have taught us these things.”

[Col. 0311A]

### Verse 4

“We have come to sojourn in your land, because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since famine has grown severe in the land of Canaan; and we ask that you command us to be your servants in the land of Gessen.”

In the world over which you rule, we have chosen not to cling but to sojourn, because the pasture of carnal wantonness—which, according to what Job says, is said to be produced for you by the mountains of Behemoth (Job XL, 10)—does not belong to us, who are made members of the flock through the glue of divine fear. For through the flowing things of lust, the mind is not filled with satisfaction but with a doubled and terrible hunger.

The land of Canaan, according to the meaning of the name, is not the land of truth but of instability and shame; whoever drinks from its water is always thirsty. We are indeed your servants because we confess that we have served you. For, according to Jeremiah, the Lord visits with famine and pestilence the nation and kingdom that does not serve Nebuchadnezzar (Jer. XVII, 8).

[Col. 0311B]

Therefore command that we be in the land of Gessen—that is, do not presume to oppose us any longer, even if you convict us of our former servitude, which we have renounced—but let us dwell in a land not of weakness but of solidity, where we may approach the touch of deceitful vices, where there is the nearness of true discernment.

Note and recall what we said above concerning the name Gessen. The request that he command is the rational response to suggestions, asking that they desist.

These five men may also be understood as the five senses, which are opposed through the authority of the intellect, when they manfully restrain themselves before Pharaoh.

[Col. 0311C]

### Verses 5–6

“Then the king said to Joseph: ‘Your father and your brothers have come to you. The land of Egypt is before you; make them dwell in the best soil of the land, and give them the land of Gessen. And if you know that there are industrious men among them, appoint them as shepherds of my livestock.’”

The king’s goodwill toward Joseph is nothing other than weakness and inability to attack.

“‘The earthliness of the world,’” he says, “‘is before you,’” that is, it is subject to your examination. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “All who trouble me are before you” (Ps. LXVIII, 21).

And since everything external is subject to your judgment, place the inner movements in the best soil—the chief state of all solidity—by the contiguous discernment of their temptations, which is Gessen. And if anything of diabolical dullness, which is “my livestock,” has slipped into you, subject it to the discipline of manly diligence.

This is the malignity that speaks through its effects: not converted, but compelled to cease and overcome.

[Col. 0311D]

### Verses 7–9

“After this Joseph brought his father before the king and placed him in his presence. He blessed him, and when the king asked him: ‘How many are the days of the years of your life?’ he answered: ‘The days of the years of my sojourning are one hundred and thirty years, few and evil; they have not reached the days of my fathers, in which they sojourned.’”

Joseph brings his father before the king when the fervor of intellectuality advances reason to penetrate the devil’s deceptions. He places him before the king when he raises reason against him through the strength of justice.

He blesses him when, in accordance with the counsels of sacred utterance, he answers his assault.

He asks how many are the days of the years of his life when he strikes the mind concerning the perfection of virtues. For “days” signify the brightness of works, while “years” signify their multiplicity.

But Jacob sets against the impulses of pride a sojourning of one hundred and thirty years. For although perfection—which is represented by the hundred—may be present in some, six times five, that is, thirty, which signifies the mind’s slipping from the solidity of the inner person into the vanity of the senses, presents itself when the mind sojourns away from itself.

The days are few and evil because virtue is so much smaller as it is more polluted by frequent invasions of evil. For this reason it cannot equal the magnificence of the Fathers, whose examples it seeks, and whose perseverance in the very place of sojourning endured with much greater strength.

167 [Col. 0312A]

### Verse 10

“After blessing the king, he went out.”

We bless Pharaoh when we turn to the rule of piety the things he introduced for our dissipation and harm, and force them to serve victory and usefulness. Then we go out when we emerge into the freedom of reason from the deceptive snare that he holds out.

### Verses 11–12

“Joseph gave his father and his brothers a possession in Egypt, in the best soil of the land, Ramesses, as Pharaoh had commanded. And he fed them, and the whole household of his father, supplying provisions to each.”

Ramesses is said to mean “pasture.” Nothing is better than the solidity of the soil—that is, of a mind that is cultivable and fertile—because there inner pasture is found.

There Joseph gives his father and brothers a possession in Egypt, because through this refection, not superficial but stable, the true increase of intellectuality grants strength to the spirit and to all its movements, as though to its sons, so that it may subject body and soul to the possession of the law of the mind; and it grants this even in the present age.

He feeds his father’s household, supplying provisions to each, when he strengthens the conscience, which is governed by being inhabited by reason, and provides each of its states with counsel by which it may be refreshed.

Pharaoh commands these things because the devil, unable to obstruct them by the power of our purpose, permits them to happen freely, whether he wishes it or not.

[Col. 0312C]

### Verses 13–14

“For there was no bread in the whole world, and famine had oppressed the land, especially Egypt and Canaan. From these he gathered all the money in exchange for grain and brought it into the king’s treasury.”

There is no bread in the whole world because the whole of our perfection, signified by the world, is in no way capable of obtaining the refreshment of inner grace.

And what will secular Egypt, which is ignorance—for it is darkness itself—and Canaan, which is commerce and shame, do if the world of the elect does not prevail over famine?

It is therefore necessary that, from Egypt and Canaan—that is, from prudence and from the shameful acts that we once practiced—he vigorously exact the money of divine knowledge.

We understand the treasury as the unfailing and, in a certain sense, inexhaustible memory of sacred eloquence. For bronze is both a durable and resonant metal. Intellectuality brings money into this treasury of the king, not because the king possesses it, but because it resounds with evident clarity in the ears of the sons of pride.
