For whatever knowledge it reaches, intellectuality does not preserve for empty eloquence, but so that it may present it from memory against Pharaoh’s persuasions.

[Col. 0313A]

### Verses 15–16

“When the money of the buyers had failed, all Egypt came to Joseph, saying: ‘Give us bread. Why should we die before you, since our money has failed?’ He said: ‘Bring your livestock, and I shall give you food in exchange for them, if you have no price.’”

The buyers’ prices fail when either knowledge of memory or memory of knowledge is lacking. Yet all Egypt asks for bread because the needs of worldly misery themselves indicate that they cry out for the gift of heavenly graces.

It is as though it says: “You see yourself perishing; why does not your natural capacity, O intelligence of whatever kind, resist death and ignorance?” [The Latin wording is defective.]

“‘Submit your dullness to me,’” he says, “‘and receive food of divine consolation. From this it will be counted for you as the price of knowledge.’”

### Verse 17

“When they had brought them, he gave them food in exchange for their horses, oxen, and asses, and sustained them that year in exchange for their livestock.”

We subject to the intellect the horses of pride, the oxen of foolishness and sluggishness, and also the asses of lust; and in the transparent days of humility, wisdom, cleverness, and chastity, we receive a full year of integrity.

“‘You who have no silver,’” he says, “‘hurry, buy and eat through faith and pious works’” (Isa. LV, 1).

[Col. 0313B]

### Verses 18–19

“They came also in the second year and said: ‘We do not conceal from our lord that, when the money failed, the livestock also failed; nor is it hidden from you that, apart from our bodies and our land, we have nothing. Why then should we die while you watch? Both we and our land shall be yours.’”

The first year, in which the livestock are given, is the first training of conversion, when the less-than-natural and, in a certain sense, bestial life is condemned.

The second is the advancement of pious will. Here, when those in need lack the money of divine eloquence but scorn brutish pursuit, the very material of the body, together with what is necessary to it, is already taken away from the wills and subjected to the intellect; and every earthliness of its affections is banished according to the intellect’s judgment.

“‘When you foresee what must be done,’” they say, “‘now that the movements of animality have been conquered, why do you permit those who obey to perish? Do not therefore allow us, while living, to descend into hell. We shall belong to you in the affection and effectiveness of the body. Buy us into royal servitude, and provide seed, lest, when the cultivator perishes, the land be reduced to desolation.’”

Spend on us the price of inner instruction, so that you may exact from us a confession of the service that we spent upon the devil; and provide the seeds of good will, lest, when the spirit lacks a cultivator through the emptiness caused by him, the cultivability and fertility of the heart be reduced to desolation, so that it lacks God as its inhabitant and bears no fruit of action.

[Col. 0313D]

### Verses 20–21

“So Joseph bought the whole land of Egypt, as each person sold his possessions because of the severity of the famine. And he subjected it to Pharaoh, together with all its peoples, from the remotest boundaries of Egypt to its farthest limits, except the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king. To them also fixed provisions were supplied from the public storehouses, and therefore they were not compelled to sell their possessions.”

Joseph buys the whole land of Egypt when, through the clarity of understanding, he subjects secular darkness to the intellect. Each person sells his possessions when the five movements of the soul, insofar as they had possessed themselves badly, surrender themselves in service to the higher love, which is nothing other than the intellect.

For famine compels them, and meanwhile they prefer to abandon their own wills rather than endure perpetually the miserable poverty of body and mind.

The exactions of both are themselves hunger and famine. He subjects Egypt and all its peoples to Pharaoh when, from his worldliness and all its vices—for this is the house and these are the peoples that the king’s daughter is commanded to forget (Ps. XLIV, 11)—the soul recognizes itself as subject to the devil insofar as these things prevail over it, according to what the intellect commands it.

This extends “from the remotest boundaries of Egypt to its farthest limits,” that is, from the furthest outlook of intentions to the ends of every kind of action; for if you attend to both, they are finalities.

### Verse 22

“The land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king, is excepted,” because the solidity of reasons, whose sacred guidance we follow in doing good, and which, taken away from the devil’s jurisdiction, has been assigned to them for possession, is excluded from this dominion. It too relies upon freedom even amid the contests of the movements.

The public storehouses from which provisions are given to them are the common counsels of the Scriptures, from which inner nourishment is supplied to them. Therefore they are not compelled to sell their possessions, because they are in no way forced, by admitting sin, to subject to the devil the one good that they possess through the virtue of discernment.

[Col. 0314C]

### Verses 23–24

“Then Joseph said to the peoples: ‘Behold, as you see, Pharaoh possesses both you and your land. Take seed and sow your fields, so that you may have crops. You shall give a fifth part to the king; I grant you the remaining four parts for seed and for food for your households and children.’”

Joseph speaks to the peoples when the intellect attempts to calm the disturbances of the soul by established laws.

“‘Behold,’” he says, “‘the devil possesses both you, insofar as you belong to yourselves, and the earthlinesses with which you are affected. Therefore, so that he may not rule you any longer, take the seeds of the divine word and allow them to be scattered over the field of the mind, so that you may have the fruits of good works.

“‘Whatever pertains to the fifth part of the external senses, through which worldly things are desired, assign to the devil, whom you serve through desires. Take the remaining four parts, by which one lives according to the four Gospels or according to the four principal virtues, for seed with which you may make your hearts fruitful; and from these nourish the households of inner states and the children of thoughts and works.’”

[Col. 0314D]

### Verse 25

“They answered: ‘Our salvation is in your hand. Let our lord only look upon us, and we shall gladly serve the king.’”

The movements of animality, led by the grasp of understanding, confess that their salvation rests in the power of intellectuality. They beg it to look upon them—that is, to let the light of truth flow to them from it—so that, with joy over their escape from the old servitude that they mystically displayed to Pharaoh, they may offer God the sacrifice of their confession.

[Col. 0315A]

### Verse 26

“From that time until the present day, throughout the whole land of Egypt, a fifth part is paid to the kings, and it became, as it were, a law, except for the priestly land, which was free from this condition.”

From that moderation of divine dispensation by which it is established that the flesh still resists reason and yet remains beneath it, reason is, as it were, a priesthood for the people until one comes to that day of divine eternity in which past things do not pass away and future things are not lacking.

A fifth part must be paid to the kings because whatever we sin through the wandering of sensuality ought to be repaid, by a fitting restoration of repentance, to the demons who rule this air and through whom we are often enticed.

“For blessed is he who shall repay them with the repayment that they repaid us” (Ps. CXXXVI, 8).

This becomes, as it were, a law throughout the whole land of Egypt when, in all our external activity, we are commanded to adhere to this rule.

The fifth part may also be understood as sight alone, which is accustomed to inflict a particularly deadly harm upon the mind. For the Apostle gives it a primary place among the three things in which are described the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John II, 16); there the totality of evil is comprehended.

But the priestly land—that is, rational virtue—never deigns to be subjected to these kings, because it belongs to rational virtue to heal through itself the things that have been injured in the realm of sensuality.

[Col. 0315B]

### Verses 27–28

“Israel therefore dwelt in Egypt, that is, in the land of Gessen, and possessed it. He increased and multiplied exceedingly. And he lived in it for seventeen years. All the days of his life were one hundred and forty-seven years.”

Israel dwells in Egypt when the spirit that rules within us with God dominates and governs like a light amid the darkness of this age. For Israel is said to mean “a prince with God”; and “to dwell” is used for “to rule.”

He moves about in the land of Gessen so that he may subtly draw near to the touch of every vice in order to resist it. He possesses it when, by the right belonging to him, he defends and retains it for cultivation even against temptations.

He increases and multiplies exceedingly because the spirit is nowhere made more abundant than through the practice of exercised discernment.

He lives there for seventeen years when, through both the Decalogue of the law and the septenary of life-giving assisting grace, we find an increase and advancement in knowledge.

All the brightness of our virtues, through the quaternary of evangelical doctrine, the septenary of divine gifts, and the denary of Mosaic instruction, reaches the right hand of eternal blessedness, that is, the hundred.

169 [Col. 0315D]

### Verses 29–30

“When he saw that the day of his death was approaching, he called his son Joseph and said to him: ‘If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand under my thigh and show me mercy and truth, so that you do not bury me in Egypt. Rather, let me sleep with my fathers; and take me from this land and bury me in the tomb of my ancestors.’”

He calls his son as the day of death approaches when our spirit, through the inner light, recurs and yearns toward the desire for intellectuality, toward the complete mortification of itself with respect to the world that seduces it, as toward a son.

He finds favor in his sight when he feels that he has the necessary alacrity. To place a hand under his thigh means to join the power of inner truth to the work, from which the seed of divine reason proceeds. It is fitting that this should depend upon that seedbed as upon a rule.

The thigh signifies propagation, and the truth of reason makes everything fruitful. He shows mercy and truth so that he may not be buried in Egypt when he completes, through perseverance—or rather, by making it persevere—the remission of sins that the intellect promises the mind from God, presenting it to himself with certainty, while he removes it from the burial of Egypt—that is, from the care of the world that buries it.

He wishes to sleep with his fathers because he desires not to be weighed down by Egyptian sorrows, but to be lulled to sleep away from external cares by the example of those who sleep while remaining vigilant in heart.

He asks to be taken from this land and buried in the tomb of his ancestors when, through the excellence of understanding, he strains to be removed from earthly affections and sheltered within the boundaries of conscience from external disturbances.

Hence it is said in Job: “They rejoice when they have found a tomb while digging for a treasure” (Job III, 21–22).

[Col. 0316B]

**VERSE 31.**—“I, Joseph,” he said, “will do what you have commanded.” And he said to him: “Swear to me, then.” When he had sworn, Israel worshiped God, turning toward the head of the bed.

The intellect affirms that it favors the purpose of reason, because without heavenly knowledge—which is nothing other than the very love of God—nothing at all useful remains for our spirit. Relying on this steadfastness, and now directed toward God according to Israel’s meaning, it humbles itself before God and inclines its mind toward him who is the head of the bed—that is, the primacy of our inward rest—for in him there is sabbath-rest from the exactions of sin.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**VERSE 1.**—After these things had taken place, Joseph was informed that his father was ill. Taking his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, he went to him.

These events pass away because, with God beneficially arranging it, periods of sluggishness and lukewarmness sometimes occur in the fervor of the soul. Joseph is informed of his father’s illness when the intellect is shaken concerning the mutability of reason. But he hastens to associate with himself those two vigorous sons, who, according to Job, possess strength (Job 36:19), begotten by a happy conscience: namely, forgetfulness of present things and the fruitfulness of things to come. Through the penetration of the intellect, he hastens to recall to reason the purpose of both.

**VERSES 1, 3.**—And it was told the old man: “Behold, your son Joseph has come to you.” He, strengthened, sat upon the bed. And when Joseph had entered to him, he said: “Almighty God appeared to me at Luz, which is in the land of Canaan; he blessed me and said: ‘I will increase and multiply you, and I will make you into throngs of peoples. I will give this land to you and to your seed after you as an everlasting possession.’”

The old man is told of Joseph’s arrival when the memory of the increase of heavenly knowledge is renewed for the spirit that is being provoked. He therefore sits strengthened upon the bed when, having recovered his powers through deep inward correction, he rises in the judicial dignity of his own conscience. To sit is the act of one who judges. That the bed signifies the mind is attested by the one who says: “Our bed is flourishing” (Song of Songs 1:15).

Moreover, Joseph enters when he is admitted into the secret place of the heart. Luz is said to mean *boja*, which we call a fetter. “In the land of Canaan,” he says—that is, in earthliness, where I endured continual movement along the downward paths of crimes, and where I was bound by the fetters of pleasures. God, who almightily leads out those bound in strength, shone upon me. He blessed the multiplication of virtue and promised with certain hope that he would create me substantial amid the disturbances of vices, and would entrust to me, for present possession, the land of this body, and afterward to my seed—that is, to my pious merit—for incorruptible possession after the condition of this world.

**VERSES 5, 6.**—“Therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came here to you, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be reckoned to me as Reuben and Simeon. But those whom you beget after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritances.”

There are two intellectual sons who so cling to the twin depths of charity that Manasseh possesses forgetfulness of present things, but they never forget the fruit of future goods. These are born in the land of Egypt before Israel comes to Joseph, because before our spirit knows what the intellect is, and before the intellect itself compels us wholly to reject worldly conduct, pious movement itself begets them within itself or from itself. Reason must choose them as its own.

Reuben is said to mean “seeing a son”; Simeon, “hearing sadness.”

“Manasseh and Ephraim,” he says, “shall be reckoned to me as Simeon and Reuben,” because the forgetfulness of things pressing upon us becomes mine through the hearing of sadness—whether of the present, by which the world is afflicted, or of the future, by which the impious will be cursed—and the whole fruitfulness of pious work comes to me through the vision of the son, that is, through contemplation of eternal things in hope.

We have often demonstrated that sons are commonly called hopes in Scripture. It is as though he were saying: “Just as I do not lack the hearing of causes, hope, and sadness, so I shall not lack the effectiveness of forgetting what lies behind and pursuing fruits directed toward what lies ahead” (Philippians 3:13). If afterward, through the powers of intellectual study, you produce something in holiness, you will have increased this for yourself toward the fullness of divine knowledge; and these things will rightly be counted under the name of brothers—that is, as sown by wisdom as mother and by the spirit as begetter—in the ordering of movements that must be subordinated.

For if you perfectly reject the world and, loving God, devote yourself wholly to the fruitfulness of good works, then whatever you finally weave into these intentions is virtue.

**VERSE 7.**—“But when I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel died for me in the land of Canaan, on the journey itself; and it was springtime. I was leaving [or entering] Ephratha, and I buried her beside the road to Ephratha, which is also called Bethlehem.”

Mesopotamia is said to mean “an exalted calling”; Rachel, “seeing the beginning.” “When,” he says, “from the divine calling by which I am raised from lowliness, I received the summons to reach the effect of grace, Rachel died for me—as far as concerns my own, that is, human uses. My earthly intention was deprived of usefulness to me, so that it might be raised toward him who is the beginning of all things and is preeminently so.”

She dies in the land of Canaan, on the journey itself, when, placed in an earthly movement from which it cannot yet be completely freed, she gradually falls away in the very desire to make progress. It was springtime when she died, and he was leaving Ephratha, because, as the fervor of faith approaches and a pious affection bursts forth into the fruit of action, the will that belongs to the flesh is cast down, while the spirit, as though released into freedom, goes forth toward the abundance of inward fullness, which is Ephratha.

She is buried beside the road to Ephratha when, beside Christ who is the way, she hides herself from worldly tumult for the sake of the fruitfulness and abundance of those who enjoy it. “Place me,” he says, “beside yourself, and let any man’s hand fight against me” (Job 17:3).

Bethlehem is said to mean “house of bread.” Thus Ephratha is called by another name, “house of bread,” because, although the fruitfulness of good actions is guided by praise, it is nevertheless in no way approved by God unless, so to speak, the super-heavenly bread is held in a settled dwelling. A house is inhabited not in the manner of a tabernacle, but with the permanence of times and ages.

**VERSES 8, 9, 10.**—When he saw his sons, he said to him: “Who are these?” He replied: “They are my sons, whom God gave me in this place.” He said: “Bring them to me, that I may bless them.” Israel’s eyes were dim because of extreme old age, and he could not see clearly.

When Israel sees his sons—that is, the effects of the intellect—the spirit carefully examines within itself their causes. But he answers himself that the sons were given to him by God in this place: that is, in the principal place, as is fitting, the good fruits of works founded in the stability of charity. That place is spacious in which David boasts that his feet have been set (Psalm 30:9). Indeed, the commandment itself is exceedingly broad (Psalm 118:96). The causes of works, therefore, are charity.

And because neither the place ought to be absent from us, nor we from the place, even for a little while, he openly indicates this through the demonstrative expression “this.” “Therefore,” he says, “if they proceed from divine knowledge, bring these same works, through the clarity of your intellect, to the knowledge in which reason can discern them, so that, once distinguished and inwardly tasted as though in a palace, I may bless them—that is, make them more numerous.”

Without the sharpness of the intellect, the eyes of Israel—that is, the faculties of reason—are dim, and through the excessive habit of temporal antiquity they are less able to direct themselves toward divine and spiritual things.

**VERSE 11.**—He brought them close to himself and kissed them; and embracing them, he said to his son: “I was not deprived of seeing you; moreover, God has shown me your offspring.”

He brings them close when he joins to himself inseparably both forgetfulness of things pressing upon him and the fruitfulness of pious actions. He kisses them because he is moved toward them not by fear but by the affection of inward love. He embraces them when spiritual vigilance, fortifying its condition on every side, watches over it.

“I was not,” he says, “deprived of seeing you,” because I do not lack the light of the intellect and knowledge, insofar as I cling to good intentions. “Moreover, God has shown me your offspring”—that is, the fruit of that transparent truth which you contain within yourself, by extending your intentions all the way to the presentation of works.

**VERSES 12, 13.**—When Joseph had taken them from his father’s lap, he bowed face-down to the ground. Joseph placed Ephraim at his right hand—that is, at Israel’s left—and Manasseh at his left, that is, at his father’s right; and he brought both close to him.

Joseph takes the sons from his father’s lap when the intellect raises the intention of works from lowly desires. The lap is, after all, a place far below the breast of the body. Therefore we understand the father’s lap as the movement of human reason. For reason is human, and it is also divine.

Having lifted them up, he bows face-down to the ground in worship, because the more he withdraws his effort from the wisdom of the flesh, the more humbly he regards himself before God while contemplating sublime things. He places Ephraim at his right hand because he establishes the fruit of good work as his hope of eternal blessedness.

But Joseph’s right hand is at Israel’s right hand because that supremacy of the intellect, intent upon heavenly things, regards as left—that is, worldly and lowly—whatever is involved in human calculations, even if it appears to possess spiritual understanding. We taste beforehand the sweetness of contemplation together with the grievous burden of vanities. For before the intellect eats, the spirit sighs. “We ourselves,” the Apostle says, “who have the first fruits of the spirit, groan within ourselves” (Romans 8:23).

Manasseh is at the left of the intellect but at the right of reason, because forgetfulness of material things, without which the virtue of contemplation does not stand out, is for the intellect the cause of the hardest labor. Yet this labor provides reason with the occasion for the keenest excellence in discerning spiritual things.

He brings both close to him when he associates with the desire of reason both powers of the intellect, without which nothing is accomplished.

**VERSE 14.**—He extended his right hand and placed it upon the head of Ephraim, the younger brother; but he placed his left hand upon the head of Manasseh, who was older, crossing his hands.

He extends his hand when the spirit of inward strength advances the exercise. The head of Ephraim, upon which the right hand is placed, is the Divinity itself, from whose head, so to speak, the effect of all our good action hangs; upon it also the hope and blessedness of our spirit are founded.

The left hand is placed upon the head of Manasseh because all the adversity of temptations rests upon the height of heavenly glory, which is the highest and chief intention of forgetfulness of present things. Ephraim is called younger and Manasseh older because worldly memory is rejected first, so that afterward one may devote oneself to eternal fruitfulness.

He therefore crosses his hands when he counts as left for the present what is right for eternal life, and rejects as right for the present what is left for eternal life.

**VERSES 15, 16.**—He blessed Joseph’s son and said:

“God, in whose sight my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked; God, who has fed me from my youth even to this present day; the angel who has delivered me from all evils—may he bless these boys, and may your name be invoked upon them, together with the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth.”

Blessing is an invocation of multiplication. We call Joseph—that is, the intellect—the son of reason, because we know that the intellect proceeds not from the intellect but from reason.

“God,” he says, “in whose pleasure”—for whatever pleases, we wish to have before our eyes—“the ancestral guardianship of the nations of the inward man, namely Abraham and Isaac, strove to advance: the hope, that is, of heavenly joy and gladness.”

“God, who nourishes me by his consolation from the growth of the steadfastness of my youthful spirit, leading me onward to contemplation of that day which is always present.”

“May the angel of divine speech, by whose announcement I am delivered from all the harms of sin, through his own effectiveness and fulfillment multiply the newness of my purpose—namely, forgetfulness of things pressing upon me and the fruitfulness of future hope—and may they experience the invocation of the perpetual desire for the intellect to be increased. And may inward devotions grow through many effects toward the surface of bodily exercise.”

**VERSE 17.**—When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand upon Ephraim’s head, he took it badly; and having grasped his father’s hand, he tried to lift it from Ephraim’s head and transfer it to Manasseh’s head.

When the intellect sometimes observes that reason is applying its effort to the good actions it performs in such a way that it neglects to rise toward the subtlety of contemplation—which is forgetfulness of corporeal things—it is distressed by the dullness of reason. Hence, restraining the right hand itself—that is, the power of the inward man—from external care, it tries to raise it from the chief intention of present activity toward the obliteration of all materiality.

For heads signify the primacy of the mind, which consists in intentions.

**VERSE 18.**—“Not so, my father,” he said, “for this one is the firstborn. Place your right hand upon his head.”

He calls him the firstborn either because man was created not for external administration but rather for divine vision, or because contemplation is more worthy than ordinary, even if good, action. This is Mary’s better portion (Luke 10:43). “Therefore,” he says, “direct the diligence of your virtue especially toward him.”

**VERSES 19, 20.**—He refused and said: “I know, my son, I know. This one also shall become a people, and he also shall be multiplied; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall grow into nations.” And he blessed them at that time, saying: “In you Israel shall be blessed.”

He refuses, asserts that he knows his primacy, and recognizes a certain singular essence of contemplation among the peoples of empty thoughts, as well as the abundance of its virtues. Yet the mind sometimes considers greater the active usefulness that chooses to benefit many; its offspring—that is, the example of its work—can be propagated into the countless edifications of many, since it is more capable of imitation.

To this meaning the complaint of Martha, who was laboring in the Gospel against her sister, corresponds (Luke 10:41). Nevertheless, he blesses them at that very time, desiring that both be multiplied in the same condition of his consideration.

“Although,” he says, “the activity of many may be beneficial, I nevertheless confess that in you, O intellect, the primacy of inward blessing consists. For the virtue of Israel—that is, of reason—overflows through you. Therefore it will be said: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh’—that is, may animality be supported by you, O spirit, as by fat and richness, fruitfully producing outwardly in manifestation, and may it be inwardly imbued with the sap of grace through the abolition from the mind of all visible things.”

He set Ephraim before Manasseh because it is necessary first to toil at good actions before the images of corporeal things can be removed from the heart.

**VERSE 21.**—“Behold,” he said, “I am dying, and God will be with you; he will bring you back to the land of your fathers.”

“Behold, through the fruit of self-restraint and contempt for tangible things, I am dying to worldly desires. And thus, O spiritual movements, once alien affections have been cut away, divine love will remain with you; it will bring you back to the land of eternal solidity, which you lost in your first fathers. For the Holy Spirit, who is love, will lead us into a straight land.”

**VERSE 22.**—“I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow.”

This portion, which is given to Joseph beyond his brothers, is knowledge of the Divinity. It is attributed neither to the vision of the eyes, nor to any of the external senses, nor to the imagination of thoughts, nor to any of the inward dispositions, however much they reason, but solely to the intellect beyond them all.

The Amorite is called “one who makes bitter”; he signifies the carnal affection hostile to the spirit. From his hand—that is, from his power and activity—the subtlety of divine love, like a gem from filth, is rescued, through the vigilance of reason, by the sword of discernment and the heavenly bow of fear; at its aspect he is given a sign to flee.

## CHAPTER XLIX

**VERSES 1, 2.**—Jacob called his sons and said to them: “Gather yourselves together, that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days. Gather yourselves together and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.”

Jacob calls his sons when reason restricts and binds the dispersion of thoughts through the providence of the bow that he previously mentioned. Above he calls this bow his own because he expressly commands its use and exercise for himself.

“Gather you,” he says, “unanimously into the bosom of reason by the glue of divine fear, so that I may announce to each movement of the mind what fortunes or misfortunes may come in the final days—that is, in the outcomes of virtues.”

Gather yourselves, because the divine voice is perceived nowhere in dissension and wandering. First obey the spirit’s admonitions as Jacob—that is, the supplanter of vices—so that afterward you may experience the peaceful fatherhood of that same victor, who through victory already possesses principality with God. For Israel is said to mean “a prince with God.”

**VERSES 3, 4.**—“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow, foremost in gifts, greater in authority. You poured yourself out like water; you shall not increase, because you went up onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

Reuben is interpreted as “seeing in the midst.” It is customary in both human and divine writings to use “midst” for what is common. “Seeing in the midst,” therefore, signifies the power of reason, which is recognized generally to care providently for everything that belongs to man.

It is therefore as though he said: “You are, for me, Reason, the dignity of providence or discernment implanted as your chief quality. Although you supply strength against emerging vices, you are nevertheless the beginning of my sorrow, because the more knowledge you add, the more sorrow you add to one who is unable to put what he knows into practice. And although you are foremost according to the excellent gift of wisdom, and greater in exacting the service of corporeality, you are nevertheless poured out through the flow of corruption into the affections. May God not allow you to grow proud in their extension. For the swollen vanity of empty joy commonly increases in wicked thoughts when an opportunity for pleasures has smiled upon them. ‘They rejoice,’ it says, ‘in the worst things’ (Proverbs 2:14), taking courage from the excess of crime.

“Turned from truth into falsehood, you, Reason, have become affection. By creeping up from below, you disturb the quiet of the mind—which is what the bed signifies—and defile the bedding of virtues through the adulterous assaults of shameful desires.”

These are the words of the spirit of the father’s inward household, complaining of the deceitful immersion of perverse appetite.

**VERSES 5, 6.**—“Simeon and Levi are brothers; instruments of iniquity are their weapons. May my soul not enter their counsel, and may my glory not be in their assembly, because in their anger they killed a man, and in their desire they undermined a wall.”

Simeon is said to mean “hearing sadness”; Levi, “added” or “assumed.”

If, according to the Prophet, it is not permitted to rejoice with the impious, the Lord says—and, according to the Fathers, joy is understood in relation to the good—that hearing sadness leads to evil, so that the cause is put for the effect. For if joy and peace are the kingdom of God, and not food and drink, as the Apostle says (Romans 14:17), then the kingdom of the devil is rightly called sadness and unrest; for the pursuit of sin produces all this.

“Hearing,” therefore—that is, understanding, or rather obediently receiving—this kind of sadness signifies the affection that is not sad because of it, but recognizes that by this means it is storing up wrath for itself on the day of wrath. When the fruit of its desire is added to it, two vessels of the worst capacity are formed, filled with wars and tumult that fight against the soul.

The spirit desires that the soul not enter their counsel when the intention of the inward man is excluded from the purpose that seeks earthly things and, after obtaining them, enjoys them lustfully. Their counsel consists in both desiring and, when the desired things arrive, indulging in them.

Hence Job says: “Because their good things are not in their hand, let their counsel be far from me” (Job 21:16). And the Lord says: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” (Matthew 24:19; Mark 13:17).

The counsel of these things, therefore, is desire, pleasure, or pride. Reason does not wish to glory in their assemblies—for these gather many other plagues to themselves, since they are the roots of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10)—because reason does not know how to rejoice in evil deeds (Proverbs 2:14), nor to imitate those who do evil (Psalm 36:1).

Their fury—that is, their vehement and almost frenzied appetite, which the Apostle calls “the passion of desire” (1 Thessalonians 4:5), and elsewhere calls “burning”—kills the one whom the Samaritan woman is commanded to call “man” (John 4:16); that is, it kills the ruling spirit.

Yet in their desire the wall is first undermined, because through pleasure, which willingly favors suggestion, inward virtue is overthrown before the ascent to madness is reached.

**VERSE 7.**—“Cursed be their anger, because it is obstinate, and their indignation, because it is harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

Their anger is cursed because it is obstinate: the excess of desire, which strives to persevere in evil, is cast down from the summit of divine advancement. For in sacred speech a curse signifies abandonment and loss.

Their indignation is cursed because of its harshness, because when they burn in that very will of pleasure against the divine commands, they raise themselves up in indignation as though those commands were unbearable. And when this carries them toward vices with a savage mind, their condition is overwhelmed by the calamity of their own obstinacy.

In Jacob—that is, in souls lively for the overthrow of sin—they are divided by such subtle discernment. But in those who are Israel—that is, those who are directed with God and, with God, exercise lordship over themselves—they are brandished with the horns of the greatest authority. Israel is said to mean “directed by God” or “a prince with God.”

**VERSE 8.**—“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you.”

Judah is said to mean “praising,” “glorifying,” or “confessing.” He is the condition of holy religion. Even if it performs some things less suitably, it piously confesses; by life and conduct it praises God, and glorifies him not only in itself but also through the examples of others.

Its true authority is demonstrated by the fact that, despite the power of unwilling reason, the necks of the aforesaid affections and evils are brought low. His brothers praise him because all who share his purpose, and also every strong act born from the same father, the spirit, and the same mother, good will, celebrate him with praise. They worship when all movements of the mind humble themselves in order to support him.

**VERSE 9.**—“Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. Resting, you have lain down like a lion; and like a lioness, who will rouse him?”

According to the natural philosophers, the lion’s cub is born asleep, but afterward is awakened on the third day by the voice of its parent. Thus the effect of true religion—Judah, that is, in his first affections—arises as though sluggish and somewhat dull through its newness. But after the recognition of the Trinity, which is God—and which is nothing other than his love, the only voice capable of being known by it—it awakens to the clarity of knowledge.

Of this voice it is said: “Everyone who hears from the Father and learns” (John 6:43), and so forth. And: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17).

He goes up to the prey because, rising above the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16), which Simeon and Levi demand, he bursts forth by steps of virtue toward bringing force to bear upon the kingdom of heaven and violently seizing it (Matthew 11:12).

He lies resting like a lion when, although he may appear secure after temptations have sometimes been put to sleep, he nevertheless remains always anxiously watchful against sudden assaults. For the lion is said to keep its eyes open even when it sleeps. “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

He is also like a lioness because the more deeply he conceives the incentive of heavenly ardor in his heart and broods over the offspring of pious work, the more fiercely he rises against vices. The nature of the lioness is indeed said to be such that, when she burns with love for the male or is intent on nourishing her young, she is even stronger than the lion.

Who, then, will rouse this Judah, who relies upon such great love, from the inward delight in which he rests in God? “Many waters could not extinguish love” (Song of Songs 8:7). His lamps are the fire and flames of that love.

**VERSES 10, 11.**—“The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations. Binding his colt to the vine, and his donkey, O my son, to the vine.”

The scepter is not taken from Judah because, from the very condition of our holiness, the rule of commanding reason is not moved in any way by the winds of opposing strengths or by the floods of lust. “The rivers came, the winds blew” (Matthew 7:25).

Judah’s thigh is knowledge of the truth, as though it were a receptacle of seed in the heart. The ruler from Judah’s thigh is therefore our spirit, begotten and strengthened from the offspring of truth in good works. This offspring proceeds from Judah because from the practice and use of holiness the hidden wisdom of the inward man is extended, as though it were a kind of ancestral line.

This takes place until he comes who is to be sent—that is, until that heavenly condition of immortality and incorruption arrives. It is awaited with prayers so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life among the nations (2 Corinthians 5:4)—that is, among inward movements.

The ruler binds his colt to the vine when he disciplines and restrains the carnal affection, impatient of yoke and burden, by the precepts of divine Scripture, which offers us a cup of the purest counsel. In the Song of Love there is a complaint that little foxes demolish these vines of sacred teachings (Song of Songs 2:15).

The donkey is tied to the vine when our will—which is nearer to reason and more consonant with the law of God—is bound to Christ, who says: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), like a beast capable of bearing a load and being handled.

Jacob, the son of the spirit, calls Judah—that is, the condition of religion—his son because he does not doubt that the exercise of all piety proceeds from him.

**VERSE 12.**—“He will wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk.”

He washes his robe in wine when our progress—Judah, the true one—through spiritual fervor and joy daily cleanses that garment received in baptism, which he is commanded to carry before the tribunal of Christ.

A cloak is customarily put on over a tunic. If, therefore, by the robe we understand the purity of the inward man insofar as possible, by the cloak we may understand the innocence of outward work. It is washed in the blood of the grape because, when he faithfully receives the sacrament of Christ’s passion, from which the fullness of heavenly sweetness has flowed down to us, he is washed from the stain of human nature.

Hence it is said: “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). For when we devoutly receive Christ’s body, we believe that we are cleansed from the necessities that intrude upon our actions.

Judah’s eyes are more beautiful than wine because he does not boast that the clarity of his mind is present in him through hypocrisy, arrogance of wisdom, or the glory of knowledge. Rather, through wine—that is, through the most sincere abundance of spiritual grace—he shows himself to abound more fully for others.

The meaning is therefore this: His superiority to others in beauty does not arise from fabrication but from the wine of divine taste and warmth.

Likewise, his teeth—that is, the powers of his words and the virtues by which they piously slaughter others and incorporate them into God—shine more abundantly than the eloquence of many because they come from milk, that is, from the fullest purity of a simple conscience, not from declamatory bluster.

“These teeth,” as it is read in the Song of Love, “went up like a flock of shorn ewes from the washing” (Song of Songs 4:2).

**VERSE 13.**—“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, and at the station of ships he shall reach as far as Sidon.”

Zebulun is said to mean “the flowing of night,” or “his oath,” or “the dwelling of strength.” When we see the night of this world flowing away through errors, we fulfill the oath that we made in the sacred promise of baptism—namely, that we would renounce its spectacles—while striving toward the dwelling of eternal strength, the enduring city.

With this consideration, our mind, avoiding the cares of the world, which are a shipwreck of the sea, chooses the shore of inward solidity. It dwells among ships—not those carried about by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14), but those by which one descends to the sea so that work may be done upon the great waters (Psalm 106:23), and those through which small animals pass with great ones.

There are, in fact, ships that are wholly faithful souls, signifying humility by their concavity, and thereby saving themselves and others. He dwells at the station of ships when he strives to live perseveringly among the examples of those who endure amid the miseries and temptations of this world.

He reaches as far as Sidon when the provident mind reaches as far as the consideration of useless profit, what alone in [lacuna] is both sought and done.

Sidon is said to mean “useless hunting”; in the Punic language it is interpreted as “fish.” Whoever lives unstained by crime amid the waves and storms of the world reaches the likeness of a fish; temptation becomes an occasion of life for him, just as the wave becomes nourishment for the fish. For one who is placed upon the earth—that is, upon earthly things—temptation ought to be the cause of vitality.

**VERSES 14, 15.**—“Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; he placed his shoulder beneath the burden and became a servant to tribute.”

Issachar is interpreted as “reward.” And it must be carefully intimated, in view of the great labors that Zebulun endures, that there is a reward. For after listing the eight beatitudes of suffering, the Lord added: “Rejoice, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew 5:12).

For this reward a strong ass must be prepared: the humble strength of endurance. He lies between the boundaries when he is commanded both to love enemies by enduring them and to love friends only for God’s sake; by these commands he is confined as though between two boundaries.

Moreover, he lies down when he does not wander unsteadily in these practices but rests, delighting in their continual performance. He sees that rest is good and the land excellent because he attends to spiritual sabbaths and perceives how useful and suitable they are in the present for abstaining from everything unlawful. Through these leisures, better than which nothing exists, the land of the living is acquired.

He therefore places his shoulder beneath the burden when, under this intention, he offers humble service of obedience to the one whose burden is light. Hence it is read: “They shall serve him with one shoulder” (Zephaniah 3:9), that is, with the unanimous resolve of obedience.

He becomes a servant to tribute when he cuts away the vices and desires that ruled him, returning to humanity only what the necessary provision of the body requires.

**VERSES 16, 17, 18.**—“Dan shall judge his people, as also the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a cerastes on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward. I shall await your salvation, O Lord.”

Dan is interpreted as “judgment,” signifying hypocrisy, by which no vice is judged—or rather condemned—more justly. Hypocrisy performs holy acts, yet, with God despised, sacrilegiously attributes the honor of holiness to itself.

It judges its own people, as do the other tribes in Israel, because it visibly discerns and restrains certain external evils of its own, just as do the elect, to whose lot it does not belong.

“Let Dan be a serpent on the road.” This means: May God will that, even if hypocrisy appears to be colored by its variety, it may nevertheless be seen how deadly an evil it is, like a serpent in the path of its own affection.

It should be noted, however, that the serpent does less harm than the cerastes, and that a road is broader and more frequently traveled than a path. The serpent on the road is the evil of hypocrisy, but it is not so pernicious in a perverse affection. For the love of praise naturally creeps in upon almost everyone. This road is therefore general. The one who says, “I will guard my ways” (Psalm 38:2), takes precautions against it.

The horned serpent (*cerastes*), which is called “horned,” an utterly deadly creature, signifies the arrogance of pride—the horn of exaltation [Col. 0327A]. The narrow path corresponds to it, indicating the singularity of insolent thought, in which one raises oneself above others by despising them all, almost comparing oneself with God himself. It bites the horse’s hoofs when an excess of arrogance corrupts in the mind the very discernment of its type, so that it does not think itself proud but considers whatever glorious thing it thinks about itself to be suitably appropriate to it. He knows how to take “hoof” for discernment who knows that a young calf produces horns and hoofs (Ps. LXIII, 32). That a horse is customarily taken as a figure of pride is attested by the Psalm, which says that the riders of horses slept because of God’s rebuke (Ps. LXXV, 7). “So that its rider may fall backward”: that is, while he is proud of the emptiness of glory, he may be overturned and fall into that from which he turned his gaze—the future age. For the Lord struck his enemies [Col. 0327B] where they pay least attention to the latter things of the life to come. But our spirit, discerning and despising these things in advance, promises God himself that it will await God’s salvation, because the more the impious and apostate man grows proud, the more the poor man is kindled (Ps. X, 23)—that is, he is rendered purer and more vigorous for doing good. While the former awaits worldly glories, the latter rejoices in expectation of salvation, that is, of Christ. Hence David, speaking of the one who prevailed in his vanity, added concerning himself—or concerning Christ and those like him: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree” (Ps. LI, 9–10), etc.

**VERSE 19.**—“Gad, girded, will wage war before him, and he himself will be girded behind.” Gad is interpreted as “raider,” through whom the carnal impulse is understood. [Col. 0327C] Girded, he wages war before Dan, because, having gathered and added to himself strength derived from empty swelling, he is accustomed to foam with the foulness of lust. Often, and almost naturally, the windy inflation of that majesty is accustomed to be blown back into corruption; and by God’s just judgment this heedless raider suddenly confronts himself, so that he who takes no account of God or human beings may suddenly see, in his most shameful fall, that he is nothing. He is said to wage war before him because one who inwardly exults beyond all measure is permitted to encounter the tumult of open assault through the sudden insolence of lust. For a stumbling block is set before those who sin voluntarily. Yet he is first girded behind, while in his own mind—toward which the hypocrite turns his back—the impulse of conceived pleasure is first armed with many contrivances of thought, in order that it may be fulfilled by cunning actions. [Col. 0327D]

**VERSE 20.**—“Asher: his bread is rich, and he will provide delicacies for kings.” Asher is called “blessed,” and no one is more blessed than the person who fears God perfectly. For him the bread is rich because, while it contains oil, he does not inwardly grow proud of virginity; the bread that descended from heaven (John VI, 41) is for him inward freedom and sap. He is fed with the fat of grain (Ps. LXXX, 17). Thus this Asher—namely, our spirit—endowed with the true blessedness of this flavor and set against the two previously mentioned figures, Dan and Gad, now provides delicacies for kings, because it supplies not uncleannesses—or rather, thorns of desire—but the delights of inward joy to those senses that once ruled us. That these are called kings is attested both by the Apocalypse and by the Psalms; their delicacies consist in nothing other than exercising themselves in the gains of invisible goods. For frequently to read, to weep, to hear the words of God gladly, to speak them, and to perform with devout intention whatever is fitting for each of the senses—these are delicacies arising from inward richness. [Col. 0328A]

**VERSE 21.**—“Naphtali is a let-loose hind, giving beautiful utterances.” Naphtali is said to mean “he conversed with me,” or “he entangled me,” or “he enlarged me.” After God, through the celebrated practice of virtue, turns the impious away from impiety, so that they are no longer impious, and entangles them in his service, he consequently [Page 176] enlarges them through degrees of advancement by the inwardness of charity. Thus our spirit, when it has attained these things, is now sent outside itself like a stag with the very powerful horns of majesty against vices [Col. 0328B] and with the most subtle senses for discerning all things—sent out through leaps and through the exhilaration of divine contemplation—where it draws in utterances of complete beauty. The more delightful these are to it inwardly, the more sweetly it offers them to others.

**VERSE 22.**—“Joseph is a son who increases; a son who increases, and comely in appearance.” Joseph is interpreted as “increase.” This increase therefore grows, and grows again, when that heavenly good—by which alone we are truly advanced—is first extended through the mind’s desire and then enlarged by a certain assurance of hope and security. Hence Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 10). And: “He made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II, 6). He is comely in appearance because, through heavenly contemplation, nothing is even now clearer, although one is not yet engaged with the realities themselves. [Col. 0328C]

“Daughters ran along the wall (verse 23). But they embittered him, and quarrelled with him, and envied him, having darts.” The wall is understood as Christ, for “the Saviour will be placed as a wall in it” (Isa. XXVI, 2). The daughters run along this wall when all sorts of weak and fragile impulses, although they trust that they stand in faith in Christ, nevertheless wander through this confidence into perverse affections and actions. Although they flatter intellectuality—which is Joseph—and soothe it, they do not soften it by that soothing; rather, they embitter it violently against themselves. Hence they also quarrel, because, having been repulsed, they are stirred up again against it with a more grievous recurrence of warfare. Concerning these daughters it is said: “Do you have daughters? Keep their body” (Ecclus. VII, 26)—that is, restrain the wicked works of the affections. They also envy him, having darts, because the tender impulses—that is, the motions—endeavour, through present desires with which they dart at it, to arouse in the intellect envy of eternal things. They are rightly said to envy because they impel it toward making it not see.

**VERSE 24.**—“His bow rested on the strong one, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob; from there the shepherd, the stone of Israel, went forth.” The bow rests upon the strong one when the intention from which the missiles of actions are directed clings steadfastly not to fragile things but to eternal ones. For this is what the word “resting” usually signifies, as in: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. I, 1). The arms signify strength; the hands signify action. When he directs these rightly, he loosens their bonds, because he now freely and firmly carries out his purposes, having been released from the habit by which he was formerly held entangled. The hands of the Mighty One of Jacob bring this about, when the spirit that supplants vices becomes the occasion of such strength and authority. From there the shepherd, the stone of Israel, goes forth when, from that same spirit, an understanding arises which refreshes the spirit itself with the bread of life and, as Israel—that is, as one who rules together with God—strengthens and establishes it like a stone; thus it is urged to proceed toward the freedom of contemplation. [Col. 0329A]

**VERSES 25, 26.**—“The God of your father will be your helper, and the Almighty will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the abyss below, blessings of breasts and womb. The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the everlasting hills should come; may they be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.” He says: The God who established me as a father and ruler, so to speak, of the spirit in a human being, and who, although by nature you are mine, nevertheless willed that you should be created from me as one superior to me in dignity—he himself will work with you in your struggles. Since he can do all things, he will multiply you through reason, as though the height of heaven—and likewise the abundance of blessing, that is, of fullness—would not be lesser in the affection subject to reason than the exuberance produced by obedience. For it is written: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deut. XXXII, 1). The spirit is nothing unless the affection obeys it; this affection is the earth, or the abyss, because of its weakness. The womb and breasts are blessed when, in the very conception of devout desire, in the determination of the purpose, and in the beginnings of the twofold love by which it is nourished in the lap of the present Church toward a truly manly future state as though at the breasts, it advances successfully. [Col. 0329B]

The blessings of the father are strengthened by the blessings of his fathers when, through the memory of the ancients who abounded in virtues, the virtues of the one who is the father of intellectuality multiply in the spirit. [Col. 0329C] This continues until the desire of the everlasting hills arrives—that is, until the abundance of heavenly glory is fulfilled, for which the devotions of the faithful, destined for everlasting excellence, sigh. Ask the Psalms what mountains and hills signify. The Sibyl, however, destroys the eternity of the figurative mountains or hills: “Now,” she says, “the mountains are made equal to the plains.” The head of Joseph is God himself, because for intellectuality—which is inward taste and knowledge [Col. 0329D] of God—God alone is the pre-eminent principal, with all passing things subject to him. The blessings are therefore established upon the head of Joseph when increases of wisdom are ascribed to God, not to our own skill.

The heavenly reward may also be understood by “head,” since it is supreme and chief for the intellect. By contrast, concerning the reprobate he says: “Their head is the circuit of them” (Ps. CXXXIX, 10). Hence “crown” is subsequently mentioned, in which God is understood to be present above the head, since he is more worthy than every gift. A Nazirite is called a flower, or purity. Thus the crown of the Nazirite is blessed when that fruitful brightness and purity by which God is contemplated by the mind is attributed to God. [Page 177] The Nazirite is “among his brothers” because the habit of contemplation, among the other states of the mind, must be pure not only from vice but also from every image of sensible things. [Col. 0330A]

**VERSE 27.**—“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils.” Benjamin is said to mean “son of the right hand.” We have often said that the son of the right hand signifies the hope of election, and many times we have explained the relations between son and right hand. The conclusion of the reasoning concerning this is therefore that the son of the right hand—namely, every elect person, whose faithful posterity has taken its place among the blessed—is taken not always from those who have acted innocently, but also from those who have done harm with wolfish cruelty. Such a person, then, when he comes to the virtues I have set forth and which I hold by right of reasoning, after receiving in the morning the illumination of God, eats what the devil had plundered from him through vices—that is, he turns it into strength for restoration, rises more vigorous from his fall, and in the evening, once the heat of temptation has been extinguished, divides among the individual dispositions of his character the spoils of salutary armour that the enemy had once possessed. For virtues, when corrupted, become vices; when restored, they are spoils to be distributed victoriously among the various states of the mind. In these final words of the argument, grace is commended for its effectiveness in the virtues previously mentioned. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V, 20). And when we consider from how great a nothing our mind has been made, we plainly perceive that it possesses nothing that it has not received.

**VERSE 28.**—“All these are the twelve tribes of Israel.” We refer the tribes to the triad of faith, hope, and charity, and twelve consists of four groups of three. [Col. 0330C] We relate this quaternary to the Gospel, or to the four principal virtues, which we make to belong through love of the Trinity and through the execution of the three relationships mentioned above, together with those abundant blessings, to that which is Israel—namely, love with God. “This is what their father spoke to them, and he blessed each one with his own blessings. And he commanded them, saying…” When the special father of our inner states distributes useful counsels to the various qualities of thoughts and affections, he takes leave of each one with its own proper blessing.

**VERSES 29, 30.**—“I am being gathered,” he says, “to my people; and bury me with my fathers in the double cave which is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mambre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a possession for a burial place.” He is gathered to his people when the spirit is wholly restricted to habits and actions worthy of reason. He is buried with his fathers in the double cave when, together with the premature movements of spiritual reasoning, he is hidden from external pleasures and from the imaginations of those external things, as though with his fathers. The double cave may also be understood as twofold fear, by which punishment is feared and the loss of the kingdom is set before the mind. Contracted, therefore, by no unjustified fear of these two things, the spirit is restrained and, joined to the examples of those whose “fatherhoods” [sic] it shares, the affection is lulled to rest away from the tumult of the world.

Abraham bought this cave from Ephron the Hittite as a possession for a burial place when the Father of the inner nations—the interior spirit—demands from the carnal affection, which inflicts dust, that is, useless cares and grief, upon him and sometimes drags him toward the stupor of a reprobate sense, the containment of the senses and imaginations, at the cost of every labor, under the pretext of inward quiet. Ephron is said to mean “useless dust,” or “dust of grief”; Hittite means “stunned” or “stupefied.” The field in the land of Canaan opposite Mambre exists because, in the earthly condition where idleness—which is contrary to the virtue of discernment and clarity—is denied by vices, the conscience that must be cultivated lies there; or it is our body, where the burial place of the double cave must be sought and purchased. For Canaan signifies “commerce” or “negotiation,” while Mambre signifies “clear,” “lucid,” or “division.” [Col. 0331A]

**VERSE 31.**—“There they buried him, and Sarah his wife; there Isaac was buried with Rebecca his wife. There also Leah lies buried.” Abraham is buried there with Sarah when reason, or the spirit—which is the same thing—together with the good will subjected to it, is hidden within the boundaries of fear from the uproar of the inner and outer senses. Isaac and Rebecca are buried together when the hope of eternal joy is secretly mingled with the patience uniquely joined to it. For he hopes in vain for the palm of reward who does not endure the adversities of warfare. Leah lies buried there because all the laboriousness of our works rests and settles down together; it neither appropriates nor desires anything external.

**VERSE 32.**—“When he had finished commanding his sons, he gathered his feet upon the bed and died; and he was joined to his people.” After giving the commands, he gathers his feet upon the bed because, after the affection has reached the instruments of virtue, he establishes within the support of a conscience now peaceful and silent those things that had flowed here and there. He dies and is joined to his people when, falling away from desires for present things, he is attached as a diligent guardian to the people of inward conflicts, to observe them carefully and vigilantly.

# CHAPTER L

**VERSES 1, 2.**—“When Joseph saw this, he fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him. And he commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father.” When intellectuality perceives that the spirit is being extinguished according to [Page 178] human cunning and the desires of the world, the purer it senses it to be, the more abundantly it customarily falls upon its face—that is, it begins ever more diligently to pursue divine knowledge. Scripture’s customary usage places “face” for “knowledge.” He weeps and kisses him when he is affected attentively and with every tender feeling of the soul toward the good of rationality. He commands his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father because the spirit commands each and every light of reason to be continually concerned with caring for those states capable of healing weakness—states in which the very truth has been known as though in the form of a most radiant face, and has been joined by kisses of inward charity—and which serve the divine intellect alone, so that they may not allow it to lie exposed to the corruptions of the world, but may embalm it with the fragrances of virtues and prayers. [Col. 0332A]

**VERSE 3.**—“When they had fulfilled his commands, forty days passed; for this was the custom of those who were embalmed. And Egypt mourned him for seventy days.” Forty days pass after the embalming when the whole of temporal prosperity is despised as transitory after spiritual gifts have imbued the mind. The number ten signifies universality, four temporality, and days prosperity. This has been treated above. Thus some firmness of the corpse—that is, of our lowest and fallen nature—is demonstrated if we desire nothing temporally prosperous for ourselves. Again, the splendors of divine gifts are signified by days. Egypt therefore mourned Jacob for seventy days when, out of the fullness of graces, the world grieved that the spirit had been extinguished. Seventy is seven times ten; and the number seven, signifying fullness, is strengthened by ten—namely, by the keeping of the holy law—because the Spirit is said to rest upon the one who trembles at God’s words (Isa. LXVI, 2). [Col. 0332B]

**VERSES 4, 5.**—“When the time of mourning had ended, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh: ‘If I have found favour in your sight, speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying that my father adjured me: “Behold, I am dying; in my tomb which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, you shall bury me.”’” The time of mourning is completed when any holy man who was once suitable to the world, and therefore was mourned as having perished from worldly honours, so humbles himself through the discipline of study that he is despised even by the world; so that the world is not only crucified to him, but he himself is crucified to the world. His intellectuality therefore speaks to the household of Pharaoh when it urges the thoughts of carnal affections to perceive what belongs to them. The meaning of the words is: If, in the very examination of your consideration, I am found to pursue and desire divine favour rather than human glory, then act, you thoughts, together with the understanding of carnal affection, and consider with it how it may assent to the paternal right—that is, to the laws of reason—because he has chosen to die to the world and, after shaking off the worldliness of the earth in which he wavered in continual movement, in accordance with the name Canaan, seeks to be hidden from external tumults. [Col. 0332D]

**VERSE 6.**—“Therefore I will go up and bury my father, and return.” And Pharaoh said to him: “Go up and bury your father, as he adjured you.” He says: I will advance from the lowest desires, so that by clinging to heavenly things I may protect the authority of reason, which gave me birth, and thus return to my homeland, as to the natural order of my condition and dignity. Pharaoh’s nod is the inability of opposition—a resistance directed against the excellence of intellectuality. The rest is as above.

**VERSES 7, 8.**—“When he went up, all the elders of Pharaoh’s household went with him, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, and the household of Joseph with his brothers, except the little ones, the flocks, and the herds, which they had left in the land of Goshen.” Although he is said to be going up, all the elders of Pharaoh’s household are said not to go up with him but to go, because, when understanding yearns for the highest things, the cooling and languid movements of the flesh are compelled, whether they wish it or not, to serve spirituality; and after it, or with it, they are dragged along irresistibly. The elders of the land of Egypt are the vices that are original and therefore older than the world. They come together because they cannot do harm. The household of Joseph with his brothers signifies those virtues that strive especially on behalf of intellectuality, such as celibacy, purity of mind, and freedom from public or worldly cares; for intellectuality is accustomed to move among these together with the goods of soul and body, with the children of justice, the mother of all.

“Except the little ones, the flocks, and the herds”: that is, except those things that are as yet immature in goodness, together with the dullnesses naturally implanted in us and external exercises. Flocks pertain to simplicity, herds to the labor of management. These are left in the land of Goshen because, through the stable subtlety of discernment by which one approaches the touch of vices, they are left to be carefully examined, since they are not capable of reaching contemplation. This is the whole meaning: the things that belong solely to practical activity, or that are utterly dull and almost animal-like, do not ascend to the heights of speculation. [Col. 0333B]

**VERSES 9, 10.**—“He also had chariots and horsemen in his company, and a very great multitude. They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan; and there, mourning with a great and very grievous lamentation, they fulfilled seven days.” He has chariots and horsemen in his company when he knows how to carry others through patience as though they were a chariot, and knows how to govern the horse of temporal glory in the manner of a [Page 179] soldier. For he knows that the Apostle has taught that the sufferings of this time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory (Rom. VIII, 18), and that one ought not to hope in the uncertainty of riches (I Tim. VI, 17). To such a person it was shouted: “The chariot of Israel and its horseman” (2 Kings II, 12). For when through patience he conquers himself together with his desire and restrains the horse of worldly wantonness, he ascends toward the vision of the deity purer than these companions, and there arises not a small but a distinguished multitude of virtues. Jordan is said to mean “their descent.” The multitude is not small, for it is commended by the greatest humility: the more beautiful the conscience, the more it knows, in accordance with the Prophet, how to descend into itself together with the sound of the name and with its own powers. [Col. 0333D]

The threshing floor is situated beyond the Jordan because, after we lay down our hearts’ love of the world and its pomp, and subject ourselves and our possessions to God’s service, we draw near to the threshing floor of inward passions, where virtue is separated from vice by the threshing of endurance. “As you approach God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II, 1). For on the threshing floor wheat is distinguished from chaff by threshing. There the funeral is celebrated with vehement mourning, because the mortification of our members upon the earth is acquired only through grief that cannot be softened by any joy of present things. [Col. 0334A] Thus the seven days are completed; while one perseveres in such things, the fullnesses of spiritual gifts are accumulated.

**VERSE 11.**—“When the inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw this, they said: ‘This is a great mourning for the Egyptians.’ Therefore they called the name of that place ‘The Mourning of Egypt.’” After those who inhabit the land and are subject to perpetual movement—which is what Canaan signifies—those who have an earthly foundation and whose citizenship is not in heaven observe the spiritual discipline of others, they greatly marvel and, in their amazement, recoil: although the joys of the world are available, these people consume themselves in unceasing grief. Hence they call them Egyptians, seeing them brought low by the darkness of perpetual sadness; and they call the monasteries where these restraints are practised a pit, where the light of transitory delight and the ranks of worldly glories do not appear. [Col. 0334B]

**VERSES 12, 13.**—“The sons of Jacob therefore did as he had commanded them. And carrying him into the land of Canaan, they buried him in the double cave,” etc. After our spirit has supplanted the vices, its sons—namely, its movements, “strong in force,” according to Job (Job 36:19)—now readily obey its commands. But, lest they become elated by the strength of their victory, they carry him into the land of Canaan, when they remind him of his earthly and changeable condition, to which he can still be subjected. He is sheltered in the cave of the containment of the senses and imaginations; this is demanded at the price of inward devotion from the power of Ephron—that is, from carnal affection, whose useless cares obscure us with dust, although there are also useful cares—and is directed opposite Mambre, that is, toward the knowledge of subtle discernment.

**VERSE 14.**—“And Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all his company, after he had buried his father.” Although our spirit is hidden from the actions of the world within itself, its intellectuality must nevertheless return to Egypt—that is, to the recollection of its conditioned ignorance and darkness—with the other offspring joined to it as kindred through the mother of charity, just as the typological Jacob was earlier carried back by his thoughts to the land of Canaan. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “My people went down into Egypt, to dwell there as a colonist” (Isa. LII, 4); and it says with the Psalmist: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul was a long-time sojourner” (Ps. CXIX, 5). [Col. 0334D]

**VERSES 15, 16, 17.**—“When he was dead, his brothers, fearing and speaking to one another, sent to him, saying: ‘Perhaps he will remember what we did.’ They said: ‘Father, before he died he commanded us to say these words to you: “I ask you to forget the crime of your brothers, and the sin and malice that they practised against you.”’” After the spirit of worldly cunning has died, the brothers fear because of the injury they inflicted, for virtues are accustomed to blush before the excellence of the intellect on account of their less than adequate stability and purity; and they rightly tremble lest they fall away punitively from its grace into vices. It is as though they were saying: The spiritual virtue from which you have your being, while it labours in mortifying the members upon the earth—a labour to which the whole of inward strength belongs—excuses the weaknesses and negligences of the other subordinate virtues, when it cannot wholly cut away what is harmful; for when the authority of the ruler is found to be weak, the soldiers’ readiness grows very sluggish. Forget, therefore, the fragile movements to which we were once subject, and, as befits you, strive toward the things above. “We also ask,” they say, “that you forgive this iniquity to the servants of the God of your father.” They ask that iniquity be forgiven to the servants of the God of their father when, through the power of heavenly understanding, they seek the expiation of the old negligence of those states of the soul that wish to serve God, the author of rationality.

**VERSES 18, 19.**—“When Joseph heard this, he wept. And his brothers came to him, and, falling prostrate on the ground, said: ‘We are your servants.’ He said to them: ‘Do not fear. Can we resist the will of God?’” Joseph hears and weeps when he pierces and moves the humility of thoughts toward the grace of the intellect. In Scripture, “to hear” means “to understand,” as when the Apostle says: “The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. II, 15)—nor does he [Page 180] hear them, that is, understand them. The brothers come to him when each of the virtues supports him successfully; they fall prostrate upon the earth when, in contemplating heavenly things, they are humbled by their own fragility, as Moses, Isaiah, and others are read to have done when God appeared to them. “We are your servants,” they say, because, keeping watch not over the lowest desires but over heavenly glory, we wish to serve intellectuality. “Do not fear,” he says; aspire to the highest things, because we cannot resist the will of God. [Col. 0335B]

**VERSE 20.**—“You intended evil against me, but God turned it into good, so that he might exalt me, as you see at present, and save many peoples.” This is to say: Whether we wish it or not, God has drawn you into his will; and although you thought about rejecting intellectuality, as though you were greedily complaining about its excess, for there are those who desire mediocrity but, under that colour, desire vices more strongly, God has shown by the very effects that led to my exaltation what good I contain and that true salvation has no place in you without knowledge of heavenly things. He has also subjected to himself, for their salvation through the taste of spiritual things, many peoples—namely, those countless insolences of the soul. Job speaks of these peoples: “Do not prolong the night, that peoples may ascend on their behalf” (Job XXXVI, 20). [Col. 0335D]

**VERSE 21.**—“Do not fear. I will feed you and your little ones.” And he consoled them and spoke to them kindly and gently. He says: Do not fear to attain the heights of divine contemplation in the name of that counterfeit and deadly mediocrity; for in me—and in you, who received from me what enables you to possess constancy in virtue—I will nourish you, together with whatever is weak in you and needs the milk of beginnings. He consoles and speaks gently when, through the incursion of saving wisdom, he makes whatever seemed difficult and incomprehensible light, so that it is now judged nectar-like.

**VERSE 22.**—“And he dwelt in Egypt with all his father’s household, and lived one hundred and ten years. And Ephraim saw children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees.” He dwells in Egypt if, for as long as he lives in the world, each person grieves, understanding himself to be placed in sorrow, tribulation, and distress. He dwells there with all his father’s household when, together with the whole company of rational states, he flees whatever seductive consolation exists in this valley of tears and judges it accursed.
