For Egypt signifies both sorrow and constricting tribulation, as well as darkness. Living in these conditions, one must say: “I have not desired [variant: longed for] the day of man; you know” (Jer. XVII, 16). Ten multiplied produces one hundred. Through the ten of the divine law, when it has reached the hundred of perfect observance, the soul of the wise man lives; and in it the days of luminous action advance into years of integrity and solidity. Ephraim is said to mean “fruitful.” [Col. 0336B]

The fruit of our devout exercise has children because it is not without the rewards of its hope. For hope itself is a child. Hence it is said: “May you see your children’s children” (Ps. CXXVII, 6)—that is, the rewards of works, or the effects of expectations. The first generation, therefore, is the good work; the second is confidence of hope arising from that same good work; the third is the arrival of hope itself at reality. This threefold generation may also be understood according to the Apostle: first calling, then justification, and finally glorification. “Those whom he called,” he says, “he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 30). Thus he regards these as children of the intellect, and consequently strives to be fruitful more ardently. But if by Ephraim’s children we understand only the benefits that arise from works, and not the works themselves, we can say: the fruit of works is the hope of rewards; the fruit of hope is the blessedness of souls; then come the resurrections of bodies. Hence the Psalm says: “You will add days to the days of the king, his years unto the day of generation”—namely, of spirits—and of generation, that is, of bodies (Ps. LX, 7). Hence also the Lord speaks of regeneration: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit…” (Matt. XIX, 28), etc.

Manasseh’s son, whose name means “forgetting,” is Machir, which is interpreted as “seeing.” For the more we forget visible things, the more intellectually we are opened to see heavenly things. Infants commonly sit upon the knees of those who cherish them, and naturally upon the knees of those who are seated. Thus the children of Machir are born upon Joseph’s knees because the fruits of speculative vision—namely, inward joy and a certain assurance of eternal salvation—proceed from intellectuality in love and from love. Unless the purity of understanding is loved utterly, neither the sublimity of contemplation nor the usefulness of the fruits mentioned above will follow. Sitting signifies humility; the bending of the knees, where the lap is enlarged to receive children, signifies the inwardness of charity. Without these, we do not believe that intellectuality can be effective or remain steadfast in acquiring such things; for “knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. VIII, 1). [Col. 0336D]

**VERSE 23.**—“After these things, he said to his brothers: ‘After my death God will visit you and will bring you up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.’” While he is extended through such a multitude of children—that is, of increases—he speaks with discerning eloquence to the virtues [Page 181] placed amid the circumstances of misery, which is Egypt, in accordance with their proper character. [Col. 0337A] He says: “After my death,” namely, when I have cut off the shoots of carnality by the vitality of my intelligibility, then you will be visited by God through the full conception of heavenly love, and from these earthly images by which you are entangled you will be raised up through Abraham, which is the fatherhood of the spirit; Isaac, which is the laughter of the hope of glory; and Jacob, which is the supplanting of every harmful action. You will be raised to that land which signifies not abasement but solidity, which God promises will be possessed by the meek (Matt. V, 4) [Col. 0337B]—namely, a purity stable and unshaken for contemplating God. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the meek” (Jas. IV, 6). For when we live by the spirit and through that same spirit walk toward the joys above with the steps of blessed hope (Gal. V, 25), we undoubtedly enjoy the successful effect of supplanting wickedness. From these three, as though from principal patrons, the grace of holiness is rightly demanded from God, by a kind of appeal grounded in divine right. For whoever engraves the divine image upon himself through devout actions claims for himself, by a just and altogether blessed violence, the grace of holiness promised by God and owed to him by right. “Be holy,” he says, “because I am holy” (Lev. II, 44; XIX, 2).

## VERSES 24, 25

“And when he had adjured them and said, ‘God will visit you; carry my bones with you from this place,’ he died, having completed one hundred and ten years of his life. And, embalmed with spices, he was placed in a coffin in Egypt.”

He adjures them when he establishes and summons the inner states to the rights of rectitude, so that, when they are tormented by the weakness of temptations, they may hear: “God visits you, so that with the temptation he may also provide a way of escape” (1 Cor. 10:13). “Carry my bones from this place”—that is, from this present wicked age, which spiritually is Sodom and Egypt—whatever intellectual virtue you possess, raise it toward the purpose of heavenly eternity; and do not have here a lasting city, but seek the one that is to come, whose builder is God (Heb. 13:14).

Everyone who does not perform his strong deeds for God but for the world has bones in Egypt. Concerning these it is said in the Psalm: “God will scatter the bones of those who please human beings” (Ps. 140:7). For bones signify the strength of virtue, while flesh signifies the burden of weakness.

Afterward, therefore, having already reached certainty of eternal perfection through observance of the Decalogue, as was stated above, he dies to the desire for all earthly things. The number one hundred plainly passes from the left to the right, because the fullness of the inner person, multiplied through the effects of the divine law, passes from the present age to the future with all the affections of contemplation directed toward the highest things.

He is placed, embalmed with spices, in a coffin in Egypt because, fortified against the corruptions of the flesh by the guardianship of virtues, he is laid down amid the storms of the present age under the stability of humility. “He is placed in a coffin” is also commonly said for “he is hidden.” And whoever wishes to be humble certainly conceals himself from every kind of public display. The very name of the act of placing suggests this. Hence the Psalm says: “He placed”—that is, he laid down—“my soul for life” (Ps. 65:9); for many are raised up for death.

The place of the elect in the present is humility. Hence it is written: “There is a place for gold, where it is refined” (Job 28:1). And: “In the valley of tears, in the place which he established” (Ps. 83:7). Therefore, although we may be fragrant with the spices of every kind of holiness, let us restrain ourselves by the smallness of this place, lest we be tossed about by the breeze of popular favor. For even if Joseph—that is, the authority of intellectual understanding—is carried to lofty things, he must nevertheless know in every respect that he still dwells in the Egypt of this age, where, unless God provides for him, he may easily be bent toward worse things.

[Col. 0337] **THE END.**

[Col. 0337]

# THE TROPologies OF THE VENERABLE GUIBERT ON THE PROPHETS HOSEA AND AMOS AND ON THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH

# PROLOGUE OF THE VENERABLE GUIBERT, ABBOT, TO THE TROPologies ON THE PROPHETS HOSEA AND AMOS AND ON THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH

[Col. 0337D] To the most beloved father and venerable lord Norbert, worthy of honor with every affection of charity, a true worshipper of all holy interiority and a teacher of true discernment: Brother Guibert, a monk in name, a sinner in deeds, wishes joy in the prosperous successes of himself and his people.

As we are about to undertake the exceedingly arduous sea of the present prophecy, an undertaking that would make the ancient masters shudder, we bring before you, most generous teacher, knowing your humility, the reasons for so bold an undertaking. I do not doubt that your modesty will receive the words of my defense in the spirit in which it is evident that I offer them to your sober ears.

The blessed Jerome multiplies the difficulty of this volume by such a dense cloud of mysteries that he admits that Origen—after the apostles supreme in doctrine—as well as Apollinaris of Laodicea, Pierius, Eusebius of Caesarea, and finally Didymus the Seer, among whom in their own time no one was more famous among the divine orators, undertook to explain this very work, yet none of them was able to complete what he had begun.

In this undertaking, it seems to me that something of hostility is generated among outsiders, who judge that these things are being attempted with an intention far different from what such great mysteries demand. But if those who hold such opinions were to weigh fairly what they wished to do and what we have subsequently attempted to pursue, they would undoubtedly withdraw from every form of foolishness involved in this unjust suspicion. For when they read that the same blessed Jerome, after saying that this book is wrapped in great obscurities, continues as follows:

“To such an extent,” he says, “that both we who attempt to explain it and the prudent reader should attend carefully together, so that, if we are unable to investigate the truth—which is most difficult—at least we may investigate what appears likely. Perhaps those who see me as rashly undertaking subjects to be feared by distinguished men will brand me with no small blemish of temerity.”

But if they considered how great the difference is between allegories—or rather between the explanations of the literal text itself—and the morality drawn from it, they would certainly restrain their judgments against us. For we treat far more securely of the nature of our own passions, which we experience within ourselves, than of the mysteries of Christ and the Church, in which, unless we are watchful, we can easily go astray.

In tropology, provided only that the obscurity of the literal text is made fully clear to our minds, the condition of the interior person may be examined with the greatest safety and without fear of error—provided, however, that we take care not to allow our understanding to be violently twisted away from agreement with the literal text. For unless you plainly recognize the literal sense, you exercise yourself in vain in the effort to seek allegory or morality; and you are greatly deceived in this inquiry if you attempt to investigate anything beyond reason or the examples of Scripture.

Moreover, if it should happen that someone judges me presumptuous in undertaking such great matters, let him know without doubt that I have penetrated these mysteries with complete certainty only through God’s prompting. And I call God to witness: he did not cease to inspire me, although no prior exercise of mine and no preparation preceded this, except insofar as the very brief delay of my secretary allowed while I was writing and dictating.

Until now, not so much through prolonged reading as through excessive continuity in writing—since I had been not only a dictator but also the tireless recorder of my labor—I had dulled the sharpness of my eyes in every way. As a result, my immoderation reduced me to having the present little work composed with a secretary assisting me, something I had never been accustomed to do, by memory alone and by voice alone, without hand or eyes.

In this matter, let the pious moderation of the reader take note: if he finds that, while dictating in a manner unusual for me, I have said something less competently than I should, let him not delay to pardon me in view of the fact that he knows I have persevered with another’s hand while he wrote what I was saying, just as I once used to do with my own hand.

For when I was writing continually with my own hand and frequently rereading what I had dictated while writing it, it was very easy for me to rewrite what had been omitted. And since I had no reason to fear the annoyances of my secretary caused by delay, I could safely apply myself with painstaking care to the elegance of my words. For I recall what must be said more freely to my mind the less I am ashamed, when I alone have leisure to consider the meaning, of the slowness of dictation.

From my experience, therefore, in the other difficult Scriptures, and relying on divine assistance, I undertake this work as well. I do not doubt that the divine majesty, which granted so much when I possessed only a lesser knowledge of its love, will not deny my mind—now more intent and more devoutly inspired in contemplating its law—better counsels for treating and considering divine matters.

Since, then, it may be asked by what name this little work should be called, it seems to me that, since I called my little commentaries on the book of Genesis *Moralia*, they ought not to be called that here; rather, with the meaning remaining unchanged while the language is altered, I think they can be called *Tropologies on the Prophets*.

[Col. 0339] **THE PROLOGUE ENDS.**

# BOOK ONE: TROPologies ON THE PROPHET HOSEA

[Col. 0341]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0341A]

### VERSE 1

“The word of the Lord that came to Hosea, son of Beeri.”

We must understand this word not as elementary, nor as something inwardly divided into parts by intellectual reasoning through the members of propositions. Rather, it is that light which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9), and of which the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7).

It is the movement of reason toward knowledge of God and toward the discernment of good and evil, implanted after God only in angels and human beings. This is the word of the Lord because it comes from Wisdom herself, the Creator, who says: “I dwell in the highest places” (Sir. 24:7). “From the beginning and before the ages,” the same Wisdom says, “I was created among the angels and human beings” (ibid., 14).

This word comes to be when the diligence of inward reflection distributes it with subtle arrangement, as though dividing it through bodily lines. It also comes to Hosea when it reaches the sole capacity of human intellectual understanding. It comes, I say, to Hosea when, with singular dignity, it gathers itself together for the instruction of our spirit, in which the sum of saving counsel resides.

For Hosea is interpreted as “savior of the Lord.” And after the Lord, to whom is the hope of human salvation more directed than to that word which, according to the Psalm, is prescribed as a lamp for our feet? (Ps. 118:105). Hence it is also called “of the Lord,” because what saves us by teaching is attributed rather to the one who illuminates than to the moon that is illuminated.

This Hosea is the son of Beeri because he draws the glory of his salvation from no other source than God himself, its proper fountain. For Beeri is interpreted as “my well.” The savior, therefore, is the son of his own well, because whatever he supplies inwardly by suggestion for our salvation comes from the abundance of the living waters that flow forcefully from Lebanon (Song 4:15).

### “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”

Uzziah means “strength of the Lord”; Jotham, “consummation” or “perfection”; Ahaz, “virtue”; and Hezekiah signifies “the dominion of the Lord.”

The word, therefore, produces a substantial effect through the reconsideration of good will in the days of the kings of Judah—that is, of confession—when, through the expulsion of sin and the virtues admitted in its place, it displays illuminations to the mind. For the beginning of good things is confession of evils. If Uzziah is the strength of the Lord, what is stronger than confessing before the Lord the injustices of which we are ashamed? (Ps. 31:5).

Then, in accordance with what Jotham signifies, since it is not only good to confess but also subsequently to sing praise (Ps. 91:2), we are consummated and perfected in the presentation of a good work, in accordance with what Ahaz signifies by his name. Virtue is necessary because, when good things abound in us, the ambition for honors and the desire for praise—which then intrude themselves improperly—must be driven away with all our strength.

When this has been done, in accordance with the meaning of Hezekiah, the Lord exercises complete authority. For whoever is in this condition can properly say: “I am yours; save me” (Ps. 118:94), especially when he admits nothing within himself belonging to the left-hand part that may exercise dominion.

### VERSE 2

“And in the days of Jeroboam, son of Joash, king of Israel. The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea.”

It should be noted that above he said that the word came *to* Hosea, whereas now he says “the beginning of speaking,” not *to* Hosea but *in* Hosea.

The Lord speaks to Hosea when our mind is pierced either by divine utterances or by some occasion presented externally. But he speaks in Hosea when the mind is kindled by its own contemplation and by the spontaneous growth of devout thought.

Jeroboam is interpreted as “temporal”; Joash as “hoping”; and Israel as “a prince with God” or “directed by God.” Israel, therefore, signifies our carnal affection. It is never ruled except with God—that is, with reason as its companion—and it is never directed by itself, because the Apostle does not even find good in his own flesh (Rom. 7:19).

Here Jeroboam and Joash have kingship because carnal affection is often oppressed by the domination or exaction of temporal advantage and worldly hope, which is always generated from it. These two have days because they investigate only the prosperities of this age.

There are therefore four kings of Judah and two of Israel because that by which reason is ruled, or which reason will rule, is fourfold and therefore solid. But that in which we swell affectively, being as far outside unity as it is, is correspondingly prone to division and envy.

As long, therefore, as temporal things and hope in temporal things rule the mind, although the power of the four preceding kings is great, the state of the mind nevertheless alternately obeys the two on either side, sometimes softly and submissively. Hence the Lord has the beginning of his speaking in Hosea when, in the inner person, four things have the first opportunities for disputing against two on account of something. This is what follows.

“And the Lord said to Hosea: ‘Go, take for yourself a wife of fornications, and make children of fornications, because the land, committing fornication, will fornicate away from the Lord.’”

The Lord speaks to Hosea when he introduces the causes of an interior act from outside. “Go,” he says, “so that you may not think more highly of yourself than is fitting, knowing that, while you live, the flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17). “But take for yourself a wife of fornications”—that is, ascribe to yourself the will, without which neither good nor evil is done, a will that revels amid the whirlpools of pleasures. “And make children of fornications”—that is, the works of various excesses.

This is the wife whom, in the Gospel parable, he commands to be sold together with her children (Matt. 18:25)—that is, to be led outside the freedom of judgment into a reprobate mind.

“Take,” he says, “a wife and make children”—that is, firmly resolve that what you think and practice is not good, but that the lusts of your thoughts and external excesses are. Nor is this unjust, for one who inwardly commits fornication and, as it were, habitually apostatizes also commits fornication outwardly (Prov. 6:12), “walking,” as Solomon says, “with a perverse mouth.”

The earth—that is, bodily appetite—is away from the Lord.

### VERSE 3

“And he went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore a son.”

He went when he withdraws from consideration of his own good action and from confidence in it.

Gomer is interpreted as “a pool,” that is, a cistern; Diblaim as “their pressed fig-cakes.” Now *palatae* are fresh figs pressed between two boards and compacted in the shape of bricks.

He takes Gomer when he attends only to wantonness, like a liquid hidden within himself. And she is the daughter of Diblaim because worldly pleasure, signified by the boards or palates, produces poisonous sweetness through its own expansion.

Yet she conceives and gives birth not to a daughter but to a son, because, while the person becomes contemptible in his own eyes, what emerges is not effeminate softness but, so to speak, masculine virtue.

### VERSE 4

“And the Lord said to him: ‘Call his name Jezreel, because, in a little while, I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease.’”

The Lord speaks to him when he shows what he ought to weigh concerning his own condition.

Jezreel is interpreted as “seed of God.” The son is therefore commanded to be called “Seed of God,” because whatever is created from the seed of humility is a robust work. For no virtue is called virtue unless it is founded upon humility.

Giving the reasons, he says: “In a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu”—that is, there will be only a brief delay of inner quiet when I begin to avenge the blood, which is the sin of violated humility. And this will be upon the house of Jehu—that is, upon the stability of conscience, which, from desire for God, constructs a kind of immobility in which it is not permitted to remain long.

For there is silence in heaven, but only for about half an hour.

It should also be noted that to call the son is nothing other than to appraise one’s own work. The word “visit,” being frequentative, is understood in two ways in Scripture, as in: “I will visit with a rod” (Ps. 88:33), and: “Visit us with your salvation” (Ps. 105:4). It also indicates the constancy of divine correction within.

We have taken Israel to signify carnal affection, which, without God, is a seducer, but with God is a prince and is directed.

God causes the kingdom to rest when he makes the turbulence and pride of that same carnal affection gentler. For he did not say “make it fail,” but “make it rest,” as in: “Sin will not rule over you” (Rom. 6:14)—plainly not saying that it will not exist.

### VERSE 5

“And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

On that day—that is, in that divine visitation—the bow of Israel is broken because the suggestions of our deceitful affection are boiled away by the diligence of heavenly love.

And this occurs in the valley of Jezreel—that is, in humility, which derives its origin solely from the seedbed of fear of God.

Observe the prophetic manner of speech: they frequently repeat “on that day,” using a demonstrative pronoun to show how constantly the presence of inner light ought to exist in the mind.

It is also customary in Scripture to use “bow” for ambushes.

### VERSE 6

“And she conceived again and bore a daughter. And he said to her: ‘Call her name Without Mercy, because I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them.’”

She conceives again and gives birth to a daughter when, after a more rigorous state, she turns herself toward weaker things—not only to be thought about but also to be carried out.

Yet God commands that her name be called “Without Mercy,” because deliberation by reason continually imposes this upon her, so that she does not attempt anything toward the mortification of the flesh under some false form of piety.

Those who keep watch are accustomed to fear for their brains; those who weep, for their eyes; those who fast, for their entire body. This does not mean that excess in these things should not be restrained, but that excessive relaxation is harmful.

To this agrees the saying: “Stretch out the skins of your tents; do not spare” (Isa. 54:2). This means: Extend in your work, without any hesitation, the examples of the saints by whose authority you are fortified.

God promises that he will not continue to have mercy on Israel when, through his own inspiration, he teaches those who profess eternal self-restraint to become hardened against themselves; and he promises that he will utterly forget them when they remove, through perpetual withdrawal, what they once erased from their hearts at the beginning of their conversion.

It should be known, however, that such repetitions of words as “living life,” “dying death,” and other similar expressions belong more to the native speech of the Hebrews than to any particular figure of speech.

### VERSE 7

“And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God; and I will not save them by bow, or sword, or war, or horses, or horsemen.”

Israel and Judah have houses because they possess states that differ from one another.

He therefore has mercy on the house of Judah because he reveres those to whom he grants the grace of devout confession.

He saves them “in the Lord their God.” This too is a Hebrew expression, meaning “in himself”: because they know that he is their Lord, they fear him; because they know him as God, they hope through love that they will possess him as their reward. The whole matter amounts to being saved first through fear and afterward through love.

Fear belongs to the Lord, as Haggai says: “If I am the Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6). Love belongs to God as to a father. Hence the same prophet says: “If I am a father, where is my honor?” (ibid.).

He does not save them by a bow, because he does not consolidate them through any labor of rigid intention. Nor does he guard them with the sword of discernment, nor in war, since, although they frequently fight against vices, he does not provide them with anything salutary through horses—that is, by restraining the wantonness of the flesh—or through horsemen, where he rides above every form of pride and animality.

The whole meaning is: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16), so that no one relies on his own discipline but on God’s assistance.

[Col. 0345C] ### VERSES 8, 9

“And she weaned her who was Without Mercy. And she conceived and bore a son. And he said: ‘Call his name Not My People, because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.’”

The daughter is weaned when one withdraws from the allurements of wrongful leniency. For we nurse ourselves when, by improperly sparing ourselves good labors, we flatter ourselves inwardly.

Then she conceives and gives birth to a son when, from experience of her own weakness, she rises into a stronger condition.

He commands that his name be called “Not My People,” because he teaches that, however much someone may exercise himself in a good work, even when he has accomplished the greatest things, he must consider himself useless, so that the security of devout efforts may not be produced in him by his people, even if he has labored greatly toward this with complete blamelessness.

Hence it is written: “We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10). And: “A human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. 9:1).

We conceive through desire, but we give birth through accomplishment.

He says, “You are not my people,” because, with the consideration of sin always placed before the eyes of the mind, he does not cease to deflate the swelling of anyone, lest that person be found reprobate.

Hence he adds: “And I will not be your God,” so that everyone who does any good at all may be taught always to fear concerning his future condition.

### VERSE 10

“And the number of the children of Israel will be like the sand of the sea, which is without measure and cannot be numbered.”

The number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea when affective instability is placed under the weight of divine fear, and inner foolishness is salted with the seasoning of divine wisdom.

For, as they say, salt is made from sea sand. Yet the sand is without measure and cannot be counted because, however much the minute particles of empty thoughts may be pressed down by the art of heavenly fear, they can never be wholly restrained or comprehended by the very person who suffers them.

Take “measure” to refer to the extent of desire’s wandering, and “number” to refer to the frequent revolutions of the inner turning that occurs through thinking.

“And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it will be said to them, ‘Children of the living God.’”

“It will be,” he says: what I say will certainly come to pass.

It is a Hebrew manner of speech, as is also that which is set forth in certain prophetic words: the use of such expressions always indicates that they are proclaiming things eternal, not things subject to change.

Our place is the fear of God. For just as joy is an outpouring of the mind, fear is its restraint. Hence it is written: “When I remembered these things, I poured out my soul within me” (Ps. 41:5), and so forth. And: “In the valley of tears, in the place which he established” (Ps. 83:7)—which is none other than fear and humility.

In this place, I say, the spiritual multitude of the mind makes us seem almost deprived of God by our own judgment.

They are called “children of the living God” because, in recompense for the labor we endure in observing humility, this fruit very often follows: when the cloud of such disturbances has been removed, an infinite calm returns, and the serenity of souls becomes greater than could have been hoped. Then the mind no longer fears that it is in danger concerning eternal salvation, but, raised by hope to heavenly things, the human being reigns and sits together with Christ, as the Apostle says (Eph. 2:6).

In this way, the condition of our mind—which, according to the Psalm, had descended into the abysses—rises up to the heavens (Ps. 106:26).

They are called children of God, but specifically “of the living God.” This has been added watchfully so that those who were awaiting death as the outcome of their interior struggle may now, by clinging to God, be assured of attaining the hope of immortal life.

### VERSE 11

“And the children of Judah and the children of Israel will be gathered together, and they will set one head over themselves, and they will ascend from the earth, because great is the day of Jezreel.”

The children of Judah and the children of Israel are gathered together when the eagerness of devout confession and the dullness of affective movements are heaped together under the bond of the one fear of God. Whatever of the babble of the foolish crowd roars inwardly is scattered through buffoonery and restrained by the confinement of holy confession.

They set one head over themselves when they gather under one ruling reason. Hence they ascend from the earth because that same reason, first enlightened by God himself, enables them to rise above the desires of the earth—that is, of the flesh.

This occurs because the day of Jezreel is great: that is, the clarity of the divine seed, namely of inspiration, through which true humility is instilled into minds and becomes known. No one despises himself in the present except through the great love of God.

# CHAPTER TWO

### VERSE 1

“Say to your brothers, ‘My people,’ and to your sister, ‘She has obtained mercy.’”

This is the voice of Israel to the children of Judah, who, after those earlier disturbances, no longer despair of their salvation, as though they were saying:

“Since, O children of Judah, we now perceive that the spiritual movements which urge us toward the purity of confession are gathered together under one head, say to your brothers”—that is, to the movements of affection now agreeing with you, as though begotten from the same mother, because you are fellow citizens under that same head.

And if some weakness has subsequently entered among you like a sister, let it not be without hope of mercy when you return to strong things.

### VERSE 2

“Judge your mother, judge her, because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.”

Although such great indulgence is shown to the sister and to the brothers, mother Reason must nevertheless be judged by her lower movements, since she ought to have ruled them.

Moreover, she must be judged—indeed, plainly judged—because she did not obstruct the beginnings of pleasure. She must be judged no less, or rather all the more, because she sometimes admitted an unsuitable work, since she conceived it from an external—that is, diabolical—seed.

“She is not my wife, and I am not her husband,” because of the infusion of such an offspring. For “everything that is born of God does not know” [or, according to another reading, “overcomes”] “the world” (1 John 5:4).

“Let her remove her fornications from her face and her adulteries from between her breasts” (verse 3). “Otherwise I may strip her naked and set her according to the day of her birth.”

She removes her fornications from her face when she removes past sins from her imagination. For when we remember our shameful acts while established in a vague condition of mind, we very easily rub our old error raw again.

The heart is situated between the breasts. For the Beloved is said in the Song of Songs to dwell between the breasts (Song 1:12).

Adulteries are therefore removed from between the breasts when whatever corruptible things can be falsely loved are withdrawn from the marital right, which is steadfast love of God.

“Otherwise,” he says, “I may strip her naked,” lest, through the habit of sinning, she be led by my just judgment through a reprobate mind into shamelessness. For no one except a person careless of himself is known to endure calmly the fact that the depravity of the senses treats things equally shameful and shameless.

Or consider the other saying: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch over his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Rev. 16:15).

God sets her “according to the day of her birth” when he does not at all diminish her original and actual evils while she receives the grace of God in vain.

“And I will make her like a wilderness and establish her like an impassable land, and I will kill her with thirst” (verse 4). “And I will not have mercy on her children, because they are children of fornications.”

A person is placed in a wilderness when he is abandoned by God, who had inhabited him. He is established like an impassable land when no trace of any teaching or of any good example is found in his heart.

He is killed by thirst when no fountain of water springing up into eternal life flows into his interior being.

God does not have mercy on her children when, for anyone sinning unto death and resisting the grace by which he could have been saved, even the prayer of the other faithful is denied, according to the Apostle John.

The whole passage should be referred to the incorrigibility of affective movements, which become hardened when God does not look upon them. Hence it follows:

### VERSE 5

“For,” he says, “they are children of fornications, because their mother has fornicated; she who conceived them has been put to shame.”

Unless the mother conscience first, straying from the love of God, had deviated from the lawful marriage bed, the thoughts and intentions that are propagated from her as children would not be called by a dishonorable name.

Because she is irrationally confounded in the very conception of depravity, the offspring must likewise be corrupted through the lineage of its begetter.

“For,” he says, “she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’”

“She said” means nothing other than “she determined within herself.”

Her lovers are none other than either demons, who support our desires by supplying causes of vice, or whatever friends or powerful people pursue wretched persons in order to obtain such things, whether through favor or through gifts.

They give bread when they administer the pleasures of temporal things. Hence it is written: “Bread is undoubtedly abominable to the just person”—that is, pleasure—“in his life” (Job 33:20).

They give water when, according to desire, they introduce carnal fluids and wantonness. Hence the spirit is said to go out and walk through waterless places (Matt. 12:43), and Behemoth is forbidden to dwell in moist places (Job 40:16).

They also give wool when they teach knowledge of secular concerns and household affairs, which are highly valued among them.

They provide flax no less when they impart either the liberal arts, which require great acuity, or the subtleties of courtroom cases.

They likewise give oil when they instruct a person how he ought to flatter the wealthy.

They also pour out drink for those whom they intoxicate with the madness of lust through persuasive and misleading speech.

The Church also makes useful use of this wool and flax, both of which she is said to have sought and worked with in Solomon (Prov. 31:13).

By contrast, the Egyptians are put to shame, who worked with flax, combing it and weaving fine cloth (Isa. 19:9)—that is, devising cunning things.

Finally, it should be noted that, while the woman boasts of her own wares, she assigns watchfully to each kind what belongs to it.

For what is more truly their own among the reprobate than that which, with God rejected, serves only the uses of vices?

### VERSE 6

“Therefore, behold, I will hedge in your way with thorns, and I will hedge her in with a wall, and she will not find her paths.”

Since such prosperity is attributed more to her lovers than to God, and is shamefully expended not for God’s uses but for her own, therefore, I say, her way is suddenly hedged in with thorns. All that softness and that intention of progressing according to these things are changed into the barbs of adversities and the hardness of stones.

Balaam, sitting on his donkey and caught in the narrow space between two walls (Num. 22:24), beautifully alludes to this tropological meaning.

Such things commonly happen to such people, so that through a sudden change of fortune they find their friends just as hostile as their enemies.

Hence she no longer finds her paths, because the byways of perverse actions and the narrow alleys of secret schemes have been blocked by the incursion of divine judgment.

### VERSE 7

“And she will say, ‘I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now.’”

“She will say”—that is, she will propose.

“I will go”—that is, I will withdraw from my involvement with such a little prosperity.

“I will return to my first husband,” because I will refer myself to the one to whom I owe my first self—and everything within me—and by whom I am ruled manfully.

“It was better for me then than now,” because after I served the original order and the law of divine and natural institution, I served error and grief in many ways.

### VERSE 8

“And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil.”

It is as though he were saying: That wretched woman, while she pursued her wicked lovers, did not know that the things she credited to them would be turned against her.

But now she rightly considers returning to her former position, because I gave her the reasons for returning to me more eagerly.

He gives grain when he supplies the nourishment of saving doctrine. And because the exercise of preaching or reading is evidently empty without divine inspiration, wine of heavenly sweetness is added, so that the sluggishness of former inertia may depart.

Oil is also given so that the sweetness of love may advance toward one’s neighbor.

“And I multiplied silver for her, and gold, which they made for Baal.”

He multiplies silver when he increases knowledge of the Scriptures or the effectiveness of instruction.

He also supplies gold with the same generosity when he provides either knowledge of heavenly things or excellence of life.

These things once made Baal because, through empty glory, they abusively transferred them into diabolical service.

Observe the prophetic manner of speech: how easily it passes from singular to plural, from plural to singular, and from one person to another. Above, for example, after saying, “I will hedge in your way,” he immediately added, “she will not find her paths.” And here, after saying that he had multiplied gold for her, he added: “which,” he says, “they made into Baal.”

### Verse 9

“Therefore I will turn back and take my grain in its season, and my wine in its season, and I will rescue my wool and my flax, which covered her shame.”

For this reason he turns back: he is recalled by consideration of the many gifts that he had bestowed upon her. Hence we repeatedly urge him not to allow those for whom he remembers that he suffered to be torn apart by the devil’s deceit. He takes his grain in its season when he preserves and retains the divine knowledge—not the knowledge she abused, but his own—to be rewarded eternally, which is “in its season.” Of this it is said: “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6).

“Time” is here placed without time, referring to the age or state, not to changing circumstances. The same understanding applies to the wine and its season. God rescues his wool and his flax when he has assigned to the heavenly reward the discipline that we have exercised concerning knowledge—represented by wool, which is of a coarser nature—and concerning the subtle understanding called wisdom, represented by flax.

He also weighs the wool and the flax when he suspends and raises whatever we know or understand temporally toward the contemplation of God even in the present. To this agrees the statement: “He who weighs,” it says, “with three fingers”—that is, with the love of the Trinity—“the mass of the earthly mind, and weighs the mountains in the balance” (Isaiah 40:12), so that the saints may receive as much inward savor as they love. For “weight” is derived from “hanging,” and whatever hangs is inclined toward something; hence one who loves is also said to hang upon what he loves.

“These things covered her shame,” because the greater the cleverness that flourishes in some people in the present, the more their license to sin seems to them to be sanctioned by the cloak of learning.

### Verse 10

“And then I will reveal her folly in the eyes of her lovers, and no man will rescue her from my hand.”

Now her folly is revealed, because in the new condition of her conversion it is made intelligible to the eyes—or understanding—of her lovers: namely, that her former pursuit was disordered and unsuitable, since it is now rejected with such severity. No one sets before the wicked livelier examples than those who withdraw from their seductive fellowship for God’s sake.

A man does not rescue her from God’s hand, because no movement of reason is so vigorous that it can say anything excusable against the threats of the eternal judgment pressing upon her heart.

### Verses 11–12

“And I will cause all her joy to cease, her solemnity, her new moon, her Sabbath, and all her festal times. And I will destroy her vine and her fig tree, of which she said: ‘These are my rewards, mine, which my lovers gave me.’”

He causes all her joy to cease when she rejects, with a sole desire for tears, whatever foolish happiness she had until then gathered from present prosperity: “My tears,” she says, “were my bread day and night” (Psalm 41:4).

Her solemnity ceases when she no longer knows the spectacles of this world, nor the very famous gatherings that chiefly nourish the eyes. The new moon, which is called the “new moon,” also comes to rest, because no change of circumstances—from the adversities mentioned above toward prosperity—raises her mind into empty hope.

The Sabbath is then destroyed when sluggishness and idleness are beaten away from her thought. For, according to Ezekiel, Nebuchadnezzar imitates the idleness of Sabbaths (Ezekiel 21:23). All her festal times are lulled to sleep when whatever pleasant and desirable thing can arise in this age dies within her intention.

Her vine is destroyed when the love of the world—from which she had drunk the wine of complete madness—is uprooted from her inmost heart. For just as the house of Israel is called God’s vineyard, so, conversely, it is called the vineyard of Sodom and elsewhere the vineyard of the earth.

Her fig tree is also destroyed. The fig tree is known to have milky juices and tender branches; it represents the perverse affection that exists toward the world or toward parents and teaches one to put God second. Through another prophet God threatens that he will strip this fig tree bare (Joel 1:7), that is, that he will remove its strength.

She had called these things her rewards because she had received this fruit of her worldliness either from demons or from friends, as she supposed—namely, because she had found in them a frequent supply of opportunities for sin.

“And I will place her in the forest, and the wild beast of the field will devour her.”

She is placed in the forest when, amid the fervor that arises for her as temptation, she lives as a stranger, according to the Apostle (1 Peter 4:12). She is devoured there by the wild beast of the field when she is gnawed by the devil’s manifold suggestions. “Wild beast of the field” is rightly said, because he is the tyrant of the world.

### Verse 13

“And I will visit upon her the days of the Baals, when she burned incense, adorned herself with her earring and her necklace, went after her lovers, and forgot me, says the Lord.”

The days of the Baals are visited upon her when she is compelled to punish with tears what she once delighted to nourish herself with through many vices. “Days” is used for joy, as in: “If only you had known, even on this day, the things that make for your peace” (Luke 19:42).

“Baals” is used for idols; it is as though he said, “the days of idols.” The term may also be interpreted as “having me” or “my men.” And what idols are greater than crimes, concerning which the Apostle says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3:5)? And elsewhere: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:19).

These are the men who do not rule us but drive us away. Of them it is said: “The one whom you have is not your husband” (John 4:18). As long as they possess us, they do not so much possess us as besiege us. Incense is then burned to them when, from the perverse heat of desire, a mist is stirred within the mind that wrongly blinds us. This is what is said in Ezekiel, where the vapor of a cloud is said to rise from incense (Ezekiel 8:11).

Nor does it hinder us that at times we gladly smell burning incense, since very often, through imaginings, we smell with pleasure things that we have seen and heard—not less vividly than if they were present.

She adorns herself with her earring when she is lifted up by the brightness of her own understanding. A necklace hangs at the lower end of the neck. She therefore adorns herself with a necklace when she takes pride in the depth of her counsel. Those who sin possess words expressing a certain reasoning within themselves, to make excuses for sins (Psalm 140:4). Under the name of humanity, which can scarcely be restrained, they customarily serve sins with greater security.

It is not surprising that we place these things among evils, since they are more frequently found among good things. In the Book of Judges we read that the Ishmaelites possessed earrings and bracelets (Judges 8:24), just as, according to the Apocalypse, there is a golden cup in the hand of Babylon (Revelation 16:19).

Hence she is now said to go after her lovers, because often, without either a human being or the devil as instigator, she voluntarily pursues a perverse habit. Thus it is said to someone: “I will cast you like a ball into a broad and spacious land” (Isaiah 22:18). A ball rolls farther than the one who throws it may wish.

Many people do not wait to be affected; they stir up affections within themselves. Therefore the one who forgets God goes after those who have turned away, because all shame is driven back when whatever belongs to God is shut out from the heart.

### Verses 14–15

“Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and I will lead her into the wilderness, and I will speak to her heart. And I will give her her vinedressers from that place, and the Valley of Achor as a door of hope; and there she will sing according to the days of her youth and according to the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.”

“Therefore,” he says, “I will allure her”—that is, I will instruct her with sweet words so that she may remember me and no longer pursue deserters. I will lead her into the wilderness because I will remove her from the noise of vices and from the crowds of empty thoughts; for she cannot be alone with herself while she is subject to so many exactors.

There God speaks to her heart when the word of sacred Scripture is sweetened in her mind through the grace of compunction. Or he speaks to her heart when those things which she scarcely deigned to touch with the tip of her ear descend deeply into her inmost being.

Her vinedressers are given to her from that place when rational movements, which had once scattered her inner faculties, are faithfully gathered together for the exercise of spiritual cultivation.

The Valley of Achor is likewise granted when the humble mind is disturbed by the bitterness of repentance. For Achor means “tumult” or “disturbance.” Hence the psalm says: “You have moved the earth, Lord, and troubled it” (Psalm 59:4), and so forth.

What disturbance is heavier, what tumult greater, than for conscience under God as judge to be gnawed and grieved by its own crimes? Yet this humility is not disturbed in vain, since thereafter, the more earnestly it wills, the more widely the hope of pardon is opened to it.

There she sings according to the days of her youth because her mind rejoices according to the brightness of renewed virtue. The more fully she reaches the day of divine knowledge and puts on the strength of inward solidity—which is signified by youth—the more gracious are the songs of joy that she pours forth to God.

She also sings according to the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt because, the more she rises above earthly desires—which Egypt signifies—through grace that gives light, the more ready she becomes to glorify and love the one for whose sake those desires are rejected.

### Verse 16

“And it will be on that day”—we have explained this above—“that she will call me: ‘My husband,’ and she will no longer call me ‘My Baal.’”

This is the voice of the woman rejoicing in the promise of God that has just been given. “When God has granted me this light,” she says, “he will call me”—that is, he will regard me as a wife—“so that he himself may be called my husband.” Former sins will not hinder her, because the worship of her former idolatry has been put to sleep.

### Verse 17

“And I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and she will no longer remember their names.”

The Lord returns to what he had begun to say above. The whole meaning is this: I will not only take away from her the worship of her former criminality, but I will also erase from her mouth the very names of vices, which the Apostle calls “shameful speech” (Ephesians 5:4). Nor will I remove only the foulness of words; I will also obliterate from her mind the memory of every obsolete deed.

Hence the Apostle says: “Let it not even be named among you” (Ephesians 5:3). And: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21).

### Verse 18

“And on that day I will strike a covenant for them with the wild beast of the field, with the bird of the sky, and with the creeping thing of the earth; and I will shatter bow, sword, and war from the land; and I will make them sleep securely.”

On that day God strikes a covenant for them with the wild beast of the field—that is, he makes a covenant over the wild beast of the field—when, through the firmness of a good intention, he arranges within that inward light that the wild beast of the field, namely savage desire, be permitted to dominate them in nothing.

Nor will the bird of the sky—namely pride—dominate them, nor the creeping thing of the earth—namely lust. Observe the distinction: the creeping thing clings entirely to the ground; the bird moves through the heights; the wild beast lifts itself somewhat above the earth.

He shatters the bow when he suppresses the ambushes of suggestions that steal into the mind. He shatters the sword when he crushes the pleasures of the flesh that disagree with the rule of reason. He destroys war when, with the highest authority of the spirit, he cuts off thoughts that plunge themselves into offered pleasure.

He makes them sleep securely when, after quieting the attacks of these three temptations—which are the origins of the others—he permits them to be free from worldly disturbances. Hence it is said: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

What is here said, “I will make them sleep securely,” is said in another translation as, “I will make them dwell in hope.” The meaning is: Whoever sleeps in freedom from suffering remains awake in hope; and he makes these people sleep securely because they already rejoice in the certainty of their reward.

### Verse 19

“And I will betroth you to myself forever; and I will betroth you to myself in justice, in judgment, in mercy, and in compassions.”

He betroths her forever when the mind of one who has pledged himself to God never wavers in the pursuit of perseverance.

She is betrothed in justice when she is most firmly strengthened to render to God and to her neighbors what she owes them. For the definition of justice is: “While preserving the common advantage, to render to each what belongs to him.”

This cannot exist without judgment—that is, discernment—for one must beware lest, by pursuing justice excessively, one become worse than the unjust person.

She is also betrothed in mercy when she considers that she has been taken from the mass of perdition not by her own merits but solely by God’s grace. Nor is this without compassions, because whatever good works she may pursue in response to God’s calling, she must firmly believe that she would in no way endure amid temptations unless she were continually assisted by the kindness of her Creator.

### Verse 20

“And I will betroth you to myself in faith, and you will know that I am the Lord.”

It is remarkable that he places faith so out of order, since all the things mentioned beforehand cannot, I do not say stand, but even exist without it. Yet we must consider that faith is added most appropriately, so that the fruit of faith itself may be signified through the merits of simple faith.

Its fruit and reward in the present is understanding. This exists not so much in knowledge as in love, because love is that substance of which the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith makes the things that are to be believed subsist in the heart of the believer with such solidity that he considers himself to possess them more certainly than he possesses anything tangible or corporeal.

She is therefore betrothed in faith when she is established in the immobility of her soul through continual contemplation of her belief. Hence what follows: “And you will know that I am the Lord.” Even if there were neither teaching nor a book to instruct her, she would nevertheless gather from the mere experience of inward sweetness that God exists.

### Verses 21–22

“And it will be on that day: I will answer, says the Lord; I will answer the heavens, and they will answer the earth. And the earth will answer the grain, the wine, and the oil.”

“And it will be”—that is, what is to be said will certainly come to pass. But here we must first consider what he answers, since nothing is added after it. We must therefore understand that he answers the faith mentioned previously.

In this light of faith he answers first, because from our heart, even when it is without works, he receives nothing more pleasing. Afterward the heavens are answered, because every virtue is pleasing when it rests upon so great a foundation, and is sufficient in itself.

It is not without reason that virtues are called “heavens,” because God is especially present in them. The Apostle says that we have been blessed in the heavenly places with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3).

“And they will answer the earth,” because the virtues do not cease to protect the substance of our body against emerging vices.

The earth answers the grain when our lower part obeys the command of spiritual doctrine without resistance. It answers the wine when the flesh itself, responding to the spirit, aspires to the joy of immortality. Hence it is said: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 84:4). This is the wine that, in the Book of Judges, is said to gladden God and human beings (Judges 9:13).

It answers the oil when, from this truly sensible intoxication, it pours forth toward its neighbor the sweetness of every benefit.

### Verses 23–24

“And these will answer Jezreel. And I will sow her for myself in the land, and I will have mercy on her who was ‘Without Mercy.’ And I will say to the one who was not my people: ‘You are my people’; and he will say: ‘You are my Lord.’”

Jezreel, as has been said, means “seed of God.” All the things mentioned above therefore answer Jezreel when, through the divine inspiration that is the source of all this good, they believe themselves faithfully to possess all these things.

Jezreel is sown for itself in the land when it is sprinkled with the fruitfulness of every holy action. He has mercy on her who was “Without Mercy,” because, once the mind that had been inclined toward vices has been purified by divine cleansing, there is no reason for the spirit to be angry with it.

The one who was not his people is called his people when the formerly wanton multitude of thoughts is restrained under God’s rule. He says, “You are my Lord,” when the lordship of God within the conscience is not mutilated by any interruption of superstition.

## Chapter III

### Verse 1

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Go again, and love a woman beloved by a friend and an adulteress, just as the Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look toward foreign gods and love the grape-cakes.’”

It is as though he said: “To someone established in so great a citadel of virtue”—for to speak of God is nothing other than to suggest something to human reason—“go again,” that is, through your reflection, consider that you may withdraw from your present state through some misfortune.

“Love a woman beloved by a friend,” that is, set before yourself a better manner of life in which, nevertheless, you do not displease God. Yet she will be an adulteress, because within the remission that appears on the surface, as though it were a certain good intention, an intention to sin will lie concealed, badly covered over.

The Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look toward foreign gods, because God often grants our affection the impulse to pray and even the grace of compunction, yet, as though she had not wept, our shameless affection returns after a moment to desire wickedness.

They love the grape-cakes because, after renouncing the world, certain people—having become contemptible to the world itself—find no sweetness or love within it, yet inappropriately desire to converse with the world and pursue worldly spectacles.

Hence in the old law the Nazirites are forbidden to eat anything from a dried grape to a grape seed (Numbers 6:4). A dried grape is one that is cooked before it is ripe so that it may remain preserved longer. What does the dried grape signify except those who are taught to sin before the capacity of age? The ripe grape signifies those to whom age itself supplies the power to sin. The grape seed signifies one who, after every pleasure has been exhausted, sins through infirmity or old age, by mere habit and mere will.

Those who love grape-cakes therefore make use of them when, merely by looking at spectacles of another’s happiness—or rather, another’s wickedness—they feed themselves in their misery.

“Na­zirites” is interpreted as “holy ones.” They are forbidden to consume grapes of any kind when, by God’s command, they are kept from imitating those who are lively with the sweetness of the present life.

### Verses 2–3

“And I dug her for myself with fifteen pieces of silver, and a homer of barley, and half a homer of barley. And I said to her: ‘You will wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man; and I also will wait for you.’”

She is dug with fifteen pieces of silver when her inner and outer senses are cultivated by the Decalogue of the law; she is truly dug when earthliness is driven away from the mind.

The division into five is signified by the five senses. Silver represents divine speech.

A homer of barley suggests the totality of animality; yet it returns to half a homer, because although the Apostle did not forbid care for the flesh—“No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5:29)—he nevertheless forbade its fulfillment in desires (Romans 13:14). See how she is dug with silver when totality is restricted to moderation.

Barley is food for beasts of burden. “I said to her” means “I instructed her.”

God waits for many days when, with God withdrawing himself in a dispensatory manner to test a human being, the mind is without the grace of compunction or even contemplation, and yet confines itself within innocence.

This is what follows: “You shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man,” while during the intervening period she is in no way separated in affection from her customary chastity for the adulterer.

But God also says that he will wait when, through this very circumstance, he makes it understood whether the soul loves him. In accordance with this the psalm says: “Do not utterly forsake me” (Psalm 119:8).

### Verse 4

“For the children of Israel will sit many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an ephod, and without teraphim.”

The children of Israel sit for many days without a king because, while God—as I have said—withdraws himself for a time, our affective movements lack the rule of reason.

They are without a prince when they fail even in good will. For, as the Apostle says, “to will is present with me, but to accomplish it I do not find” (Romans 7:18). This is Sarah, whose name means “princess,” under the exalted father Abraham—that is, acting under the authority of the spirit.

They are without sacrifice, that is, without the vow of inward desire, which slays us inwardly. They are without an altar, that is, without the fervor of faith. For there could be no altar where there was no fire with which to burn the flesh; nor is there faith that lacks the warmth of devotion.

They are without an ephod when they lose “the charity of Christ, which surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:19); for the ephod is called the garment worn over the priestly clothing.

They are without teraphim because they do not live according to any representation of heavenly things. The teraphim were those figures that, under the appearance of cherubim, the Lord commanded Moses to make in the tabernacle.

All these things signify that [lacuna] they conduct themselves without regard for any form of spirituality.

### Verse 5

“After this the children of Israel will return, and they will seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they will fear the Lord and his goodness in the last of the days.”

It often happens that even the carnal affection is terrified by its excessive wandering. Thus Israel gathers itself together again for reflection upon God, together with its children—that is, the multitude of thoughts.

Hence David the king is immediately sought, when reason—the strong hand that alone resists carnal and diabolical assault—is restored to its former rule.

They fear the Lord when, withdrawing from illicit wandering, they restrain themselves humbly at the command of the one who can punish them as Lord. For what is contracted by servile fear is often loosened with great ease when the opportunity arises.

It is rightly added: “And his goodness in the last of the days.” If punishment is feared, it is much more generous to desire the reward.

They therefore fear God’s goodness at the end of the days when that unique good of the final recompense is brought forth by fear and awaited with joy: “Let my heart rejoice,” he says, “that it may fear your name” (Psalm 86:11).

## Chapter IV

### Verse 1

“Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the earth.”

The children of Israel hear the word of God when the arrows of the Mighty One, according to the psalm, pierce the hardness of their carnality (Psalm 120:4).

And rightly, he says, it must be heard so that affective desire may be restrained. For when the Lord judges the world at the end, he will not judge alone, but also the inhabitants of the earth—namely, those who have ruled their earthliness well—and they will likewise be granted judicial dignity. Hence possession of this earth is promised to the meek (Matthew 5:4).

“To inhabit,” from *habeo*—“I have,” “you have”—means, through repeated use, “to rule,” as in: “Inhabit the land, and you will be nourished by its riches” (Psalm 37:3).

“There is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land.”

What is truth except the identity of one thing without any wavering? It is not in the earth, which is continually subject to vanity; for the Apostle himself did not find good in his flesh (Romans 7:18).

There is no mercy because, always inclined toward its own desires, it looks upon all the anxieties of others with complete indifference.

There is no knowledge because discernment arises in the mind from that lower part without any discrimination.

### Verse 2

“Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.”

Since, therefore, there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the earthly mind, cursing consequently overflows. Where the heart is not governed by the bridle of divine fear, the shameless tongue is carried toward the savagery of evil speech; and when it disparages others, it lies with even greater security.

This is hardly surprising, since it is scarcely—or not at all—subject to human power, but only to divine power.

When freedom is surrendered to cursing and lying, it is necessary that one easily break out into crimes—murder and theft—and into disgraceful acts—adultery.

Observe that one passes from the iniquity of words to the cruelties of deeds. Then rage foams into sordid action.

“Blood has touched blood” when a sin negligently committed—which kills its author, as blood signifies—often leads him knowingly to repeat the same death.

### Verse 3

“Therefore the land will mourn, and everyone who dwells in it will grow weak, together with the wild beast of the field, the bird of the sky, and the fish of the sea; they will be gathered together.”

Therefore the earth mourns—that is, it makes itself worthy of mourning—because no intellectual vigilance restrains it.

Everyone who dwells in it grows weak, because whoever strives to oppose its movements must often be endangered by the distress of thoughts rushing upon him from his own condition.

This occurs through the wild beast of the field and the bird of the sky, because at one moment he is stretched by desire, and at another tossed about by the lightness of pride.

The fish of the sea are also gathered when the ticklings of the flesh, nourished in the waters of pleasures, mass together against the spirit exhausted by them.

### Verse 4

“Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be rebuked.”

It is as though he said: Although the power of human understanding, tested against so many vices, almost gives way, nevertheless the person who judges one who is weakened in such circumstances acts unjustly.

Nor should he accuse the one who ought to be called a man because he bears and tolerates what is being tested in him as best he can. He should attend not to the measure of the temptation but to the strength of endurance in the one who is tempted: “Considering yourself,” he says, “lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

### Verse 5

“For your people are like those who oppose the priest. And you will fall today, and the prophet will also fall with you.”

Your people, O Israel, are like those who oppose the priest, because the enormity of your movements, O carnal affection, is truly like those who continually set themselves against sacred leadership—that is, against reason.

“You will fall today,” that is, on account of the cause of the temporal pleasure or present glory that you pursue.

“The prophet will also fall with you,” because, since you do not reach forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3:13), your lack of foresight will make you blind.

“I have caused your mother to be silent by night.”

The mother of this people is reason. God therefore makes the mother of this people silent by night when, in his just judgment, he denies her the strength with which she ought to resist the insolent multitude of thoughts.

Hence what follows:

### Verse 6

“My people have become silent because they have lacked knowledge.”

God’s people become silent when they do not rebuke the evils arising in the heart with appropriate severity. This is because they have lacked knowledge—that is, they have lost the power of inward discernment.

“Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve as priest to me.”

It is as though he said: Because you have neglected to bring your habits and movements into balance by the scales of judgment, and have not wished to learn how you ought to govern yourself inwardly, you have surrendered yourself to a reprobate sense, so that you do not know how to provide for yourself or measure your own condition.

“And because you have forgotten the law of your God, I also will forget your children” [elsewhere, “you have forgotten,” feminine].

The law of God is understood not in literary knowledge but in natural experience. Whoever forgets it—that is, whoever does not recall what he once knew and possessed—justly reaches the point at which God does not remember his children, that is, his evil works, for his own correction.

Spontaneous ignorance gains no advantage; innate ignorance, however, is spared. Hence it follows:

### Verse 7

“According to their multitude, so they sinned against me.”

A person is “many” when, even without an abundance of teaching, he possesses the resources of a discerning intellect. Those who possess multitude therefore have the sharpness of their original understanding because of their learning.

Their sins are weighed according to their cultivated—even if through negligence dulled—and natural prudence, because they are judged according to what they knew or could have known.

“I will change their glory into shame.”

Their glory is the liveliness of their understanding. It is changed into shame when what they desire to have counted as their praise is charged against them as disgrace because of the dishonor of their studies.

### Verses 8–9

“They eat the sins of my people, and they lift up their souls toward their iniquity. And it will be: As the people, so the priest.”

They eat the sins of God’s people when they take the falls of various good people as support for their own error and, as it were, feed upon them. So that they may persevere more securely in evil, they take root, so to speak, in the example of those whom they had once considered good.

Their souls are lifted toward their iniquity when those whom they hated as spiritual, after they have become worldly and committed worse deeds, are immediately raised up by favorable excuses; and they “give life” to souls that do not live, according to the prophet (Ezekiel 13:18).

“And as the people, so the priest” applies when the one who approves the sinner is guilty of the same crime, if not a greater one, than the person who sins. For he administers a priesthood appropriate to his own condition when he teaches in defense of such a person.

### Verse 10

“And I will visit his ways upon him, and I will repay his thoughts to him. And they will eat and will not be satisfied.”

Following prophetic usage, he passes from the plural to the singular. He visits his ways upon him when he condemns him by burdening him with his actions. He repays his thoughts to him when he openly pours back upon him, through punishment, the sins of his hidden apostasy.

Observe, however, that “people” is a collective singular, and therefore the numbers may perhaps change.

Above he had said that they eat the sins of his people; here he adds that they eat and are not satisfied. Although they desire to obtain consolation from another’s iniquity, it can offer no nourishment to their biting conscience, by which they are continually shaken inwardly.

“They committed fornication and did not cease, because they abandoned the Lord by failing to keep him.”

They commit fornication when they are alienated from God through love of present things. They do not cease when they do not strike back against the vices that rule them with any authority of reason.

“Because,” he says, “they abandoned the Lord by failing to keep him”: they showed no reverence for the divine regard and provided no guardianship for the mind.

### Verse 11

“Fornication and wine and drunkenness take away the heart” [elsewhere, “take away” plural].

The meaning is: When someone is cut off from God and, having put God aside, desires the pleasures of the world and is overwhelmed by them with reason buried, his heart is taken away, because afterward nothing in him remains attentive or restrained in the face of crimes.

### Verse 12

“My people consulted their own piece of wood, and their staff will announce it to them” [elsewhere, “announced it”].

The people consult their own piece of wood when the mind, noisy and agitated, does not turn for advice toward the line of what is just and right from which it has turned away, but toward the customary stupidity to which it is wholly devoted.

His staff announces it to him when some person of similar ignorance and foolish will supplies more deadly counsel concerning the things that lie close to his heart.

“For the spirit of fornications deceived them, and they committed fornication against their God.”

If we understand the spirit of fornication as the demon, we surely seem to excuse their error by assigning the devil as their instigator. But we can understand it otherwise.

In Scripture “spirit” is used for pride, as in: “You take away their spirit, and they fail” (Psalm 104:29); and: “He takes away the spirit of princes” (Psalm 76:13). Saul, when he threatened to strike, is also said to be “breathing” threats (Acts 9:2).

The spirit of fornications therefore deceived them because, while they were proud of their perversity and rejoiced exultantly in the worst things, the depravity of their mind surrounded them. “It deceived” is said as though it had completely seized them [perhaps, “seized”].

The preposition *de* is sometimes used intensively, as in *deame* and *deiero*.

### Verse 13

“They sacrificed upon the tops of the mountains and burned incense upon the hills, beneath the oak, the terebinth, and the poplar, because its shade was good.”

They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains when, imitating the pride of the rich, they slaughter themselves through the ruin of every vice.

The tops of the mountains—that is, the arrogance of the powerful—are imitated by the poor or the person of moderate means, so that what is done in the powerful by wealth is done in these others by the mere desire for wickedness.

Incense is burned upon the hills when, following the example of their contemporaries and equals, someone is, as it were, sprinkled with the fragrance of those who have departed from the fire of another’s desire.

They themselves burn incense upon the hills when, by their association with such people, they conceive and kindle the heat of perverse fervor.

They do this beneath the oak when, through a swinish imitation, they submit themselves to every wallowing-place of vice. For the oak, being acorn-bearing, feeds pigs.

The one who does this beneath the terebinth sins in a somewhat more careful and familiar manner, after the ugliness of the act has been removed. For the terebinth is beautifully shady and of pleasant fragrance.

The poplar is indeed fruitless, but spreading in branches and tall; its leaf is white on one side and black on the other. It clearly signifies those who speak with an appearance of honesty outwardly, but secretly affect others with perverse persuasion toward every evil.

Hence it follows: “Because its shade was good”—that is, because one could more quietly engage with such people in any sort of discussion concerning error.

“Therefore your daughters will commit fornication, and your brides will commit adultery.”

When the authority of another’s way of life is shamefully regarded, the daughters commit fornication because inward softness is entirely laid aside from divine strength.

The daughters commit fornication when hearts, fragile in themselves, are also injured by external weakening.

The brides become adulteresses when wills already corrupted in one direction plunge much more disastrously into another by imitating others.

## VERSE 14

“Upon your daughters I will not visit punishment when they have committed fornication, nor upon your brides when they have committed adultery, because they themselves consorted with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men, and an unintelligent people will be beaten.”

God does not visit punishment upon the daughters who commit fornication when he does not correct those conditions which, as though they had been deprived of their virgin integrity, are not amended through the grace of compunction, or chastise them with any sort of scourging. The same applies to the daughters and, in the same way, to the brides. They consort with prostitutes whose hearts are offered to every disgrace solely for the price of pleasure. Or certainly they consort with prostitutes over whom desire and lust chiefly rule. They sacrifice with effeminate men who, having no share in the seed of God’s word and having renounced themselves to feminine softness, prostrate themselves like victims before the devil’s will. An unintelligent people is beaten because indiscriminate thought ulcerates the surface of the mind with the wounds of vices.

## VERSES 15–16

“If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not offend.”

This is to say: If you, O carnal affection, stain the bed of divine love through illicit wanderings, nevertheless see to it that you do not lose the refuge of confessing your sins.
