“And do not enter Gilgal, and do not ascend to Beth-aven, nor swear, ‘The Lord lives.’ For Israel has turned aside like a wanton cow.”

He enters Gilgal who is thrust into the filth of disgraceful acts; for Gilgal is interpreted as “a place of rolling.” One ascends to Beth-aven when the mind is marked with the titles of arrogance. Beth-aven is called “an unprofitable house”; and what is more unprofitable than not seeing the shamefulness of one’s own conscience and wishing to make oneself a spectacle to the eyes of others?

“‘The Lord lives’:” whoever swears in this way claims through hypocrisy that the Lord lives in him, and, by adding certain works, declares and confirms it. Therefore one is forbidden to swear, “The Lord lives,” because Israel is turned aside like a wanton cow. He is rightly forbidden both to ascend and to promise himself a life he does not possess, since he is shown to bend his flanks like a horse and a mule.

“Now the Lord will feed them like a lamb in a wide place.”

Yet the Lord now feeds them when, through the Scriptures, he instructs them in the present. They are fed like a lamb in a wide place when, following the broad and spacious way (Matt. 7:13), they encounter sacred discourse in the likeness of the elect and the innocent. Hence it continues:

## VERSE 17

“Ephraim is a partner of idols; let him alone.”

Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitful.” Our will is called fruitful when, receiving a seedbed from the spirit, it becomes our wife within the sides of our house, like an abundant vine (Ps. 127:3). This Ephraim—that is, the will—is a partner of idols when, inclined solely toward display for the sake of coveted praise and worldly expectation, it is shaped by ostentation. An idol has the appearance of a human being, but is not a human being; nevertheless, it is much more ornamented than a human being.

The will is therefore a partner of idols when it desires outwardly to appear what it provides not in reality but through external adornment. To this agrees the saying of Zechariah: “O shepherd,” he says, “O idol abandoning the flock” (Zech. 11:17).

Judah—that is, the vow of pious confession—is therefore told to let him go, because it is exceedingly difficult and unusual for someone whom a likeness of such great splendor has transformed to wish to become a confessor of something shameful, if such a thing lies hidden within him. He is therefore commanded to be dismissed who is forbidden to imitate.

## VERSE 18

“Their feast has been separated; they have committed fornication with fornication; they have loved to bring disgrace upon his protectors.”

Their feast—that is, the feast of hypocrites—is separated because what they are accustomed to feed upon most wickedly, namely, the favor of external approval, is rarely detected by human beings. Therefore they commit fornication with fornication, because their inner corruption—whose hardness is indicated by the repetition of the word—grows all the more fiercely and hides itself as all the more incurable, the less it becomes known to human senses. For if it became known, it would more quickly be exposed to some form of treatment.

They love to bring disgrace upon his protectors when the movements of his carnal cunning—which protect his simulation so that it may not be recognized, placing a veil of wickedness over it and striving to arrange it—are plainly revealed by God’s just judgment through his iniquity being uncovered. They did not cultivate it for its honor, but for its disgrace.

## VERSE 19

“The spirit has bound him with its wings, and they will be confounded by their sacrifices.”

The spirit binds him—that is, Ephraim—with its wings when the breeze of pride, of which we spoke above, couples the will, carried about by every wind, to its own levity. It is not that pride, as a guest, leads him; rather, pride itself flies about with him in whatever direction it wishes. Therefore they are confounded by their sacrifices, because, by delivering themselves over to demons through every kind of crime, they are carried headlong while they imagine that they are being lifted up.

# CHAPTER V

## VERSES 1–2

“Hear this, priests, and attend, house of Israel, and listen, house of the king, because judgment is for you, for you have become a snare for contemplation, and a net spread over Tabor. And you have turned victims toward the depths, while I am the instructor of them all.”

God’s word urges the priests to listen—not, of course, others than those whom he had previously called “protectors” ironically—for, in the very manner by which they protect, they are accustomed to offer guidance that is not sacred but accursed.

The house of Israel is also commanded to attend, and the house of the king to listen, so that affection may be warned to direct its intention and reason to obey together with its movements. “For judgment is for you”: that is, it is yours to discern what I say.

They become a snare for contemplation when they obscure with the common mist of thought whatever they could contemplate within themselves through the ray of understanding.

Tabor is interpreted as “coming light.” And what light is this except that which is marked upon us from the face of God? And from whom does it come except from him who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9)? A net is therefore spread over Tabor when human ingenuity is laid over the light-bearing power of reason, and a person prepares to devote himself to slander against his neighbors by means of what ought to have served the contemplation of truth. A net made for catching birds and beasts is sometimes used as a figure for the craft of fraud. Hence Isaiah says: “Those who spread a net over the river will wither” (Isa. 19:8). He spreads a net over the river who proposes to exercise his cunning amid the concerns of this world.

Note that “contemplation” does not refer only to that which is directed toward God, but also to that which concerns the contemplation of truth and the discernment of spirits.

Victims are turned toward the depths when those who had prostrated themselves before the devil through every kind of wickedness are lowered by evil persuasions into the abyss of despair or of hardness of heart, over whom, according to the Psalmist, the mouth of the pit is pressed (Ps. 68:16).

And God is the instructor of them all, since there is no one who can hide from his heat (Ps. 18:7). Yet the wickedness in which they seem shamelessly to be suffocated is not obscure to themselves, because reason repeatedly scintillates: however they turn themselves away, the evils in which they are are repeatedly forced upon the mind, even against its will. Hence it continues:

## VERSE 3

“I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me.”

God knows Ephraim when he causes us, through reason’s prompting, to know our will, which ought to have been fruitful like an abundant vine. Israel is not hidden from God when our affection cannot remain hidden from us through the ray of enlightened reason. For reason, which is recognized to have God principally dwelling within it, is sometimes put for God, as in the passage concerning the fellow servants who report to the king—without doubt, to God—about the servant to whom he had forgiven ten thousand talents, but who had strangled his fellow servant over a hundred denarii (Matt. 18:24).

For what else does this mean than that they reconsider the wickednesses they have seen while God presides over their reason?

It continues: “For now Ephraim has committed fornication; Israel has been defiled.”

As though he were saying: I will set Ephraim and Israel against their own face, and I will make him know that now Ephraim has committed fornication and Israel has been defiled—that is, the will, in its love of present things, which is signified by “now,” has completely departed from the line of pious intention; and then the worse affection, by rolling itself into the foulness of crimes, has proceeded shamelessly.

## VERSE 4

“They will not give their thoughts to return to their God, because the spirit of fornications is in their midst, and they have not known the Lord.”

They do not give their thoughts so that they may return to God because they consider it difficult to abstain, for the love of God, from the pleasures of their imaginings. Nor do they value God highly enough to be willing, for his sake, to expend what they inwardly handle with pleasure.

To such a person it is said: “You have cast me behind your body” (1 Kings 14:9). This happens because the spirit of fornications is in their midst—that is, pride, which specially expels us from God. It does not preside secretly in a corner, as though stealing upon us, but in the midst, like a king ruling openly, it governs the whole understanding.

Therefore they do not know the Lord—that is, they do not conceive him through inward savor—because when someone’s palate has grown bitter from fevers, nothing, even if naturally sweet, tastes sweet to him.

## VERSE 5

“And the arrogance of Israel will answer to his face; and Israel and Ephraim will fall in their iniquity; Judah also will fall with them.”

The arrogance of Israel answers to his face because the inner affection, wandering through illicit things, is accustomed to break forth most shamefully into what is externally improper. It answers in the face when it is late in becoming ashamed outwardly of what it long cherished arrogantly in the mind.

Israel and Ephraim, who seemed inwardly to stand firm in the great conceit of their haughtiness, will fall deservedly because of their iniquity. Then, from the ignobility of their fall, they will infer what they desired long ago and what they nurtured by prolonged longing.

Alas, Judah also falls with them, because, according to the saying of the wise man, “Confession perishes from the dead” (Sir. 17:27). For one whose sin has turned into shamelessness is unlikely, or only with difficulty, to recover for the grace of confession.

## VERSE 6

“With their flocks and with their herds they will go to seek the Lord, and they will not find him; he has been taken away from them.”

They go with their flocks when, through an uncorrected inner foolishness, they sometimes show that they wish to turn back to God. Sheep are sometimes used as a figure for useless simplicity. Hence: “Like sheep they are placed in hell” (Ps. 48:15). David, too, was taken from the flocks of sheep, from following the ewes that were nursing their young (Ps. 77:70).

These are the movements carried away by every wind of temptation.

They go also with their herds when, without any spiritual liveliness, they shake off their customary dullness of mind and their burdensome concerns. Therefore they do not find the Lord, because corporeal things cannot grasp what is intellectual; nor does what is intellectual dwell in a body subjected to sins, since it continually withdraws from thoughts that are without understanding.

God is taken away from them when that whatever will seemed to be giving birth to something good is lost.

### VERSE 7

“They have transgressed against the Lord, for they have begotten foreign children.”

As though he were saying: In this very matter—that although they propose good beginnings as signs of an undiscerning conversion, they easily abandon themselves from their purpose—they deserve to be regarded before God as transgressors. And this happens because they have begotten foreign children.

If they are foreign, how are they children? They are both children and foreign.

They are children because they are works. Hence: “May you see the children of your children” (Ps. 127:6), that is, may you experience the rewards of works. And these works are foreign—that is, adulterine—not begotten from the seed by which they ought to have been begotten, namely, intention. They were either begun out of fear of some earthly disadvantage, as happens very often, or pursued perfunctorily or lukewarmly, without a will to persevere.

“Now the month will devour them with their partners.”

Since “now” signifies the present time, it indicates that something momentary is meant here. “Now,” therefore—that is, suddenly—the month devours them when a monthly religion, which greatly differs from the year of God’s goodness, causes the mind to grow worse than it had been. Nor is it inappropriately said to “devour,” since nothing consumes whatever good remains in a person so completely. From crime audacity is gained when good beginnings are openly despised.

Their partners are devoured together with them when natural goods, if any exist, are rejected—goods that seemed to contribute their partnership to that transitory conversion.

[Col. 0363] **THE FIRST BOOK ENDS.**

# BOOK TWO

## CONTINUATION OF THE TROPOLOGICAL INTERPRETATIONS OF HOSEA

[Col. 0365]

I am invited to expound the blessed Hosea morally not by confidence in my own knowledge, but by purity of faith. For the experience of past labors, in which divine inspiration deigned to grant me good results, has bestowed upon me the faith to undertake no lesser things, since I know that he who gave an ass things contrary to nature (Num. 22:30) will give greater things in a human being.

Let us therefore repeat the same Spirit by whom he spoke, so that he who is recognized to have burst forth wondrously in that heavenly flute may deign to cause the breath to resound in us through the same whistle by which he once spoke to Elijah (1 Kings 19:12).

## VERSE 8

“Blow the horn in Gibeah, and the trumpet in Ramah; howl in Beth-aven behind your back, Benjamin.”

This is addressed to preachers, whose duty is to sound differently against different errors.

The horn is blown in Gibeah when moderate sins are confronted in measured speech. Gibeah is interpreted as “hills,” and hills are said to be moderately extended ridges of land. The horn belongs to shepherds and watchmen. Therefore we use the horn against the hills when we deal with moderate offenses in a more restrained manner.

Ramah, however, is interpreted as “exalted.” We must therefore rise against swollen and elevated minds with something like a military apparatus, not fearing their power, but using unflinching authority because they are richer, lest the same vices spread to those subject to them. For we use the trumpet in wars.

It should be considered that he is silent about the lowest, and teaches that only the moderate and the exalted are to be rebuked—plainly because our haughtiness is accustomed to attack the poor, whom we in no way respect.

But in Beth-aven, which is interpreted as “house of the idol,” one must howl, not preach. For toward those who are completely turned away from God, whom the Psalmist calls the willows in the midst of Babylon, not only are our instruments hung up (Ps. 136:2), but they are also mourned by those who think soundly, as Lazarus was mourned by the Lord (John 11:35), with a compassion befitting the dead. Their apostasy is indicated by the idol.

And this is “behind your back, Benjamin.” Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” And who is the son of the right hand except that principal offspring of our mind, namely, the rational movement, to which the effect of every prosperity is always joined?

The house of the idol is therefore behind Benjamin because such great forgetfulness of God arises only from the fault of reason badly directed.

It should also be noted that, after saying that one must howl in Beth-aven, he immediately added an apostrophe to Benjamin, as though crying out. It is as if he said: Alas! Reason is the cause of so great an evil when you turn yourself away from right consideration.

### VERSE 9

“Ephraim will be in desolation.”

When Benjamin turns his back, Ephraim is made desolate, because whatever is fruitful in our will is scattered when the spirit of prudence has departed.

“On the day of correction I will reveal faith among the tribes of Israel.”

The day of correction is the return of light-bearing reason. In this return faith is revealed among the tribes of Israel when the truth of the words spoken above concerning the spirit’s turning away is made clear: namely, when carnal affection is corrected through all its movements, as though through tribes, according to the rights of reason.

As though he were saying: It can be known from this that, when Benjamin turns his back, Ephraim is made desolate; that, when the day of inward inspiration has been restored, the tribes of Israel are corrected. In this, I say, the faithfulness of this word is revealed.

## VERSE 10

“The princes of Judah became like those who assume a boundary; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water.”

The princes of Judah became like those who remove a boundary when the principal movements that urge us toward true confession are created in a good intention. And “like”—that is, truly—they assume a boundary when, having confessed well about complete amendment from God, they presume upon it.

A boundary is assumed when a limit is set in the mind against all errors. It should be noted that all this takes place on the day of correction.

God’s wrath is also poured out upon them like water when the judgment of divine chastisement that comes upon them is frequently considered in the mind. Yet this wrath is poured out like water because, through such consideration, the conscience is washed clean of the filth of sin.

## VERSE 11

“Ephraim suffers oppression, broken by judgment, because he began to follow filth” [al., “filths”].

Ephraim suffers oppression when, in the fear of divine judgment, our will is harassed by the disturbances of thoughts and is often even drawn away from the good it has begun. Hence he is also said to be “broken by judgment,” because amid such repeated disturbances the sharpness of our discernment is blunted.

“For,” he says, “he began to follow filth”—that is, he began to turn his mind toward the foulness suggested to him and hurled at him by the devil.

## VERSE 12

“And I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah.”

God becomes like a moth to Ephraim when, amid temptations, the mind wastes away through excessive listlessness. For one is consumed as if by a moth when, under the pressure of grief, he is stirred by no zeal for reading or prayer, but “their soul abhors every kind of food,” according to the Psalm (Ps. 106:18).

He becomes decay to the house of Judah when confession itself—through which the inner dregs are so often vomited out—seems to stink in the sight of the mind. For when it is shaken by troubles, nothing that is of God is found not to be foul-smelling.

## VERSE 13

“And Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond; and Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king. But he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able to loosen your bond from you.”

Ephraim sees his sickness when he cherishes awareness of his condition’s helplessness within the breast of a wavering conscience and is unable to resist. Judah looks upon his bond when reason itself, entirely bound and torn away from its proper authority, is in no way able to exercise the powers of confession.

Assyria is interpreted as “court.” And what is signified by a court except the tumult of temporal wantonness? Such spectacles rage in courts.

Ephraim therefore goes to the court when, by attending to worldly matters, he separates himself from his own care. He sends to the avenging king when he directs the destination of his worst desire toward the devil—the most cruel avenger of this desertion of his. Alas! The embassy of our intention is sent to him, and he avenges this very thing upon the one who sends it.

He will not be able to heal us, since it is his nature even to render the healthy wounded. Nor can he loosen our bond, since it belongs to him alone, if he is permitted, to leave no one unbound. In all this, a remedy is sought from the one by whom everyone who flees to him is slaughtered.

It continues:

## VERSE 14

“For I am like a lioness to Ephraim, and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah.”

He had often said: “I am like a moth to Ephraim and like decay to the house of Judah.” Now he adds that he will become like a lioness to Ephraim and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah.

There is no doubt that moths and decay silently and secretly consume clothing and wood, whereas a lioness and a lion’s cub leap upon their prey openly and inflict injury visibly. This means nothing other than that those whom God permits to be destroyed through hidden temptation he afterward permits to be torn apart through manifest vices.

There is a distinction between these two kinds of temptation, so that one thing may be understood by the moth, another by decay, another by the lioness, and yet another by the lion’s cub.

A moth is alive and arises from the very thing it corrupts. The moth, therefore, is any vice of the mind that does not arise from an external cause but receives its seed internally from its own condition, such as listlessness, vainglory, pride, or any other inward vice.

Decay is nothing other than torpor and idleness, from which corruption gradually enters the mind, as though through the evil of decay. The three evils mentioned above are therefore, as it were, living and possessing movements within the mind, whereas idleness is as though lifeless.

What, then, is signified by the lioness except the manifest wickedness of any crime? And what by the lion’s cub except negligence that is slight, newly arising, and easily bent?

This is to say: After the hidden plague of the mind, by which it is first gnawed when any vice strikes it, there follows the carelessness of the spirit, through which it is corrupted of its own accord. But after the mind has departed from God and turned toward the embassy of the avenging king, it is struck outwardly with every evidence of some most atrocious crime, as though by the attack of a lioness. For a lioness, especially when she is raising cubs, is said to be stronger and fiercer than a lion. By this Ephraim—that is, our will—is torn apart on every side.

Afterward the lion’s cub encounters Judah, because the shame that extinguishes the grace of confession is very slight. It is indeed slight, because as soon as the spark of penitence has glimmered in the heart, the first will to confess immediately presents itself spontaneously. For just as fire cannot exist without heat, so sincere repentance cannot exist without the desire for confession.

“Behold, I will seize and go away; I will take away, and there is no one who can rescue.”

God seizes when fear of heavenly strictness intercepts the mind wandering away from itself. He goes away when he causes us to depart from our former error. The word “behold” indicates the outcome of sudden inspiration.

Such plainly are the falls of the human mind: one who has just begun to stand may soon succumb when his conscience grows weak or vice stumbles him—and this happens not once, but repeatedly through many returns. In this way “the righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24:16). When he falls, he is not dashed to pieces, because, as we began to say, “the Lord places his hand beneath him” (Ps. 36:24).

He takes away when he lifts the soul of this mortal life away from its desires. “There is no one who can rescue,” because no temptation attacking the heart so greatly can, by any deceit, snatch a person away from God when God fully possesses him.

## VERSE 15

“Going away, I will return to my place until you fail and seek my face.”

God again goes away when, after grace has been received, he withdraws from us for a time in a providential manner, in order to show us what we are from ourselves; yet he does not abandon us altogether.

Going away, therefore, he returns to his place when we are repeatedly commanded by him, as needy and deserted people, to return to humility, which properly is our dwelling place in the present.

Certainly, when we are thus deserted, we are brought nearer to him more beneficially. This happens until we fail, for the Psalm says that sinners fail from the earth and that the wicked are no more (Ps. 103:35). A person fails from the earth when he becomes free from earthly vanity, so that what he once was is no longer present.

In this way, then, once we have failed, we seek his face when our inner poverty compels us to seek it again with more ardent longing.

# CHAPTER VI

## VERSE 1

“In their tribulation they will rise early to me.”

The tribulation of holy men is nothing more specific than deprivation of this inward sweetness. One rises early in this tribulation when one hastens with complete diligence to receive its grace. “Early” is sometimes used to mean diligently or promptly, as in the Psalms: “And my chastisement,” he says, “was in the mornings” (Ps. 72:14); and: “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the earth” (Ps. 100:8).

## VERSE 2

“Come, and let us return to the Lord, because he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike us and will cure us.”

This is the voice of those who rise early to God from tribulation.

“Come,” they say—that is, all of you who are held by the same error as we are, or all of you whose inward movements have gone away to Assyria, or who have sent to the avenging king: gather yourselves from the dispersion into which you have been scattered, and let us now turn our faces with more sensible minds toward him to whom, together with the aforesaid Benjamin, we had turned our backs.

For he has seized us by the bridle of the tribulation inflicted upon us; he has restrained us from wrongful license. Above he said: “Behold, I will seize.” Then he heals us, something he could not do unless we were restrained and returning.

Finally, he strikes us either through adversities that he sets before us when we are unbridled and carried about by every wind of vanity, or he strikes us when he shows us wounded by sins, or even struck by our very susceptibility and mortality. He laments these things as follows: “For,” he says, “your arrows are fixed in me” (Ps. 37:3).

He cures us either by softening adversities, by forgiving sins, or by changing natural necessities into perpetual incorruption. He also cures us when, through inward diligence and the long guardianship of the movements subject to us, he leads us to the rule of complete integrity.

## VERSE 3

“He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we will live in his sight. We will know, and we will follow, so that we may know the Lord.”

He revives us after two days when, after the grace of conversion, he stirs us to pursue the virtues. On the third day he raises us up when he lifts us to the summit of perfection—or rather, to the heavenly prize.

These three states are represented under the names of Job’s three daughters: one is called Day, the second Cassia, and the third Horn of Plenty. Beginnings, progress, and ends are observed in the conduct of each person. This is to go out from Egypt, wander through the desert, and enter the promised land.

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Today I cast out demons, tomorrow I perfect healings, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13:32).

We live in his sight when we either perform deeds worthy of his regard—for we gladly behold what pleases us—or are refreshed by his eternal vision. “We will live” is rightly said, because whatever condition we may possess in the present, we never remain in the same state; so to speak, we are always dying.

We will know when, in our very return to the Lord, we obtain complete discernment of spirits, having acquired knowledge of that word which reaches “to the division of thoughts and intentions.” Then we will follow when knowledge of that word has gone before our feet like a lamp (Ps. 118:105).

Then we will know the Lord when we have reached the inner chamber of his love, which is true knowledge—or rather, as he himself testifies, eternal life (John 10:28).

“His going forth is prepared like the dawn, and he will come to us like the early and the late rain upon the earth.”

He explains in detail how he heals and what care the Lord gives to our wounds.

God goes forth when a new ray of divine inspiration arises in the mind. That going forth is prepared as though it were dawn when it expands gradually through the progress of a faith that is growing together. Dawn does not burst forth all at once; rather, as the darkness slowly weakens, it admits the radiance of the morning.

His going forth is therefore prepared like dawn when the covering of ancient ignorance is uncovered after many ornaments of penitence have been placed beforehand. John the Baptist is sent ahead in the minds of believers to prepare this dawn.

He comes to us like the early rain when he teaches us how we ought to exercise the condition of our mind in the present. Rain is called “early” when preaching, extended outwardly by teachers, or the inward anointing sprinkled through the Spirit of God, is applied to heal the inward passions that we suffer temporarily.

The late rain belongs to the earth when the word concerns eternal things that are awaited as the world grows old toward evening. They are called “earth” because there can be no greater solidity there; for no element is more stable than earth. Hence it is written: “But the earth stands forever” (Eccles. 1:4).

## VERSE 4

“What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like the dew that passes away early.”

As though he were saying: What reward do you await, O will and reason, for this very return of yours to God?

I know that the mercy which you desire to be shown to you according to your animal movement is superficial, like a morning cloud, since you seek external advantages instead of inward good, and, although you are thought to labor for eternal things, you desire to prosper in the present.

A morning cloud is scattered when dawn appears, and dew is dissolved as the heat rises.

This is to say: You do not bend your intentions to perform my acts of righteousness for the sake of the reward that is given in eternity; rather, you consider piety a profit.

Understand this mercy to be no other than that of which it is said: “You received good things in your lifetime” (Luke 16:25).

## VERSE 5

“Therefore I have hewn them through the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgments will go forth like light.”

For this reason he hews them through the prophets: so that they may not seek temporal things as though they were the reward of merit, he cuts away from us some foolish expectations of empty hope and preserves others. A tree is cut with an axe so that its knots may be removed and it may be prepared for suitable straightness.

No one doubts that prophets are so called from prophesying, and that in former times they were also called “seers” because of the subtlety of their understanding. He therefore hews through the prophets when he cuts away earthly things from our prudence and preserves eternal things, which alone ought to be hoped for.

He slays them by the words of his mouth when, through the words of preachers—who are called the mouths and lips of God in the Scriptures—misdirected desire is condemned.

His judgments go forth like light when the discernments of reason, illumined by God, are sent out toward works of light that edify our neighbors.

## VERSE 6

“For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.”

God desires mercy and not sacrifice when he seeks more eagerly that a person first have mercy upon himself and afterward extend that same mercy to his neighbors than that he offer victims of irrational animals. For it is said: “Have mercy on your soul while pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24).

This mercy, therefore, is no less pleasing to God when directed toward oneself than when directed toward one’s neighbor, and is more acceptable than the slaughter of the external body.

Here, however, a question arises, one also raised by many: “Obedience,” they say, “is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15:22). The question is therefore whether the sacrifice of the Lord’s body outweighs obedience, or obedience outweighs the sacrifice.

We answer this without prejudice to a better judgment. We certainly know that disobedience is compared to the sin of divination. But it is not the act itself that makes disobedience, but its cause. If it had consisted in the act itself, Adam would not have paid the penalty for a most worthless apple, nor Saul for mute animals.

The cause therefore made it disobedience, because God’s commands were set aside. Yet what belongs to God is recognized to have assumed the person of the Church’s teachers. Whoever therefore disobeys them—whatever it may be that he offers, I say confidently—gains nothing for himself by slaughtering it in disobedience. It would be better for him, though I do not know whether for others, to obey without any sacrifice than to sacrifice while disobeying.

I do not wish to discuss here whether the substance of the Lord’s body is consecrated through such people and through any others who have been condemned [Note: He treats this in Book II, *On the Relics of the Saints]. Nevertheless, I will say that whatever the disobedient have done is entirely void of benefit to them.

## VERSE 7

“But they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; there they were faithless to me.”

Above he had said that he desired mercy and not sacrifice, so that, by contemplating his own misery and being compelled to have mercy upon himself, a person might not be aroused toward the desire for another’s possessions. It is therefore rightly added: “But they transgressed the covenant.”

As though he were saying: When I urged them to look upon themselves, they, like Adam, thought upon the transgression of greed. While divinity seemed desirable to him, scarcely any human being remained.

“There,” he says, “they were faithless to me,” because in accepting this suggestion they resisted my admonitions.

## VERSES 8–9

“Gilead is a city of those who work an idol, trampled down by blood. And like the throat of men, of robbers.”

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Gilead is a city of those who work an idol when the mind is inclined toward earthly imaginings. An idol is called a form. And what is it to recall various forms except a certain creation of idols before oneself?

Gilead is therefore a heap of testimony because it is certainly broadened below and narrowed above, and is employed as a kind of testimony: namely, that whoever pursues the broad and spacious things of this world is narrowed in the love of God. Nor can such a person be like a city without tumult or be free from the mental representation of material things if he does not remember to withdraw himself, even for a little while, from care for worldly matters.

This city is undermined by blood because through such affections it is very frequently overthrown by deadly sin.

It is like the throat of robbers when it greedily swallows with insatiable appetite what it cruelly snatches from the weaker. Two things must be considered here: in the robbers, the atrocity of plundering; in the throat, the gluttony of gulping down what has been seized.

“An accomplice of priests on the road who slaughter among the peoples of Shechem, because they have committed a crime.”

This city is an accomplice of priests who kill among the peoples from Shechem on the road, when the cunning of perverse impulses—like certain sacred leaders who reason inwardly about mitigating their crimes—slaughter, by their reconsideration, those thoughts that strive to obey the divine words, and mortify them in their action, as it were on the road. They are compared to that conscience which delights in the fantasies of earthly images. For Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder,” in which the endurance of obedience is signified.

Those, therefore, who proceed from Shechem are killed on the road when these impulses—which wish to submit themselves to God and to their teachers through obedience and desire thereby to make progress—perish through the noise of an insolent mind and the foul recollections of things seen. Thus the inhabitants of the city commit the same crime there as those of Gilead, when they are not allowed to bring to completion the desires to which some good has been added, because an inner tumult obstructs them.

**VERSE 10.**—“In the house of Israel I saw something horrible: there are the fornications of Ephraim.”

It is no wonder, he says, if whatever good will is in the heart is killed, since horrors of vices are seen stored away in the affection—which is Israel—which rules execrably without God; from this there arises in Ephraim, that is, in the will, the fault of fornication, that is, inward estrangement from God.

**VERSE 11.**—“Israel is defiled. But you also, Judah, set a harvest for yourself, when I restore the captivity of my people.”

That is to say: Israel indeed has fallen into defilements of this kind; but you, Judah—that is, rational confession—set a harvest for yourself, that is, set before yourself the reading of sacred discourse. Yet you have no ability to do this until I restore the captivity of my people. The captivity of the people is truly restored when the one who held them captive is himself taken captive by the one who was formerly captive; and it is restored within us when the state of the mind is changed from what had stood wrongly.

### CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.**—“When I wished to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickedness of Samaria was revealed, because they practiced deceit.”

When God wishes to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim is revealed, because when the carnal affection is corrected according to the rule of reason and is, in some measure, crushed by God’s judgment, the will—which, through the habit of its ancient practice, is inclined toward evil—is suddenly revealed. For when it is compelled to think unfamiliar thoughts and is removed from what delights it, the disease of impatience is branded upon its spirit.

The wickedness of Samaria greatly assists this disease: namely, that of those priests who, as the worst counselors, arise inwardly to offer excuses for sins (Psalm 140:4), when those who wish to appear as leaders in the mind, smoothing away its vices, display themselves as though proclaiming that imitation of the former state ought to be postponed. Somer, from which Samaria is derived, is plainly interpreted as “keeper.” For perverse cunning falsely promises the mind protection, when it is accustomed to pledge security not to God but to the world, and fears disgrace not before God but before the world. This occurs because they practice deceit: they are covered, that is, with hypocrisy. For what is more deceitful than wishing to appear to be what one is not?

“And a thief has entered, despoiling; a bandit is outside.”

It is as though he said: Whatever external vigilance may be applied, a thief will nevertheless enter—that is, inward betrayal, which admits the devil as a plunderer. He will rage within, and once the human being has been disemboweled of his familiar possessions, the bandit outside, who strips him of external respectability, immediately rises up. For when a tree is corrupted at its core, the entire surface of its branches dries up and is destroyed.

Observe the distinction between a thief and a bandit. A thief acts secretly; a bandit acts by ambush but openly. Hence the Lord says: “That one is a thief and a bandit” (John 10:1). The thief climbs up from elsewhere; the bandit, after entering, rages among the household’s possessions.

**VERSE 2.**—“And perhaps they will say in their hearts: ‘He has remembered all their wickedness’; now their inventions have surrounded them; they have been made before my face.”

It is as though he said: Perhaps, when they reflect upon the progress or decline of their mind, they will say that I have wished to heap up all their wickedness as though for a final punishment. They are wholly mistaken. But now—that is, in this condition of hypocrisy, in which depravity has enclosed their understanding—their inventions have surrounded them: the fabrications of a deceitful way of life have thrust them into the pit of this labyrinth.

The inventions produced through hypocrisy are rightly called inventions, because scarcely any works of truth are adorned with so much cosmetic artifice. Therefore God declares that they have been made before his face, because nothing so greatly offends God’s sight as those things which are thought to be done for God, while by this very means their agents seek nothing but worldly glory. To wish to attribute to oneself what is offered to God is a wicked kind of idolatry.

**VERSE 3.**—“In their wickedness they have made the king glad, and the princes in their deceit.”

If we understand the king as the devil, the interpretation stands; for he is “king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25). If we understand the princes as his demons, it likewise holds together. But let the matter be confined within us.

They make the king glad in their wickedness when secretly committed evils, which fear no external judge, delight the zeal of an exalted reason. He is called a king because he is lifted up by private pleasure: whoever acts through hypocrisy lies in all his activity.

They make the princes glad in their deceit when, by deceptive works through which they draw the foolish crowd to reverence them, they amuse and cheer their own senses—which rule them badly, as the Samaritan woman’s senses did—by the bestowal of honor. These are the princes who persecute us without cause (Psalm 118:161).

**VERSE 4.**—“All are adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker.”

All these princes commit adultery when, before the eyes of others, they display the appearance of humility assumed for God, while thereafter they desire to please someone other than God.

They are like an oven heated by the baker when, beneath a kindly face, they carry within their minds the enclosed fires of fiercely burning desires. An oven burns inwardly, and the more chambered it is, the hotter it becomes. Hence the Poet says (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 4.64):

> And the more it is concealed, the more fiercely the hidden fire burns.

The baker is none other than the person who is himself the kindler of such ambition.

“The city rested for a little while from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened.”

The city rests for a little while when, at the beginning of the hypocrisy that has been undertaken, the force of its inward desire is not excessive, nor is the city permitted to resound with constant clamor, because it has ceased to consider the process of its recent fermentation. No one doubts what leaven signifies. This plague first attacks the mind under the appearance of holiness; but once a sinister intention has occupied the breast, the whole is said to have been leavened.

**VERSE 5.**—“The day of our king.”

This is the voice of a deceived thought. Above we said that the king is reason filled with arrogance. “O, the day of our king!” he says, as though he were saying: Behold, our king has a day, because our spirit appears radiant in the prosperity of its own favor.

“The princes began to rage from wine.”

When the mind boasts of its own praises, our outward senses rage from wine: they lose the awareness of themselves through the favor of another’s voice. It belongs to madmen neither to recognize nor to fear themselves or anyone else, and not to know what they are suffering. Thus those who rage from wine are drunk with external flatteries: they attend not to what they are, but to how they are praised.

**VERSE 6.**—“He stretched out his hand with mockers, because they applied their heart like an oven when he was lying in wait for them.”

The king stretches out his hand with mockers when, to satisfy the will of his flatterers—or rather of his mockers—he strives to enlarge his actions, by which he may be more greatly exalted.

Our spirit magnifies its fringes, according to the Gospel (Matthew 23:5), when it celebrates any of its works, however insignificant. It enlarges the phylacteries that are accustomed to be hung from the neck or breast (ibid.) when it displays, with trumpet-blast, knowledge or doctrine as though it were the protection of those who obey.

“For they applied”—there is no doubt whom he means—“their heart like an oven”: the mockers, judging themselves worthy of praise and miserably mocking themselves, worse than their external appearance, bend their heart—that is, their reason—which is heated everywhere by such flatteries, and humble themselves before them as though rejoicing in their presence.

This, he says, the thoughts do when the king himself lies in wait for them: that is, when the very spirit whose office it was to govern them seeks present pleasures, submitting itself to them for the destruction of those whom it ought to have saved.

“All night the baker slept, cooking them; in the morning he himself was kindled like a flame of fire.”

The baker sleeps all night while cooking them when, in total blindness, he buries himself—as though in a process of cooking—for the destruction of those inward impulses that might have possessed sound judgment.

He himself is kindled in the morning when, as the dawn of some prosperity rises upon him, he is set aflame by excessive desire. Hence it is said under the image of a certain bird in Job: “When the time comes, he raises his wings on high” (Job 39:18).

He is like a flame of fire when he burns with the very plague by which he boils over, while outwardly he teaches those whom he strives to illuminate; or he is like a flame of fire when the mind, secretly kindled by the desire to sin, blazes openly as an example to others.

**VERSE 7.**—“All of them grew hot like an oven, and they devoured their judges.”

They all grow hot like an oven when reason, will, and affection, together with the impulses subject to them, boil over through the zeal of foolish desire.

They devour their judges when the heats of vice annihilate all the impulses of the spirit. These are called judges because from them proceed the judgments and restraints of our entire inner life.

“All their kings have fallen; there is no one among them who calls upon me.”

The kings of our interior life are all the dispositions of mind that compel a person to think upon God. Hence the Psalm says: “His spirit was not faithful with God” (Psalm 77:8).

These kings fall when they cast themselves down to desire earthly things. There is no one among them who calls upon God—no one, that is, who, after the losses caused by delight or consent, strives to return to a resolve of repentance. For who cries out more pitifully than the person who weeps over his own calamity?

**VERSE 8.**—“Ephraim himself mingled among the peoples.”

Ephraim himself mingles among the peoples when the will, which ought to have been fertile in moderation, is scattered among the multitude of insolent thoughts.

It should be noted that the pronoun *ipse* (“himself”) is deliberately added, as though it said: Ephraim himself—who is nothing other than the will, which ought rather to have agreed with reason—has thrust himself into the popular crowds of thoughts; and the one who was trusted so greatly, who ought to have stood firm because of his proximity to reason, has, alas, flowed away.

“Ephraim has become like a cake baked under ashes, which is not turned.”

Ephraim becomes a cake baked under ashes when the will, rekindled by the memory of past crimes, grows hot. And rightly so, because when images of past evils press upon it, repeatedly renewing the pleasures of the excess it has experienced, it is not turned, since what has once been conceived is never driven back from the mind.

**VERSE 9.**—“Strangers have devoured his strength, and he himself did not know; moreover, gray hairs have been scattered over him, and he himself did not know.”

Strangers devour his strength when demons and the impulses of the flesh—nothing being more alien to our salvation than these—erode whatever virtue is established in our will.

He himself does not know when, through the power of discernment, he has no knowledge at all of the harm he is suffering.

Gray hairs are scattered over him when whatever pious newness exists in him is changed by a certain old age of hypocrisy. For gray hairs are white and signify old age. Whiteness therefore pertains to what is displayed, while old age pertains to what is deprived of true newness. Old things are present realities; new things are future ones. Ephraim does not understand this because he does not consider whether he is forgetting the condition in which he is—namely, the present—and striving toward what lies before him.

**VERSE 10.**—“And the pride of Israel will be humbled in his face; yet they did not return to the Lord their God, nor did they seek him in all these things.”

The pride of Israel is humbled in his face when our affection, ruling without God, is said to fall knowingly through an open crime. Israel is humbled in his face when the swelling of our desire—which, though shameful, had raised itself up because of its supposed chastity—is deflated by the experience and shame of its sin.

They do not return to the Lord their God when their emotional impulses, not even frightened by the collapse of their crimes, are not turned back so that thereafter they may think upon God. They do not seek him in all these things when, even amid the evident reversal of their crimes, they do not rise again through repentance toward divine purity.

**VERSE 11.**—“Ephraim has become like a dove deceived, without understanding.”

Ephraim becomes like a deceived dove when he does not lament the corruption of his works, as though they were his offspring. For, unlike other birds, the dove does not make a commotion over the removal of its young. Thus the dove is called deceived as though reduced to insensibility.

For what is more insensible than that will which does not know how to grieve over its unworthy works? Although it is said of other doves that they have no gall, of this one it is said that it has no heart, so that the enormity of its rejected understanding may be shown: it is not moved by pity for its evils.

“They called upon Egypt; they went away to the Assyrians.”

Egypt is interpreted as “tribulation” or “darkness”; the Assyrians are interpreted as “courtiers” or “those who direct.” They call upon Egypt who, after committing sin, rationally drive their spirit toward the darkness and tribulation of sorrow.

For the desire for pleasures, according to that saying of Boethius, although full of anxiety, is nevertheless a satisfaction of repentance (*The Consolation of Philosophy*, book 3, prose 7). Thus, after calling upon Egypt—that is, crying out in conscience over the bitterness of repentance appropriate to sin—the voice of blood morally crying to God—they immediately go away to the Assyrians.

For the thoughts that excuse and mitigate sins, having cast aside fear, instead offer counsel, and through them people believe themselves to be directed, while they call the foulness of their crime courtly refinement. Earlier he called these thoughts “priests” and “protectors,” by the same abuse through which he also calls the prophets Ezekiel and Jeremiah such things.

**VERSE 12.**—“And when they have gone forth, I will spread my net over them; like a bird of the air I will bring them down.”

They go forth when they wander away from consideration of the wickedness they have committed.

God’s net is spread over them when, by divine judgment, obstacles are placed in the way of their wantonness, by which the impulse of their levity is suddenly restrained.

They are brought down like a bird of the air when their pride—which walks above itself amid marvelous things—is overthrown by a sudden fall. In the bird, levity is signified; in the sky, pride.

As it is written: “The birds of the air devoured it” (Mark 4:4).

“I will strike them according to the report of their assembly.”

God strikes them when he permits them to be afflicted by dangers, whether by tortures of their thoughts or by bodily illnesses. This striking is according to the report of their assembly when the punishment of blows and pains proceeds all the way to their understanding of every movement of their mind—what had persuaded them to go to the Assyrians. Otherwise the striking would in no way be beneficial unless the one being struck recognized why he was being struck. Hence it is written elsewhere: “Only affliction will give understanding to the hearing” (Isaiah 28:19).

**VERSE 13.**—“Woe to them, because they have departed from me.”

Woe, therefore, to them, because they depart from God, while they perceive that eternal misery threatens them on account of their desertion. They already have their “woe” in the present, since they fear that it is owed to them unless they correct themselves.

“They will be devastated, because they have transgressed against me.”

Those who seemed to be courtiers are devastated when they are utterly desolated by the continual tumult of lusts. For whoever transgresses against God—that is, deviates from divine rectitude—is consumed by the very place from which he thinks he will obtain an increase of pleasure.

**VERSE 14.**—“And I redeemed them, yet they spoke lies against me. They did not cry out to me in their heart, but they howled upon their beds over grain, and they ruminated over wine.”

God redeems them when he frees them from the hardships that had arisen. Yet they speak lies against God when they judge that their deliverances should be attributed to their own foresight or to chance rather than to divine intervention.

Or they also speak lies against God when they do not think that God is so provoked by their crimes that, on account of them, he wishes severe judgments to be exercised against them; and when such judgments occur, they consider them nothing more than accidental misfortunes. They bring forward as an argument that many people persist with impunity after dreadful crimes. Wretched people would easily refute this if they considered the causes of universal judgment and remembered that the rich man had received good things during his lifetime (Luke 16:25).

They do not cry out to God in their heart when they offer no thanksgiving for heavenly benefits. For they would cry out if they could breathe again.

But they howl upon their beds when, within their deadly hearts, they rage and burn with every kind of savagery, wickedness, and rapacity. Howling belongs to wolves and dogs. In sacred Scripture, beds are customarily used for hearts, as in: “When you pray, enter into your room” (Matthew 6:6).

They howl upon their beds, therefore, who grieve in their hearts that they are not permitted to sin less. “Under their tongue,” he says, “are labor and sorrow” (Psalm 89:10).

They ruminate over grain and wine when they reconsider and debate heavenly doctrine and spiritual knowledge. For to ruminate is “to bring chewed food back to the mouth in order to grind it again.”

Thus they ruminate who presume to examine and scrutinize the ecclesiastical doctrine that they have once absorbed, and to bring back into discussion as though it were something new what has been defined by God and the Fathers.

Grain is used for doctrine, as the Gospel bears witness in the passage about giving the measure of grain at the proper time (Luke 12:42). Wine signifies the force of spiritual knowledge, just as milk signifies the gentleness of simple instruction: “Buy wine and milk without any exchange” (Isaiah 55:1).

We see this even today in the controversies of certain grammarians, who strive to flash with blind eyes not only in divine speech but also in every heavenly mystery.

**VERSES 15–16.**—“They departed from me, though I instructed them; I strengthened their arms, yet they devised wickedness against me. They returned so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow.”

It is as though he said: Although I instructed them and strengthened their arms, they departed from me.

God instructs them when he fills them with saving wisdom. He strengthens their arms when he consolidates the strength of their natural understanding, or their activity itself.

“And they devised wickedness against me,” he says, when, relying upon their instruction and upon an impious strength directed against justice, they wage war against me.

They return so as to be without a yoke when, having been struck and warned by divine inspiration concerning repentance, they grow foolish again and return to the delusions of their former vanity, so that they may not possess the rule of any rationality by which they would become more fearful in pursuing worldly license.

Certain people promise in the Psalm that they will tear away and cast off these bonds and this yoke (Psalm 2:3).

They became like a deceitful bow: a bow that strikes the very person by whom it is drawn. They are plainly drawn by God when their hearts are restrained as if by a double knowledge. From this the arrow of their understanding is discharged; although it ought to strike the enemy, it is often carried as far as insults against divinity. A deceitful bow is one that wounds the person by whom it is drawn.

“Their princes will fall by the sword because of the rage of their tongue.”

Their princes fall by the sword when their thoughts entangle themselves in deadly evils. The sword is used for mortal sin, as in: “Deliver me from the evil sword” (Psalm 143:10).

This happens to them because of the rage of their tongue, since their senseless conscience rages against the mysteries of the holy Church more by inward than by outward verbosity. For you will rarely find a heretic whom some shameful crime or disgraceful act does not either follow or precede.

“This is their mockery in the land of Egypt.”

This is their mockery in the land of Egypt when the conduct of those who do not think rightly about God’s goodness (Wisdom 1:1) is worthy of ridicule even among outsiders.

What follows:

### CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Let there be a trumpet in your throat, like an eagle over the house of the Lord.”

This is God’s voice addressed to reason itself. By the throat, from which the voice is emitted, we understand speech itself. The trumpet is an evident sound.

Yet by the throat—which is beneath the tongue—thought itself can also be understood, just as the mouth is customarily used for the mind, as in: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom” (Psalm 36:30).

It is as though he said: Let the thought of your heart, or the speech of your mouth, be governed with such balance that whatever you think or say may be proclaimed everywhere without bringing you shame.

Many founders of heresies teach their doctrines in corners, from which they do not dare to mutter them openly. Therefore let there be a trumpet in your throat, so that whatever you have conceived with a faithful mind you may declare with a confident cry amid the conflict with the devil’s satellites. Be, that is, like an eagle over the house of God: let your steps be preceded by the eyelids of discernment.

The house of God is a good conscience. We exist over it like an eagle when we examine with the sharpest insight toward what direction our faith is tending. For, apart from lynxes, nothing has sharper sight than the eye of an eagle.

**VERSE 2.**—“Because they have transgressed my covenant and violated my law, they will call upon me: ‘My God, we know you, Israel.’”

God’s covenant is what we promised him through faith in baptism; the law is whatever we receive through the divine words as a commandment for living well.

A person transgresses the covenant whenever he is shown to deviate from the rule of faith that he professed. A person violates the law whenever he voluntarily deserts the discipline that he undertook.

Thus, having transgressed the covenant and violated the law, they will call upon me, saying: “My God.” That is, although they have failed in faith and life, they will themselves be deceived if, in some necessity, they wish to boast of me as their God.

“We who are Israel have known you.” Israel, as was said above, is interpreted as “upright with God” or “a prince with God.”

Some people, confused by the dullness of their understanding after long-standing crimes, pay no attention to their ancient sins, in which they have spent nearly their whole lives, but only to the momentary breathing-space in which they turn to God on account of some adversity. They declare themselves upright, princes with God, and already acquainted with God, measuring the superficial piety of a single day against the crimes of their entire lifetime (Titus 1:16).

**VERSE 3.**—“Israel has cast away the good; the enemy will pursue him.”

Israel casts away the good when, having taken it up under the pressure of danger, he rejects it when prosperity returns. Therefore the enemy pursues him: when the affection of every good intention fails, no constancy of inward virtue resists the enemy.

**VERSE 4.**—“They themselves have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know.”

A person reigns but does not reign from God whenever, under the pressure of distress, he rules over his own wicked habits, while nevertheless, in the corners of his conscience, he preserves—if freedom should smile upon him—the desire to return to his vomit (2 Peter 2:22).

They become princes, but God does not know them, when their outward senses for a time rule themselves under the royal authority of reason, but God does not know the causes of this restraint, because he does not approve them.

Of such people it is written: “When he slew them, they sought him and returned” (Psalm 77:34).

“They made silver and gold into idols for themselves, so that they might perish.”

A person makes his silver and gold into idols for himself whenever, with perverse intention, he expends his knowledge of divine speech or the wisdom pertaining to the knowledge of God.

For what else is it than to construct an idol when someone desires to be honored by these gifts—not God—and does not return to God what he has received from him, but rather wishes to display himself as a kind of image?

This has produced many heretics in former times and continues to produce them today: those who hide because of the obscurity of their birth and life, yet desire to be celebrated for their efforts to devise new doctrines.

They do this so that they may perish, because according to God’s judgment it happens that, while they desire to be proclaimed and to shine everywhere, they bring themselves down to the disgrace of their final destruction.

**VERSE 5.**—“Your calf has been cast away, Samaria; my fury has been kindled against them.”

Samaria, as has been said, is interpreted as “guard.” And what is this guard except that which is arranged as a precaution for the propagation of one’s own name?

The calf of this Samaria is cast away when the glory of its reputation—in which it desires to revel—is not only condemned but also rejected as filth.

It should be noted that he does not say that God is raging, but that God’s fury is angry with them. First he places anger, then fury, to show that God was initially angry with them because of the wickedness of their conduct; afterward, because they wished to arrogate to themselves a name from the blasphemy of God—a thing whose very remembrance was impious—he was rightly turned to fury in order to overthrow them.

“How long will they be unable to be purified?”

**VERSE 6.**—“Because it is from Israel; and he himself is the artisan.”

It is as though he said: How long will this perversity of theirs remain uncorrected? As though the answer were: For a very long time, because it is from Israel, and he himself is the artisan.

Israel, as was mentioned earlier, is also interpreted by certain ancient authorities as “a man seeing God.” Therefore they are not easily purified, because the artisans of such idolatry are usually drawn especially from those who boast above others of their knowledge of God through the Scriptures. They cling more tenaciously to their sect precisely because they twist sacred Scripture according to their own desire as though they understood it more sharply, and they attract others to themselves more securely because they hear themselves called more discerning in divine speech.

Therefore the artisan himself is from Israel, because an author of such fables usually arises only from those endowed with great sharpness of intellect.

**VERSE 7.**—“He made it, but it is not God, because the calf of Samaria will be like a spider’s web. For they will sow the wind and reap the whirlwind.”

A person makes a god, but it is not God, whenever he circumscribes God according to his own capacity and imagination, attempting to reach an exposition of God’s nature—something that is in no way comprehensible to human beings and therefore cannot be God. For whatever you are able to perceive, you falsely regard as God.

“Because the calf of Samaria will be like a spider’s web”: that is, the wantonness lying beneath that externally whitewashed guard—since they do many things under the appearance of hypocrisy in order to deceive more effectively—will be annihilated and vanish like a spider’s web.

For what is more foolish, and what resembles the levity of a calf more closely, than to weave books which the authority of all Christianity rejects and hisses away? They are spider’s webs because they are produced by those who cast away their inner life into their outward life; and they are quickly scattered because they take root no otherwise than illegitimate shoots, as it is written (Wisdom 4:3).

The spider, being a poisonous creature that produces its work from venomous entrails, unfolds nothing except what exhausts itself through empty efforts.

They sow the wind who consider it more important to scatter the clouds of error and useless trifles. They reap the whirlwind when they encounter blindness of mind and the movement of external adversity.

For this is characteristic of heretics: while they desire to make a name for themselves through doctrinal difference, they soon become exposed to everyone’s contempt and hatred.

“A standing stalk is not in it; it will produce no grain.”

The stalk stands when the arrogance of speech grows luxuriantly. For it is customary among them to serve the pomp of words and to handle everything through dialectical arguments.

In the stalk there is emptiness; in standing, the vitality of speech. But in the things signified by the stalk’s summit there is no germ, because in the words of a vapid heart there is no power to bring life to others.

It produces no grain because speech gives birth to no sweetness of inward richness. For what is understood to be done solely for the favor of the crowd is scarcely ever, or never, received gratefully by the minds of listeners.

Or certainly it produces no grain when it expresses nothing fruitful except what can be repeated to its own praise.

“And even if it should produce something”—that is, if it should say something useful—“strangers will devour it.” Its eloquence is clearly reserved for diabolical nourishment, by which our pride is especially fed. Hence Solomon says: “Let strangers not share in you” (Proverbs 5:17).

**VERSES 8–9.**—“Israel has been devoured; now he has become among the nations like an unclean vessel. For they themselves have gone up to Assyria; Ephraim is a solitary wild ass for himself.”

Israel is devoured when those who judge themselves upright because of their knowledge of God, compelled by sin, descend into complete dullness of understanding. For whoever abuses knowledge given by God must, through the prolonged practice of wickedness, continually be changed for the worse.

Now—that is, through love of present things—he has become among the nations like an unclean vessel, when, amid the foreign origins of every kind of vice, he offers himself as an open receptacle for them all.

In the ancient law, a vessel without a cover was commanded to be considered unclean. Likewise, the mind of a person who does not ward off from itself the fall of an invading crime is rightly condemned as impure.

“For they themselves have gone up to Assyria”: that is, by the steps of wickedness they have seized the chambers and palaces of lust.

Ephraim immediately becomes a solitary wild ass for himself when the abode of the will, exiled from God, is found intent upon itself alone—that is, upon carnal wantonness, which is signified by the wild ass.

“They gave gifts to lovers” (verse 10). “But they also hired nations for a price.”

They give gifts to lovers when they expend themselves upon, and are expended by, demons or wicked people who provide them with the resources either of rapacity or of obscene pleasure.

Hence it is that, after making a covenant with wicked spirits, they sometimes submit themselves to them as human beings and learn necromancy from them, by which they become more effective in the mystery of iniquity.

But they also hire nations for a price when they do certain things that serve as incentives to their vices—for example, when some people chew garlic and spices of a hotter nature, by which they become more aroused to wantonness. Understand the same of the other vices.

“Now I will gather them, and they will rest for a little while from the burden of king and princes.”

God gathers them when, amid countless crimes, he recalls those who have wandered back to consideration of themselves.

This happens “now” because the whole of that recollection passes away from the sight of reason like something superficial. Nor does this occur without a definite judgment upon them, because their spirit, though it senses with God, was not trusted by them (Psalm 77:8).

They rest for a little while from the burden of king and princes when, as the mind returns to itself, it is for a time relieved from the arrogance of pride—which viewed everything loftily—or from carnal affection and the dispersal or oppression of the outward senses.

**VERSE 11.**—“Because Ephraim multiplied altars in order to sin, the altars became for him an occasion of guilt.”

Ephraim multiplies altars in order to sin when, through the changes of the mind, he repeatedly alternates and serially renews countless purposes of evil.

According to the various dispositions that arise from this diverse mixture, now anger, now lust, now pride, now ambition, and all the other things that change inwardly take their turn.

He worships as many altars as are the desires to sin that he introduces into himself.

For this reason altars become occasions of guilt for him: even the good of pious recollection that arises from the spark of reason is rejected.

“Delictum” (“guilt” or “offense”) derives from abandoning, since the good that ought to be done is deserted. Thus offense follows sin when, as its punishment, even the rejection of a good will commonly arises.

**VERSE 12.**—“I will write for him the many things of my law, which have been regarded as something alien.”

God writes his many laws for him when he inserts both the natural law and the written law fully into his memory, so that he may be condemned all the more justly because before God he is in no way excused by ignorance.

Yet these laws are regarded as something alien when they are held to be exiles from his mind—or rather from his will, which is signified by Ephraim—as though they had neither been known nor heard.

[Col. 0382D] **VERSE 13.**—“They will bring offerings [variant: offer them], they will sacrifice flesh and eat it, and the Lord will not receive them.” They bring offerings who propose public penances from time to time, and the other ceremonies of ecclesiastical observance, more from mere general custom than from religious devotion. They sacrifice flesh when, by detesting carnal sins, they seem to slaughter them through acts of confession. Yet they eat them, because they do not cease to gorge themselves on their use. God therefore does not receive these offerings, because he pays no attention to external observances unless they proceed from the innermost heart.

“Now he will remember their iniquities, and he will visit their sins; they themselves will return to Egypt.” “Now”—that is, in this condition of theirs—he remembers their iniquities, when, through the infliction of any scourge, he appears to recall their long-standing wickedness. For God is thought to forget those whose errors he temporarily refrains from punishing. He visits their sins when, through the repetition of adversities, he frequently demonstrates that he has seen them. The verb “visits,” being frequentative, signifies the constancy of his seeing. They themselves return to Egypt when, instead of the light of correction, they are enveloped in the darkness of obstinacy, which Egypt signifies.

**VERSE 14.**—“Israel forgot his Maker, and built shrines, and Judah multiplied fortified cities.” Israel is made by God when, through the fear of God, he is created and established in true being, having been brought forth from his own emptying through vanities. For one who loses the substance [Col. 0383B] of living intention is, as it were, nonexistent—the substance which the prodigal son squandered on prostitutes. Hence the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “To all who are among you” (Rom. XII, 3), clearly implying that some among them were not what they ought to be according to this standard. Israel was made according to this standard when, through the perception of inward grace, he was consolidated into solidity. Accordingly it is also said: “Let Israel rejoice in him who made him” (Ps. CXLIX, 2).

Israel forgets this Maker of his when he turns away from him who could restore him from his annihilation. He builds shrines when, once the Lord has departed in devotion, the most wicked enemy immediately enters his conscience as though it were his own temple; for the mind cannot exist without one or the other guest. Then Judah multiplies fortified cities when rational devotion—which properly urges us to confess God—has fallen into perversity and, whether through negligence or shame, blocks and hardens itself against the piety of confession. He builds fortified cities when, for every crime he has committed, he sets up the barrier of obstinacy and raises the wall of a vicious—or proud—conclusion.

“And I will send fire into his cities, and it will devour his buildings.” Fire is sent into his cities when, in the hidden madness of one who admits no breath of any good opening, the more severe fire—or ardor—of desire burns up from its concealment. It devours his buildings when inward ardor, through lack of self-control, manifests itself in the outward display of the bodily members. For it cannot be prevented that what is conceived within for a long time should not emerge through some sign, by way of whatever disposition of the senses [Col. 0383D].

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 1.**—“Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult like the peoples, because you have fornicated away from your God.” Israel is forbidden to rejoice when the one who once used to take delight in the vision of God is reproved because he exults in the prosperity of his worldly condition. “Do not,” he says, “exult like the peoples”—that is, do not regard the foolish joy of those who have never understood anything of God; do not imitate their license or conform yourself to their commonness. For those who never even began to possess good things will receive a far more merciful judgment than you, who have already clung to your God through knowledge and have now committed fornication.

Note that “to rejoice” pertains to the interior, while “to exult” pertains to the exterior. Since the ungodly are not to rejoice, both are forbidden. “You loved the payment above all the threshing-floors of wheat.” He loves the payment above all the threshing-floors of wheat—namely, that by which he previously hired the nations—more than all the pages of Sacred Scripture distributed among the books. These are the threshing-floors, as it were certain portions of land cut up separately. The threshing-floors of wheat are therefore the books of divine utterance; the more one cultivates each of them, the richer the fruits of heavenly understanding one discovers. Wheat is that with which, according to the Psalm, the valleys abound (Ps. LXIV, 14), and with whose fatness the sons of Zion are satisfied (Ps. LXXX, 17).

The payment is loved above all the threshing-floors of wheat when, above everything found in the Scriptures, flatteries and divinations—through which a greater access to crimes is opened—are desired more than exercises in the word of God. For things that delight either through use or through curiosity are commonly purchased at the cost of sacrileges against our faith [Col. 0384B].

**VERSES 2, 3.**—“The threshing-floor and the winepress will not feed them, and the wine will deceive them. They will not dwell in the land of the Lord.” The threshing-floor signifies the divine books, from whose cultivation we draw the manifold and refined fruits of allegory and tropology. We experience this frequently in the prophetic and apostolic writings. The winepresses signify those who know how to extract from the Scriptures the intellectual meaning that we call anagogy, which pertains to the contemplation of God.

The threshing-floor and the winepress do not feed them—that is, neither what is extracted, as from the threshing-floor, nor those who extract it, as from the winepress—because they neither understand treatises on moral knowledge from the threshing-floor nor take care, by laboring, to draw from the winepress anything of the heavenly wisdom with which they are instructed concerning God. For what is more blessed than to draw from the Scriptures the wine of inward sweetness and, by drinking it, to erase from one’s mind the love of present things? The wine deceives them because their mind is deprived of the taste and warmth of eternal seasoning.

The Lord’s land is the body which, once its passions have been overcome, is subjected to the dominion of reason subject to God. They do not dwell in this land because they are not meek and do not have God as its inhabitant; they are therefore unable to dwell in—or possess—their own bodies. For the disobedient veils his body, which obedient Adam had possessed, with fig leaves. “Your good Spirit,” he says, “will lead me into a level land” (Ps. CXLII, 10)—which is level because it belongs to the Lord.

“Ephraim has returned to Egypt, and in Assyria he has eaten polluted food.” Ephraim returns to Egypt when our will, which ought to rejoice in the harvest of eternal bread, turns in every direction toward Egypt, the land of sorrow and distress—that is, toward the cares and labors of the world. Hence it is said to certain people: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. II, 28). He eats polluted food in Assyria when, with those who are in royal houses, who do not pursue narrow ways but clothe themselves in soft garments (ibid., 8), and who, according to Job, live in ease, in whom wisdom is not found (Job XXVIII, 13), he does not cease to stuff himself with the obscene dishes of desire. Asshur is said to mean “court,” which is ordinarily royal.

**VERSE 4.**—“They will not pour wine to the Lord, and they will not please him.” No one pours wine to the Lord who does not burn before God with the sweetness and warmth of divine love.
