Hence such people cannot please him either, because whoever is not led by God to beseech God is certainly not recognized by the Son—who is unquestionably God—because God the Father has not drawn him, much less is he thought pleasing (John VI, 44).

“Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourners.” Under the old law, whoever ate of a sacrifice for the dead was himself unclean, and the offering was considered empty. Their sacrifices are therefore like the bread of mourners, because whatever they offer to God, whether in prayer or by giving alms, is compared with their life, which is worthy of no imitation. They have touched none of the taste of heavenly joys, and their pursuits can be called nothing better than material for tears.

Bread is used for life, as in: “Let us cast wood into his bread” (Jer. II, 19). “All who eat it will be defiled, because their bread is their own life; it will not enter the house of the Lord.” Those who eat that bread are defiled because those who assimilate their examples into themselves are condemned by the same foulness of life as they are. The same thing is signified by the law’s prohibition against touching a carcass (Lev. XI, 24). For “their bread,” understood as “the sustenance of their souls,” is the nourishment of their life, as it were a kind of food for their souls. Just as poison is life to a serpent, so to every wicked person his wickedness is nourishment.

Hence Solomon says of detractors: “They provide flesh for eating” (Prov. XXIII, 20). In contrast, it is said to the holy: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). Morally, it is also customary to say that a person is fed by what delights him. Thus, when bread nourishes bodies, it is said to belong to their souls because, by signifying temporal pleasure, it is recognized as food for the animality of the wicked. It does not enter the house of the Lord because such joy is most strictly excluded from every heart inhabited by God. Hence the saying of Job: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and food that was previously desirable” (Job XXXIII, 20).

**VERSE 5.**—“What will you do on the solemn day, on the day of the feast of the Lord?” The solemn day of the Lord is when, after enemies have been placed beneath his feet, he has handed the kingdom over to God the Father (1 Cor. XV, 24–25). Understand the solemn day, therefore, as the time when the wicked are submerged; and the feast as the time when the elect are advanced to contemplate the appearance of God. What, then, will you do when such a separation comes between the two destinies?

**VERSE 6.**—“For behold, they have departed from devastation: Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them.” He returns to describing them. Above he had said that their bread would not enter the house of the Lord, as if he were saying: Since there is no harmony between light and darkness (2 Cor. VI, 14), nor between pleasure and temperance, they depart—that is, they wander away from right consideration—and this happens to them from devastation, because the mind incurs solitude away from God.

After saying above, as though correcting them, “What will you do on the solemn day?”, he immediately adds their insolence: “And behold, they depart from devastation”—that is, impatient of correction, they straightaway become alienated from themselves. Egypt gathers them when worldly ambition unites them to itself. This means: Although they are separated from their own reason, they are nevertheless heaped together under Egyptian care. Memphis is interpreted as “from their mouth.” They are buried when their understanding is overwhelmed by every kind of holy vitality. This also comes upon them from their own mouth, when the punishment for the sin by which they deceive others into doing evil through corrupt speech befalls them.

“Their desirable silver will be inherited by the nettle; the bur will be in their tents.” The nettle inherits their desirable silver when what the wicked most highly and gloriously esteem—namely, that the knowledge of divine Scripture should be accompanied by more distinguished and abundant eloquence—descends to the extremes of utter worthlessness and wickedness. For the nettle is a thoroughly contemptible and fiery plant.

The nettle therefore inherits their desirable silver when the desired price of affected eloquence is not only despised because of the shamefulness of life, but also scorches and afflicts others with its cunning, deceit, and obscene bitterness. It is said to “inherit” because it holds their ways in miserable perpetuity, or because an heir survives the one whose place he succeeds. Let this be referred to the heretics mentioned above and treated here as well: their writings are condemned not only for their contemptibility but also for their innate bitterness against everything agreeing with the faith.

And because they often excluded those who were approved in silver—that is, those who were tested and genuine—while controversies remained in the books of those who had fought most vigorously against their errors, their little works were erased because of their uselessness. This has been proved everywhere in the case of the ancient heretics, whose volumes disappeared like spiders’ webs, as we discussed above. In our own times, booklets have been made by certain parasites; though exceedingly thin, they have been consumed immediately, in their very novelty, because of their unworthiness, in opposition to the mysteries of our faith.

The bur is in their tents because, unless they were subjected to the impurities of carnal desires—which are severe goads—they would never be turned toward such disgrace of a corrupt mind as to think wrongly about divine things. The tents themselves are bodies, in which we wage war either against the flesh or against the spirit, or in which we are presently pilgrims.

**VERSE 7.**—“The days of visitation have come; the days of recompense have come.” The days of visitation are when God sends scourges in the present upon the unrepentant. The day of recompense immediately follows, when he assigns to those who persist in their begun filth or faithlessness the lot of unchangeable misery. For God is accustomed to crush such people with a twofold contrition.

Does he not crush those whom, while they live, he exposes to the detestation of all, and after their death stains and casts away their memory, together with all their work and teaching, like a menstrual cloth?

“Know, Israel: the prophet is foolish, the spiritual man is mad.” “O Israel,” he says—meaning, apparently, the movements of your affections, which, under God’s judgment, are abandoned to the error of your senses—you could now, in this destruction of yours and extermination of reason, learn what foolishness and what madness lies hidden in the spirit that ought to have ruled you. If you had wished to subject yourselves to it and be ruled by it, you would never have come to such an incongruity of vices or faithlessness. “Because of the multitude of your iniquity and the multitude of your madness.” Because you have strayed greatly from goodness and faith, God has handed you over, without distinction, to shameful falls. It is as though he said: Because, when you sinned, you did not think that God took notice, God gave you over to a depraved mind.

**VERSE 8.**—“The watchman of Ephraim is with my God. The prophet has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways, and madness is in the house of his God.” Ephraim—that is, the voluntary disposition of the mind—has become a watchman so that he may desire the things pertaining to God and propose what ought to be done for God: “To will,” he says, “is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it” (Rom. VII, 18).

In Scripture, “will” is frequently understood in relation to the good; and because of the foresight by which he detects sins and adversities, he is called a prophet. Yet, alas, he becomes a snare of ruin: he ensnares himself by withdrawing counsel from himself, and gives others examples of wickedness, causing them to fall. He becomes a snare of ruin upon all his ways—that is, upon all his own ways. For this is a feature of Hebrew expression, as in: “Ethiopia will hasten its hands to him” (Ps. LXVII, 32), meaning “its own hands.”

“With my God” means that in all his intention—whose inward ways run outward into works—nothing but the fall of sin is found, and every access to counsel, signified by the neck because the word passes through it, is blocked. Madness is in the house of his God when his most wicked zeal for crimes, which his devotion regularly practices as though it were the worship of God within the house of his conscience, is wholly devoid of every measured and disciplined concern, and the mind plunges into such madness that secret desire bursts into open insanity.

**VERSE 9.**—“They have sinned deeply, as in the days of Gibeah.” Whoever longs for sin with the whole deliberation of his mind sins deeply. He appears to touch upon the history of the Kings, when Saul was taken from Gibeah and made king (1 Sam. XI, 4), after the command of God had been shaken off for the sake of the custom of the nations alone. Saul is interpreted as “desire,” and Gibeah as “hills.” Saul is taken from the hills to the kingdom when desire arises from great swellings of the soul—not a desire that is subject to us, as the Lord says to it, but one that most shamelessly rules us. For when we conceive arrogance, we immediately desire things greater than are suitable for us.

“He will remember their iniquities, and he will visit their sins.” After iniquity has been turned into stupidity, so that sin is committed with wicked freedom, God is, as it were, roused by some cry to hasten to vengeance. Hence the voice of Abel’s blood (Gen. IV, 10) and the cry of Sodom are mentioned. When sin is committed quietly, God seems to forget. He therefore appears to remember when he attacks the sinner with adversities. He visits sins when, by punishing them repeatedly, he demonstrates that he has seen them.

**VERSE 10.**—“Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; like the first fruits on a fig tree at its summit I saw their fathers.” Israel is found like grapes in the wilderness when our carnal affection, scattered away from itself, is gathered together by the breath of divine fear. He is found like a grape in the wilderness when the sweetness of inward compunction is perceived in a mind that was once desolate.

Their fathers are seen like the first fruits of a fig tree when rational movements, by which the intemperance of the affections is restrained, are first recalled from their former bitterness through God’s indwelling and sweetened by the maturity implanted in the mind. These first fruits are found at the summit because the principal pursuits of our heart are founded upon the heavenly intention that is recognized as superior to our inward self.

The fathers of Israel are therefore dispositions of mature reason that generate devout affections. In Scripture the fig tree signifies love of neighbor, just as love of God is expressed by the vine. The first fruits of the fig tree are therefore superior exercises of mercy. The fathers are likened to the first fruits of the fig tree because we are first urged to bestow benefits upon the brothers whom we see, so that afterward we may reach God, whom we cannot see.

Children are compared to grapes because our affections, as though arising from paternal generosity and from the milk-like innocence figured by the sap of the fig tree, are more eagerly steeped in the richness and taste of love of God. For the spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; from heaven, consequently, so that God may be loved.

“But they themselves went to Beelphegor, and were alienated in shame, and became abominable like the things they loved.” They enter Beelphegor when, having forgotten the choice of themselves that we have described, they throw themselves into a labyrinth of utter disgrace. It is rightly said that they “enter,” because they plunge themselves into the entire experience of lust. Beelphegor is said to mean “man of itch,” by which the shamelessness of detestable disgrace is indicated.

They are alienated in shame when, the more shameful the things they perpetrate, the less they think they are doing anything shameful. Hence certain people are said, in the Apostle, to glory in their own shameful things (2 Cor. XI, 18). They become abominable when they lose every fortune belonging to the good person. For what is it to be abominable except to lack prosperous success in the advancement of a devout work? And this is “like the things they love”: just as the vices they pursue are, even by name alone and without the deeds of goodness, a horror to the memories of people, so are those who entangle themselves in traffic with them. For if every filth is foul in itself, surely those who willingly throw themselves into its mire are fouler still.

**VERSE 11.**—“Ephraim flew away like a bird; their glory is from birth, from the womb, and from conception.” Ephraim flies away like a bird when, touched rationally from time to time, the alacrity of the will aspires toward the desire for good, but, withdrawing itself with sudden lightness, does not at all persevere in what it had begun.

“Their glory,” if I approach the passage in reverse order, begins with conception when the particular grace of the states of that same will—which frequently alternate within it—is present in the first breathing of God, by which we first take delight in living well. The Apostle calls this the glory of the saints because of the testimony of conscience (2 Cor. I, 12).

After conception comes the womb: the longer gestation within the mind of a good intention before the work is displayed. For what is faithfully reconsidered through a solid deliberation of counsel is, as it were, fostered inwardly; the body of action, divided among the members of discernment, is strengthened. Then it is brought forth when it is presented to human sight in the pursuit of a good exercise.

Because Ephraim therefore flies away like a bird through exaltation even to birth—that is, until he can be seen by human beings—his inward glory endures until then; the sword of human praise immediately cuts it down.

**(VERSE 12.)**—“But if they rear their children, I will make them childless among human beings; and woe to them when I depart from them!” They rear children who advance by progress in works of devout conduct. They become childless among human beings when, amid human approval, they servilely surrender the freedom of mind given to them to the breath of the crowd [variant: of the crowd’s breath]. But woe to them when God departs from them, because nothing remains of any good hope; indeed, it is the extreme misfortune of condemnation when the rectitude of intention is perverted. God departs when the good that is done is not done with regard to him.

**VERSE 13.**—“Ephraim, as I saw him, was Tyre, founded in beauty.” The literal sense is: “As I saw”—that is, “as I beheld”—“Ephraim was like Tyre, founded in beauty.” Ephraim is Tyre because that fruitful will which, while rightly directed, served its own benefit and that of many others is now confined in narrowness, while it advances in poverty of hope toward human favor alone. For Tyre signifies “narrowness.”

It is the voice of God: “As I saw,” he says—that is, as I weighed him in the consideration of my divinity—“Ephraim was comparatively Tyre.” And this Tyre was founded in beauty because he had placed the foundations of his intention in the outward appearance of the work he had begun, by which he had resolved to please himself and others, so that in what he displayed outwardly it was not God’s power but his own beauty that might appear.

In contrast, the Psalm says: “So I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power” (Ps. LXII, 3)—not that the glory was mine, but yours.

“Ephraim will bring his children to the slayer.” Ephraim has children when the will produces good effects. Yet he brings them to the slayer when he exposes them to the tongues of flatterers, to their own destruction.

**VERSE 14.**—“Give them, Lord. What will you give them? Give them a womb without children.” This is the voice of the prophet, or of any holy man provoked by such hypocrisy: “Give them, Lord”—that is, inflict some present harm upon them. And what could you more fittingly give them than that they should not have a womb—that is, a receptacle—in which to receive the freedom of a willing act? For it is better never to have desired a good work than to lose a desired work through some imitation of a false one.

If they are called “children” because they are not subjected to servile work, then the works marked out for them are free because they are not done for human praise. “Dry breasts” are likewise given when there is a lack of spiritual understanding, by which inner and outer sensuality is offered to God in another way. Or the breasts are dry when knowledge of both Testaments is annulled in the mind.

**VERSE 15.**—“All their wickedness is in Gilgal, for there I hated them.” Gilgal is interpreted as “a place of wallowing.” All their wickedness is therefore in a place of wallowing, because all their vicious activity habitually slackens and wastes away in the sole vice of lust. However great the faith of anyone, however great his proud majesty, it is recognized as finally foaming away and swelling up into such softness. The great ferocity of Alexander, the great ferocity of Caesar, has often everywhere experienced the temper of Sardanapalus; and what once stretched to the Indian Ocean was miserably circumscribed by the sight of worthless little women.

God hates them because he does not tolerate the frenzy of unrestrained license. Note the causes of the Flood, and how the prophet calls this plague nothing other than the hammer of the whole earth.

“Because of the wickedness of their inventions I will drive them out of my house; I will no longer love them.” When someone sins habitually, it is in some measure tolerable; but when new forms of crime are invented and someone transgresses the laws of nature, it is unheard-of to all good people, let alone to God, who slays the inventors of evil with such atrocious punishment that he makes them memorable as an example of an extraordinary death. This is evident throughout the testimony of Scripture.

He drives them from his house when he excludes them from the fellowship of the good, who are his house. He does not add “to love them,” because he rightly hands over to a depraved mind those who have labored for the corruption of others, or who, not content with their own destruction, have brought about the destruction of others.

“All their princes are those who depart.” As often above, “princes” signifies the external senses. These are “those who depart,” since they never restrain themselves within themselves but scatter themselves through external things. Hence, shortly above, he also threatens to drive them from his house; this happens when, under God’s judgment, sensuality is expelled from the mind—which ought to have been God’s dwelling—for the handling of external things alone.

**VERSE 16.**—“Ephraim has been struck; their root has dried up; they will produce no fruit.” Ephraim is struck when the state of the will, which ought to have been fruitful, is crushed in its willing of the good. Their root—that is, its motive—is dried up when the intention, withered away from the greenness of divine hope, is rendered fruitless. It is rightly called the root because from it emerges everything vital that is accomplished. They will produce no fruit because, just as their thoughts, so their works fail of every usefulness.

“Even if they beget, I will slay the beloved things of their womb.” They beget when, compelled by nature—which cannot be without some good—they act devoutly. But God slays the beloved things of their womb when he disperses and destroys whatever in the conscience could have stood either according to the honesty of the world or according to natural goodness, turning it into an accumulation of judgment. He calls the things of the womb “beloved” because whatever more pleasing thing pertains to moral integrity can be held within the bosom of the soul [Col. 0391A].

**VERSE 17.**—“My God will reject them, because they have not listened to him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.” Because they do not listen to God, God rejects them: since they refuse in any way to obey God and close the ears of their minds to him, he displays them as rejected because of the reprobation of their life. They are wanderers among the nations when they scatter themselves through every vice. That “nations” signifies vices is indicated, if not elsewhere, at least by the peoples whom the Lord overthrew before the children of Israel.

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.**—“Israel is a leafy vine; fruit has been made equal to him. According to the abundance of his fruit he multiplied altars.” Israel is a leafy vine when those who boast, through knowledge of the Scriptures, of the vision of God—that is, of knowledge of him—heap up for themselves a multiplicity of words without works. Israel becomes a leafy vine when he covers himself with the mere pomp of empty eloquence. Thus, just as Israel is so in name alone, so the vine is without work.

Fruit is made equal to him when a succeeding work corresponds to empty loquacity, in complete falsity. According to the abundance of his fruit he multiplies altars—that is, in proportion to the quantity of exercises performed through hypocrisy, he accumulates for himself titles of popular flattery.

“According to the fertility of his land he abounded in images.” The land abounds when our body is full of distinguished but false works. The body acts, but not the mind, when something good is done with an empty and senseless mind merely so that it may be seen. Therefore, as many works as there are, so many images are erected, as it were, for human approval.

**VERSE 2.**—“Their heart is divided.” Their heart is divided when one thing is practiced in the work and another is considered in the mind. For in intention they seek praise while outwardly, at least in appearance, they strive to display labor fitting for God. Hence the Apostle says that the one who is with a wife and concerned about worldly matters is divided (1 Cor. VII, 33), since, while he attends to marital obligations on one side, he is sometimes admonished to turn his attention toward God on the other.

“Now they will perish; he himself will break their images; he will lay waste their altars.” **(VERSE 3.)** “For now they will say: We have no king.” They will perish now—that is, they will perish in this very condition in which, having set God aside, they devote themselves to earthly regard [Col. 0392A]. He himself breaks their images when the spirit, leaping toward shameful deeds as it bursts forth from the burning pyre of crimes, diminishes whatever was falsely represented. He lays waste their altars when he makes their purposes and institutions feeble, and renders void the things on which they had relied as supreme and principal.

“For,” he says, “now they will say.” This means: Because they are now perishing, they will say, “We have no king”—that is, because our displays have dragged us into the punishment of inward blindness, there is no one within us to rule us. For what the spirit is, that is the king; and that is also the measure. “For we do not fear the Lord; and what will the king do for us?” It is as though they were saying: Since we have been stripped of the fear of God, what measured and disciplined thing can reason, which consists solely in the fear of God, bring us, now that it has been deprived of what supports it? Unless we make reason an appendage of God, we call it reason in vain [Col. 0392B].

**VERSE 4.**—“You speak words of a useless vision, and you will strike a covenant; and it will sprout like bitterness.” This is said to Israel, whose name is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” It is as though he said: You are a leafy vine; under the honored name of “vine,” your mind is devoted to babbling. Concerning the knowledge of God—which is vision—you speak useless words. They are plainly useless because boastful speech produces sound without mind.

These words are spoken, as it were, ironically. “And you will strike a covenant”—namely, concerning the continence of your body, by which you may appear more glorious, when you establish agreements with your mind. But this covenant sprouts like bitterness because the instability of the heart and the wantonness of the flesh, through the irruption of every impurity, suddenly embitter their mutual agreement. This is the germ of hypocrisy, which, with God as avenger, reveals in an instant the state of the impious mind. Hence it follows:

“Judgment,” he says, “upon the furrows of the field.” The furrows of the field signify the body’s affliction on account of God. Hypocrites make furrows in their field when they inflict suffering upon their bodies through abstinence. Judgment falls upon these when, with God making it manifest, clear evidence of false holiness is given to all.

Solomon testifies that the furrows of the field are customarily understood in this way: “Diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. XXIV, 27). And concerning God’s horse, Job says: “He digs the earth with his hoof” (Job XXXIX, 21); “when he hears the trumpet, he says: ‘Ha!’” (ibid., 25).

[Col. 0391] **HERE ENDS THE SECOND BOOK.**

**CONTINUATION OF THE THIRD BOOK OF TROPES ON HOSEA.**

[Col. 0391]

[Col. 0391D] Undertaking a third little book on the blessed Hosea, we pray—not so much with words as with melodies—that God, who is the Trinity, may not allow me to remain hidden from his illumination and warmth. He who has always spoken, and will always speak, what he wills through whom he wills, and who knows that I have undertaken such great difficulties of the mysteries solely through the favor of his mercy, not through presumptuous security, may deign to grant access to the harbor of prosperity to one who is already clinging there, yet fearful [Col. 0393A].

**THE CHAPTER FOLLOWS.**

**VERSE 5.**—“The inhabitants of Samaria worshiped the cows of Bethaven, because his people mourned over him, and his temple-wardens exulted over him in his glory, because it had departed from him.” Bethaven is interpreted as “house of an idol”; Samaria signifies “guardianship.” The inhabitants of Samaria therefore worship cows when those who think they rule over their outward guardianship, and ascribe the continence of their bodies to their own power, do not abandon inward wantonness—indeed, embrace and cultivate it—in Bethaven, that is, in the house of an idol, namely, in the conscience in which the worship of God is transferred to the devil [Col. 0393B].

That cows signify wantonness is attested by: “The assembly of bulls among the calves of the peoples” (Ps. LXVII, 31). He inhabits Samaria who reckons that he can live chastely by himself. “To inhabit” is used for “to rule,” since it is derived by inflection from *habere*, “to possess.” Since he had signified the desire for lust by calves, he now indicates that he is repeating that plurality in the singular.

“He mourned over him,” he says; but it should be noted that “because” is placed first. The meaning is: They were guardians of external conduct, and this precisely because the people of their thoughts mourned—that is, murmured, longing for the one who restrained the desire outwardly. His people—that is, his desire—is so called because such concupiscence inwardly produces many disturbances.

Moreover, his temple-wardens exult over him in his glory when crafty and deceitful movements, which guard external behaviors, likewise rejoice together over the honor and glory of praise bestowed from outside. They exult, I say, in his glory because he has departed from him—that is, all that praise is alienated and, as it were, emigrates from the awareness of that desire which burns most shamefully in the mind.

The whole meaning is this: The precautions of the mind, which watch over bodily appearance, rejoice that the foolish crowd has been removed far from knowledge of its inward condition—a condition that could have been deeply displeasing.

**VERSE 6.**—“Indeed, he himself has been carried away to Asshur, a gift for the avenging king.” Whatever outward glory may accompany such a person, he himself is nevertheless carried away to Asshur—which means “into the court”—that is, he is secretly plunged into the haunts of vice. And he is not merely made into a gift, but as though into the devil’s proper gift, becoming the devil’s own possession; the one to whom he is given takes vengeance on the very thing that is offered.

“The confusion of Ephraim will seize him, and Israel will be confounded in his will.” The confusion of Ephraim seizes him when obscurity of discernment intercepts our will, which ought to have been supported by reason. Israel is confounded in his will when, so to speak, because his reason and will have already inclined toward evil in willing—or rather desiring—there is no measure or order maintained in his affection.

### Verses 7–8

“Samaria caused its king to pass away like foam upon the face of the water. And the high places of the idol, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed.”

Samaria causes its king to pass away when the prudence of the outer man, which disguises itself as reason—or rather, worldly cunning—compels him to go beyond the unworthy acts toward which he is carried through the waves of pleasures, borne about by every wind of temptation, and, as it were, to foam away; for it happens often that hypocrisy cannot restrain itself for long. The high places of the idol are destroyed when proud thoughts, which had taught the mind to apostatize from God, are brought to nothing. They are called the high places and the sin of Israel because they arise from the perverse freedom of the affections.

“Burdock and thorn shall ascend upon their altars.”

Burdock is a lowly herb; thorn grows up among shrubs, but both are roughened with prickles. By the burdock, therefore, is signified luxury, always shamefully low; by the thorn, covetousness, which stretches itself out and strives to expand. These ascend upon their altars because they now visibly creep over what they have set forth as religious undertakings.

“And they shall say to the mountains: Cover us; and to the hills: Fall upon us.”

Those who once were mountains—that is, who had swollen up within themselves through excessive arrogance—now, deflated by the emptiness of hope, desire to be covered and protected by the true mountains, namely, the saints; and they plead with the lesser elect, who are the hills, to fall upon them—that is, to bend over them in pity.

The whole meaning is this: Those who had thought that they could become holy by their own guardianship—which we said was signified by Samaria—now, attending to the true holiness of others, brought about by God’s help, do not doubt that they themselves were false in their own estimation.

### Verse 9

“From the days of Gibeah Israel sinned; there they stood.”

Gibeah, as has often been said, is interpreted as “hills.” By the hills here we understand the private fears of the mind. Israel therefore sins from the days of these hills, because from the time when the wretched mind began to prosper in its pride—what the days signify—the affection subjects itself to perversity. “There they stood,” that is, they persevered. “To stand” is used for “to persevere,” as in: “They drew near and stood against me” (Psalm 37:12).

Note that when Israel and Ephraim are used in the singular, they are said to figure separately those two dispositions of the mind, namely, affection and will; but when they are used in the plural, the movements of those same dispositions are understood.

### Verse 10

“Battle shall not overtake them in Gibeah against the children of iniquity. According to my desire I shall chastise them.”

Battle does not overtake them in Gibeah because where there is no temptation, there is likewise no rebellion against any vice. And how can someone be said to be tempted when, before the devil suggests anything to him, he is already inflamed with the zeal of every wickedness? This battle is against the children of iniquity, that is, against the works whose mother is iniquity. Scripture frequently uses “children” for “works.” For the Lord commands that the debtor’s wife and children be sold (Matthew 18:25), that is, that the will and works be brought under the harshness of the understanding and withdrawn from the freedom of choice.

God chastises them according to his desire because, in accordance with his will that all people should be saved and return to the knowledge of him (Titus 1:1), he punishes them in the present in order to correct them. For what he desires above all is that those whom he chastises should come to their senses.

“Peoples shall be gathered against them when they are chastised because of their two iniquities.”

The two iniquities are, first, the committing of sin, and second, the possession of an impenitent heart. They are chastised because of these two iniquities when they are divinely pierced and shaken loose from their obstinacy and customary wickedness. Then peoples are gathered against them when vices long grown old pursue the mind with greater insolence than usual. These are the Egyptians who appear to press upon the Israelites who had departed from them all the way to the crossing of the Red Sea.

### Verse 11

“Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck.”

It is the nature of a threshing heifer willingly to return to the task in which, when driven rapidly, it has sometimes been accustomed to taste the work of threshing. We think that “heifer” is used here not only for wantonness but also for fruitfulness.

Ephraim, therefore, is a heifer trained to love threshing when our will, made fruitful through divine correction, is now ready to separate good from evil as grain from chaff. For our beginnings, according to blessed Gregory, are mixed with evils.

God passes over the beauty of her neck when he permits the newness of her purpose—which, so to speak, has just become beautiful through a recent conversion—to be trampled down, through certain temptations, by lofty consideration. It is customary in Scripture to say that God does what he permits to be done.

The neck may also signify not only purpose, whose channel it is—for the purpose of the righteous is a resolve to act well—but also the stiff neck of elation, which often creeps upon those newly converted. God passes over this neck and the beauty of the purpose when, by permitting both to be tested, he casts them down.

“I shall mount upon Ephraim.”

God mounts upon Ephraim when he makes reason, which is God’s proper seat, ride over the now truly fruitful will.

“Judah shall plough, and Jacob shall break up his furrows.”

Judah ploughs when sincere confession of repentance turns and wears down the surface of body and mind. Jacob breaks up his furrows for himself when, by supplanting sins, he does not cease to level a kind of smooth plain of inward peace.

He is said to break them up for himself because whatever the piety of repentance accomplishes through holy labor, it performs for its own inward benefit, not for the praises of the crowd. Jacob, moreover, is called “supplanter.” For Judah ploughs to no purpose if Jacob labors too laxly in breaking up the furrows, and especially in supplanting.

### Verse 12

“Sow righteousness for yourselves in truth; reap mercy in your mouth; renew the fallow ground for yourselves.”

Whoever resolves to render to God and neighbor what is fitting for each, preserving common equity, sows righteousness for himself in truth. To sow is to propose. But whoever, without craving praise, decides to perform this good deed for himself alone, conscious of it before God, sows for himself in truth.

He reaps mercy in his mouth when he does not cease to declare to others what he has conceived in his heart, in the hope of reaping mercy. We also reap mercy in our mouth when we cause a sinner to turn back from the error of his way: we undoubtedly free his soul from death and cover the multitude of our own sins.

Whoever, on beginning a religious life, begins to examine the secrets of sacred speech renews the fallow ground for himself. In these fallow fields, as is said elsewhere, there is much food, since suitable teachings for every manner of soul and way of life are there, as it were, laid out like dishes (Proverbs 13:23). For wherever the spirit goes, the wheels go there also.

“But it is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness.”

You must practice these things that have been said, he declares, because the fitting time is smiling upon you: the time for seeking the Lord has come, especially when the Spirit of divine compunction has already come to you. Without a teacher and without a book, he will lead you into all truth, as it is written elsewhere (John 16:13), and this is what he here calls righteousness.

Hence it is also said: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27). And the Apostle warns us that we have not received this grace of heavenly infusion in vain (2 Corinthians 6:1). The whole meaning is that the time for seeking the Lord is when he himself is present to breathe upon us.

### Verse 13

“You ploughed impiety; you reaped iniquity; you ate the fruit of falsehood, because you trusted in your ways, in the multitude of your strong men.”

He ploughed impiety who once, through hypocrisy, devoted his body to self-mutilation, although what ought to have been done for God alone was required of him. And what is so impious, what so godless, as to slaughter one’s own flesh not for God? Who deserves to be called more truly a nobody than one who hates his own flesh under such a pretext?

He reaped iniquity who thereafter sacrilegiously appropriated to himself the praises that should have been given to God. Nothing is less just than to place God after one’s own honor. He therefore reaped unjustly who first assigned to himself such a profane reward.

He ate the fruit of falsehood who, while his conscience accused him, learned to feed upon the deceptive flattery of ordinary people. “Because you trusted,” he says, “in your ways”—that is, without looking toward your inner emptiness, you directed your eyes only toward those things that were emptily proclaimed about your superstitious work outside you. For just as a road is outside a person, so the works in which a hypocrite trusts are outside him.

He also trusts in the multitude of his strong men when he places his hope in the purpose of an arduous way of life scarcely tolerable even to holy men, without considering toward what he is aiming, but only what he foolishly performs.

### Verse 14

“Tumult shall arise among your people, and all your fortifications shall be laid waste, as Salman was laid waste by the house of him who judged Baal in the day of battle, when the mother was dashed against her children.”

Tumult arises among the people when the insolence of former license breaks out again in the hearts of those newly converted. Or tumult arises when a grave movement of repentance emerges in their thoughts.

All his fortifications are laid waste when all the barriers of the mind—which had formerly concealed the gloomy recesses of crimes in their hiding places—are dragged forth into the light of pious confession.

Salman is interpreted as “the shadow of hindering” or “of commotion.” “As Salman was laid waste by the house of him who judged Baal in the day of battle” means: as that wicked obscurity which had hindered the approach of divine light to the mind ought to be consumed, and which, lest he remain in misery, had continually harassed him with repeated disturbances, is laid waste by the house—that is, by the conscience—in which Baal judges, as it were, on the day when flesh and spirit contend, and condemns the man.

Of this it is said: “The one whom you have is not your husband” (John 4:18).

This occurs when desire is crushed together with its works, “the mother” being dashed upon her children. Baal is interpreted as “husband” or “one who has,” that is, one possessing dominion; it signifies the dominion of error.

### Verse 15

“Thus Bethel has done to you, because of the face of the wickedness of your crimes.”

Although Bethel is interpreted as “house of God,” it is nevertheless profaned because of the idol that Jeroboam had set up there.

The meaning, then, is this: Bethel has produced for you these opposing strongholds by which your hearts were fortified against God—namely, the conscience which God ought to have inhabited but which the devil’s fantasy had imbued—and this “because of the face,” that is, because of the consideration of the enormity of your crimes. For “wickedness” here denotes the excessive practice of crimes.

## Chapter 11

### Verse 1

“As morning passed away, the king of Israel passed away.”

The king of Israel is our spirit, whose task it is to rule whatever lies under the affection. According to the etymology often mentioned, he himself rules together with reason, as it were with God; otherwise, he serves.

This king passes away like morning when, after the rejection of ignorance and the fog of thoughts, like the pallor of dawn, he reaches the grace of fuller understanding and tranquility, like the radiance of the sun.

“Because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.”

Israel is a child, and for that reason he is loved by God, because after returning to the newness of life he cannot fail to please God. He also calls his son from Egypt when God leads back and raises up from the daily darkness—which comes either through imposition or by nature—our spirit, which is begotten in us from the true light like a light.

### Verse 2

“They called them, and so they went away from their presence.”

What he had indicated above in the singular through the king, he now applies in the plural because of the various movements of rational faculties. For although reason is one, there are nevertheless many reasons because of the many causes involved.

It is as though he said: Although God himself reveals us from our blindness, the rational movements themselves nevertheless sometimes strive to awaken us from our body. But because “a person’s way is not in himself, nor in a man to direct his steps” (Proverbs 16:9), those movements withdraw when God providentially holds us back, and thus make us experience what we are of ourselves.

They go away from his presence when the obstinacy of their thoughts excludes them from giving an account of their reasons.

“They sacrificed to the Baals, and sacrificed to images” (verse 3). “And I was like a nurse to Ephraim.”

They sacrifice to the Baals when, often yielding to temptation, they perform many things of God, but not for God’s sake. They sacrifice to images when, while their inner condition is endangered, they display themselves to the eyes of people in a manner far different from what is actually taking place within.

“But amid these things,” he says, “I was a nurse to Ephraim,” while I always strive to remind the mind of resurrection after its fall; thus our will is not shattered, since the Lord places his hand beneath it. He nourishes us in this way, teaching us through both our falls and our recoveries.

“I carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I was caring for them.”

He carries them in his arms when he lifts them up to divine strength. “Arm” is customarily used for “strength.” They do not know that he cares for them because, almost despairing under the weight of temptation, they do not understand that, in his providence, he presses them down through hidden shipwrecks so that they may not become proud of the prosperity of their virtue.

### Verse 4

“With cords of Adam I shall draw them, with bonds of love.”

In another translation, where “Adam” is read here, “human beings” is found there, for that is how the term is interpreted. Thus also in Genesis, where it says, “He called their name Adam” (Genesis 5:2), it is likewise transferred as “human beings.”

He therefore draws them with human cords when, through fear of suffering and human troubles, he seizes them for himself. Hence it is said: “Their infirmities have been multiplied”; afterward, as though he were saying, “They hastened to the physician” (Psalm 15:4).

But afterward what was first undertaken through fear is turned into love, and therefore it follows: “With bonds of love,” which casts out fear (1 John 4:18). The cords themselves are the affections by which we are led to desire something without anyone compelling us.

The fear mentioned above is not without love; otherwise it would not possess these cords. Hence the poetic line: “Each person is drawn,” he says, “by his own pleasure” (Virgil, Eclogue 2).

“And I shall be to them like one lifting the yoke above their jaws, and I bent down to him so that he might eat.”

He is like one lifting the yoke above their jaws when the true substance of the mind raises the prominence of its fear above their intellectual senses. God had raised his yoke above the jaws of the one who, like swelling waves towering over him, had always feared him.

The yoke is raised all the more as one advances further in inner virtue, while what has once been tasted of eternal love is feared always to be lost. We understand “jaws” as the intellect, because with them, like teeth, we grind hard things.

He bends down to him so that he may eat when God, through that fear by which the mind is healthfully humbled, also bends down to us so that we may be nourished by his inspiration.

“I shall dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20).

When above he speaks to “him” in the singular, although he had previously mentioned certain things in the plural because of the various movements, understand a single disposition of mind, since we know that God does not descend to dine amid the divisions of minds.

### Verse 5

“He shall not return to the land of Egypt, and Assyria itself shall be his king.”

He does not return to the land of Egypt when he no longer permits himself to return to former sins. Yet Assyria—that is, the familiarity and acceptance of courtiers—appears to him highly desirable.

This is still visible today in certain men of our order, who, while restraining themselves from worldly foulness, nevertheless burn irreparably to thrust themselves into the solemnities of courts. Assyria, as it is no burden to repeat, is a court.

“Because they refused to return” (verse 6), “the sword began in his cities, and it shall consume his chosen ones and devour their heads.”

The meaning is: Because they refused to return from Assyria—that is, from the utterly empty feeding of their eyes—the sword began in his cities, that is, in their minds, because the unfamiliar conflict of the flesh against the spirit arose throughout all his sensual faculties, which, according to the Gospel, are cities.

The sword signifies division, as in: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). Explaining this, he says: “I have come to separate” (ibid., 10:35), and so forth.

“And it shall consume his chosen ones,” that is, it shall annihilate whatever is more eminent in his inner condition. “It shall devour their heads” when it consumes the summits of both the cities and the chosen intentions through the rust of temptation [perhaps “fire” or another reading; the printed text has *aurugine*].

### Verse 7

“And my people shall hang upon my return.”

Although their heads are devoured and a grievous titillation sinks into the mind, nevertheless the spark of reason sometimes tends to revive. This is why God’s people are said to hang upon his return: after so many evils have descended upon them, pious thoughts customarily become inclined toward God’s saving visitation.

As we said elsewhere, lovers are said to hang upon one another, and therefore the expression is used for love.

“But a yoke shall be imposed upon him at the same time, and it shall not be removed.”

The yoke is imposed upon him when the mind is depressed by fear of the temptation it has experienced. This yoke is not removed because no security ever cuts away boldness from the neck of the mind.

### Verse 8

“How shall I give you up, Ephraim? How shall I protect you, Israel? How shall I make you like Admah? How shall I set you like Zeboiim?”

It is as though he said: Into what condition shall I transfer the human will? By what art shall I protect affection that wanders through so many departures and returns?

By these complaints he indicates how great is the difficulty of governing the condition of our interior life. If it is raised up to virtues, it swells with pride; if it weakens into perceptions, it perishes through insipidity; if it falls into crime, it rots.

“I know,” he says, “what I shall do, because I shall make you like Admah and set you like Zeboiim.”

Admah is interpreted as “earthly.” Zeboiim is interpreted as “its station,” “sea,” “their goat,” or “doe.”

First, then, the human mind is set, like Admah, for its own protection, so that, whatever virtue it may excel in, it may unceasingly remember the earthliness in which it dwells. But it must not grow sluggish in considering this weakness; rather, it must establish its station in the sea, so that amid the assaults of temptation it may learn to stand rather than fall. When struck, it must neither turn aside nor collapse, but, like a goat, must always stretch its mind toward the heights of a good purpose, while in that purpose it must in no way lose the sharpness of discerning subtlety.

For the goat desires steep places, whereas the doe derives its name from its great sharpness of sight.

“My heart is turned within me; at the same time my compassion is disturbed.”

God’s heart is turned toward him when he is moved not by the example of someone else but by consideration of himself toward the inward parts of mercy. It is human to be broken by regard for and reflection upon another. His compassion is likewise disturbed because, while he repents of an expressed judgment, he is also mercifully affected by the other troubles that we suffer in human fashion.

God speaks in human fashion, although nothing of this kind occurs in him; nevertheless, no one doubts that he grieves over the calamity of his elect.

Or otherwise: The elect themselves are God’s heart, concerning whom it is said: “His heart drew near after the wicked were divided from the anger of his face” (Psalm 54:22). His heart, therefore, is turned toward him when those to whom he has made known everything he heard from the Father (John 15:15) strive, under the guise of their earthliness—which is Admah—to turn toward the height of contemplation, which is the goat and the doe.

Then God’s compassion is likewise disturbed when the pain and difficulty of their long disgust with the present age are added to the repentance that God first implanted in them.

### Verse 9

“I shall not carry out the fury of my anger; I shall not turn to destroy Ephraim, because I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst, and I shall not enter the city.”

The anger of God is the movement of worthy retribution against our vices; fury, however, is the being girded against human obstinacy through the imposition of a reprobate disposition.

He does not carry out the fury of his anger when he does not take away from us the remnants of good thought; for these keep a festival for themselves.

God turns to destroy Ephraim when he appears to imitate in the mind of the one being tempted what seems entirely to consume the effort of his good will from the roots.

“I am God,” he says, “and not man.” The meaning is: A human being stubbornly carries through whatever he has begun, but I, God, know how to suspend even an impending judgment through myself.

The Holy One is in the midst of Ephraim when God inserts himself into the very center of his reason, within his will, as a king surrounded by an army. He does not enter the city because he does not inhabit it; indeed, he scarcely breathes upon the conscience when it is deafened by the tumult of vices.

### Verse 10

“They shall walk after the Lord; he shall roar like a lion, because he himself shall roar, and the sons of the sea shall fear.”

The reasons implanted in the will walk after the Lord when reason is first subjected to God, and afterward the disposition of the will obeys reason.

Reason itself—which above is called holy because of its firmness—roars like a lion when, through the cry of the one upon whom it rests, namely, the divine word, it terrifies and shakes bestial movements from every direction with something like royal authority.

Itself, I say, shall roar, and the sons of the sea shall fear when, either through the severity of inward judgment or through remembrance of sin, reason rises turned toward itself and makes the sons of the sea—that is, worldly movements—afraid. The more it is imbued with either of these, the more whatever temporal and transitory thing resounds in the mind is terrified.

### Verse 11

“And they shall fly away like a bird from Egypt, and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians, and I shall settle them in their houses.”

The sons of the sea fly away from Egypt like a bird when the impulse of pride, figured by the bird, lifts itself from the lowest desires and changes present sorrow into spiritual joy. Egypt signifies sorrow.

It flies away from the land of the Assyrians like a dove, without gall but, when deceived, without heart, when it removes from itself everything that it considers more pompous and courtly in this world. For this has the sound of a court.

He settles them in their houses when he gathers them back to their conscience after they have been recalled from their dispersion.

### Verse 12

“Ephraim surrounded me with commerce, and the house of Israel with deceit.”

Ephraim surrounds God with commerce when he constricts the reason presiding over him in God through the commerce of empty glory. For what is it to engage in commerce if not to do good for the sake of popular favor?

Ephraim therefore surrounds God with commerce when vanity persuades and incites the spirit of the will, which perceives God, to receive praises for good deeds.

The house of Israel surrounds him with deceit when, on the surface of thought, Israel—that is, the will inclined toward carnal desire—pretends to obey the command of reason, while nevertheless lying in wait for an opportunity to sin, if permitted.

“But Judah, a witness, descended with God, and was faithful with the holy ones.”

The meaning is this: Penitential confession, which condemns together with God what God judges in us—for “if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31)—descends with God as a witness in this very matter, that is, it is humbled, because from Ephraim and Israel, both proud and deceitful, one returns to this in simple lowliness.

And it is faithful with the holy ones when it glorifies the humility that God now commands them in the exaltation of the age to come. It is therefore called faithful because it carries out for the saints, with everlasting fidelity, what it now promises.

## Chapter 12

### Verse 1

“Ephraim feeds on wind and follows the heat.”

Ephraim feeds on wind when he attributes causes for the promotion of his praises to windy people—that is, talkative people eager for novelties. Ephraim is said to do this because it is agreeable to the will to wish to be praised.

He follows the heat because the more he is outwardly restrained, the more inwardly the heat of carnal incentives burns.

It is as though he said: He seeks favors outwardly, but the more harshly his wantonness burns him.

“All day he multiplies falsehood and desolation; he made a covenant with the Assyrians, and he carried oil into Egypt.”

He multiplies falsehood all day who continually supplies, through his hypocrisy, opportunities for others’ lips to lie. But he multiplies desolation because the more he hears himself exalted, the more he expands the deserts of inward desolation, while, amid the flowering abundance of words, he consigns unseen things to negligence.

He makes a covenant with the Assyrians when he becomes united with those who glory in temporal things. He carries oil into Egypt when he does not fear that he has received the grace of God in vain (2 Corinthians 6:1). He carries oil into Egypt when, from the refuse of his virtues, he desires to please worldly people in a worldly fashion.

### Verse 2

“Therefore the Lord has a judgment with Judah, and visitation upon Jacob.”

The Lord’s judgment is with Judah because, in the virtue of confession, the subtlety of discerning spirits is supremely necessary. Visitation comes upon Jacob when, in supplanting vices, fear of divine vengeance is always present to our reason. “Visitation” is sometimes used for punishment.

“According to his ways and according to his inventions he shall repay him.”

He is repaid according to his ways when our understanding is pierced in proportion to the measure of each error and, as though being beaten for the offense, presents to the former wantonness of the mind a retribution of inward pain.

His inventions are whatever in human practices exceeds what nature requires. He repays these to him when that intellectual judge restores them to him under the bitterness of repentance.

### Verses 3–4

“In the womb he supplanted his brother; and in his strength he prevailed with the angel. And he prevailed against the angel and was strengthened.”

He supplants his brother in the womb when, within the conscience, he casts down the rigidity of carnal desire. In his strength he is directed with the Angel when the freedom of choice, than which nothing is stronger, leans unwaveringly upon the divine word, which is God’s messenger to us.

He prevails against the Angel when, through frequent engagement with the divine word, spiritual strength grows day by day against opposing powers. He is strengthened when, amid the assaults of temptations, the firmness of his mind is permitted nowhere to waver.

“He wept and pleaded with him.”

In weeping, inward moisture is drawn out into external expression. He is therefore said to weep who strives to drain away every inward softness. He pleads with the angel who holds the word of God in the highest veneration and reverence.

“He found him in Bethel, and there he spoke with us” (verse 5). “And the Lord God of hosts, the Lord is his memorial.”

Bethel is interpreted as “house of God.” He finds the Angel in Bethel when, having God as an inhabitant, he examines through God’s inspiration the mysteries of the divine word, and by the author of that word comes to know what has been uttered.

For whoever thinks that he can unlock the mysteries of Scripture without the Spirit of God is plainly like a blind man groping in error along another person’s walls without lamps.

There he speaks with us because, according to the way the reader’s heart is imbued by God, whatever had long obstructed understanding is immediately disclosed clearly, with the judgment of sacred Scripture agreeing with it.

It should be noted that, speaking of himself in the singular, he added at the end: “with us.” He who is found in Bethel speaks with us because, when something obscure in sacred Scripture has become clear to a holy conscience that rejoices to have God as its guest, that conscience, unable to bear concealing from others what God has granted it without envy, will gladly disseminate it without delay, either by speech or in writing.

And not only the Angel but also the Lord God of hosts speaks with us, because whatever is found in that same sacred word is undoubtedly disclosed by him who is shown to be the kindly instigator of our earlier exercises, and who approves that what is expended in these holy studies belongs to him.

“Hosts” derives from exercising, and God is the God of hosts because the exercises of souls serve under him. “The Lord is his memorial”: above he had said, “the Lord God of hosts”; now he repeats “the Lord,” thereby indicating that the Lord who supplies us with zeal for sacred study is the same Lord who once spoke through the mouths of the prophets those things that we anxiously seek in their books as manifestations of his grace.

His memorial means that he who once foretold marvelous things through those ancients is to be believed even today to exercise no lesser power in us, granting it to those who humbly seek to enter the inner chambers of so great a plan.

“We have,” says the Apostle, “the same Spirit; we believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians [the supplied citation reads “XIV, 13”]).

### Verse 6

“And you shall return to your God; preserve mercy and judgment, and hope in your God always.”

There is no doubt that Jacob or Judah returns to his God when reason, always confessing penitentially, is admonished to look toward him from whom heavenly gifts are bestowed.

He is commanded to preserve mercy and judgment so that, if he keeps good watch in the present, he may not despair of finding God’s mercy; but if he does not, he may await a judgment that will show him to be wretched in the future. Thus, established between hope of mercy and fear of judgment, he may be found more inclined toward hope, so that he may be drawn more by love than by fear. For no one hopes for anything except under love.

This is what is meant by: “Hope in the Lord your God always.”

### Verse 7

“Canaan has a deceitful balance in his hand; he loved oppression.”

Canaan is interpreted as “merchant.” Above we said that commerce pertains to hypocrisy. In the hand of Canaan, therefore, there is a deceitful balance because in the work of hypocrites there is nothing measured or moderate.

If they weighed things well, they would never sell to their trumpeters the emptiness of their mind or work. If you wished to equate such great emptiness with the name of holiness, which outweighs every treasure, it would not merely fail to stand; it could not exist, because no comparison can stand between nothing and something.

He also loves oppression because whoever desires to be raised up by external favors must necessarily envy all those whom he hears praised either more highly or equally. If he envies them, he certainly soon goes on to disparage most bitterly those whom he has envied.

### Verse 8

“And Ephraim said: Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself.”

What he called Canaan he also indicates through Ephraim. If the former is a merchant and the latter is fruitful, then the commerce of hypocrisy plainly arises only from the surface of the action that is thought fruitful.

It is as though he said: However deceitful the balance of my disposition and external appearance may be, I nevertheless become rich when I am advanced through the daily increase of rumor on everyone’s lips.

“I have found an idol for myself,” because I have displayed an image of holiness that is honored by everyone.

“All my labors shall not find in me the iniquity that I have committed.”

The meaning is: I engage in every care and labor in the appearance of religion so that the inner iniquity of mine may not come to the notice of any of those who exalt me. What he says, “shall not find,” is as though he said, “shall conceal,” as in: “He did not open the prison to those who were shut in” (Isaiah 14:17), which means, “he closed it up.”

### Verse 9

“And I am the Lord your God, who brought you up from the land of Egypt; I shall still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the feast.”

God brought us up from the land of Egypt when he called us from the darkness of vices into his marvelous light.

He will still make us dwell in tents when, as long as we are pilgrims away from the Lord and as long as we groan, weighed down in this tent, he will keep us depressed by due humility, which is signified by sitting.

“Rise,” he says, “after you have sat” (Psalm 126:2).

Tents belong to pilgrims or soldiers. “The life of man is warfare” (Job 7:1). We do this as in the days of a festival when, in the present, we truly compensate our depression with the joy of that luminous hope, as with a feast.

### Verse 10

“I spoke over the prophets, and I multiplied vision, and in the hand of the prophets I was likened.”

The Lord speaks over the prophets when, beyond the insight of all our foresight, he deigns to teach us by his inspiration alone.

He multiplies vision when, through that same impulse, he increases the sharpness of discernment in our understanding. He is likened in the hand of the prophets when the exercise of our foresight strives to rise toward contemplating even the appearance of divine exaltation.

Observe how carefully he says “represented.” Everything similar is not the same as that to which it is said to be similar. God is therefore accustomed to be likened in the hand of the prophets when all the activity of our contemplation strives to shine toward God, although what it sees is not God himself.

### VERSE 11

“If Gilead is an idol, then they have become worthless, sacrificing oxen in Gilgal.”

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” This is to say: If those who spread themselves below and are wrongly constricted before God devote themselves to vices as though to the worship of idols, they ought to consider that they are plunging themselves uselessly into the whirlpools of vice, since they accomplish nothing except changing the mind’s vision into bestial dullness by slaughtering it.

For Gilgal is interpreted as “whirlpool.” Thus they sacrifice to oxen in a whirlpool, so to speak, when with spiritual eagerness they shamefully handle themselves—like stupid animals—by recoiling from the weight of the flesh.

“For their altars are like heaps upon the furrows of a field.”

Above we said that their altars signify the proposals of hypocrites. Whatever any one of them wishes to be honored for—for example, this man keeps vigil, that one abstains, another remains silent; whatever practice, I say, he wishes to be considered distinguished in—he sets up as an altar, upon which he is to be revered by the frivolous crowd.

These altars become like heaps upon the furrows of a field when they make those to whom they preach, and over whom they desire to preside with the authority of teachers, into heaps like the furrows of a field. For if a heap lies upon furrows, it never allows them to reach the usefulness of any crop. And those who falsely preside, while displaying doubtful examples, do not so much instruct the simple as weigh them down.

### VERSE 12

“Jacob fled into the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch.”

Jacob flees into the region of Syria when our spirit—which has the duty of supplanting vices—rises beyond the body’s sensuality into the lofty disposition of mind that surpasses temporal things and, according to the Apostle, exceeds toward God (II Cor. 5:13). He is said to have fled because David also testifies that, fleeing from the tumult of the forum, he withdrew himself far away (Ps. 54:8).

Syria is interpreted as “lofty.” There he serves for a wife when, in order to subject his own will to himself, he abandons himself. For our wife is our will, since nothing is good except what is done willingly. Without it, therefore, our spirit—which is the man—accomplishes nothing. But whoever serves gives himself over to another’s authority. Thus, in order to possess this will, he renounces his desires.

But what does he flee? Clearly, the conformity of those whose assembly sacrifices to oxen in Gilgal, and who are like heaps upon those furrows of the field which, according to Job, lament together while the earth cries out against its cultivator (Job 31:38).

Jacob kept watch for a wife—without doubt, for Laban’s sheep—when through companionship with his good spouse he restrains the flock of pious thought.

### VERSE 13

“But through a prophet the Lord led Israel out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved.”

Israel is led out of Egypt through a prophet when, through foreknowledge of the future judgment, our affective nature is withdrawn from worldly pursuit. For unless Christian prudence looked ahead to both good and evil, it would nowhere be drawn or driven away either by love or by fear.

Having been led out of Egypt through a prophet, Israel is also preserved, because without such foresight the constancy of perseverance is not maintained in those who are beginning to despise present things.

### VERSE 14

“Ephraim provoked me to anger by his bitterness, and his blood will come upon him, and the Lord his God will repay him for his reproach.”

Since we have already brought forth Ephraim as signifying hypocrites, it is our wish, so long as the text does not prevent it, to continue what we have begun.

Ephraim provokes God to anger by his bitterness when those who boast of their own fruitfulness irritate him through the bitter corruption of their inner wickedness. His blood comes upon him when the prolonged concealment of his sins overwhelms him by rising above him. It is also commonly known that “blood” is used for sin.

The Lord repays him for his reproach when the things they continually commit as an insult to God are exposed, through the most manifest falls into disgraceful crimes, to their perpetual dishonor.

## CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 1

“When Ephraim spoke, terror seized Israel, and he sinned in Baal and died.”

Ephraim speaks and terror seizes Israel when, as the eloquence of hypocrites thunders in their expositions of Sacred Scripture and argues with great subtlety about morals, a great terror shakes those who desire to be directed with God beneath their preaching. For the more pitiable they wish to appear in the eyes of the crowd, the more they display their eloquence by treating of subtler matters.

Yet amid these things he sins in Baal when, bringing none of what he says near to his own mind, he exposes the Lord’s words to his hearers like an image, concerned only with the wonder it produces. And he dies because, forgetful of what he has said, he is turned into the stupor of insensibility.

### VERSE 2

“And now they have added to sinning; they made themselves a molten image from their silver, like the likeness of idols; the whole thing is the work of craftsmen.”

“And now”—that is, in this very purpose of preaching—they add to sinning when, attributing to themselves the good things they have spoken, they do not cease adulterating the word of God.

For although they speak from God, they do not speak before God. They make a molten image for themselves from their silver when, out of their eloquence, they strive to cast for themselves a crowd of foolish commoners. “Silver” signifies eloquence, as in: “The sayings of the Lord are silver tested in the fire” (Ps. 11:7).

This molten image is like the likeness of idols because that whole aggregation of the worthless rabble exists solely as a fiction of their display; and, as far as its author is concerned, it is a sacrilegious transfer of something from the worship of God to the worship of the devil.

“The whole thing is the work of craftsmen,” because whatever they perform outwardly is fitted together entirely without any firmness of truth, according to a certain outline of falsified composition.

“To them they say: Sacrifice human beings who adore calves.”

The whole meaning is this: What do such people do to those images of holiness which they appear to exhibit, except that by their deeds they cry out that calves should be adored, and that they sacrifice to them the very thing they are—human beings?

Whoever subjects himself to worldly wantonness adores calves. Yet it is the nature of a calf to be heavy because of its innate sluggishness, but wanton because of its age. This is evident in hypocrites, whose maturity flourishes outwardly in their bearing, while inwardly it reeks of goatlike wantonness.

Thus these calves are adored—or, by such an example, people are urged to adore them—when such a state of theirs is commended as worthy of veneration for the glory of their name. Hence people sacrifice human beings to them when they slaughter their rationality beneath such great bestiality.

### VERSE 3

“Therefore they will be like a morning cloud, and like the morning dew that passes away.”

Because, he says, they desire to become renowned in such a way for the destruction of others, they will become like a morning cloud on account of their own merit: their tasteless praises, with their superficial pomp, will fail in a moment when God exposes their wickedness.

A morning cloud soon ceases to exist as the course of dawn advances. Likewise, dew customarily disappears as the sun grows warm. This requires no explanation, because it shines forth almost continually in the very outcomes of hypocrites.

“Like dust carried away by a whirlwind from the threshing floor, and like smoke from a chimney.”

Our threshing floor is the holy Church, or the religious profession of any form of life. Dust is carried away from this threshing floor by a whirlwind when the instability of minds, driven by the devil’s breath, is moved away from its purpose toward unlawful acts.

They are also like smoke from a chimney, because when they have sought high things through favors, they suddenly disappear. Just as smoke burdens and stings the eyes of those who look at it—or rather, those who stand around it—so feigned virtue sometimes obscures the understanding not only of the simple but also of the clever.

Hypocrites are rightly compared with these things: through unexpected falls they are suddenly blown away from their own swelling pride.

### VERSE 4

“But I am the Lord your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt; and you shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior except me.”

There are many who put forward good things truthfully and persist in this for some time; but when they hear themselves praised, they transfer themselves, with their intention changed, to the desire for glory.

It is therefore as though he said to them: You ought to have remembered that long ago I transferred you from the power of darkness into the kingdom of my love (Col. 1:13). Once you had come to know me, every other god ought to have been excluded by you, and your salvation—which you attribute to your own foresight and effort—ought above all to have been attributed to me, because if you wish to be saved while leaving me aside, you are deceived.

He knows God without God whose vice is more closely worshiped than God.

### VERSES 5–6

“I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude. According to their pastures, they were filled, and they were satisfied, and they lifted up their heart, and they forgot me.”

He knew them in the wilderness—that is, he approved them as long as they held worldly company in hatred. For to know, in God’s case, is to approve.

A person is known in the land of solitude when, through the instability of the mind dwelling with itself—for the earth stands forever (Eccl. 1:4)—he is graciously accepted by God.

It should be noted that, in the Hebrew manner, he passes from the second person to the third.

Those are known according to their pastures who faithfully and humbly delight in the nourishment of divine reading. But they are filled when pride is conceived from an abundance of knowledge. They are satisfied when, either out of disgust or pride, like people who know everything, they do not even deign to look upon the sacred volumes, so that, in the words of the psalm, “their soul abhors every kind of food” (Ps. 106:18).

They lift up their heart when they proclaim their wisdom everywhere. “Heart” signifies wisdom in Scripture, because God “speaks peace to those who turn to the heart” (Ps. 84:9), or certainly because we understand through the heart.

They forget God when everything confused is carried about in their hearts without the authority of reason.

### VERSE 7

“And I will be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians.”

God is like a lioness to them when, from the good work that appeared to be theirs—and which, insofar as it is the work itself, belonged to God—pleasure arises in the licentious mind, while cruelty of indignation and envy toward others is also generated.

God therefore becomes this to them because he provides the cause of its effect; hence the psalm declares that he becomes perverse to the perverse (Ps. 17:26). A lioness is a cruel and wanton animal.

He is also like a leopard to them on the road of the Assyrians when, because of the variety of their diseases—by which they eagerly seek to please others—he allows those who pursue the broad and spacious way to suffer the punishments of sudden ruin. For the leopard is both a variegated animal and, because of its excessive speed, one that rushes headlong into death.

### VERSE 8

“I will meet them like a bear deprived of her cubs.”

God meets them like a bear deprived of her cubs when he sends upon them persecutions and troubles from those who used to praise them, as well as contempt for their work.

A bear is fiercer when her offspring have been taken from her, and nothing weighs more heavily upon their minds than being deprived of the praise of their works. Thus he is said to meet them like a bear when judgment is exercised upon them in keeping with their bestial nature.

“And I will tear open the inward parts of their liver; and I will consume them there like a lion; the beast of the field will tear them apart.”

According to the natural philosophers, we love with the liver. God therefore tears open the inward parts of their liver when, as though disemboweling them, he exposes everywhere the wantonness of the hidden love with which the insolent mind takes pleasure.

There he consumes them like a lion when he empties out the state of those who seemed to themselves to be something—that is, there, in the foulness of this carnal fall. He does this like a lion, namely by an open attack, not from the tail—that is, secretly, like a dragon.

Nothing is more closely opposed to the rigidity of pride than its customary dissolution beneath such softness.

By “field” is understood a disordered mind ignorant of Christian civility. By “beast,” whose wild and untamed nature is recognized, is understood desire.

Thus the beast of the field tears them apart when bodily desire, whether they wish it or not, makes them unable to bear their innate concupiscence and, as though eviscerating them, reveals what they are regarded as being in themselves.

### VERSE 9

“Your destruction, Israel, is only in me, your help.”

Above we said that Israel signifies those who faithfully depended upon the mouths of such hirelings and, according to the etymology of the name, desired to be directed with God.

Here it says, “Your destruction,” as though it said: You think yourself lost because it has happened to you, by the example and admonitions of such condemned men, to conceive willingly some shuddering that leads to repentance.

Since, therefore, you see them languishing in their sluggishness, you must turn your help solely to me.

### VERSE 10

“Where is your king? Let him save you now, especially in all your cities.”
