It is as though he said: You wished to rejoice and exult in your own teaching, and you had begun to say, “I belong to Paul, I to Cephas, I to Apollo” (I Cor. 1:12). And behold, you see that your king, in whom you had falsely hoped, has fallen through hypocrisy.

He was especially necessary for you so that, in all your cities—that is, in the receptacles of your consciences—he might fortify you with a saving example.

“And your judges, of whom you said: Give me kings and princes.”

It is as though he said: These are the men whom you used to boast would sit with the Lord at the final examination, because of their voluntary poverty and renunciation of the world.

This is said concerning those who knowingly favor hypocrites and, under the pretext of such discipline, desire to attach themselves to their favors. “Your judges,” as you imagine—not God’s judges.

Of these you said, “Give me kings and princes”; that is, you desired such men to rule and govern you, men who would train you in their discipleship to love and seek services and praises.

Even now we frequently see this happen: people immerse themselves not only in the company of hypocrites but also in that of reputable men, so that in some manner they may share in the honor shown to the latter.

### VERSE 11

“I will give you a king in my anger, and I will take him away in my indignation.”

Do not complain, I say, that you have lost glorious kings; rather, complain that a king has been given to you in my anger—the reprobate mind, namely, which is inflicted upon the wretched as punishment for sin.

And if any spark of a truer understanding, which might still govern you, remains in you, it will justly be taken away by the judgment of indignation.

### VERSE 12

“The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hidden.”

Ordinary sinners are very easily led to the grace of confession; a hypocrite scarcely ever, or never. For the person who labors to be honored by the name of holiness is never induced to confess anything shameful about himself.

The iniquity of Ephraim is therefore bound up because it is never loosened from his hardened heart by any word of purity. His sin is hidden because his way is not revealed to God at all, since he is separated from nothing whatsoever except from God, and from the world alone.

### VERSE 13

“The pains of a woman in labor will come upon him; he is himself an unwise son.”

The pains of a woman in labor come upon him when the most acute prickings of the flesh tear apart the womb of his mind.

Yet amid these things he himself is an unwise son, because although he rejoices that he is commonly proclaimed to be a son of God, he is nevertheless unwise, since he pleases God the Father in nothing. For, according to Solomon, “a wise son makes his father glad” (Prov. 10:1).

“For now he will not stand in the contrition of the sons.” (VERSE 14.) “From the hand of death I will deliver them; from death I will redeem them.”

“Now”—that is, at the present time, while it is called “today”—he does not stand in the contrition of the sons, because the Lord does not chastise them as sons when they are not in the labor of men (Ps. 72:5), since he does not receive as sons those whom he does not accept.

For he crushes his sons in this world whom he has chosen to raise up to eternity.

He delivers these from the hand of death whom he now saves from the commission of sin. “Sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Rom. 5:12): he has put the effect in place of the cause.

Those whom he delivers from the hand of death he also redeems from death, when those whom he had stripped of their works he likewise absolves from the deadly punishment of that same perpetual death.

“I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell.”

He explains how he delivers them from death. God is the death of death when, entering into the insensibility of minds, he rekindles whatever there is that is torpid, whatever lacks the movement of pious rationality.

If the soul of the just is called heaven, then every wicked person is not inappropriately designated by the name of hell. God therefore becomes the bite of hell when, through the entrance of his inspiration, he offers himself to be tasted beforehand by the heart of any sinner.

### VERSE 15

“Consolation is hidden from my eyes. For he himself divides among the brothers.”

Above he had spoken of the contrition of the sons; now he repeats and develops the same subject.

Consolation is hidden from the eyes of God when holy men, amid the adversities of the present age or any other scourges of God, do not allow any temporal comfort to enter into them.

By the eyes of God are understood the saints and the learned, who provide the way for the body of the Church; or else the intellectual clarity of our understanding illuminated by God.

All consolation is therefore hidden from these eyes because they utterly reject prosperity in this way, or even a brief respite amid divine blows.

Thus Rachel did not wish to be consoled (Matt. 2:18), because the just know that ineffable rewards are prepared for them. Even hell itself, which has already tasted him in part, as though by biting him, divides among the brothers how sweet the Lord is—that is, it receives the reward of the blessed portion among those who are and are called holy.

“The Lord will bring a burning wind, rising from the wilderness; and he will dry up his veins, lay waste his spring, and he himself will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.”

Therefore let hell not be terrified or despair because of any difficulty—hell which was once of one kind but has now tasted God beforehand—for the Lord will bring a burning wind, namely a spirit that dries up whatever foul moisture is within.

This wind rises from the wilderness: from the mind, that is, for which the world is exile, or rather solitude, it emerges. The bride in the Song of Songs calls it by name and asks it to come to blow through her garden (Song 4:16).

It dries up his veins when it blocks the channels of thought through which he once allowed ancient wantonness to flow. It lays waste his spring when it burns up the origin of worldly intention beneath the simplicity of a single desire.

For wherever there is a multiplicity of desires, there is, as it were, a multitude of inhabitants. The spring is therefore laid waste when the memory of the world is no longer frequented by the habits of thought.

Then hell itself, having first been made heaven, plunders the treasure of every desirable vessel when it draws into itself, with a purified heart, Christ, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom (Col. 2:3), and from whose garments myrrh, drop, and cassia flow (Ps. 44:9)—that is, every kind of virtue.

It should be noted that he says “plunders.” To plunder is to carry away into various parts. He therefore plunders the treasure of every desirable vessel who draws into himself, from every direction, the examples of all the saints and of all the virtues that are reckoned in Christ.

## CHAPTER XIV

### VERSE 1

“Let Samaria perish, because she has stirred her God to bitterness.”

It is as though he said: Let that perverse guardianship of the outward person perish from serving as an example to the faithful, because, by not guarding her inward God—so to speak, by saying vigilantly, “Not some external being, but the inward Judge”—she has provoked her God to bitterness.

“Let her perish by the sword; let their little ones be dashed in pieces, and let her pregnant women be ripped open.”

Samaria perishes by the sword when that subtle vigilance in watching herself is abandoned by the multitude of her flatterers, who used to fawn upon her. For it often happens that such craftiness is discovered; hence discord is signified by the sword. Their little ones are dashed in pieces when, dashed against the rock, they are broken by the hardness of their own dullness. Little ones are those still untrained in this occupation. Her pregnant women are ripped open when those who have been schooled by long practice in this art and have already conceived hope of gain are publicly exposed, as it were through opened fissures, together with the purpose for which they do these things. Of such pregnant women the Gospel says: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” (Luke 21:23)!

### VERSE 2

“Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have fallen in your iniquity.”

He addresses those upon whom he had pronounced an imprecation. It is as though he said: Since you have fallen in the iniquity by which you wished to be directed with God and to become like the Most High, while arrogating to yourself the honor due to him—that is, since you have fallen away from vain hope—at last return to the Lord your God: to him, namely, not whom you are equal to, but under whose power you are subject, and who, insofar as he is God, is the judge of your secret and the witness of your pretence.

### VERSE 3

“Take words with you, and return to the Lord.”

In both secular and our own writings, “words” are customarily used for trifles and tales. Hence Ovid: “Every lover gives words.” And David, to his brother who rebuked him: “Is there not,” he says, “a word?” (1 Sam. 17:29). He takes away words who despises the blandishments of a praising crowd. But because he takes nothing away who does not also take himself away, “with you” is added, so that the falsity of deeds may be driven away together with the flatteries of words. They return to the Lord when they turn themselves wholly to pleasing him henceforth. For this is signified by the prefixed preposition con-.

“Say to him: Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good; and we will render the calves of our lips.”

The Lord is asked to take away iniquity when, after duplicity has been removed from the good work performed, its due purity is sought. He is also asked to receive good—that is, the pursuits of good practice, whose praise and glory had been defrauded. We render the calves of our lips: those very calves whom we impiously cried should be worshipped, so that human beings might be sacrificed to them, when through confession we present to God the wantonness of inward frivolity by which we rejoiced in popular favor and which we were accustomed to incite with our own lips.

### VERSE 4

“Assyria will not save us; we will not mount a horse; nor will we any longer say, ‘The works of our hands are our gods,’ because you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you.”

Assyria does not save us when royal acquaintance and courtly advancement no longer occupy our minds with any hope, so far as temporal salvation is concerned. We do not mount a horse when we reject the nobility of worldly eminence. We no longer call the works of our hands gods when, for the display of our good conduct, we by no means enlist the allurements of ridiculous popularity as though for the worship of some idolatry. I had overlooked the testimony of divine speech that the horse signifies the arrogance of temporal glory, as in: “At the rebuke of the God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell asleep” (Ps. 75:7). God has mercy on the orphan who is in him, because after the mind lays aside every consolation of the present age, loses of its own accord the support of the devil as father under whom it had been nourished, and admits itself into the bowels of the merciful God, then indeed he has mercy upon it, because no alien kindness is hoped for.

### VERSE 5

“I will heal their bruises; I will love them freely.”

He heals their bruises when, by restoring, he makes good the losses of former sins. He loves them freely when he binds them to himself not superficially, but wholly and perseveringly. This seems to look back a little to that Gospel passage. When a young man asked the Lord by what deeds he might gain eternal life and the Lord set before him the commandments of the Law, the young man replied that he had observed these same things from early youth. It is then added that Jesus, looking upon him, loved him. Yet when afterwards he proposed to him the precepts of the new Law concerning renunciation of the world, he is immediately said to have gone away sorrowful because he was rich and possessed many things (Matt. 19:16–22). I should like to consider whether he deemed both this love and that perfunctory humility of the faithless king Ahab—which the Lord once praised because he had bowed his head—worthy of free love, as is read here. If what is free is what is done with no one compelling and with no causes underlying it, it seems to me greater in God than if it were from merit. For what is referred to merit is owed, but what is gratuitous is innate. When someone loves service, affection usually grows weak when the service ceases; but gratuitous affection endures with the same spontaneity with which it began. Therefore, in my view, he is said to be loved freely who is known to be chosen without any preceding good. But in God nothing is perfunctory or liable to change, so that what he has once loved could immediately be annulled when a cause arises. Rather, the statement that he loved him shows that, on account of his outward conduct, the young man could have been loved by those who saw him. This sense is supported by the words: “Jesus looked upon him.” Not without purpose; for he did not fail to know him. Similar is what is said of the centurion’s faith: that he marvelled (Matt. 8:10). What did he marvel at in a centurion whom he knew had nothing that was not from himself, except that the same man was shown to be worthy of wonder?

It follows: “Because,” he says, “my wrath has turned away from them.” God’s wrath turns away from them when the obstinacy of a heart hitherto unrepentant is removed. For in nothing does God rage more against a human being than when he does not soften the hardness of a wicked conscience.

### VERSE 6

“I will be like dew; Israel will blossom like a lily, and his root will burst forth like Lebanon.”

God is like dew when the moderation of his grace cools the fiery movements of the mind. Israel blossoms like a lily when he burns most flourishingly with the desire for holiness, without which no one will see God. Here it should be noted that a lily is cultivated with a hoe and sometimes moistened with manure. This is not unfitting for chastity, which requires both the spade of abstinence and, for its own safer preservation, the recollection of former sins. Thus in the Song of Songs the lily is called “the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1), because chastity cannot endure unless it is fortified by a profound contempt for itself.

Israel’s root is nothing other than steadfastness of intention. This bursts forth like Lebanon, or, as it is in another translation, the Septuagint: “He will send forth his roots like Lebanon,” when, in accordance with the excellence of outward work, the firmness of thought rooted by God through charity is established. For the height of cedars is said to have exceedingly deep roots. A great weight of tree cannot stand if a short and weak root is placed beneath it.

### VERSE 7

“His branches will spread.”

His branches spread when works, orderly distributed, make progress. And rightly after the height of the root he adds the extension of the branches, because whenever anyone stretches himself out in the exercise of beneficence, he must first, if he intends to persevere, be grounded in deep deliberation of mind.

“And his glory will be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon.”

His glory is like an olive tree when he abounds in works of mercy. For the olive is rich in oil, and while he kindly refreshes others, he supplies the weak with ointment by which pains are soothed. Or his glory is said to be like an olive because the brightness of inward glory, signified by oil, is called by the Apostle the testimony of conscience (2 Cor. 1:12). His fragrance is like Lebanon when whatever he does, says, or thinks is either prayer or contiguous with prayer. For Lebanon is interpreted as frankincense. Hence in the psalm: “Let my prayer,” he says, “be directed as incense” (Ps. 140:2). And: “The fragrance of your garments,” that is, of your works, “is like the fragrance of incense” (Song 4:11).

### VERSE 8

“They who sit in his shadow will return; they will live on wheat, and they will blossom like a vine.”

Those sitting in his shadow return when those who attach themselves to their example are changed to the life of holy conduct. They sit in Israel’s shadow who humble themselves under the protection of one who is directed with God. For sitting belongs to humility, and God customarily covers heaven—that is, protects it—with clouds of this kind. They live on wheat, namely on that grain which, dying after it had fallen into the earth, bore much fruit (John 12:24–25), and by which the valleys are also said in the psalm to abound in grain (Ps. 64:14), because grace is given only to the humble mind. They blossom like a vine, or, as another translation has it, flourish, when they continually aspire to the joy of the heavenly homeland and everywhere drive away the poisons of vices by the fragrance of their own virtue. For this is known to be the nature of flowering vineyards: if swarms are nearby, they customarily put serpents to flight.

“His memorial will be like the wine of Lebanon.”

The memorial of any just person is nothing other than the glorious reputation of spiritual conduct, richly fragrant with the seasoning of intellectual perfumes, and especially of outstanding discernment. Wine of Lebanon, according to the letter, is said to be mixed with spices.

### VERSE 9

“Ephraim, what have I further to do with idols?”

It is as though he said: O you badly fruitful one, who value and boast of yourself as a falsely fruitful olive tree in the house of God, since, as you hear here, “the just person will be in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. 111:7), and the just person’s everlasting remembrance is with praises, why do you strive through vain zeal to raise for yourself a statue of enduring praise? And note that “to me” is added, as though it were said: This idol of your singularity which you celebrate you set before me rather than before anyone else.

“I will hear him and direct him.”

The sense is: You, Ephraim, seek a name for yourself; but the greater the noise with which you proclaim yourself, the less you should know yourself to be known, heard, or even directed by me, since you think yourself your own author and desire to direct yourself through yourself. But Israel, by contrast, who seeks these very things from me alone, I will both hear and direct.

“I am like a green fir tree; from me his fruit is found.”

“I will direct him,” he says, “like a green fir tree”: the more humbly he thinks of himself in the present, the more I will raise him to lofty majesty and bestow upon him the greenness of blessed perpetuity. And not without reason. For his fruit is found from me: whatever pious pursuit grows in him proceeds from my dew.

### VERSE 10

“Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them?”

The wise person understands these things because undoubtedly, unless someone has first seasoned the palate of his heart with heavenly savor, he will never be able to attain understanding of what has been said. The discerning person knows because through the subtlety of discernment he reaches knowledge—that is, experience—of holy action. What these things are which must be known, he proceeds to explain.

“For,” he says, “the ways of the Lord are straight; the just will walk in them, but transgressors will fall in them.”

The ways of the Lord, since according to the psalm they are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10)—mercy, by which sinners are brought back through repentance to pardon; truth, by which the just are drawn to glory according to faith in the promises—are straight, because neither is the sinner, if he repents, excluded from glory, nor is the just permitted to enter that same glory except with the greatest labor. God so orders this that neither prejudices his equal: the just person has what he has innocently earned, nor does the other possess less, who by doing violence to the kingdom of heaven violently seized it (Matt. 11:12). The just walk in them because, whether one is a sinner or just, after he dwells in them through either repentance or justice, brought with equal lot to God’s hand, he bears the name without distinction. But transgressors fall in them who do not fear to nullify either the laws of living justly or those of subsequently repenting.

We give thanks to the all-powerful kindness of the Holy Spirit, whose inspiration, though we are unworthy and undeserving, he has deigned to receive in the pipe of our mouth. May he therefore, whose purity is not weighed down by our filth, so extend to the minds of his elect what he has spoken through us that through these very things he may bestow on them the seasoning of his sweetness.

**Here ends the third book on the prophet Hosea.**

# Preface of the Venerable Guibert to the Tropologies on the Prophet Amos

[Col. 0415]

We undertake the holy Amos with the same intention with which we have labored over the rest, invoking with heartfelt sighs him who transferred Amos from the flock to the herds and raised him from being rough and rustic into the princes of the spiritual court, so that with the blasts of his intellectual trumpet he may shake off the torpid deafness of our mind, and so infuse that Spirit who became Amos’s inward sound that he may impart to our voice—which, with undoubting faith, we believe we draw from him—the voice of life-giving power for the instruction of all who read.

To you, therefore, revered master [Note: [Col. 0415] He means St. Norbert.], in whom we have placed not only our work but ourselves, who share the infinite riches of knowledge with all without envy, we commit the entire task of correcting our discourse, so that you may confidently expand or reduce it if, in your judgment, we may be found to have said anything too much or too little.

**End of the Preface.**

# Fourth Book: Tropology on the Prophet Amos

[Col. 0415]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0415C]

### Chapter I

#### Verse 1

“Words of Amos, who was among the shepherds [or: pastors] of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam, son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.”

Amos is interpreted as “a people torn away.” That people torn away is the multitude of thoughts, which is attached to the world by no roots of intention but, wholly withdrawn from its love, rests solely upon intellectual understanding. These are the words of this Amos: whatever keen perceptions of spiritual movements can treat of the nature of the virtues concerning the discernment of spirits. He also remains among the shepherds, because while he labors at such studies in the pasture of God’s word, no hunger afflicts him.

Tekoa, moreover, is translated as “trumpet” or “bugle.” And what trumpet can resound more loudly in the mind than the understanding of the divine page, which, reproving the sleepy states of the soul, summons us with a terrifying voice to look again toward divine things? It sees these things concerning Israel, because through the examination of these words it shines forth how one may be directed with God. For Israel is said to mean “directed by God,” or “with God.”

The words are seen to occur in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, because unless the mind first learns to command itself by the authority of reason, it cannot in any way attain spiritual things. Uzziah is interpreted as “the command of the Lord.” He is king of Judah because, driven by such governance, the conscience is led to a true confession of sin. For the beginning of good things is confession of evils. Judah indeed signifies “confession.”

Jeroboam is likewise interpreted as “judgment of the people,” and Joash as “the dwelling of the Lord.” Thus the words come to be spoken in the days of Jeroboam, king of Israel, when, from inward discernment—as though from the judgment of the people—contemplative perceptions emerge. He is called the son of Joash because whatever good subtlety is born within us arises from the divine dwelling in our hearts. He is king of Israel because he is the particular guide and stimulus of our direction toward God.

The words are seen two years before the earthquake when, before we advance in the virtues or attain the goal of perfection, those two things—when they have wholly taken possession of our soul—shake our earth, that is, our flesh, from its own weight, so that they make it rejoice with its heart in the living God. For in the very beginning of our renewal, when the tumult of vices has been lulled for a while, the mind’s gaze is sharpened for the examination of itself.

#### Verse 2

“And he said: ‘The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice.’”

The Lord roars from Zion when, at the very beginning of our conversion, after we have begun to measure and, as it were, observe our condition, we roar from the groaning of our heart while considering ourselves. The Lord gives his voice from Jerusalem when, through perseverance in the experience of inward sorrow, as though having obtained a vision of peace, nothing bestial or savage—which the roar signifies—is now felt, but everything human and serene, which the voice expresses.

God roars within us when, through the repentance infused into our heart, he introduces the causes of our roaring.

“And the beautiful places of the shepherds mourn, and the summit of Carmel is dried up.”

The beautiful places of the shepherds mourn when, through hearing the divine voice of sacred Scripture—than which nothing is more beautiful for inward nourishment—the occasions of mourning are disclosed to us. For unless God has first sounded in the mind, there will be no fruit for those who read the sacred page.

The summit of Carmel is dried up when the inward stiffness of softness, by which it had once swelled against God while languishing amid vices, is hardened by the spirit’s rebellion, now undertaken against its own flesh. For Carmel is interpreted as “soft.”

#### Verse 3

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn it back, because they threshed Gilead with iron wagons.’”

Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood” or “the eye of blood.” By “the eye of blood” is signified an intention inclined toward sin; it drinks blood when it gorges itself on the desire for sin.

Damascus has three crimes when, after suggestion, it submits to pleasure and consent. But for four crimes it is not turned back, because it is exceedingly difficult to return to the freedom of the will after one has advanced into the execution of a sinful deed. For when someone has fallen by the will, he is now dragged by necessity into habit.

Gilead is interpreted as “a heap of testimony.” It threshed Gilead with iron wagons when, through the malicious revolutions of its thoughts, it destroys and tramples within itself the testimony of a good conscience—which, according to the Apostle, ought to have been its glory (2 Cor. 1:12). Iron is customarily used to signify malice.

#### Verse 4

“And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the houses of Ben-hadad.”

Hazael is interpreted as “seen by God,” and Ben-hadad as “a willing son.” Fire is sent into the house of Hazael when reason itself, which once seemed marked by the vision of God, is permitted to seethe with the desires of vices. The houses of Ben-hadad are devoured when the habits of carnal affections—which are created like sons from a corrupted reason and which voluntarily, as though naturally, are carried toward evils—are swallowed up in those same desires.

#### Verse 5

“And I will break the bar of Damascus, and destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol, and the one who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure.”

The bar of Damascus is broken when, once God has been made propitious, the obstacles of the mind are dissolved through admitted repentance. The inhabitants of the plain of the idol are destroyed when the license of the mind—which wandered here and there through the appetites of crimes and seemed to serve every familiar vice as though it were an idol—is cut away from this unlawful dwelling.

The one who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure is destroyed when the principality of the intention, whose supreme purpose was to subject the conscience to pleasure and make it, as it were, a tenant of pleasure, is entirely removed.

“And the people of Syria will be transferred to Cyrene, says the Lord.”

Syria is interpreted as “the exalted”; Cyrene signifies “an heir.” Thus the people of Syria are transferred to Cyrene when the arrogance of common movements within the soul is brought back to seek the rights of an eternal inheritance.

#### Verses 6–8

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn her back, because she carried away a complete captivity, to enclose it in Edom.’”

Gaza is interpreted as “her strength.” If Damascus, through “the eye of blood,” signifies a perverse intention, Gaza, through its strength, undoubtedly signifies that same intention when hardened in the opposite direction.

God turns back for three crimes—that is, transgressions of understanding, memory, and use—because he is more quickly propitiated by inward things, and by those that are not carried through into the display of action, than by those that are led toward the corruption of others through example. But for four crimes he is not turned back, because once that inner trinity which we mentioned—reason, will, and affection—has advanced to bodily exercise, which is administered by the four elements, there will be no easy return to the condition of integrity.

“For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34), and from experience of its former poisonous sweetness he cannot be forgetful. For we report things touched and sensed in one way, and things conceived in thought in another.

“I will not turn her back because she carried away a complete captivity”—that is, whatever virtue, whatever profession of goodness, remained in the soul, she has transferred into the devil’s and vices’ servitude. And she has done this “to enclose it in Edom,” that is, to restrain the soul without any reconsideration by the spirit under an earthly way of conduct; for Edom is interpreted as “earthly.”

“And I will send fire into the wall of Gaza, and it will devour its houses. And I will destroy the inhabitant from Ashdod and the one who holds the scepter from Ashkelon.”

Fire is sent into the wall of Gaza when desire is permitted to be introduced into the outward restraint adopted, under the pretext of secular propriety, to conceal perverse strength. It devours its houses when it overturns and devastates whatever is beautiful and seemly in that outward manner of life.

God destroys the inhabitant of Ashdod when whatever can rationally dominate foolish movements through the inward power of the mind is miserably disturbed and destroyed, so as to suppress the fire of temptation. He also destroys the one who holds the scepter from Ashkelon when, by his just judgment, he extinguishes the spark of good will that is recognized, according to the custom of that region, as restraining the flame of infamous desire. Ashdod is interpreted as “burning,” and Ashkelon as “infamous fire.”

“And I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines will perish.”

God turns his hand against Ekron when he does not turn away from our minds the inward consolation that is the highly useful instruction of sorrow. For Ekron is interpreted as “instruction of sorrow.” The remnant of the Philistines perishes when the small earthly thoughts accustomed to intoxicating the mind with the drink of pleasure are blotted out and fall away.

#### Verse 9

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they enclosed a complete captivity in Edom and did not remember the covenant of brothers.’”

Tyre is interpreted as “anguish.” And what greater anguish is there than that of which it is said: “He will rescue you from the narrow mouth into broad spaces” (Job 36:16); and David says: “Let not the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16).

Thus three crimes of Tyre in the mind, and four in bodily action, do not allow it to be turned back—namely, crimes that enclose it without any breathing-space of confession within the abyss of its own sins. Gaza earlier carried away captivity “to enclose it”; Tyre has enclosed it, because through the growth of wickedness what the former disposition of the soul proposed, this one completed with a hardened face.

They do not remember the covenant of brothers because carnal reason and appetite, arising from the same mind like a brotherhood of blood, do not consider what they owe one another in mutual watchfulness and obedience.

#### Verse 10

“And I will send fire into the wall of Tyre, and it will devour its houses.”

This means: I will permit every outward caution by which it provides for its respectability to be openly devoted to shameful desires. Thus I will plainly subject the whole circumference of its sensual faculties to destruction.

#### Verse 11

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated his mercy, prolonged his fury, and preserved his indignation to the end.’”

Edom is interpreted as “earthly.” After the mind has been inwardly constricted by the love of God, it must immediately be dispersed through earthly desires.

Thus for three crimes and for four—which can sufficiently be explained in the twofold manner given above—it is not turned back, because once pleasure has been imbibed inwardly and then passes into bodily use, the more customary it becomes, the more tenaciously it binds.

Edom, therefore, the earthly affection, pursues his brother with the sword when it attempts to cut off the spirit arising from the same conscience through deadly evils. It violates his mercy when, by continually infecting and disturbing what ought to have been pleasing to God as mercy shown to one’s own soul (Sir. 30:24), it corrupts it.

It prolongs its fury when it burns to fulfill whatever it desires—not through the enticement of ticklings, which is natural, but through the furies of perpetration, which is diabolical. It preserves its indignation to the end when it sins not through ignorance or weakness, but turns away its ear so as not to hear the law of God (Prov. 28:9).

#### Verse 12

“I will send fire into Teman, and it will devour the houses of Bozrah.”

Teman is interpreted as “the south wind”; Bozrah signifies “tribulation.” Fire is sent into the south wind, which is a warm wind, when a relaxed and vapid mind is nourished by the severity of temptation. The houses of Bozrah are devoured when the immoderation of the outward senses is hemmed in by insatiable snares of evils.

To this Job’s saying corresponds: “Consider the paths of Teman, the roads of Sheba, and wait a little” (Job 6:19). And “when the house has been swept with brooms, the sevenfold spirit enters the vacant house” (Luke 11:26).

#### Verse 13

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their border.’”

Ammon is interpreted as “a people of sorrow.” If discipline in the present is sorrow that produces a most peaceful fruit (Heb. 12:11), and if it is said of married people that “such persons will have tribulation” (1 Cor. 7:28), what do you think occurs among those who serve disgraceful deeds, under whose tongue, according to the Psalm, are labor and pain? (Ps. 10:7.)

They have these reasons for not being turned back: namely, that they rip open the pregnant women of Gilead—that is, they cut apart with the sword of a wicked eruption the rational movements that naturally conceive certain good things, as usually happens, in order to enlarge the territory of their wickedness.

Gilead is interpreted as “a heap of testimony.” It is nothing other than a certain accumulation of good thought, whose being brought to effect is witnessed before God by the mind. But the one who burns toward the fulfillment of a perverse purpose enlarges the border.

#### Verse 14

“And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbath [or: Rabba], and it will devour its houses amid wailing on the day of battle and amid a whirlwind on the day of commotion.”

Rabbath is interpreted as “multitude.” Fire is kindled in its wall when, amid the multitude and tumult of wicked thought, a conflagration is stirred up—whether of pride, empty glory, lust, or greed—all of which are called fire—in that which makes a miserable obstacle between us and God as though it were a wall.

Its houses are devoured amid wailing when its members, which are upon the earth, are engulfed by an immense appetite. For to howl is wolf-like. The day of battle is the evident conflict between flesh and soul. A whirlwind follows it, because blindness is created in the mind by the excess of temptation. The day of commotion is added when the mind is recognized as having been manifestly shaken from its stability through the indications of its deeds.

#### Verse 15

“And Melchon will go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord.”

Melchon is interpreted as “your king.” It is as though he said: Not only is the spirit—which ought to have ruled you—now banished into the service of sin, but with it also are its princes, that is, the sensual faculties that once pursued you freely.

### Chapter II

#### Verse 1

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes.’”

It should be noted that the phrase “Thus says the Lord” is frequently repeated solely to indicate that whatever we examine by reason, we conceive as though God were speaking to us.

Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” and also as “lawless.” For one who is born from the devil as father—I cannot know by what law he is bound—does not turn back because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes.

This means that he brought to utter destruction the reasons—which I express in the plural, not because there is more than one reason, but because of the multiplicity of causes whose office is to restrain carnal movements, just as bones support flesh—after the commission of sin. Ash remains as though the sole memory of fire that has been exhausted. Therefore he burns the bones to ashes who, after demolishing the powers of the soul that consolidate carnality, leaves behind, once the fire of desire has been spent, a residue of satiety for late repentance.

#### Verse 2

“And I will send fire into Moab, and it will devour the houses of Kerioth, and Moab will die amid the sound, amid the blast of the trumpet.”

He sends fire into Moab when he permits greater heats of incitement to arise from those born of the devil and, so to speak, from laws of their own.

Kerioth is interpreted as “the meeting of fire.” Fire therefore meets the houses that are to be devoured when an occasion of desired appearances approaches to inflame the senses with a more powerful desire.

He dies amid the sound of Moab when, under the disgrace of a filthy way of life, he is proclaimed far and wide as shameless and insensitive. He also dies amid the blast of the trumpet when others are terrified both by the example of such great abomination and by the dreadful cry.

#### Verse 3

“And I will destroy the judge from his midst, and I will kill all his princes with him.”

The judge is destroyed from his midst when reason—which ought to incline neither to the right nor to the left—is deprived of the judicial throne of discernment. What was signified above by Melchon is represented here by the judge; the princes likewise are understood in the same way.

#### Verse 4

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments.’”

Judah is interpreted as “confession.” Judah is not turned back because he rejected the law of the Lord, since confession is annulled in the one who does not at all seek to remember the divine law. For how can he confess to the one whose commandments he detests, the one to whom confession is owed?

“For their idols deceived them, after which their fathers went.”

Their idols deceive them when the imaginings either of their own crimes or of those of others obstruct them. Their fathers went after these things when either the authorities of reason, or those whom they profess to imitate, were deceived by these same things.

#### Verse 5

“And I will send fire into Judah, and it will devour the houses of Jerusalem.”

Fire is sent into Judah when someone does not confess out of sorrow for sin, but does not hesitate to publicize what he has secretly committed in order to incite another’s wickedness.

Hence it is said to a certain person through Ezekiel: “You displayed your fornications to every passerby, so that you might become his” (Ezek. 16:15). The houses of Jerusalem are consequently devoured when whatever could remain established in the mind or in the senses is severed from the vision of inward peace.

#### Verse 6

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals.’”

Israel is not turned back because he sold the righteous for silver, because the one who ought to be directed with God is all the more reluctant to return to God after his fall, the less he loves the righteous—that is, righteousness—in comparison with silver, that is, knowledge or eloquence.

He also gives away the poor for sandals when the spirit exchanges humility for dead works.

#### Verse 7

“They crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble.”

The heads of the poor are the intentions of the soul’s movements, which simply measure their poverty before God. They crush these heads upon the dust of the earth when they subject the principal dispositions of the inward person to earthly triviality.

They turn aside the way of the humble when, through worldly diversion, they corrupt the intention once assigned to humility.

Let the diligent reader note that in these eight sentences, corresponding to the eight provinces, something may figurally be understood according to the number of the eight capital vices.

“And father and son went to the girl, to profane my holy name.”

The father and son are reason and affection, because there is the greatest regard for the subordination of the lower to the primacy of the higher. They go to the girl when they descend without any discernment into the softness of inward weakness. From this they profane God’s holy name when, so far as lies in them, they diminish the reputation of complete holiness.

#### Verse 8

“And upon garments taken in pledge they reclined beside every altar, and they drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their God.”

Garments taken in pledge are garments handed over as security for a debt. Upon these, therefore, they recline beside every altar when they take the works of sin, entrusted to us as a pledge of forgiveness through confession, and—by reclining beside the purpose that is the altar of complete repentance—apply them to themselves, that is, lay them beneath themselves for perverse imitation.

They drink the wine of the condemned in the house of their God when, in their own conscience—which ought to have been the house of God—they greedily and indecently seize as an example the pleasures of those whom they know to have been condemned for those same pleasures.

#### Verse 9

“But I destroyed the Amorite from before them; his height was like the height of cedars, and he himself was strong like an oak.”

The Amorite is interpreted as “the embittering one,” as though he said: They make themselves hostile to me through so many offenses; but they ought to have remembered how, at the beginning of their conversion, I destroyed for certain people the proud arrogance that embittered God—namely, in the hearts of those who rejoiced in their own contemplation as though in cedar-like height, and boasted of the invulnerability of their flesh as though of the imperishability of that same tree, while, when adversities arose, they thought themselves steadfast like the strength of oak.

“I crushed his fruit above and his root below.”

The fruit of the Amorite is crushed above when worldly prosperity is annulled by advancing misfortunes. His roots are worn away below when even hopes of future gain are now utterly buried.

#### Verse 10

“I am the one who made you come up from the land of Egypt and led you through the desert for forty years, so that you might possess the land of the Amorite.”

This means: I raised you from the sorrow and present distress of the world—which is called Egypt—and led you out, through the Ten Commandments of the Law and the teachings of the four Gospels, into the singularity of the desert from vices. Thus I formed within you years restored by virtue, as though by the brightness of days, so that you might transfer the land that persisted in pride, embittering God by its rebellious movements—that is, your body, which had been rebellious up to that point—into the rights of intellectual understanding.

#### Verse 11

“And I raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men.”

Prophets are raised up from sons when, from inward movements—which are the offspring of reason—perceptions of sharper understanding are brought forth. Nazirites are made from young men when manly dispositions of soul extend themselves toward the purity of holiness.

For Nazareth signifies “flower,” or “purity,” or “holy.”

“Is it not so, sons of Israel, says the Lord?”

It is as though he said: Have you not once experienced such a condition in your minds, when you were intent that your spirit should be directed with God?

#### Verse 12

“And you gave the Nazirites wine to drink, and you commanded the prophets: ‘Do not prophesy.’”

This means: You had no perseverance in these conditions. Rather, to those movements in which the desired purity was earthly pleasure, you brought wine so that they might be made foolish; and you wickedly closed within yourselves the eyes of providence, so that they would not look toward eternal things.

#### Verse 13

“Behold, I will creak over you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay.”

He says: Now, impatient with your apostasy and, as it were, harshly intent upon punishing your wickedness, I will display against you—or rather, openly—the clamor of retribution, so that it may become clear to all how reluctantly I bear the multitude of your frivolities, like heaps of hay.

#### Verse 14

“And flight will perish from the swift, and the strong will not retain his strength.”

Flight perishes from the swift when one swift in understanding does not at all escape the dullness of a rejected sense. The strong does not retain his strength when, trusting in his own invulnerability, he cannot contain himself even for a moment as soon as adversity strikes.

#### Verse 15

“And the robust man will not save his life, and the one holding the bow will not stand.”

The robust man does not save his life when the one who had grown hard against the softness of sin through prolonged celibacy, once attacked, in no way restrains his own animal nature.

The one who holds the bow does not stand because, in temptation, the person who rashly claims for himself knowledge of the divine law quickly falls.

“And the swift will not be saved by his feet, and the rider of a horse will not save his life.”

The swift is not saved by his feet when, surpassing many in cleverness and cunning, he achieves nothing by appearing to hurry forward—for it is recognized as belonging neither to the one who wills nor to the one who runs, but to God who shows mercy (Rom. 9:16).

The rider of a horse does not save his life when the one who strives to dominate the movements of his animal nature solely for the sake of worldly respectability does not restrain the levity of his soul, which in the Gospel we are commanded to hate: “his life” (John 12:25).

#### Verse 16

“And the strong-hearted man among the mighty will flee naked on that day.”

It is as though he said: Whatever superior good arts a person may possess without God is esteemed as nothing and has no force. But the one who has assumed strength of heart not among the glories of the world, but among strong states of soul, flees naked on that day—that is, in that manifest crisis in which God in the present both casts down and raises up the lives of people—when, conscious of his humility, he hides himself from God’s judgment.

### Chapter III

#### Verse 1

“Hear the word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, sons of Israel, concerning the whole family that he brought up from the land of Egypt.”

It means: You, whose spirit ought to be directed with God, weigh the word of inward rationality on the intellectual balance, because this word stands over you—that is, unless it is heard and thoroughly absorbed in its full savor, it presses upon you and burdens you—so that the whole family of inward good arts, which I once brought out from worldly earthliness, may strive to persevere in the same resolve.

#### Verse 2

“‘You alone,’ he says, ‘I have known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you.’”

Because, he says, I approved you, movements of reason, above all the movements of animality, which savor only the earth—this is what it means for God to know—therefore do not be surprised if I visit you in your iniquities, since it is mine to rebuke those whom I have loved (Heb. 12:6).

#### Verse 3

“Will two walk together unless they have agreed?”

Two walk together when the spirit of God and human reason dwell together in agreement. This does not happen unless they agree—that is, unless, by clinging to one another, they become, according to the Apostle, one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). They are said to walk because each makes progress through the other.

#### Verse 4

“Will the lion roar in the forest unless he has prey?”

The lion does not roar in the forest unless he has prey, because the devil does not emit the roar of any temptation in the heart that has already abandoned the love of the world unless he finds an occasion of human sluggishness to lie in wait for. Thus he may also prevail in disturbing that agreement between God and humanity.

“Will the lion’s cub give a voice from its den unless it has seized something?”

It is as though he said: It is not surprising if the devil, being a spirit, hunts for the causes of temptation in us, since even a lion’s cub—that is, any son of the devil—does not dare to produce from the den of the heart, in which it is nurtured under the devil as its author, the voice of insinuation by which it attempts to draw someone away from the right path, unless it has first estimated through conjectures where it might deceive someone.

#### Verse 5

“Will a bird fall into a snare on the earth without a bird-catcher?”

A bird does not fall into an earthly snare without a bird-catcher, because the mind, lifted up on the wings of the virtues, is in no way entangled in earthly affections unless the impulse of some wicked suggestion has preceded it in the manner of a bird-catcher.

“Will the snare be taken away from the earth before it has caught something?”

The snare is not removed from the earth before it catches something, because the occasion of temptation does not cease in our body until something substantial belonging to true spirituality is set against the devil’s counsel.

The snare catches something when, amid the vanities it introduces, the state of eternal truth always returns to the mind. For the snare is sins, and sins are nothing; hence good things are, as it were, a substance. Thus it is said: “Without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

#### Verse 6

“If the trumpet sounds in the city, will the people not be afraid?”

The trumpet sounds in the city when the authority of divine truth proceeds in the mind. The people are afraid of it because the insolence of their thoughts flees from its knowledge.

“If there is evil in the city that the Lord did not make [or: will not make].”

Evil occurs in the city when the immoderation of temptation operates in a person. God makes this evil when he permits it to occur, whether for testing or for a fall, according to his dispensation.

#### Verse 7

“For the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets.”

The sense is therefore this: God makes evil, but the divine purpose generally does not remain hidden from the patient soul. For nothing of this kind occurs as a word in the conscience—that is, nothing is brought into effect—whose cause he himself does not reveal to our foresight. In this they prophesy: they deliberate to serve him according to his providence.

#### Verse 8

“The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?”

This means: Since the devil possesses such subtlety and such spiritual power, when he himself roars with excessive greed, who, hindered by human flesh, will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken through his Apostle: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Who will not apply foresight to this?

#### Verse 9

“Make it heard in the houses of Ashdod and in the houses of the land of Egypt.”

Ashdod is interpreted as “burning.” Under prophetic speech our understanding is admonished to make heard, in the houses of Ashdod—that is, in our bodily members, which are burned by continual desires—and in all the corners of the conscience, which are continually darkened according to the name of Egypt by distresses, the intelligible meaning of what follows:

“Gather yourselves,” he says, “upon the mountains of Samaria, and see the many insanities in its midst, and those suffering calumny in its inner chambers.”

They are commanded to gather upon the mountains of Samaria when they are warned that they ought to rise above the proud conceptions of outward restraint, which is called hypocrisy, through the height of contemplation. For Samaria is interpreted as “custody.” Thus they are to see many insanities in its midst: they are to weigh, in intimate discernment, that they intend one thing inwardly while wishing to appear to desire another outwardly.

And they are to see that the thoughts themselves bring calumny upon one another, when they consider that they think worldly things and do divine things, each contrary to the other.

#### Verse 10

“And they did not know how to do what is right, says the Lord, storing up iniquity and acts of plunder in their houses.”

They do not know how to do what is right because they disdain to do, in accordance with what they understand, the righteousness that they perceive through however little reason they possess. It is customary in Scripture for “not to know” to be used for “to disdain”; ordinary speech likewise says that a good man “does not know how to lie.”

They store up iniquity and acts of plunder in their houses: namely, they store up as something precious the iniquity of hypocrisy—because they do good while intending evil—and the plunder of another’s praise.

“Its midst,” “its inner chambers,” or “its houses” signify the conscience.

#### Verse 11

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: ‘The land will be afflicted and surrounded; your strength will be dragged away, and your houses will be plundered.’”

This means that, according to the judgment of reason itself, the earth of their bodies may be surrounded by many tribulations—abstinence, vigils, and the other hardships with which hypocrites customarily afflict themselves. But the inward strength directed toward outward approval does not cease to be dragged away, and the love of praise plunders whatever is contained in the houses of their minds.

#### Verse 12

“Thus says the Lord: ‘As a shepherd rescues from the mouth of a lion two legs or the tip of an ear, so will the sons of Israel who dwell in Samaria be rescued, and those in the region of the bed and on the couch of Damascus [or: on the couch of Damascus].’”

The shepherd rescues two legs from the mouth of the lion when God, the shepherd within, extracts from the devil’s mouth the extremities of the pleasures that hypocrites had possessed in their desire for praise. For when what they desire is not available to them, they often return at last to the line of right intention.

The tip of an ear is some portion, however small, of sounder understanding. Thus the sons of Israel who dwell in Samaria are rescued when either the fruit of their own ambition is taken away from them, or some seed of divine eloquence is left behind, like a spark by which they may grow warm.

The sons of Israel are movements directed toward God. Samaria is outward custody, with the inward custody rejected. They are rescued in the region—that is, in the region of the bed—where their mind thought it would find more powerful nourishment for sin.

The region of the bed is therefore a byway in the mind that aims at human praise, as though it were a place of rest. Damascus is interpreted as “the eye of blood.” It is treated as a couch when the perverse intention sometimes seems to soothe the wretched even by a false hope.

#### Verses 13–14

“Hear and testify in the house of Jacob, says the Lord God of hosts, because on the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel, I will visit him and the altars of Bethel; the horns of the altar will be cut off and fall to the ground.”

The prophetic word therefore admonishes them to hear—that is, to understand—and, instructed by what they hear, not to neglect bearing witness to others. The Lord of hosts says this, as though he said: There will be no lack of power to avenge the crime.

“For,” he says, “on the day”—that is, in manifest vengeance—“when I begin to open the cosmetic disguise of their hypocrisy, I will visit the altars of Bethel,” which is called “the house of God,” that is, the purposes of those who strive to be believed by the common people to be temples of God. I will visit them—that is, I will judicially press upon them more frequently—so that the horns of the altar may be cut off, namely, the proud heights of concealed wickedness, and may fall to the earth, that is, may be exposed to complete contempt.

For the altar of the hypocrite is whatever in his pursuit is outwardly impressive.

### Verse 15

“And I will strike the winter house together with the summer house, and the ivory houses shall perish, and the many buildings shall be destroyed, says the Lord.”

The winter house is the conscience, which is accessible to the torpor of every greed and wickedness. The summer house is the outward appearance of works that seem good, as though overflowing with a certain spiritual grace. The ivory houses perish when those who display the appearance of holiness and the whiteness of celibacy pass over into open disgrace. The many buildings are destroyed when the many externally contrived images of an affected composure are demolished.

## Chapter IV

### Verse 1

“Hear this word, you fat cows who are on the mountains of Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your lords, ‘Bring, and we shall drink.’”

The fat cows are wanton and proud hypocrites. They are on the mountains of Samaria because they swell with pride over the external observance of restraint; for this is expressed by the name “Samaria.” They oppress the needy because whatever they do for glory they do against the protests of their sounder understanding—and therefore against one who is truly needy. They crush the poor when they bury within themselves thoughts that sometimes counsel humility. They say to their lords, “Bring, and we shall drink,” when they demand the favor of those whose approval they desire to serve through good works, and on whose approval they depend as though they were drinking it down. These fat cows are warned to hear this word so that they may carefully weigh what is threatened against them.

### Verses 2–3

“The Lord God has sworn by his holiness: Behold, days are coming upon you, and they shall lift you up on poles, and your remnants in boiling pots. And you shall go out through the breaches, one opposite another, and you shall be cast into Armon, says the Lord.”

The Lord swears by his holiness when, in his true holiness, he summons the hypocrites’ pretended appearance before open judgment, so that the truth of their lives may be revealed. Days come upon them when the disclosures of their hidden depravity confront them. They are lifted up on poles when they are carried in the unstable condition of pride. For whoever sits upon a pole never rests securely. Their remnants are lifted up in boiling pots when all their sensuality, glowing with desire, is made public through the pursuit of a shameful deed. “Remnants” are customarily used for works, since they remain above thought, as it is written: “The remnants of thought shall keep festival for you” (Ps. 75:11).

Note that the text now passes into the feminine gender, in order to show them unmanned and weakened from the vigor of justice. They go out through the breaches, one opposite another, when, as the pots of their wanton senses crack and collapse, their vices expose one another and they rush into disgrace. One goes out opposite another when one exposes his own shamefulness for the other to see. They are also cast into Armon when, taking boldness from their crime, they exalt themselves on account of their own disgraceful acts; yet, according to the Psalm, they are to be cast down into the depths of a reprobate mind while they are exalted (Ps. 72:18). For “Armon” means “height” or “exaltation.”

### Verse 4

“Come to Bethel and act impiously; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression.”

They are ironically urged to come to Bethel, so that they may display themselves to the eyes of the people as temples of God. “Act impiously,” he says—that is, in this very celebration of your name, know yourselves to be doing nothing other than denying God, who is truth. Gilgal means “a place of rolling.” They come to the place of rolling and multiply their transgressions, because by a just judgment it happens to those who voluntarily fall that they do not remain in their miseries (Ps. 139:11).

### Verse 5

“And offer your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes after three days. And sanctify praise from what is leavened; and call for voluntary offerings, and proclaim them.”

They offer sacrifices in the morning when, as the dawn of favor breaks forth, they strive to slaughter their own bodies more and more. They offer tithes after three days when they assert that they live lawfully, not for human praise but solely out of love for the Trinity. They sanctify praise from what is leavened because in every exercise they mingle depravity into their intention. They call for voluntary offerings when they loudly proclaim that they undertake this labor not to blot out their own evils—which they wish to be considered nonexistent—but solely out of love for God and virtue:

> “The good hate sin for love of virtue.”  
> *(Horace, Book I of the Epistles, Epistle 16, line 52.)*

They proclaim them when they celebrate their hidden deeds. For thus you wished it, children of Israel: thus it pleased you to act according to your own desire.

### Verse 6

“Therefore I also gave you dullness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

Therefore God gives them dullness of teeth in all their cities when, in all the inward states of their minds, he produces a dullness of understanding. With these teeth we grind every roughness, as it were. The lack of bread in all our places exists when the nourishment of divine consolation, by which our hearts are strengthened, is absent from all our spiritual movements. For whatever is rational is the place of one’s own soul.

### Verse 7

“I also withheld rain from you when there were still three months until the harvest; and I rained upon one city, but upon another I did not rain.”

It is as though he said: Because after my correction they dissimulated and refused to return to me, I also withheld rain from you—that is, the temperate influence of heavenly inspiration. And I did this while there were still three months until the harvest, when their hearts were still distant from every expectation of good hope—in its beginning, progress, and perfection—that is, before they proposed anything good under God’s prompting. Such things are sometimes beneficially and providentially withdrawn from the saints, though they are not entirely abandoned.

He rains upon one city when he fully drenches the reason so that it may see what must be done. But he does not rain upon another when he leaves a corrupt affection in the hardness of obstinacy. Hence, in the office of the Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany, prayer is offered that they may see what must be done and grow strong to do what they have seen.

“One part was thoroughly watered, and the part upon which I did not rain withered.” One part is thoroughly watered when benevolence is attributed to reason; the other part, which was not watered, withers when, according to the Apostle, it was not granted to the affective faculty to accomplish the good (Rom. 7:18).

### Verse 8

“Two and three cities came to one city to drink water, but they were not satisfied; and you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

Two and three cities come to one city to drink water when either the affection or the will—or, when the three are formed, reason joined to the understanding, whose proper function is to perceive divine things—take refuge there so that they may drink together the drops of saving wisdom. But they are not satisfied because they are not brought to any abundance of efficacy that might cool their burning thirst.

### Verse 9

“I struck you with scorching wind and with blight, the multitude of your gardens and your vineyards.”

It is as though he said: Because even then you did not return to me, I struck you with scorching wind—that is, with desire burning beyond measure—which not only dries the inward parts by its own spirit but also darkens the outward parts. The multitude of gardens and vineyards is struck with blight when the abundance of original and actual goods, and also that understanding with which we are inebriated by God, is changed into the pallor of hypocrisy. For this is the nature of blight: in human beings and in herbs it changes into a whitish color.

“Your olive groves and your fig trees the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

By the olive groves, whose fruit is healthful and light-giving, the disposition of mercy toward us is signified. By the fig trees, whose sap is milky, is signified the piety by which one’s neighbor is nourished with affection. “Have pity on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24). For unless we first have mercy on ourselves, we do not condescend to our neighbor.

The locust is a bristly and troublesome creature. Hypocrisy, however, which is said to consume these things, does not abandon the person whom it once infects. As many hairs as the locust has, so many movements toward the inflation of empty glory does hypocrisy have—perverse movements that swell the soul.

### Verse 10

“I sent death among you on the way of Egypt; I struck your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses; and I caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

God sends death against them on the way of Egypt when, in a worldly intention—at whose entrance death has been placed—he permits the light of our knowledge to be darkened. He strikes our young men there even to the captivity of the horses when he allows whatever pious vitality is established in the soul to perish, from whatever source, even to the point of incontinence by which the bodies are taken captive. Horses and beasts are bodies, as it is written: “He shut up their beasts in death” (Ps. 77:50).

He causes the stench of their camps to rise into their nostrils when he permits the foul odor and evil reputation of the bodily vices they have committed to overflow into their own shameful embarrassment. It is obvious that “camps” may stand for bodies: “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. 13:13).

### Verse 11

“I overthrew you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire.”

God overthrows them as he overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah when, through the rebellion of the people’s thoughts, he diminishes them inwardly by an enduring silence in which no revolt remains against vice. For “Sodom” means “a silent beast,” and “Gomorrah” means “the rebellion of a people.”

They become like a brand snatched from the fire when, scorched everywhere by the pyres of vices, they retain nothing within themselves of sap or generative seed. In a brand neither sap nor shoot remains. The person snatched from the fire is not voluntarily restrained from vices by himself, but is violently pulled away by another’s discipline. Nor does the one whose will does not provide him with the habit of doing good out of delight bear much fruit.

### Verses 12–13

“Therefore I will do this to you, Israel. And after I have done this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel. For behold, he forms the mountains, creates the wind, announces his word to humanity, makes the morning mist, and walks upon the heights of the earth; the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

It is as though he said: I will inflict upon you according to your merits what I have foretold. But after I have inflicted it, receive God, who comes to you through scourges, with a good disposition of soul. For behold—that is, you have at hand—the one who forms the great-hearted through an abundance of virtue, yet then knows how to cause the excellence he has granted to breathe out through the whirlwinds of temptations. Nevertheless, he does not alienate those whom he has struck; rather, in their need he supplies them with the word of inward consolation.

He indeed makes mist in the morning, so that our beginnings may be mingled with certain evils, because no one suddenly becomes perfect. For it is necessary that he walk upon the heights of the earth, that is, suppress that crude and tender excellence of our earthliness. “The Lord God of hosts is his name,” because he is powerful to avenge the transgressions of any crime.

## Chapter V

### Verse 1

“Hear this word that I raise over you as a lamentation, house of Israel.”

They are commanded to hear the word that God raises over them when they are warned to understand the intellectual order of the mind—namely, how God humbles the mind and by what consolations he lifts it up. This word is a lamentation for the house of Israel because those who wish to be directed to God do not know whether the temptation itself is ruin or salvation.

“The house of Israel has fallen; it shall not rise again.”  
*(Verse 2.)*

“The virgin of Israel has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up.”

The house of Israel falls when the one who ought to rule with God amid temptations is unable to stand. For Israel means “one who rules with God.” It does not rise again when, despairing through its own sluggishness, it never breathes again toward better things.

The virgin of Israel is cast upon her own land when the barrenness of their spirit is brought down under their own recklessness. There is no one to raise her up because the rational movement that could make such a conscience flourish again is extinguished.

### Verse 3

“For thus says the Lord: From the city from which a thousand went out, a hundred shall be left in it; and from the city from which a hundred went out, ten shall be left in it, in the house of Israel.”

A thousand go out from the city when the totality of pious devotion proceeds from a firm conscience. That fullness is reduced to a hundred when, with spiritual abundance removed, it is restricted to external—and, so to speak, publicly human—goods. For a hundred is a tenth of a thousand, and the human being is the tenth within rational creation.

A hundred are also reduced to ten when, after even the common and natural good has been cast aside, one is brought down to the pure dullness of sensuality. The number ten is found to suggest this because the number five itself is doubled in inward and outward sensuality. Hence, for the sake of his profit, dominion over ten cities is assigned to a certain person (Luke 19:17).

### Verses 4–5

“Seek me and you shall live. And do not seek Bethel, and do not enter Gilgal, and you shall not cross over to Beersheba, because Gilgal shall be led captive, and Bethel shall become useless.”

This means: If you, who ought to have considered it worthwhile to be directed toward God, were to seek me, you would undoubtedly perceive what is vital. But because you presumptuously desire to appear to hypocrites as the house of God, secretly entangle yourselves in the places of vice, and plunge yourselves with miserable greed into the seventh well, which is Beersheba—or the well of satiety, that is, the abyss of human appetite, composed of the outer four and the inner three—you should know without doubt that your hidden impurities will be brought into public view, and that the temple of God which you pretend to be will profit you in nothing.

### Verse 6

“Seek the Lord and live, lest perhaps he burn like fire the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be no one to extinguish Bethel.”

Joseph is interpreted as “increase.” Therefore the conscience whose entire intention serves the increase of outward reputation is burned when it is given over inwardly to desires. The house of God—which is Bethel, not true but imaginary—is devoured so that it no longer exists, because it is deprived of the fruit of its great reputation.

### Verses 7–8

“You who turn judgment into wormwood and abandon justice on the earth; who make Arcturus and Orion, who turn darkness into morning and change day into night.”

They turn judgment into wormwood who, by a perverse judgment, do not fear to twist the sweetness by which God’s goodness is tasted in advance into temporal glory, by which God is made bitter. For wormwood is whatever is sought through the fruitless punishment of bodies. They abandon justice on the earth when, remaining in earthly desires, they despise the true essence of justice itself, which is God.

This justice makes Arcturus and Orion when it creates and instructs in its subjects whatever of most illustrious holiness is found in their leaders. It is not unfitting to understand Arcturus as referring to leaders if you consider the Bear together with the wagon. It turns darkness into morning when it reduces the obscurity of consciences to the dawn of divine inspiration. But it changes day into night when it condemns the brightness of hypocrisy either by the present exposure of its own wickedness or by perpetual blindness in the future.

“He who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out over the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.”

He calls the waters of the sea who draws together and raises hearts that flow astray toward love of self, embittered by inward diseases and by insatiable desire. He pours them over the face of the earth when he extends their contemplation toward consideration of their former delinquency. “Earth” is used for the sinner, as in: “You are earth.” His name is “Lord,” because he can make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21).

### Verse 9

“He smiles upon devastation against the strong and brings desolation upon the mighty.”

He smiles upon devastation against the strong when he exposes to the laughter of all the one who arrogates to himself the glory of inward strength, declaring him infamous through public desolation. He brings desolation upon the mighty when, reducing to outward weakness and the impotence of vice the inner resources of virtue that they pretend to possess, he empties them.

### Verse 10

“They hated the one who reproves at the gate, and they abhorred the one who speaks with integrity.”

The one who reproves at the gate is the one who judicially convicts someone. For it is well known that judgments were customarily carried out at the gate in ancient times. Therefore they hate the one who reproves at the gate when they resent the person who speaks not rashly but truthfully. They abhor the one who speaks with integrity when, accustomed to the flatteries of others, they curse those who sincerely reprove their vices.

### Verse 11

“Therefore, because you plundered the poor and took away the chosen spoil from him, you shall build houses of squared stone but shall not dwell in them.”

He plunders the poor who drives someone away from a good intention and disperses him. He takes the chosen spoil from him who overturns by perverse discouragement whatever is more precious and excellent in a human being—namely, spiritual goods. They build houses of squared stone when they show their consciences rising up as though established by the authority of unimpaired virtues. But they do not dwell in them because, while God reveals their vices, they persist in their possession only in a very superficial manner.

### Verse 12

“You shall plant delightful vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine, because I know your many crimes and your mighty sins.”

They plant delightful vineyards when they propagate spiritual goods with wondrous eagerness and with the gratification of many who see them. But they do not drink their wine when they do not refresh themselves with any spiritual reward directed toward an outward recompense. He knows their many crimes—many more, of course, the more hidden they are; and the more hidden, the less corrigible.

Their sins are mighty because, being spiritual, they are no more exposed to correction than they are to shame. “Enemies of the righteous, receiving gifts and oppressing the poor at the gate.” They are enemies of the righteous—that is, of justice—because they receive a gift from the richer person and therefore oppress the poor at the gate, that is, in judgment.

### Verse 13

“Therefore the prudent person shall be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.”

The prudent person is commanded to be silent at that time because, figuratively, the musical instruments are hung upon the willows in the midst of Babylon (Ps. 136:2). It is an evil time—not the time that has not yet come for the Lord and his members, but the time that is always prepared for the reprobate (John 7:6).

### Verse 14

“Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said.”

It is as though he said: You attribute to yourselves that God dwells in you—something you have already heard expressed under the figure of Bethel—but this is false. Seek good rather than evil if you wish to live, and then God will truly not be absent from you.

### Verse 15

Therefore, hating evil and girding your loins, love good; holding lamps, establish the judgment of discernment at the gate—that is, at the entrance of thought—in the hope that God may perhaps have mercy on the remnants of Joseph.
