This means: perhaps he may deign to support some remnant of good intention in those who strive after worldly increase.

The use of “perhaps” is characteristic of Hebrew usage: uncertainty is put for certainty and certainty for uncertainty, as in: “Perhaps I would have humbled their enemies” (Ps. 80:15).

### Verses 16–17

“Therefore thus says the Lord: In all the streets there shall be lamentation, and in all that is outside it shall be said, ‘Alas, alas’; and they shall call the farmer to mourning, and those who know how to lament to lamentation. And in all the roads there shall be lamentation, because I shall pass through the midst of you, says the Lord.”

There is lamentation in all the streets when, in every dispersion of mind and action, no joy of heaven is sought, but in every matter only things worthy of mourning are handled. “Alas, alas” is said in all that is outside when misery is summoned—or repeated—not only in the enormous expansion of souls signified by the name “streets,” but also in every outward administration of souls and bodies.

The farmer is called to mourning when every preacher, recognized as one to whom the cultivation of minds is entrusted, is moved by dreadful compassion for the hardened. Those who know how to lament are called to lamentation when those in whom God has implanted pity shed compassionate tears over the destruction of others.

There is also lamentation in the roads—in all those, that is, who know how to instruct others by life-giving examples. God passes through their midst when he does not remain even for a little while in the heart of any one of them.

### Verse 18

“Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you desire it? The day of the Lord is darkness and not light.”

The one who desires the day of the Lord is deluded by empty favors and, hearing himself praised by the people in some fashion, believes himself to be what he is said to be. He desires his own woe and darkness when he looks not to his conscience but to fables.

### Verse 19

“As when a man flees from the face of a lion and a bear meets him, and he enters the house, leans his hand upon the wall, and a serpent bites him.”

A man flees from the face of a lion when many fear to undertake the arduous condition of life, fearing that they may provoke the devil against themselves, who would press them with the greater force of temptations. Thus, as though they were avoiding the devil, a bear meets them—namely, some carnal desire, slower than a lion but extremely powerful for subduing them.

Then, fearing this, he enters the house when, from outward diffusion, he gathers himself within the boundaries of his conscience. There he leans his hand upon the wall when he thinks that, by means of an obstacle—as though it were an invisible conscience—he can conceal the intention of his work. But there he is bitten by a serpent when, arranging himself for the eyes of human beings, he decides to act more negligently within before God. Thus, while he guards against each individual danger, he comes to perish through the venom of inward sluggishness.

All this applies to hypocrites. While they fear to provoke the devil by genuine devotion, they care little that, before human beings, under a concealed appearance, they are corrupted within the recesses of their minds. Hence it follows:

### Verse 20

“Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and not brightness in it?”

This means: You speak of the day of judgment as though it were your final destiny; but know that the day of the Lord is present, and that it does not shine upon you for salvation. Rather, through the imposition of a reprobate understanding, it grows dark within you.

### Verse 21

“I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not accept the odor of your assemblies.”

God hates and rejects their festivals when, by exposing their iniquities, he shows that he detests the empty works that hypocrites solemnize before the eyes of the people. He does not accept the odor of their assemblies when he indignantly excludes from himself, as though from the perception of the divine majesty, whatever benefits they appear publicly to accumulate.

### Verse 22

“Even if you offer me burnt offerings and your sacrifices, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the vows of your fattened animals.”

They bring burnt offerings to God when, in every appearance and through innumerable crosses—crosses that you would scarcely see the saints bear, or see them bear only with great difficulty—their bodies are afflicted. Do not be surprised that these things are said to be offered to God, even though they are not offered to God but to the people. You should know that many things in Scripture are presented not as they are in reality but as they are held in opinion.

Their gifts are not accepted, and the vows of their fattened animals are not regarded, because whatever is performed in God’s name, even at great expense, and whatever abundant generosity, like fatness, is bestowed upon one’s neighbor, is not regarded by God if it is done outside charity, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 13:3).

### Verse 23

“Take away from me the tumult of your songs; I will not hear the songs of your lyre.”

Whatever hypocrites produce by composing books to prolong their own memory is nothing but tumult in the ears of God, whose only fruit is momentary praise. Their lyre’s songs are not heard when their affected eloquence, which serves preaching, is rejected from the ear of God. In contrast, it is said to a certain chosen woman: “Let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet” (Song 2:14).

### Verse 24

“Judgment shall be revealed like water, and justice like a mighty stream.”

Judgment is revealed like water when the truth of their condition, unstable and superficially concealed as though covered only by a thin layer of water, is quickly stripped bare. Justice becomes like a mighty stream when, through God’s just examination, the entire image of this counterfeit holiness is swept away as though by a swift current.

### Verse 25

“Did you offer victims and sacrifice to me for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?”

The house of Israel does not offer victims and sacrifice in the wilderness for forty years when, although they abandon God and are abandoned by God, they appear to live evangelically and according to the law. They make neither the victim by which they might subdue the hostile devil nor the sacrifice by which they might willingly serve God, though they wish to appear to be directed toward God.

### Verses 26–27

“You carried the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. And I will cause you to migrate beyond Damascus.”

They carry the tabernacle of their Moloch when they do not fear to make their mind a shrine of lust, even though outwardly they wrap it in the appearance of a continent body, as though in the goodness of a tabernacle. Moloch himself, however, is Priapus.

They also carry the image of their idols and the star of their god, which they made for themselves, when they occupy the mind with an almost indelible devotion to vices. More particularly, they desire to be marked by a kind of star-like splendor of conceived pride, as though by a conspicuous celestial quality.

He causes them to migrate beyond Damascus when he permits them to carry the intention of their criminal will beyond the boundary into the execution of the deed—which is “beyond Damascus,” that is, “the eye of blood.” For the eye of blood is the intention of sin.

## Chapter VI

### Verse 1

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, nobles and chiefs of the peoples, who enter the house of Israel pompously!”

They are wealthy in Zion who perceive themselves as surpassing others in the fullness of divine contemplation; and they trust in the mountain of Samaria—that is, in the excellence of outward vigilance. Woe threatens them, namely, the judgment of eternal condemnation.

These are the nobles and chiefs of the peoples who think nothing about themselves except what is supreme and, always impatient of companionship, desire to be preferred to everyone both in position and in reputation. They enter the house of Israel pompously when they fill the mind—which ought to have been stretched out toward God—with affection for pomp alone.

### Verse 2

“Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to great Hamath; descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to the best of all these kingdoms: is their territory broader than your territory?”

They are commanded to cross over to Calneh and see so that they may measure, as far as possible, the condition of all other minds. Calneh means “all.” From there they are to go to great Hamath, as though they were to observe individually those who are undoubtedly magnificent in the perpetration of crimes. Hamath means “blood,” and blood is sin.

From there they descend to Gath of the Philistines when they come to consider those who are intoxicated by temporal desires and yet find pleasing nothing except what is extorted either by force, secretly, or by begging. Gath means “winepress”; the Philistines, or Philisthaeans, are “those who fall through drinking.”

The best of these kingdoms are the foremost purposes of each person’s life. They are therefore commanded to consider whether their territory is broader than that of the others—whether, that is, the arrogance and ferocity of the desire of those who openly commit crimes are as great as what is known to rage and expand in the minds of hypocrites. For the breadth is as great as the ambition of extending their reputation, which in these people is found to be much more vehement than in great Hamath or in Gath of the Philistines.

### Verse 3

“You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity.”

They are set apart for the evil day who, through their present moral divergence, are so distinguished from the good that, carried from here to the evil day, they will then be made still more completely separate from the company of the good. He draws near to the throne of iniquity who knowingly immerses and entangles himself now in the kingdom of the devil.

### Verse 4

“You who sleep on beds of ivory and indulge yourselves on your couches.”

He sleeps on beds of ivory who rests in a false security while living in the supposed safety of chastity. For the elephant, from which ivory comes, is an animal of cold nature. They indulge themselves on their couches who, under a reputation for restraint, propose to devote themselves all the more freely to wantonness and pleasure.

### Verse 5

“You who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd, who sing to the sound of the psaltery.”

He eats a lamb from the flock who strives to incorporate into himself, for imitation of his wickedness, other inexperienced people as well. He eats calves from the midst of the herd who takes into his sect any dull and wanton persons, removed from the conformity of those who know only how to perceive mature things.

They sing to the sound of the psaltery, but not in the psaltery, who perform good works but do not perform them for the sake of the intention of the good work. Throughout the Psalms, “to sing with the psaltery” is found to signify a good work.

“As David, they thought they had vessels of song.”

It is as though he said: What David instituted—indeed, what he carried out as a sign of holy action—these people attribute to themselves as a cause of boasting and pride.

### Verse 6

“Drinking wine from bowls and anointed with the finest ointment, they suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph.”

They drink wine from bowls when, from the fragile example of temporal things, they take for themselves the material of pleasure by which they become intoxicated into forgetfulness of God. They do this while anointed with the finest ointment—not with virtue itself, but adorned on the surface of the skin by the likeness of virtue.

They suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph when, striving after worldly increase, they are not at all saddened by the loss of spiritual advantage.

### Verse 7

“Therefore now they shall migrate at the head of those who migrate, and the company of those who indulge themselves shall be removed.”

They migrate at the head of those who migrate when, surpassing the other transgressors, they both transgress and sin. The company of those who indulge themselves is removed when the entire pretense of those who boast of their chastity while risking their modesty is stripped bare and exposed as the reality of their shameful condition.

### Verse 8

“The Lord has sworn by his own soul, says the Lord God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob, and I hate his houses, and I will deliver the city with its inhabitants.”

God swears by his own soul when at last, by breathing upon them, he calls such people back to the ordinance of his will. He detests the pride of Jacob when he shows that those who arrogantly claim to have overcome their own vices are worthy of detestation by themselves. He hates their houses when he shows that the chambers of their minds, in which they glorify themselves before themselves, deserve hatred.

Hence he delivers the city with its inhabitants when he compels the conscience itself, together with all its conduct, through confession to betray itself.

### Verses 9–10

“And if ten men should be left in one house, they too shall die. And their relative shall take them and burn them, in order to carry the bones out of the house.”

Ten men are left in one house when, in a single conscience, the two fives of sensuality remain—as though alone—after the evil deed has now ceased following confession. They too die when they are slain by their customary greed. Their relative takes them when reason, more closely related to them than anything else, lifts them away from their lowest appetite.

He also burns them when, in the heat of pious desire, he strives to examine them thoroughly. He does this in order to carry the bones out of the house—that is, to expel outwardly whatever inward hardness lies hidden through confession.

### Verse 11

“And he shall say to the one who is in the innermost rooms of the house, ‘Is anything still with you?’ And he shall answer, ‘The end has come.’ And he shall say to him, ‘Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord.’”

He speaks—without doubt, the relative, namely our spirit—to the one who is in the innermost rooms: the carnal affection implanted in the marrow of our being. He asks whether anything still remains with him—some remnant, that is, of the scruple of sin that inwardly gnaws at him.

That one answers, “The end has come,” because the fire of desires has been put to sleep. The other then tells him to be silent, namely, not to exalt himself in any way over such a small and perhaps momentary quiet of spirit. He forbids him to remember the name of the Lord. This means nothing other than that he must not in any way consign this very matter to forgetfulness. For we are said to remember what we have forgotten. Therefore, whoever, after sometimes forgetting him, finally recalls him, undoubtedly does not pray without interruption.

I certainly do not consider him to have remembered the name of the Lord who is read as having feared God as though he feared waves swelling over him.

### Verse 12

“For behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the greater house with ruins and the lesser house with fissures.”

The Lord commands when he mercifully inspires. He strikes the greater house with ruins when he shakes and overwhelms that more diffuse and spacious disposition of mind called carnal desire. He strikes the lesser house with fissures when he divides reason itself—because it is subtler and, by the nature of its inward discernment, somehow more elevated—against its own movements in continual conflict.

**Verse 13.**—“Can horses run upon the rocks, or can one plough there with oxen?” Horses do not run upon rocks when, after minds have become hardened by God against vices, wild and wanton impulses do not intrude upon them. One does not plough with oxen when a mind, through unrestrained movements and impatient of the yoke, is in no way touched by any overturning of devout thought.

**Verse 14.**—“For you have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood. You who rejoice in nothing, who say: ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?’” It is as though he said: At one time, when you were still following the manner of the world, you were turning the sweetness of your reason into the bitterness of worldly affairs; and what could thereby have arisen in you as the fruit of righteousness, you were accustomed to turn into wormwood—which Scripture elsewhere calls onions and garlic (Num. XI, 5)—rejoicing for a moment in this temporal existence, which can be called nothing, and boasting that you had taken for yourselves the horns of power by your own strength and intellectual acumen.

**Verse 15.**—“Behold, I shall raise up a nation against you, O house of Israel, says the Lord of hosts, and they shall crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of the wilderness.” God raises up a nation against the house of Israel when, with God willing to direct it, a new kind of thought is brought to life in the mind after having been conceived through repentance. Hamath, as I said above, is interpreted as “blood.” From the entrance of Hamath, therefore, to the torrent of the wilderness they are crushed—that is, from the first delight in sin until, through complete renunciation of the world, the secular wisdom within us is dried up by the swelling waters of divine love.

## Chapter VII

**Verse 1.**—“The Lord God showed me this: and behold, the maker of locusts at the beginning of the sprouting of the late rain; and behold, the late rain after the king’s shearer [or: shearing].” “The Lord God,” he says, “showed me what I am about to say.” “Behold,” he says, “the maker of locusts at the beginning of the sprouting of the late rain”—namely, God, the fashioner of temptation for our testing. For he dwells with us both in Sinai, which means “temptation,” and in the sanctuary, that is, in holiness, at the beginning of our formation, when we begin to be pierced by divine love. This is the late rain, at whose movement we burst forth into the bud of every virtue.

“Behold,” he says, “the maker of locusts.” It is as though he said: “You have approached the service of God; stand in justice and in fear” (Eccli. II, 2), because—behold!—that is, suddenly, although by God’s command, the biting force of an evil suggestion will leap upon you. A locust injures with its mouth, becomes numb in the cold, and is moved by warmth; so temptation, when admitted into the heart, consumes it, is checked by adversity, and is stirred by prosperity.

The king’s shearer was literally called a *brucus*, and it was called a shearer because it seemed to cut down the remains of the locusts right to the ground. It is called the king’s shearer because it was not permitted to do anything without the permission of the king of all. The *brucus*, then, is the shearer when the unceasing practice of any capital vice invisibly remains upon the mind in order to devastate it. [Col. 0439C] After this shearer, the late rain returns when, because sin has become exasperating—or rather pressing—the whole mind suddenly yields, as though to the final medicine of repentance. We know, moreover, the nature of the *brucus*: it does not move at all from the place on which it has settled until it has rendered it consumed.

**Verse 2.**—“And it came to pass, when he had finished eating the grass of the land, that I said: ‘Lord God, be merciful, I beseech you. Who shall raise up Jacob, because he is small?’” He finishes eating the grass of the land when temptation weakens the greenness [or vigor] of inward hope. Jacob is not raised up because he is small, since a raw mind, not yet recovering manfully from its old habit, is never lifted from its torpor unless it is supported by an influx of grace.

**Verse 3.**—This voice is the spirit complaining to God of its misery within itself. He therefore has mercy, intending afterward to show the mind another kind of fall.

**Verses 4, 5, 6.**—“And behold, the Lord God was calling judgment to the fire; and it devoured the great abyss and consumed part of it at the same time.” If we put the cause for the effect, we may understand “judgment” as “reason.” The Lord therefore calls judgment to the fire when he condemns the authority of reason to the flames of desire. He devours the great abyss when, by darkening, he annihilates precipitous dispositions and the extreme depth of a certain penetrating insight. He consumes part at the same time because, although the mind may still measure and grieve over its condition insofar as it is falling away, nevertheless, as though partly blind, it does not recognize where God’s permission is leading it or what outcomes the evil it has begun will have.

To restrain, therefore, the frenzy of impending death, our spirit, crying out its smallness, repeats its plea to God; and, with grace soon following, it dictates that what it had proposed must not be done. Hence it is necessary that he show us other things by which we may be instructed.

**Verses 7, 8.**—“And behold, the Lord was standing upon a plastered wall, and in his hand was a mason’s trowel. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A mason’s trowel.’” The Lord stands upon a plastered wall when, intending to bring assistance, he makes himself present upon the defenses of our mind, with which we prepare to resist the devil, giving us a sure test of our spirits. He calls it a plastered wall because God smooths it by removing the roughness of vice and fortifies and strengthens it against the rains of temptations. The mason’s trowel is in God’s hand because the effectiveness of our protection lies in his judgment.

Amos is interpreted as “the people who have been torn away.” For one is torn away whose thought is led from the love of the world by the intervening space of the fear of God. Amos, then, is asked to consider what he sees, and he answers that a mason’s trowel is seen, because by God’s workmanship the lime of divine warmth, joined to our earthliness, is shown to be constantly applied to our minds for their protection.

“And the Lord said: ‘Behold, I shall place the trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall not continue to plaster him further.’”

**Verse 9.**—“And the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste, and I shall rise up with the sword against the house of Jeroboam.” The Lord speaks when he suggests to the mind what it must answer to its own movements. It should be noted that “Behold” is placed before each vision, so that it may indicate the sudden arrival of temptations or of various dispositions upon the human mind.

God places the trowel in the midst of his people Israel when he openly sets before everyone the ministry of his support, by which he is prepared to assist all who are tempted. He will not continue to plaster him further when, judging in his own mind according to the person’s merit, he considers someone worthy of having God withdraw the obstacle of his assistance. For the cement by which a wall is fortified against the assault of a storm seems to signify this.

The high places of the idol are demolished when the distinctiveness of pride is brought low as the devil strikes us. For what is the high place of an idol except a certain spectacle of distinction? Hence we also call those “spectable” whom we admire because of their own reputation.

The sanctuaries of Israel are laid waste when the dense appearances of religions and the shadows of a great name are reduced through daily decline. One rises with the sword against the house of Jeroboam when one wages war against the conscience that aspires, through hypocrisy, only to temporal things, while vices ride alongside it. The sword signifies a grave sin. David asks to be delivered from the evil sword (Ps. CXLIII, 10).

**Verse 10.**—“And Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: ‘Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot bear his words.’” Amaziah is interpreted as “strong and cold”; Jeroboam as “temporal.” The priest of Bethel is strong and cold when someone, strong in action but cold in mind, hypocritically promises that he can offer sacred leadership—as though he were the temple of God. He sends to Jeroboam king of Israel when, through love of temporality, he commits himself to be directed by him, although he ought to be directed by God.

“Amos,” he says, “rebels against you in the midst of the house of Israel.” Your thought, plainly, wishing to be torn away from the world’s wantonness, is rebellious against you within yourself. “The land cannot bear his words”: the frailty of the human body cannot tolerate the excess of his continence.

**Verse 11.**—“For thus says Amos: ‘Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall go into captivity away from his land.’” It is as though he said: The love of temporality always falls back into a capital evil, and fictitious Israel will be deprived of the freedom of his body by departing into captivity.

**Verses 12, 13.**—“And Amaziah said to Amos: ‘You who see, go away and flee into the land of Judah; eat bread there, and there you shall prophesy. But at Bethel you shall no longer prophesy, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of his kingdom.’”

“You who see,” says Amaziah, “go away”—that is, you who perceive that all can be saved through penitential confession at the end, use your own laws meanwhile, while you are safe. Flee into the land of Judah: reserve your salvation for your final confession. Eat bread there: in this intention, plainly, satisfy yourself with temporal pleasures. There you shall prophesy: undoubtedly, you will remain under the foresight of this hope.

“At Bethel you shall no longer prophesy”: content with the honor of the present, you will cease to discuss the future against customs which all judge worthy of God as a guest. “For it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of his kingdom”—that is: if God did not regard us, who are praised in this way, as holy, and if he had not chosen to reign in us, such great praise would never have followed our actions.

**Verses 14, 15.**—“And Amos answered Amaziah: ‘I am not a prophet, and I am not the son of a prophet; but I am a herdsman, plucking sycamores. And the Lord took me when I was following the flock.’”

Amos speaks to Amaziah when our spirit, reasoning as though under the impulse of hypocrisy, resists. “I am not,” he says, “a prophet”: I have no prominence whatever by which, relying on my own judgment, I may determine my end. “I am not the son of a prophet,” because I have received no seed—or even beginning—of prudence by which I might be wise.

“But I am a herdsman, plucking sycamores”: undoubtedly, in work and word I pursue the discernments and judgments of every wise person. I pluck sycamores—which blessed Jerome calls “brambles”—not discussing future things, which I do not know how to reach, but treating morally with myself concerning the present passions of my soul. For it is not lawful to think about tomorrow where the evil of the day is sufficient for itself.

Passion is rightly signified by a bramble, which is known to be red in leaf and fruit. “The Lord took me when I was following the flock”: he lifted me from the world when, despising it, I was following worldly dullness. A flock properly refers to sheep, just as a herd refers to cattle; and sheep are used for foolishness, as in: “Like sheep they are placed in hell” (Ps. XLVIII, 15).

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’” The Lord speaks when he prompts reason regarding what must be perceived. “Go,” he says, “away from inept simplicity, and, for caution, look ahead to the people of thoughts who seek to be directed with God.”

**Verse 16.**—“Now hear the word of the Lord: You say: ‘You shall not prophesy against Israel, and you shall not drip upon the house of the idol.’” He hears the word who understands it. He does not prophesy against Israel who corrects the mind with no foresight. He does not drip upon the house of the idol whoever does not strive gradually to bend a conscience given to sin. “To drip” is commonly used for “to fall.” He therefore drips upon the house of the idol who, in his own consideration, weakens the power of hypocrisy.

[Col. 0442B] **Verse 17.**—“Therefore thus says the Lord: ‘Your wife shall fornicate in the city, your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword, your land shall be measured with a measuring cord, and you shall die in a polluted land, and Israel shall go into captivity away from his land.’”

The wife of hypocrisy is the pleasure of the will. She fornicates in the city when she prostitutes herself in the mind to foreign praises. Sons and daughters fall by the sword when strong and weak dispositions of the soul alike collapse into the evil of crime. Her land is measured with a cord when the function of the body is not refused for the amount of any sin that is to be committed. He dies in a polluted land when the whole spirit is extinguished in the execution of carnal desire. Israel departs into captivity from his land when the mind, failing in direction, is separated from its inward solidity, which is signified by “land.”

## Chapter VIII

**Verses 1, 2.**—“The Lord God showed me this, and behold, a hook for fruit. And he said: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A hook for fruit.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘The end has come upon my people Israel.’”

The Lord shows these things when he proposes them to the mind for understanding. “And behold, a hook for fruit,” because he suddenly strikes the mind when representations of various merits are considered. Fruit is drawn as if by a hook when, with the mind contracted by fear, one looks ahead to the lot into which one is going to fall.

He is asked what he sees when, having been brought by thought before God’s judgment, he examines within himself what he thinks about himself. But immediately he is shown what fruit of his action he should expect. “The end,” says the Lord, “has come upon my people,” when a restraining limit comes to the perverse thought that has inserted itself into the heart up to that point.

**Verse 3.**—“I shall not continue to pass over him. And the hinges of the temple shall creak.” God no longer passes over the one whom he now drenches with a local inspiration. The hinges of the temple creak when the innermost perceptions of a good conscience howl in the presence of its former error. For in Greek, *kardían* (καρδίαν), from which *cardines*—“hinges”—are also named, means “heart.”

“In that day, says the Lord, many shall die; silence shall be cast forth in every place.” Many die in that day because, in that illumination of the inner person, the superfluous thought suffers sudden destruction. In Scripture, “silence” is spoken of when no one speaks to God either by prayer or by life. Hence: “While profound silence held all things” (Wis. XVIII, 15). This silence is cast forth in every place when this perverse muteness is regarded with abhorrence by every mind that serves God not by the hour but in every place.

**Verse 4.**—“Hear this, you who crush the poor and cause the needy of the land to fail.” This means: Let those understand who, through the pride of hypocrisy, trample upon poverty of spirit, and cause those movements that confess themselves needy of divine help and frequently plead their own earthliness to fail before God.

**Verse 5.**—“When, they say, will the month pass and we shall sell our merchandise?” They desire the month to pass who wish this collection of virtues to be emptied within the bosom of the mind; and the affections commonly burn with longing for this. They sell merchandise when minds greedy for praise display the works of good conduct for the price of receiving that praise.

“And the Sabbath” [understand: “when it comes”] “and we shall open the grain, so that we may diminish the measure, increase the shekel, and put false balances underneath?” The Sabbath is sought when, under the law of the members, a pitiable rest from good work is seized. Grain is opened when inward fruitfulness is expanded for the profits of favor. The measure is diminished when the standard of a holy purpose is lowered in the intention itself. The shekel is increased when the coin of diabolical suggestion is gladly admitted into one’s conduct. A false balance is placed underneath when we use the Scriptures “to excuse our excuses in sins” (Ps. CXL, 4).

Balances are therefore mentioned in the psalm: “The children of men are deceitful in balances” (Ps. LXI, 10). For there we weigh our deeds. Indeed, when we wish to grow sluggish in devout zeal, we are accustomed to say that saying of the wise man: “Do not lift a burden upon yourself,” even though we have not yet, in truth, begun the rudiments of a good beginning.

**Verse 6.**—“And that we may possess the needy for silver, and the poor for sandals, and sell the refuse of grain.” They possess the needy for silver when, through false interpretations of Scripture, they twist people of teaching and reason toward a more relaxed life, and by incorporating them into themselves thereby possess them. Likewise, they possess the poor for sandals when they strive, through the seductive charm of their words, to hand over friends of true humility to dead works. They sell the refuse of grain when they expound the final and apparently carnal examples of Scripture to the disparagement of their hearers.

**Verse 7.**—“The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: ‘If I shall forget all their works to the end.’” God swears by the pride of Jacob when, summoning to the law of deserved vengeance the fear of those who glory in the supplanting of vices, he breathes against it. He does not forget all their works to the end because, even if he seems meanwhile to forget them, in the end—that is, in every respect—they are by no means permitted to be erased from his judgment.

**Verse 8.**—“Shall not the land be shaken because of this, and shall every inhabitant of it mourn?” The land is shaken because of this when every mind of the sinner is terrified under so great a threat. And what wonder if the sinner fears, when even every inhabitant of that land—that is, the one who wholly dominates sin itself—will flee? “Land” is commonly used for the sinner, and “to inhabit” for “to dominate.”

“And it shall rise like a whole river, and shall be cast out, and shall flow down like the stream of Egypt.” It rises like a whole river when that inhabitant himself, not partial but entire, bursts upward in the likeness of a river sweeping everything away in its current of adversity toward the heights of virtue. He is cast out when he is excluded from his former earthliness or sin. He flows down like the stream of Egypt—without doubt, the land that ought to be inhabited, that is, possessed—when the delight of sin, which is derived from the Egypt of the present age, fails within itself.

**Verses 9, 10.**—“And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, that the sun shall set at midday, and I shall make the earth dark in the day of light.” “It shall be”: true essence, plainly, shall be established in that day—that is, in the inward light which must always be kept before the eyes, and which is therefore indicated by the demonstrative pronoun. The sun sets at midday when the heat of temptation subsides under the warmth of heavenly inspiration. The earth is darkened in the day of light when, as the conscience grows hot with love of God, the works of darkness that a person has practiced become foul and make him ashamed.

“And I shall turn your feasts into mourning,” when the joys of the world are reduced to the goad of repentance. “Your songs shall be turned into lamentation” when worldly delights in any matter are unable to find any refuge in spiritual lees (*amurca*).

“And I shall bring sackcloth upon every back of yours, and baldness upon every head; and I shall make it like the mourning for an only-begotten son, and its end like a bitter day.” God brings sackcloth upon all their backs when, in their perverse endurance by which, according to another prophet, they are always bent for the passage of demons (Isa. LI, 23)—for this is what “back” signifies—the harshness of sin’s yoke is rubbed against them.

Baldness is brought upon every head when discriminating thoughts, which take care for our shame and, like hair, fortify the forehead, are disgracefully cut away from the mind, which is the head. God makes it like the mourning for an only-begotten son when he subjects the conscience signified by the head to the singular loss of fallen reason.

Note that he passes from one grammatical gender to another, as in the passage where David, seeking a tabernacle for the Lord, is said to have found “her” in Ephrata (Ps. CXXXI, 5–6), inserting the thing signified in place of the signifying term.

He makes its end like a bitter day when he makes the satiety of sin, which the bitterness of repentance commonly follows, be given over most bitterly to the pains of suspicion. It is rightly called a bitter day: the gaiety of pleasure has gone before, and sorrow follows.

**Verse 11.**—“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God.” “Behold”—that is, in this very condition of such great torpor—days are coming, not of illumination but of the manifestation of evils. From inward misery I shall send the poverty of outward desolation in action, where no one understands—not bodily hunger for food, but a lack of the word of God, that is, of inward sweetness to be tasted from the marrow of the soul.

**Verse 12.**—“And they shall be moved from sea to sea, and from the north to the east.” They are moved from sea to sea when, from the anxiety of a crime committed, they are driven by continual agitation of heart all the way to fear of the final judgment. They proceed from the north even to the east when they strive to breathe from the frost of diabolical despair toward the east of God’s mercy.

“They shall go about seeking the word of the Lord, and shall not find it.” They go about seeking the word of the Lord but do not find it when they desire God to enter into them by divine action, yet do not cease to go about through worldly desires. They do not find him because they seek him in a manner different from that in which he ought to have been sought.

**Verse 13.**—“In that day the beautiful virgins shall fail, and the young men shall fail in thirst.” In that day—not of inward light but of manifest vengeance—the beautiful virgins fail when the more subtle and, as it were, more delicate gifts of our spirit, which the Apostle calls “the better gifts” (I Cor. XII, 31), perish. The young men also fail in thirst when all that is strong but done through hypocrisy collapses from inward dryness.

**Verse 14.**—“Those who swear by the guilt of Samaria,” because they choose to persevere firmly without inward fruit in the semblance of outward observance. For Samaria is interpreted as “watch.”

“‘As your god Dan lives,’ they say, ‘and as the way of Beersheba lives; and they shall fall and shall not rise again.’” Dan is interpreted as “judgment”; Beersheba as “the well of satiety.” It is as though they said: Those who, after a long period of hypocrisy, promise themselves God’s mercy at the end say: “O terrible judgment, your God lives—the one who promised salvation to anyone who should groan at any hour; he lives, because he is the same yesterday and today” (Hebr. XIII, 8), capable of doing what he promised. But “the way,” that is, the activity, of the well of satiety, that is, of temporal glory, also lives, possessing great power over weak minds through its usefulness to them.

Therefore, says the prophet, “they shall fall and shall not rise again,” because they must not restrict divine judgments according to their own will.

## Chapter IX

[Col. 0445D]

**Verse 1.**—“I saw the Lord standing upon the altar, and he said: ‘Strike the hinge, and let the lintels be shaken.’” The Lord stands upon the altar when, aggrieved by the harsh judgment proposed, he assails perversity. For hypocrites regard as an altar whatever they consider great in themselves under a new institution: “He who stands in the assembly of the gods himself judges” (Ps. LXXXI, 1).

He commands the hinge to be struck so that the lintels may be shaken when he orders hearts to be wounded by the darts of preaching, to such an extent that even the outward appearance is changed.

“For avarice is at the head of all, and I shall kill their end by the sword.” What he calls the hinge above, here he calls the head; what he calls the lintels, here he calls the end. Avarice is at the head of all when ambition for honor and favor lies beneath the principal intention of minds. Their end is killed by the sword when the body—which is called “the end” because it is recognized as being more contiguous than the mind—is handed over to deadly sin.

“There shall be no flight for them. He shall flee, and none of those who flee shall be saved.” There is no flight for hypocrites when they tremble there through fear where fear does not exist. For flight is fear of the spirit. Yet they flee because they fear only the losses to their own praise. Whoever flees is not saved because anyone who fears in this way is in no way protected from God’s judgment, which usually exposes sins.

**Verse 2.**—“If they descend as far as hell, from there my hand shall lead them out.” They descend to hell who do not recover toward the Lord through any act of piety. The hand of God leads them out from there, for the more desperate they are, the more easily he does so—he “who brings out the bound in strength and releases those dwelling in tombs” (Ps. LXVII, 7).

“And if they ascend as far as heaven, from there I shall drag them down.” He who ascends to heaven is dragged down from there when, lifted up in pride so that, according to Job, his head might touch the clouds (Job XX, 6), he is finally destroyed like dung.

**Verse 3.**—“Even if they are hidden on the summit of Carmel, from there I shall search them out and remove them.” Carmel is interpreted as “soft”; the summit signifies pride, as in the psalm’s expression “the crown of the hair” (Ps. LXVII, 22). They hide on the summit of Carmel who rejoice in their thought over their fragile work. God searches them out and removes them from there when, within themselves, examining their shameful deed through the central faculty of reason, he moves them away from their former filth.

“Even if they hide themselves from my eyes in the bottom of the sea, there I shall command the serpent, and it shall bite them.” They hide themselves from God’s eyes in the bottom of the sea who, in the most extreme and contemptible vices of the world—by which they embitter God—separate themselves from the regard of divine visitation, having entirely rejected confession. There God commands the serpent and it bites them when he orders our carnal affection, by stirring it up, to torment the miserable reason whose cunning has so far concealed it badly, as it disdained what it had done. This is the serpent that deceived Eve—that is, the will—and daily lies in wait for her heel.

**Verse 4.**—“And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I shall command the sword, and it shall kill them.” They go into captivity before their enemies who, stripped of the freedom of their own will, decide within themselves to sin even more than the demons who captured them suggest. There God commands the sword and kills them when he loosens the opportunity for them to sin in their misery and hands them over to destruction.

“And I shall set my eyes upon them for evil and not for good.” God sets his eyes upon them when he regards these five aforesaid ways of sinning, not so much in a spirit of punishment as with mercy. He does this for evil and not for good when he considers not the good things they carry out through hypocrisy, but the evil intentions with which they did them.

**Verse 5.**—“And the Lord God of hosts, who touches the land, and it shall melt; and all who dwell in it shall mourn.” “The Lord,” he says, “is the God of hosts, who is effective over every power as he pleases.” Hence, when he touches the land, it melts: when he puts his hand through the opening of the conscience, according to the saying in the Song of Songs (Cant. V, 4), and his touch causes the sinner’s belly to tremble, the sinner melts, as it were, through self-examination.

“For he touches the mountains and they smoke” (Ps. CIII, 32); he looks upon the land and makes it tremble. All who dwell in it mourn when even those who govern their bodies well see nothing in their entire good action except what is worthy of mourning. “If the righteous man is scarcely saved” (I Pet. IV, 18), it is therefore no wonder if sinners fear.

“And it shall rise like every stream, and shall flow down like the river of Egypt.” This verse, and half of the preceding one, have been explained above. It rises like every stream when everyone who chastises his body and brings it into subjection (I Cor. IX, 27) is carried toward God by the full force of his intention. It flows down like the river of Egypt when that cunning by which he was conformed to worldly knowledge wholly perishes in him.

**Verse 6.**—“Who builds his ascent in heaven, and has founded his bundle upon the earth.” He builds his ascent in heaven when, in the breast of the elect—who, like heaven, are seats for him—he multiplies the instruments of virtue, through which he not only advances in their understanding but also causes them themselves to advance toward knowledge of him.

He founds his bundle upon the earth when, in our body, he binds and strengthens the material of every good practice through the bonds of holy religion.

“Who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.” The Lord calls the waters of the sea when he summons all who are light and unstable, and bitter with the bilge-water of a foul way of life, to the pursuit of his instruction. He sweetens them so greatly with the seasoning of his grace that he pours them out upon the face of the earth—that is, he sets them forth as examples before all the good who, according to the Apostle, are God’s cultivation (I Cor. III, 9). Nor is this unjust. He is himself the Lord, in reality as in name, and it lies within his power to do this whenever he wills.

**Verse 7.**—“Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me, O sons of Israel? says the Lord.” The sons of Israel become sons of the Ethiopians to God when those who ought to rule their own movements with God persist unchangeably in the blackness of sin. “Israel,” meaning “prince with God,” is said to the obstinate hypocrites.

“Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene?” God causes Israel to ascend from the land of Egypt when he causes him to rise from the sorrows and darkness of the world in order to see God. The Philistines are brought out of Cappadocia when some are led from the coldness of unbelief so that they may fall through a share in worldly pleasure. The Philistines are called “those falling by a drink”; Cappadocia is a northern region.

The Syrians are likewise summoned from Cyrene—or, to speak according to another translation, the Septuagint, from the pit in which they were held—when proud people are dragged out from the depths of vices; or, since *Cyrene* has the sound of “inheritance,” when they are removed by baptism from the devil’s hereditary lot, yet are permitted to remain within the height of pride.

The whole passage is as though he said: Do not become exalted because I brought you out of Egypt. You must remember that I have often also transferred other ordinary persons from serious evils to easier ones.

**Verse 8.**—“Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I shall crush it from the face of the earth.” “Do not be exalted,” I say, “you hypocrites, because of your counterfeit continence. For behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom”—that is, the judicial discernment of God is upon those who seem to have ruled themselves outwardly and yet, by that very rule, are plunged into the pit of exaltation.

The kingdom is crushed from the face of the earth when, by God’s just judgment, even chastity displayed for human purposes is brought to nothing.

“Nevertheless, crushing, I shall not crush the house of Jacob.” It is as though he said: Although I permit you to possess a great deal of sanctity and allow my elect, who strive to supplant vices, to fall at times, yet, while crushing them outwardly, I shall not crush them inwardly at all; rather, I shall make their fall material for standing. Jacob means “supplanter.”

**Verse 9.**—“Behold, I shall command, and I shall shake the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is shaken in a sieve, and not a pebble shall fall upon the earth.” God commands when he does not forbid something to happen. He shakes the house of Israel among all the nations when he usually collides the hypocrite’s conscience among nearly all vices. This happens as grain is shaken in a sieve, in which the fruits of natural goods are cleansed from the chaff and filth of vices by God’s discernment.

But no pebble falls upon the earth, because the hardening of the mind does not go so far as to reach knowledge of sin and of its own earthliness.

**Verse 10.**—“All the sinful people of mine shall die by the sword, those who say: ‘Evil shall not approach; it shall not come upon us.’” This means: Whoever promises himself immunity from the punishment of sin, as though on account of the merit of his life, shall, because of his security, be cut down by the sword of capital crime.

**Verse 11.**—“In that day I shall raise up the tabernacle of David, which has fallen, and I shall rebuild its breaches, and I shall restore what had collapsed.” In that day the fallen tabernacle of David is raised when, in that inward illumination by which, while the impious man is proud, the poor man is set ablaze like gold for his own brightness (Ps. IX, 23), the holy warfare of anyone strong-handed, which had ebbed away through sloth, is renewed.

He rebuilds its breaches when he joins together the gaps in the mind through which evil suggestion was admitted, filling them with virtue. He restores what had collapsed when he repairs the losses caused by sin through the expenditure of repentance.

**Verse 12.**—“And I shall rebuild them as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnants of Edom and all the nations, because my name has been invoked upon them.” He rebuilds them as in the days of old when he forms and reforms, after the model of the heavenly Jerusalem—whose days, that is, whose virtues, if I may so speak, possess nothing more eternal—those who ride in that army.

“So that they may possess the remnants of Edom and all the nations”: namely, the earthliness of their body and the desires wandering through the body. And this is “because my name has been invoked upon them”—that is, they did not ascribe the victory over sin to their own name, but, rejoicing, sent their crowns before the throne of God to him alone, in gratitude for the pursuit of their labor.

### Verse 13

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when the ploughman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him who sows the seed.” The days come when inner illuminations succeed in the mind. The ploughman overtakes the reaper when the practice of good works, even before zeal has advanced, already begins confidently to anticipate the harvest of good works. This seems to contradict that condition in which, as we have learned, the dwelling in the heavenly homeland was customarily denied even to the most perfect before Christ’s coming. The treader of grapes overtakes him who sows the seed when the one who draws and elicits from his mind the nectar of divine grace through the feeling of a new compunction strives, in the fervor of pious desire, to equal him who scatters the seed of saving doctrine.

“And the mountains shall drip sweetness, and all the hills shall be cultivated.” The mountains drip sweetness when those who excel in contemplation gradually discourse, with a certain slowness of words, on the joy of heavenly glory. These are the sparks of gleaming bronze in Ezekiel (Ezek. 1:7). And who else seems to drip sweetness than one who is not at all permitted to elaborate what he perceives concerning God? All the hills are cultivated when, from their dripping, nothing wild, nothing unusual, and nothing disordered is seen to remain in the minds of their subjects.

### Verse 14

“I shall turn back the captivity of my people Israel, and they shall build the deserted cities and inhabit them.” God turns back the captivity of his people when the animal impulses that had led our captives away are themselves led captive to the rational commands of free will. Hence it is said: “He led captivity captive” (Eph. 4:8). They build the deserted cities when they restore, against every assault of vanity, the sensual faculties that had been bereft of fellowship with God. They inhabit them when, frequenting them with watchful guardianship, they subject them to their own authority by fixed determination.

“And they shall plant vineyards, and drink their wine, and make gardens, and eat their fruits.” They plant vineyards who, by piously laboring together, propagate the causes of eternal joy. They drink their wine when from them they anticipate the joy of everlasting hope. They become intoxicated from it when, pressing toward what lies ahead, they forget what is behind (Phil. 3:13). They make gardens when they rush toward courageous pursuits and even toward the disciplines of bodily exercise. They eat their fruits when, from strenuous labor and from the expenditure of benevolence toward one’s neighbor, security concerning the heavenly reward even in the present grows within the mind.

### Verse 15

“And I shall plant them upon their own soil, and I shall not uproot them again from the land that I gave them.” He plants them upon their own soil when he grants them immovable dominion over their bodies, so that these may no longer become rebelliously excessive. He does not uproot them again from the land he gave them, because he permanently established for them, by an eternal right, the land of their bodies—that is, the land he promised the meek to possess (Matt. 5:4).

[Column 0449] **AMOS THE PROPHET ENDS.**

## PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTH BOOK

[Column 0449C] 243 The most blessed Jeremiah, who was sanctified from his mother’s womb and appointed as a prophet to the nations, entered upon his age and prolonged it under evangelical virginity. In accordance with the purity innate in him, he hastened inward with all the greater keenness because, owing to the adversity of the times and his most chaste heart, he was more withdrawn from external fellowship and worldly prosperity.

Therefore, applying the misfortune of the holy city to the downfall of the inner person, he employed an alphabet of four letters for mystical sorrows, so that he might heal by an evangelical poultice the one whom he had discovered to have fallen through the excesses of the four elements, and so that the one who had trampled upon the Decalogue by transgressing its twofold character might restrain himself under the evangelical duality. For since there are twenty-two letters, he marks by the number twenty the excess of the *deuteresis*—the repetition—which had corrupted the integrity of sacred law through the novelty of traditions. But when the contrite mind, tearfully remembering its ruin, is brought back to the love of God and neighbor, the inward destruction is repaired by the brevity of the twofold commandment.

Therefore, omitting the *deuteresis* and taking up hypocrisy, which doubles so many people in the Church in their own colors, let us carefully examine the falls and losses of minds that we continually suffer in daily devastation. Let us also examine the wrinkle of dissimulation by which we are indeed narrowed toward God, but toward the world are folded back through the worst multiplication of twenty; going forth from ourselves toward God, let us extend ourselves with abundant generosity in every direction toward friends and enemies. Therefore, amid the ruin of cities, let us contemplate the ruins of souls and see what the first letter suggests to us, since from it, as is clear concerning the others, the meaning that follows depends. Let us then proceed, girded by the Holy Spirit.

# FIFTH BOOK OF THE TROPological INTERPRETATION OF THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH

[Column 0451]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Column 0451A]

## ALEPH

### Verse 1

“How does the city full of people sit alone? She has become like a widow, the mistress of nations; she has become a princess among the provinces, under tribute.” *Aleph* is interpreted as “doctrine.” The city full of people sits alone when the mind, crowded with throngs of thoughts, sits solitary and unattended, without the support of meditation on saving doctrine, while it is unable by its own power to rise up to restore the mind’s tranquility and calm its tumults. Hence it is said to a certain evil virgin: “Sit in the dust” (Isa. 47:1). For no one is truly alone who is inwardly composed of the sacred utterance.

The mistress of nations becomes like a widow when reason, which ought to preside over the nations of vices with the scepter of discernment, is deprived of divine seed and lacks God as husband. She becomes a princess among the provinces, under tribute, when she is made subject to the provinces of the external senses, which are called five cities in the Gospel (Luke 19:19). Concerning this tribute it is said: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17).

## BETH

### Verse 2

“Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks.” *Beth* is interpreted as “confusion.” He weeps in the night who, in the confusion of sin, weakens the sharpness of the mind—like the eyes of the head—with the moisture of compassion. Her tears are upon her cheeks when the inner parts of souls flow outward into manifest ruin. Hence it is said of any wicked person: “In his life he cast away his inmost parts.”

“There is none among all her loved ones to comfort her.” There is none among all her loved ones to comfort her when, from the whole company of virtues in which alone true charity is found among us, no remnant appears that seems to restore us to hope. “All her friends have despised her and have become her enemies.” All her friends despise her when the rational impulses—which, if they restrained themselves, she could have as true friends—shame the mind by detesting it because of the foulness of its conduct. They become her enemies when, although they abhor what they do and think, they nevertheless remain enemies by failing to come to the aid of her infamous activity.

## GHIMEL

### Verse 3

“Judah has migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude; she has dwelt among the nations and found no rest.” *Ghimel* is interpreted as “retribution.” Judah migrates because of affliction and the multitude of servitude when, because of the very frequent recurrence of shameful deeds and crimes in the mind, the virtue of confession is entirely lost. For this is how Judah is interpreted, and thus a wicked life is condemned by the retribution of a worse meaning. She dwells among the nations while, by sinning, she frequents the barbarism of an evil way of life. She finds no rest because she does not remain in misery.

“All her persecutors have seized her amid her distress.” The mind is distressed when it is harassed by perverse desire rushing upon it from every side. Amid these distresses her persecutors seize her when whatever vices rush upon her do not cease to subjugate her.

## DALETH

### Verse 4

“The ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the solemn assembly.” *Daleth* is interpreted as “fear.” The ways of Zion mourn when those purities of a clean heart, by which one travels toward divine contemplations—which is what Zion means—taste nothing of heavenly joy, but, conscious of their evil condition, know nothing except how to give birth to continual fears. They mourn because there are none who come to the solemn assembly, for the cause of joy’s removal is that no breathing of virtue comes forward to lead us toward contemplating the frequency of the spirit, the soul’s thoughts, and its intentions, as though toward the attendance of a solemn day.

“All her gates have been destroyed.” All her gates are destroyed when the whole of sensuality collapses from the state of its proper restraint. Concerning these it is written: “Lift up your gates, princes” (Ps. 23:7, 9).

“Her priests groan; her virgins are defiled.” Her priests groan when her intellectual faculties, whose duty it was to provide her with sacred guidance, persist in handling nothing except what is worthy of groaning. Her virgins are defiled when faith and hope, which alone seem to have remained incorrupt, are continually handed over to the filthiness of vices. Nor is this unjust, for she herself is oppressed by bitterness. She is oppressed by bitterness who is seasoned by no affection for heavenly sweetness.

## HE

### Verse 5

“Her enemies have become her masters; her enemies have been enriched, because the Lord has spoken against her.” *He* is interpreted as “to be.” Her enemies become her masters when we admit into the mind—which governs the members as the head, and in which, so to speak, we receive the substance of truly being in God—the siege, indeed the possession, of sins. For one may be said not to be who does not coexist with the inner truth by living sincerely. Hence it is said of the devil: “Let his companions, of him who is not, dwell in his tabernacle” (Job 18:15).

His enemies are enriched when the demons boast of the virtue they have stolen from us. This happens because the Lord speaks against her—that is, because a sentence is issued against her, deservedly, for the oppression of her on account of her wickedness.

“Because of the multitude [elsewhere: ‘on account of the multitude’] of her iniquities, her little ones have been led into captivity before the face of the one who afflicts.” Her little ones are led into captivity when any uninstructed persons, through their deviations, are brought outside the freedom of the will, so that they sin by necessity what they contracted by choice. This happens to each of them on account of the multitude of their iniquities, so that each may feel himself taken captive from the jurisdiction of his own understanding. They are led before the face of the afflicter when the impulse of the one wishing to sin is more ardent, while the devil’s attacking suggestion follows from a distance. For, according to that saying of Isaiah, they are thrown into a spacious and broad land, “like a ball” (Isa. 22:18). They are also said to generate for themselves the breath of an evil inspiration.

## VAU

### Verse 6

“And all her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion; her princes have become like rams finding no pasture.” *Vau* is interpreted as “he himself.” “He himself” indicates the proper character of the one about whom it is said. Thus all her beauty is said to have departed from the daughter of Zion when, from that mind which either once was, or could have been, the daughter of the heavenly contemplatives if it relied upon God, an inner pest removes the grace of God—the very thing that constructs and builds for itself in God’s sight a personal and, so to speak, substantial character, and the only beauty that he himself desires.

Her princes are like rams when her external senses become the leaders of all her activity. Rams customarily provide leadership to the flock, and the Samaritan woman had this fivefold husband (John 4:18). These rams find no pasture—namely, anything life-giving—and do not even desire to seek nourishment.

“And they departed without strength before the face of the pursuer.” They depart without strength when, without any resistance, their spirit yields to the devil’s suggestions. They depart before the face of the pursuer when, before experiencing the evil exhortation, they voluntarily succumb through their own impulses, as though to the presence of his face.

## ZAI [elsewhere: ZAIN]

### Verse 7

“And Jerusalem remembered the days of her affliction and the transgression of all her desirable things, which she had possessed from ancient days.” *Zai* is interpreted as “hither,” implying that the fallen soul ought to remember from where and to where it has fallen, and that it must always turn its eye hither. “My people,” it says, “shall turn hither” [elsewhere: “here”] (Ps. 72:10).

Jerusalem remembers the days of her affliction when the mind, which once attained the vision of peace, recalls its own degradation. It remembers the days—that is, every kind of discernment—before the eyes of its intentions grew dim, which usually happens at the beginnings of temptations. It remembers the transgression of all its desirable things when it appears pitifully, though without any result, to call to mind the treasures of inner wealth that are now disturbed by the transgression of souls and that were possessed from ancient days—that is, before the mind became wholly darkened.

The desirable things are nothing other than inner goods, which the Apostle calls “the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12:31), and which are “the glory of the king’s daughter within” (Ps. 44:14).

“When her people fell into the hand of the enemy, and there was no helper.” Her people fall into the enemy’s hand when the crowd of wanton thoughts, its good purpose broken, yields to the devil’s party. There is no helper when the spirit that resists is absent.

“The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths.” The enemies see her when the evil dispositions of her mind in no way displease them. They mock her Sabbaths when they rejoice to have her acquiescing in them and refraining from every useful endeavor.

## HETH

### Verse 8

“Jerusalem sinned grievously; therefore she became unstable.” *Heth* is interpreted as “stupor.” Stupor is insensibility, and insensibility is nothing other than a reprobate mind. Therefore, by an antonomasia, sin sins in Jerusalem, and she becomes unstable because, after the mind has fallen from the vision of inner peace, it runs about wandering here and there through the impulses of its tempters.

“All who glorified her have despised her, because they saw her disgrace.” Those who glorified her are the virtues of the soul. They despise her when they show her worthy of contempt by the evidence of their desertion. “Because,” it says, “they saw her disgrace”: they made her appear infamous, namely through obscene conduct. Such sayings accord with this: “My garments will abhor me” (Job 9:31).

“But she herself, groaning, turned backward.” She groans when the wretched mind encounters difficulty in doing evil. “Under her tongue,” it says, “are labor and pain” (Ps. 10:7). She turns backward when she is turned back toward former pleasures rather than reaching forward in hope toward what lies ahead.

## TETH

### Verse 9

“Her filth is upon her feet, and she did not remember her end; she has been cast down exceedingly, having no comforter.” *Teth* is interpreted as “exclusion.” Her filth is upon her feet when the intentions of sin do not cease from her affections. She does not remember her end when she is excluded from considering her evil condition; this is noted in the preceding letter. She would attend to her end if she considered what the fruit of her endeavor would be.

She is cast down exceedingly because she is never raised up to desire eternal things. She has no comforter when, amid so many miseries, she lacks even some virtue by which she might breathe—in fact, she is deprived of every consolation of the Holy Spirit.

“See, Lord, my affliction, for the enemy has exalted himself.” This is the voice of some holy person who is afflicted by another’s fall. The enemy is exalted in proportion as she, as was said above, is cast down exceedingly.

## IOTH [elsewhere: JOD]

### Verse 10

“The enemy stretched out his hand toward all her desirable things, because he saw nations entering his sanctuary, concerning whom you had commanded that they should not enter your church.” *Joth* is interpreted as “desolation.” And she is plainly desolated when power—which is the hostile hand—wanders through the inner goods believed to be more desirable to God. This happened to her because he saw nations entering his sanctuary: that is, he tolerated with equanimity whatever wickednesses occupied the conscience, which ought to have been the temple of God. For we customarily say of what we hate that we cannot bear to see it. God commanded concerning these things that they should not enter his church; he also commanded that the eyes be turned away lest they see vanity, much less admit vanity itself into the mind.

## CAPH

### Verse 11

“All her people groan, seeking bread; they gave every precious thing for food to revive the soul.” *Caph* is called “bent down,” and not without reason. For all her people groan and seek bread when the whole of thought, suffering beneath the burden of desires, carries about the nourishment of temporal pleasure. In contrast, it is written in Job: “Bread becomes detestable to him in his life” (Job 33:20).

They give every precious thing for food when, in exchange for worldly wantonness, they distribute inner goods at the great price and wicked commerce of the transaction. They do this to revive the soul—that is, to serve the appetite of their animal nature with a momentary draught of whatever pleasure.

“See, Lord, and consider that I have become vile.” There are some who, concerning this bending down of theirs and as though concerning their vileness, breathe again by crying out to God from the depths. God sees when he makes us see; he considers when he brings us back to consideration of ourselves.

## LAMETH [elsewhere: LAMED]

### Verse 12

“O all you who pass along the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow.” *Lameth* is interpreted as “the heart of servitude.” By the heart, through which we understand, intelligence is signified; by servitude, subjection to sin is signified. The knowledge of a perverse humility toward sin is therefore signified by the heart of servitude.

Hence, through her works, she cries: O all you who pass along the way—who, being formed by Christ, who is the way (John 14:6), pass through life—attend and make me your lesson and example, and see how great a madness it is to be given over to these sorrows. For while others grieve over the sin they have committed, in me, alas, there arises not so much grief as rage: because I am unable to sin at will.

And this is because “the Lord has harvested me”: he has stolen from me the fruits both of every pious exercise and of heavenly sweetness. “On the day of his anger the Lord”—she says these things when, in the manifest sentence of his punishment, both sin and the penalty of sin are laid bare together, as though in daylight.

## MEN

### Verse 13

“From on high he sent fire into my bones, and he instructed me.” *Men* is interpreted as “from themselves.” It is plainly “from themselves,” because whatever inner damage exists comes about through their own merit. Thus fire is sent from on high into the bones when, amid the very beginnings of a fall, the fire of vainglory arises, taking its origin from the strength of the virtues. It comes from on high—that is, it is likewise generated from the pride of arrogance.

The prophet testifies that fire is understood in this way: “At the sound,” he says, “of a great utterance, fire blazed in it” (Jer. 11:6). It instructs him when, through the fall into any sin, he is taught from what good he has fallen. Hence Balaam also says of himself: “He who falls, and so his eyes are opened” (Num. 24:4).

“He spread a net for my feet; he turned me backward; he set me desolate, exhausted with sorrow all day long.” A net is spread for the feet when a stumbling block is placed before those who sin voluntarily; and while one tries to extricate oneself from it, one becomes still more entangled in the stains of the evils that press upon one. He turns backward when he is thrown back toward former sins. He is set desolate when, empty of God as inhabitant, he is prostituted to the devil’s will. He is exhausted with sorrow all day long when, groaning beneath an earthly burden all day—that is, continually—he is exiled from eternal rejoicing.

## NUN

### Verse 14

“The yoke of my iniquities kept watch; in his hand they were entwined and placed upon my neck.” *Nun* is interpreted as “unique.” Above she had said that, from the height of her own estimation, the fire of vainglory had blazed in the bones of her inner steadfastness; therefore she considered herself unique and singular.

Accordingly, in God’s hand the yoke of her iniquities keeps watch, because the practice of committed wickedness, which continually oppresses and bends us down, harasses us with cares from which there is no remedy. For to keep watch is to be troubled. These iniquities are entwined when iniquities are added to iniquities. They are placed upon the neck when everything is dragged into the habit of oppression.

“My strength has been weakened; the Lord has delivered me into a hand from which I shall not be able to rise.” Her strength is weakened from that point onward because there is no power of heart that can resist the vices arising within. The Lord delivers us into a hand from which we cannot rise when, once we have become slaves of sin, we cannot tear ourselves away from the authority of the one to whom we have submitted ourselves.

## SAMECH

### Verse 15

“The Lord has removed all my mighty ones from my midst; he summoned a time against me to crush my chosen ones.” *Samech* is called “firmament.” The Lord removes the mighty ones from our midst when the principal impulses—through which great things are accomplished in our midst, that is, in reason itself, and through which, according to the meaning of the preceding letter, we are strengthened in the love of God—are withdrawn by God’s judgment.

He summons a time against us to crush our chosen ones when, stirring us through temporal desire at the devil’s instigation and permitting such things to be supplied opportunely by him, he demolishes and scatters whatever is more distinguished and whatever is more excellent in the soul.

“The Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah.” The juice of any substance is pressed out in a winepress. The Lord therefore treads the winepress when, by his judgment, he presses out those passions which draw from us the moisture of complete piety and increase through their innate stubbornness. This happens to the virgin daughter of Judah—that is, to a confession that is not manly, one that proposes to confess against itself, but is unfruitful, since it is a virgin and barren; by returning its offspring to vomit, it makes it effeminate or destroys it.

## AIN

### Verse 16

“Therefore I weep, and my eye pours out water, because the comforter who turns my soul has been put far from me.” *Ain* is interpreted as “eye.” He weeps who removes from himself the impulse of inner tenderness. His eye pours out water when the intention that illumines thoughts gradually rejects from itself the fountain of saving wisdom.

This is why the proposed letter signifies “eye”: the one who had dissolved the firmament of the virtues consequently weakens the eye of intention itself. This happens because the comforter has been put far from him; for when the spirit of consolation is expelled from the soul, whatever remains inwardly is hardened by eternal obduracy. That comforter turns the soul back, because without his inspiration the wretched soul does not return from its own impulse.

“My children have become lost because the enemy has prevailed.” The children are lost when the enemy has prevailed—when what appear to have been well done are not done for God, or when what was done for God is deprived of its reward because the devil introduces wickedness.

## PHE

### Verse 17

“Zion stretched out her hands; there is none to comfort her.” *Phe* is interpreted as “he went astray.” Explaining this error, he adds: Zion stretched out her hands when the one who had hitherto directed himself toward contemplating God—for this is what Zion signifies—strives to display his works through hypocrisy, by which no one strays worse from the truth.

Therefore there is none to comfort her because, concerning these labors that she undertakes in vain, she is sustained by no hope before God.

“The Lord commanded enemies against Jacob all around him; Jerusalem became like a woman polluted by menstruation among them.” The Lord commands Jacob’s enemies against him when he arouses the hostility of temptation against the one who boasts of overthrowing vices. For his commanding means permitting something to happen. He sends them around him when he also plainly permits the outward person to be hindered. Jerusalem is like a woman polluted by menstruation among them when, struck from within and without, she suffers especially inwardly through obscene thoughts.

## SADE

### Verse 18

“Righteous is the Lord, because her mouth provoked him to anger.” *Sade* is interpreted as “justice.” Hence what follows: The Lord is righteous, because her mouth provoked him to anger; that is, he justly led her into outward impropriety, because, by not doing divine things for God, she cursed God, as though to his face.

“Listen, I beg you, all peoples, and see my sorrow.” She entreats all peoples to listen when, through the infamy of her wicked conduct, she urges everyone to consider the sentence of God pronounced openly against her. “See my sorrow,” she says—not the sorrow by which, alas, I grieve over my own miseries, but the condition that I consider worthy of sorrow.

“My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity”—which is to say: If anything incorrupt, if anything strong and steadfast, had remained in my mind, the ancient enemy has taken it captive by leading it away from every pious disposition.

## COPH

### Verse 19

“I called my friends, and they themselves deceived me.” *Coph* is interpreted as “conclusion.” He is plainly shut in for whom no place is found where he can breathe. For he calls his friends and they deceive him when he even seeks to make demons favorable to himself, so that they may supply vices more familiarly; but in this very matter they fatally deceive him.

“My priests and my elders have perished in the city, because they sought food for themselves to revive their soul.” The priests themselves are the rational impulses that bring guidance to the mind. The elders are likewise impulses that excel either in understanding or in the body with greater gravity. These perish in the city when, within the conscience where they originate, they are endangered by famine of the divine word.
