They seek food for themselves to revive the soul when they pursue temporal things by which they may raise up their animal natures.

## RES

### Verse 20

“See, Lord, for I am in distress; my belly is troubled, my heart is overturned within me, because I am full of bitterness.” *Res* is called “head.” He asks God to see because he is distressed when, repenting from the depths, as we said above, he repeatedly cries out to God to make him see—that is, understand—the death that advances within.

The belly is troubled when the mind is darkened so that it cannot assess what it suffers. His heart is overturned within himself when reason—which in the letter prefixed above is called the head—is confused in its own reasoning against vices. He says that he is full of bitterness because no grace of heavenly sweetness refreshes him.

“Outside, the sword kills; and indoors, death is like it.” The sword kills outside when bodily efficacy destroys her through the execution of some capital offense. A similar death is found indoors when, while the sinner is outwardly available to opportunity, there is inwardly a savage eagerness to sin.

## SIN

### Verse 21

“They heard that I was groaning, and there was none to comfort me.” *Sin* is interpreted as “upon the wound.” It is “upon the wound” when, in addition to the injuries of the inner person, bodily adversity also inflicts itself. In the Scriptures, “to hear” is used mystically for “to understand.” They hear that she groans because the fallen soul strives to breathe again toward God. They also hear that there is none to comfort her—that is, no mind remains capable of comforting her concerning inner virtue.

“All my enemies heard of my evil; they rejoiced because you did it.” This means: All the enemies of the inner person rejoice when they understand that God permits them to tempt the person, because it is as though you had granted them the opportunity.

“You brought the day of consolation, and they shall become like me.” Nevertheless, if God at some time introduces some consolation into the captive mind that is returning to its senses, it is clear that all the movements of its affections, which had wandered here and there, are immediately reduced to conformity with it. For once reason has been corrected, everything is drawn together into the same condition.

## TAU

### Verse 22

“Let all their evil enter before you, and strip them bare, as you stripped me bare because of my iniquities.” *Tau* is said to mean “he completed.” What is assigned to any end is completed. This happens if all the evil of the devil’s will is heard before God—which is what “enter” means. Let them be stripped bare—that is, let all their delight in me be annulled, just as they themselves annulled me because of my wickedness.

My groans are many, and my heart is grieving; many indeed are the labors over which I groan, and reason itself, which does nothing except what is worthy of mourning, is disturbed.

## CHAPTER TWO

## ALEPH

### Verse 1

“How the Lord in his fury has covered the daughter of Zion with darkness; he has cast down from heaven the renowned Israel, and on the day of his fury he has not remembered the footstool of his feet.” *Aleph*, as above, is called “doctrine.”

The soul therefore complains and wonders how the Lord in his fury has covered the daughter of Zion with darkness—how, that is, through the irrevocable sentence of his punishment, he permitted the heavenly Zion of old, the daughter of contemplation, to be darkened, and cast her from heaven, that is, from heavenly conduct, into earthly desires: the soul that had begun to be directed with God.

He is said not to remember the footstool of his feet on the day of his fury when he appears to forget the ancient compassion by which the one coeternal with the Father accepted, on earth and from a mother, flesh for the salvation of humanity. The footstool of his feet is understood as his blessed flesh’s Mother. Hence it is said: “Adore his footstool” (Ps. 98:5).

The letter placed above expresses doctrine, which, covered with darkness, perished; toward it the mind of sound understanding directs itself as toward a lamp shining in a dark place (2 Pet. 1:19).

## BETH

### Verse 2

“The Lord cast down and did not spare all the beautiful things of Jacob; in his fury he destroyed the fortifications of the virgin daughter of Judah; he cast them to the ground and polluted her kingdom and its princes.” *Beth* is called “house,” undoubtedly the house of God. He casts down all the beautiful things of this house, once overthrowing vices, when he weakens the distinction of every virtue. He would spare it if even a pious intention remained.

The virgin daughter of Judah is an unfruitful confession. Her fortifications are destroyed in fury when overflowing wickedness demolishes the strongest arguments by which she confessed her injustices against herself. He casts her to the ground when he abandons her to savoring only earthly things. He pollutes her kingdom and its princes when he permits the seat of intellectuality, together with all sensuality, to be handed over to depraved pleasures.

## GHIMEL

### Verse 3

“He broke in the anger of his fury every horn of Israel; he turned his right hand backward from the face of the enemy, and he kindled in Jacob, as it were, the fire of a devouring flame all around.” *Ghimel* is interpreted as “fullness,” namely the fullness of which it is said: “The iniquities of the Amorites have been completed” (Gen. 15:16).

According to this fullness, not in the anger of correction—in which he is angry yet not angry—but in the anger of fury, which does not turn back, every horn of Israel is broken when whatever in the mind could have transcended the flesh and savored the things above is overthrown.

He turns his right hand backward from the face of the enemy when, amid temptations in which the enemy’s power is especially recognized, the memory of holy perpetuity is struck back from the heart. For we recognize by the face, and we are chosen by the right hand.

He kindles in Jacob, as it were, the fire of a devouring flame all around when bodily desires are permitted to blaze through the senses and limbs in the one who formerly used to overthrow them.

## DALETH

### Verse 4

“He bent his bow like an enemy, fixed his right hand like a foe, and killed everything beautiful to behold in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion; he poured out his indignation like fire.” *Daleth* is interpreted as “of the doors,” undoubtedly of the external senses, through which we often admit our destruction.

The Lord bends his bow like an enemy when he does not cease to threaten the future judgment, as though aiming an axe at the root. Hence it is said: “You gave a sign so that they might flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. 59:6). He fixes his right hand like a foe when, in view of our wickedness, he indicates that he will close the heavenly homeland to us, like—in fact, truly—a foe.

He kills everything beautiful to behold in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion when he permits everything that could have pleased either God or humanity in outward works to be lost in the one who ought to have resembled the heavenly Mother. He pours out his indignation like fire when he grants that everything be brought to completion in crimes.

## HE

### Verse 5

“The Lord has become like an enemy; he has cast down Israel, cast down all his walls, destroyed his fortifications, and filled the daughter of Judah with humiliation, both man and woman.” *He* is called “receiving,” plainly referring to nothing other than what the devil, entering in, wishes to thrust upon her.

Thus he is said to have cast down Israel when whatever direction can be possessed in the mind with God is bent downward. “Directed by God,” or “with God,” is what Israel signifies. All his walls are cast down when the outward beauty of his restraint is dissolved. His fortifications are scattered when the established safeguards of spiritual custody are annulled.

He fills the daughter of Judah with humiliation, both man and woman, when, with the spirit cast down and the will also cast down, an effeminate confession fills the languid mind in place of the destroyed fortifications. For the daughter of Judah is an unprofitable and wicked confession.

Note the Hebrew manner of expression: “He filled the daughter of Judah with the humiliated man and the humiliated woman,” as elsewhere: “He filled the flesh for her” (Gen. 2:21), where we say: “He filled the daughter of Judah with the humiliated man and the humiliated woman.”

## VAU
## VERS. 6

“**He has scattered his tent like a garden; he has demolished his tabernacle.**”

Vau is interpreted as “possession,” which is none other than the one himself who is here compared with a garden, in whom a life-giving fruit had once grown. Therefore he scatters his tent like a garden when, having torn away the surrounding enclosure of vigilance and fear as though it were a hedge, he deprives the mind of its useful resources, as a garden is deprived of its fruits. And rightly he calls it a tent or tabernacle of conscience, not a house, because it has established nothing lasting or stable within itself, weakening its own condition through such ready abandonment; for both are temporary dwellings for pilgrims and soldiers.

“**The Lord has consigned festival and Sabbath to oblivion in Zion, and in the indignation of his anger he has delivered king and priest to disgrace.**”

God consigns festival and Sabbath in Zion to oblivion when he permits the continual practice of every virtue and the cessation of sin to be erased from a mind once devoted. The psalm appoints this solemn day “in the thick places” (Ps. CXVII, 27). He also delivers king and priest to disgrace when, with spiritual government altogether extinguished, he likewise annihilates the divine teaching that leads and instructs us in all holiness.

## ZAIN

### VERS. 7

“The Lord has rejected his altar, he has cursed his sanctification; he has delivered the walls of its towers into the hand of the enemy; they raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.”

Zain is interpreted as “nourishment.” The Lord rejects his altar when he despises the mind from which he had received the nourishment of good will and faith, once evil has arisen. He curses his sanctification when he brings to the deterioration of daily decline that which had once rightly been marked by the title of holiness. For “curse” is used for decline, just as “blessing” is used for increase.

By the walls, restraints upon the senses are signified; by the towers, the eminence of virtues. He delivers these into the hand of the enemy when he permits the devil to enter and occupy them. They raise their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day when, through the madness of depraved senses, they exult in the worst things. He does not say “on a solemn day,” but “as on one,” because some have no joy in accomplishing good works equal to their joy in carrying out evil.

## HETH

### VERS. 8

“The Lord has thought to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion; he has stretched out his measuring-line, and has not withdrawn his hand from destruction; and the outwork mourned, while the wall likewise was destroyed.”

Heth is interpreted as “fear,” and this arises from nothing other than the fact that the Lord thought to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion—that is, the continence of those imaginations that wander here and there. Hence the Lord says: “When you have shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. VI, 6).

God stretches out his measuring-line when he weighs sin and the punishments of sin upon us with an even balance. He does not withdraw his hand from destruction because, when the mind does not entreat God concerning its own ruin, manifest vengeance follows upon the divine thought. The outwork mourns when the outer sense, in sorrow, lies subject to desire. The wall is likewise destroyed when the license of imaginations, released everywhere, is scattered.

## TETH

### VERS. 9

“Her gates are driven into the ground; he has destroyed and shattered her bars, her king and her princes among the nations.”

Teth is interpreted as “good.” Her gates are driven into the ground when the obstacles of reason, which oppose vices—and which are the supreme good of the human being—are overwhelmed by earthly desires. Her bars are lost and crushed when spiritual impulses, without which reason cannot possess strength, are consumed. He loses her king and her princes among the nations when he submerges the spirit, whose task it is to govern all that is ours, in the passions of the senses and in monstrous vices.

“There is no law, and her prophets have found no vision from the Lord.” Where the spirit is not king, there is no law of any moderation. Her prophets do not find a vision from the Lord because they foresee nothing through inward providence except what benefits the world.

## JOD

### VERS. 10

“The elders sat on the ground and were silent; the daughters of Zion scattered ashes upon their heads, the virgins of Jerusalem.”

Jod means “confession”—certainly that confession which perishes with the dead (Ps. VI, 6). Hence the elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground and are silent, because, while they cling wholly to earthly things, like the one who sat in the seat of pestilence (Ps. I, 1), the more mature movements of the soul, which the consciousness of sin usually bites most terribly, fall silent instead of confessing.

Consequently, the virgins of Jerusalem scatter ashes upon their heads when those fallen and barren movements of former reconciliation are stained by the mind’s renewed rubbing against sin. For in Scripture it is a familiar usage for minds to be marked by ashes upon the head, signifying the memory of a sin once committed.

## CAPH  
*(The Vulgate places this before the following verse.)*

“**The virgins of Judah girded themselves with sackcloth; they cast their heads upon the ground.**”

Caph is said to mean “heart.” This is entirely appropriate, because everything that follows the letter consists wholly in damage to the interior. They gird themselves with sackcloth whose loins are pricked by the tickling of lust; the point being supported by the fact that it is a wanton animal, from whose hair it is woven. The virgins of Judah are the unfruitful duties of confession. For it is good to confess, provided that one also sings psalms. They cast their heads upon the ground when the principal movements of the mind, which sometimes admonish one toward confession, plunge themselves beneath a shame that is morally distorted.

### VERS. 11

“My eyes have failed because of tears; my inward parts have been troubled.”

The eyes fail because of tears when, through overflowing inward gentleness, the sharp points of the whole rational faculty fall away. The inward parts are troubled when, likewise, the inner vitality is drenched and overwhelmed by true discernment.

“My liver has been poured out upon the ground over the destruction of the daughter of my people, when the child and the suckling fainted in the streets of the city.”

According to the physicians, we love with the liver. Therefore the liver is poured out upon the ground when heavenly love is changed into earthly love. And this happens over the destruction of the daughter of the people, because such falls are nourished by the broken softness of thought. It also happens when the child and suckling faint in the streets of the city: that is, when scant faith and an appetite for worldly sweetness, through the cares of the world, produce the causes of destruction.

## LAMECH

### VERS. 12

“They said to their mothers: ‘Where are grain and wine?’ when they fainted like the wounded in the streets of the city, when they breathed out their souls in the bosoms of their mothers.”

Lamech is interpreted as “speech.” They say to their mothers, “Where are grain and wine?” when, at times, weary of pleasures, they demand from their consciences not only the consolation of the divine word, which the preceding letter signifies,[^c0043-250] but also an impulse of divine inspiration by which they may be made more energetic.

They faint like the wounded in the streets of the city when, struck by the arrow of diabolical desire, they perish through excessive license in worldly life. Here “city” and “town,” as elsewhere “court,” signify the world; the street of the narrow way is opposed to it. They breathe out their souls in the bosoms of their mothers when, within consciences—which are the mothers both of good and of evil interior realities—they strangle themselves in the noose of desire.

## MEN

### VERS. 13

“To whom shall I compare you? Or to whom shall I liken you, daughter of Jerusalem? To whom shall I equate you, and console you, virgin daughter of Zion? For great as the sea is your destruction. Who will heal you?”

Men means “inward parts,” plainly those of people who feel compassion for the misfortunes of those who are endangered in this way. The sense is therefore as though they said:

“You, soul, who ought to have been strengthened by devotion to your heavenly mother, by inward peace and contemplation of God—by comparison with whom could I lighten your fall, when your destruction, through a despairing forgetfulness of yourself, is swallowing you up? And when you no longer remember yourself, who will heal you by preaching to you?”

## NUN

### VERS. 14

“Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not uncover your iniquity, so as to summon you to repentance.”

Nun is interpreted as “their pasture,” undoubtedly referring to those who fed upon the lies of others. Our prophets see foolish and empty things for us when our worldly clevernesses not only promise false gains, as they usually do, but also, making conjectures about the future, advance us proudly in hope.

What follows is clear: although they ought to set before themselves the things in which they sin, they strive instead to think proudly. “They saw for you false assumptions and expulsions.” Assumptions are those by which they believe that they will be raised to worldly heights. But all these things are nothing other than expulsions, because, while they seek outward increases, they prostitute themselves through the most certain expulsion from the true good.

## SAMECH

### VERS. 15

“All who passed along the way clapped their hands over you; they hissed and shook their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem.”

Samech is interpreted as “help.” They clap their hands over her who once remained in the help of the Most High, rejoicing in her pious works according to what the letter had foretold. For clapping signifies rejoicing together; hands signify working.

All who passed along the way did this because, while the mind was in a good condition, all who eagerly aspire through Christ, who is the way, toward the homeland, rejoiced with her.

One who hisses blows out breath with a tightened mouth. And one who wisely praises someone for a good work speaks partly and partly refrains from speaking. “Do not praise a man during his lifetime,” it says (Eccli. II, 30). Yet he should certainly be praised, as Paul also does (I Cor. XI, 2), so that he may be encouraged; nevertheless, this should be done sparingly, lest he become overconfident. Hence they are said to shake their heads: although we marvel at the glorious way God works in them, meanwhile, because the end is uncertain, we must restrain our words.

“‘Is this the city,’ they say, ‘of perfect beauty, the joy of the whole earth?’”

The same shaking of the head is made over Job (Job XLII, 11) and over Jerusalem. But after her fall they lament that she had been a city of perfect beauty, remembering and proclaiming the beauty of her former condition with a now useless confidence. That perfect beauty, however, is changed into the joy of the whole earth when an example of ruin or obstinacy is thereby supplied to all who seek earthly things.

## AIN  
*(In printed editions, Phe is found in place of Ain, and Ain in place of Phe.)*

### VERS. 1

“All your enemies opened their mouths against you; they hissed, gnashed their teeth, and said: ‘We shall devour her. Behold, this is the day that we awaited; we have found it; we have seen it.’”

Ain is interpreted as “question.” And what greater question is there for the wicked than that something said or done by holy men should be found less reasonable? Therefore the enemies open their mouths against them—mouths which, while they were managing their own condition well, they had kept closed. Or they open their mouths when they expose biting consciences.

They hiss when, because of the fall of one person, they judge that the resolve of the whole of justice should now be rejected and cast down. For we hiss at those things that we utterly repudiate. They gnash their teeth when they strive to digest—or, to speak more precisely, to chew up—whatever other good may remain in them. And in another sense the enemies open their mouths over her when, having overrun her, they now reveal, as though freely, the counsels of the ancient enemy. They hiss when they sweetly murmur accusations. Yet they gnash their teeth because, amid the infliction [possibly: tickling] of pleasures, they grind the miserable mind with the hammer of the whole earth.

“‘We shall devour him,’” he says, that is, “we shall incorporate him into ourselves.” For thus the day—that is, the brightness of our prosperity—is both eagerly awaited and desired: long sought, finally found, and at last seen through experience.

## PHE

### VERS. 17

“The Lord has done what he thought; he has fulfilled his word which he commanded from ancient days; he has destroyed and did not spare; he has made the enemy rejoice over you; he has exalted the horn of your enemies.”

Phe is interpreted as “mouth.” With the mouth we bring to completion the secrets of our mind. The Lord does what he thinks when, through the pious execution of a work, he reveals those things that he insinuates into our heart by inspiring it. He completes his word when he himself accomplishes in us, and himself presents as an example, those things that he sows in us through his spirit.

He had commanded this from ancient days because through it he had instructed us by the earliest saints. For these are the days that are formed in the book of God. Through these days, by word and deed, command is given, by which our mind is illumined through the conception of the word.[^c0043-251]

But after this brightness the Lord destroys and does not spare when he permits those who had ascended to the heavens suddenly to fall into the abysses. He makes the enemy rejoice over her when he holds her beneath the enemy—that is, beneath the enemy’s will—and joyfully weighs her down. He exalts the horn of the enemies when he denies their pride the strength to resist. For our horn is the spirit’s rising above the flesh; the devil’s horn is the tossing of the miserable heart here and there.

## SADE

### VERS. 18

“Their heart cried out to the Lord over the walls of the daughter of Zion.”

Sade means “consolation.” Their heart—namely, the hearts of those who had earlier clapped their hands—cries out to the Lord over the walls of the daughter of Zion when, through frequent reflection, it weeps over the oppression of the fallen conscience. And what greater consolation can there be for any miserable soul than to know that it is cared for by holy men? This is what the letter signifies.

“Let your tears flow like a torrent by day and by night, and give yourself no rest, nor let the pupil of your eye be silent.”

This is the voice of those whose heart cries out to the Lord for the daughter of Zion. It is as though he said:

“Lead forth from your inner conscience into a manifest work of mercy, as though into a torrent that sweeps away every obstacle of vice, the tears of your inward breathing toward God—not only through the day of prosperity—for some confess when God has benefited them (Ps. XLVIII, 19)—but also through the night of adversity, in which his song was most clearly retained in the ears of God. Nor should you give yourself rest, that is, security, so as to presume upon the continuance of your sorrow; nor should the pupil of your eye be silent, that is, your spiritual sharpness should never assent to a depraved conscience, but should always remain watchful over its developments.”

## COPH

### VERS. 19

“Arise, praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches; pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord.”

Coph is said to mean “look.” The one addressed above is asked to look at where and how, and toward whom, he ought to arise from his former fall.

“Praise,” he says, “in the night,” that is, never depart from God in temptation. And do this “at the beginning of the watches,” namely, at the beginning of conversion, or in the earliest period of life itself. He is commanded to pour out his heart like water before the presence of the Lord because it is pleasing in no other way than when the conscience, inwardly—where God alone sees—becomes thin and clear, without scruple or any grossness of thought.

“Raise your hands to him for the souls of your little ones, who fainted from hunger at the head of all the crossroads.”

He raises his hands to him who exalts the good done in God’s name, not in human praise, and does not bend the work toward such praise. This is done for the souls of the little ones—that is, for the life of disciplines recently begun in holy profession. They faint from hunger who perish through lack of the word of God. “At the head of all the crossroads” means in the resolve governing all worldly actions.

## RES

### VERS. 20

“See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested.”

Res signifies “spirit.” Therefore those mentioned above cry out to the Lord to see and consider whom he has thus harvested—that is, to make us see and attend with our deepest heart how he has stripped the spirit, which properly desires against the flesh (Gal. V, 17), of so many fruits of vital light.

“Shall women then eat their fruit, the children scarcely a handbreadth in size? Shall priest and prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord?”

This means:

“If the guidance of sacred Scripture, which is a lamp to our feet (Ps. CXVIII, 105), and the providence that stands above our actions, is overthrown in the sanctuary of the Lord, which is the mind, I should like to know whether the weak minds signified by women—within whom these two things perish—will eat, that is, consume within themselves, the fruits of all their good action, recently begun and not yet reaching any perfection.”

The palm signifies a beginning; the cubit signifies fullness.

## SIN

### VERS. 21

“Child and old man have lain on the ground outside; my virgins and my young men have fallen by the sword. You killed them on the day of your anger; you struck them and did not show pity.”

Sin means “life”—not the life that is hidden with Christ in God (Col. III, 3), nor that by which we dwell in the present and are buried together with Christ himself (Rom. VI, 8, 4). Hence it is said that child and old man have lain on the ground outside.

Child and old man lie outside upon the ground when not only the carnal affection—which, like a child, is nothing more unstable or fickle in a human being—but also reason itself, which ought by its seniority to restrain the fleeting dispositions of the soul, cling wholly to earthly things.

Virgins and young men fall by the sword when, if any good has remained undefiled in the soul, and if anything strong and vigorous has endured in its conduct, all of it succumbs to some capital sin. He kills “on the day,” that is, in the manifestation, of his anger when he shows the inner downfall through the evidence of the outward ruin. He strikes and does not show pity when he permits one to fall but does not immediately grant contrition after the fall.

To this agrees the saying: “When the righteous man falls, he is not shattered, because the Lord supports his hand” (Ps. XXXVI, 24).

## THAU

### VERS. 22

“You have summoned, as for a solemn day, those who would terrify me from every side; and on the day of the Lord’s anger there was no one who escaped or was left behind.”

Thau is interpreted as “signs”—the signs prescribed upon the forehead, according to Ezekiel (Ezek. IX, 4, 6), of those who are shown to mourn over the evils of others. These are rightly set against the condemned here, who do not pity even themselves in their own punishment.

They are summoned as for a solemn day by those who terrify her from every side when, as though to a festive spectacle, those are summoned who outwardly pursue and accuse the miserable with threats and reproaches for their guilt.

On the day of the Lord’s anger there is no one who escapes and is left behind because, in this manifest vengeance, there is no movement of the soul that withdraws itself from sin and is reserved for repentance.

“Those whom I raised and nourished, my enemy has consumed.”

They are raised who are removed from temporal things and from desire for them. They are nourished when that same condition of ours is conducted under the fostering care and guardianship of reason. The enemy consumes them when he introduces a chaos of darkness into a mind that until then had been discerning.

# CHAPTER III

## ALEPH

### VERS. 1

“I am the man who sees my poverty beneath the rod of his indignation.”

In this third alphabet it should be observed that in each verse every letter is repeated three times. From this it may be inferred that, although there are four modes of sinning—suggestion, delight, consent, and action—greater caution of reason and teaching must be applied to consent alone. For if you restrain consent through the rebellion of the spirit, the shameful action that would cause you grief will never intrude upon you.

There are therefore some who fall but measure their fall with the greatest discernment. Here such a person speaks. He sees his poverty beneath the rod of God’s indignation: he attentively observes the poverty of his mind and the devastation of his inward powers while divine correction rages within him. Yet unless repentance intervenes, the mind itself does not discern this for long. Hence he is called “a man,” because he contemplates his losses with a mournful conscience. But it follows:

### VERS. 2

“He threatened me, led me into darkness, and not into light.”

He threatens when revived delight withdraws and separates the mind from consideration of itself. He leads into darkness when he drags it into ignorance of itself. To such a person it is said: “I will set you before your own face” (Ps. XLIX, 21). He does not lead into light when he is stripped not only of knowledge of himself but also of the pious instruction of all sacred Scripture, which our letter has expressed.

### VERS. 3

“He has turned and turned his hand against me all the day.”

This means:

“When God ought to have taken action against the vices that oppress me, he has instead allowed those vices, once raised up, to act only for my oppression. Nor is this all: he has turned his hand throughout the day, continually withdrawing from me the help of inward consolation after I had become hardened.”

Hence it is said that the beloved puts his hand through the opening (Song V, 4).

## BETH

### VERS. 4

“He has made my skin and my flesh old; he has shattered my bones.”

Beth means “confusion.” Our skin becomes old when our affection—by which nothing in the inner person is more quickly harmed—is worn away by the long accumulation of repeated falls, together with the flesh, that is, the will, which stands midway between skin and bones, that is, between affection and reason.

“For what grows old and becomes aged is near destruction” (Hebr. VIII, 13).

The bones are shattered when the firmness of the rational faculties, which ought to govern all that is fragile within us, is broken. Behold the evident confusion in the mind.

Observe the distinction between affection and will: we are affected by many things that we do not will, and we will many things by which we are not affected. The Apostle has the willing of the good according to the law of the mind, but according to the law of the members—which is affection—he does not find the power to accomplish it (Rom. VII, 18). We have discussed these matters more fully elsewhere.

### VERS. 5

“He built around me and surrounded me with gall and labor.”

He builds around us when he multiplies on every side the things we desire, by which we become more inwardly obstructed. He surrounds us with gall and labor when the sin he commits becomes harshly bitter, yet he nevertheless labors to commit sins.

### VERS. 6

“He placed me in dark places, like those who are eternally dead.”

He places us in dark places when God condemns the soul to confusion no longer as something temporary, but as though it were established permanently; and he does this as though to those eternally dead, that is, to those who have never recovered enough to perform any good acts.

## GHIMEL

### VERS. 7

“He built around me against me, so that I could not go out; he made my fetter heavy.”

Ghimel means “fullness.” He builds around us against us so that we cannot go out when, by a just judgment, he supplies from every side occasions for wrongdoing, by which we are bound irreversibly to vices as though in the prison of the body. He makes our fetter heavy when the weight of carnal desire burdens the liveliness of the spirit.

### VERS. 8

“Even when I cried out and pleaded, he excluded my prayer.”

Behold the fullness of evils. We cry out when, because of the atrocity of sin, we pour forth groans from our heart. We plead when, with whatever—even though dull—condition of mind, we practice not so much prayers as mere imitations of prayers. Yet the prayer is excluded when it is made under the affection of sin, according to the psalm (Ps. CVIII, 7).

### VERS. 9

“He enclosed my ways with squared stones; he overturned my paths.”

Our ways are enclosed with squared stones when, abandoning the example of those who are said to roll upon the earth, we diminish our ways—that is, our wicked actions—by imitating instead those who cling utterly to the earth on every side. The paths are overturned when the intentions, which are less conspicuous, are likewise corrupted.

## DALETH

### VERS. 10

“He became a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hidden places.”

Daleth is interpreted as “birth.” And what is it to be born except to be fashioned for crimes through the conception of an evil will? Job and Jeremiah curse and detest this birth (Job III, 1; Jer. XX, 14).

God therefore becomes for such a birth first a bear lying in wait—that is, a savage desire subjugating all our inward parts to itself. For it is the nature of bears to trample whatever they have seized with their feet. It is said that God does this because he permits it to be done. Hence in Hosea he testifies that he will become like a bear when its cubs have been taken away (Hos. XIII, 8).

He becomes a lion in hidden places when he drinks in whatever evil is suggested with insatiable greed. For it is the nature of a lion to drink all the blood of offered livestock before touching the flesh. Thus the bear lying in wait is the outer sense, lying in ambush; the lion in hidden places is the ferocity of the mind, seeking to satisfy itself.

### VERS. 11

“He overturned my paths and broke me; he left me desolate.”

The paths are overturned when, before the ruin, private exaltation is usually brought to confusion. Then one is broken when whatever was distinguished within is laid down. One is made desolate when deprived of God as its inhabitant.

### VERS. 12

“He bent his bow and set me as a target for the arrow.”

He bends his bow when he brings forward the sentences of Scripture that correspond to our condition. He sets us as a target for the arrow when, under continual fear, he declares that the darts of divine vengeance are being aimed at us by God.

## HE

### VERS. 13

“He sent the daughters of his quiver into my kidneys.”

He is interpreted as “salvation.” For what is more salutary than always to be driven on by fear of divine blows? The daughters of the quiver are, literally, nothing other than arrows. He sends the daughters of the quiver into the kidneys when he pierces the delights of our thoughts, or even of our body, with the judgments of heavenly counsel.

### VERS. 14

“I have become a laughingstock to all my people, their song all the day.”

He becomes a laughingstock to his people when his own thoughts promise his spirit no good success from what it has begun. He becomes their song all the day when, through the continual recurrence of thought, whatever good intention is grasped is judged to be about to pass immediately into the common tale, as something ridiculous.

### VERS. 15

“He filled me with bitterness; he made me drunk with wormwood.”

He is filled with bitterness who is constrained by remorse for crimes committed, though only for a moment. He is made drunk with wormwood who burns with desire and groans over what he has admitted. For, as someone has said, the desire for pleasures is full of anxiety, but satiety is full of repentance.

## VAU

### VERS. 16

“He broke all my teeth; he fed me ashes.”

Vau is also said to mean “and he.” The sense is:

“And he—the one who inflicted the things mentioned above upon me, though not unjustly—broke my teeth with gravel, that is, all of them: the intellectual faculties with which we grind whatever we think worthy of scrutiny. He feeds us ashes when he implants within us, with delight, the renewed rubbing of sin.”

He does this who permits it to be done.

### VERS. 17

“My soul has been rejected; I have forgotten good things.”

Our soul is rejected when its salvation is consigned to negligence. He forgets good things who, although oppressed by inward evils, in no way takes pleasure in remembering the good things he has done or may receive as a reward.

### VERS. 18

“And I said: My end and my hope from the Lord have perished.”

He says that his end has perished when what he had once proposed to do for an eternal reward becomes empty in his inmost self. His hope from the Lord also perishes when, occupied by temptations and as though unworthy of heavenly help, he now prepares even to depart from him.

## ZAIN

### VERS. 19

“My memory will remember, and my soul will waste away within me.”

[^c0043-Note: In Sixtus’s edition this verse is numbered 20, and the following verse 19.]

Zain is interpreted as “lead yourself.” It is as though he said:

“You said that your hope had perished, but do not remain in this folly. Rather, lead yourself—that is, advance yourself—so that you may strive toward the inner things.”

Hope is called *spes*, as though it were “there is hope.” With this admonition he adds:

“My memory will remember”—understand, one must not despair because of a fall, but rather cling to hope, so that the soul may waste away; that is, the animal part, which does not grasp the things of God, may, when the spirituality of holy hope arrives, fail within itself.

Thus he now begins to pray.

### VERS. 20

“Remember my poverty and my transgression, wormwood and gall.”

It is as though he said:

“Lord, you ought to remember that up to now I have sinned because of the poverty of my inward powers; and you ought no less to remember that I have endured that fall with the greatest anguish, and have been able to recall it only with immense bitterness.”

There appears to be a certain distinction between wormwood and gall. Wormwood can be taken as a drink: it produces heat and calms the blood; gall cannot do so at all. In wormwood, therefore, is the sorrow of a deed recently committed, which reheats us toward God and calms the incentive to crime; in gall is the memory of sin after repentance, utterly intolerable and unworthy of the mind.

### VERS. 21

“Remembering these things in my heart, therefore I will hope.”

This means:

“While I review these things in my thought, I summon myself to hope.”

Hence it follows:

## HETH

### VERS. 22

“The mercies of the Lord are many, for we have not been consumed, for his compassions have not failed.”

Heth is said to mean “narration.” And what is this narration except to weave together, before the eyes of the heart, the mercies of God experienced even while sinning?

These mercies are therefore present because we have not been consumed, since he brings us, even in the sinful act itself, nearer to salvation. Otherwise they would certainly fail if his mercies yielded to our iniquities.

### VERS. 23

“I know at daybreak: great is your faith.”

This means that God says to the soul:

“From your diligence and vigilance I know that you possess great faith.”

For “morning” is frequently used for diligence, as is “daybreak.” If, according to certain copies—though I do not know whether they are corrupt—the reading is *novae* (“new”) rather than *novo* (“anew”), it may be explained in this way:

“The former mercies are those often bestowed upon the ungrateful, and these are only temporal. The new mercies are those that shine like daybreak through a fresh illumination in the minds of converts, and these are eternal.”

Then what follows will be an apostrophe by him to God, as he rejoices in this way over the mercies.

### VERS. 24

“The Lord is my portion, said my soul; therefore I will wait for him.”

He says:

“I do not await temporal mercies from God; rather, I take God himself as the retributive portion of my soul. Therefore, with living hope, I await not something transitory belonging to him, but him himself.”

## TETH

### VERS. 25

“The Lord is good to those who hope in him.”

Teth is interpreted as “good.” For the more ardently you go toward God in hope, the more deeply and ineffably you will understand that he is good.

### VERS. 26

“To the soul that seeks him. It is good to wait silently for the salvation of the Lord.”

For the soul that seeks nothing except God—for one who strives in two directions cannot rightly be said to have sought God—it is good, without any preparation, not to grow weary of God’s service amid the labors of the day. For thus one sleeps “in the midst of the lots” (Ps. LXVII, 14). What is called “silence” here is called “sleep” there.

### VERS. 27

“It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth.”

He bears the yoke from his youth who, in response to the impulses of youth, chastises himself beneath the discipline of divine fear.

## JOD

### VERS. 28

“He will sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself.”

Jod is interpreted as “beginning,” though this beginning refers not so much to an initial point as to a certain primacy. He appears to be explaining the yoke in detail.

He sits alone who restrains himself in humility, removing himself from earthly commotions. He is silent when, after putting to sleep the trifles of thoughts and imaginations, he speaks in prayer to God alone. This could happen in no other way than by lifting himself above himself—that is, by subjecting his animality to spirituality.

### VERS. 29

“He will place his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there is hope.”

He places his mouth in the dust who, however exalted his conduct may be, nevertheless always recognizes himself as dust—that is, as a sinner. For it was said to the sinner: “You are dust” (Gen. III, 19). He does this “if perhaps there is hope,” so that he may always seem to himself to hope for rewards from God as though the matter were uncertain.

### VERS. 30

“He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches.”

Anyone gives his cheek to the one who strikes him when he exposes to those wishing to inflict injuries, rather than defending, whatever is presently known to be dearer and more esteemed by him. He is filled with reproaches who considers the insults themselves his highest refreshments.

## CAPH

### VERS. 31

“For the Lord will not reject forever.”

Caph is said to mean “bent down,” though not toward earthly things; rather, he is depressed by a salutary consideration for his own self-contempt. It is as though he said:

“He is not unjustly humbled, because he is not rejected forever, even though he may seem to be handed over to present lowliness. For the ends of the earth are in God’s hand—those, namely, who consume earthliness within themselves. Although he has cast them down in this world by afflicting them, he will nevertheless have mercy in the future according to the multitude of his compassions.”

### VERS. 33

“For he has not humbled from his heart, nor cast away the children of man.”  
[Other copies: “children of men.”]

God humbles from the heart those whom he punishes in the present in such a way that he punishes them even more at the time of retribution. For the present he scourges and rejects the children of man only in appearance, when he makes the children of the Redeemer exiles from worldly joy.

He did not say “of men,” but “of man”—plainly of the one who said: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV, 20).

## LAMETH  
[Other copies: LAMED]

### VERS. 34

“To crush beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth.”

It is said to the servant; yet we preserve what we have as a mystery. The mystery is that we are worn down by the pressures of this age, while we are uncertain about the condition of the life to come.

The sense is therefore:

“He does indeed cast away the children of man, in order to crush all the prisoners of the earth beneath his feet, so that all who are bound by the affairs of this age or by any vices may be broken under the example of his preachers.”

This means:

“If the children of God and man, insofar as they appear to the eyes, are cast away, how much more do the children of the devil deserve, once they have been brought back to adoption as children of God, to be shown as not merely belonging to God but also to his servants, who are his feet because they carry him about by preaching—not as existing or standing, but as crushed, that is, utterly humbled?”

The Lord leads out the prisoners “in strength,” according to the psalm (Ps. LXVII, 7).

### Verse 35

“**To turn aside the judgment of a man before the presence of the face of the Most High.**”

The judgment of a man is turned aside before the presence of the face of the Most High when we know without doubt that we are devoted to good works, yet do not know whether we are worthy of hatred or of love (Eccles. 9:1). We therefore turn our judgment toward the face of the Most High when we reserve for his balance whatever measure we take of ourselves.

[Col. 0472D] **Verse 36.** “**To pervert a man in his judgment: the Lord did not know.**”

He cast away, I say, the sons of man in order to pervert a man in his judgment, so as to show that God had not ordained matters in such a way that good things would presently be repaid to those doing good things. For human custom has become so ingrained that they scarcely consider anyone good who is oppressed by evils to have proved himself good; this had grown strong, indeed, in the opinion of Job’s friends. But the Lord does not know this, since he often grants evils to the good and good things to the wicked, and at times grants to both what corresponds to their deserts.

### MEM

**Verse 37.** “**Who is he who said that it should happen, when the Lord had not commanded it?**”

Mem is interpreted as “the inward parts.” The prophet therefore cries out against those who complain about such things; [Col. 0473A] according to them the psalm was composed: “How good is the God of Israel!” (Ps. 72:1). He says that something happens without the Lord’s command who, seeing those whom he knows to live wickedly nevertheless healthy, unharmed, and prosperous, believes that they are governed by fortune rather than by God’s judgment.

**Verse 38.** “**From the mouth of the Most High neither good things nor evils go forth.**”

Neither good things nor evils go forth from the mouth of the Most High, because it is never believed that, strictly speaking, good things have presently come to the good by decision, nor, again, evils specifically to the wicked. In both cases they fall short, because such things are common to both.

**Verse 39.** “**Why does a living man murmur, a man because of his sins?**”

A living man [Col. 0473B] murmurs because, while he lives in sins, he does not look at the sins he commits when some adversity overtakes him; instead, he justifies himself by comparing himself with those who seem to do worse things. A man also murmurs because of his sins when, while suffering, he does not accuse his own sins but assails God, who strikes excessively, with complaints.

### NUN

**Verse 40.** “**Let us examine our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord.**”

Nun means “everlasting.” If we are punished for a time on account of sin, it is not fitting for us to murmur, but rather to hasten toward the everlasting one, who is God. Therefore let us examine our ways—that is, let us scrutinize our actions. Let us also seek the Lord and return to him: let us apply ourselves attentively to the Scriptures [Col. 0473C], seeking there the things by which we may be pierced with remorse and, through preceding contrition, be led to him.

**Verse 41.** “**Let us lift our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens.**”

We lift our hearts with our hands when, together with the execution of our works, we raise our understanding to God, without aspiring to any lowly praise, extending it solely in hope of heavenly things.

**Verse 42.** “**We have acted wickedly and provoked to anger; therefore you are inexorable.**”

The matter is clear; let us continue with the rest. Yet this seems worth considering: here God is called inexorable on account of iniquities, and elsewhere is said not to hear sinners (John 9:31). This is resolved in a single statement: namely, that as long as they are proved to persevere in the intention of sinning, they both make God inexorable and are by no means heard.

### SAMECH

[Col. 0473D] **Verse 43.** “**You have covered us in fury, struck us, killed us, and have not spared.**”

Samech is interpreted as “hear.” For, however much more inexorable he is thought to be, he must hear if he is called upon with greater insistence, once the dense mass of depraved desires has been removed. We are covered in fury when, as the cloud of crimes rushes upon us, we are crushed by the night of folly. We are struck when we are cast down from all integrity. God kills and does not spare when he extinguishes the spirit from his own light; yet he would spare us if even a spark of some good will remained in us.

[Col. 0474A] **Verse 44.** “**You have set a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through.**”

A cloud is set before him when the obstacle of our evil intention is stretched out between us and God. Prayer does not pass through when the thickness of ill will has beaten it back.

**Verse 45.** “**You have made me eradication and rejection in the midst of the peoples.**”

He did not say, “You have eradicated me,” but “You have made me eradication.” Eradication or rejection becomes or is imposed upon that mind which makes itself a pestilence to all inward goodness. For he eradicates and rejects when he tears out from himself the good things naturally implanted in him and arrogantly excludes them. This happens in the midst of the peoples, amid the din of the many vices that surround the ears of the mind.

### PHE

[Col. 0474B] **Verse 46.** “**All our enemies have opened their mouth against us.**”

Phe is interpreted as “mouth.” And what mouth is this, except the one that whispers all obscene actions to the mind already wholly inclined toward perversity? All our enemies open this mouth against us when they burst forth unhesitatingly to inflame our conscience through every kind of crime.

**Verse 47.** “**Prophecy and contrition have become for us a snare and dread.**”

The order is: “Prophecy and contrition have become for us a snare and dread.” Prophecy occurs when a mind possessed by vices promises itself prosperous outcomes and hopes of glory. But contrition follows this prophecy, because the more it exalts itself without regard for itself, the more grievously it is suddenly oppressed by sin. Both then become dread and a snare for the wretched soul: fear of biting guilt interrupts its prophecy, while the snare of despair lies beside its contrition and closes off the spirit of confession.

[Col. 0474C] **Verse 48.** “**My eye has brought down streams of waters in the contrition of the daughter of my people.**”

The waters are divided when whatever spiritual subtleties of understanding may have remained are scattered. The eye brings these down while the people are being crushed, because, when the acuity of intention begins to lie beneath crimes, it is gradually weakened within and pours itself out externally.

### AIN

[Col. 0474D] **Verses 49–50.** “**My eye is afflicted and has not kept silent, because there was no rest, until the Lord would look down and see from the heavens.**”

The eye is afflicted and does not keep silent when intention is worn down by vices, nor does it restrain itself from the tumult of desires, while conscience also afflicts itself by accusation. This happens because there is no rest—that is, no moderation from the inner heat—until the Lord looks down and sees from the heavens; that is, until the Lord takes pity and approves our conversion through imitation of a heavenly way of life.

**Verse 51.** “**My eye has plundered my soul among all the daughters of my city.**”

Ain is interpreted as “eye.” And what is the eye except that same intention, which plunders the soul by taking away, through its own transgression, all that it once seems to exercise well, while it pursues outward praises?

[Col. 0475A] But this happens only among the daughters of its city—that is, in the softness of the dispositions of our conscience.

### SADE

**Verse 52.** “**My enemies have hunted and captured me like a bird, without cause.**”

Sade is called “justice,” though this justice seems to me to be nothing other than what is repaid to each person, even in the present, according to merit by the just judgment of God. Hence he complains that he has been captured by his enemies through hunting like a bird, because, through the fickleness represented by the bird, he is ensnared without cause and without any profit by empty favors from those who seek only carnal things. And rightly does he call them enemies, since, according to the prophet, in declaring him blessed they prove to be deceivers (Isa. 3:12).

[Col. 0475B] **Verse 53.** “**My life has fallen into a pit, and they have placed a stone over me.**”

Life falls into a pit when our condition inclines toward an inextricable labyrinth. A stone is placed over it when the hardening of the mind is brought upon thought submerged in the lowest things. Hence the psalm says: “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16). What there is “to close over,” here is “to place a stone over.”

**Verse 54.** “**The waters have flooded over my head. I said: I am lost.**”

The waters flood over the head when the flow of carnal pleasures accumulates upon the mind beyond what it can contain. Hence he says that he has perished, because he does not know how he might escape.

### COPH

[Col. 0475C] **Verse 55.** “**I called upon your name, Lord, from the lowest pit.**”

Coph means “calling.” We are called when, amid inward troubles, we are rationally admonished to have recourse to the divine oracle. “I called upon your name, Lord,” means nothing other than “From the depths I cried to you” (Ps. 129:1). What is “from the depths” is here “from the lowest pit.”

**Verse 56.** “**You heard my voice; do not turn your ear from my sobbing and cries.**”

The voice of one crying from the lowest pit is heard when an inward groan from an almost despairing condition is admitted into the divine ears. For God to hear means to raise, even slightly, the desire of the spirit against the flesh. Sobbing occurs when the mind is first shaken by the anxiety of fear; a cry occurs when it is lifted up by the vehemence of fervent contrition. God’s ear is not turned away from these when both are supported by the nourishment of his inspiration.

[Col. 0475D] **Verse 57.** “**You drew near on the day when I called upon you. You said: Do not be afraid.**”

This is to say: When the pit was growing dark for me, you granted me the day of inner light through your nearness. You did not say, “Do not cry out,” but rather, “Do not be afraid,” so that what you conceived through fear you might manifest through love.

### RES

**Verse 58.** “**You have judged, Lord, the case of my soul, my Redeemer of life.**”

Res is called “primacy.” Nor is this unjustly said. For after divine hearing, the mind’s principate of free judgment, which it had lost, returns to reason. The Lord judges the case of our soul when he distinguishes the claims of flesh and spirit. He is therefore called the Redeemer of our life, because in his mercy he deigns to rescue from ancient miseries the movements of reason, without which one does not live.

[Col. 0476A] **Verse 59.** “**You saw, Lord, the iniquity against me; judge my judgment.**”

The Lord sees the iniquity against us when he makes us see bodily impulses riding above the spirit. He judges our judgment when, by his inward visitation, he illumines our understanding so that it may discern all things.

**Verse 60.** “**You saw all their fury, all their thoughts against me.**”

The fury [Col. 0476B] of vices is what, in Job, is called the cry of the exactor (Job 39:7). “Their thoughts” are those things which they heap up before the eyes of the mind through an imagination of every kind. For *cogito* is a frequentative from *cogo, cogis*—“I compel, you compel”—and means nothing other than “to gather together.” Hence the saying: “Gather the assembly” (Isa. 16:3). God sees these thoughts, I say, when he sharpens our discernment to foresee them.

### SIN

**Verse 61.** “**You heard their reproaches, Lord, all their thoughts against me.**”

Sin is called “over a wound.” Morally, it is appropriate that a poultice be placed upon a wound. This means nothing other than what follows: whatever is deliberately committed as sin is always loved, and therefore is less charged as a reproach. God therefore hears their reproaches when he makes them understand, through the fullness of repentance, how reproachful and shameful they are.

It should be noted that he repeats what had been said in the preceding verse, and perhaps not without reason: “All their thoughts against us.” For the more ashamed we are of them, and the greater our rebellion against these same things, the sharper the inward assaults we shall experience.

[Col. 0476C] **Verse 62.** “**The lips of those rising up against me, and their meditations against me all day long.**”

The lips of those rising up against me are nothing other than the murmurs of emerging suggestions. For silent temptations are nothing other than words; what others accomplish through words, temptations accomplish through the seduction of images. Their meditations are known to be the reconsiderations, or rather the delights, of images. These occur all day long, undoubtedly without interruption.

[Col. 0476D] **Verse 63.** “**Look upon their sitting and their rising; I am their psalm.**”

Their sitting is the counterfeit repose of vices produced by diabolical cunning. For temptation rests for a time in order unexpectedly to overthrow what it has permitted to live securely for a while. Their rising, moreover, is the sudden invasion of minds. We ask that God look upon it—that is, that he make us discern it—so that, while we are lulled in some superficial peace, we may never be suddenly thrown down and crushed.

Finally, he becomes their psalm when the intention of the suggestion is nourished by the foolish reconsideration of the hearts of those who are tempted. For a psalm is nothing other than what is commonly called a *ladius*, which is produced without the exercise of the voice, by strings and hands. Thus, just as a psalm delights the ears, so the revolving of thought is recognized as soothing and nourishing images of evil spirituality.

### THAU

**Verse 64.** “**Repay them their recompense, Lord, according to the works of their hands.**”

Thau is interpreted as “has completed.” God completes those whose prolonged wavering he determines with a fixed end. He repays recompense according to works when, night after night, he suggests baths of tears for washing the bed.

[Col. 0477A] **Verse 65.** “**You will give them a shield of the heart, your labor.**”

The labor of God occurs when vices are resisted with appropriate vigor. This labor becomes a shield of the heart, by which every dart of the devil is turned back. It is repaid to them in place of their works, so that from the place where they had entered arrogantly they may be driven out with deserved severity.

[Col. 0477B] **Verse 66.** “**You will pursue them in fury and crush them beneath the heavens, Lord.**”

They are pursued in fury when they are extricated from the soul by complete divine punishment. They are also crushed beneath the heavens when they are broken under the authority of the virtues. He calls the virtues “heavens,” in which alone God gladly dwells.

## CHAPTER IV

### ALEPH

**Verse 1.** “**How the gold has grown dark, the finest color has changed, the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street!**”

Aleph, as above, signifies doctrine [Col. 0477C], the explanation of which may depend upon the following verse. The question, then, is how gold becomes dark—that is, how the knowledge of God, which is nothing other than love, than which nothing is more precious, and in which we are taught everything that must be known and done, is so greatly weakened in the mind from its former appearance.

The finest color changes when the purity of thought is turned aside. The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street when the brightest and clearest rational faculties in all holy prudence are divided from their simplicity toward God by the pleasures and glories of the world—for these are the primary purpose of all worldly license.

### BETH

**Verse 2.** “**The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed with the finest gold [Col. 0477D]: how have they been reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of the potter’s hands?**”

Beth means “confusion.” For who is more justly confounded than one who is reduced from such great worth almost to nothing? The illustrious sons of Zion are intellectual movements, entirely free through masculine virtue. They are clothed with the finest gold when they are adorned with the privileges of divine wisdom. They are reckoned as earthen vessels when they have already fallen into fragile works. They are the work of the potter’s hands because, through such a perverse way of life, they now have the devil as their creator. That Pharaoh signifies him who compelled the Israelites to serve in mud, brick, and straw.

### GHIMEL

**Verse 3.** “**Even the lamias expose the breast; they suckle their young. The daughter of my people has become cruel, like an ostrich in the desert.**”

Ghimel means “retribution.” Since our merits demand such things, we receive the infamies of our falls as retribution. It is therefore as if he said: They do not merely fall into earthly pursuits; having become lamias, they also expose the breast when, under the appearance of kindness, they compel others to perpetrate the same things they themselves do, through the poisonous sweetness of words and a certain feminine flattery.

A lamia is a monster that has a woman’s form as far as the waist. They therefore expose the breast when they proclaim doctrine in order to propagate the things they do. They suckle their young when, by their seductions, they entice others toward beastlike practices.

“The daughter of this people is cruel [Col. 0478A] like an ostrich in the desert,” because those who above were called sons are now, through the feminization of their conduct, designated by the name of daughters. They are cruel [Col. 0478B] because those whom diabolical persuasion has begotten they hide beneath earthly frivolity. For the nature of the ostrich is to lay its eggs on the ground and leave them covered with dust. It is also said to feed on iron, undoubtedly because such people are filled with malignities as though with food.

### DALETH

**Verse 4.** “**The tongue of the suckling has clung to its palate in thirst. The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.**”

Daleth is interpreted as “tablets.” And who are the tablets except those who, having cut away from themselves the strength of inward fullness, are weakened by thought and action from the hardness of virtue?

The tongue of the suckling clings to its palate in thirst when, as the water of saving wisdom [Col. 0478C] fails, the speech of one nourished on monstrous milk restrains itself in conformity with the one from whom it had received the saliva of poisonous teaching. For saliva proceeds from the palate, and the tongue is bound to the palate when the words of the disciple are carved out by the wickedness of the teacher.

The little ones ask for bread when those who are more innocent and less imbued with perversity demand life-giving instruction, but expositors are altogether lacking.

### HE

**Verse 5.** “**Those who ate delicately have perished on the roads; those who were nourished in saffron garments have embraced dung.**”

He is said to mean “this.” And what is “this” except the present things? One eats delicately who takes pleasure in the divine utterances only for the sake of present glory. Such a person perishes on the roads because, adulterating the word of God concerning the things that pertain to God [Col. 0478D] and seeking favor, he departs from himself and is lost.

Saffron is golden in color and fragrant. One is nourished in saffron garments who glories either in the appearance of holiness or in the reputation of wisdom. Such people embrace dung when, wanting great things to be understood about themselves, they suddenly rush down with shameful eagerness to the lowest things, which the Apostle considers to be dung (Phil. 3:8). Our present text looks toward this.

### VAU

**Verse 6.** “**The iniquity of the daughter of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and hands did not seize it.**”

Vau is interpreted as “he himself,” undoubtedly the same one who, as we said above, signifies the present things; he is found to desire them.

The iniquity of this daughter of the people [Col. 0479A] becomes greater than the sin of Sodom, because just as the weight of silver differs from the weight of lead, so the sins of the simple and dull plainly differ from the sin of those who eat delicately and are nourished in scarlet.

Sodom is interpreted as “a silent beast.” And what is a beast except inborn stupidity, whose understanding has no voice? This Sodom is overthrown in a moment because it is easily overthrown and prone to fall if anyone attacks it in any way. “Hands do not seize it” because whatever enters such a mind is gladly admitted as a shameful deed. Hands also do not seize it when they desire to do more than the capacity for action can bear.

### ZAIN

**Verse 7.** “**Her Nazirites were whiter than snow [Col. 0479B], brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire.**”

Zain means “the nourishment of the world.” And by whom is the world nourished more than by the illustrious sons of Zion, who are clothed with the finest gold? He therefore continues by describing them.

Nazirite is interpreted as “holy.” It is as if he said: Those who once flourished in the purity of holiness—for these three things are signified by “Nazirite”—are whiter than snow through their desire for heavenly glory, since snow falls from heaven; brighter than milk through the innocence of simple action, since milk is born from flesh; and redder than ancient ivory through their endurance of bodily stimulation, being more thoroughly tested than some ancient holy person by the very incentives that provoke them. For the elephant, from which ivory comes, is of a cold nature.

Finally, they are more beautiful than sapphire [Col. 0479C], and more worthy than the many whose way of life is said to be in heaven (Phil. 3:20); for sapphire is of an ethereal appearance.

### HETH

**Verse 8.** “**Their face has become blacker than coals, and they were not recognized in the streets. Their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood.**”

Heth means “life.” If pride, by which we fall, produces death through its ruin, humility, by which we are truly lifted up, strengthens life.

Thus their face is darkened above coals when all their beauty is judged worthy of being despised in their own consideration, even more than that of those sinners who are reckoned to have been extinguished by sin. Hence the bridegroom’s locks are said to be black like a raven (Song 5:11).

They are not recognized in the streets [Col. 0479D] because they are not seen amid the broad and spacious concerns of this world. Their skin clings to their bones because affectivity, and even the ease of sensation itself, has joined itself indivisibly to the strength of reason. It dries up when it is emptied of every flow of wantonness, and becomes like wood when it grows firm into the hardness of impassibility.

### TETH

**Verse 9.** “**It was better for those killed by the sword than for those killed by hunger, because these wasted away, consumed by the barrenness of the earth.**”

Teth is called “exclusion.” It is better for those killed by the sword than for those killed by hunger, because it is lighter to fall through a sudden lapse into sin without any deliberation than gradually to grow sluggish through prolonged failure.

For these have wasted away, consumed by the barrenness [Col. 0480A] of the earth, because they have been handed over to the stench of vices through the uncultivated state and prolonged neglect of their mind. Hence these are deservedly excluded from the preceding people, according to the meaning of the letter already mentioned, because no fruitfulness of the heart—earthly not, but stony—follows them.

### JOD

**Verse 10.** “**The hands of compassionate women cooked their children; they became their food, in the contrition of the daughter of my people.**”

Jod is desolation. And what is more desolate than what is emptied of God as its guest?

The hands of compassionate women cook their children when the works of men who have rejected the faith, possessing nothing of intellectual character, soften those whom they have drawn into conformity with their examples, bringing them into conformity with themselves by the fire of deceitful persuasion.

[Col. 0480B] They are ironically called “compassionate women,” because on one side they deceive through the softness of seductions, while on the other they intrude under the guise of kindness, indeed as though offering counsel. Their children become their food when they strive to incorporate them into themselves. From this the daughter of the people is crushed, since it is not the son of reason—who, according to the Apocalypse, is brought to the throne of God (Rev. 12:5)—but the unstable daughter of inward vulgarity who is continually overwhelmed.

### CAPH

**Verse 11.** “**The Lord has fulfilled his fury, poured out the anger of his indignation, kindled a fire in Zion, and devoured its foundations.**”

Caph is interpreted as “operation.” This operation is said to be nothing other than a certain effect of the iniquity previously described, just as the punishment of sin is produced from sin.

Therefore the Lord completes his fury [Col. 0480C], so that he who was angry at sin may now, in his fury, inflict the sentence of punishment. He pours out the anger of his indignation when he exposes the wretched conscience to the mockeries of temptation. He kindles a fire in Zion when God permits the flames of carnal wantonness to be inserted into the mind accustomed to contemplate God. He devours its foundations when he consumes and abolishes the subsistence of every good intention.

### LAMED

**Verse 12.** “**The kings of the earth and all the inhabitants of the world did not believe that an enemy and adversary would enter through the gates of Jerusalem.**”

Lamed is called “the heart of servitude.” The heart of servitude is understood as the understanding that is possessed not through reason, which commands, but through sensation, which serves.

[Col. 0480D] The kings of the earth are rational movements that dispose all our earthly things. The inhabitants of the earth are our members upon the earth, or any bodily dispositions. They do not believe that an enemy and adversary will enter through the gates of Jerusalem, because, already made sluggish through the quiet of former habits, they did not suppose that the ancient enemy, followed by the hostility of natural appetite, would attempt to suggest anything through the senses once dedicated to the vision of peace.

### MEM

**Verse 13.** “**Because of the sins of its prophets and the iniquities of its priests, who poured out the blood of the just in its midst.**”

Mem means “the inward parts.” And what are the inward parts except the very intention of thought [Col. 0481A], which, like the inward parts in the body, lies hidden beneath thoughts in the mind? Hence the Apostle calls the Holy Spirit the discerner of thoughts and intentions (Heb. 4:12).

The sins of the prophets and the iniquities of the priests are therefore the cause of inward punishment. The iniquity of the priests—that is, of the rational movements that ought to have guided us beneficially—is that they do not judge equally between the impulse of flesh and spirit.

The sins of the prophets—that is, of foresight—are that they do not look ahead to punishments or rewards in the future age, but promise themselves in the present whatever boastful things might arise by chance. These pour out the blood of the just in their midst when they turn into sins the things that could naturally have accorded with justice within them.

### NUN

[Col. 0481B] **Verse 14.** “**The blind wandered in the streets; they were defiled with blood. And when they were unable to do so, they held their garments.**”

Nun is called “their pasture.” Their pasture is whatever worldly cares is available to them. Hence the blind wander in the streets because, without any light of discernment, they have scattered themselves among worldly affairs. They are defiled with blood when, amid those affairs, they are infected by every contagion of crime.

And when they have no opportunity to sin, they hold their garments, because they never endure being without intentions of sinning. For just as a cloak is fastened by its strips, so worldly care is entwined with depraved intentions.

### SAMECH

[Col. 0481C] **Verse 15.** “**Depart, you defiled ones,” they cried to them; “depart, go away, do not touch.” For they quarreled and, stirred up, said among the nations: “He will no longer continue to dwell among them.”**

Samech is called “hear.” They are plainly urged to hear, since those defiled with blood are shouted at to depart from their pollution. Those who cry out are either the divine words that thunder forth or the intellectual faculties that naturally rebuke what is done wickedly.

They depart if they withdraw from perverse execution; they go away if they recover from the vanities of their intentions. They are forbidden to touch when they are commanded not to direct their affection toward that thing.

They have quarreled when, through their perception of the divine utterance, they conceive inward disputes against their own senselessness. They are stirred up when they are troubled in the very course of their debate. Hence they are said at once to turn back toward eternal pursuits—that is, they resolve that God will no longer dwell in them among the nations [Col. 0481D]: namely, that God will by no means enter again to remain in minds once possessed by so many crimes.

### PHE

**Verse 16.** “**The face of the Lord divided them; he will no longer continue to look upon them. The faces of the priests did not blush, nor did they have pity on the elders.**”

Phe is interpreted as “mouth.” The mouth, however, is nothing other than the very face of God joined to it. “The face of the Lord,” he says, “divided them,” because, while in that inward conflict they picture for themselves in the mind, on one side, tears of repentance and, on the other, worldly wantonness, they seem to set their faces before the face of the heavenly Judge. When they have perceived the difficulty of holy conduct, they turn back, as though from the mouth of God, to easier purposes.

And because they are thus carried toward sins by deliberation, God does not continue to look upon them through the presentation of repentance. The faces of the priests did not blush when they shamelessly resisted reason admonishing them together with God. Nor did they have pity on the elders when they sometimes offered incentives to sin even to mature states of life that had grown weary of sins.

### AIN

**Verse 17.** “**While we still endured, our eyes failed for our empty help, when we looked attentively toward a nation that could not save us.**”

Ain is called “fountain” or “eye.” In either the fountain or the eye, intention is understood, from which everything we conceive in the mind emerges.

Hence, while we still endure [Col. 0482B]—that is, after abandoning God, when we decide to restrain ourselves from crimes solely for the sake of worldly respectability—our eyes fail for our empty help when our intentions, resting upon a fragile support, suddenly wither.

For a person restrains himself only briefly when it is not God but Egypt that offers aid; indeed, Egypt pierces the hand of the one leaning upon it. Egypt not only cannot save, but foolishly condemns its own work before God.

Yet something should be observed in these two later alphabets, which differs from the earlier ones, and certainly not without reason. In these later alphabets, the two characters—Phe and Ain—are transposed; in the earlier ones, Ain is properly placed before Phe.

I recall having said that in this lament [Col. 0482C] four kinds of sin are indicated four times. Moreover, in the two final letters—the penultimate and the last—consent and action are understood, just as in the two earlier letters suggestion and delight are understood.

In the first pair, therefore, Ain is placed before Phe, to indicate that in suggestion and delight the mind does not exceed its order, since intention appears to precede whatever action of the little delight may follow.

But after consent and action have succeeded in the mind, the eye of perverse foresight goes downward, because the whole mind passes into outward affections. For what does intention do there, where action itself, having been placed after it, is already raging?

Consent is plainly a component of execution [Col. 0482D], as is shown in the Gospel by the young man carried out beyond the gate (Luke 7:12). Therefore, in consent and action there is a proper alteration of the order of the letters, so that intention subsides precisely where the whole mind has already advanced itself into the pursuit of action.
