The threefold arrangement that is placed first in the third alphabet is nothing other than the instruction of sacred speech for the protection of thought, speech, and actions; for these are necessary in three ways to restrain falls. Just as modesty is useful before a fall but, after a fall, becomes an obstruction to holy confession, so intention requires much watchful care before sin; but once it passes into perverse action, it remains sluggish and almost nonexistent, because after it has satisfied its own will it has nowhere toward which to direct itself.

### SADE

[Col. 0483A] **Verse 18.** “**Our footsteps slipped on the path of our streets; our end drew near; our days were completed, because our end came.**”

Sade means “justice,” which, as above, refers to the just judgments of God.

Those who had looked toward a nation—that is, toward the cleverness of human foresight, which could not save them—now say that their footsteps slipped on the path of their streets, when they perceive their affections being undermined through investigations born of worldly cares.

Their end draws near when the sin that the mind had determined is completed in action. Their days are completed when their virtues are consumed. And this happens because their end has come—that is, the complete abandonment of their minds.

### COPH

[Col. 0483B] **Verse 19.** “**Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven; they pursued us over the mountains and lay in wait for us in the desert.**”

Coph means “conclusion.” We are plainly enclosed when we are constricted by the multitude of vices.

Hence our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven when the incentives of the flesh, which naturally weigh upon us, become through habitual use even more ravenous than the demons themselves. Eagles signify this because of their rapacity.

They pursue us over the mountains when they destroy us in our very pride. They lie in wait for us in the desert when, because of our crimes, they seize upon us as people deserted by God.

### RES

[Col. 0483C] **Verse 20.** “**The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, has been captured in our sins. To him we said: In your shadow we shall live among the nations.**”

Res is called “spirit.” The breath of our mouth, however, is the understanding of our heart. “Mouth” is used for “heart,” as in: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom” (Ps. 36:30), and: “Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing” (Ps. 118:108).

That Spirit is called Christ the Lord because it especially belongs to him to be anointed by God, and it is no less fitting that he should rule. He is captured in our sins when, as their servitude overtakes him, he is deprived of the freedom of his own judgment.

“To him we say” means that we attribute to him the fact that we can live in the nations under his shadow: namely, that under the appearance of reason, and not in the unleavened bread of sincerity, we are able to conceal ourselves among vices by that worldly caution [Col. 0483D] of which we spoke above.

### SIN

**Verse 21.** “**Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, who dwell in the land of Uz. The cup will also reach you; you will become drunk and will be stripped bare.**”

Sin is called “life.” The daughter of Edom is therefore commanded to rejoice and be glad while the earthly mind, buried in the foreskin and sins of its flesh, encounters things nearer to salvation and finds occasions for the body and soul to breathe again into life—for the sake of both of which she is commanded to rejoice and be glad—when, having come to Babylon, she begins there to be freed.

Edom is interpreted as “earthly.” The daughter of Edom is the affection generated by a carnal mind. She dwells in the land of Uz, which is interpreted as “hasty,” and which signifies sin undertaken too quickly [Col. 0484A]. For the Apostle does not find good in this land—that is, in the flesh (Rom. 7:18).

The cup also reaches her because, just as it interrupts reason, so the judgment of good breathing cuts off affection through shame over sin. She becomes drunk when she is removed from the awareness and practice of ancient evils. She is stripped bare when she is clothed in the truth of pious confession.

### THAU
### Verse 22

“Your iniquity is complete, daughter of Zion; he will not continue to lead you into exile. He has visited your iniquity, daughter of Edom; he has uncovered your sins.”

*Thau* is interpreted as “he went astray” or “he completed.” Error is truly completed when even the affection that is more inclined toward evil is overwhelmed by shame at its own error. Therefore, when affection—namely, the daughter of Zion—does not lead intellectuality into exile, that is, does not draw it away from its proper state, it certainly brings its iniquity to an end. The daughter of Edom visits its iniquity when, because it does not judge the inner movements equally, it also strongly accuses the disgust of carnal appetite. For unless it felt disgust at its sins, it would not uncover them.

## The Prayer of the Prophet Jeremiah

### Verse 1

“Remember, Lord, what has happened to us; look and behold our reproach.”

God remembers what has happened to us when he makes us remember our falls. He looks upon our reproach when he urges us to consider or grieve over that defect of ours, than which nothing is greater. Hence also the seven women in Isaiah say: “Take away our reproach” (Isaiah 4:1).

### Verse 2

“Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners.”

Our inheritance is our bodies, which have been promised to the meek for possession under the figure of the earth. This inheritance is turned over to strangers when any vice abuses those bodies. Our houses are turned over to foreigners when our consciences are directed toward those who have no right over us except what they obtain through our betrayal—namely, the demons.

### Verse 3

“We have become orphans without a father; our mothers are like widows.”

We were without a father because we had as our father the devil, who, according to his true essence, ceased to exist. For it is written of him: “Let his companions dwell in his tabernacle, he who is not” (Job 18:15). Our mothers are like widows because they lack as husband God, who alone truly is.

### Verse 4

“We bought our water with money, and we acquired our wood at a price.”

He drinks his water with money who, through costly animal-like stupidity, purchases his vapid condition, alien to the warmth of spiritual wine. For *pecunia* (“money”) is derived from *pecus* (“cattle”), since it used to be made from the hides of cattle. We acquire our wood at a price when, by paying the price of our entire rationality, we acquire insensibility and the brutish dispositions of mind and body.

### Verse 5

“We were driven by the neck; no rest was given to the weary.”

He is driven by his neck whom pride rules. For we call the proud *cervicosi*, “stiff-necked.” Rest is not given to the weary when, according to the Gospel, no refreshment of inward rest is granted to those who labor and are burdened (Matthew 11:28).

### Verse 6

“We gave our hand to Egypt and to the Assyrians, so that we might be filled with bread.”

He gives his hand to Egypt who attributes his zeal for action to the world. He gives it likewise to the Assyrians who secures for himself courtly favors and empty titles; for this is indicated by *Assur*, which is said to mean “court,” through the burden of courtly honors. And this happens so that they may be filled with bread—that is, that they may rejoice for a time in earthly pleasure.

### Verse 7

“Our fathers sinned and are no more; and we have borne their iniquities.”

Our fathers are those whose examples we imitate. They sin, and therefore they are no more, because they are banished from true being. We bear their iniquities because we are struck by severe punishment, since we are not corrected by the penalty of another’s sin. “For sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 4:24).

### Verse 8

“Slaves have ruled over us, and there was no one to redeem us from their hand.”

The slaves are vices, if the cause is put for the effect, because they make us slaves: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). There was no one to redeem us from their hand because intellectuality, which did not possess true being and lacked within itself the subsistence of God, could not thereafter make us free.

### Verse 9

“We brought bread to ourselves in our hands, in the presence of the sword in the wilderness.”

We bring bread to ourselves in our hands when, from our zeal for our works, we extract nourishment for ourselves from some worldly prosperity. And this occurs “in the presence of the sword in the wilderness,” that is, under the pressure of sin’s necessity, in which, when its refreshment has been withdrawn, we are abandoned by the Lord. For the sword is sin.

### Verse 10

“Our skin has been burned like an oven by the face of the storm of hunger.”

Our skin is our affection, which, like the skin of the body, is more readily injured in the mind. For we are affected by many evils that we shudder at by our will. Thus we distinguish these two things: we desire good through reason, but we are not distressed by it.

This skin is burned like an oven, burning all the more furiously as it is more tightly closed, after the manner of an oven. It is burned by the face of the storm of hunger when it is consumed by the onset of inward disorder, which gives birth to hunger for the word of God.

### Verse 11

“They humbled the women in Zion and the virgins in the cities of Judah.”

They humble the women in Zion when they subject the state of conscience wherever some fertility of good will was beginning to smile. The virgins in the cities of Judah are likewise humbled when confession—the sole remedy that remains after sin—is condemned to sterility within the receptacles of the mind.

### Verse 12

“Princes were hung by the hand; the faces of elders did not blush.”

Princes are hung by the hand when our sensibilities are restrained from the accomplishment of carnal desire—not by desire, but by lack of ability. Their faces do not blush when more mature dispositions of the soul, which at times feel more modestly, are invaded by the levities of the senses. It is beyond doubt that “face” in Scripture is commonly understood as presence or knowledge.

### Verse 13

“They abused the young men impiously, and boys fell upon the wood.”

We become young men when we grow to a certain strength of mind. But we abuse this youth shamelessly when we turn the health of the liberal arts into opposing kinds of strength. We experience this frequently when we now see, most impudently, those whom we once knew to be discerning before God becoming more cunning toward the world. Boys fall upon the wood when those who had attained no strength or subtlety devote themselves, through excessive practice of shameful acts, to shamelessness and insensibility.

### Verse 14

“The elders have failed at the gates, and the young men from the choir of singers.”

The elders fail at the gates when intellectualities, in which a delineation of souls is inscribed, succumb under the judgment of inward examination. For solemn public judgment used to be exercised at the gates of cities. The young men perish from the choir of singers when lively skills depart from unanimity in well-doing.

### Verse 15

“The joy of our heart has failed; our choir has been turned into mourning.”

The joy of our heart fails when the testimony of conscience, which is our glory (2 Corinthians 1:12), grows silent within us. Our choir is turned into mourning when the concordant goodwill of the soul becomes entangled in works worthy of grief.

### Verse 16

“The crown of our head has fallen. Woe to us, because we have sinned!”

The crown of our head falls when all hope of our reward, if we once did any good, is made void. For in ancient times a crown was given to victors, but there is no victory when it has been nullified by failure.

### Verses 17–18

“Therefore our heart has become sorrowful in grief; therefore our eyes have grown dark. Because of Mount Zion, which has perished, foxes have walked upon it.”

This is to say: Because we have been deprived of the crown and have come to woe on account of our sins, we therefore incur sorrow through the biting suspicion of daily falling. Accordingly, our expectations grow dim with respect to the foretoken of some future good, since no hopes of pious merit present themselves.

And this happens because of Mount Zion, which has perished—that is, because of the excellence with which the mind was once imbued through divine contemplation, but which, because of the vices pressing upon the mind, deserved to be blotted out. For Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.” Foxes walk upon this mountain because the cunning of demons and the works of darkness trample upon this superficial holiness. For the fox is a deceitful animal, and one that delights in burrows.

### Verse 19

“But you, Lord, remain forever; your throne from generation to generation.”

It is as though he said: Their holiness, lasting only for a moment, has vanished; but you—that is, those who are yours, incorporated into you—intend to serve you not temporarily but eternally. And those over whom you deign to preside and reign as upon a throne perpetuate their service not only in this present generation in which they are born for you, but also in the subsequent regeneration of this age.

### Verse 20

“Why will you forget us forever? Will you abandon us for the length of days?”

If, he says, you grant these things to your elect, so that here and hereafter you may bestow upon them indivisibility with you, why do you take away from us—whom you see to be foolish apart from you, though you can make us recover our senses—the desire to serve you here and the lastingness of inexhaustible light there? This is the voice of those who doubt their salvation.

### Verse 21

“Convert us, Lord, to yourself, and we shall be converted; renew our days as at the beginning.”

Certainly, he says, if you were to breathe into us the grace of conversion, without doubt we could do nothing except turn to you, as they too have done. Renew our days as at the beginning—that is, restore in us that brightness of holy desire which has now become a haunt of foxes, so that we may be permitted to return to the beginnings of the sweetness and joy once experienced.

But through obstinacy you repel us and show yourself irreparably angered.

Since our discourse has at last swum through the immense gulfs of mysteries, this little work of fearful labor having been completed, I shall say with the most confident boldness that, in crossing so dreadful a sea, I had God alone as oarsman and helmsman. For I call him to witness, in whose harbor I have brought the anchor of my intention to land, that from the very beginning of this whole course the sharpness of my intellect grew so dull whenever I directed my mind’s edge to investigate these matters that, unless I looked back tearfully to him—whose countenance’s light is marked upon our heart, and whom I knew, with a good conscience, to have prompted me to undertake this task—I would certainly have desisted in great confusion from what I had begun.

But to you, God, infinite thanks are due for this experience: you so imbue us by your gift that it is in no way hidden from us what we understand from you and what from ourselves.

## Epilogue

Since, therefore, under God’s guidance we have reached whatever kind of harbor after crossing this most turbulent strait, we finally lay before you [Note: The author addresses St Norbert.], reverend master, as upon the most solid shore, the wares we have purchased with great sweat of heart and body. I do not doubt that judgment of complete sincerity presides in you.

Nor do we choose you rashly as the appraiser of this collection of ours, but rather as its most vigilant examiner. I know that it is entirely foreign to you to hurl a censor’s judgment at anyone without regard for complete equity; indeed, the eyelid of intellectual counsel has habitually preceded the steps of your work without interruption.

It is not absurd, I say, that I have decided to bring this little work before your investigations, especially since I have undoubtedly recognized that no one in all the regions adjoining us possesses greater power of discernment concerning the condition of the inner person. And not unjustly. For what spiritual matter could you not know, when you exercise yourself without ceasing in examining this very matter? In these treatises you join night to day; in the ray of this contemplation you strive with delight in the whole inward disposition.

But if I were to propose spiritually perceived matters to teachers of the merely animal nature, whose number is infinite, and who are known to be entangled in their own sensations, I would plainly scrutinize my own undertaking most seriously, considering their sluggishness.

To you, therefore, who examine all things spiritually and are judged by no one, I direct myself without fear, because you will be able to penetrate everything thoroughly, and matters greater than these, since what you live is nothing other than divine and spiritual. If, therefore, you perceive anything here that ought to be corrected, do not disdain to correct it after consulting with the Scriptures, whose use is by no means unfamiliar to you. Know with certainty that you will in no way find me ungrateful if you mark anything here for obliteration—or rather, for alteration.

Do not be surprised, however, that I have wished to say nothing concerning the literal sense. For what Blessed Jerome has made sufficiently and more than sufficiently clear is readily available, and it would certainly be superfluous for me to fill pages by repeating it.

Whatever, therefore, I remember having accomplished according to my capacity, with good intention and under the inspiration—as I believe—of God, though I am an unworthy sinner, I have transmitted for confirmation and authorization not so much through your reading as through your prayer.

**Here ends the fifth and final book of the Tropologies.**

# The Treatise of the Venerable Abbot Guibert on the Incarnation against the Jews

## The Author’s Dedicatory Letter

To Bernard, father and lord, dean of the holy Church of Soissons, Guibert, most unworthy, bearing a name greater than his deserts.

I delayed your holiness’s request for two years, but now I do not know whether I have obeyed worthily. I confess to you, before the Lord whom I call our common Lord, that I was greatly ashamed of this request, since I perceived that your opinion of me was greater than I deserved.

For I had been terrified by my weakness in knowledge. While I was being required to undertake matters untried and capable of frightening Gregory and Jerome, I feared falling beneath the burden I had shamefully assumed and, as far as I could, avoided your pressing demand through delays until now.

To refute unheard-of and excessively subtle controversies directed against our faith requires the purity of a most penetrating mind. For the sincerity of the Lord’s Incarnation is perceived by the eye only of those whose imagination is more refined; and since I know that I am sharply impeded by such imagination, I was certainly greatly troubled when I was compelled to undertake this task.

For if I were to do it and the matter proved contemptible, I thought—judging according to human standards—that this could harm my reputation. Indeed, what is more to be feared, a lukewarm treatment of such matters might injure the Church’s teaching.

Nevertheless, reflecting that you had so earnestly asked me to precede the work with prayer, I directed my heart toward him who had until now helped all my undertakings. At last I attempted to labor, insofar as I could, on your behalf.

If I was able to do anything well in it, I attribute this to you, because I resolved humbly to obey your profound humility.

When I was a boy and lived under a tutor, it happened that I repeatedly recited certain rather worldly little writings [Note: On these matters Guibert speaks at length in his Life]. When this same teacher took it badly, an old man with white hair appeared beside me while I was sleeping and said: “I want you to give me an account of the writings; nevertheless, the hand that wrote them does not belong to the person who wrote them.” When this was reported to me by the man himself, I understood that God was offering me some inward light, so that my hand might serve holy works.

# Book One: On the Conception of the Son of God within the Virgin

## Chapter One

### The Author Explains Why He Undertook the Treatise

It is tolerable enough when our faith is attacked by those who have not accepted its doctrines at all. But when those who appear to have been reconciled to Christ by grace sharpen against it the teeth and swords of controversy, all pious lovers of goodness waste away at such an accusation.

Although Jewish inertia murmurs against the conception of the Son of God within the Virgin, the matter is unfamiliar to that people, and it considers it shameful to have impressed upon it when it hears that the God who came to it as Savior was handed over to the cross by its own forefathers.

But a Christian who does not reject being designated by that very name, who, although wretched and lukewarm, nevertheless enters churches [Note: The author here means John, Count of Soissons.]; who sometimes honors altars and priests while participating in the Eucharist of the faithful and in the confession of sinners [Note: See Guibert’s Life, book III, chapter 15, below.]; who worships the memorials of the Lord’s Passion and at times also desires to give alms—why, I ask, does such a person incline himself to Jewish arguments? Why does he adopt and strengthen their contentions against us?

He supports with his own power the whispers of those who do not dare to mutter for themselves, a power which, with God as judge, will soon flourish briefly. What they scarcely speak in their throats, he proclaims; and, astonishingly, he is accused of superstition because of his own words, takes offense, scarcely endures it, and loudly calls himself a Christian.

What madness is it that one who refuses to be regarded or called a Jew or pagan should defend their ceremonies and institutions, direct hatred against Christian laws, and even condemn the very thing he worships?

While I was discussing this very matter with a certain exceedingly witty Jewish woman, she said: “It is the height of madness for a human being to worship the images which he calls those of the Savior, and then, as soon as he has withdrawn, to mock the very thing he worshipped.”

I shall not unsuitably call this man a *Neutericus*, using a new word: one who follows neither side, since he does not pursue the principles he praises, and does not praise the principles of Christian devotion which he appears to pursue.

This utterly wicked man therefore draws from Hebrew conversation words that are impious and most grievous to our chaste faith, not only to utter but even to hear. Certainly, until now we had believed—for we had read it—that that unique Virgin, the God-bearing one without precedent, had destroyed heretical perversions throughout the whole world.

Indeed, the One born from her “smashed the heads of his enemies” (Psalm 67:22); she herself is the dragon’s heads “given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73:14) [the printed wording is grammatically irregular]. And whence could incapacity come upon this most powerful Lady? Indeed, he “crushes the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Psalm 77:22).

Whoever disputes against the Virgin’s childbearing blasphemes against the Holy Spirit. No sane person doubts that this blessed woman was made fruitful by the Holy Spirit; therefore this blasphemy is not remissible.

We had heard of the blessedness of the pure in heart, who are to see God in this way (Matthew 5:8). John, who is second to no one among those born of women, professes himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Jesus’ sandal (Luke 3:16).

Those who do not judge the Savior’s birth to differ from that of others, nor to possess mysteries, cook the flesh of lambs in water, and the sandal strap is shamefully scattered by them. In considering this sacrament, the intellectual purity of all the saints from the beginning of the world—both those who foresaw what was to come before grace and those who treated what had occurred under grace—grew faint.

Even if some pious contemplator possessed a spark of momentary attention toward it, he nevertheless lacked prayer concerning what could not be comprehended. Rightly, therefore, human perceptiveness fell silent concerning this matter, since the example of their entire nature was absent.

No spiritual subtlety was sufficient to grasp this. For, the prophet says, “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Will a human being also say: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5)?

If, then, none of the pure in heart, not even John the Baptist, the knower of the womb, nor prophet nor apostle, presumed to say anything concerning so great a matter, what understanding, I ask, will belong to a mind stained by enormous impurities, in which shameful transactions have left nothing untouched?

If Paul, even when caught up to the third heaven, did not dare anything of this kind, is it fitting now for the most disgraceful of men to discuss these matters? If he himself praised out of affection, his praise would fail within him; for “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15:9)—let alone when the most filthy of all reproaches the beginnings of our salvation and defames a birth more worthy of heaven and earth.

I would discuss his character and conduct, unless the following material were itself to provide me with a fuller opportunity. But we know with even greater certainty that he fell into this supreme blasphemy through continuous movements of enormous crimes and lusts.

Let us now present some of his curses, and because they have emerged from the foulest Jewish source, let us answer them in such a way that we may silence the whisperers of impure doctrine together with their promulgator. May it belong to Mary that we, her suppliants, obtain favorable outcomes.

## Chapter Two

### The Jew’s Question

“None but a madman,” they say, “believes that God wished to lower himself into the vileness of a woman’s womb and endure the delays of ordinary growth. Most horrifying of all is that the one who was called God should be poured forth through a virgin woman’s organs. When he was born with limbs no different from those of humanity, he likewise made use of the organs of generation, and, being subject to the necessity of eating and drinking, was also subjected to the hardships that follow from these things.

“Thus it is altogether ridiculous that such a one should be regarded as God, since he appears to differ in no respect from ordinary miseries. Moreover, if it is said that he was born of a Virgin, it is utterly false, because a human being weighed down by such weakness could not be born contrary to the laws of nature.

“Finally, the greatest strength was added to this opinion by the fact that he himself died together with thieves, with the death of thieves. How could he have been able to raise himself from evil, when he was unable to avoid the outcome of so foul a death?”

That is what he says. But we respond:

### The Solution to the Question Follows

#### The Incomprehensible God, Containing and Filling All Things, Cannot Be Polluted by Bodily Things

O God, to whom no one is like, “do not be silent or be restrained”; rather, “fill his face with disgrace” (Psalm 82:2, 17), for he diminishes your name. “For it is no concern of mine to judge those who are outside” (1 Corinthians 5:12).

Let us nevertheless ask both groups whether they believe that God is unbounded and rules all things. If they say that he is bounded by some corporeality, however great, and fashion him majestically as though he were a glorious old man from the book of Daniel—as they are accustomed to do, since they find eyes and ears, hands, a womb, and feet attributed to God throughout Scripture (Daniel 10:6)—then we too shall call him some kind of bird, since he is read to have wings and to have flown: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 17:8); and, “The children of men will hope under the covering of your wings” (Psalm 36:8). “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew” (Psalm 18:11).

But if any of them is ashamed of this statement and grants that God is incomprehensible, as he truly is, let him answer me whether he who is wholly everywhere and universally fills what he has created is polluted by bodily things in the world, or even by spiritual impurities.

For, as we have said, being wholly everywhere, he contains and fills all things. If he says—which is true—that that impenetrable nature cannot be defiled by the diversity of another nature, we consequently infer that God could not, and ought not, be burdened either by his own humanity or by that of his mother.

### Interrogation

#### God Created Creatures Good

The following question should then be raised: Did God make the things he created good or evil? There is no doubt that he made them good, and very good, as he asserts (Genesis 1:31).

Although Moses, after the creation of humanity, omitted the customary words, namely, “God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:10), and although it is clear that this was not done without a mystery, it would nevertheless be utterly absurd if humble creatures made to assist human beings were called very good, while the one created in the image of God became inferior in goodness.

Indeed, humanity excels them greatly. For the Creator would have ordered things perversely if he had preferred brute creatures to intellectual ones. If, then, the nature of mortal beings was created good by God—as it certainly was—why do you reject the fact that the pious Author entered into a conditionally good creature?

#### On Original Sin: Circumcision and Sacrifices Benefited the Jews through Faith

But if the question concerns the contagion of original sin, about which there is nevertheless silence among the Jews, we shall say that all who needed this remedy were cleansed by their own faith or that of their parents, rather than by circumcision or ceremonies.

For example, when faithful Jewish women once gave birth to newborn daughters who died and were not even brought to the Temple with offerings, did those girls perish? Certainly faith did not derive its power from sacrifices; sacrifices derived their power from faith. And there was no place for circumcision in the case of females.

“For God looked upon Abel, and then upon his offerings” [variant: “and toward his offerings”] (Genesis 4:4). Therefore, whoever at that time was saved either in circumcision or in the foreskin deserved to be saved through his own faith or that of his parents.

Accordingly, it is not without reason that it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “Cleansing [variant: purifying] their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9), although this passage is by no means acceptable for refuting our enemies, since Scripture is not at all agreeable to them.

Without faith, even in baptism, the other sacraments are rendered void. Therefore the Virgin who was to bear God obtained purity for herself by faith, so that she might receive God. But let us now return to the sequence we had undertaken.

## Chapter Three

### The Question Continues

You believe in almighty God. And certainly he would not have been almighty if, out of compassion, he had been unable to move toward receiving for redemption the human being whom he had made good. To sin is weakness; to be overcome by compassion is power. In this weakness which you allege, he was able to do more. For he did what he ought to have done.

Indeed, God is especially a debtor of mercies. Why do you not set before us the fact that, although you were rebellious through continual obstinacy of murmuring and complaint, he carried you around in the wilderness like an eagle carrying its young and, though condemned through repeated idolatries of many kinds, nevertheless nourished you in the promised land?

In your Law and Prophets he is called not merely merciful—what belongs to nature—or compassionate—what belongs to activity—but Mercy itself in essence. Even if he had acted otherwise, he would certainly have denied himself.

You say, therefore, that the lowliness of a woman’s womb is incompatible with divine sublimity. Why, I ask? Because there are so many weaknesses especially in the female sex that nature itself often becomes foul to it. And since humanity itself is indignant at its own condition because of the frequent miseries with which it is burdened, it is weak to believe that divinity would ever permit itself to become involved in such things.

### Solution

#### Why God Assumed Human Rather Than Angelic Nature

You have understood these matters well. God ought, then, in order to avoid the foulness of flesh, to have prepared angelic wombs for himself. Perhaps you will be able to judge them more suitable for his conception.

By no means. Have you not read that “the heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job 15:15), and, “Among his angels he found perversity” (Job 4:18)?

If the issue concerns dignity, nothing in creation is worthy of the Creator. And since the purity of the Creator is so great that all the justice of created beings has something by which to displease him, he joined to himself, by the most fitting reason, that rational nature which appeared weaker; there, apart from any hope of merit, the grace of his condescension alone appeared.

For if he had taken hold of angels, a certain similarity might have appeared in the assumption of a nature contiguous to his own, since they are incorporeal. Hence, in your books too, divine comparison is frequently introduced through things that are most unworthy, so that whatever is considered more noble among human beings is brought low in comparison with God. Where things precious to human beings are given as likenesses of God, they are not at all to be considered as things that can be compared with him.

Hence: “I shall groan beneath you as a wagon groans beneath a load of hay” (Amos 2:13). And: “The Lord was roused as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine” (Psalm 77:65).

#### Fragility Is Understood in Two Ways

Why do you complain about fragility? It is commonly understood in two ways. For both the necessity of food, drink, and sleep, and the liability to fall into sin, are called fragility.

Certainly, while sin and death still hung over paradise, those first ancestors of our race were fragile through the necessity of eating, drinking, and sleeping. Would that fragility have produced sin for them if they had not transgressed the commandment? From your book you have: “Eat from every tree of paradise” (Genesis 2:16). And: “The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam” (Genesis 2:21). These things were said to him; these things happened in him while he was free from sin.

What does God abhor in human beings? Certainly not the nature he himself created, but the evil that humanity added. If he abhorred nature, he would most justly expose his own handiwork to contempt. For if he himself abandoned what he had established by disavowing and devaluing it, he would make himself a transgressor.

But let this madness cease. It is most prominent in your books that God frequently calls human beings both sons and gods. Do not attend to the corruption of flesh and the foulness of the womb. Do not think that anything except sins stinks to God. God does not have nostrils like yours.

You have read that Noah, after the Flood, built an altar and offered a burnt offering from birds, and that God inhaled an odor of sweetness (Genesis 8:21). What pleasure could there be in such vapor? Perhaps you imagine God to be a glutton, delighted by smoking dishes and gladly consuming the fragrance of roasted meat.

Certainly, among sober people even the food prepared for use and the smell of kitchens are unpleasant—how much less could the stench of burned birds please God? Do you think that what is foul to human beings smells sweet to God?

Put away the swine’s head and reject the judgment of the flesh. Compare spiritual things with spiritual things. God is spirit, and he inhales the odor of virtue alone; only the vices of conduct are foul to him.

Therefore, where God had gathered together every good of the soul, he ought in no way to have recoiled from the bodily fragility of a little virgin.

## Chapter Four

### The Question

#### Human Beings Cannot Offer Worthy Thanks for the Incarnation of the Son of God

Who among you, however, can accuse the woman herself of sin? But since no basis for accusation is available, the sole cause is said to be the unworthiness of nature and sex.

If God had descended to human beings in his own person, or had joined to himself some divine person—from whom, I do not know how, he would be born—while diminishing nothing of his majesty in himself, he would have earned sufficiently moderate thanks from human beings.

But because he devoted his whole being to their salvation, there is nothing that human beings can return worthy of his humility and grace. Nothing could have instructed humanity more effectively.

### Solution to the Question

#### God Appeared in Human Form; It Follows That It Was Not Absurd for God to Assume a Human Body

Did God not appear in your ancient Law to Abraham in human form in the valley of Mamre? (Genesis 18:1.) And he who for the sake of one human being wished for a time to clothe himself in our likeness—ought he not at some point truly to have done this for the salvation of his own image?

The benefit to the whole human race ought certainly to have surpassed the benefit to one individual. Did not unleavened bread, butter, and meat from a calf get brought to that one whom you call God? Then he is read to have eaten and to have stood beside Abraham as he reclined at table (Genesis 18:6–8).

And lest you say that he was an angel, read that God departed after speaking with Abraham (Genesis 18:33), and that two angels are expressly said to have gone toward Sodom (Genesis 19:1). Consider, therefore, that God, before becoming embodied, indulged in bodily food and drink.

And if you believe that this was God, then, insofar as humility is concerned, I do not consider him to have done anything less than what he was later seen to do when he assumed a human being. For, according to your opinion, it is believed that he temporarily assumed a body formed from air.

If, then, you believe that the incorporeal God ate corporeally for a time, why do you disbelieve that, for so great a matter of human salvation, he wished to assume a body for a while? Or was more owed to that person—however distinguished in faith—for the announcement of a son than to the salvation of the ages?

Moreover, all the nations were to be blessed in his seed (Genesis 22:18). You do not understand this because you do not believe.

## Chapter Five

Why, then, are you indignant that he was poured forth through the childbirth of a woman? I am compelled to speak of unusual matters, and with the greatest shame; but, to use the words of Blessed Gregory, “I reproach this very shame in myself.”

Whoever does not endure with the greatest grief such insults against the pious Redeemer; whoever does not refute with the bitterest indignation unheard-of abuses against the most pure Mother; whoever hears these things with equanimity—plainly, he is not a Christian. Indeed, it is much more rightly said to such a person: “You have been impious here, if you wish to be pious.”

Why should I not be inflamed by vehement zeal [Note: Guibert discusses these matters at greater length in his Life], when I see those who abandon the most beautiful and honorable marriages, and who even live under elderly wives while pursuing women covered with wrinkles; those who, in abusing such women, do not spare rivalry with their own brothers; those who fear no woman betrothed to God; those who are driven not by any zeal for faith but by perjury and betrayal; whose fathers, and those from whom these men descended, persisted in destroying the mother Church and loved the slaughter of the sacred order?

These men, I say, to increase their depraved way of thinking, debate the divine birth. Having taken the Jews as their defenders, and with their tongue having passed over the earth, they have now set their mouths against heaven (Psalm 73:9). They measure divine mysteries according to their customary filth, and, when they begin to feel disgust at the foulness of practiced lust, their defeated wickedness vomits the drunkenness of its own crimes upon Christian purity—indeed, upon the purity of heavenly realities.

It is therefore no wonder if they disparage God, whom they do not see, since such men exist among themselves as implacable enemies of one another. Yet there is one who says somewhere: “You thought that I would be like you; I shall rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX, 21).

I therefore ask those who, while attending to the most shameful practices, fail to recognize the glory of virginal and impassible purity: Why did Adam and Eve, after transgressing the commandment, cover their nakedness with leaves? Before that they were naked and were not ashamed. Whence came shame? It was right that, so long as they obeyed God, their bodies should be subject to reason and should not possess a rebellious concupiscence; but when they put God behind them, they immediately seethed with foul movements within themselves. These are the movements that transmit original sin into the souls and bodies of those who are begotten. David therefore complains that he was conceived in iniquity (Ps. L, 7). They were rightly ashamed, then, when they realized that they were no longer masters of their own members.

## Why the shameful members of the body are covered

Some therefore ask why we cover those members so carefully, when we do not conceal any other parts of our body for that reason. Indeed, we hide not only those parts but also the areas near them, such as the navel and the thighs, which we scarcely permit to be seen. Why is this?

When my finger, my eyes, or my lips move, they move at my nod and by my will; and because they act peacefully under my authority, they cause me no shame (Rom. VII, 23). But because the parts of which we are speaking are carried along, with a kind of unbridled freedom, contrary to the laws of the whole reason, and because, according to the Apostle, there is in our members a different law, warring against the law of our mind and taking us captive under the law of sin which is in our members (ibid.), we are rightly ashamed: whether we wish it or not, we see these parts shamefully become erect through the passion of desire.

For example, suppose that I have a servant who is otherwise useful but insolent. In the presence of strangers I refrain from giving him orders or conversing with him, and I conceal him as much as I can, because, if he proudly raises himself up, I regard it as contempt for me. Rightly, therefore, both by law and by force, the contumacious thing is covered with clothing, because it is raised up to the greatest insult of both flesh and spirit. But let us return to the subject.

# CHAPTER VI

## There was no shame in the state of innocence. Whether our first parents would have turned to generation had they remained obedient

Adam and Eve, then, before their transgression, were free from these movements and were blessedly without shame. Something very similar is seen when we observe infants and generally young children walking naked without embarrassment. If they were subject to any such titillations, they would fear either themselves or those who might happen to be present. Blessed, therefore, was the original condition of the first human beings. Happy also is the ignorance of little children, because, surrounded by the defenses of impassibility, they rejoice with angelic security.

But it must be asked whether, had they persisted in obedience, the two alone would have inhabited paradise, or whether they would have cared for posterity—in fact, for offspring. Posterity cannot be spoken of where there is no predecessor; yet, unless they procreated, they would not increase their number, and unless they increased their number, they would not be sufficient for the purpose for which they had been made.

We must therefore consider what method of generation they would have had, when neither would ever have felt any incitement to act or to undergo the act. Freedom from sin would have existed in both. But sin is concupiscence. If, then, they would have generated without concupiscence, while all other evils were likewise absent, I wonder—but I do not dare to decide—whether the virginity of both would also have remained unharmed. For virginity is a good; therefore its loss would be an evil. Good Jesus! Although we have deserved greater things through you, what purity and tranquility did we lose in our first parent?

## The delights of virginity provoke contempt

With filthy mouths, therefore, the enemies of the divine birth loudly proclaim their putrid words. I shall say—and certainly establish—that those members which would then have served that birth were more worthy than the most foul mouths that fill themselves daily with frauds and luxuries and deride the life-giving sacraments.

What, I ask, is displeasing in those members except the fulfillment of foul pleasure? Remove the suspicion of lust, and there will be nothing for you to shudder at but something to venerate. You who love shameful acts will rightly be condemned, because you condemn the very members that make you shameful.

Almighty God, what can be more pleasing, what sweeter to a good mind, than true virginity and an undefiled spirit? We had heard from Hosea that wine and drunkenness take away the heart [al., “takes away the heart”] (Hos. IV, 11). Joel also speaks of your people, associating fornication with drinking: “They have placed the boy in a brothel, and sold the girl for wine, so that they might drink” (Joel III, 3).

Tell me what wine it is that “makes virgins bud” (Zech. IX, 17), when other wines commonly cause the loss of chastity. I know that you do not know; and I shall add further that it is the same wine which, in the Book of Judges, is said to gladden God and human beings (Judg. IX, 13). Do you think that God ever drank, since you fail in understanding according to the literal sense? I shall explain your own words to you; meanwhile, if you wish, keep babbling.

## What the wine that gladdens God and human beings is, and how it makes virgins bud

The wine that gladdens God and human beings is the Holy Spirit, who joins the Father and the Son in love and joins human beings to God. But what is love except joy, and what is joy except in love? This wine—that is, spiritual fervor—makes virgins bud, because the ardors of the flesh can never be quieted except by the flame of heavenly desire.

If this is God’s good, this is his beauty, so that nothing better or more beautiful should be thought to exist with God, who would dare to shudder at a virgin’s womb? Who would find fault with the emergence of a virginal birth? If you wish to detest this on account of natural passages, oh, how often have you vomited from your most fetid mouth the previous day’s gluttonous excesses of meat? How often have you discharged foul vomits and phlegms more horrible than that fluid? I answer according to your own sense.

But in God, the author of such things, I know of nothing unbecoming except sins.

## That God contracted no stain in the Virgin’s womb

You therefore have in our first parents a model of generation without passion, which he who could have brought it into effect had they persevered reproduced in his own mother. Although it ought to be enough that God cannot in any way be touched by human filth, hear still more.

You believe, I suppose, that the sun is by nature most pure. Every day you see its rays pass through public heaps of dung and illuminate whatever is putrid and unworthy even of sight. It would be madness to think that from the things over which it passes it contracts any stain.

Further: if you pour oil or balsam into water, neither is confounded with the water, but each nature remains solid in itself. Consider again: when my mind, reflecting and repeatedly recalling in imagination things it has seen anywhere, remembers a leper swollen with bloody ulcers, or swarms of worms pouring from a torn corpse, or heaps of dung lying about everywhere, what stain, I ask, does the mind in its revolving motion carry away from these things, except as much as it would carry if it passed in a single movement over the most beautiful bodies of women or men, or revisited metals of splendid workmanship?

Bury gold in black rubbish: although the decaying earth may soil it, the nature of gold will not thereby fail. Learn, wretched man, from material things how to measure spiritual realities; and, since you have examples in earthly matters, consider what Divinity is capable of in eternal things.

# BOOK TWO  
## WHETHER GOD ASSUMED EVERYTHING HUMAN OR NOT

[Col. 0499]

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0499A]

## When sin is absent, the members are holy

Furthermore, when the Son of God came in the flesh, if he had the members appropriate to a body, the composition of those members did him no harm. There is no reason to be ashamed of what did not shame him. And what could shame him, when nothing in him was not holy?

If everything that exists is good except where sin is present, then the members that are good in themselves are holy when sin is absent. Our members serve our weakness; and when our ears, mouths, or nostrils serve the necessary discharge of bodily matter, what evil do the other members do when they expel the burden of the intestines below?

## God assumed everything human

Ask, you most foul and wicked man, concerning our Lord whether he spat, whether he blew his nose, whether he drew the mucus from his eyes or ears with his fingers; and understand that, just as honorably as he performed these upper functions, he performed the remaining ones.

Or tell me: the God of yours who appeared to Abraham—where did he deposit the things he ate? And how, or whether, did what naturally followed take place? I tremble while discussing these matters; but you, sons of the devil, compel me. May God demand an account from you; he knows with what disposition I do this.

Briefly understand that God humbly assumed everything human, and feared nothing human except sins. If you wish to grasp this rationally, the arguments given above ought, I think, to be sufficient for you. If it is for you as it was for your fathers—if, I say, you do not believe—you will not understand.

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 0499C]

## Arguments concerning how the Virgin gave birth

As I am about to treat the remaining question concerning the virginity of blessed Mary—namely, the claim that a virgin could not give birth contrary to nature—I should rightly be judged insane if I seem to reason in this way with the insane. Yet my reasoning is this: even if I am mocked by the mad, I may at least be found, among those who know less than I and desire to learn, to possess for a little while an understanding of the faith.

She who is truly the Mother of God can herself provide us with strength against our adversaries. Why do you argue about nature? Was it nature that Adam suddenly emerged formed from clay? Was it nature that man then took his origin from earth? It was not nature, insofar as nature’s ordinary operation is concerned, by which one human being proceeds from another.

You will therefore believe in a creation that you have not seen and for which no examples at all are offered to you among human beings. You will plainly believe not so much in God as in your Moses. You also do not deny that a woman was built from a rib. That too was not according to nature.

Come, then: can you believe that anything is born except through the introduction of suitable seed? Certainly, we have discovered that cats conceive from catmint [Note: Or nepeta, a kind of calamint], she-goats from vervain [Note: Or “vanelli,” birds; but here the word is taken for a quadruped], and vultures conceive and give birth without intercourse. Could the Son of God not be conceived through the Holy Spirit for the sole reason that your envy refused it?

Bees produce offspring from the seed of their little works, while smaller flies repeatedly rush upon one another in intercourse. Was God the Father powerless to prepare conception for the Son, and the Son for himself, when he has given growth to so many lesser things without their own seed of propagation?

## God prepared seed in the Virgin’s womb. The Jews of that time differ from the contemporaries of Christ

But you say: “God could indeed have done this for himself and for anyone else; but the one whose mother, as you claim, was to be made fertile by the Spirit without a man’s seed was neither God nor the Son of God. Therefore God did not do it for him, nor could he do it for himself.”

You are lying. Tell me: after Isaiah said that the people of the nations who had walked in darkness had seen a great light, and that light had dawned upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death (Isa. IX, 2), who is that little one of whom he says, “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (ibid., 6), and about whom he speaks afterward?

I know what you will say, just as you said when I was disputing this saying with some of you: “The son who is said to be born is a human being.” And when you said that these things concerned the Messiah, I drew this conclusion against you. According to your opinion, the Messiah will be a mere human being.

“God and man?” “Far be it,” you say, “that divinity should be ascribed to one who is human!” He will be a wise man, destined to reign for some time, and afterward destined to have an end both of his reign and of his body.

Behold how great is the foolishness—or rather, the dullness—of the Jews of the present day, compared with those who were contemporaries of the Lord Jesus. The latter said: “We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever” (John XII, 34); these assign him the boundaries of death. Consider, I say, unhappy men, how absurdly you think.

Continue with what follows. “And the principality,” he says, “was made upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the future age, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX, 6). The one who above is asserted to have been born, to be a son, and to have been given to us is now called God and Father of the future age.

And lest the divinity itself be thought merely figurative, as in the words “Apply him to the gods” (Exod. XXII, 8), or “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII, 1), the perpetuity of his power is added: he is called Father—not Lord—of the future age (Isa. IX, 6).

There, plainly, is the Wisdom that now “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII, 1). Finally, after the multiplication of his dominion, after the perpetuity of peace, and after the establishment of David’s throne in judgment and justice, his indefectibility is again proclaimed: “From now and forever” (Isa. IX, 7).

Will one such as this be able to prepare a little place for himself in a womb, while he who rules the future age will not be able to provide himself with so small a place in this age?

I am compelled, to restrain your obstinacy, to give examples from the most trivial things. Physicians report, and the truth of historians confirms, that in a certain province mares conceive from the wind. Nature, then, prevailed over the Holy Spirit—or rather, the powers of God were surpassed by the privileges of places and of the air.

# CHAPTER III  
## Also concerning the preceding subject

## He proves the virginal conception from the Old Testament

Do you still deny the Virgin? Acknowledge the saying of that same prophet Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14).

But you say that *almah*, a Hebrew word, means among you not “virgin” but “young woman”; and a young woman can plainly be not a virgin. Yet Jerome (*On Isaiah*, book III, chapter 7, after the middle), whom you are accustomed to attest as a most learned interpreter, and whom one of your number, when disputing this matter with me, cited because he did not wish to deviate at all in the controversy from Jerome’s translations, asserts not only that the aforementioned word means “virgin”—the word you call *betulah*—but that it specifically denotes a virgin who remains always hidden from the sight of men.

But, remembering your old obstinacy, you retain the ambiguous term, namely “young woman.” For if you agreed with us, this single word would seem greatly to subdue you.

Let us therefore suppose that the word there means “young woman.” Tell me what is meant by what precedes it: “Behold, the Lord himself will give you a sign” (ibid.), followed immediately by, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” with no preceding indication of the man by whom the young woman would conceive.

And even if the one who conceived were not a virgin, because she conceived of herself, it would be a sign. But one of them, older in stone—that is, hardened in antiquity—objected to me that this same young woman was the prophet’s wife and that she was the woman whom Isaiah mentions at length in what follows: “I took faithful witnesses for myself, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Barachiah, and I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (Isa. VIII, 2–3).

In our books under grace I find women called prophetesses, such as Anna, daughter of Phanuel (Luke II, 36), and the virgin daughters of Philip, who are called prophetesses (Acts XXI, 9), not because they had prophets as husbands, but because they themselves prophesied. For the Book of Kings calls Huldah under King Josiah not a prophetess but a prophet (IV Kings XXII, 14). I do not know whether I have read this word elsewhere in the old books. I do know, however, that Huldah’s husband Shallum is not called a prophet (ibid.).

Let us suppose once again, I ask, that she was the prophet’s wife. I know for certain that among us neither an abbess nor a deaconess is the wife of an abbot or deacon; nor would a virgin or widow lose the title of countess if she governed a county. In the same way, a woman has the title “prophetess” from her own office, by which she is so called.

But let us grant them this escape, so that for a time we may drive them into an awkward position. What, then, does it mean that Isaiah approached his wife, as you say, in the presence of two faithful witnesses? “Approach” is commonly used in Hebrew custom for intercourse, as in Ezekiel: “You shall not approach a menstruating woman” (Ezek. XVIII, 6).

If, then, you say that Isaiah had intercourse with his wife—that is, with the prophetess—in the presence of the faithful witnesses Zechariah and Uriah, and that she conceived and immediately gave birth, with what words ought you to be spat upon, with what dung pelted, since you thereby inflict the most disgraceful dishonor upon a most holy man and on the other hand construct a most powerful falsehood?

If this position cannot stand, let us at least concede, according to you, that a young woman conceived. Why was it not stated from whose seed she received the thing that she conceived? Yet if this had been done, the sign that was promised would no longer have been a sign.

Therefore either the father must be declared, or, if a virgin—or young woman—conceived and gave birth, it is a sign. But if it is a sign, it is contrary to the ordinary course of nature.

Since, then, what was conceived and born is called Emmanuel—that is, “God with us”—and since God provides this as a general sign for the house of David, that is, for the Church, understand, or be convicted, you wicked men, that whether you wish it or not, he who is the author and disposer of nature prepared for himself what he willed in nature, even beyond nature.

And he who ordered it, and who was born in it, and who himself founded it, could choose nothing except what was purer. It is therefore established that she was not a young woman, not merely a virgin, but a most chaste virgin, above the ordinary purity of human beings.

And the one whom she bore stood as a sign of the peoples, as the prophet continues (Isa. XI, 10), because no one except the one who looked toward him merited salvation.

Tell me, you who seek to establish your mastery of the law, what rational harmony is there in the statement that this child, when he is to be nourished, eats butter and honey so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good (Isa. VII, 15)? Is butter eaten so that hatred of all wickedness may follow, and does the eating of honey pass into the soul in such a way that it fills us with the choice of good?

I confess that until now I have hated butter and cared little for honey. From now on I shall snatch both with eager jaws, since you have taught that they possess such power.

I know that at this point you will, according to your custom, crow like crows. Listen, even if you turn away, to what is true. Butter is made from flesh; honey is produced from heavenly dew.

By butter, therefore, the humanity of the Savior is understood, by whose gentleness the harshness of our sins is tempered. By honey, his divinity is signified, by whose wisdom the understanding of our reason is sweetened.

That blessed Child ate these things because in his one person he united both substances, of God and of man. Through his human nature, by which he offered examples of virtue, he “knew”—that is, he caused us to know—the foulness of crimes; and through the draught of his divinity he made known the charity of inward sweetness.

But what I have said has been offered for your mockery.

# CHAPTER IV

## He presses on and continues Isaiah’s prophecy

The same prophet continues after many other things: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1).

Why a rod? Because it is stretched out straight, singular and unique, in complete purity and delicacy.

Tell me: although you do not wish to admit any allegories in the five books of Moses, do you not nevertheless acknowledge that the prophetic books are filled with mysteries? Tell me, I say, what is the rod? What does “go forth” mean? What is the flower that rises not from a branch but from the root?

There is certainly no doubt that you think this was spoken of our Messiah. I therefore ask you to state it according to the division I have proposed.

If you call the Messiah the rod, who will be the flower? Consider whether what I say will appear even plausible. If rods were spoken of in the plural, from which a flower would arise, they would rightly be thought to signify married persons. But since it is a single rod, it seems to indicate simplicity.

If you understand a father without his marital partner, we know that, according to nature, a male does nothing by himself. If you understand a mother without a father, according to your opinion there is nothing; according to mine—indeed, according to the prophetic meaning—there is something.

She went forth because she was shown as preeminent and without precedent in the whole human race. If he had said, “A rod shall go forth, from whose branch a flower shall rise,” perhaps someone would have thought of a husband and of his lateral rib, namely his own. But it does not rise from a branch or from an equal partner; it rises from the root of the rod, formed from the blood of the Virgin mother alone through the Holy Spirit.

But why a flower? Because of the fragrance of all virtues, because he is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3), and because fruit rises from a flower. For he is the tree planted beside flowing waters, which gives its fruit in its season (Ps. I, 3).

## The fullness of the whole divinity dwells in Christ, whereas in other human beings it is present according to the measure of virtue

“Upon this flower,” he says, “the Spirit of the Lord shall rest” (Isa. XI, 2), and so forth.

Since we agree that these things are to be understood as spoken of Christ, while you believe that Christ will live for a definite period and then come to an end, and that he will be born from a man and a woman like other human beings, I cannot suppose that such abundance and continuity of graces could exist in any mere human being, especially since the Spirit is said not merely to come upon him but to rest upon him.

Although it is written that the spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha, it is one thing for the spirit of a human being to come upon another human being—indeed, Elisha is read to have received a double portion—and another thing to possess the fullness of the entire divine gift.

Of servants it is plainly said: “He gave them his goods, to each according to his own ability” (Matt. XXV, 15). But of Christ, God does not give the Spirit by measure.

Since you do not accept examples from our Scriptures, attend to what follows, because it appears more than human: “He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of his ears” (Isa. XI, 3).

What human being ever judges justly except concerning those matters approved by sight and hearing? And why are three or two witnesses, upon whose testimony every word stands, commanded in your law (Deut. XVII, 6), except concerning things that are heard and seen?

The meaning, then, is this: Human beings judge matters grasped by the senses, caring less for what is inward. He, however, judges inwardly, both when he judges the humble—that is, when he justly distinguishes the merits of each and distributes to each his due—and when he reproves on behalf of the meek of the earth in righteousness, chastising those whom he loves so that he may teach goodness and discipline, and making them earth rather than dust carried away by the wind, by giving drink in tears by measure.

“And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked one” (Isa. XI, 4).

How does Christ, whom both you and we understand here, strike the earth with the rod of his mouth if he is a mere human being? To strike the earth with the rod of the mouth is either to call forth famine upon the earth or to punish the sins of human beings by various corrections. To strike the earth with the rod of the mouth is to terrify the minds of sinners by the power of his speech.

“With the breath of his lips he slays the wicked one” (ibid.), when the understanding of prophetic utterance destroys you yourself from the state of sin.

If this is understood according to what is said in Job—“You are not wicked; who, then, is he?”—the lips of Christ are the prophets. Their breath is the inward meaning; for you follow the body, that is, the letter.

“With the breath of his lips he slays the wicked one” (ibid.), namely the Antichrist whom you await as the Messiah; for “by the manifestation of his coming he will destroy him” (ibid., cf. 2 Thess. II, 8).

Does it seem to you that any human being could do this? And how could justice and faith become the belt of his loins, when in material things there is no mixture of one material thing with another? It is as though he were saying: Whatever is thought carnal in that person of God and man is entirely surrounded by spiritual power.

The loins, moreover, and the regions of the kidneys, which are known to be places of pleasure, are rightly taken as representing carnality. Perhaps you laugh at my view; I ask you to substitute your own judgment for mine. But it can in no way be said that all this suits a mere human being: earthly power may strike the earth with the mouth or make it tremble by looking upon it, but it will not kill the wicked one by the spirit, nor gird its loins with faith and justice.

I would append the lower passages that follow, concerning the dwelling together of contrary substances, if I did not consider it superfluous. For if anyone wishes to gather from these and similar passages, by a friendly exercise of reason, that Christ was foretold, he will easily be able to see the diverse things that are peacefully joined together. The whole is expressed in the words: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord” (Ps. LXXXV, 9). And: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. XVII, 45).

# CHAPTER V  
## Also concerning virginity

What, then, is asked concerning the virginity of blessed Mary, when it is plainly known that, where Christ the Son chose to be born, the place ought to have been prepared in the purest and most excellent manner? Certainly, that womb was purer in proportion as it was more free from passion.

Virginity is greatly worthy even when it is scorched by temptations; but it is far more glorious when, after all movements have been overcome and quieted, it is compared with the original condition of our first parents.

You plainly believe that the Spirit of God once inhabited holy men and often stirred them not only to live well but also to prophesy. Since he is God, he was not at all constrained by law from filling even wicked men and sharpening them for prophecy, whenever he wished.

For if the same Spirit transformed Saul, whom the spirit of wickedness had long possessed, and his attendants who had come to slaughter David—overturning their former madness—so that the treacherous king, naked among the prophets, prophesied by day and by night, why do you strive to argue that something contrary to nature took place in the Virgin’s conception?

What is more contrary to nature than for God, the author of purity, to enter filthy breasts? Certainly you know that your ancient history contained many holy men to whom, as you read, angels never appeared. Yet you read that Daniel, most worthy in every way of celibacy, grew weak and fell ill for many days because of the vision of Gabriel, if I am not mistaken.

But you know that the ass, when an angel visibly appeared to it, did not limp even for a short while. Is an ass more worthy than a prophet? Is a brute animal holier than those holy men who saw nothing of the kind? I say nothing of the fact that it spoke, which is contrary to nature; but I will say this: for any irrational creature to recognize intellectual and angelic realities is much more contrary to nature.

Cease, obstinate men; let your verbosity be silent, because your whole argument lies prostrate. How can you perceive the causes of God’s sacraments and the sacraments of his causes, when you twist your hearts around thefts and usury?

Does that tiny amount of human seed outweigh the omnipotence or will of God, so that unless it goes before him God can accomplish nothing—as though the author of nature needed the aids of nature?

I strive in vain against your obstinacy, because unless you believe in this one whom we believe to be Christ, you will never be able to abandon this argument against us, nor will you think rightly of his mother, since you shudder at the Son.

Nevertheless, what will not benefit you will not harm the faithful to have learned. Let us now pass on to other matters.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0505]

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0505C]

## Concerning Christ’s human life among human beings on earth

What do you say about the long dwelling of the Lord Jesus Christ among human beings, when you admit that your own God lived among you for forty years?

David plainly reads: “For forty years I was near that generation” (Ps. IX, 10). And in the Book of Kings: “I walked,” he says, “in a tabernacle and in a tent, through all the places which I passed through with all the children of Israel” (II Kings VII, 6).

In Deuteronomy also: “You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the necessities of nature, carrying a stake on your belt. When you sit down, you shall dig around and, after removing the waste, cover the hole with the earth by which you were relieved; for the Lord your God walks in the midst of the camp, to deliver you, so that your camp may be clean and nothing filthy may appear in it” (Deut. XXIII, 12–14).

You therefore boast that God lived among you for so long, to govern your camps and lead you from land to land. Why, then, will it seem absurd to you that the Son of God endured the discomforts of humanity and common companionship in order to restore the nations to knowledge of God and call you to more spiritual things?

If you object to the filth of living together, because you once carried stakes on your belts and covered the holes with excavated earth so that you might prepare a clean camp for the God who walked there, surely your little children and wives were exempt from carrying stakes, yet they nevertheless relieved their bowels of urine and excrement.

God, then, who was moving suddenly here and there amid encounters, either did not see these things at all, or he endured the filth of the men with difficulty while being in no way burdened by that of women and children.

What of the fact that livestock and herds remained there? Why did the vigilant diligence of your good ancestors not collect, in the tracks of the herds, the pellets falling from the hindquarters of goats and sheep, and bury, so to speak, the calves’ droppings in a tomb, lest, while God wandered about, cow dung soil his valuable shoes?

Surely we know also of the incontinence of infants in their cradles, and that mothers or nurses washed away such filth. Who can say how often God stood at the doorway where these things were happening, not at leisure?

And did those other abominations that are customarily committed in the inner rooms of bedrooms cease to occur while God was going around?

Most wretched of human beings, who think that God, who is spirit, inhaled these stinks of bodies! Was it surprising if the embodied Son of God endured these things, which you claim that the incorporeal God did not tolerate among you for forty years?

Certainly, the God-man endured nothing more burdensome than your God endured then through your grumbling. He truly carried you on his shoulders as an eagle carries its young, yet the food sent from heaven, the frequent miracles, the continual embassies of God, and the announcements of future blessings could not restrain you from complaint.

We know that our God more easily carried his own flesh—indeed, rather, the cross—than your God carried your restlessness. For when he was killing you, you sought him, loving him with your lips while lying in your hearts.

Let us now touch upon something concerning his passion.

# CHAPTER II  
## Concerning Christ’s passion

“His appearance,” Isaiah says, “was without honor among men, and his form among the sons of men” (Isa. LII, 14). His appearance and form, by which he is beautiful beyond the sons of men, are still despised by the Jews, while divine works are suppressed and communion with the flesh and death are proclaimed.

“This man sprinkles many nations” (ibid., 15). With what will he sprinkle, and what will he sprinkle? Clearly with that hyssop which grows on the wall, with which David wishes to be sprinkled so that he may be cleansed, and with which lepers were sprinkled according to the law. He will sprinkle blood—his own blood—but “many nations,” he says, not all, for “the Lord knows those who are his.”

“Before him the nations [al., kings] shall hold their mouths” (Isa. LII, 15). None of them, even among the holiest, who govern themselves completely, dared to violate the mysteries of his dispensation. “Those to whom it was not told about him shall see” (ibid.).

We are the ones who see, because we believe in him, although at times we do not possess a full understanding of the faith itself. Nevertheless, we tenaciously follow the faith of the Fathers and, as though without a preacher, embrace it.

“And those who had not heard shall contemplate,” for before the eyes of our mind he has been set forth through the love of faith. Even if almost no one proclaims him, devotion nevertheless longs for him. Or this whole saying may be understood: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24). Yet they possessed both, because they believed in what was to come.

Hence the same prophet says: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. LXIV, 1). He rends the heavens who brings into effect the prophetic promises concerning himself.

Then follows the voice of believers complaining about you: “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1).

“Some,” they say, “scarcely wish to believe the things we have heard—that is, understood—and in the weakness of a human being the strength of God is not recognized.”

“And he shall ascend like a young plant before him” (ibid., 2), because he appeared humble and because he is the one in whom the Father was well pleased.

He also ascended “like a root from thirsty ground” (ibid.), because he allowed himself to be recognized only slowly. He alone plainly remained almost like a living grain; once dead, he brought forth much fruit (John XII, 24).

Or he ascended “like a root from dry earth,” because in Mary he was his own origin, since no stream of human seed flowed into her.

He has neither appearance nor beauty. We saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him: one despised and last among men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, and as one whose face was hidden; and he was despised, so that we did not esteem him (Isa. LIII, 2–3). In these words, where not his person but the contemptibility of human sufferings in his person is thus marked, a question arises: the one whom he calls desired, shortly afterward he reports as not esteemed. He was desired, I think, when they said to him: “How long do you take away our soul? [Col. 0508A] If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X, 24). He was not esteemed when he was called a glutton, a drunkard, and demon-possessed, or when he was mocked upon the cross. “We thought,” he says, “that he was like a leper, and stricken by God, and humbled” (Isa. LIII, 4); and the Jews loudly proclaimed that he was not of God and was a sinner because he had not kept the Sabbath, and that he had been struck down for his arrogance because he had called himself the Son of God.

“He himself was wounded for our iniquities, and crushed for our crimes. Truly he bore our infirmities himself, and carried our sorrows himself. The discipline of our peace was upon him” (Ibid., 4–5). For he himself taught and accomplished the means of reconciliation with God. “And by his bruise we were healed” (Ibid., 5).

Why should I continue, killing my own words with those of another? [Col. 0508B] To whom do you attribute, Jew, what I have brought forward, 270 and what follows? Who is he in whom God placed the iniquity of us all? He was offered because he willed it, and did not open his mouth; like a sheep led to slaughter, and like a lamb he was silent before the shearer (Ibid., 7).
