He was taken away from distress and judgment (Ibid., 8), yet he has such a generation as cannot be recounted. He, according to your opinion, cut off from the land of the living, will nevertheless give the wicked for his burial (Ibid., 8–9), in order to draw them away from ungodliness by burying them with himself in baptism; and he will kill the rich one (Ibid., 9), namely, the devil, with the price of his death.

Who is he, I ask—passing over much of what follows—“who was reckoned among criminals” (Ibid., 12), who bore the sin of many, who prayed for transgressors (Ibid.), so that they might not perish? Will that Messiah whom you await to reign prosperously be thought to have been signified here by you? You do not attribute this to him, so as to believe that a mere human being would carry your sorrows and sins, die no less willingly than simply, be counted among criminals, and pray for transgressors so that they might not perish.

A mere human being could not make satisfaction for sins.

And since, according to you, this does not pertain to him, into what person will he appear to have entered, in whom such things have come together—misery and power alike? For he who is so great that, with God transferring them to him, he supports the sins of all is, I think, not human but God. For if not even an infant of one day is pure before God, if his life is upon the earth—especially since he is conceived from unclean seed—what shall we say when David, whom God had found according to his own heart, says: “If you observe iniquities, Lord, who will endure?” (Ps. CXXIX, 3). And Isaiah says: “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth in your sight” (Isa. LXIV, 6). Even Moses, who pleaded against the destruction of others, obtained nothing for them and, when guilt demanded it, was deprived of the promised land.

If, I say, all are impeded by their own guilt, who is capable of bearing the weight of everyone’s sin? For if it is true that there is woe to the praiseworthy life of human beings if it is judged without mercy—for “in your sight no living person is justified” (Ps. CXLII, 2)—how will one who is insufficient for himself alone plead before God concerning the evils of a few, let alone of all? But if the matter concerns the magnitude of sins, we carefully affirm that no sin can be called small when it is recognized as committed in contempt of God. By what satisfaction, then, can anyone make amends, unless he has as his advocate with God the one whom he has offended, and that advocate is merciful?

It was therefore just that the one who could die as a human being for human beings should act on behalf of humanity; yet, being free from sin, he should bear the sins of human beings; and, insofar as he was God, he should reconcile them to God and to himself, since they are one. See, then, where your wicked prophet is aiming, Jew: here he does not even wander through prophetic riddles, but narrates almost as history. If you do not know anyone in the past to whom this applies, and do not recognize anyone in the future, hold fast to the one upon whom we rely, in whom what was foreshadowed is plainly and evidently fulfilled. Examine the Gospels; examine what we believe: Christ has opened the prophet’s meaning to us by his deeds.

## CHAPTER III

### Whether Christ could die, or not

Christ is God and human being, without confusion of either nature. Therefore it was necessary that the human being who is God should die for all.

But if, because you hear him called God, you therefore raise an objection concerning death—for death is not fitting to God—you should know that God, who assumed humanity, in no way confused God with humanity or mixed humanity with God. Rather, with each nature remaining stable within himself, he existed as one person from two natures and in two substances.

Therefore, in that part by which he was human, he rightly presented himself as mortal, so that, since death had come through sin, he—free from sin—might, when he voluntarily handed himself over to death (which, since he had not sinned, he nevertheless endured undeservedly), free all who were subject to that wretched condition. For no nature other than the one that had sinned could make satisfaction for the same sin. Yet it would not have been fitting for what humanity had committed to be expiated by someone from the angelic order.

Justly, therefore, it was a human being who should take up the cause of all before God, yet one who was without any stain of guilt. For since he owed nothing, and when attacked by the devil was compelled to pay what he had not stolen, he overthrew the one who had attacked him, though unjustly, and expelled him from possession of the human race. Thus, when by dying as a human being he stripped the devil of dominion [f., “mastery” or “possession”], and when, in the matter in which he was weak according to your opinion, the enemy’s pride was confounded by his own humility—as was right—strength increased for us.

You may perhaps say: Could the one who was God not do this unless he died? He could, I say. Your God also, when he appeared to Abraham in the valley, could return fasting to heaven. If you tell me the reasons for the meal, I promise that I can state much clearer reasons for the punishment. If you were to say to me: “Your God, who, if he wished, could—as the saying goes—turn beans into gold, why did he command fraud to be practiced upon the Egyptians concerning gold, silver, and clothing? And why did the avenging angel spare the firstborn after the blood of a lamb had been smeared upon your doorposts?”—I would explain to you most brilliantly the reasons for the Passion. But I know that unless you bring the heart of faith to the matter calmly, you will not be able to accept a rationale for something you hate.

Daniel’s prophecy concerning Christ is examined.

And since we have already begun to confront you with prophetic oracles and to renew your memory of your own books—for we are accustomed to examine the songs of others more sharply than our own—listen to Daniel, who declares the events themselves and the times of those events:

“Seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be erased, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX, 24).

Understand the angel speaking to the prophet as though he were saying: “Because you complain about the removal and dispersion of your people, know that God has shortened the periods required for applying the remedy and has become propitious, so that the people may indeed transfer themselves from the righteousnesses of the flesh to spiritual worship; and that city, now made holy by Christ’s blood, may exchange its old condition for new honors; so that the guilt of Adam, the transgressor, may weaken, and that which is preeminently called sin—idolatry and unbelief—may come to an end. Whatever is done against one’s neighbor without righteousness may be lulled and cease; and there may be brought in not the profane, secular thing spoken of by the Apostle (Heb. IX, 1), but everlasting righteousness. For holiness befits this house, to endure through length of days, so that its fulfillment may be revealed, having been delivered over to the accomplishment of visions and prophecies. And all this will happen when the anointing of the Holy of Holies is celebrated with the oil of gladness above his companions.”

“Know and understand,” he says: “From the issuing of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt until Christ the prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks” (Dan. IX, 25). From the issuing of the decree by which Darius ordered the city to be restored, you have the number of years extending specifically to Christ the prince. Understand the weeks as weeks of years, not of days. As for how the first seven weeks and the remaining sixty-two weeks are to be carefully distinguished, let the reader inquire in Jerome (Commentary on Daniel, Book I, chapter 9), where a compilation of very many authors has been made. To recognize it briefly, however, the seventy weeks, unless I am mistaken, contain four hundred and ninety years.

“And after the sixty-two weeks Christ will be killed, and his people, who will deny him, will not be his; and the people with the coming leader will destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed” (Ibid., 26).

“After this sequence of years has been completed,” he says, “the very one who is to be called [f., ‘who is to be vacated’] will be killed essentially as Christ; and the people who will say, ‘We have no king but Caesar’ (John XIX, 15), will cry out to Pilate, ‘Do not write: King of the Jews’ (Ibid., 21). Against this stands the Psalms’ title-inscription, “Do not destroy.” They will be of their father the devil, not his [people]; why? Because he did not recognize the time of his visitation (Luke XIX, 44). And the Roman people, with the leader Vespasian, will destroy the city and the sanctuary; the end of this will create perpetual devastation there for Jewish habitation.”

“And after the end of the war” (Dan. IX, 26), making firm what he had said, he repeats: “The extermination will be confirmed by the decreed desolation. He will confirm a covenant with many for one week; and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease; and in the temple there will be the abomination of desolation, and desolation will continue until the consummation and the end” (Ibid., 27).

For what is the week in which he confirms a covenant with many, except what is elsewhere called “a time, times, and half a time” (Rev. XII, 14)—namely, three and a half years of the Lord’s preaching, followed by three and a half years in which especially the apostolic band, together with the entire body of disciples, labored among the Jews and drew many away from error? Yet all their teaching was a seedbed of the Lord Jesus.

In the middle of that week sacrifice and offering ceased, because, once the body that is Christ had been presented, the shadow of calves and bulls was no longer of any benefit. In the temple there was the abomination of desolation, because where God is not, there is neither any good omen nor can it be said that anyone dwells there, since no one is present. For because the devil is not truly present where true essence is absent, it is wretched solitude: “Behold,” he says, “your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38; Luke XIII, 35). For how could the shadow exist without the body? Therefore nothing there was not superfluous.

And so that we might hold with complete certainty what we have now seen to have persisted for a thousand years and more, he repeats the sentence of desolation for a third time: “Desolation will continue” (Dan. IX, 27), until the consummation and end—that is, of the ages—arrive.

Tell me, profane and obstinate people, to whom will you judge these things to belong? Perhaps to Hyrcanus, whom you had as the last king together with the high priest [f., “with the pontificate” or “with the office of pontiff”]. But what do these things have to do with him? Did the people who belonged to him deny him? Had not his [parchi] cut off his ears—not with iron but with their teeth—so that he might be excluded from the priesthood? For he was deprived neither of life nor of kingship by the people.

I would very much like to know from you what, after the shortening of the seventy weeks, are the consummation of transgression and sin, the end that then occurred, the removal of iniquity, and the one who then brought everlasting righteousness. Compare the matters, liars, and certainly you will be unable to find anything that in any way fits that period. Indeed, under new kings, according to the histories, the most numerous residues of wars and slaughter raged savagely.

I marvel at what you think concerning the vision and the prophet, since nothing new, according to your opinions, happened to them in those days. And since the limit of years was fixed so evidently that knowledge of the times cannot waver, while you yourselves do not assert that anything prophetic or corresponding to the vision occurred at that time in that place, what will be the anointing of the Holy of Holies? If he is the Holy of Holies, he is the chief of all the holy ones; I do not know whom you understand this to be. This, however, I do know: if he is so preeminent, he can be none other than Christ. But if he is Christ, and it is proved that such a one was killed at the time specified, then the people’s rejection and denial, and finally the destruction of the city and sanctuary, wholly agree with him and with the leader mentioned above.

The confirmation of the covenant—which is nothing other than a promise—is also the confirmation of the heavenly kingdom: “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” [al., “has drawn near”] (Matt. III, 2). And in the middle of the week, when Christ offered himself to the Father, sacrifice and offering ceased, and finally the condemnation of the place was repeated three times by its inhabitants.

What will you say, when you cannot bring forward anyone to whom these things apply except him? Either explain your Scriptures to me, so that your explanation does not diverge from the sequence set out above, or submit to Christian understanding, from which the prophet’s intention does not recoil.

If these matters are not sufficiently clear to you, receive something more evident:

“I was watching,” the same prophet says, “in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he came up to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him; and he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him” (Dan. VII, 13–14).

There can be no doubt that you understand the Ancient of Days himself to be God. But who is the son of man who comes to him? Will a human being be compared with his Maker? For power, honor, and kingdom in that eternity are given to no one except one who is regarded as God. There no peoples, tribes, or languages serve anyone except the one whom they know to transcend all the rights of humanity.

Therefore they present him before God, because all the faithful believe that he alone is visible to the Father and specially pleasing to the Father. “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. IX, 27). He also adds there: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Ibid.). And: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

Thus he comes to the Ancient of Days, because the one who had placed his tabernacle in the sun, who had gone forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, who, being more than human and therefore a giant, had rejoiced to run his course, whose going forth was from the summit of heaven, also had his meeting at its summit—that is, with the Father (Ps. XVIII, 5).

[Col. 0512D] He was coming in the vision of the night like a son of man upon the clouds (Dan. VII, 13), because in prophetic expressions he was foretold as coming in complete obscurity, like a mere man; or like a son of man—that is, truly a son of man, which means nothing other than the Virgin’s son. As in the phrase: “Like the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John I, 14).

It follows: “His power is an everlasting power, which will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 14). If he is the son of man, and his power is everlasting, immovable, and incorruptible, then he is God and human being. He is the human being “free among the dead, without help” (Ps. LXXXVII, 6).

Who also, in this same prophet, is that stone cut from the mountain without hands, which crushed all the kingdoms of the earth? (Dan. II, 34–35.) Does he not add the following when explaining it? “The God of heaven will raise up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and its kingdom will not be handed over to another people. It will crush and shatter all these kingdoms, and it itself will stand forever” (Ibid., 44).

If you do not deny that all human beings are mortal, and believe that everything possessing a body is transitory, what kingdom will have eternity? Do you think that stone is some stupid object? But if it became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole earth, where then will human beings dwell? You see that history rejects you and that a type is being brought forth most openly.

Accept, then, that otherwise you will not be able to understand the name of Christ, because it is he who cannot be utterly obliterated through an external religion. He was cut out without hands, begotten by no sexual act. He crushed kingdoms because he is the one who inherited among all nations. His kingdom is not destroyed and is not handed over to another people, because the righteousness introduced through the Holy of Holies is established in eternity. Nor is it corrupted by the alien transmission of some heresy, so that it might be handed over to another people who would be changed when faithlessness arose. “Holiness befits the house of the Lord throughout the length of days” (Ps. XCII, 5).

You see, O minds more crooked than any sickle, in these few testimonies the clarity of the Christian faith. They are not few because they are rare in your books, but so numerous that no one’s knowledge would suffice to unravel them, and all eloquence would be blunted in attempting it. If you possessed the Spirit who leads the good into the straight land, you would certainly taste, with the same seasoning, what he himself spoke through his prophets. But because you think of nothing at all except thefts and interest-bearing loans, you pursue nothing belonging to pious subtlety.

If it is true that “the Lord did whatever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6), and if God, existing plausibly as God, assumed humanity, what scruple is there, I ask, in the fact that he allowed humanity to be humbled—not without a saving mystery—and afterward exalted it as he wished?

Explain what the Lord Jesus himself set before his contemporaries. “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1), and the rest of the psalm, which is very much opposed to your error. Let your discernment either say or learn what that Davidic statement means: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 7–8).

And if he is David, how is he the Son of God? I ask what meaning “Today I have begotten you” has for you. Were the nations his inheritance from the Father or from his mother? And I question you at length about the possession of the ends of the earth. Although he may plainly have made neighboring districts of the Palestinians or Ammonites tributary, it is contrary to the truth that he held nations as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession, rather than merely as tributary territories.

He also says: “You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people; you will set me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me,” and so forth, “As the Lord lives” (Ps. XVII, 44, 46).

Certainly, even if he had opponents, they were not the people but the son of Absalom, who was plotting revolution. But let it be granted: where was he set as head of the nations? I will not say of nations, but not even of one nation. Will you say that when he, fearful of Saul, withdrew to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, he was appointed head of the nations? Yet he was not head even of a tenth part of them.

Who was the people whom he did not know? Certainly the Philistines—but he knew all of them. And from where is such obedience of theirs commended, so that they are said to have obeyed at the sound of his ear? Did not Abimelech’s officers, when he was about to fight against Israel, say to him concerning David: “David will not go out with us, for he could not please his lord better than by attacking our heads”? (I Sam. XXIX, 4.) These are not the words of members concerning their head.

“Foreign sons lied to me” (Ps. XVII, 46). Are foreign sons repeated a second time, and called aged and limping, because after Absalom’s death they are called by him “his bone and his flesh”?

Give up, I ask, because reason has abandoned you. Who, then, is head of the nations? Christ, certainly: “The scepter will not be taken from Judah, nor the leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLVI, 10). He is the one who stands as a sign for the peoples, whom the nations will entreat (Isa. II, 10).

Read Isaiah, recall the Psalms: what do they sound forth other than the calling of the nations, which will hope in the name of Christ? It must be declared among the nations that the Lord has reigned: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord will be worthy of praise, and he himself is exalted above the nations” (Ps. CXII, 3–4).

And when your temple was already deprived of priest and sacrifice, Malachi adds: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is presented to my name, because my name is great among the nations” (Mal. I, 11). Yet when we ask you why you lack a temple, a pontificate, and an altar, you immediately blame the land in which you live as unclean; but the prophet just mentioned does not support you in this.

What moreover of that diviner Balaam? “A star,” he says, “will arise from Jacob, and a staff will rise from Israel, and it will crush all the leaders of Moab; it will lay waste all the sons of Seth; and Edom will be its possession. The inheritance of Seir will fall to its enemies. But Israel will act bravely” (Num. XXIV, 17–18).

What is the star? Mary, illuminated by the true sun, from whom light arose in darkness for the upright in heart—“merciful and gracious and just” (Ps. III, 4). From her the staff then rises: namely, Christ himself emerges as the singularity of all uprightness.

Observe in these examples, taken from your own books, how purely, without any mention of father or seed, the origin is proclaimed. Hear the star that emitted that light without diminishing itself. But because the light was not visible to weak eyes, the star’s offspring is changed into a staff, which directs the straying, casts down the proud, and becomes a support for the weak.

[Col. 0515A] This staff crushes the leaders of Moab in their most wicked rigidity—namely, the Gentiles who are without the law and have the devil as their father. For Moab is said to mean “from the father” or “lawless.” But Eth is interpreted as “stunned.” Who are the stunned except the Jews, who have neither known nor understood and walk in darkness? These are sons, but lying sons, alienated sons.

The staff lays them waste because Christ truly gives the Gentile people the knowledge of the law that Judaea falsely claims for itself. “For there is a cup in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine mixed with spices, and he poured from this to that people. Yet its dregs have not been emptied; all the sinners of the earth will drink them” (Ps. LXXIV, 8–9).

Edom is his possession, because the more earthly a mind is, the more rigorously it turns to God. “As Mount Zion, so are the sides of the north, the city of the great King”; for where sin abounds, grace abounds all the more. Seir is said to mean “hairy”: hair grows excessively on the body and signifies the substance of the world.

What is the inheritance of Seir except the law, or the very kingdom of the Jews, which the Christian people now possess? But how does this interpretation fit the literal sense for you? You will accept nothing significant in the Pentateuch. In those lands, certainly, the Assyrians, Parthians, Arabs, and Franks have recently taken turns in victory, yet not even the names of these nations have remained there.

What, then, will your Messiah do? It follows:

“But Israel will act bravely” (Num. XXIV, 18). Israel is said to mean “straight with God.” And who is made straight with God except the one who follows the rule of faith? He acts bravely who defends the Christian faith even amid savage tortures.

“From Jacob one will come who will rule and destroy the survivors of the city” (Ibid., 19). This is to say: Although the courage of martyrs is praised among the nations, nevertheless from Jacob—that is, from the Jews, who rejoiced that through their acceptance of the law they had supplanted Esau, that is, the nations—the Lord Christ arises. Hence above there is a star from Jacob and a staff from Israel.

For Mary indeed derives her origin from the Jews, but the people of the nations, made straight in a special way with Christ, chiefly displays Christ’s strength. He destroys the survivors of the city because, although he is a human being born from a woman, through the power of his divinity he can punish with everlasting torments those whom he judges exiled from the city of God.

What does all this mean? The one who will put on the lowliness of the Jewish race will possess such greatness of the Lord—which concerns the ungodly, for fatherhood concerns the pious—that, seeing some unworthy of his citizenship, he will be powerful enough to destroy them in everlasting fires. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 12).

There is, moreover, a Jerusalem “which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXII, 3). I wonder what blessednesses of yours you understand here in the literal sense. But if this is how you are deceived, attend to what follows shortly afterward. Balaam, taking up his parable again, says: “Alas! Who will live when God does these things?” (Num. XXIV, 23). By prefacing “alas,” he clearly promised that he would speak of things worthy of lamentation.

“They will come,” he says, “in ships from Italy; they will overcome the Assyrians and lay waste the Hebrews” (Ibid., 24). You have proved this desolation, which he proclaimed beforehand for you, by its continuation for a thousand years already.

## CHAPTER IV

### On Christ’s resurrection

Having therefore the arguments and examples concerning the assumption of humanity by God, concerning the Passion, resurrection, and ascension—so numerous, certainly, that their abundance produces a poverty of speech, and whose multiplicity even the less learned have readily at hand and the Church sings—I have been pleased to set forth only those that demonstrate God in a human being.

But if the eternal God is proved by the clear testimony of your Scriptures, what great thing did he do by restoring a suffering body to life, when even the corpse of Elisha did the same? You hear David, when he complained of the excessiveness of his distresses, which commonly provoke wakefulness among human beings: “I slept,” he says, “and was overcome with sleep, and I arose” (Ps. III, 6); elsewhere asserting that his hands and feet were pierced (Ps. XXI, 17). In Hosea, God presents himself as destined to become death to death (Hos. XIII, 44). Again, in a psalm God is said to have ascended amid jubilation and at the sound of the trumpet (Ps. XLVI, 6). Elsewhere he is said to have ascended on high, led captivity captive, and given gifts to human beings (Eph. IV, 8), although, according to the Apostle, it is certain that no one ascends except the one whom it is established had descended (Ibid., 9).

### On the calling of the nations

Since testimonies of this kind from your Scriptures flash everywhere like sparks, it is supremely clear that the calling of the nations, celebrated throughout the prophetic books, plainly appears to have been fulfilled. “Their sound has now gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 4).

No one can object to us on account of the apostasy of certain nations, any more than one can object to Isaiah, who called the Jews “a sinful nation, a wicked seed, and criminal children” (Isa. I, 4). Later he says: “Hear, Israel, my servant, and [reading uncertain: ‘rectissime’], whom I have chosen” (Isa. XLIV, 1). If they were a wicked seed and a sinful nation, how was the one whom he had chosen upright? But you know that in your Scriptures and ours it is customary for the whole to be taken for a part and the part for the whole, as in the statement: “All flesh will come to you” (Ps. LXIV, 2), which we understand in no other way than as though he had said: “From every flesh they will come to you.”

To the one who would rise from death it is said: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you will inherit”—not all nations, but “among all nations” (Ps. LXXXI, 8). And when Elijah complained that he alone had been left (I Kings XIX, 10), he heard of seven thousand who had not bent their knees to Baal (Ibid., 18).

For if you were once called God’s people, although the greater part of you had gone astray, you did not lose what you were called on account of regard for the good part. Thus, even if a great part of the world has since fallen away, it has nevertheless not diminished Christ’s power through its former apostasy.

## CHAPTER V

### He addresses the Jews

Therefore, since we have brought forward against you certain authorities and arguments, I will now address you with a few questions.

With what intention do you cling to that law so carnally? I know what you will say: “How can we change a law given by God from heaven—or rather, written by his own finger—proclaimed amid terrors of voices, flashes of lamps, and exhalations of the mountain, a law never given to any nation since the beginning of the world? And if human laws endure, who will set aside God’s commandments?”

He responds to the Jews and proves by scriptural authorities that God has abrogated the law.

To this I will reply: Whatever terror and whatever outward magnificence are known to have accompanied the giving of the law are not greatly significant; such things are often employed even in lesser affairs. Clearly, when Samuel was objecting to the Jews who desired royal dignity, he said: “Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and he will give thunder and rain, and you will know that you have done a great evil” (I Sam. XII, 17).

Certainly Uzziah, the king who rivaled the priestly headdress, when he presumed to enter the holy places, experienced great earthquakes, of which Amos speaks, and the most precipitous clefts in the earth also opened. Nothing happened there that could not have happened more easily elsewhere.

If Moses postponed his fast for forty days, we know that Elijah did the same for a lighter reason. If Moses spoke with the Lord face to face, and Isaiah professes that he saw the Lord of Hosts with his own eyes, whom he had seen seated upon a lofty throne, some others among the prophets did the same. What of the fact that God is said both to have appeared to Balaam the diviner and to have come before him repeatedly? Thunder and such noises result from disturbances of the air, occurring in some provinces in winter and in others in summer. If not, let them produce a portent.

Let this alone, therefore, be at issue: that God gave those commandments. If they are judged immutable for that reason, let us see from the very beginnings of the ages what he instituted, and what institutions he changed according to places, times, and persons.

Certainly, in the creation of the first human beings, after Scripture had said that he placed them over earthly and aquatic creatures, it added that God likewise said: “Behold, I have given you every plant bearing fruit upon the earth, and all trees that have within themselves the seed of their own kind, so that they may be food for you” (Gen. I, 29).

But after the floodwaters had subsided, when he had again spoken the words of the same dominion to Noah and his sons, he added: “All the fish have been delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives will be food for you, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood” (Gen. IX, 2–3). You have here God changing his decree, so that he might release us from grasses to the eating of meat. Finally, under Moses, when he dealt with the distinction of foods, as though forgetting what he had granted to those men—namely, everything that moves and lives—he forbade it to be eaten [the phrase “in munera” is uncertain].

When Adam had been given his wife, he also said: “A man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife” (Gen. II, 24). He did not say: “A man, then full of God and wisdom, will cling to wives,” but “to his wife,” although afterward we read that the flood came on account of numerous marriages, and yet that Abraham had Hagar from the side of Sarah, with God also arranging this for him several times. We know that Jacob, Moses, and many others highly esteemed under the law had a number of wives without contradiction of the law.

We unquestionably take Adam’s words as God’s words, since we know that Adam was then God’s intimate inhabitant of paradise. The Lord Jesus also attributes these words to God.

God had said to the woman who had persuaded her husband to disobey: “You will be under your husband’s power, and he will rule over you” (Gen. III, 16). The same God speaks to Abraham: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Gen. XXI, 12). Behold how great and how remarkable an authority he assigned to a woman, although he could have instructed her directly.

[Col. 0518B] You know from where Cain and Seth, Adam’s sons, obtained wives for themselves: plainly, from their own kinship. God could have created wives for them from elsewhere, but he himself arranged that this should necessarily happen. The same is entirely true of aunts, both paternal and maternal. Yet all these things, which God had first established by command, were afterward most harshly forbidden by the Mosaic decree.

What of the fact that he himself soon afterward permitted the one rib that he had taken from the man and built into a woman to be divided into so many, so that now not two but very many would become one flesh?

The angel found Hagar the servant, driven away by her mistress Sarah, and ordered her to return and humble herself under her mistress. Finally, when Isaac had long since been born and Ishmael had grown older, Sarah could scarcely bear their games; and, although Abraham was unwilling, the servant woman was ordered to be driven away with her child. The divine voice, which above had commanded her to be reconciled to her mistress, entered into this dispute and, as though forgetting its former counsel, set Abraham aside and commanded obedience to Sarah in everything.

God moreover commanded that no graven image, no cast image, no likeness, and no sign should be erected in your land; yet, at the Lord’s command, Cherubim were carved in the tabernacle. What shall I say about the bronze serpent set before the fiery serpents, toward which, if anyone who had been bitten looked—raised up before the whole army—he would be saved? Was it a sign, was it a likeness? And certainly, as the Book of Kings testifies, the Jews continued to honor it by burning incense until the time of Hezekiah; and God, the institutor of that portent, was surely not unaware that this tendency of theirs toward idols would contribute greatly to error. This, I say, God commanded contrary, if I may dare say so, to his own decrees.

But Solomon abandoned the tabernacle itself, which God had fashioned from its foundations to its heights with his own word, through a new construction, to such an extent that, after the temple’s dedication, anyone who paid any cultic attention to those places would be judged guilty of sacrilege, indeed of idolatry. Hence it is repeatedly said against it as an accusation: “Even still the people sacrificed in the high places” (IV Kings XIV, 4). Yet divine favor was not lacking toward that temple, either before or after its construction.

God had commanded you to receive on loan gold, silver, vessels, and garments from the Egyptians, 276 which, having been granted to you humanely, you took, as it seems, sufficiently inhumanely—though God permitted it. Hence it is said: “God gave you favor before the Egyptians” (Exodus XII, 35–36). Later, when he himself proclaimed the judgments of that law, he prohibited theft, fraud, and covetousness.

## CHAPTER VI

### Although God is immutable, he appears to change his judgments in adapting himself to human mutability; this is confirmed by arguments.

You have, I think, many examples of changes in divine judgments, from which you may infer that God, although immutable, has given judgments adaptable to human mutability, in order to educate human beings through successive developments. Just as you see little children instructed by one set of rudiments in infancy and by other teachings when they have grown; and, after they have fully matured, governed by stricter discipline; while with old men the deepest matters are discussed—so understand that God has acted in accordance with the progressions of this age.

For just as it is fitting for a small child to be formed in the rudiments of speech through the constant chatter of bearers and nurses, and, as he grows, to be restrained from the license of infancy by sterner schooling, and, when he reaches the age of puberty, to be entirely restricted from childish behavior, while youth, fully educated, is governed of its own accord and by its own seriousness, without the rod, through love of virtue—so, at the beginning, God accustomed the newly formed age to his own voice and that of the angels, and, as though by the pattern of his speech, corrected the world’s babbling lips. Thus what is not granted even to the best now was then provided to the worst, and even to the animals themselves. When the world had advanced somewhat, as in the times of Noah and Abraham, he began to chastise it in a few matters and to mark it out with signs. Under Moses, as though lifting an adolescent somewhat above its former baseness, he compelled it to perceive something of the dignity of a human being.

### The perfect age began with Christ. The old law teaches the pursuit of temporal things, but Christ teaches the pursuit of eternal things.

Moreover, under the grace of the Redeemer, as though with a mind now more weighty and capable of understanding his entire divinity, and as though he were revealing the precipitous depths of his inner counsel—for those who serve their masters out of love alone are usually told their secrets more readily—he says: “I will no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John XV, 14).

What rewards does God promise you in your law? Possessions, fullness of belly, wives and children, longevity—and he threatens nothing except things opposed to these. About eternal things there is silence. The rewards of heaven and the punishments of hell are left unmentioned. Just as a virgin alone is offered to a young man burning with lust, and dishonorable speech is kept from his ears, so they were driven away from vices by torments or death; toward whatever goods were offered, they were drawn not by desire or admonition but by the allure of such rewards.

I am lying unless the law itself bears witness to this: “The Lord brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey,” it says, “so that you might observe his commandments, and so that the law of the Lord might always be in your mouth” (Exodus XXXIII, 3). The Psalm likewise says: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples, so that they might keep his justifications and seek his law” (Psalm CIV, 44).

The threats found in your books against sinners include: “Your body shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (III Kings XIII, 22). And: “Because Ahab humbled himself before me, I will not bring evil in his days” (III Kings XXI, 29). Many gentile philosophers held in contempt the things that were promised to you, and, like Diogenes, rejected them even when they possessed them. And when supreme power weighed upon certain men, as upon Caesar Octavian, they treated it as insignificant.

What shall I say to you? Is that a good law whose rewards promise nothing stable? Why do you weigh the thousands of victims? Hear the Lord in Isaiah: “I am full,” he says. “I did not desire the holocausts of rams and goats” (Isaiah I, 11). He adds the reasons: “Your hands are full of blood” (ibid., 15). And he immediately explains what he wants: “Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes. Cease to act perversely” (ibid., 16), and what follows.

Another says: “I will not rebuke you for sacrifices, because your holocausts are subject to my disposal. I will not receive calves from your house. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls? But sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God; pay your vows to the Most High in addition to sacrifices” (Psalm XLIX, 8–14). The same speaker says: “You will not delight in holocausts. The sacrifice to God is a spirit troubled” (Psalm L, 18–19).

As for your circumcision, put away your trifles. Do not the law and the prophets alike sing to you that you should remove the foreskin of your heart? If they loudly demand circumcision of your heart and senses, they are merely marking that circumcision of the flesh as a figure of the interior one.

What are you doing with the fasts in which quarrels and murders seem to occur? In opposition to this the prophet says: “Loosen the bonds of wickedness, the bundles that oppress” (Isaiah LVIII, 6), and the rest of what God there recognizes as worthy of esteem in fasting.

You display much diligence in observing the Sabbaths. But perhaps you believe that God rejoices in your leisure and spectacles. Nor is it far from this what the same prophet thinks: “If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath, so as not to do your will on my holy day, and you call the Sabbath delightful, and glorify it while not following your own ways” (ibid., 13).

277 You perhaps think that turning the foot away from the Sabbath means refraining from traveling. What will you say about restraining the will? But if you turn to active desires, hear what follows: “And your will is not found, so that you may speak a word” (ibid.). No law requires you to abstain from conversation on the Sabbaths. Indeed, we are already compelled to this by necessity, so that we may regard the Sabbath as delightful in this alone: if, in a more spiritual way, we divide our tongue and mind away from evils that are not forbidden by the law.

Consider, then, the most illustrious authors of your law, and how greatly they differ from your understanding. Regarding bodily exercises as nothing, they attended only to spiritual marrow. For in those observances there is only an affliction of the flesh—at least for those who have perceived nothing of spirituality.

Although it is said in your law, “Whoever does these things or those commandments shall live by them” (Leviticus XVIII, 5), no one should ever be believed to have lived, as far as the soul is concerned, if he did not cling to those ceremonies through love and faith. Hence it is written in Ezekiel that, when God reproached them for the transgressions committed by them in the wilderness, for their incursions into idolatry and their neglect of the Sabbaths, he finally added: “Therefore I also gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they will not live; and I defiled them through their gifts, when they offered everything that opens the womb, because of their sins” (Ezekiel XX, 25–26).

Why were they not good, when, according to our apostle, the law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good? (Romans VII, 12.) They were not good for those who gnaw the bark and bones; they are useful to those who pluck out the interior and make use of the marrow. These are the enemies in the Psalm who “lick the earth” (Psalm LXXI, 9).

“I defiled them through their gifts,” even when they were fulfilling the legal commandments themselves—namely, by offering everything that opens the womb—because he showed them to be defiled by those gifts when they offered nothing for the interior things but only for the exterior. Hence it says: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psalm CVIII, 8): let him seek from God temporal gain rather than God himself.

Life would indeed be found in those commandments if someone loved God with his whole heart, if he cared for his neighbor, if theft were avoided, if lying and fraud were not practiced. But when, after these things have been set aside, the superstition of empty rites is celebrated, the flesh is afflicted without producing fruit in the mind.

Since, therefore, you pursued the whole visible body and held the hidden soul as worthless, God finally wanted to produce for us—or, if you had wished it, for you—not merely representations of the realities but the realities themselves, nearer to salvation. He had already foreshadowed them for you through the prophet mentioned above:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, the covenant which they made void. But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel: After those days I will give my law in their inward parts, and I will write it on their hearts; and they shall no longer teach one another, a man his neighbor and a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest, because I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah XXXI, 31–35).

When a new covenant is said to be made by God with the house of Israel, life is already being lived by you under the old covenant familiar to you. To use the words of our Apostle: “By saying ‘new,’ he has made the first old; and what is becoming old and aging is near destruction” (Hebrews VIII, 13). But why is it called old, unless because it promises things that are fleeting and soon to perish—namely, visible things?

The other is rightly called new because it promises incorruptible things, visible only to immortal eyes and not subject to decay through any use. Nor is it like the covenant made with your fathers in the wilderness, because there, with threats and terrors attached to every commandment, “I am the Lord” is proclaimed; here, however, “Our Father” is preached as the one to be addressed (Matthew VI, 9).

Here the Holy Spirit, who is love, is employed as teacher. Here the law is written not on stone but on hearts and inward parts, because, as the same prophet elsewhere testifies, the heart, the stone having been removed, is filled with a new spirit (Ezekiel XXXVI, 26).

The evidence of our faith is now so great through God’s grace that no one need now be instructed about knowledge of the incarnate Son of God. For the uneducated know as well as the learned that he is the one who came to wash away the sins of all. Instruction should now be given openly about correcting works and conduct.

## CHAPTER VII

### He likewise demonstrates Christ’s coming from the Old Testament.

Since, therefore, the testament once given to your fathers has been transferred—not buried—to an understanding of healthier observance, what are you objecting to me, wicked Jew, concerning the pig, the hare, and the oyster, which we eat? No trace of your temple remains; the pontificate has collapsed, so that almost the whole stock of your nation appears abolished, and dispersions wander throughout the world. With sanctuary, priesthood, kingdom, and almost the entire nation vacant—or rather destroyed—what part of the law remains? For almost the whole law depends upon devotion to the temple and priesthood.

After God himself, and no other, has overthrown this central substance of the entire law, what will you say about the minutiae of the remaining precepts? You hear of the covenant of a new star [possibly: “of a new covenant”], at whose arrival no one doubts that the old order is annihilated.

To whom do you attribute what is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”? (Psalm CIX, 4.) Whose person do you think speaks to God in the Psalm? “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you fashioned ears for me. You did not request holocaust and sin-offering; then I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Psalm XXXIX, 7–8).

If you refer these words to David, for whom God fashioned ears—that is, gave obedience—because he neglected sacrifices, the meaning will be equivalent to the statement: “Obedience is better than victims” (I Kings XV, 22). If you refer them to the Messiah, whom you vainly await as your own, it is false, because you imagine that he will serve those ceremonies with the utmost submission.

But if you refer them to Christ, he alone clearly learned obedience from the things he suffered (Hebrews V, 8), because he had learned that the Father could in no way be pleased by holocausts or sin-offerings.

Although there were many priests, which of them existed forever? Who is eternal except God? Yet you will nowhere find God called a priest, as I think, unless you understand Christ. Christ, therefore, is the one priest who said, “Behold, I come” (Psalm XXXIX, 8), because he offered himself as a victim to the Father for sin.

“Because you complain,” he says, “about a futile sacrifice, I now come to offer myself to you, Father. For I am the one of whom it is written at the head of the book that I should do your will” (ibid., 9).

This meaning has now departed from the person of David. What is the head of this book? “Blessed is the man who has not gone,” and what follows, up to “everything that he does shall prosper” (Psalm I, 1, 4). Who is the one to whom the present verse sings, so that, according to its type, he has not gone, has not stood, and has not sat?

If, in the third matter, some pure human being might perhaps be able to remain free from it, no living human being has been able to be exempt from either of the first two. Who is the one who has meditated on God’s law day and night—that is, without ceasing? Does not Jeduthun sing: “For every living person is altogether vanity,” and “Passing away like a shadow, he is troubled in vain”? (Psalm XXXVIII, 6–7.)

You will accept Christ, whether you wish it or not—whatever you find there that exceeds the human. He is born not “upon the courses of waters” but beside them, because he is not propagated in a nature made fluid through sin, but is seen only in the likeness of sinful flesh. And rightly, not a pool but the flow of waters can be understood as the virgin who gives birth, where no filth remains.

She was the planting of blessing and gave fruit—not her own, but in its time and in its proper season. Every good person gives fruit, but not his own, for without God no one can do anything. He, however, produced his own fruit in a proper sense, because what he did could not have been done except by God, and he had from himself what he did.

Its time was also its own, because he who was born when he wished also died when he wished. Its time was its own when, with the arrival of the fullness of time, he granted the blind world the light of knowledge of himself. Its leaf will not fall, because although heaven and earth will pass away, his word will not pass away (Matthew XXIV, 35). All his works will prosper, for God’s right hand will guide him wondrously. It is enough to have pursued these matters at such length.

## CHAPTER VIII

Behold your prophets, most impure man—or rather, prophets who oppose your observances through God—to such an extent that one who sacrifices and one who brains a dog are placed on the same level. Why do you make your pigs grunt at me and your hares squeal? Why do you repeat the matters concerning chewing animals and divided hooves, when you see so clearly that the pontificate and temple, from which all the force of your law arises and in which its purpose is contained, have been utterly abolished? What force do you think the lowest members will have, most wretched man, when the head has been cut off?

Listen, if you still have too few witnesses for this, to what we seemed a little earlier to have touched upon. God speaks in Isaiah, rejecting carnal things and choosing spiritual goods:

“To whom shall I look,” he says, “except to the humble and contrite in spirit, and to the one who trembles at my words? He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man; he who slaughters a sheep is as one who brains a dog; he who offers an offering is as one who offers swine’s blood; he who remembers incense is as one who blesses an idol” (Isaiah LXVI, 2–3).

But you say: “Certainly it cannot be denied that God forbade the eating of pork.” Certainly, I reply; it is no less established that he commanded bulls, rams, and the other animals to be sacrificed, and that later, as you hear from the prophets, he himself declared these things void.

But perhaps, once sacrifice and temple have been rejected, abstaining from pork outweighs everything else. If you condemn us for eating pork, although nothing has been commanded to us, why do you not wear the blue fringes on the four corners of your garments? The same God who commanded that the pig not be eaten also commanded that fringes be worn (Numbers XV, 38). We eat pork for a very different reason from that for which you have torn away the fringes.

You are therefore transgressors, because you plainly neglect what was commanded to you. We omit nothing, because we have received no commandments concerning those matters. You devote yourselves to theft, piling up interest upon the necks of the needy. You set aside loving God from the heart, loving your neighbor as yourself, and the other useful things, and you whirl around trifles.

Do you interpret in the merely outward sense what is said: “If, while walking along the road, you find on a tree or on the ground a bird’s nest, with the mother sitting on the chicks or eggs, you shall not take her with her offspring, but shall let her go, while taking the chicks, so that it may be well with you and you may live a long time” (Deuteronomy XXII, 6–7)?

Has God forgotten the command he gave to Noah: 279 “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; just as I gave you all green plants, so I give you everything” (Genesis IX, 3)? Is he now promising us prosperity and long life if our hand spares the mothers of chicks?

What rational purpose is there in the command that you carry a stake on your belt (Deuteronomy XXIII, 13), so that you may cover your excrement and prevent any filth from appearing before the eyes of God? If I, the least of human beings, were to bring forward something of this sort in public, my hearers would perhaps not easily believe that I was weaving these things together pointlessly or without hidden meaning. Even if some people value me as having neither dignity nor importance, so that they think my words devoid of weight, can you imagine God to be a flute-player, so that his statements vanish into chatter? The less, therefore, divine speech agrees with human reasoning, the more it overflows with intellectual subtlety.

Come to your senses, overcome at last by such a mass of testimonies and witnesses; and, having cast off the flesh, become capable of holy interiority. Come with the prophet Hosea, and let us return to the Lord whom, thinking that you were following him, you flee. For he began, from the origin of the world, with predestination and promises, and at the end of time he will save us through the efficacy of his Passion; he will strike us—that is, by teachings powerful for our souls he will lay bare our wounds. Finally, he will not delay to heal those struck with blood and water:

“He revived us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. We shall know, and we shall follow, so that we may know the Lord. His coming is prepared like the dawn” (Hosea VI, 1–3), and so forth.

But with these statements sufficiently established, as we think, let us pursue other matters.

## CHAPTER IX

### The Jews are refuted for accusing Christians of idolatry.

You also attack us on the ground that we adore images of the crucified Lord Jesus, or the wood of the cross itself, and thus accuse us of a kind of idolatry, as though this were prohibited by your law.

We, on the contrary, consider only God’s very substance worthy of worship. Even if we are seen to venerate certain external things, we do not worship what is visible but what we infer from visible things.

Certainly, Nathan the prophet is recorded among you as having prostrated himself before King David while petitioning on Solomon’s behalf (III Kings I, 23); yet it would be impious to believe that he perceived anything divine in him. Joshua, seeing Israel fleeing and cut down by the inhabitants of Ai, is said in the Book of Judges to have continued the day in vigils, lying prostrate before the ark of the Lord (Joshua VII, 6). Was the ark a goddess or a god, or had some part of God been hidden in it?

Daniel, after the king’s decree had been proclaimed that no one should petition any god, with the windows of his upper room open, three times during the day facing Jerusalem, knelt, worshiped, and confessed his God (Daniel VI, 11). Was Jerusalem, or the temple, for whose sake that kneeling occurred, God, because he had decided to worship in that direction?

Are all the things reported as having been worshiped among you therefore believed worthy of divine worship?

### How Christians worship images.

We therefore worship, in visible signs, the invisible things signified; indeed, by the sudden sight of paintings, as by a kind of reminder, we restrain our wandering mind and direct it toward inner things.

Why was that bronze serpent set before you, which you later worshiped, unless so that you might ask what such a portent meant? Nor did the Cherubim stand uselessly prominent in the temple and tabernacle. Oxen and lions also deserved to be carved there in particular not without purpose; they gave you suitable occasions for inquiry.

Laugh, if you wish, at our worshiping the weakened and bloodless man Jesus on the gallows. Surely anyone with sense can see how much more ridiculous in faith your parents were, who worshiped Beelphogor—that is, the idol of lust, which is Priapus.

You too deserve laughter—or rather weeping—because many of you fully understand the truth of Christian teaching and yet do not abandon your error. Know, however, that for us, to whom God has imparted knowledge of the Scriptures and, even after imagination has been removed, has given the wing of faith and contemplation, the appearance of sculptures is not necessary. It is necessary only for those who are ignorant and dull, who learn through such aids what they cannot reach through letters.

## CHAPTER X

### The author shows that Christians do not worship three gods. He proves the Trinity in God.

There remains the final question that you propose for debate. You say that we worship three gods because you know that we pronounce the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit under a threefold distinction.

From the mass of testimonies above, it has been sufficiently proved that God has a Son and that this Son became human. It is also readily apparent that the Holy Spirit is mentioned throughout your pages. Therefore, just as we speak of three persons, so you openly accuse us of worshiping three gods.

Do you believe God to be unbounded and incomprehensible? If so, why do you construct three thrones of persons, or limbs, in your imagination? If you consider God to be spirit, and the Son, as we believe, belongs to him, he cannot be a son unless he is what the Father is; otherwise he is not God. In a human being there can be something that is not human, but in God there is nothing that is not God.

For if someone is just, devout, and wise, these qualities are one thing and the human being another; a human being exists even without them. But when these qualities are said to exist in God, they are understood not as accidents but substantially as God.

### The Son is the Father’s will; the Holy Spirit is his power.

If, then, you accept the Son, do not understand him as one whom the Father begot outside himself; perceive instead that he is begotten within him. Accept the Son, therefore, as though he were the Father’s will. This will came to evident effect when he entered into flesh.

But this will, directed by God toward us, must have power, through which it can accomplish what it wills; and this power is the Holy Spirit, who creates a body for it in the Virgin. For human will is idle unless the ability to act follows it. The Father’s will, therefore, is accompanied by possibility.

In the Scriptures the same Spirit is called both love and power, as in the words: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 32). And: “The power of God works for salvation in everyone who believes” (Romans I, 16). The Father’s will is therefore brought to effect in this way through power, and from it the effect that has been given to our knowledge proceeds.

It is not permitted to anyone to dispute about God. But when examples are offered from the things around us, this is done to show that three things can cling to one another inseparably. When this is done, “faith no longer has merit,” as it is written, “when human reason provides the proof” (St. Gregory, Homily 26).

This Trinity is spoken of by us in this world more by designation than substantially, since, to instruct our understanding about the persons, we necessarily join their names together through moments and syllables, because we cannot do otherwise. But when we have drunk from the fountain of life and seen God in God, in the light that is light, we will need no gradation of speech in naming these things.

If our mouth, tongue, and spirit move together for the use of speech, none of them being absent or superior, it is the height of madness to deny that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exist, and can act indivisibly. For if we said that there were three gods, we would plainly assign to each of them a portion of the world’s government. None of them could be supreme if he had others equal to him in action and name.

And while we favored now one, now another, according to the alternation of their portions, we would perhaps regard as less suitable, value less, or openly disparage whichever one seemed to have the lesser kingdom. Yet you have encountered none of this in our doctrines, nor will we discuss it at length with you, because while we deal with these matters, we become a source of laughter to minds made obstinate. Those who deliberate about believing will not lack teachers capable of instructing them.

### The Lord truly rose again.

Hear this, whether you wish it or not: our Redeemer, whom you falsely claim to have rotted, lives, and on the last day—which you too believe—we shall rise from the earth. In our flesh also we shall see God, namely Jesus, whom you interpret as “Savior.”

Can someone who is in the flesh see God, even if he has already passed beyond corruption—something that will scarcely be possible even for angelic spirits, who behold him with flashes of light? For the angels desire to look upon him. Desire seeks fulfillment. How, then, will he see him? Existing in the flesh, he will be able to behold the one who is carnal, namely the Son of God, now immortal because he has risen incorruptibly.

Both realities—the human being in himself and God—are the Son of God. If he lacked this name, he would have been neither dead nor buried.

It can also be understood very clearly that Job promises to see his Savior in his own flesh, that is, in the same human nature in which he himself exists. Marking the indivisible subject of mortal and rational nature, he repeats what he said: “Whom I myself shall see,” he says, “and not another” (Job XIII, 27). That “other” would undoubtedly exist in some sense if, after stripping off the human being, the spirit remained.

Finally, he repeats this a third time: “And my eyes shall behold” (ibid.). By expressing the eyes so emphatically, he made it known that what he would see would plainly be the body of God. But it is not permitted for divinity to be seen by a body.

Behold, against the enemies of God, against the adversary and defender, we have taken up weapons—using what we could, not what we ought. We have suppressed many things because we refrained from adducing ambiguous testimonies from their books. An example that resolves one dispute by another accomplishes nothing.

If what I have done seems empty to the faithless and mockers, perhaps I have deservedly pleased the faithful, who either do not dare or do not know how to debate such matters, because, if not very usefully, at least very faithfully, I have completed what was imposed upon me.

If infamy or praise is acquired for this, it is rightly ascribed to you, Father, who commanded it. If it was done well, it is the fruit of your faith and prayers; if badly, the venture was rash on both sides. Let no one accuse me of rebuking the most disgraceful errors, since I am insignificant and foolish. Let him remember the prophet’s she-ass rebuking folly. For although I am a bad human being, I am better than a good she-ass.

## CHAPTER XI

After this discussion, whatever its quality, I think I must not leave unmentioned a report concerning a certain Jew, which may be judged more powerful than any contest of words. As he testifies, while still a little boy he was at Laon and heard, in a certain house, a cleric disputing with a Jew.

When the cleric could not resist that faithless man’s windy bluster, he said: “In the name of Jesus the Lord, I will take a burning brand by its flaming, burning end with my bare hand and carry it outside the door of the house.” (A hearth was near [read: “close by”].) The Jew did not object, waiting to see whether he would be burned in the faith of his Jesus.

The cleric, blazing with wondrous ferocity, took the glowing, charred brand in his right hand, carried it as far as he wished with deliberate slowness, and, having thrown it down, showed that his hand was unharmed by the fire. The wicked man was amazed, but the miracle did not move him to faith. The same event was attributed by the person who reported it to me to nothing but magic tricks.

Tell me, most wretched men: is not that the name of divinity which the elements obey? But you say that, while placed on earth, he never called himself God. For when someone asked whether he was God, he replied: “You say it” (Matthew XXVII, 11)—that is, “It is as you say,” as though he were saying, “You say it, but I do not.”

O senseless men! Attend to what follows: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God and coming on the clouds of heaven” (Matthew XXVI, 64). He said the same thing, clearly indicating the betrayer, when the latter said, “Surely it is not I?” and he replied, “You say it” (Matthew XXVI, 25)—with the understood meaning, “You say what is true.”

I say nothing about the other passages, since they attend to bodily actions. Read John, in whom almost nothing other than his consubstantiality with the Father is proclaimed. “You believe in God,” he says, “believe also in me” (John XIV, 1). “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. Whoever believes in me sees the Father” (John IX, 10), and thousands of similar passages.

**[Col. 0527] END.**

**[Col. 0527]**

# LETTER OF THE VENERABLE GUIBERT, ABBOT, ON THE MORSEL GIVEN TO JUDAS AND ON THE TRUTH OF THE LORD’S BODY

**[Col. 0527D]** To SIGEFRID, father and lord, prior of Saint-Nicholas [another reading: “to SIGEFRID, abbot of Saint Vincent, brother, etc.”], Guibert, minister of God’s household which is at Nogent, seeking and embracing simply the things that are God’s.

I do not know whether I can even see clearly, much less explain fully, the question that your holiness has placed before me. At the outset, I am also horrified lest I say anything in which I might appear to oppose the judgment of the Fathers. Therefore I ask that, if I say anything that nevertheless does not depart from the rule, you listen to it with the intention in which I shall say it. I shall speak without prejudice to a better opinion, probing rather than asserting.

## CHAPTER I

### QUESTION I

The question is whether the more distinguished teachers of the Church—Augustine, namely (Exposition on Psalm X, volume VIII, and Tractate 26 on John, volume IX), and Leo (Sermon 3, On the Passion of the Lord)—agree that Judas received the Eucharist from the Lord’s hand together with the other apostles. Hilary of Poitiers (Commentary on Matthew, Canon 30), and Victor of Capua, dissent from this interpretation of what he received. If I am not mistaken, they base their view on the fact that, while the others were participating in the sacrament, the Lord marked out his betrayer by offering him the morsel, which was simply bread.

### QUESTION II

Some also customarily object, as a foreshadowing of our sacrifice, that this sacrament was more a sign than a reality, and that therefore the Lord gave the same thing irrevocably to Judas, whom he had previously called the devil. This is how it is proposed in the letter you sent me.

To this I add that both the ancient and modern authorities who argue and dispute about this matter consider the circumstances of the readings less fully than they should. For, while the apostles were dining at the ancient Passover according to Matthew’s account, it is said, with no one excepted: “Take and eat” (Matthew XXVI, 26; Mark XIV, 23; Luke XXII, 14). Later, when the cup had been handed around, it is stated even more explicitly: “Drink from this, all of you” (ibid., 27). Mark likewise says: “They all drank from it” (Mark XIV, 23).

Luke, after first asserting that he had reclined for the eating of the Passover, and that the twelve apostles were with him (Luke XXII, 14)—which Matthew and Mark also say—adds, after the giving of the cup: “Take this and divide it among yourselves” (ibid., 18). It is also recorded that he gave them bread after giving thanks and breaking it.

If, therefore, all drank from the cup after it had been divided among them, Judas was in no way excluded. Nor is he excluded by John from the washing of the feet, even though he was already conscious of his betrayal.

Even if no authority supported the point, much reason would nevertheless be available: a person should in no way be excluded from his rank or from the common favor of his comrades merely because he had conceived a crime that his openly displayed actions did not prove. For he himself had said—and could not deny it: “Do not judge” (Matthew VII, 1). Since the sin was still hidden and concealed, the one who had come to summon everyone to salvation ought not at that time to condemn it.

What is said about the cup is equivalent to saying the same thing with equal clarity about the bread, since the dignity of both is equal—indeed, identical.

For the one who had granted him, along with the others, the authority to baptize, cast out demons, and cure diseases, if at the end he had withdrawn from him the grace granted to the others for carrying out an evil deed, he might perhaps have increased the reasons for carrying out the betrayal. For what is the power that, according to the Apostle, works for the salvation of every believer (Rom. I, 16), unless it is the Holy Spirit, from whom power over demons and for curing illnesses arises? “He gave them,” he says, “power and authority over all demons” (Luke [Col. 0530A] IX, 1), and so forth. Although, being the spirit of discipline, he avoids hypocrites insofar as concerns their own salvation, he nevertheless supplies assistance for the faith of others. Since, therefore, he did not deny Peter the Spirit he had given him for miracles, rightly he did not refuse him the mysteries shared with the others.

But if the matter concerns the morsel that was dipped and handed to him, it was a sign—and not a sign: plainly, a sign of the betrayer, but not a sign of the sacrament. Indeed, before the handing over of that new sacrifice, according to the testimony of Matthew and Mark, while they were asking who the betrayer was, it was given (Matt. XXVI, 22; Mark XIV, 19). If it possessed anything holy in itself, it perhaps received it not through any change in itself, but through the touch of the Savior. And he deserved the entry of the devil not so much because he received the morsel unworthily as because of his shamelessness and incorrigibility toward the Lord who rebuked him.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the apparent discrepancy among the Gospels regarding that passage: “Nevertheless, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke XXII, 21), which Matthew and Mark place earlier (Matt. XXVI, 23; Mark XIV, 19), whereas Luke connects it with the handing over of the Lord’s body. If I answer you, I shall linger around a cheap and obvious matter, since almost laughable is the person who asks about this as though he had found a knot in a reed. For if you seek in the Gospels the order of passages that say the same things, or that differ among themselves, you will find them so transposed and so altered that you may think that folly has called teachers to account over a matter so trivial. Whether this saying precedes or follows makes no difference.

But in the parts with which we are concerned, the controversy that seems so great requires not a letter but a necessary book. Certainly, both at the banquet of the old Passover and after the handing over of the new mystery, the betrayer sat for some time at that table and placed impudent hands upon both foods. Or what is surprising if one evangelist has put one time in place of another, so that “was” is said instead of “had been”? You should know that here the abundance of things to be said makes me poor.

## CHAPTER III

He argues against the Berengarian heresy.—But since the author of the letter says that objections are raised concerning the Lord’s body, on the ground that it is a sign and not the reality, let us consider a few things about it, though they are slight and meager. If it is a shadow and not a body, we have fallen from shadow into shadow, or rather we have descended into things much worse. If oxen, rams, goats, turtledoves, pigeons, and sparrows were formerly sin-offerings—sacrifices, that is, for sin—so that they were called the justice of the flesh, and could not save the one who served them according to conscience, how much less, if an appearance is believed and not the reality, will that exceedingly small and miserable quantity of bread be worthy of any remedy for souls? If we eat of it, we shall not abound; if we do not eat of it, we shall certainly not fail.

If, therefore, both are appearances and there is truth in neither, it will be made equal to the new baptism of John. In the old there will be no inward benefit, but the value of the material will prevail—just as animals, and those things which are bought as flesh, surpass lifeless matter, and as such things surpass loaves worth a coin. Certainly, the old will also be shown superior in another way. If what the authorities transmit is true—and nothing is more true—original sin was forgiven through sacrifices before circumcision. But if this sacrifice of ours, after the Lord had suffered once, is merely the figure of his suffering, as is said, I do not know whether it accomplishes anything true. And if it is merely a memorial of that death, it is like some image of God or of a saint that is ordinarily painted in a church: it is perfunctory. Whatever, therefore, presents only a memorial to the eyes of the unlearned offers little or no assistance to the wise.

But I should like to know why the chalice is called the chalice of the blood of the new and eternal covenant (Matt. XXVI, 28; Mark XIV, 24; Luke XXII, 20), where something is renewed and antiquity is abolished. “That which is becoming obsolete and growing old is near to disappearance” (Heb. VIII, 13). If antiquity lies in sin and newness in grace, grace itself is nothing unless it can endure unto eternity. Yet it bears witness to and pledges something eternal. It is therefore productive of some great good, not empty or shadowy.

Hence, in the consecratory canon, this same chalice is called “the mystery of faith.” For “mystery” is understood not only in what is good but also in what is evil and in what is trivial. The “mystery of iniquity” is also spoken of; and when a comedy is being performed, if you see it, you ask what that action signifies. Both, therefore, are mysteries, but faith is not required for the utility of those seeking anything in them. What, then, does the adjective “of faith” mean? It is plainly as though he were saying: “The secret of the whole faith,” in which, that is, the majesty of all our belief lies hidden. Thus, as what follows says, the chalice itself bears within it no fruit except the divine one, namely, the remission of sins.

Let them say, then, what kind of shadow it is that gives birth to so great a truth. I am also astonished at the ears with which they hear the words of Truth himself: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI, 56). Where there is something “truly,” how can it be merely an appearance or merely a shadow? Certainly, if after the priest’s prayer the appearance of bread were changed into flesh, the dispute would be brought to an end. This is why the objectors concern themselves with appearance.

But if it is an appearance and possesses nothing more than the rock which, according to the Apostle, is Christ (I Cor. X, 4), I wonder why we do not pursue rocks, woods, and the other things said in Scripture to signify Christ with the same regard and praise with which we pursue that little offering of bread and wine prepared on the altar. Why do we not call them “blessed, inscribed, ratified,” and again “pure, holy, and immaculate,” “of eternal life,” or “of perpetual salvation”? And finally, after it has been carried “to the lofty altar of God by the hands of an angel” through the priest’s prayer, which is nothing other than the body of Christ, without which every sacrifice is empty, why do we not call it again sanctified, enlivened, and blessed?

If, then—to leave the rest aside—the sacrifice is said to be enlivened through sanctification, and the Lord’s saying applies to it, “Whoever eats not something else but me lives because of me” (John VI, 58), let the shadow cease, let the appearance cease; let the soul perceive in these mysteries something productive of life and salvation. And, O folly! Through the invocation of the Trinity so much is ascribed to the element of baptism that simple water is made fruitful and enlivened for washing away sins, while to this sacrament, which is effected by God’s own word, only a foolish figure is attributed!

Let those who assert this sign without the reality say whether the Lord’s own body, while dwelling on earth, was a sign, since one thing was apparent and another hidden. Shall we then deny the Lord hidden within the human being?
