When he rose from the dead, he did not show his disciples the glory that he had promised to those who would rise, although before his passion he had shown it when he was transfigured on the mountain before Peter, John, and James. He displayed, by a dispensation, the humble condition so that he would not show the inexperienced anything unknown or unusual, thereby blunting more severely the senses of those whom he ought to instruct.

What of the fact that, being placed in heaven, he did not even wish to cover his wounds or remove the servant’s form that he will display at the future judgment? Rather, after the judgment, as he passes from the human state into the divine, he will again alter himself. If in that substance which is God and human there was, is, and will yet be so great a change of appearances, is it surprising that in this—provided in the present meanwhile as a defense and consolation for our misery, a new creation and a union of God and human beings—God should exercise our faith by leaving it under the very appearance of bread and wine, because of the horror of human perception?

Certainly, the Trinity itself, which in this life is necessarily spoken of for our sake, is not substantially predicated of God; for our sense, which here is instructed about God only through syllables and intervals, is filled in that eternity, without any pauses or names, by seeing light in light with the recognition of divinity. If we believe these and other things that we do not see—such as remission in baptism, punishments in hell, and rewards in the kingdom—why, when brought to this point, do we say, “How can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. LXXVII, 19.) And if we believe many good and evil things that we have not seen, why do we take offense at one thing and say that God is powerful elsewhere but powerless here?

Let us not, therefore, fall away from his presence as though we were his enemies. Let us confess that God’s truth and mercy are in Christ, and that because he came in the name of the Father, his horn is exalted above carnal sacrifices.

## CHAPTER IV

The author alludes to these ideas in what is said to Elijah in the Book of Kings: “Withdraw from here,” he says, “and go toward the east, and hide yourself in the torrent Carith, which is opposite the Jordan, and there you shall drink from the torrent” (III Kings XVII, 3).

Elijah, whose name is interpreted as “My God is the Lord,” signifies the Jewish people, to whom “I am the Lord” is frequently impressed upon their own law. They are commanded to withdraw from here—that is, from unbelief—which is known to have happened first in Abraham. He is ordered to go toward the east, that is, to direct himself toward knowledge of God. For *contra* is often used not only for opposition but also for direction.

He is hidden in the torrent while he is protected within knowledge of the law from the many vices forbidden by the law. The torrent itself is rightly so called, since it is given not immutably but perfunctorily and, as it were, for a time. Hence Paul also calls it “holy and worldly” (Heb. IX, 1). It was called Carith, which is interpreted as “the encounter of fire,” because the more one was restrained from unlawful things by the command of the law, the more one was struck by the assaults of desires. For fire is desire. Hence the Apostle says: “I would not have known desire unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire’” (Rom. VII, 7).

It is opposite the Jordan because it is nothing other than a foreshadowing—or rather, an auspicious beginning—of those who wish to live according to the grace of baptism. For “the law was our pedagogue in Christ.” “He drank from the torrent,” he says, while the people draw from knowledge of the law whatever stagnant understanding they can.

God commands ravens to feed him there, while he enjoins priests, rapacious through excessive greed for sacrifices, to teach him; concerning them the Lord says: “You have made this house a den of thieves” (Matt. XXI, 13). Elijah also remains in the torrent while the people, to speak according to the Apostle, rest in the law.

“Ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening” (III Kings XVII, 6), while in prosperity and adversity—what morning and evening signify—they promise the people temporal enjoyment through the constant repetition of sacrifices and carnal observances. “After some days the torrent dried up” (ibid., [Col. 0533C] 7), because after the illumination of the Gospel, the rudimentary instruction of legal doctrine appeared to believers insufficient for salvation. “For it had not rained upon the earth” (Gen. II, 5), because the coming of the Savior had infused no understanding into the ancient books, which seemed to promise nothing but earthly things. Hence: “He will proclaim the power of his works to his people, that he may give them the inheritance of the nations” (Ps. CX, 6).

Then the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “Rise, go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and you shall remain there” (III Kings XVII, 8–9). The word of the Lord comes when the invisible Word appeared made a creature. He urges him to rise because he is encouraged by a new grace to aspire from lower things to higher. He is ordered to go to Zarephath when he is admonished to know that within himself there is a tribulation of bread—that is, a scarcity of divine understanding. For Zarephath is interpreted as “tribulation of bread.”

What is understood in the Gospel by three loaves because of the Trinity (Luke II, 5) is understood here singly because of unity. This Zarephath belongs to the Sidonians, because this poverty by which one is afflicted exists especially among those who uselessly pursue carnal things. For Sidonia is interpreted as “useless hunting.” He is also commanded to remain there, while he is taught to persist in this reflection not by the hour but in a fixed station.

“I have commanded a widow woman there to feed you” (III Kings XVII, 9): that is, I have commanded the Church, widowed by the death of the crucified Lord, without any remembrance of morning or evening bread and meat, to instruct you through the example of simple faith.

When he had come to the gate of the city, a widow woman appeared to him gathering sticks (ibid., 10). The gate of the city is the one who says, “I am the door” (John X, 9). The Church is a city because there those who have one heart live their lives together. Rightly, therefore, one first comes to the gate; then the widow woman appears, because Christ is first recognized and only then does what the Church is become clear.

She gathers sticks because she unites both peoples in herself. What a wall signifies elsewhere, a stick here not inappropriately displays: the two pieces of the cross signify the two peoples, one extended piece indicating the Jews as if they were one-horned, and the other transverse piece showing the Gentiles as though introduced from the opposite direction.

“And he called her and said to her, ‘Give me a little water in a vessel, so that I may drink’” (III Kings XVII, 10). He calls her when he openly learns the cause of the calling of all the faithful. He asks that water be given him in a vessel to drink when he earnestly requests from the primitive Church instruction no longer flowing uncertainly through the *deuteroses* (secondary traditions), as it formerly did, but restrained and stable in Christ, who is the chosen and specially chosen vessel, in whom “all the treasures of wisdom are hidden” (Col. II, 3).

And while she was going to bring bread, he called after her, saying: “Bring me, I beg you, a morsel in your hand” (III Kings XVII, 11). She goes to bring it when, according to the Apostle, she attends to reading in order to teach. He calls after her when some part of the Jews, after the apostles had turned away from them and said, “Since you have rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46), humbly entreats her to teach them as well.

It is as though he were saying: “Until now the ravens have fed me with the flesh of sacrifices. From now on let your teaching supply me not with bread but with a morsel of bread, something able to be tasted beforehand rather than to satisfy. For in the Lord’s body, which is taken from his table, it is wicked to presume anything bodily flavorful or anything that expands through an external sanctity [al., satiety], because what has been provided for the spirit alone must be entirely distinct from bodily pleasure.”

The morsel, therefore, which is commonly called *bucca*, is requested from the widow when it is not shoulders or just any pieces of meat that gratify the appetite of the throat, but the smallness of the bread and wine changed substantially into divine flesh through the Lord’s words, which passes beneficially into the mind no less in its smallness than in its greatness. For what does quantity matter where the entirety of salvation is established even in an atom?

It should be noted that he asks her to bring it in her hand, because whatever is received from it lies within the power of those who use it. If it is in our power to become children of God, it is no less within our choice to be inwardly united to so great a mystery through the love of faith. But whoever disputes about this matter never counts himself among those receiving this inward gift.

If someone does not take its food—which is why we call it a morsel—with the required moderation, but rather with a destructive excess presumes to consume whatever else, he condemns body and soul in that he brings the antidote of the soul into the taste of the throat and, according to the Apostle, does not distinguish the Lord’s body from common foods (I Cor. XI, 29).

“‘As the Lord lives,’ she said, ‘I have no bread, except as much flour as a handful can hold in a jar, and a little oil in a flask’” (III Kings XVII, 12). She says that the Lord lives when she faithfully perceives him as effective for so great a change from substance into substance. She declares that she has no bread except as much as a handful of flour can contain, because with a faithful mind she affirms that in this sacrifice there is nothing of the essence beyond the appearance of bread, except what the invocation of the Trinity without any scruple administers to the faithful—which the flour signifies. For it is as though it were ground, so that no hand of understanding is hindered by any resistance. Hence the frequent trinities of crosses are made in the sacrificial canon, because just as the Trinity wrought flesh in Mary, so on the altar the Trinity works this mystery. By a handful we mean the three foremost fingers.

A handful can also be understood as Scripture, because we write with those fingers. It is as though she were saying: “I do not possess, or understand, this thing that appears on the altar as substantially bread, except insofar as it can be grasped from the testimony of the sacred page.” No eloquent person is unaware that a jar is a water vessel. In the jar is the spiritual knowledge of this fragile way of life; for water is customarily used to signify knowledge. Oil is added to this knowledge because it is seasoned with divine charity, lest it puff itself up. The *lecythus*, or oil flask, signifies the same thing as the vessel in the Gospel, and the jar signifies what the lamps signify.

“Behold, I am gathering two sticks so that I may enter and make it for myself and my son, that we may eat and die” (ibid.). This means: “Behold, I embrace the love that is extended toward God and the love that is extended toward friend and enemy alike. Through these the soul is restrained from every wantonness, as though crucified. I embrace two sticks so that, restrained by them from my wandering, I may return to myself and make—that is, engrave figuratively—not bread, but what is signified in the bread, not so much for myself as for those whom I have begotten in faith, so that we may eat what is consumed not by the mouth but only by devout affection. And let us die—that is, let us be conformed to the death signified by this sacrifice itself. ‘Have you sat at a great table?’ (Sirach XXXI, 12); you must prepare similar things.”

## CHAPTER V

“‘Do not fear, Elijah,’” he says, “‘but go and do as you have said. Nevertheless, first make for me from that little flour a small cake baked under the ashes, and bring it to me; afterward you shall make one for yourself and your son’” (III Kings XVII, 13).

It is as though he were saying: “Do not fear the changing of David’s countenance before Abimelech—that is, the transfer of our priesthood to the order of Melchizedek—but go, that is, advance in faith, so that in your conduct you may be conformed to Christ’s passion, to which you have begun to teach corresponding sacraments.

“Make for me, as I recover from carnal observance, something solid and coherent in the little knowledge of this new mystery, as though from fine flour. I have already discovered this flour to be more healthful because more true than the useless ceremonies of former times. Make a bread from it: bind the wavering and mobile mind, light as dust, with reason, as though by the sprinkling of water.

“Make it small, preserving in the presentation of your teaching the measure of my capacity, which has not yet matured. Yet make it a cake baked under the ashes, never taking away from me the remembrance of sins, even though I have been washed in baptism, because ashes signify the sharpness of penitence, for which ashes and sackcloth are fitting.”

Here it is rightly noted that “first” is placed before it, because the grace of God is accustomed to overflow especially for those who have lived most wickedly both in Judaism and in paganism. Among them we recognize Paul, who confesses himself first among sinners, saying, “that in me Jesus Christ might first display the riches of his mercy” [Col. 0536B] (I Tim. I, 16). Hence: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V, 20). The same became fully evident in Matthew and Magdalene. Understand the saying, therefore, as applying to them and those like them.

He asks that this bread be brought to him—that is, that it be brought in through an exposition into the inner chambers of his own understanding. What follows is understood as applying to the righteous, those coming from the fulfillment of the law, such as Peter, Andrew, and James the brother of the Lord. “You shall make one afterward for yourself and your son,” that is, for those whom you will bring into conformity with yourself from the innocence of the law, and whom you will recognize, after conversion from more serious sin, as able to subsist through the indulgence of grace wherever they may be. Hence Paul says: “I did nothing less than those who are super-apostles” (II Cor. XII, 11). And: “I labored more than all of them” (I Cor. XV, 10).

“And the Lord God says this: ‘The jar of flour shall not fail, and the flask of oil shall not diminish until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth’” (III Kings XVII, 14).

It is as though he were saying: “Although I have received explanations from your instruction, O primitive Church, concerning the New Testament, nevertheless I have discovered from legal and prophetic reading that God established the knowledge and contemplation of this faith, which is in the Lord’s body, as exceedingly subtle and never-ending.

“The holiness of the Lord’s house is fitting for enduring length of days” (Ps. XCII, 5), and the priesthood of Melchizedek possesses eternity without repentance of an oath. The gift of grace, like the oil flask, will emerge in the mind of the Church in perpetual abundance until that day without night when the spiritual stream will no longer be secretly offered to us, but, after the resurrection, the knowledge of God will pour itself upon us visibly, like rain, through the incorruptible eyes of the body.

“Then the face of the earth will be enriched so greatly that what the mind, however sincere, can scarcely now manage to make sparkle, the eye of the flesh will then never cease to behold with an unremoved and unobscured gaze.”

She went and did according to the word of Elijah (III Kings XVII, 15), and he ate, and she, and her household. She goes when the primitive Church advances through the conversion of Paul and of many other wise men from the Jews. She did according to the word of Elijah when she received as teachers even those whom she had accepted to be instructed. He ate because he did not learn these things to proclaim them with word or tongue, but retained them always to be chewed over inwardly by the mind for its satisfaction. She and her household ate when she abundantly supplied others also with the life-giving dish in which she firmly believed.

[Col. 0537] END.

[Col. 0537]

# THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE GUIBERT, ABBOT, ON THE PRAISE OF HOLY MARY

287 ## CHAPTER I

The Blessed Virgin never rejects those who praise her.—Let us praise with wholly faithful lips, though insufficiently capable, that woman who, after her Son and through her Son, was blessed above all creatures and, under God’s worship, most worthy of all creatures.

Although the dignity of heavenly beings is judged incapable of being enhanced by her praise, much experience has nevertheless made it known that human praise and devotion are most pleasing in her sight. Nor is this unjust. Since she cannot deny that she is human, how could she—far from despising human beings, especially those for whose benefit she was made and in whom she shone forth—fail to love them more dearly than all creatures?

Moreover, she was appointed, indeed set above others, for the human race for this purpose: that she might be sufficient for giving birth to God. From that by which she provided for the healing of others, she herself first received the beginning of redemption. Will she not, then, love in others that which first benefited herself?

And she who, by believing, equaled the glory she possessed in giving birth to the Son of God—a glory that no one could hope to equal from the beginning to the end of the ages—how could she not rejoice ineffably in our faith, which has that very God as the Son and reward of its faith?

Her faith.—At the announcement of her conception, no powers of intellect can comprehend that miracle: that a girl, timid because of her sex and inexperienced because of her age, could give faith so swiftly when an angel promised her things unprecedented and unheard of. We shall certainly not be able to repay this by admiration in any other way unless we first understand that among all human beings she alone had been uniquely nourished by the Holy Spirit.

For unless, beyond what human custom permits, she recognized within her little mind from earliest childhood something divine and majestic, she would not have believed with such ease. For the extraordinary greatness of the promises could not have been contained in a heart subjected to vanity. Where no merits have preceded, the rewards of great hope are not available.

Who, then, can weigh—indeed, what angelic nature, surpassing humanity, can conjecture—what purity, what weight, what glory had been nourished in that, so to speak, heavenly conscience, which, with no examples of Scripture previously set before it and no images of similar events from the ages presented to it, opened the bosom of its faith to such a privilege of words?

If Sarah, and Manoah and his wife, in comparison with this event something entirely familiar, could scarcely establish or scarcely believe such a thing, how could such faith so quickly enter this young woman, utterly inexperienced in all things, especially in matters pertaining to women, through such simple words of the angel?

If Moses, after the effectiveness of so many divine signs—he who spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks to his neighbor—made a distinction—hesitating in his speech—at the waters of contradiction, although it is said of his excellence that “he was the meekest of all who dwelt on the earth” (Num. XII, 3), and although God struck Miriam with leprosy because she disparaged him against Aaron, what do we suppose was the source, what an infinite fountain of holiness, from which there proceeded her opening her ear so obediently and her mind so readily not to just any conception but to a divine one, as though it had always been foretold to her?

Certainly Zechariah himself, the father of John, most learned in the law and the prophets, hesitated pitiably when the extraordinary origin of his son was announced to him from heaven. But she stood more quickly than speech itself when told that a virgin would conceive from the Spirit, not a woman from a husband. To this judgment agrees the fact that the fullness of grace is proclaimed to her by the angel. For unless the abundance of divine power had flowed into her completely, she would never have offered obedience in conceiving the Son of God to the totality of all good things—something that foolish minds would regard as fabulous.

By a gift of heavenly infusion, which had been uniquely impressed upon her from the beginning, she was not stunned by such a message; rather, she gratefully received the overflowing abundance of the entire divinity, as though she had known it from eternity. The Holy Spirit had always instructed her for this very purpose.

How excellent was her assent to the angel.—When the angel plainly said, “Behold, you will conceive and give birth” (Luke I, 31), she would never have objected, “How can this happen, since I do not know a man?” if she had known that she was to conceive from the husband to whom she appeared to be betrothed.

Who, then, would not draw an inference from this extraordinary question: that, from an ancient experience of miraculous grace, she had chosen to devote herself to perpetual virginity, since she did not at all suppose that she would give birth from the man to whom she had already been entrusted?

Because she herself was the beginning of new grace, it was entirely fitting that she should have the distinctive profession of something new, since by a new manner of giving birth she was to bring forth the author of all holy newness.

The angel therefore did not find her heart crude or unprepared when he announced to her things so unexpected [f. *insperabilia*] to all who were then living. She gave assent to them with the greater fidelity because she sensed that human nature possessed within her a more exalted desire.

God gives grace to the saints according to measure.—In the minds of other saints, particular measures of spiritual gifts, not their fullness, are granted in the present age. For this reason it is said, by contrast, that in the future God will be “all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28).

If, then, the sparks of all virtues now shine in them, at that time they will flash throughout them in their fullness, without any interruption of light. For what is said—“God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John III, 34)—pertains to the Son, to whom the whole Spirit belongs.

But what is given to each according to his own virtue pertains to the fact that the heavenly distributions are granted to the faithful, according to the Apostle, in proportion to the measure of faith (Eph. IV, 7). This is very similar to what is both believed and proclaimed concerning this altogether incomparable and blessed Virgin.

To her, plainly, nothing was given by measure, since the wondrous Virgin carried within the enclosure of her womb, whole and entire, him who was wholly present with the Father.

## CHAPTER II

The Blessed Virgin substantially contained all of God within herself.—On this matter a question arises, worthy of every contemplation. Of no saint do we dare think or say that, in that everlasting blessedness—much less in this mortal life, whatever his excellence—he has all of God substantially within himself.

For even if every accumulation of virtue within anyone is judged to exist most perfectly, nevertheless the totality of the divinity is not recognized as essentially infused into anyone as it is. For what is meant by the future statement that God will be “all in all” is nothing other than that God, who ennobles each saint in this world through each individual virtue, will then illuminate them all by pouring over them the totality of his graces.

It is one thing, therefore, to overflow with grace; it is another to be filled ineffably with incomprehensible substance. The woman of whom we speak, singularly blessed, possessed both in such a way that she overflowed with the fullness of grace and, alone among all creatures, carried the uncircumscribed one wholly within herself—not merely in his gift, as the others do, but in himself entire.

Her state in this mortal life was superior to her state in heaven.—Hence it is asked, and weighed by us with due humility, whether that most holy woman, while still established in mortal limbs and carrying God, possessed more than she now possesses while co-reigning with her Son in the heavenly places.

I think this can plainly be understood without prejudice to a truer understanding: that she possessed much more in corruptible flesh, when the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily within her (Col. II, 9), than she now possesses, although she co-reigns with her Christ.

For although she experiences blessedly that she is more powerful than all creatures, nevertheless what she already possesses in the manner of the abundance of all graces and glories—indeed, with a richness superior to that of every creature—cannot, it seems to me, be compared with that former state in which, although mortal, she contained within herself all that God is.

For it is one thing to be the place in which someone dwelt whole; it is another, even though supremely blessed, to be filled by him only in part. I would therefore say that ineffable Mary, in a certain respect, was happier in the present when she conceived God than she is in the future, with nearly the same inequality by which a part is thought to differ from the whole.

For to what person other than this one can you attribute that God gave himself wholly and personally into her? You will not find even in the future anyone in whom he formed a conjoining of that inaccessible majesty.

If nothing is happier than God, and if those are called blessed who are poor in spirit and who are meek (Matt. V, 3–4), whom the splendor of some virtue illuminates, what in heaven or on earth is happier than that heart and womb into which the omnipotent summit of that creative essence gathered itself wholly?

The author answers objections. The Blessed Virgin is shown to be supremely wise and powerful.—But at this point let the mind recover itself and bring against the most holy mother the ignorance and apparently ordinary weaknesses attributed to her. Let it say: Since she, having conceived God, ought to have known all future things, the angel should not have been troubled so often to instruct Joseph.

Let memory answer in opposition that which is said by the archangel during the annunciation: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35). And what was that overshadowing except to cover from the eyes of the mind the immensity of that uncircumscribed light?

The power of the Most High overshadows her when the Holy Spirit, whose special gift is humility, diminishes the brightness of glory before the sight of inward reason. Therefore, just as her dignity in that regard was incomparable, so a weakness not unlike that of others obscured the power of that dignity.

Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Place your shadow like the night” (Isa. XVI, 3). “Like,” he says, not truly—for we must attend not to what makes us shine but to what makes us grow dark.

Perhaps, therefore, she could not be ignorant of anything, since she gave birth to God who knows all things. Yet wisdom, and likewise the power proceeding from God united to her flesh, lay hidden in her by such a dispensation that she lacked neither knowledge nor ability, while nevertheless the concealed power served the appropriate time.

For just as in the child Jesus wisdom, age, and grace gradually grew together before God and human beings (Luke II, 52), so in the mother, as the Son matured and revealed through teaching and signs what he was, whatever had been done in her beyond nature and had remained unknown became apparent.

As time proceeded, and the efficacy of the dispensation that had begun unfolded, both the mother’s weakness and the child’s lowliness became manifest through the wondrous revelation of the mysteries. In a certain way, we think that consideration was shown to her fragile sex and, if I may say so, unstable age in this matter: so that an excessive power might be borne within the mind through the frailty of the body, it was moderated by domestic poverty and by the general condition of knowledge and outward conduct.

With the Son, then, freed from temporal misery, the glorious [Col. 0541A] Mother is raised beyond the estimation of all the faithful: she was indeed able to suffer things like ours, and to be shut off by the impediment of the body from that complete knowledge which God is; yet from what could she have been shut off, when what she had borne was, without doubt, always kept fixed in her mind? If, because of his self-emptying, his assumption of the form of a servant, and his obedience to the cross, the Son is exalted above every name, then, since a mother’s affection could not have concealed his insults and death, a corresponding effect in some way succeeded the Son in his Mother. For just as humility preceded glory in the Son, so sublimity—which flowed back from the Son—plainly followed the Mother’s humility. The more inward her glory, the more subtly was it directed toward the contemplation of God; and the more despised her lamp was in the thoughts of the rich, the more prepared she was for the appointed time of her Son. Hence he himself says: “My time has not yet come” (John VII, 6).

When, therefore, the scapegoat had been sent into the wilderness, and the moon had been placed beneath the feet of the Mother herself, and she had likewise been led into that desert, her magnificence and, from the Son and after the Son, her omnipotence are now properly disclosed by numerous manifestations. In visions of the saints and in the efficacy of signs, through the appearance of heavenly spirits, the patronage of human beings, and the exaction of the underworld, she reveals herself everywhere, from the circumstances surrounding her, as Queen of heaven and earth. O glory from within! O how God regarded the singular humility of his handmaid! If you now consider him who “passed a sword through your soul” [Col. 0541C] (Luke II, 35), you will rejoice with much more eager joy over the fruit of your womb!

O woman truly ineffable even to angelic understanding, who, still enclosed within a bodily wall, bore that incomprehensible light which no human or heavenly spirit could, not to say wholly endure, but even fully behold! For although one is permitted, in some manner, to see one’s Creator, nevertheless to comprehend and behold him fully is in every way forbidden. Hence it is that “the angels desire to look into him” (I Peter I, 12), since, because of his incomprehensibility, they do not cease to yearn for him insatiably.

Let us therefore consider, while she conceives him, how much more excellently than every creature she saw him, since she was permitted to bear what no one else was permitted to bear. Hence that saying was wonderfully meaningful: “He did not know her until she had given birth” [Col. 0541D] (Matthew I, 25). For the pregnant woman’s appearance differed so greatly from the appearance her face had possessed before conception as the sun’s power differs from the rays of the moon. If it is said of the righteous man that he “makes his face cheerful with oil” (Psalm CIII, 15), that is, that he brightens his outward appearance through the Holy Spirit, what splendor do we suppose was added from innate majesty to the appearance of that glorious woman, who shone with a glory surpassing angelic beauty? If Stephen was so greatly illumined by God while sitting among those assembled in council (Acts VI, 15), to what light can this woman, illumined from the fullness of divinity, be compared?

## CHAPTER III

### Solomon’s throne is ivory

“This is the throne which Solomon made, great, of ivory; and he covered it with exceedingly pure gold” (III Kings X, 19). The Wisdom of God the Father, first of all, according to the Apostle, “peaceable” (James III, 17)—that Wisdom is Solomon. It makes a throne of ivory for itself when it establishes for itself a seat in the Virgin, than whom nothing was ever more chaste. For the elephant, whose bones are ivory, represents a continent and pure nature. Moreover, it is “great,” namely, because through the Son it presides over heaven, earth, and the underworld. He covers it with exceedingly pure gold when he fills her inwardly and outwardly, not with sparks of virtues as in others, but substantially with his own divinity.

“It had six steps, and the top of the throne was rounded at the back” (III Kings X, 19). The six steps are fear and piety, knowledge and fortitude, counsel and understanding; by these she reached him who specially presided over her—the Wisdom, Christ. The top of the throne is the singular eminence of the Mother of God. It is rounded at the back because, while she lived, she was contemptible for human purposes, like a carpenter’s wife; but now, where God alone sees, she shows herself, in a manner somehow equal in miracles to the omnipotence of God, since, as we have already indicated, she encompasses the threefold structure of the universe by her power.

“And two hands on either side held the seat” (ibid.). The two hands are the two operations in Christ. The operation of the flesh, although initially subject to weakness, is nevertheless that which says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew XXVIII, 18). The operation of divinity is this: “Through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made” [Col. 0542C] (John I, 3). Both operations, belonging to one person, strengthen her—who merited to give birth to him—on either side with the dignity due to her. Since he is one, they possess equal powers, both according to God and according to man.

“And two lions stood beside each hand” (III Kings X, 19). The lion signifies royal dominion over the movements of the flesh in each believer. The two lions, therefore, are the two orders of the Church: prelates and subjects, who govern themselves. Two lions stand beside each hand when certain members of these orders cling actively to that holy humanity. Others excel by devoting themselves to the highest contemplation. Hence the saying: “You established summer and spring” (Psalm LXXIII, 17), that is, “You appointed contemplatives and active workers.”

[Col. 0542D] “Twelve young lions stood upon the six steps, on either side” (III Kings X, 20). Through the number twelve they are instructed in faith in the Trinity and made square by the fulfillment of the four Gospels. These young lions, alongside the other innocent ones and rulers of themselves, stand upon the six steps when they strengthen themselves with the six virtues mentioned above. They are on either side because each, according to his capacity, inclines himself in one direction or the other. Hence it is said of both: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Psalm CXX, 6). This means: the excess of the glory and splendor of divinity will not harm you while you contemplate. Moreover, the humanity of Christ, if you are less perceptive, does not hinder you.

“There is no such work in all the kingdoms,” because neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor beneath the earth has anything like this occurred: that God should deign, by assuming the form of Abraham’s seed, to take up not angels but the Virgin’s womb.

## CHAPTER IV

### The eastern gate in Ezekiel XL, 6

This is also that gate in Ezekiel which looked toward the eastern road: “And behold, the glory of the God of Israel entered by the eastern road.” O gate through which God enters to us! O gate through which the mysteries of faith are unveiled! A beautiful gate, I say, through which the city of God is opened. It looks toward the eastern road because whatever she is, and whatever was done in her, indicates nothing other than the activity of the divine light.

When we believe that she was thus blessed among women, behold, as soon as she is loved in this way, the glory of God enters through that road by means of her. For the more we embrace her in the arms of our inward veneration, the more clearly we recognize the honor of her exaltedness; it is penetrated not by changing it, but by loving it.

“And its voice was like the voice of many waters” (Ezekiel XLIII, 2). To that God of Israel—whose name is interpreted as “of those directed with God”—this woman is glory, because when we consider from what great humility God raised her up and what he did in her, our mind fails entirely in contemplating her excellence. Her glory has a voice like that of many waters (Psalm XCII, 4), because although there is one truth—that she is always virgin and Mother of God—nevertheless, according to the differing qualities of those who diligently seek and love her, there will never be a lack, so long as the present age continues, of those who proclaim her most welcome praise in words and writings.

### The Church is illumined by Mary

“And the earth shone with his majesty” (Ezekiel XLIII, 2). Exclude Mary from the Church: what will the Church be except misery? If she had not given birth, what mention of redemption would there have been? But because she gave birth, see what most flourishing beauty of the glory of hope has emerged in the minds of all the devout. And who among Christians is so wretched that he does not at least bear the name of wondrous Mary upon his lips, or invoke it amid dangers?

Therefore, when the greatness of her motherhood is contemplated—although it cannot be fully conceived—the Church is sprinkled with that splendor, because everything by which she is established as so greatly honored is in every way directed toward the Church’s beginning, propagation, and glorification. The Church is the earth to which it is said: “You are God’s cultivation” (I Corinthians III, 9), and further:

“And I fell upon my face” (Ezekiel XLIII, 3). We fall upon our face when, in conscience, we blush before the greatness of the kindness bestowed by Christ. “What shall I render,” he says, “for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm CXV, 12.) “The majesty entered the temple” (Ezekiel XLIII, 4) when we are shaken by worthy shame, because we cannot render anything worthy to Mother and Son. The majesty of God enters the temple when, in our contemplation, our affection is greatly enlarged by considering what God did for us in the Virgin.

“And he entered the temple by the way of the gate that looks toward the east” (ibid.) when, through faith in the dispensation accomplished in Mary—which is a singular way and inclines toward the understanding of the true light—he inspires the mind.

“And the spirit lifted me up” (ibid., 5). The spirit lifts us up when the understanding, through the filling of the conscience—which is the temple—is advanced to the eminence of contemplation. “And he brought me into the inner court” (ibid.). We are brought into the inner court when we are admitted to the innermost embraces of divine love. Outwardly, love is love of neighbor; for the more we contemplate the humility of the Son from the Mother and the power of the Mother from the Son, the more fervently we burn with love for them.

Hence it follows: “And behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord” (ibid.). In sacred Scripture, the glory of God is understood as the joining together of heaven and earth, but more properly as the entering of divinity into humanity for our salvation. Hence, when the Psalm said that God had done wonders, it declared: “His right hand saved him” (Psalm XCVII, 1)—that is, the human race. And again: “Let glory dwell in our land” (Psalm LXXXIV, 10). For nothing is more glorious about God than what is most lowly concerning him among unbelievers, humblest among the good, and most useful for all who are to be saved.

Glory is a widespread opinion about someone accompanied by praise. In what, then, will God be more glorious to us than in this: that for our sake he became, not without his own immense sufferings, more bowed down? Therefore, after the house of conscience has been brought into the King’s chamber—which is the inner court—it is suddenly filled when, through remembrance of divine mercies, the inward descent of the Holy Spirit makes it rejoice in glory. For nothing more strongly invites the Spirit of God to visit us than the mind’s recollection of the labors and gifts of its Redeemer.

After some further material, he added:

“I turned toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary, and it was closed” (Ezekiel XLIV, 1). The way of the gate is consideration of Mary; the outer sanctuary is the beauty of her bodily virginity. It is closed, fortified on every side by every circumstance of chastity; it is not opened because it is not loosened in any way for any enticement. “No man passes through it” (ibid., 2), because no marital intention falls upon it. “The Lord God entered through it, and it shall be closed to the prince” (ibid.), because although divinity penetrates the mother’s conscience, the very one who is prince in being born from the Virgin does not diminish the guardianship of her chastity.

“The prince himself shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord” (ibid., 3). To sit is the action of one who reigns. He therefore sat in her who entered her, with virginity unharmed, as king of natures. There he ate bread before the Lord because he incorporated all the elect into himself in that same womb. “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John IV, 34)—which is “before the Lord.”

“He enters through the vestibule of the gate and goes out by its way” (Ezekiel XLIV, 3) when the Virgin becomes pregnant through humility, which properly clothes the souls of the saints; and after that same sanctuary has been exhausted, life is spent under the same way, that is, under the same intention. The Gospel bears witness to the lowliness in which she conducted herself when the child was carried to the temple in accordance with the duty of his parents.

### She sees and knows God more clearly than every creature

After much else, the following is added: “The gate of the inner court, which looks toward the east, shall be closed for six working days” (Ezekiel XLVI, 1). The inner court is that which burns most fervently within in loving God. The gate of the inner court, therefore, is the Virgin who has given birth, through whom access to divine knowledge is made for us: no one is known by one who does not love him.

She is therefore the gate of the inner court, through whose innermost love we hasten toward the understanding of the purest faith, which is the fruit of that faith; through it we perceive how, under the same person, he is both God and man. Moreover, the gate of the inner court is she who was admitted, not merely earlier, but more excellently than all others, to the highest knowledge of God; and by the same Spirit with which she perceived, she gave us the means to perceive the same thing.

She looks toward the east because she freely fixed her mind upon God, the author of light, toward the place where scarcely any mortal—indeed, scarcely any rational creature—has been able to cast even a spark of light. She is closed for the six working days because the mystery of her conception, through which the entrance to life was opened to humanity, has been and will remain hidden from every nature in the present age—since the six days customarily signify this age. If no one is worthy to loosen his sandal strap, and there is no one greater among those born of women, whom do you suppose is worthy while he lives?

### On the beatific vision

“But on the day of the Sabbath it shall be opened” (ibid.). If the six days signify the present age, in which we have the exercise of perfected works, and the Sabbath signifies the rest of souls, then the mystery of the closed gate is opened at that time. For when the wall of the flesh has been removed, what is now seen “through a mirror and in an enigma” is perceived to a great extent. The simpler our spirit becomes, without its accustomed coverings, the sharper it becomes not only for knowing hidden things but also for the very vision of God.

“But on the day of the Kalends it shall be opened” (ibid.). The day signifies the open comprehension of God and of all divine things. Hence Paul says: “I pursue, if I may comprehend; and then I shall know even as I am known” (Philippians III, 12). The Kalends, so called from a convocation, signify the day of our regeneration. On that day, without doubt, just as the fullness of glory will be completed for souls, so also for the body there will be granted a complete knowledge of Christ’s incarnation in the Virgin and of his dispensation in humanity. In this way the fullness of the inner light is opened, since whatever is to be known about his divine and human nature is known.

“And the prince shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the outer gate” (Ezekiel XLVI, 2). The vestibule may be understood as our body. Just as a vestibule is placed before a house, so the soul is obstructed by the flesh. Its way is sensuality itself. Although sensuality is bodily, once it has been transformed into incorruptibility and impassibility, the more it already surpasses through spiritual power, the more—if I may dare to say so—it is sharpened into the subtlety of reason by the force of the resurrection and is able to contemplate the face of God more purely. The less it suffers outward distractions, the more it is gathered into one and clings outwardly, immutably, to him for whom it inwardly yearns.

The outer gate itself is the entrance and exit of the Virgin, just as the inner gate may be understood as an exit from the secret essence of the Father. The prince, therefore, enters by the way of the vestibule of the outer gate when the power and truth of the virginal conception are penetrated through the bodily senses themselves, which are no longer passive.

It follows: “And he shall stand upon the threshold of the gate” (ibid.). The threshold of the gate is the summit of virginal obedience. The prince will stand there when, through the power of divinity—which, once all things have been moved, always stands—he himself shows that he made the virgin fruitful, and shows how he made her fruitful through the Holy Spirit and left her a virgin.

“And the priests shall make his burnt offerings and his peace offerings” (ibid.). A burnt offering is wholly consumed by fire. His burnt offerings are made by the priests when, considering that humanity so wonderfully assumed from the Virgin, we who have now been made kings and priests by God marvel at it; and we do not cease to burn with perpetual fires of desire because the Author of all things endured things lower than the angels.

His peace offerings—that is, the prince’s—are likewise made when the saints rest in the unchanging contemplation of such great sweetness and in an already undisturbed security.

### Obedience is proved by humility, and humility by adversity

“And he worshiped upon the threshold of the gate, and he went out” (ibid.). Above, we called the threshold of the gate obedience. This obedience cannot be called obedience unless it is established upon certain humility. Certain humility, however, is recognized as existing only when it is proved through adversity arising in the course of obedience. Just as the threshold of a gate lies beneath it like a foundation and is open to all who enter, so the ineffable Virgin, although she is otherwise regarded as wholly inimitable, is set before all as an example in this matter alone, or almost alone.

In the preceding discussion we proved that a mighty miracle occurred: the mind of that blessed young woman was able to bend so swiftly, without prolonged exhortation and without anyone’s offering an example, to promises so unsuspected by all mortals. To this obedience itself we add something no less astonishing.

If ordinary virgins were promised by some omen that, from the noblest husbands they might marry, noble sons would be born, surely both the pleasure of distinguished husbands and glorious offspring would entice them beyond doubt. But here the situation was utterly different. For she had devoted her mind to perpetual virginity, as was argued above; and although, in outward appearance, she had already passed into a husband’s legal power, how, I ask, could she obey so readily? Certainly, as a human being, she feared the scandal of the one who appeared to be her husband, even if not that of others. She knew nothing of his touches and was not involved in that union; and this circumstance, the more it had been hidden from him, the more it ought, by human custom, to have troubled him when the secret was disclosed.

Where, then, there was nothing in the conception to delight her carnally, but rather a mystery exposed to the ignorant to suspicion or disgrace, her marvelous obedience is proved under this humility. In such a vulnerable—or rather angelic—chastity, she seems utterly unconcerned about all popular infamy. For the more chastity fortifies the mind, the more shame is accustomed to torment it even over the most false and rare rumor.

Yet in this her faith is especially approved: whatever God’s promises might be, just as she believed them without hesitation, so she likewise knew that he would order, honorably, properly, and suitably, to govern them through the age. Christ therefore worships upon this threshold when he impresses upon every mind the obedience of such great humility, which deserves to be venerated with the deepest affection. She rightly deserves to be honored: she believed what surpassed her, and in what was promised to her she observed that there was nothing pleasing to the flesh, but rather something by which she would excel spiritually.

## CHAPTER V

### The Blessed Virgin is shown to have been full of grace not temporarily but continually

But someone worse than an unbeliever may object that the young woman, wholly ignorant of divine matters, was filled by the Holy Spirit only perfunctorily and for a time. If this is so, I ask, what does it mean that she is said to have “found grace” with God? Clearly, if she is said to have found it, she cannot be said to have found it unless it is understood that she had sought it. Therefore, if she found grace, she had sought it in some way. And how could she be the handmaid so often named in the Psalms and the Gospel if she had been idle in every service? I cannot express the servitude of one who renders no service to her lord or lady.

There was unquestionably great humility in the handmaid whom God so greatly honored that he is said to have regarded her. If, then, humility is a merit—and not merely a common good, but something surpassing other goods in the highest degree—which God is proved to have regarded, how can it be true that the Holy Spirit filled her suddenly? If the miracle occurred only temporarily, as in Balaam prophesying, the donkey speaking, and the angel appearing (Numbers XXII, 23), then Christ was conceived insensibly, which would be the greatest indignity to Mother and Son.

Suetonius records that in a dream a certain lame man was ordered to go to Caesar Vespasian, ask him to touch the lame man’s injured thigh with the big toe of his right foot, and thereby regain the proper balance of his steps; and this was done. If, therefore, before the conception the Virgin knew little or nothing of God, what more did she possess than Vespasian and the lame man?

If God is said to have prepared a lamp for his Christ (Psalm CXXXI, 17), was not her mind and womb prepared, into which Christ himself came in order to be universally born? The ancient righteousness of Elizabeth herself is certainly not passed over in the Gospel: she was filled with the prophetic spirit together with the child she bore. Is religious intention before conception to be taken away from this woman?

If the prophet calls him Emmanuel, which means “God with us,” and no one disbelieves this; if the angel who preceded his greeting said to her, “The Lord is with you” (Luke I, 28), then does he lie? And what ignorance of the love of God was in her if the Lord was with her in an abundance of grace?

If the Lord himself goes to prepare dwelling places—that is, minds in which he may dwell—was the Virgin’s life, before the angel’s words, so devoid of divine savor that he would not grant to himself what he does not deny to others, who are altogether lesser by comparison, by fitting her to be his mother? If it belongs to a philosophical mind to create solitude for itself amid crowds, while nevertheless being unable to be alone apart from the company of reason, what cleansing do we suppose the Son of God accomplished in that woman’s heart? How could he have withdrawn even for a moment from illuminating her whom he chose for the future honor of her own motherhood and of all Christianity? And how could he have been absent from her even for an instant from the time she was born, he who united to the Word—which he himself is—even before the ages what he was going to take from her? For he is called in the Apocalypse “the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” [Col. 0548B] (Revelation XIII, 8).

It should also be noted that it does not say, “Hail, who will be filled with grace,” but “full of grace.” It should be observed no less carefully that, before announcing to her the conception and birth, the angel teaches that the fullness of grace is already in her, lest, after the announcement, anyone should suppose that grace had suddenly been poured into her when she had not possessed it before that hour.

Faith, certainly, consists above all in free will aided by prevenient grace. How, then, is she called blessed by Elizabeth because she believed (Luke I, 45), if the merit of her admirable faith is in no way to be proclaimed in her? Moreover, why is she called blessed among women by the same angel before he announces the cause for which he had come, except because in this her, so to speak, fitness for receiving the Son of God is marked by a singular preeminence?

If such a great matter is demanded from a sluggish virgin who merely follows the custom of the others, it does not appear to be a greater glory, as far as the Virgin is concerned, than what is foretold in Isaiah concerning what was to be done with Cyrus. These words are added: “I girded you, and you did not know me” (Isaiah XLV, 5).

Nor would this be anything greater than what is celebrated in the rods of Moses and Aaron, one of which was changed into a serpent and the other produced an almond. If this grace burst upon her suddenly, what blessedness could have reached her mind, when neither the novelty of so great a good had previously given any sign within her, nor, once its task was completed, did it continue any longer than a spark?

If her breast had been foolish from the beginning, how is it that she sings so wisely of the mighty being cast down from their seats and the humble being exalted? (Luke I, 52.) If she conceived with such ease, she would perhaps have tossed about the mystery that, according to the objection, she had received so unexpectedly, with childish frivolity; but, according to the Gospel, she “kept all these things, pondering them” (Luke II, 19). Therefore, the mother of Samson is subjected to ritual observances for the sake of reverence toward the one who was to be born (Judges XIII, 13–14), while the mother of the Author of all things is suddenly seized as though she were demented?

### Why the Blessed Virgin is troubled at the angelic greeting

This too must be considered: after the angel’s greeting, it is added, “When she had heard this, she was troubled at his saying and considered what kind of greeting this might be” (Luke I, 29). Note the character of these words, unusual to our customs and almost to everyone’s. She hears herself so highly praised, and by one whom she undoubtedly recognized as an angel. What was the cause of her movement, the cause of her trouble? Although she may have been able to wonder, as is thought, she ought not to have been troubled.

It is something that even very holy men are often cleverly robbed of: when they are praised by an unstable crowd, not without flattery, they are immediately bent inwardly almost to their very core. But here, something more wonderful than every wonder is that the angel, truthful in himself in every respect, speaks to her also according to the judgment of God, and yet she is troubled at so great a testimony.

The matter must therefore be contemplated with a more attentive mind. The nature of the most perfect good is such that, the more abundantly it burns with love of virtue, the more the misery of its frailty—or even the least fault to which it still thinks itself subject—overflows in its contemplation. It does not consider what it possesses, but to what necessity it remains subject. Although it is continually nourished inwardly by the nectar-like sweetness of divine inspiration, it does not rejoice over the things that are present to it; rather, it laments that tiny thing which still seems to obstruct it.

Hence David repeatedly calls himself needy and poor (Psalm LXXXI, 4). Jeremiah cries: “I am a man who sees my poverty” (Lamentations III, 1). Yet one had heard, “I have found a man according to my heart” (Acts XIII, 22), and the other, without doubt, “Before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah I, 5). Nevertheless, the humility to which each subjected himself is evident.

John was not unaware of what the archangel had said about him, almost on a level with Christ himself; nevertheless, by word and deed he displayed whatever was more humble.

### The higher anyone is in holiness, the humbler he is in himself

But to some it seems impossible that, while someone has acted better than others, he should think worse of himself. This can be proved by simple examples. You see a man greedy for money, overflowing with splendid treasures and pouring out riches useful to no one. The more abundant he sees those riches to be, the more eagerly he rushes in spirit to possess them and the more needy he hastens to become; he does not value what he has while aspiring to what he wants to have. Thus, the richer he is, the poorer he considers himself, while desiring what belongs to others.

Look elsewhere at someone in the gestures of love, in the direction of missiles, in distinctions of voice, in the turns of choral or musical discipline; and, not to delay, everyone who is exercised not only in any useful skill but even in a frivolous art is accustomed to swell with pride over his own, however ignoble, accomplishment and to prefer himself in knowledge even to respectable people.

If the miser becomes poor, as it were, because of his abundance, how much more does the love of virtue, drawn on by inward sweetness, make a person become empty in his own sight? For if it is true—as it is—that wherever you direct your intellect, there it becomes effective, and that everyone intoxicates himself with a true or false intention, then, in the pursuit of that thing, he thinks himself superior to the rest. While he directs his eye solely toward that in which he seems, even vainly, to excel, and neglects the usefulness of others, he is driven mad by his own arrogance.

### The reason for the Blessed Virgin’s supreme humility

There are therefore men of great ability and renown who, the more learned they are, consider themselves the poorer in knowledge. For them there is that philosophical saying: “This alone I know: that I do not know.” Moreover, the one who first led others to contempt sees everything sublime; hence the word “to despise” is said to mean “to look downward,” because he looks below himself upon those whom he despises.

The Virgin, therefore, more excellent than every creature, is troubled by the extraordinary favor of the archangel. The more richly she is adorned in herself with merit, the more unworthy she considers herself on account of her supposed uselessness. She was the one who, more uniquely than every angel and human being, approached the feet of the Lord, according to the Mosaic saying; she received more specially than the others from his teaching, which sounded nothing but the humility of her Son in word and deed. From him she had learned to be gentle and humble of heart. She had drunk in the fullness of his grace before he was born from her.

She is therefore troubled not by the angel’s sight but by his words, since she considers herself in every way to possess none of the things that were being proclaimed. Do not suppose that she even attributes to herself the virtue of humility when she says that God regarded her; rather, she calls “humility” (Luke I, 48) nothing other than the lowliness of herself.

She is troubled, I say, whose conscience is not penetrated even by heavenly praise. O immeasurable strength of soul, to which the archangel could not flatter even if he wished! O extraordinary strength of the blessed woman, who is troubled even by God’s own approval! Yet although, before God, when she hears herself exalted, her devout intention suffers the shame from which she is troubled, she nevertheless considers “what kind of greeting this might be” (ibid., 29). For a virtue without understanding can neither be spoken of nor exist.

Although she does not cease to shrink from what is praised, she nevertheless examines the causes arising from her merits, which are sometimes enacted under the divine ordering. She was plainly destined to give birth to the Wisdom of God; she did not understand foolishly, but in examining the outcomes of divine arrangements she was, through her own marvelous humility, discerning. This is and is fitting in all holy men. Even if that most blessed woman seemed to regard her state as insignificant, she did not consider empty the special gift of divine love bestowed upon her above all others.

Unless she clearly discerned what was taking place within her, she would in no way possess the mastery of inward virtue. She presided over her mind’s contemplation with such majestic authority that, confident in the incomprehensible purity of which she was conscious, she assented immediately to the angelic message.

### Grace is understood as the remission of sins. According to Plato, spirits are created before bodies

But it must not be allowed to slip away what the grace proclaimed to her is. Nor should we overlook what the fullness of that grace is. Grace is used for the remission of sins, as in the apostolic letters: “Grace and peace be multiplied to you” (I Peter I, 2). For when sins have been remitted, we are reconciled to God.

If the matter concerns either original or actual sin, it is cleansed by the Holy Spirit who was joined to her from the womb. If every faithful person is commanded to prepare a way for God by which he may come to the heart, will the mother into whom he came to be generated be left to filth and negligence? [Note: See note 1 at the end of the Works.]

Certainly, if, according to the Platonic opinion, our spirits are created before our bodies, God could give some spirit the choice of the mother from whom it wished to be born. If this were done, what sort of person do you think that spirit would be conscious of itself to be? I shall say nothing of bodily form and condition. Whatever honesty and prudence his mind and character would carry, nothing would assuredly detract from her so as to prevent her being enviable to others.

If the human spirit thus adorns the city of the virginal womb which the Most High builds for itself, according to the spirit’s greater power, does not the Spirit of God adorn it much more? I say confidently: if the instruments of all the heavenly citizens were to undertake to express the arrangement of her heart, they would fail before they could speak words worthy of it.

For if, according to the Apostle, “the manifold wisdom of God has been made known through the Church to the principalities and powers” (Ephesians III, 10), how could the mystery enacted in Mary be expressible to them, when John, greater than those born of women, cannot unravel even the smallest question concerning it (Matthew XI, 11)? If they learned, from what God did around us through the Son, things they had previously not known, how could they comprehend what Christ did in himself?

Let us therefore understand grace in this way: whatever she was, we should believe that she was singularly chosen from all human descent, since by an unheard-of privilege through the ages she knew that she had been appointed by the Father and by the Son for himself, and through the Holy Spirit chosen for such great services. I do not doubt—if I dare to say so, and I shall say it—that among all creatures she was, while she lived on earth, second to no one but God alone, and is now second only in heaven.

Grace, however, was the whole of this, although it pursued this through every encompassing virtue. For no virtue, no exercise, and no labor of any merit whatever, undertaken by any woman, would have sufficed to merit the conception of God, unless grace—and not merely ineffable grace, but grace inconceivable to every nature except God—had gone before.

But we must likewise consider what this fullness itself may be; for perhaps the special quality cannot be attributed to her which is attributed to many. For if she is called “full” (Luke 1:28), and Elizabeth is also said to have been “filled” (ibid., 41), and the same is abundantly found elsewhere concerning many others, nevertheless the difference among these fullnesses is recognized to be almost as great as the variety of good dispositions everywhere. For however many are the capacities of innumerable vessels, [Col. 0551D] so nearly numerous are the kinds of inner states. It is according to each person’s own virtue, in accordance with the Gospel’s measure of talents (Matt. 25:15), and according to the measure of faith, as the Apostle says (Rom. 12:3)—that is, according to what it is possible for each person to contain—that God’s munificence is given. The capacities themselves also either deteriorate or increase according to the ages of bodies and souls. John, for example, perceived one way as a child and understood another way in his mature body.

Fullness, therefore, occurs in many forms according to the qualities of minds, since each person receives more or less in proportion to God’s gift and his own devotion. Just as the bellies of those who eat are stretched to entirely unequal degrees by the quantity of food, so minds apprehend God’s grace through a distribution far more unequal. The more a person is enlarged by love of God (examplatur; perhaps exampliatur), the more capacious, so to speak, he is found to be for divine reception. For some, only sparks of compunction suffice; others bear the hearth-fires of heavenly contemplation. Thus, according to the narrowness of understanding and faith, some are filled with little, while others, according to the breadth of their capacity, are extended toward the infinite. You see, then, how the Virgin, blessed among creatures, possesses a fullness of grace extraordinarily distinct from that of others: she who, having become heaven, contains in her blessed womb the Author of all grace.

Finally, although it may seem a small matter, I shall not omit that the angel’s presenting to the Virgin the conception of the aged Elizabeth, as though to establish her faith, would never have been introduced by him except so that it might seem a great thing to the Virgin. Yet what was great for God, if a virgin’s womb swelled by the Spirit, who once hovered over the waters in order to make them fruitful? To grant conception to an old woman was subject to no lesser ease. But among us this matter is not least constrained, since the difficulty—or rather the impossibility—of the whole of nature is indicated. If the Virgin is made fruitful by God, it is not surprising, because the example of creatures that give birth without males makes the matter easier to understand. Only the preservation of virginity after childbirth is esteemed incomparably great. Nothing at all can be compared with it, because what is conceived and brought forth is divine, and because it has no example in nature.

But in old people, when generative power has been withdrawn from both sexes by exhausted bodies, I esteem it no less a wonder if they beget children than if such fertile intercourse should occur in the years of childhood. Indeed, I esteem it much less; for in children heat naturally grows together and, in physiological terms, aids the ineffectiveness of the aged in begetting: what the freezing of blood prevents in the latter, youthful fervor unfolds in the former. In the utterly decrepit, therefore, the matter becomes readily miraculous, since on the one side women, trembling already with extreme old age, are free from any intervening illness, and on the other side men are drained of their customary heat and moisture. Certainly nothing remains that might awaken the impulse—not to speak of desire, but even of the faintest inclination.

Hence Paul especially proves Abraham’s faith in this matter because he saw “his own body already dead and the deadness of Sarah’s womb” (Rom. 4:19), and “against hope believed in hope.” If what is described in Jerome—that a nine-year-old boy had intercourse with a young woman and produced offspring—is judged by everyone to be beyond nature, then, so to speak, it is far more beyond nature that those whose every inborn fervor has grown cold, and whose vitality cannot be restored to full vigor in either one, should, though both are numb, awaken one another to conception.

Elizabeth, then, is not proposed without reason as Mary’s kinswoman; for unless the event had been wholly unexpected to everyone and contrary to physical nature, Zechariah would never have so obstinately disbelieved Gabriel’s words. Nor should anyone, in the example employed, brand the most blessed Virgin with a blemish, as though it implied some disparagement of her faith—a faith which, as we remember, we rightly praised for its readiness. Rather, let him understand that the angel, out of an abundance of prudence, reported a miracle performed in an old woman, both to provide support for Mary’s faith and to enable her to rejoice in such an outcome for her kinswoman.

Indeed, the two women would also thereby safeguard each other’s modesty: Mary had conceived without the knowledge of the man to whom she was betrothed, while Elizabeth had returned to youthful fertility contrary to everyone’s expectation. Hence Mary proceeds into the hill country in haste and chooses to remain with her kinswoman for three months, while Elizabeth conceals herself for six months, lest she cause astonishment to those who saw her or shame to herself. “And you shall know,” he says, “that this will unquestionably come to pass for you and for that old woman, because no word will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37)—with God who, whenever he wills, releases a virgin just as readily as a barren woman into childbirth.

## CHAPTER VI

### “This is the day which the Lord has made,” referring to Blessed Mary

This, then, is the most blessed day of Blessed Mary, which the Lord specially made: “Let us rejoice and be glad in it.” For when he had spoken of the Son, as though of the stone that was made the head of the corner (Matt. 21:42), and had declared that “this is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. 117:23), made by the Lord, he immediately transferred his words to this day. This, I say, is the day that brought forth the sun of righteousness, who from his own munificence established in the Church the most splendid hours of dignity.

She is also the gate of the Lord Jesus, through which the righteous enter; for no one attains righteousness unless he enters through faith in his incarnation. Upon the threshold of this gate the prince previously expounded by us in Ezekiel, and still to be expounded, adores. He inspires those who adore—not the lintel of its dignity, but its threshold of humility, which is accessible to all—that is, those who hold it in every form of veneration. God is rightly said to do what he administers to others as something to be done.

But let us return to the hours of the aforesaid day. This most flourishing day, after it had produced that greater light which illuminates both itself above all, and the moon of the Church and the stars of the faithful with the rays of wondrous understanding, let us consider how many determinations of happiness it likewise admitted. For it was both their origin and their official cause. The Son of God did not wish—or rather, he ought not and could not—go forth to us in any other way, because he neither ought nor could violently violate the rights of the devil, to whom man had voluntarily surrendered himself. But, in the words of blessed Leo, “By the great right of equity, it was fitting that the contest should be waged there.” He therefore set before the devil the woman from whom he was to be created, so that, when he seized him, he would think that nothing other than a man had been taken.

### He brought forth twelve blessed hours

The first hour, therefore, is that he cast out the prince of this world, conquered the world, and, by giving himself over to the cross, rescued us from the enemy.

[Col. 0554A] The second is that, through the water flowing from his side on that same cross, he consecrated baptism. In that passion he stripped the devil of his ancient strength so completely that he had already begun to be punished before the day of judgment. For the great Origen says that after the passion itself, whenever a holy martyr or confessor departed victorious from the present world, just as the saint went forth to his crown, so the enemy who had spiritually attacked him immediately entered eternal torments, never again to harm anyone. This, he says, is what the demons themselves said to the Lord: “You have come to torment us before the time” (Matt. 8:29).

For this reason, too, we see that the great powers which they once used to exercise have been blunted; and it is no wonder, when we believe that after so many victories of the saints, so many of the more powerful demons have fallen into punishments.

The third is that, through the resurrection, he brought the elect out of the underworld, and added so great a privilege to its glory that, according to Prudentius, a holy and noble man, there are beneath Styx renowned holidays of punishment even for spirits that have often done harm:

> On that sacred night when God returned from the Acherontic pools to those above.

The fourth is that through it he opened the kingdoms of heaven to believers.

The fifth is that he brought our humanity, personally identified with the Word who is himself, to the right hand of the Father.

The sixth is that he who had taken flesh from us returned his divinity, which is his Spirit, to us.

The seventh is that he not only granted that same Spirit to be enjoyed, but also ordained that through the hands of the apostles, and from them through bishops, it should be given to others.

The eighth is that through the teachers of the Church he judged that sins—which belonged to him alone to forgive—should be forgiven.

The ninth is that he granted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to Peter, and in Peter to the rulers of that kingdom. Hence, at a certain place in Rome, this is written of him:

> The power conferred on Peter terrified the angelic ranks—  
> such power to unbar the heavens and feed the flocks.

The tenth is that he did not entrust the mysteries of handling his body and blood to angels, but to human beings, even though they are sinners. The same was likewise done with baptism.

The eleventh is that in the resurrection he will conform our body to the body of his glory.

The twelfth is that in that same resurrection, just as every principality and power in heaven will venerate and adore our flesh in the Son and in the mother, so also those who are in Christ “will rise first” (1 Thess. 4:15). Hence the steward of the household began to give the denarius to the last ones. This statement is supported by the fact that we read that their name will be honorable before him. If the Christian name is honored under so great an author, it is certainly necessary to understand that, with justice, a more glorious reward is otherwise granted as a privilege to all those who have lived well under grace.

### She is the light cloud that poured forth the rains. How exalted a glory she possesses

Let us therefore see with what joyful pious compunction we should congratulate this day, which is suffused with so radiant a sun, with heaven, the underworld, and the earth. Through it that sun gained entrance to us, and, for the infinite brightness of that day itself and the glorification of those dwelling under it, he brought the gifts of our perpetual nobility and his own.

This is that light cloud which the true sun mounted, according to Isaiah, in order to illuminate the dark Egypt of this world (Isa. 19:1). Its rain softened the clods of earthly hearts with every kind of inner fruitfulness; for it opened the cataracts of all health-giving teachings, especially when it set before the world the bread of angels. It possessed within itself a lightness free from every addition of sin as great as the dignity of Christ’s most holy flesh and soul deserved.

Let us consider, then, what excellence she possesses from whom we draw such honors of soul and body, since she bestowed the Son of God bodily in her flesh. If, after the court of her most blessed womb had been emptied, she perhaps suffered some loss of the glory which she had fully tasted, let that idea be rejected! I shall speak of this confidently: if she was joyful when she took in what no other creature was ever permitted to take in, she was surely more joyful when she saw him crowned with glory and honor seated beside the eternal Father with the apostles. As long as she remembers that she gave birth to God, she could never feel diminished, even for an instant, in the fruit of joy that she possessed in conceiving him.

If Christ God is exalted because he humbled himself, then she likewise possesses the glory that remains eternally from having borne the whole of God. Indeed, she is advanced in glory; for it is far more glorious for a queen to see her Son reigning than to know herself pregnant by him.

Let the prince, therefore, adore upon the threshold of this gate—that is, let him inspire those who adore in spirit and in truth. Hence the psalm says: “Adore his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98:5). For if it is said of Christ as man, “Adore him, all his angels” (Ps. 96:7), no one doubts that they adore him as God. What is more holy, what more worthy of adoration, than the flesh from which Christ is begotten, which has identity with her and is united to the Son of God?

And certainly, when he was placed in the world and was subject to his parents as a child (Luke 2:51), in accordance with what the ordinances of his own law required, he honored them.
