It is therefore not surprising if he adores that very thing which he placed in her in virtue and glory, and which the threshold of the gate signifies. For “to adore” is used sometimes for divine worship and sometimes for reverence shown to human beings, as the prophet Nathan is recorded as having adored David (1 Kings 1:23). Hence Jacob is also said by the Apostle to have adored the top of Joseph’s staff (Heb. 11:21)—that is, to have held in great veneration the summit of his power, which is so inseparably established by God.

If it is said of the saints, to whom divine sonship is promised, that their name will be honorable before him (Ps. 71:14), while Christ honors in them what he himself has granted, will he not in his mother venerate his own nature, from which he is bound to her by debt? For whose sake is the reward of long life granted to others, if not to the one from whom he suffered himself to receive what makes him human? If she is honored by the one from whom she received all that she is, she ought to be so much more honorable to us, inasmuch as no one can hope that any woman was more necessary to her own salvation and to the salvation of all.

He adores, therefore, upon the threshold of the gate in Ezekiel (Ezek. 46:2), when, dwelling especially within her mind through humble obedience, he glorifies himself in her glorification.

### Blessed Mary avenges the injuries inflicted upon her by heretics and evil people

Then he goes out (ibid.), because what he advanced within himself in that blessed woman, in the blessed interiority of his heart, he reveals publicly—or rather, so to speak, as a second authority of omnipotence after himself, he discloses among human beings. For who, however dull, does not know that she is the one who through her Son presides over heaven, rules the earth, and constrains the underworld? The prince therefore goes out when the power of the Prince of the Mother is sent forth through the Prince.

“But the gate shall not be shut until evening” (ibid.). Here the shutting does not refer to virginity, which has been discussed repeatedly. The gate, therefore, is not shut until evening because access to her mercy is not closed until the end of the age to anyone who devoutly asks. When it is said that it “shall not be shut,” this means that it shall be opened. For she who, after the giving of the Holy Spirit, was known to have poured forth salvation for us all, in the manifestation of her glory thereafter suffered no decay. Just as faith in her Son could not be deprived of strength by any storms of persecution, indeed never ceased to advance, so the honor of his blessed Mother—I do not say ceased to grow warm, but could not fail to be exalted day by day as time progressed.

For if, in each generation of the faithful, Christian judgment is strengthened the more it is tested, and, once examined, has learned to give no answer other than what is solid, so her virginity, destined to be glorified throughout the ages, and her fruitfulness, which no heresy could violate, never succumbed even to a momentary shadowing. Rather, as the avenger of her injuries, she has through the revolutions of time most imperiously revealed, by marvelous manifestations, how greatly she reigns everywhere.

### It is proper to her to show mercy, since she is the mediator between God and human beings

Hence it follows: “And all the people of the land shall adore at the door of the gate” (ibid., 3). If the prince adores what he received from her—that is, the covering of his own humanity—and thereby indicates to his members that it should be adored, then the people of the earth, not of dust—people steadfast and fruitful in faith, not flighty—most rightly adore her as more glorious than the heavenly creatures. For she is the author and nourisher of the new creation of the Son of God; she is honored not merely as the other saints are honored, but is adored as being, so to speak, equal to Christ’s humanity.

The doorway is the approach to the gate of Mary’s sweetness, standing wide open to all. For what mercy would not flow to that blessed woman from whom the fountain of all generosity and grace flows to all sinners who tenderly repent? To whom, when the whole of mercy has poured itself forth, would she be opposed who contains within herself the one who poured it forth upon us?

It is plainly her special property to show mercy, because she, who understood that she had been mercifully chosen by God for so immense an office and made a mediator between God himself and human beings, rightly possesses such special compassion toward us. Through this compassion, and for our sake, she has been made so singularly excellent that we might obtain mercy.

For since no one has any ability at all adequate to approach the Son and intercede with him as is fitting, what eloquence of any mediator could be more pleasing—or rather, could be so greatly pleasing—to him than that of the woman whom he is compelled, so to speak, to honor both by the bond of kinship and by the authority of his own law? If he were to withdraw his hearing from her in any matter, no one could approach to ask without being miserably rejected.

Certainly, he who established nature and consequently instituted the laws of nature left no doubt that maternal personhood would have weight with him, since an inborn custom preserves this among mortals in all good households.

## CHAPTER VII

### The Gospel customarily read on the Assumption of Blessed Mary is explained

Moreover, many people are accustomed to ask why, at her Assumption, that chapter of the Gospel is customarily read: “Jesus entered into a certain village” (Luke 10:38). The more this seems, according to the outer shell of the historical account, to be remote from her, the more fully it remains within her according to the moral meaning and the state of contemplation. If God grants that we speak according to the truth, the following points will be able to demonstrate this.

“Jesus entered into a certain village.” We usually say “a certain” concerning something that we do not wish, or are unable, to express. A village, however, is constructed of a rampart, a wall, and a tower; and it is called *castellum* from *castrare*, “to cut off” or “restrain.” The fortress of that blessed woman’s conscience, then, was such that she never ceased utterly to repel whatever could displease God in her.

But first it has a rampart, since above all it never lacked the lowest foundation of complete humility. Finally, it is surrounded by a wall when her most blessed mind, inwardly watchful for her good, is fortified by the external guardianship of the bodily senses. A tower is erected within when, in a humble heart and with the body already disciplined, hope in God is stretched upward in its full height.

For when the infusion of the Lord’s entire majesty had been announced to her, what sounded in her mouth except the humility of a handmaid? What was her entire subsequent life except silence and modesty?

### Her most holy acts are described

Hence it is said: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Here we should consider within what lofty fortress that woman, destined to be set above the angels, concealed herself. Although she already carried God himself in mind and womb, she restrained herself with an incomparable abasement.

When she declared that all generations would call her blessed, and was conscious of such great glory, it was especially marvelous that she contained herself with such humility—a humility that could have been greatly praised in any sinner.

What her external conduct was may be inferred from the solitude in which she was found by the angel. He found her offended neither by the presence of chatterers nor of lovers, but content with the contemplation of God, in which she had been nurtured.

Moreover, it is remarkable with what haste she climbed into the hill country and chose to remain for three months in the dwelling of her aged kinswoman; this was no small distinction for a young woman. It was a sign of an unusual celibacy that she not only endured the weight of old women’s manners and severe movements, but that youthful eagerness most eagerly sought them, even though she had conceived, with an ineffable affection, such great joy of majesty.

With what magnanimous regard she contributed to the overflow of the glory bestowed upon her is revealed by what she sang: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1:47–48), and so forth.

You have, then, the wall above and the tower here. It is therefore a certain fortress—one that no one can conceive, much less express—which, as the Mother of God, possesses such magnificence outwardly and such worth within.

### How Martha, who was troubled, applies to Blessed Mary

### Her active life

“A certain woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). By “woman” is signified active fruitfulness, or rather activity fruitful in good works. She is called Martha because she is provoked by many bitternesses. Hence it is said to her: “You are troubled about many things” (ibid., 41). Her name is interpreted in accordance with this.

She received him into her house when the Virgin, more blessed than all human nature after the Son, conceived the Son of God. The house was both the house of the soul and the house of the womb.

But we must investigate what kind of activity could have existed in that receiving woman. Other saints render ministries of generosity to their fellow members; she, however, ministered in a special way to her own Head and the Head of all, whereas others generally offer such service at his feet.

If you give a tunic to an ordinary poor person, she fashioned for the almighty Son, from the Spirit of God and her own blood, a bodily form. If you offer bread, she supplied her Creator with nourishment from her blessed breasts. If you provide consolation to someone grieving, she wiped away the little tears that nourished universal joy with the soothing tenderness of a mother. Whatever benefit you might be able to confer, she surpassed it by her blessed service.

Do you wish to hear the bitternesses by which, in accordance with the etymology of her name, that glorious woman who so served was vexed? “Your own soul,” it is said, “a sword will pierce” (Luke 2:35). As many insults as the Son endured while preaching, so many sword-points pierced her—far more grievously than the one who endured them, or rather the one to whom they were inflicted.

### Her contemplative life

“And she had a sister named Mary” (Luke 10:39). It is everywhere well known that the grace of contemplation is signified by Mary. The two are called sisters because they are generated within the conscience from one seed of divine love.

We believe that this blessed woman, above all human beings, was imbued with the glory of this virtue. For the fullness of divinity had entered her wholly—not for an hour, as in others, nor by touching her with only a part of itself.

Hence what follows: “Who also, sitting at the Lord’s feet, heard his word” (Luke 10:39). She sat beside his feet when, in receiving Christ’s humanity, she humbled herself with the humility that was due; for sitting is humbling oneself. Hence: “Rise up after you have sat” (Ps. 126:2).

The Lord’s feet are his humanity, just as his head is his divinity. Hence she is also called his footstool (Ps. 109:1), and the Psalm commands that she be adored (Ps. 108:5). In her, Christ’s flesh is unfolded as a kind of extremity of him.

That blessed woman therefore quite rightly sat beside these feet, because, while she considered the greatness of the one conceived by her, she clung, through the vision of her incomparable abasement, to the one whom she bore or carried, as though by the outermost points of contact. The more reverently she handled his flesh, the more spiritually was she sharpened for the vision of the divine substance, which is the Word.

For if holy men, by loving and believing in Christ’s humanity from the depths of their hearts, gradually arrive at contemplating the appearance of his divinity, what could be hidden from the glory of God by her who begot within herself God and man and possessed the whole of him without distinction? The more secret her blessedness was in this contemplation, the more abundantly her understanding, through a simple and wholly undivided intention, penetrated divine realities.

In spiritual matters, seeing is nothing other than hearing, and hearing nothing other than seeing. What, then, is hearing the Word except understanding God? She sits and hears the Word because divinity, through the grace given to the humble, imbued the mind of the most blessed Virgin Mother—not by giving her a foretaste, but by pouring itself into her universally.

If divinity can conceal itself from itself, and if anything divine could be hidden from one more blessed than all the blessed, then perhaps something of whatever God is could have been hidden from her heart and womb. But nothing of it was absent there.

### Martha was busy with much serving

“But Martha was busy with much serving” (Luke 10:40). The “much serving” around which she is busy is the very solicitude for the care of the Lord’s body. In the blessed Virgin, activity ministers in such a way that she believes she must sometimes devote herself more to the service of the external man than to contemplating God. For what she had begotten bodily and always had before her eyes, she constantly embraced with especially fervent devotion.

What is present to the hand is plainly desired more intensely by the mind; what lies less close to the senses is penetrated with difficulty by the power of understanding. To gather the mind for contemplation requires quiet attention away from external disturbance. Hence she is also said to stand, because she is burdened by frequent conflicts.

When he is sought for execution by Herod, when he is attacked by the Jewish envy of youth, when he is threatened with being thrown headlong, when he is overwhelmed with insults, when at last he is handed over to the cross, her active life is stretched upon the battlefield of the mind by many struggles.

“Lord,” she said, “do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve?” (ibid.) This is what she says to the Word himself, for whom contemplation has leisure to listen:

“Although I am occupied with the continual duties of infancy and with the misfortunes of youth, worn down by constant distress and compassion, there is now no place here for contemplation and inner peace, since the confinement of repeated labors and sorrows besieges her. And because it is certain that through these things she is made to go outside herself, whether she wishes it or not, command her to be restrained within the single duty of activity.”

No one doubts that there was a great dispute in the heart of the most blessed Virgin between these two states: on the one hand, she delighted in seeing God; on the other, she was distracted by the bodily care of him.

But attention must be given to the word “alone.” If activity alone ministers, contemplation is certainly idle. Whenever contemplation bends itself toward activity, it is undoubtedly nullified. Therefore, since she is not permitted to do anything without inner quiet and is troubled about many things, she is not raised to spiritual matters.

How, then, can the woman who complains that she has been left alone be helped by that which has no place amid troubles? Yet activity itself appears to receive help from contemplation when the mind uniformly carries out what predominates within it. For when activity turns elsewhere and the mind, eager for contemplation, seeks solitude, then, by withdrawing from the multiplicity of cares, it ceases, as it were, to assist its active sister.

It would therefore help her if it ceased desiring contemplation. It does not leave activity alone if the mind that had proposed to contemplate does not flee the cares of activity. As long, then, as contemplation is at leisure in gazing upon God, it does not assist activity when activity is alone. But when the mind grows weary of the love of contemplation, to the extent that it withdraws from it, it now devotes itself more freely to activity and thereby assists the one who is alone.

### If God had not clothed himself in flesh, he could never have been endured

Nevertheless, the Lord declares that one thing is necessary. To say nothing of that glorious woman who, through the ministry she offered to that most holy flesh, reached the height of divinity, every saint arrives at knowledge of divinity only through faith in and love of humanity.

Hence it is said: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7). Approving also the services that were offered to his body while he lived, he says: “You always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (Matt. 26:11).

What, then, was more necessary to that blessed woman than the covering of the Lord’s body? While she clothed him in it, the sacrament of the heavenly divinity provided her with great assistance in reaching the inner light. For if Christ did not conceal himself in flesh, how could that pure fire of divinity be endured? Indeed, even that flesh itself, with God hidden within it, would not have been bearable unless the power of the Most High overshadowed the bosom of her mind.

### Blessed Mary was placed on earth in continual vision of God

“Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Although, then, the most blessed Virgin might appear to have been excessively distracted by the bodily troubles of her sweetest Son and occupied with external duties, no sound-minded person could believe that she, who had received within herself the God who is the author of the universe, was ever deprived, even for an hour, of continual contemplation of the one whom she had once wholly imbibed—something permitted to no other human creature.

Whatever pains of the Son might trouble her, the fervor of her faith in him whom she undoubtedly knew to be God never grew cold, especially since the hidden ordering of his dispensation was by no means unknown to her.

For although it is not believed of any other saint, there is almost no doubt that she retained so much of the fullness of divinity that, wherever she turned herself, she never withdrew from the vision of God. She who possessed more on earth than an angel ought not to have been less than an angel after the blessedness of such a birth.

For if, among the angels who are sent to minister to those who are to be saved (Acts 2:2), an unmoving continuity of contemplation keeps watch wherever they turn, what must have been at work in so great and ineffable a Mother, who therefore reigns above the angels? In her holy mind—indeed, as I might say, her almost divine mind—it is absurd to suppose that, after the place of so great a sanctuary had been emptied, any loss occurred, so that she lost by giving birth what she had possessed in labor.

And if she is recognized to have conceived the fullness of divinity bodily, so that she did not possess, after giving birth, the whole of what she had borne, nevertheless the faithful do not judge that she possessed anything less of what pertains to the grace and glory of the heart.

Just as the Holy Spirit, when he appeared over the apostles and believers through tongues (Acts 2:3), remained in their hearts through knowledge, strength, and love without diminution after the miracle had passed, so, after the heavenly birth had been displayed, the excellence of divine greatness remained in the virginal mind without any reduction of its former contemplation.

It was therefore rightly said, “It shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). For just as things occurred in her unlike anything in the events of any age, so the eminence of mind with which she was once imbued remained with her. Otherwise, if it had ceased after childbirth, the virtue previously mentioned would appear to have been only temporary.

Even if this grace flourished in the Virgin at the time of conception on the condition, so to speak, that it would grow lukewarm or cease afterward, whence did she possess in heaven such power over earth and the underworld, beyond all human measure? Certainly, where beginning and end correspond to such privileges, I confess that the intervening period was never exposed to any loss.

The choice of the better part therefore fell to her, because whatever services Martha performed within her, her choice was always turned toward the kernel of inner sweetness. Hence Mary is called “star of the sea” or “illuminatrix.” In the sea, namely, from which she is troubled about many things, she is a star and illuminatrix, because amid the temptations of the world, which she sometimes suffers while serving active duties, she is sustained by the perpetual and unconquered light of contemplation amid the storms.

Let what has been said about the present chapter suffice, so that we may show how it applies to the preaching of this ineffable Lady.

## CHAPTER VIII

Moreover, we think it worthwhile to examine that passage of Isaiah, if perhaps it agrees with what has been said:

> “As the rain and the snow descend from heaven and do not return there any further, but water the earth, soak it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. 55:10–11).

The rain descends when the angel lays down before the Virgin the words concerning incarnation. Snow comes from heaven when the Holy Spirit poured himself into her from the Father—not to remove her virginity, but to increase the radiance of her purity beyond all measure.

For he who was able to grant conception in her first through faith ([1 [Note: With smaller typefaces the reader is referred back to the notes published separately after Guibert’s works]), when the actual conception occurred, abolished original sin. He does not return there any further because the mind of that blessed woman is never deprived of the privilege of spiritual grace once received.

He would return there if what had been received in vain, without the fruit of the recipient, were carried back to God who had given it. And this is Mary’s portion, which shall not be taken away from her (Luke 10:42).

He makes the earth drunk when the Holy Spirit renders Mary’s conscience insensible to all the movements of inward passions. For drunkenness removes awareness of inflicted pains. He then pours it in when he imbues her, not from elsewhere but from himself, with the capacity to conceive.

[Note: This is what the text says. If he were speaking according to the literal order, he would have written “first he pours in, afterward he makes drunk.”]

He makes it germinate when, without seed, he draws forth from her the pledge of our redemption. When she is said to germinate without any previous mention of seed, the singular purity of blessed Mary in conception is undoubtedly indicated.

He gives seed to the sower when she who conceived spiritually sends forth, together with the one whom she bore, spiritual seed as well. Seed is given to the sower from this point onward (Isa. 55:10), when the general preaching of the saints, arising from Christ’s incarnation, is scattered; but this pertains to the teachers.

“And bread to the eater” (ibid.), namely the one who descended from heaven (John 6:33), and who is requested by us as our daily bread—owed to no one except the one who embraces him with the eager mouth of the heart.

Thus shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth—not explained by any movement of words, but set apart from human efforts by the mystery of unbounded reason. This is that book which the same prophet is commanded to take, “Take for yourself,” he says, “a large book, and write in it with a human stylus” (Isa. VIII, 1). This Word, indeed, could be grasped by God alone, with God, by the stylus—that is, the understanding—of God; [Col. 0562D] but, so that it might in some manner be grasped by man, he willed that it be circumscribed in human form. This Word therefore goes forth when he deigns to present himself visibly through the flesh; and he goes forth from the mouth—that is, from the spirit—for it is with the mouth that we emit the spirit. He goes forth from the mouth because he is conceived in the Virgin from the purity of the spirit alone: “He shall not return to me empty” (Isa. LV, 11). He would plainly return empty if the Son of God had proved ineffective for that which he had begun.

Note that above it is said that he does not return, and here likewise, but “not empty”: for she never turned her mind away from virginity, even for a moment; but, as she was found when the Son was announced, so she grew continually more flourishing in herself until her own end, with the same glory of soul persisting; the Son, however, although he is said not to return empty, is said to return because the visibility which he had assumed necessarily had to be restored to the Father’s right hand. He accomplishes whatever the Father willed, while carrying out human salvation not without his own blood, and this is why he did not return empty. In those matters for which he is sent, he prospers, especially since he is wondrously led forth from his own right hand—that is, from his divinity—for, because of what he suffered, no one who believes in him devoutly fails to be saved.

The same author says something not very different elsewhere: “Drip down, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. XLV, 8). What are the heavens except the hidden counsels of divinity? Hence the Son himself says: “I am from above” [Col. 0563B] (John VIII, 23). The heavens, therefore, are said to drip down when the divine mercies bend themselves to show favor toward human beings. The clouds rain when the prophetic words clearly show that what they contained within themselves is born concerning Christ. The earth is opened when, at the angelic words, the womb—or rather, the bosom of the blessed mind—of the blessed Virgin is obediently opened.

This is that earth of which it is said: “You blessed, O Lord, your land” (Ps. LXXXIV, 1); from this blessing—that is, from the fruitfulness implanted by God—the captivity of Jacob is turned away. This is also, according to the Book of Wisdom, the earth set in the arid waste of immense chastity, and the field which no plowshare of marriage had cut, bringing forth of its own accord from the depths of humility (Wis. XIX, 7). Note the propriety of the word: it is said to “bring forth” not of sown things, but of things growing spontaneously; this refers to the Virgin.

## CHAPTER IX

### How pleasing it is to the Son to exalt his Virgin Mother with praises

We have touched upon these very small matters in praise of our common Lady; and although we have done little, we have nevertheless shown our devotion. Although we can in no way grasp the fullness of her glory, still less express it with our tongue, we nevertheless think that the effort itself is not without great reward, even though no service of speech adequately commends the devotion of the mind, and our limited ability supplies little with which to complete what we feel. Yet to cherish that woman and embrace her with heartfelt love is gratifying not only to her herself, who extends the breasts of infinite compassion to all, but also provides a singular approach, through her honor, to the Son, who is recognized to accept whatever reverence is shown to her with no less willingness than if his own praises were being sung.

For if God is commanded to be praised in his saints (Ps. CL, 1), this is because what is recounted of their virtue is rightly carried back to God, who gave it. In her, his praise is more particular: she excels not only in being a mother, but also in being ineffably inclined to relieve our misery. This, certainly, is owed to her, because those whom the Son liberates by his blood it is fitting that she should cherish with a more serene favor; plainly, even among human beings, the female sex is usually fuller of compassion.

Since, then, she is full of God, who is wholly mercy, and since nature itself makes her inclined to the practice of compassion, she ought by right to love that for which the Son gave himself to the gallows. Let us therefore fasten the anchor of our intention upon her, whose voice surpasses the intercessions of all when she comes before him. And since, with her generous Son in this world, the authority of the mother usually prevails to such an extent that she commands rather than entreats—he who once does not deny that he was subject to her cannot, I say confidently, deny himself to her in anything; and whatever, speaking in human terms, she may have brought about not by prayer but by a nod, will undoubtedly stand firm. And who among the saints will remain silent at her indication? She is believed to be visible and revered by the entire host of heaven above, and, together with the other saints, she is not denied a ready hearing from the Lord for her petitions. Then, after the Son, whatever she wishes is granted before all others, since she is superior to all in obtaining what is asked.

### Why the blessed Virgin performed miracles in those times

Hence it is that the faith we have concerning her excellence is now established, above all, by wondrous signs displayed in our own age. By the expenditure of unusual acts of generosity she recalls and warms hearts grown numb through the abundance of iniquity; for these same signs, which in ancient times served to build up faith, now serve to raise up the same faith—scarcely constant without works—and to strengthen morals. Therefore, mindful of her innate kindness, she now celebrates wonders of no lesser glory than those she once used to perform for a world still more faithful.

Thus she teaches that, after the name of Jesus the Lord, she is the one refuge to which we should turn, and she indicates to an age sinking toward its final necessity that her intervention has become more necessary. Since today there is no preacher who even murmurs, she announces through signs that she herself ought to be sought and that she is willing to help even without being asked. Therefore, since we have wished to signify how great she is and how great she was shown to be by the proclamations of the ancients, it is fitting also to weave in what she has done in our own age. The place of the event and the witnesses are rendered credible by such close proximity, and are so numerous as to be beyond suspicion, that not even a madman ought to cling to doubt.

## CHAPTER X

### The miracle of a woman named Teodeberta, delivered from fire

[Note: [Col. 0563D] See Herman, Book III, chapter 27, in the Appendix.]

Chiviacus is a village belonging to the bishopric of Laon, situated about two miles from the town itself. A certain man lived there with his wife, and is known to have had a daughter by her among their other children. When she had reached marriageable age, and circumstances had then smiled upon a more agreeable period of life, she was given in marriage to a certain young man. The affection of both parents drew him to themselves with such great love that, without expense to their private property, the young man and the girl had table and bed under the same roof as her parents.

While she was living there with her husband and her mother was cultivating him with astonishing maternal diligence for the sake of her daughter, no greater love could be found in the girl for the young man than in the mother-in-law for her son-in-law. She adorned him in festive garments, took pains to provide lavish meals, washed his face and hair, spread soft coverings for those going to bed, was the first to stand by him when he called for a servant, anticipated her daughter in every service except the marriage chamber, and, to sum it all up, displayed not the authority of a matron but the bustling activity of a maidservant. Yet this care was not plotting adultery. She was not being drawn away from her daughter in order to thrust herself upon him, but so that she might commend her daughter to an unstable young man by her own services, and attract the young man’s affection toward her daughter by attending to him with every courtesy.

Meanwhile, the cunning subtlety of the devil twisted to an evil interpretation everything done with benevolent intent, and branded the mother-in-law with the stain of much foulness through malicious slander: namely, that she did these things not out of affection for her offspring, but in order to exchange herself for her daughter in his regard. As the bitterness of this baseless rumor increased day by day and shook the woman’s mind, the more innocent she felt herself to be of the reproach heaped upon her, the more painfully she endured that what she practiced out of devotion should itself be turned by the common people into a scandalous tale.

Overcome by these troubles after some time, she began suddenly to loathe the young man whom she had loved so greatly, fearing that she would thereafter live under suspicion if she kept him daily before her eyes. Thus she resolved not merely to separate him from her company, as would have been sufficient, but now to kill him. She would have acted wisely if she had only removed him from her presence; but she resorted to the sword, preferring to eliminate the man rather than expose herself to an obscene suspicion.

### The woman orders her son-in-law to be killed

When autumn had advanced, she made an agreement with two young men, promising each of them twenty solidi if they would murder him, as the following events will show. They were, it is said, of Nervian origin; driven by the profits of the harvest, they had come into the province of Laon. After they had stayed there for some time, attracted both by their wages and by the novelty of unusual food, the woman mentioned above approached them with the promise; and they, fierce by nature and sharpened by determination and payment, armed themselves to carry out the crime.

One day she deliberately sent her husband outside to do some task, and, by a false pretext, likewise sent her daughter elsewhere. Once they had departed from the house, she secretly opened the storeroom, brought in the hired accomplices, and, after bolting the door from the outside, immediately began urging her son-in-law to bring out wine for those about to dine. He quickly took up a jar and opened the cellar, but before he could pour the wine into a vessel, those who had been hiding rushed in, and he was strangled at once.

When she learned that this had been done, she ordered the perpetrators of the crime immediately to remove the body, carry it to the upper part of the house, lay it on the bed where he had been accustomed to sleep with her daughter, and cover it with a sheet and clothing as though he were asleep.

After a short time had passed, the master of the house returned, along with his daughter, and they began discussing the meal together. As they hurried toward their accustomed domestic routine, the girl’s mother said to her: “Go and hurry to wake your husband, who has just lain down to sleep.” The young woman proceeded as far as the bed, called the sleeping young man by name, and also tried to rouse him by touching him. When he did not answer his wife, even though she called and shook him, she cried out, striking her hands together, that he was dead.

The household was thrown into commotion, and the neighborhood gathered, weeping over his sudden misfortune all the more miserably because they more justly grieved that he had died without a will. When the funeral lament had been proclaimed by all with genuine sorrow, the mother-in-law—or rather, the murderer of her daughter—made a great show of mourning with feigned grief, wailing more calmly than the others. She followed with still more lamentation the man’s good qualities, his charm of character, the elegance of his speech, the distinction of his handsome appearance, and, above all, his hated gaze, the more she feared that the attempt at such an ill-fated cruelty would become known.

### She repents and confesses the crime to a priest

After the man had been carried out with such rites, the woman kept silent about the whole affair. But, conscious of her foul crime, the woman came forward first, driven by unproductive repentance, and consulted the priest in whose diocese she lived, making a confession of what had happened. By him she was assigned fasts appropriate to so great an evil, and for some time she remained hidden beneath the same burden of spiritual medicine.

After a long period had passed, disputes happened to arise between her and the priest. Since the priest was impatient of canonical discipline, he hurled at her, with all the severity he could muster, the most atrocious reproach: he charged the woman with the murder of her son-in-law. The young man’s parents, as though awakened by a terrifying thunderclap, brought the matter before Ibert, the vicedominus of Laon. As much more vigorous as he was in military affairs, so much more ferocious did he prove in the public administration of the bishopric.

Why should I draw this out with scraps of words? The vicedominus entered the village, seized the woman, brought her before the law, and demanded the case. The woman did not deny it, and the sentence was deferred to be delivered at Laon.

While the same legal official was subjecting some of her relatives to the same charge, she said: “Against me alone, strike these weapons for these children. Know for certain that no one else is conscious of the alleged crime.” At that time Elinandus was bishop, a man plainly as weak in learning as he was not unfamiliar with secular administration, and especially with ecclesiastical discipline.

When the bishop’s sentence had been transferred to the court, and the vicedominus was considering what action would be appropriate, a grammarian suggested to him that such a crime deserved to be punished by fire. When the vicedominus read this with eager approval, because of the harshness of his own character, he strengthened it with his own assertion as a public judgment.

But when she saw that such a sorrowful sentence had befallen her—she who had long been weary and grieving over what she had done—she was now shaken more miserably, despairing of this world. The more everything was cut off from her in the present, the more completely the whole force of her mind was exposed to the judgment to come.

### She implores the help of the Mother of God and remains unharmed in the midst of the fire

She therefore asked the officers to allow her to go to the church of our most merciful Mother at the cathedral. Who, even if profane, would refuse this? Accompanied by a large crowd that had gathered to watch the death of the woman to be punished, she proceeded, piteously escorted, and, in the middle of the basilica, to complete her purification, confessed her own guilt before the general assembly.

Afterward she prostrated herself on the ground to implore the compassion of the common Lady of the ages. How deeply she sighed to her, who turns away no one in misery, and with what anguish she groaned, the following event itself bears witness. Then, summoned by her executioner, she asked for punishment after prayer.

The church of Saint Justus stands on a slight slope of the hill and serves as an oratory for the Britons living around it. There the vicedominus’s servants had a hut ready. They bound the woman, wearing only a single undergarment, by her feet and arms to its forked support, using reeds and thorns taken from the nearby vineyard. They packed its hollow interior tightly with a great heap of brushwood and set fire beneath it. When the pile of material had been consumed and reduced to embers and ash, the woman appeared standing unharmed in the midst of it, freed from her bonds.

But the parents of the son-in-law whom she had killed, envious of her safety and attributing her deliverance from the fire to negligence, sacrilegiously rushed back to the branches and brushwood. They rebuilt fires all around her, and, refusing to believe that she had been freed by a miracle—though she could have been suffocated merely by the fumes of the smoke—with savage cruelty beat her with poles thrust through the fire.

This alone seriously injured her amid the otherwise harmless fires; for when all this burning had been beaten down, she remained once again free from danger. The vicedominus, astonished at the sight of so great a novelty, unheard-of in all the persons and regions of our land, immediately recoiled from the barbarity of the peasants. With the heroic severity that was proper, he drove them away from the holy woman and ordered his officials at once to put out the fires and bring her to him.

When she had been presented to him, he examined her all around, seeking to understand the event from its circumstances. He found that not merely her undergarment, but not even the smallest part of her hair or eyelashes had suffered the slightest injury. In this he was especially amazed, since the flames had affected only the bonds.

Taking her with him, the vicedominus himself then hastened to Laon, and entered the city amid a considerably larger crowd, to glory, whereas earlier he had left it for punishment. Although the vicedominus could have taken her to his own home and cared for the wounds inflicted upon her, that blessed woman refused. She said that she would go nowhere else except to the one who had saved her.

She therefore turned her steps back toward the church, and, in the middle of the basilica, fell prostrate before her Lady to give thanks for benefits unheard-of in our time. It cannot be said what tears she poured out there. We shall say nothing of the jubilant cries that breathed forth from the multitude of sobs, since the crowd of onlookers could nowhere restrain itself; to them, an outstanding example was being offered generally concerning the aid given to so great a sinner.

Then, while she lay clothed only in linen and clung to the pavement, the vicedominus covered her with the cloak lifted from his shoulder. After unceasing prayers and thanksgivings, he raised her from the ground and led her home. Since she had been injured by the thrusts of the spears and stained by the ashes of the fires, he soothed her with baths, whatever remedies he could provide, and the softness of bedding. While he thought he was restoring her to health, God, after three days, provided for her eternal salvation; for on the third day she confidently surrendered her spirit into the hands of her savior.

She could indeed have begged to be spared bodily death, but she deserved to be blessed with freedom bestowed upon her soul. From this also the extreme mercy of her blessed heart became clear: although she had shown that woman such compassion in an external danger, after she had experienced her grace she did not wish her to be defiled again by worldly conduct. Instead, the woman whom she had purified, as it were, by burning without injury, she immediately led to the summit of ultimate liberation.

The woman was named Teodeberta [Note: [Col. 0567] Herman, Book III, chapter 27, in the Appendix, calls her Soiburgis.]

## CHAPTER XI

### The miracle of a man who, because he had ordered plowing to be done on the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene, was punished and restored to health

In the territory of Grenoble, a certain man had a stepson by a widow whom he had married. The stepson served his stepfather as a herdsman. When the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene arrived, and the young man had heard from priestly proclamation that he was forbidden to perform fieldwork, he appealed to the reverence owed to the prohibited solemnity against his stepfather, who was ordering him to plow.

His name was Peter. The stepfather’s angry command prevailed. Yoking the oxen to the plow, he proceeded with curses against the work itself and against the animals. When he assailed it with uninterrupted maledictions, his wish was uselessly heard. For, when the elements were stirred by a sudden thunderclap, the oxen and the implements were consumed by lightning, and the man who had demanded that this be done was condemned to a more atrocious punishment because it lasted longer.

The heavenly fire had devoured the dumb animals and the wooden implements; the same fire immediately seized his foot. After quickly consuming it, it passed through his shin and likewise seized the upper part of his leg. Devouring the flesh, while the hardness of the sinews lay hidden beneath wasting fluids, it exposed the bones, and by the ordinary course of the disease scattered them here and there as far as the knee. Moreover, as the flesh of the leg failed, the limb, now hanging painfully from the bare bone as far as the adjoining parts of the buttocks and groin, was subjected to the same sentence.

When, because of his miserable condition and his stench, he began to be a source of misery and shame to his parents, he entrusted himself entirely to divine assistance. He asked to be carried to a certain church dedicated to the name of blessed Mary Magdalene. This was not unreasonable: since the violation of whose feast had been the occasion of his punishment, it was fitting that she might at last become the cause of a remedy for him.

A more fortunate outcome than most had expected accompanied his hope. For the sacred fire, which had now reached the upper parts of his body, was extinguished through the merits of her who deserved to have the fire of desire extinguished by her tears at Jesus’ feet.

Meanwhile, already presuming still greater things from this single experience of compassion, although he was utterly useless in his extremities, he learned that a certain church of the Mother of God, the common Lady, was everywhere renowned for frequent miracles. It also held a memorial of the martyr Hippolytus. When he had obtained permission to be carried there, he entered a boat. As he attempted to board it, the dry bone that protruded was struck against the stern by some misfortune and separated from its joint. When he had taken it and reached the basilica, he hid it in an opening in the church wall.

There he began to address the Queen of the world with frequent entreaties, asking that she not refuse him, utterly powerless as he was, what she bestowed upon those who were stronger. Christmas was near. A soldier who often saw him creeping into the basilica advised him, out of charity, to withdraw into his own house.

After he had stayed there for some time, one day he had drawn himself toward a nearby stream and was washing with water drawn in his hands the blood that was dripping from a small vein of the old wound. A bold woman observed this and said: “You are striving in vain, Peter, because you will never again have either a thigh or a shin.”

Peter received these words with the deepest distress. At that time the soldier’s wife mentioned above was lying in childbirth, and the soldier had moved into another house so that she could manage the matter more privately. During the night, some maidservants went from the chamber into the outer house to do something or other, and they heard Peter groaning with repeated lamentations. The cause of these groans was this:

The Virgin and Mother, blessed above all, had stood in a vision beside his bed with the blessed martyr Hippolytus. She commanded the martyr, as he appeared to the man lying there: “Restore him to his former strength.” The martyr humbly obeyed the command. Gathering together the thigh, shin, and foot, which had formerly been scattered in every direction, and which by divine power were compacted in an instant in the likeness of the future resurrection, he began to attach them to Peter’s body as one attaches a shoot to a tree.

During this joining, Peter was tortured by such anguish that, groaning through clenched teeth, crying out at intervals, and indicating by the repeated opening of his mouth and movements of his limbs what he was suffering, he summoned the maidservants mentioned above, who were moving about the house.

They rushed in. Bringing a torch from the adjoining room, they looked around and found that Peter had two feet and two legs. Such astonishment immediately deprived the women of their senses at this sight that they thought themselves not to be the women who had entered, but to have been changed into others. They touched him and felt that the limbs they had touched were real. Yet they were burning with anxiety over how such an unprecedented thing had happened to them.

At last, when Peter had been awakened only with great difficulty, the women repeatedly asked who had restored what he had lost. He said: “The accursed woman had told me that I would never again have a thigh, shin, or foot.” When he opened his eyes, he still thought that the blessed Virgin was standing with the martyr beside his little bed. When they vanished invisibly, he related the event.

Meanwhile, someone ran to the master of the house and reported this astonishing event to him. He hesitated for a long time, thinking the reports were nonsense; finally overcome by the testimony of those who asserted it, he entered his house, saw the man, and scarcely managed to restrain himself from believing out of sheer astonishment.

The soldier had one brother in the same town. He immediately sent him a message about this extraordinary occurrence. The brother, thinking of the feast held the previous day after the soldier’s wife had given birth, called him drunk; but on the following day, when the townspeople were already rushing there, that brother was able to see the event for himself and believed it.

A further astonishing feature was added to the miracle: this new work of God, unequal to the other in its childish softness and altogether lacking in comparable strength, was found to possess a less fitting majesty. The thigh was separate from the old one, and, because of the roughness and thickness of the other leg, the composition appeared very different. This strongly supported the faith of those who had not known him before. Nor could it in any way equal the old leg in supporting the body. Nevertheless, wherever he went or appeared, the whole matter served the praise of God, since what had been so wondrously established in his flesh was celebrated everywhere.

For a full year the magnificence of the miracle limped along in the man. When that year had passed, she who is blessed above all creatures after the Son and through the Son, together with her Hippolytus, returned on the same night and in the same form in which she had first come. When the most blessed martyr, at her command, began to touch the man’s new creation, whatever that year-old formation lacked—except for the tenderness of the skin and the appearance of newness—was made fully similar to his former limb.

When Peter awoke and perceived the truth of the vision from the improvement of his former condition, he announced the repetition of the heavenly spectacle to everyone by his gestures. He thereby both strengthened belief in the event and proclaimed, before God and before God’s works, that nothing imperfect exists.

### Bishop Leodegarius of Viviers investigates the miracle

Moreover, as news of this extraordinary event spread everywhere, a report reached Leodegarius, the present bishop of Viviers: the same thing had begun in the territory of Grenoble, from which the man originated, but had reached its conclusion in the diocese of Viviers.

The bishop was therefore greatly stirred by the unprecedented rumor. One day, when a large gathering of nobles had come before him to conduct business, the man in whose house the event had taken place also appeared with his own brother. The bishop addressed them as follows:

“Since I know you, among all the men of my diocese, to be truthful and of legitimate conduct, I adjure you, in the presence of these credible persons, to report in the hearing of everyone present whatever you can say most faithfully about that sign which is said to have occurred among you.”

They rose and related everything as it had been reported. After they had finished, the bishop, to remove any doubt among those standing by, demanded an oath confirming the truth. When it had been given, the bishop and the nobles immediately postponed the cases they had intended to discuss and went together to the fortress. There they found Peter in the church, surrounded by a crowd.

The bishop approached Peter. First asking about his misfortune, he heard the causes together with their results. Then, inquiring into the course of the recent recovery, he received the account with his own ears and observed the matter with his own eyes. He investigated again whether Peter could determine by any arguments whether the limbs now attached to him were the same ones he had possessed before or different ones.

Peter replied that he did not know. “I cannot,” he said, “torment myself by examining this way and that because of the novelty of the leg itself. You should investigate instead; and if you find a scar on it, know that it is the very limb I once had.”

They examined it more carefully. Before long they saw the marks of the wound and did not deny that God was wondrous.

When the bishop departed, Peter reflected on what return he should make to God for such great grace bestowed upon him. At last he resolved that, since he had become a spectacle to everyone everywhere in the public world, he would withdraw into seclusion and live for God alone. Since God had done unheard-of things for him, he considered it fitting that he should do something corresponding to God’s munificence.

While he was thus devoting himself to contemplation of God and seeking no human rewards for divine favor, the devil found something to devise against his immunity. He knew perfectly well that this miracle had given everyone the greatest incentive to seek the Mother of God and to hope more and more for her mercies. Therefore he attempted, through some corruption of Peter’s morals, to defile what had been accomplished by God through her. The one whom God had healed with extraordinary compassion, the devil assailed with even more extraordinary persecution.

At an untimely hour of a certain night, as Peter was preparing to lie down, the appearance—or rather, the actual figure—of a naked woman suddenly appeared before him. She shamelessly exposed every part of her body, especially the disgrace of childbirth, and tried by seductive arts to lure him into foul acts. When blandishments achieved little, she attacked the man with terror. When she could accomplish nothing by either method, she also laid hands upon him and attempted to entice him by force. The more vigorously he resisted the outrage, the more rabidly the pest pressed upon him from both sides.

From that night onward, the woman appeared to him every night and, by whatever tricks she could, branded him with shameful license. She wearied him so greatly that in the morning he could scarcely answer those who came to visit him and could scarcely explain what he was suffering.

While many people were becoming doubtful about what Peter reported, the bishop of Viviers mentioned above happened to come to that fortress. That very night, some soldiers, carrying candles out of reverence for the nearby basilica to which Peter’s cell was attached, were keeping vigil in its vestibule.

And behold, from the inner little house where Peter lived, the usual uproar about which the crowd had heard arose. They therefore rushed to the window, looked inside, and saw Peter struggling with the woman. Already growing exhausted, he cried out more forcefully at the sight of them: “For God’s sake, quickly bring me a priestly stole from the church!”

When it had been swiftly brought to him and thrown around him, he wound it around the throat of that diabolical harlot. He twisted her throat with such force that he threw her to the floor and completely suffocated her.

The soldiers reported this to the bishop on the following day. The bishop arrived and marveled at the victory which God had achieved through Peter. He sent his own attendants, who uncovered the roof, lowered a rope, fastened it around the woman’s throat, and pulled out an enormous old woman. They carried her out of the town and condemned her to be burned in fierce fires.

After Peter had suffocated her in the cell, such a stench overwhelmed both him, who had killed her with the sacred weapon, and those standing nearby that no one could doubt that it was the corpse of some exceedingly foul creature which the devil had put on. This opinion was supported not least by the fact that torn and rotten pieces of cloth were found in the little latrine window. Who could think that these were anything other than the pieces which that most impure corpse had around itself as wrappings? Indeed, she had been accustomed to enter through that window.

Finally, some people add—and it is also established by a written account—that, after the devil had been defeated in this way, Peter abandoned his seclusion on the advice of the bishops of Grenoble and Viviers, as though it were a more dangerous condition, and entered a monastic community for the sake of nearby companionship and consolation.

This is less reliably established because the bishop of Viviers, who had himself seen most of these events, is known to have reported them to our most excellent lord, King Louis, in the presence of the venerable Guillelmus, bishop of Châlons, without saying anything of the kind. The bishop of Laon, Lord Bartholomew, very recently heard this from the bishop of Viviers; and when the bishop of Châlons himself told me about it a few days ago, I had mentioned to him, as I had heard from others, that Peter had become a monk. He replied that the bishop of Viviers had said nothing about this.

It is of no concern to me or to anyone else whether Peter is a monk or not, since it is worthwhile to believe that he possesses a good purpose under whatever way of life he follows, he to whom God granted such a triumph after displaying signs in him.

Behold how this blessed woman brings about what is most desperate among human beings. Certainly, if she had accomplished such a thing in some holy man, you would rightly have acclaimed the deed. But in a simple herdsman, ignorant of everything, what will you say except that it was her customary grace? For rarely does she glorify herself by miracles elsewhere than among those who do not know how to ask her, or who are sinners of the utmost degree.

Nor is this unjust. What will she give to the righteous person who obeys her, if she is so compassionate and tender toward one who turns away? Nor does she degenerate in this respect. Her Son came to call not the righteous but sinners (Luke V, 32). In what way, then, will she show herself more truly a mother to the human race than by drawing the offended to herself without their merits?

## CHAPTER XII

### The miracle by which the Blessed Virgin converted an adulteress

[Col. 0573A] There is also another brief event to relate, but magnificent in its example, to which the ears of all sinners ought to be opened. According to the report of the bishop of Arras, there was a woman who was enticingly drawing a certain married man away from his own wife. Although she was driven either by payment or by pleasure and did not refrain from daily adultery, and although the memory even of his wife had nearly disappeared from the mind of the wretched man wrapped in foul love, nevertheless, whenever she went to church, before she uttered any prayer, whenever it happened that she first saw an image of our blessed Lady, she offered the angelic salutation to her with whatever reverence she could:

“Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

The wife of the man, therefore, grieving that adulterous embraces were preferred to her own, burned with the bitterest anger against her rival. Out of fear of her husband she dared do nothing against the woman; but to the extent that she was not even permitted to growl against her publicly, she raged all the more furiously in private.

Thus her entire devotion toward the most blessed Lady was directed toward this: through the power of that Lady, she prayed for heavenly anger against the woman who was defrauding her of her husband, and she could not tolerate the foul rivalries of that little woman going unpunished for long.

When she thought that she had gravely provoked the most merciful feelings of the Queen of Heaven against the adulteress by her continual complaints, the blessed Lady herself graciously appeared to her in a vision and said:

“Why do you seek vengeance from me against that woman? I plainly can do nothing against her, because by her daily devotion she announces to me that joy of mine which I cannot hear from any creature in a more pleasing way. Do you think that I ought to be angered against her on your behalf, when, as though recalling my ineffable glory, she urges me to rejoice in glory?”

From the time of this statement, the woman’s mind had entirely ceased its customary curses. One day it happened that her rival came to meet her; and, as though she had now despaired of divine judgments, she assailed her with insults:

> “O most shameful woman, how many anguishes you inflict upon my soul—you who, by your seductions, tear my flesh away from me, and, by meeting me, thrust your presence upon me, which I hate beyond comparison! How gladly—or rather, how deservedly—I would bring evil upon your evil body, since you never cease to inflict daily pain upon my mind, ears, and eyes! For when neither bed nor table is free from continual rancor, what is more cruel than this hostility which you impose upon me? One sole hope remained: that the Virgin, Mother of God, would hurl against you some avenging sentence. But I have now been wholly deprived of this hope, for she herself told me that the very *Ave* which you hasten to utter to her every day so delights her that she is unable to inflict anything adverse upon you.”

When the other woman heard this, she most carefully questioned her about whether it was true and whether she had really heard such things from the Virgin. When the first woman affirmed it, the other replied:

> “From now on, know that your husband will in no way henceforth lie with me to your injury; and on this matter I pledge him my chastity, since she has granted such great indulgence for so small a service of mine.”

Thus it came about that, from the moment the latter gave herself to chastity, the former abandoned her hostility; and the Blessed One arranged the whole matter for the salvation of them both.

## CHAPTER XIII

Since the devotions of this sinful soul were so generously received, and since the salvation of bodies is also at issue—though in it nothing is sought except the common well-being of souls—let us once more turn our discourse to her praise.

“Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Ps. XLVII, 1). And when he is called great, how can one express how great he is? Let him speak who understands better. To me, God seems greater in nothing than in this: that he deigns to stoop to us in human fashion. For if, as it is said, “He manifests his omnipotence especially by sparing and showing mercy” (*Orat. Dom.* 10 after Pentecost), I too shall say that nothing in God is more exalted than that, having become human, he humbles himself. In this respect, namely, that he is “meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29), he sets himself forth as the one whom we are to imitate; and in this he shows the way in which we are to be magnified in him. Hence the omnipotent Word is said to have come from the royal seats (Wis. XVIII, 15). For he whom neither heaven nor earth can contain—what is more wondrous than that he should be conceived in a girl’s womb? Nor, as it seems to me, is he more omnipotent in any other respect than in this: that the Creator of the creature is contained within the creature. Nor is he more worthy of praise than in that respect in which he became more merciful.

But this is in the city of God, of which it is said: “Glorious things are spoken of you” (Ps. LXXXII, 3), in which the human being was born, although the Most High himself founded it. And what more glorious could be said of it than that it contained within itself the glory of the entire kingdom of heaven? And what is the mountain of the city except the Son of virginity? He is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which filled the whole earth (Dan. II, 34–35).

“This is founded as the joy of the whole earth” (Ps. XLVII, 3), because through the Holy Spirit he is raised up in her as in a mother—he who is the oil of all ecclesial joy. Hence the words:

> “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty” (Ps. XLIV, 4).

He is girded with a sword upon the thigh when, through the Holy Spirit, he is circumscribed by a body formed for himself; and this is upon the thigh because, from his divinity, whatever is outwardly assumed from his mother precedes it. He also does this most mightily—nothing more so, certainly, than in becoming little within the Virgin.

“Mount Sion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. XLVII, 3). If it is the city of God in which God dwells, let us see of what its inhabitant consists. If the mountain signifies divinity, then the sides of the north are consequently called humanity. For every array of spiritual beings strives toward the excellence of divinity, because Sion is interpreted as “contemplation.” The sides of the north are the lack of foresight belonging to the ancient enemy. Whatever is at the side is inferior in advancement: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8). Hence the captured man is also said to have been taken, because by his own impulse he is given over to cowardice.

The mountain, then, and the sides of the north are God, together with the covering of the body by which the blind greed of the robber is deceived. And why not “side,” but “sides”? Because there are two matters in which he was without foresight. First, by the unlawful seizure of the Son of God, he was losing the right over human beings which he had usurped. Second, he was about to undergo everlasting torment before the appointed time.

To this city flow those who rush headlong into the labyrinth of every crime. Here are the foreigners who do violence to the kingdom of heaven and, having become piously violent, seize it (Matt. XI, 12). Here is Tyre, which casts off every weight and the sin that clings closely around it. Hence Tyre is interpreted as “anguish.” Here is “the people of the Ethiopians” (Ps. LXXXVI, 4), blackened, that is, by the soot of sins; whatever is most monstrous among sins plunges itself all the more readily into the safer bosom of this Blessed One, safer than every city.

She herself is the city in which those who do not dwell through affection have lives of no account. She is also “the city of all those who rejoice” (ibid., 7), because whoever from the depths of the heart enters into her most merciful presence is not deprived of joyful hope.

And what are the gates of Sion, which the Lord loves (ibid., 2), except eternal virginity, which the first desire possessed—a humility unmatched in such sublimity, a virtue of faith and obedience transcending all things? What is Sion except her most blessed soul, in which the glory of divine contemplation of the one whom she contained within herself shone forth above all else? Through these gates of outward example our understanding learns how great was the heavenly courtesy that flourished in her inward disposition. Nor can Jacob’s tents reach these gates (ibid.), because whatever is practiced outwardly is perfunctory, and spiritual realities are in no way equal to bodily ones. Especially since “her foundations are in the holy mountains” (ibid., 1): that is, since the fathers Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David—from whom Christ came—preceded this blessed daughter of theirs not so much in ceremonies as in spiritual virtue.

Therefore “the desert and the pathless land rejoice” (Isa. XXXV, 1). And what is more desert-like than Mary, whose mind, like that of an angel, was deprived of every sense of pleasure? What is more pathless than she, who never admitted into her mind even the consent of lawful marriage? Desire may indeed be absent from someone’s mind, while the approach of the marital way nevertheless remains open. Hence it follows: “And the solitude will exult” (ibid.). She who was desert through insensibility to passion, and pathless through contempt for what was lawful, now exults in such great solitude because she stands without the example of those who preceded or followed her. Hence she sings that all generations shall call her blessed (Luke I, 48). For who is so solitary as she who surpasses everything that exists in creation?

“And it will flower like a lily” (Isa. XXXV, 1). The nature of the lily is such that, when its stalk is cut off level with the ground and earth is heaped around it, or water is brought up from below, its crown blossoms as though it remained rooted. The Virgin lacked a root, because in conceiving the Son of God the use of nature entirely failed. When the human mass is therefore cut away, the earth of humility—that is, what is lower and inward—is buried, and at the same time moistened by the Holy Spirit. From there emerges the whiteness of that divine humanity, by whose singular fragrance the whole company of the faithful is nourished. Its leaves spread openly, because the brightness of her virtues turns itself toward our examples. Within, the finest rays of the little branches display a golden color, because all her inward movements reveal the glory of heavenly wisdom.

Thus she who germinated without human seed will, through the same Spirit, germinate the members of her Son—that is, she will be established as the cause of their germination. “It will exult rejoicing” (ibid., 2), since outwardly she expresses not so much joy as the likeness of joy. But she praises when, inwardly, she glorifies God with ineffable sound. Hence “her soul magnifies the Lord, and her spirit rejoices in God” (Luke I, 46–47), which is to sing with the spirit and to sing also with the mind (I Cor. XIV, 15).

“The glory of Lebanon has been given to her” (Isa. XXXV, 2). Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness.” The glory of Lebanon is the heavenly beauty of the kingdom. This is given especially to that Blessed Lady, to whom the King of glory himself is chiefly indebted, as is recognized from the sharing of his own flesh.

And what in heaven does not obey her, when she almost commands her own Creator and that of all things? Good God! How great is the mind within that woman, who, although proportionately, is wholly something divine.

“And on earth the beauty of Carmel and Sharon is given to her” (ibid.). Carmel means “knowledge of circumcision,” and Sharon “prince of sorrow.” By Carmel understand the righteous; by Sharon, penitents. For God speaks peace “over his holy ones and over those who turn their hearts” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9). The knowledge of circumcision is experience of the complete cutting away of vices; this applies to the holy. But the princes of sorrow are those of whom one says: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (I Tim. I, 15). Here sorrow is placed for its effect: sin is sorrow. Those, therefore, are princes of sorrow who do not deny that they are above all sinners.

The whole meaning is this: whatever beauty the innocent and the penitent sinner can possess before God, let them refer the entire origin of their goodness to the grace of so great a Mother; for unless she had given birth in this way, neither the righteous nor the penitent would in any way have shone in this manner.

“These shall see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. XXXV, 2), because they shall eternally embrace in vision her in whose womb-chamber he gloried in his marriage, when they behold the fruit of her Christ and of those whom he redeemed. They shall also see “the beauty of our God” (ibid.), namely, that flesh already glorified, to which, by God’s favor, we shall be worthy to be conformed.

## CHAPTER XIV

### An Apostrophe to the Blessed Virgin

For a while, Blessed above all women, we delighted in your praises; at last, though sinners beyond measure, we turn our thoughts and words toward you. We cannot satisfy our desire to praise you and embrace you, yet from the depths of our being we ask you to make us capable of this. The storms of carnality beat us back; yet the sweetnesses we have always experienced in you summon us to dispel them. To be filled with these, to drink them in with the most eager hearts, is better than life itself. And who lives except one who feels you with affection? Who, unless mad, would not desire to die if by dying he could purchase the sight of you?

Is it not the consummation of our glory if we can have you as mediatrix between ourselves and your Son? It is your duty, Lady, to remember us; for this you were made, for this you were chosen: to plead our cause most mercifully before your sweetest Son.

Plant in our hearts and mouths an unceasing remembrance of your name. To whomever you grant this, I say confidently, that person is already beginning to taste heavenly glory. For what is sweeter than you, what safer than remembrance of you? For you have it at hand not merely to pray, but everywhere to command.

Command, therefore, that in our present misery you become inwardly present to us, and misery will no longer exist. Make it so that whatever we are, we may be from you; and when you have made us yours, let nothing remain of us except what belongs to you.

### A Rhythm to the Blessed Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist

Bearing entrails full of hardships and sorrows,  
from the detestable pit of my sins,  
whose harms I suffer, wretchedly, whether I will or not,  
I invoke you as savior, Lady of purity.

I turn to the remembrance of your deeds.  
I reckon you my singular hope, you my salvation.  
Do not disdain or despise me when I call upon you, Mother.  
Though I am unworthy, do for me what you would for a son,

O Blessed One, more precious than the price of the whole world!

You were foretold by God’s voice at the world’s beginning;  
Your childbearing is proclaimed by the entire assembly of prophets;  
You alone are the portion desired by the Christian people.

Virgin, rich in piety in former days,  
In these days give no lesser signs of mercy.  
For if you are silent, O wondrous one, what hope of pardon will there be?  
How cruelly will miseries crush us when we are rejected!

My offenses are grave; appease God, Lady,  
If the Egyptian prostitute once found you merciful,  
And the man who had denied you and your Son,  
Why will you defraud of pardon one who seeks you with his whole heart?

It has never been your custom to despise the wretched,  
But often you have been accustomed to visit them unasked.  
How much more, then, ought you to be present when requested,  
You who are called upon by the deep wound of my mind [variant: “inmost being”],  
Full of God, and wholly full of the inmost feelings of the devout,  
Beyond all that human speech can accomplish.

Now the splendors of your gifts shine forth.  
Adorn my character, caring for whatever is deadly in me.  
There has never been, nor is there now, anyone equal or similar to you.  
For you surpass the whole of creation in nobility.

Before God your voice is so effective in obtaining what it asks  
That none is so well suited to reach the ears of the King of kings.

Look upon us, then, with maternal inward feeling,  
And commend our sighs to your Son, who is yours;  
Moderate the flow of the flesh and its wandering desires;  
Always refresh this breast with the dew of chastity;  
Bury whatever evil you abhor in us;  
Gather together fitting conduct, a quiet heart, and all that is holy.  
Driving away its poison and deceits, resist Satan.  
Do not allow us to yield to his enticements.

For if you alone rise in the assembly of heaven,  
About to entreat the merciful Father with your most sweet Son,  
The united assembly of the saints will immediately cry out to you,  
And whatever is requested will lie beneath your authority.

And you, John, who, conscious of such great chastity,  
By Christ’s gift became the son of so great a Mother,  
Hear, I pray, my vows together with hers, with attentive ears,  
And turn me away from every evil deed.

You, who were wonderfully dear to the Lord while dwelling on earth,  
Were made worthy of so fortunate a privilege.  
Speak before him for the remedy of your people,  
Breaking the kingdoms of death, and subject us to his rule.

The nearer you are to the Word whom you proclaimed,  
The more earnestly provide your intervention.

May your holy prayers benefit this wretched man who bewails himself.  
Pray always for one conscious of the sins of many.  
We greatly need the gift of your generosity.  
Why delay saying what may release offenses against God?  
For whatever you ask, you will easily obtain.

Therefore, at last entreated, look upon the unhappy.  
Grant the enduring chastity of the body which you loved,  
And free us from all adversities that trouble us.  
Increase understanding, strengthen peace, remove whatever harms.  
Restrain me from future wrongdoing and wash away past deeds.

O Queen, now invoked by this present song,  
And you, Apostle, its powerful guardian and minister,  
Act before him who approved you above all others,  
That he may deign to raise our minds to himself.

You are surely mindful of the suffering Christ,  
Beside whose cross you stood in grief.  
By the sorrow of that holy death, therefore, I ask you both  
To obtain for us the grace of merciful Jesus.

O Mary, although I name you with a polluted mouth,  
Hear me nevertheless, and grant respite from my sins.  
Grant also, in this life, continual remembrance of you.  
Grant, wholly sweet Mary, glory in the life to come.

O John, greatly worthy to be called the grace of God,  
Free us and all who seek you from dangers.  
Though the body is afflicted, drive harmful things from the mind,  
And let it be proved by its effect that grace is in you.

Grant, Mary, purity of soul to your servants.  
Grant, John, victory over the troubles of adversity.  
Lead us both back to the path of virtue,  
That we may be found worthy to be joined to heavenly glory.

## END

[Col. 0579]

# A SHORT WORK ON VIRGINITY

## Dedication Letter of the Venerable Abbot Guibert for the Short Work on Virginity

[Col. 0579A] 311

### How humbly the author thinks of himself

Although we both believe—and wish others to believe—that we are almost entirely devoid of this outstanding virtue, if it is impossible even to conceive, much less to explain, the height of its glory in full, nevertheless we know of nothing that should be denied to your affection, even if you demand of us what exceeds our strength. Especially since you ask us to encourage you by our prayer toward the pursuit of purity, we judge that it would be impious not to obey your petition, although it is clear that we shall speak about this matter awkwardly and unworthily.

We have indeed touched, however faintly, upon knowledge of the divine Scripture.
