Having learned its commands by word but, I confess, not by practice, we have learned them chiefly to our own condemnation if we delay distributing them—not, I do not say, to those who reject them, but to those who devoutly ask for them. Therefore, if concern for salvation or reward does not summon us, at least, despairing in every way and as though certainly destined for punishment, let us gain this one thing amid all that punishment: that, when we are punished for other evil deeds, our hellish pain may not be increased by the inertia of blessing others. For it is not without remedy if, amid deaths, we redeem ourselves from even a single blow.

We therefore propose humbly to obey you, although to others it might seem presumptuous. Yet you—or anyone else—must not reproach us when we are found lacking the very virtue about which we wish to write, since we have done the same thing under compulsion. Certainly, if we had undertaken this of our own accord, simply and not as though with the authority of a teacher, our spontaneous good deed ought not to have been attributed to arrogance or rashness, but received with gratitude.

[Col. 0580A]

There is also another reason, not at all empty. If anyone seems unfit to proclaim sacred doctrines and has resolved to remain silent because of the accusation raised by an evil conscience, he appears to me excessively timid. He must change this useless attitude and, even if he cannot correct the fault completely, act nevertheless for the sake of the person whom he represents. Let him not bury his talent in the earth; even if he does not perform the office of teacher or preacher, let him cry out lest others perish with him by pursuing the worst things—or let him do so at least as one who wishes to fortify them.

### A learned man, although subject to sins, ought by his words to urge others toward better conduct

For example, suppose the son of some rich man, after consuming his father’s money and squandering the estates left to him, plunged entirely into gluttony and, reduced to poverty, became an infamous example of how to live. If such a man, repentant of his error but unable to return to his former condition, warned some wealthy person not to squander his riches through excessive extravagance, saying, “Take care that, by devoting yourself to your belly or to useless generosity, you do not sink so far as to become like me,” who would consider him ridiculous?

Certainly he should be heard differently from the man whom the Terentian character Parmeno is read to have mocked:

> “A clever fellow, by Hercules,” he said, “who turns utterly foolish men into madmen” (Ter. *Eunuchus* II, 2, 23).

The former, by boasting of the fortunes lost through his gluttony, provokes his unfortunate listener; the latter would teach him cautiously to avoid imitating himself, lest he rush into disaster.

But because you know us, and because, knowing what we are, you wish to be admonished by such men, we have cast off our shame and sing to your ears—not with the voice we ought to have, but with the voice we can.

# A SHORT WORK ON VIRGINITY

[Col. 0579]

## PREFATORY NOTE

[Col. 0579C]

### The author was more pleased with poetry than was proper

I completed this work when I was still in very tender adolescence. For since I devoted myself more than was proper to the art of meter, which is usually the companion of swelling language and wantonness, one of my companions, a man devoted to literary studies without envy, who at his own request had drawn several little poems from me, urged me also to say something about virginity. As I approached this task—unusual as it was—with trepidation, I shrank from it in two ways: my mind, devoted to the sport of verse, had scarcely attained the serious gravity of prose; and the subject proposed for treatment was difficult even for the understanding of old men.

Let the curious reader therefore judge how I have explained it, attributing to God whatever I have understood well, and to my youth whatever I have understood otherwise than I should.

## CHAPTER I

### How excellent and arduous virginity is. The pleasure-loving cannot understand how it can be maintained

What wonder is it if that blessed name of integrity possesses such glorious praises among human virtues, since human beings, still clothed in their own ashes and groaning beneath the burden of this corpse-like body, strive to follow their Creator by an imitation sufficiently arduous and almost exceeding their strength?

It is indeed arduous—and no small matter—when we see those who ought already to have grown weary through long experience of the flesh not merely unable to resist such an appetite, but unwilling to do so, so that they even marvel at those who abstain from this matter and can restrain themselves. This evil is often found more fiercely and more uncontrollably—shamefully—in those whom old age exhausts, whose heads have grown white through a most wretched longevity.

### Whoever preserves virginity imitates God

As I have said, the virgin follows God by an imitation almost exceeding human strength, since, against the goad of natural heat and the sharp points of innate stimulation, she continually struggles not against another but against herself—something more difficult.

In overcoming any external matter, clever intelligence, the strength of weapons, engines, and the hardships of sieges often prevail. Meanwhile, many accomplish through verbal deceit what they cannot accomplish through battles. But none of these things helps in inward struggles. Each person has himself within himself—or rather carries himself within himself—for no one is anything other than what he is; nor can he be divided into two so that one part may oppose the other.

A person can scarcely overcome himself to such an extent that he would more readily believe his members could be cut apart from himself than that he should refuse to do what nature itself has chiefly taught him to will and desire.

When, therefore, the mind voluntarily longs for something—here I speak of the desires that affect us by origin—and the love of the entire body immediately attends the mind’s will; when the veins burn, when the strength of the heart grows weak, when the inward fire loosens the weary viscera, when flesh and spirit rush together in miserable union, I ask: in that one man, overwhelmed by so many blows, what part remains that can bring a remedy from elsewhere? From where will he draw even the smallest drop with which to suppress the mind’s fire, when he is wholly flame?

It is certainly astonishing that one element within a person can rise against himself in a war of his own will, so that he commands himself not to do what he has especially failed to resist desiring.

The living wisdom of the ancients, exercised by such conflicts, searched out what ought to distinguish human beings from beasts. It prudently discovered that body and spirit must not be one thing in us, so that the spirit accomplishes nothing except what serves the body’s use, as is plainly evident in the life of animals. It taught us that neither should alternately subdue or prefer the other, but that the governance of the whole mortal body should remain permanently with the spirit; and that, divided against himself, a human being should recognize the perpetual hostility of these two while he lives.

But, with God’s help, it will be possible to treat these matters more fully elsewhere. Let us return to the beginnings of the earlier statement that we introduced.

## CHAPTER II

### Virtues possess something resembling God

Since “every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17), every prudent mind ought to consider how each of the virtues that we receive from this source always possesses something resembling its giver.

If our God, as it is written, is “a consuming fire” (Heb. XII, 29), I do not think it inelegant to say that these little fires, like rays of that eternal sun, draw us toward the one from whom they are infused. Consideration of this matter plainly declares both that the goods within us ought to be believed to proceed from him and that no good ought to be believed to be good if it presses our thoughts downward toward what is low and earthly, even under the appearance of piety.

For if this material flame always indicates the quality of its nature in such a way that it continually strives upward, how much more ought portions of that incorruptible fire—that is, the virtues implanted in us by God—to imitate him and fly toward him?

These are the likeness of God according to which humanity is read to have been made in Genesis (Gen. I, 26). This is the light of his countenance marked upon us (Ps. VII, 4). Hence the poetic line:

> “He gave the human being an uplifted face  
> and commanded him to look upon heaven,  
> raising his countenance toward the stars”  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*).

Thus, as one destined to inhabit that region, he might frequently direct toward it the gaze of joyful hope.

All virtues, then, since—as we began to say—they indicate something resembling their giver, possess this quality. The integrity of which we are speaking preserves the mind of its human being and purifies the body completely; through a kind of twofold office it strives after the likeness of its Creator. And, as I think, it does so more especially than the others.

Most of the other virtues belong so entirely to the mind that, if they are fully possessed in the soul, then even though diverse and often wholly contrary manifestations appear outwardly, the mind nevertheless retains the stronghold of its goodness without any loss through deprivation.

For example, someone prays while working and, with his mouth closed and lips unmoving, while his limbs are engaged in every kind of bodily labor, prays to God through meditation alone. Another chastises his son for a crime he has committed. Some superior gnashes his teeth fiercely at his subjects and, as it is thought, more harshly than is just; yet neither exceeds the balance of discretion, if he knows how to strike down crimes rather than satisfy anger.

### Vigilance must be constant if chastity is to be preserved

This integrity, with the greatest vigilance, devotes itself to cleansing the heart. It watches over the members of the whole body as though they were officials placed in charge of their own household, lest through their negligence or lust any diminution occur in the inward substance.

Although the mind often promises to remain at peace and professes that it wishes nothing except chastity and peace, it nevertheless does not permit the members to relax in any security of their own. It strives to imitate even amid the frequent insults of the flesh the serenity of the citizens of heaven, as though concealing the noise of its thoughts; indeed, it strives to imitate that highest bosom of eternal peace into which no admixture of inconvenience enters.

In that peace integrity exists essentially, properly, and not comparatively but naturally. To him who exists through himself, from himself, and in himself, nothing of those things made through something or from something necessarily happens; nor is the Creator upheld by any assistance. Outside him no created thing is contained at all.

A truly happy rival, admitting nothing foreign into itself and fleeing whatever corrupts it, pursues impassibility of spirit and flesh. Happy—indeed, a thousand times happy—is the audacity which, not content with being made like the glory of the heavenly spirits, even envies excessively the blessed tranquility of the Creator himself, wondrous though that may be to say—not hoping to acquire the same nature that God possesses, but hoping to enjoy that rest and peace by which the saints are deified through adoption as God’s children.

This is the “strength of the ass,” placed in the blessing of Issachar (Gen. XLIX, 14), not because of irrationality but because of gentleness and endurance. Seeing the rest from the battle of carnal tumults, and that it was good, and seeing the earth—that is, the body in which he now dwells as an exile—which will be given into the possession of the meek because it is good, he set his shoulder to bearing the burden of the day and the heat. He was held in contempt, as though the luxury of the world were a burdensome annoyance.

These are the first conceptions of this holy virtue: just as its author is recognized as free from every movement and superfluous thought by essential power, so integrity should make each person devoted to it, insofar as a human being placed in corruption can become so, immune from every disordered impulse. In this respect, then, I would call it like God.

## CHAPTER III

### The temporal generation of the Son of God

To this especially notable argument another, not altogether to be rejected, may be added: namely, that the indisputable birth of the coeternal Son from the Father’s eternity was not accomplished from an external substance brought in to cooperate with that birth, nor through the office of our human generations or marital unions, nor through corruptible seed. Rather, from that inscrutable sanctuary and treasure of the Father there proceeded not something other than, or different from, what he himself is, nor a mere image, but his own Wisdom and Power, without which he did not exist even for a moment.

This occurred according to a mode of generation appropriate to him, so that he might surpass in purity the glories of all that he purifies, and so that the Son might proceed from himself, namely as a life-giving fire that warms all things, as radiance proceeds from its source.

By such arguments Christian vigor is instructed to strengthen continence. Yielding the enjoyment of temporal pleasure to others, it weakens everything of worldly love that steals into it and, resolving to wither in perpetual sterility, fruitless for the world, becomes spiritually fruitful for God, excelling in joyful hope more pleasing than every flower through the reward of unblemished chastity.

Since, therefore, Scripture’s testimony shows that it accepts God as a kind of fire from which nothing except what is spiritual is certainly generated, it is not absurd for the virgin to compare herself to him. While she voluntarily deprives herself of the offspring of flesh that will perish, she becomes all the more diligent in giving birth, through the proofs of faith, to as many as she can for God; and she pours forth not seed destined to die and bring sorrow, but seed destined to live eternally and bring joy.

It is a wicked thing if any Christian resists so blessed a manner of life, excuses it as excessively arduous, or contends that it need not be preserved, when it is clear from the evident example of pagan literature that it was observed among the ancients.

They wished Vesta to be a goddess, whom they also called the Great Mother and about whom they invented countless other stories. Because she was a virgin, they added virginity to the miracles of her power and attributed to her the divinity of fire. For fire generates nothing; neither does a virgin. Thus, when they established virgins to serve in her shrine, they opposed their wantonness with such severity of discipline that they enacted laws stating that a Vestal virgin accused and convicted of sexual misconduct was to be buried alive with the man who had violated her. The Romans devoted great care to investigating this matter most attentively and leaving it unpunished.

If, then, in those times even something as worthless as glass was preserved with such care lest it be broken—although it had no particular brilliance and, while intact, was not worth even two worthless coins—what protection ought that pearl, more precious than every topaz, to receive, especially among us, who so often read of its rewards in our hearing?

Let virtue therefore have a place in the Christian breast, since Christ invites those whom he promises the kingdom and glory. If it flourished among pagans, when it compelled miserable groups by punishment alone, without any reward in either life, then let whoever has until now lacked marital companionship embrace his solitude. Made wiser by the troubles—or rather the miseries—of married people, let him never, I pray, begrudge his own peace, or rather his blessedness.

The Apostle clearly knew this when he cried out that such people would have tribulation (I Cor. VII, 28), but he did not conceal how good it would be for them to remain as he himself remained (ibid., 7). O how many wings of eagerness—by which he might enter heaven—does the man cut away from himself who plunges into such a burdensome exchange!

## CHAPTER IV

### The reason by which virginity is commended

That mystery which had been purposed from the ages—the incorporation of the Word—was accomplished from no other source than the sacred womb of the precious Virgin. Every faithful mind rejoices in the joyful fruit of its salvation, and this awakens, with complete justice, the affection of every devout person toward love of this virtue.

For whoever, placed in uncertainty about preserving virginity, observes the most exalted dignity of such a birth—who, whether man or woman, would not immediately aspire to follow the footsteps of so great a Mother?

If we could sufficiently contemplate this miracle, we would have abundant reason to marvel that God values the good of human continence so highly. For, compared with his purity, all our cleanliness is judged by the prophet to be “like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV, 6); and those things that we generally think will please him least—or, indeed, what must be considered as nothing without punishment (Luke XVII, 10)—although among us they are nothing or worthless, he nevertheless deigns to accept so greatly.

Since divinity could have brought itself forth in many other ways, and from elsewhere, in a manner far nobler and more exalted than feminine virginity, although she was a virgin, nevertheless, because she was a woman, the dignity of her womb adds nothing to God, who was coming to make known to mortals the glory of every virtue.

He praised this singular condition, lest marriage seem to defile it, but he did not establish it as a command. He showed how worthy of reverence and wonder it should be considered by, so to speak, the mere indication of his choice.

He therefore chose the body of a Virgin for his own body, silently suggesting to us what seems to be openly expressed in these words:

> “Although, because of your weakness—or rather lest you think marriage an evil—I hesitate to command you to pursue virginity, nevertheless, through the evident signs of my conception and life, I indicate what you ought chiefly to desire. I came to you through an intact woman; I lived among you in complete integrity; and among those whom I had gathered into the school of my teaching, although I loved all especially, I admitted more familiarly to my affection the one who had been a virgin. You ought therefore to weigh more clearly than other things how highly I regard the merits of their sincerity, since you see that I honor them with more exceptional privileges.”

These examples of virginity could be sufficient.

## CHAPTER V
## God Chose Pure, Bodiless Angels as His Ministers. Angels Surpass Human Beings in Dignity; the Blessed Virgin Far Surpasses the Angels

I think it worthwhile not to pass over another point: that One who is singularly pure—indeed, who is both above and beyond the world, and whom nothing can in any way trouble with corruption or vice while He governs corruptible things—chose no others for more familiar service than creatures of incorporeal substance. Just as an eternal will to obey God, which has already rendered them immutable, and the excellence of their nature make them perfectly free from everything unbecoming, so their glorious order has adhered more closely to their Author than that of other creatures. How great their number is, and how eminent their dignity, can be chiefly judged from the fact that it is known with certain authority that no human being can attain such a degree of holiness as to surpass the least of the angels in the measure of glory. Yet she is excepted who brought forth from herself the Lord of glory—the Virgin, to whom we have learned, by ancient and well-attested testimony, that nothing heavenly is not subjected through her Son.

[Col. 0585C] We must therefore examine with every acuity of mind the fact that, when God established ministers for Himself, He then prescribed, for the human race still to come—whose future sinfulness He knew—a kind of silent rule in His angels: that when human beings observed the court of their King and its several officials, and admired in His chamberlains, cupbearers, and, so to speak, more intimate attendants a singular radiance of purity, they should infer that they could in no way be admitted into the fellowship of His palace unless they first took the greatest pains to become participants in that same brightness and chastity which the angels naturally possess. He did not create them burdened with the weight of flesh, so that they would have to wrestle against flesh and blood and, after prolonged violence and a very great struggle, finally reach, like us, a state beyond suffering. Rather, creating them without sex and without external or internal affliction, He set them before us as an image of the perfection whose conformity we should strive toward with unceasing diligence, as far as our dust permits.

Yet this family of the divine King, of such great beauty and dignity, to which nothing after its Creator can be compared, is subject to the virginity of her who is blessed among women and who bore her God. And she herself is truly exalted because she is humble: while she adores the dispensation of her Creator, she consequently honors the minister of that same dispensation. Gladly she subjects herself to the one through whose service she recognizes with joy that the losses of her own order are repaired by the increase of the human race. It is wondrous, indeed, but full of truth, that the Virgin should rule over the angels.

But I know that someone may object that it is not to the Virgin, but to the Mother of the Lord, that the angels are subject, and that I am trying to exalt the matter excessively. Granted; nevertheless, it is certain that if they are subject to the Mother of the Lord, and the Mother of the Lord cannot be other than a virgin, then they are plainly proved to be subject to a virgin. The privilege is indeed to be ascribed to her power as Mother, but in such a way that virginity is likewise acknowledged to be honored. For her praise and integrity—namely, her purity—might be sufficiently established by the fact that God was born from one undefiled. But why should we seek so anxiously to have the great honor her due bestowed upon her by eminent persons, when the King Himself, by His own act, so lavishly honors her with gifts that the affection which He showed to the blessed Apostle who reclined upon His breast at supper could suffice the Mother for the glory of all? We are reluctant to add the other marvels, which almost exceed the limits of happiness. We leave them to the discerning reader to weigh; and if he fully considers them, there will be no need to inquire about John’s honor: a virgin succeeded the Son of the Virgin under such a succession of adoptive motherhood. There can therefore be no doubt that the angelic majesty venerates the entire order of virgins above all others, since nothing among the saints of any virtue is considered nobler or more like itself.

## Why Paul Occupies the Right-Hand Place and Peter the Left-Hand Place in Paintings

[Col. 0586C] We may also add, in excess of what is necessary for this praise, what is reported about certain ancient paintings in Rome: the image of the Savior is said to have Paul painted on its right and the Apostle Peter, in what is considered an inverted arrangement, on its left. When I asked prudent men what significance that apparently disordered order might have, I was told that Paul was on the right because he had been a virgin, and Peter on the left because he had been married. No one hesitates about Peter, whose mother-in-law we know from the Gospel, and whose daughter Petronilla we know from the Acts. But Paul may cause considerable scruple for some people. Yet if we wish to consult his own words on his behalf, I confess that we find something quite clear. When he was giving advice to those who were marrying and taking wives, he concluded by saying that it would be better for them to remain as he himself was (I Cor. VII, 40). From this, the opinion is not considered entirely idle. For since he testifies that, before Christianity, he had served his ancestral God without reproach (Phil. III, 6), and recalls that he had surpassed his contemporaries in zeal for the divine law and his ancestral traditions (Gal. I, 14)—and this during his youth, at which time he was also called to the faith—it will be thought unreasonable that, once a Christian, he should have subsequently abandoned what he had observed as a Jew.

[Col. 0587A] The judgment, therefore, which took shape in so famous a city and in so important a place within that city—namely, the Church of the Blessed Peter—under the wisdom of so many pontiffs must be accepted by us as certain. When Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Ecclesiastical History, discussed the Apostle’s statement concerning the authority to lead about a believing sister as a wife (I Cor. IX, 5), he most absurdly called the sister Paul’s wife. We refute this just as we refute what he wrote concerning the letter of the Lord to Abgar. Thus, then, Paul is not without reason placed before Peter in that very basilica.

# CHAPTER VI

## Chastity after Marriage or a Fall Must Be Held in Great Esteem

[Col. 0587B] It must be understood, amid these praises of virginity, that continence either after marriage or after a fall should likewise be exalted with great praises. It is rewarded with rewards as great as the fiercer fires of experienced pleasures by which it is assailed. For the heavier the battle of the one who struggles, the more welcome is the increase of glory that follows, although no one can come to the triumph of the immaculate by any exertions.

I think these two orders can be understood as represented figuratively by the types of those two leaders, Moses and Joshua, whom no one in former times doubted were placed over the Hebrews. Let us therefore believe that Moses, whom we know to have had two wives, signifies the life of those who have experienced the sins of the flesh. Fleeing from Egypt with the army of the children of Israel, he crossed the Red Sea, whose waters stood on either side (Exod. XIV, 22). This means that when someone, placed in the sorrow and darkness of the world, blushes at the foulness of his conduct and abandons that same world, he leads with him, as it were, a people of God: all the thoughts by which he shapes himself toward the vision of God. He leads them through the Red Sea—that is, through bitterness and the abundance of tears by which he cries out that his sins be forgiven, saying: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God” (Ps. L, 16). He has its waves like walls on his right and left, because whether he is tempted or enjoys rest of mind, in prosperity and adversity alike, he never ceases to fortify himself with sighs and prayers, without any relaxation.

[Col. 0587C] When these waters have overwhelmed the Egyptians—that is, the crimes of his former life—he reaches the solitude of the desert, namely, a certain serenity of heart, where, removed from worldly urbanity, he may live more freely for God and for himself. There, occupied in battle with himself alone, he often suffers the importunities of his thoughts—like the complaints of an unruly crowd—to such a degree that, unless he frequently returned to the Lord’s oracle, that is, to prayer, he would in no way be able to endure the force of temptation. There the calf of pride, made secretly by him himself, is erected, but is immediately broken up and consumed by its own makers. There Beelphegor—that is, Priapus, the leader of secret lust—is admitted by a shameless crowd, though soon to be driven out; and even the victories, whenever they are celebrated, are generally achieved not without loss and with some difficulty.

[Col. 0587D] For God knows that it is often advantageous for those who, after their sins, turn back to Him and reach some height of perfection to be frequently oppressed by adversities. Just as the poor who suddenly become rich by whatever means easily grow proud, so such people, unless they are constantly worn down by punishments, raise their necks, forgetting their former error. Hence they possess only a rare and short-lived power of contemplation. Even when it is granted to them from time to time, this is believed to happen so that, when they have touched something heavenly in mind for an hour, yet are unable to return to the same state after losing it whenever they wish, they may blame their sin for their diminished ability to see heavenly things. This is suggested by the fact that Moses is commanded to climb the mountain so that he may contemplate the promised land, yet is not permitted to dwell there. For “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). But although all burn with desire for that place in their minds, not all dwell there equally through the gift of contemplation.

## Joshua Represents Those Who Have Preserved the Whiteness of Baptism

[Col. 0588A] Joshua, who remained in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the service of the divine army—and, under a kind of virginal reverence, always adhered undividedly to the Mosaic discipline, remaining unmarried and bound to no marriage, seems to me to bear the likeness of those who possess integrity of body and mind. He circumcises the people a second time—thereby showing that those who have stained their baptism with some blemish must cleanse their conscience through confession—and receives command over Israel at the entrance to the Jordan. This means that such people, who have conceived divine love from the beginning of their lives, when they reach their descent—that is what “Jordan” signifies—namely, the humbling of their thoughts, not through fear of punishment but through desire for the kingdom, immediately submit the movements of mind and the impulses of the body to the command of the spirit, like the light-minded tumult of a crowd.

[Col. 0588B] Through the waters of the Jordan, I think, there is plainly meant that wholly appropriate compunction which is not embittered, like the sea, by the memory of a crime committed, but which confidence in attaining eternal joy makes more pleasing than any food or drink. In accordance with the etymology of its name, it bewails the prolonged delay of its descent into the valley of this life; yet, through hope of receiving its fruit, it often triumphs with the greatest joy.

[Col. 0588C] While this Joshua explores the depths of the blessed river, he finds twelve precious stones there. For he learns that the Decalogue of the Law—or rather, all the commandments of Scripture, which are marked by the number ten because of their perfection—are fulfilled by the two commandments of love. For when anyone’s mind is repeatedly pierced by such sincere compunction, you will find nothing in which one learns so much about God.

[Col. 0588D] Finally, purified by these waters, he enters the promised land, because, established in the ether of contemplation, he moves about like a noble eagle in singular expansiveness. Such a person is not only raised by himself to so great a height, but through him the same grace is imparted to others, when, by powerful teaching, he often stretches out the thread of speech according to the capacity of each hearer, explaining what the unfailing goods of the heavenly kingdom are. Yet although he does not disdain to adapt himself to the mediocrity of all, he chooses and assigns to himself, like Joshua of old, lofty and mountainous things, in keeping with the excellence of his way of life.

[Col. 0589A] If the dangers of attack arise, they immediately reach a blessed triumph with as much eagerness as no flame of virginity kindled by the experience of pleasure could arouse. Although the battles are frequent, losses there are altogether rare; there is no memory of murmuring, nor any oft-repeated tale of returning to Egypt, as occurred under Moses. The battles, I say, are indeed constant, but they are no longer against the fires of the flesh; they are against the spiritual wickedness of the rulers of this air, which inflicts attacks from outside. I have said these things not by comparing the two men in order to prefer one to the other, but to append to my work something typologically drawn from the deeds of the ancients.

# CHAPTER VII

## How the First Parents Would Have Devoted Themselves to Procreation Had They Not Sinned

[Col. 0589B] Amid these considerations, the question of the created human being comes very suitably to mind: if he had persevered in paradise, what sort of life would he have had—or rather, what sort of propagation would have proceeded from the wife given to him—if he is believed to have been created without sin? If he had obeyed God and had not sinned, he would have lived perpetually without the loss of all the good of his origin, which suffers no damage except through sin, and he would have enjoyed the joyful delight of that place. It would certainly also be established that he would have generated children without sin, if we dare say that such an act could have been performed in such a place and by such persons.

But if it is said that they would not have generated children in that place, whatever sort of place it might have been, and if it is asserted that such intercourse—which is now considered entirely unclean—could not have been practiced by people so pure, it will seem absurd to say that God created two human beings so that two alone might rule the whole earth, and that He uselessly said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen. I, 28).

## Even If They Had Procreated, They Would Nevertheless Have Remained Virgins

[Col. 0589C] But since it is extraordinarily absurd to think this, let us consider what manner of generation could have taken place without guilt. It requires no argument to say that a human being, if created without the contagion of sin, was without sin. If he was without every evil, then he was also entirely without the stimulus of the flesh, which is evil. If he was without carnal movement, then undoubtedly, had he obeyed God’s word, he would have remained eternally a virgin—and yet something much more than a virgin. For among virgins, pleasure is extinguished only through great exertion. In him there was neither anything that would tempt him nor anything that would need to resist the tempter. But this would have been something new and uniquely wondrous: Adam, a virgin, generating children; Eve, a virgin, giving birth.

[Col. 0589D] Hence that age would have been blessed and happier than any happiness human beings can now possess—if only it had existed. For, as it were, it did not exist: as soon as it began to exist at its very origin, it ceased to exist. It is certain that those members which perform the functions of generation are not ordinarily moved without an evil heat, and that the movements which we now experience as natural cannot occur without sin. All of this would then have been so alien to us that, just as a foot or hand or any other limb is often moved innocently within us, so the entire process would have drawn neither the mind nor the flesh of those performing it away from any good affection. And just as no passion would have ruled in either party during generation, so in childbirth the emission would have caused no pain.

## The Origin of Original Sin

[Col. 0590A] After the original state had fallen through disobedience, that ancient sin passed from the parents to those who are born through the pleasure of intercourse, so that wretched humanity might always weigh the immensity of the ancient loss through its new and daily corruptions, and discern the inward baseness of the soul from the body’s so sordid generation. At least belatedly, therefore, let a person fear voluntarily plunging himself into evils, even those he considers slight, since a very large structure can often be burned by a spark of very small size if it is badly tended.

[Col. 0590B] For this reason David, not unaware of the corruption of his origin, laments that he was conceived in iniquities (Ps. L, 7). He asks to be sprinkled with that hyssop which, shaping us according to its humility and cleansing the swelling of pride from our lungs, teaches us to think soundly; and he testifies that, washed in baptism, he was immediately made whiter than snow with glorious confidence (ibid., 9). To this the intention of this noble virtue responds: it reaches back to the beginning of humanity’s first creation. While it laudably strives after things greater than itself, things which it cannot fully attain in the present, it deserves to possess something singular among the glories of the other virtues. For while it eagerly pursues what it remembers having lost in its ancestors, it finds more effectively what no one who seeks differently can attain in the same way.

[Col. 0590C] Those who have adhered to this purpose also contemplate the fact that, in that part of the human being upon which the image of God was properly impressed, a certain integrity and angelic sincerity remains. Although the body, which is corrupted, weighs it down (Wis. IX, 15), and an earthly dwelling depresses it, there is nevertheless nothing that can tempt it when freed from the body or bend it further toward the vices of the flesh. Having been made wholly suited to the fellowship of angels, it flies in the greatest purity to its Creator. Since the Godhead made it eternal and incorporeal, I have not called it improperly marked with His own likeness.

[Col. 0590D] Every mind devoted to purity therefore turns the power of its reason toward the nature of the soul. When it recognizes that an exemplar has been set before it within itself, and observes that it consists of two elements—one lowly and dependent upon corruptible things, the other spiritual and required to strive toward eternal things—it devotes itself entirely to the better part. It wisely transfers the rule of its whole being to that part to which the glory of incorruptibility more properly belongs, which no frailty of bodily flux can besiege.

For unless the soul slipped through the softness of the flesh, and were always permitted to exist outside the body, in what would it differ from the angels? I do not see what could be more equal to it, or what could be more whole, in a certain sense. Each devout person therefore inclines toward his corruptible element so that he may subject it to his incorruptible part—namely, his spirit—as to a more perceptive and more sensible guide, to be governed by it.

[Col. 0591A] Thus, by right consideration, the flesh strives toward the imitation of its superior. For when it is perhaps impossible for a human being to contemplate higher or heavenly things in the mind, he finds within himself, by God’s work—for God made all things providentially—a prescribed and entirely proximate form. There he reads what must be done and directs the perversity of his conduct toward it as toward an established rule.

Finally, for commending the glory of this virtue, it is useful that God, with an especially gracious delight, has become accustomed to call the holy Church—a Church for whose redemption He expended His precious blood—a virgin. In this it is also perfectly clear that He Himself delights in the observance of chastity, since He so often applies this distinctive name to all His faithful generally. The blessed Apostle betrothed this virgin to that one man who alone is sufficient for all, presenting her chaste to him (II Cor. XI, 2). Even if bodily integrity were not present in all these people, the inviolability and solidity of undefiled faith would nevertheless not be lacking.

[Col. 0591B] This virtue, therefore, prepares for those who undertake it a reward almost beyond expression compared with the other virtues. Yet without the most vigilant diligence and unremitting watchfulness over oneself, it scarcely, or never, remains unharmed to the end. For the more glorious it is in beauty, the more sensitive it is to the useless cares that must be endured; and as transparent as glass, so intolerant of every disturbance is it, bordering on weakness. But let us now proceed to explain it more fully.

# CHAPTER VIII

## By What Means the Virtue of Chastity Must Be Guarded: 1. Humility; 2. Submission of Mind; 3. Meekness; 4. Compunction; 5. Patience

[Col. 0591C] The mind of anyone who has been animated by the teachings of so many and such great considerations reaches the love of purity as though borne on very light wings. But we have resolved not to pass over the question of what nurse should nourish so great a love once it has been born.

Since no virtue can be a virtue if it lacks the virtue of humility alone, I dare unhesitatingly to declare that without humility nothing is of any value at all. Even if something appears for a while to retain its position, it must not be believed to possess a true position if it has already willingly accepted the impulse of pride, from whose punishment it may fall into the foulest sin. In the minds of such people there is no knowledge of the experience of pleasure, while they examine the falls of others and their often fragile and useless lives; while, hearing of the shameful acts of anyone, they seem to bring horror into a pure heart; and while, under the zeal for purity which they consider excellent, they curse and drive away not only those acts but also their perpetrators.

[Col. 0591D] They conceive the arrogance of boundless swelling when they elevate their own sanctity by comparison with the disgraceful conduct of others. Before long they succumb to the very ruin they had despised. I do not say that evil acts should not be rejected; rather, the person’s wicked deeds should be rejected generously, lest we be drawn into imitating them, but the person should not be despaired of or despised according to the measure of his crimes.

[Col. 0592A] I confess that this is not unjust. I myself have often brought such a severe judgment upon the disorderly frivolity of others, while I myself, as I think, was troubled by the same passion, or by an even worse one. Their temptation seemed to me not human, nor something to be corrected with moderation, but impious; and it wearied me even to look at them. But when, by God’s grace, I was not entirely blind, I presented to my shameless thoughts the fact that the same enticements—indeed, much more troublesome ones—often assailed my own mind. Thus I understood that I abhorred others more from the zeal of curiosity than of charity.

[Col. 0592B] Only after much struggle and much turning over of thoughts, by which I showed myself excusable and them deserving of contempt, could I, as though drawn out of a thick darkness, begin to sparkle in the ray of reason. For this is a vice deeply implanted in human character: each person lightens his own errors in his private judgment, while he attacks others with the utmost severity even for the smallest faults.

This virtue, therefore, is very often and especially recognized as adjacent to this disease. For when it sees itself freer in this respect, it miserably believes that all those in whom it detects any trace of intemperance are completely enslaved, while it has no care at all for itself. When it hears of or considers the perverse acts of others, it commonly happens that the mind’s attention turns back to its own impure thoughts, which perhaps are not absent. Weighing its own thoughts and the deeds of others on the same scales, it judges its own so light and those of others so heavy that it freely grants itself whatever indulgence in thought it wishes, as though it were already secure from itself, and as though it were saying:

“Since this one and that one are always rolling about in the activity of their own crimes, it is entirely human and wholly pardonable if my mind, as though merely strolling, should sometimes stray into such a thought; and even if the mind should briefly fall into it, as commonly happens, it would never approach a movement of the flesh—let alone the act itself, which could not possibly occur by any means.”

[Col. 0592C] Through such underground passages lust creeps toward the walls of the heart that is trying to remain continent. Thus the mind, curious and more concerned with another than with itself, is forced to slip into a relaxed order of life, indeed into a fall of extreme ruin. Everyone must therefore think humbly of himself. Special attention must be devoted to meekness. Foolish gaiety must be restrained, and the threshold of anger must be blocked at its very beginnings.

[Col. 0592D] Often—and even had it never been written, experience in our own conduct would teach us this—we find that the gravest swelling of pride tends to subside into the softness of lust. Foolish joy likewise serves that vice no less; and anger, as the blessed Augustine is said to have held, if it does not destroy its beginnings, sometimes lacks the strength to bear the weight of lust.

## The Lily of the Valleys

This is the lily of the valleys; this is the flower of the field. Although he had first said “the flower of the field,” he added, not without reason, “the lily of the valleys” (Song II, 1), lest by speaking simply of a flower he might be understood to mean certain useless and beautiful flowers, such as mallows and thistles. He added “of the valleys” in order to designate something excellent in whiteness and nectar-like fragrance.

[Col. 0593A] In my view, “field” can be understood as bodily endurance. When the outward human being is beaten by the frequent occurrence of adversities, like a field prepared for the Lord’s sowings, he produces more abundantly a flower of chastity that gives off an extraordinary fragrance. Indeed, many kinds of flowering grass are cultivated. But the lily is born in the valleys—that is, in the innermost parts of the conscience. For there is no integrity of the flesh unless it proceeds from love in the mind.

The “flower of the field” may instead be understood as that integrity which exists in immature age—namely, in children and young girls—from natural innocence alone; or rather, that which is often found in certain people whose bodies are cold and who are less pressed by an inborn temperance against these movements. Such people possess something great without severe exertion, and they often exercise themselves in other forms of good living. But scarcely anyone among them is found to devote himself to perfection. Hence eunuchs, through a certain security concerning themselves, are recognized as turning aside toward tepidity of mind.

[Col. 0593B] I confess that I once saw two brothers of the same parentage. One, although he belonged to the priestly order, could not restrain himself from marriage. The other, a layman, was accustomed to claim that he had such a cold nature that—something astonishing to say—he was entirely free from this stimulation. If, then, the incontinent man had devoted himself to the pursuit of continence, how much better would he have become than that cold man?

By “the flower of the field,” therefore, let us understand not the lily, as we interpreted above, but any flower whatsoever, provided it is good; this is the kind of virginity intended here. This interpretation agrees with the fact that a field is customarily understood as uncultivated land. Thus the field has a flower without the hand of a laborer, when someone rejoices that he is a virgin without temptation.

[Col. 0593C] But the lily, which, as we have prescribed, is cultivated both by digging around it and by applying manure, and which flourishes most abundantly—what does it signify except the vowed chastity of soul and body, which is not won without a difficult battle? It breaks up earthly thoughts with the hoe of reason, and brings faults contracted elsewhere to the mind for weeping, as manure with which it may be fertilized. Thus, in that valley which always abounds in the grain that, having died, brought forth much fruit (John XII, 24), it gradually migrates toward the perfect flower of total integrity in a glorious exaltation through humbling itself.

## The Pre-eminence of Humility

[Col. 0593D] This exalted humility, without which the integrity we are discussing cannot stand at all, except at its summit, must also be investigated with particular care. One thing is especially recognized as contributing to its praise: the devil’s neck is not crushed, nor the edge of his cunning blunted, by any art of human exercise or, to put it briefly, by the assistance of any virtues except this one. As soon as humility is set against him, whatever his savagery contrives becomes immediately powerless, and he finds himself unskilled in attacking it, because he has no knowledge of the height of such a stronghold.

[Col. 0594A] Since he is sustained by a spiritual creation and, through the subtlety of his nature, is not subject to bodily necessities, what can a human being—earth and vile mud—do against an invisible enemy, from whom he cannot flee locally, against the almost impenetrable sharpness of so great an enemy? He is scarcely able to keep himself safe even from a human being whom he can see and evade and who is generally his inferior in intelligence. Yet God, who established a remedy for every earthly and spiritual evil, also taught by what diligence this enemy could be defeated.

[Col. 0594B] Because he fell solely through the occasion of his own swelling, the spiritual strength of that enemy is most readily seen to be overcome by ashes and mud—or rather, by those who recognize themselves to be ashes and mud, with divine assistance. For the lower each person is in his own estimation, the more effective he becomes at shattering the crown of the enemy.

What better shield can anyone use to protect the continence of the flesh, which the devil especially provokes with his fires, than always to think humbly of himself while he remains in the flesh—something that the devil himself neglected to do in his own case when he was a spirit? When the sense of the flesh is restrained, the power of the wicked spirit is annulled. The flesh itself, by suffering the rule of the mind or reason, is made gentler; the arrogance of its innate pride, indeed the outward joy by which it is often shamefully relaxed, and the inward wantonness of wandering thought by which it runs about foolishly, are cut away.

[Col. 0594C] Since so great an offspring is nourished under this nurse, as has been said, it is necessary that another virtue be sought to serve as its bearer after her. For infants of noble birth are usually assigned, besides nurses, larger maidservants or attendants who may carry them wherever they go. It is not fitting that a virtue so singularly noble should lack such an ornament.

# CHAPTER IX

## Modesty and Vigilance Are Necessary for Guarding Chastity; Harmful Familiarities Must Be Avoided

[Col. 0594D] After the devout mind, conscious of its own lowliness and as ready to submit as it is subject to accidental injury, has subjected itself to itself, it is necessary that, whatever it does and wherever it goes, the gravity of its conduct should always accompany it as nurse and guardian, restraining incongruous movements and everything juvenile.

After prayers amid long fasts, after tears and devout sighs, when one returns to external occupations and ordinary conversation, a certain joy is often displayed—perhaps to relieve the mind of weariness or to show goodwill and cheerfulness. Although it seems to begin honorably, it often slips into shamefulness. For when delight is multiplied through a cheerful exchange of words, playful chatter gradually approaches. Then, as stories of shameful things begin to follow one another, the rigor of the mind, warmed—or rather loosened—by pleasing amusements, grows soft with an unexpected and almost irresistible pleasure toward thinking about the things to which it voluntarily lends ear and tongue.

[Col. 0595A] Thus, I say, while the falsely sweet conversations—which could nevertheless easily be resisted—are sampled, death follows, a death which neither mind nor reason is sufficiently capable of driving out.

The mind, then, wounded by this grievous arrow, and its thought wandering here and there according to the movement of its pleasure, becomes wholly absorbed in amorous trifles. To speak of these things and seek after them becomes its most ardent occupation. Even when it returns to itself, it humanely lightens this fault within itself by many excuses, charming itself with the claim that it is doing this not out of love for vice or for anything obscene, but rather through indulgence in social activity and cheerfulness.

From there, little by little, one comes to harmful familiarities. These often begin with such an appearance of religious sincerity—almost through the exchange of prayers or the offering of edifying conversation—that they seem even to arise from compunction. But afterward, through habit and the frequent use of amorous flattery, one proceeds to light words and jokes, by which fires are built up in the unwary mind.

[Col. 0595B] When the torches of conversation and play have been applied for a little while, the shameless mind begins to feel its own ruin. If a spark of wrongly conceived love, long cherished, bursts into destructive flames, who would be surprised? Then the diseased conscience is forced to experience the passions which fatal love contains within it. Then, according to the saying of Terence, it is compelled, even unwillingly, to pay out in such an affair enmities and reconciliations revived for its own destruction, suspicions, fears, anger, and quarrels.

For so great is the affliction of that pestilential association that, although it sometimes soothes through habit, the difficulty of enjoying the object loved often aggravates matters so much that it makes the bloodless and languishing lover more cruelly fevered than by any fever. But when he tries to break away peacefully and honorably from what he loves, without anger or disturbance toward the person, he is miserably bound even more tightly.

[Col. 0595C] One must not flatter the ears of a wife inclined to wantonness with charming words; her back must be severely flayed with blows. In the same way, when the mind inclines toward perverse affections—or when, having inclined, it delays correction by promising that it will easily straighten itself whenever it wishes—one must not merely refuse assent to it. Even disregarding everyone’s hatred, one must immediately impose so strict a restraint upon its lust that the service of the entire body must be denied altogether to its impure desires.

For to whom except a hopelessly sick person would harmful food be given, however eagerly he might eat it—and who except the most insane would give it? Sick people are often accustomed to say: “Allow us to eat what we want. Whatever we willingly consume will contribute to our health.”

[Col. 0595D] Lovers also say: “We are acting most beneficially if, while the mind remains in its proper state, we at least test through simple conversation and outward companionship how burdensome and oppressive it is to serve wandering loves. When we have considered how harmful the matter is, we shall despise it all the more detestably because we have experienced it.”

When some people have attempted to do this—already weary of what they had loved—and, as though by mutual agreement, have wished to separate under a kind of peace, they are nevertheless so entangled by the customary enticements, from which it is now harsh to abstain, or by the soothing words of the person involved, that with hardened minds they descend into the abyss of every kind of destruction. Without reverence or hesitation, they shamelessly burn for what they had begun to love gradually and, as it seemed, religiously and innocently.

[Col. 0596A] But whoever feels himself being drawn by any love—whoever it may be—and recognizes that his heart is being separated from God by some cares, must reject the person from himself, however worthy and suitable that person may seem, even if doing so brings infamy or loss upon him. He must know that it is a matter of reward, not offense, if by such hatred he reconciles God to himself while offending that person.

He must not proceed weakly or playfully, or with the kind of anger about which that Chremes in Terence’s *Andria*, if I am not mistaken, says to Simon: “Anger among lovers is a renewal of love.” Rather, he must flee with such a sharp and abrupt separation that no hope remains of restoring the love again. Indeed, he must flee not only in mind—which is known often to be changeable and deceitful—but also, according to the Apostle’s prudent saying, most swiftly in bodily presence.

# CHAPTER X
[Col. 0596B] **One should by no means devote oneself to elegance of face and the care of clothing.**—Moreover, there is no doubt that it sometimes happens that, when the mind has begun gradually to be scorched by the first sparks of this fever, even though no heat of any temptation is outwardly perceived, it nevertheless becomes so intent on adorning its own face and on winning the praise of elegance that it pants after amorous pleasure. Finally, by fitting garments to the shape of the body, so that all human ingenuity is occupied in serving these pursuits, it carefully investigates how its beauty is received by each person; and while it disparages in itself—or rather, before itself—whatever is considered beautiful, it longs especially and uniquely to be praised and desires above all to be loved.

[Col. 0596C] Thus, while it loves to be loved and burns most eagerly to acquire the favor of persons, it thirsts, as is natural to that condition, for the desire of many the more widely it insinuates itself among them. And while, I say, it succeeds in obtaining someone it has desired, it is carried away by the most adhesive love for the one to whom it has clung; and, whether it wishes it or not, conquered by desire, it loves to love. Certainly, if its wandering conscience had not pursued the disorderly favor of the crowd—an impulse not without a shameful kind of pride—it would never have fallen into this most tenacious fetter of love, by which it is dragged into the accomplishment of every disgrace, even knowingly, which is worse.

Thus excessive attention to clothing and appearance, since they bear the signs of a lustful breast just as smoke bears witness to fire and wind to rain, must be driven from outward practice and, even more, must be excluded from the entrance of the mind, as the fuel of crimes.

[Col. 0596D] We are not discussing the wantonness of those who are outside—that is, of secular people—for that is not our concern; rather, we offer some counsel to those whose way of life is silent concerning the world’s external cares. This vice makes its devotees wandering and unstable, not only in heart but also in body, as Solomon says of the chattering woman: “She is restless and unable to remain at home” (Prov. VII, 11), and so forth.

Otherwise the matters would contradict one another: to make oneself beautiful and adorn oneself beautifully, yet not wish to be seen by those whom one pleases. From this arise the most disgusting features of the outer person: an absurd stiffness of the eyebrows, an indecent rolling and shameless, brazen—indeed, meretricious—movement of the eyes and gestures of the limbs; unbecoming laughter, ready for every [Col. 0597A] subject; a stupid throwing about of the feet while walking; words at first wanton and redolent of the love burning within, but afterward openly belching forth the shamelessness of an already flagrant obscenity.

But the inflated and most impatiently stretched rigidity of such behavior, and the accursed swelling of this pleasure, suddenly perish; and while it triumphs, an intolerable pain tears apart the affection and leaves it mournful and languid. For amid its apparent successes, when such persons see themselves not merely desired by others but, with haughty disdain, placed below them—or not even looked at—by those very persons whose loves consume them, then, even if all the world’s beauty and pleasures were available to them, none would suffice except those they pursue; and the lusts already present do not cure them, while the pride of others has not yet been subjected to them.

[Col. 0597B] Among the ancient pagans, Cupid, son of Venus and Vulcan, was commonly depicted winged, holding a torch and an arrow. This was not done without a mystery appropriate to the present work. For when the flame of that heat generated from an adored beauty—represented by Vulcan, the god of fire—serves as its attendant, desire is born, that is, the burning of lust. Cupid is first depicted winged because lust lifts the unhappy person whom it seizes to such levity that no hypocrisy of the mind can restrain its exultation over the outcome of its love.

He was also depicted with one foot, signifying the instability of such loves. He was blind as well, because foresight has no part in them. Finally, he was a child, because deeds and words of this kind are undertaken without reason. [Col. 0597C] He holds a torch and an arrow because he miserably sets aflame and simultaneously wounds the heart he pierces. According to the poet Ovid, two kinds of his arrows are read of: one compels love; the other causes love to grow cold when it strikes.

Thus, when the breast has been pierced to the marrow by one or the other of these fatal wounds, it suffers; and while it tries to heal itself by changing its loves, the wound grows worse. Change aggravates it; complete abandonment heals it.

I would wish those persons who are loved to be struck by the arrow that is said to drive love away, so that, when they saw their lovers rejected, they might at least repent through shame. I would wish that Cupid might turn upon such men Apollo’s most bitter misfortune: when the aforesaid hero was proudly exulting in youthful triumph over that divine dragon’s defeat and no longer feared Cupid’s arrow, [the wording is corrupt: Apollo/Daphne is] struck by the leaden shaft that drives love away, and Apollo is immediately and most shamefully despised by her.

[Col. 0597D] O God, may it thus befall those who love badly and presume upon themselves, who are well represented by proud Apollo. Above all, we declare and advise all who care for their own good that, however much the lover and the loved one may excel in virtue, however impenetrable their hearts may be, the intimacy of both should be severed in such a way that it may be understood to work far worse than that frequent association which begins on both sides with the lightest of causes.

[Col. 0598A] Let no one object to me the coldness of an aged body or long experience in religion; let no Ethiopian ugliness be opposed to what I see more frequently practiced. With the devil, who is hot and skilled in his own arts, and who does not spare either age or beauty or ugliness, I can find nothing safe.

## CHAPTER XI

**How those who have professed an austere life miserably fall into the vice of the flesh.**—Meanwhile it is often asked, and is regarded by some as a very great marvel, when a person of either sex who has professed continence or virginity falls into vice—especially one whose discipline of abstinence is so rigorous that he abstains from everything cooked except bread and eats nothing on three days of the week. For many this is usually a grave wonder and a cause of despair.

[Col. 0598B] I say nothing of those whom youth excuses if they fall. I shall address those who have passed beyond the misfortunes of youth and who, when the maturity of age ought to have exhausted the swellings and humors of passion, have become perverse and, already old in years, plunge into youthful filth. But if they knew how to weigh and examine the cause of such ruin—which I consider not sudden but contracted from material long prepared beforehand—they could grieve over their falls without being astonished by them.

I do not dare to say that anyone can fall by a sudden assault—I neither remember experiencing nor reading that this can be definitively established. What are called sudden falls seem to me usually to arise either from ingrained negligence or from an old pride growing together inwardly. For when the mind begins little by little to relax from its rigor through the smallest concessions, and by daily decline falls into the worst tepidity, then, as the force of temptation succeeds it—for temptation is never absent from a relaxed mind when the devil lies in wait for it—it soon becomes accustomed to being agitated toward worse things.

[Col. 0598C] From there, not through an unexpected thought but through indulgence in a thought already badly habituated, one runs into action as the penalty of sin; and what had been shamefully conceived and hidden from human sight under hypocrisy is brought forth by God’s just punishment. It also often happens that many who live apart from secular companionship are led by the conversation of worldly people—those who think about and pursue earthly things—to the extreme depths of madness and the abyss.

**Those who watch over chastity must conduct themselves with great circumspection.**—Let us therefore understand that we have said these and similar things, whose folly does not accord with seriousness, in such a way that from the opposites we may appear to have suitably and beneficially indicated what ought to be done by the prudent. If, for example, I said to someone, “You are destroying yourself because you live badly,” he would undoubtedly understand nothing other than, “Save yourself by living well.”

This maturity of conduct is a complete moderation of action: insofar as humanly possible, nothing less or excessive should appear in the gaze, speech, or movement of the limbs; even one’s step should display nothing superfluous outwardly. Above all, the inner rule of the mind should proceed with such subtle forethought that through no sluggishness is it permitted to deviate from the order of equity. Therefore nothing that the flesh eagerly desires should be admitted within the gates of the mind, nor should one turn one’s eyes toward those things whose desire is known to be forbidden to a Christian heart.

[Col. 0599A] Under such a nurse and guardian—for I confess that this is the best provider of all—the honor of this holy virtue is advanced. What is not yet strong enough to proceed by itself, nor sufficient to stand by itself, is supported and surrounded as though by the arms of holy seriousness and withdrawn from sudden collapse and impending harm. Thus, as though strengthened from the beginning of youth under its guidance, when it reaches a more advanced state, and pious practice has become habitual, it grows everywhere stronger by itself.

But since we have assigned a nurse and guardian according to our modest ability, it is better to say briefly what teacher can subdue a young girl shaken by wantonness or pride, and, having interrupted or opposed her, subject her, return her to her task, and restore her to obedience.

**One must devote oneself to the fear of God.**—I consider nothing more suitable for such a task [Col. 0599B] than the continual remembrance of divine fear. At first, indeed, fear of judicial punishment, if present, does no harm; rather, it helps, affecting the beginnings of conversion with salutary grief and usually becoming the first material for desiring virtue.

But that holy fear which endures forever and ever (Ps. XVIII, 10), by which the devoted mind fears offending the grace of its Father, is so necessary for preserving integrity that without it none of its glory can stand—none, I say, which without this intention of divine love cannot withstand the smallest assaults of any temptation. From this hope of obtaining God’s love strength arises in pious souls against every danger.

[Col. 0599C] That is the chaste fear of adoption, not of slavery (Rom. VIII, 15): while it bends the wandering movements of mind and flesh beneath a generous command, it makes the soul safe when danger attacks. It gives no place anywhere to negligence, because the person fears losing the one good; nor does such a person approve himself if he is permitted to do some evil with impunity. Therefore one who approaches the service of God must stand “in justice and fear” (Eccli. II, 1). “Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. XXVIII, 14).

[Col. 0599D] **From the love of God comes continual joy.**—But who, formed by the eager pursuit of so great a lesson of discipline, will be joined by a marital bond unless he is one from whose seed there continually comes to him nothing other than the perpetual joy of offspring—that is, the love of God, which is called charity? Since continual joy is recognized to be present in it through purity of conscience—for if secular love makes its devotees rejoice vainly, how much more spiritual love will do so—what will that person be when, freed from this valley of tears and deprived of every cloud, he is entirely joy and delight in beholding God?

Virginity brought to perfection is therefore joined not to any transitory virtue, such as faith and hope, but to that spontaneous love which never fails (I Cor. XIII, 8). Begun now, it will be perfected in the possession of the kingdom and will rejoice with God, gloriously and without limit, over its happiness.

[Col. 0600A] After so many and such serious conflicts of flesh and spirit, after the tumult and most importunate voices of trivial desires, which are usually restrained with such great exertion, it is just that after so many battles, when God grants peace, all the earth should be silent before the face of the victorious spirit. And, as the reward for a war well fought, the ruling spirit should possess a quiet and solid little dwelling of flesh, without the assault of any insolence, and should rest from the whole conflagration of passion, which it has repressed in battle with such abundant sweat.

**How much good the chaste person draws from the same love.**—When the soul, still confined by its bodily condition, reaches the glory of impassibility, it is drawn toward complete purity by such great and affectionate love that not only does something pleasurable seem almost natural to it, but it appears to itself like an incomparable paradise or delight; and what had previously been almost unbearable now becomes lighter beyond all estimation.

[Col. 0600B] Virginity is therefore joined to this as to a perpetual husband, after those previously mentioned tutors who, by the disciplinary right they exercised over her as a still youthful pupil, broke her neck; so that, even through a very great force of love, it may presume upon security regarding its perseverance in this world. In accordance with a certain saying of the glorious Antony, it should no longer fear God but love him; it should strive to pursue the good not so much for the reward of the good itself as for the sake of what is good; and it should flee sin not because of the punishment it deserves but solely from the desire to preserve its own goodness.

But let us proceed to the rest.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0600C]

**Objections commonly made against the virtue of chastity are answered.**—To you, then, O soul devoted to holy integrity, longing for a state of such eminence, accept eagerly, now that you have begun to live sincerely, the arguments that will benefit your perseverance.

[Col. 0600D] Many who profess any form of religion commonly object that continence of the flesh need not be taken very seriously, since it is scarcely upheld anywhere by the example of the ancient books and nowhere imposed on anyone as a command. Indeed, at the beginning of human creation, man was produced not without woman, with limbs suited for begetting, and it was said to them: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 28). A fool is anyone who is persuaded to take up such a yoke.

There is no need to labor at length in refuting these objections. Let them nevertheless hear briefly that God gave commands to the ages according to time and circumstance; that at the beginning, when the race was being propagated, the ancestors were permitted to make use of multiple wives; but that as the human race grew, people were reduced to single, lawful marriages. Under the same principle, pagan license was restrained. Roman generosity also consented to the union of marriage on the same grounds, even before Christianity.

Thus the command concerning multiplying the race remained in force as long as it was necessary. Yet although Scripture said nothing about virginity lest marriage be defamed, it was nevertheless fitting that the Son of God should display something greater than marriage, which is good and lawful. If not by commanding it in words, then by indicating it through examples, Christian faith gathered this from Christ’s imitation and singular purity and strove to practice it with exceptional devotion.

[Col. 0601A] Nor does it invoke the shameless argument of the reproductive organs to defend its lust; rather, it prudently removes from itself what is permitted but not expedient, so that it may become stronger for overcoming what is not permitted.

“It is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII, 9)—that is, for those whom neither profession opposes nor a vow, whether their own or that of a parent, binds.

By a parent’s vow I mean one which the canons have decreed may be made up to the age of twelve.

[Note: [Col. 0601] Council of Toledo IV, canon 48; Council of Tribur, chapter 6. See Menard, on chapter 66 of the *Concordia Regularum*.]

For these persons to withdraw from their vow is the greatest sacrilege. But for those who endure the burden and heat of the day (Matt. XX, 12), that is, the anxieties of this life’s temptations, there is a great—indeed special—reward: they are granted to sing the new song apart from the others (Rev. XIV, 3). In that song their singular joy in bodily integrity is signified, in comparison with those who lack this privilege; and they follow the Lamb’s footsteps wherever he goes (ibid.), because, while they desire to be conformed to Christ in the remaining virtues, they also watch more keenly to follow his steps in this matter.

[Col. 0601B] But this is its most common praise. Let us advance to other matters.

## CHAPTER XIII

**Those who have professed the monastic way of life should conduct themselves cautiously.**—The order of those who live in this manner in holy Church is not very numerous. But who are they? Either they are offered to God by others at the beginning of life, or they offer themselves. Let us briefly touch upon the purity with which the life of such persons begins and the caution by which it must be protected.

[Col. 0601C] First, in the very beginnings of childhood, unsuitable familiarity must be rejected, and a slippery and deceptive instruction—although otherwise most useful—must be refused. For at the beginning there is often gathered what later harms the whole of life. But the very entrance into adolescence, if it has the fear of God as its companion, easily drives away temptation when it encounters it.

For the more a person experiences carnal things, the lighter are the dangers suffered from bodily desire. For what is more dangerous than the memory of past pleasure? To those, plainly, in whom the dangerously sweet taste of deadly food has not yet lodged, if they reject the enticement of seductive companions, conceal wandering glances, and know how to call back the errors of their thoughts to the right path, whatever temptation comes upon them becomes easy.

[Col. 0601D] Nevertheless, through excessive confidence in themselves and a certain curiosity to see attractive forms, they commonly allow their gaze greater freedom than is right. While they hunt after other people’s faces, while they remove the shield of their eyelids from their eyes too recklessly, they turn against the light of the heart the cruel dart of the stimulus with which they gaze improperly. Thus they are often dragged through this into the abyss of every evil.

It can also happen that sight does not greatly inflame them but quietly persuades them to love what they have seen; that conversation, or even touch itself, does not altogether rush into disgrace; and therefore that foul movement of the flesh displeases them only slightly. But the mind, on some occasion, comes to regret the deed and is led by grief over its guilt to repentance.

Yet, lest it incur the disgrace of treachery toward the person to whom it had promised lasting love, the mind advises it, as though it were now acting soberly with that person, not to abandon the practice of conversation. Thus it happens that love, wrongly renewed, boils over without any hesitation and rushes most greedily into the lowest depths of abrupt destruction. From this the prudent reader should understand with what vigilance the first assaults of temptation must be rejected, however flattering they may be.

[Col. 0602A] The seductive and deceitful persuasion of demons, or of the flesh itself, must therefore be guarded against, lest, while we display our virtues to ourselves and trust that we shall walk across level fields, we miserably fall into pits covered by the enemy’s deceit.

One must also attend with every effort and extraordinary care lest, while the shifting mind burns fiercely—as it usually does—to see what it desires, eyes enslaved to desire obey the mind. For if what we look upon innocently often harms us terribly, how much do we think that which is done with a mind already evil wounds the unhappy soul?

It sometimes happens that things seen move the viewer to no harmful heat, but a boldly presumed touch plunges him into such a furnace of lust—even while the mind vainly resists—that he can scarcely, or not at all, digest the fires conceived without contamination. I admit that the mind then resists in vain to extinguish the fire, when the hand is voluntarily extended to kindle it.

[Col. 0602B] Finally, not only must sight be restrained and touch avoided more than any fire, but proximity itself and conversation must be avoided with the greatest care.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0602C]

**By what means virginity is defiled.**—It is also often asked by some through what kinds of sin virginity is considered lost. This inquiry appears excessively obscene, since they ought rather to have investigated by what zeal for virtue it might be obtained more fully than by what danger it might be lost. The former question belongs to a lax spirit; the latter to one burning with zeal.

Yet, since a woolen weft should not be inserted into a linen warp, and the grossness of a corrupted body ought not presume to glory in the hope of virginal refinement, each person should consider not how far he may go but what he must avoid.
