Anyone devoted to attaining this purity should watch over the restraint of the heart’s wantonness so carefully that the flesh scarcely, or as little as possible, or as rarely as possible, experiences such pleasure, lest consent be added to pleasure by any force.

It is the judgment of blessed Gregory, not my own, that consent does not differ from the effect of guilt, since the wretched will inwardly carries out what it cannot do outwardly, if God should nevertheless decide to judge this strictly.

What hope of virginity, then, can rejoice there where the theater of every foulness resounds? For such people an open fall would, I confess, be more useful: it would prevent the mind from swelling with false hope, and the experience of falling would most sharply deter them from seeking such things thereafter.

[Col. 0603A] Since, then, we do not know what God will judge justly and piously, let us therefore know that no reward of virginity awaits those who are shown to obey the lust of the mind.

It would be pointless to speak of the external stain, which is sometimes extracted through shameless conversations and dishonorable touches; by these even someone naturally castrated, possessing bodily integrity from birth, would undoubtedly lose it through this most filthy corruption of the mind.

## CHAPTER XV

**By how many evils one ensnared by carnal pleasure is afflicted.**—But since we have barked sufficiently up to this point about these misfortunes, let us contemplate the glory of this integrity in relation to the misery that follows whenever it suffers a fall. The noble author Boethius says this (*On the Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, meter 7), when he was discussing pleasure as a robber of modesty:

[Col. 0603B] “Every pleasure has this characteristic:

It drives the raging with goads,” and so forth.

But with what goads? With what insanity of pain, I ask, does it tear apart the languid breast? And while frenzied remedies are sought for a frenzied desire in order to increase its madness, the mind, lacerated on every side and scattered, is driven toward utter collapse and bloody tortures.

Even if it sometimes repents when driven by pains, the exactors of Pharaoh soon return and force the wretched, scourged heart to its accustomed payment, always adding harsher demands and driving it to hasten its tribute. From there one soon comes to hatred of the whole of religion: the holy cloisters and brotherly fellowship stink; whatever resists perverse love, however excellent, is cursed; and repentance for every good undertaken follows.

[Col. 0603C] The author whom we mentioned earlier, I believe, fully elucidates in the preceding passage the first advances of this worst hemlock, and its foul odors and deadly juices when it is crushed:

“What shall I say,” he says, “about pleasures? Their desire is full of anxiety, but their satisfaction of repentance” (Boethius, prose III, 7).

From what has been said you have the anxiety. But what is that satisfaction? It is the taste of that poisonous and savage bloody banquet, whose belches are so foul that their reputation most horribly torments those who hear of them.

For the consummation of that feast, a moment is almost sufficient to produce its effect; but the grief of infinite pain follows immediately upon the shortest pleasure.

And what grief? The sharpest, not comparable with the sadness of any temporal loss. It is accustomed to drive its author with the goad of anguish to such a degree that he chooses with his own right hand to plunge himself into the peril of death. Since he believes that no one besides himself is aware of the crime he has committed, the unhappy mind is gnawed so cruelly by the tooth of suspicion that, now bloodless and fearful among all those with whom he lives, it awaits judgment concerning itself, while its crime still remains hidden.

To be subject to such punishments—what should it most plausibly be considered except a kind of imagined hell?

[Col. 0604A] Yet after the fall, when a person is sometimes intensely ashamed to confess what he has done, he professes a certain continence before himself and promises that by his own power he will restrain himself as much as even his own pastor would restrain him if he had confessed it to him.

But this deceptive presumption immediately ceases to propagate the badly nourished crime into multiple crimes. While hidden iniquity delights the heart, by some sign or deed it is made known to everyone. Then shamelessness and, together with it, hardening follow; and the process ends in a rejected mind and despair.

Before sin, I would generally call modesty a useful fear, like the fear of a servant; after guilt, however, it is much more harmful, insofar as one who does not confess appears more cautious in protecting an evil shame of his own.

Let us therefore love the confusion that brings glory; for to have come to Babylon in this way greatly contributes to our liberation.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0604B]

**Monastic discipline and flight from secular associations are the best remedy for preserving virginity.**—Let no one wonder that we have decided to remain entirely silent about the measure of the heavenly reward owed to virgins, because it is hidden from us, we are incapable of expressing it, and things not visible to the eyes excite lukewarm hearers less. Things whose harsh experience is evident, and which are very often shown by anyone to be bad in ordinary practice, seemed to me more deserving of an example, so that the mind might at least shudder at seeking a little honey in the bee’s mouth while considering the sting contained in its tail.

[Col. 0604C] It is also not beside the point to insist that, for those stirred by that goad, nothing is more useful than the permanence of the cloister and monastery; flight especially from conversation with secular persons; avoidance of rumors; and whatever else the flesh eagerly embraces as its choice.

Among these things, the greatest moderation must be exercised in consuming food and every provision; diligent attention must be given to much servile labor; and ferocity must be bent beneath the yoke of frugality, lest, while purity of heart is sought without abstinence from external pleasures, the desired result be frustrated, as it rightly must be.

**Temptations must be disclosed to the spiritual father.**—Above all this, I consider it supremely and urgently beneficial to reveal to one’s own pastor, whose particular responsibility is to care for the soul, every movement of whatever wantonness creeps into the soul, as soon as it arises and at the very beginning of the suggestion.

[Note: [Col. 0603D] See chapters 4 and 7 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

This must not be done summarily or deceptively; rather, one must lay bare one’s thought as completely as possible, so that the whole self may offer itself to be governed by the judgment of the director. For no one can be well subject to a ruler or superior whose conscience he himself does not know.

If, then, a sick person wisely provides for himself when illness begins, he must declare to the physician of the mind the substance and manner of his disease and surrender his whole self to him. These things are difficult in practice, but the more difficult they are, the more useful they are.

**How much good and peace come even in this world to one devoted to purity.**—I therefore dare to set before the virtue of so slight a labor a reward of marvelous power and sweetness even in this world, in comparison with which that slight labor may truly be considered slight.

[Col. 0605A] No one familiar with this kind of torment, I think, is unaware of how great a whirlwind of suspicions torments the wretched mind—whether lust is still being nourished while the heart conceals it, or whether it has been carried out in deed—and with how many anxieties it troubles a person held captive.

Lust, once passed through, as someone has said, always leaves behind repentance for itself. And a mind conscious of wrongdoing, as another has said, is always driven by its own goads.

But when a pious person devoted to purity shakes the refuse of such filth from his innermost being, begins to rule over bodily movements, and by a certain imperial force quiets the tumult of his worn-out crowd of passions, who could adequately describe what light, peace, and security immediately arise in the heart which is not stained by the foulness of a contemplated crime, is not scorched by the heat of shameless desire, and is not stretched apart by any longing that separates it from God?

[Col. 0605B] This is the oil with which the mind, gloriously anointed, gladdens its face by contemplating its Creator (Ps. CIII, 15). It is also the oil of joy with which the Holy of Holies is anointed above his companions (Ps. XLIV, 8).

This, I say, is the oil that heals inward pains, by which our bones—that is, the hidden parts of our virtues—are watered and strengthened, in accordance with the contrary statement in the psalm: “Like oil in his bones” (Ps. CVIII, 18).

It is likewise said elsewhere that our head must be made fat, signifying the mind (Ps. XXII, 5).

What, then, could I say is sweeter than a good conscience, or happier as a present reward? Although it is sometimes obtained through devotion to the other virtues, it is acquired above all through this virtue of chastity.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0605C]

**By the purity of certain animals, human beings are urged toward chastity.**—Who would dare resist continence, so highly praised and endowed with so many privileges, when the Savior not only taught clearly that it should be imitated through examples proper to himself and to human life, but also did not refuse to celebrate it through the example of wild beasts and birds?

Let us consider beavers, which we commonly call *beveres* [French: *Bieures*]. Their testicles possess considerable medicinal value, and because of them they are said to endure the greatest persecution in their native regions. [Col. 0605D] When they see themselves being pursued more fiercely for these organs, and realize that flight alone cannot suffice for their safety, they throw themselves to the ground, bite off the members for which they are being chased, and leave them to their pursuers as a kind of ransom for themselves.

What will you do, Christian person? Will you place the love of your practiced lust before your life? Cut away from yourself what the devil’s wickedness demands from you. It desires to rejoice and feed on your luxury; cut it away, I say, and cast it from you, lest you enter hell with it (Matt. V, 30). You can live without lust; with it, though alive in body, you live unhappily in soul.

It finally happens to the same animal that, after losing that part of its body, it is again attacked by some who do not know what has happened. But when it begins to tire, it flees, turns over with its hind legs spread apart, and, displaying that it no longer possesses what they seek, declares the fact; thus it is released.

[Col. 0606A] Let us also, whenever some evil thing is suggested by Satan and he presses us fiercely, humble ourselves beneath the mighty hand of God (I Pet. V, 6), reject earthly affections, and raise our gaze to heaven, proclaiming through our deeds: “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14). “Get behind me, Satan, with your trifles. Your lust has long since been castrated in me by heavenly love.”

If the beaver willingly deprives itself of the organ by which it reproduces, an organ so useful, and gladly gives up what is especially important for life, how much more gladly should a human being cast away what harms him more than it benefits him?

[Col. 0606B] We also know that vultures, cruel though they are, in their own manner both conceive and produce offspring without intercourse. If God has implanted this glory of integrity in the most wicked of birds, why do you, rational soul, from whom the reward of virginity is not hidden, shrink from the discipline of continence?

**What one who watches over chastity should avoid.**—But since this virtue cannot be effective unless the highest affection for God is burning, a certain fire—not honorary but continual—must always be kindled in our breast, of such a nature that it extinguishes whatever harmful thing burns elsewhere.

[Col. 0606C] Let our soul therefore glow by burning with love for that one Beloved, and let it earnestly seek the kiss of his mouth, panting with desire. I mean that kiss which is accomplished through the innermost inpouring of heavenly inspiration, by which one drinks from the mouth of those ineffable lips and from the breath—so much more wondrous and sweeter the more secret it is.

According to blessed John the Apostle, this kiss should awaken in us everlasting desires; and there we are tinged with the saliva of his mouth, sweeter than every honeycomb, which renews in our mind the saving taste of the whole divine word.

Thus, when the mind, stirred by a singular and tantalizing wantonness, wishes to wander persistently after the blandishments of another’s mouth, let the sweetness recalled to memory make bitter, through contemplation of the inspiration already experienced, everything that outwardly nourishes wandering eyes.

But when an indecently gentle and dishonorably pleasing touch is suggested to our mind, let there be no lack in it, nor let the opening of that aperture be blocked by any vice, through which the Beloved may put in his hand, at whose touch the belly—that is, the fragility of our flesh—may tremble (Song V, 4), and, with Ezekiel, may always be strengthened by that same hand accompanying us and may constantly reject everything soft and yielding (Ezek. III, 14).

[Col. 0606D] If embraces and the other frequent pleasures of the world invade the inner eyes and wish to turn them toward themselves, let us imitate those sixty mighty warriors, the nobles of Israel, who surround Solomon’s bed, all holding swords and highly trained for war (Song III, 7–8).

Those sixty, through the perfection of pious work, now deserve the denarius that remains for laborers after their toil; and therefore they watch over Solomon’s bed—that is, his holy soul, in which true peace and Christ the peacemaker rest—with all the greater vigilance the more they devote themselves, as exiles from external things, to inward care.

And they do this not without swords: that is, with great points of discretion, by which on one side they cut away superfluous thoughts [Col. 0607A] and on the other resist the sudden assaults of harmful deeds with a kind of military diligence.

“Each one’s sword is upon his thigh because of nighttime fears” (Song III).

By the sword here, it seems to me, perseverance amid adversity may be understood, because from its transverse hilt and projecting part it presents the figure of the cross, in which endurance is signified; and by its lower length it is considered to indicate perseverance in suffering.

To this should be added that a point projects from the top, because there is no doubt that all our endurance amid hardships descends from hope of the heavenly prize.

[Col. 0607B] With this sword, therefore, the thigh of carnal desires must be restrained without remission. Nor is it without reason that it excludes nighttime fears: extraordinary vigilance must be applied to ward off the devil’s deceits.

Then, if a cloud and a dense mass of every obscene motion should assail the soul, it is necessary for the resisting spirit to sing:

**326** “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Cedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song of Songs 1:4).

“Black,” she says, “like the tents of Cedar,” since amid the darknesses of worldly life I serve in the gloom of storms that break forth, under hope of the city that is to come, and am necessarily still troubled by the cloud of bodily affliction. But although at times I submit unwillingly to these things, nevertheless I am beautiful, “like the skins of Solomon,” because I undertake something resembling the work of martyrs, while striving, through combat, to obtain the triumph which they sought against principalities and powers, against the rulers of visible darkness and their inciters, having laid aside their bodies and fought in coverings—that is, in the skins of their souls. I, too, strive to obtain this triumph against flesh and blood, laying aside the weight of vices, shaking off the sin that surrounds me, and fighting through prolonged conflicts, not without sharp injury to the flesh and anguish of spirit.

God providentially arranges matters so that, whenever my conscience is at times clouded by the guise of temptation, it may, through fear, fall away from the pride that might perhaps steal upon it; and the more it grieves, in its own judgment, to have lost its customary brightness, the more beautiful it may appear before its innermost examiner. For just as the lily among thorns (Song of Songs 2:2), even when struck by their spines, does not thereby diminish the power of its fragrance, so the mind already endowed with love for the eternal Bridegroom stands among those daughters whom the king of Egypt desired to cherish, after carefully killing the males (Exod. 1:22)—that is, among fleeting and soft thoughts—as though a royal virgin of purity, distinguished by the glory of beauty and honor, stood among shameful little women.

Let us therefore awake, exact from ourselves every kind of labor as tribute, and apply ourselves to cleansing the mind. Let us not suppose that virtues will spontaneously grow within us through idleness. Just as it is commonly said jokingly of priests that they work while wearing the mitre and eat with their arms folded, so let us imagine that, with our hands extended for the exercise of bodily pleasure and our senses lulled to sleep in divine duties, we can earn God’s favor by dreaming. But the reality is far otherwise [Note: [Col. 0607C] The author notes the profound humility of spirit.].

I have been compelled, O holy soul, excellent in every pious exercise, to bark vehemently against myself in warning you; and while I distinguished the vices of souls for you at such length, I have, whether I wished it or not, laid myself open before you. But if I have said anything about the pursuit of virtue, you ought to ascribe it rather to the power of nature, which is never entirely deprived of goodness, than to any experience of mine in such pursuits. “The narration of a fool,” as someone says, “is like a burden on the road” (Ecclus. 21:19). Yet I dare presume that you will excuse me for my verbosity, since I did what I dared chiefly at your request. Others give you books painted and splendid in abundant ornament; would that I might bring something useful before your eyes! Accept, then, one who warns you concerning your salvation; and although you know that I act otherwise than I speak, do not disdain what is uttered for your salvation. I shall gladly do whatever you command. At least grant me the reward of this labor in your prayers.

**THE END**

[Col. 0607]

# ON THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS

[Note: [Col. 0607] In this document, numbers appearing in brackets, for example (2), refer to notes that appear as a separate document in this volume, beginning at column 1021.]

## DEDICATORY LETTER OF THE VENERABLE GUIBERT, ABBOT, ON THE FOUR BOOKS ON THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS

[Col. 0607D] **327** To the lord and father Odo, abbot of Saint-Symphorian (2): Guibert, if only a minister and servant of the Mother of God, wishes you joyful progress in the service of God.

### The author explains the circumstances of his undertaking

Since many questions concerning the tooth of the Savior—which our neighbors, the people of Saint-Médard, claim to possess—were making a commotion around me, and since some people had been making strenuous efforts over the matter in ordinary conversation, I judged that I should touch briefly upon this subject in writing and declare, while leaving aside the opinions of others, what my own mind thought about it. When, therefore, I began the matter itself at the very beginning of the little book, and was laboring to dictate what I had conceived, scarcely filling a whole page, such an abundance of things related to what had to be said flowed in upon me that the subject begun was soon abandoned without conclusion. When I pursued another subject, though not unrelated to this occasion, I first brought forth the little book in an imperfect form, with the discourse I had undertaken unfinished. In the following work, where the subject I had vowed to discuss had already been touched upon, when mention was made of the Lord’s body, everything that we had then begun to say about the tooth also slipped from our mind. Thus, after I had dealt with the matters that had rushed upon me in discussion, I finally exercised my attempt in a third work. But I do not know whether I have explained anything that could satisfy a prudent person.

### An objection made against the author

#### 1. That he called the body of Christ in the Eucharist Christ’s substitute

For the rest, whatever I have thought, I have put forward what I thought with the full security of faith; if anyone thinks better, I should be pleased. Nevertheless, one of my kindly readers noted in the second little book that I had called the mystery of bread and wine Christ’s substitute. This seemed to him less suitably expressed because whatever is called a substitute is in some way regarded as less than that of which it is the substitute.

But if he had attended to my statements, by which [lacuna] the identity of that which is from the Virgin and of that which is signified, which [lacuna], is repeatedly declared by me, all his ambiguity would immediately have been dispelled; since the Lord’s own words, immediately added there, command [lacuna] to be done in remembrance of himself, no question of substitution would ever arise. For who doubts that a substitute for representing anything renews the memory of that which is represented? [f., *vicarium*; f., *repraesentatam*].

It seems rather that the matter lies in the fact that the Holy Spirit is called the “Pledge” (Eph. 1:14), that the Son himself is called “the brightness of glory and the figure of the substance” (Heb. 1:3), and elsewhere “the image of God” (2 Cor. 4:4). Certainly, I do not see what prevents that from being called a substitute which he himself also calls “daily,” as though he were suggesting that we should use it in the present, while it is called “today,” in such a way that it may lead us to the eternal enjoyment of that which sits at the Father’s right hand. I cannot but think that absolute truth itself, though wholly present, appropriately bears the appearance of a certain substitution, since he commands this to be done in this age in such a way that, in the ages of ages, once we have reached the reality of this source, it will no longer need to be done.

I therefore decided to appoint you, most beloved man, as judge of this little work. The sharpness of your ever-alert intellect has taught you to examine not only the condition of the letter, but the persistence of contemplation has accustomed you to seek out the spirit of the letter itself, so to speak. I have therefore chosen you confidently, since I have learned that you proceed even to correct hostile writings only from the innate humility bestowed upon you.

#### 2. Because he wrongly interpreted Wisdom 5:3—a point he chiefly refutes in *The Interior World*

Moreover, when you were present, someone [lacuna] [f., “a rival”] objected to me—quite ready to speak, but less careful to defend what he had barked out—that I had said, contrary to the Book of Wisdom, that those who are or will be in hell possess, and will possess, an impenitent heart. The passage reads:

“They will say within themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit: ‘These are the ones whom we once held in derision’” (Wis. 5:3), and so forth.

With such an argument, if I am not mistaken, I shall close the matter. I remember that I proved in the same book which I called *The Interior World* that their mind had fallen into diabolical fury and obstinacy. If not there, I nevertheless concluded the matter by the sole force of a contrary comparison: just as Christ, with what benevolence he unites and incorporates his fellow members to himself in heaven, so the devil, with a similar likeness of madness, makes those of whom he becomes the head conform to himself and enfolds them within his own entrails.

**328** No one doubts that it is exceedingly absurd and inconsistent with every rational principle that one who departs this life malevolent should recover there what he did not care to possess here while he lived. Otherwise Solomon’s saying is empty: that a tree, whether it falls toward the south or toward the north, remains immovably wherever it has fallen (Eccles. 11:3). It would not remain so if it departed from the conformity and condition of its head, whether good or evil. But since it is wholly impious to recognize oneself as absent from the meaning of so great a book, let us discuss their repentance in such a way that we do not deny the perpetual impenitence of those people.

We attribute to them the ability to repent only in this one respect, although their repentance bears no fruit whatsoever: amid the bitterness of their punishments, they so loathe the sins for which they are being punished that, when the fruitlessness of such great grief immediately presents itself to their minds—since it can in no way be changed—the fury of despair overturns their hearts. They hate so intensely what they are that they regret having been less sinful and less savage in their pleasures while they were alive.

Isaiah’s saying agrees with this: “Affliction alone will give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28:19). What is called repentance in the Book of Wisdom is called understanding by Isaiah. And although Solomon declares that neither reason nor knowledge will exist in hell (Eccles. 9:10), nevertheless they are known not to be without understanding in this one respect: they always discern for what they are suffering. But while they suffer, because there is no benefit from their discernment, they relapse into the madness of obduracy and contempt.

Hence there is the passage in Job, when he described the land of misery and darkness: “Where the shadow of death and no order dwell, but everlasting horror” (Job 10:22). There would plainly be order if the one who repented withdrew from the effect—and indeed from the disposition—of the thing for which he was repentant. There is therefore no order there: on the one hand he repents because of the punishment for evil; on the other, inflamed by the desire for evil, he rages in despair. That fury is signified by the everlasting horror which burns with monstrous intensity in minds made cruel by complete alienation from hope. All of this is most clearly weighed in the deed of Judas the betrayer: although he repented of the betrayal he had committed, he nevertheless did not restrain his hand from his destruction by taking up an earnest desire to correct his guilt.

Certainly, if the man who tried to bind me with this little question were present, I would ask him—and much more appropriately than he asked me—what he thought about the words of the foolish virgins in the Gospel. They ask the prudent virgins to give them oil and ask the bridegroom to open to them after the door has already been closed (Matt. 25:8, 11), although no one doubts that, after the resurrection evidently implied there, no one—whether destined for salvation or destruction—can be left in doubt about his condition. Since Scripture sometimes calls the day of each person’s death the day of judgment—for at the very moment of our departure we receive the sentence of either our salvation or our condemnation—it can in no way be hidden from anyone what inheritance he is to receive in the future. Once the spirit has been stripped of the body’s covering, there is no obscurity concerning the knowledge of either the good or the evil of eternity.

If, then, nothing remains hidden from one newly stripped of his body concerning the lot allotted to him, and after the resurrection the condition of the life to come is much more clearly revealed through the experience of body and soul, where neither false piety nor flattery—I do not say advances itself, but cannot exist—how do these words stand in that truth which, if uttered in the vanity of this age before any wise person, would not stand? For who in the present life, if he thinks soundly, would testify concerning another’s conscience that he could not, if he judged rightly, testify concerning his own? Who, then, would foolishly expect anything from God or demand anything from a human being at that time, when he does not know how to measure himself in the present? Lies will not be able to be offered to the one before whose judgment all things will be naked.

Elsewhere too we read that many will say: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” (Matt. 7:22). Will they, at that supreme examination, contend with God, the witness of hearts, in elementary words, as though ignorant of themselves? Since the letter therefore tends toward absurdity, we must observe what meaning reveals itself in these words. It will not be what the discerning spirit then says or thinks, but what can be considered by a person in the present who is astonished by the great virtues attributed to hypocrites, or what can be felt by those hypocrites who seek the praise of people blinded by them and believe that what people celebrate about them is established before God. Hence the words: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord!” (Amos 5:18). The blind person hopes for rewards which, deceived by the flatteries of the wretched, he judges himself worthy to receive.

Thus those who are in hell “repent within themselves,” since through reflection upon themselves and through the example of their condemnation they compel others to repent when the excellence of the saints is considered. For if we understand that those who are punished in hell grieve because the Sun of Justice has not shone for them, then we must also understand the word of the Wise Man: “From the dead confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26); and the Psalm: “Who in hell will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6); and: “There is none in death who remembers you” (Prov. 18:3). “When the impious comes into the depth of evils [al., sins], he despises.” We obscure this through a perverse understanding. For where do the saints stand “in great steadfastness” (Wis. 5:1), if not amid the adversities of this life? Here the impious “took away their labors” (ibid.), when they said that they labored so greatly for God in vain. Let us therefore weigh similar passages in Scripture; otherwise many contradictory statements will stand against one another.

## BOOK ONE: ON THE SAINTS AND THEIR RELICS

[Col. 0611]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0611C]

If it is wrong to err about the condition of the general resurrection of all, it is much more perverse to take anything away from the very Head who rises again. Since the efficacy of this entire hope depends upon his example, the whole consequence of this promise is undoubtedly weakened if the one who made the promise should falter in the ability to accomplish it, or if anything that was promised should in any way be nullified in him. For when the one who promises does not fulfill his promises, he is either accused of falsehood or shows himself less able to do what he had said he would do for others. Therefore, since it is horrible even to conceive of God in this way, let no one attribute to himself under the name of piety what is most demonstrably impious according to every rational consideration and what answers to an insult against the faith of all.

### Whoever falsely attributes something to the Church dishonors it

If they claim for themselves, on account of the singular excellence of their churches, the grounds by which the rights of our faith chiefly collapse, this honor must be regarded as utterly detestable: it gives birth to deviations and falls in the hopes of all. Certainly, if you were to load the right hand with so much gold that the strength of the whole body was weakened by that ornament, such beauty would be greatly useless, since it would hinder the whole in favor of a particular adornment—just as the frequent growth of shoots causes the destruction of a branch, indeed of the entire body of the tree.

### The different customs of the churches do not harm the Catholic faith

Moreover, even in those things that are held or taught ecclesiastically, such moderation has by now become firmly established that no one dares promulgate anything unless a more exacting judgment confirms it as consonant with Catholic agreement, whether by reason or by example. There are certain things that are held but not taught, such as customs concerning fasting or psalmody. Although these differ in practice, they nowhere disagree with the meaning of the faith; nor can one who acts differently be accused of being absent from the understanding of one who abstains or sings differently. Otherwise, anyone who maintained diversity in the frugality and duties of a similar faith could rightly be called a schismatic because of the singularity of his privilege [f., “because of faith through diversity”]. If, then, you sing something different and fast differently, it is neither suitable nor proper for you to proclaim or impose this upon others who are pursuing no lesser goods. Hear the Apostle: “He who eats, eats for the Lord; and he who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord” (Rom. 14:3). It is easy to make the same judgment about similar matters.

### Without baptism and the Eucharist the faith cannot subsist; their form is everywhere the same

There are, moreover, things that are both held and taught, such as the sacraments of baptism and of the Lord’s host. Since these are so common to Christianity that our faith cannot subsist without them, they are always held by unchanging authority, everywhere in the same manner, so that everywhere and always the same doctrine accompanies, precedes, and follows a form that is alike. I say “a form that is alike,” so that the discourse of those who teach may proceed in accordance with what is pronounced outwardly.

Yet there is this difference between the two: a Christian cannot be one without water or blood, whereas he can be without the Eucharist, provided that he remains steadfast in faith in it. This can be proved in the case of many martyrs and hermits. The former never received it; the latter received it once or very rarely, and thereafter, incorporating themselves into it through holy works, were sanctified in long solitude.

### At times faith without works is reckoned as righteousness

The same is true of the commandments: when other things are absent, faith is to be held and taught as sufficient for salvation. Hence the Apostle says: “To the one who does not work, faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4:4). Nevertheless, greater precedence is attributed to charity: it is placed before faith and hope; it alone is regarded as standing for all; it alone is proclaimed almost antonomastically as “the work”: “Direct the works of our hands over us” (Ps. 89:7). These are the common exercises of every good profession. And “direct the work of our hands” (ibid.) means: teach us better gifts, namely, the more excellent way. These things are both held and taught among us, and held by being taught.

Furthermore, there are certain things which, although they belong among what is supremely necessary to our salvation and are the matters under discussion, are not counted among those without which one cannot live rightly. Nevertheless, they are both held and preached in the churches, although many have lived and are living good lives without their use and presence. Such things include the corpses of the saints and relics—namely, objects that were used by them. These are held in reverence and honor by us, as examples and safeguards provided by them.

In their case, the only authentic principle that ought to be observed is this: only the person should be called a saint whom not opinion, but the certain tradition of antiquity or truthful writings, establishes as such. For how, if I may put it so, can someone be sanctified whose authoritative memory is nowhere known, much less one who is not confirmed by writings or by the manifest experience of miracles? I speak of writings effective for strengthening the case. There are indeed very many accounts concerning various saints through which their praise could rather have been made impious among unbelievers than in any way illuminated. For even when they relate what is true, they present it in such a ragged and pedestrian style—or, to use a poetic expression, in language crawling along the ground—and indeed bark it out so incoherently that, although the things themselves are not false, they are believed to be utterly false.

How could the discourse of such authors, with its most unworthy crudity, support a falsehood when it places even the truth itself in doubt? And whom do we think spared the infliction of this blemish when we see that not the lives, but rather the dirges, of certain apostles have been darkened by such great soot? The whole revolving wagon of these fables is worse than the screeching of any cart. What edification will it bring to the pious when it even supplies the impious with an incentive to blaspheme? What is the story of Thomas to be called except a din in the ears, a story against which Augustine objects not once but in many places? (Job 13:7.) (3) Did God, or their saints, perhaps need lies, in accordance with that passage of Job, so that they might speak deceit on his behalf? If the holy apostles themselves, who clung to the supreme Head like hair or a beard, were not free from such deceptions, and if our knowledge of them did not shine forth from the Gospels and from their own deeds, such fabrications would disturb the minds of some.

What shall I say about those who have gained renown through no other testimony and who, because they are thought to be celebrated in writings of any sort, are chiefly shrouded in darkness? What shall I do about those whose beginnings and middle are known to no one, and whose end—the subject of all their praise—is entirely unknown? Who will entreat them to help him, when he does not know whether they have any merit before God? Does not a person’s conscience suffer serious offense when he presents to God as an intercessor someone from whom he expects nothing great? Does he not blunt the edge of his prayer—or rather of his intention—when he does not know whether the one whom he invokes has anything in common with God?

Certainly, I have seen some people who, after having for a very long time regarded as a confessor a certain man brought, as they said, from Britain and considered a saint, suddenly changed their minds and celebrated him as a martyr. When I asked their reasons, they said nothing more worthy concerning the man’s martyrdom than that his confession had been omitted.

I testify before God that I read—and, with excessive disgust, reread before those who were present—the following passage: in the *Life of Samson*, a most renowned saint among the Franks and Britons, the reading calls a certain abbot Saint Pyro (4). When I was properly following the account of his end, thinking I would find a holy conclusion, I came upon the culmination of his sanctity: namely, that the man, drenched in drunkenness, fell into a well and was thereby killed.

(5) Nor has this escaped me: Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury among the English, later put a question to his successor Anselm, then abbot of Bec, concerning one of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0613D] Named Ælfheah.], who had been thrown into chains and was killed because he refused to redeem himself with money.

### Before anyone is invoked, his sanctity must be established

(6) What shall I say about those saints whose end is plainly evil, or whose end is hidden so that it is uncertain whether it was good or evil, or about whom there is doubt between the two? Merciful Jesus! What sort of saint is one whose end is acknowledged to be ambiguous? Before I pray to him, it is necessary for me to dispute the truth of his sanctity.

I shall dare to call it profane that men whose time, birth, and life, and even the day and character of their deaths, reside in the memory of no living person, occupy behind the sanctuaries of altars lofty thrones resembling the highest tribunals. Although the faithful honor them because of the name of sanctity, priests nevertheless—and let me say this with their pardon—do not judge rightly when they fail to correct and amend the common people, who are carried about by the wind of their own opinion.

For if no one is lawfully advanced to the highest ranks without testimony, such people will be marked with rash, indeed sacrilegious, titles and set before all mortals as eminent, although perhaps they have been banished to places of punishment or led away lost into Tartarus and, if they knew that it would profit them and had the means, would beg help from mortals together with that rich man.

### It belongs to the prelates of the churches to ensure that the people duly attend to the worship of the saints

(7) Let the bishops therefore look to this; let the guardians of God’s people look to it, so that they may provide for those entrusted to them. If they have zeal for God, let them be permitted to have zeal only according to knowledge, lest they sin by offering correctly but not dividing correctly.

If, according to the prophet, “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5:20), what greater perversity is there than to thrust such people into the sacred altars, whom it would perhaps have been appropriate to drive out from those very sacred precincts?

If those from whose bodies miracles flowed after death were not free in soul from torments, as we read—for experience has taught us that the righteous person is scarcely saved—what may we hope concerning those whose glory is supported by neither sight nor hearing, neither writings nor miracles? And certainly it is exceedingly difficult to believe in signs apart from those which a good end, continued from a good beginning, has produced.

### External signs are not indications of sanctity

These things are considered so ambiguous, if I may put it so, that they are said to furnish glory both to the right and to the left. The one who divided the Red Sea for the children of Israel also divided the Pamphylian Sea for Alexander the Great. Read Suetonius to learn how Vespasian lifted up a lame man by pressing upon him with the toe of his foot. There are also signs readily observed at the birth of powerful rulers, such as the aforementioned Alexander, Julius Caesar, and Octavian; and other signs preceded the deaths of Charles and of his son Louis and served as portents.

Thus in our own time we have often seen comets arise at the deaths of our own kings and of the kings of Lorraine or England, and at changes of kingdoms.

### Louis the Fat, or Louis VI, cures scrofula; this was denied to his father Philip, who was burdened with crimes. The English king does not possess this power.

What of the fact that we see our lord King Louis using a customary marvel? (8) I have seen crowds of those who suffered from scrofula around the neck or elsewhere on the body hasten to his touch, together with the sign of the cross. I remained beside him and even tried to restrain them. Yet, with his natural generosity, he gently marked them with the sign of the cross, extending a serene hand toward them with the utmost humility.

When his father Philip eagerly exercised the glory of this miracle, he lost it because of certain faults that intervened—I do not know what they were. I shall pass over how other kings conduct themselves in this matter; but I know that the English king does not dare to do such things at all.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0616B] **§ I. Signs and visions often serve the benefit not of those through whose ministry they occur, but of others**

It must therefore be understood that the gifts of signs are distributed in many ways. There are some through whom, as through channels, the same marvels are conveyed; and while these marvels serve the benefit of others, the people through whom they occur are themselves excluded from their benefit. This can be inferred with complete certainty from the speech of the ass, the vision of the angel, and the prophecy of Balaam (Num. 22:27), as well as from Caiaphas (John 11:51), because what sounded outwardly was entirely alien to them.

Thus we also see many things concerning the future foretold by people of every degree of merit who are dying, and much declared about the condition of the age to come. In the same way, we are accustomed to value the words of utterly innocent children, for concerning events involving themselves and others they often utter, as if through dullness, sayings full of foreknowledge. The following example will make this clear.

### A little child sees a priest celebrating the sacred mysteries holding a child in his hand in place of the host

Very recently, namely on the actual day of the past Easter celebration, when the same festival was being observed in the city of Soissons near us (9), a certain woman brought her own little child to church so that he might receive communion. When the time for consecrating the Eucharist approached (10), and the child, still ignorant of everything, was standing behind the priest in the presence of his mother, he saw, in the middle of the altar while the divine service was being performed, a child more beautiful than any other being raised between the priest’s hands.

As he watched this with childish curiosity—for what he sees does not permit him to remain silent—he cried out to his mother, within the hearing of the church: “Lady,” he said, “do you not see what a beautiful child the priest is holding upon the altar?” But when the mother looked, she saw nothing of this vision. A little later, when the priest lowered the sacrament after the elevation and covered it with a linen cloth, the child cried out again: “Look,” he said, “he is wrapping him in a white cloth.”

As he repeated these things before everyone who heard him, certain people of greater understanding observed that the child’s innocence was looking upon that beautiful child with one set of eyes, while with another he was attending to the material pall with which the intellectual reality was being wrapped.

Behold: the one who saw these things is being nourished for this world, and is not thought likely to attain the better life that follows in hope. Hence it is unquestionably known that this vision neither discloses the merit of the one who saw it nor increases his glory; it adds magnificence instead to the faith of those who heard it. And how can one be said to have seen it for his own benefit or glory when, being scarcely—or not at all—above the level of understanding, he is known barely to remember what he once saw?

### § II

There are also others for whom this occurs neither because of preceding merits nor according to the judgment of reason, but who, without regard to any zeal or labor, receive almost the whole glory of righteousness. This is evident in the case of the holy innocents, who, having suffered without contemplation either of God or of the reward, obtained as their reward whatever belongs to God. For it belongs to the potter’s power “to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. 9:21). He himself is the one who says: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will?” (Matt. 20:15). “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). Nor is an example from our own time lacking in this matter.

### An acolyte addresses an image, which itself gives him a reply

Near the town of Saint-Quentin, a certain little boy had likewise been brought by his parents’ decision into the clergy; and, unless I am mistaken, he had already entered the rank of acolyte. On a certain solemn day, at the hour of sacrifice, he stood before the front of the apse—that is, between the altar and the apse—to perform his service. He was carrying the paten with the host that was to be offered.

An image made of plaster projected from the front of the screen, presenting the appearance of the crucified Lord. It stood not far from the tomb of the martyr Quintinus. As the boy stood before the image and carried the offering, he said to it, in both childish words and childish understanding: “Lord, do you want some of my bread?” The image deigned to answer him with complete clarity: “I,” it said, “will soon give you some of my bread.”

After hearing these words, the boy was seized by illness, and within a very few days, stripped of the little body he had briefly inhabited, he became possessed of the heavenly robe. He was buried before the image that had promised this to him.

I learned this from the clergy of that church, who reported it, and, with the tomb bearing witness, I saw and believed the event. I heard the first account I related from the lord archbishop of Reims, Ralph. The clergy and people of Soissons and Laon also bear witness to it.

Seneca says in his books *On Benefits*: “For whoever returns a favor equivalent to another’s generosity is equal to merchants; but whoever gives freely imitates God.” I shall certainly say without hesitation that it is much more natural for God to bestow grace than to respond to anyone’s merit.

### III

There are also some whose faith earns much from divine mercy, so that he whose food is to do the will of his Father (John 4:34) attributes the efficacy of their salvation especially to those whom he finds bolder in faith in seeking what they have undertaken. Hence his familiar saying to many is: “Your faith has saved you” (Mark 10:52). This means: “The persistence of your faith pleases me so greatly that, in my place, your health depends upon you yourselves.” He also demonstrated this in a new example in our own times.

### A girl who, after indulging in pleasures and confessing her sins, deserved by her faith to be rescued from the greatest danger to her life

Near the borders, if I am not mistaken, of the provinces of Cambrai and Ader, a young man and a girl, closely related by blood, lived in the countryside under the same roof. As constant companionship produced familiarity, and familiarity gave boldness to the foolishness that had arisen, shameless incest suddenly violated their ill-guarded relationship. No sooner had the girl perceived that she had conceived from the intercourse than the two began to lament continually to one another, with murmuring and tears, fearing the disgrace of their family and the eyes of their relatives.

They therefore decided to leave their native soil. But the girl, deeply fearful of her own guilt, hurried to a priest and confessed her deed with bitter sorrow. After this, both of them left the countryside by night, intending to withdraw to a foreign region. As they traveled beyond those fields, they came upon the edge of a long-abandoned well, accessible from the road.

The young man said: “Let us sit down, so that by resting upon the rim of the well you may ease the heaviness of your womb.” She believed his deceit; and when she had sat down beside the wicked and foolish young man, the villain thrust her from his breast and hurled her into the well.

When, shortly afterward, she recovered her senses and groaned over the treachery of so great a fall, he began to call down to her, as though asking whether she was alive. Hearing the murmuring of her plaintive voice and realizing that she was alive, he began gradually to throw stones down at her. The little woman immediately fell silent and withdrew into a corner of the well—not so much to rest there as to escape the stony rain. When he could hear neither her breathing nor even any movement from her, he supposed that she had died no less from the fall than from the blows of the stones.

He therefore departed and returned to his own home, happier because of his crime. As for the girl, apart from the fact that she had left without a companion, there was little unusual in the story.

Therefore, settled in the hollow of that cavern, when in utter despair she no longer awaited food from God himself, she felt a drop of liquid fall repeatedly from the clod that hung over her head. Placing her mouth beneath it, she was refreshed by that tiny trickle—enough, one might say, to equal the resources of Sardanapalus. What need is there to delay? She spent almost forty days there, sustained by no other nourishment than the drop we have mentioned. Meanwhile, on a certain day before the fortieth, swineherds and shepherds were driving their animals through the fields, which provided pasture on every side, near the well. As they moved about those places, they heard from the depths the voice of someone grunting there. Lowering their heads over the mouth of the well, they perceived from the voice that some human being was groaning within. When they called out repeatedly, they recognized that it was a woman. They asked who she was; and with a great outburst of shouting she proclaimed both who she was and whose family she belonged to.

On hearing this, the shepherds hastened to the nearby village of Pegasca and announced that they had found the woman whom almost everyone believed either to have perished miserably or to have gone into exile. Immediately the rustic population rushed there; a crowd of women hastened forth. Neither tenderness for their children nor the sluggishness imposed by old age held anyone back: everyone hurried as quickly as possible. Someone was also sent to raise the woman from the well with ropes and display her to the waiting crowds. When she had been brought up and the event of so great a salvation had been reported, the fame of the miracle did not confine itself to that countryside, but spread into distant regions—a deed wholly unfamiliar to that age.

Behold what faith accomplished in repentance. Behold what perseverance accomplished in the intention to correct one’s life. A person has faith in repentance who, after receiving the grace of confession, never loses confidence in pardon because of the assurance arising from the amendment he has undertaken. This, then, is the faith that the Apostle commends with such repeated emphasis in almost all the patriarchs mentioned above, so that he even counts Rahab and Jephthah among them (Hebr. XI, 31–32), although they have circumstances in their lives far more obscure than those of the others whose faith he so greatly praises.

Yet the principal feature of the little woman’s faith, as it seems to me, was this: her faithful and undaunted appeal to God in her need. Nevertheless, such faith is so powerful with God that heavenly compassion cannot refuse assistance even to those whose correction will in no way follow. Hence the prophets repeatedly press this upon him: “Do not delay for your own sake,” they say (Dan. IX, 19); and, “For the honor of your name, deliver us” (Ps. LXXVIII, 9). Therefore I shall say with complete certainty that God, who is compassion, cannot deny himself (II Tim. II, 13), and that he assists even those who will become alienated from him more promptly than the just: he tests the just for their salvation, while granting to the others what they seek more quickly, for their own judgment.

§ IV. Concerning Erlebald, dean of Cambrai, distinguished for holiness and learning.—There are, finally, others who do not deserve sudden honors for faith alone, but earn modern and heavenly glory through the long duration of holy labor. In the Church of Cambrai, about two years ago, there was a dean who had also been the chief custodian of the church. His name was Erlebald. In many sermons that he preached to the people throughout the surrounding region, in order to demonstrate the fruit of true confession, he used to relate the same example that we have just reported.

He chastised his own body beneath the heavy burden of strict abstinence and wasted away in the perpetual filth of a hair shirt, in which he scarcely ever had any cleanliness. In it such a swarm of vermin bred and multiplied that it was astonishing how human flesh could endure it, since he never went without it—not even in bed. He never used a mattress, but had a bench, almost without any support or bedding, for his bed; and he never lay down naked.

When he was approaching the end of this life, he began to be gravely harassed in spirit by demons and dragged about by them as if through muddy channels. When those who visited him asked the cause of this suffering, he said that the demons chiefly reproached him for not having exercised complete discipline over the clergy entrusted to him.

After his death, when he had appeared in a favorable form to many people, and especially to the bishop, the bishop asked him in this manner how he was being treated. He replied:

“For the past thirty days,” he said, “I have been punished each day by the blows of scourges.”

The bishop asked him: “And, my lord, for what reason?”

“It is remarkable that you have asked this,” he replied, “when you know that a human being, even though holy, is subject, willingly or unwillingly, to so many falls through weakness. But you ought also to have considered the matters that you confessed both to God and to me, so that you might be corrected, as you had promised me. Therefore do not delay being corrected, because it is good for you to do so.”

His end had come, then, on the Nativity of the Lord.

When this vision and the other visions had subsequently been made public, and when, in accordance with their sequence and with the piety of his life, everyone had come to believe everything about him with good hope, Easter had already passed. Behold, in the monastery of Brotburg, which is a place of great religious devotion for holy virgins, there were two young women of outstanding character. When one of them died before the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the other summoned her companion and bound her by many entreaties that, once she had laid aside the flesh, if God permitted her spirit to do so, she would return to her and tell her what good or evil was happening to her. For they had bound themselves to one another by such great mutual affection, and while they were alive had each been aware of all the other’s affairs, that they did not wish death to separate them entirely.

Thus, several days after the girl’s death and after the feast of Easter, when the surviving young woman had gone to the dormitory for some purpose or other, behold, her most loving companion suddenly stood before her, displaying nothing funereal or dreadful, but shining with an appearance most pleasing to the senses. The living girl was overcome with boundless astonishment, yet, with hesitant voice, asked her how she was faring.

“I am well,” she said. “For on the day of the holy Resurrection just celebrated, Erlebald, dean of Cambrai, and I were received into the presence of almighty God amid the joy of an immense heavenly multitude.”

She spoke and departed; but the one so quickly deprived of her presence was immediately overwhelmed by excessive grief. This man, in addition to the priesthood with which he shone, was rich in knowledge of Scripture and was very closely connected with me in friendship. As I ought, I rejoice in his supreme honor; may I now be found pleasing to him. This active faith deserved its reward, having made God its debtor through the exchange of devout labor.

When I had heard this from my lord Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, almost as many witnesses from the surrounding region subsequently followed who sounded in complete agreement about this blessed man as I can no longer enumerate from memory.

§ V. Just as the true deeds of the saints redound to God’s honor, so false ones redound to disgrace.—But since I have related these signs not so much because of their novelty as in order to explain the diversity of the causes themselves, I think I should add this: just as what is evident and indubitable ought to be embraced with all the heart, so things adorned with some false embellishment—things not done but fabricated—ought to be punished with dreadful condemnation. For whoever attributes to God what he has not even imagined compels God, insofar as he can, to lie. If someone accused me, a mere little man, of some falsehood, or charged me with having done what I had not done, it would fill me with great horror and hatred. What, then, could be more deadly, desperate, or damnable than to stain God himself, the fountain of all purity, by the mere ambition of a most filthy will?

A dead boy is imprudently venerated as a saint.—Certainly I saw—and I am ashamed to report it—that a certain ordinary boy, said to have been the armed attendant of some soldier, died on Good Friday, two days before Easter, in a village near Beauvais. He belonged, moreover, to a certain very renowned abbot. Gratuitous sanctity began to be attributed to the dead boy on account of the sacred day on which he had died. When the peasants, eager for novelty, had celebrated this, offerings and candles were suddenly carried to his tomb from all the neighboring rural districts. What more need be said? A tomb was built over him, and the place was enclosed by a constructed house. From the very borders of Britain, bands of peasants—and no groups of nobles—came on pilgrimage to him.

That most wise abbot saw these things, together with his religious monks, and, charmed by the multitude bringing gifts, tolerated fabricated miracles as though they had actually occurred. Thus, in the avaricious hearts of the profane crowd, fictitious deafnesses, feigned madnesses, fingers deliberately bent back toward the palm, and twisted footprints beneath the buttocks could all be accepted. What does the modest and wise man do when, while presenting himself as a supporter of such things, he gives precedence to a purpose of holiness?

We often see such things worn away by gossip, ridiculous processions of biers being carried about, and, through the lies of those whom Jerome calls “bawlers” who declaim in their frenzy, we see the depths of another person’s purse stripped bare each day. We are shaken by their immense knavery and swept along by their excessive flattery of divine things, so that, according to the teacher mentioned above, they surpass buffoons, gluttons, and lapdogs in their greedy licking, and outdo crows and magpies in their importunate chatter.

§ VI. What was done concerning false relics in Guibert’s own presence.—But why should we add this crime to the list unless we introduce something specific for condemning the error? A certain very famous church was conducting such processions and, by employing a spokesman to solicit gain, was seeking to repair its losses. When he had swollen beyond measure in his speech about the church’s relics, he brought out a reliquary and said:

“I myself was present. Know,” he said, “that inside this little box there is a piece of that bread which the Lord chewed with his own teeth. Although you may believe this only with difficulty, behold this nobleman”—and by this he meant me—“whom you testify to be highly learned in letters. If necessary, he will rise as a witness to my statement.”

I confess that I blushed when I heard this. If I had not been restrained by the presence of those whom he appeared to have as his authorities, I ought to have exposed him as a falsifier—acting, as I should, out of respect for their good faith rather than for the speaker himself. What shall I say? Not even monks, let alone clerics, restrain themselves from this disgraceful profit, so that, even while I am listening, they proclaim heretical claims concerning matters of our faith. For, in accordance with that saying of Boethius: “I would rightly be judged insane if I were to quarrel with the insane.”

# CHAPTER III

§ I. Who should be considered enrolled in ecclesiastical registers.—But so that the matter before us may be examined more freely, we must first discuss those who are called saints. Certainly, since we regard the apostles as saints, and those whom the Church has safely approved as martyrs, a later judgment may be passed concerning confessors.

Martyrs, plainly, even if written testimony is silent, have been exalted by the sole privilege of their blood; and one does not inquire what life preceded martyrdom, since blood itself is sufficient to erase the crimes of the most ancient offenses. Good Jesus! Why should this not be so, when punishment itself is capable of providing everything necessary for glory once sins have been abolished? For punishment, just as before baptism, so also after baptism, wipes away sins and performs the office of washing and salvation—indeed, it produces the most certain glorification.

I speak of punishment preceded by a thoroughly just cause. Hence the canons prescribe (Council of Elvira, canon 60) that if someone is found destroying idols and happens to be killed for this very act, he is not to be regarded as a martyr for such a death. Certainly, the cause here appears good; but what if the intention behind the cause is sometimes corrupted? The Donatists suffered things no less severe than martyrs, but because they were exiles from charity, they suffered in vain. The remaining Manichaeans were once burned at Soissons through the zeal of God’s people; but because they were alienated from a just cause, they brought harm only upon themselves through their condemned bodies. I have spoken at greater length about these matters in the books of my *Monodies*.

Guibert published a book of *Monodies*.—If, then, judgment is pronounced with such uncertainty concerning the sanction of a martyr, what judgment should be made concerning confessors, whose end is at times less certain? If the judgment of the entire Church agrees concerning Martin, Remigius, and others like them, what shall I say about those whom the common people create every day as rivals of the men mentioned above, throughout villages and towns? When some people saw that others possessed great patrons, they too wanted whatever kind they could obtain, and made them their own. Thus, when poets had first produced distinguished little works, afterward, driven by rivalry with them, crowds of idle people—“learned and unlearned alike,” as Horace says—“wrote poems everywhere.”

The ancient discoverers of the arts, and those who led golden ages in their own times, were raised to the rank of gods and goddesses. Later generations accumulated such a multitude of deities that their successors, abolishing some, separated others and called them the chosen gods. The Samaritans, after the Jews had been deported to Babylon, manufactured gods for themselves: “Each nation,” it says, “made its own god” (IV Kings XVII, 29). The Babylonians made Succoth-benoth for themselves, the Cuthites Nergal, and others made other gods.

Saint Gregory states (Pastoral Care, part II, chapter 11, beginning) that when someone who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the angered person’s mind is provoked to something worse. Yet everyone denies that they have chosen such displeasing patrons.

Whoever prays to someone he does not know to be a saint sins.—Let them tell me, then, how they suppose that person can act as their patron when they are ignorant of everything that must be known about him. Nowhere will you find anything written about him except his name. Meanwhile, while the clergy remain silent, old women and troops of worthless little women invent stories about such patrons and sing them after the *insubuli* and at the *litiatoria*. If anyone refutes their assertions, they attack in defense of them not only with insults but with the rays of their distaffs.

Since no trace remains from which one might even form a suspicion of what sort these patrons were, who except someone utterly mad would summon them to intercede on his behalf? And what value does that prayer have when complete uncertainty concerning the one whom the petitioner presents to God on his behalf continually gnaws at the petitioner’s mind? What benefit, I ask, can come from a prayer that is never without sin? For if you pray to one whom you do not know to be a saint, you sin precisely in the matter through which you ought to obtain pardon, because you do not rightly divide your offering even while offering it rightly.

In this very respect, when you pray, you do not placate God at all; but while you distrust your petition, you provoke him. For it is an insult to the one to whom the intercessor is directed that the intercessor is unknown. And how can someone intercede for you when you regard him with suspicion? If you do not think well of him, what do you believe you will deserve from him? Ambrose says in one place: “The one to whom I am preparing to entrust myself must stand above me.”

If, then, you are altogether uncertain about someone’s condition, is it not utter madness to ask such a person for help? If you do not know whether he is better than you, why do you ask that he stand before God on your behalf? Consider the Lord commending the merit of faith to the point of moving a mountain and openly forbidding hesitation of heart (Matt. XXI, 21). It is as though he said: If you propose something great, whatever it may be, and hesitate even a little, you lose it. It is much more tolerable for each person to distrust his own merit than to despair of the one on whom his hope before God depends—namely, his patron. For because you attribute less to yourself, you employ him; and you certainly know that if your interpreter is convicted of falsehood, you will lose whatever you might have obtained.

The glorification of the body of the Blessed Virgin cannot be asserted by clear arguments; yet it would be impious to believe that the Son left it subject to corruption. Reason suggests that she was assumed into heaven.—But why should I linger long over these matters, when there is such modesty in the mouth of the entire holy Church [10*] that it does not even dare to say that the body of the Lord’s Mother was glorified through resurrection, precisely because it cannot prove this by necessary arguments?

That vessel which, after the Son, was more excellent than every creature, which brought forth the Lord of the majesty of all things—something that had never been permitted to any creature, not even to the angelic nature—to believe that he left it unrewarded and dishonored, exposed to corruption, would be impious. This is especially so because, being bound to return to his glorified body what it had received from its mother, from whose body it derived what it is, he ought to do the same for her maternal body. Yet we do not dare to say outright that she was resurrected, for no other reason than that we cannot affirm it by probable indications.

Although in other discussions of sacred Scripture reason alone may sometimes be sufficient, and reasoning supported by the Scriptures may contain examples within itself, here reason may indeed bring together from every side the most suitable arguments by which she would be shown to have been raised bodily in her entirety. But because clear proofs are lacking, we may silently believe whatever is most glorious concerning her, yet we are by no means able to approve it publicly.

Reason plainly seems, beyond doubt, to offer evident support for this: since many bodies of various saints are believed to have risen with her Son, how could she—whose flesh is none other than the Son’s flesh, especially since at his conception she knew no generative agency of a father except that of the Holy Spirit—have remained under the laws of the ancient curse in the dust of the earth? She bore, by singular election, the author of blessing. If I may say so, the Son’s flesh could not remain undiminished if he left his Mother’s flesh to the common lot and granted to foreign flesh a privilege that he denied to his Mother, his own true flesh. We are not forbidden to hold this inwardly; yet because supporting testimonies are not available, we are forbidden to assert it.

The author refuses to write uncertain and unknown deeds of the saints.—If we cannot teach the things stated above concerning her whose glory no creature is capable of measuring, what else should we do concerning those whose salvation or destruction is uncertain except impose perpetual silence? Moreover, certain writings about particular people exist that are much worse than nursery tales and should not even be forced upon the ears of swineherds.

Certainly, since many people attribute the greatest antiquity to their saints, they now demand that their lives be written. This has often been requested of me. Yet I am mistaken even in matters that lie before my eyes; and concerning things that no one has ever seen, what truth can I profess? If I were to repeat what I have heard said—and I have even been asked to speak in praise of people so ignoble, and indeed to declaim publicly before the people—then both I, if I said what was requested, and those who urged me to say such things, would equally deserve public branding.

§ II. Concerning the relics of the saints about which there is absolutely no doubt. The monks of Constantinople and Angers testify that they possess the head of Saint John the Baptist.—But leaving aside those whom their own authority deprives of authority, let us turn to those whom certainty of faith follows. Yet even concerning these there is boundless error. One person claims to possess this relic, and another claims to possess the same one. For example [11], when the monks of Constantinople say that they possess the head of the Lord’s Baptist, the monks of Angers testify that they possess the same head. What could be more ridiculous to say about so great a man than that both groups claim that he has two heads?

But let us set aside the jokes and attend to serious matters. Since it is clear that something which could nowhere have been doubled cannot be possessed by both groups, it is evident that either the one party or the other has succumbed to extensive falsehood. If, in a matter wholly devoted to piety, they contend with one another through mutual arrogance and falsehood, they are acting demonically in place of divinely. Thus each side, deceived and deceiving, improperly venerates precisely the thing of which it boasts. And if what they venerate is something unworthy, behold how great a danger is imposed upon the entire succession of those who obey it. Even if it is the relic of some saint rather than of John the Baptist, it remains no small evil of falsehood.

No evident testimony exists in the Church of Amiens for the presence of Saint Firmin’s body; rather, such testimony is found in the monastery of Saint-Denis.—What shall I say about the head of John, when I hear the same sort of claims daily concerning countless bodies of saints? [12] My predecessor, the bishop of Amiens, once believed that he was carrying the body of the martyr Firmin from one shrine to another. But he found no label there, not even the testimony of a single letter, identifying who lay within. I report what I heard from the bishop of Arras and from the bishop of Amiens himself.

For this reason the bishop of the city immediately inscribed on a sheet of lead that Firmin, martyr and bishop of the people of Amiens, had been buried there. Before long, however, the same claim began to be made in the monastery of Saint-Denis. When the body was being lifted from there in a more splendid coffin prepared by the abbot, and the head was removed along with the limbs, a little membrane was found in the martyr’s nostrils, on which it was stated that he was Firmin, martyr of Amiens.

Since the people of Amiens have nothing in this important matter to support their claim, while the others on the opposite side possess at least some sort of testimony, let reason, I ask, sit in judgment over everyone’s case. Should not whatever has been written on the leaden sheet by the lord bishop rightly be annulled, since that writing provides absolutely no testimony? Certainly, the men of Saint-Denis, however imperfectly they may mutter, have at least the support of some written letters.

Those, therefore, who venerate what they do not know, even if it is something holy, are never free from great danger. In another situation, they are guilty of enormous sacrilege. For what is more sacrilegious than to cultivate as divine something that is not divine? Whatever pertains to God is divine. And what belongs more to God than those who are one body with God?

§ III. In place of Saint Exuperius, the body of a peasant named Exuperius is substituted.—Listen to an account that illuminates our complaints and enables judgment concerning the matters just mentioned.

Odo, a certain bishop of Bayeux, natural son of Count Robert of the Normans and natural brother of William the Elder, king of the English, was exceedingly eager to recover Saint Exuperius, his predecessor, who was honored with the greatest devotion in the fortress of Courbeil. He gave the sacristan of the church over which he presided a hundred pounds of denarii so that he might receive the saint from him. But the sacristan, wickedly advised, dug up the tomb of a certain peasant named Exuperius, taking advantage of the name, and brought the body to the bishop.

The bishop asked whether what he had brought was the body of Saint Exuperius or not, and even demanded an oath from him. “I shall affirm this to you under oath,” he said, “that it is the body of Exuperius; but I shall never swear to its sanctity, since this name is attributed to many people whose standing is far removed from sainthood.”

Thus, in this way, the bishop was deceived by the thief and remained at peace. But the custodian’s commercial transaction concerning the town’s patron became known to the townspeople. When they summoned him, he replied: “Examine again the signs of his bier, and unless you find them undamaged, I shall pay the penalty.”

Behold how great a disgrace to the whole of religion was produced by the bishop’s purchase, when this rustic Exuperius was advanced so profanely and brought to the sacred altar of God into which he had been intruded—a contagion perhaps never destined to cease. [13] So many similar events everywhere present themselves to my memory that I would lack both time and strength to report them, especially since frauds are committed not only concerning entire bodies but in equally great measure concerning limbs and fragments of limbs [14], when ordinary bones are distributed for sale as relics of saints.

This is plainly done by those who, according to the Apostle, “consider piety a means of gain” (I Tim. VI, 5), turning into refuse for their purses what, if they had wisdom, would be useful to the salvation of their souls.

# CHAPTER IV

§ I. The bodies of deceased saints ought not to be enclosed in gold or silver.—But all these things arise from a perverse root, namely, that the same bodies are deprived of what the whole human race ought to receive according to the common lot of nature.
