If it is absolutely certain that human beings originate from the earth and, once the debt of death has been paid, fall back into it according to the laws of the first condemnation—especially since it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go”—then, in my judgment, God has said neither to anyone in the present nor to anyone in the future: “You are gold or silver, and into gold or silver you shall go.”

Why, I ask, is a human being torn away from his nature, indeed from God’s command, so that what belongs conditionally to no one is inserted into golden or silver shells?

If a wise man knew of other receptacles for human bodies besides the earth, he would not say: “A heavy yoke has been placed upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until they return to the mother of all” (Eccli. XL, 1). Notice how elegantly he says “their mother” and “the mother of all.” If she is called my mother because she provided the chamber of the womb—and this chamber is immutable, incapable of alteration—then more appropriately she is also the mother who gave mortals the material of being. Indeed, she is more than a mother, because, unlike ordinary mothers, she receives us back a second time.

Whatever arrangements of sarcophagi you may wish to use to remove yourself from contact with the earth, whether you wish it or not, you become earth. And what dignity is there in enclosing someone in gold or silver when the Son of God was shut in by a most worthless stone? This practice is not known to have been adopted even by the proudest kings from the beginning of the ages, and my memory supplies not a single example of it. Although they immersed countless treasures in tombs, I do not remember ever having read that they replaced pure marble with golden or silver coffins.

What kind of rivalry with God is this—though not according to knowledge (Rom. X, 2)—that, in our time, a faith producing no fruit but generating much indecency should invent what we know to have been offered by no religion and nowhere by any wealth from the beginning of the world?

Guibert does not approve of bodies of saints being dug from their tombs.—Certainly, if the bodies of saints had preserved their proper places—their tombs—in accordance with nature’s due, the errors I have just listed would have been absent. For once they are dug from their tombs, carried here and there limb by limb, and the pretext of piety provides an occasion for their circulation, wickedness begins to twist the uprightness of the original intention, so that almost every practice formerly performed simply becomes corrupted by greed.

If the burial of the dead is attributed to Tobias as a merit of such magnitude that Raphael himself specially praises it among the other benefits of his humanity and says that it was carried most pleasingly before God’s eyes (Tob. XII, 12–13), what impiety and guilt must we suppose belongs to someone who deprives bodies of the debt owed by nature and harasses them on any trivial pretext?

And what occasion is there—not merely more trivial, but more importunate—than to place the disciple before the teacher? The former is thrust into stone, while the latter is enclosed in gold; the former is scarcely wrapped in a fine linen cloth, while the latter is girded with cloaks, silks, or woven gold.

[17] In the presence of the most glorious Pope Gregory, those who unknowingly looked upon the bodies of the Apostle Paul and the martyr Lawrence were punished with the greatest severity. What judgment should be pronounced concerning those whose only motive is avarice, and who cause the bodies of saints to be dispersed restlessly—or, to put it this way, cause them to be displayed daily solely for the bringing in of offerings?

They customarily cover the bare bones of saints with ivory or silver boxes and then uncover them at a fixed time and hour when payment is offered. The spirit of Samuel, which, because it possessed the natural vigor of a spirit, complained through the witch that it was being disturbed by being summoned (I Sam. XXVIII, 15); should not material bones, exposed to dispersal here and there, complain justly, if they could?

Jacob and Joseph give such strict commands concerning their burials (Gen. XLVII, 30; L, 24), and all the saints prepare tombs for themselves and arrange for their bones to be carried back to their native soil. They seem almost to fear being buried outside their own house—that is, among their own family and kinsmen—as though this were nearly a condemnation. What else does this indicate except that they regard with the utmost seriousness the bodies that are to be transformed for the glory of the resurrection?

If no one—that is, no rational person—hates his own flesh (Eph. V, 29), but supplies it with the food and drink required by daily need, how much more deeply should he cherish that body in which no luxury mingles with necessity, as it sometimes does in the taking of food, and which ought, even amid the sumptuous preparation of this sad ministry, as the poet says, to build up and extend hope toward the state of a better life, where, freed from the winter of the world and safe from the rain of present disturbances, it may await the voice of the archangel commanding it to rise?

If the Apostle calls such people “those who sleep” (I Thess. IV, 12), I consider it impious to disturb them, especially since in this very rest they await no one else who might compel them to awaken except the one who makes the living rise from the dead.

Let each person say what he thinks. I shall state confidently that it was never pleasing either to God or to the saints themselves that the tomb of any one of them should have been opened or his little body cut into pieces. Among the pagans, in view of the complete poverty of human concern, the offices of embalmers and grave-diggers were generally performed, as were those of the common bier; and, of course, their hope perished along with the body. Yet we dig up the graves and divide the limbs of those whom we have learned, through many proofs, to be angered by such disturbance.

Gregory plainly, when the head of the Apostle Paul was requested from Augusta, if I am not mistaken, Tiberia, replied that he absolutely did not dare to do this, invoking the punishment mentioned above concerning those who had discovered the bodies.

Edmund, a king and martyr of no small renown among the English, exists. I wish that the other saints would imitate his zeal in protecting his body. Remaining until now in a state very like sleep, he allows no one to see or touch him.

In our own age, to say nothing of what is read in the account of his passion [20], a certain abbot of that place, excessively curious to know whether, as was commonly said, his head had been reunited to his body after its beheading, attempted to investigate this after preceding fasts, with the assistance of one of his monks. But that attempt was immediately punished by such a severe illness that afterward neither of them retained any useful power in his hands.

If everyone were permitted to remain quiet in his own tomb, all dispute over the exchange of bodies or sacred relics would fall silent. Neither group would say that it possessed one body, nor the other that it possessed the same body, if everyone’s monuments remained intact, as justice required. If all rested unmoved in the earth assigned to them, the frauds we have mentioned concerning their manifold distribution would not occur, nor would the unworthy occupy the places of the worthy.

§ II. Those who venerate the relics of one saint in place of another do not sin.—Some also ask whether, when one set of relics is honored in place of another and the relics are not those of the person they are thought to be, the worshippers should be considered to incur some harmful consequence.

I do not think so. When the Lord says of them, “that they may be one, just as we are one” (John XVII, 22), and when the entire body of the saints under Christ the head is, as it were, a single identity of body, and the spirit of one who clings to God is one with God, there is no error in venerating the bones of one saint in place of another, since they are recognized as fellow members in the body of their creator.

This seems consistent with the fact that the feast of the Four Crowned Martyrs is commemorated, by Roman authority, under the names of five other martyrs (8 November).

Whoever regards and venerates someone as a saint, though he is not one, receives the fruit of prayer before God.—But someone may perhaps ask whether God hears simple people when he is invoked through those who are not demonstrably saints.

The answer should be that, just as the person who asks God for something through one whose status he doubts provokes God, so the person who faithfully believes a non-saint to be a saint and prays through him pleases God.

For example, suppose someone thinks that almsgiving is a sin. If he knowingly gives alms, he certainly sins in the judgment of his conscience, even though the act he performs is truly good in another respect. In the same way, if someone regards as a saint a person whom he hears called a saint, although it is not established that he is one, and appeals to him wholeheartedly and according to faith, then before God, who is the cause and fruit of prayer, the petitioner’s entire intention is fixed. However much the mind may appear to err through simplicity concerning its intercessor, what is honored in the hope of good is never deprived of the reward of good.

For if you receive a prophet in the name of a prophet—that is, if he presents only the name, without the reality, of either a righteous person or a prophet—you will receive the reward and merit of a prophet or a righteous person (Matt. X, 4), whereas the man who merely assumes the name and appearance of either a righteous person or a prophet is deprived of that reward and merit.

Certainly, many people who are barely literate frequently make mistakes in their prayers, but the divine ear measures intentions rather than words. If, when you ought to say, “May he be present,” you say, “May the power of the Holy Spirit be absent from us, Lord,” this does not harm you if you pray with sobs. God is not concerned with grammar: no voice penetrates him; he attends to the heart.

**THE FIRST BOOK ENDS.**

**THE SECOND BOOK. Concerning the body of the Lord, divided into two parts—namely, the principal and the mystical.**

# CHAPTER ONE

Therefore, having brought these matters to a close as though they were the preface to our future discussion, let us place the precious stones of faithful speech upon the foundation that we laid at the beginning. Let us seek out the kernel of the most difficult question, proposed to me by many people, by grinding it and, as it were, breaking it open with our teeth. For this reason we exhausted the dense rubble of the preceding treatise, so that we might work more freely upon the knot—which, God willing, may be capable of being untied.

Having said thus far what ought to be thought and done concerning the relics of the saints, one matter has entirely been left over for our consideration: certain people in our vicinity claim to possess a tooth of the Savior, which perhaps, compelled by nature, he may have shed at the age of nine. Nor are there lacking others who say that they possess the excess of the navel, which is cut away from newborn children; there are also those who assert that they possess the Lord’s foreskin. Concerning this the great Origen says: “There were some who were not ashamed to write books about the Lord’s circumcision itself.”

Omitting, then, the two matters that follow, let us remain with the first chapter, which presses us more closely. Once this has been abolished, the remaining matters too will be emptied out more clearly. Even if it can be proved that this remained on earth from what was his own, I marvel at what substitute he did not wish to leave us in the figurative body—figurative, I say, which becomes a shadow according to its appearance, so that in efficacy of power it does not differ from the preceding truth. The preceding truth, however, is the personal truth itself, to which the signified thing is referred and identified. For what he handed down to be done in his memory represents the unquestionable presence of his own property.

Yet if this presence here were something other than the property itself, it would be no greater than the significance of a wedding ring in the possession of a wife. For, in memory of her husband, the ring would become a substitute for the husband. Thus the one, just as it preceded the other by being born of the Virgin and suffering on the cross after a short interval of time, supplied the causes for the other; and the other succeeded to its vicarious identity, so to speak, under its example.

Hence I call that first thing above all “truth,” from which the sacraments with which we are dealing flowed forth for our consideration. Whatever truth the thing sent down from the first under a figure may receive, the first nevertheless is principally true, since it supplies the cause for that which is derived from it. For that is without doubt both principal truth and properly called such in which nothing else is shadowed forth except what can be grasped by the senses and intellects of those who observe and handle it.

In the other, although every kind of truth must be present, it is nevertheless not principal, because it is bent away from what is principal and must always be referred back to that of which it is the likeness and relative counterpart.

[Col. 0630C] By “likeness” I mean not particularity but the figure presented by outward usage, since this whole thing is what its preceding reality is. Hence in the Psalm the principal Spirit is called Father (Psalm 50 [51]:14), not because, according to the divine essence, he is principal over the Son and the Holy Spirit, but because the origin of the Son and the Holy Spirit is derived from him.

Thus he who is called “principal” in the Psalm is nevertheless named last among the persons, since from his mouth the Son is placed first in the three names, so that the prophet clearly indicates that in that nature nothing is earlier and nothing later. Yet pleasant frivolity tries to posit something like origins among substances and subsistences, although neither seems capable of being comprehended in the divine essence, since, when we speak of divine matters, it is more fittingly judged that essence alone should be named. For when subsistence is said by some to be the origin of substance, let anyone who is carefully watchful consider how “to stand beneath” and “to subsist” can apply to God, since the capacity of the human mind and the liberty of human speech can say nothing about God more suitably than essence.

## CHAPTER II

### § I

Having said these things by way of digression, let us at last return to what was omitted. If that principal body, which supplied the material for the sacraments that followed, left a remnant of itself on earth, while one part was carried upward to heaven, what necessity was there for us in this life to be pledged to the mystery of another body, when it would have been entirely sufficient to rejoice in the remnant of his own flesh?

And certainly, without any sharpening of intellectual perception or any experience of contemplation, it lay before the eyes of our flesh to look upon and touch with our fingers the particles of the Lord’s flesh that I mentioned. There was no need, through the material of wine and bread—namely, things that appear—to exercise the substance of our faith, according to the Apostle (Hebrews 11:1).

For the mind is exercised greatly, and as though it goes out beyond the camp of its own dwelling, when it is taught to contemplate invisible things through the intention directed toward visible things. It is plainly gracious, and worthy of being desired with every surge of longing, to have before one’s eyes the very thing that is to be cultivated, without types and without the veils of figures; to burn for it in one’s inmost heart and embrace it with the arms of the heart.

Since God is not unaware that love for things seen and accessible to the senses settles more affectionately and clings more firmly in human judgment, it was never fitting that, although we are always able to delight in him as our own possession, we should be wearied rather than gladdened by his shadowy representation.

Since, then, that tiny remnant—if it can be called tiny, seeing that it outweighs the whole world—would have been sufficient for universal joy and the continuity of faith, why does the Lord Jesus once again give his flesh to mortals as a pledge in a figurative sacrifice?

I shall say confidently that he left a substitute body in memory of himself in vain, since he left on earth so many portions of himself as would have been sufficient to make mention of him. “Whenever you do this,” he says, “you shall do it in memory of me” (1 Corinthians 11:25).

I should like to know what sort of memory of himself he desires to be held, and why he introduces other things by which he might be celebrated more among his own people, when—not to speak of so many and such great portions—even a single particle, like an atom, of his body, which the Virgin conceived from the Holy Spirit, would suffice for the gathering together of the whole world.

It seems to me that he is saying something like this: “Since nothing remains on earth from which my memory may grow warm among you—for where nothing is supplied to your sensuality that may renew my presence and display it to your intellect—it is fitting that something of this kind should be made for you by me, whereby I may restore myself to you in place of myself, and diminish nothing of my presence among you, which you loved and still desire.” If you attend carefully, what else will the speech quoted above seem to proclaim?

Are there, then, two bodies appointed for us to impress this memory upon us? Does he not say to the apostles—but speaking against Judas alone—“You always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (John 12:8)?

But lest this be thought contrary to that promise, “I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), we must undoubtedly understand the former of spiritual protection, insofar as he is God, and the latter of bodily presence.

If the matter concerns this bodily presence, then the person who claims for himself his tooth, or navel, or what is read as having been circumcised, is plainly lying through and through. For the word “me” embraces whatever was ever humanly his.

If you deny that those particles are himself, perhaps you do not know that a part can be put for the whole and the whole for a part. It is obvious to everyone that not only Scripture speaks by synecdoche, but that even illiterate and ordinary people use this figure of speech.

If, by some accident, you injure your foot, hand, or the very end of your nail, and are asked what has happened to you, will you not immediately reply, “I have injured myself”? And what proportion does the nail constitute of the whole? If you do not deny that you have been injured when a very small part of you is shaken, then the word “me,” which admits that the whole cannot always be possessed by them, must be understood in the same sense.

If we customarily call friends—the halves of our souls—and blood relatives “our flesh,” when each of us says “me,” what else do we express than the whole that is in us and comes from us? Certainly, if you draw blood, cut hair, or trim a nail, and someone asks whose these things are, you would answer either that they are yours or that they came from you.

If a piece were cut from a field or from leather, no one except a madman would assert that what had been cut away was not from the field or from the leather.

### § II. How inequality of merits operates in the reception of Christ’s body

Listen further, before we proceed against you to narrower arguments, to what bears upon your position. The Lord himself says elsewhere: “Whoever eats me lives because of me” (John 6:58).

See how, just as we said above, “I am with you” (Matthew 28:20) and “You will not always have me” (John 12:8) have different meanings; so the first “me” signifies something different from the second.

The meaning is this: “Whoever eats what is outwardly mine—namely, my flesh and blood—lives because of that very thing which, by illuminating the inner person, gives him life.” Since it cannot literally happen that someone eats the whole of him unless the part is taken for the whole, this is readily accomplished according to the inner meaning, especially since the faith of the body is held in such a way that what is offered in small portions is held wholly in its smallest portions.

For just as it is read of the manna in Exodus: “The one who gathered more had nothing extra, and the one who prepared less had nothing lacking” (Exodus 16:18), but each received according to what he was able to eat, so this kind of sacrament is either diminished or increased according to the capacity of understanding in each person.

It is diminished according to the more obscure understanding of one’s own faith, although the sacrament’s usefulness is not thereby less; but it is increased according to the capacity of the faithful intellect, in which the equality of the sacred food for salvation remains the same as it does among the simple. For all, according to the measure of devotion granted by God, the sufficiency of so great a gift is in no respect defective.

In every material thing, greater and lesser are recognized because the quantities of bodies in different natures cannot possess equal dimensions, and what is contained in the enormous bulk of greater masses cannot at all be contained in the smallness of lesser ones.

In the mystical arrangement of this sacrifice, however, the measure is quite different, especially since, although there is a disparity in that distribution not unlike the disparity found among other quantities, nevertheless, according to the judgment of the inner eye, the person who takes everything that is consecrated there brings no more away from the altar than the person who receives an utterly tiny portion.

If you set many loaves upon the altar, do you suppose that each of them makes a separate body of the Lord, rather than that however great the number of hosts may be, they are reduced to one image of inner contemplation?

### Bread left in a pyx on the altar without the priest’s knowledge is not consecrated, because the intention of the one offering is required

This too must be noted, although it is less relevant to the subject, because I have learned that some have gone wrong in this very matter. Someone had left sacramental loaves in a pyx on the altar while the solemn rites were being performed, without the priest’s knowledge, and after the divine rite had been completed he discovered that they had remained there.

The case was brought before the judgment of the clergy who served that church. The conclusion of their ruling was that whatever was contained in the pyx which had remained on the altar during the sacred rites should be regarded as a completed sacrament and offered as the Eucharist to those who were to receive Communion.

Anyone who doubts that this was done most absurdly is dull-witted. For where no intention of the one praying or offering was directed—indeed, where there was not even memory or knowledge—how can it be believed that anything was consecrated?

Certainly, if something had been placed beneath the corporal cloth without the priest’s knowledge, or if a drop had been seen hanging in some part of the chalice after the mystery had been completed, beyond what he himself had set forth, no wise person would think that anything there pertained to the sacrament.

Nothing is done there except in that which the faith of the one making the petition touches; nor does anything become sacred from elsewhere except that alone to which the Lord’s word, which alone makes the sacrament, is joined.

What an unbeliever or catechumen does in the church after the Gospel, that is what bread placed there heedlessly does, or a drop accidentally hanging in some part of the chalice during the sacred rites.

### Whoever receives the Eucharist eats the whole Christ, that is, man and God

But setting these matters aside, let us return to what I had begun. “Whoever eats me,” he says, “lives because of me” (John 6:58).

If you understand Christ to be eaten in such a way that you believe him to pass, in that distribution, through limbs and fragments of limbs into the mouths of those receiving—so that, for example, one person receives a finger and another a part of a finger, and thus one proceeds through the individual parts of the body and again through fragments of the parts—then Christ’s word plainly does not agree with this interpretation.

When he says “me,” therefore, he signifies the totality of the substance that then existed, indeed that which existed from both natures. It is as though he said: “Whoever eats me insofar as I am human lives because of me insofar as I am God.”

For since he is God in two natures and from two natures, by one he gives life to what is mortal in us, and by the other he glorifies what is living in us.

This is why he gives his body and blood, which he hands over separately: so that what pertained to raising our bodily lowliness from natural afflictions might be introduced into our use through his body, which was given for us; and, according to what is read in Leviticus, “For the life of every flesh is in its blood” (Leviticus 17:14), so that through his blood he might cleanse inwardly the souls within us.

He shows this more clearly than daylight when, in presenting the body, he brings forward nothing other than: “This is my body, which will be given for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24). Yet this addition itself comes from the Apostle Paul.

With regard to the blood, he treats the matter more broadly, since he considers the soul more precious than the body. For he says that it is to be poured out both for those to whom he was speaking and for many, for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28).

If, then, the blood is offered for washing souls from sins, it is plainly demonstrated that no sin exists in souls except what is carried out by the desire and consent of those very souls. For just as a handle without iron accomplishes nothing, so the body, without the will of the soul, does not sin except through original sin.

If you still ask for examples, very similar ones are readily available. When John had said, “Many of the Jews believed in him,” he added, “But Jesus did not entrust himself to them” (John 2:23–24).

According to blessed Augustine, he does not entrust himself to them because, although they may believe, he entrusts the Eucharist of his body to no one except the baptized.

He also says elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John 12:44). Elsewhere too: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood” (John 6:54), and so forth.

## CHAPTER III

### § I. The remaining sacraments flow from the sacrament of the altar

Since, then, we have begun to speak of the Lord’s twofold body—namely, the true body, which above we called principal, from which these subsequent sacraments flowed, and the mystical body, which above we called figurative, in which Truth, purer than all light, is made under the shadow of bread and wine—before we undertake to discuss the tooth and relics of the Savior, we wish to examine, on the basis of the testimonies already given, the questions that commonly arise from this matter; yet I do not know whether we shall be able to define them.

The question is whether the body received from the altar bears the appearance of the living or the dead Lord. We know that, while living, he always had God dwelling personally in himself; and, even when dead, he did not lose the name of the Son of God, nor, together with the name, the reality itself.

Since, then, he asserts that he is to be eaten, he plainly seems to display the indivisible unity of his person. Yet personally he is God and man. What reason, then, would permit God and man to become edible? For the saying, “Whoever eats me” (John 6:58), seems necessarily to be understood in this way.

Yet more moderately he says there: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me” (ibid., 57). What controversy, then, ought to arise among sane-minded people from this?

If Christ’s soul had God dwelling within it, who would dare say that the mystery of that simple creature, which is purely employed in sacred rites, does not possess God as its life-giver? For he who was created from the Holy Spirit and virginal blood and manifested the indivisible person of God and man—ought he not to have infused into the substances of bread and wine, for the representation of himself to us, the most abundant entrance of the whole divinity?

### This sacrament removes all sins

If the water of baptism is called not merely “giving life through the Spirit” but also “life-giving,” will that nature, which is wholly changed into the divine, be thought lifeless because of the heavenly presence and the perfect indwelling of God?

That water, destined to rush through sewers, receives from the Spirit’s fertilizing power a temporal, indeed hourly, capacity for washing away sins; but this host, whether received for the salvation of enemies or presumptuously received by sinners and the unworthy, is always brought to the throne of glory and carried forward without end. I say confidently that it is received into the body from which it came, never to suffer any indignities or unworthy humiliations from the wicked.

For if it is received worthily by anyone, what else happens than that he is immediately made a member of that supreme Head through the flesh of the Head itself, which he receives? In what way, indeed, is anyone more transferred into the body of Jesus than by being joined to it through communion with this flesh and blood?

### Christ suffers no injury from unworthy recipients

Moreover, if you receive it wickedly, you certainly condemn yourself, because you receive sacred things sacrilegiously; and, insofar as it concerns you, by not discerning the Lord’s body (1 Corinthians 11:29), you despise and dishonor that very body. But an altogether impenetrable immunity protects that supreme excellence from your injuries.

### § II. Objection 1

Some wrongly thought that Christ was not received by such people; Guibert refutes them below.

Let no one be troubled if I seem to argue at somewhat greater length in the person of someone who thinks differently.

It is supposed, I say, that the sacrament is present—or, as it were, fails—according to the faith or faithlessness of those who receive it: in the case of one who receives it unfaithfully or contemptuously, insofar as, if he is a believer, he does not reverence or honor it, and insofar as, if he is an unbeliever, he disbelieves and rejects the Lord’s body in his mind.

According to my own judgment, therefore, I do not see how it can be applied to the souls or bodies of such people. For if, in the sacrificial canon, prayer is offered only for those who are orthodox, who worship the Catholic faith, and especially who are servants and handmaids of God, what merit would be sufficient for this purpose—let alone when it is added: “Whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is known”? What does the unbeliever have here? What does the rejected Christian have?

If that blood is poured out for you, O apostles, and for the other holy disciples, and for many, for the remission of sins—that is, for many, not for others than the elect—then any wicked person may indeed have the capacity to receive the sacrament outwardly, but he does not possess the reality of the sacrament.

They receive what is visible alone; but since they are not nourished by it toward everlasting life, what is invisible and beneficial is emptied out for them. And how can so great a thing be adapted to them, a thing given to those who receive it for eternal life, if they are irreparably prepared for the fire of Gehenna?

If a catechumen of good faith who has not yet been baptized is ordered to abstain from the divine sacrifices, how can they benefit someone who approaches them unbelievingly or shamelessly? Indeed, how can they not add to his condemnation?

When the evangelists were instructed to say, upon entering a house, “Peace to this house,” it was added: “If there is a son of peace there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke 10:5–6).

If the preacher’s benefit, bestowed fruitlessly upon the rejected, returns to the one whose merit it is, do you suppose that so great a gift is shut up in the foulest prison—in the body of one who receives it ineptly and irrationally and in the soul of one who handles it sordidly—and detained in so filthy a place?

If the Holy Spirit of discipline flees what is feigned and does not dwell in a body subject to sins, indeed is driven away by the arrival of iniquity (Wisdom 1:5), how will that divine substance, which through the fullness of the same Spirit and the identification of the Son’s person becomes the body of the Son of God, enter that most filthy heart whose dwelling cannot endure the uncleanness of the holy Spirit?

### § III. Objection 2

But someone may say: “If, then, whoever receives such a thing has neither the sacrament nor the reality of the sacrament, why is he subject to condemnation?”

To this I shall reply: if that bread contained nothing sacred in itself except ordinary bread, yet the person who received it, believing it to be the Lord’s body and shamelessly thrusting himself forward to take it, would undoubtedly fall under no lighter judgment than if it were the very body of Jesus.

It therefore seems to me profane to say that such great dignity—which in an improper place brings no benefit, but rather the causes of every curse and of this wicked betrayal—is condemned by such an intrusion. It in no way contributes to its honor that this grace, which nourishes all purity, should be overwhelmed by the contagions of a shameful conscience and that the wretched man should be punished under this presumption.

### § IV. Objection 3

Do you suppose that, if an unbeliever receives it, it is the Lord’s body? And how is it the Lord’s body for one who receives it in mockery or ignorance, when he has no faith concerning the mystery itself?

Even if it is presumed by a child or by any senseless person who cannot discern whether it is a sacrament, is such a person charged with having insolently received the Lord’s body? I do not agree at all.

I shall say, without prejudice to a better opinion, that this body, whether rightly or wrongly received, ought to be imputed to no one except one who was first able to recognize, at least in part, its faith.

Certainly no one dares to impute to natural fools or to those who have fallen into madness, for condemnation, even the gravest sins that they commit in dementia and foolishness; nor should anyone condemn as sinful a person who does not perpetrate evil with a conscience capable of discerning it.

It is plainly beyond doubt that there have been countless men of episcopal and of the second order who celebrated these sacred rites for the people and nevertheless possessed no internal faith at all in the truth of those same rites.

Do you suppose, then, that when they performed these acts, without possessing the conviction concerning what was outwardly visible, they accomplished anything heavenly, so far as they themselves were concerned? Certainly not.

Nor was the substance of bread and wine changed among them, because no faith of the mind accompanied their outward act, through which the mysteries are completed; faith alone specially earns the secret of spiritual transformation.

### § V. Objection 4

But in this matter, especially where divine power shines forth, the following is effective: that grace which escapes fictitious priests does not abandon faithful people for whom these things are administered. The same body, which is not a body among those who administer it unbelievingly, is sacrament and reality of the sacrament among those who, although the ministers are unbelieving, nevertheless stand there faithfully.

For example, if some Jew receives baptism—which often happens—with a deceitful mind and for the sake of gain, does he obtain freedom from sins? And when a feigned and malicious person approaches such great purity, was the Holy Spirit himself, whose power it was to sanctify baptism, in no way able to forgive him any sin, even the smallest?

If he could have done so, it would certainly have been not power but impotence, and an unjust impotence at that. For, as it seems to me, to pardon guilt to a heedless and unrepentant person is nothing other than to offer, through indulgence, a malign favor to criminals and the proud.

And how will God be God if he remits their crimes with impunity to those who persist in them? The feigned person certainly received baptism—that baptism which the Holy Spirit, at the invocation of any priest, undoubtedly imbued and made effective—yet the one who approached deceitfully found it ineffective.

See how clearly it appears that where faith is absent, the sacrament too becomes powerless.

Nor should anyone object to me that a pagan or heretic also baptizes, because the authority possessed by the giver differs from the confession of the divine name in the recipient. The outward ministry is referred to the giver and sacrificer; efficacy, however, is attributed to Christ, to whom, as it is said, “This is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33), it is also attributed that he alone sacrifices.

If, then, the givers—that is, the ministers—are commended by Christ’s unique authority, because he retained it for himself, there is nevertheless much uncertainty in discerning confessors while we are in this world.

Hence the Psalm says: “He established the waters as in a wineskin” (Psalm 77 [78]:13). If the waters are spiritual gifts, of which it is said elsewhere, “The river of God is filled with waters” (Psalm 64 [65]:10), or if they signify baptism itself, God pours these into whom he wills and closes them off from whom he wills, according to the intention and merit of the person approaching; he restrains them and grants them.

### § VI. Objection 5

This too, no less than the preceding arguments, may serve the present case. We know and hold by many canons that those ordained simoniacally, whether bishops or priests, receive nothing from their ordainer; and that, when they have ordained others or celebrated the sacrifice for that reason, because they received from no one the power either to perform or to give such things, they are unable either to perform or to give them.

Yet divine providence intervenes in this grave danger in such a way that, if something sacred is received through the laying on of hands of people who are not known to be Simoniacs, the poison of that entire heresy is emptied out through the faith of the recipient who is ignorant of the disease. Thus what the Simoniac himself does not possess, although he may appear to have bestowed what he did not possess, is nevertheless shown to be valid solely through the faith of the recipient.

Let us also suppose, on the other side, some holy man entirely free from the plague of simony, whose subordinates—archdeacons or deans, for example, hired in a simoniacal manner—bring people to him for ordination. From that holy man, however holy and legitimate the thing he gives may be, they receive nothing; but, like lifeless bodies beneath the sun, they neither see nor feel.

If these things, insignificant by comparison with the divine sacrifice, are both taken away and given on account of the enormity of a single sin, and are altered by divine judgment according to the grace of the recipients, is the just person not distinguished from the condemned in that most holy mystery?

I know that in this I do not oppose the blessed Doctor of the Gentiles, who says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29). For whoever does not doubt the truth of the Lord’s body and nevertheless communicates it with the depravity of a savage or criminal mind—to use an ecclesiastical expression—while showing no reverence to so great a person, I should like to know what sacred or beneficial thing he brings away from the altar.

Granted: let it be even the sacrament, although received insolently and foolishly—not so much taken as presumed upon. Yet even if this is granted, it does not appear how he can bring away from it the reality of the sacrament. If the reality of the sacrament is absent, what benefit is there in having received the sacrament?

### The word “sacrament” is used in three ways

The word “sacrament” is used in three ways. It is used for an oath; it is also commonly used for a sacred thing; and it is also taken to mean a mystery.

Let it therefore be a sacred thing, and let it be a mystery: once the reality of the sacrament is removed, the whole becomes punishment for the unworthy. Shall we then say that the majesty of so great a gift, worthy of adoration by heaven and earth, willingly immerses itself in the most foul breast of some criminal, solely so that it may burn the wretched heart of a man destined for condemnation?

Far be this from the most merciful soul of kindly Jesus! In heart I believe and with my mouth confess that the person who approaches these sacred things presumptuously is most deservedly punished; but I would in no way dare to profess that the dignity of so great a truth is held in infamous places.

“Although we have known Christ according to the flesh,” says the Apostle, “yet now we know him no longer in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16). Shall he, then, now advanced to the seat of equality with the Father, be reduced again to enduring insults, so that, on account of the vicious person who once had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), he must now grow old in a sordid lodging?

I dare say this, and I have good faith toward God: I therefore say more safely that the Lord Jesus could more easily have carried the cross than endured human society amid foul morals.

Would returning misery therefore bring him back to this, so that he should be reluctant to return to bear again the errors of our race? Does he perhaps find his own inability wearisome and, unable to endure rest, long to depart again into the troubles of the body he once customarily inhabited?

[Col. 0639A] I should like to learn from someone what this means: “Whoever eats me lives because of me” (John 6:58). What is “to eat”? What is “me”? It is ambiguous, and the Lord can be eaten well or badly when the statement is taken absolutely; the Apostle, however, states it conditionally.

But what is eaten? “The bread,” he says, “which I shall give is my flesh” (ibid., 52); and the Psalm says: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77 [78]:25).

To eat seems to me to mean nothing other than to reproduce the life of Jesus within oneself as an example. This is what he means by “me,” as though he were saying: “He does not eat me who, by joining himself to me, is not made one body with me.”

Let no one believe me unless the Lord’s words are shown to agree with mine. “Give us,” he says, “our daily bread today” (Luke 11:3). In whose person is this spoken? Clearly, in the person of those who say and can say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9).

Whose Father, do you suppose? Certainly the Father of the elect, who strive to be conformed to the character of God the Father. “Be holy,” he says, “as I am holy” [also read: “because I am holy”] (Leviticus 11:44). These sons, I say, cry out, “Our bread,” as though they were saying: “By our works and truth we confess you as our Father; give us bread, not the bread of outsiders, but our own proper bread.”

Whose prayer is this? Undoubtedly, that of those who are to be saved. For they say, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), that is, “Let the holy Church, which is God’s special kingdom, grow together”—the kingdom which, as he says elsewhere, is not of this world. For if it were of the world, the world would love its own (John 15:19).

Who, then, would dare say that this bread, which is also called “of angels” (Psalm 77 [78]:25), belongs to any of the rejected? It is granted solely to the lot of the elect.

“Whoever, therefore, eats me lives because of me” (John 6:58), that is: no one communicates in my flesh and blood except the one whom the inward inspiration of me gives life.

Consider, if you wish, what this condemned man possesses, whom the devil kills by feeding him with vices for Gehenna. Since it is for God alone to discern such a person, and since it is evident that he has been destined for death, I cannot see how he could worthily participate in those sacred things even once during his life.

It is certain, beyond doubt, that he cannot be made one body with the bread that is given for eternal life and is called the pledge of eternal salvation. I therefore judge him to be as far removed in this world from the complete reception of the true sacrament as it will be evident in the future that he is an exile from the reality of the sacrament itself.

For I say—and no sane person will be able to deny it—that whoever has once received it worthily will in no way be deprived of eternal salvation, of which it is the most certain pledge.

You see, then, for whose benefit, in its entirety, this eating is intended.

### § VII. Objection 6

If any uncertainty still gnaws at your insolent mind, read the book of blessed Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*. There, unless I am mistaken, you will find that certain people who had fallen during the persecution and had tasted the blood of the sacrifice later, during the time of peace that had been granted, entered the churches of the faithful as though innocent and received the same sacrament of the Lord’s body just like the others. Some men and women—I do not know which—carried it home in shining linen cloths, as was customary at that time, and placed it in their chests for safekeeping.

Not long afterward, when they returned to take it, they found that it had been reduced to ashes and cinders. Even little children who were carried to the Eucharist in their mothers’ arms, after receiving it in their mouths from the priest’s hand, coughed it back out—if they too had swallowed anything of the sacrificial blood.

What, then, is the Lord’s body doing as ashes? What reason did it have for punishing its own body, when it ought rather to have taken vengeance on those who had defected from his body? Certainly, the one who elsewhere attributes so much honor and human protection to his body ought never, if it were his body, to have allowed it to be reduced to ashes.

Tell me, whoever you are, why, when the Lord was about to depart from the world, he made for us a substitute body to enjoy in the meantime. I shall answer plainly: for common consolation, for his own memory, and also for the exercise of faith.

If these three appear to be the reasons, then where they are proved to be absent, Christ’s substitutions are understood to be entirely void—especially where there is consolation for no one, where there is no memory, and where the faith of the one who ought to exercise it, or even wishes to do so, is not present.

We see this not only among pagans but also among Christians who have turned away from God, whom the Apostle calls worse than unbelievers (1 Timothy 5:8). Where, then, there is no faith to be assisted and no devotion that demands it, I do not know what substitution the body of Christ can effect there.

See, therefore, that this mystery belongs only to the faithful, and to those among them who belong to the portion of those to be saved. As for the person who presumptuously makes use of it—for the opportunity is meanwhile supplied to good and bad alike—I do not know whether he even receives the sacrament itself; I do know that, because he judges it to be a sacrament, he condemns himself.

## § VIII. Objection 7

What of the fact that we have heard that it is consumed by mice and dogs, that through the negligence of its custodians it perishes, rotten or moldy, that it is subjected to various accidents, and that finally it is burned by flames? Is what mice have gnawed and dogs have licked to be applied to the most holy body, so that what the magnanimity of our faith could scarcely secure for the use of the soul rather than the body should be freely prepared for the teeth of mice and dogs? Shall we therefore say that the teeth of worthless little beasts happen by chance to grind what Christian prelates, together with their devout flocks, immolate with such devotion and so many tears, although Christ presides over the sacrifice? May this, I ask, be utterly erased from the minds of all the saints.

It has already been established, in whatever manner it has been proved, that this gift was provided by God as a support for true faith; and what is attributed solely to the merit of faith cannot nourish any creature here unless it is truly faithful. Since the true faith of certain people is nourished by this single food, it cannot in any way be established that it is a sacrament, much less that it supplies the reality of the sacrament, once it is transferred to impious souls and brute animals. But if this mystery is ascribed to our redemption, a very ridiculous case is advanced against our belief by its opponents. For if those who willingly argue about the Lord’s body and wish it to be a figure rather than a reality can be taunted with the fact that the same thing is common to beasts and human beings, they will easily subdue us by this argument and convict us merely through shame at our stupidity, saying that our sacraments are common to humans and beasts.

Wherever, therefore, faith is found, let the truth of the sacrament be present. In cases involving the accidents of beasts or of any others, since there is no faith to which it may adhere, let the substance that previously existed be retained rather than have that one and only purity branded with so great a disgrace. For if, while it is being burned, decaying, gnawed, and licked, it everywhere proceeds with the same majesty, such great glory passes away subject to every misery. And although it may appear to have been handed over to such dangers, those who seem to have been appointed guardians of so great a thing are nevertheless not free from the grave destruction of their souls; they truly betray the Lord’s body when they deprive it of the observance it deserves. Yet this is not a sacrament while it passes into external food; for those to whom the care of this matter was entrusted, it is instead a betrayal of the entire true mystery and the crime of dreadful desertion.

## § IX. Summary of the objections

Since, by wandering farther than we had intended, we have treated these matters, let this conclusion be appended to our discussions on the subject: let no human, indeed no earthly creature, be believed capable of receiving this food—insofar as it is called supersubstantial—as nourishment except for the truly faithful and those predestined to eternal life. But if it should come to someone else, let it be thought nothing other than pure bread. I do not hesitate to repeat this statement, because if an unbeliever or someone altogether unworthy approaches, he burns himself by insolently thrusting himself into matters that do not belong to him. Yet it cannot be believed that so great a dignity is joined to so foul a habitation. Rather, just as holy baptism is holy and makes the well-disposed holy, so for the ill-disposed, apart from the guilt of their fraud, it does nothing other than make them public water. I say this according to my understanding, and, with God as my witness, I say it for the sake of faith. If anyone thinks otherwise, let him take care to think soundly.

# CHAPTER IV

## § I

Against these assertions, made with insufficient moderation, I shall respond with a shorter—and therefore more temperate—argument.

[Col. 0641D] It is certainly most true that the Eucharist is, strictly speaking, the nourishment proper to true faith. But against the claim that for the unworthy it is not only not the reality of the sacrament but not even a sacrament, we resist not merely by authority but also, even if authority were lacking, by numerous arguments.

### The objections are refuted. Christ is received in his entirety by the worthy and the wicked.

First, because it is highly inappropriate to attribute mutability and alternation to such great mysteries, so that what supplied both sacrament and reality of the sacrament to Peter should, at the same moment, have been established as neither for Judas; and so that the water of baptism, which after the completion of the sacrament, when mixed with underground streams, no longer differs from ordinary waters [*differt*, “differs,” E. P.], should seem to have no superiority at all, while what is something for one according to his worthiness immediately becomes nothing for another according to his unworthiness, and the wickedness of a miserable little man suddenly deprives it of the eminence of so great a majesty.

For he who, present in this world, showed himself no less accessible to Judas and his persecutors than to Mary and her companions; who also graciously admitted to his discipleship those who were later to turn back (Mark VIII, 33); who even now, reigning together with the Father, gives his sun equally to the good and the wicked (Matt. V, 45); who also, according to the Book of Daniel, assigned angelic protection to the faithful just as to the faithless—as he shows in Michael, the prince of the Hebrews, against whom the prince of the Greeks resisted (Dan. XI, 13)—must never be believed to exclude anyone from his sacraments at this time, especially since it is a time for mercy (Ps. CI, 14), when he excludes no one from his generosity.

### Innumerable errors and difficulties would flow from the proposed view, if it were admitted.

But if he were now to make them exiles from this gift, what would he demand from them at the judgment, when in the present he had entrusted them with nothing concerning this grace? Even if the opinion were established among the wicked that their wickedness overturns the sacraments, their minds would fear their own foulness in vain, since they would regard the Lord’s body, because of their wickedness, as returning to its former substance.

For example, suppose—I do not know whether I deserve hatred or love—that, conscious of my weakness, I approach those sacraments (Eccl. IX, 1). What hope or benefit could I believe I would bring away from them if, because of my sins, I recognized in a despairing mind that so great a reality had been nullified? And who, while living in the flesh, does not sometimes distrust his own election? Whenever, therefore, the misery of my humanity overwhelms me, will the Lord’s body be neither sacrament nor reality of the sacrament for me when I approach the Lord’s table?

Let the wise person consider how many improprieties arise from this opinion, and let him hold with the utmost firmness, without any perverse interpretation, that “whoever eats the same body unworthily, according to the Apostle, certainly eats judgment for himself” (1 Cor. XI, 29).

## § II. God alone knows who receives the grace of the sacrament.

Having therefore removed those investigations that are most pernicious and the cause of infinite error, let this alone be considered: for the worthy, the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament are present; for the unworthy, without the reality of the sacrament, there is a simple sacrament. But how it exists in the minds and bodies of the unworthy, he alone knows whose substance, wherever it is distributed, can neither perish nor anywhere grow obsolete, whatever may happen to it as a result.

To him Solomon’s parable can aptly be applied: “Lots are cast into the lap, but they are directed by the Lord” (Prov. XVI, 33). Let these lots be understood as nothing other than the distributions of this gift, known to God alone. They lie hidden within the lap because, closed together, they contain one another beneath the divine mysteries. Hence they are said to be vigilantly and beautifully directed by the Lord, because many are thought to receive these things without the reality of the sacrament, yet, while God provides for their correction, they are thereby nourished toward eternal life. For something very different rests in God’s judgment from what human rashness supposes, when good beginnings are changed by a wicked end, or good beginnings are spoiled by an ignoble conclusion. Thus heavenly mercy directs what unreflective severity does not fear to judge—or rather to prejudge—for itself.

“Lots are cast into the lap” (ibid.), because he forms human hearts individually (Ps. XXXII, 15); but intellectually, after we enter the sanctuary of God (Ps. LXXII, 17), he will cause the works of each person to be distinguished. Hence the Holy Spirit cooperates for good (Rom. VIII, 28) not only with those who love God, but also with those who are presently held in whatever crime yet will at some time come to love God—even in their receiving the gift of this Eucharist.

Let whoever wishes object to me the ashes of Cyprian, which that contentious fellow set against me, and the visions of that old man of whom we read in the *Deeds of the Elders*: he saw coals being offered by an angel to the unworthy when the sacrament returned to the altar. My faith, however, can never waver on this point.

## § III. Christ suffers no injury or disgrace when he is eaten by criminals or beasts, or when the appearances of the sacrament are corrupted.

Furthermore, if the matter concerns mice or beasts, or something that seems to be accidentally consumed somewhere, we do not presume to affirm anything other than that we should in no way believe that the substance which God implanted in that appearance can be taken away. Some have written that our eyes are deceived concerning the great corruption of the mystery that appears to occur, and they introduce the eyes of Cleopas and Mary Magdalene as having been temporarily withheld from recognition of the Lord. I do not know whether these arguments will ever be sufficient for me or for many others.

This, however, we know: insofar as it is an appearance, it is thought to be subject to accidents of this kind; but insofar as it is the truth, that which is joined to its principal reality, seated at the Father’s right hand, is mutilated by no harm. From these accidents, therefore, which among unbelievers lie open to the disparagement of our mysteries and cannot be adequately defended by authorities, let those who are not foolish hold this opinion: that they should reserve this remnant, as though this had been said specifically about it, for the fire; and let them regard it as having returned from the dead in such a way that whatever belongs to it, they perceive nowhere except in its glorified body. Let them no more shudder at the bellies of mice than at the minds of criminals, which provoke God more greatly, because wherever it is carried, by returning to its own origin it is protected from every injury. Nor should someone be called a heretic if, in defense of so great a reality, so that it not be assigned to base places, he offers an opinion somewhat more freely than is proper.

## § IV. It is exactly the same in the sacrament as in heaven.

Since we have already begun to speak of the conformity of this body that is made on the holy table, we must define that what is done there entirely corresponds to that body which now reigns immortal and incorruptible with the Father.

Let no one object to me that, when the same God and Lord was delivering these mysteries, he said: “This is my body, which will be handed over for you” (1 Cor. XI, 24). And: “This is the blood which will be poured out for you and for many” (Matt. XXVI, 26; Mark XIV, 24). As though he were teaching that what he was handing over had to be determined according to the condition in which he then existed. Let him consider this false, because he who through the union of divinity was always immortal—he did not undergo death as a debt, but assumed it by deliberate choice—handed over these things in an incorrupt condition, which he immediately displayed on the mountain to Peter, John, and James (Matt. XVII, 2).

# CHAPTER V

## The Lord in the Eucharist is neither passible nor mortal.

But because I have heard that one of my friends, a man especially learned in letters, has deviated very far from this position, saying that “the mystery of that body, which by the faith of priest and people, with the word of God preceding, is made on the altar, has the form of Christ’s passible and mortal flesh,” it seems fitting to me that we address this matter with a somewhat broader inquiry and show that, on so great a subject, he thinks less competently and astutely than would befit a man of such learning.

For if he had attentively considered what I said briefly above, he would have spoken very differently about the passibility or mortality of our Lord Jesus. Without doubt, if he had examined with due subtlety what the Savior himself says—“No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John X, 18)—he would never have so rashly branded the Lord with the mark of suffering and death.

Certainly, it is possible for a human being to have his life taken from him, since in suffering and dying he is continually exposed at every hour and moment to accidental experience. But he of whom it is repeatedly said that “his hour had not yet come” (John II, 4)—to whom, of course, the outcome of hours and the hours of outcomes are immutably subject—lays down his life because, when he wishes and how he wishes, he releases what he took up in himself and created from himself.

From human beings life is forcibly taken; but from him, whose entire being is from himself and in whom nothing occurs except what is voluntary, life is freely assumed and freely relinquished. What necessity of dying could there have been for him whom, in his second birth, the freedom of the Holy Spirit always accompanied in the womb of the one conceiving? Hence he is said to have “paid what he did not take” (Ps. LXVIII, 5), he alone among the dead having paid the penalties of sins he had not committed (Ps. LXXXVII, 6).

If the necessity of sinning contracted by us through the corruption of nature consequently imposes on us the necessity of dying, by what law could he, who was stained neither by original sin—for he was born of the Spirit and the holy Virgin—nor by any sin he himself had added, be touched by the law of sin? By what penalty, moreover, was he compelled to pay the debt of sinful nature? Where he is recognized to be free from the guilt both of origin and of action, what exactions can death and passibility be permitted to have?

For if death is introduced into our humanity through sin (Rom. V, 12), where there is no sin, the operation of death is proved to be annulled, since there can be no doubt that the removal of the cause brings about the extinction of the effect.

In the original state of the first man, if no event of sin had occurred, no assault of suffering or death could certainly have intervened. Nor would any sort of ancestral age have entered through the propagation of his descendants, where no cruelty of concupiscent disobedience would have destroyed the mind. For what is new, what is vigorous, what is sound there, where anxiety gnaws at the feeling of a biting conscience?

If, according to Solomon, “a joyful mind makes an age flourish” (Prov. XVII, 22), and if that is understood to be paradise which the Lord planted at the beginning (Gen. II, 8)—namely, what he first planted in the intellectual minds of angels and human beings, even though for many angels he provided stations of transient service—an uncertain, textually difficult phrase—soon to pass away, so that no one could in any way rejoice continually in the impassibility of his mind and body—what must be judged concerning the mind and body of the Son of God, in whom not only humanity but also the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in the unity of the person? (Col. II, 9) Even of a mere human being, one who did not learn to live without sin, it is said that his life, as a kind of kingdom of God, is peace even in the present and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. XIV, 17).

The first man, I say, before sin, if I may dare to say it, was both passible and impassible, mortal and immortal. Through sin he could fall into suffering and death by an abuse of his will, though not by a free will; but if he had wished to keep himself within true freedom by not sinning, he would undoubtedly have remained impassible and could in no way have died.

The second man, Jesus the Lord, succeeded him in an almost similar form, though with a nature all the more impassible because he was born more freely—or rather, through the ineffable birth of God and man alike. How could he be called passible, when the complete removal of sin both in origin and in action would not allow the penalty—which is suffering and death—to approach him at all?

If the first man, by restraining himself from sin, could be impassible and immortal, should the Son of God, having united to himself the substance of our weakness, not make it far more impassible and, so to speak, more immortal? Thus, formed without concupiscence solely from the Holy Spirit within the virginal womb, he was born into the world naturally impassible and immortal.

So impassible and immortal, I say, that just as the first man through disobedience willingly lowered himself into suffering and death, so this second man, for the restoration of justice, voluntarily lowered himself to endure pains and death, for neither of which he was in any way a debtor. For unless he paid on behalf of human beings penalties he had not deserved, he could in no way free those who did deserve them and were liable to punishment.

Therefore I want you to believe that he was passible and mortal for this one reason: because he wished to suffer and die for the redemption of humanity, not because he had drawn from the inheritance of the first parent any debt of nature that required him to suffer and die.

[Col. 0646A] He suffered and died, therefore, because he wished to do so, not because he owed it by the law inherited from Adam. What likeness, then, do you attribute between Christ’s passibility and mortality and the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, when you should have known him to be immortal and impassible from definite statements spoken by his own mouth?

“No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13); and elsewhere: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10). Before he departed from this world he commended many things of this kind concerning his consubstantiality with the Father. If the Son of Man is in heaven, and there is one with the Father—for elsewhere he says, “I am from above” (John VIII, 23)—what is this other than if he had said, “I am in the principal Spirit, who is the Father”?

What passibility, what mortality are you attempting to impose upon him who, whenever he is found in Scripture to be called passible and mortal, is without doubt called so only because, according to the choice of his will, he exposed himself to death and did not succumb to any necessity?

There is therefore nothing passible or mortal in Christ that you ought to compare with those life-giving sacraments. If you consider the matter with faithful and unyielding attention, you will find in him nothing at all except what is incorruptible and immortal—except that he freely wished to die. For one thing is what we do willingly and gladly; another is what we are forced to complete under compulsion, as though driven by debts. But on this point, let what has been said suffice for the wise.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0646C]

## § I. The author refutes someone who asserts that Christ is crucified daily on the altar.

Some of the associates of this same friend of mine have also reported to me that he is accustomed to say—not merely in consultation or in discussion with learned acquaintances, as is customary, but openly, while disputing in the midst of large gatherings of wholly ignorant and uneducated people—that in the making of the saving host Jesus the Lord is crucified daily on the altar.

We Catholics and all who think devoutly ought to abominate this with as much indignation as our Lord must be defended by authority against the charge of utter impotence or eternal misery. For what could be more unworthy and more miserable to think about God than that God should become eternally miserable for our blessedness? What could we attribute to God that is more impotent than that we should need his daily punishments continually as an aid to our restoration?

Certainly, if the matter were as he says, so that the cruelty of daily suspension slaughtered the Author of life, nothing in the heavenly reward would be so blessed or glorious that it would not become cheapened by contemplating so prolonged a calamity in Christ, the guarantor of that reward. And who would not accuse that death of great uselessness which is known to be repeated each day not merely many times but ineffably infinitely? And what of the fact that in each individual church, indeed even on each altar, several sacrifices are offered?

Thus, if this is so, that utterly powerless Savior would be said to be fastened to as many gallows as there are Masses celebrated everywhere on the altars.

Certainly, even if no support from Scripture were available, universal reason would overwhelm all this folly. For although the act of ecclesiastical institution that occurs during the sacrifice undoubtedly suggests the likeness of the Lord’s Passion and is believed to take place in commemoration of our Lord, it is nevertheless impious to say that he is crucified whenever this is done.

Although signs are sometimes set before the things signified, the things that foreshadow in shadow are not therefore identical with those that follow in reality. For example, the triple immersion in baptism signifies the Lord’s three-day burial, yet we do not say that whenever someone is baptized anywhere, Christ is buried everywhere.

Although that host plainly refreshes our memory through daily approaches to its reality, it inflicts no repeated injury on God, who will never again die, through the image of his Passion. “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. VI, 9–10).

If, then, having risen, he does not die, yet according to your opinion is crucified every day on every altar, I should like to know how your prudence understands the Apostle’s “once,” by which he is said to have died to sin—that is, to have been made a sacrifice for sin. And how does he live to God when, by countless repetitions of his suspension throughout the world, he is subjected to such torment?

[Col. 0647C] If, according to the Apostle Peter, who treats this very subject in these words, “Christ died once for our sins, so that he might offer us to God” (1 Pet. III, 18), how can one who has been subjected to so many instances of punishment raise anyone up when offering him to God?

If he dies once and through that death restores us to eternal salvation, the mystery he celebrates is certainly worthy and fitting for divinity. But if, after dying and rising again, he continually, so to speak, makes himself flesh through the infliction of crucifixions, then, having become miserable, he plainly supplies no one with a blessedness that he himself does not possess.

“For Christ,” says the Apostle, “did not enter into holy places made by hands [others: ‘holy things made by hands’], representations of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us; nor that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer frequently from the foundation of the world. But now, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared once for all, to abolish sin, through his sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many” (Heb. IX, 24–28).

Behold, you see clearly—unless your mind’s sight is found to be blinded by sin—how the apostolic word cries out against your errors. But I should like to ask you whether, in your view, the New Testament outweighs the Old, or the Old the New. I do not doubt that you will say the New.

If you consider the New to be superior, why do you so thoroughly empty the authority of Christ’s death through his daily crucifixions that the high priest’s yearly entrance into the holy places for his own sake appears far more authoritative than the unceasing death of our Savior every day? If, according to Scripture, you believed the effective punishment of his first Passion, you would never extend his reproach—which, if you think soundly, he endured for you—into suspensions coextensive with the age.

As for the fact that the same sacrifice is repeated daily, this does not refer to the daily repetition of his punitive crucifixion. Rather, it means that the daily variety of offenses is washed away by the daily representation of so great a mystery. We do not torment him who accomplished this work once by continually carving the same thing again, but recall our fluid memory to renew in our minds the origin of what we know was once accomplished for the salvation of all, without any need of repetition.

## § II

I also think it should be asked whether that body which, as you say, is always being crucified is the very same body that is known to have been born of the Virgin and to have hung upon the cross.

I know that you will answer that it is the same. Therefore, if it is believed to be the same, and if what is made on the altar is believed—as you teach—to have to conform to this passible and mortal body, I should like to be instructed whether the body that you describe as passible and mortal is the same body as that which is recognized to have already taken its seat, impassible and immortal, at the Father’s right hand.

If you say that they are not the same, two bodies of Jesus the Lord are introduced. One will be subject to suffering and death; the other will plainly have reached the stronghold of incorruption. Thus, when the mystery of the sacred bread and cup becomes a sign of corruptible flesh, the indivisible substance of the Savior is divided into a perverse duality.

But if you are ashamed to say this and confess that there is one body—the passible body on the altar and the body that sits with the Father in heavenly glory—take care, according to the Apostle cited above, lest you crucify Christ again after he has become incorruptible and immortal and expose him to public disgrace (Heb. VI, 6). Indeed, take care lest, as is more consistent with the truth, you make yourself a laughingstock to all who think worthy thoughts about God.

[Col. 0648D] These discussions, as I think, should suffice for you if you apply your mind to correction. But if you choose to harden yourself, you may perhaps laugh at these things, which ought not to be rejected by the faithful, as though they were fables. Let those who weigh the Lord’s states therefore cease asking whether this sacrament performed among us corresponds to the passible or the impassible Christ, to Christ dead or living.

## § III. The body of Christ in the sacrament is such as it was after the resurrection.

For they understand that it can in no way be understood otherwise than that it must be received in the condition in which he was when he presented that same body to the disciples to be eaten. For, they say, if he had commanded these things at the meals he held with them after the resurrection and had said that this was his body, no one would rightly have understood any other body than the one he then had when he said these things.

Indeed, he is remembered as saying while dining that he would not drink again from the fruit of the vine until he should appear to drink it with them in his kingdom (Mark XIV, 25); and that kingdom is nothing other than the glorification of the body after it had suffered. Hence it is said: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 39).

Thus, they consider that the body which provides a life-giving food from the altar is of the same kind as he was when he declared such things as: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me” (John VI, 57), and “Whoever eats me will live because of me” (ibid., 58).

But the question concerning the likeness of the dead Jesus is empty, because the one who died is, in his very death, none other than the Son of God. He who is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world, before he was born in time, and who is read to have performed the deeds done with the patriarchs (Rev. XIII, 8), was, so to speak, before he existed, and was therefore always the same in death as he had been in life. Nothing should be distinguished between the living one and the dead one.

He himself, through the Apostle Jude, led the people out of Egypt a second time (Jude 5). And Paul says that Christ was tested by the Israelites in the wilderness (1 Cor. X, 9). The same mysteries are made alive through the complete abundance of divinity, as the sacramental canon itself clearly shows, if nowhere else: “You sanctify, enliven, bless, and bestow upon us.” Through these words it makes him effective in omnipotence.

## § IV. Guibertus maintains that Christ left no part of his remains in the world.

Let us therefore set these matters aside and return to what had been omitted concerning the Savior’s tooth and navel. First, this must be noted: just as it is said concerning the Holy Spirit, “It is expedient for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come” (John XVI, 7), so those who claim such relics for themselves, as it seems to me, weaken the words of truth.

For what does “if I do not go” mean except “unless I withdraw my bodily presence”? The Paraclete therefore does not come unless this presence is withdrawn—as though, unless everything bodily belonging to him is removed from memory, the mind could in no way be raised to the faith of contemplation.

It was said above that, for the exercise of our faith, our Lord wished to transfer us from his principal body to the mystical body, and from there to train us, as though by certain steps, in understanding divine subtlety.

Thus, as though he had withdrawn us from the density of external vision to the subtler sight of imagination, and as though from hemp to flax, he advanced us from the appearance of his bodily form to recognition of this mystery, so that, when we recovered from tangible flesh, promising—or rather containing—something else, another appearance might be formed.
