For when an untrained person, ignorant of allegorical forms, observes those two material things placed on the altar—bread and wine—and is taught to perceive in them the body and blood of Jesus, to what height of divine courtesy do we suppose he is raised?

But if God commanded this to be done with such labor, while nevertheless the world was not deprived of the first portion of his body, then God has three bodies. First, there will be the body conceived from the Virgin; second, that which is enacted under the figure of bread and cup; third, that which, impassible—or rather already glorified—sits at the Father’s right hand.

If anyone wishes to oppose this view by saying that the one born of the Virgin and hung upon the cross is the same as the incorruptible one exalted to the Father, he is mistaken. For although the property of the same person exists, the essence is nevertheless found to be very different in the qualities of the natures. Once glorified, no power of death or suffering can thereafter rule over him.

Bringing this little book to a suitable conclusion, let us now undertake another beginning. Taking up again both what we are setting aside for the present and other matters that, with God inspiring us, we believe we shall add, we gird ourselves against not their relics but their blasphemies.

# BOOK THREE

Against the monks of Saint-Médard, who assert that they possess the Savior’s tooth.

[Col. 0649]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0649D]

## § I. When devotion attributes false things to God or the saints, it detracts from divine honor. An error is corrected with great difficulty once it is believed to be religion.

Devotion toward God and his saints must be approved in every respect. But when devotion arrogates to itself as much as the rule of religion in no way supplies, then, whereas any pious worshiper of divine things might have expected a reward, something pitiable occurs: from that very devotion he incurs the penalty of a most wicked error.

For when something is worshiped or said concerning God that plainly conflicts with the testimonies of his own truth, it naturally happens that the mind is shown to be all the more seriously and incurably wrong when it begs under the appearance of piety. Nothing is worse than to do evil and to judge the very things done thoughtlessly to be an exercise of good works.

How, then, and when will this error be corrected, when it is not only not believed to be an error but is even regarded as a prerogative of divine favor?

Every correction of sin is brought into the mind of the offender either by fear or by shame. Fear is fear either of divine rejection or of extreme punishment; shame is either the biting guilt within the conscience or the timid face turned toward human beings because of public rumor.

Where, therefore, the mind is troubled by no ambiguity of thought and the face is flushed by the sight of no one, no material for repentance is offered. Whatever is blameworthy, filled with estrangement from God, and wholly opposed to ecclesiastical authorities, when it is proclaimed as though praiseworthy and attributed to the privilege of some singular distinction, is never corrected according to the rule of true discipline.

For wherever fear presses upon the inner chambers of conscience because of some offense, it stirs great hope of correction; but where the cultivation of holiness is put forward, although the mind’s intention is thereby drawn away from the equity of sound belief, it never rises to the line of amendment.

## § II. The monks of Saint-Médard of Soissons claim to possess the Savior’s tooth.

This is why our neighbors, the monks of Saint-Médard, have grown hardened in an ancient falsehood among their dull hearts, while they attribute to themselves something concerning the Savior’s tooth, which he produced naturally at the age of nine. By this they cast down, as though with a fiery dart, the pillar and summit of universal hope; and while they desire to celebrate themselves, they overturn the principal defenses of the common faith.

For once the recognition of faith has been gained, if the strength of hope is overwhelmed, what else is cut away than the root of every good desire and practice? If I possess the sap of sound belief and send forth branches of holy acts in every direction, once the root of hope has dried up—the root by which trunk and branches are moistened—I shall expect nothing throughout the whole structure of the tree that is pleasing or useful.

If you sow well, if the growth of the seed prospers well, and hail destroys the whole crop while you are bringing in the sickle, what profit will you pursue from it?

[Col. 0651C] Guibert proves that Christ left no tooth anywhere on earth.—I should like you to acknowledge what you think about the resurrection. To say nothing of that which is to occur at the end of the age, you certainly do not deny that the Lord himself, whose tooth you claim to have in your possession, rose again. If he rose, did he rise in part, I ask, or wholly? If you testify that he rose wholly, where will the parts you claim for yourselves be? If only in part, what benefit will the promises he made concerning us, who are to rise, bring? Clearly, if it can be proved that he did not fulfill in himself what he had promised concerning us, he will appear to introduce no small ambiguity into our hopes. Someone will reason as though presenting the following argument: “What,” he will say, “will he do with the others who follow, if he does not establish the truth of his own words in himself?” [Col. 0651D] He had said that not a hair of our head would perish (Luke XXI, 18), and yet he, as though making a mutilation of his own body, consigns portions to the earth, brings the remainder into heaven, and declares that he has risen? If he proves incapable of gathering up his own things, how will he gather our members, scattered here and there through human carelessness?

While you wish to raise up your church with foreign treasures, and to boast that your status is far nobler and far superior to that of others, you have burst forth into the utmost madness, to the full measure of your depraved understanding, so that you wish to summon not only—something considered wicked to say, yet worth saying—the prophetic words themselves, but the Lord Jesus himself, as a witness to falsehood. If the Prophet says, “You will not give your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm XV, 10), then surely the Prophet is not unjustly charged with falsehood, since God himself is undoubtedly consigned to perpetual corruption. And what is more exposed to corruption without hope of recovery than that God whom you acknowledge to have been excluded from the glory and incorruption of the resurrection?

My God, what misfortune befell that tooth? I will never admit that it was generated with the rest of the body from the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb; rather, it came from elsewhere and adhered to the Lord’s jaws, as though a grafted shoot from an external tree. That tooth is therefore corrupted, because, to unfold the matter in the terms themselves, when it is torn away from its body and, while that body is glorified, is left on earth and condemned to everlasting misery—or, if not otherwise, is burned with heaven and earth at the end of the age. Thus you are charged either with arrogance or with falsehood—and not with just any falsehood, but with that which makes you blasphemers against God and, if you resist more obstinately, heretics regarding catholic doctrine.

A greater hope is therefore suggested to us than to Jesus the Lord, the father and author of our hope, while we believe that through him we shall be gathered from the dispersion of our bodies, whereas we see him himself undermined! And behold, for your sake we are greater than Jesus here. Complete regeneration awaits us, whereas his has become so partial that either it will never be completed eternally, or it must remain unfinished until the common resurrection [Col. 0652C]. Then perhaps Jesus, when he comes, will make room for the tooth; or his still-gaping jaw will then receive the tooth that has wandered until that time. Thus the tooth and the navel, and whatever else there may be, will undergo a repeated glorification, just as there was once a second circumcision.

§ III. He vehemently attacks the monks of Saint-Médard.—Consider, falsifiers, how small a fire this error of yours is, and how much of the vigor of Christian truth it consumes. Even if no testimonies were available apart from the prophetic one we cited above—especially since the most blessed Peter himself brought forward the same testimony against the Jews in asserting the Lord’s resurrection (Acts II, 27)—it would at least be fitting for you, placed in such a difficult position, to offer a substantial answer concerning this passage. Since it is the height of frenzied madness to refute so distinguished a Prophet and an apostle of such high rank, I marvel how you dare say what so clearly contradicts such great authorities [Col. 0652D]. Certainly, even if many other arguments converged in your favor and could in some way or for some moment support this assertion, your consciences ought nevertheless to shudder greatly at undertaking it; for against men of much lesser glory you would rightly remain silent on this matter.

But if you say that it is not corruption, it plainly is—or, even if it has not yet been corrupted, it must necessarily be corrupted. And how could it be corrupted in a worse manner than by being abandoned to the squalor of perpetual despair after the whole body has been glorified? And how do you dare assert something so absurd? Since you do not deny that he rose, how did it happen that he forgot his own tooth? If it slipped from his memory, or if he voluntarily left it behind, what will he do at the resurrection, when, gathering the members of others, he himself goes about with one part of himself lost?

The same reasoning applies to the navel attributed to the Savior.—Let us suppose, then, that it is possible for you to be enriched by so great a gift. I ask you, therefore, to deign to answer: to whose body will the tooth—and whatever else you suppose—belong at the resurrection (22)? For among us the question concerns the navel and the other things said to have been taken from him no less than the tooth. What is said plainly of one extends to the others. Where, then, will the things preserved from the Lord Savior go when that final day arrives? If they are to return to the former body [Col. 0653B], where will they enter? What places will open themselves to receive them? Or has the glorified Savior remained toothless until now in order to preserve a place for the tooth that is to come? And certainly a place suitable for so small a tooth could not at all be found in the manly jaw of the Lord. Let it be so. Where, I ask, will the navel put itself? Are two glorifications to be celebrated in the same body? This is something nowhere read of and supported by no testimonies. What, then, are you introducing, when you see that everything surrounding your opinion is being weakened and made ridiculous?

§ IV. Moreover, why do you stamp such a blemish of unbelief upon the Lord himself, to say nothing of the prophets? If you had him present now, would one of you accuse me of sin? (John VIII, 46.) He declared that what is weakest and most insensible in a human being would not perish in us; yet, to his own confusion and to the distrust of us all, your wisdom constructs for him such a remnant—not of his hair, but of his flesh and bones. In this distrust, however, an evil consideration emerges on both sides, because to think and speak in this way openly attacks the truth of the divine words and thickens, with no small storm of thoughts, the eye of a feeble understanding, while people fear that God’s promise cannot be fulfilled in them, although they implicitly suggest that he did not make it beforehand in himself. For if you promise someone an abundance while you yourself cannot remedy your own poverty, it is certain that the confidence of the person to whom you have promised it is weakened in you.

[Col. 0653D] I grant that this might at times harm weak or deceitful minds; but because, by God’s mercy, we see no one among us whose cunning regarding such a view is sharpened—I say rather, we see it blinded—this will not be attributed to your prudence, which, contrary to the prohibition of the law, is not afraid to dig so deep a pit (Exodus XXI, 33), into which the fall of any kind of brute animal may open. Certainly, even if, through God's agency and because our age sets less store by this doctrine, no one is permitted to be harmed there, your guilt of shamelessness is nevertheless no less increased, because you continually furnish an occasion by which some unwary person may be endangered.

§ V. Above all, this is charged against you: although you customarily teach these things openly before everyone, and hear that wiser people resist them daily as a sign to which opposition is made, you have never, I say, sought a weighing of the better opinion, nor considered how discordant it is with the Scriptures. For if you had even lightly tested their statements concerning the condition of his resurrection and ours, immediately the spark of the truth of which we speak would have shone forth clearly. And what is more insane than to proclaim to the ears of the Church something that cannot be established by any assertion in debate? Paul went up to Jerusalem and conferred with Peter and the others about the Gospel, lest he should be running, or should have run, in vain (Galatians II, 1–2); yet your prudence is ashamed to learn where it hesitates? Turn your minds to that line of Horace:

“Why,” he says, “do I perversely prefer not to know rather than to learn?” HORACE, *Ars Poetica*, 88.

Yet you are not of such complete dullness that you cannot fully grasp how one part might migrate to the Father’s throne while another part of so great a body might remain, destined for corruption. What reason could tolerate one part being reserved for such glory while another remains, banished from so great a body and destined for corruption?

Even if no authority supported our words, the very difference of the parts would be sufficient, since it cannot endure such a division in the majesty of so holy a body. If, in the bodies of pure human beings, there will be such uniformity at the resurrection, when we are changed, that, with the whole of the members glorified, not even an atom’s measure of unworthiness from the former state will remain anywhere, what madness will make us judge anything incongruous in him who is personally both God and man—so that something in him should be worthy, while something else is excluded from what is worthy? If, through the mouth of the Doctor of the Gentiles, in whom Christ speaks, we are promised that he will reform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory (Philippians III, 21), how will he raise the contemptibility of human corruption to conformity with his glory, when he showed himself as though powerless to take up again what belonged to him?

See, then, lest, while you arrogate to yourselves the members of God—as an honor, a distinction, and a special prerogative for your church, because you think that by this opinion you are contending for your own honor—you should humble God, so to speak, all the way to the earth, the God whose tooth you boast of possessing. If you seek honor from God, what God, I ask, will you be able to believe him to be, when you plainly appear to accuse him of falsehood? If your honor redounds to the disgrace of the one from whom you desire to receive honor, what gratitude do you return in place of honor? And how is your service reasonable if you worship and urge others to worship what provides no proof of faith? The Apostle calls it a reasonable service (Romans XII, 1), in which the mind is freely exercised only after the truest reasons have been given. For when someone venerates and praises anything while unaware of the reasons for his veneration and praise, he is easily shaken or proceeds haltingly.

And certainly, although the opinion of this boastfulness is widespread among everyone, the credulity of any wise person is very rarely available to that statement. Since your reasoning wavers in every respect on this matter, scarcely anyone but an inexperienced and ignorant person can be found whom it might instruct to believe; and where every suspicion of a subtle mind arises, who but a shameless and perverse person bursts forth to publish discussions of this sort? Shame alone ought to have restrained this loquacity, lest someone attribute to dullness what sound minds recognize cannot be considered credible. But if the arguments offered are by no means sufficient for minds of whatever kind, behold, on behalf of your position I am ready to present to myself the arguments that might support your doctrine, and afterward, without any pretense, to refute the arguments presented with complete impartiality.

# CHAPTER II

§ I. The first objection of the monks of Saint-Médard.—This, then, is how your opinion is thought to proceed—or rather, how your assertion appears to arise from such arguments—not because I have ever heard any such reasoning from you, but because, through the conjectures of my mind, I have supposed that something of this sort might be said—or rather barked—by anyone against this little disputation of mine. For I have heard nothing from you worthy of a good person’s hearing; I have learned that this is what you are accustomed to answer those who ask you. “Did he not, in accordance with the natural custom of childhood, shed teeth at the age of nine?” To this, I say, I agree; but many other arguments present themselves, and they tell of things far different from what you report.

In saying this, I feared that I was stirring up a sea of controversy, keeping in mind that saying of Boethius: “I should rightly be judged insane if I intended to speak against the insane.” For in whatever outweighs each person’s mind according to his will, he gives little thought to how he should answer; his heart is occupied only with subduing the opposing view by obstinate shouts. It seems proper to the wicked to thunder so absurdly, substituting one thing for another, that what they cannot obtain by reasoning they may at least seem to have secured by continuous clamor, as though thereby brought nearer to victory. Come, then, and let our speech be exercised on your behalf.

§ II. The second objection.—If you say that God and our Lord left the mystery enacted at his table as a remembrance of himself for his own followers and their successors, so that, when absent, he might provide by a vicarious gift the consolation that his own had received from the companionship of his presence, we do not understand this to mean that, beyond the mystery's provision for its immediate purpose, superfluous portions of that body, as we may call them, given for the completion of universal joy, ought therefore to be absent. We call the sacrament perfunctory precisely because he himself calls the bread daily bread (Luke II, 3)—that is, necessary only so long as, according to the Apostle, it is called “today” (Hebrews III, 13). This, then, is said to be celebrated in his memory in such a way that the possibility of possessing those things is by no means denied; for although there is a general benefit in being united through the sacrament to Christ’s body, the glory of private individuals ought nevertheless not to be deprived of the majesty of their privileges. Just as the privileges of individuals cannot make a common law, so common glorification in no way takes away the distinct radiance of any private person.

§ III. The third objection.—If the visible remembrance of the sacrament represents Christ as having suffered for the world, although this figure is clear to every wise person, why did God not allow these things, fallen from his flesh and, as it were, excretions of his body, to be possessed for the consolation of those for whom he undertook these things? If the blood and water flowing from his side on the cross perhaps touched the earth or a stone, and if it happened to be destroyed by absorption or friction of some kind, how do you suppose that those things which you previously called “excrescences,” as though pledges for renewing our faith, could not have been left to be honored with greater reverence? Those sacraments, therefore, rightly benefit us in his memory, because by receiving them they also produce in us union with the Lord Jesus; but these things furnish minds less capable of understanding with visible and tangible rudiments of faith in invisible things, so to speak.

§ IV. The fourth objection.—There are, then, certain stages by which this truth is to be recognized: that visible and tangible tooth and navel might educate the simple concerning the mystery performed at the altar [Note: Something is missing here.], exercise imagi—[f., *imaginationes*, “imaginations”]—and then, as though ascending to the third heaven, contemplation might sharpen itself toward him who sits at the Father’s right hand. Since flesh and blood could not be suitable for ordinary consumption, the Lord changes them into a sacrament adapted to human use. The sacrament itself, therefore, appears to present something different from the flesh or the tooth said to have remained from the resurrected one. Those remnants themselves suggest the reality of the flesh once presented; but the mystery of the flesh signified becomes effective for those who, through its use, are incorporated into the divine flesh and live. Thus the tooth and navel are a plausible indication, toward the end of our times, of the dispensation once undertaken, and the sacrament generally assists the salvation of souls.

§ V. The fifth objection.—But if it is thought controversial that this remnant exists after the resurrection, baptism after baptism is likewise assigned to the controversy. The baptism which Christ received could appear more glorious than the one that followed, since he himself succeeded what came before in a far better condition. Likewise, if, when Christ rose, he left behind him certain things pertaining to himself as a memorial for our changeable minds, will he, after the judgment, be unable to insert these same things, once glorified, into himself, who will then be more glorious? For we say that although he rose, he did not advance his resurrected body to the glory of immutability that it will possess after the judgment. If it had been completely glorified, the side that he showed open to Thomas would not have remained (John XX, 27); nor would the open wounds of his feet and hands have continued until now, wounds which he preserves for his seat at the Father’s right hand, so that on the day of judgment he may display them preserved both to those who pierced him and to all the reprobate. Where, then, the scar is not covered, no perfect glorification has been applied to a body that has been only partially changed, so to speak; and where the complete restoration from corruption is not yet present, what is evidently less complete in him must in some way be supplemented.

Why, however, should I discuss supplementation, when the very form of a servant—which will be equally visible to the just and the reprobate while he judges—will after the judgment be entirely transferred into the divine form? Hence also the saying: “And passing by, he will minister to them” (Luke XII, 37). We ought to understand this passing as nothing other than that the whole ministry of the human dispensation manifested in him will be reduced to the state—or rather, the dominion—of that divine majesty, in which transition he ministers to the vision of his chosen ones, supplying them with the satisfaction of contemplating him, a satisfaction they will never find wearisome.

Where, then, the transfer of the servant’s form into the appearance of divinity is to occur, and where the covering of the scars is to come through the proper transformation, why do we hesitate to say that the taking up again of whatever we believe remains will immediately follow? When the hollows of the wounds are leveled and smoothed into an even surface, what wonder if what has meanwhile been entrusted to us for the consolation of our faith is joined to the same body from which it plainly derived? Certainly, if anything greater or lesser can exist with God, he does not judge it greater to close the gap of the scars than to attach to himself, through the invisible contraction by which he gathers together whatever has been dispersed, the remnants deliberately applied to human affection by the provision of his design.

§ VI. The sixth objection.—If the Son of God himself testifies concerning the Jews, his enemies, as shown to him by the Father: “Do not kill them,” he says, “lest my people ever forget” (Psalm LVIII, 12). While the presence of the Jewish people, whom we have before our eyes, renews in us the memory of the crucified Christ and makes the ancient books written about and addressed to them more authoritative, through the misfortunes foretold there that have befallen them and through the favorable outcome of our own fortunes, who will be able to obscure our opinion concerning that tooth, or likewise concerning the navel? Indeed, just as that mystical body is known to have been instituted for union between him and us, so whatever of it—the principal part, as we call it, not because it precedes in majesty but in time—is said to remain on earth is recognized as serving to prove the dispensation he undertook and to strengthen the faith of the weak.

# CHAPTER III

§ I. He answers the first objection.—What faith is.—To this we may reply: if anything is believed to remain from his principal body, as though to provide evidence of the humanity once assumed, nearly the whole strength of catholic faith is overturned. For “if faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews II, 1), how do the things to be hoped for subsist, or continue to subsist, in the heart of any believer, if the understanding of his thoughts concerning invisible things returns to visible things? For “who hopes for what he sees?” (Romans VIII, 24.) If faith and hope consist only in something to be desired by the intellect, then, just as they are nourished and advance through the inner vision, so they grow sluggish and fail through bodily habit and attachment to the senses.

If the Savior had left something of his body, it would impede the exercise of faith.—Faith must therefore be something substantial in a person’s mind, so that what it contemplates in the spirit may be held within the mind as something solid. How, then, is the sharpness of faith directed—or rather, what is hoped for and what is believed—when the hoped-for and believed thing is materially present before the eyes of the observer? What exercise of the mind will take place there, where its consideration is exercised upon things subject to sight? Why, unless he first withdraws himself, does he declare that the Paraclete will not come, if he leaves the remnants of his body on earth precisely so that belief in his incarnation may be implanted more firmly in human hearts? He declares that he will absent the presence of his flesh from the disciples so that spirituality may present itself more abundantly to the understanding (John XVI, 7); we must in no way believe that he wished to weaken his words in any respect, namely by wishing, according to you, to leave a remnant of himself on earth.

Indeed, he would plainly have contradicted his own words if, after saying that the Paraclete would not come unless he went away (ibid.), he had left among us a part of the same body toward which the human mind might again be directed. It would be the same as doing and, so to speak, undoing the same thing, if he withdrew his own body in order to discipline us toward spiritual things, yet left behind one part after withdrawing another. Nothing contradictory, nothing discordant, is found in the Lord’s words; the whole mass of evangelical sayings is always clothed in unchanging harmony.

§ II. The hairs, blood, water, and other things that fell from the Savior’s body did not perish.—Therefore, if the question concerns blood and water, and it is objected that they were effaced on earth, the answer must plainly be no different from that concerning the little hairs shed in infancy as the body grew larger—although no one has a fixed opinion about where they flowed or into what they were changed—just as with the stream of water and blood mentioned above. Do you suppose, then, that they were lost? If your tooth, which you arrogate to yourself, does not continue even now in misery, how, do you think, will the other teeth, which it is established he produced under the same natural condition, be believed to have been scattered here and there through negligence? A more fortunate breeze smiled upon the tooth you possess, while, according to the consequences of your words, the others are assigned to fetid squalor, and this one alone shines, adorned with gold and snowy gems. And it is strange that, although he produced several and equal reverence is owed to all, you boast that you alone possess this single one while the others are buried.

If, then, hairs, teeth, streams of water, and the blood of the fourfold wound—which undoubtedly could have dripped all the way to the earth—have settled amid earthly debris, there to decay at the end, I do not see how the condition of the human resurrection and the promise proceeding from the Lord’s mouth of conformity to its likeness can stand without enormous falsehood. And I say this with greater caution than foolishness, because if someone deviates in any portion of his promises, it becomes entirely doubtful that he will fulfill the straightforwardness of his promise in the rest. And if it is granted that so much of the body of him who is the author of the promise will be corrupted, then by an easy little argument whatever is said to have been done in him or to be done concerning us can be nullified. For if firm expectation of future gifts arises from the reception of present gifts, and if one who is deceived at the beginning of his speech is disregarded as the discourse proceeds, it is surely clear that, if he consistently displayed in his own restoration what he promised, he bound without doubt to the faith of his words all those for whom he offered himself as guarantor. But if he is recognized to waver in the truth of his promises, everything that stands out in the structure of his words is immediately overcome by the instability of the whole.

§ III. He answers the third objection.—No one would have collected the bodily matter shed from the infant Christ; why.—But even if we had no answer available to this, it would be sufficient above all to maintain that, during the Lord Jesus’ childhood, there was certainly no one who would have wished to collect such things shed from his most sacred head, especially since at that time no one thought more highly of him than of any other child of the same age. And who would then have attended to the remains of humankind (*generis*; read *corporis*, “body”), when among the Jews it was considered utterly profane to preserve anything from a person's body after death? And what was more defiling among them than to touch the bones of a dead man, when they were commanded, at every such contact, to remain outside the camp for a time and to use waters of purification? Apart from the tablets of the Testimony, the golden urn, and Aaron’s rod, nothing is known ever to have existed as a memorial received from the ancients. And who would have thought that the things pertaining to that child should be preserved, when he was judged in no way more worthy than ordinary estimation?

§ IV. The Blessed Virgin did not do this. Her milk is said to be preserved in the church at Laon; Guibert disproves this.—But if it is objected that the blessed Virgin Mother could have preserved these things and wished, as though out of superstition, to pass them on for the worship of her descendants, the matter will be received in the same way (23) as it is said that at Laon among us her blessed milk is still kept in a crystal dove. How far this departs from truth, and even from probability, is clear from an easy argument: she did not preserve it, especially since during Jesus’ infancy she never had so much leisure or security that she could value his memory so highly as to take care of producing her milk for future ages; at that time she could scarcely live, scarcely remain within her native land. And who could have found even a sign of such arrogance in her blessed character or in her worshipful demeanor, from whose mouth nothing but the humility of a handmaid ever sounded? This substance could even less have endured under any protection for many generations—I say not many, but even a few years—the more so because such coagulated matter is continually consumed by natural instability.

But let us grant the point. What examples of antiquity were available to that most mature mind, greedy of no praise, for observing relics of this kind, so that she might begin, as though for the first time, an image of some vanity concerning something she had never seen done or heard had been done until then? And if, through the same Spirit from whom she had conceived, she could not fail to know that the one whom she had borne through faith was to fill the whole world with his dispensation, why should the little tooth, the navel, or any of the other things have been guarded—things which, in view of the immense glory of her Son, she would have thought no more capable of serving any purpose, even if they could be preserved according to some ancient custom, than a lamp is useful at midday beneath the sun?

Let us therefore know with complete certainty that the Lady of the ages never devoted herself to such childish trappings. They would indeed be childish trappings if he who publicly proclaimed himself God and man to the world through miracles fully worthy of faith desired to be celebrated through such fragments and trifles, entirely useless for every purpose. But if she did not do this, who could have done it, since at that time there was no one who would have valued such things, much less cherished them with affection?

# CHAPTER IV

§ I. He answers the fourth objection.—Christ’s body was completely glorified in the resurrection, although it appeared no differently than before.—But after setting these matters aside for a little, let us return to the subject. If, then, you say that the Lord’s body after the resurrection was not yet wholly changed and not yet fully glorified because it had not covered the openings of the scars, you demonstrate, I confess, the undeniable dullness of your understanding in this very matter. If, therefore, he was not completely glorified because he did not cover them, then I will not say completely, but not even to the slightest degree was he changed or glorified, since after the resurrection he showed the disciples no signs either of change or of glorification. For he appeared to them altered in no respect from the form they had previously been accustomed to see. Therefore, since the resurrected one presented them with no new brightness, someone could say that, in rising, he received nothing greater from the Father than he had possessed before he suffered.

Certainly, not even at the very hour when he ascended into heaven did he present anything of a newer appearance, so that in the very manifestation of the resurrection he showed himself to be none other than the same person he had been before he died. For if he had displayed something unfamiliar by shining forth, he would never have been believed to be returned flesh, but rather, as they suspected, to be another person or a spirit. Hence the words: “It is I; do not be afraid” (John VI, 20). And: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV, 39). It was therefore fitting that he should continue to appear to those same inexperienced disciples simply in the form to which they were accustomed, lest, through an unfamiliar brightness, he lead minds of limited capacity into an error concerning his outward identity.

Why the Lord, when raised, showed the apostles the scars of his wounds.—He who appeared in an obscure form, as though by his own choice, already diminished in glory—what wonder if he displayed to them the places not covered over by the nails? But to whom? Clearly, first to the apostles, and afterward to Thomas, and on both occasions to those who were hesitating—and this only once. Consider whether he revealed anything that needed covering as evidence at the feast for the two going to Emmaus; consider whether he did so in the frequent meals over the forty days; consider whether he appeared with the marks of his passion to the women holding his feet, or to anyone else. What, then, did it mean to offer the hollows of the scars for doubtful people to touch, unless it was to show the identity of his person not by the customary appearance of his face but by the more recent signs of his death? (24) What would those wounds, preserved after the resurrection, signify if they were still to remain even now? Was it so that he might remind the Father, as though he were a forgetful man, through the same dispensation undertaken for human beings? Let it be so. Certainly, while the Father attended to other matters, his flesh seated at the Father’s right hand without wounds would alone have been sufficient to remind him.

§ II. He answers the fifth objection.—Will the marks of those same wounds not be seen in Christ on the day of judgment?—But you object that the reprobate and the impious will see him on the day of judgment—him, that is, whom they pierced. If you were to see, without any reminder of the injury you had inflicted, the one whom you remember having wronged, would you not immediately recall, by seeing him, the crime committed against him? And what will a lacerated side do to you, or what will the nail-holes in his hands and feet do, when the sign of the Son of Man appears? How will the horror of the fivefold wound be fitting on the throne of his glory? And certainly, when he ate and drank with the disciples and handled food with his hands, was pus then flowing from an open ulcer? The absurdity is infinite.

He who, as proof of the true flesh he had resumed, ate frequently with his own people—not from necessity but as a dispensation (Luke XXIV, 43); he who entered to them through closed doors by power alone, not by nature (John XX, 26)—for the weight of flesh and bones does not pass through the spaces between walls, nor does such bodily substance naturally endure an ethereal dwelling, all of which is attributed to the power of the resurrection; he who pretended that he was going farther when he was compelled by the two men mentioned above to remain (Luke XXIV, 28)—could he not for a moment have presented the recently made marks of the passion to any doubter, by which both his nature and his person might be proved? Was not the transfiguration before Peter, James, and John on the mountain merely provisional (Matthew XVII, 2), so that it might demonstrate the condition he would have after the resurrection, a condition which, once he had risen, he nevertheless refrained from showing as it truly was, out of consideration for the weakness of those who saw him? It was as though he were saying: “Because it is not useful for you that I, having returned from the dead, should show you the glory of the changed body—for you would not grasp it with a suitable understanding—I now display it to you while I am still alive, so that you may learn to weigh and remember it, when I have veiled the excellence of glorified nature beneath a humbler, and therefore darker, appearance.”

## § II. Response to Objection 6: How Christ Will Change the Form of a Servant at the Final Judgment

Moreover, concerning the transfer of the form of a servant into the form of divinity: if you understand this to mean that he is changed into another appearance, so that then, with the scars covered over, that tooth and that navel, and whatever else remains, are attached like a grafted shoot to an old trunk, we plainly say that, if this is how matters stand, there will be two resurrections of Christ, and he will be changed twice. If so great an error takes root in the head, what can anyone believe about the resurrection of the limbs? [Col. 0662B]

We understand that Christ’s passage from form to form as nothing other than death being swallowed up in victory (I Cor. XV, 54), and, once the wicked man and his wickedness have been driven out—namely, once his heart draws near, divided from the wrath of his countenance (Ps. LIV, 22)—the elect alone are admitted to behold the glory of his divine vision, while the foolish wicked man is excluded so as not to see his glory. Hence, when Judas goes out, he says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified (John XIII, 32).” He plainly passes into this glorification when he causes us—namely, the elect alone—to pass from the form of a servant, which the just and unjust alike share, into the eternal vision of himself. In this transition he ministers to them (Luke XII, 37), when, after rejecting the reprobate, he satisfies them with his own countenance. Christ therefore passes over when, after the day of judgment, he also excludes the form of a servant from the sight of the reprobate, opens himself to be seen by the eyes of the elect, and indeed brings them over to himself through seeing him.

# CHAPTER V

### § I. The people of Saint-Médard produce a certain miracle performed in the time of Louis the Pious. It does not prove that the Savior’s tooth exists there.

Having thus spoken against the advocates of this opinion, let us observe that in the church of Saint-Médard they loudly proclaim miracles of great importance concerning that tooth. The first—unless I am mistaken, and the one that most readily comes to mind—is this: among the chaplains of the Emperor Louis the Pious, in the emperor’s own presence, the matter was being debated. Since they strongly opposed the monks’ opinion, maintaining that nothing had remained of the body which the Virgin’s womb had brought forth on earth, it is reported that they proceeded to the celebration of Mass. There, during the sacred rites, a reliquary is said to have remained suspended above the altar; they say that this was an argument for themselves and for some who witnessed it. But what, I ask, was the argument? What heavenly voice, I ask, what angel, I beg, thundered that this was then the Savior’s tooth—the tooth which the tender child had produced? But what have I to do with an angel, or with a voice? Even if thrones and dominions asserted this, no minds truly belonging to the faithful—though possessing knowledge of the faith—ought in any way to assent. For, as we said above, and consider it necessary to repeat a thousand times, if he asserts that not even a hair of ours will perish, if he has any remnant on earth, he commands those who believe in him, by his own example, to despair of it rather than believe such things on the authority of doctrines. Certainly, the one who allows his own decaying remains to be carried here and there after the resurrection never gathers up the ashes or bones of the martyrs scattered throughout the world. [Col. 0662D–0663A]

But it is worth considering how dull that miracle itself was, since those who observed it were unable to understand what its suspension signified. For what flew up from the altar into the air, rising, so to speak, from the sacred toward the unsacred, seems to show that it bears the holiness of the altar impatiently. And if we wish to attend to the very word *suspension*, what appears to have been suspended is thought to be ambiguous. But why do I call it ambiguous, when properly speaking something is ambiguous if it can both be and not be? This, however, is in no way possible—unless the God who is truth wishes to deny himself. So deafeningly foolish is the miracle, and it contributes so little to the proof of this matter, that, although it was foolishly written, the person who reconsiders it is still more foolish. [Col. 0663B]

### § II. That tooth may belong to some saint. Faith is often the cause of miracles.

Other things follow, no less doubtful. I called them doubtful for this reason: they are entirely silent as evidence for proving the matter. The object to which the sign is attributed may be holy for another reason; but the thing that is said to exist cannot be what it is claimed to be. And even if it were, the testimony of such signs could not establish that it was the Lord’s tooth.

Let that tooth, then, be believed to belong to some saint, through whose merit perhaps such a thing was granted. And if it certainly belonged to no saint, the faith of those who believed would plainly have demanded that what was hoped for should occur. For many things can happen not so much through the merit of the person through whom the favor is granted as through that of the one upon whom it is bestowed. [Col. 0663C]

### § III. In the city of Luni, a boy announces that pirates are present in the harbor while the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord is being celebrated (Isa. XL, 1).

Something is known to have happened several years ago in the city of Luni.  
[Note: [Col. 0663D] Commonly called Luni, a town of Etruria situated by the sea.]

The faithful people there were celebrating the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. Meanwhile, a pirate fleet was approaching the harbor called Portus Veneris, intending to ravage the city with sudden attacks while the nighttime divine office continued. While they hastened forward in swift *myoparones*—light pirate vessels—whose beaks were racing to cut through the shallow sandbank, a boy in the cathedral church climbed the pulpit to read the first, or perhaps the second, lesson of the first nocturn.

Having received the blessing, he was beginning to read: “Comfort, comfort my people,” when immediately the Holy Spirit, dividing the sentence, added from his mouth: “At the harbor of Venus, Salandra.”  
[Note: *Salandrae* is said to mean ships, called so from *saliendo*, “leaping” or “springing.”]

When everyone ordered the words to be repeated and corrected—not in murmurs but aloud—the boy repeatedly said the same thing. At once the dean of the church, grasping the meaning of the utterance, roused the people to arms and ordered them to go to the harbor of Venus. There, with a mighty trumpet-call sounding along the shores, the crowd went out to meet them and resisted; armed by God, they quickly secured the city against the enemy, who was about to overrun it, after routing him. Thus, just as this did not at all pertain to the merit of the boy who spoke, so many times a benefit is extended not through the person by whom it is thought to be granted, but toward the one who is worthy to receive its fruit. [Col. 0663D–0664A]

### § IV. Concerning a certain fornicator swallowed by the waters

But the authority of those signs seems to me extremely slight; indeed, the worthlessness of that written account is proved to be exceedingly great. For in their little book, which deals with this tooth and with the miracles of the saints of the place, they report of a certain monk that he was accustomed to consort with a prostitute. Yet as he was traveling at night, he necessarily had to cross some nearby waters; during that crossing, the weight of his sin killed him amid the waves. By the abbot’s judgment, he was excluded from the cemetery of the brothers.

But, as that page relates, some saint is said to have appeared there to the abbot and is said to have told him: “Admit him with the others, because he died in your obedience.” In what obedience, I ask? Had the abbot ordered him to enter the danger of the river and pursue intercourse with an unchaste woman? Certainly, however much he may otherwise have obeyed the abbot, in this matter he cannot be said to have obeyed, because obedience can be understood nowhere except in what is good—unless the word is being abused. In what obedience, then, did he die? Indeed, if there is doubt about the meaning of the word *obedience*, let him hear the Apostle concerning the Son of God himself: “From the things he suffered, he learned obedience (Heb. V, 8).”

It may therefore be inferred that things to which such claims are attached contrary to the whole measure of reason are wholly unworthy of faith and therefore of acceptance. And certainly we see that, although it is decorated with gems and pearls from foreign shores—  
[Note: [Col. 0664B–C] Better *perulis*, that is, “pearls”; Gallic *perles*.]  
—what has been received by tradition as the memory of the tooth is not the tooth itself, and that what lies inside the same reliquary is proved solely by the reasoning of those who succeed one another, not by the experience of those now present. Thus they venerate in two ways what they do not know: they are completely unaware of what is enclosed by that gold and stone, and it cannot in any way be established that the case itself contains what it is thought to contain. [Col. 0664C]

### § V. The Blessed Virgin preserved no relics of the body of her Son for posterity. The Savior first does not appear to his mother because she certainly knew of the resurrection.

Will Mary therefore be accused of having been able alone to preserve what is said to be possessed by those people? How, then, could the one who recognized in advance the future state of her Son, whom the Holy Spirit had instructed above all angelic and human nature—indeed, above everything that exists after the Son—have been ignorant of the order of the resurrection? For if she had been ignorant, it would certainly have been fitting that he should appear first to her in order to establish the credibility of his resurrection.

But why would he appear to her, when she unquestionably knew, before he suffered and rose again, that he would rise? And certainly the saying is known: “A sword will pierce your soul” (Luke II, 35). Hence, preserving both the event and the words of those who spoke about it, she pondered them in her heart (ibid., 19). Since no one was regarded as sufficiently trustworthy to whom she could entrust so great a matter, it was surely not unfitting that she should conceal within herself her own thoughts and experiences. Therefore, since she herself was not ignorant of his future state, and since no one who could have distinguished him from the common mass of humanity preserved these things for posterity, everything that anyone has presumed concerning so great a body must be regarded as entirely superfluous.

For among us there stands the Apostle’s brief but decisive statement: the same body “was announced by angels, preached in the world, and taken up in glory” (I Tim. III, 16).

To pursue profit from the relics of the saints is sacrilegious. [Col. 0666A]

As for the others, we define the matter as follows. If the canons have decreed that someone who is killed while destroying idols is not to be numbered among the martyrs—since he may have been led astray by some other error—then no one, however much he may outwardly display the appearance of goodness, should readily be regarded as a saint unless he is proved so in some way by divine revelation.

But learn how sacrilegious it is to seek profit either by carrying the saints’ relics about or by displaying their bones, if you wish alike to censure the saints and avarice.

# BOOK FOUR  
## Concerning the Interior World

[Col. 0665]

# CHAPTER ONE

### § I. Whoever devotes himself to contemplation ought to renounce earthly things.

The state of the interior world—which external vision cannot grasp and no imagination can conceive—is reached solely by the power of contemplation. For where nothing material is found, nor anything subject to the senses, one penetrates by the single sharpness of the intellect: by that one eye, that one lock of her neck—that is, by the unique and indivisible concentration and restraint of thought by which the bride in the Song of Songs is recognized as pleasing her bridegroom above all (Song IV, 9).

Just as we cannot possess its vision in things that can be handled, so we cannot in any way perceive bodily places, or the places of bodies, in contemplating it. As in any page, if you attend to its contemplative meaning, you inspect the letters in which the meaning is contained with one set of eyes, while with another you contemplate the meaning itself, which is gathered by reason alone. [Col. 0665B–C]

No force of imagination contributes to this. For where neither temporality nor any mass subject to temporality intrudes upon the mind, nothing seen—or capable of being seen—admits anything external into itself. Imagination, which receives only forms and the habits of corruptible things, is always unable to endure subtlety and grows dense through the recollection of familiar things. If it wishes to rise toward some form of subtlety, it can be directed toward discerning intellectual realities only after the persistent intrusion of external vision has been expelled.

Hence we are commanded to pray to the Father with the door closed (Matt. VI, 6). This is the manner in which the first, second, and third heaven of which the Apostle speaks (II Cor. XII, 2) are to be understood. In this way, then, when spirituality advances as though toward a certain ethereal heaven, alone and unaccompanied by all earthly things, it compares spiritual things specially with spiritual things, examining by intellectual subtlety those incorporeal forms of the interior world. [Col. 0665D]

### § II. The visions in sacred Scripture present only corporeal images to the mind.

But the histories of the visions in the Old and New Testaments seem greatly to impede what we are saying, since, although raised to that state, they report having seen nothing except the bodily images of those things. When Ezekiel, in the vision of God, saw a storm wind, the north wind, a great cloud, and fire enveloping it, brightness all around, and four living creatures possessing a fourfold form (Ezek. I, 4–5), and when he also saw a building being measured on a mountain (Ezek. XL, 5), what did he see other than the prescribed images of corporeal things?

There were thresholds, gates, vestibules, and windows; there was a man in the appearance of bronze; there was a measuring reed and a measuring cord. What more need be said? There bodies or likenesses of bodies are observed, and nothing else is perceived that does not reproduce, in one way or another, the forms of present things.

Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and any others to whom God presented himself as visible speak in the same way—not in terms of truth, but through signs and figures—when they proclaim that they saw the throne of God and compare the appearance of the throne with sapphire and chrysolite. [Col. 0666B–C]

When, therefore, they represent the divine form either as fire or by distributing it into human shapes through the arrangement of individual limbs, there is nothing there that can be said concerning the true simplicity of almighty God, since whatever is done concerning the unbounded one is thought capable of being contained within bodily limitations.

Nothing there is expressed according to the purity of the eternal essence. Rather, everything is so constrained by figures and enigmas that nothing proper to his nature is proclaimed; only what allegorically pertains to his limbs is spoken of. Since everything consists in signs and figures, and nothing essential concerning God can be found in the writers of the Old Testament apart from this: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III, 14), the other things reported about him so strongly bear the odor of human custom in their words and deeds that, in every passion except sin, they conform to our habits or movements.

We know that nearly all these things happened figuratively among the ancients, and we have the Apostle as our witness to this (I Cor. X, 11). But in the New Testament, too, matters are not very different, since everything said in the Apocalypse seems in no respect to differ from external forms. Consider, then, what form, and as though of what outline, he saw on the Lord’s Day.

Yet one must pay the greatest attention to what is said: “I was in the spirit” (Rev. I, 10). What does “I was in the spirit” mean? Clearly, it means “in contemplation of spiritual things.” For he would not have been in the spirit unless he had something spiritual as an object of sight. If, then, nothing but spiritual things was visible to him, why could he speak only of corporeal forms, which alone he had before his eyes? [Col. 0666D–0667A]

Attend, then, to the merely human manner of the divine description. Attend to the two-edged sword, the lampstands, and the stars; and, to return to his appearance, to the hair white as wool and the feet fashioned of brass. Turn through the whole volume: nowhere will you find anything expressed except in a human manner. Nowhere—I do not say is anything substantial, but even anything essential—concerning God brought forth. Whatever is stated there is veiled beneath a thick covering of allegories.

Whatever is proclaimed there concerning the state of holy Church is also shaded by colored language. And although the one who saw is said to have been in the spirit, whatever spirituality lies hidden within speaks of nothing except corruptible form and corporeal things. [Col. 0667B]

### § III. The things in this world suggest nothing but material realities.

Since, then, those who pass from seeing present things to seeing interior things bring back nothing other than what they were accustomed to see in the world, someone might suppose that the same forms exist among spiritual beings as appear to exist among those above—or rather among those below, which is what we are.

If this uniformity of forms is so—and this is in no way to be believed—then there is neither distance nor difference between body and spirit. Indeed, to gather everything together briefly, spirituality itself is nothing. For if there is no intervening degree between the two, and if one passes from one into the other as from body into body, there is never a transition from the present, however limited, good to something better.

The things created by God are good, but they are imaginary. We use them for the time being, until we are granted enjoyment of those things which, because these are transitory, are called eternal. [Col. 0667C]

### § IV. Those who reported their visions displayed things resembling bodily realities.

Finally, what we have already suggested also seems supported by the fact that, according to blessed Pope Gregory, all those who were carried from this exterior world into that interior one and then returned remembered seeing nothing except things resembling those to which they had been accustomed here.

If some reported bridges, rivers, sulfurous stench, pleasant fields, houses built of golden bricks, and other such things, they must surely have inferred them from the likeness of the present state. Nor should you think that these things appeared only to certain persons in the sequence of the *Dialogue*, and not rather throughout all the visions that I remember—not merely reading, but also hearing. [Col. 0667D]

For what of Bede? In the *Deeds of the English*, when he inserts revelations once manifested to his people, full on one side of fear and on the other of glory, he says that nothing appeared except what was most suited to our usages.

There are mountains, castles, harsh weather, leaden chests of the damned, the torn shins of those placed in punishments, certain places exhaling stench and prepared as a punishment for the tormented, the genitals of a certain prince gnawed by the daily bite of some animal—I do not know what kind—and mountains of money as well; cloaks and silks, richly woven fabrics, and multifarious furnishings, set before those undergoing that examination as evidence of their perversity—namely, those who gladly accept gifts in order to pervert judgments.

Nor are modern examples lacking. Whenever something concerning the state of souls is seen even today, it differs in no way from the manner we have described. [Col. 0668A]

### § V. The Lord likewise uses material examples in the Gospel.

Moreover, in addition to all these things, what does the Lord Jesus himself seem to threaten except a material punishment? When he commands that hands and feet be bound, orders someone to be cast into the outer darkness, and declares that there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there (Matt. XXII, 13), what does he display other than the sufferings familiar to us?

And certainly, if we think that criminal souls—or souls that have sinned more lightly—are tormented by the same material punishment by which bodies are tormented, we do not, in accordance with the Apostle, compare spiritual things with spiritual things (I Cor. II, 13). This is nevertheless better demonstrated by the example that follows.

How many people sacrifice themselves to punishments and various labors in order to acquire earthly possessions?

Consider a man held captive by an infinite desire for profit, eagerly submitting himself to the most bloody labors in order to obtain what he desires; consider how he torments himself with hunger, how many sleepless nights and how many sweats he endures. If such endurance were imposed upon someone unwilling, it would certainly bring his life to a swift end.

This is made clear by considering the endurance of captives who are tortured for money. We see them being flayed by tortures so monstrous, suspended by their thumbs and genitals, having their teeth pulled out with pincers, their nails crushed by the pressure of wood, their heels smeared with salt and licked by the tongues of goats—and enduring all these things with such equanimity, indeed with such delight of spirit, that you could suppose their minds, exulting in their hidden recesses through the hope of treasure laid up, to be soothed by it. [Col. 0668B–C]

We have certainly learned by experience that a tower of extraordinary size, glowing with fire, could be entirely extinguished by a certain person with his moistened tongue, and that he demanded payment in money solely for undertaking this feat. If, then, when the body is worn down by such miseries, the mind, intoxicated by the joy of a hidden hope, rests from the same distress, it is easy to see that, just as the flesh is driven by torments while the soul is for a time free from such whirlwinds, so, when the body is in no way troubled, the soul is often slain by the mere conception of sadness. [Col. 0668D]

The holy martyrs compare spiritual things with spiritual things; the idle and hypocrites do otherwise. Holy men who consider their daily mortifications.

Comparing bodies with bodily things and spirits with spiritual things, as we have stated above, we see that each endures its own crosses without the other, according to place and time. This is clearly displayed in the holy martyrs, whose interior rejoices amid the sufferings of their outward person.

On the other hand, in those whom the sharpness of accidie consumes, it is evident by how many anxieties the wounded breast is torn apart, while, as one supposes, the body rests externally. In hypocrites you see fasts, endurance of cold, vigils during the day scarcely relieved at night, and at night watchfulness as though for unbroken prayer; yet the greed for empty glory considers these things very light.

In the minds of holy people, too, the sweetness of expectation of what is above makes the daily deaths of their flesh brief and momentary. Let it therefore be established as proved that, just as an external punishment is known to render bodies corpse-like, so spiritual vigor—or a hidden vice of the mind—either nourishes or torments what is within us. [Col. 0668D–0669A]

# CHAPTER II

### § I. The prophets and holy men were often unable to disclose the knowledge they received from God.

Having examined these matters under this arrangement—namely, how the punishments of souls should be thought to differ from bodily torments, and why the Lord himself and all the saints spoke, not merely thought, of that state in such a carnal manner—let us address the matter in turn.

If we are concerned with their understanding, prophetic perceptions were far more spiritual than they were able—I will not say obliged—to communicate to their hearers in the course of the argument already begun. I will nevertheless say, and assert without doubt, that they were neither able nor obliged to do so.

For if they had been able, they would have proclaimed publicly what they knew in part concerning Jesus who was to be born and the mysteries of the Church, if they had possessed permission to express what had partly shone within them.

Hence the Psalmist says: “You have manifested to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. L, 8). If things were uncertain even to him from whose seed the one to be born would come, what benefit would there have been if they had been proclaimed as doubtful teachings? Moreover, if hidden things are hidden because of their uncertainty, they are all the less to be disclosed. For the more hidden something is, the more dangerous it is to publish it if uncertainty arises.

Thus, what had indeed been manifested to them but remained uncertain and hidden to others, they had decided to keep silent about in a most fitting act of dispensation. Hence the Apostle says: “I heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (II Cor. XII, 4).

We can understand this in two ways. It is as though he were saying: such things are not in themselves permitted for a human being to utter; for what we speak we do not ordinarily write to anyone—“not to speak to a human being,” that is, not to explain them to another person. [Col. 0669B–D]

It is not within human free will to possess contemplation of God or knowledge of sacred Scripture.

They were therefore unable because they were not permitted. For unless the spirit of the prophets had been restrained by them as a horse is restrained by a bridle, the mystery they had conceived in their minds would no longer have been a mystery. They could not disclose what they had held under the seal of so great a dictator.

For if it is not within human free will or human power to possess contemplation of God or sacred Scripture whenever one wishes, then they could in no way have been permitted to think as much as they wished about future mysteries, nor even to penetrate completely what they were to say.

Just as in visions that come from God we are often informed about events concerning us, yet cannot gather from them how or when those events will occur, so their hearts were touched in particular ways that left them no power to explain what they had seen.

Their inability was nothing other than a matter of what was not permitted. Hence it is said of the Lord that he could perform no sign in Capernaum (Luke IV, 23). “He could not,” therefore, should be understood as “he was not permitted”; for it was not permitted that he should bestow the benefits of signs upon those whom he could not attach to his faith. Hence he also forbade pearls to be cast before swine (Matt. VII, 6), because the brightness of divine speech is wholly unsuited to filthy minds. [Col. 0669D–0670A]

### § II. He proves again that human speech is inadequate for the knowledge of God obtained in contemplation.

To return, then, to the sequence of the argument: whatever was said bodily about God by the prophets—rather said than perceived—is clearly an accommodation to human understanding. For they themselves could not find words by which to comprehend the nature of the divine essence, nor did they have hearers capable of grasping what was said—even if anyone could in any way say it.

Those who could neither speak nor hear these things were rightly silent concerning the nature of God. What necessity would have compelled them to speak, then, except that, if they had not spoken according to the custom of human language, they themselves would have failed in their speech like madmen? And if they had said things above themselves, then, just as they themselves would not have understood their own words, so they would have found no interpreters of what they said.

Hence they sometimes attribute to God comparisons and likenesses unworthy of him, saying that he is like a cart loaded with hay (Amos II, 13), or describing him as a powerful man drunk with wine (Ps. LXXVII, 65). [Col. 0670B–C]

Because they were not capable of what lay beyond them, they could proclaim only bodily things familiar to our usages. They did not hesitate to attribute even to God things that seemed less suitable to good human beings, so that, by composing things unworthy of the highest majesty, they might show that whatever can be greater and more worthy among us is altogether unworthy of God if it is applied to him.

Hence Ezekiel displays bodies resembling four monstrous living creatures, with faces more portentous than those of Janus—for they are shown as fourfold (Ezek. I, 5–6)—so that from a form enormous in our eyes we may understand that intellectuality alone is to be sought.

For if he makes his angels spirits (Ps. CIII, 4), and if only spiritual beings exist in the heavens, it is exceedingly unworthy to believe that such bodily forms are found among heavenly beings. Angels plainly please us by the brightness of their glory, whereas these figures displease us by the horror of their excessively dreadful appearance. Since the literal meaning fails, the only thing left is to seek what they signify. [Col. 0670D]

Human beings speak only of corporeal things.

Human beings therefore speak to human beings only about corporeal things, because, even if they perceived something intellectual, they were in no way able to express what they perceived. Hence one must suppose that those who go out into the interior state of that age, yet return to us, cannot see anything except what is familiar to those living bodily, and that through the image of earthly things a few rays of eternal realities shine upon us.

For if they were able to grasp things in that way, so that they did not return to this age, then, while still placed in this flesh, not only their words but also their subtle and formerly acute intellects outside the flesh would grow dull, and what they saw would perish within them, let alone that they could explain to others things incomprehensible even to themselves.

When they return from interior realities, then, they can speak to human beings in terms resembling what human beings see externally, because all the saints, whatever they were at some time—or even for a moment—able to see in divine contemplation, never had the power to convey it in speech or writing. [Col. 0671A]

When, therefore, in a vision they perceive the glory of the saints through scents, or hear hymnic choirs, or absorb radiances, all these things are presented not according to the truth of spiritual nature, but according to the qualities of visible things with which they are familiar.

Whatever among human beings is more beautiful, more precious, or more delightful is shown to us in interior visions, so that from the things we chiefly value among ourselves we may derive indications of the glory granted to the saints.

Hence in the Apocalypse they are said to be clothed in white robes, to carry palms in their hands as signs of victory, and to have golden crowns on their heads, as befits those who reign (Rev. VII, 9). What is signified by pleasant places, flowers, and splendid forms does not revive the fables of those heretics called Chiliasts, who promise a thousand years of carnal pleasures after the resurrection. Rather, the sequences of these visions display such things—things with which human beings are accustomed to delight—as signs of the glory of the saved. [Col. 0671B–C]

Moreover, what we say about the revelation of the glorified is what we also think about the condemnation of the punished. When, according to Scripture, souls are often seen being burned by fires, consigned to scourges, submerged in foul waters, and subjected to the things presented by Gregory and Bede, the teachers, these are nothing other than the punishments customarily inflicted bodily upon criminals. They suffer them spiritually.

Nor would we, to whom such things are announced, believe ourselves condemned to be tormented by such miseries unless we recognized the punishments that we ourselves have continually been accustomed to experience. Since we cannot hear that spiritual language in which spiritual things answer spirits, we extract, as it were, the colors of intellectual realities from our knowledge of corporeal things, and from the things by which bodies are known to be afflicted we perceive souls to be constrained. [Col. 0671C–D]

### § III. If souls are not afflicted by material punishments, by what punishments are they afflicted?

Since we do not believe that pure souls can be restrained by bodily punishments, let us consider by what punishments they can and ought to be distressed. Above I said, on the authority of the Apostle, that spiritual things must be compared with spiritual things. It is very astonishing if an incorporeal soul is said to be afflicted by tangible torments.

To begin, however, we should speak of that world which, as the Apostle says to the Gentiles, “are called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision” (Eph. II, 11), is called interior in relation to this exterior world.

For just as, within my body—which is visible to everyone—there lies the invisible soul, so beneath this material creation, which is visible to rational and irrational natures, there lies another structure. It is visible and accessible only to rational beings stripped of immortality. No mind occupied with images of visible things can measure its state; it lies open only to the eyes of souls freed from the filth of this age. [Col. 0671D–0672A]

Just as we call something a spiritual word when it is produced by breath, tongue, and teeth—hence the Apostle says, “I will sing with the spirit” (I Cor. XIV, 15)—so there is, if I may put it this way, a mental word, which is arranged or expressed by thought alone while the lips are silent, and even an intellectual word, which is treated through the purest contemplation without any inner arrangement of words.

So, too, this world in which we live can be called visible and imaginary, because it lies beneath our gaze and, when our eyes are empty of other things, its corporeality can be recalled by the mind. But that interior world is penetrated with greater difficulty, because it contains and enacts nothing of bodies, places, or times. And the more it differs from our practice—for we scarcely ever fix the gaze of the mind anywhere except upon the things to which we are accustomed—the more earnestly we must break through the mists of our attention in order to see that interior world. [Col. 0672A–B]

# CHAPTER III

## Whether the demons inhabit this world

The question arises whether this world is generally habitable by the devil and his angels, since the Lord calls him the prince of this world in which we act (John XII, 31). The Apostle also calls him “the prince of the power of the air” (Eph. II, 2), “the prince of the darkness of this world,” and “spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12).

The question, then, is whether the one who, because of his dwelling within this air, is called aerial and wanders invisibly among us is also considered contiguous with that world.

The first point raised in response is this: however great the dignity and purity of that world may be, I would not dare to say that it was not common to good and evil alike. For since the nature of demons is sharpened by innate liveliness, their keenness of perception—or rather the agility of spiritual power—means that, however much they may wander through the exterior world, they maintain their proper dwelling in that interior world to the same extent that they possess a greater communion of nature with it.

For if the world is spiritual, and if the devil does not consist of a denser corporeality, then, since the identity of substances is recognized in both, apart from rationality, one is not permitted to be absent from the other. [Col. 0672B–D]

The world is accessible to the devil for now.

Before the day of judgment, that interior world is accessible to the devil because, for souls being thrust into eternal punishment, he is the exactor and servant of God in that space; and freedom to perform this office is granted to his cruelty until, when the grain is separated from the chaff, his power is taken away.

Indeed, I consider him, together with his deadly army, to be an inhabitant of the hell of this world. Why should he not be, since those banished to prison are separated from the present state of the age only by their punishments, so that whether their children are noble or ignoble, they are said to be unknown to blessed Job? (Job XIV, 2.)

That other world is nevertheless distinguished from the likeness of this one by the fact that in this world good and evil are held together indiscriminately, whereas there the saved and the lost are shut away in an infinite separation from one another.

After the Day of Judgment, by no means: for the world will become pure. The saints themselves will then inhabit it. —After the final day, therefore, the devil himself, together with his accomplices, having shared their punishment, will no longer be able to find passages by which to exercise his former plague; and the world will become all the more uniform in its accustomed purity, since no polluted being will thereafter be able to pass through it. Hence, when a new heaven and a new earth have been made (Rev. XXI, 1), both the inner and the outer world will be accessible and habitable to the saints. For when the saints have been purified both by fire and advanced through the blessed transformation of their bodies, and when the age—or rather the world itself—has been consumed by the conflagration of its ancient defilements and restored to an incorruptible condition, the state of the habitation and of its inhabitants will everywhere correspond. Once purification has been accomplished in both places, dwelling-place and dweller alike will flourish. And just as body and soul in the saints will rejoice beneath the glory of a single blessedness, so the outer and inner world, reduced to a single purity by the burning away of the other, will display splendid, unhindered movements to the saints, who will triumph everywhere.

## CHAPTER IV

### § I. Neither do the elect possess bodily glory in heaven, nor do the reprobate possess bodily punishment in hell

Let us return, then, to the matter with which we began. If we wish to determine whether those punishments which we say are inflicted upon the reprobate in that more hidden world are bodily or incorporeal, we can arrive at a better understanding by considering the contrary. We must first ask plainly whether the elect attain bodily or incorporeal glories in the heavenly kingdom.
