If we judge their glories to be bodily—that is, if we suppose that they devote themselves to pleasures, taste, and banquets—we explain nothing; rather, we oppose the Scriptures. “Do not rejoice,” he says, “over the spirits that are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). Certainly the apostles themselves, still inexperienced, say to the Lord: “Lord,” they say, “show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 8). And likewise: “But I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice” (John XVI, 22). If the glory of the inhabitants of heaven consists in such things, what earthly thing is being sought here? What bodily pleasure is to be supposed in the vision of God the Father? Further, what does the psalm say? “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth? God,” he says, “is the God of my heart and my portion” (Ps. LXXII, 25–26). If, therefore, “whoever sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life” (John VI, 40), and if nothing is sought in heaven or on earth except to possess God, I ask: what place is left for bodily pleasures?

364 Since no examples are available by which anyone might understand anything carnal in heaven, it is strange if someone judges otherwise, as though seeking falsehood in truth itself. If, therefore, everything that exists in God’s reward is spiritual, it seems to me to follow that what is administered by spirits, even evil ones, in the spiritual world must likewise be considered spiritual insofar as it concerns the punishment of wicked spirits. For just as we do not believe that angels are burdened by human stench, so we say that souls cannot be tormented by bodily punishments.

### § II. What are the weeping and gnashing of teeth in hell?

But, as I said above, we can approach the matter more effectively from the opposite side. If, according to the Apostle, “the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV, 17), let us examine, by contrast, what a condition utterly different from these—namely, eternal turmoil, perpetual agitation, and sadness—prevails in hell. “There,” says the Lord, “will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII, 12). What is the weeping of souls except their heartfelt and inward sorrow? Weeping, which is emitted only by embodied beings, and gnashing, which properly belongs to beings furnished with teeth, are referred to the pain, madness, and fury of those incorporeal beings themselves. For when gnashing is spoken of a human being, it belongs to those who rage. It is therefore the pain of misery endured and to be endured forever. There is also gnashing when the soul, made a fellow-member of the devil and now a despiser of all divine things, begins to regret that it did not make itself worse than it did.

Hence the saying: “When the wicked has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). “Every tree,” he says, “that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10). It is cut down, that is, from the power of sinning—which means the same as if he had said: “Bind his hands and feet” (Matt. XXII, 13). To be thrown into the fire means to be consumed by the perpetual desire to do evil. Hence also the saying: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. LVII, 9). For if it is true—as it is—that in that inner world they desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve, although rejoicing is wholly unsuitable to the wicked, nevertheless three of these things cannot be absent from them even for a moment. I do not mean merely that they are subjected to the same passions to which they were once subject, but that they experience them all the more furiously the more spiritual they are, so that these passions themselves— not merely one, but passions of every kind—become in them nothing other than an unquenchable and ever-burning fire.

### § III. Blessed Gregory says that souls are tormented by material fire

If someone objects to me that blessed Gregory says that souls are punished by bodily fire (Dialogues, Book IV, chapter 29), let him attend to what is said there. “We say,” he states, “that the spirit is held by fire,” so that in the torment there is fire both seen and felt. For it suffers fire by the very fact that it sees, and because it beholds itself being burned, it is burned. The whole matter is this: because it sees itself condemned, it is boiled by the savage exacerbation of the mind. Consider a man confined in an eternal prison: deadly weariness destroys him. This year I saw a certain man who, unless his own people rescued him, had put a noose around his neck out of fear of poverty. From his circumstances, therefore, according to the blessed pope, the spirit has something by which it may be tormented.

But if the rich man’s punishment is alleged to be bodily fire, I should very gladly ask the holy pope, were he present, whether, if that fire is bodily, as he says, taste, finger, and tongue are likewise bodily. Since we consider it impious not to agree with so great a teacher, yet do not know how to mingle bodily things with spiritual things in that wholly interior realm, let us entrust to God what we have not yet been able to experience. For we oppose no one; we simply state our perceptions, with sincere intent and according to the measure of our understanding.

## CHAPTER V

### § I. What is the activity of the saints in heavenly glory, and what is that of the impious in eternal torments?

The devil’s food is to suggest sins. —It is therefore clear that, just as the benevolence of the saints continually increases with immeasurable sweetness when they attain the vision of God, so the souls of the reprobate, united to their head, the devil, burn with a far more vehement desire to sin, not without the most atrocious torment, in proportion as they differ in no intention from him whose food is to suggest sins. And just as the saints regret, when they behold the glory of God, that they did not labor more earnestly to attain it, so the impious grieve most bitterly that, before coming to those punishments, they did not serve their malicious pleasures more fully. Why should they not? Of the living impious person it is said: “Under his tongue are labor and pain” (Ps. X, 7). Labor, namely, because he sweats in the pursuit of doing evil; pain, because he cannot accomplish the crimes he has desired. And what can be said of him who is incorporated into Satan? How great will the intensity of the worst desire be in him? If the saints burn with everlasting ardors toward God, the wicked gnash with perpetual furies.

### § II. Why does the rich man ask that Lazarus, not himself, be sent into the world?

The Gospel passage about the rich man and Lazarus also supports our opinion. If it is examined carefully, it reveals a great deal about the condition of the inner world. First, if you consider what it means that the same rich man asks not that he himself be raised and sent to his father’s house, but that Lazarus be sent (Luke XVI, 27), you will find that he had departed from this life with the most wicked will. He knew for certain that, if he were raised and returned to the world, he would have no desire to correct himself; nor did he in any way intend to abandon the same perversity from which he could not be separated amid his torments. He also plainly understood that, if he were restored to his former condition in the world and did not conduct himself better than before, he would ultimately fall back into the same torments, with his condemnation multiplied a hundredfold. He therefore confidently asks that Lazarus be raised, since nothing else was expected of him than that he who had lived piously amid illness and poverty before experiencing glory could, upon returning to life, become only better than he had been.

### § III. Why does that rich man show such concern for the salvation of his brothers?

Our opinion is also supported by the fact that the man who, according to Solomon, possessed neither wisdom, nor knowledge, nor understanding in hell (Ecclus. IX, 10)—the man, that is, whom the fury of the devil’s purpose drove—why did he ask so benevolently on behalf of his brothers, lest they too should be lost? If benevolence is a good thing, and this very thing is subject to punishment, then surely wisdom, knowledge, and understanding are also present there, contrary to what the aforementioned wise man said. But since the Holy Spirit cannot lie in this matter, it is easy to see how futile this request is.

It was said above that the reprobate in hell will not merely not lack carnal affections, but will also grow hardened in perverse loves. The rich man understood this when he feared his brothers’ arrival. He knows that, with each of his brothers, his punishment would be doubled; and because he turned away from divine love in the worship and desire of them, he is equally inflamed and maddened by their condemnation, which he sees prepared for them. Since, therefore, he fears that his hell will, so to speak, be multiplied fivefold, he asks that his brothers be kept away from his company by the teaching of Lazarus.

Someone may object that this punishment could not have been avoided without a good act; therefore he was not without benevolence, since he preferred that they act more correctly. We reply: there are many things which we seem to desire, although it is plainly recognized that we do not desire them. If, for example, you suffer an incurable disease in a finger and a surgeon advises that it be cut off, you say that you would rather have the finger amputated than be deprived of the use of the whole hand as the disease spreads. You say that you prefer this to that, although in truth you desire neither. Such was the will of the rich man: in desiring, he did not desire, and in not desiring, he desired, preferring this to enduring an increase of his punishment. Thus, whoever the impious loved against God, they see being tortured before them by a just judgment, and they continually reflect their punishments back upon themselves.

## CHAPTER VI

Souls are not bodily, nor are they capable of sensation except in a spiritual manner. What is the spiritual worm? —I do not know what bodies souls possess. This, above all, accords with my judgment: what is said by the Lord’s mouth should be understood figuratively: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 24). If blessed Job rightly said of the putrid and decaying body, “Those who consume me do not sleep” (Job XXX, 17), I do not see how this can refer to the spirit, since we have not yet heard that worms are born from the spirit or that worms bite the spirit. Since, therefore, a spiritual worm departs from the letter—a worm which is the sting of perpetual anguish and an always fruitless remorse—let us understand it as fixed in the soul, whose fire is never extinguished, because it is consumed by unfailing anxiety until the end of its utterly hopeless misery.

What are the torments of the condemned? —If you think that those who are in hell suffer too little pain and torment, what do you consider worse than being driven mad by infinite rage and being conformed in all folly to the devil and his angels? Their madness is plainly just, for those whose eternal despair consists in the absence of every refreshment throughout the ages of ages: what else is there for them but a rage that is always renewed? If, as the Apostle testifies, the sadness of this age is called “working death” (II Cor. VII, 10), since a person may be driven by conceived resentment and excessive grief to lay hands upon himself, what bitterness of unremoved death must the ferocity of those minds foster, which cannot endure even a single moment’s rest? In this life the mind is sometimes soothed by hopes, even false ones; there, the inward severity is so complete, without the flattery of any foolish thought, that no emptiness capable of pleasing the wretched even for an instant can steal in.

## CHAPTER VII

How those who were freed from hell by the Lord are said to have been established in darkness. The chief punishment of the reprobate in hell is eternal deprivation of the contemplation of God. —Moreover, if those who were brought out of hell when the Lord rose are said, while they were there, to have been established in darkness, although they suffered there no darkness except that of sheer weariness—darkness increased daily by prolonged deprivation of the divine vision, though they were not entirely deprived of the hope of possessing it one day—what could be darker, I do not say to their eyes but to their hearts, for those upon whom the density of such despair is laid? Let others speak of fires, allege sulphur, and add the spirits of storms as well. I state my judgment confidently: there is no abyss worse, no destruction more cruel among them, no torment more grievous than every torturer, than that they are hopelessly to lose so loving and serene a Lord, whom they will not see in their uttermost unhappiness and misery. They would not be wholly darkened if they had any possibility of breathing again elsewhere.

366 For if “whoever sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life” (John VI, 40), and “this is eternal life, that they know you, God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3), so that the everlasting vision of God alone is sufficient for the blessedness of the saints, who would dare oppose or resist the claim that the principal—or rather the unique—cause of the condemned’s misery is that they are eternally excluded from the contemplation of God? Nor does this seem absurd in any respect. Rather, both truth and probability establish it: what grants life to the saints, as brightness grants clarity to the eye, inflicts death upon the reprobate, as the deprivation of light brings night.

## CHAPTER VIII

### § I. Souls are proved to be incorporeal

Furthermore, some people describe the form of souls in such a way that they attach human figures to them. I neither hold nor understand this opinion. If you ascribe to them an ear and an eye, a nostril and a lip, a breast and a womb, kidneys and thighs, feet and shins, you plainly make them bodily. But if they are bodily, how do they fit within a body? And if they fit within it in the way that smaller vessels are contained within larger ones, I should like to know how two bodies are confined within one another under such constraint. I say this not against those people, but rather according to their own words, for they wrote that souls possess the figures of their bodies. Such are the people whom I consider it rash to refute. If, then, body is inserted into body, it must necessarily be fitted together so that mouth is joined to mouth, hand to hand, and each limb to its corresponding limb—so that, if it should happen, as it commonly does, that one is cut off, two would be amputated instead of one.

Finally, even if you believe that souls are formed in this way, you must necessarily confine them both to places and to intervals of time, and remove from them everything that belongs to and is called spirit. What will their size be, if it is greater than that of the body? What will their agility be? If it is assumed as an argument that they appear in visions according to the forms of bodies, the argument is easily overturned: what is seen in this way is neither body nor soul, but only the image of the thing seen that is carried back to the mind.

What of the water which the rich man asks for in his torments? —Let them suppose, then, that the rich man in hell had a tongue and that Lazarus had a finger (Luke XVI, 24), and that this supports their position. But I should like to ask them whether there was water in that spiritual world. If there was, then its inhabitants required material things such as these. Let it be so. But how could they have been so effective in extinguishing the fire of Gehenna? My God, what would a drop accomplish there, when the Ganges and the Indus flowed uselessly into that tongue? We therefore understand the tip of Lazarus’s finger as bringing a drop when, through even the smallest intention of his, the gift of whatever slight indulgence was administered to the rich man. This is the smallest finger which the Pharisees and scribes, after laying heavy and unbearable burdens upon people’s shoulders, are unwilling to move in order to lift them (Matt. XXIII, 4).

But if the human image is still defended, what will Germanus accomplish in the fiery sphere according to blessed Gregory (Dialogues, Book II, chapter 35)? In what direction will Scholastica, transformed into a dove, proceed (ibid., chapter 33)? Let the whole controversy therefore be brought to this single point: we should attribute to them neither a human, nor a fiery, nor a dovelike form, but strip them entirely of every bodily thing and likeness, and devote them wholly to intellectual subtlety. For it is incongruous to say that a spiritual habitation has bodily inhabitants. If, indeed, these are the words of the Lord Jesus: “My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world” (John XVIII, 36), and “I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until I drink it new in my kingdom” (Matt. XXVI, 29), and if this same kingdom is daily requested to come (Matt. VI, 10), then we state without hesitation that heaven—that is, the higher part of the threefold structure of the universe, which is also called the seat of God because of its more worthy portion—is nothing other than this spiritual interiority. In it, as though outside this world, the Lord declares that he reigns, because here the ruler of this air, together with his followers, greatly opposes him, whereas there he possesses all things in peace.

This kingdom—that is, those over whom he has reigned and reigns through charity—after he “has handed it over to God and the Father, then God will be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 24). Hence he says to the thief: “Today you will be with me”; he does not say, “in heaven,” but “in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). For paradise is where the constant vision of Christ is, and this exists nowhere except in that spiritual age. Nor did he ascend into heaven before the eyes of the disciples so that, with the lower part left vacant, he might sit in the upper part; rather, he showed himself to occupy the more worthy place, from which he indicated to those of lesser understanding that he presides with the Father, since in that inner world there is neither high nor low, nor anything local—especially since it has neither times nor places.

Just as sensuality by itself not only does not subordinate reason and understanding to itself, but does not even penetrate them—for “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of God” (I Cor. II, 14)—while reason and understanding not only discern these things beneath themselves but also enter into divine things, so God and the saints, like understanding and reason, judge all bodily things, yet in such a way that those bodily things touch neither of them.

These matters have been pursued thus far without prejudice to a better opinion. We defend them not with verbal ornament, but by faith alone.

[Col. 0679] THE END.

# THE HISTORY CALLED THE DEEDS OF GOD THROUGH THE FRANKS, WRITTEN BY THE VENERABLE GUIBERT, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY AT NOGENT

## GUIBERT’S LETTER TO LYSIARD, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

367 To Lysiard, father and lord, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons, Guibert, forever indebted to his generosity, whatever is believed sweet and unique in affection.

### Lysiard, distinguished by nobility and learning. —Why the style of this history is more elegant than in Guibert’s other works

When my friends often suggested that I should not mark the present little work with my own name, I continually rejected the proposal, plainly fearing that I might disgrace a pious history with the name of an objectionable person. But thinking that the work itself, already distinguished, could be made more distinguished by the title of a distinguished man, I finally brought it to you, and, with the mark of its author suppressed, placed before the work a most delightful luminary. For since your ancient nobility is joined by literary learning, a particular serenity, and moral moderation, it is rightly believed that God, the disposer of all things, provided that the dignity of the episcopate should dignify a gift of such reverence. Let the following little document therefore bloom beneath your embraceable name. In itself it is uncouth, but may it be refined by love for you, to whom it is written, and strengthened by the authority of the office in which you excel.

There were, indeed, other prelates whom the ideas, or even opinions, of this and my other writings had touched. Setting these aside, however, my chief desire was directed toward you. In reading this work you should consider that, if I sometimes happened to depart from ordinary grammar, I did so because I was correcting the defects—or rather the earth-creeping style—of the preceding history. I see villages, cities, and towns fervently devoted to grammatical studies. Therefore, if I had possessed the ability, I would not have wished to differ from the ancient historians. Finally, consider that amid the concerns of household administration and frequent hearings of cases, my intention was feverishly occupied with dictating—or, more burdensome still, translating; and while I was compelled to listen outside to various matters, not without biting annoyance, I was obliged inwardly to hold firmly to what I had begun.

Let no one be surprised that I used a very different style from that employed in the Expositions on Genesis or in my other treatises. It is fitting, and entirely permissible, that history be adorned with the laborious elegance of words; but the mysteries of sacred discourse must be handled not with poetic chatter, but with ecclesiastical simplicity. I therefore ask that you receive this graciously and preserve it as an enduring memorial of your name.

[Col. 0679] THE LETTER ENDS.

# PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING HISTORY

368 In carrying out the present little work, I received much encouragement not from any confidence in literary learning—for the extent of that learning in me is admittedly very slight—but from the authority of spiritual history. I have always held it certain that whatever history was completed by God’s sole power and through those whom he chose, he also wished to have written through those whom he chose, even if they were unlearned. For he who led them through so many difficulties of travel, who cut down before them so many remnants of war, could surely have no difficulty in placing the truth of the events, in whatever manner pleased him, within my work, nor in denying it the appropriate ornaments of language.

### The style of the earlier account was excessively simple. What style suits a historian and one treating divine matters?

The same history already existed, but it was woven in words that were too simple and often exceeded the rules of grammar, and whose vapid and tasteless expression could frequently exhaust the reader. To the less learned, and to those who do not care about the quality of expression, it seems sufficiently suitable because of their love for this new account; and they suppose that it could not have been expressed by its author in any other way than they themselves understand it.

But to those for whom the nourishment of eloquence is considered honorable, when they weigh what has been expressed less appropriately, they note that a graceful manner of narration is required where the subject demands it, and that a concise presentation appears where the expansive variety of persuasive eloquence would have been suitable. When they see the sequence of the matter undertaken proceeding in bare footsteps, they either fall asleep or laugh, in the sense of the poet; indeed, when they consider that the badly assumed discourse ought to have been sung in a very different manner, they resent it. Speech must plainly be adapted to the condition of the matters and persons being treated, so that the sharpness of words may convey martial deeds, while what pertains to divine things should proceed with a more measured step.

If I had possessed the ability to do so, I ought to have ranged through this field of work in both forms, so that insolent Gradivus might recognize the distinction of his deeds, which should not be recited in mismatched words, and so that, when piety is at issue, Mercurial modesty might never exceed the tone of gravity assigned to it. Although I have not been able to fulfill these things according to my intention, I have nevertheless learned to approve, and no less to commend, for the most part, what was well done by another.

### The study of grammar was then flourishing

I therefore confess that, in my very rash and impudent exposure to the judgments of others—rash, but arising from love of the faith—I have taken a risk. For since my studies have found me engaged in this work out of a desire to correct it, perhaps what is second may be judged worse than what came before. Since we see grammar flourishing everywhere, and know that this discipline is open even to the most worthless people because of the great number of schools, it seemed shameful not to write, even if we neither ought nor were able to do so, the glory of our age. Indeed, I saw that it would be disgraceful to leave beneath the roughness of uncouth language a history concerning which God had accomplished in these days deeds more marvelous than anything he had done in the past, allowing such a jewel to be scattered in the dust. Unable to endure so great a contempt, I took care, with whatever eloquence I could command, to complete what had been handed over to neglect—something more precious than all gold.

### Guibert had devoted himself excessively to poetry

Nor did I undertake this merely presumptuously, from my own impulse; some people had also faithfully urged me to do so by their requests. Some asked that I write in prose, while most urged that it be done in verse, since they had learned that, in my earliest beginnings, I had celebrated this kind of study more than was proper. But now, advanced in age, rank, and experience, I judged that it should not be expressed in flattering words or in the clatter of verses. Rather, if I may say so, I thought it worthy of being arranged with greater maturity than all the histories of the Jewish war, if God should grant anyone the ability to speak about this matter.

I do not deny that, after the capture of Jerusalem, when those who had taken part in so great an expedition began to return, I turned my mind to writing about it; but because obstacles arising from certain importunities concerning the matter stood in the way, I postponed it. Since, however, by God’s permission—though I do not know whether by his will—an opportunity has been offered to my desire, I have entered upon what I had devoutly longed for, perhaps to be laughed at by everyone, passing beyond the laughter and derision of some, so long as I might somehow make an outlet for the long eruption of what I had conceived.

And if there is someone who laughs, let him not disparage one who acts according to his ability and strives for what is sound; let him not prematurely brand my words with a blemish. But if he utterly rejects them, then, setting aside quarrels over words, let him write the matter anew, badly argued though it may be, and provide examples of how it should be dictated.

### He composed the history from an account

If anyone complains that something has been expressed somewhat obscurely, let him beware of inflicting upon himself the mark of dullness, since I know for certain that no person trained in letters could justly raise a question concerning what I have said in the following book. As I undertook to correct—or, I do not know whether, to corrupt—the exemplar of the history itself, I first set forth the causes and necessities that pressed toward the undertaking of this expedition, as I had heard them, and then, after displaying the circumstances, attached the account of the deeds.

I learned the course of these events, related by the earlier author whom I am following with much variation [another reading: truth], from those who had taken part in the journey. I frequently compared what was reported in the book with the words of those who had seen the events, and I discovered beyond doubt that neither account differed from the other. Whatever I added, I either learned from those who had seen it or came to know through my own experience.

### It is therefore not surprising if he is mistaken in some matters

If anything should prove to have been said otherwise than the matter actually stands, an ingenious discoverer of faults will have accused me in vain of lying, since, under God’s testimony, he can know that I said nothing from a desire to deceive. For what is surprising if we are mistaken when we report the deeds of others, when we cannot, I do not say express in words, but even gather silently in our minds, our own thoughts and actions? What shall I say of intentions, which are so often shown to lie hidden that they can scarcely be discerned even by the acuity of the inner person? We should not therefore be judged too severely if, through ignorance, we slip into error in our words. But what must be beaten down by inexorable censure is falsehood woven deliberately, either from a desire to deceive or from the purpose of someone’s subornation.

### Why he used more recent terminology when citing proper names

Regarding the names of people, provinces, and cities, I have an innate difficulty. When I recognize that certain names whose form I have encountered were badly expressed by that author, I have no doubt that names farther removed, and therefore more unfamiliar, were pronounced with the same corruption. For example, we call the Turks by their everyday name; we call Corozania a name of recent coinage. Since the antiquity of these names lies almost entirely hidden by oblivion, I preferred, after setting aside every ancient form—even if it had been fully available—to say only what is commonly repeated.

If I were to write Parthians rather than Turks, as some believe, and Caucasus rather than Corozania, I would become obscure by pursuing supposed authenticity and would expose myself to criticism from those who dispute the proper names of regions. Above all, I consider that, just as lands in these provinces are known to have been marked by new names, so we must not doubt that foreign lands have likewise changed. If what was once called Neustria is now called Normandy, and what was Austria is now called Lorraine in consequence of certain changes, why should we not believe that the same thing has happened among eastern peoples? Indeed, some claim that Memphis, once Egyptian, is now called Babylon. I therefore preferred to express certain things in the vulgar manner rather than become obscure or provoke dispute by setting down different names.

I was long uncertain about the name of the bishop of Puy—commonly, *le Puy*. Only at the end of this work did I learn it, for it was not found in my copy.

Let the reader also pardon my negligence in composition, knowing without doubt that the moments available to me for writing were the same as those available for dictating. I did not carefully revise what should have been corrected on wax tablets; instead, I set it down on parchment as it was available, badly uttered. I gave the work a title free from arrogance and beneficial to the honor of the nation, namely:

# THE DEEDS OF GOD THROUGH THE FRANKS

# THE DEEDS OF GOD THROUGH THE FRANKS, OR THE JERUSALEM HISTORY, BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE

### [I.] The virtue of those living in our own time must by no means be blamed

It is a defective habit, though not an invariable one, that has grown into the character of certain mortals: they blame the deeds of modern people while exalting ages past. Certainly, the happiness tempered by the moderation of the ancients and the vigor moderated by reconsideration of their plans deserved praise. Yet no sensible person should in any way place their worldly prosperity above whatever virtue may belong to us. For although purified virtue prevailed among the ancients, the endowment of nature has not entirely died out in us, even though the end of the ages has come down to us.

Because of the novelty of the people involved, deeds accomplished in ancient times are rightly praised; but those things that are usefully accomplished by the unlearned while the world is sliding into old age deserve to be proclaimed with much greater justice.

We sigh for foreign kingdoms once distinguished by mighty wars. We recount Philip's slaughter and victory, pitiless everywhere and achieved amid continual bloodshed. We weigh in thunderous language the madness of Alexander, rising from the furnace of the Macedonians to the destruction of all the East. We measure the forces of Xerxes at Thermopylae and of Darius against Alexander, together with the detestable slaughter of innumerable nations. We admire Chaldean pride, Argive severity, Egyptian depravity, and unstable Asia through the investigations of Pompeius Trogus and other eminent authors. We embrace the earliest institutions of the Romans, established under the judgment of common utility and the expansion of empire.

And yet, if the essence of all these things is examined thoroughly, their boldness is not merely found praiseworthy among all decent people; rather, the persistent madness of waging war without any reason, from the sole desire to rule, rightly lies open to infamy.

### The martial deeds of Christians surpass those of the pagans

Let us look back—or rather, let us come to our senses—and examine the fetid dregs, so to speak, of this age which we despise. Then we shall be able to find our little finger thicker than the backs of the fathers whom we exalt beyond measure, in accordance with the saying of the foolish king. For if we consider the battles of the pagans and the kingdoms acquired through immense military labor, we shall judge that none of their strength and none of their exercises can, by God’s grace, be compared with ours.

If we have heard that God was magnified among the Jewish people, we have learned through certain proofs that Jesus Christ is as powerful and active among modern people today as he was among the ancients yesterday. Kings, generals, dictators, and consuls, whenever they were about to fight, assembled the multitudes of peoples and, through powerful decrees, gathered numerous armies from every nation:

> Yet these, these come together, driven by the terrors of men.

What shall I say of those who, without a lord, without a prince, driven solely by God—in fact, advancing not only beyond their native province and beyond their original kingdom, but even beyond the multitude of intervening nations and languages—extended the lines of their camps from the farthest shores of the British Ocean to the very center of the whole earth?

We are speaking of the new and incomparable victory of the Jerusalem expedition. Its glory among those who are not foolish is so great that we rejoice that our times have been marked with such a title, a distinction which no earlier ages deserved. Our people were not driven to undertake this by empty fame, by money, or by the ambition of extending their boundaries—motives upon which almost all who move, or have moved, arms against anyone else rely.

To them the following poetic words may appropriately be applied:

> What madness, citizens, what such license of the sword,  
> To offer your own blood to hated nations?

It seemed good to wage wars destined to have no triumphs. For if they undertook the cause of defending liberty or safeguarding the commonwealth, they could certainly put forward an honorable excuse. But whenever an invasion by barbarian peoples or pagans is feared, no soldier ought to be barred from the right to bear arms; and, when these circumstances are absent, wars undertaken solely for the protection of Holy Church have nevertheless customarily been conducted with complete legitimacy. Yet because this pious intention has now died away in everyone’s hearts, and the desire to possess everything has seized them all, God established holy battles in our time so that the military order and the wandering populace—who, following the example of ancient paganism, had been engaged in mutual slaughter—might discover a new means of earning salvation. Thus they would not be compelled to abandon the world entirely by choosing the monastic life, as usually happens, or by adopting some other religious profession; instead, under their accustomed license and dress, they might obtain some measure of God’s grace through the very duties of their own station.

People of every status and condition renounced everything in order to set out to war against the faithless. — Thus, with God as their instigator, we heard [al.: saw] nations in motion, hardening the innermost entrances of their hearts against every kind of attachment and affection, and seeking exile with such eagerness in order to overthrow the enemies of the Christian name, going beyond the Latin world and even beyond known lands, as no one had ever seemed to us to approach banquets or holidays with such enthusiasm. The highest honors, and lordship over castles and cities, were scorned; the most beautiful wives became loathsome as though they were something putrid; the sight of children of either sex, once more pleasing than every jewel, was rejected; and toward that which no mortal could have compelled them to undertake by command or driven them to by persuasion, they were carried by the sudden obstinacy of minds transformed. No ecclesiastical person needed to deliver speeches in the churches to stir up the peoples for this purpose, since each person, at home and abroad, proclaimed to another the vows of departure no less by exhortation than by example. The zeal of each burned, and those who had no resources for expenses seemed just as capable of undertaking that journey as those for whom the sale of vast possessions or stored-up treasures furnished the richest provision for travel. One could plainly see Solomon’s saying fulfilled: “The locust has no king, yet it goes forth, all of it, in its companies” (Prov. 30:27).

This locust had made no leap toward good works as long as it had lain numb under the long frost of iniquity. But when the heat of the sun of justice had grown hot [al.: flared up], it immediately sprang forth in the natural flight of migration: it departed from its father’s house and kindred, and through the adoption of a holy purpose was changed in its conduct. It had no king, because every faithful soul lacked any leader except God alone, considering itself his companion and having no doubt that he was its guide. It rejoiced that it had begun through his will and prompting, and that he would be its consolation in its hardships.

But what is the “whole” that goes forth, except that simple-mindedness which turned the hearts of countless multitudes toward seeking one and the same thing? Although the apostolic see had issued a summons concerning this matter specifically to the nation of the Franks, that people, living under Christian authority, did not at once produce its companies; and while it considered that it owed God the same faith as the Franks, it strove and sought, with whatever strength it could, to share the Franks’ danger.

One could see bands of Scots—fierce among themselves, though otherwise unwarlike—sliding down from their marshy borders, bare-legged, in shaggy cloaks, with psitarcia [provision-bags; al. sytarchia] hanging from their shoulders, and presenting us with the aid of their faith and devotion, armed with an abundance of weapons that would have seemed ridiculous to us. I call God to witness that I heard of men of some barbarian nation who had landed at our seaport. Their speech was so entirely unknown that, in the absence of a common language, they indicated the sign of the cross by turning their fingers over one another; by these signs they showed what they could not express in words: that they were setting out for the sake of the faith. But perhaps we shall discuss these matters in their proper place at greater length; for now let us say something about the condition that the Church of Jerusalem, or of the East, then possessed.

## CHAPTER II

### [II.] The wavering faith of the Eastern peoples. The origin of heresies.

From the time of the faithful Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, basilicas had been established by that same Augusta throughout the places marked by the traces of the Lord’s dominical sufferings [al.: the traces of the Lord’s sufferings], together with services worthy of those basilicas. We learn from ecclesiastical history that this order of establishment continued for a long period, through the successions of the Roman Empire, after the deaths of the aforementioned rulers.

The faith of the Eastern peoples, however, since it has always remained wavering and has been changeable and unstable in devising new things, has always strayed from the rule of true belief and departed from the authority of the ancient Fathers. These people, because of the purity of the air and sky into which they were born, are of lighter bodily constitution and therefore more lively in intellect; for this reason they habitually misuse the ray of their perceptiveness in many useless speculations [al.: because of the keener perceptiveness of their intellect, they habitually misuse it]. And while they disdain to obey the teaching of their elders or contemporaries, “they searched out iniquities; they failed while searching with scrutiny” (Ps. 63:7 [Vulg. 63:6]). From this arose heresies and monstrous kinds of every sort of pestilence. Their destructiveness and inextricable labyrinth became so great that nowhere could the most uncultivated soil be more fiercely overgrown with brambles or even nettles. Let all the catalogs of heresies be read, and let the books written by the ancients against heretics be reviewed: I shall be astonished if, apart from the East and Africa, scarcely any can be found anywhere under the Latin world.

### Pelagius, Arius, Manes, Eunomius, Eutyches, and Nestorius, heresiarchs.

Unless I am mistaken, I have read somewhere that Pelagius was a British heretic; but I do not believe that anyone has ever been able to collect either the errors of those men or the men themselves in their entirety. They were a land accursed through the work of their own teachers, bringing forth thorns and thistles for those who worked upon it. Arius emerged from Alexandria; Manes from Persia. The madness of the former tore and bloodied the garment of Holy Church, which has neither stain nor wrinkle, with such persistent violence that, by comparison with it, the persecution of Decius seems to have been shorter in duration and narrower in extent, since, after Greece, Spain, Illyricum [al.: the Illyrians], and Africa completely succumbed to it. The fable of the other, although laughable, blunted the acumen of even the sharpest men far and wide, as though by certain magical tricks. Why should I speak of Eunomians, Eutychians, and Nestorians? Shall I enumerate thousands of monsters? Their senseless obstinacy against us was so persistent, and victory over them proved so difficult, that heresies seemed to be beheaded not with swords but with clubs.

Let us recall the ancient histories of the origins of kingdoms, chatter about the ridiculous condition of kings and Asian fickleness, and marvel at the sudden deposition and restoration of rulers.

### The erroneous doctrine of the Greeks.

Therefore, whoever wishes to learn about their shameful instability should review the revolving kingdoms and the Antiochuses and Demetriuses who succeed one another. Whoever today he sees flourishing in imperial power, the fickleness of his subject peoples will scatter him not merely from his office but even tomorrow, as an exile, from his native soil. Hence their frivolity, both in secular affairs and in Christian profession, has flourished so greatly down to the present that they have almost nothing in common with us, either in their confession of the Eucharist or in their subjection to the apostolic see.

But if their making the sacraments from leavened bread can be defended by an appropriate or plausible argument—because what is done with right faith is not harmed by the admixture of material leaven; and because, when the Lord, affirming the ancient ceremonies, had eaten the lamb with unleavened bread, he then entrusted the sacrament of his body from that same bread, since no other was available and, according to the law that he was fulfilling, another could not at that time be introduced; so that the use of unleavened bread, which was then present because of necessity, does not seem to them to belong to the institution of the mystery, just as the dipping of the morsel was not performed in order to enact the sacrament but to identify Judas the betrayer—if, I say, these or any other arguments can be advanced, whether falsely or truthfully, what will they say about the Holy Spirit? Even now, following the remnants of the Arian heresy, they profanely maintain that he is lesser than the Father and the Son.

Since they disagree with the ordinances of the paternal canons and with the pious rite, understanding, and manifold practice of the Western Church, they have added this further heap to their condemnation: they declare that God, by having an inequality of his own nature imposed upon him, limps. For if, according to the command of the Son of God, one must be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19), and this is because these three are one God, then whatever is asserted of one of these three as less than another is certainly not God.

### Because of their sins, various provinces were handed over to foreign peoples.

Thus this gathering of bulls among the cows of the peoples has even now driven out those who have been tested by silver (Ps. 67:31 [Vulg. 67:30]), while some of our countrymen, provoked by this dispute with the Greeks, have produced illustrious books on the procession of the Holy Spirit. But because God places a stumbling block before those who sin willingly, their land vomited out its inhabitants: first they became deprived of knowledge of true belief, and then, deservedly and by right, exiles from all their earthly possessions. For while they departed from faith in the Trinity, so that “those who are filthy might become filthier” (Rev. 22:11), they gradually reached the extreme losses involved in embracing paganism. As the punishment for sin advanced, foreign peoples invaded, and they lost even the soil of their homeland; or, if anyone happened to remain there, the native inhabitants submitted themselves to outsiders under the payment of tribute.

The cities of Antioch, Jerusalem, and Nicaea, of renowned nobility, and the provinces—Syria, Palestine, and Greece—where the seedbeds of the new grace had sprung up, withered from their inner vitality to the very roots, while Italy, Gaul, and Britain flourished in their place as abortive growths. I say nothing of the fact that, in the very refuse, so to speak, of their churches, such great abuses have taken root that in most of their regions no one is advanced to the priesthood unless he first takes a wife, so that the Apostle’s statement may be fulfilled concerning “the husband of one wife” who is to be chosen (1 Tim. 3:2), although the authority of the Western Church most firmly maintains that this saying refers not to one who has and uses a wife, but to one who has had a wife and dismissed her.

I also say nothing of the fact that, contrary to Latin custom, persons of both sexes, including those of Christian rank, are bought and sold indiscriminately as though they were brute animals; and that they are sent for sale far from their homeland, to increase their cruelty, so that they may become slaves of the pagans.

### The unspeakable crimes of the Eastern peoples.

Finally, this seems to outweigh all the rest: among those people, it is generally established by imperial law that, as if a lawful license had been granted everywhere, one of all the daughters of a family must be taken to undergo prostitution. For example: suppose someone has three or four daughters; one of them is exposed to a brothel, and from that foul profit, obtained through the suffering of those unfortunate women, some portion—whether what fraction I do not know—is carried to the miserable emperor’s treasury; another portion is retained for the expenses of the woman who has shamefully earned it. Behold the cry of the Lord of Hosts rising with dreadful violence to his ears.

Moreover, the priests entrusted with handling the divine sacraments prepare the Lord’s body after meals, in places where, as I have heard, this is commonly done, and offer it to be consumed by anyone who is fasting. While they stray in these and similar ways of wickedness, while they walk in their own inventions (Ps. 80:13 [Vulg. 80:12]), God appointed a new lawgiver over them: “Let the nations know that they are but men” (Ps. 9:21 [Vulg. 9:20]). And while they knowingly transgress the boundaries of their fathers (Prov. 22:28), they have deservedly fallen so far that, having become more wanton than animals, they are held in disgrace.

But it must be explained briefly: since it is known that the Eastern nations once abandoned Christian worship and returned to paganism, upon whose authority they rely.

## CHAPTER III

### [III.] The doctrines of Muhammad.

It is a common opinion that there was a certain man—if I represent his name correctly, he was called Mathomus [Muhammad]—who once drew them entirely away from belief in the Son and the Holy Spirit [Note: Concerning these matters and the origin of Muhammad, see Cedrenus and John of Damascus, *On Heresies*, near the end], and taught them to rely upon the person of the Father alone, as upon the one God and Creator. He declared Jesus to be a mere human being and, to summarize his doctrine briefly, while prescribing circumcision, loosened the reins of every kind of sexual immorality.

I consider this profane man to be of little antiquity, principally for no other reason than that I find no ecclesiastical teacher who wrote against his impurity. Since I have learned his character and life from no written source, but only from what I have commonly heard certain more eloquent people say, no one should be surprised if I wish to speak of them. Whether these matters are true or false may be examined by anyone; but one need attend only to what sort of teacher he was, given the reputation for such noble deeds that has been propagated about him. Anyone may safely sing ill of a man whose wickedness surpasses and exceeds whatever evil is said of him.

### [IV.] From where he drew his poison.

It had been established that the patriarch of Alexandria had died at some time, and, as usually happens, while the Church was vacant, it had been torn apart by great diversity of opinion. Each person, with excessive freedom, pressed toward the individual whom he desired, and attacked those who held different opinions with sharper severity.

Not far from there lived a hermit, toward whom the consideration of the greater part of the people had been directed. When some of the more perceptive among them frequently visited him in order to discover his character and essence, and to learn his knowledge and eloquence, they inferred from his conversation that his understanding was not in harmony with the Catholic faith. Once this became known, they immediately withdrew entirely from the choice of the man they had been considering and, in the deepest grief, settled upon his rejection.

As contempt, accompanied by anguish [al.: grief], tore him apart with cruel violence, and he could not rise to the position he desired, he began anxiously to ponder, in imitation of Arius, how, by pouring out the poison of the faithlessness he had conceived, he might everywhere pervert the teachings of the Catholic faith in revenge. Such men, whose entire purpose is inclined toward human praise, are mortally wounded and roar intolerably if they perceive that their reputation has been diminished by any circumstance.

When the ancient enemy saw this opportunity, he approached his hermit with these pitiable words:

“Suppose you wish to find consolation for your evident rejection and to exercise an authority among those who come near you far greater than you would have possessed as patriarch. Carefully identify, among those who will soon come to you, a young man of such clothing, such appearance and bodily form, and also of such a name. Since he is sharp-minded and suited to your character, instruct him in the doctrine that lies close to your heart. Treat him, through your office, as the most faithful hearer and propagator of your teachings.”

### The hermit provides him with a wife, a widow. He falls into epilepsy.

The hermit, made anxious by this oracle, looked among the arriving crowds for the signs foretold to him. He recognized the young man, received him affectionately, and infected him with the plague from which he himself was wasting away. Since the young man was poor, and a poor man had little authority available to him, the hermit immediately procured wealth for him in the following way.

A very wealthy woman had become a widow when her husband died. The utterly filthy hermit brought her to the young man through a messenger and suggested that she marry again. When she said that, given her honorable status, she had no one available whom she could marry, he replied that he had found a prophet suitable for her, and that, if she consented to him, she would live entirely happily through marriage to that man. By much circumlocution he ensnared the woman, and, promising that that prophet’s foresight would serve her in both the present and the future age, he opened the woman’s heart to love for a man whom she did not know.

Lured by hope of foreknowledge concerning everything that had happened and everything that was to happen, she was joined to her seer. And the former wretch Mathomus, with fortune glittering from every direction, was advanced to unexpected dignities—perhaps not without incredible astonishment on his own part.

But when the couch repeatedly received the intercourse of both of them, the excellent prophet began to be violently afflicted from time to time by epilepsy, which we commonly call the falling sickness, while the prophetess looked on. His eyes rolled back, his face grew livid, foam covered his lips, and the chattering of his teeth terrified her. Frightened by this unexpected event, she returned to the solitary and described the misfortune that had befallen her. Completely overwhelmed by anguish of mind, she confessed that she preferred death to enduring the detestable marriage to a man possessed by such a seizure.

### His wife says that Muhammad must be repudiated, but she is deterred by the hermit’s persuasion.

In countless forms of complaint she reproached the hermit for having given her such wicked advice. But he was equipped with incomparable cunning:

“You are foolish,” he said, “you senseless woman, to attribute to your own injury what is a sign of brilliance and glory. Do you not know, thoughtless woman, that whenever God enters the minds of prophets, the entire mass of the human body is shaken, because the weakness of the flesh cannot bear it when divine majesty joins itself to it? Come to your senses at last, so that you are not frightened by unfamiliar visions, and observe with gratitude the blessed convulsions of the holy man, especially since at that time spiritual power is instructing him about everything that it is useful for you to know and do in the future.”

Her feminine fickleness was relieved by these words, and she now considered everything that had previously seemed foul and contemptible not merely tolerable but also sacred and admirable. Meanwhile, through the heretical hermit, that instrument of the devil was instructed in profane doctrines, and, with the prophet’s proclamation preceding him in every direction, he was believed by everyone.

### By what cunning he promulgates his law.

When he had become famous far and wide, as his reputation advanced in everyone’s opinion, and when he saw that the peoples of nearby and distant provinces were inclined toward his teachings, he wrote a law after taking counsel with his teacher. In it he loosened the restraints on every kind of depravity, so that his followers might be more readily drawn to him.

After doing this, he gathered an infinite multitude of common people. To deceive their wandering hearts more effectively under the guise of the religion he had introduced, he ordered them to fast for three days and urged them attentively to beseech God for the reception of the law. He also gave them this sign: if it pleased God to give them a law, he would give it to them in an unusual manner and by a hand from which it was not expected.

Meanwhile, he had a cow which he had so accustomed to his hand that whenever it heard his voice or saw his presence, scarcely any force could restrain it from running to him with an extraordinary eagerness. He therefore tied the written document around the animal’s horns and hid it in the tent where he was staying.

Finally, on the third day, rising above the whole assembled people, he climbed onto a platform and began to address the crowd in a loud voice. When his speech had, so to speak, reached the summit of its verbal sound, the cow immediately came out from the tent below and, passing through the middle of the gathered nations with the document placed upon its horns, hurried to the feet of the speaker as though it were coming to congratulate him.

Everyone marveled. The document was quickly unrolled and displayed to the panting crowd. The permission granted by the shameful law was received with joy. What more is there to say? The miracle of the book that had been presented was celebrated with favor multiplied a hundredfold.

The new license for indiscriminate intercourse was spread among all nations as though it had come from heaven. And the more abundant the supply of permitted pollution became, the more the grace of God—who was said to be granting times of greater indulgence—was proclaimed, without naming the foulness involved. The entire judgment of Christianity was condemned with a thousand insults, and everything that had once been established from the teaching of the Gospels as a matter of chastity and strength was called cruel harshness.

But the command that the cow had delivered was called universal, and this freedom alone was said to have been commended by God. Neither the antiquity of Moses nor the Catholic novelty was taken into account. Everything before the law and under the law, everything under grace, was branded with inexpiable falsehood; and, to use a psalm in a manner not entirely appropriate, they sang that God “has not dealt thus with every nation, nor revealed his judgments to any other people from the beginning” (Ps. 147:20).

The more lavish opportunity to satisfy lust, now surpassing even the appetite of beasts, and pleasure in the number of prostitutes rather than in marriages, was disguised under the superficial pretext of producing children. But while the flow of nature was not at all restrained in matters that are regarded as ordinary, they rushed toward acts that are improper and ought not even to be named among us—acts unknown even to brute animals.

The obscurity of this wicked institution then covered the Christian name and still blots out almost all the regions of the East, Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Libya, and the remotest parts of Spain near us. But it must be told what end removed this great and extraordinary lawgiver from the world.

Since he often collapsed from sudden epileptic seizures, the disease that we said above afflicted him, it happened once, while he was walking alone, that he was struck down by the same illness. He was found while still tormented by the seizure and was so torn apart by pigs that no remains of him were found except his ankles.

Behold the most excellent lawgiver: while he tried to raise up—or rather, completely raised up—the Epicurean whom the true Stoics, namely the worshipers of Christ, had killed, the pig itself was exposed to be devoured by pigs, so that the teaching of obscenity might end, as was fitting, with the most obscene conclusion. He rightly left his ankles behind, because he had imprinted the traces of faithlessness and depravity upon souls that he had miserably deceived.

In honor of his ankles we composed a four-line poem, following the poet [Horace, *Odes* III.30.1–2]:

> More lasting than bronze,  
> and higher than the royal structure of pyramids,

so that this remarkable man, already happier than every pig, might say with the same poet [ibid. 6–7]:

> I shall not wholly die, and a great part of me  
> shall escape Libitina.

This means:

> He who had called the pig his own is chewed by its mouth;  
> his blessed limbs are renowned, poured forth from its rear.  
> Let the worshiper who celebrates him with worthy honor  
> bear to the mouth the ankles, and to the nose what the sow discharged.

But if the accusations against the Manichaean sect are true—that in everything eaten a certain part of God remains defiled; that this part of God is cleansed by the crushing of the teeth and the digestion of the stomach; and that, once cleansed, it is transformed into angels, who are said to emerge from us through belches and flatulence—are we to believe that the pigs which fed upon this man’s flesh made it into angels and emitted still more of them here and there through their blasts?

But setting aside the jokes spoken for the mockery of his followers, this must be made clear: they do not consider him a god, as some think, but a righteous man and also a patron through whom divine laws were transmitted. They assert that he was taken up into heaven, and that only his ankles were left behind as a memorial for his faithful, who visit them with infinite veneration. They rightly and for good reason reject the eating of pork, since pigs consumed their master with their bites.

## CHAPTER V

### [V.]

The peoples we mentioned above, after the error of their beginning paganism had grown strong over a long period and through many generations, overran Palestine, Jerusalem, and the Lord’s sepulcher, and possessed Armenia, Syria, and part of Greece almost as far as the sea called the Arm of Saint George.

Among all the kingdoms of the East, the Babylonian Empire had been most powerful from ancient times and had ruled over many kingdoms. Nevertheless, the kingdom of the Parthians, whom we call Turks by a corrupted name, surpasses it in military affairs, equestrian skill, and strength of spirit, although it extends over a smaller area of land.

The Babylonian emperor had therefore occupied the provinces mentioned above with a great army; but as time passed, when the power of the Turks arose and the Assyrians had been defeated, he lost them.

### The Greek emperor asks Robert, count of Flanders, for assistance.

These peoples, more vigorous in arms and more accustomed to using daring, were pressing upon the Empire of Constantinople and seemed almost ready to break into that city and besiege it. Terrified by their repeated threats and constant incursions, the Greek emperor sent to France, writing a letter to Robert the Elder, count of the Flemings, and laying before him many reasons by which his mind might be stirred to defend endangered Greece.

He did not appeal to this man because he thought that the assistance of Robert alone would be sufficient for so great an undertaking, although Robert was extremely wealthy and could have assembled a large force. Rather, he knew that if so powerful a man undertook that journey, he would attract to himself, simply because of the novelty of the enterprise, very substantial assistance from our people.

This count was as shrewd in military matters as he was perceptive and witty in letters. Having once traveled to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, and perhaps having Constantinople on his route, he spoke with the emperor himself. Thus, having gained greater confidence with him, he proceeded to seek assistance. I have been unwilling to insert the letter itself into this little work, but I have wished to present some of the things said in it, clothed, however, in my own words.

### The emperor’s letter.

“There is a complaint concerning the churches which the pagans, after overthrowing Christianity, held and in which they constructed stalls for horses, mules, and other animals. This was so true that they even established there their own shrines, which they call *Mathomaria* [al.: established them], and conducted there innumerable transactions of sexual immorality, so that they became not basilicas but brothels and theaters.

“As for the slaughter of Catholics, I would speak of it in vain, since for those who died in the faith an exchange for eternal life seemed to be at hand, while the survivors continued their lives under the wretched yoke of servitude, a life more bitter, as I believe, than death itself. For captured virgins of the faithful were ordered to become public prostitutes, while nowhere was regard shown for modesty or the honor of marriage. Mothers were violated in the sight of their daughters through repeated intercourse with different men, while the daughters, standing nearby, were compelled during such acts to dance and sing obscene songs before them. Immediately the same suffering—which is both painful and shameful to describe—was turned upon the daughters, and even this defilement was adorned with the obscene songs of their unfortunate mothers. In short, reverence for the entire Christian name was handed over to the brothel.

“And when the female sex was not spared, although this might still be excused as belonging to nature, they crossed over into bestiality with males, breaking the laws of humanity.”

Therefore, to disclose the wantonness inflicted upon the middling and lowly by the execrable and altogether ear-intolerable enormity of a single crime, he says that they had subjected a certain bishop to Sodomitic abuse [al.: killed a certain bishop].

“And how should that headlong lust, which must be preferred to every kind of madness, restrain itself from human beings? It is always fleeing counsel and shame, driven forward by perpetual impulse; and the more frequently it is extinguished, the more vigorously its flame is rekindled. Yet it is sullied by unheard-of unions with brute animals, unions forbidden to the Christian mouth.

“And although the wretched are permitted, according to their own judgment, a multitude of women, it is not enough for them unless the dignity of males is also defiled in the filth of such depravity. Nor is it surprising that God could no longer endure their worn-out wickedness when it had been turned into a cry, and that, following the ancient pattern, the earth vomited out such abominable inhabitants.”

When he was discussing at length the siege of Constantinople, which he feared above all, and which threatened it once the Arm of Saint George had been crossed, he added, among other things:

“If no other opportunity for assisting itself seemed available to us, at least on account of the six apostles whose bodies are buried there, that most famous city deserves every kind of aid, lest they be burned by the impious in a fire or plunged into abysses.”

And certainly nothing could be more true. For that city, distinguished not only by the monuments of those saints but also glorious through the merit and name of its founder—especially since, by heavenly revelation, he transformed it from a very ancient town into a city admired by the whole world and a second Rome—was worthy, if it could have been achieved, of the gathering and support of the entire world.

### The head of John the Baptist at Constantinople. The author does not approve of the display of sacred relics. Why.

After the translation of the apostles, he goes on to say that “the head of blessed John the Baptist is kept among them.” Although he falsely says: “Even today it appears to be marked by hair and skin as though he were alive.” If this is true, the monks of Ageria must be asked whose John the Baptist’s head they boast of possessing, since we know for certain both that there were not two John the Baptists and that one and the same man—something impious to say—could not have become two-headed.

On this occasion we should also consider a very widespread but not harmful error which has occupied chiefly the churches of Gaul concerning the bodies of the saints [Note: More extensively on these matters in the treatise *On the Relics of the Saints*, book I]. Some boast that they possess this saint and others that one, whether martyr or confessor, although one complete person cannot occupy two places.

The whole evil of this dispute originates in the fact that the saints are not allowed to enjoy the rest of their proper and unchanging burial. I do not doubt that it arose from piety that their bodies are covered with silver and gold; but now the display of bones and the carrying about of biers to collect money are plainly and excessively serving greed. All these practices would have ceased if their limbs, like those of the Lord Jesus himself, had been enclosed behind a strong, immovable barrier in a tomb.

But let us set these matters aside and take up what follows.

### How perverse the emperor’s mind was.

Furthermore, he adds that “if the restraint of so great an evil did not move them, and if love for the saints mentioned above did not encourage them to this very thing, at least the desire for gold and silver, of which innumerable supplies are found there, would entice them.” Finally, he introduces something incompatible with the frugality of good men, namely that “besides all these things they should be drawn by the pleasure of exceedingly beautiful women,” as though the appearance of Greek women were so great that they could in any way be preferred to women of Gaul, and as though the Frankish army were being led into Thrace for their sake alone.

While that utterly filthy tyrant was proclaiming these things, he ought to have remembered that this very reason was the chief cause of the adversity that arose against him and his people: by a celebrated edict, he ordered that, from among the daughters of numerous families, one should be prostituted throughout his entire empire and that the profit from this most foul suffering should be brought into his own treasury.

No less significant was his command, authorized by an official order, that from among several sons one should be made a eunuch, rendering the bodies of males powerless, enervated, and effeminate by removing their strength. Such bodies were no longer considered useful for military service; indeed, to complete the accumulation of harm, the future offspring itself was cut off in them, although through its increase assistance against the enemy might have been hoped for.

Therefore, whoever has voluntarily condemned his own possessions is justly compelled to seek those of others.

But it must also be noted that this emperor himself had not received the purple by legitimate succession. Rather, while he was one of the palace officials under the emperor who, unless I am mistaken, was called Michael, 376 and while he was in command of a considerable contingent of western soldiers—men whom their innate integrity had made more distinguished in the eyes of the Greek emperor and closer to his personal protection—he began, gathering boldness from the soldiers subject to him, to plot revolution against that same emperor.

[Col. 0696B] Having overrun the city of Constantinople against the emperor, he immediately and savagely deprived the captured emperor of his eyesight, confined him under strict guard in a certain town, and usurped the rights of the entire empire, though he had no right to them. He did indeed seek the Franks, compelled by the necessity I have described; but after he saw that nobles of such great dignity had assembled, so well equipped with discipline and arms, and that they were horsemen, he envied their numbers greatly, but their prudence much more. Once their purpose had reached its fulfillment, the magnitude of his envy of our men’s effectiveness increased, since after the victory at Jerusalem he feared that their victorious arms might be turned against him—especially since he had learned that among all the nations there was no rival whom he considered more powerful than himself.

[Col. 0696C] It is nevertheless certain that we heard that, before the beginnings of this expedition became known, his mother had been a fortune-teller. She often foretold to him that, since he traced his origin to the Franks, a Frank would deprive him of empire and life. Perhaps Bohemond is striving to bring her prophecy to fulfillment. He presses him so insistently that, engaging him in battle on many occasions, he has compelled him to turn his back and has added a very large part of his provinces to his own dominion. Since Bohemond derives his lineage from Normandy, which is acknowledged to be part of France, he will for this reason above all be considered a Frank, because he is now joined in marriage to the daughter of the king of the Franks.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0695]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0695D]

### [1.] Praises of Pope Urban. Famous for miracles after his death.

Before becoming pope, Urban was called Odo. He was descended from a noble Frankish family, from the territory and clergy of Rheims, and, as they say—unless they are mistaken—was the first pope from among the Franks. At Cluny he was made a monk from the clerical state; afterward, following an abbot of glorious memory who assisted Hugh, he not long afterward held the office of prior. Then, as his merit advanced, by order of Pope Gregory VII he was appointed bishop of Ostia; finally he was placed over the Apostolic See as its supreme pontiff.

How great his magnanimity was became known through the motive that prompted this expedition: when he himself first set the example of how it should be undertaken, the whole world was astonished. The end of his life, radiant with miracles, bears witness to the state of his mind. For after he had died and been buried, as the bishop of Ostia who succeeded him wrote, when many miracles were already occurring, a certain young man stood beside his tomb and invoked the loss of his limbs upon himself if any sign had ever been or should ever be performed through the merits of Urban, who was called Odo. He had not yet withdrawn his foot from the place when, having lost the power of speech and having been struck by paralysis affecting one side of his body, he himself, on the following day, bore witness to Urban’s miraculous powers by dying.

### Roman pontiffs have long been accustomed to seek assistance from the Franks.

This exceptional man, therefore, while he was being honored with splendid funeral rites by Alexius, the Greek emperor, and was being impelled by prayers—but much more strongly by the general danger of Christendom, which was being diminished daily by the incursions of the pagans—for he was hearing that Spain too was frequently being disturbed by Saracen invasions, resolved for this very reason to travel to France in order to stir the people of his own nation to action. For it had long been customary for the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, whenever they suffered any trouble from a neighboring people, always to seek assistance from the Franks.

The pontiffs Stephen and Zachary, both under the kings Pepin and Charles, took refuge with them. The former of the kings, accompanying the corresponding pontiff, undertook an expedition as far as Pavia and restored the Church’s patrimony to its proper see; by the mere threat of arms he compelled King Desiderius, who had inflicted the violence, to return what he had plundered. For this same people behaved with greater fear and humility than the other nations toward blessed Peter and toward pontifical decrees, and did not wish, with the recklessness customary among others, to seize upon freedom as a cloak for wickedness against God.

[Col. 0697C]

### The Franks’ continued devotion toward the supreme pontiff.

We have seen, after several years had passed, the Teutons—or rather the entire kingdom of Lorraine—resist the commands of blessed Peter and his pontiffs with a kind of barbarous obstinacy, and prefer either to remain subject to a prolonged or perpetual anathema than to submit. Last year, while I was arguing with a certain archdeacon of Mainz about their rebellion, I heard that he had so despised our king and his people, solely because he had received Pope Paschal 377 and his nobles graciously everywhere, that he called them not merely Franks.

I said to him: “If you consider them so sluggish and feeble that you distort, by shameful babbling, a name celebrated even as far as the Indian Ocean, tell me: to whom did Pope Urban turn when he was gathering forces against the Turks? Was it not to the Franks? If they had not gone before and constrained, by their vigorous industry and fearless strength, the barbarism of the peoples flowing together from every direction, there would have been no assistance from your Teutons, whose very name was not heard there.”

This was my answer to him.

### How firm and enduring the Franks’ faith is.

I confess, and it is credible to all, that God reserved this people for so great a task, especially since we know for certain that, from the time they received the sign of faith through blessed Remigius, they have never accepted or tolerated even for an hour the contagion of any faithlessness, at a time when scarcely any nations remained—or remained at all—untainted.

These are the people who, while still sunk in pagan error and subduing the fields of the Gauls, though those Gauls were Christians, by determined warfare, never inflicted punishment or death upon anyone for the faith of Christ. Instead, those whom Roman severity had punished with sword and fire, the people’s innate generosity enclosed in gold and silver and covered with gems and amber. Nor did it strive only to surround with these honors those who had suffered among them; it also cultivated with such eager affection those brought from Spain, Italy, or any other peoples that the love of the martyrs or confessors whom it so greatly cherishes made them famous and illustrious, endowed them with an unbroken steadfastness of faith, and finally raised them up in the triumphs of this victory at Jerusalem.

Because it bore the yoke from its youth, it will sit [Col. 0698B] solitary—a noble people among the distinctive qualities of all nations: wise, warlike, generous, and refined. Since they have a name peculiar to themselves, people of whatever nations are honored by borrowing—or rather, receiving—their surname. For when we see Britons, Englishmen, or Ligurians of good character, do we not immediately call them Franks? But let us now return to the subject at hand.

## CHAPTER TWO

### [II.] The pope comes to Gaul and convenes a council at Clermont. How many bishops were present there. The pope’s eloquence and fairness.
