Pope Urban, then, entering the borders of our kingdom, was welcomed with such joy and such a gathering of the cities, towns, and villages as had been unknown in the memory of all who were alive, since it seemed that a pontiff of the Apostolic See had at last come to these regions. The year 1095 of the incarnate Word was hastening toward its end when that prelate made great haste to convene a council. At last he gave it a place in the Auvergne city glorified by the most learned of all bishops, Sidonius; although its name is known to have been changed to Clermont.

It was all the more celebrated because it was more desirable to see the face and hear the words of so eminent and extraordinary a person. There, besides the assemblies of bishops and abbots—some had counted approximately four hundred of them, distinguished by their croziers—the learned men of all France and of its attached counties streamed together. One could observe with what serene dignity and weighty courtesy he presided and, to use the words of the aforementioned Sidonius, with what “peppered eloquence” the most eloquent pope thundered against every matter brought before him. It was noted with how much moderation the illustrious man endured the loquacity of those who noisily pressed their own cases upon him, and how little he valued anyone’s personal standing unless it was in accordance with God.

### [III.] He excludes King Philip from the company of the pious.

From there he excommunicated Philip, king of the Franks, who was then reckoning the thirty-seventh year of his reign. Philip had abandoned his lawful wife, Bertha by name, and had bound himself to the wife of the count of Anjou, named Bertrada. He excommunicated him with such authority that he disregarded the intercessions of distinguished persons and the presentation of numerous gifts, and did not fear what lay within the boundaries of that king’s realm.

At this same council, just as he had proposed before departing from the city—and for this reason he had sought the Franks—he delivered a speech to the great assembly assisting him. Among other things that exceeded the memory of his hearers, he argued with the following purpose. His agility cooperated with his learned eloquence; for in pursuing Latin expression, his fluency seemed no less than the speed that any advocate might display in his native language. The multitude of disputants did not dull the speaker’s talent. Although he seemed surrounded by the elegances of eloquent grammarians, clouded by the fogs of emerging issues, overflowing with the resources of orators, and believed to outstrip every wit of speech with his learned brilliance, he nevertheless used the following words—or at least the following intentions.

### The speech delivered by Pope Urban at the council.

“If, among the Churches spread throughout the world, some deserve greater reverence than others because of their persons and places—because of their persons, I mean, when greater privileges are granted to apostolic sees; and because of their places, when the same dignity that is granted to persons is accorded to royal cities, as is the case with the city of Constantinople—we ought above all to honor that Church from which we received the grace of redemption and the origin of all Christianity.

“For if what is said by the Lord is true, namely, that salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22), and if it is established that the Lord of Hosts left us a seed, so that we should not be like Sodom or become like Gomorrah (Romans 9:29), and if Christ is our seed, in whom there is salvation and the blessing of all nations, then the very land and city in which he lived and suffered are called holy by the testimony of Scripture.

“If this land, the inheritance of God and the holy temple, is read of in the sacred and prophetic pages even before the Lord walked and suffered there, what holiness and reverence must it be believed to have possessed when the God of Majesty was embodied there, nourished, grew to maturity, and in bodily growth walked or was carried here and there? And, to compress into suitable brevity all that can be narrated in a long circuit of words: where the blood of the Son of God, holier than heaven and earth, was poured out; where his body, while the elements trembled, lay dead at rest in a tomb—what veneration do we think it deserved?

“If, when our Lord himself had only recently been killed and the city was still possessed by the Jews, the evangelist calls the holy city holy when he says, ‘Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose, and came into the holy city, and appeared to many’ (Matthew 27:53); and when the prophet Isaiah says, ‘His tomb shall be glorious’ (Isaiah 11:10)—since the holiness once imparted to the city by God himself, its sanctifier, cannot be emptied of its meaning by any subsequent evil, and the glory of the tomb likewise remains indivisible—you must labor with the greatest zeal, dearest brothers, so that the holiness of the city and the glory of the tomb, which the frequent presence of pagans continually pollutes as far as it can, may be cleansed if you aspire to the Author of that holiness and glory, if you love the signs of his footsteps that remain on earth, and if you desire it, with God leading you and fighting before you on your behalf.

### Reasons by which the pontiff exhorts Christians to take up arms for the expedition to Jerusalem.

“If it once greatly benefited the Maccabees to their praise for piety that they fought for the ceremonies and the temple, then you also, O Christian soldiers, are lawfully permitted to defend the freedom of your homeland through the zeal of arms. If you consider even the thresholds of the apostles or of any saints worth seeking with so much toil, why do you refuse to recover or visit the cross, the blood, and the tomb, or to spend the price of your souls for their recovery?

“Until now you have waged unjust wars; at times you have turned weapons against one another for the sake of mere greed or pride; from this you have earned perpetual destruction and the certain ruin of damnation. Now we propose to you wars that contain within themselves the glorious reward of martyrdom, wars that leave behind the title of present and eternal praise.

“Let us now suppose that Christ was neither dead nor buried in Jerusalem, and had never lived there. Certainly, even if all these things were lacking, that one fact alone ought to have stirred you to come to the aid of the land and city: that the law went forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isaiah 2:3). For if whatever belongs to Christian preaching flowed from the Jerusalemite source, let the streams scattered in every direction throughout the entire world turn the hearts of the Catholic multitude back toward it, so that they may carefully consider what they owe to so abundant a fountain.

“If rivers return to the place from which they flow, in order to flow again, as Solomon says (Ecclesiastes 1:7), it ought to seem glorious to you if you can cleanse that place from which it is evident that you received the cleansing of baptism and the instruction of faith.

“It must also be weighed with the utmost deliberation whether, if through your efforts the very Mother Church of the churches should flourish again in Christian worship, with God acting through you, she may perhaps wish to restore some regions of the East to the faith before the nearby times of Antichrist. For it is clear that Antichrist will not wage war against the Jews or against the pagans, but, in accordance with the etymology of his name, will overrun Christians.

“And if Antichrist finds no Christian there—as scarcely anyone is found there today—there will be no one to oppose him or whom he may rightly overrun. For according to Daniel, and Jerome, the interpreter of Daniel, he is to fix his tents on the Mount of Olives, and in Jerusalem, in the temple of God, it is certain, as the Apostle says, that he will sit as though he were God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). According to the same prophet, he will undoubtedly first kill three kings—those of Egypt, Africa, and Ethiopia—on behalf of the Christian faith (Daniel 7:24).

“This, however, cannot happen unless Christianity is established where paganism now exists. Therefore, if you devote yourselves to the exercise of pious warfare, so that just as you received from Jerusalem the seed of knowledge of God, you may there restore a return of the grace you borrowed, so that through you the Catholic name may spread and oppose the faithlessness of Antichrist and the antichrists, who cannot fail to imagine that God—whose abundant power surpasses the hope of all—may through your spark consume so vast a thicket of paganism that Egypt, Africa, and Ethiopia, which have departed from the fellowship of our faith, may be enclosed within the beginnings of this law, and that the sinful man, the son of perdition, may find some rebels to oppose him?

“And behold, the Gospel cries out that Jerusalem must be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). The times of the nations may be understood in two ways. Either they are so called because the nations have dominated Christians at will, pursuing every kind of disgraceful excess according to their own desires, and in all these matters have encountered no obstacle—for those to whom everything is available according to their wishes are said to have their own time, as in the saying, ‘My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready’ (John 7:6), whence it is also customary to say to pleasure-seekers, ‘You have your time.’

“Or again, the times of the nations are the fullness of the Gentiles, which will enter in before Israel is saved. These times, dearest brothers, may perhaps now be fulfilled, while through you, with God cooperating, the power of the pagans is driven back; and while the end of the age is already near, even if the nations cease to convert to the Lord, because, according to the Apostle, an apostasy from the faith must occur (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

“Nevertheless, according to the prophets, before the coming of Antichrist it is necessary that in those regions, either through you or through whomever God pleases, the rule of Christianity be renewed, so that the head of all evils, who is to have his throne of rule there, may find something belonging to the faith against which he can fight.

“Consider, then, among yourselves that perhaps the Almighty has prepared you for this purpose, so that through you he may restore Jerusalem from such trampling underfoot. I beg you to weigh with what hearts those joys will be conceived when we see the holy city raised up with your assistance, and the prophetic—indeed, the divine—utterances fulfilled in our own times.

“Let it move your memory that the voice of the Lord himself says to the Church: ‘From the East I will bring your seed, and from the West I will gather you’ (Isaiah 43:5). God brought our seed from the East, because that eastern province produced the first growth of the Church for us in two ways. But he gathers it from the West when, through those who were last to receive the teachings of faith—namely, the westerners, which we think can happen through you with God’s favor—he restores the losses of Jerusalem.

“If the sayings of Scripture do not stir you, and our exhortations do not penetrate your hearts, let at least the great misery of those who desire to visit the holy places stir you. Consider those who make the pilgrimage and travel there across the Mediterranean. If they are wealthy, consider how many ransoms and acts of violence they endure, being compelled to pay charges and taxes at almost every mile, and to pay redemption fees at every city gate and at the entrances of churches and temples; and whenever they migrate from place to place, how, on any accusation whatsoever, they are compelled to buy their freedom.

“And when they refuse to give gifts, how, as the officials of the pagans are accustomed to do, are they savagely driven on by beatings? What shall we say of those who possess absolutely nothing and, relying nakedly upon their poverty, undertake that journey while appearing to have nothing besides their bodies that they could lose?

“When money that does not exist is demanded from them through intolerable tortures; when the calluses of their ankles are cut open and torn away, to investigate whether perhaps they have sewn something into them; when the cruelty of the wicked proceeds so far that, supposing the wretches to have swallowed gold or silver, they force them to drink scammony until they vomit or even discharge their entrails; or, what is unspeakable, having cut open their bellies with iron and stretched apart the wrappings of their intestines, they expose by horrible mutilation whatever nature keeps hidden—remember, I beg you, the thousands who have perished in this detestable way.

“Act on behalf of the holy places from which the beginnings of your piety came. Believe without doubt that, when you are sent into his wars, Christ will be your standard-bearer and your inseparable forerunner before you.”

### [V.] The cross is affixed to the soldiers’ clothing.

The illustrious man had finished his speech. He absolved all who had vowed that they would go, by the authority of blessed Peter, confirmed the same by apostolic authority, and established a sign fully appropriate to this most honorable profession. As though giving the mark of the Lord’s Passion as a military belt—or rather, as the insignia of those who were about to serve God as soldiers—he ordered the figure of a cross, made from cloth of any material, to be sewn onto the tunics, cloaks, and mantles of those who were going.

He ordered that anyone who, after receiving this sign or after publicly making this vow, should withdraw from this good undertaking through wicked repentance or affection for some of his own people should be regarded forever as an outlaw, unless he repented; and that he should disgracefully undertake again what he had abandoned.

Moreover, he condemned with a terrible anathema all who dared to inflict harm, for the entire period of three years, upon the wives, children, or possessions of those who undertook this journey of God.

Finally, he entrusted responsibility for governing the expedition to a man deserving of every kind of praise, the bishop of the city of Le Puy, whose name, I regret to say, I have found nowhere [Note: [Col. 0701D] He was called Adhemar or Aymar.] and have not heard. He entrusted to him his own authority over the instruction of the Christian people wherever they might come. He also laid his hands upon him, together with a blessing, after the manner of the apostles. How wisely that man carried out his charge is shown by the marvelous outcome of so great a work.

## CHAPTER THREE

### [VI.] The expedition to Jerusalem.

When the council held at Clermont had ended—it had convened around the octave of Saint Martin, in the month of November—a great report spread throughout all the regions of France. Everyone to whom the swift rumor first conveyed the pontiff’s command concerning the proposed Way of God—for so it was called by antonomasia—began to stir up all those nearby and familiar to him.

The intention of the counts of the palace was already itching to act, and the modest means of the mounted men had already begun to give birth to an enterprise, when suddenly the eagerness of the poor aspired to this purpose with such desires that none of them considered the smallness of his resources or took care to sell his houses, vineyards, and fields at a suitable price. Instead, they sold the best proceeds of their possessions for far less than they would have fetched if each of them had been confined in the prison of the most savage captivity and threatened with the necessity of an extremely rapid ransom.

At that time, because of the general failure, there was also a great shortage of grain even among the wealthier, although some people here and there had enough money to buy it; nevertheless, they had no grain—or scarcely any—from which to make their purchases. The flocks of the poor had already learned to live on the roots of plants growing wild, while they compensated for the scarcity of bread, which was exceedingly rare, by eating whatever foods they could obtain from anywhere.

Misery, loudly proclaimed by everyone’s judgment, was plainly before the eyes even of the powerful. While each person observed the torments of the lowest common people through cruel hunger, he feared laboring with great exertions under imposed frugality lest his wealth be squandered through easily incurred expenses.

The thirsty hearts of the avaricious, who rejoiced when the times smiled upon bloody interest-taking, considered, while they measured out bushels of grain stored for a long time, counting the repeated returns of the years, what they could add to the mountains of money by selling it.

Meanwhile, while the former were afflicted and the latter pursued their aim, suddenly Christ thundered through the ears of almost every heart, “crushing the ships of Tarshish with a violent wind” (Psalm 47:6). He who “leads out the prisoners in strength” (Psalm 67:7) shattered the adamantine bonds of greed with which the hearts of desperate men were entangled.

For, as I said above, when that unproductive season was constricting everyone’s resources and had stirred countless people toward voluntary exile, the various possessions of many were brought into the open. Things that had seemed valuable, while no one was moving, were sold at a low price once everyone had been moved to undertake this journey.

And while many hastened to arrange this departure, let me express the sudden and unexpected cheapness of what was being sold by one example: an extraordinary thing to report, seven sheep were sold for the price of five denarii. The shortage of grain was turned into abundance; provided that anyone could gather even the smallest amount of money by any means, he gave up whatever he seemed to possess—not according to its value, but according to the buyer’s assessment—lest he be the last to undertake the Way of God.

It was therefore possible to see a marvel: everyone buying dearly and selling cheaply. They bought dearly the things needed for the journey, because they were in a hurry; but they sold cheaply, because they were amassing the expenses of their travels. Everything that neither prisons nor tortures could previously extort from them was soon obtainable for a small number of coins.

[Col. 0704A] Nor was this less ridiculous: many who had not yet been touched by any desire to go, while laughing today at the complete sale of others and declaring that they would go miserably and return even more miserably, on the following day, suddenly inspired, sold all their possessions for a few coins and traveled with those whom they had mocked.

Who could say that boys, who could say that old women, were moving to war?

Who could count the maidenly hands?

Who could recount old age, wasting away with trembling weakness?

All sing of war, though none admits that they will fight.

They promise martyrdom, saying that they will offer their necks to the swords.

“ You young men,” they say, “will handle swords with your hands,

but allow us here to merit Christ by enduring.”

Although they seemed to possess zeal for God, it was not according to knowledge. Yet God, who is accustomed to turn many things begun in vain toward a pious end, granted salvation to their simple hearts from their own good intention.

One might see something strange and entirely suited to laughter: certain poor people, having yoked oxen to a two-wheeled cart and shod them in the manner of horses, carried their little possessions and their children in the wagon. The children themselves, whenever they encountered any castles or cities along the way, asked whether this was Jerusalem, toward which they were traveling.

### [VII.] While everything was burning with war, the wars were immediately extinguished when the supreme pontiff proclaimed the expedition to Jerusalem.

At that time, before so great an expedition of the nations took place, the whole kingdom of the Franks was thrown into turmoil by the greatest mutual hostilities; brigandage was frequent everywhere, and the roads were blockaded. Fires without number were heard of everywhere, or rather were being set; battles were being constructed for no reasons except sheer, unrestrained greed. To sum it up briefly, whatever lay before the eyes of the greedy was exposed to plunder, without anyone considering whose property it was.

Then, moved by a marvelous and incredible change of heart precisely because it was unexpected, they sought to have the sign prescribed by the pontiff’s command—the crosses—placed upon them by bishops and priests. And just as the force of the swiftest winds is often restrained by no great fall of rain, so immediately it happened that the disputes and wars of all parties were quieted by the inspiration implanted in them, unquestionably by Christ.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### Peter the Hermit, commander of the army. He spreads the word of God through Gaul. His manner of life. Hairs from his mule were taken out as relics.

While the princes were slowly and carefully arranging their affairs, since they required great expense and the extensive services of their attendants, the common people—poor in material resources but exceedingly numerous—attached themselves to a certain Peter the Hermit and obeyed him for the time being as though he were their teacher, while the matter was still being carried on among us.

We learned that he was born in the city of Amiens, unless I am mistaken, and that in some upper region of Gaul he had led a solitary life under the monastic habit. After he departed from there, we saw him travel around cities and towns on the pretext of preaching, surrounded by such great multitudes of people, presented with such great gifts, and acclaimed with such great praise of holiness that I do not remember anyone else being held in similar honor.

He had been very generous in distributing to the poor much of what was given to him. By providing dowries from his own resources, he married prostitutes to husbands, and everywhere, with astonishing authority, restored peace and treaties among those in disagreement. Whatever he did or said seemed almost divine, especially since even hairs from his mule were pulled out as relics. We report this not as truth, but as the behavior of a populace that loves novelty.

He wore a woolen tunic next to his skin, a hooded garment reaching to his ankles over it, and a cloak above these; he wore no breeches and went barefoot. He was nourished on bread, scarcely ever fish, and never wine.

### [VIII.] The disorders of the soldiers traveling through Hungary.

This man, having gathered an enormous army partly through reputation and partly through his own exhortation, chose to depart through the land of the Hungarians. When these untutored common people found its regions extremely rich in everything necessary for food, they began to run riot in extravagant luxury, contrary to the gentleness of the inhabitants.

They saw the wheat harvests of many years standing throughout the fields in the form of towers, as is customary in that land—heaps that we commonly call stacks. Since supplies of various meats and other foods, in which that fertile land abounds, were available, they were not content with the inhabitants’ hospitality. In extraordinary madness, these foreigners began to trample upon the natives.

Although the natives, as Christians welcoming Christians, willingly offered them everything for sale, the foreigners, unable to restrain their lusts and forgetting pious hospitality and kindness, attacked them in gratuitous warfare. They thought that the natives would dare nothing against them and would be entirely incapable of fighting.

Thus, with accursed frenzy, they set fire to the public storehouses I have mentioned; girls were seized and violated; marriages were dishonored by the repeated abduction of women. They plucked out or burned the beards of their hosts. No longer did anyone discuss purchasing the necessities of life; instead, each of them, as he could, strove after plunder and slaughter. In this way, with astonishing recklessness, they freely threatened that they would act against the Turks.

Meanwhile, they came upon a certain castle through which they had to pass and whose passage they could not possibly avoid, for the terrain is so situated that, like a narrow lane, it offers no turning either to the right or to the left. With their customary insolence they began to besiege it. But when it was nearly captured, suddenly—whatever the reason may have been—they were so overwhelmed that some fell by the sword, some were drowned by the river’s waters, and some returned to France without any pay, indeed in shameful poverty and, still more, disgrace.

Because they called that castle Moysson and, after returning to their own people, said that they had reached as far as Moysson, they were received with great mockery by everyone.

### [IX.]

When Peter was unable to restrain that undisciplined crowd, which behaved like slaves and public servants, by any exhortations, he escaped with whatever remnant of the Alemannic contingent and our own dregs he could gather, and reached the city of Constantinople on the Kalends of August.

A great host of Italians, Ligurians, and Lombards, together with men from the regions beyond the Alps, had preceded his arrival. They had decided to await there his company and that of the other princes of France, for they did not think that they possessed a sufficiently numerous army to pass through the province of the Greeks on their way to fight the Turks.

By the emperor’s order, they were instructed to trade freely in all the merchandise sold in the city. But on the advice of the emperor himself they were forbidden to cross the Arm of Saint George, which bordered the territory of the Turks, because he had said that it was dangerous for the few to confront countless enemies.

### The Franks’ insolence.

But they were restrained neither by the kindness of the inhabitants nor in any way softened by the emperor’s affability. They behaved with excessive insolence, pulled down the palaces of the city, set fire to public buildings, and, after stripping the churches that were roofed with lead, offered that lead for sale to the Greeks.

The emperor, disturbed by such a shameful presumption, ordered them, without further delay, to cross the waters of the aforementioned Arm. Once transported across that strait, they did not cease repeating on the far side the very actions they had committed on this side. Although they had undertaken by vow to fight the pagans, they fought against people of our faith through the enormity of their conduct, devastating churches and plundering the possessions of Christians.

For, since they experienced no severity from a king who would turn them back from their deviations by judicial force, and did not conceive reverence for the divine law, which restrains the levity of minds through mature reflection, they suddenly fell into ruin. Death confronts the undisciplined, and whatever possesses no restraint or moderation lasts only a short time.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### [X.] At last, when they reached Nicomedia, the Italians, Lombards, and Alemanni, unable to endure the Franks’ arrogance, separated from them.

The Franks, in accordance with the nature of their name, are indeed distinguished by the title of great vigor, but unless they are restrained by firm authority, amid the crowds of other nations they are more fiercely disposed than justice permits.

The Transalpines whom we mentioned, therefore, having separated from the Franks, entered the province called Romania under a certain Rainald, whom they appointed as their leader. After passing Nicomedia by a journey of four days, they came upon a certain castle, which its author had given the agreeable name Exorogorgum. Since it had been emptied of the protection of all its inhabitants, it immediately lay open to the invading crowd.

The inhabitants had fled, driven out by fear of those who were approaching. Since they had despaired of their own safety, they had taken no care at all to transport their abundant possessions, which were very considerable. Consequently, when the newcomers found there a great abundance of provisions, they were fully refreshed.

[Col. 0707A] **Conflict with the Turks, who kill many of the Christians. Lack of water in their camp.**—When the Turks learned that the Christians had taken the fortress, they surrounded it with a powerful siege. Before the town gate there was a well, and beneath it, not far from the walls, another spring flowed. Having stationed his men there, their leader Rainald lay in ambush and watched the Turks as though he were shrewdly observing them. Before long, those who were being watched came upon them. On the day when the memory of blessed Michael is celebrated, their leader broke through with his companions, killed many of those who had lain in ambush for him, and forced the others shamefully to retreat within the fortifications.

The Turks immediately surrounded the place and pressed it with such a violent assault that the besieged were completely deprived of the means of drawing water. Such was the parching of their thirst that, after their horses and asses had been bled with a lancet [Col. 0707B], they were compelled to drink the animals’ blood. Others lowered belts and little pieces of cloth into the pool and, squeezing them into their mouths, seemed to obtain some small relief. Others—and it is horrifying to say this—drank the very thing they had urinated. Others dug into the earth and, immersing themselves in what they had dug, covered their parched chests with the freshly excavated soil, believing that by this means they could somewhat temper the heat within them with a little moisture. Yet the bishops and priests who were present and suffering the same things did not fail to provide consolation. The more terrible they saw the dangers and the more human assistance was denied, the more earnestly they strove to promise them heavenly aid, lest they should fail.

[Col. 0707C] **[XI] Duke Rainald, abandoning his faith, makes a pact with the Turks and hands his army over to them.**—This distress continued among them for eight days. Meanwhile, although all appeared to be equally subject to misery, they did not all alike sigh for God’s mercy; rather, those who had been commanders devised for themselves the protection of treachery. Rainald, who had led them in prosperity, secretly secured the Turks’ favor by a shameful agreement, promising that he would betray to them the entire army he commanded.

He therefore went out to them as though he intended to fight. But while affecting to arrange his battle line, he fled with many of his men to their side, intending to remain with them forever. The rest were taken captive. Some of them were questioned about their faith and ordered to deny Christ; but those who confessed Christ with unbending love, in heart and voice, had their heads cut off.

And now Christ will bestow honors like those of the ancients,  
adorning our age with new martyrs.

How fragrant are the times they bear, marked by laurel,  
who prepare to bear a brief thing upon a severed throat!

They called those happy who endured these things  
from moment to moment; a sure faith holds them in eternal life.

Now we may no longer despair of our own refuse,  
since it has dared what is scarcely imitable by anyone.

The other captives were divided among the Turks—some through a concession granting them life, or rather a slower death, but more through violence—with the intention that they should perform grim service under bloodstained masters. Some were exposed somewhere as targets and shot with arrows; others were given away as gifts [Col. 0708A]; others were sold. Those to whom they had been given led them away to their own settlements; some to the region called Corozania; others they dragged to the city of Antioch, where, according to the character of their wicked masters, they were to endure a miserable slavery.

I confess that these went to a more prolonged punishment  
than those whose heads the sword carried off at once.

The cruel master drives this one on and assigns him  
to hard labor; though devoted, he serves everywhere under an ungrateful lord.

The dutiful servant is beaten, nor are torments lacking  
for the faithful man, in whatever task he performs for greater profit.

Whatever he sees or hears, whatever deed he performs day by day,  
because he is unmarried, becomes for him a cross amid shameful things.

I would not hesitate to say that these are tortured  
far more cruelly than a rack could torture them over three days.

[Col. 0708B] God made these men the first martyrs of our new age and of the almost desperate condition of our present life.

Meanwhile that Peter whom we discussed above, often troubled by the great folly of his companions and confounded by their repeated slaughter, had finally entrusted the leadership of his people to a certain Transalpine, a man of known lineage and, so far as he himself was concerned, vigorous in arms, named Walter [variant: Gualtero]. He did this so that those whom he could not restrain by instruction might at least be curbed by Walter’s military authority.

Walter was therefore hastening with that foolish army of his to reach Civizum [variant: Cizicum], a certain city said, by virtue of its geographical position, to stand above the city of Nicaea. When the Turks discovered this by tracking the footsteps of our men, they hurried there with a great eagerness for the worst intentions. [Col. 0708C] While they were on the march, they encountered the aforementioned Walter with his numerous company in the middle of the journey and killed him together with most of his men.

Peter, however, whom they surnamed the Hermit, since he could not restrain the madness that had gathered in his people, had prudently withdrawn to Constantinople, fearing that he might be swept up in their unbridled and heedless folly. The Turks therefore unexpectedly poured upon them and found some asleep; others they found not only without weapons but even without clothing, and they immediately consigned them all alike to death.

Among them they happened to find a priest celebrating Mass. They killed him at the very moment when he was performing the sacred mysteries; and while he was offering sacrifice to God, they sacrificed him before his altar [Col. 0708D].

What more pleasing victim could have been offered  
than one whose flesh becomes a victim for his Lord?

What prayers did he pour from the depths of his heart  
when battles thundered with the great trumpet?

The victors tear them apart; weapons resound;  
the grieving crowd of fugitives howls.

The excellent priest had surrounded the altars,  
embracing the sacred rites of God from the depths of his heart:

“Jesus,” he said, “be present as my good protection;  
now that I hold you, let hope of flight perish.

I shall now join an everlasting covenant with you;  
I am being killed: God, complete the sacred rites begun.”

But those who were able to escape fled into the city of Civizum [Col. 0709A]. Others, whom flight could not protect, were swallowed by the precipice of the sea, since they preferred to choose death rather than succumb to the one who was attacking them. Others, seeking the mountains, were sheltered among the rocks; others hid in the forests.

Before long, after seizing or punishing those whom they had found outside, the Turks attacked those who had taken refuge in the fortress and enclosed them in a siege, even to the point of bringing together wood with which to set the fortress on fire. The besieged then set fire to this wood; and, by God’s judgment, while the Turks supposed that those inside would be burned, the whole force of the flames turned upon the Turks and consumed some of them, but did not touch a single one of our men.

Then, as the attackers pressed on, the town was captured. The living men whom they sought were seized [Col. 0709B] and, just as they had previously dealt with others, divided among them and sent to the provinces from which the enemies had come, destined to remain perpetual exiles. These events took place, as described, in the month of October.

But the treacherous emperor, having learned of the Christians’ misfortune, was lifted up by wicked joy and ordered that the survivors be given resources to return to the parts of nearer Greece, after crossing the Strait of Saint George. When he saw them back in territory under his rule, he demanded, as necessity now required, that they sell him their weapons.

Such was the outcome of Peter the Hermit’s companions. We have followed their story without interruption from the material of another subject so that we might show that they had provided no assistance to the others but had added courage to the Turks. We shall now return to those whom we had omitted, [Col. 0709C] who followed the same road by which Peter had gone before them, but with far greater discipline.

# CHAPTER VI

**[XII] On Godefrid, who, with his two brothers, proceeds to Jerusalem after assembling a powerful army.**—Duke Godefrid, son of Eustace, count of Boulogne, had two brothers: Baldwin, who ruled the city of Edessa and, after his brother, became king of Jerusalem and still reigns; and Eustace, who presides over his paternal county.

They had a powerful father, a man of secular intelligence; and also a mother who, unless I am mistaken, was learned in letters and nobly descended from Lotharingia, but who excelled above all in innate serenity and great devotion of spirit toward God. To her long and conspicuous religious observance, we believe, the joy of her sons was owed.

The duchy among the Lotharingians had come to Godefrid, the one of whom we have begun to speak, through his maternal inheritance. These three men, in no way degenerate from their mother’s simplicity, flourished with great glory in arms and with no less modesty.

The noble woman used to relate that, when she marveled at the outcome of this expedition and at the success of her sons, she had heard such a prophecy from the mouth of the duke’s son long before any beginning of the pilgrimage had been made. He had said that he desired to set out for Jerusalem, not in the ordinary manner of others, but, if the opportunity were granted him, with the force of a great army. [Col. 0710A] In accordance with the divine inspiration by which he perceived it, a marvelous opportunity later smiled upon this desire.

These three men therefore set out, having forgotten the greatest honors they possessed. But, as he was more prudent than his other brothers, so Duke Godefrid proved more powerful through the larger number of his troops. Baldwin, count of Mons, son of the younger paternal uncle of Robert, count of Flanders, joined him.

With a noble display of cavalry and a splendid multitude of very brave young men, they entered the land of the Hungarians. They nevertheless possessed the discipline toward their soldiers that Peter had been unable to maintain. Two days before the Nativity of the Lord, they were the first of all the princes of France to reach Constantinople [Col. 0710B], but they lodged outside the city.

The treacherous emperor, terrified when he heard of the arrival of the famous duke, paid him respect—but respect extorted by threats—granting him permission to remain before the walls, in the suburb of the city.

After accepting lodging at the emperor’s command, the duke and each of his men sent their own armed servants to gather straw wherever they could find it and to obtain what the horses required. While they thought they could lawfully and safely go wherever they wished, that wicked prince secretly ordered those around him to kill the duke’s servants indiscriminately wherever they could reach them.

When this became known to Baldwin, the duke’s brother, he exposed the ambush. Finding his men being harassed by the violence of the Turcopoles, [Col. 0710C] he attacked them with the greatest vigor, as was fitting. With God granting success, he won so great a victory that, after capturing sixty of them, he killed some and presented the rest to his brother the duke.

When news of this reached the impious emperor, he was tortured by deep indignation. The duke, made more cautious by the prince’s anger, withdrew from the city suburb where he had previously stayed and pitched his camp outside its boundaries.

But the prince, not forgetting the injury inflicted upon him, sent against the duke, as the day was declining toward evening, whatever army he could assemble, challenging him to battle. The duke met them with vigorous force and, having driven them into flight, pursued them and forced them into the city, killing seven of them.

After these events had ended happily, the duke returned to his camp and remained there for five days, until he and the emperor were reconciled [Col. 0710D] to peace. But the anxious prince required the duke, under threat, to cross the Strait of Saint George, promising that he would order all provisions available in Constantinople to be conveyed to them and would also provide alms for their poor. This was done.

# CHAPTER VII

**[XIII] Aimarus, bishop of Le Puy, distinguished for piety and learning.**—Since we have spoken of the duke and of the provisions he had so far obtained, we must now return to the nobles of inner France and touch, at least in part, upon who they were, where they went, and what outcomes they experienced.

The bishop of Le Puy was a man admirable in life, learning, instruction, and the sagacity of military organization. With an innumerable multitude of his own people, he chose to travel through the region of the Slavs. Since I had earlier lamented my ignorance of his name and could not learn it through the history of which I seem to be the interpreter, I finally came to know it through those who had known him and served under him on that expedition. That precious man was called Aimarus.

**[XIV] Hugh the Great, most vigorous.**—Among the other princes, it seems to me that I should begin with Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the Franks. Although some surpass him in wealth and power, no one, so far as origin and integrity of character are concerned, is considered his equal.

His vigor in arms, his serenity together with the majesty of his lineage, and, beyond these, his humility toward the entire sacred order—which was nevertheless seasoned by the honorable dignity of his own self-restraint—are rightly celebrated. Certain nobles relied upon him and were considering making him their king if, by the right of war, they happened to conquer and retain the pagan peoples.

**[XV] Stephen, a very wealthy and very generous count.**—After him came Count Stephen, a man endowed with such power that, as report attests, he possessed authority over as many castles as the year contains days honored by the calendar. While he lived, his generosity was exceedingly remarkable and his personal bearing sufficiently pleasing; his judgment in every matter was maturely balanced.

In the art of warfare he excelled with such nobility [variant: mobility] that the entire holy army, when it was preparing for battle against the Turks, made him its dictator and commander [variant: had made him].

He had as his wife one of the most discerning of women, the daughter of William the Elder, the king who subjected the kingdoms of the English and Scots to himself. If we wished to praise her prudence, generosity, munificence, and wealth, I fear that we might cast a shadow upon the magnificent man by transferring to his wife the praise she deserved even in widowhood.

**On Robert of Flanders. The princes leave behind their wives, possessions, and so forth.**—To augment the strength of these men, Robert the Younger, son of the elder Robert to whom the emperor’s letter had been sent, was impelled with all the vigor of his spirit. He exchanged the county of Flanders, over which he had presided with great martial courage, so that he might be called a fellow soldier of those who had chosen to become exiles for Christ.

The continuation of the present history will show how perseveringly he devoted himself to the enterprise he had begun. These men, leaving behind illustrious wives and beloved sons, placed before everything dear to them their chosen exile. I say nothing of their honors and possessions, which lie beyond our subject. But this produces wonder in us: how could the love of husbands and wives, bound together—or rather fused—through their children, be separated from one another without danger to either?

**[XVI] Praises of Robert, count of Normandy.**—Finally, it is by no means fitting to remain silent about Robert, count of Normandy. The weight of his body, the gentleness [variant: lightness] of disposition that he possessed, and the excessive outpouring of money from his generously inclined spirit—together with no small amount of sleepiness and a more conspicuous impetuosity—he atoned for by the perseverance and courage with which he served in the Lord’s army.

Natural clemency was so deeply implanted in him that he would not permit himself to take revenge on those who had fallen under his authority through the guilt of treason and the judgment of death; indeed, if anything happened to them, he wept over their misfortunes.

His courage in military matters and, so far as wicked schemes are concerned, his complete lack of the cunning by which we see many men disgraced would rightly be praised, were he not burdened by certain indignities that must be kept silent. Yet all this ought now to be forgiven him, because, as God temporarily repays him for these and similar deeds, he is kept in prison, having lost the entire honor of his county [Col. 0712B].

# CHAPTER VIII

**[XVII]** Along with the renowned ranks of those whom each of these men had brought with him from his own province, a multitude of lesser princes also set out. Since their number seems to obscure our account, we suppress it for the present, perhaps intending, as the history proceeds, to name some of them for a particular purpose. For who could count the lords of one, two, three, or four towns? Their number was so great that the Trojan siege could scarcely be thought to have assembled as many.

At that time, when the matter of this expedition was being discussed among the leading men of the kingdom and they were holding a conference in Paris with Hugh the Great in the presence of King Philip, on the third day before the Ides of February, the moon began, before midnight, gradually to be veiled in a bloody color as it underwent an eclipse, until it was transformed entirely and horribly into the deepest red.

When, at the dawn’s first light, it returned to its natural state, an unusual brightness appeared around the lunar circle. Then, on a certain summer day, as evening approached, so great a blast appeared to flare up from the northern quarter that many people rushed from their houses, asking what enemies were ravaging their provinces with so severe a burning.

Not long afterward, in the month of April, stars were seen at night as though they were falling densely like rain from heaven. This was regarded in many churches as something resembling—and in fact constituting—a portent, so that they instituted litanies to avert the calamity signified by it and recorded the time and event in writing.

Again, in the month of August, on the sixth day before the Ides, shortly before sunset, nearly half of the moon was turned black while many people watched. Although the moon naturally undergoes eclipses at full moon, some omens are nevertheless discerned in these very changes of its color. Hence such events are also customarily recorded in the histories of pontiffs and kings. Many other things were seen, which we omit from our account.

**[XVIII] Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles sets out with the others.**—Finally, Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles is placed last, not to his disparagement, but as the culmination. Since he lived at the farthest edge of France [Col. 0713A], the less knowledge he had previously provided us of his deeds, the more he ennobles the whole course of this history, from beginning to end, as a memorial of his great courage and steadfastness.

Leaving the county he governed to a certain natural son of his, he took with him his own wife and the only son whom he had by her. He was more mature in age than the princes mentioned above, and in military force inferior to none—except insofar as the noisy customs of the men of Provence are concerned.

When, therefore, the very numerous band of brave soldiers had reached Apulia by the road along which we usually travel to Rome, countless men contracted deadly sickness and death from the unusual heat of the summer then prevailing, from the corruption of the air, and from unfamiliar food. They therefore dispersed in different directions [Col. 0713B], intending to cross the sea at the ports.

Brundisium receives many; trackless Hydrus (Ydrons) receives these,  
while the fish-filled waters of Bari lay open to the others.

**[XIX]** But Hugh the Great, without waiting for the assembly of his men, his soldiers, and his fellow princes, acted most imprudently and with excessive haste. He entered the port of Bari and, with a favorable voyage, was carried to Dyrrachium [Col. 0714A].

He ought to have considered that the foundations of all Greece, so to speak, had trembled in expectation of such eminent persons and such great forces of cavalry and infantry. Although the authority of the other nobles was considered much greater among us than his, abroad—especially among the most sluggish of peoples, the Greeks—an immense reputation for the brother of the king of the Franks had gone before him.

When the emperor’s duke, who resided there, noticed that this distinguished man was accompanied by only a small retinue, wickedness seized his mind, taking advantage of such an opportunity for isolation. He seized him and ordered that he be conducted to the emperor at Constantinople with great provision and respect, solely in order to give the anxious prince assurance that through him Hugh’s life [Col. 0714B] and honor would remain wholly unharmed.

This misfortune of the illustrious man caused the courage of the nobles who followed a very great weakening. The fraud of the treacherous prince compelled the other leaders to do the same thing that he demanded of Hugh, whether by force, secretly, or through entreaty. But now let this little book draw to its end.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0713]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0713C]

**386 [I] On Bohemond, son of Robert, or Wiscard.**—When an innumerable army had arrived in Apulia from nearly every region of the western lands, news of the approaching multitude reached Bohemond, son of Robert called Wiscard, a man of singular magnificence. At that time he was pressing the Amalfitans under siege.

When a messenger came to him with news of the people who were gathering, he asked the reason for their journey and learned that they were hastening to free Jerusalem—and, more precisely, the Lord’s Sepulchre and the sacred places there, which were being held in disgrace—from the control of the nations.

Nor was it concealed from him how many men of every kind and of what distinction, having left behind, so to speak, the majesty of their honors, were hastening with unheard-of eagerness to accomplish this. He then asked whether they carried weapons, whether they bore bags, or whether they displayed some emblem of this new pilgrimage that they would proclaim as their battle cry.

The answer was: “They carry weapons, as is customary among the Franks. They have been instructed to sew the shape of a cross onto their garments, whether on their shoulders or elsewhere, using whatever material or cloth they wish. Setting aside the arrogant variety of signs, they will proclaim humbly and faithfully in battle: ‘DEUS ID VULT’—‘God wills it.’”

At this, inspired in the depths of his heart by God, he was moved to compunction and ordered that a most precious cloak be brought to him. He had it cut into little crosses and, after placing one upon himself, distributed them to his men, who desired to pursue the very vow he had made, so that they too might attach crosses to themselves.

For the soldiers who were serving him in that siege suddenly changed their minds and set out on the journey with him, since he was their own lord. So great a multitude of soldiers then gathered to make this vow that his brother Roger, count of Sicily, was deeply distressed because in that siege he was deprived of almost all the assistance of his faithful men.

**[II] The deeds of Bohemond the Norman.**—It must be explained briefly from what stock he sprang and by what stages Bohemond was advanced to such honor.

Robert, whom we have said was surnamed Wiscard, was born in Normandy and came from a sufficiently humble station. Whether he left the native region we mentioned earlier voluntarily or was driven out, I do not know; he went on foot to Apulia. There he acquired, by whatever skill he could, horses and weapons with which he might become a mounted warrior.

Afterward, having gathered from every direction brigands to assist him, he seized certain castles—not without the stain of treachery—and occupied others that had likewise been weakened by repeated raids. He also besieged cities that were well fortified and forced them to surrender.

To sum it up briefly, this newcomer extended his dominion so greatly and subdued whatever he wished to such an extent that, as it is said in the verses of his epitaph:

He drove from the city the man  
whom the Ligurians have as king, and Rome as a German (*Lemannus*, probably *Alemannus*):

namely, Henry Augustus, a man fortunate in countless, indeed almost uninterrupted, victories.

Neither the Parthian, the Arab, nor the Macedonian phalanx protected Alexis,  
the prince of the Greeks who often deals with us. [Col. 0715A]

But he repeatedly subdued him; and, had a draught of poison not suddenly taken his life, he would, as they say, within a few days have brought his crowned head into the seat of Constantinople.

Let anyone who wishes look today upon the power of his son Bohemond, who, having erased the disgrace of his ancestors’ lowly condition, married the daughter of King Philip of the Franks and attempted to seize the empire of the aforementioned Alexis by force.

While his brother Roger was returning to Sicily, grieving that he was losing almost the entire people of his nation, since all of them seemed destined to go to Jerusalem:

**On Tancred, Bohemond’s nephew.**—Bohemond gathered the forces necessary for so great an expedition, boarded ships with his army, and, with a favorable breeze assisting, was carried safely to the Bulgarian shore [Col. 0715B], where he disembarked.

His company included both many excellent cavalrymen and no small number of men of princely rank. Among them we recognized Tancred, son of a certain marquis by Bohemond’s sister, unless I am mistaken. Tancred’s brother, named William, had gone ahead with Hugh the Great. We also recognized a certain Richard, who was said to be “of the First City,” a man striking in his handsome appearance, whom we saw carry out an embassy to the king of France on behalf of Constance, Bohemond’s wife.

When he entered Bulgaria with his men, they found abundant supplies of provisions. When they reached the valley of Andropolis, they waited there until their entire fleet had sailed in and come alongside [Col. 0715C].

When the whole people had therefore been assembled, he called the nobles together and shared counsel with them. He ordered, with the unanimous agreement of all, that as they passed through Christian peoples they should conduct themselves kindly and innocently and should not lay waste the homeland of those whose support they ought to have come to seek. They were to take only what could suffice for provisions, and to take it peacefully, though at a price.

They proceeded from there and, as they passed from city to city, from countryside to countryside, and from town to town, they found everywhere an abundant market, until they reached the province called Castoria. There they solemnly celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and remained for several days.

They then sought to conduct trade with the local people, but the latter refused their consent, fearing them because they regarded them as soldiers rather than pilgrims and believed that they wished to destroy the land and put its inhabitants to death.

The pilgrims’ discipline, however, turned into fury, and they plundered horses, oxen, asses, and whatever else seemed useful to them. At last they left Castoria and came to Pelagonia, where they found a certain fortress belonging to heretics. They attacked it on every side, forced it to submit to their authority, set it on fire, and burned the fortress together with its inhabitants.

From there they reached the river called Baudarum [variant: Bandarum]. Bohemond therefore advanced with part of his soldiers, while he left the remainder under the command of one of his counts [Col. 0716A].

When the emperor’s army, which was not far away, learned of this, it attacked the count, who had been left without the support of the duke who had gone ahead, and the count’s companions were thrown into confusion by the sudden attack of the enemy.

News of this reached the ears of the very brave Tancred. He immediately turned back, threw himself into the aforementioned river, swam across to those who were under attack, and gathered nearly two thousand auxiliaries who had swum after him [variant: had swum across].

He found the enemy fiercely engaged against his men and attacked them with an even fiercer courage, as was fitting. Before long he subdued them. Many of them were captured, led before Bohemond, and thrown into chains.

The prince said to them: “Why do you pursue both Christ’s people and mine? I am plotting no destruction against your emperor.”

They replied: “We are doing nothing by our own decision. We have entered military service in order to earn the prince’s robe [variant: to obtain his request], and whatever he orders us to do, we shall necessarily carry out.””

When the excellent man heard this, he immediately released them to depart without punishment or ransom. This battle is said to have taken place on the fourth feria, which among Christians is called the Head of the Fast.

# CHAPTER II

**[III] The emperor fraudulently makes a pact with Bohemond.**—When the emperor Alexis learned of the distinguished man’s achievement, he instructed one of his close advisers, on whose counsel he chiefly relied, to escort the high-spirited duke and his army honorably through his territory until he reached Constantinople and the emperor’s presence [Col. 0716C].

As the army passed through the towns and cities of the empire, the emperor ordered the inhabitants of each region by an imperial edict to take care to bring the army an abundance of everything available for sale from every direction.

The army was allowed to hurry through the provinces in such a way that none of those attached to Bohemond was permitted to enter within the walls of any city. But these soldiers began to break into a certain fortress that seemed at that time to be rich in goods appropriate to their needs.

The illustrious man forbade this, partly so as not to disturb the rights of the land, partly so as not to offend the emperor’s still-sensitive feelings, and above all so as not to annul the agreements recently made with him through intermediaries. He therefore bitterly regretted the foolish action that had begun and, angry with those who had initiated it, especially Tancred, restrained them [Col. 0716D].

This had happened in the evening. But when morning came, the men of the fortress came out, carrying before them banners of the cross, and proceeded to Bohemond with great humility and reverence. He received them graciously and gently, granted them his favor, and sent them away rejoicing.

At last they came to a certain city called Serra, where they pitched their tents. During those days they did not lack suitable provisions. There Bohemond returned to concord with two palace prefects. Accordingly, in accordance with their new agreement and to preserve the rights of the province, he ordered that whatever had been taken from the inhabitants as plunder be restored.

From there they reached the territory of another city called Rusa. Behold, a mixed crowd of Greeks ran out to meet the noble man, bringing whatever goods were then available for sale. There they set up camp three days before the day of the Lord’s Supper.

Bohemond, leaving his own company there, went to Constantinople with a few soldiers in order to confer with the emperor. Meanwhile Tancred managed the army. When he saw how difficult it was, now that the purse was exhausted, to purchase the necessities of life, he proposed to himself that he should abandon the well-traveled road and turn his men toward regions less frequented by travelers, where a more abundant supply of things for purchase would be available to all.

He therefore led them away from the public road and entered a valley rich in various kinds of food [Col. 0717B], providing for the poorer among his men. There the people celebrated the Lord’s Easter with him in due devotion.

When Alexis learned that Bohemond was coming to him, he ordered that the approaching man be shown the greatest respect and that lodgings be provided for him in the city’s suburb. After Bohemond had been received there, he was summoned to a conference; when he came, he was admitted to a private meeting with the emperor.

**[IV]** Meanwhile Duke Godefrid, with his brother Baldwin, and afterward the count of Saint-Gilles, each with a substantial force, reached the suburbs of Constantinople [Col. 0717C].

Then the treacherous Alexis, who had formerly been thought eager for assistance against the Turks, ground his teeth with the bitterness of resentment and repeatedly considered by what fraud he might hurl into a shameful destruction so many armies that, as he thought, were advancing against him.

But God, by whose inspiration those pious forces were led, protected them so completely that no opportunity was left to the wicked man to harm them; indeed, every possibility having been cut off, great fear was inflicted upon the wretch.

Finally, when the people of Constantinople saw the converging columns, they were thrown into confusion and gathered together to seek counsel. Fearing that the city might be overwhelmed by the multitude of those arriving and that their province might be given over to devastation, they found, in the discussion of the counsel they had taken, that the tyrant demanded an oath from the Franks “that they would never harm him or his people.”

When this became known to the leaders of our people, it was immediately met with great mockery and contempt. They had plainly considered that, if somehow the first armies could be made to stray from the undertaking they had begun, then, having been deprived of pay, so many and such great soldiers would be obliged to wage war against the treacherous prince in violation of the oaths they had sworn.

“And certainly,” they said, “if no fear of the future burdened us, the mere fact that we should be compelled to swear by these utterly sluggish little Greeks would be an everlasting disgrace to us. We have no doubt that they will say that, whether we wished it or not, we had obeyed their imperial authority.”

The emperor then approached the very brave Bohemond and prepared to entice the man whom he feared most with gifts. Bohemond had often defeated him in war, and therefore Alexis pressed him more than the others, recognizing him as his particular rival.

He promised, therefore, to give him territory extending fifteen days’ journey in length and eight in breadth, beyond Antioch. The illustrious man’s severity was broken by this promise. He did not delay to swear oaths to the tyrant, and he consented to swear in the same terms as Hugh the Great had sworn under the pressure both of necessity and of money: “If Alexis broke the terms agreed by oath [variant: what had been promised to the man], Bohemond would be free from the obligations he had confirmed by oath.”

But if anyone asks why he and the others were diverted from their former rigor into offering oaths to the tyrant, let him know that the nobles were responding to the necessities of their fellow soldiers in the Lord, who were suffering great want if they were denied pay when they went to market.

Alexis, for his part, had likewise given our men an oath of faith: “He would come with them, accompanied by his army; he would assist them by land and sea; he would order that provisions purchased for their sustenance be conveyed by both routes; and, if any losses happened to them, he would restore them in full, without diminution, to make good the loss [variant: to the utmost]. In this expedition he would neither wish nor permit anyone to be harassed, injured, or killed, insofar as his power allowed.”

# CHAPTER III
[V.] Moreover, when the count of Saint-Gilles had occupied the suburbs of Byzantium with his camp, while part of his army had not yet assembled in full, the tyrant began through a messenger to urge the count to allow him, as the others had done, to perform homage to him. The insolent tyrant’s cunning dictated this proposal; but the prudent mind of the glorious count had already begun to consider how he might avenge the wicked man’s spite. [Col. 0718C] The princes, however—Duke Godfrey, Hugh the Great, Robert of Flanders, and the others—said that they would never bear arms against anyone who was reckoned by the name of Christian. Bohemund added that, if the count made war upon the emperor and rejected the oaths of security, he himself would support the imperial party.

Accordingly, after taking counsel also with his own close companions [alternative reading: *cum suis consilio*, “with his men’s counsel”], the count swore to the impious Alexius “the safety of his life and honor,” namely, that “neither by his own action nor by helping another would he favor Alexius’s destruction.” When they repeated to him the word concerning homage, he said that he preferred to undergo the danger of losing his head rather than become subject to him in such a manner.

[Col. 0718D] Meanwhile Bohemund’s army was approaching the fortifications of Constantinople. Tancred, therefore, having learned the oaths demanded by the emperor, quickly crossed the Arm of Saint George with almost all of Bohemund’s host which he was leading. The army of the count of Saint-Gilles, meanwhile, was dispersed by pitching its camps around the borders of the same city. The count decided to remain there for a while with his forces. Bohemund also stayed with the emperor, so that he might negotiate more freely with him, asking that by imperial decree the peoples settled beyond Nicaea be notified to transport provisions from every direction.

Duke Godfrey, who had gone ahead, reached Nicomedia with Tancred. With Nicomedes as authority—who is sung in a triumphal song as famous for having subdued Caesar, rather than triumphed—each remained there for three days with his forces. [Col. 0719A]

The duke perceived that certain obstacles blocked the roads and that there was no way for so great a multitude of troops to reach Nicaea. The path by which Peter the Hermit’s men had passed could in no way be traversed by so large a multitude. He therefore sent three thousand men ahead with axes and hatchets, to cut away the obstructions of the narrow roads and make the route passable by opening the defiles as far as Nicaea.

The road was extraordinarily steep, exceedingly rocky, and ran through mountains of threatening height. Those who had been sent ahead widened it by cutting down the rocks and set iron and wooden crosses upon tall stakes, so that our men would not stray from the path when they saw the signs of the stakes from a distance. [Col. 0719B] At last they came to Nicaea, the metropolis of all Romania and the capital of Bithynia, famous for the synod of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, but even more renowned for the assertion of the Homoousion and the condemnation of Arius. On the day before the Nones of May, the third day after their departure from Nicomedia, they pitched camp around the city’s territory.

Before Bohemund’s army arrived, there is said to have been such a shortage of bread there that one loaf was sold for either twenty or thirty denarii. But when Bohemund arrived, he conveyed [alternative readings: *convexit*, *contraxit*] by land and sea immense supplies of every kind of merchandise, and suddenly an abundance of everything suitable for use flowed together.

## CHAPTER IV

### [V.] Nicaea Is Besieged by the Franks and Captured

On the Sunday of the Lord’s Ascension, they began to attack the city from every side before its walls, to set up engines, raise siege screens, restore the *phalaricae*, and strike the circuit of the walls and towers all around with repeated ballista shots. The siege of the city began with such vehemence of spirit that within only two days they had undermined the walls.

The Turks who held the city sent messengers to other cities, asking them to come to their aid. Their plan was certainly that they should enter without fail through the southern gate, since that side was free from the siege and no one there would hinder those wishing to bring assistance. Accordingly, on that very day—the Saturday after the Lord’s Ascension—the count of Saint-Gilles and the bishop of Le Puy were fortifying the approach to the gate. [Col. 0719D]

There occurred there a deed worthy of a famous name. The distinguished count, confident in God, brave and skilled in arms, and accompanied by a thoroughly equipped army, encountered the battalions of auxiliaries hastening toward the city. With his spirit resting upon the aid of divine strength, he attacked and defeated the Turks, forced them to flee, and cut down most of them.

But, shamefully repulsed, they began to assemble new forces. Trusting in their support, they resolved with great exultation to renew the battle, bringing ropes with them so that they might bind our men and drag them away to Chorozania.

While they were being lifted up by this empty hope, they began slowly to descend from the summit of the mountain overlooking the city, one after another. [Col. 0720A] Our men welcomed them gladly, as was fitting, and they left behind their severed heads as testimony to our victory. After their flight, these heads were hurled into the city with ballistae and slings, to terrify the gentiles.

The bishop of Le Puy, of blessed memory, and Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, set about weakening the city’s defenses. They began to undermine a certain tower adjoining their camp by digging tunnels beneath it to weaken its foundations. Miners were assigned to carry out this work, while crossbowmen, archers, and those who strained the cords of slings were likewise stationed to ward off the defenders of the excavation.

When the tower had been cut away down to the limits of the sinking ground, they temporarily supported the wavering wall with beams and planks; then, once the building’s mortar had been completely destroyed, they set fire beneath it with beams placed below:

> But when the cloudy night imposed rest on both sides,  
> the undermined tower suddenly collapses in ruin.  
> Yet because the hours of night are less suited to combat,  
> the Franks desist, lest they provoke the Turks by night.

Nevertheless, the Turks, concerned for the preservation of their lives, rose with every kind of ingenuity and rebuilt the wall there with such strength and such speed that the next day our men could find no place from which they could harm them.

Meanwhile, newly arrived men, most distinguished for the glory of their arms and exceedingly wealthy counts, of whom we spoke above, came with the numerous military companies attached to them. At their arrival the whole army of the Lord rejoiced together: Robert, count of the Normans, and Stephen, count of Chartres. [Col. 0720C]

### [VI.]

Bohemund therefore besieged the city from the front, Tancred from the side; in the third position was Duke Godfrey, in the fourth the count of the Flemings, in the fifth the Norman count, and in the sixth the count of Saint-Gilles and the bishop of Le Puy. They intended to besiege it in such a way that the besieged could find no avenue for entering or leaving.

There one might see assembled the flower of the whole Frankish army, nobility, prudence, and military renown. Those accustomed to estimate the size of armies reckoned the mounted armored and helmeted men at approximately one hundred thousand. As for the multitude of the infantry and the number of those who followed the cavalry, I do not think that anyone could fully count them. [Col. 0720D] Indeed, such people brought not merely the services ordinarily supplied to military men by retainers or slaves; in sieges and battles their courage, and their lion-like boldness, were so necessary to their superiors that their hands often performed whatever arms or implements were useful in war or labor.

### [VII.]

> No speech will be able to say  
> how great, throughout that time,  
> the splendor of the mighty in arms was there.  
>   
> Never, anywhere in the world,  
> had any land seen gathered together  
> so noble a stock. If you wish,  
> I shall unfold every kingdom  
> and tell of the battles fought everywhere:  
> no one would be able to compare  
> his lineage or strength with theirs.  
>   
> Behold: they have left their parents’ homes;  
> they shun marriage covenants;  
> children are despised,  
> households are counted a punishment.  
> In every soldier burns  
> the concern for martyrdom.  
>   
> Though a multitude is drawn onward  
> by the omen of shed blood,  
> who could find a sluggish man?  
> Each one advances with a lion’s heart.  
> Therefore it is pleasing to behold  
> the walls of Nicaea encircled.  
>   
> The field shone with the splendor of horses;  
> the form and sound of the trappings  
> delighted everyone. The gleam of the breastplates  
> passed forth more beautiful than the captured sun.  
> The helmet and shield of yellow bronze,  
> and the shining rim of the same metal,  
> stood out brilliantly.  
>   
> You would see these men, like a whirlwind,  
> repeatedly battering the walls with a ram.  
> Their Frankish spear-point found  
> their hard bows [alternative reading: *artus*, “limbs”].  
> A wound upon bone repeatedly  
> blunted the sharp swords.  
>   
> A wooden tower compelled the Turks  
> to yield at the high walls.  
> Hand-to-hand battles raged among them;  
> each man hurled his missiles at the other.  
> The force of the projectiles was empty in its flight;  
> sudden death struck each man down.  
>   
> Heavenly glory had made our strong men brave;  
> then they offered their bodies to fate.  
> They rejoiced to seek rewards through death.  
> Every man, once sluggish, was made  
> keen and daring there,  
> whom the choice of a better life  
> would rightly have approved.  
>   
> Far from them were the crimes  
> of a mind greedy for empty praise.  
> Everyone believed that Christ would aid them  
> if they prepared battles for the renown  
> of a worthy name.  
> No one, whoever had done anything honorable,  
> claimed the deed for himself.

> We cannot compare to these men  
> the Scythian triumphs over Darius,  
> nor can the enterprises of Cyrus be known—  
> enterprises worthy of the man whom Thamyris  
> had enclosed in a skin of blood.  
> You may mourn the outcome, good Pyrrhus,  
> while defending Tarentum.  
> In vain you boast of undertaking  
> new battles with elephants.  
> Hannibal’s companions cut down the Romans,  
> once, twice, and three times,  
> like a standing crop; yet, defeated,  
> they withdrew from the city.  
> If a ten-year battle under Caesar  
> was without loss, let the dwelling  
> across the Gallic fields be the price.  
> The time for this work was brief;  
> all things prospered when God was present in them.  
> The best outcome proves everything.  
> Whoever receives death, when glory comes with martyrdom,  
> is fortunate; whoever is needy,  
> is judged, because punishment releases him from his crimes.

### [VIII.]

A portion of the same city was surrounded by an obstacle of stagnant water extending far and wide. Thus the enemy, having lowered boats into it, seemed to possess a free passage for going in and out; through it they also obtained firewood, fodder, and the transport of every kind of useful thing. [Col. 0722A]

Therefore the nobles, having convened a council, unanimously resolved that an embassy should be sent to the prince of Constantinople. It was to urge that as many ships as possible be brought as far as the city of Civizena [alternative reading: Cizicena], where a harbor was known to exist; then that innumerable pairs of oxen should be gathered to drag them through the mountains and forests until they could be placed in the lake mentioned above.

There was no delay. The rapid execution of the work, which had been planned and requested, proceeded as the prince hastened it; at the same time those called Turcopoles—by whom we understand members of his household troops—were sent. When the ships had been brought forward as the prince’s command required, they remained silent there during the day on which they were transported, but at night they pushed them into the lake, together with the Turcopoles, fully equipped with arms. [Col. 0722B]

At dawn, when the fleet had been arranged, they set out toward the city with great composure, as though they were transporting the goods of their own tax revenues. The Turks, who watched this spectacle, were amazed, uncertain whether the transport belonged to themselves or to the emperor. When they realized that what they had seen was hostile, they wasted away in deadly fear. Our men, however, indulged in an equal measure of joy and repaid God with applause and thanksgiving.

This misfortune left the enemy weakened everywhere. Now despairing of their own strength and that of their auxiliaries, they sent an embassy to the emperor and promised that they would surrender the city if he could obtain permission for them to depart among the Franks with their wives and children, carrying their possessions with them. [Col. 0722C]

The tyrant, favoring their request most gladly, not only granted them immunity but also drew them all the way to Constantinople, to bind them to himself by the strongest affection. His deceitful mind had this principal intention in the undertaking: if any opportunity should ever open for danger to threaten the Franks, he would have the men at hand to throw against them at a suitable moment.

They were held in this siege for seven weeks and three days, and many of our men there received the gift of martyrdom. Of these it will undoubtedly be said that those who exposed themselves to death for the justice of the faith were certainly reckoned among those with God who, giving blood as the price, earned heavenly rewards.
