[Col. 0722D] Nor would I call them inferior to those who perished from the misery of hunger. For in this way a very great multitude died there.

If, as the prophet says—so far as it is permissible to state it historically—“It was better for those slain by the sword than for those killed by hunger” (Jeremiah IV, 4), then those who were tortured in dying by a longer torment will not, as it is right to believe, be without the nobler crown of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER V

### [IX.]

After the city had been restored and the Turks had been brought to Constantinople, that tyrannical prince, rejoicing excessively at the recovery of the city, bestowed countless gifts upon our leading men, and abundant alms were distributed to the poorest. [Col. 0723A] As a result, deep envy and hostility arose among the ordinary members of the army, whom that generosity appeared to pass over, directed as it was toward the princes. Nor was this entirely unjust. These men had fought the battles; to them belonged the whole labor of the siege, the transport of the siegeworks, and the striking of engines and ballistae. These men, in short, had borne the burden of the day and the heat.

On the first day after they departed from the recovered city, they found a passable bridge and remained near it for two continuous days. On the third day, when the thin dawn was already bringing forth the twilight, our men arose. While they were still blinking in the uncertain light, they split at a fork in the road and proceeded for two full days in two separate columns. In one column were Bohemund, Robert of Normandy, and Tancred with a very large force. The other was led by the count of Saint-Gilles, Duke Godfrey, the bishop of Le Puy, Hugh the Great, and the count of Flanders, by certain trackless routes. [Col. 0723B]

### The Turks Attack the Franks

On the third day, an immense multitude of Turks suddenly and terribly collided with Bohemund and his counts—an encounter almost impossible to endure. You would have seen them theatrically mocking our men, whom they believed to be afraid, thinking that they had been terrified by the unexpected attack, and shouting the customary battle signal in terrifying cries in their own language.

Although that distinguished man was attacked by an enormous force, he did not lose his judgment through fear. He immediately ordered everyone to halt, and, with the tents rolled down, commanded that the camp be spread out quickly. Before the orders could be carried out, he said to his own soldiers: [Col. 0723C]

> “If you remember the military service which you have professed, then, considering the necessity that presses upon you, go and meet them manfully; defend your honor and your lives alike. You infantry, however, stretch out the tents carefully.”

The words had scarcely been carried out when the Turks suddenly swooped around them, cast their missiles, and, following their customary flight-fighting, drove arrows into the breasts of those pursuing them. The Franks, mindful of the faithfulness of their purpose and not ignorant of their own celebrated courage, clearly recognized that they were inferior to such a multitude; nevertheless, with lively courage they strove to meet the raging enemy.

There the count of Normandy, remembering as was fitting his father’s warlike spirit and his ancestral nobility, immediately offered our somewhat frightened army an example of defense through great military skill and the repulsion of the enemy. [Col. 0723D]

God also saw to it that the women who accompanied them did not fail them there in their attentiveness. They diligently carried water to refresh the soldiers; yet through their exhortations and admonitions they made them much more vigilant and more skillful than the newly supplied water itself could make them.

When Bohemund began to be warned of the disproportion in this battle, he immediately sent word to the count of Saint-Gilles, Raymond, to Duke Godfrey, to Hugh the Great, to the bishop of Le Puy, and to the other members of their company, urging them to hasten their arrival—not for any other reason, but for the battles that threatened. [Col. 0724A]

> “If,” they said, “you desire to see the first beginnings of battle with the Turks, what you seek is already at hand. Come quickly.”

Godfrey, worthy of the name of duke and an example of military skill, and Hugh the Great, who was not degenerate in the courage appropriate to a king—indeed, possessing, so to speak, the courage of a leopard—rushed forward with their leading troops in a kind of festive eagerness. Then the bishop of Le Puy fortified him not only with the many weapons in which he excelled, but also with sacred admonitions and prayers:

> And if the army was lukewarm,  
> he compelled it to grow fervent.

At last, the count of Saint-Gilles, Raymond, older in years, better equipped by experience, and therefore more secure in counsel, burst forth with the support of companies from his Provençal countrymen. [Col. 0724B]

When our men had surveyed the enemy army, such amazement grew among them that they wondered at nothing except where in the world or in what land such an infinite multitude had gathered. They were Turks, Arabs, and Saracens, whose numbers and rank stood out among the enemy. A less conspicuous multitude consisted of auxiliaries and less celebrated peoples. You would have seen the mountain ridges and rounded hills thickly covered by this profane gathering, and every plain occupied by innumerable crowds.

### The Leaders Encourage Their Soldiers to Battle

The leaders therefore addressed an exhortation to those under their command: [Col. 0724C]

> “If you have devoted this military service to God, as you practice it; if you have despised your homelands, your homes, your wives, your children, and finally your own bodies, and if these alone have been left to be offered to glorious martyrdoms, what, I ask, could terrify you when you consider these men? The faithful sagacity granted by God to one of you is stronger than the superstition of all this most worthless rabble.  
>   
> “If you must die here, the heavenly kingdom awaits you, and you will die a blessed death. If you must live, then, if you trust in the faith, certain victory awaits you; after victory, glory; after glory, greater courage. In addition, abundant wealth will come from the riches of the enemy.  
>   
> “Whichever outcome occurs, security is present for you in both. You have nothing to fear anywhere; let no hesitation or doubt now hold you back. Therefore devote your minds and bodies to the faith of the Lord’s cross, and take up arms against this heap of straw—against such tiny, almost nonexistent men.” [Col. 0724D]

The battle lines were then arranged in order. On the left wing were the magnanimous Bohemund, the count of the Normans, the fierce soldier Tancred, and Richard, who is called “of the First City.” On the opposite side, the bishop of Le Puy advanced through the mountains, encircling the Turkish army. Count Raymond also rode alongside that left-hand division. On the right were Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, Hugh the Great, and the remaining mighty host of those who were to fight for Christ.

O good God, knower of hidden things, what tears were poured out to you amid such preparation? What pious contrition and confession arose from everyone’s heart in that array? [Col. 0725A] And who, as is fitting, could weigh with worthy consideration how tenderly the hearts of all depended upon hope in you alone? With what griefs did the justice or sins of each person cry out to you, Christ? They had wept and were still moving Christ, most compassionate, with pious sighs, when suddenly, with the seal of the cross leading every brow—not, I say, with the courage of lions, but, more appropriately, with that of martyrs—the densely massed standards were carried against the enemy.

> Soon the Arabs, Persians, and fierce Turks withdrew;  
> before the faithful peoples the savage turned his back.  
> Flight began; the wretched army scattered and stretched away;  
> the Arabs fled in every direction like hares.  
>   
> What a fleeing army! Their slaughter became lavish;  
> our swords could scarcely keep up with the deaths.  
> Every sword was blunted by the damage it inflicted on limbs.  
> Like crops with a sickle, so they cut down men.  
>   
> One cuts off a head, another noses, another throats,  
> another ears; one tears open a belly,  
> and every man who meets him departs—or dies [alternative reading: *obit*, “dies”].  
> Hands were stunned; arms stiffened with slaughter.  
> No one repelled them, and each one carried death.  
>   
> For dullness had taken possession of those profane minds;  
> their blinded breasts received the approaching evil.

### [X.] The Franks Win the Victory

The number of the defeated enemy is reported to have been four hundred and sixty thousand, apart from the Arabs. Their multitude was so enormous that its very size overwhelmed our men. At first, having loudly proclaimed the loss of hope for their safety, they hurried in alarm toward their own tents as quickly as possible. There they seized whatever lay to hand and fled. Our men pursued them relentlessly for an entire day. [Col. 0725C]

As the enemy withdrew, our men were filled with the spoils they had seized. After innumerable outpourings of blood, they enjoyed the consolation of abundant money, precious clothing, many animals, and whatever else the fugitives had carried away. From the third hour until the ninth hour the fire of this battle—or rather, of the Arab slaughter—burned fiercely.

Two nobles of revered name among our men fell there: one Josfred, surnamed of Mount Scabious, and William, whom we mentioned above, Tancred’s brother, together with very many others whose names have been entrusted to the knowledge of God alone. [Col. 0725D]

Here, plainly, here we experience the marks of Christian valor. While we marvel at the unequal battle of a few against countless multitudes, we are compelled to attribute the whole matter necessarily to the aid of Christ alone. For if it is said in the ancient Scripture of those Jews who had not yet turned away from God, “One pursued a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 30), then I think the same must be understood of this victory, where human ingenuity and human expectation failed entirely to discover by what art countless enemies could be overcome by so few men.

Perhaps someone might object: “It was a rustic force, the refuse of common soldiers, gathered from every direction.” [Col. 0726A] Certainly the Franks themselves, who exposed themselves to such danger, openly confess that nowhere could a race of men comparable to those Turks be found—so clever in mind and so vigorous in arms. Indeed, when they first began to engage them in battle, they nearly despaired because of the novelty of their weapons.

Our men had no experience of such agility in horsemanship, or of such astonishing speed in avoiding their attacks and blows, especially since the Turks customarily discharged their arrows only while fighting in flight. They are of the opinion that the Turks are related to the Franks, and that, above all other peoples, military distinction belongs especially to Turks and Franks.

## CHAPTER VI

### [XI.]

After the Turks had been repulsed in this way and were fleeing day and night from the face of the Franks, it happened that the duke who had ruled Nicaea, after the end of the siege had passed, encountered ten thousand Arabs in a state of extreme and foolish fear. They said to him: [Col. 0726B]

> “Why in the world are you fleeing so miserably terrified?”

He replied:

> “I had thought that I had utterly scattered and destroyed the Franks, and I believed that their entire host had already been given over to everlasting captivity. While I expected to subdue them gradually as they approached in companies and squadrons, and to lead them away bound into foreign lands, suddenly such a numerous army appeared that, with the fields and mountains filled by the enormity of their numbers, nowhere did their multitudes seem to leave any land free in our regions.” [Col. 0726C]

The captivity he claimed to have produced must be understood as referring to Peter the Hermit’s army; the multitude that followed must refer to those who had recently subdued the city of Nicaea.

> “When we saw,” he continued, “such swarms of peoples and such battalions multiplying like crops, we did not presume to defend ourselves with arms; nor did we consider it safe to escape the death that stood before us, or even think ourselves able to do so by the aid of our feet. Therefore, I confess, although we are far away, we are shaken by the dreadful memory of those whom we saw, and we still fear the ferocity of those whom we experienced, even if only for a moment.  
>   
> “If you would trust my experience, you should withdraw from this place as quickly as possible. For if you fall into their hands, you will undoubtedly have to pay manifold penalties for your imprudence.” [Col. 0726D]

Hearing this, and judging that those who had experience should be believed, they quickly turned everything backward and spread themselves throughout Romania.

### [XII.] The Turks Pretend to Have Defeated the Franks, Enter the Cities, and Plunder the Churches

Meanwhile our men took care to follow the fleeing Turks closely. The Turks went ahead of them, and as they passed through cities and camps they loudly boasted everywhere that they had defeated the Franks. Thus they deceived the inhabitants of the lands through which they traveled with lying words:

> “We have repulsed the Christian armies and have taken away from them all further courage to engage us. Admit us, therefore, into your cities, and gladly welcome those who defend you so effectively.”

When they entered the cities, they plundered the ornaments of the churches, stripped the public buildings of their wealth, and sought to seize gold and silver, animals of every kind, and whatever useful things were available. [Col. 0727A] They also carried away the children of Christians as slaves, consuming by fire whatever other goods were less open to plunder, and always fearing the arrival of our men, who were advancing ahead of them.

Our men searched for these profane people along the trackless ways of the wilderness and entered a deserted, roadless, waterless land (Psalm 62:3), from which they themselves scarcely emerged, pitiable. On one side hunger and on the other thirst drove them with want. Nothing suitable for food could be found, except that at times their cruel starvation seemed to be moderated by rubbing grain from ears of corn.

Many men of equestrian rank are known to have died there, as the harshness of the wilderness took life from their horses and the difficulty of the roads killed those accustomed to luxury. Hence great scarcity compelled them at that time to make pack animals out of oxen, goats, rams, and—more astonishing still—dogs; they used all these, according to their capacity, to carry whatever bundles they had. [Col. 0727B]

### The Franks Enter Iconium after Expelling the Turks

After this they happened to enter a wealthy province, rich in things useful for living, and reached the city of Iconium, famous for the endurance and writings of the apostle Paul. The provincials warned our men in advance to carry water with them in skins, because throughout a day’s journey no water at all could be found.

They did so, until they reached the bank of a certain river. There they took lodging for two days. Those who served as scouts went ahead and reached Erachia, where a very large phalanx of Turks had gathered, waiting only for an opportunity to disturb the army of Christ. Our men found them and, fearless in their customary courage, broke through them. The enemy quickly escaped in flight: [Col. 0727C]

> No differently from an arrow released  
> by the cast of a Balearic sling.

### When the Turks Flee, the Citizens of Tarsus Voluntarily Surrender to Tancred; Likewise Athena and Mamistra

With the way into the city now open, our men entered and remained there for four days. Tancred, Bohemund’s nephew, and Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, had left the company of the army—not from reluctance toward military service, but because of the sharpness of their spirit—and entered a certain valley called Botentroh in that language.

Tancred, being impatient of a partner, separated even from the aforementioned brother of the duke and attacked Tarsus with his men, a city distinguished by the revered birth of our particular apostle. [Col. 0727D] The Turks came out of the city to meet the approaching men and rushed into battle; but when the clash drew near, they fled back to the fortifications of the city from which they had emerged.

Tancred, having driven his horse after the enemy, blocked the city gate by placing his camp there. Soon Baldwin arrived and likewise settled on the opposite side to besiege the city. He asked Tancred to allow him a share in capturing the city, which he would seize with the assistance of his own army. Tancred rejected this with great indignation, desiring to claim for himself both control of the city and the marks of victory. [Col. 0728A]

Night then came, and the Turkish populace, unable to endure the siege and unaware of the obstinacy and courage of its besieger, fled away altogether. After they had been driven out, those who remained in the city—the native inhabitants of that land, namely Christians—came out to our men by night and cried:

> “Franks, hurry to enter the city, for the foreigners are fleeing. They have conceived such fear of your courage!”

When daylight appeared, the leading men of the place voluntarily surrendered the city. To those whom they had discovered quarreling over its lordship they said:

> “We choose to have that man rule over us whom we saw dealing so fiercely with the Turks yesterday.” [Col. 0728B]

Baldwin, however, continued to press Tancred to enter the city with him and to apply himself, according to each man’s ability, to plundering its spoils. Tancred replied, not without reason:

> “My purpose is to attack the Turks, not to plunder Christians, especially when they have chosen freely and wish no one other than myself.”

Although he said this, he nevertheless saw that Baldwin was superior through the strength of his larger army. Whether he wished it or not, he yielded to that man for the time being. As Tancred then departed, two excellent cities surrendered themselves to him: Athena and Mamistra, together with very many fortresses.

### Baldwin’s Deeds Briefly Recounted

Since perhaps no further opportunity will later arise to speak of Baldwin himself, I wish briefly to indicate how fortunate his career was.

At Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia, as we have learned from those who lived there, a certain man held the dignity of duke. He had protected the Christian province he governed not so much by arms against the incursions of the gentiles as by payments of money. As old age increasingly weighed upon him and made him feeble, and since he had a childless wife, herself now an old woman, when he learned that the Franks were near the borders of Mesopotamia he repeatedly desired with great longing to have one of the Frankish nobles adopted as his son, so that what he himself defended with money, that man might defend with arms and strength. [Col. 0728C]

Meanwhile it happened that a certain soldier who was familiar with him and knew of this desire held a conversation with this Baldwin. When the soldier gave Baldwin hope of obtaining the duchy if he allowed the old man to adopt him, the count believed him and went with the soldier to Edessa. [Col. 0728D]

The old man received him with extraordinary affection, beyond what had been expected, and both husband and wife adopted him as their son. The manner of the adoption is said to have been as follows, according to the custom of the people. Having made Baldwin enter naked inside the linen garment which we call a shirt, the old man embraced him; he confirmed the whole act with a kiss, and the woman afterward did the same.

When these matters had been completed and the citizens saw that the old man had been cast down from the height of his former rank and was now a private citizen, they secretly formed a conspiracy and suddenly besieged the court in which he was staying with Baldwin. [Col. 0729A] They remembered certain evils that he had inflicted upon them.

When the old man had been besieged, his new adopted son prepared to resist with Frankish courage. But the old man restrained him with remarkable loyalty, saying that he knew for certain that he could not in any way be rescued from their hands, whereas Baldwin could easily place himself in danger while defending him.

He therefore extracted from Baldwin, by endless prayers, a promise that he would cease resisting. When Baldwin, weeping bitterly, said that he preferred to die with him, the old man sent him away and negotiated with the people besieging him, asking them to spare the new prince but to kill himself as they wished. This was done.

Having killed him, Baldwin vigorously held the duchy that had come to him through the adoption, and, mindful of the treachery he had recently experienced, he employed Frankish horsemen and servants to guard him. Not long afterward, however, when Christmas Day arrived, they resolved, in a renewed conspiracy, to kill the new duke on the very solemn feast day. Their plot did not escape the duke’s notice. He therefore himself suggested to the Franks who were in his following that, clad in cuirasses and helmets for the Church’s festivals—or rather as though prepared for battle—the horsemen should stand by him, while the foot soldiers armed themselves with spears, swords, and battle-axes, and that they should proceed everywhere in this fashion.

When this had been done, [Col. 0730A] the townsmen realized that the duke had forestalled them; for he proceeded to the church with a large throng of armed men and attended the sacred office. On that very day, however, he kept silent. The next day he summoned the Edessans and brought charges concerning the treachery. When he compelled them by legal means to confess, they were not at all permitted to deny what they had proposed. Thus, once all the leading men of the city had been convicted, some had their feet cut off, others their hands, others their ears together with their noses, and some their tongues together with their lips; the organs of generation were removed from all. Nevertheless, all were dispersed far and wide into various exiles. Finally, when no one remained who could again stir up a crowd against him, only then did he safely experience what the fruit and happiness of so great a duchy might be.

He therefore lived with abundant wealth and prosperity [Col. 0730B], ruling many cities, among which the ancient and renowned Seleucia stood out, until, after his brother Godfrey, who had reigned at Jerusalem, he passed from the duchy to the kingdom; but from that point onward he received no increase of earthly happiness, rather the exercise of blessed labor on behalf of God, since continual battle with the gentiles is his lot.

# THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0729]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0729C]

### [I.] The author answers the objection that he did not himself hear what he narrates

No one, as I judge, can justly mock me for undertaking this work. For although I have neither gone to Jerusalem nor, until now, happened to know most of the persons or even the places themselves, I do not think this harms the general usefulness in any way, since it is established that what I have written, or shall write, I heard from men endowed with the testimony of truth. If it is plainly objected to me that I did not see these things, it cannot be objected that I did not hear them, since I have certainly believed that hearing is in some way equal to sight. Although indeed

> Things poured in through the ear stir the mind  
> less readily  
> than those placed before faithful eyes,

[Col. 0729D] nevertheless, who would doubt that historians, and those who have published the Lives of the saints, wrote not only what they had seen with their own eyes, but also what they had learned from the reports of others? For if, as one reads, a certain truthful man “testifies to what he has seen and heard” (John 3:32), then, unquestionably, an authoritative account by truthful speakers is accepted as genuine where seeing is not available. If, then, there is someone who criticizes or despises what has been begun, he certainly has the free choice, if he wishes, to correct it; and those to whom our work is displeasing may write their own.

### Raymond, Bohemond, and Godfrey enter Armenia; then Caesarea of Cappadocia

Accordingly, the Christian army, with its leaders Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, Bohemond, and Godfrey, together with many others, entered Armenia and rejoiced in the prospect of Turkish incursions, should any occur. As they proceeded, they came upon a castle whose access was so difficult that any attempt to assault it there seemed futile. There was there a certain Simeon, distinguished by the Christian name, a native of that same province, who had sought from our nobles dominion over this region so that he might protect it from Turkish attacks. They did not delay in granting him the office he had requested; and he settled there, intending to provide the land with a defense.

At length our men advanced and reached Caesarea of Cappadocia. After leaving the Caesarean province, they came to a city of great beauty and exceptionally fertile situation. A Turkish army had besieged it for three weeks before the arrival of our expedition reached them, but the siege had produced no result for the Turks. When our men arrived, the city was received through the voluntary surrender of its citizens. A certain knight called Peter of the Alps requested it from the princes as a benefice, so that, in accordance with the faith pledged to the Greek emperor and to our nobles, he might defend the region. Since the petitioner’s earnestness deserved such a grant, it was conceded to him.

Night had already fallen on that day when Bohemond heard that the enemy who had earlier besieged that city, following behind in frequent but not large detachments, had moved ahead of our men. Content with the contingent of soldiers belonging to him alone, he went forward, but did not find those whom he was seeking. They also reached the city called Coxon by its inhabitants, [Col. 0731A] where they found an abundance of every kind of useful possession. The natives of that place, therefore, gladly admitting our men within the city gates, strengthened them with a sufficiently ample supply of provisions for three days.

### [II.]

The count of Saint-Gilles further heard that the Turks who had customarily provided the garrison of the city of Antioch had withdrawn from its defense. He therefore sent ahead part of his army to seize it and preserve it under his authority. Selecting four men from the leaders of his own soldiery—three of them bearing the same name, namely Peter, while the fourth was called William of Monte Pislerii, who among us was considered more renowned for arms—he dispatched them there with five hundred horsemen.

Not far from the city mentioned above, they entered a valley, and in the valley itself found a castle. There they learned that Turks were stationed in defense of the city of Antioch with a considerable force. They also discovered that the Turks were equipping themselves with the greatest array of weapons and men against the Franks, should the latter ever attack them.

Peter, therefore, one of those whom we stated above were called Peter, who also bore a surname from the place called Roasa, separated himself from the company of his comrades and entered the valley of a certain city called Rugia. When he found Turks and Saracens, he engaged them, killed very many of them, and pursued the others. The Armenians, observing this and rejoicing in the man’s courage because of his extraordinary boldness against the Turks, placed themselves under his dominion. Without delay, by the surrender of its inhabitants, he was placed in charge of a city called Rusa; and he was likewise received in many castles.

The rest of the army, departing from Coxon, the city mentioned above, proceeded along a narrow and extraordinarily rugged path through certain mountains. They were so steep that no one could pass the man who went ahead in any way; rather, it was necessary for them to proceed one after another, singly and little by little. Beneath the narrow and excessively rocky path there was a tremendous precipice [al.: “of the greatest magnitude”]; if one horse happened to strike against another, it would immediately perish in an irretrievable plunge.

You might have seen the military column—men who, through the hardships of travel and hunger, had recently been changed from cavalrymen into foot soldiers—afflicted with savage sorrow: beating their fists, tearing their hair, and, having wished death upon themselves, selling cuirasses and helmets and every sort of weapon, without regard for their value, for three, four, or five denarii. When no buyer was available, they threw shields and other excellent possessions into the depths, provided only that they might extricate bodies scarcely capable of sustaining themselves from so great a danger.

At last, after emerging from these crags and cliffs through intolerable exertions, they entered a city called Marasim. Its citizens came out joyfully to meet them and brought abundant goods for sale to the armies. The exceedingly fertile land revived the exhausted men until the presence of their lord Bohemond, who was following behind and whom they were awaiting there, should restore them.

## CHAPTER TWO

### [III.] At last the Franks reach Antioch, which they also storm

At length they reached those plains where Antioch, the most renowned metropolis of Syria, is known to be situated. Besides the privileges by which it flourished in this age, its special distinction is that the glories of the Christian name sprang from it. The river of that city is called the Pharphar.

When our men reached the places adjoining its bridge, some of those whose duty it had been to go ahead of the army encountered a large force of Turks, who, laden with numerous supplies, were hastening to bring assistance to the besieged. When our men saw them, they rushed upon them with Frankish ferocity and, subduing them almost without any interval of time, scattered them in every direction.

They tore the wretches apart like rams, and threw down the weapons that shortly before might have inspired terror. The common crowd fled through the ranks; they wounded and overwhelmed them, while the allied troops hurried about in confusion. The formerly proud fury now experienced humiliation, and those who had expected to rejoice in the slaughter of our men were glad if they could rescue even their bodies, and that with shame.

Those who had come to offer aid in storming the city immediately became a foul heap of corpses, and the supplies they had brought for the besieged the Almighty destined, by a more merciful design, to be furnished to the besiegers. Thus, when they had been crushed like crops by hail, much booty remained for our men; countless stores of grain and wine were left behind, and horses, camels, and asses became a resource for the foot soldiers. Our men therefore established their camp along the bank of the river mentioned above.

[Col. 0732C] Bohemond, however, taking with him four thousand of the finest soldiers, positioned himself opposite one of the city gates. To prevent anyone from leaving it or entering it, he maintained watches there throughout that night. The next day, on reaching Antioch itself—twelve days before the Kalends of November, on a Wednesday, when half the day had already passed—the army halted. With the besiegers’ diligent efforts, the entrances of three city gates were obstructed; the fourth remained unoccupied, because no place suitable for besieging it could be open to them, the great height and narrowness of the adjoining mountains standing in the way.

Such fear of our men was instilled not only in the citizens but also in the Turks who held authority there that no one among them came out against us, and no one attempted any hostile action against them, as though they had come to conduct a market rather than to wage war. This superficial appearance of a disguised peace continued for nearly fifteen days, as though the city had already been declared dead.

Around the city itself, however, the opening days of the siege were exceedingly fertile. Abundance of every kind of thing suitable for use was boiling over, since the season of fresh produce had recently taken place there. They found vineyards filled with hanging grapes—though I marvel at the season—and grain stored everywhere not in granaries but sunk into pits and tunnels. Nor were the trees lacking fruit, and every convenience of life flowed together, supplied by the exceedingly fertile soil.

The Armenians and Syrians, of whom the entire city consisted, apart from, so to speak, its Turkish occupants, lived within the city and boasted of their Christian status. They frequently visited our men, learned the strength of all of them, and reported to their own people what they had discovered among us.

For while they enticed the Franks with the glue of constant conversation, and while they had murmured into our ears, with much flattering charm, that they were fleeing from the face of the Turks, they nevertheless did not allow their own wives to leave the city at all. After departing from the Franks, they returned to those wives and conveyed to the Turks whatever they could infer from what was happening there, especially the weaker points of the Christian side.

Once their purpose had been discovered, and the matter had been learned by the Syrian interpreters [f.: “known”], the Turks began repeatedly to sally from the city, to steal something from our men while they were wandering about in search of provisions, to block the familiar paths, to burst unexpectedly upon those making for the mountains and the sea, and to leave no opportunity free from ambushes and attacks.

Not far from there stood a castle called Areg. The Turks of exceptional ferocity whom they had stationed there for the defense of the garrison repeatedly inflicted the turmoil of frequent incursions upon the Franks when the latter were less cautious.

The princes, unable to tolerate such injuries, gathered a considerable force of horsemen and foot soldiers and sent them to discover where those who inflicted so many evils upon their people habitually concealed themselves. When their hiding place had been found, they first presented themselves openly to them; afterward, however, by cleverly pretending flight, they allowed themselves to be led by their pursuers to the place where they knew without doubt that Bohemond lay hidden in ambush.

There, while the Turks were pursuing them, two of our men fell. But Bohemond, bursting from his hiding place, met the enemy with due severity. He brought back those who had appeared to turn their backs and engaged them in a most closely joined clash of arms. He killed very many of them and led others away as captives. He dragged those whom he had captured to the city gate and there ordered their heads to be cut off, to terrify the watching citizens.

Some of the townsmen, however, climbing to the top of one of the gates, harassed our men in every direction by showers of their arrows, so much so that a cloud of missiles poured within the enclosure of Bohemond’s camp, and a woman there fell beneath an arrow strike.

At length the princes shared counsel and decided and arranged that a castle should be built on the summit of a certain mountain, which they called Malreguard, [Col. 0733D] whose garrison might enable them to remove the fear of the Turks. The stronghold was therefore being constructed; but there, above all, one could see the hands of the leading princes laboring to carry stones.

No needy laborer could complain there that he was being forced by the power of his superiors to endure some compulsory service, when he observed those who ruled him refusing themselves leisure in any way, even in the completion of the most arduous work. For, prompted by an instinct of their pious nature, they knew—although they had not read it—that Marius, according to Sallust, said:

> “If you conduct yourself gently, while compelling the army by command, this means being a master, not a commander.”

When the castle had been completed, the princes took turns guarding it.

[Col. 0734A] Christmas was approaching, and grain and the other foods for the body had begun to diminish severely. Meat had become so expensive that everything in the entire army was being sold. There was no opportunity to wander even a little farther in search of provisions; within the boundaries of Christendom itself scarcely anything relevant to use [al.: “eating”] could now be found. Moreover, no one could advance into the Saracen territory except with a very large expedition.

Thus, as hunger pressed upon them, the nobles called a council and debated how such a great multitude of people might be provided for, since, unless it were aided, it was about to undergo the danger of the most terrible famine. At length, after consultation on both sides, they found a solution: one part of the army should devote itself to procuring wages or supplies from wherever possible, while the other remained free for the siege already begun.

[Col. 0734B] At this Bohemond said:

> “If it seems safe to you, valiant soldiers, I shall, supported by the contingent of the count of Flanders, undertake the procurement of provisions.”

This was received by the younger men with as much rejoicing as they had previously been overwhelmed not only by dryness but by every kind of food shortage. Thus they celebrated Christmas with whatever devotion and eagerness they could muster. On the following day, a Monday, the two princes mentioned above, having gathered twenty thousand foot soldiers and horsemen, began to ravage the provinces of the Saracens.

## CHAPTER THREE

### [IV.]

Meanwhile, the Turks and Arabs, the Saracens, and other gentiles who had gathered from Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo, and other peoples, massed together with equal determination to bring aid to the same garrison, were hastening toward Antioch with an immense host.

They had already learned that the Christians would hurry into their territories to gather crops and other useful goods. While the twilight was still uncertain, they advanced against our men with their battle line prepared, at first eagerly, though their eagerness was soon to be changed into sorrow, toward the place where they had learned that our men would await them.

They divided themselves into two battle formations, sending one ahead of our front while the other, moving behind, attempted to surround their entire army. The count of Flanders, however, in no way distrusting divine power, fixed the sign of the cross upon his heart and body. Relying on the illustrious Count Bohemond, he met the enemy with the high courage befitting such men.

Battle was joined, but at the very first attempt of the encounter the fleeing enemy was turned back. Battles were transformed into trophies, and as the bodies of those turning their backs were struck down, the frequently scraped spear was shattered in many places. The enemy’s great shields repeatedly received long ash spears, and, struck with great force, they were splintered into little shafts by the multitude of blows.

A helmet covered with blades did not protect the back of the head from wounds; the coverings of cuirasses thought impenetrable exposed their thinness. The defenses of the body, whatever the Barbarians judged secure, proved inadequate; whatever the Franks touched was torn apart.

The surface of the plain was strewn with countless corpses, and the frequent heaps of the dead roughened the level of the formerly grassy field. The earth, everywhere stained with the hated blood of the gentiles, grew black.

Those who had survived the slaughter of our men purchased life for themselves by the swiftness of their feet, and rejoiced to be relieved of their own possessions—not out of kindness toward these men, but because of their own speed. Thus the condition of our men was transformed into another state: fear was roused into boldness, battle into victory, sorrow into joy, hunger into abundance. The naked man was enlarged by clothing, the barefoot by conveyances, the poor by money, the rescued by gifts, and the victor by celebrations.

### [V.]

Meanwhile, while these events were taking place, the Turks who held authority at Antioch learned that Bohemond and the count of Flanders were absent from the siege. Made much more secure by their absence, they went out more frequently and carefully challenged our men to battle, seeking to discover which part of the besiegers might be weaker.

At last, seeing a suitable day for testing their strength—it was a Tuesday—they suddenly attacked the less prepared and killed very many of the foot soldiers and horsemen while they were completely unafraid. The magnificent bishop of Puy also lost his major-domo, who was at the same time his standard-bearer, among those who were slain.

And if the riverbed, between them and the bank on which the camp had been established, had not stood in the way, the slaughter of our men would have been considerable and very widespread.

At this point the excellent Bohemond had returned after ravaging the Saracen provinces, and was revisiting the mountains where Tancred was staying, thinking that he might find there something useful to the besiegers of the city. For although each of our men had plundered whatever lay before his eyes, many nevertheless found nothing and returned empty-handed, particularly lacking the things necessary for food.

Bohemond, however, never lacking counsel, saw them wandering about foolishly and attacked them, saying:

> “If you are seeking the necessities of life, if you are properly providing for your bodies as hunger presses you, act in such a way that, while food is being sought, the life of those seeking food is in no way destroyed. Stop roaming through the trackless mountain regions, since you know that your enemies maintain hidden lairs in solitudes unknown to you.

> “Let the army advance together—for each becomes stronger through the other—so that, if force is brought to bear upon one part, it may be able to experience the support of the other. For just as a sheep, if it strays from the hand or presence of its shepherd, is recognized as exposed to the jaws of wolves, so a soldier, if he goes out alone from the company of his comrades, is unquestionably left as a plaything for any robbers.

> “It is therefore better for you to be fed among your own people and with your own people on scanty food than, condemned to inextricable captivity, to eat richer fare. Thus to go together and return together, to delight in assemblies, and to do nothing presumptuously are the judgments of the good; freely to wander about belongs to those who wish to perish.”

He spoke and returned to his companions, but by his return did not make the besiegers in any way wealthier.

The cunning of the Armenians and Syrians, however, seeing that food was being depleted in the army and that the goods for sale were being exhausted, went about through every place known to them and brought to the army, which was suffering from want, the grain they had purchased all around the region. They sold it with such exorbitant greed that a single ass-load of grain was sold for eight of their bezants, which they call “purple” coins there and valued at one hundred and twenty solidi of money.

Here one may estimate how terribly those men had succumbed to the danger of hunger when no means of paying were available to them. And when lack of money had already begun to constrict the princes, what was the man to do whom, although previously surrounded by every kind of wealth, extreme poverty now pressed?

### [VI.]

> Great torment had plainly racked them,  
> scanty food confined the exhausted,  
> their strength poured out, the frenzy of hunger  
> reduced them to the lowest state.
>
> The stores of bread had been removed;  
> there was no ox meat, nor was there pork.  
> Everywhere the hands of the needy had plucked  
> every kind of grass.
>
> Whatever food might have existed,  
> no one could finally find available.  
> Their limbs had relaxed, and slackness had taken away  
> the boldness of their breasts.
>
> The dreadful skin is stretched into swelling;  
> it has retained no proper use of food.  
> Food has failed, the means of living have perished:  
> these things bring death.
>
> A brief anguish releases all those who are killed,  
> but pains torment those touched by hunger.  
> Hence deaths prolonged in this way bear  
> better rewards.
>
> The food of angels plainly nourishes these men;  
> they rejoice in the excellent reward of their labors,  
> by which it is evident that they have endured  
> the weight of their sufferings.
>
> The others fight and strive to endure  
> various misfortunes. They scarcely offer  
> any favorable outcome to the grievous;  
> they judge sad things better than joys.
>
> Now they seek to follow Christ  
> by bearing double crosses;  
> they gladly undertake what is preferable to commands,  
> when the one who ordered them has ordered the same person to bear one.
>
> For this man dreadful hunger gnaws at an empty heart;  
> his dry stomach, long since, grows weak.  
> The passion has made a slaughter of the entrails  
> and ruins of the brain.
>
> Within, this corruption exhausts the spirit;  
> from outside, the savagery of wars afflicts it.  
> Day and night, full of cares,  
> presses upon it with slaughter.
>
> The mind remains sharp, and the strength is slight;  
> yet the sick mind’s vigor is restored,  
> and they have the least fear of proceeding  
> to shed blood.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### [VII.] William, who had vaunted himself without reason, secretly fled

Meanwhile there was a certain William who was called Carpentarius—not because he was a carpenter, but because in battles he persisted in cutting down men in the manner of a carpenter. He was a man from beyond the Seine, powerful in words but sparing in deeds, the shadow of a great name, a man undertaking things greater than himself and leaving nothing completed.

When he too was about to undertake the journey to Jerusalem, he had prepared an impious travel fund by plundering the small possessions of the poor who lived near him. This man, then, unable to endure the hunger that he saw men far more needy than himself bearing with the utmost faith, silently fled.

His glory in arms existed only in the boastfulness of his words, never in an accomplished deed. When the Frankish expedition was staying in Spain to turn back the pagans who had gathered there from Africa, this man, whose entire courage consisted in words, shamefully withdrew and deceived countless people by his retreat.

[Col. 0737B] It is believed that this did not happen without an evident judgment of God: divine judgment exposed as the worst of all and the least able to endure labor those whom popular fame had made most renowned. Nor did this portent become clear only in his person. The same thing was evident in others, whose names I shall pass over, so that those whose ferocity in arms had here among us been extraordinarily terrifying and famous became in that Christian army a gentleness pitiably more peaceful even than hares.

The farther this was from what was right, the more contemptible it ought to have been considered. For if, while stationed here, they had been timid when they fought without right and when they wickedly made the poor their prey, they would plainly have been timid with good reason, in view of the damnation of their souls. But where there was complete security of eternal salvation [al.: “inward security”], there indeed was criminal timidity.

### [VIII.] Peter the Hermit, turned to folly, departed

To this was added the appearance that even the stars, according to the Apocalypse, were falling from heaven: that famous Peter the Hermit, of whom we spoke above, himself also turned to folly and departed:

> What are you doing, Peter, by this counsel? Why do you stand forgetful of your name?  
> If a rock is established as Peter’s origin, what, then, does “solid” signify?  
> Why do you wish to remember flight? A rock does not know easy movement.  
> Halt your step; recall the old desert, the ancient fasts.
>
> Until now you have joined bone to skin; you ought to have sustained  
> your collapsing stomach on a slender root and eaten the grass of cattle.  
> Why do you remember excessive feasting? The monastic order knows nothing of such a thing;  
> neither does your birth teach you this, nor should your doctrines urge you on.
>
> As though you were driving peoples toward that journey, you even compel them to become needy.  
> Thus, proceeding now, you bear the laws that you once imposed by teaching each person.
>
> Once a fugitive from Ceres, he used to consume fish and wines.  
> For a monk, more holy food would be leeks, cresses, turnips,  
> cardoons, nuts, hazelnuts, the fruit of gruel, lentils, and herbs,  
> with fish and pure wine set aside, though a piece of bread might still be added.

### [IX.] Tancred forces William and Peter to return

Tancred, a man of unyielding steadfastness in this undertaking of Christ, pursued these fugitives from the pious siege—or rather from the holy suffering—captured them, and, as was proper, brought them back, not without inflicting many insults upon them.

Although they promised in words that they would return, he postponed believing them until each had confirmed by an oath, with faith pledged between them, that they would return to the fellowship of the army and submit to the judgment of the princes concerning their desertion of military service.

William, therefore, whether he wished it or not, was compelled to return and was handed over to keep watch there throughout the night before the court of the magnificent Bohemond. On the following day, when the edge of dawn had grown bright again, he was brought before that illustrious man.

With the shame he deserved suffusing him, the elder spoke as follows:

> “When the name of France, royal among all peoples, stands out in majesty among all kingdoms; when, after God, the Mother of God sends here men of the utmost integrity in courage and steadfastness; you, babbling scoundrel and most impure of all, you had she brought forth for her disgrace and infamy, and henceforth she should regard you as a portent.
>
> “O good Father of all things, what sort of Carpentarius did we have—the man who, as an architect with a chisel wears down wood, would wear down the backs of gentiles with spears and swords? Behold: by the constant repetition of his blows, this same craftsman had blunted a thousand swords in a day, and alone had cut down crowds of pagans while we rested.
>
> “Where is that arrogant sternness, and that loquacity nurtured beside the Loire and the Seine? Where is the frugality of action known to reside, and the uninterrupted thunder of your chatter that crackles on? Alone this man could have come to the aid of the suffering moon (Juvenal, Satire 6), yet, shamefully sluggish in action, he displays nothing effective.
>
> “And certainly it was fitting for such great strength of yours that you, who had proved a traitor to the Lord’s people in Spain, should here in Syria have sought the culmination of the honor you had begun to acquire. So be it. It plainly suited you to do nothing else, and therefore, despite so shameful a crime, you shall be granted the most generous pardon.”

[Col. 0738D] The Franks standing around him had now begun to feel embarrassed by this exceedingly mocking speech, and they scarcely obtained from the indignant man that he should be silent. The illustrious man’s severity spared the wicked one, not unaware of propriety, and was content with this condition: after making him swear an oath, William promised never to withdraw from the journey to Jerusalem, whether prosperity should meet him or a time of want confront him.

Tancred himself, who had restrained him from evasion, also promised that he would thereafter be his friend, provided that William steadfastly remained manly. Both sides agreed to these terms.

Not long afterward, however, that remarkable Carpentarius, who once, when placed in safety, had threatened to act as a butcher against the Turks, incontinent in his oath and prodigal of faith, did not delay to repeat his secret flight.

[Col. 0739A] No one should find it surprising that such hardships befell the army itself, although it was pious, since it can unquestionably be believed that the great crimes of those men opposed the prosperity that divine providence would not have withheld from them had they acted well.

For when such extreme poverty pressed upon them, and each man was savagely beaten down by the denial of food, if anyone happened to go farther away from the army, some person—though no one other than one of our own men—would kill him if he found him alone, for the sake of a small price.

Thus misfortune raged everywhere through them, so that scarcely a thousand horses could be found in so great a host. Hence a terrible scarcity of bread tormented everyone; yet this did not restrain some men, but drove them more fiercely toward crimes.

Since these divinely inflicted scourges were being added to their sufferings, there is no doubt that many of them were brought back through repentance to remembrance of themselves, and, despairing of their own strength, were moved by a better hope to await solely God’s aid amid such misery.

The events plainly made them wiser, so that the more they saw either their forces diminished or their courage weakened, the more they were taught to submit with due humility to God, whom they believed capable of everything.

### [X.]

Moreover, there was also a certain man, unless I am mistaken, among the envoys of the tyrannical emperor called Tetigus, who was taking part in that siege. He was a man advanced in years, but his nose had been cut off on some occasion unknown to me, and for that reason he used a golden one.

Compelled on one side by fear of the Turks and constrained on the other by the danger of hunger, adorned with a great deal of polished deceit, he approached the elders:

> “Necessity, great and pressing, compels you, excellent leaders, to learn how we are weighed down by what anxieties within us and by what terrors outside us. When battles are taking place outside and the pains of hunger do not cease tormenting us within, no means of escape seems open anywhere, and no relief lies near that might allow us to breathe.
>
> “But if you judge it suitable to your wisdom, let me have permission to go into the regions of Romania. I shall arrange for grain, wine, barley, meat, flour, cheese, and other things useful for various purposes to be brought from there in a very large and frequent fleet. I shall also arrange for a continuous supply of all kinds of merchandise to travel across the seas, with the emperor’s edict everywhere preceding it.
>
> “All the advantages of horses, and of whatever other animals and means of transport there may be, the whole province of the Greeks will convey to you by land. The emperor himself, who has hitherto been unaware of your want, will hasten with the utmost speed to bring assistance for so great a need as soon as he learns of it.
>
> “And I shall affirm to you by oath that I shall faithfully fulfill all these things as I have said. Once I have accomplished them, I shall in no way fear presenting myself again for the labors of this siege already begun.
>
> “But if you fear that I might shrink from your fellowship and from sharing your hunger, behold my tents; behold, my household will remain with you. Even if I leave them for a time, I shall not be able to disregard them forever.”

He spoke and enticed the ears of the nobles with the charm of much elaborate circumlocution. The man therefore departed, utterly unafraid of the crime that overtook him when he shamefully perjured himself; and thereafter he never approached what he had promised, having lied about everything.

### [XI.] The besiegers of the city are tortured by enormous hunger

The pressure and force of the enemy had begun to constrain them so severely that no one among our men dared, for any business whatsoever, to leave his tents or the common camp. Besides this, a domestic pestilence, entirely pitiable and resembling madness—the pestilence of hunger—harassed them.

For if, as someone says, “Nothing is more troublesome than hunger that is forced upon an unwilling man,” what tortures do we think were suffered by those continually given over to torments, who, relieved by no hope, however slight or false, sat daily before those truly impregnable walls?

The common people, consumed by utter poverty, wandered through various provinces. Some had begun to go to Cyprus, others to Romania, and some to wander through the mountains, as insufficient food narrowed their circumstances. The sea route, moreover, had been everywhere closed by the frequent encounters with Turks. Finally, no exit lay open anywhere for our men.

### [XII.]

Meanwhile, Bohemond heard that countless Turkish forces were approaching the camps of our men. He approached the other princes and said:

> “Since our army is now so small that it already seems weak and insufficient for completing a single battle, much less for being divided in two to fight two engagements, we must reconsider this: if we go out with whatever army we have to meet the Turks who are advancing against us, who meanwhile is left to besiege this city whose siege we have begun, and who is left to defend our tents?
>
> “If, therefore, it seems right to your judgment, let us select the better part of the foot soldiers and send them to guard the city under siege; as for the horsemen, since they are stronger, we think they ought to be matched against the fury of the Turks.”

He had spoken, and none of the princes dissented from his counsel.

## CHAPTER FIVE
[XIII.] Bohemond attacks the Turks. He exhorts the soldiers.—

The enemy’s swarms had already pitched camp beside a fortress adjoining the city, called Areg, beyond the Pharphar. The day was declining toward evening, and Bohemond went out of the camp with his entire army, hastily summoned, and advanced to encamp between the river and the neighboring lake. When morning dawned, he sent scouts with all speed, ordering them to assess the number of the Turks and promptly report how they were disposed and where they were staying.

They had gone on for a short distance and had begun to search for the enemy, whose approach was loudly announced, when suddenly they saw their innumerable swarms emerging, divided into the legions of two battle lines; behind them, a vast multitude followed slowly. At this sight they returned as quickly as possible, saying: “The enemy is already upon us; see to it that they find you brave and prepared.”

Then Bohemond, rousing his brothers-in-Christ and fellow soldiers, spoke:

“Brave soldiers, the frequent outcome of your victories supplies you with no small opportunities for courage. Until now you have waged wars of faith against treachery, and amid every danger you have enjoyed fortunate outcomes. You ought surely already to have been delighted by the repeated, evident proof of Christ’s strength, especially since you know with absolute certainty that, in those battles which pressed hardest upon you, it was not you who fought, but Christ. How, then, can the madness of despair creep into your minds because of some assault, when no evils hitherto attempted against anyone have overcome you, with God raising you up, and when triumphs impossible for human beings have come to pass for you? I ask, therefore, that tested faith may now profit among you to such an extent that no human strength hereafter can resist you. Make your spirits more secure by this means; advance cautiously; and now take care to pursue and acclaim Christ with all the keenness of your minds, as he customarily bears your standards.”

They loudly declared that they would act faithfully, vigorously, and prudently. Trusting Bohemond, as one most experienced in war, to distribute their battle lines, he ordered each of the princes to gather his contingents around him and arrange his own line. Six battle lines were therefore deployed, as he had said, each formed into separate wedges for penetrating the enemy. Five advanced with the greatest caution. Bohemond followed behind with his own force, ready to provide support if necessity arose.

When our men had thus been divided and, packed closely together, marched toward battle with spirits aflame, each man, touching the side of the next, urged his companion on, so that no one, insofar as it depended on him, would allow the fighting to falter. But when the struggle began to be conducted hand to hand:

> Without delay the enemy approach, their spears bent low;  
> Their spirits burn, and they press their horses with the spurs;  
> On both sides the air is shaken by savage cries;  
> The lines collide, and the Turks hurl their javelins.  
>   
> The Franks, striking with their spears, pierce their breasts.  
> The sword’s blows had blunted the edge; the clashing steel  
> Made a din, while the iron forged wounds,  
> And the swift right hand thirsted for foul blood.  
>   
> As when you see swarms of crows in motion,  
> Or when a thrush advances in an immense flock,  
> So then the arrows covered the light of heaven,  
> Thickening the blind air with a hailstorm of missiles.  
>   
> Weapons ring, the charge carries off the horses, and the bronze resounds.  
> Those struck down suffer, the victorious rejoice; discordant voices rise.

But when the entire weight of the army that followed the foremost lines had poured into that most savage battle, the edge of our men’s strength began to be blunted by the enemy’s heavy assault, and, as the enemy’s numbers increased, our men began somewhat to bend from the valor they had undertaken to display. Observing this, Bohemond—who was watching the rear guards in order to bring assistance—growled in deep displeasure. He therefore summoned his own master of the stable, Robert, the son of Girard, and sent him forward, saying:

“Go now and employ the magnanimity that you ought to possess and that this great undertaking demands. Set before yourself the purpose of the labor you have assumed, knowing that the cause for us and for you is the aid of all Christendom: to redeem Jerusalem for God and free his Sepulchre. You know no less surely that this work is accomplished through divine assistance rather than human. Go, then, and now offer your courage to the suffering Christ. Let not this timely opportunity find you sluggish; perhaps God has prepared it for your honor.”

Roused by these words, and relying upon God with all his mind,

> He sprang forth and cleft the dense ranks with his sword;  
> He bore the commander’s standards, which the enemy feared,  
> So that, while they led the way, our side might be strengthened in vigor.  
>   
> He raged no differently than a lioness bereft  
> Of her cubs, accustomed to kill whatever is placed before her.  
> The sword opened paths and split the crowded host;  
> He crushed whatever confronted him and taught the following wedge to advance.

The Christians win the victory.—

At this point, when our men saw that Bohemond’s familiar standard was in no way wavering and that the aforesaid master of the stable was raging against the Turks with such ferocity, they recovered their courage together and drove the enemy back with such violence that the Turks were forced to place their hope only in flight. Our men pursued the fugitives and, as they hurried away in disorder, did not cease cutting down and dismembering them until they had driven them headlong to the narrow passages of the Pharpharean bridge.

After suffering this slaughter, the Turks entered the fortress I mentioned above, Areg; they stripped it of everything and set fire to the town attached to it. They then scattered, never to return there again.

The treacherous Armenians and Syrians, who stood between the two peoples and watched for the outcome of the battles so that they might attach themselves especially to whichever side won, observed that the Turks were defeated. They attacked as though to block the paths and kill the Turks passing by.

Thus, from the goods taken from the defeated enemy, our people’s cruel want was relieved: they were supplied with horses and provisions. Moreover, as the outcome of their victories increasingly favored them, they came to despise Turkish ferocity. Accordingly, after the victory, they cut off the heads of one hundred of those who had fallen in battle and hung them before the walls of Antioch, to terrify the Turks who were under siege. It is the custom of the gentiles to preserve and display the heads of the slain as a sign of victory.

The emperor promises to embrace the faith if what was taken from the Turks is restored to him.—

Meanwhile, while our men were carrying out these actions, the Babylonian emperor had sent an embassy to the princes of our army. Through the ambassadors he congratulated them on what they had accomplished against the Turks and likewise, though falsely, promised that he would become a Christian if our people took from the Turks what they had plundered from his empire and restored it to him.

We have already stated above that the Babylonian empire was far more powerful than the eastern kingdoms, but that the Turks, fiercer in arms and spirit, had usurped much of it. Those who had been left behind to besiege the city also fought fiercely with its inhabitants—not in one place only, but before almost all the gates of the city.

This triumphal day was the fifth day before the Ides of February, the day before the beginning of the fast. And not unjustly: on the day when Christians are owed a feast before the fast itself, they were to be filled above all with the slaughter of their wicked enemies.

The Franks therefore, exulting in the fervent rejoicing of so great a victory and thanking God, their helper, with many expressions of devotion, returned to the camp, not without a very substantial share of the spoils. The Turks, unable to bear being seen in their shame, would have crawled back to their homeland through tunnels and caves, if they had been able.

## CHAPTER VI

[XIV.] A fortress is established near the gate of the besieged city.—

Finally, the senior leaders of the army, repeatedly considering the many indignities of incursions they suffered from those inside the city, summoned a council and determined that, before their forces were diminished by any misfortune, they should establish a fortress at the city gate where the enemy’s shrine stood and where, it is agreed, there was also a bridge. From there they could restrain the enemy’s attempts to some extent.

All the younger leaders agreed with this decision. Then the count of Saint-Gilles spoke first:

“I will provide the pay,” he said, “and I will also guard the fortress. Only assist me in building it.”

Bohemond replied:

“If it pleases you, I promise that I will go with this count, who has offered himself first, to the port of Saint Simeon. There we will jointly protect those engaged in this work. Let the rest attend to the siege and prevent the city’s enemies from going out through its gates.”

The count and Bohemond therefore proceeded to the port of Saint Simeon, as they had proposed. Those who remained behind began to establish the fortress, but the Turks disrupted the beginnings of this construction with a most violent assault. Bursting upon our men in a sudden attack, they forced them to turn their backs, killed many of them, and brought a day of mourning upon the Franks.

The Turks make an incursion and kill some of the Christians.—

The next day the Turks learned that some of the leaders were absent from the siege and had gone to the port of Saint Simeon. They equipped themselves with a large force and suddenly confronted those returning from the port.

When they saw the count and Bohemond approaching with a considerable body of soldiers, they began to utter hideous shrieks and cries, surround our men from every side, hurl missiles and arrows, and savagely kill them even after inflicting wounds. Their assault was so fierce that our men barely escaped headlong through the neighboring mountains, wherever an exit was open.

Whoever could pass the others—so to speak, his horse flying with speed—escaped; if the gentile vigor of the enemy found anyone slower, he perished. In this great calamity, as it was thought, the number of our dead exceeded one thousand. Those among them who were found, in the testimony of faith, approved, according to the Apostle (2 Tim. 2:15), received after death the glorious rewards of their suffering. If they had needed to pay any penalties for sins, the shedding of blood alone had the greatest power to cleanse every offense.

Bohemond pursues them and puts very many to death.—

Bohemond, worn down by boundless anxiety over such a disaster, took a shorter route away from his companions and reached the siege with a few horsemen, whom he found gathered together there. Their spirits inflamed by rage over the destruction of their comrades, and Christ provoked by the bitterest sobs of the faithful, they reached the battlefield, united in their determination to attack those who had inflicted such calamities upon them.

The enemy cohorts stood confidently opposite them, emboldened by their recent victory and believing that they would accomplish against these men what they boasted of having accomplished against the count and Bohemond. But while the wicked were plotting their evil, the benevolent God mercifully arranged the remedies that the grieving required.

The distinguished men, driven by compassion for their murdered brothers, fixed the sign of the Lord’s cross upon their foreheads and in their hearts, and poured out all their strength against the enemy. The Turks, immediately perceiving their unanimity, gave way and hastened toward the Pharpharean bridge, intending to cross through its narrow passages.

The mass of those crossing was compressed as their flight hastened. Since the wedge of infantry and cavalry was crowded into too small a space, each man, attempting to overtake his companion, knocked him down. Nor did our men lack vigilance regarding this [alternative reading: “these men”], so that wherever the multitude of the fleeing crowd seemed to grow dense, the issue was decided not by wounds but by a fall.

If anyone, immersed in the waters, tried to emerge onto dry land by climbing along the bridge’s pillars or swimming with his hands, our men surrounding the riverbank immediately forced him, once overcome, to swallow the midstream waters.

So great, it is known, was the renewed slaughter that the water of the Pharpharis seemed to be blood rather than water. The defeated and the victors raised such shouts there, and such a terrible din arose from those perishing and those forcing others to perish, that one might believe the heights of heaven itself were being struck by the noise.

The air became clouded by the frequent throwing of spears and other missiles, and the sun’s bright sphere was covered by the dense flight of wandering arrows. The native women of the city, who were indeed Christians, fed their eyes on this spectacle around the defenses of the walls. As they watched the Turks being killed and subjected to so many misfortunes, they groaned outwardly; but with their faces turned away, they secretly applauded the Franks’ favorable fortunes.

The Armenians and Syrians, although they were Christians, were compelled to shoot arrows at our men; some of them did so willingly. Twelve of their leading men fell there. In a Chaldaean term they call them *satraps*, “admirable men” according to their barbarous usage [the Latin wording is uncertain]. Many others among their most powerful and capable men also perished, those upon whom the city’s entire defense rested. They were said to have numbered fifteen hundred.

Those who remained from this destruction ceased, as they had previously been accustomed to do, to insult our men. No more of their chatter or mockery appeared; this day changed their long-standing joy into grief.

> Then night came and parted the two crowds,  
> And their hands ceased, though their minds still brandished weapons.

This victory benefited our men so greatly that the enemy never again seemed to possess such strength and power, and their mocking voices fell silent. Moreover, God being favorable, the want that was pressing our people in many respects was abundantly relieved.

The next day, when daylight had come, some of the Turks came out of the city and gathered the bodies of their dead. They found some of them; others, carried away and lost within the riverbed, had disappeared. Those they were able to find they buried beside their shrine, which they call Mathomaria, beyond the Pharpharean bridge, at the gate of Antioch.

In their tombs they placed cloaks, gold *bezants*, arrows and bows, and many other implements, which we omit describing. When our men learned of these burials, they went to that mournful cemetery, relying on a large supply of arms, ordered the graves to be broken open and the bodies removed, and threw them in a heap into the bottom of a pit.

They nevertheless cut off their heads and had them carried to their own tents, so that an exact count could be made of those who had fallen, except for four horse-loads of heads which the envoys of the Babylonian emperor had carried away as testimonies of the victory achieved against the Turks.

When the Turks observed this, they took the exposure of the bodies much worse than they had taken their slaughter. They no longer restrained their grief with moderate tears; casting off shame, they proclaimed it with wailing.

Three days afterward they began to build the aforesaid fortress, using the stones they had taken after breaking apart the gentiles’ sarcophagi. When the fortress was completed, the besieged city began to be constricted, so that the pride it had formerly possessed now began entirely to deflate.

Our men, however, were given free opportunity to go wherever they wished, and the mountain paths—formerly difficult—now became convenient for seeking provisions. Thus, with all the roads in every direction closed to the advantage of the Turks, one section beside the river, where the fortress and a church stood next to it, still seemed to offer a possibility of exit or entry.

If that fortress, since it belonged to our side, had been fully fortified by our men, none of the enemy would now have dared to attempt going out freely. The nobles therefore summoned a council and reached this decision: they should choose one of their own number to be placed in charge of the fortress, fortify it diligently, and defend it faithfully, so that every excursion of the pagans wandering through the mountains and fields might be prevented in every way, and access to and exit from the city might likewise be cut off.

While a suitable person for so great an undertaking was being sought among the princes, Tancred—the man who, in the wars of the Lord, has until now deserved and continues to deserve the distinction of being the most perceptive of young men—could not contain his own energy. He immediately came forward, saying:

“If I knew what benefit would later come to me from undertaking such a great labor, I would, with appropriate care and supported by the company of my household, strive to strengthen this same fortress and, with God’s help, attempt to close the roads along which our enemies customarily have permission to travel.”

The princes, pleased by his willing proposal, immediately promised to provide him with four hundred silver marks. Tancred accepted the promise reluctantly, since it seemed small in proportion to his zeal. Nevertheless, lest he be accused of inactivity if he withdrew, he promptly and confidently took with him the knights and retainers who were closely attached to him, assumed control of the fortress, deprived the enemy of the ability to leave the city’s gates, and imposed the greatest scarcity upon everything connected with fodder for horses, as well as a very severe shortage of wood and other necessities.

The excellent man therefore chose to remain there steadfastly. By cutting off supplies, he began with every form of vigilance to surround—or rather, block—the city.

On the very day when he entered that fortress, a large company of Armenians and Syrians was coming through the mountains, bringing the besieged city supplies of various kinds of food. That excellent knight, so that the undertaking he had begun might have a successful outcome, met them—not so much by chance as through God’s prompting—and, after capturing them, plundered a great quantity of grain, wine, oil, and other necessities no less important.

The good man could not complain that, while engaged in so pious an undertaking, he had been divinely forgotten. Rather, at this first good fortune he learned that he would never be in excessive need of bodily necessities, and that afterward, once the supports of the flesh had been supplied, the fruits of eternity with God would not be lacking to him.

Thus the Turks’ power to go outside the walls or conduct operations was entirely cut off. They were compelled to be content with whatever could be found within the city’s walls, until Antioch was captured.

## CHAPTER VII

[XV.] Christian piety flourishes in the camp.—

During this same siege, the vigor of Christian law was great. If anyone was found to be convicted of any crimes, he was subjected to the severest sentence by the judicial judgment of the army’s princes.

In addition, offenses of bodily immodesty were specifically ordered to be punished; and rightly so. Those who were surrounded by terrible shortages, and who seemed each day to lie exposed to the enemy’s swords unless God protected them, certainly ought not reasonably to have entertained thoughts of wantonness. What access to pleasure could there be where the suspicion of death was unceasing?

Thus no mention of a prostitute, nor even the name of a brothel, was tolerated there, especially since they feared that for this very crime they might, with God judging among the gentiles, be consigned to the sword. If any woman was found to be pregnant who was known to have no husband, she was handed over, together with her pimp, to savage punishments.

Meanwhile, a certain monk from a monastery highly renowned above all others, who had fled beyond the enclosure of his monastery and undertaken the expedition to Jerusalem, provoked not by piety but by recklessness, happened to be discovered there with a woman. He was convicted, I believe, by the judgment of red-hot iron; finally, by order of the bishop of Le Puy and the others, that wretched woman and her lover were led naked through all the streets of the camp and brutally beaten with whips, as a terror to those watching.
