[XVI.] Moreover, so that they might become more patient under their shortages and more vigilant against vices, the aforementioned bishop of Le Puy devoted himself in many ways to exhortation. No Sunday or Christian festival passed without the authority of the divine words being preached throughout every corner of the camp. This duty was entrusted by the same bishop to bishops, abbots, or clerical persons who appeared more learned, whenever any such persons happened to be present.

[XVII.] The fraud of a certain abbot, which nevertheless greatly benefited the Christians. He becomes archbishop of Caesarea.—

Since the name of an abbot has entered into our work, I consider it worthy of report that there was an abbot there who, when the beginning of this journey was still being discussed among us and he discovered that he did not possess the means appropriate to so great an undertaking, carved the sign of the Cross—which was customarily attached to garments after being made from some material—into the middle of his forehead by I know not what artifice, so that it was not merely painted but inflicted with iron like a military brand.

Once this had been done, to secure his fraud with a lie, he proclaimed that an angel had impressed it upon him in a vision. Nor was this hope, whatever its worth, without its reward. For when the ignorant and novelty-loving crowd understood what he implied, many people followed him, within and beyond his own region, with numerous gifts.

Yet such a deception could not escape the careful scrutiny of observant people, since the line of the cross violently inscribed upon him seemed openly to drip with poison. Eventually, after he had set out and was present at the siege of Antioch, he revealed what he had falsely invented, although others had discovered it long before, and he did not conceal his intention of profit.

He conducted himself honorably there and benefited the Lord’s army greatly through many useful services. He had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10:2); yet he acted altogether in this way. He distinguished himself to such an extent that, after Jerusalem was captured, he was appointed abbot of the church of Blessed Mary, situated in the Valley of Jehoshaphat; later, he was made archbishop of Caesarea, the metropolis of Palestine.

Many attain the palm of martyrdom.—

It is certain beyond doubt that, unless the frequent consolations of the divine word had been supplied to them, their endurance would never have persisted amid such dangers of famine and war. Therefore we say that those among them who were upright in life and endowed with knowledge were no less, indeed more, powerful than those who wielded weapons against the enemy with their own hands.

“For he who strengthens a failing spirit by admonition is certainly greater than he who supplies strength by his encouragement, especially when those who gave the admonitions shared in the same endurance in every respect.”

What shall I say, finally, about those who in this very expedition were consecrated in various places by the confession of martyrdom? What shall I say of the fact that not only priests and learned men, but also military men and common people—of whom no hope of confession might have been expected—were raised to this glory?

We have heard that many of these were captured by the pagans and, when ordered to deny the sacraments of the faith, preferred to expose their heads to the swords rather than betray the Christian faith with which they had once been imbued.

What the nobleman named Matthew accomplished gloriously.—

Among these I have chosen to relate in particular the story of one man, a soldier indeed, noble by birth, but, among all the men of his family and rank whom I have known, more distinguished in character than any other.

I had known him from childhood and saw him grow in a holy disposition, especially since he came from the same district as I did, and both he and his parents had held benefices from my parents and owed them homage. He grew up with me, and throughout his life his character and pursuits were entirely open to me.

By then he had distinguished himself in the knightly office and was singularly renowned for arms. Yet he was free from every fault of wantonness and highly celebrated in the palace of the emperor of Constantinople, Alexis, in whose service he had been accustomed to travel diligently.

Insofar as his station allowed, although he was outwardly blessed with abundant means, he was regarded as exceptionally generous in almsgiving and so devoted to the divine mysteries that his life seemed not that of a soldier but rather of a bishop.

When I recall his constancy in prayer, his piety in speech, and his kindness in giving, I rejoice exceedingly in his holy purpose—but I grieve no less for my own. For I experienced in him a pattern of conduct that deserved no other end than martyrdom.

I certainly glory—and may anyone who was able to attain knowledge of him glory; I do not presume to say friendship—for whoever saw him should know beyond doubt that he had seen a martyr.

He gives Christ a distinguished testimony of faith after his head is cut off.—

This man was captured by the pagans. When he was compelled to deny the faith of Christ, he asked the unbelievers for a delay until the following Friday. They readily granted it, supposing that a longer period of reconsideration would cause him to change his mind.

At last, when the appointed day arrived and the fury of the gentiles pressed him to yield to their decision, he is said to have spoken as follows:

“If you think that I delayed the sword hanging over me for this reason—that I might gain a few small lights of these intervening days—and not rather so that it might happen to me to die on the very day on which my Lord Jesus Christ was crucified, then it is fitting that what a Christian mind thinks should be made clear. Rise up, therefore,” he said, “and kill me in whatever manner you wish; only let me restore my soul to him, slain for his sake, who today offered up his own for the universal life of all.”

After saying this, he extended his neck beneath the threatening sword and, his head cut off, was sent to the Lord whose likeness in death he had longed for. His name was Matthew—truly, according to the interpretation of his name, given not to another but to God.

# BOOK FIVE BEGINS

## CHAPTER ONE

[I.] With what intention the author writes history.—

Apart from whatever spiritual benefit this little work of mine may provide, my intention is to speak in the way I would wish another person to report the matter to me if he were writing about the same subject.

Such is the inclination of my mind that it desires what is somewhat obscure, while it avoids what is crude and inelegantly expressed. I value more highly those things that can exercise my mind than those that are easy to understand; things that are always readily grasped offer nothing memorable to a mind greedy for novelty.

Although I have written and continue to write many things, I have cast them all out of my mind in such a way that I think they will benefit me alone; I do not concern myself with whether they will please anyone else. I have therefore set aside everyone’s opinions and, secure—or heedless—of myself, await being beaten by the blows of anyone’s words. Let us continue, then, with what we have begun, and endure with equanimity the judgments of men tearing us apart.

[II.] He continues the account of the siege of Antioch.—

We consider that the events of the siege of Antioch cannot be fully related by anyone. Among those who were present there, no one could have been found who was able to see and comprehend in its entirety everything that took place around that same city, in the exact order in which the events occurred.

But since the hardships they suffered amid shortages and the various accidents of war have been touched upon only briefly, it now seems suitable to gather, however we can, the end to which they came through the siege and the reward they obtained for so great a labor.

In those days, on a certain night, something glowing like fire flashed above our army and at the same time displayed unmistakably the form of a cross. All the wise men there interpreted the fiery apparition as referring to the wars that were to come, in which the cross seemed to indicate that certain salvation and a coming victory would be present.

[III.] Pyrrhus, leader of the Turks, hands the city over to Bohemond.—

One of the leading men who governed the city for the Turks was called Pyrrhus. In some way he had gained Bohemond’s friendship, and through messengers traveling between them he began to seek his conversation more frequently. The two men also often exchanged counsel about what was being done on either side.

Meanwhile, as trust grew through their constant conversations and strengthened the bond of affection, Bohemond gradually began to urge him to subject the city—over much of which he evidently exercised authority—to Christian rule. He also persuaded him to accept Christianity, promising that, if he consented to both of these things, he would provide him with substantial profit and greater honor than he had previously enjoyed there.

After these promises had been pressed upon him not once but many times, Pyrrhus finally consented, enticed by the prospect of gain, and sent him instructions of this sort:

“I am in charge of the guard of three towers. I will hand them over to your control, and at whatever hour you wish and find convenient, I will gladly admit you—or anyone you choose—into them.”

This hope began greatly to raise Bohemond’s spirits. As he more confidently awaited entry into the city, he displayed the joy conceived in his mind with an outstanding expression on his face.

Fearing, however, that when Pyrrhus betrayed the city one of their princes might seize the governance of the entire city from him, Bohemond craftily approached the senior leaders of the army:

“You are not unaware, most excellent counts,” he said, “of the hunger, the cold, and the savage watches we have endured while besieging this city. You know that deadly weariness weighs equally upon people of every rank—great, small, and middling—and that no remedy is available.

“Therefore, after taking counsel among yourselves, I ask you to consider whether you would allow any one of us to obtain dominion over this city if someone should happen to bring about its betrayal.

“It seems to me not unreasonable that, whether by force, secretly, or by entreaty, whoever obtains entry into it should unquestionably be granted dominion over the city by everyone.”

The leaders’ judgment was quite different, and they opposed his opinion with a stern expression, saying:

“It is not sufficiently appropriate that, where equal labor and fear have been endured, and where the request has been made at great cost, and where danger has hung in an equal balance over everyone, authority over the city—won through the suffering of so many—should be assigned to one individual.

“Who would not consider it just that, where the struggle of all has boiled over, there should be general rest for everyone and that each should lawfully receive a share after the victory?”

Bohemond received this response with displeasure and, weighing what he had heard with a troubled mind, withdrew.

Soon word reached the leaders that an army of innumerable barbarian nations was being assembled to come to Antioch’s aid. Their minds suddenly changed, and, after summoning a council, they spoke among themselves:

“If Bohemond should seize the city by any stratagem, let us patiently allow him to retain what has been handed over to him, on this condition: if the emperor provides us with the aid he has promised and fulfills with suitable generosity what he has likewise promised and sworn, the city itself, when we hand it over, shall pass under the emperor’s authority. But if he deceives us, let the whole city be granted to Bohemond, as he himself desires.”

When this became known, the distinguished man confidently renewed his pleas to Pyrrhus every day and surrounded him with much flattering talk of promises:

“See, excellent Pyrrhus,” he said, “you perceive what opportunity smiles upon us for accomplishing these things. Do not, I beg you, delay, lest—if what we are jointly contriving for our benefit should be discovered by anyone, God forbid!—you lose it.”

Pyrrhus, rejoicing at Bohemond’s embassy, announced that he would in no way delay offering his aid. And, so that he would not leave the illustrious man suspended in uncertainty through a prolonged wait, Pyrrhus secretly sent his own son to Bohemond and instructed him to hope confidently for the surrender of the city:

“Tomorrow,” he said, “as soon as daylight first appears, gather the entire body of the Frankish army into one force with sounding trumpets, and order them to advance some distance from the camp, as they customarily do when they intend to plunder Saracen lands. Then turn back immediately to the right through the mountains.

“I shall await your arrival inside the city. Without doubt I will receive your men—whoever you wish to send—into those towers that appear to be subject to my authority.”

[IV.] Bohemond hastened to carry out without delay what he had heard. He summoned one of his retainers and ordered him, as though acting in the office of a herald, to go around the Frankish camp and announce to everyone that they should prepare themselves with the utmost diligence, as though they were about to advance into Saracen territory.

Without delay, the servant’s ingenuity irreversibly obeyed the prince’s command, and the Frankish expedition did not refuse to comply.

Bohemond revealed to Duke Godfrey, count of the Flemings, and likewise to the count of Saint-Gilles and to the bishop of Le Puy what joyful hope he was conceiving for himself. Now made more confident by Pyrrhus’s promises, he declared that Antioch would be handed over to him that night.

Once the army had been arranged in the formation described above, the soldiers were ordered to walk across the plains, while the mass of infantry advanced through the mountains. They completed their route throughout the night and, before dawn produced the first twilight, took their positions before the towers that the fortunate traitor guarded in sleepless watchfulness.

### [V.]

There Bohemond leapt down from his horse and, with an authority now unusual in him, thundered at the Franks, saying:

“Advance, and breathe again after the distress you have endured for so long. Climb the ladder set up before you, and, lest I delay you long, seize Antioch, which you have desired for so long; for the city that previously lay subject to the Turks will shortly, if God so wills, pass into your custody.”

The Franks reached the ladder. Leaning against the city walls and firmly fastened to them, it immediately offered ascent to sixty men; once they had been admitted inside the towers, the man entrusted the towers’ guards to them. But Pyrrus, observing that so few of the Franks were climbing, was not— as later became clear—so much afraid for our men as for himself. He feared that the outcome of the treachery he had begun might falter to his own destruction. Thus he growled most severely in the Greek language at those present:

“We have too few Franks.”

After saying this, he loudly summoned Bohemond, plainly hastening the enterprise that was under way lest it become known to the citizens before the Franks had assembled. Then a certain Lombard among the servants, understanding that Pyrrus was complaining about Bohemond’s absence, hurried as quickly as he could to the man being sought:

“What are you doing so stupidly? Why are you pursuing so difficult an undertaking with such sluggishness? Look: we already hold the guards of three towers, while you stand watching the outcome of this affair from a distance as though it were still uncertain. Wake up, lend a hand, and involve yourself in the midst of the action.”

He hastened more quickly with his men to the ladder and raised the resolve both of the good traitor and of those who had climbed.

At once those who had entered Pyrrus’s towers, noticing Franks streaming together from every direction, began to shout their customary signal with great jubilation:

“God wills it! God wills it!”

Those who were standing before the walls, preparing to climb, repeated the same words in loud acclamations. Then each strove with boundless eagerness to outstrip the other in ascending the ladder; and everyone who was carried up occupied the towers and other positions as quickly as he could. Whoever encountered them was delivered to death. Among them Pyrrus’s brother was also killed.

Meanwhile the ladder broke, and the entire multitude of our men beneath it, including those who had gone before, was wounded by profound anguish. Those above feared that help would be delayed for them, while those below were afraid to withhold support from those who had climbed. But ingenuity quickly found a way forward. A gate, closed and adjoining the place, lay hidden on the left. The obstruction of night prevented it from being found; even during the day, because it stood in a deserted spot, it was not very conspicuous. Nevertheless, with anxiety pressing them, they discovered it by feeling their way. Everyone immediately ran toward it; its bars and bolts were broken, and it was opened. It was made passable when 408 Franks burst through.

### [VI.]

You could have heard the whole city being thrown into confusion by a dreadful uproar. While some rejoiced together over the end of so great a labor, others wept over the wholly unexpected overthrow of themselves and all their people. Nowhere among victors or vanquished did anything remain moderate. Immediately Bohemond, wishing to make the city his own, ordered that the well-known and utterly recognizable Turkish banner be planted at the summit of a certain mountain, in full view of the fortress that had still resisted capture—his own, of course.

The city was overwhelmed by an immense multitude of wailings. As fugitives everywhere met one another in the narrow streets and the victorious pursuers urged them toward slaughter, a deathly and savage shouting was carried throughout the city. As they remembered the hardships they had endured during the siege, and the famines more bitter to them than death itself, they judged every punishment they could inflict insufficient for the guilt of their enemies.

The treachery of the Armenians and Syrians, deservedly reckoned equal to that of the pagans, was punished with every penalty. For when the Franks discovered that these people had zealously assisted the Turks in laboring for their own destruction, they were unwilling to exempt them from punishment. Yet I confess that they would have spared countless numbers of them if they had known how to distinguish between pagans and people of our faith. In such total confusion of time and circumstance—for it was night, and the desire to plunder the entire city, together with impatience of delay, had thrown everything into disorder—perhaps nothing permitted the differences of clothing to be recognized, and nothing allowed the barbarian character of the people to be discerned.

Our men, meanwhile, constantly stationed on alert, had at first been surrounded by the terrible appearance of emaciated, exhausted faces. Following the Frankish custom, each had delayed shaving his beard, through the long neglect brought about by their wandering. The bishop of Le Puy noticed this and, fearing that they might rush into mutual slaughter if they should ever happen to fight, mistaking one another for Turks because of their similar barbarous appearance, ordered them frequently to shave and commanded that silver crosses, or crosses of any other material, be hung around each man’s neck, so that one might not be intercepted by another as though a foreigner.

But those who had remained in the tents, when at dawn they heard the townspeople agitated by the most violent tumult, came out of their pavilions. They saw Bohemond’s banner fixed on a high mountain before the walls of the fortress, which had not yet been captured. They hurried there, burst through the city gates, and struck down the Turks and Saracens whom they found, except those whom they spared because they had entered the fortress. Some Turks, realizing that the Franks had taken possession of the city, escaped through other gates.

Within the city, however, the distinction between the sexes was indiscriminately destroyed, the fragile hopes of youth were cut down; and since no aged and withered person was spared, it cannot be doubted with what ferocity the young, fit for war, were slaughtered.

### [VII.]

Meanwhile Cassianus, who had ruled the city of Antioch, fearing that he would fall into the hands of the Franks and wishing to preserve his life by the aid of flight, arrived with many companions not far from Antioch, in the territory of Tancred. As they hurried to escape, they had utterly exhausted their horses, which were now no longer able to proceed; therefore they turned aside into a dwelling of some mountaineers.

When the inhabitants—Armenians and Syrians—learned that their monstrous enemy had hidden in a poor hut, now that fortune had turned against him, they seized him and cut off his head. They carried the severed head into Bohemond’s presence, hoping thereby to obtain from him the favor of freedom as an unusual gift. They removed his belt and dagger-sheath and assessed them for sale at the price of sixty bezants.

These events took place on the Nones of June, when it was Thursday.

You could have seen the city, after the slaughter had been completed, overflowing with intolerable stench. The marketplaces, streets, courtyards, and vestibules of the houses—formerly distinguished by marble inlays with great elegance—were now uniformly fouled by the most dreadful blood. Heaps of innumerable corpses lay scattered everywhere; savage spectacles and the deadly horror of corrupted air infected the senses of the eyes and nostrils with miserable force.

The narrow lanes were strewn with heaps of rotting bodies. Since there was neither any means of carrying away so many corpses nor anywhere safe to turn aside from the stench, the constant sight and breathing of them gradually dulled the horror that had first overwhelmed the senses. Thus no one feared to walk across the very corpses with which the paths were covered, custom having supplied the courage.

## CHAPTER II

### [VIII.] Curbaran, commander of the army of Persia, advances against the Franks with a very large army.

A certain man called Curbaran, chief minister—or rather commander of the army—of the king of the Persians, whom they customarily call by the old Sogdian name, just as the Romans call their rulers Caesars, was still staying within the kingdom of Persia, in the province they call Corozania. Some say that the land around the Caucasus is called Corozania, the name having been corrupted by ignorant people.

The aforementioned Cassianus, prince of the city of Antioch, repeatedly urged him by messengers to come to his aid, since he was confined under such severe pressure of siege. He promised that, if Curbaran drove away the Franks, he would either surrender the liberated city to his authority or repay the labor of the relief expedition with gifts of the greatest value.

When this commander of the army, enticed by the hope of this promise, had already assembled a very large army, and had sought and received from the supreme priest of his error— for they too have a pope of their own, after the model of ours—permission to kill Christians, he hastened to rescue Antioch, advancing with an endless column of reinforcements.

The prefect of Jerusalem—whom they call Admiravisos in that barbarous language—immediately enlarged the approaching force with a very substantial army. Likewise, the king of Damascus gathered no small expedition and brought it to Curbaran’s aid.

Besides Turks, Saracens, Arabs, and Persians—peoples whose names are well known to historians—the nations summoned by that profane prince were designated by novel names: Publicani, Curti, Azimitae, and Agulani, together with countless others, not really nations but monsters. They are said to have numbered three thousand of those whom they call Agulani. These men fear neither swords, spears, nor arrows, nor any weapons whatsoever, because both they and their horses are entirely covered with iron. In battle they use no weapon at all except swords.

Curbaran, therefore, with such a display of nations, was making his way to drive the Franks away from Antioch. When he had already drawn near the city, behold, the son of the deceased Cassianus, named Sensadolus, met the prince and said to him with great sorrow:

“Since great renown is attributed to your courage, and an incomparable reputation for your victories spreads everywhere among the nations, I, most invincible man, may surely hope for your protection. For since I see that your assistance fails no one, and since your power is everywhere held in reverence because of your deeds, it is no more than a source of shame for me to lament my misfortunes before you, when I am certain that whatever I ask will in no way go away empty-handed.

“Your glory remembers how many embassies you received from my father Cassianus while he was besieged in Antioch. When you had decided to come to his aid, you heard that the city had been captured by the Franks. Now, with my parent killed, I am besieged inside that same city, undoubtedly awaiting for myself the same fate that I know befell my father.

“If they have overrun Antioch, and have done the same to many towns and cities of Romania and Syria, it is surely beyond doubt that they have likewise resolved to do the same to you and to other people and places of our nation. Let your Excellency therefore be roused, bringing forces against such savage audacity, and cut off the opportunity of these wretched men, who wish to seize everything. For me, amid my misfortunes, the hope of your aid alone remained.”

To him, as he magnified his complaints, Curbaran replied:

“If you want me to ward off these dangers that press upon you and devote myself more attentively to your interests, surrender to my authority the town that you are defending and for which you plead. After I have placed my own guards in the fortress, you will then discover how earnestly I labor for your advantage.”

Sensadolus answered:

“If you utterly destroy the Franks for me and hand over to me their severed heads, I will admit you into the town; and after doing homage to you, I will preserve the fortress under your authority.”

Curbaran said to him:

“You will not deal with me on those terms; you will surrender the fortress immediately.”

What more is there to say? The demand of the profane prince prevailed. The young man, withdrawing himself from possession of the fortress, persuaded the one who was extorting it that he would not enjoy it for long.

### [IX.] Curbaran besieges Antioch.

The third day after the Franks had burst into Antioch was under way when, behold, the Turkish forerunners ran before the city walls, while the rest of the army in great numbers pitched its tents at the Pharpharic bridge.

They therefore attacked as quickly as possible the tower adjoining the bridge. After it had been stormed with great exertion, they killed everyone whom they found inside; no one’s life was spared except that of their lord. Later, however, when our men fought against these people, they found him fettered in iron.

On the following day the army hurried to the city. Choosing a site for their camp between the two rivers, they remained there for two days. After the fortress had been captured—the commander of which, as we have said, had been thrown into chains—Curbaran summoned one of his nobles, whom he knew to be intelligent and loyal to him, and ordered him:

“Go, and defend this town for me with the loyalty that you owe and that I expect from you.”

The man replied:

“I shall obey your command concerning this matter only with difficulty. Nevertheless, I will carry it out on the following condition: if victory goes to the Franks, I must be granted permission to surrender the fortress to the victors.”

Curbaran answered:

“I know you to possess such firmness of purpose and constancy that, whatever you then wish to do, I shall safely approve.”

After completing the fortification of that fortress, the grim prince returned to his own camp. Some of his Turks, having newly seized the weapons of a certain poor foot soldier, displayed them before his eyes in mockery of our men: a sword rough with long rust, a bow black like soot, and an unpolished spear stained by the smoke of many years. They jeeringly said to him:

“Look at the weapons with which the army of the Franks will conquer us.”

Curbaran smiled at them and said:

“With such bright and powerful weapons will they lay waste the East? With such forces will they subdue the farthest regions of the Caucasus? Will the completely unarmed Franks perhaps be able to take from us those lands that the Amazons possessed in ancient times and that our ancestors once claimed for themselves?”

He spoke, and immediately summoned a notary and said:

“Write down these same words as quickly as possible on separate tablets, to be sent throughout the provinces of Persia—to our pope, to our lord the king of the Persians, and also to the prefects and fellow soldiers of the various regions. Their substance is as follows:

### [X.]

“To the magnificent lord, the king of the Persians, to the most blessed pope, and to all who profess the holy warfare against the Christians, Curbaran, commander of his army: greetings and victory.

“I give thanks to the supreme divinity, fathers and lords, because it continually supplies us with times suited to joy and everywhere grants victories over the enemies of nations. We are sending you these three weapons, which we took from the Franks, so that you may see what sort of armor is possessed by those who desire to drive us from our homeland.

“But I want you to know that I hold the Franks, who threatened destruction to all of us, shut up inside Antioch itself, which they had begun to seize. I also possess the fortress that dominates the city from the opposite side, facing those who are besieged. Since it lies entirely within my power either to slaughter those shut inside or to consign them to the extremity of captivity, do not, meanwhile, until I return, torment yourselves with any anxiety on our account. Know without doubt that we have utterly mastered them.

“Therefore devote yourselves to pleasures with greater security than usual; celebrate richer banquets; apply yourselves to propagating your race through multiplying the gynaecea of wives and harlots; and let the increasing number of sons be able to oppose the Christians—now even their very name.

“Yet I call the supreme Thunderer to witness, with the most blessed Mahomet as his patron, that I shall not again appear before your majestic eyes until I have brought under my authority the royal city—Antioch—and its appendage, Syria; the Greeks and Epirotes whom they call Bulgars; and until I have subjected the Apulians and Calabrians as well, to increase your glory.

“Farewell.”

### [XI.] Curbaran’s mother tries to dissuade her son from destroying the Christians.

At that time Curbaran’s mother, who was staying in the city of Aleph, came to him and sadly suggested:

“I would like to know whether the reputation about you that people proclaim is, as they say, well founded.”

Her son replied:

“What reputation?”

“They believe,” she said, “that you are going to wage war against the Franks.”

“Nothing is more certain,” he replied.

“My son,” she said, “best of men, by the most generous qualities implanted in your character, I beg and adjure you not to attack them and not to incur damage to your reputation. Since the renown of your arms shines as far as the remotest ocean of upper India, and the farthest Thule responds to your praises, why do you desire to stain your swords with the blood of poor men, whom it is a pointless punishment to attack and no glory to overcome? Since you are able to terrify distant kings, what pleasure do you take in provoking miserable foreigners?

“I admit, my son, that you may rightly consider their persons contemptible; but know for certain that the authority of the Christian religion is exceedingly great. Therefore I beg you not to attempt what you will afterward regret having begun, when it is too late.”

He refused to heed his mother’s warnings. When he had heard this, he looked at her with a fierce expression and began:

“Why do you weave these old-woman’s tales for me? You are, I suppose, out of your senses, and, having fallen into madness, you utter words without understanding. More lords of cities serve under me than the Christians themselves are able to produce as men throughout the whole of their army; and you, delirious in mind, think that the boasts of the Christians have covered over the proofs of my valor?”

“My dearest son,” she said, “I make light of the names of the men of whom we are speaking; but I beg you in every way not to shrink from their author, Christ. They may have no power with which to fight you, but victory belongs certainly to their God if he chooses to grant it. He is accustomed to defend his own, even when they are sluggish and cowardly, for the sake of his own glory alone; and he watches over those whom he knows—or remembers—as entrusted to his care, indeed as their shepherd and Redeemer.

“Do you think that he who bent the empires of his faith to his will, who has allowed them to prevail against us up to this point, cannot even now with the greatest ease remove your efforts? To him, as though to God rising from the dead, the Father says:

“‘Arise, O God; judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations’” (Psalm LXXXI, 8).

“If, therefore, he judges the earth—that is, distinguishes and separates some from the mass of the lost, while rejecting others—and if he does not inherit all nations but, taking a portion from the whole, inherits among all nations, let your prudence hear, my son, how severely he punishes those whom he allows to remain without a share in knowing him. The prophet David says:

“‘Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name’” (Psalm LXXVIII, 6).

“You do not despise these Franks because they are foreigners and you are gentiles; you do not reject the obscurity of their arms or the poverty of their lives, but rather shudder only at the Christian name that is in them. And certainly the one who is despised in them will, when necessity arises, fight on their behalf with poured-out wrath.

“If the prophetic mouth promises them that the name of the Lord will be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting, and that he is proclaimed exalted not over the Jews but over all nations (Psalm CXII, 3–4); and if by the very mouth of God the people that had not been his people is now called his people, and the unloved is called beloved (Romans IX, 25); if what had existed among the Jews is transferred to the nations by the grace of adoption, and God’s countenance is prepared for the remnant of those Jews, who but a madman attempts to attack the sons of God?

“I plainly foretell to you that, if you attack them in war, you will bring upon yourself immense harm and disgrace. You will suffer certain losses to your army; you will even enrich them by the seizure of your spoils; and you yourself will fall through departing in shameful flight.

“Death does not, in fact, await you in this battle. Yet know for certain that, while life remains with you, the present year will not pass you by. For their God does not immediately avenge the crime that has been committed; rather, until the offense has fully ripened, punishment is sometimes postponed for the guilty. Therefore I fear, my son—God forbid!—that, while it is delayed, your death may become violent.”

### [XII.]

At this, Curbaran was rendered dull with astonishment at his mother’s extraordinary speech, and, bloodless and enfeebled at the mention of his approaching death, began:

“I would like to know how you obtained knowledge of these things: that the Christian people would summon such forces against us, defeat us in the battle that is now approaching, carry off our spoils, and that I would fall into the snares of sudden death in the present year.”

“My son,” she said, “it is known that nearly a hundred years have passed since it was discovered in certain hidden books of the pagan sect that the Christian people would rise to wage war against us, completely subdue us, and establish kingdoms for themselves wherever we now exercise dominion, so that paganism would become subject to the faithful.

“But our knowledge is darkened on this point, because we do not know whether this will be fulfilled now or after a long time. I too, investigating the astronomical discipline with the greatest care and considering the conjectures of countless divinations, have learned from a balanced comparison of them all that we must surely be defeated by Christian men. Therefore I grieve for you from the depths of my heart, because it is certain to me that I remain almost deprived of you already.”

“Mother,” he said, “I want you to explain certain matters about which I am uncertain.”

“Ask without hesitation,” she replied, “for whatever I know is ready at your disposal.”

“Tell me, mother, I beg you,” he said, “whether Bohemond and Tancred are to be regarded as gods or as men; and if they make the Franks victorious in battle, declare that to me.”

“My son, Bohemond and Tancred, like us, are subject to common mortality. But because they act on behalf of their faith, they have earned the glory of a famous name, with God cooperating with them. They profess God the Father, whose Son they likewise venerate as having become human for their sake; yet they are believed to be one and the same in the unity of the Holy Spirit.”

“Since, mother,” he said, “you testify that they are not gods but mere men, entirely like us, nothing else surely remains except that we should match ourselves against them in battle and test our forces.”

### [XIII.]

When the mother realized that her son was inclined to wage war against the Franks and unwilling to heed her counsels, she gathered whatever forces could be found around her and withdrew to the city of Aleph mentioned above, being exceedingly suspicious of her son.

Three days later Curbaran took up arms, and a great multitude of Turks came with him to the city, on the side where the fortress stood—the one they had recently captured and fortified for themselves. Our men, believing that they could resist them, drew up their line against them. But their numbers were so great that our men possessed neither the strength nor the courage to withstand them. Forced to retreat, they returned to the city.

As they entered the gate in a fleeing, tightly packed column, the entrance was so narrow that many suffered death through mutual compression. It was then Thursday. Some were fighting outside the city gate; others, fighting against the townspeople within, continued the battle until evening.

## CHAPTER III

### [XIV.] Some Christians, terrified by fear, flee.

But Christ, who once knew those whom he had chosen, knows them even now. That night some who—as I may put it—were not of the number through whom salvation would come to Israel, seeing themselves surrounded by the Turkish army, and seeing

> The battles of the day scarcely closed within the boundary of night,  
>  
> They trembled; empty fear penetrated their hearts,  
>  
> And beneath their gaze death alone stood before the terrified.  
>  
> Their life utterly hung in the balance before those inert men;  
>  
> With trembling minds they now look only upon the Turks.  
>  
> They already reckon themselves struck by the enemy’s sword.  
>  
> Each despairs there of assistance from his own weapons.  
>  
> He therefore thinks of flight; those who have despised hope in God  
>  
> Shamefully enter foul sewers as fugitives.  
>  
> A fitting end was theirs, since they gave such an example  
>  
> To armies that ought to be held in reverence. Crawling, the fugitives  
>  
> Reach the sea, and lose the skin torn from hands and feet;  
>  
> With the flesh eaten away, they scrape their bones  
>  
> Against the rocks. In the manner of the teacher Paul,  
>  
> Whom flight through a wall enabled to escape Damascus,  
>  
> They marked themselves out with these neatly arranged latrines.

### [XV.]

Those who had withdrawn were a certain William from Normandy, of entirely noble birth, together with his brother Alberic. From earliest youth Alberic had been given to the schools and made a cleric, but afterward had apostatized from the clergy disgracefully and shamefully, abandoning it for love of military service.

I would name the town from which they took their surname, if, overcome by the friendly closeness I had with their family, I had not decided to spare their shame. A certain Guy, also called Trossellus, renowned for the dominion and power he held over towns beyond the Seine, and distinguished by birth throughout all France, likewise bore the mark of that flight.

There were other deserters from this holy army who, when they had returned to their homeland, were held up to disgrace and execration and everywhere proclaimed infamous. We do not know the names of some of them; but with regard to others, whose identity is readily known, we have not wished to detract from them.

### [XVI.]

They therefore reached the harbor called Saint Simeon and found ships and sailors. They said to the sailors:

“What are you unfortunate men waiting for here? Know that all those for whom you used to carry provisions have been destined for death. The Turkish army has besieged the city and the people within it, and we have barely stripped our own bodies from their destruction.”

Struck through by the dart of this sad report, they remained for a long time stunned among themselves. At last, placing their safety in flight,

> They boarded the boats and sought the open sea.

No sooner had they begun cutting through the waves than the Turks arrived. They killed those whom they found there, burned the ships they discovered in the shallow water, and plundered the belongings of those whom they had slain.

After those degenerates, fugitives from heavenly aid, had withdrawn through the most shameful places, as they say, the survivors who had chosen to persevere could no longer endure the hostile weapons without any respite. They therefore built a wall between themselves and the enemy, which they guarded night and day with continuous watches.

There their oppression became so pitiable that they were driven to eat disgraceful food: the flesh of horses and asses.

### [XVII.] Christ appeared in a vision to a priest and declared that he would come to the aid of the Christians.

Meanwhile, on a certain day, when the commanders of the army were stationed before the fortress besieged within the city and were utterly distressed in spirit because of all the misery they endured, a certain priest appeared before them and said:

“Lords and elders, I shall report to your Excellencies a vision which, if you believe it, will, I hope, benefit your consolation. When I was sleeping one night in the church of the Blessed Mother of God, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to me together with that most holy Mother and the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles. Standing beside me, he said:

“‘Do you know who I am?’

“‘Not at all,’ I replied.

“He had spoken, and behold, in the halo around his head, as is customary in paintings, the form of a cross appeared. The image of the Savior then repeated the question:

“‘Do you still not know whom you see?’

“‘No, Lord,’ I said. ‘I recognize you in no other way than by seeing the image of a cross hanging over your neck, the sign by which your image is customarily marked wherever it is painted.’

“‘You are not mistaken,’ he said. ‘I myself am he.’

“Immediately, mindful of the distress we were suffering together, I fell at his feet and earnestly begged him to come to the aid of the calamity of those who were fighting together for the faith.

“‘I have observed well what you have endured,’ he said. ‘From now on I shall not delay in helping you. At my prompting you took up the vows of this expedition; with me as conqueror you seized the city of Nicaea; under my leadership you have won many victories; and since I have brought you this far, I have grieved over the hardships you endured while besieging Antioch, as well as those which you are now suffering within the city.

“‘But although I have raised you up through so many benefits and such great triumphs, brought you into the city as victors, and preserved you safe and unharmed, you have abused my gift: you have acted wickedly both toward Christians and in your most shameful relations with pagan women, sending up to heaven the stench of excessive clamor.’

“The invincible Virgin of mercy, Mary, ever the interpreter of the human race before God, and the heavenly key-bearer Peter, the special bishop of the Antiochenes, then fell at the feet of the most merciful Lord, beseeching and asking him to grant his consolation to the suffering people.

“Then that wonderful Peter himself added:

“‘Your majesty remembers, Lord, with what shameful filth the pagans defiled my house in this city. It redounds to the insult of your divinity that they filled your sanctuaries with crimes and slaughter. Since, in your mercy, you have at last driven them out and brought joy over this matter to heaven, will you, regretting so pious a deed, allow their arrogance to return to its former state against you?’

“Moved by these words, the Lord said to me:

“‘Go, and tell my people to turn to me from the depths of their hearts, and I promise that I will return to them with all my compassion. Within five days I will provide you with the greatest assistance. Let them therefore institute litanies, and let all the clergy sing this Responsory:

“‘“Our enemies have gathered together and glory in their strength. Crush their power, O Lord, and scatter them, so that they may know that there is no other who fights for us except you, our God. Scatter them by your strength and destroy them, O Lord our protector.”’”

After bringing these words to an end, the priest added:

“If any doubt about what has been said has entered your minds, I, in the name of this truth, will submit myself with complete faith to whatever examination or judgment you wish—whether fire or precipice. And if I should happen to be harmed, add to me a punishment more severe than the injury you can inflict.”

But the bishop of Le Puy, a man altogether canonical in character, ordered the Gospels and a cross to be brought forward, so that an oath might establish the credibility of his words.

### [XVIII.] The besieged commanders swear to one another with courageous resolve that they will endure.

When this had been done, the commanders, after consulting together, exchanged oaths, namely:

“Neither death nor life would compel them to withdraw from the defense they had begun, no matter how great a necessity might happen to press upon them.”

First Bohemond, then the count of Saint-Gilles, Hugh the Great, Robert the Norman, Duke Godfrey, and the count of Flanders swore with equal determination that they would never abandon what they had begun.

Tancred, however, swore on this condition: as long as he could rely on the support of forty knights, he would neither withdraw from the siege in which they were then suffering nor be diverted from the journey to Jerusalem, except by death itself.

When this became known to the lesser men, it produced great courage in the hearts of the entire multitude subject to them.

## CHAPTER IV

### [XIX.] Blessed Andrew showed someone, in a vision, the lance with which Christ’s side was pierced, hidden in a church of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0761D] See below, Book VI, chapter 1.]

Before the city of Antioch was captured, the apparition of the blessed apostle Andrew appeared to a certain man from the army, named Peter, and said:

“What is happening with you?”

The man, bewildered, did not answer the question but asked who he was. The apparition did not conceal that he was the apostle Andrew.

“And know, son,” he said, “that when, with God opening the way, the valor of the Franks has entered the city, you will go to the church of my fellow apostle and brother, the blessed Peter. There, in such-and-such a place, you will be able to find the lance with which it is said that the side of our Savior Jesus Christ was pierced.”

He spoke and, adding nothing further, departed.

At that time the man did not wish to make anyone aware of the vision; nor did he value it so highly that he thought it worth more than the mockeries of dreams, which afflict us almost without interruption. Yet, while speaking with the apostle, he had not been entirely forgetful of himself, and had said:

“Lord, if I were to tell our people what you have commanded, what sign of faith could I offer to convince those who doubt, so that they might be compelled to believe?”

At these words the glorious apostle rebuked the man and spiritually transported him to the basilica of the blessed brother, to the place where the lance had been deposited.

After the city had subsequently been captured, when God’s people were being subjected to the disasters we have recounted [Col. 0762B], that same memorable apostle, who had rightly begun in every respect to become the administrator of those matters which he had recognized as pertaining to the adornment of the house of his dearest brother, appeared again to that man Peter:

“Why,” he said, “have you delayed making known what I commanded? When you see your people here endangered by the hardship of famine and there almost falling into the pit of despair as the Turks press upon them, you ought to have announced to them what you had learned through my foretelling. Without doubt, it is fitting that they should know that wherever they carry this same lance, certain victory will come to them.”

After receiving this apostolic admonition for the second time, he began to proclaim to our men the sequence of the words he had heard in the vision. But the people, rejecting the man’s statements [Col. 0762C], thought them something like a lie; for, with evils surrounding them on every side, they could not in any way conceive hope from such a matter. Yet he, persistent and made more steadfast by the authority of the apostolic speech, insisted that the apostle had appeared to him and had said twice in a vision:

“Hurry, and do not delay telling the Lord’s endangered army, so that, once fear has been shaken off, it may cling with unwavering faith to God, who promises assistance. Within five days the Lord will reveal something of such a kind that he will open their hearts to great joy; and if battle should come upon them, with this sacred sign going before them, every hostility will soon lie conquered beneath them.”

Meanwhile, through that man’s diligent persuasion, they began to be summoned to belief in his words and, through his repeated admonition, to be assisted by some breathing-space of hope [Col. 0762D]:

“We must not be so foolish,” they said, “that God—who has hitherto granted so many victories—would expose us, shut in as we are for the defense of the faith, hoping in him and yearning toward him with groaning hearts, to be cut down by the swords of the Turks. Rather, it must certainly be believed that, after sorrowful times, he will show us the light of his mercy and impose his fear upon those nations that have not sought him.”

## CHAPTER V

### [XX.] The Turks who guarded the fortress harass our men so severely that they shut three soldiers inside a certain tower overlooking the fortress.

The Turks guarding the fortress had surrounded our men with such pressure that they shut three of their soldiers inside a certain tower which stood within sight of the fortress. For the pagans coming out of the fortress attacked our men with such a furious assault [Col. 0763A] that they could scarcely endure it at all. Thus two of the soldiers whom they had shut in, having been wounded, fled; the third continued the day in defense of himself against the enemy, to such an extent that he killed two of them on the wall-walks, after cutting through their spear-shafts. Those three soldiers had rendered the Turks’ spears useless by cutting through their shafts with their hands.

That soldier’s name was Hugh, and he was surnamed “the Madman.” He belonged to the household of a certain Josfred, who bore the byname of Montescabioso.

### [XXI.] By what stratagem Bohemond rouses the soldiers to battle.

The memorable Bohemond, when he could scarcely persuade anyone to attack the fortress [Col. 0763B]—for some who were hiding indoors were being constrained by lack of bread, while others were terrified by the rage and numbers of the pagans—summoned by severe command, ordered a fire to be set in that part of the city where the palace of the recently deceased Cassian had stood.

When everyone saw this, abandoning everything that was burning, some fled from the fire toward the fortress; others gathered at the gate of the Count of Saint-Gilles; some joined Duke Godfrey; each went to the people among whom he was thought to be a native. Soon, to increase the abandonment that had begun, an extremely violent storm arose, so that the force of the winds became such that scarcely anyone could walk upright.

Meanwhile, while Bohemond saw the city being completely stripped by a horrible conflagration, he began to be exceedingly anxious for the church of Blessed [Col. 0763C] Peter and Saint Mary, and for the other churches. From the third hour, however, until midnight, the raging flame reduced two thousand churches and houses to ashes. Around the middle of the night, therefore, the violence of the furious fire subsided.

### [XXII.] Fire falling from heaven foretells the destruction of the Turks.

Moreover, the defenders of the fortress were tormenting our men most cruelly. They struck those who were in the city, exhausted by continual pressure and famine, both by day and by night; and nothing separated the two armies except spears and swords. Seeing, therefore, that they were being held in an unceasing struggle and that, even if every supply of provisions were available to them, no opportunity at all was granted them for eating or drinking [Col. 0763D], our men began building a fortress between themselves and the enemy with cement and stone, and hastened to surround it with numerous engines, so that they might thereafter be somewhat safer.

Some of the Turks remained in the fortress and were accustomed to provoke our men almost every moment with attacks; another group lodged in the field near the fortress. On the following night, therefore, the appearance of a fire slipped down from heaven from the western region and descended by falling into the enemy camp. This event presented a very remarkable miracle to both sides. But when morning grew bright, the Turks withdrew as quickly as they could from the place where the heavenly flame had fallen, and pitched their camp before the gate that Bohemond had occupied. If they had understood it, that portent plainly seemed to announce the destruction that was threatening them [Col. 0764A].

The townsmen, moreover, who were attacking our army with frequent incursions, pressed upon our men’s wounds and deaths almost without any interval of time, with bows drawn. Those who had surrounded the city from outside and covered the territory adjoining the walls far and wide had blocked all the city’s entrances with such vigilant guard that no one could go out or enter anywhere except at night, and then only secretly.

For the enemy had gathered there in such numbers and with such luxury that everywhere nothing seemed visible except men and tents, costly furnishings, the splendor of various garments, and herds of cattle and livestock for provisions. In addition came wives adorned, so to speak, in the likeness of a temple; and, moreover, to complete their ostentation, maidens bearing quivers and bows arrived, so that a new likeness of the ancient Diana might be seen in them. They seemed to have gathered not for the purpose of waging war, but rather under the pretext of making a display.

It is plainly asserted by those who took part that, after the greater battle had been fought, even newly born infants were found lying abandoned in the grass in the middle of the open ground. Their mothers had given birth to them during the very preparations for the expedition, while they hurried forward because of the urgent pursuit by the Franks and, unable to endure delay and the burden, rid themselves of them—carelessly casting them away because they feared more for themselves than for the children.

### [XXIII.] The besieged suffer the greatest scarcity of food.

In this manner, then, as we have said [Col. 0764C], with the Turks preventing our men from coming out on every side and all outside provision of necessities being entirely denied them, the dangers of famine spread through almost the whole army, and the cruel excess of starvation afflicted the hearts of all the poorer men.

When the Franks, while besieging Antioch, had deprived the citizens of every supply of food that could be gathered, they found the resources within the captured city all the more restricted, because the besiegers themselves kept more careful guard lest the Turks fortify themselves against them. At last, when everything useful for consumption had been exhausted, a small loaf of bread was bought for one Byzantine coin.

The scarcity of grain and the meagerness of seasoning, after producing extreme distress everywhere, deprived many of life, as they swelled from want [Col. 0764D]. I need say nothing about drinking wine, for it had generally disappeared from everyone’s lips. Indeed, the man who had nothing to eat would drink anything.

With the proper accompaniment of food now failing, scarcely anyone hesitated to eat horseflesh. Many were saddened by the frequent meat-stalls and by the small number of donkeys, sought out and bought at a higher price. A chicken was sold for fifteen solidi, an egg for two, and a nut for a denarius. For wherever there was a multitude of people and a shortage of every kind of food, it necessarily followed that everything there was expensive.

Figs, cardoons, and vine leaves had become ingredients of stews. People had already ceased looking for fruit on the trees. In place of vegetables, various cooked preparations of every kind of leaf were used. The flesh of horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, and buffaloes was carried away for food by wealthy persons; but their dried hides, cut into pieces like cuttlefish and boiled while being cooked over a long fire, provided the poorest people with an exceptionally careful cuisine [Col. 0765A].

### [XXIV.]

Let the besieged cities of every nation be read about, and let the whole body of ancient histories be reviewed: what peoples shall we be able to find who, exiles from their ancestral land, could have remained so steadfast and hardened amid such great want?

Certainly, if the famous siege of Troy lasting ten years is brought forward, we repeatedly acknowledge that truces offering reciprocal security were granted here and there, during which the sharpness of blunted forces was restored and an abundance of pay was supplied through the cooperation of land and sea [Col. 0765B]. And if some besieged people somewhere ever happened to endure the dangers of famine, they surely endured it in defense of liberty, since “the defense of body and homeland must be placed before absolutely all other things.”

These men, driven from their native soil not by any desire to possess more, but rather under the pretext of acting for God, endured—in order to remove the injuries done to the churches of God—the miseries of food, sleeping, watches, cold, and rain, together with the anguish of unceasing fear, such as no one has heard or read that any peoples ever suffered.

And what is recognized as the greater miracle: while they were still within their own borders, they scarcely endured tents for three days in the army of their own king, even when they were not compelled to leave the province. [Col. 0765C] No one, I think, who was subjected to that danger existed who could recall the anxieties of mind and torments of body that happened to them there.

This ordeal lasted for twenty-six consecutive days.

## CHAPTER VI

### [XXV.] What Count Stephen of Blois did outside Antioch.

At that time Count Stephen of Blois, formerly a man of great moderation and wise counsel, whom the whole army had chosen as its commander, claiming that he was held by a serious illness, had withdrawn, before the entrance to Antioch had been opened to our men, into a certain small town which is said to have been called Alexandriola.

After the city had been captured [Col. 0765D] and besieged again, when he learned that the Christian counts inside the city were being pressed by terrible calamities, he delayed until this point—whether from necessity or from choice—giving assistance to those who were awaiting it.

But when he learned that swarms of Turks had settled before the city walls, he proceeded craftily toward the mountains and observed what forces the enemy possessed. When he saw the countryside covered with countless tents, moved by human reasoning, he withdrew, judging that no human power could help those shut up in the city. For he was a man free from all frivolity, fleeing cowardice and outstanding in his love of truth. Since he judged that he could in no way help them, and did not doubt that they would die, as the circumstances showed, he thought that, if he looked after himself meanwhile, he was doing nothing worthy of infamy [Col. 0766A], provided that he reserved himself for a more opportune time.

And certainly I consider his flight—if it corrected an indecorous act by the repayment of martyrdom—much better than the perseverance of those whose return led them into the depths of every kind of filth and crime; although perhaps it ought not to be called flight, since, as is said, a genuine illness could be alleged.

Who would say that Count Stephen and Hugh the Great were comparable to certain of those who persevered, merely because the former seemed to have returned, when their integrity had always been so great? The conclusion of the execution of this matter for which they are accused became so clear that secure praise can now be sung about them; but the life of the others should be the shame of all good men.

Let us consider those who boast of the captivity of Jerusalem because they were present there, and we shall see [Col. 0766B] that, in crimes, betrayals, and perjuries, none of them allows himself to be second to anyone else.

The beginning and end of these men are proved to give off the fragrance of integrity. The others, “because they saw Jerusalem and the tomb, think that thereafter they may safely persist in crimes,” and reproach holy men for returning in comparison with themselves; nor do they consider that the end of those whom they suppose to be stained by countless crimes ought to be proclaimed.

But let us set these matters aside and attend to the thread of the narrative we began.

### [XXVI.] Count Stephen reaches the city called Philomena.

Departing, therefore, from his town of Alexandriola, that count reached the city called Philomena. The tyrannical emperor had already been informed that Antioch had been captured, and he was hastening there with many forces, judging that he would undoubtedly recover it from the Franks [Col. 0766C].

### The emperor is known to persecute the Franks out of hatred.

When the count met the exceedingly eager prince, and the latter questioned him about the condition of the Christian army and the betrayed city, the count certainly did not conceal that the city had been captured; but he stated that the Turks still held the fortress.

“But, alas!” he said, “the joy of having obtained the city has been disturbed by a renewed siege, since those who had previously besieged the Turks are now, in a pitiful reversal, surrounded by the Turks. I do not know, however, how they have fared since I withdrew from there.”

The count communicated these things privately to the prince. But when the emperor heard them and fell from the hope on which he had relied, he summoned Guido, Bohemond’s brother [Col. 0766D], a man distinguished for military vigor, along with certain others, and disclosed the situation to him as much worse than the count had reported it.

“What do you decide must be done?” he said. “The Franks are being pressed by a most savage siege of the Turks; or perhaps they have already fallen beneath their swords, or even been scattered through various provinces and condemned to the yoke of perpetual captivity. Since, therefore, no power or opportunity seems available to us for bringing them aid—and especially since, if we advance farther, we must fear that we shall perish when the Turks meet us—if this seems suitable to your prudence, let us turn back.”

As he said this, the most treacherous man was undoubtedly rejoicing, because he had heard that those whom he hated with no less envy than the Turks had perished.

### [XXVII.]

When Guido heard of the danger facing his brother Bohemond and the Franks, both he and his household and companions lamented with the most violent cries. Having already taken up, as they thought deservedly, the boldness of quarrelling even against the Lord himself, they complained, saying:

“Almighty God, whose judgment never deviates from what is right, who in no way leaves the scepters of sinners over the lot of the just: why have you exposed to the swords of wicked men a people who had abandoned parents, wives, children, distinguished honors, and their native soil—or rather, who for desire of you had daily surrendered themselves to crosses and death—without the assistance of your protection?

“If it should prove true that you have allowed them to be handed over by profane hands to the destruction of slaughter, whom will you henceforth find willing to obey your commands, when everyone must now judge that you are powerless to defend your own people? But so be it. If you wished them to be killed for your sake, you will crown them with glory and honor. Certainly, even if you bestowed upon them kingdoms multiplied a hundredfold, you would nevertheless have made a man of your faith, and the stirring-up of his head, a perpetual reproach among the nations.

“You have thrust the whole world of the Christian name into the pit of extreme despair and unbelief, while you have granted the most wicked of men unanswerable boldness against your own people forever. There will no longer be anyone who presumes anything great about you, when he sees those who thought they served you more specially than all mortals brought down by so shameful an end.

“Tell us, therefore, most merciful one: with what face will your people henceforth call upon you [al., invoke you], when they await such ends for your people?”

This and other expressions of anxiety and dreadful lamentation [Col. 0768A] were brought forth by the fiercest grief, to such an extent that throughout the entire army led by that tyrant scarcely any bishop, abbot, cleric, or layman dared invoke God for several days, being overwhelmed by the excess of their astonishment.

Guido, recalling his brother’s unity of spirit and the magnanimity of so great a prince, repeated the man’s finest qualities with pitiful emphasis and gave voice to his innermost sorrow through many cries.

Moreover, as the emperor was preparing to return, fearing that, once the obstacle presented by the Franks had been broken, the Turks would soon wander freely everywhere, he ordered the men serving under him:

“Go,” he said, “and by imperial edict compel the people of this entire region; lay waste to all the places of Bulgaria [Col. 0768B], so that when the Turks roam about to devastate our provinces, they may find nothing there that is useful.”

Thus, willingly or unwillingly, those Christians who had been hastening to join our men were compelled to return with the emperor. The soldiers hurried to fulfill the tyrannical command; the foot soldiers followed the army by forced service, and, while striving to keep up with the speed of the cavalry, they plunged themselves into an inescapable impediment of weakness.

Everywhere, unable to endure such labor, they collapsed, and while traveling countless numbers of them succumbed, seized by illness. Finally, when the tyrant returned to the city of Constantinople, each of the others returned through Greece to the places from which they had come.

Here, then, let this little book come to an end.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0767]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0767C]

When, with God as author, we read of wars carried out in the authentic histories of the holy Fathers, and consider that such things happened through the almost nonexistent faith of such small numbers of men—not that we call the most blessed Joshua, David, and Samuel “small,” but because, apart from their merit and that of the others whose glory the Church of God has proclaimed down to our own time [Col. 0767D]—we regard as contemptible the vanity of the Jewish people—most wretched of men, serving their bellies alone instead of God; were reason not to stand in the way, we might consider them more pleasing to God than these men, whose entire service had been spiritual.

For the former, protected only from idolatry, had everything turn out favorably: frequent victories and great abundance. For the latter, however, victory came with difficulty; while they were conquering, losses were frequent; wealth was rare; and continual, indeed most cruel, poverty prevailed, even though they were leading a life that was not military but monastic, insofar as it concerned frugality and holiness.

Reason most pleasing to us explains all this when we attend to the words: “God chastises every son whom he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). To those from whom he withdraws temporal things with the severity of discipline, he arranges spiritual things with the affection of eternal sweetness [Col. 0768C].

### [I.] The lance found, as recorded in chapter 4 of the preceding book. Peter the Hermit is sent to the Turks.

After the words of that Peter, through whom we said that the revelation of the Lord’s lance had been made by Blessed Andrew, the Christian people grew strong with great rejoicing and emerged from the depths of despair at the sight of the great event for which they had been waiting [Col. 0768D].

At the indication of that man, everyone ran to the place he had designated, and an excavation was ordered to be made in the church of Blessed Peter beside the Lord’s altar. After thirteen men had been bringing out earth from the first light until evening, the man himself found the lance.

When everyone saw that what had happened corresponded in every respect with the vision they had heard about, they conceived great joy, and no lesser joy at the prospect of now facing every enemy’s boldness. Having taken up the lance in this manner, they carried it out with immense glory, and from that day began confidently to make plans for waging war.

Finally, while the leaders of the Christian army, having assembled in council, were considering by common agreement what ought to be done, they decided that before fighting they should first approach the Turks through a formal embassy, so that the Turks might desist from occupying Christian territory and might not wish to make Christ’s servants exiles or condemn them to death, but remain within their own region, content with their own boundary.

They therefore summoned that Peter, the hermit well known at the beginning of this undertaking, and assigned to him a certain Herluin, an interpreter skilled in both languages. They sent both men to the pagan prince and gave them the substance of their speech.

When they had reached that gentile’s tent and, having been admitted, stood before the dreadful sight of the diabolical man, they spoke in the following manner.

### [II.]

“You should know that the minds of our princes have been greatly astonished that you have begun so irreverently and wickedly to enter and usurp land which, from ancient times, was possessed in solid freedom by the Christian name [Col. 0769B].

“Since you have certainly known, from the frequency of the victories we have heard about against you, that Christ’s power has in no way failed, and since you have experienced how little strength you possess against him, they in no way think that, having so often been driven back in battle, you would dare to repeat the madness of fighting against God.

“Therefore, we now unanimously judge that your wisdom has gathered here for no other reason than that, through the Christian bishops who are with us, you may be instructed in the doctrine of our faith. For we know beyond doubt that you care nothing for your salvation, but [al., if] are attempting wars against Catholic belief.

“We therefore ask you, in concern for your ignorance, to cease from this presumption, knowing that Blessed Peter the Apostle, by God’s grant, claims for himself that Church of which he knows himself to be the first bishop; and, through our ministry, although we are sinners, he intends to restore it to the worship of God, in which he instructed it.”

“Your princes also grant with the utmost generosity that you may retain all the property you have brought with you. If you depart peacefully, none of our men will attempt to inflict any injury upon you.”

But Curbaran, inwardly wounded by the magnificence of Peter’s words, while the Turks who stood nearby were now raging with savage pride after hearing them, said:

### [III.]

“We shall prove that the land which you say has been subject from ancient times to your Christianity is ours and is owed to us by every right, especially since we have taken it from a nation scarcely equal to women through our marvelous valor [Col. 0769D].

“Moreover, we consider it evidence of immense foolishness that you, coming from the farthest ends of the earth, threaten us concerning our own possessions—or rather, that with the full deployment of your strength you attempt to drive us from our seats—when you possess neither wealth, nor arms, nor numbers sufficient to accomplish this.

“As for the Christian name, we not only do not accept it, but reject it with the most abrupt contempt.

“To end briefly what you have brought us: you who are carrying out the embassy, return quickly to your princes and tell them this: If they desire to become like us in our condition and to deny Christ, toward whom they seem inclined, we will give them not merely this province but also land of greater wealth and extent [Col. 0770A]. We will freely distribute these castles and cities to them, suffer none of them to remain foot soldiers, but make all of them horsemen; and when we have rites equally indifferent, we shall rejoice equally in mutual friendship and proximity.

“But if they decide to depart from the judgment they have proposed, they will undoubtedly soon encounter the destruction of an unwelcome death or undergo the exile of eternal captivity, serving both us and our descendants throughout the ages.”

He said this, and the embassy quickly returned; everything was reported to the leaders of the Christian army.

## CHAPTER II

### [IV.] The Christians take refuge in God through pious exercises.

The army, therefore, being placed in the greatest straits, harassed on one side by cruel famine and on the other gnawed by dreadful fear of the pagans who had entirely surrounded it [Col. 0770B], finally turning to divine assistance, celebrated three-day fasts under the direction of the distinguished Bishop of Le Puy.

They carried supplicatory litanies from church to church, cleansed themselves through sincere confession of sins, and, having subsequently received absolution from a bishop or priest, received the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood with complete faith. Each person gave alms according to his ability, and everywhere they entreated that divine sacrifices be offered on their behalf.

Finally, having gained security from these observances, they proposed battle, and immediately arranged six battle-lines within the city.

### [V.] The battle-lines are arranged for combat.

In the first battle-line—namely, among those who would receive the first force and blows of the Turks [Col. 0770C]—stood Hugh, truly great in accordance with the quality of his name, with the entire Frankish army joined to his command, and, besides the others, the Count of Flanders.

I heard concerning this same nobleman that, before battle was undertaken, his steward had purchased a camel’s foot for him at no small price, since he had been unable to find anything more suitable for his food. This lord had been so weakened by the scarcity of provisions that he could scarcely ride. When it was suggested to him that he should not go out to battle but should remain in the city, perhaps with those besieging the fortress, he replied eagerly:

“Far from it! I shall certainly go, and would that I might there meet a blessed death together with those who are to die!”

### [VI.]

In the second battle-line, the outstanding Duke Godfrey [Col. 0770D] was stationed with his army. Count Robert formed the third with his Northmen’s contingent. The fourth was commanded by the distinguished bishop of Le Puy, carrying with him the lance that had recently been found belonging to the Savior. This line consisted of his own retinue and that of Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles.

Raymond himself remained in the city in order to attack the fortress and prevent the townsmen from rushing into the city. Tancred was in the fifth battle-line with his army. In the sixth, Bohemond came last with his own troops.

### [VII.] The ecclesiastics go before them dressed in sacred vestments.

The bishops, presbyters, clerics, and monks, adorned in ecclesiastical garments, proceeded ahead together with crosses, striving to aid those about to fight with tearful prayers; they too awaited the gift of martyrdom if it should happen that their own people were cut down [Col. 0771A].

Some watched the outcome of the battle from the height of the walls, displaying the signs of the Lord’s cross in their hands and marking with them the army proceeding from there.

In the order we have described, they advanced through the gate before their temple, which our men call the Mahomery, so slowly and cautiously that even for any sick old woman it would scarcely have seemed necessary to adopt a more measured pace.

Almighty God, with what cries of the soul were you called upon there! As the bodies of some wasted away from prolonged hunger, the distress of their wretched hearts rose with irresistible force, from the urgency of fear, into your highest ears [Col. 0771B]. With what anxieties was the mind then driven within the remaining body! And when weakness compelled them to despair of victory, the only thing considered in everyone’s mind was pious endurance for your sake, O God.
