Their hearts were shaken by grief, and the dryness of tears beat upon heads drained by long famine. As the substance of the outward person failed, the violence of spiritual desires resounded.

Good God, what could you deny to devotions of this kind, when you saw—or rather caused—men burning with such fires? For when I consider in them, on the outside, military ferocity, but inwardly, the modesty of martyrdom outweighing all else, I judge and maintain that through all the ages no army had shown equal steadfastness in either respect.

I would truly say that these men then cried out to heaven; I confess that these men sounded forth upon sacred trumpets. They were exercising themselves not through strength of bodily power but through the singular boldness of the mind.

### [VIII.] Curbaran mocks the Christians; nevertheless, struck by fear, he considers flight.

Meanwhile Curbaran saw them coming out. When he noticed one group following another in slow departures, he mocked what he thought to be their small number:

“Let those who are coming out proceed,” he said, “so that, when they flee, they may be more effectively prevented from returning to the city.”

But when the entire army had passed beyond the gates, Curbaran looked upon the Frankish people, powerful in order and number, and only then was he terrified. Immediately, wavering already over flight, he ordered the commander of his household that, if he saw a fire being kindled at the first part of the camp, he should immediately announce by herald throughout the scattered enemy that the Frankish column had won trophies.

Meanwhile Curbaran began gradually to draw back, making for the mountains, while our men pressed upon their pursuit without yielding.

Moreover, the Turks divided themselves through needless cleverness. Some moved about near the sea; another part waited motionless for the Franks who were advancing, thinking that our men could be enclosed by such an encirclement.

When our men noticed this, with a kind of presumptuous boldness they likewise separated themselves from the others, forming a concentrated line against them. By this insolence of theirs, however, they alone caused damage to our army that day, since scarcely any of their foot soldiers escaped alive apart from a few horsemen.

The instigator of this rashness, together with certain others, was one of our men named Clarembald of Vendoilo, who was extremely famous among them but accomplished nothing useful in those provinces.

### The Christians join battle.

Meanwhile, a seventh battle-line was formed against those by the sea from two battle-lines—namely, those of Duke Godfrey and the Count of Normandy—and a certain Count Rainald was placed in command of it.

There the fighting was at its fiercest that day, for they killed many of our men with showers of arrows. From the river Pharphar, however, the enemy cavalry extended as far as the mountains, which were separated from one another by a distance of two miles.

The pagan phalanxes therefore sprang forward from both sides and pierced with arrows and javelins the Frankish column, which our men had placed against the first attacks of the Turks as though it were the stronger [Col. 0772B].

But Hugh the Magnificent, of kingly spirit and not fallen away from his ancestral magnanimity, cried out to those beneath him amid the enemy’s missiles:

“Endure,” he said, “and await the second and third blows boldly, because these men will soon withdraw.”

### [IX.] Christ fights on their behalf.

And behold, innumerable forces began to emerge from the mountains. Their horses and standards shone with great whiteness. At the sight of them, immense astonishment grew among our men, who feared that they were coming to assist the opposing side, until they learned that the assistance of Christ had been visibly granted to them.

They thought that the leaders of these forces were the glorious martyrs who had followed the military life: George, Mercurius, and Demetrius [Col. 0772C]. Many of our men saw these things, and when they reported them together with other matters they had witnessed, they were believed with complete faith, as was fitting.

If it is recorded that, long ago, when the Maccabees were fighting for circumcision and pork, an evident heavenly aid appeared to them, how much more ought it to have appeared to these men, who, for the purification of the churches and the propagation of the state of the faith, offered to Christ the service of their shed blood!

Those first enemies, therefore, who had taken their position on the side of the sea, unable to withstand so great an obstacle from our people, set fire to piles of brushwood, thereby signaling flight to those who were guarding the tents while the battle was being fought.

Moved by that signal, the latter took flight after plundering the most valuable things. The Franks, however, once they had recognized their own superior strength [Col. 0772D], made for the enemy’s tents.

### What the Turks customarily do while fighting.

Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, and Hugh the Great attacked with joined efforts those who were riding alongside the riverbank. These three men, together with their followers, keeping before their eyes the Son of God crucified for them, plunged bravely into the entire multitude of the enemy.

When the rest of our army saw this, they too threw themselves with all their courage into the opposing lines. From the other side, the enemy multitude also rushed forward, shouting with intolerable fury.

Their custom when drawn up in battle is to produce endless crashes with bronze pipes, which they use in place of spear-shafts, with the clanging of cymbals, and with terrifying cries [Col. 0773A], so that horses and men can scarcely withstand the terror of such a great sound.

But at that time none of their efforts availed; their endeavors were completely emptied of power. Once our men had begun the battle, they routed the enemy in the first clash, and they were quickly driven toward the flight they had long had in mind.

Our men nevertheless pursued them relentlessly through the middle of their camps. They were not snatched away by desire for the spoils lying here and there, preferring to feed solely upon the blood of Christ’s enemies.

They pursued them as far as the bridge of Pharphar and as far as Tancred’s castle. Thus, when the enemy withdrew, the field was occupied by the great glory of the spoils. There stood tents rich in gold, silver, and very many ornaments, though empty of people; sheep, goats, and cattle were scattered everywhere; there were abundant supplies of horses, mules, and donkeys; and provisions of grain, wine, and flour had been heaped together without order [Col. 0773B].

### The Turks made an attack. — The Christians give thanks to Christ and enter the city in triumph. — But the Syrian and Armenian settlers who were living in those regions, learning that an unexpected victory had fallen to the Franks, presented themselves everywhere in the path of the fleeing Turks, hastened into the mountains, and killed everyone they caught.

Our men, moreover, returning and rendering immeasurable praises with immense joy of heart to Christ, their fellow-worker, entered the city with the honor of heavenly triumph. But the man who was in charge of the city’s garrison, seeing the commander of the army turn his back while our men pressed forward, trembled utterly. And realizing that the defense of the fortress would henceforth be less secure for him, he requested, without delay, the standard of one of our princes.

The Count of Saint-Gilles, who was nearby where this was being requested, quickly ordered his own standard to be handed to the petitioner. When the latter had received it, he fixed it upon the tower. But the Lombards, jealous of all the others in their favor toward Bohemond—for they relied upon his patronage—shouted to the commander of that fortress: “This standard,” they said, “is not Bohemond’s.”

When the commander asked whose it was and learned that it belonged to the Count of Saint-Gilles, he took it down and returned it to the count. After requesting and receiving Bohemond’s standard, he also received security: among those who were with him in the town, if any wished to join our faith, they would have permission to remain with Bohemond; otherwise, they could depart without any harm to themselves.

Thus, when the fortress had been surrendered to Bohemond’s authority and men had been brought in, at his direction, to guard the town, after a few days the man who had handed over the fortress received baptism, together with any others who had preferred to associate themselves with the Christian name. Those who wished to adhere to their own laws were allowed to do so freely, and they were escorted as far as the land of the Saracens under Bohemond’s protection.

[X.] This battle was fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, on the eve of the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, who pitied the misery of that city and could not endure the destruction of its new citizens—those peoples who had expelled the nations that had polluted the holy temple of God. They rightly ought to have pitied those whom both apostles had taught by preaching.

Indeed, in the churches stables were being established for horses, and in part of the very principal basilica of blessed Peter they had erected a house for their Muhammad. At last, when the defeated enemies fled here and there, the mountains and valleys, fields and groves, paths and trackless places were filled with some half-dead, others dead, and countless wounded.

Then, visited by God’s sudden mercy, they swiftly exchanged the calamity of prolonged famine for prosperity, so that where an egg had previously been sold for two solidi, an ox could scarcely be sold for twelve denarii. To conclude briefly: where the fury of starvation had raged, such abundance of money and of every kind of food arrived that, as though by a sudden emergence, every fullness of goods seemed to arise everywhere, and the Lord seemed to have opened the cataracts of heaven.

There were so many tents that, after each of our men had plundered the shelters and all had been enriched, and after they had already grown weary of the bundles of booty, scarcely could anyone be found to carry it away. Nor, when a poor man had taken possession of something, did any richer newcomer inflict violence upon him; rather, each yielded to the other without dispute.

## CHAPTER III

### [XI.] The Christian leaders offer Antioch to the emperor.

After this, our princes—the Duke Godfrey, the Count of Saint-Gilles, Bohemond, the Count of Normandy, Robert of Flanders, and all the others—having taken counsel together, sent Hugh the Great, Count Baldwin of the Mounts, and several other men of illustrious name to the emperor, so that he might receive the city of Antioch and fulfill what he had promised our men.

They did indeed set out, but afterward delayed returning to those by whom they had been sent. For, in a certain place, they were overtaken by Turks whose horses were ready at hand. They escaped, while those who were farther away were either carried off as captives or met their end by the sword. It is still not at all clear to us what misfortune befell the Count of the Mounts.

As for Hugh the Great, some think that the following was the reason why he wished to avoid returning. Although otherwise endowed with immense vigor, in securing what were thought sufficient supplies for the needs of so great a man he showed himself less diligent. Thus, a man honorably accustomed to refinement, he feared suffering want among those who were either more miserly or more energetic in acquiring such provisions—men to whom he was either superior or in no respect second.

Yet no one ought justly to have complained about his return, since later, making this same return once more, he fell—destined to be distinguished by the name of martyr and always excellent soldier.

### [XII.] They deliberate concerning the journey to Jerusalem. Various raids by Raymond against the Turks.

Not long afterward, finally, they discussed how the journey to Jerusalem, for which they had endured so much and toward which they had striven so earnestly, might be brought to completion, and how the same people, who desired it most passionately, might meanwhile be governed until the undertaking could be carried out.

The nobles had clearly realized that in that region there was much lack of water during the summer season. For this reason, the departure was judged to be postponed until the Kalends of November. Meanwhile, since everyone agreed to this plan, the senior leaders of the army divided themselves among the cities and towns that they had distributed and acquired for themselves, and ordered heralds everywhere among the peoples subject to them to proclaim that anyone in need should attach himself to the more powerful under an agreement of payment.

Among the others was a knight of the military order, outstanding above all in the practice of arms and belonging to the foremost retainers of the Count of Saint-Gilles. His name was Raymond, surnamed Pilitus, and very many cavalrymen and infantrymen joined him.

Thus, with many men gathering to him both because of his generosity and because of his natural resourcefulness, and with a considerable army assembled, he entered the land of the Saracens and attacked a fortress called Talamania. The townspeople, however, being Syrians, were immediately received by the aforesaid man through their own voluntary surrender.

While he remained within that same town for eight days, he was informed that not far away there was a Saracen fortress crowded with an innumerable multitude. As they rushed to storm it with the swiftest assault, God entered into the matter and it was subdued. After the inhabitants had been seized, those who consented to receive the Christian sacraments were spared unharmed; those who refused were killed.

When this had been accomplished, they returned to Talamania, giving thanks to God. On the third day after departing from there, they made for a city called Maarrat, exceedingly fierce in its fortifications and proud in the concentration of various peoples.

It was adjacent to the fortress mentioned above, and from the surrounding camps and cities—especially Aleph, the cesspool of the Saracens and Turks—a great crowd had flowed into it. A mass of pagans advanced to meet them, prepared to fight; and our men, thinking that they could engage them in battle in the customary manner, were deceived by their swift withdrawal.

Nevertheless, those same enemies, coming out repeatedly, did not cease provoking our men. Thus the entire day passed, occupied by alternating attacks and counterattacks on both sides.

At last, when the heat was scorching our men and the innards of everyone were cracking from unusual dryness and thirst, with no remedy available, they decided to pitch their tents beside the same city that night.

But when the townspeople perceived that our men were wavering to some extent—for the Syrians were the first to begin preparing for flight—they became more fiercely emboldened against them by the cowardice they had observed and no longer feared pressing the attack.

Harassed by this assault, very many surrendered their souls to God, driven out by zeal for piety. This is recognized as having been the final day of those men, the fifth day of the month of July.

The Franks who survived returned to Talamania and remained there for many days with their leader Raymond. Those who stayed at Antioch, meanwhile, lived in great tranquility and abundance.

### [XIII.] Aimar, bishop of Le Puy, departs this life.

But God, by a hidden dispensation unknown to us, immediately disturbed their serenity with the darkest cloud. For the man who had governed them, who had most devotedly cherished them inwardly and outwardly, a man esteemed by God and the world—the bishop Aimar of Le Puy—fell ill. The Almighty, in his most generous mercy, determined to wipe away for him the labors of pious toil with the Sabbath-rest of perpetual repose.

Accordingly, he died on the feast called the Chains of Saint Peter. He found the one to whom belong the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the powers of binding and loosing, and he deserved to be admitted by him as an introducer through the heavenly gates.

At once, throughout Christ’s entire army, there arose an excess of the sharpest grief and sorrow. As each person recounted the frequent acts of kindness of that most merciful man, people mourned inconsolably, while no relief was expected.

The outcry of the princes themselves at his funeral was so great and so heartfelt that it seemed as though a general destruction had been announced to them. So much money was offered at his bier, before he had even been buried, by the entire people whom he had governed as a father, that, as I believe, no one anywhere had ever seen so much carried to any altar in the same span of time.

All of this was immediately distributed to the poor for the sake of his soul. While he lived, he had cared for them with such concern that he continually impressed upon the rich above all else that they should love the needy and devote themselves to acts of mercy toward them, declaring that the poor were the guardians of their own lives.

### Aimar’s excellent sayings concerning the relief of the sufferings of the needy

> [Note: [Col. 0775D] Aimar’s sayings are missing in the Reims manuscript.]
>
> “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy. For unless you extend the embrace of humanity to your inferiors—who are nevertheless your equals by sharing the same nature—and unless you share with them what you know was created by God alike for you and for them, though seized by you unequally, you will undoubtedly close against yourselves the door of divine mercy.
>
> “Refresh, I say, those whose favor sustains you with portions of your possessions. Be certain that just as they cannot live in time without you, so you cannot live eternally without them.”

The remarkable man recalled these and similar sayings to them in frequent exhortations.

## CHAPTER IV

### [XIV.] Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, captures the city of Albara and arranges for a bishop to be placed over it.

Then Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, entered the provinces of the Saracens and led his army to a certain city called Albara. As soon as he laid hands upon it, he captured it and killed all the Saracens and women whom he found there.

Having immediately subdued it, he restored it, as best he could, with faithful settlers. After consulting prudent men, he judged that a bishop ought to be appointed to the city, one who would gradually instruct the pagans in the teachings of the faith of Christ and, after first purifying their temples, administer the ministries of piety and the mysteries of rebirth.

They therefore chose a man suitable in age and commendable in learning and brought him to Antioch for consecration. Once instituted as bishop, he did not on that account neglect the expedition to Jerusalem. Rather, after appointing a certain man who had voluntarily offered himself for this duty as commander of the city’s garrison, he departed with the others.

The latter, displaying there a very unusual boldness, had taken only a very few companions, since the poverty of the revenues required it, and began to hold the city’s citadel. Since the place was now becoming deserted by the Saracens, the very few pagans who remained submitted themselves to his authority and provided him with revenues from their own labor, merely so that he would allow them to live.

### [XV.] Dispute between Bohemond and Raymond concerning possession of the city of Antioch.

Meanwhile, since the Antiochenes were flourishing in abundance and prosperity on every side, the feast of All Saints was approaching, the date set for renewing the expedition. Suddenly the princes, mindful of their purpose, gathered together at Antioch and began to seek counsel from one another as to how they might more quickly carry out the journey for which they had come.

Before the army of the Lord set out, Bohemond opened negotiations concerning the surrender to him of the city that they had agreed upon. But the Count of Saint-Gilles in no way gave his consent to Bohemond, fearing the oath he had sworn to the emperor.

Therefore the nobles, proceeding between the two men as mediators, repeatedly assembled in the church of blessed Peter. Bohemond stated that, since the city had been betrayed to him by Pyrrus, all its territories had been granted to him through the generosity of the princes themselves.

The Count of Saint-Gilles, on the other hand, replied that he had bound himself by oath to restore the city to the prince of Constantinople, while preserving the fulfillment of the agreements made with him—and that all this had been done on Bohemond’s advice.

Meanwhile the bishops who had undertaken to settle the dispute, after summoning Duke Godfrey, the Counts of Flanders and Normandy, and adding the other elders, withdrew separately. They heard each man’s statement separately, intending, after examining the matter through a comparison of the arguments, to deliver judgment.

But after weighing the statements of the disputants, and appearing to favor neither side in the matter, they returned to the assembly and, fearing to offend such great men, postponed judgment.

When the count himself realized that this had been done deliberately, he said:

> “Let us not allow the present dispute to generate disorder among Christ’s faithful, nor let the freedom of the Lord’s sepulcher appear to be delayed. Let us not be judged blameworthy on either side because of the stain of greed. I declare that I shall submit to the judgment of my peers, the princes who are present—except for the matter that you, brothers and lords who are here, know I unwillingly promised to the prince of Constantinople.”

Without delay, Bohemond himself agreed to words of this kind. Thus both men, with every dispute now set aside, placed their right hands in the hands of the bishops in pledge of faith, asserting most firmly that the army of God would in no way henceforth be disturbed by their quarrels.

Bohemond therefore, after taking counsel, fortified a mountain fortress with men and provisions. The Count of Saint-Gilles likewise consulted with his own men about filling with abundant supplies the palace of Cassian, which in the native language they call Admiravisus, and the tower that overlooked the bridge gate, on the side, namely, of the port of Saint-Simeon.

## CHAPTER V

### [XVI.] Description of the city of Antioch. The bishop distinguished by the honor of the patriarchate. He has one hundred and fifty-three bishops under him.

Antioch had been under siege for eight months and one day.

### Concerning the unfortunate death of Pyrrus

The city of Antioch is incomparably beautiful, second to none in the grandeur of its buildings, pleasing in its situation, blessed with a temperate climate, fertile in vineyards, and rich in the abundance of its territory.

On the eastern side it is enclosed by the heights of four mountains. On the western side, the river called the Pharpar, well known from sacred Scripture (2 Kings 5:12), washes its walls with waters exceedingly rich in fish.

On the highest of the mountains a castle rises, worthy of wonder, but yet more remarkable for its impregnable security. Below it lies a city filled with every glory, still proud among its nobles of the monuments of its ancient splendor, and encompassing within its circuit three hundred and sixty churches.

The bishop of the city, distinguished by the honor of the patriarchate through apostolic succession, is elevated by privilege over one hundred and fifty-three bishops attached to him.

The city is surrounded by a double wall: one of moderate size, the other incredibly broad and unusually high, built of stone and furnished with enormous blocks. Four hundred and fifty towers are set around it with imposing grandeur.

Jerome, in the fifth book of his commentary on Isaiah, reports that the city of Riblah, where King Nebuchadnezzar put out the eyes of King Zedekiah and killed his sons, is this Antioch.

It is said, however, that it was founded by that earlier Antiochus, whose power has left many monuments, and constructed through the cooperation of fifty subordinate kings, whom its municipal records also name, with such outstanding defenses and such variety of buildings.

This, however, is false, since Pompeius Trogus most truthfully states that it was founded by King Seleucus under his father’s name and subsequently enlarged by that king or by his successors, just as he founded Laodicea under the name of his mother Laodice, and Seleucia from his own name.

No siege engines or ballistae of any kind could accomplish anything against this city. If Pyrrus’s betrayal had not assisted the besiegers—indeed, if God had not assisted them through those whom he chose—Frankish courage would have suffered in vain the hardships of hunger and all the other miseries there.

Our men remained there, pressing the besieged city, for eight months and one day.

### [XVII.]

Afterward they themselves were confined there for three weeks, while an innumerable host of pagans gathered against them. Once they had finally overcome those enemies, they remained there again for five months and eight days, while that same people were being urged by their princes to go to Jerusalem.

But since the memory of the aforementioned Pyrrus seems to me unlikely to have any further place later on, I must explain what end he met.

Bohemond had plainly professed Christianity after receiving the sacraments and had taken his name in the sacred font from the man who received him. He had served as a companion and fellow-worker to our men during the siege of Jerusalem, and after its capture he had returned to Antioch.

There he issued a proclamation that anyone in the city or its vicinity who was in need should come with him to his more distant homeland, where he possessed many estates. He promised to enrich each person with splendid gifts. By this hope he gathered an immense crowd around himself, and is said to have led them away, deceived, into the region he had mentioned.

When he reached his own towns, he betrayed some of the soldiers accompanying him to exile and others to death. If word of the treachery had not reached the others, whose great number had been lodged outside the fortress, and if they had not been able to escape or hide through a pitiable flight, the freedom of all would have perished either by the sword or in captivity.

There, having utterly abandoned Christianity, he resumed the pollution of his former luxury and paganism. And not unjustly. For if *Pyrrus* means “red” in Greek, and the mark of unfaithfulness is branded upon the red-haired, he is consequently shown not to have strayed far from his own line.

## CHAPTER VI

### [XVIII.] Bohemond attacks Maarrat.

Then Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, led his army away from Antioch, when November was already hastening toward its end. Having passed between the two cities, Rugia and Albara, he finally reached the city of Maarrat on the fourth day, as November came to an end.

A great force of Saracens, Turks, and Arabs had gathered there. The count prepared to attack it on the day after his arrival, committing all his strength to the assault.

Without delay, Bohemond followed the count with his army and, on a certain Sunday, pitched his camp near him.

On the following day they rushed toward the city walls with such determination that ladders clung to the walls and they strove to mount the very battlements by means of steps. But the townspeople, wholly free from cowardice, resisted with such persistence that none of our efforts could accomplish anything that day.

Then the Count of Saint-Gilles, seeing his men expend their labor in vain, ordered them to erect a wooden fortress of great height, requiring much work. This machine moved upon four wheels. A multitude of soldiers stood at its summit, while armed troops below pushed it with great force toward the city wall, beside a certain tower.

In opposition, the townspeople quickly built a device for hurling stones, with which they attempted to weaken the fortress by throwing enormous rocks. The frequent impacts of the stones threatened both damage to the machine and death to our men.

They also tried to set fire to the structure by casting Greek fire upon the mass of soldiers; but their God frustrated their efforts in this matter.

### A fierce engagement

The structure therefore rose above the city wall. Amid these clashes between the two sides, the tumult of a blaring trumpet stirred the courage of the combatants.

Meanwhile, certain soldiers from our side, occupying the upper platform of the same structure—William of Montepislerium among them, together with many others—struck those who were defending the walls with enormous stones. They hit them so forcefully that when a shield was struck, both shield and its owner often rolled uselessly away from the wall.

Others, carrying iron hooks on poles, attempted to hook the Saracens defending the battlements and drag them toward themselves.

The fighting on both sides scarcely ceased until the evening hours. Behind the fortress, priests, clerics, and monks, each adorned according to his rank in sacred vestments, prayed to God with the utmost attention for the immediate undertaking, asking that he deprive the pagans of strength and increase the power of the propagators of the faith.

On the opposite side of the machine, other soldiers, having placed ladders, hung over the battlements. Nor did the pagans lack the energy to drive them back with the most furious ferocity.

But a certain Guilferius, unable to tolerate their resistance, was the first to climb the wall with a force that was small but very brave. At once the townspeople were seized by such fury against men who had dared so boldly that, by assailing them with spears and arrows, they terrified some of them into lowering themselves from the wall.

But the portion that remained stood amid the enemy’s missiles for as long as it could, refusing to yield, and repelled their attacks by skill at arms until those below tunneled under the wall.

As soon as the townspeople saw that the wall had been undermined and ruined, relying now only upon flight as their defense, they withdrew into the inner parts of the city.

The day on which this occurred was a Saturday, when the declining sun was already seeking the western setting, eleven days having passed in December.

Immediately, through an interpreter, Bohemond approached the leading Saracens and instructed them to gather with their own soldiers, children, and women, together with all their collected property, inside a certain palace situated above the city gate. He promised that he would fully protect their lives and defend them and their possessions.

When the city had been obtained in this manner, whatever they found in pits or houses, each man claimed as his own property.

Then, after the night had passed, at dawn the crowd of our men ranged everywhere and slaughtered any pagans they happened to find. No portion of the city, however small, was free from the slaughter of Saracens, nor could the city’s alleys now be traversed, because the corpses of the pagans filled the public roads.

But Bohemond invaded those who, at his own command, had crowded into the palace mentioned above. He took away what they possessed, condemned some to death, and ordered others to be led to Antioch and sold.

The Franks remained there for a full month and four days.

And there the people endured severe hunger.

Some of our men, while they lacked certain necessities—in fact, all necessities—and had nothing nearby suitable for plunder, are said to have cut open the bellies of dead Saracens and dared to search their intestines, because they had heard that those reduced to extremity commonly swallowed gold and silver in order to keep it safe.

Others, cutting pieces of flesh from the corpses, are said to have cooked and eaten them. Yet this was so rare and so concealed that almost everyone doubted whether such a thing could in any way have occurred.

## CHAPTER VII

### [XIX.] The quarrel between Bohemond and Raymond flares up again.

Meanwhile Bohemond did not entirely set aside the quarrel that had arisen between himself and the Count of Saint-Gilles. Since the count would yield to him in no respect, he returned angrily to Antioch.

Without delay, the count sent envoys to that city and summoned Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, the Count of Normandy, and finally Bohemond to a conference at Rugia—the city mentioned above.

When they hastened their arrival, a general council considered how they might unite with such harmony of mind that the expedition to Jerusalem would not be delayed any further.

Bohemond was found to be altogether vehement and insolent in conducting the reconciliation, unless the count favored his will and ceded to him the part of Antioch over which he ruled. The count, on the other hand, was found to be more rigid in these matters, pleading the oath he had given to the emperor.

Thus divided by this bitterness of mind toward one another, Bohemond and the Count of Saint-Gilles, together with the duke, returned to Antioch.

Bohemond again entrusted to his soldiers the guard of the palace and of the fortress that overlooked the bridge gate of the city, and then returned to Maarrat, which he had captured earlier.

Nevertheless, not entirely lacking reason and considering the common losses caused by his stubbornness, since the freedom of the Lord’s sepulcher was forced to be delayed because of his obstinacy, the excellent man departed barefoot from the city of Maarrat on the thirteenth day of January and reached Capharda, where he remained for three days.

There the Count of Normandy, abandoning his quarrel, joined him.

### [XX.] The king of Caesarea asks to make a treaty with our men.

Moreover, the king of Caesarea had repeatedly urged that Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles enter into a firm peace agreement with him. He promised that everywhere in his kingdom he would provide assistance to Christians and would not deny them supplies of food, clothing, horses, or anything else required for their use.

Delighted by this promise, our men chose a place for their tents near the city, since the river Pharpar flows not far from the city walls. But the king of the city, seeing so great an army, was not pleased by the proximity of such a camp. He took it badly and forbade them to hold a market unless they withdrew from there immediately.

On the following day he sent two of his men with our forces to show them a ford of the river and lead them to a place where they could seize some booty.

Accordingly, these men showed them a valley below a certain town belonging to our people. There they found a great number of animals and captured nearly five thousand of them. They also discovered a very large supply of grain and other useful goods, from which that entire cavalry force was fully replenished.

The same fortress was also transferred into the count’s possession by its own surrender. A considerable amount of gold, together with horses, was provided from it, and our men were promised complete security on the condition that they would never harm the inhabitants.

They remained there for five days. Departing from there, they reached another town inhabited by Arabs. When they had pitched their tents around it, the lord of the town came out to meet them, and an agreement was made with the count.

### Several Christians capture cities.

At last, after hastening the movement of their camp, they reached a very beautiful city called Kephalia, rich in every good, situated in a certain valley.

But when the inhabitants learned that the Franks had arrived, they abandoned the city. Its houses were filled with an abundance of food, and its gardens everywhere overflowed with fruit, but they chose to preserve their lives by flight alone.

On the third day after leaving that city, they climbed exceedingly steep and rocky mountains, and afterward descended again into another valley, no less fertile than the place where Kephalia stood. There, refreshed by its richer resources, they restored themselves for nearly fifteen days.

They were then informed that a certain fortress was near those places and that a very large crowd of pagans had gathered there. When our men had surrounded it in a very swift siege, they were ready to subdue it, when suddenly the townspeople brought out a considerable herd of cattle. By this lure they temporarily induced them to abandon the siege.

But at first light our men brought their tents up to the fortress and prepared to besiege it. When the pagan people perceived their intention, they withdrew in swift flight and abandoned the town empty.

The Christian army entered and found an abundant supply of grain, wine, flour, and oil, as well as whatever other necessities there may have been.

### The Christians refuse peace to the king of Tripoli unless he gives his allegiance to Christ.

There they celebrated the feast of the Purification of blessed Mary with complete devotion. There also they received envoys from the king of the city of Camela.

That king agreed through a separate embassy to provide the count with horses, gold, and silver, promising that he would offend Christians in no respect but would show them the reverence owed to them.

The king of Tripoli also sent word to the count that he would gladly enter into an agreement with him if the count wished, sending him ten horses, four mules, and a considerable amount of gold.

But the count replied that he would in no way act peaceably with him unless he received the sacraments of our faith.

They left the very fertile valley that I mentioned above and reached, on the Ides of February, which fell on a Monday, a naturally very strongly fortified stronghold situated at the summit of a rock, called Archas. They occupied the vicinity of the town with their tents pitched.

An innumerable multitude of pagans had filled the place—Turks, namely, Saracens, and Arabs. In addition to the protection afforded by its location, they had made it much stronger in every respect by their sheer numbers.

It happened there that fourteen mounted men from the Christian army set out toward the city of Tripoli, which was near that fortress—not, if I am not mistaken, for any other reason than to obtain something useful for food.

These fourteen, I say, encountered approximately sixty Turks, accompanied by others. The Turks were driving before them more than one thousand and fifty people and animals that they had captured.

The fourteen, becoming instruments by their deeds of the Lord’s promise that “two shall put ten thousand to flight, and one a thousand” (Deut. 32:30), and engraving the sign of the cross upon their devout minds, overcame them with incredible boldness, God supporting them. They killed six of the Turks and captured an equal number of horses.

### The Christians obtain the city of Tortosa.

Furthermore, from the cavalry of the Count of Saint-Gilles there came that Raymond whose excellence frequently demands mention in this little work, whom we have said was surnamed Pilitus. He was a man exceedingly distinguished for sharpness of spirit and skill at arms.

Together with another man of the same name, who held the office of viscount, he made for the city of Tortosa. In the first assault, which they launched with great ferocity, they terrified the inhabitants of the place to no small degree.

An incredible multitude of pagans had flowed into the city for its defense, which seemed very strong, like flies. On the following night they withdrew to a certain part of the city, intending to lodge there—or rather, to pitch their tents. They established innumerable fires throughout the watches, as though the entire Frankish army were present.

The pagans were terrified and collapsed into utter despair. Realizing that they could not protect their lives with shields, they decided at last to avoid death by any means, even on foot.

Thus, silently escaping by night, they left the city—filled with the riches of every kind—inferior to no other in wealth, empty of every inhabitant. In this they fulfilled the pious saying of Scripture:

> “For skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2:4).

This city has an excellent harbor in its suburb, since it lies beside the sea.

On the following day our men assembled, intending to overrun the city with all their strength. But at the very moment of their approach they found it utterly empty of people.

They entered it, therefore, and remained there until they afterward set out to besiege the town mentioned above, Archas.

There is another city adjacent to this one, called Maraclea. Its governor, whom they also call Admiravisus, immediately prepared to make a treaty with our men.

As soon as he received them and their standards, he brought them into the city.

## CHAPTER VIII

### [XXI.] The fortress of Archas is besieged.

Meanwhile Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, and the Count of Flanders arrived together at Laodicea. But Bohemond, unable to tolerate the division of Antioch that had been made for him, separated from the company of the men mentioned above and returned to that city.

The others, with equal purpose, proceeded to besiege a certain city called Gibellum.

A report reached Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, that an enormous multitude of pagans, greatly increased in number, had planned to fight against him. He quickly summoned the leaders of the entire army he possessed and asked them what ought to be done.

That council replied that it could think of nothing more useful for this undertaking than to summon the companions of the Lord’s journey and the other leaders to his assistance.

He sought their advice, and immediately put the plan into action.

When the princes—namely Duke Godfrey and Robert of Flanders—learned of the need of their companion, they made treaties with the man who ruled the city of Gibellum, accepting magnificent gifts of horses and gold, and came to the count to offer assistance, abandoning the city they had begun to besiege.

But rumor, the bearer of news, disappointed their expectation of battle. Therefore, united in purpose, they decided together to return to the fortress of Archas.

When they had remained there with minds resolutely fixed against it, they soon desired to visit the Tripolitans after moving their army. They found, however, that the enemy had placed before the walls of the city, for its protection, a hostile force of Turks, Saracens, and Arabs.

Our men attacked them with the punishment they deserved and immediately compelled them to resort to the final remedy of flight.

[Col. 0784B] There occurred there not merely a great slaughter of the city’s nobles, but something like a butchery of livestock, so that even the current of the river flowing into the city ran red with blood poured into it indiscriminately, and, polluted by such gore, would have soiled any of their cisterns. From this there soon arose in their minds a deadly terror, and such goads of fear oppressed the spirits of the survivors that none of them dared, for any reason whatsoever, venture outside the city walls or attempt an escape.

On the following day our men advanced beyond a certain valley called Desen. We have already said above that on the third day after the capture of Befalia [al., Cephalia] they had come to it, found it extremely fertile, and remained there for fifteen days. Having found cattle, asses, sheep, and many other animals there, including three thousand camels, they returned joyfully, carrying off abundant plunder from all these things.

[Col. 0784C] They therefore besieged that same fortress continuously for three months, less one day. There they celebrated the Lord’s Easter on the fourth day before the Ides of April. Meanwhile, while the delay of the siege held them there, their fleet, which was accustomed to serve in transporting provisions, sailed into a nearby harbor, bringing a considerable supply of grain and wine, meat and cheese, barley and oil; from this the Lord’s expedition was abundantly replenished.

Although they did not happen to suffer any shortage there, nevertheless, to have spent so long in useless labor over such a trifling matter seems to me to have exceeded the bounds of sound judgment.

[Col. 0784D] [XXII.] The Lord’s Lance is called into question.—After the death of that remarkable man, the bishop of Le Puy, who by pastoral love and severity had bound the hearts of all to one another with the glue of concord and unanimity, disagreements and insolence began occasionally to arise among the princes. Among the lesser and common people, moreover, liberties appeared that ought not entirely to have been tolerated, so that the saying from ancient history seemed at times to be fulfilled: “Because there was no king in Israel, but each man did what seemed good in his own eyes” (Judges XVII, 16).

For although other bishops remained there after the death of that glorious man, who had been appointed their particular father and leader, they did not esteem those others so highly, especially since they remembered that they had not been entrusted to him in the same right in which they had been entrusted to that one man. [Col. 0785A] Thus, since they obeyed no one individually and everything among them was considered equal, unsuitable judgments were frequently made when the appetite of the common people prevailed.

Accordingly, after the Lord’s Lance had been revealed—a lance which the deceased bishop had received with complete devotion—a shameful murmur of disbelief arose. Some said that he had not found it truthfully but by trickery, and that he had produced not the Lord’s Lance but merely some ordinary lance. Thus the crowds of the enormous common people began to mutter everywhere, and by their persistent deceitful words they corrupted those who had believed and chosen to venerate it. They demanded proofs of the object’s discovery and subjected its discoverer to divine judgment. The man was compelled to give proof of his claim to those who doubted; what they extorted from him, he was forced to undergo solely in order to remedy their unbelief.

At his command, therefore, two pyres were prepared, scarcely a very short cubit apart. The people, eager for novelty, piled up great heaps of wood, and when flames streamed from both sides, a very narrow path was left between the burning logs. He therefore called upon God, who is truth and without whose will he recognized that he had done nothing in this matter, with a pitiful prayer, as was fitting; then he flew with all his vigor through the dark passage of the raging pyre and immediately returned by the same path through which he had entered.

**The truth is confirmed.—**The whole force of the Western army, which at that time was encamped nearby, was present at this spectacle, and all awaited the outcome of the unprecedented undertaking, each with different expectations. Finally, when, as I have said, he had returned, innumerable ranks of the surging people received him as he emerged from the flames. When they saw that he had passed unharmed through the fires, they tugged him from this side and that, each wishing to retain some part of him—whether his body or his clothing—as a relic, and pulled him in different directions. Thus, amid the great tumult of those who were tearing and pushing him, they deprived him of life.

For, having leapt from the flames—so to speak, half alive—from the fear and wonder of the impending destruction, unless God showed mercy, on the one hand, and of his sudden deliverance on the other, while the assaults of the crowd pressing upon him from every direction closed him in, and already trembling from exhaustion caused by his former anguish, he could not difficultly have had his breath choked off.

Once the man had died, the slippery and fickle crowd began again to be stirred by a much worse confusion. Some proclaimed that the judgment of fire which the man had undergone had turned out one way, others another: some said that he had been burned, others that he had emerged from the flame unharmed; some quarreled with the others and reproached them for having killed a man for nothing.

But whatever course popular opinion took, we know that that glorious prelate embraced the all-holy Lance with every form of veneration, to such a degree that, at his own command, the body of that same bishop was buried in the very place where the Lance had been found. This is how the matter stood.

[Col. 0786A] [XXIII.] Ansellus of Ribodimonte.—While the long siege at Archas detained our men there to no purpose, and the tents of the besieging army stood far below in the valley before the fortress, which rose upon the summit of a certain rock, Ansellus, surnamed of Ribodimonte—for he had been lord of that fortress and of other great possessions—a liberal and altogether generous man, remarkably skillful in directing an army, seeing the difficulty of capturing the stronghold and unwilling to endure the delay of a prolonged encampment, advised our men to prepare engines for hurling stones and fire-darts.

They had indeed begun, by means of an exceedingly long network of tunnels, to undermine the tower situated on the height, and every day they persisted in enlarging the excavation by scraping it out, supporting the exposed sections with beams and posts. Even women and the wives of the better men carried away the earth that had been dug out and removed, on feast days, in their gathered garments or little cloaks.

When those in the garrison discovered this, they immediately opposed our efforts, not without danger to those who were attempting to thrust themselves into the excavations. When all the work of undermining the tower had consequently come to nothing, Ansellus then arranged to advise our men to construct engines for shooting bolts. Once these had been set up and the tower was being battered by frequent discharges of stones, behold, the besieged began to construct similar devices opposite them.

**Ansellus was struck and died in the Lord during the siege of Archas. He sent an account of what had happened in writing to Manasses, the archbishop.—**When the engine had been erected and was hurling enormous stones against our men, Ansellus himself was struck, either first or among the first, to the greatest loss of the entire Frankish army.

Since he had conducted himself with the utmost faithfulness and steadfastness in the Lord’s campaign, he displayed, among the other distinguished signs of his intelligence and powerful faith, something admirable and deeply cherished by all literate men: he clearly disclosed, in letters sent once and again, everything our men had done during the siege of Nicaea, while traversing Romania and Armenia, and finally while attacking and capturing Antioch and defending it after its capture; he also described how, during the same period, they had fought against the king of Galapia, against the Damascene, and also against the king of Jerusalem, whom he repeatedly calls an adulterer, sending this account to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, a man of blessed memory who had died almost two years earlier. [Col. 0786D]

As a testimony of the pious love he bore toward the martyr whom he honored, he also caused the annual day of blessed Quintinus’s passion to be celebrated there with whatever honor he could provide, summoning clergy from every direction; and he supplied worthy gifts to those who celebrated it. It also happened there that many others happily suffered martyrdom and, by the short path of sacred death, earned the kingdom of heaven.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0787]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0787A]

[I.] How great were the faith and devotion of the Christians in the Jerusalem expedition. They abandon the siege of Archas and proceed to Jerusalem. They make an agreement with the king of Tripoli.—No small encouragement to our faith is provided by the fact that, through the labor of the faithful from the West, the Church of the East is restored.

We see battles undertaken with the most devout intention toward God alone, in which the entire army burned with the love of martyrdom, and in which their own devotion to salvation alone served as their advance guide, without king or prince. We read that Gauls migrated even to the farthest regions of the East for the sake of warfare; and we know that the treasures plundered from the sacred precincts after they had explored the secrets of Delphic Apollo were cast into the marshes of Toulouse.

We understand that all these forces were assembled by the exactions of their princes at that time; here, however, we have heard of not one man being compelled by any lord of his own to depart against his will and resistance. Here, amid arms, tears, confessions of sins, renunciations of possessions, rejection of wives, and flight from children, one ambition surpasses all others in the minds of everyone for the love of God: the sole desire for blessed death.

Here, I say, we may marvel at God, who once strengthened the minds of martyrs to endure torments through love of invisible things, and who in our own time implanted in the hearts even of savage and greedy men such contempt for present things—something no one could have expected and which would have been considered ridiculous to say—and accomplished so much through so few men that, leaving aside the praise of those who performed these deeds, it is certain that God alone did them.

This is evident from the fact that whenever their repeated victories gave rise to arrogance, or whenever they became puffed up against one another’s princes, or whenever some insolence happened to stain them, the gentiles would immediately find them almost powerless and, so to speak, like beasts. But whenever they were brought to repentance and mindful of themselves, they were at once restored to their customary fortunes and pious successes.

Let us therefore rejoice that the present age has been marked by divine power through battles begun and completed solely from spiritual desire—battles such as have never occurred since the beginning of the world—and let us not marvel at the wars of carnal Israel for the sake of the fullness of their bellies.

The king of Tripoli, therefore, did not cease to assail our princes with frequent embassies, asking them to withdraw from the fortress and join themselves to him. When the leading men of the army learned this—the duke namely, Godefridus; Raimundus, count of Saint-Gilles; and the two counts Robert, the Fleming and the Norman—and when they considered that the provinces were already overflowing with new crops, for by the Ides of March the beans sown earlier were plainly edible, while by mid-April grain could provide porridge, they judged together, after considering the condition of the land, that it would generally be advantageous for them to undertake the journey to Jerusalem with whatever fresh supplies might be available.

They therefore abandoned the siege of the fortress and, in accordance with the decision mentioned above, reached Tripoli on Friday, the thirteenth day of March, and remained there for three days. Having made peace with our leaders, the king of Tripoli immediately released more than three hundred men whom he had captured from our forces and thrown into chains. As they departed, he distributed fifteen thousand Byzantine coins to them as a mark of goodwill and likewise gave them fifteen horses of excellent value.

He also provided our men with a most ample supply, offering horses, asses, and everything that could be useful in passing to so great an army, so that the Lord’s expedition might be fully replenished for the present. Finally, he added to the agreement he made with them that if they defeated the war of the Babylonian emperor—which was frequently reported to be in preparation and to be of the greatest magnitude—and if they captured Jerusalem, he would immediately submit himself to the Christian cause and add both himself and his territory to them.

Having departed from that city, on the second day of May they traveled through a harsh and narrow road by night and day. Then they reached a fortress called Bethlon. Afterward, arriving at a city situated near the sea called Jebari, they suffered greatly from thirst, until a river, soon arriving to their aid, provided a timely remedy; its name was Braim. [Col. 0788C]

On the night of the Lord’s Ascension they climbed a certain mountain with a path narrow in every respect. There they were extremely afraid that they might encounter enemies at the exits of those narrow passes; but, by God’s providence, no one dared present himself to meet them. Our soldiers who had gone ahead cleared the road of enemy attack.

Finally they came to a maritime city called Baruch; from there they went to Sarepta, formerly a city of the Sidonians, famous for Elijah’s nourishment by a widow; then to another city called Sur; afterward they reached Accaron, once the metropolitan city of the Philistines.

**A bishop is appointed at Ramatham.—**Finally, proceeding along a pass called Caiphas, they came upon a fortress, until they subsequently arrived at the notable city of Caesarea, itself also a city of the Philistines. There they celebrated Pentecost for three days, before May had come to an end.

After this they reached the city which some call Ramatham, famous because of Samuel, while others, more knowledgeable and more curious about the places, assert that it was Ramoth-gilead. The conflicts for its possession brought the utterly wicked Ahab to ruin when Ben-hadad, king of the Syrians, prevailed. When its inhabitants learned of the arrival of the Franks, they fled.

Although this city might have been distinguished by monuments of the most ancient memory, its present reality would nevertheless seem to me to be wholly overshadowed by that of the most celebrated martyr George, whom they assert to have been buried there. When the settlers had departed, a great abundance of almost every kind of provision was found there, and it provided general assistance for the armies lodging there for many days.

There the leaders, consulting the clergy and the bishops who could be present, with their approval appointed a bishop for the city itself. They enriched him with the tithes of their possessions and also with gold and silver; they supported him with horses and animals, so that he might conduct himself with his household without difficult want and without dishonor to his high office.

He remained there with every joy, intending to obey the command of the princes, who had earnestly requested that this be done out of reverence and love for the martyr: to defend the city, above all to govern the basilica, and to establish the officials of the Church.

## CHAPTER TWO

[II.] The Christians besiege Jerusalem.—And behold, at last they reached that city which had produced so many hardships for them, which had so long and so frequently brought forth such thirst and hunger; the cause of so much nakedness, sleeplessness, and cold; the occasion of unceasing fear; the most alluring incentive to endure misery; the enticement to death and wounds.

At that city, desired with a thousand thousand desires, hailed, as it came into view, with such great sorrows and rejoicings, they finally arrived—Jerusalem. Of it, just as it is written of the resting places of the Lord’s body, “They ate and worshiped,” so it can also be said of these men: they worshiped it and conquered it.

On the eighth day before the Ides of June, when it was Tuesday, the city was besieged with remarkable courage. On the northern side, Count Robert of the Normans besieged it near the church of blessed Stephen, where he was buried beneath a shower of stones by the Jews because of the Son of Man whom he had loudly proclaimed that he saw standing at God’s right hand.

On the western side stood Duke Godefridus, Count Robert of Flanders, and Tancred. On the south, Count of Saint-Gilles besieged it on Mount Zion, near the church of blessed Mary, Mother of the Lord, where the Lord is said to have reclined with his disciples at supper on the day before he suffered.

On the third day after their arrival at the city, that Raimundus whose deeds in the Lord’s expedition had shone with no small distinction—he, I say, whom they surnamed Pilitus—went some distance from the place of the siege with a certain namesake of his, likewise a distinguished man, and many others, in case they might happen to find some of the enemy wandering about, as was their custom, and lying in wait for our men.

And behold, suddenly a band of nearly two hundred Arabs presented itself to them. When Raimundus saw them, he attacked them with leonine ferocity, and, with God pressing upon them, all their boldness was subdued. After killing many of them and capturing thirty horses, they carried back to the army a joyful victory, celebrating the brilliance of the deed.

At dawn on the second day of the following week, the outer wall of the city was attacked with such force and unanimity that, if equipment of ladders had not been lacking, the city together with its suburbs would immediately have fallen under Frankish rule.

The entire outer fortification was therefore broken into, and, through the breaches of the smaller wall, with the way forward now fully open, the single ladder that was available was extended to the battlements of the larger wall. Some of our soldiers climbed it swiftly and began to engage in combat at close quarters. When missiles were exhausted, the entire struggle was conducted with lances and swords; the city’s defenders and their besiegers fought face to face with steel. Many of our men fell, but more of theirs.

[III.] It should be known, however, that while Antioch was still under siege, this same city was held under the rule of the king of Persia by the Turks. [Col. 0790B]

Now, when the Babylonian emperor, as we related above, had sent envoys to our army, it is clear that he had done so solely to investigate the condition of our forces. For when they saw the Christian army being worn down by the most grievous want, and discovered that the nobles generally, deprived of their horses, had already become foot soldiers, they began to despise all that belonged to us and, trusting in our forces that were engaged against the Turks—whom they especially had as enemies—to undertake new measures against the Turks.

The king of Persia had usurped a large portion of the Babylonian empire, which was said to be exceedingly broad in every direction; for he possessed a more skillful people in the art of war. When that Babylonian prince finally learned that the Franks—or rather, through the Franks, God—had subdued Antioch, and that at Antioch, before the walls, Curbaran himself had been confounded together with all the pride of Persia, he immediately took courage, declared war on the Turks, and besieged Jerusalem, which they controlled.

When it had been recovered—I do not know whether by force or by some alliance—they left many Turks in the very tower called David, which we think should properly be called Zion, I do not know whether for its defense or for its possession. It is certain of them that, during the siege, they did no harm at all to any of our men; they peacefully devoted themselves solely to guarding the fortress to which they had been assigned.

Our men therefore came into conflict in this war with the Saracens.

[IV.] The Christians are afflicted by the greatest want of every kind.—During that siege, bread for purchase could not be found, and for about ten days there was widespread difficulty in obtaining this food, until God came to our aid and our fleet reached the harbor of Joppa.

The pressure of thirst was equally severe, so that not only did the men themselves miserably languish under this affliction, but they also led their horses and other beasts of burden a distance of six miles to drink, amid the great fear of the enemies roaming about.

The spring of Siloam, known from the Gospel account of the healing of the blind man, which rises from the roots of Mount Zion, sustained them. Its water was sold among them at an extremely high price.

After an embassy had arrived and announced that the ships had reached Joppa, the elders, having taken counsel together, proposed which soldiers should be sent to the harbor to protect the ships and the men aboard them. At first light, when the faint dawn was already bringing forth the twilight, Raimundus, whom we frequently mention in our narrative, selected one hundred horsemen from the army of his lord, the count of Saint-Gilles, together with two other nobles, and proceeded to the harbor with his customary authority.

Of these, thirty soldiers immediately separated themselves and, departing from the others, encountered approximately seventy [al., seven hundred] Turks, Arabs, and Saracens whom the king of Babylonia had sent to lie in wait for the movements of our men.

Although greatly outnumbered, our men charged their wedge with immense courage. But such were the enemy’s valor and ferocity that they already pressed upon our men from every side, almost to their destruction. Thus they killed one of the two nobles, a man named Achardus, and some of the poorer soldiers and more distinguished footmen.

When they had surrounded our men, pressing them as they were enclosed by weapons on every side, and when they were already almost collapsing in pitiable despair, someone came to the aforementioned Raimundus to tell him of the necessity suffered by his companions:

“What are you and your soldiers doing lingering here?” he said. “Behold, your men who recently departed from you are being savagely surrounded by a mass of Turks, Saracens, and Arabs. Unless you bring them aid quickly, know for certain that they are about to die—if indeed they have not already died. Fly, therefore; hurry, for I confess that every speed will be too slow.”

Raimundus, with his entire company, hastened as quickly as possible to the place where these events were occurring. But as the battle was being prepared, he placed his hope of assistance not in weapons or strength, but in faith in the Savior.

When the phalanx of the gentiles saw Christ’s army, it immediately divided into two battle-lines. Our men, calling upon the aid of the Most High, then attacked them with such violence that each man struck down the enemy who rushed toward him. The pagans, realizing that their strength could not long withstand the Christian assault, withdrew and, by a swift flight, took counsel for their unbearable fear.

Our men followed them with rapid determination and drove them for a distance of four miles, killing many of them and bringing back one hundred and three horses as tokens of victory. After the others had been killed, they left one survivor and brought him with them. From him they learned everything that was being planned among the enemy and what the Babylonian prince had proposed to do against our men.

[V.] They are tormented by thirst. Their endurance is praised.—Meanwhile, the army was horribly oppressed by the excess of thirst, to such a degree that they sewed together the hides of oxen and buffaloes, in which water was carried for six miles. They used such skins as vessels for transporting water; softened by the moisture of fresh hides, they caused some the greatest misery of famine, yet were compelled to be used by the army along with barley bread.

How many throats and gullets of so many noble men were scraped by the roughness of that coarse bread! How many of their delicate stomachs must have been twisted by the sourness of foul liquids! Good God! What endurance do we suppose existed there, where none of them had forgotten the dignity once possessed in their homeland—a dignity that had usually been seasoned by no small measure of pleasurable repose—while neither hope nor the consolations of external gain softened what they suffered, and the heat of the cruelest labors consumed them day by day?

This is my judgment, my sole judgment: never, since the beginning of the ages, have there been men such as these, who for the mere expectation of spiritual profit exposed their bodies to so many torments. The affections for their distant children, the pleasures of wives, and the splendor of possessions burned in their minds; yet, as though they intended to remain there forever, they did not cease to pursue the service of Christ.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0792B]

[VI.] The sacred army presses the siege.—The Saracens therefore continually kept watch in ambushes around the springs and rivers; everywhere they longed for the slaughter of our men; they plundered whatever they happened to encounter; and they carried off stolen animals or anything else into tunnels and caves.

Around the city, as the army remained encamped for action, the savage bitterness of hunger and thirst raged; and the more rabid malignity of the enemies roaming on every side thundered all around.

The princes of the sacred army, seeing that so great an affliction could scarcely be endured much longer by so many people of such varied origins, considered by what engines the city might be more easily conquered, so that, after enduring such hardships, they might be able to be present in worshipping the memorials of the Savior’s Passion and burial.

Besides many other instruments by which the walls might be shaken by the blows of rams or the towers and battlements battered by frequent discharges from ballistae, they ordered two wooden fortifications to be constructed, which we customarily call *phalas* [or *falas*, that is, wooden towers].

Duke Godefridus was the first to build his fortification, together with other suitable engines, and Count Raimundus of Saint-Gilles, who would suffer no one to be his equal, likewise constructed his own. Then the Saracens, seeing the engines being raised, the fortifications advancing, and the siege machines being brought up to the strongholds, themselves began to raise the walls, shore up what was collapsing, and extend the tops of the towers to an unusual height.

They worked to complete all these things during the night; by day they astonished our men with the novelty of the constructions. The timber from which our men built either their fortifications or their various machines was transported from a more distant province.

The leaders of the Lord’s army therefore considered which part of the city was weaker. One Saturday night they transported that same fortification, together with certain engines, to that location. At first light it was raised on the eastern side, and on the first, second, and third days they devoted themselves to fitting and securing it. The count of Saint-Gilles was also rebuilding his machine on the southern side.

While such great zeal for the siege was burning, the dryness of intolerable thirst nevertheless scorched everyone’s innermost parts, to such a degree that not even enough water could be obtained for refreshment, so to speak, at the price of a single coin.

Finally, on the fourth and fifth days, they resolved, joining their strength in unanimity, to attack the city, which was surrounded on every side. But before the planned assault took place, the bishops and priests proclaimed litanies to the assembled people and ordered fasts, prayers, and almsgiving to be observed.

Remembering the former fall of Jericho, and that the Israelites had once brought down the walls of the faithless city by marching around it seven times to the sound of trumpets and by carrying the sacred Ark around it, the prelates went around Jerusalem in procession, performing acts of penitence with great contrition of spirit and body, tearfully invoking the names of the saints, and practicing barefoot processions. Both the elders and the people joined in the same necessity, imploring heavenly assistance.

**The efforts of the Christians accomplish nothing.—**When these actions had finally been completed with the deepest devotion to humility, it happened that Friday arrived. On that day, although they attacked the city with fierce determination, and although their combined efforts achieved absolutely no result, behold, a stupor of such despair entered the minds of the entire army that everyone’s strength vanished, and the hearts even of the boldest generally collapsed, shattered by repeated misfortunes.

I heard—I call God as my witness—from certain men endowed with truthfulness who had been present at that divine undertaking that, when the Christian army returned from attempting to storm the city’s walls without any result, one could see the best of the cavalry recoil from their encounters with the walls, clap their hands, cry out with dreadful lamentations, and groan as though they were now utterly abandoned by God.

I have also learned from no less trustworthy a report that Robert, count of Normandy, and the other Robert, prince of Flanders, came together in equal grief and, amid copious tears, loudly declared themselves most wretched, saying that the Lord Jesus judged them unworthy of seeing and worshiping his cross and, indeed, venerating his tomb.

But as the hour approached at which that true Jesus, who on a second occasion led the people out of the prison-house of Egypt, is believed to have been lifted up upon the cross, Duke Godefridus and his brother Count Eustachius—who had in no way ceased to fight from the fortress and were striking the lower walls with the repeated blows of a battering ram—pressed the Saracens who stood above defending the battlements by throwing stones and various missiles against them, while swords were also ready on every side, and those men fought fiercely for the protection of their lives and homeland.

## CHAPTER FOUR

[VII.] Finally, the Christians enter the city by force of arms through the walls.—Meanwhile, Letaldus, one of the horsemen, destined to be celebrated in succeeding times for so bold and remarkable a deed, was the first to leap upon the city walls, and by this fortunate presumption shook the minds of the gentiles to the greatest astonishment of those standing around.

When that man had climbed up, all the young Franks, whom pious courage had already long since made more illustrious, rushed forward. Although they seemed reluctant to be seen below the one who had gone before them, they likewise climbed to the top of the walls.

I would insert their names individually on this page, if I did not know that after their return they incurred such infamy for their many disgraceful deeds and crimes that, according to the judgment of God and of those who love God’s name, I seem not unjustly to have remained silent about identifying them.

As soon as the Saracens saw that the Franks had flown onto the walls, they immediately took flight along the walls themselves and through the city. When all of them had withdrawn, our army poured in at once: some through openings made by the blows of the battering rams, others flowing in over the tops of the engines.

A dangerously hasty rush to enter then took place, and while each man desired to be found first, one trampled another by mutual pressure. Moreover, around the entrances of the city gates, where the Saracens had shut themselves in, a concealed ditch was discovered—a deception devised by those same Saracens. There the fall itself endangered many, apart from the danger caused by the narrow entrance when the men impatiently rushed in.

The Franks therefore pursued the fleeing pagans fiercely, and, slaughtering all whom they encountered without distinction, the killing extended through the streets, crossroads, and lanes all the way to the place called the Temple of Solomon. There the outpouring of human blood was so great that the flowing stream nearly submerged the feet of those advancing.

Thus the matter proceeded with success.

[VIII.] Raimundus, however, that count of Saint-Gilles, brought his army up from the southern side. An enormous engine mounted on wheels was likewise being carried toward the wall, but between the engine called the fortress and the wall there lay a very deep ditch.

The prince therefore, acting quickly, ordered a proclamation to be sung throughout the army, announcing how that steep place might be filled without a long delay, so that whoever carried three stones to the same ditch should know that he would receive one denarius.

The filling could scarcely be completed within three days, and the work could not be interrupted even at night. When the ditch had been filled in this way, they brought that engine up to the walls.

Those who had taken responsibility for defending the interior of the city resisted our men—not, I say, with courage, but with the most stubborn rage. They battered the carriages of the engines with castings of what they called Greek fire and of stones; yet the Franks repeatedly evaded their blows and attacks by remarkable ingenuity.

Meanwhile, when the city had been breached on the eastern side, as I have said, nothing but the tumult of battle brought word to the aforementioned count that the Franks seemed to be running about throughout the captured city, slaughtering everywhere.

“Why,” he said to his men, “are you lingering here? Do you not see that, having obtained the city, the Franks are already triumphing in a celebrated plundering of its spoils?”

The count therefore rushed into the city with his men as quickly as possible. Since he had learned that some Franks were roaming and fighting fiercely through the urban palaces, others at the Lord’s memorial, and not a few around the *pastophoria*—to use the old term, the Temple’s sacred chambers—of Solomon’s Temple, he did not wish to remain without a share in the rule of the captured city.

He therefore spoke with Admiraviso—for that is what they call him—who was in charge of the citadel of David, which is called Zion, and demanded that he surrender the citadel to him.

The satrap, after an agreement had been made between them, opened for the count that gate through which, until then, pilgrims entering Jerusalem had been compelled, most unjustly and cruelly, both to enter and to pay the dues they customarily called *musellas*.

When the Provençals entered—namely, the army of the Count of Saint-Gilles—and all the others entered the city as well, an indiscriminate slaughter of the pagans began. Neither tenderness nor beauty nor dignity nor any strength was spared from destruction: a dreadful ruin threatened everyone alike, universally and inevitably. But those [Col. 0795B] who had taken refuge in Solomon’s Temple held our men at bay for the entire day by fighting against them. Our men, however, unable to tolerate the desperate men’s half-dead yet insolent boldness, joined together in determination and pressed forward; forcing their way into the temple approaches with united strength, they penetrated within and tore the wretched people apart in so great a slaughter that the blood of the slain, beyond counting, almost rose above the edges of their shoes.

Thus, after an innumerable multitude of both sexes and every age had been poured out throughout the temple, they left some survivors alive, granting them a temporary interval of life and safety until they themselves removed from the temple the corpses of those who had been killed, whose loathsome heaps lay scattered here and there.
