When these had been removed, those survivors too, as had the earlier ones, fell beneath the swords.

But those who had climbed to the highest parts of the temple, an endless crowd of the undistinguished populace, took up the banners of Tancred and Gaston as a sign of the peace temporarily granted to them. This Gaston was a distinguished and exceedingly wealthy man; whether he was from Gascony or from Bascony I do not remember precisely, though I have retained with certainty that he was from one or the other.

As the army swept through the city, the whole city was plundered. Once the palaces and every kind of dwelling had been seized, a rich booty of silver, gold, and silk garments was carried away; an abundance of horses and mules appeared, and in the houses supplies of every kind were found in plenty. This was the rule and equalization of the Lord’s army: “whoever, even the poorest, encountered anything good, that person would unquestionably possess it without question,” whatever his condition might appear to be, if it had first come to his hand.

And now, leaving these matters aside, they hastened together toward that object for which they had thirsted with such intense desire, mingling joy and sorrow alike.

### [IX.] They hasten to the Lord’s sepulchre and weep for joy.

They therefore approach the Lord’s sepulchre, and greatly rejoice with him over the freedom obtained for the blessed places—he who had accomplished through them such great things as could be measured neither by those through whom they had been performed nor by any human being. They remembered the anxieties they had endured for this very purpose; and as they contemplated these anxieties transformed into unforeseen triumphs, and considered deeds unknown to the ages that had been accomplished and could be comprehended by no one except themselves, they could not restrain their weeping, so blessed did they make them.

Almighty God, what depths of feeling, what joy, what grief were there, when, after unheard-of sufferings, like the pangs of childbirth—sufferings untested by all the armies of the world—they saw themselves arrive at the new joys of the long-desired vision, as though at the sight of sons newly born? They grieve, therefore, and yet, with tears poured forth, they rejoice together in things sweeter to each of them than all bread. At every moment of remembrance they embrace Jesus, most compassionate, the cause of their prolonged labors and tortures, as though he were hanging upon the cross, as though he were still held within the covering of the tomb, with the richest affections. Magnificent offerings of gold and silver are paid; but inward devotion, more powerful than every gift, is brought forth.

[Col. 0796B] ### [X.] The Saracens who had fled to the upper parts of the temple are killed.

At last the following morning dawned, and behold, the Franks, grieved that those who had climbed to the highest parts of the temple still remained—those to whom Tancred and Gaston, as we said above, had extended their own banners—rushed fiercely across the roofs of the sanctuary. They tore the Saracens apart and killed them, women together with men. Some of them, choosing death rather than bringing it upon themselves voluntarily, threw themselves headlong from the roof of the temple. Tancred, however, because of the display of his banner and the pledge that Gaston and he had made, was deeply distressed by this slaughter.

Our men therefore ordered certain Saracens to carry out the dead, since the corpses burdened them with a most foul stench. [Col. 0796C] For the city was so filled with corpses that the Franks had no possibility of going anywhere except over the bodies of the slain. The pagans therefore, carrying the bodies of their people out of the city, piled up mountains of corpses before its gates and burned them on pyres heaped beneath them.

We rarely read that such slaughter of gentiles occurred anywhere; we have never seen it. God was repaying them in kind, restoring with a fitting recompense to the most wicked the punishments and deaths of so many pilgrims who had suffered there for so long on his behalf. No one under God can comprehend how many tortures, labors, and deaths were inflicted there by the insolence of the gentiles upon all who sought the holy places. It must be believed with surer faith that God grieved over these things than over the cross and sepulchre held captive by profane hands.

### Solomon’s Temple did not then exist.

Before turning our pen to other matters, this must first be made clear: that temple of Solomon, of which we spoke above, is not truly the same building that Solomon made. That building, as the Lord foretold—“not one stone here will be left upon another”—has been destroyed. This was plainly its likeness, constructed by I know not whom as a testimony to the nobility of the ancient house.

The place itself was one of infinite beauty, furnished with gold and silver of incomparable value and no less incredible variety; its walls and doors were extended by the attachment of sheets of precious metal. Count Raymond, however, had that prefect who was in charge of the citadel and to whom he had entrusted his standards sent out from the citadel by night, and had him conducted safely and securely to Ascalon with all who belonged to his company.

# BOOK EIGHT

## [XI.] The Count of Saint-Gilles rejects royal dignity. Godfrey is chosen king of Jerusalem. His illustrious deeds.

Furthermore, after the city and the holy places had been restored to freedom, alms and prayers were immediately ordered throughout the entire army of Christ, so that heavenly unction might deign to suggest to their minds whom they ought to choose under royal dignity to govern the rights of the holy city.

On the eighth day after its capture, they offered this office to the Count of Saint-Gilles in view of his magnificence. But he, mindful of his accustomed greatness and unwilling to submit himself to so burdensome an undertaking upon the advice of wiser men, refused it. He was indeed advanced in years and one-eyed, though he had distinguished himself wonderfully in arms and skill.

At last they approached Duke Godfrey, and by the unanimous plea of all who pressed the matter upon him, they placed upon him the burden of this labor rather than the honor. He would have to endure, against the exceedingly numerous forces of the gentiles, the unremitting severity of warfare and perpetual favor toward the Christianity surrounding him.

Although he had slender limbs, he was of very suitable height; in speech he was graceful and of extraordinary serenity. In that expedition of the Lord’s army he displayed such conspicuous valor in arms that a remarkable deed is sung of him in truthful testimony: it is said that near Antioch, upon the bridge of Pharpharis, he encountered an armored Turk mounted on horseback, and pierced his groin so powerfully with his sword that, when the trunk of the body fell to the ground, the horse carried away the seated legs as it passed onward.

For the Lotharingians commonly possess swords remarkable both for length and for sharpness.

### [XII.] Another deed of his, no less glorious, worthy of narration and every kind of celebration.

They had taken Nicaea and were hastening to besiege Antioch, since matters had proceeded favorably at Nicaea. While traveling, whenever the opportunity for safety permitted them to advance beyond their usual marching order, they hunted wild beasts in the adjoining thickets. The woods of that region did not have the same thickness or height as those of our country.

Once it happened that a bear of enormous bulk emerged from the bushes, and the army, discovering this, searched for it on every side. The bear, sensing the crowd of men shouting, immediately returned to the woods from which it had emerged. After many had been circling about in every direction, when nothing appeared, it happened that some unfortunate man reached the beast’s lair.

When the bear attacked him unawares, it overpowered him with its arms and immediately seized the thigh of the fallen man with its teeth. And behold, while the duke was wandering apart from his men, he came upon them alone. When the wretched man caught sight of him, weeping from the circumstances of his pain and fear, and invoking the man’s innate generosity, he called upon him to provide help.

The duke, whose nature was almost entirely composed of courage, did not hesitate to assist him. With all the strength he possessed, he drew his sword from its sheath and struck the beast upon the head. Because of the resistance of the bone, the blow irritated rather than wounded it, and the beast turned upon the duke.

Nevertheless, the duke’s first stroke caused the fierce creature to release from the man’s leg the teeth with which it had pierced him. The man quickly escaped, and, concerned for his own safety rather than for reporting the ensuing struggle to the duke, abandoned both of them in the conflict he had begun.

Then the beast, maddened by that blow,

> Leaps upon the duke and seizes him with its hooked claw;  
>   
> Throws him down and holds him beneath its cruel arms;  
>   
> Tears at his thigh with its rabid mouth;  
>   
> But his royal mind, suffering no disturbance  
>   
> From the sudden fall,  
>   
> Did not cease to hold the sword he had drawn.

When he had been knocked down and the beast began to twist the hip it had seized, the duke, not forgetting his own necessity, placed his sword at the very junction of the beast’s neck and shoulder and drove the blade into its vitals with the full force of his sword point.

When the creature sensed the iron sliding down into the depths of its entrails, it finally released the jaws with which it had clamped the flesh of his thigh. As the duke saw himself freed from the beast’s mouth, but noticed that it did not move from its place, he pushed it away with both feet. Yet in that act of repulsion, he almost fatally cut the backs of his own legs against the edge of the sword projecting from the beast’s chest.

He therefore fell much more grievously than when the beast had crushed him; and, his entire body now weak and bloodless, he was scarcely found by his men at last. The duke repented too late of his solitary wanderings, when, as a result, losses befell the contingent of the army attached to him and the whole sacred expedition. Until the end of the siege of Antioch he could scarcely be carried except on a litter. And because he could provide for neither himself nor anyone else, he soon lost nearly fifteen thousand men who had been attached to him and who, because of his incapacity, had withdrawn from him.

### [XIII.] A Christian deed of King Baldwin.

But since we have once begun to speak of a bear, we wished to anticipate what Baldwin as well—his brother, who still reigns at Jerusalem—did, because perhaps no other suitable occasion for reporting it will present itself.

In rescuing one of his infantrymen, whose courage was of great assistance to him, Baldwin had likewise received a very serious wound in battle. His physician, exercising prudent care, was afraid to cover it externally with poultices and form a scar over it; for he knew that the wound had penetrated more deeply into the interior of the body, lest, when the surface of the skin was closed, a mass of pus should be retained within.

He explained that this was so by an admirable conjecture and with commendable experience. He asked the king to order some person among the Saracens held in custody to be wounded in the same condition and at the same place where the king himself had been wounded—and then, after the wound had been inflicted, to order that person killed. It would then be possible to examine the wound more freely in the body of the slain man, or rather to determine from the dissection of that body how the royal wound was situated internally.

At this the king’s compassion, recalling the ancient examples of Constantine, recoiled greatly:

> “He denies that he will in any way become the cause of anyone’s death, even of a man of the worst possible condition, for the sake of such a small and uncertain hope of safety.”

Then the physician said:

> “If you have resolved not to deprive anyone of life for the sake of restoring your health, at least order a useless bear, fit only for spectacle, to be brought before you. Have it raised upright with its forefeet extended upward and struck with a sword. When it has been killed, I shall examine its entrails and, as best I can, measure how far inward the wound has extended and how great your injury is.”

The king replied:

> “The beast will be available when it is needed. Consider it done.”

When the physician’s wish had therefore been carried out upon the beast, he discovered that the king would suffer the danger we have described if the wound were closed too quickly, unless the purulence were first drained and the torn internal part allowed to knit together.

Let what has been said about the piety of kings suffice. Their glory, I confess, would have advanced equally if the papal election—and indeed the papacy itself—had not faltered.

[Col. 0799]

>

>   
> So that it may be lawful for the good to approach Jesus’ cross,  
>   
> And to bow the pious head beneath the sepulchre.  
>   
> I shall proclaim that our times have discovered  
>   
> What no school of historical annals will teach.”

### [XIV.] A certain Arnulf seeks and obtains the patriarchate of Jerusalem.

But since, while temporal matters are being arranged, they are thought to require royal administration, the inward matters belonging to priestly office must not be neglected. Once a king had been created as best they could, they consequently considered the appointment of a patriarch.

At that time there was a certain man living under clerical discipline, though I do not know his rank, whose name was Arnulf. He was not dull in dialectical learning; and since he was not at all untrained in grammatical studies, he had long taught the king of England’s daughter, the nun whom we mentioned earlier, in discipline. Through his sister, the Count of the Normans had promised her that he would confer episcopal honor upon her if one of his bishops should happen to die.

Meanwhile, when the opportunity for the journey to Jerusalem arose, Bishop Odo of Bayeux, a man of great wealth, vowed to undertake that journey. Since he was the brother of the elder King William of England and, in addition to his pontifical dignity, held the county of Kent among the English, he seemed so daring in his hopes of acquiring incomparable treasures that he even began to contemplate an attempt against his own brother’s kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0799] Thus write the English historians William of Malmesbury, Matthew of Westminster, and Polydore Vergil.]

The king forestalled him, committing the man to prison and keeping him there until his own death. After that had occurred, the same bishop returned to freedom and honor; and, as mentioned above, when the trumpet of this journey resounded, relying upon the multitude of his own people, he proceeded with immense wealth.

Arnulf joined his company. When this bishop’s death occurred somewhere, unless I am mistaken, short of the borders of Romania, he made Arnulf, from the enormous estate he left behind, almost the chief heir of all his precious possessions.

Since Arnulf was very capable in literary knowledge and was not lacking in eloquence of talent, and since greater abundance was already making knowledge more effective, he began to encourage our people with frequent speeches and to spread his reputation in such matters. The scarcity of learned men had made him more famous; and, while attention was paid more to speech than to life, he was summoned to become patriarch of Jerusalem. For some time, therefore, he displayed the appearance of a bishop in name alone; nevertheless, his declamations benefited that novelty.

### [XV.] The pope opposes Arnulf because he was the son of a priest. Daibert is substituted in his place, but is expelled through a conspiracy against the king.

At last, after some time, when the election that had been made had become known even to the Apostolic See, Pope Paschal, following the death of the Bishop of Le Puy, entrusted the responsibility for the Lord’s army to Archbishop Daibert of Pisa.

After Jerusalem had been captured and a king promoted, Daibert arrived with a very large fleet. Not long afterward, when he investigated the election that had been made concerning Arnulf, he judged that it had to be rejected according to the law of the canons. On examining the man’s lineage, he was found to be the son of a priest. Such a man is ordered not only to be barred from the sacred grades, but, according to the decrees of the Council of Toledo (IX, chapters 10 and 15), to become the perpetual servant of that church to whose injury he had evidently been born.

Excluded on this ground, Arnulf pressed his claim and defended himself vigorously. When the nobles wished somehow to remedy the disgrace caused him by his rejection, they asked him whom he thought should be chosen. Immediately envying his equals and juniors, as is the perversity of human nature, he said:

> “Accept this very Pisan, who is serving as legate.”

The princes agreed with his words. Seizing the archbishop, and scarcely even asking his consent, those same princes themselves carried him into the church and placed him upon the very chair on which he was sitting.

Not long afterward, following the death of the glorious King Godfrey, when his brother Baldwin—who had governed Edessa—was reigning, they accused this same man of treason. Having thus condemned him on a definite charge, they deprived of the patriarchate the man who had ceased to be metropolitan.

When the election for appointing a pontiff was discussed again, Arnulf took care to promote a man who would in no way dissent from his authority. He favored one of his companions, whom he knew would obey him in everything—a simple and unlearned man named Ebremar.

Later, when Ebremar conducted himself religiously and, as we suppose, did not entirely fulfill Arnulf’s wishes, they accused him at the Apostolic See. But they failed shamefully in the very course of their accusation. As a result, he incurred such hatred with the king, together with the accomplices who had labored with him in the accusation, that the king barred him from custody of the sepulchre and even expelled him from the city itself.

The pontiff, however, having given thanks to the authorities of the Apostolic See, returned to Jerusalem, to the great disgrace of his many persecutors. Let what has been said about the election and deposition of that imaginary patriarch suffice. That election, which the judgments of all good men should have annulled, broke out on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains; but since it possessed no supports of a pious life, it passed away.

The same city was captured by the Franks on the fifteenth day of July, when it was Friday, at almost the very hour at which Christ was lifted upon the cross.

# CHAPTER II

### [XVI.] The Emperor of Babylon declares war on the King of Jerusalem.

Not long afterward—indeed, only a few days later—envoys arrived from the city of Neapolis, anciently called Shechem or Samaria [alternate reading: which, unless I am mistaken, was anciently called Emmaus]. They urged Tancred and Count Eustace—the brother of the man formerly duke and now king, distinguished and very brave men—to set out for the aforesaid city with a large supporting force, plainly intending to receive it into their own jurisdiction.

They set out, taking many men with them, including a considerable number of infantry, and reached the suburb of the city on horseback. The townspeople opened the garrison and submitted voluntarily.

Other messengers also arrived and reported to King Godfrey that the Babylonian emperor was preparing great forces to wage war against him. The king, immediately becoming more resolute in response to what was reported, sent word to his brother Eustace and to Tancred concerning the news he had received, ordering and beseeching them to hurry back to Jerusalem as quickly as possible. He also announced to them that the place of battle had been designated near Ascalon.

When those invincible men learned this, they entered the hill country more quickly than the word could be spoken. Expecting that the Saracens would engage them in battle on the way, they found none and reached Caesarea of Palestine.

From there they advanced toward the city we mentioned above, Ramoth, famous for the memory of blessed George and situated near the sea, and turned their steps there. They encountered a considerable number of Arabs, who were scouts [alternate reading: sentinels] of the aforementioned battle.

When our men joined with them and observed them, they attacked with united force, compelling the enemies to give way in flight. Many were captured alive, and from them they learned everything the opposing side had planned concerning the imminent battle: where their army had now assembled, how large their number was, and what place had been designated for the battle.

After learning these things, Tancred sent messengers to Godfrey, king of Jerusalem, and informed him of what he had discovered. He also sent word to Arnulf, distinguished by the name of patriarch, and to the other nobles:

> “Know that a great battle awaits you. Since it is now recognized as imminent, hurry to Ascalon, trusting in the strength that your skill will be able to assemble in superior form.”

The king, second to no one in judgment after his trust in God, urgently summoned the entire army of God to this undertaking with great authority, and designated Ascalon as the place where they should advance against the enemy’s preparations. He himself, after summoning the patriarch and Count Robert of Flanders, left the city on Tuesday.

### [XVII.] The king prepares for war and sets out.

The Count of Saint-Gilles and the Count of the Normans told the king that they did not yet wish to proceed until they knew whether the war truly appeared imminent. They therefore said that they would meanwhile return to Jerusalem, asserting also that they would not be slow to appear when needed.

The king departed. When he saw the enemies at a distance, he promptly sent word to those who had remained in Jerusalem that they must know what had occurred. He immediately summoned a certain bishop and sent him to the city, urgently appealing to all his people to come together without delay to meet the present necessity.

On Wednesday, therefore, all the princes, having generally assembled the Lord’s expedition, had moved the camp away from the city. The same bishop, who had carried the king’s words to those remaining in Jerusalem, was returning to the king when he was intercepted by Saracens. It is not known whether he was killed or carried away captive.

[Col. 0803B] ### Peter the Hermit organizes public supplications in the city of Jerusalem.

Peter the Hermit, who had thus far carried out this pious work, remained in the city with Greek and Latin clerics, organizing processions, composing litanies, instituting prayers, and urging almsgiving, so that God might deign, as though granting a final victory, to crown the victories of his people.

Moreover, the ecclesiastical men who could be present, proceeding in sacred vestments as though to sacred mysteries, went as far as the Lord’s Temple, conducting masses and prayers with their whole hearts and leading men and women along, entreating the deliverance of God’s exiles.

Those who were present under the name of patriarch, and any bishops who happened to be there, gathered together with the various princes at the river known to lie beyond Ascalon. There, through the treachery of the gentiles, many thousands of animals had been exposed—herds of oxen, camels, and sheep. When the elders learned that these had been sent out to lure our men with the abundance of booty, they proclaimed throughout the camp that no one should find any part of that booty in his tent except whatever proved necessary for the immediate need that had been stated.

Meanwhile, three hundred Arabs presented themselves to the sight of our men. Our men immediately pressed them with such ease that they captured two after putting the rest to flight, pursuing them all the way to their camp.

### [XVIII.]

As that day drew late, the patriarch ordered that a perfunctory chant be sung throughout the entire army, so that at dawn the following day everyone would be ready for battle. He imposed an anathema forbidding “anyone, while fighting, to persist in seizing booty,” but ordered each man to defer his zeal for collecting booty until the battle had ended.

He urged them so insistently to devote themselves to striking down the enemy that they should not turn aside here or there for worthless gains, lest they incur the loss of the victory already begun because of anyone’s greed.

Friday had dawned, and behold, a most beautiful valley appeared before our advancing army. There, upon the plain beside the neighboring sea, they set their battle lines against one another.

The duke, now changed into a king; the Count of Flanders; likewise the Count of the Normans; the Count of Saint-Gilles; Eustace of Boulogne; and Tancred and Gaston together, along with some individual commanders and some pairs of commanders, took charge of the arranged divisions.

Infantry archers and spearmen, who were to precede the armies, were assigned their positions. King Godfrey was placed at the head of the left wing with his considerable force; the Count of Saint-Gilles was stationed beside the sea; the Flemish and Norman counts rode alongside the right wing; Tancred and the others advanced in the middle between the two sides.

### The battle begins. Our men emerge victorious after routing and slaughtering the gentiles.

Our men therefore advanced little by little toward the enemy’s formation, while the gentiles prepared themselves for battle and did not move from their position at all.

You could see vessels hanging from their shoulders, containing cold water in small skins; they believed that they would drink from them after driving our men into flight.

But God had planned something very different from what the hostile people intended.

Meanwhile the Normans and Count Robert, having seen from a distance the weapon of the army’s prince—a weapon that seemed to gleam beneath much silver and whose rounded tip was adorned with a weight of gold—urged on their swift horse with repeated spurs. They charged the prince, beside whom the spear we have mentioned stood as his standard, with a rapid attack, and wounded him grievously.

On the other side, the Count of Flanders, with his rein slackened, poured himself into the dense enemy. Tancred, finally, rushed with a great charge toward the tents. Everywhere the ranks raged with their own commanders; the fields and plains of the place became bloody with slaughter.

This immediately became an unbearable disaster for the enemy, and in despair they soon began to flee. As the multitude of gentiles had been enormous, so consequently the slaughter too became enormous.

For although the waves of the sea had been great in their rising, the Lord showed himself far more wondrous in the heights. Thus, to make it clear that so great a battle had been accomplished by God rather than by human hands, one could see the blind fleeing with open eyes; and, while they thought they were avoiding weapons, they threw themselves against armed men.

When no place of escape was open to anyone, a lofty tree offered an unsafe refuge to most, nor could they hide from our arrows. Struck, they plunged headlong into great falls. All whom flight did not shelter, whether dead or half-dead from javelins or swords, our men’s weapons overtook, and slaughtered them as though among cattle.

The Count of Saint-Gilles, however, beside the sands of the neighboring sea, where he had deployed his own division against the enemy, attacked them with such violence, like a storm, that a considerable band of them, while avoiding the destruction of the iron, voluntarily plunged into the sea.

# CHAPTER III

### [XIX.] Why the victory must be ascribed to God.

When the victory had thus been completed with God as its author, the Babylonian commander, whom the native language calls Admiravisus, was confounded and, unable adequately to comprehend the misfortune that had befallen him, uttered many complaints.

He considered the countless troops he had brought, their joyful youth, their noble weapons in strength and appearance, the wealth of his fellow soldiers, and, so to speak, all the resources of cavalry. He considered also what usually gives the minds even of the most cowardly a great sense of security: that they had fought before the gates of their own city, in their own province, where they had reliable refuges.

But he saw the Franks with forces inferior in every way: their youth weakened by prolonged famine, their swords covered with rust, their lances blackened, their armor thin and deprived of the strength of soldiers; all those who seemed distinguished above the rest were sluggish from harsh want, and their horses were exhausted by every kind of squalor.

In short, he marveled that the poorest of all, an exiled band, had defeated innumerable natives, or rather that the glory of the entire East had fallen through the most despised of men.

The victory of our men was also greatly aided by the flight that was proclaimed throughout the hostile army. When that Admiravisus who was in charge of Ascalon saw the Babylonian commander turn his back, he ordered all the fugitives to be barred from entering their own city.

The same enemies were also exceedingly astonished that the Franks had not chosen to fight before the walls of Jerusalem, as though for the sake of nearby protection, but had advanced almost two days’ journey to meet them.

### [XX.]

While the Franks were rightly rejoicing exceedingly over so great a victory granted by God, Count Robert of Normandy, a man never lacking in his extraordinary generosity even amid the poverty of that exile, bought for twenty silver marks the spear we had said was adorned with silver, the spear that had stood planted before the Babylonian prince like a standard, from someone who had seized it. He gave it to Arnulf, called patriarch, to be set up at the Lord’s sepulchre as a testimony to so great a victory.

They say that the sword belonging to the same prince was bought by someone for seventy bezants.

Moreover, a very large fleet that had followed the army landed at the port of Ascalon. It had come there for this very purpose: once the Franks had been defeated and thrown into captivity, the fleet intended to buy them from the victors and disperse them for sale throughout the farther kingdoms of the East.

When these men saw the Egyptians fleeing disgracefully, they immediately removed their sails and advanced into the open sea.

Finally, after the Franks had carried out a dreadful slaughter of the Saracens—especially of the Ethiopians—they returned to their now-deserted tents and refreshed themselves with an immeasurable quantity of booty.

From Gaza they brought forth an abundance of silver and gold, the wealth of Assyrian nobility, and every kind of precious equipment. Animals of every sort and implements of various weapons were gathered together. Whatever was suitable for use they preserved; whatever was foreign to their needs they burned with fire.

They returned triumphantly to Jerusalem with unimaginable joy, filling the memory of the Lord’s passion and burial with countless thousands of tears of gratitude.

So great was the abundance bestowed upon the Franks by the events of this heavenly fortune that those who had set out on this journey once utterly destitute and lacking even provisions returned with great wealth of gold and silver and with an impressive train of horses and mules:

> The day of August that immediately precedes the Ides  
>   
> Was granted to behold such glory of war.

# CHAPTER IV

### [XXI.] Various oracles of the prophets.

But since at the beginning of this volume we offered certain examples from Scripture that we thought suited the great undertaking we have explained, we must now consider whether anything corresponding to the siege of Jerusalem can be found in the prophet Zechariah.

“He says,” the Lord says, “stretching out the heavens and founding the earth, and forming the spirit of man within it” (Zech. 12:1).

He stretches out heaven who enlarges the Church, so that, just as according to Isaiah he brought forth its seed from the East through the apostles, so through these men he should gather it from the West (Isa. 43:5). He founds the earth when he permits the perfidy of the gentiles to become hardened in their inmost hearts. He forms the spirit of man within it when he shapes the mind of each believer through the gift of implanted reason.

“Behold, I shall set Jerusalem as a threshold of drunkenness for all the peoples round about” (Zech. 12:2).

A threshold rises above a doorway; through a doorway one enters a house; drunkenness harms the stomach. If by “doorway” we mean the faith of the Lord Jesus, through which we come to the Father, then we may rightly call the Jerusalem church a threshold, because the law and the word of the Lord went forth from it and because it provided the beginning of these teachings.

For Paul returned to it after fourteen years in order to compare the Gospel with Peter and the others, lest he had run or should run in vain (Gal. 2:2). But this threshold is drunkenness to all the surrounding peoples, because it is clear that all those nations, on account of the things that remained there, disdain and execrate the traces of our belief as though nauseated.

But also, “Judah shall be in the siege against Jerusalem” (Zech. XII, 2). He says: It is not only an object of horror to foreigners, but Judah also—that is, the faithful people, truly confessing the one trampled by the nations—will besiege it. “On that day I shall make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all the peoples” (Zech. XII, 3). If, according to the usage of Scripture, a part may be put for the whole, Jerusalem becomes a burdensome stone for all, because it has recently imposed upon all the peoples of the Christian name the burden of the greatest labor for its liberation: “All who lift it will be torn apart by laceration, and all the kingdoms of the earth will be gathered together against it” (ibid.).

Who are those who lift Jerusalem, except those who, when the times of the nations have been fulfilled, raise her from her trampling? “Jerusalem,” says the Lord, “will be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled” (Luke XXI, 24). These men are torn apart by laceration, because it is impossible even to say—or rather, to imagine—how great was the misery of hunger and thirst, or with how many sufferings from labors and wounds they were plainly tormented while besieging her. And, to speak in the words of Ezekiel: “Every head was shaved, and every shoulder was stripped of hair” (Ezek. XXIX, 18)—whether from other causes, or from the frequent blows of siege engines, or from carrying loads.

But once Jerusalem has been lifted up, “all the kingdoms of the earth will be gathered against her” (Zech. XII, 3). This is not to be understood as an allegory, but is set before our eyes as a recent historical report. For what kingdom of the East was there whose people did not come to that war? Those who had brought with them every kind of siege engine necessary for besieging the city—something I omitted above—and who, besides armed men, had also brought merchants for the purchase of Franks, plainly presumed upon victory because of their excessive numbers, perhaps with a greater sheer majesty of numbers than that which Curbaran had learned that man to possess.

“On that day, says the Lord, I shall strike every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness” (Zech. XII, 4). If the horse is understood as temporal rank, the rider of the horse, who rises above it in dignity, is doubtless meant. Every dignity is bewildered, because whatever authority exists anywhere, whatever kingdom there is, has been made dull against this hand of God’s new army and dares nothing. Every prince is turned to madness, because he is without counsel and has nowhere to turn—being, as he is, without strength—whoever experiences the might of this army of the Lord.

“And over the house of Judah I shall open my eyes, and I shall strike every horse of the peoples with blindness” (ibid.). If I call Judah, the confessing people, especially those confessors who are read as having never strayed from the faith from the beginning of their belief, then I shall certainly mean the Franks, upon whom the whole course of this undertaking rests. God opens his eyes over them when he shows them, through the very events themselves, the grace of his own benevolence; he strikes the horse of the peoples with blindness when he punishes the pride of the nations by subjecting them to a reprobate mind.

In the sacred page, the horse often stands for pride. What is more blind than to bring war upon the sons of God without regard for God? What is more reprobate than not to acknowledge God, to grow proud through that very ignorance, and to make war against the faithful? But how far does the freedom of allegory run through the folds of words, when historical truth restrains us, lest we seem to wander everywhere through mere opinions? Did we not say above that the enemies had been struck with blindness and covered with bewilderment by the swords hanging over them? And I marvel how the seeing horse conducted itself when the rider of the horse had fallen into evident madness.

[Col. 0807D] 439 “And the leaders of Judah will say in their heart: ‘May the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened for me in the Lord of hosts, their God’” (Zech. XII, 5). Whom should I call the leaders of Judah except the princes of that faithful army? They pray that the inhabitants of Jerusalem may be strengthened for them, when with all their affections they desire that that holy city be restored through the strength of the Christian army, so that Christianity may be propagated, the Lord’s memory honored, and paganism pressed down on every side.

But their strength is said to be in the Lord of hosts, as is seen even today, when a hand of men incredibly small engages all the kingdoms of paganism—something presumed upon entirely through the sole power of him who presides over the powers of heaven. “Their God” is rightly added, so that they may not be thought to rely upon God as upon just any author, but upon their own God, that is, the God of the Christians.

“On that day I shall make the leaders of Judah like a furnace of fire among wood and like a torch of fire among hay; and they shall devour all the peoples around them, on the right and on the left” (Zech. XII, 6). On this day, I say—whether of faith or of divine prosperity—those leaders who will govern the Christian people, either outwardly by arms or inwardly by spiritual teaching, will be a furnace: burning inwardly with heavenly love, they will consume the wood of sinners among the nations; and, as regards outward matters, they will kindle wars against all the reprobate as against hay.

For we know beyond doubt that God did not begin these things merely for the liberation of one city, but that he cast these seeds, destined to bear fruit far and wide, against the fury of the coming Antichrist. Thus they devour all the peoples around them on the right and on the left, when on the one side they incorporate the elect, signified by the right hand, into Christian piety, and on the other they lay waste the reprobate, who are known to belong to the left, with a punishment of slaughter appropriate to them.

“And Jerusalem will again be inhabited in her own place, in Jerusalem” (ibid.). If Jerusalem is the Church, her place is the faith of Christ. Jerusalem, therefore, is inhabited in Jerusalem when that earthly city is restored for this purpose: that it may gaze intently upon the vision of heavenly peace. It possesses its place because it clings immutably to Christ.

“And the Lord will save the tents of Judah as at the beginning, so that the house of David may not glory magnificently, and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not rise against Judah” (Zech. XII, 7). The Lord saves the tents of Judah as at the beginning when he himself, who performed wonders with our fathers, is also glorified in our times to such an extent that these people of the present seem, under hardships and calamities, to have accomplished altogether greater things than the Jews of old are thought to have fulfilled with their wives and children, with the continual fullness of their bellies, under the leadership of visible angels and amid frequent miracles.

These, I say, he saves more truly, because he truly receives as sons those whom he permits to be killed bodily and scourged temporally. “So that the house of David may not glory magnificently”—that is, so that the ancients, who excelled in the victories of wars, may cease to be proud when they consider that these new men have undertaken greater things.

The glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem is likewise raised against Judah, when the arrogance of those who ruled there and accomplished certain illustrious deeds is set against the men of the present. Through David, who above all others was able, whatever they possess as a cause for greater pride is expressed. It is as though he said: Even if David was most renowned in arms, and some of the kings who succeeded him sought some glory, nothing is found by which they can be equated with our people.

We say that “to inhabit” means “to rule”; hence we derive it repeatedly from the verb *habeo*, “I have,” *habes*, “you have.” It is also said that David glories magnificently against Judah, and that there is glory among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, because they themselves provide material for boasting to those who wish to diminish the deeds of our people.

[Col. 0809A] “On that day the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Zech. XII, 8). Does he not protect them even today, when he defends a very small wedge of men in the midst of an immeasurable mass of paganism? Every day they provoke the neighboring nations with bold arms; and for those nations it is enough if they fortify themselves against their incursions, much less do they dare to besiege them.

“And it shall be that whoever among them stumbles on that day will be like David; and the house of David will be like God, like the angel of the Lord, before him” (ibid.). David is scarcely ever found to have committed any grave offense whose punishment he is not subsequently read to have received in the present life. Therefore, whoever among our people stumbles will be like David, since God himself does not leave unpunished either their lusts or their pride in their progress, as the deeds mentioned above contain; rather, amid the beginnings of their sin, he quickly repays them with the torments they have deserved, whether of hunger or of any other hardship.

Thus the house of David becomes like God, because through the immediacy of divine correction one returns to the conception of spiritual grace. For those upon whom God, as once upon David, imposes fatherly discipline, he does not immediately cast away from the embrace of his inspiration. A man also becomes like an angel in the sight of God, because, when he sees through the scourges threatening him that he is being freed from his passions by God’s agency, he immediately aims to love God more ardently. For when he recognizes that he is chastised as a son, he loves as an angel. The sight of God, however, is the pious affection of the human interior.

[Col. 0809C] “And it shall be on that day: I shall seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem” (Zech. XII, 9). We generally seek those things which we are certain are not before our eyes. But what does it mean for God to seek except to set before himself, under the call of eternal providence, what is to be done? God therefore seeks to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem, and this “on that day,” because by his subtle judgment he foresees and orders either that those who act contrary to the faith be destroyed by eternal condemnation, or, insofar as concerns the testing of their own weakness, that they be weakened.

Hence it is said: “You will shatter them like a potter’s vessel, those whom you rule with an iron rod” (Ps. II, 9). Yet God does this through an inward illumination, which is plainly the day—but the kind of day that cannot be expressed by any reasoning.

“And I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication” (Luke XII, 10). I would call the inhabitants of Jerusalem themselves the house of David. Almighty God has granted them frequent victories and still grants them victories, yet through very frequent misfortunes he has subdued and resubdued them. Since he permits them neither to despair through the continued succession of evils nor to grow proud through the constant succession of blessings, the Spirit of grace and supplication, now necessarily a merciful dispenser, pours itself out upon them. Thus, since no prosperity—which even loosens the firmness of the perfect—seems to smile upon them without adversity immediately accompanying it, the mind, always fearful of troubles, is compelled to sigh in tribulation toward him who is a helper in times of need.

Behold now, with every mystery set aside, that material Jerusalem: how often do we think she must exist amid uncertainty and fear, when, according to Ezekiel (chap. V, 5), she observes herself placed in the midst of the nations and, looking around at the nations surrounding her, considers the infinitude of the neighboring peoples and the smallness of her own city?

And while they continually fear the invasions of barbarian nations, unless they are miserably foolish, they are never without the grace of the fear and love of God, since they are never without material for pious affection and prayer. The Almighty is accustomed, through the goads of adversity, to rouse his own people to remembrance of him; he is accustomed to brand their minds with the prickings of the flesh, so that, while they fear ruin, they may always be found inclined through vows and prayers toward God’s aid.

## CHAPTER V

### [XXI.] The calamities of the Christians are recalled

We have said not once but perhaps many times—and we are not weary of repeating it—that nothing of this kind has ever happened anywhere in the world. If the sons of Israel are brought forward against me with the miracles that the Lord performed before them, I shall establish something much more wondrous: a sea of the most densely packed pagan world opened before these men. For them I shall point to the cloud of divine fear supplied by day from a pillar, and by night the light of divine hope; Christ himself inspired in them examples of uprightness and strength as a pillar. He strengthened them with the word of God, as with heavenly manna, as their sole nourishment [al. consolation], without hope of any earthly support.

The Israelites grew disgusted with the food supplied from heaven; they repeatedly recalled Egypt, which they had abandoned, in their minds and with their voices. These men, on the other hand, just as they never undertake anything that turns backward, so they embrace whatever poverty and necessity may assail them with vigorous spirits. Certainly the calamity celebrated at Antioch, which was almost yawning from its repeated fasts, is reported not to have existed without certain noble spectacles. With what courage do we suppose they conducted themselves amid the afflictions of that utter destitution—when nothing is customarily endured with greater difficulty among human beings—those who did not disdain the Christian theaters appropriate, beyond doubt, to that time and place?

### The little children who went to Jerusalem with their fathers. The army of those children

It is plainly reported by those who were present that, while the same city was being besieged and the besiegers and townspeople were mingling in frequent engagements, it very often happened that, when the men on both sides gave way and alternately checked the attack by judgment and reason, groups of children would come out from the city on one side, while groups of our people’s sons would gather against them from the other; and they would engage in battle, each side fully worthy of expectation.

For, as we related at the beginning of this history, when the expedition to Jerusalem had become widely known in the western regions, fathers with their little sons undertook this same journey. Consequently, when some parents died, the boys themselves continued with the army, grew accustomed to hardship, and, so far as endurance of poverty was concerned, were in no way inferior to their elders.

These boys, therefore, having formed a column of their own, had created leaders from among themselves: one bore the name of Hugh the Great, another that of Bohemond, this one that of the Fleming, that one that of the Norman, and others bore the names of other persons. Whenever they saw those subject to them being harassed by a scarcity of provisions, they went to the leaders mentioned above to ask for food. Those nobles gave them abundant supplies, by which their weakness could appropriately be nourished.

Such an army, then, so remarkable in appearance, frequently challenged the city’s children; they used long reeds as weapons, wove shields from wicker, and carried little bows and missiles, each according to his ability. When these boys and the townspeople had met in the middle of the field, with old men watching on both sides, the townspeople waited from the walls, while our men waited before their tents.

There one could see attacks shouted against one another and blows made bloody, though without any suspicion of deaths. These frequent preliminaries stirred the hearts of the adults to renew the conflicts. When they saw spirits boiling too fiercely beneath their limbs [al. beneath powerless limbs], when they observed the unarmed boys, whatever their weapons might be, eagerly moving their arms, and when the different groups of spectators groaned over the injuries inflicted by either side, the elders, having removed the children from the midst, would come together for their customary wars. Thus it scarcely happened that the army of the Lord was found at rest: while some were being trained, others were exercising themselves every day.

### [XXII.] The army of the barefooted, and their manner of life

There was also another kind of people in that army who went barefoot, carried no weapons, and were not permitted to possess any amount of money at all. Completely filthy from nakedness and want, they went ahead of everyone, living on the roots of plants and whatever cheap growths they could find.

When a certain man born in Normandy, of no obscure origin, as is said, but having become a foot-soldier from a knight, saw them wandering without authority, he laid aside his weapons and the clothing he wore and wished to declare himself their king. From that time he began to be called King Thafur in the barbarian tongue.

Among the gentiles, *Thafur* is what they call those whom we, speaking too literally, call *trudenues* [al.: *trudennes*, French *truands*]. They are so called because they *trudunt*, that is, “they pass lightly through,” traveling everywhere across the years (*annos*; perhaps read *agros*, “fields”).

It was this man’s custom that, whenever the people under him came to the crossing of some bridge or reached some narrow place, he would hasten to occupy the entrance. Having examined each of his men individually down to the last detail, if it happened that any one of them possessed the value of two solidi, he would immediately exclude him from his jurisdiction and, ordering him to buy weapons, separate him for service in the armed fellowship of the army.

If he saw that any who loved their accustomed poverty had neither saved nor desired any money at all, he would admit them as special members of his own company. Someone might perhaps think such men entirely useless to the common good, and that they consumed food without benefit, food that could have supplied the expenses of others. Yet in transporting provisions, collecting pay, and even hurling stones during the siege of cities, it cannot be said how necessary they were: in carrying loads, they went ahead of asses and pack animals; and they matched the crossbows and siege engines in their frequent throws.

Moreover, when, at Maʿarra and elsewhere, pieces of flesh taken from the bodies of pagans were found after excessive hunger had pressed hard, a thing which is acknowledged to have been done by these men both secretly and very rarely, a dreadful rumor spread among the pagans that there were certain men in the Frankish army who eagerly ate the flesh of Saracens.

Therefore, when this opinion had resounded especially loudly among them, they roasted the mutilated body of a certain Turk, as is said, placing it before everyone on a fire as though it were edible meat, in order to terrify them. When the Turks learned of this, and, thinking that what was fabricated was entirely true, had become convinced of it, they feared the insolence of Thafur more than, in a certain sense, the violence of our princes.

The Turks, plainly following the custom of the ancient pagans, are tormented by unburied corpses to such an extent that no Christian seems to think or grieve so earnestly over souls condemned. Therefore, to stir up their bitterness most fiercely, during the siege of Antioch the bishop of Puy, after consulting our nobles, issued an edict and ordered it to be proclaimed throughout the army: whoever brought him the severed head of any Turk would immediately receive twelve denarii as a reward.

For when the bishop had received their heads, he ordered them to be fixed on enormous stakes before their eyes, in front of the city walls. They used to be tortured and terror-stricken most bitterly when they saw this.

The bishop also did something else there that should not be passed over. Acting with the advice of our nobles, when the townspeople perceived that our men were suffering from a scarcity of provisions, our men proposed, on the contrary, that they should yoke oxen to the plow, plow and sow in sight of the city, so that the townspeople might understand from this that men making arrangements for the harvest of the coming year would by no means abandon the siege they had begun.

These and other marvelous and wondrous things were done in this same expedition. We think that no one could possibly comprehend them all, just as no one in the history of the world is known to have heard of a people leaving its own regions without a king or prince; of great and small alike learning, under God alone, to bear the yoke as equals; of a servant not looking to a master, nor a master claiming anything from a servant except brotherhood.

As, then, we cannot produce examples from the past for such things, so we think that similar events will never occur in the future. We infer this for the most part from the fact that, after the capture of Jerusalem, we saw such movements among Christian peoples; we learned that so many persons of no lesser dignity, so many cavalry units of a name not to be despised, and so many infantry forces migrated after those who had gone before and prepared the road for those who would follow, that we undoubtedly judge them to have been almost equal to the earlier people both in wealth and in number.

For who could count, when Count Stephen—whom we discussed above—and Hugh the Great, brother of King Philip, again began the journey to the Lord’s Sepulchre, how great a multitude of the most ordinary and lowest sort proceeded from the regions of France alone? I say nothing of the duke of Burgundy; what shall I say of the count of Poitiers? Besides the great mass of soldiers whom he had decided to lead with him, he had also gathered groups of girls.

When the ambition of his majesty resounded everywhere as its own witness, he came to Constantinople and held a conference with Alexius, that most faithless of men, the tyrant. Before that count had departed from the royal city, the utterly wicked traitor reported his arrival to the Turks by letters.

“Behold,” he wrote, “the fattest sheep from the Franks are advancing toward you, though they are ruled by a shepherd of little foresight.”

What more need be said? The count had passed beyond the tyrant’s territories when a Turkish army suddenly appeared before him. Weakening the man’s forces, which were, as might be expected, newly arrived and disorganized, it scattered, plundered, and defeated them.

There Hugh the Great, struck in the knee by an arrow and weakened by a prolonged illness, finally died, obtaining the rights of burial at Tarsus in Cilicia. They report that these events took place in the province called Satyria.

## CHAPTER VI

### [XXIII.] The treacherous emperor deceives the Frankish leaders

Meanwhile Count Stephen, with certain bishops of our kingdom—including Hugh of Soissons and William of Paris, men of distinguished character and lineage, who in the first flower of their age served their episcopal offices with the most illustrious morals, and Engelram of Laon [al.: Ingelram], a man conspicuous in form and eloquence—if only he had been equally so in religion—entered within the walls of Constantinople with great dignity from every order.

The emperor summoned them to him and honored their leaders with splendid gifts. When they were consulting whether they should follow the route of the earlier army or proceed by another road, he truthfully declared that they did not possess enough cavalry to be able to take a route different from that of the earlier army.

They, thinking that they would achieve something new and greater than their predecessors, declared that they would travel through foreign regions. At the same time they requested from the emperor that everywhere, by his command, they should be allowed to have a general and universal market throughout Greece. He promised this; and, knowing that by this insolence they had, as it were, conspired toward their own destruction, he gladly consented to the error he had foreseen so well.

They were therefore advised to enter some desert through Paphlagonia, a province known hardly at all—not merely to ordinary travelers, but scarcely even through written records. The emperor forbade them to carry provisions except what would be necessary for forty days alone. Moreover, he almost discouraged the carrying of provisions by promising magnificently that they would be able to obtain supplies throughout the entire land.

### The Frankish army is delivered over to slaughter

As they went on and had already advanced into the farther reaches of the deep wilderness, the common people, who had proceeded carelessly without provisions in reliance upon the promised market, began day by day to be oppressed by the most violent hunger, to swell up, and to die. The army, too, was harassed by the stench of corpses lying everywhere.

Several times, when the leaders of the impoverished multitude were punishing the rearmost members of the army so that they would not follow the cavalry ahead too slowly, lest the Turks swoop down upon them, those men, driven by the tortures of hunger, wished with vows and prayers that the Turks would come.

They had almost reached the borders of Armenia. The men were exhausted and the animals were dying from starvation when suddenly numerous thousands of Turks burst upon them. But the Franks, who at that time appeared to be holding the army’s first line of defense, easily blunted their efforts at once, although they themselves were exhausted.

On the following day, when the Turks saw that the Franks had withdrawn from the front, and that Lombards, Ligurians, and Italians—alas!—were occupying the forward positions, they attacked. Having perceived the cowardice of the men in front, the fiercest of enemies fell upon them. When those who were leading and carrying the standards disgracefully turned their backs, the entire army lay open not so much to flight—for flight was very slight among men wasting away from hunger—as to pitiable slaughter.

Those who fled did not return by the route they had come, nor did they gather together even in groups so that they might flee collectively. Each turned his steps wherever his spirit carried him, plainly destined to die. Their slaughter and pursuit continued for almost eight uninterrupted days.

There was in that army [al. in that danger] an archbishop of Milan who had brought with him the chapel of Saint Ambrose—that is, a chasuble and a white garment, and I do not know what else—adorned with gold and gems of such great value that nowhere on earth could anyone have found another capable of matching it.

The Turks seized and carried it away. God thereby avenged the folly of that prelate, who had brought so sacred an object into barbarian lands, through such a loss.

So great was the slaughter there of Christians of both sexes, and so great the discovery of money, clothing, gold, and silver, that, considering the damage which the first expedition had inflicted, this one victory alone could have been sufficient consolation for the Turks.

For although there were said to be two hundred thousand, and according to some more than that, of the Christian name there, scarcely seven thousand remained. Count Stephen, however, was there with many powerful men, including the magnificent Harpinus of Bourges and Count Stephen from beyond the Arar; they likewise reached Jerusalem.

When they were settled there, and the army of the Babylonian emperor had offered battle to Baldwin, now king, at the city of Ramoth, the aforementioned Harpinus told the king to postpone the battle until he had gathered whatever forces he could. The king said: “If you are afraid, flee to Bourges.” Having spoken these words, he engaged rashly and immediately lost all his forces, driven into the aforesaid city; he alone escaped. Many were then led into captivity; concerning the end by which many others perished, we remain uncertain to this day.

### Harpinus of Bourges assumes the monastic habit

Harpinus was carried away captive. Later, having been released from captivity and returning to France, he became a monk.

Nothing certain is known about Stephen of Chartres, except that he is believed to have been killed, though without any evidence. He was captured with countless others inside a certain tower near the aforesaid city; whether he was assigned to the fate of captivity or of death, we have so far been unable to learn from reliable authorities. We are inclined to believe in his death because he never appeared again.

The Turks, plainly, customarily condemned the corpses of the slain after victory by cutting off their heads, and carried them away as a sign of triumph. Once these had been removed, it was extremely difficult to recognize the identity of any person from a headless body. The same uncertainty has likewise persisted until now concerning certain other very distinguished men.

Meanwhile the king himself, who, as has been mentioned, had escaped alone, was mourned by his people not only because of the common destruction that threatened, but was also loudly proclaimed dead by the pagans with mocking laughter. Proceeding through certain rugged mountains known to only a few, he finally, after two days, if I am not mistaken, entered Jerusalem, which was awaiting him amid despair and already extreme dangers, with the griefs that were due.

He quickly gathered whatever cavalry he could and, as far as his resources permitted, selected the best infantry. With the Lord now more merciful, he prepared to engage in battle with the victorious pagan forces—though their victory did not last long. When they thought the king dead, he suddenly appeared with his forces restored, fought with authority far different from before, and drove them into flight, blowing back their renewed fear with the sting of a most savage slaughter.

### [XXIV.] The death of King Godfrey

But since, because the order of the subject took precedence, we did not previously report the death of King Godfrey, the brother of this Baldwin, it is appropriate briefly to explain how he died and where he was buried.

It is said that gifts were sent to him by a certain prince of the neighboring pagan people, gifts infected—as became clear—with deadly poisons. Taking them incautiously, since he suspected the sender of being a friend, he fell ill with a sudden sickness and, without delay, died lifeless.

There are also those who, rejecting this opinion, say that he died a natural death.

He was buried near the place of the Lord’s Passion, as a testimony to the eternal redemption he had merited by his faith and life. There he possessed a monument in every respect, in the very place which he had rescued and defended from the trampling and invasion of the pagans.

His remarkable humility, and the modesty worthy of imitation even by monks, marked the period of his kingdom with this very praiseworthy distinction: he never wore the royal crown within the city of Jerusalem, evidently out of consideration for the fact that our Lord Jesus Christ, the universal author of the salvation of all, had worn there a crown of thorns in human mockery.

### Baldwin, the brother of Godfrey, succeeds Godfrey

When this had been completed, as we have said, and since we in no way believed that Baldwin would prove degenerate from his brother’s moderation and prudence, they brought him from Edessa and appointed him to reign over that holy new colony of Christianity.

They had observed certain qualities of the utmost distinction in the nature of those men, and, having observed them, had loved them: calm manners, entirely free from every kind of ostentation; unremitting courage, more than was appropriate even to royal majesty, with scarcely any fear of death; arrogance removed from all their bearing; and a generosity wholly munificent, beyond the resources of their wealth.

Baldwin’s faithfulness toward his people and his contempt for himself can be inferred from one deed: while he was conducting an expedition against the enemy, he exposed himself to such danger in rescuing a certain foot-soldier that, after receiving a very serious wound, he scarcely escaped the perils of imminent death.

## CHAPTER VII

### [XXV.] Prophecies concerning the Christian expedition to Jerusalem

Meanwhile there was something which greatly terrified the innumerable surrounding nations, lest they rise against the smallness of our people, and which is recognized as terrifying them no less even today. The science of the stars is weaker and rarer among Westerners, but among Easterners, where it originated, it is known to burn more intensely through constant use and frequent recollection.

The pagans themselves testify that they had received a clear prognostication from it, and that long beforehand, through this foreknowledge, they had learned of the disasters that would come upon them because they would be subdued by the Christian people. Yet through their knowledge of the art they could not be instructed fully as to the time when these events would be fulfilled.

### [XXVI.]

For almost twelve years before our nobles undertook the journey to Jerusalem, Robert, the elder count of the Flemings, whom we discussed in the first book of this work, went to Jerusalem with many riches for the sake of prayer.

While he remained in the city for several days, desiring to see the holy places, he was permitted, on account of his generosity, to have the opportunity of learning many things, including what was being done among the pagans. One day, as I learned from those who had provided the count with familiar attendance there, almost all the citizens of that city gathered at Solomon’s Temple. After holding a very large assembly there throughout the entire day, they finally returned toward evening to their own lodgings.

The count was then staying with a Saracen of advanced age and more experienced judgment, who, insofar as could be said among that people, was of holier life. “Servant of God” was his usual name. When he asked the count, on his return home, what they had wished to sit for so long in that temple discussing, and what they had treated in such an extended debate, the man replied:

“We have observed certain unusual signs in the courses and recourses of the stars. From these we have drawn a very certain conjecture: men of Christian condition will come into these provinces, and we shall be overcome by continual battles and frequent victories. Yet whether this will be greatly delayed in the future or is to happen soon remains entirely uncertain to us.

“Nevertheless, it has become clear to us from the astronomical prediction itself that those very men who, by a judgment from above, are permitted to overcome our people and drive them from their native lands will finally be defeated by us and expelled by the right of war from the homeland they will usurp.

“To this heavenly indication, a reading drawn from the oracles of the ancients of our sect, taken everywhere from various volumes, immediately gave its harmonious testimony. It openly confirmed the same thing that the ethereal radiance had signaled through its more obscure signs.”

The words of this pagan agree with those reported above as the words of Curbaran’s mother. Nor is there any doubt among us that, by the same reasoning through which she dissuaded her son from making war against the Christians, these men too are restrained who long for the destruction of Jerusalem, lest they enter into wars against what has been shown to them as a fatal decree.

For although at first they persist in harassing our people with repeated battles, they now act against them with so much greater restraint, since they perceive that it is not our people but the Lord who is being exercised and fighting on their behalf.

If it should seem incredible to anyone that a person can foresee future events through the astrological art, let this provide us with clear evidence: through such a discipline the emperor Heraclius foresaw that a circumcised people would rise against the Roman Empire. Yet by that expertise he could not foresee that it would not be the Jews but the Saracens who would carry out these actions.

Let us also consider the magi. When, upon the sudden appearance of the star, they perceived that a king had been born—and this king both God and man—they also knew in which regions he would reign.

[XXVII]—In this very new campaign of God against diabolical men, this too deserves attention: the event seems in every respect to correspond to Gideon’s [Judges 7]. For when our countless forces were thought to be unanimously resolute in undertaking the proposed enterprise, they were tested at the waters—that is, at pleasures and luxuries—so that those who chose to follow God would not yield to the torments of hunger and thirst or to various kinds of death; while those who would place God after their bodies would incline feebly toward passing desires, as the bent knee there signifies. Those who drank by thrusting their hands to their mouths are the ones who, like Diogenes, with every concern for luxuries set aside, satisfied nature in whatever manner while serving God.

The three hundred who were approved under Gideon signify those who, both outwardly and inwardly, are shown to bear the cross, represented by the letter Tau, which is valued at three hundred. Why, then, did many of our people disgracefully withdraw from the Lord’s service? Was it not because they were steadily worn down by severe hunger? And because, as Terence says, “without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold” [Terence, *Eunuchus* IV.5.6], no capacity for the practice of lust remained in their weakened bodies; and even if it had remained, no suitable opportunity was available.

These men, therefore, who were found approved, “hold trumpets” in their hands, because they express in their deeds the divine word by whose consolation they are refreshed amid so many dangers. They “hold jars,” because, stationed in continual readiness for battle, they keep themselves from every bodily defilement. Within the jars they “have lamps,” because in the earthen vessels of their bodies treasures of devout intention shine more brightly than every light.

“Gideon divides them into three companies”: Christ gathers some of them to the crown through the shedding of their own blood; he leads others, as though to the cultivation of the promised land, to guard the holy city, through whom even today that very small number resists the whole power of the East; and he permits the rest to return to their homeland as witnesses to so great a victory and as examples for imitation of this devout exile.

“When the jars are broken, the lamps shine,” because, when their bodies have been killed, their spirits, burning with divine love, depart directly to the Lord with upright purpose. The enemies are thereby terrified and overcome, because they rightly fear those who, made bold by hope of eternity, embrace death more dearly than life itself.

“For the blood of those animals,” as the Apostle says, “whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest, their bodies are burned outside the camp” [Hebrews 13:11]. Hence the Lord suffered outside the gate. Therefore they went out to him, outside the camp—outside, that is, the desires of the flesh—“bearing the reproach of his cross” [ibid., 13], preserving mortification in their vices and desires.

## CHAPTER VIII

[XXVIII] But how powerful the undertaking of so great a labor was when joined to good will may be gathered from the single example set out below. We have decided to present it so that we may clearly weigh how greatly the devout undertaking of this pilgrimage benefited those who confessed their sins sincerely and truly repented, since it is shown to have been so powerful, and to have struck such terror into the devil, even in the case of those almost entirely deprived of repentance and confession.

[XXIX] A certain man, having undertaken the journey to Jerusalem and confessed his sins there to a priest, is freed from diabolical deception.—A certain man of the equestrian order, from the coastal regions, if I am not mistaken, had lost his own brother through violence inflicted by an enemy. He had borne his brother’s death so bitterly that he was wasting away in inconsolable grief. The man who had killed him seemed to possess greater power, so that the mourner had no hope of avenging the dead.

Thus, weakened by intolerable pain and following his brother in his grief at every moment, he found the bitterness of his irreparable loss renewed day by day. Without any thought of consolation, the unavoidable memory of it tormented the unhappy man’s lacerated heart; and as the difficulty of pursuing vengeance to the end multiplied his constant anguish a hundredfold, the devil—clever through long experience and, in spiritual quickness, more agile than any mortal nature, always watching for occasions and causes—smiled upon this opportunity for grief.

One day, then, when he was riding his horse and leading it to the water, breathing out the sighs of profound exhaustion, inwardly squalid with the decay of madness, he saw a demon standing across from him on the farther bank of the river. It appeared to him in the form of a certain man whom he had often been accustomed to see with his legs contracted. The figure too appeared as a rider, carrying a hawk in his hand and wearing a tunic of a muddy color, as he described it.

When he looked at the figure from a distance and, recognizing the familiar man whom he believed it to be, recalled his customary weakness and appearance, he was stunned by the force of the unexpected novelty. The evil spirit, mindful of its ancient boldness, spoke first:

“I am not,” it said, “the one you think. Know, however, that I am the devil, sent to offer remedies for your long torment. My master, who compassionately deigns to assist all who are in sorrow if they consent to him, has sent me to you; and if you are willing to accept what I shall tell you, he will not delay to offer you consolation.

“Since he is generous and possesses no lack of the infinite wealth he gives, he is lavish in the assistance of his gifts to those who desire riches beyond what can be estimated; to the needy he does not postpone aid beyond what they might hope for. You, however, who continually lament an old misfortune with an ever-renewed grief of spirit—if there is anything for which you complain, declare it, knowing beyond doubt that you will receive much more than you presume to ask.

“If you bring forward the murder of your brother, you will learn that the sentence of vengeance will be hastened; if you ask for any kind of increase, you will marvel at what is done. Whatever you wish or command, the means will be available according to your desire.”

He had observed an exceedingly strange creature and was astonished to hear the devil speaking with the greatest amazement; but to the extent that he was drawn on by the allure of the promise, he was frightened by the wickedness of the promiser. At last ambition for the promised benefits prevailed, and he admitted that he would gladly accept what was offered.

“Nevertheless,” said the devil, “if the fruit of my promise delights you, and the free benevolence of my prince, who sent me to you, has in some way attracted you; when you have proved by the actual results that what I foretold concerning both vengeance for your brother and success in your fortunes is true, my master himself demands this from you: that you do homage to him and promise that, having transferred your Christian faith, you will cling to him indivisibly and persistently abstain from whatever he forbids.

“There are, however, certain specific things from which he wants you to refrain completely once you have joined him: namely, that you never enter a church, and that you never receive anyone baptized from the sacred font.” He likewise forbade a third thing, which had slipped from the memory of the man who told me the story.

The man replied: “I can easily observe these commands without any delay; but regarding the performance of homage, I ask that some postponement be granted.”

While still exercising his free reason, the man greatly recoiled from being asked to transfer his allegiance to so execrable a faith; but he judged it more tolerable to abstain from Christian observances than to be deprived of the foundation of his belief.

Thereafter, at the prompting of the evil one, an opportunity for vengeance upon his brother was supplied to him so abundantly that, as good fortune continually increased, his desires were entirely surpassed. As the remedy thus succeeded, the ferocity of his grief was gradually blotted from his mind, while in the meantime he did not presume in any way to attempt the things the devil had forbidden him.
