Meanwhile, the ancient enemy of human nature carefully continued to appear to the man—not only, as usual, seeking out his solitude or secret places, but suddenly approaching him even amid the crowds of the public. It proposed the benefits he had already experienced, promised greater ones in the future, and persistently urged him to transfer his faith. He, rejoicing in every way at the generosity he had experienced, promised perpetual service to so generous a prince, but continually begged for postponement concerning the homage-payment that was so frequently demanded of him.

As this man was pressed by extremely frequent apparitions, which approached him invisibly even amid crowds, by God’s will the report of the journey to Jerusalem spread throughout the Latin world. Everyone who realized that he was entangled in some crime was directed there, as God opened new paths of repentance. Among them this man chose to set out, but he did not disclose in confession the wicked pact he had already made, for the most part, with the devil.

Thus, although he possessed zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, and although confession of his sins had not preceded the beginning of his good works, such an abundance of God’s grace accompanied him along the way, and the labor pleased God so greatly—though undertaken with an imperfect devotion—that during the journey itself the deadly exactor did not dare to trouble him with any demands. Rather, as though he remembered nothing of the pact made with him, he did not appear to him in a vision in any form.

At last, when Jerusalem had been captured, while he was staying for a time in the city with the others, one night, when he was thought to be sleeping with certain soldiers, he grew concerned about his own horses and those of his companions, which, according to the custom of the region, were staying outside under the open sky. He looked toward them and, seeing what appeared to be a standing man among them, rose, suspecting a thief, and anxiously asked who he was.

The figure immediately assumed the appearance it had been accustomed to bear and, as though reverent and bashful, said: “Do you not recognize me?”

But the man, as though an old reproach were being renewed against him, answered much more sternly: “I recognize you.”

After these words had been spoken on both sides, the apparition added no further question after the inquiry, and the man added nothing to his reply. Although this appearance seemed pointless as far as the man was concerned, by God’s providence it nevertheless signified something of importance to us: namely, that the devil had not forgotten the man, but by showing itself and by what had happened had declared what it wanted, while by its silence it revealed that it had been unable to obtain it.

What more is there to say? The man returned, but even during the return journey the devil nowhere made itself visible or troublesome to him. Once he had arrived at home, however, the companion of his wicked purpose was immediately revived for that pitiable person, so that scarcely a short time passed before he was again troubled by such admonition.

“Human beings may be separated from those they fear by certain intervals, and rooms and walls may distinguish them from disturbances; but spiritual wickedness is kept from its assaults by neither the presence of crowds nor the defenses of enclosed chambers.”

While that man was enduring—and fatally detesting—a robber so inseparably attached to him, it happened one day that he encountered a certain priest of Christ, outstanding in learning, kindness, and devout cheerfulness, named Conon. Since, given the hardship of the time then prevailing—for everyone was occupied with his own journey—he had disclosed to him the misery he was suffering, that good man offered him whatever consolation he could in the circumstances and, after receiving a promise that he would return, dismissed him.

Yet the bloodthirsty beast did not remain silent; meanwhile it did not cease provoking him through the allure of its repeated enticements. Before long, unable to endure the troubles and almost daily harassment, the man returned to the physician. He made a full confession, undertook penance with his whole heart, and, once he had undertaken it, never again saw his own persecutor.

Let us consider, then, how greatly this pious pilgrimage availed the pure, and how much protection and security it brought to the impure.

[XXX] The deeds courageously accomplished in the East must be attributed to God alone.—It is also clear, and worthy of the closest consideration, that kings were excluded from the favor of this expedition for a reason: lest the exalted dignity of a conspicuous person should seem to claim the heavenly results for itself. Praise, therefore, must be referred to the heavenly Lord, while the human agent must be entirely passed over in silence.

No individual commander gathered so many armies or earned these triumphs. Regulus subdued the rebellious Carthaginians, and the praise for his enterprise is attributed to him. Alexander, exhausting the eastern kingdoms through immeasurable slaughter, succeeded in acquiring the name “the Great.” Here, Count Stephen, to whom the supreme direction of the sacred army had been entrusted, is cast aside as though he had rashly usurped what belonged to God alone, as though condemned for cowardice; and Hugh the Great, as a man of royal name, is set apart.

Once the shadows of great names had been driven away and the power on which the army had relied had been removed, that little flock remained dependent upon God’s help alone. When the decisive moment came, in accordance with the saying of Scripture, “The unsuspected man bore the crown” [Ecclesiasticus 11:5]—not from lineage, but because God had chosen him.

God, who works wonders, did not wish the honor of his name to be assigned to another. He alone was their leader; he ruled them, corrected them, directed what had been begun toward accomplishment, and extended their kingdoms to this point. Thus, from wolves whom he had made, he gathered lambs in his own strength, not theirs; he lifted them in the protection of his bosom and, filled with the joy of devout hope, carried them to see what they had desired.

## CHAPTER IX

[XXXI] Fulcher of Chartres is censured and corrected. 1. His assertion that many were divinely marked with the cross is refuted.—As, with the world’s Creator graciously disposed, we are about to place the finishing touches on the body of the present history, we have discovered that a certain Fulcher, a priest of Chartres, who had formerly been the chaplain of Count Baldwin, commander at Edessa, has reported certain other matters unknown to us, and also some matters differing from our account, though few, in a deceitful and crude style like that of the others. Although we have judged that not everything he wrote should be exposed, we have decided to uncover and join some of it to this little book.

Since this man casts out inflated expressions and words a foot and a half long [Horace, *Ars Poetica* 97], and displays the lurid colors of empty figures of speech, I have preferred to seize the bare limbs of the events themselves and wrap them, whatever the quality of my eloquence, in a sack rather than weave them into ornament.

At the beginning of his little work, if I am not mistaken, he is said to report that certain men who appeared to have undertaken the journey to Jerusalem entered the sea in hired ships at the strait that separates Apulia and Epirus. I do not know whether they committed themselves to the uncharted sea or sank their vessels through their excessive numbers; it is certain, however, that nearly six hundred men there suffered shipwreck.

After all had been killed by the storms of the turbulent sea, they were soon cast upon the mainland by the impatient surge of the waves. There, still wearing the cloaks, mantles, and tunics that they had customarily used, they were discovered to bear the sign of the cross visibly upon the surface of their shoulders.

No faithful person may doubt that this sacred mark could have been divinely impressed upon their skin to demonstrate the reality of their faith. Nevertheless, the writer of this account, if he is still alive, should carefully consider whether the matter truly happened in this way.

For when the beginning of this road had spread throughout Christian peoples everywhere, and it was being proclaimed throughout the Roman empire that it was undertaken not without the will of God, people of the lowest class—and even women, in their unworthiness—claimed this miracle for themselves in many forms and places.

One man displayed for a while streaks woven into his eye by an effusion of blood, asserting that they formed a cross. Another, pointing to a disfiguring spot on the pupil with which he saw poorly, presented it as a heavenly sign summoning him to depart. Someone else, using the juice of new apples or some other kind of coloring, tried to make the appearance of a cross on some part of the body, so that, just as the seats of the eyes are customarily painted with stibium, the spectacle of the divine sign in him might appear green or red—a display produced by fraud and fabrication.

Let the reader remember that abbot whom I mentioned above [Book IV, chapter 7], who carved his forehead with iron and whom I later said was made bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. I call God to witness that, while I was staying at Beauvais at that time, I saw clouds, turned somewhat obliquely toward one another in the middle of the day, which scarcely seemed to display anything larger than a crane or the shape of a stork. Suddenly, however, the urban crowds everywhere shouted that a cross had been sent to them from heaven.

What I am about to say is ridiculous, though the event was attested by authors who were not ridiculous. A certain little woman had begun to advance upon this very journey. A goose, furnished with I know not what novel rudiments, wandered after her, contrary to the laws of sluggish nature. And behold, flying rumor, driven by Pegasus-like movements, filled both camps and cities with the report that God had destined even geese to redeem Jerusalem.

The poor woman was not merely said to be leading the goose; rather, she was said to be led by the goose. This was confirmed at Cambrai to such an extent that, while the people stood on either side, the woman proceeded through the middle of the church toward the altar, and the goose followed behind, directly in the woman’s footsteps, without anyone urging it on.

Not long afterward, as we learned, it died in Lorraine by a death of its own. It would more properly have gone to Jerusalem if, on the day before its departure, it had offered itself as a festive banquet to its mistress.

We append the whole story to our history for this reason: so that all may know themselves warned “that Christian seriousness should in no way be made frivolous by attributing faith to the fables of the crowd.”

[XXXII] The claim that Christ appeared a second time to Pyrrhus so that he might surrender Antioch is proved false.—Finally, the same author again asserts that God appeared to Pyrrhus, the traitor of Antioch, and commanded him in a vision to betray the city to the Franks.

This was easy for one who had made himself audible to Cain and Hagar and had made an angel visible to the donkey. But all who returned after the holy city had been taken, and all who sent us letters about what had happened, especially Anselm of Ribemont, said nothing of the kind. Indeed, that same man did not even mention Pyrrhus, though he did not conceal that the city had been handed over by three of its citizens.

He also reports that, before those three nobles had seriously discussed the city’s surrender, they offered our men a deceptive peace, promising that they would soon return the city. This mutual security was so effective that they repeatedly received Franks within the city walls, and frequently mingled gatherings of their own people with ours.

While the army, because of excessive confidence, was paying insufficient attention to itself during these events, the Turks, laying ambushes, killed several of the Franks; yet they themselves did not escape unharmed. There they lost a young man of outstanding character, named Walo, who had been constable to the king of the Franks.

[XXXIII] His rejection of the Lord’s lance, thirdly.—He is said to invalidate the discovery of the Lord’s lance, and, because he was liable to falsehood, to testify that the condemned man was burned by the presumed ordeal of fire.

Not only do the testimonies of modern people contradict him on this matter; the most ancient witnesses also, with the fullest confidence, affirm that when they formerly visited the holy places—before the Turks overran the kingdoms of the East and Syria—they used to venerate and kiss that same lance in the same city.

Will the cleverness of Fulcher, the priest—who, while our men were endangered by hunger at Antioch, was feasting in idleness at Edessa—prevail over the understanding of so many prudent men who were present when it was found? Even Baldwin, who later governed the aforementioned Edessa after King Baldwin, declares in his letter to Archbishop Manasses that, when the lance was found through the revelation of blessed Andrew, our men were emboldened by confidence in it to fight against the advancing Turks.

Should that distinguished bishop of Le Puy be thought to have been so foolish as to carry an uncertain lance with such reverence when he went out to engage Curbaran?

There, certainly, a memorable event is known to have occurred. Curbaran had ordered a fire to be set to some grass, and the same bishop saw the faces and eyes of the Franks hastening to battle flooded by the density of the smoke. Carrying the sacred lance on one side and, with his devout right hand, tracing the figure of a cross against the rising clouds on the other, he tearfully called upon the help of almighty Jesus. More quickly than words can say, God’s mercy turned the ball of dark vapor back upon those who had sent it forth.

Moreover, if the discussion concerns the death of the discoverer, who is said to have lived only a few days after the trial by fire, I confess that I shall say how this man died—though it is uncertain whether he was injured—if Fulcher will tell me why the man who had received all tongues from blessed Gregory tore his own limbs apart with his teeth.

[XXXIV] Fourthly, that a radiant beam in the form of a cross appeared during the siege of Antioch.—Furthermore, while they were staying at the siege of Antioch, he asserts, if I am not mistaken, that at night a radiant beam, like fire, flashed above the army and displayed, in unmistakable form, the appearance of a cross.

All the wise men who were there interpreted this conflagration as a sign of future battles, in which the cross seemed to indicate certain salvation and forthcoming victory. We do not refute this; it is fully confirmed by abundant testimony. I say that Parmenon, full of cracks, could have kept silent about this.

A similar event is also known to have occurred at the very beginning of this journey, which I happened to pass over above when I was speaking about eclipses and the motions of the stars, whose falls were seen [the text has *visus est*, perhaps *visi sunt*].

One summer evening, a conflagration appeared to burst forth so fiercely from the northern quarter that many people rushed out of their houses, asking which enemies were devastating their provinces with so severe a burning. We unquestionably regard all these things as portents of future wars.

But now, leaving aside the matters that we have judged should be touched upon only selectively, let us continue the sequence of our narrative.

## CHAPTER X

[XXXV] Again concerning the siege of the city of Jerusalem.—When the city of Jerusalem was besieged, it is impossible to express with what determination its citizens defended it. You could see them cover the walls with beams against the siege engines by which they had learned that stones were hurled, and throw Greek fire onto the machines with mats—especially since they understood that the scarcity of timber created the greatest difficulty for the siege.

But because France excelled in ingenuity, the flames were checked by sprinkling vinegar, and whatever seemed to hang over the walls was cut away with a very sharp sickle. They attached iron hooks to long poles, by which they seized the armored defenders of our side from the siege engines; our men, with drawn swords, turned the poles into clubs.

The Sarracens’ vigorous persistence was especially evident in this: if one of their men happened to be crushed by a blow from our people, another immediately seized the stricken man’s shield and set it in the very place from which he had fallen [variant: restored it], so that our men would understand, to their dismay, that none of them had been harmed by their missiles.

[XXXVI] Bohemond was not present at the siege itself. He asks to go to Jerusalem.—When the city had therefore been successfully captured, Bohemond—who had secured his rule at Antioch through the hunger, bloodshed, and cold endured by the Franks—preferred to remain there while the others departed rather than suffer hardship for the liberation of the Lord Jesus’ tomb.

And while he foolishly contended for the custody of a single small tower and building, he seemed to have lost the fruit and joy of all his previous labor. For what did it profit him to run where he did not wish to attain his goal?

Nevertheless, since up to that time he had contributed greatly to the Lord’s army by arms and counsel, it is not inappropriate to relate briefly how he came to go there.

He therefore sent an embassy to Baldwin of Edessa and urged him to come with him to visit the Savior’s tomb. Baldwin himself had not joined the siege of the city because he was held back, not by greed, but by the defense of his own city. It was plainly a Christian city, and it frequently suffered hostile attacks from the pagan peoples around it.

When Baldwin promised that he would go, they gathered immense forces of cavalry and infantry, especially since not only their own safety but that of the entire neighboring region was weighing upon them, and they undertook the journey to Jerusalem.

When they had joined the separate groups into a single camp and numbered nearly twenty thousand men, cruel scarcity of provisions began to press upon them as they traveled, so that they had neither seasonings for the bread nor bread for the food. Their provinces, exhausted by the long duration of various sieges and by extended campaigns far and wide, were utterly unable to provide supplies for so great a multitude of men and animals.

Bohemond is taken captive by the Turks. After being granted his freedom, he returns to Gaul, marries the king’s daughter Constantia, and is killed by poison.—Thus the multitude, constrained by pitiable hunger, returned to the food of donkey and horse flesh that they had learned to eat on other occasions. Nor did this calamity cease from such use, even with the restraint appropriate to such circumstances, until they reached the city of Tiberias, celebrated under the Lord for its pasturage and containing five thousand inhabitants.

There the more abundant food somewhat quieted the wasting illness [variant: frenzy] from which they were suffering. At last they reached Jerusalem, but found it so filled with the stench of recently slaughtered corpses that nowhere could the air be drawn into the nostrils or mouth except in a state of utter corruption.

They were joyfully received by King Godfrey and attended the approaching celebration of the Lord’s Nativity. As the judgment of reason required, the feast was held at Bethlehem. Not only because of the mutual sight of those who had gathered, but even more because of the victory unexpectedly granted to their age, the event was a cause of rejoicing for the Franks beyond what can be believed.

After they departed and each returned to his own place, Bohemond was attacked by a great force of Turks as he approached a certain city and was carried away captive to the remotest regions of Persia.

When the illustrious Tancred learned of this, he hastened to occupy Antioch and fortified the citadel of Laodicea; for both cities paid their due services to Bohemond.

Robert, count of Normandy, had formerly possessed Laodicea, but when the citizens could no longer endure the exactions of that extravagant man, they expelled the guards of the principal citadel, deprived him of its lordship, and, out of hatred for the man of Rouen, renounced the use of Rouen’s coinage.

Bohemond, however, after spending several years in prison, was finally released, partly by agreement and partly through a monetary ransom. Not long afterward, once Antioch had been entrusted to Tancred, he crossed by ship to Apulia and came to France. Having obtained from her father, King Philip, Constantia, the king’s daughter, with a great sum of gold, he celebrated their wedding at Chartres with great splendor.

He then returned to Apulia, subdued a large part of the Byzantine emperor’s kingdom, and, after having two sons by the king’s daughter, ended his life by poison.

[XXXVII] The deeds of King Godfrey are briefly summarized.—As for Godfrey, whose excellence in knightly glory was so great, since much has already been related above, a concluding account of his praise may be gathered from the words of the aforementioned Baldwin.

He was the son of Count Hugh of Reiteste. When he was later placed by King Baldwin in charge of the duchy of Edessa, he had already, alas, fallen into the hands of the Turks. Kept imprisoned for a long time, he escaped alive from their hands with God as his protector.

His account of him survives in the following judgment, clothed, of course, in my words:

“It was the feast of Saint Denis, and that same king was returning from one of his cities, called Morocoria. Behold, one hundred and twenty Turks were lying in wait for him, while only twenty horsemen accompanied him.

“When we saw them,” he says, “we cast aside fear and seized our weapons. They, because they had suddenly fallen upon us, thought that we would flee because of our small number. But we, taking constant courage from the help of God that we had experienced, relying above all upon his Spirit, attacked the barbarians and raged against them with such slaughter that, after eighty of them had been killed, we captured ninety horses as well.”

After some further remarks, when he had mockingly recalled those who had fled from Antioch and those who had delayed their return while serving as ambassadors to Constantinople, he continued as follows, to encourage the Franks who had remained in France concerning their prosperity:

“We are very well supplied,” he says, “and, to say nothing of the treasures of others, the ten castles over which I alone rule, together with one abbey, pay me fifteen hundred marks annually.

“And if God smiles upon my capture of Aleppo, I shall soon have one hundred castles under my authority.

“Do not believe those who have gone backward and celebrate that we are wasting away from hunger; believe my written words instead.”

## CHAPTER XI

[XXXVIII] Concerning King Baldwin.—When King Godfrey departed this life after a noble career, destined for greater blessedness, the people of Jerusalem, not forgetting his moderation and serenity and fearing that they themselves might fall short of him, sent interpreters to summon his brother, the duke of Edessa, to royal rule.

In the duchy he had conducted himself with such splendor that, whenever he traveled, he had a golden shield carried before him bearing the figure of an eagle. It was in the Argolic style. Following the custom of the pagan peoples, he had continued to walk about in a toga, had grown his beard long, bowed to those who worshiped him, and took his meals only upon carpets spread on the ground. Whenever he entered a municipality or city under his authority, a double trumpet sounded from the mouths of two horsemen before his advancing carriage.

Obeying the embassy, he began to depart for Jerusalem. But when the neighboring pagan people, having learned of his intention to depart, saw him on his way, they boarded their Liburnian ships. While the breeze vainly favored them and the duke hastened along the sands of the same sea with a fairly modest escort, they competed to confront him and hurried to bring their fleet to shore, rowing vigorously and cutting through the waves with their beaks.

But the duke, powerless against all that mortal hands could accomplish, driven by inward grief, called upon the Most High and laid before him the royal enterprise he was about to undertake obediently for the sake of defending his faith.

And behold, the ships that had been carried swiftly by their winged movement resisted with muddy sluggishness. The more each ship strove to advance while sweeping the sea with its oars, the more eagerly, in a ridiculous reversal of their hopes, they turned from prows toward sterns.

Thus, their wicked effort having been scattered, the duke obtained the freedom he deserved and received from heaven a clear omen concerning his assumption of the royal purple.

I had passed over the fact that the Pisan bishop Daibert, with a considerable number of his people and accompanied by a certain Apulian bishop, had already gone ahead to Jerusalem with Bohemond and this same duke.

After assuming the kingdom, Baldwin restrains the Arabs.—His first campaigns after receiving the kingdom are said to have been conducted within the Arabian region. When he advanced as far as the slopes of Mount Sinai, he found an uncultivated people resembling the Ethiopians. Out of consideration for their rustic way of life and unusual ugliness, he spared them the gift of life.

There he prayed in the church called Saint Aaron’s, where God had uttered his oracles with the patriarchs and had given the army drink from the Spring of Contradiction. Because Moses had shown hesitation in speech and had not sanctified God before the children of Israel, God kept him from the land of promise.

There, too, the opinion of my presbyter faltered: for it is recognized that the mountain was not Sinai but Mount Hor, once bordering the Arab city of Petra, where Aaron put off his human life and where water emerges from the depths of the rock that had been struck.

[XXXIX] A perpetual miracle in Jerusalem: light kindled by divine power.—In that holy city of Jerusalem, a certain ancient miracle had taken root. I call it ancient because almost the entire Latin world is unaware of when it began to occur.

But by conjecture we judge that, after the pagan peoples began to trample upon those places before our own times, the Lord granted this sign on behalf of his servants who lived there or who came there during that period: namely, that on the very Sabbath of Easter the lamp of the Lord’s tomb is seen each year to be kindled by divine power.

It was the custom in the city for the pagans to go around to all the houses, extinguishing the hearths of each one down to the ashes. They did this with as much vigilance as they believed the same thing was being done through the Christians’ deception rather than through faith.

Thus, when Vulcan was banished from the town in this manner, at the hour when the observance of our religion commands the Catholic people to attend the solemn service of the Resurrection and baptisms, you would have seen pagans roving throughout the basilica with drawn swords and threatening death to each of our people.

You would have seen the native adherents of our faith tortured by profound grief before God, while all those whom vows of prayer—or the desire for the miracle—had drawn there from the hidden regions of the world prayed with a single purpose for the gift of light.

Nor was there then any troublesome delay before the petition, heated by longing, was relieved by an eager fulfillment.

I heard from elderly persons who had gone there that once the papyrus or wick—for I do not know which of the two, or both, they use—was removed from the box of a certain pagan, and the iron remained empty. But when the miracle descended from heaven, light emerged from the iron.

While he sought to weaken the power of heavenly miracles through fraud, he learned that “nature, contrary to its own character, serves its own God.”

## [XL.] It Is No Longer Seen Because of the Sins of the Christians

In the following year after the aforementioned king had assumed the scepter, it is said that the difficulty of the miracle was so great that the prayers of those praying and weeping could scarcely be fulfilled as night approached. The aforementioned prelate’s sermon to the people urged confession of sins. The king and the prelate pressed for the restoration of peace; they promised that whatever was inconsistent with faith and honor would be corrected. Meanwhile, under the pressure of the circumstances, so many enormous crimes were confessed there that, unless repentance followed, it would have seemed appropriate for the holy light to be removed without delay. Yet even then, after the rebuke, its kindling was not postponed.

But in the following year, when they had reached the hour at which the heavenly flame was to make the glorious tomb, the prayers of all rose wholly upward. Greeks and Syrians, Armenians as well as Latins, each calling upon God and his saints in the idioms of their own languages; the king, nobles, and people accompanying the clergy with repentance and the groans of their hearts—everyone was tormented by wretched anguish, because in that city, now possessed by Christians, events were occurring which they had never heard of happening under the pagans.

Meanwhile Fulcher of Chartres, taking with him the chaplain of Patriarch Daibert, set out for the Mount of Olives. For there the lamp of God was accustomed to arise whenever it was not present in Jerusalem. But when they returned and brought no welcome news to the ears of the church that awaited them, prayers from different quarters were repeated before the people—not prayers that comfort the sick, but incitements to mourners. That day ended with the matter unresolved and sent everyone back to his proper place; a second night fell, and sharp sorrow tormented the hearts of all alike.

On the following day they decided to proceed as far as the Temple of the Lord, with the grief that was their due. They had gone forth, utterly forgetful of Easter joy, while no one’s clothing differed from that of Good Friday, when suddenly, behind the backs of those following, a song was heard from the church’s custodians: the lamp of the holy monument had been lit.

Why delay? On that day grace shone forth with such abundance—its richness increased by the success that followed the delay—that the brightness of God, not all at once but successively, touched nearly fifty lamps within the church of the tomb. This happened not only during the sacred mysteries, but also when the king was dining in the palace after the services had been completed: compelled by repeated messengers to go and see the newly kindled lights, he rose from the table.

It cannot be said with what consolations that sorrow was relieved, when on that day the king himself consented, something he had never before presumed to do, to be crowned within that same city, in the Temple of the Lord, in favor of this gift.

## [XLI.] The Franks, Returning to Their Homeland, Are Slaughtered by the Turks

The Franks, who had redeemed the holy city with their own blood, longed to return by the route through which they had come—through the interior regions, that is—to see their parents, children, and wives. Perhaps trusting in their numbers and courage, they decided to retrace their steps. While they thought they could pass freely through the territories of Nicaea, which they had formerly conquered, the Turks whom, as I said earlier, the emperor had kept in reserve to be thrown against the Franks once the city had been restored, confronted them with a fierce force. As my priest, unless he is mistaken, reports, they slaughtered one hundred thousand in a monstrous battle.

But in expressing so great a number, I fear that the man is mistaken, because he is known elsewhere to have been even more ready than was reasonable in his calculations. For example, he himself dares to estimate at six hundred thousand those who set out for Jerusalem. I wonder whether all the kingdoms of Cisalpine Gaul—or indeed of the entire West—could have supplied such a number, since we know beyond doubt that at the first battle before the walls of Nicaea there are said to have been scarcely one hundred thousand who possessed a complete mounted equipment.

And if he is plainly speaking of those people, perhaps counting among them those who did indeed set out to go but who, scattered in every direction through various provinces, by land and sea, succumbed to disease and hunger, even so they would certainly not have sufficed to make up so vast an infinity of men.

Thus, as has been said, after the Franks had been struck down in a savage slaughter, most of the survivors returned to Jerusalem, having lost their possessions. The most generous king both deeply grieved for them, bestowed many benefits upon them, and urged them to return to their homeland by sea.

# CHAPTER XII

## [XLII.] The Turks Are Defeated by the King of Jerusalem

The Babylonian prince, distressed not so much by the loss of Jerusalem as by the proximity of the Franks who had settled there, repeatedly attacked the new king in frequent expeditions and attempted a more substantial incursion through the port of the city of Accharon.

Robert, count of the Normans, had besieged Accharon while the army of the Lord was hastening to besiege Jerusalem; but Duke Godfrey, considering the more fruitful undertaking, had drawn him away. The Babylonian therefore sent enormous forces and challenged the Christian king to battle.

The king gathered his humble flock, to which the Lord says, “Do not be afraid” (Luke 12:32), and, arranging it in battle lines as best he could, attacked the profane enemy. Without delay, as though slaughtering dumb cattle, he scattered them like a whirlwind scattering dust.

A second time the enemy sent nine thousand soldiers, beneath whom there were nearly twenty thousand Ethiopian infantry, a common mass of troops. To meet them the pious king had scarcely gathered a thousand horsemen and foot soldiers; nevertheless, after arranging them in seven divisions, he threw himself with bold confidence into their densely packed phalanxes.

There the same prince, seeing from a distance a certain mounted pagan, burst forward with such force that, after thrusting his weapon through the man’s chest, he drove in with it the banner attached to the weapon. When the spear was pulled out of the wound, the banner remained held in the man’s chest. Terrified at the courage of their own and their companions, the enemies first gave way; but as their courage returned in view of their numbers and strength, they attacked our men together and forced them to think of flight.

They wisely attributed this misfortune to the fact that the Lord’s cross had not been present with them for so great an undertaking. The cross itself, they say, was discovered—hidden in certain places, as the lance had formerly been—through the guidance of a certain Syrian, or perhaps Armenian; I do not know which.

Thus made more chastened, when forces no smaller than those of the Babylonian prince’s earlier army appeared for the third time, the excellent king met them with as large a force as he could muster, yet more confident because of God. After arranging his ranks according to his ability, he engaged them on every side with such fury that, although the contest was very unequal, both sides were cut down in so great a slaughter that six thousand from the pagan army and one hundred soldiers from among the Franks were killed.

And because they had not cared to be marked by the proud emblems of eagles or dragons, but had carried before them the humiliation of the humble Crucified One—that is, the cross—they immediately became most glorious victors and compelled the enemy to turn their backs.

## [XLIII.] The Franks Besiege and Capture Caesarea

After these forces had been thoroughly dispersed, as was fitting, the king immediately assembled as large an army as he could and encircled Caesarea of Palestine, that distinguished city, with a siege—not relying on the sight of its thousands, but rather on the hope placed in his own strength.

The construction of siege engines was hastened; numerous ballistae were extended around the walls. The device they call a battering ram was brought forward: a beam plated with iron at its front. Camps of battle formations were established opposite the walls, but they did not advance as a single body. Standing beside the fortifications of the walls, they not only pelted the Saracens with a rain of missiles of every kind, but at times also slaughtered them with drawn swords.

There you could have seen engines boiling with enormous stones, not merely battering the outer wall but also striking the palaces of the city with tall, powerful masses of blows. They repeatedly battered houses and walls with stones, and scattered cords carrying lumps of glowing iron together with molten lead, so that the town might be set ablaze.

Meanwhile the battering ram was driven against the walls, and while it sought to create an opening below, the entire solidity of the surrounding fortification was loosened as it began to crumble. While the Franks strove to reach the inner parts and their effort to inflict damage drove the Saracens toward the exterior, they carried on mutual slaughter.

There also, when an engine collapsed, the loss of many of our men aroused the courage of the opposing side. For although the Saracens are sluggish in exposed battle lines, within their defenses they are astonishingly resourceful in resistance.

On the twentieth day of the siege, when the king, relying on a picked body of young men, was pressing the townspeople hard, he suddenly leaped from an engine onto the wall. The soldiers rushed after him and drove back the fleeing enemy.

As the Franks followed the king with complete eagerness, an innumerable crowd was killed throughout the city; no one was spared, except that girls found suitable for service were kept alive. Treasure was sought everywhere. Not only chests but also the silent throats of the Saracens were searched: the throats that had swallowed Byzantine gold disgorged it when struck by the fist, and those who had usurped inappropriate offices in those places poured out, in gold, the fruits of women’s childbirth.

Without delay, a colony of Franks was left in the captured city to inhabit it. Not long afterward he attacked Accharon and, after exhausting it through prolonged efforts, brought it under his own authority. It is also known that he later captured several other cities, but they are situated so deeply amid that savage pagan people that it is scarcely possible to imagine anything there as safe for our colonies [variant: “colonies”].

Nevertheless, continuous warfare and their frequent victories rendered the Saracens so contemptible to Christian soldiers that last year we learned that something remarkable had occurred.

# CHAPTER XIII

## [XLIV.] A Certain Soldier Behaved Toward the King More Insolently Than He Should Have

A certain soldier, whom the king himself had appointed over the city of Tiberias, had behaved toward the king more insolently than he should have. The king, therefore, summoned him and, angered by the man’s arrogance, ordered him to leave the territory under his authority.

As he hurried away with two mounted companions, accompanied by an equal number of squires, he suddenly encountered immense forces of pagans. Distrusting his own numbers but looking, however imperfectly, toward God, he cut open his shirt—the garment called a tunic—and fastened it to a spear in place of a banner; he ordered his companions to do the same.

They did so, and, raising a shout, pressed their horses with their spurs and charged the enemy before them. Terrified by the sudden boldness, the enemy thought that they were being followed as a vanguard by numerous cohorts. They took flight and exposed themselves to be slaughtered by those three men.

Many were killed, and more spoils were seized than the men were able to carry. Struck by this favorable outcome, the soldier returned giving thanks to God, prostrated himself before the king, and faithfully promised that he would obey him thereafter.

## [XLV.] Money for Paying the Soldiers’ Wages Is Miraculously Found

On one occasion the same king was afflicted by a great shortage of money, so that even the monthly wages owed to the soldiers were lacking. Then, behold, divine clemency showed itself to him in a marvelous way.

The soldiers were already suffering to such an extent that the king’s guards and troops were considering abandoning him. At that moment, young men from Joppa, who had gone into the sea not far from the shore to bathe—or rather to play—found one day, at the very place where the sand and saltwater meet, bags filled with great weights of gold. The Venetians had lost them; it was known that they had suffered shipwreck there.

When the bags were brought to the king, they offered an ineffable miracle and consolation to the king, who was almost in despair, and to the new Christian community.

## [XLVI.] Why the King Divorced His Wife

Because the matter is known to be open to slander, since it is said that he repudiated his wife, the reason is handed down as follows.

The woman herself was born of one of the best pagan families of the land. After her husband’s command, she traveled toward Jerusalem and reached the port of Saint Simeon by sea. There, transferred to a faster ship while she was trying to hasten her voyage, she was carried by the violence of the winds to a certain barbarian island.

The islanders seized her, beat a certain bishop of her company together with his attendants, detained her for a long time, and afterward allowed her to depart. When she had reached her husband, the king, reasonably suspecting pagan incontinence, kept her entirely away from his own bed. Changing her clothing, he placed her with other nuns at the church of Blessed Anne, the Mother of God and Virgin Mother.

He himself rejoiced to live unmarried, because his struggle was not against flesh and blood but against the rulers of the world (Ephesians 6:12).

## [XLVII.] A Soldier, Pierced by Arrows and Beheaded, Earned the Palm of Martyrdom

Around the feast of Easter in the previous year, that aforementioned soldier whom we said had been appointed prefect of Tiberias, and to whom that victory had come, was captured in a battle that had gone badly for our side. He was taken alive by the pagans to one of their cities.

While they were celebrating certain sacrilegious festivals there, they compelled the aforementioned knight, who had been brought before them, to deny and renounce the grace of his own faith. But he, rejecting with a firmness of spirit entirely worthy of him such an impious abuse, shrank completely even from hearing it.

Without delay, that man—now deserving of every honor by which he ought to be named—was seized. Bound to a stake, as they say, he was set up in the middle of the field and pierced from every side by a dense hail of arrows.

Then, after the crown of his head had been cut off, his head was severed from his body with a saw; it was fashioned like a drinking cup and presented to the king of Damascus, by whom these deeds were carried out, as though he were thereafter going to drink from it, for the terror of our people.

As he died under the vow of an unbroken confession, he transformed the soldier who had been proclaimed into a martyr to be proclaimed throughout the ages. His name was Gervasius, nobly born near the castle of Basilicas in the district of Soissons.

# CHAPTER XIV

## [XLVIII.] What Guibert Reports He Learned from Men Endowed with Sincerity and Faith

Thus far, by God’s favor, we have learned these things from men endowed with complete sincerity. If anywhere we have followed the opinions of others and gone astray, we did so with no intention of deceiving.

We give thanks to God, the Redeemer of that holy city, for the efforts of our people. For when the siege of the city had begun, he revealed to a certain hermit living at Bethany—as was certainly reported to us—that the city was indeed to be besieged with urgency, but was to be attacked only on Good Friday and captured at the hour when Christ was led to the cross, so that he might show himself to be the one who would redeem it anew from its sufferings through the pain of his members.

This man disclosed the revelation to certain leaders of our side whom he had summoned; the manner in which the city was captured confirmed all of it. We likewise give thanks to God, who composed his deeds through his Spirit and by means of our mouth.

Moreover, if anything seems to have been explained less fully here than Julius Caesar usually explains, together with Hirtius and Pansa, in his histories of the Gallic, Spanish, Pharsalian, Alexandrian, and Numidian wars, one must carefully consider that the very men who carried out those wars and wrote about them were present in them. Hence nothing is omitted from their accounts of what was done generally and in detail: how many thousands were on this side, how many on the opposite side; which praetors and legates commanded this or that division; which generals and which princes from elsewhere were in charge; what the cavalry and light-armed troops accomplished; how many shields were pierced by spears; and, to use their own words, “after the consuls, or proconsuls, had sounded the retreat,” how many were missing after the battle had been broken off and how many were wounded.

We who write these things are occupied by another profession, and the direct sight of events gives us no license for boldness. In reporting what we heard, we have therefore judged that we should sometimes be sparing.

Under the military discipline of the Julians, Roman citizens, legionary soldiers, squadrons, maniples, and cohorts were each compelled to stand by their own standards. Because of the advantageous locations, they enclosed their camps with ramparts and towers no less than towns or cities; wherever the deployment of battle lines was imminent, they occupied the neighboring hills and overcame the extreme disadvantages of the terrain. There were numerous services of camp followers and sutlers, and the baggage of the army was richly supplied.

Among our people, however, scarcely anything of this order—or rather, of this careful organization—existed. The undertaking was carried out not by Frankish rashness, but by awakened faith and strength.

Let those who wish say that I have omitted more than I wrote; I preferred to be brief rather than excessive. If anyone knows of other deeds, let him entrust them wherever he wishes them to be written.

Let us rejoice in God and in such great victors, who, driven by lack of grain, learned to live on roots dug from ditches. If anyone is uncertain about the Parthians, whom we have called Turks, or about the name Caucasus, let him consult Solinus, *On Remarkable Things*, Pompeius Trogus, *On the Origin of the Parthians*, and Jordanes the Goth, concerning Baetica.

May God, then, at last set a boundary to this pious labor. Amen.

**HERE ENDS BOOK VIII OF THE DEEDS OF GOD THROUGH THE FRANKS.**

# BOOK IX, PUBLISHED BY ANOTHER AUTHOR

## Concerning King Baldwin. He Makes Peace with the Babylonian Emperor

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1112, King Baldwin, after repeatedly provoking his enemies, had inflicted many slaughters upon the people of Ascalon. But because the gifts with which the foreign soldiery were rewarded had run out, he was very much afraid that the appearance of his glorious achievements might be altered. With careful deliberation and the more serious advice of his nobles, he considered suspending the conflict.

At that time a considerable embassy of Saracens had gathered in Jerusalem to request peace. Therefore, judging the cessation of war requested by the barbarians to be just, he announced to the embassy that both sides should meet at a suitable place, thinking it “fair to negotiate a peace treaty at the borders of the kingdoms.”

The messengers returned and instructed their prince in the terms; the proposed agreements pleased him, and the announced day was awaited. When it approached, the place designated by both rulers was visited. A considerable number from our side came with the most Christian king; from the profane nation, however, an immense multitude appeared with its emir.

When the barbarian and the king of Jerusalem were stationed opposite one another at no great distance, the barbarian sent word through interpreters that the king should state whatever agreements he wished, and that he would carry them out in every respect.

Then the king said:

“We have heard that, according to his own rite, he is a sufficiently strict man, and that he would prefer to be killed rather than betray a pledge of security once given. Let him, according to his rite or custom, confirm faith and security concerning the protection of provisions and merchants’ goods by land and sea; concerning not harassing those who transport timber; concerning the prevention of nightly and repeated acts of robbery; and concerning the extension of peace everywhere. When we have confirmed these same pledges with an oath, we shall call down heavenly vengeance upon anyone who violates the treaty.”

At these words, approval arose on both sides, and the princes immediately withdrew into mutual conversations.

## The Emperor Himself Deceitfully Visits the City of Jerusalem

When the barbarian had gained access to the king’s greater confidence, he said:

“Since we have sometimes removed the causes of war by laying aside our weapons, I have acquired a great desire to see Jerusalem. We have heard that, since the time when we lost it after it was conquered by the Franks, it has been restored to a better condition. I ask to be admitted within the city with as many companions as I wish. Let me see it only once, and I shall consider having seen it sufficient for me.”

The king did not refuse, since the man’s deceitful fraud was hidden from him. The entire barbarian force returned to Ascalon. The emir, retaining very few men, accompanied the king as far as Jerusalem.

They remained silent that day. On the following day, surrounded under the pretext of honor by certain of our nobles, the emir proceeded not merely to view the city but to inspect it. When he saw the shining temples and churches, the ancient shrines of his people overturned, the altars destroyed, and the city’s condition transformed according to Christian custom, he is said to have wept bitterly.

Our people, who suspected no evil of the man, regarded such weeping as piety. Finally he said to the king:

“The rumor that had reached your glory did not deceive us, since I have now seen with my own eyes things better than I had heard. I openly confess that, although I may seem to detract from our side, the city now enjoys far happier prosperity than it did in our times.

“But in return for your generosity, we shall contribute fully to this glory. We have sent merchants to transport Babylonian wealth to them, and we shall bring it into this city to be sold at a sufficiently low price. You should know that, through the abundant variety of these goods, they will permanently benefit you in proportion to how much you need them.”

He said this and, protected by royal attendants, was escorted back to his own people.

## An Ambush Is Prepared for the King of Jerusalem

Without delay, he attacked the Babylonian prince through intermediaries by means of letters:

“Since the name of your exalted dignity, spread throughout the world, inspires terror in so many nations, it is an eternal disgrace that Christian newcomers have mutilated the borders of your kingdom. Behold, the greater part of the Babylonian empire, subdued under foreign laws, is deprived of the ancient rites and sacrifices of the gods, and of the luxury and pleasure in which we were accustomed to live.

“I fear that the gods are angry, and that Muhammad does not wish to offer his protection. But if you resume your strength and arms and wish to drive the Christians from the land and cities, the gods will hear you and Muhammad will help you.

“Provide assistance. Load camels with weapons, and send as many thousands of armed men as you can. We have obtained a two-year truce from the king of Jerusalem; we have seen the city itself without defenses and the light-armed troops and auxiliary forces scattered. We promised him gifts of your wealth and a market, so that we would make them suspect nothing about us. If, instead of merchandise, you send them bundles of weapons, the city will easily fall into your hands.”

When he heard this, the tyrant was encouraged by the hope raised by these words. One would have marveled at the boldness of the soldiers, the quantity and varied splendor of the weapons, the boundless number of herds and provisions, and the immense amount of gold and other wealth. All these things were carefully prepared, placed aboard ships, and not long afterward unloaded at Ascalon.

## The Ambush Prepared for the King Is Exposed and Dissolved

When the promised day for carrying out the undertaking was approaching, the tyrant sent to the king and requested that someone from the king’s side accompany the men who were to transport the merchandise. At that time, however, the king had withdrawn to the fortress of Cavas, situated in Arabia. He had built it not far from Mount Sinai to protect the region, for he had extended his kingdom as far as that place.

While the king was absent and the royal affairs had to be managed, a certain highly trustworthy and vigilant-minded man was carrying out the office in Jerusalem. We do not know his true name, but by some circumstance we learned that he was called Mathonius.

He had once been captured as a young man by Christians and had received baptism. He had grown not only in bodily grace but also in the moral character of the profession he had embraced. The citizens therefore assigned him this task above all because he was highly skilled in the barbarian language.

Meanwhile, among the Saracens, such a fraud was being contrived that anyone might have thought that those who had arrived were not soldiers but merchants, and that they carried not weapons but merchandise, from which five hundred bundles were assembled.

When Mathonius arrived, he was received courteously and was excluded neither from their banquets nor from their councils, since they thought he did not understand their speech. By carefully inserting himself, unsuspected, into the gatherings of those who were making their plans, he easily discerned the deception.

Nevertheless, concealing that he knew what was happening, he led a thousand men with five hundred bundles to Jerusalem. After distributing the bundles among the lodging houses adjoining the Tower of David, Mathonius went to Arabia, where the king was staying, and said:

“There are extremely deadly merchants in Jerusalem. They have brought us not bundles of wealth but bundles of weapons. Unless you come to our aid quickly, I fear that both the people and the city will be destroyed.”

The king therefore abandoned the undertaking and hurried back to the city. He summoned the merchants and ordered the goods to be displayed in the marketplace. They insisted that this could not be done in any way until those whom they had preceded—their associates or the owners of the merchandise—arrived, and they resisted vehemently.

But soon the king placed them all under guard and ordered the bundles to be opened. What more is there to say? Weapons of both remarkable brilliance and variety appeared. Among them they also found a trumpet distinguished by its gold, gems, and novel workmanship.

“These,” said the king, “are merchandise both sufficiently dangerous and useful. Dangerous, if we do not resist the evil that has been prepared; useful, because they will serve the purposes of war. Therefore, brave men, take counsel among yourselves concerning them.”

To this Eustachius, count of Caesarea, replied:

“Once these have been brought out, condemn them all to death. Preserve one man who can explain the whole affair.”

This was done, and one man was granted his life on condition that he reveal everything in order. He said:

“We enclosed the weapons in the bundles so that we might deceive you under the appearance of merchandise. We came ahead so that, through a planned stratagem, we might open the tower and the adjoining gate to the army that was to arrive, at night, while you were asleep.

“Those who were to enter, however, were not to do so until, when twilight came, they heard from the top of the tower the trumpet known to them. They were not to enter in a rush but one by one, as men who were unarmed. The tower was to be seized by some, while others immediately took these weapons for your destruction.”

When they heard this and accepted the plan, Eustachius said:

“The only thing that remains for us to devise is how to repay them in kind.”

When the entire barbarian army had assembled, night fell and it settled around the city in profound silence. Most of our men, equipped with the new weapons of theirs [Note: [Col. 0835D] Up to this point, unpublished.], kept watch over the gate.

When that trumpet sounded at first light from the tower’s guards, they opened the gate. The men entered slowly, without hindering one another. After the predetermined number of a thousand had been admitted, they closed the gate, raised an uproar, and cut down the profane intruders.

When the outsiders heard this, they believed that their own men were attacking to the destruction of our people. But after the day grew bright with the spreading sun, the king, knowing that it was unsafe for a few to confront countless numbers, ordered the heads of the slain to be hurled into the enemy camp by slings and Balearic slingers, so that the survivors, terrified by the deaths of their companions, might be forced to flee.

When this had been done, such terror seized the multitude that suddenly every thought of every other matter left them except flight; they considered it a gain if they could escape even after mounting their horses.

As they fled and our men pursued them, such a slaughter of the pagans took place that our men followed them all the way to Ascalon, killing everyone, and scarcely found anyone left to strike down.

When they returned as victorious men, with the highest praise and rejoicing, those who were present testified that no heart could imagine, nor tongue tell, how much wealth our people carried away from the Babylonian tents.

This confusion Christ brought upon his enemies and this victory upon his faithful, when he wished both to cast the former into the trap they had prepared and to preserve the latter from evils they had not deserved.

## [Col. 0837] THE END

# [ON HIS OWN LIFE]

# THE THREE BOOKS OF THE VENERABLE GUIBERT OF HIS OWN LIFE, OR OF HIS *MONODIES*

[Note: [Col. 0837] In this document, the numbers in brackets, e.g. (25), refer to notes included as a separate document in this volume, beginning at column 1047.]

# BOOK ONE

In this book the principal subject is his own life.

## CHAPTER ONE

## He Laments the Sins of the Three States of His Life

I confess to your greatness, O God, the course of my countless errors and my very frequent returns to the inner mercy that you nevertheless inspired.

I confess the evils of my childhood and youth, still boiling within me even at this mature age, and the long-established pursuits of depravity that have not yet ceased beneath the torpor of an exhausted body.

Whenever I recall my most persistent impurities, and remember how you have always granted me remorse for them, I marvel beyond what can be imagined at your exceedingly patient compassion toward me.

If remorse and the affection of prayer are never possessed without your spiritual infusion, how can you permit yourself to enter so graciously into the hearts of sinners, and lavish such great grace upon those who have turned away from you—or rather, who provoke you?

You know, O Father of immense greatness, how obstinate are the hearts we bear against those who incur our displeasure, and how reluctantly we forgive those who once or repeatedly direct against us either looks or words.

But you are not merely compassionate; you are compassion itself, indeed its source. Although you proceed most universally toward all, can you not be sufficient for each individual? Why not?

When the world lay in ignorance of God, when it dwelt in darkness and the shadow of death, when universal silence held sway while night completed its course, by whose merit, by whose voice, could your almighty Word be summoned to come from the royal throne? (Wisdom 18:14–15.)

And since you could not then be prevented from having mercy by the negligence of the whole human race, it is no wonder if you are compassionate toward one sinner, however greatly he has sinned.

I cannot say that you have mercy more readily upon individuals than upon all, since in both cases it is certain that you close off no facility at all; nothing is easier for you than what is easy.

Since you are a fountain, and (25) since what flows from you is owed to all, you plainly do not withhold from individuals what belongs to everyone.

Thus, always sinning and always returning to you amid my sinning, shall mercy, when I flee the merciful one or abandon mercy and then return to mercy, lose what it is, and, even overwhelmed by manifold offense, be found unaccustomed to me?

Is it not said to you: “You will not restrain your mercies in your anger”? (Psalm 76:10.)

The same singer says that these mercies will exist not only in the present but also forever. You know that I do not sin because I perceive you to be merciful; rather, I openly confess that you are called merciful because you are ready to those who ask forgiveness.

I do not abuse your mercy (26) whenever I am compelled to sin by the necessity of sinning. But it would be a most profane abuse if, because the return to you after sin is very easy, I were always delighted by the excess of sinning.

I do indeed sin; but, having regained reason, I repent that I have passed into the inclination of my heart, and my mind, unwillingly, sinks heavily beneath such filthy baskets.

But amid these daily sicknesses, what should I do when I experience some kind of resurrection from my fall? Is it not much healthier to strive toward you for a time, to breathe toward you even for a moment, than entirely to forget the remedy and despair of grace?

And what is despair except to throw oneself deliberately into the whirlpool of every crime? For there the spirit no longer resists the flesh in any way, and the substance of the unhappy soul is overthrown by the loss of pleasures. This is the man who is submerged in a storm of waters, swallowed by the deep, while, to complete his reprobate condition, the mouth of the pit presses down upon him from above.

Therefore, good God, when after these intoxications of my inner man I come to my senses, if I make progress in no other way, at least for the moment I do not fail to know myself.

For how could I sparkle with knowledge of you if I were blind to seeing myself? If, plainly, according to Jeremiah, “I am a man who sees my poverty” (Lamentations 3:1), it follows that I should diligently seek the things by which that want may be supplied.

Conversely, if I do not know what is good, how will I be able even to know evil, much less to detest it? If I do not know beauty, I shall never shudder at ugliness.

Since, therefore, both are established—that through knowledge of myself I should seek knowledge of you, and that, enjoying knowledge of you, I should immediately not lack knowledge of myself—it is worthy and supremely salutary that the obscurity of my reason should be wiped away through such frequent confessions and through the continual seeking of your light. Thus, once firmly illuminated, it will never thereafter be ignorant of itself.

## CHAPTER TWO

## He Recalls the Benefits Conferred on Him by God and Gives Thanks for Them

It is therefore fitting first to confess to you the benefits you have bestowed upon me, so that those servants of yours, O God, who will read these things may understand how cruel my ingratitude is.

For if you had given me nothing other than what you distribute to other human beings, would you not still have exceeded what I could have deserved?

You added very many things that are praiseworthy because they come from you, but nothing that comes from me; and there are other matters that I think should be passed over.

For if birth, wealth, and beauty—to say nothing of whatever else there may be—are given by you, Lord, as their author, they receive no praise among the good except when those to whom you have given them restrain them under the rule of moral integrity, or when, because of their changeable nature, they are regarded as utterly contemptible.

What have I to do with things that, by their own colors and names alone, provide causes for wantonness and pride; things that are so intermediate that, according to the disposition of minds, they can be directed toward good or evil; things that are endowed with flexibility in proportion as their transience makes them suspect?

If no other argument occurred concerning these matters, this alone would suffice: no one has fashioned either his own lineage or his own appearance, and in these matters especially he possesses nothing that he has not received.

There are certain other things whose acquisition human effort can sometimes assist, such as wealth and intellectual abilities. Solomon bears witness to this: “Iron,” he says, “when it has become blunt, is sharpened with much labor” (Ecclesiastes 10:10).

But this too is entirely overturned by an easy argument, because unless the light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9) imbues the mind with reason, and unless Christ, with the key of knowledge, opens the doors of learning, there is no doubt that every teacher expends a futile effort upon foolish ears.

Therefore, let every prudent person consider it folly to claim for himself anything except sin.

### Guibert’s Mother, Beautiful and Adorned with Virtues

But leaving these matters aside, let us return to the subject begun. I said, piously and reverently, that I rejoiced in the benefits you had bestowed upon me. First and foremost, therefore, I give you thanks for having granted me a beautiful but chaste and modest mother, one exceedingly God-fearing.

I would certainly have spoken of her as beautiful in a worldly and foolish sense, unless I had confirmed this empty name by the sternest face of steadfast chastity. For just as fasts appear forced in the case of the utterly poor, who lack the means to obtain food and are therefore less praiseworthy, whereas the frugality of the rich possesses value because of their abundance, so beauty is the more desirable when it has held firm against deceptive adornments (*fenocinia*, reading uncertain), and is therefore raised higher under the title of every virtue. Sallustius Crispus, unless he had considered beauty without morals worthy of praise, would never have said of Aurelia Orestilla: “In her, he says, no good man ever praised anything except her appearance.” If he asserts that her appearance was praised by a good man, while nevertheless saying that she was disgraceful in all other respects, I may safely speak for Sallustius as though he meant this: she was rightly endowed by nature and approved by God, although it is clear that she was defiled by every kind of added impurity.

Thus, in an idol of whatever material, the form corresponding to its proper parts is praised; and although, so far as faith is concerned, an idol is called nothing by the Apostle (I Cor. 8:4), and although nothing more profane is thought to exist, nevertheless that fitting arrangement of the limbs is not without reason praised.

### Beauty Is to Be Praised

And certainly, although beauty is fleeting and changeable because of the instability of the flesh, it cannot, according to the customary manner of treating imaginary goods, be denied to be a good. For if whatever has been eternally instituted by God is beautiful, everything that is temporarily beautiful is as it were a mirror of that eternal beauty. “For the invisible things of God are understood and seen through the things that have been made,” says the Apostle (Rom. 1:20).

Angels also, when they presented themselves to human sight, always brought exceptionally radiant faces. Hence Manoah’s wife said: “A man of God came to me, having the appearance of an angel” (Judg. 13:6). Conversely, demons, who, according to the words of the First Epistle of Peter, “are kept under darkness for the day of the great judgment” (II Pet. 2:17; Jude 12), usually appear with the most frightful faces—not when they deceitfully transform themselves into angels of light (II Cor. 11:14)—and not unjustly, since they have withdrawn from the glory of their noble fellow citizens.

Moreover, our body is said to be conformed to Christ’s body of glory (Phil. 3:21), so that the ugliness contracted through accident or natural corruption may be corrected according to the pattern of the Son of God transfigured on the mountain. If, then, the internal exemplars are beautiful and good, whatever things present their image—especially when they do not differ from their order—are good from the same source from which they are beautiful.

Indeed, Blessed Augustine is remembered, if I am not mistaken, as having said in the book *On Christian Doctrine*: “He who has a beautiful body and a deformed soul is more to be mourned than if he also had a deformed body.” If, therefore, appearance is rightly mourned when it is defective, it is unquestionably a good thing that is corrupted by the admixture of some depravity or increased by the steadfastness of moral goodness.

### He Continues to Praise His Mother’s Deeds

I thank you, therefore, God, who had joined virtue to her beauty. The gravity of her bearing could convey contempt for every kind of vanity: the weight of her eyes, her sparingness in speech, and the difficulty with which she moved her face did not at all indulge the frivolities of those who looked upon her.

You know, Almighty One, that you had implanted in her a fear of your very name as though from the beginning, and a rebellion of the soul against every form of seduction. It is noteworthy that hardly ever, or nowhere, among women of high standing is one found who, while possessing within herself so much of your gift, was so sparing in censuring the incontinent. Whenever such a tale was mentioned by outsiders or members of the household, she herself would turn away, withdraw, and become irritated by such whispering, as though her own person were being censured along with the other.

True God, you know that it is not private affection—namely, love for my mother—that compels me to report these things, but rather that the matter itself can be regarded as surpassing the force of my words. Certainly, I see the rest of my kindred as far from you—some animal-like and ignorant of God, others savage with weapons and guilty of slaughter—unless, as is your custom, you greatly pity them.

But perhaps a more suitable place in this work will open for discussing her life. Let us now proceed to our subject.

## CHAPTER III

From this woman, as I believe and hope, you granted me, the worst by far of all whom she bore, to be born. I was her last child in both respects: for my brothers and sisters departed in the hope of something better, while I remain alive amid every form of despair.

While I am still living amid these evils, all hope of salvation has rested in her merit—after Jesus, the mother of Jesus, and his saints. I know—and it is not permissible to doubt it—that just as she loved me more dearly and honored me more conspicuously while she was in the world (for mothers treat their youngest children with greater affection), so now, being more present to God, she does not neglect me.

She had plainly been a fire of God in Zion from her youth, since concern for me never ceased in her mind, whether sleeping or awake. But now that death has overtaken her, and the interval of flesh has been broken, I know that the furnace burns more powerfully in Jerusalem than can be expressed—especially since, being filled with God there, she is not unaware of the miserable condition in which I am entangled. Though blessed herself, she groans over me as I wander astray, insofar as she sees me departing from the counsels, conduct, and footsteps she so often repeated to me.

Father and Lord God, through this woman, truly good and not deceptively so, you granted an origin to me, who am evil, in the manner and measure you know; and through her merit you also gave me hope, although I would never presume to possess it unless, out of fear of my sin, I could breathe for a little while under your grace.

You likewise introduced into my wretched heart—I do not know whether hope or the likeness of hope—the thought that you had granted me to be born and also reborn on that holy, transcendent, and most desired day for all Christians. My mother had spent almost the whole of Lent in the extraordinary pains of labor—pains that she also often reproached me with, since I was wayward and pursuing slippery paths—until at last the solemn Saturday, that is, the vigil of Easter, dawned.

### His Mother Endured Severe Torments in His Birth; He Is Dedicated to the Service of the Blessed Virgin; How Small He Was in Body When Newly Born

After being tormented by prolonged pains, and with her sufferings increasing as the hour approached, when it was thought that the birth would naturally be accomplished, I was turned back upward toward her inmost organs. By then sorrow over both of us had crushed my father, friends, and relatives: for while the child hastened the mother’s death, the child’s own destruction likewise seemed imminent, since he was unable to emerge, giving everyone cause for compassion.

It was the day on which, apart from the solemn office celebrated uniquely at its appointed time, the services ordinarily performed for family members were not being held. Necessity led to a decision, and everyone hurried to the altar of the Lord’s Mother. To her who alone had given birth while remaining, and destined always to remain, a virgin, vows of this kind were pronounced, and this offering was placed upon the altar of the pious Lady in place of a gift: namely, that if the birth resulted in a male child, he would be handed over to the clergy, to serve God and her; but if the outcome were worse, he would be entrusted to a suitable religious profession.

Nor was there delay. Something feeble, like an aborted fetus [read: “abortion,” *abortionis*], was expelled; and what had been expelled was for the time being, as was proper, cast aside like dung, while joy was felt solely because the mother had been saved.

The frailty of that little man newly brought forth was so pitiable that he was thought to look like a tiny corpse born prematurely. Indeed, around mid-April, the extremely thin reeds that grow in that region had to be placed beside his fingers so that they might appear more substantial.

On that very day, while I was being carried to the saving font, a woman—something repeatedly related to me in jest during my childhood and even adolescence—took me from hand to hand and said:

“Do you think this one will live, whom nature, almost failing, brought forth without limbs, giving him more the semblance of an outline than a body?”

All these things, my Creator, were signs of the condition in which I seem to live. Could the truth of your service ever be found in me, O Lord? I had nothing solid, nothing steadfast, in you. If I seemed to display any work openly, my intention repeatedly made it less upright and exceedingly slight.

I said to you, God of supreme goodness, that you had bestowed upon me, born and reborn in anticipation of so joyful a day, hope—or at least some tiny image of hope—and had offered me to the Queen of all, after God. Lord God, do I not already gather from the reason you gave me that the day of birth brings nothing more useful to those who live fruitlessly than the day of death?

If it is established and indisputable that no merits can precede one’s birth-day, whereas they can precede one’s death-day, then, if life is not spent under good conditions, I confess that glorious days will be of no benefit at all—just as neither the day of birth nor the day of death is beneficial in itself.

For if it is true that he himself made me, and that I did not make myself; if I did not appoint the day, nor earn the right that it should be fixed in advance, then the day granted to me by God gives me neither hope nor honor unless, by observing the religious character of the day, my life commends whatever the day signifies.

Our birthday would then truly shine because of the festal character of the time, if the zeal of our conduct were guided by the virtue desired in its fullness. The glory of one’s entrance into life would rightly seem granted to a person if a mind persevering in righteousness glorified the end of life.

If I am called Peter or Paul, if I am named Remigius or Nicholas, it will not help me—to speak poetically—

> “The name descended from great Iulus will avail nothing”—

unless I carefully carve again in myself the examples of those whom providence or fortune made my namesakes.

Behold, my God, how everything that was swelling in my soul is deflated; how that which seemed to extend itself into arrogance can be reduced to nothing.

### The Author Gives Thanks for the Favors Received from the Mother of God

And O Lady of the world and of the heavens after your only Son, how well those men understood you who, under that necessity, vowed me to you! And O how much better I myself would have understood it, if, once grown up, I had built my heart under the judgment of that vow which was always upon me!

Behold, I profess myself to you as one specially given by gift, yet I do not deny to you that I have often sacrilegiously and knowingly stolen myself away from you. Did I not take myself from you when I preferred foul desires to your fragrance?

Yet although I repeatedly withdrew myself from you by this fraud, I nevertheless returned more securely to you, and through you to God the Father and your only Son, by virtue of the consideration of this offering. And when I wasted away under the burden of sins repeated a thousand times, security arose for me from your inexhaustible compassion; I was reminded by the benefits of your ancient mercies to hope.

But why do I call them ancient? I have experienced, and experience daily, so many constant acts of your mercy; with you rescuing me, I have escaped so many captivities into which I had fallen, that I am now inclined to keep entirely silent about former mercies, where such an abundance of deliverance prevails.
