And when the repetition of sins produces a savage hardening in my heart, as though naturally implanted in me, an immediate return to you softens me. When, looking upon myself and considering my sufferings, I nearly fail in despair, I feel—whether I wish it or not—that confidence in breathing toward you is born within my wretched soul.

For this is so fixed in my thoughts that, whatever evils entangle me, you cannot, if I dare say so, fail to meet my necessities as though bound by obligation. For if you do not look favorably upon me, cast from the womb into your care; if you do not receive me when I return, I shall rightly attribute the causes of my destruction to you.

Clearly, since you possess the power to do what you wish, and since the power of the Son is known to overflow into his mother, from whom could I demand my salvation more than from you, to whom, so to speak, I cry out by the condition of kindred servitude: “I am yours” (Ps. 118:94)?

But I shall reason with you about these matters elsewhere, as gladly as possible. Let us touch upon the remaining matters.

## CHAPTER IV

### The Infant Is Deprived of His Father; Had His Father Lived Longer, He Would Undoubtedly Have Harmed His Salvation

Having been born, I had scarcely learned to cherish my baby rattles when you, merciful Lord, who were destined to be my father, made me an orphan. For after a period of almost eight months had elapsed, my father according to the flesh died. I therefore give you great thanks, since you caused this man to die in a Christian frame of mind—a man who, if he had lived, would undoubtedly have harmed the providence you had for me.

For since my appearance and a certain natural liveliness suitable to my tender age seemed fitted for this world, there was no doubt that, when the suitable time for learning letters arrived, he would fulfill the vows he had made concerning me.

Good Provider, you arranged both matters beneficially: I was not to be deprived of the beginnings of your discipline, and he was not to violate the promise he had made to you.

### He Is Given Over to the Study of Letters on the Feast of Saint Gregory

Thus that truly widowed woman of yours raised me with great care. At last, when she was about to entrust me to school, she chose the day of the feast of Blessed Gregory.

She had heard that your servant, O Lord, had excelled wonderfully in understanding and flourished in boundless wisdom. Therefore, by accumulating many alms, she repeatedly sought the intercession of your confessor, so that he to whom you had granted understanding might obtain for me the desire to acquire intellectual ability.

Once entrusted to letters, I had reached the rudiments of writing as best I could, but scarcely knew how to join the elementary characters, when my pious mother, eager for my education, decided to place me under the charge of a teacher of grammar.

### The Scarcity and Ignorance of Grammarians at That Time

(27) Shortly before that time, and still partly during my own period, there was such a scarcity of grammarians that scarcely anyone could have been found in the towns and hardly anyone in the cities; and those who happened to be found possessed only slight knowledge, not even comparable with that of the wandering clerics of our own time.

The man to whom my mother decided to entrust my education had begun to learn grammar only when already advanced in years. He was therefore all the more unskilled in that art because he had absorbed less of it in childhood. Yet he possessed such modesty that he made up in honorable conduct for what he lacked in learning.

### Guibert’s Teacher Was a Man of Highly Commendable Life

Accordingly, when my mother, through the mediation of certain clerics who familiarly celebrated God’s offices for her as chaplains, was urging that schoolmaster, he had undertaken the guardianship of one of my cousins. Because this cousin was necessary to certain relatives of mine, in whose household he had been raised, the teacher considered the entreaties of the woman who was urging him, as well as her honorable character and firmness. Although he feared offending my aforementioned relatives, he resolved to join my mother’s household and live with her.

He was compelled to do this by the following vision.

While he was sleeping at night in the room—which I also remember—in which the general school of our entire town was conducted, the figure of an old man with white hair and an altogether venerable appearance seemed to take me by the hand and lead me into the room. When he had stopped at its entrance, he showed me his little bed to me, who was observing this, and said:

“Go to him, because he will love you greatly.”

Then, releasing the hand with which he had held me, he let me go. I ran to the man, and while I was covering his face with frequent kisses, he awoke and was seized with such affection for me that, rejecting all hesitation and casting off his fear of my relatives—whose entire household was dependent on them as much as he himself was—he went to my mother to live with her.

The boy whom he had until then been escorting was handsome and noble, but extremely averse to the liberal arts, unstable in every discipline, a liar for his age, and a thief, so that, since supervision accomplished nothing, he was scarcely ever found in school but hid almost every day among the vineyards.

When the teacher had grown weary of the boy’s childish stupidity, and when the timely familiarity of my mother had pleased him, and the tenor of the vision just mentioned had driven the matter he desired deeply into his heart, he abandoned the boy’s company and likewise left the masters under whom the boy had lived.

He would not, however, have done so with impunity had not my mother’s authority as well as her power protected him.

## CHAPTER V

### Guibert Is Instructed in the Best Practices and Morals; He Is Restrained under More Severe Discipline

Once I had been placed under his authority, he taught me with such purity and restrained me from the insolences that tend to arise in early youth with such sincerity that he kept me entirely away from the common wolves. He permitted me to go nowhere without his company; he allowed me to take no food except at home, nor to accept anyone’s gift without permission from him; and he required me to act temperately in everything—in speech, in appearance, and in conduct—so that he seemed to demand of me not clerical but rather monastic discipline.

While my peers wandered everywhere at will and were granted the freedoms appropriate to their age, I was held back from such behavior by constant restraints. Wearing the clerical tonsure, I sat and watched the groups of children at play like a trained animal. Even on Sundays and feast days of the saints I was compelled to study under the discipline of the school, and scarcely on any day or at any time was I permitted to be free from work. I was always driven in the same manner toward undertaking my studies.

Undertaking to teach me alone, he allowed himself to have no one else to teach.

Although he pressed me in this way, and anyone observing my little intellect under such intense pressure would have thought it greatly sharpened, everyone’s hopes were disappointed. For he was entirely lacking in the knowledge of dictation and versification. Meanwhile, almost every day I was pelted with a cruel hailstorm of blows and words, while he compelled me to learn what he was unable to teach.

### He Makes Little Progress in Letters but Much in Moral Conduct; the Mind Oppressed by Excessive Study Is Dulled

I spent almost six years with him under this empty struggle, but, considering the length of time, I brought away from it nothing worth the labor. In every matter that contributed to the beginnings of complete moral discipline, however, there was nothing he did not devote to my benefit. Whatever modesty, chastity, and outward elegance there was, he instilled into me with the utmost faithfulness and affection.

But I perceived that he had shown little consideration and moderation in the danger he had created for me, since, supposedly under the pretext of learning, he drove me relentlessly and busily. For the more any nature—not merely that of a child, but of any human being—is stretched by the constant exercise of meditation beyond measure, the more it is dulled; and the more fiercely the mind is inflamed by severity toward perseverance in study, the more, its strength being subdued by excess, the mind turns from rigidity to sluggishness and grows cold in every respect.

### Alternation of Exercises Should Be Applied So That the Intellect May Become Sharper

It is therefore necessary for the intellect, still weighed down by the covering of the body, to act with greater moderation. For just as the strength that remains undiminished during life cannot possess the gift of contemplation if silence falls for half an hour in heaven, so an intellect laboring in any kind of thought cannot endure constant, so to speak, obstinacy.

We therefore believe that, for those whose hearts are intensely devoted to any particular matter, alternations of concentration should be applied, so that, while we treat different subjects in turn with the mind, we may return to the one to which the soul should chiefly be attached as though refreshed by an indulgence . . . [lacuna] and renewed.

Let weary nature occasionally find relief in some variety of its activity. Let us remember that God did not establish the world uniformly, but delighted us with changes of time under days and nights, under spring and summer, under autumn and winter.

Let everyone, therefore, who bears the name of teacher observe how he moderates the disciplines of children and young people, since we do not think that those in whom full gravity flourishes, even in the manner of old age, should be treated differently.

### Guibert’s Tutor Was Unlearned and Ignorant

I therefore felt toward that man a fierce affection; his excessive severity did not seem unjust in his blows. Nevertheless, his complete diligence in carrying out his work was evident.

I was certainly beaten less deservedly, because if he possessed the teaching skill he claimed, I was certainly, as a boy, very capable of grasping what he said correctly. But since he spoke not according to knowledge, and since what he was trying to express was not at all clear even to himself concerning something lowly but not evident—which he could neither gather nor understand—his empty speech went around in a circle.

He was so unlearned that he retained incorrigibly what he had badly absorbed once, as I have already said, when he was advanced in years. If he happened to utter something rashly, so to speak, he considered all his thoughts authoritative, defended them, and supported them with blows. Yet, I think, he would undoubtedly have spared a stupidity so great [Note: [Col. 0845D] Something is missing here], for, as that same teacher says: “Before nature has absorbed knowledge, it is no greater glory to say what you know than to remain silent about what you do not know.”

When, therefore, he harshly punished me because I did not know what he himself did not know, he ought plainly to have considered that it was a very bad thing to demand from a fragile little breast what he had not placed within it.

For just as the words of madmen can be gathered by sane people only with difficulty or not at all, so the statements of those who do not know, yet claim to know and teach others, grow darker through their own explanation. You will find nothing more difficult than trying to expound what you do not know: obscure to the learner, still more obscure to the listener, just as though both were returning a stone.

I say this, my God, not to brand so dear a friend with a mark of disgrace, but so that anyone who reads may understand that we should not wish to teach as certain everything we suppose, nor envelop others in the fogs of our conjectures.

For I have undertaken to season the present subject, slight as it is, with some reasoning, so that if one matter is judged less worthy of esteem and rightly counted so, the other may occasionally be considered worth the labor.

## CHAPTER VI

### The Teacher Held Guibert Dearly; Guibert Returned His Affection

Although he oppressed me with such severity, in other respects he made it abundantly clear in every way that he loved me with almost no less affection than he loved himself.

He watched over me with such vigilant concern; he took such care for my safety because of the envy of certain people; he taught me with such authority to beware the antiquated habits of certain persons who were held up for my observation; and he pressed my mother so insistently concerning the careful arrangement of my clothing that he seemed to be guarding not my body as a tutor but my soul as a parent.

Although, for my age, I was dull and small, such a reciprocal affection had arisen between us that, even though he often gratuitously marked my tender skin with many welts, I obeyed him—not because of the fear customary among boys of my age, but because of some love implanted deep in my marrow, having entirely forgotten all his harshness.

Indeed, the same teacher and my mother often tested me in many ways. They saw that I showed each of them the fear due to them, and wished to discover whether, when commanded by one of them in the same matter, I would dare to prefer the other.

At last an occasion arose on which, without either of them doing anything in the matter, the test was established beyond all ambiguity.

Once I had been beaten at school. The school, however, was nothing other than a dining room in our house. For the sake of me alone, he had given up the care of the other boys whom he had occasionally accepted as pupils. My mother, prudent in increasing his income and mindful of preserving his honor, had required this of him.

After that uncertain study had ended in the evening, I approached my mother’s knees, having been severely beaten, and even beyond what I deserved. When she began, as was her custom, to ask whether I had been beaten that day, I denied the matter completely, so that I would not appear to have informed on my teacher.

But, whether I wished it or not, she threw back the undergarment called an *interula*, or rather a shirt, and saw my little back bruised, its skin everywhere raised by the blows of the rods.

When she was inwardly grieved that such cruelty had been inflicted on my tender body, she became agitated and hot with anger, and, her eyes filled with sorrow, said:

“You will never become a cleric after this, nor will you suffer punishment any longer in order to learn letters.”

I looked back at her as attentively as I could and replied:

“Even if it should happen that I die for it, I will not stop learning letters and becoming a cleric.”

For she had promised that, if I wished to become a knight when I came of age, she would provide me with the equipment and weapons of military service.

### He Refuses to Become a Knight

When I rejected all these things with no small disdain, that servant of yours, O God, received her injuries so gladly and was made so cheerful by her own contempt that she repeated to my teacher the very answers with which I had opposed her.

They were both delighted, therefore, because I seemed eagerly to aspire to what had been my father’s desire. The more quickly I embraced the study of letters, even though they were not well impressed upon me, the less I entangled myself in ecclesiastical offices—or rather, when the hour summoned me or necessity required it, I by no means preferred meals to such a place and time.

Yet then, my God, you knew how far I later departed from this intention of mine, and how mournfully I proceeded toward divine things, scarcely consenting to attend even when driven there by blows.

Those impulses were not religious ones descending from any intellectual understanding, Lord, but merely childish urges that compelled me at that time. But once adolescence had exhausted the wickedness implanted in me from birth and had burst forth, through its conceptions, into every kind of moral ruin, that old devotion completely withered.

Even if, my God, good will—or rather the likeness of good will—seemed for a moment to flare up, it soon happened that, obscured by showers of the worst thoughts, it fell away.

## CHAPTER VII

### His Mother Tries to Obtain a Benefice for Him

(28) In the end my mother strove by every means to insert me into ecclesiastical benefices.

The first reason for this insertion was not merely bad but wicked. A certain adolescent brother of mine, a knight and citizen of the castle of Clermont [Note: [Col. 0847D] Something is missing here], was awaiting money—two [years?] before that time—from the lord of the town, which lies between Compiègne and Beauvais, whether as a gift or as a feudal obligation, I do not know.

When he appeared unable, as I suppose, to provide the money that was to be given, certain relatives of mine advised him to suggest that the lord give me a canonry—what they call a prebend—of the church in that place, which was subject to his authority contrary to the canons, so that my brother would no longer be troubled by demands for repayment from him.

### On Married Priests

(29) At that time a new attack by the Apostolic See against married priests was taking place. Consequently, such fury burned among the common people, who were zealous for the clergy, that they loudly demanded, in a hostile spirit, either that such priests be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices or that they be barred from the priesthood.

In this matter, a certain nephew of my father—a man distinguished both by his power and by his prudence—was so peculiarly devoted to the work of Venus that he showed no consideration whatever for any woman’s kinship. Yet he raged against the clergy over the aforementioned canon with such insistence that one would have thought that a singular chastity had driven him to detest such things.

Although he was a layman and could not be restrained by the laws applicable to his own class, the looser those laws were, the more disgracefully he abused them. He could not be held in the nets of marriage, since he had never allowed himself to be caught in such bonds.

Thus, although a foul reputation concerning these matters was scattered everywhere about him, and although the secular wealth in which he excelled protected him, he never ceased to thunder against the sacred order with his obstinacy, using his own impurity as a weapon.

Having therefore found an opportunity by which he might advance me through the loss of a certain wealthy priest, as people reported, he acted with the lord of the castle, with whom he had considerable influence, since he was so necessary to him. He arranged for the lord to summon me, while the cleric was absent and entirely unheard, and to grant me the investiture of the aforementioned canonry.

That church had been improperly entrusted by the bishop to the lord as an abbey, contrary to right and justice, and a non-canon was demanding canons from the canons.

Since, therefore, at that time not only sexual relations among the persons of the three higher orders and among canons were charged as an offense, but also the purchase of ecclesiastical offices below the governance of souls—such as prebends, cantorates, provostships, and other offices of that kind—was considered no less criminal, not to mention honors whose holders were ordered to conduct internal business, those clerics who favored the side of the man who had lost the prebend, together with many of my peers, began to raise frequent whispers about simony and the excommunication that had recently become widespread.

Since that man was a priest and had a wife, yet could not be deterred from his office by her, he had indeed ceased to celebrate Masses.

For, since he had put his own body before the divine mysteries, he was rightly subjected to the punishment which he had thought to escape by renouncing sacrifice.

Thus, deprived of the canonry, because he no longer had anything by which he could be restrained, he freely celebrated whatever Masses he wished, while retaining his wife.

From this arose the widespread rumor that, amid those same sacred rites, he was destroying my mother and her household by repeated excommunication day after day.

But my mother, always fearful of divine things and dreading both the punishments of sins and the occasions for sin that follow from them, immediately renounced the prebend that had been wrongly bestowed and, in the hope of the death of the clerics concerned, secured another for me from the lord of the castle.

Thus we fled iron weapons and fell into a bronze bow. (30) For to give something in anticipation of another person’s death is nothing other than to order someone to become a daily murderer.

My Lord God, at that time I was so wickedly entangled in those hopes, and I was in no way restrained by expectation of your gifts, which I had not yet learned to experience.

That woman of yours had not yet understood what hopes and assurances she ought to have regarding my sustenance from you, nor did she know what benefits you had prepared for me. Since she was still living somewhat in the world and felt the things that belonged to the world, she sought for me what she herself had chosen to provide for herself—worldly advantages, as she thought, for one who would also seek worldly things.

But once she had observed the danger to her own soul and had gathered the countless chambers of her heart together in lamentation over her former life, as though saying, “What I do not want done to me, I will not do to another,” she judged it the height of madness to do for others what she had rejected for herself. What she had ceased to desire for herself, she considered wicked to desire for another’s ruin.

It is clear that many act quite differently: we observe them utterly rejecting their own possessions under the pretext of poverty, yet burning with excessive eagerness to procure things for others—not only for their own people, which is itself bad, but also for outsiders, which is worse.

## CHAPTER VIII

### Concerning Those Who Restored or Repaired the Monastic Life

But since the subject turns back, insofar as mention is made of our own time, I wish to touch somewhat more fully upon the condition of religious institutions and of the conversions that we witnessed. From these, this very [church?] . . . [lacuna], as well as many others, happened to take examples of good change.

There is an abundant report in the writings that the monastic way of life flourished in ancient times. Since I remain silent about foreign regions, it is known that under certain kings of the Franks we cultivated the rules of this institution, with different people constructing various houses. In some of them such a vast multitude of devout people gathered that we marvel how the narrow capacity of the places was able to contain so great a crowd.

Among these were certain monasteries distinguished by a special strictness. They often nobly restored to proper order monasteries in which the fervor of the discipline had grown lukewarm. Such was once Luxeuil (*Luxovium*) (31) in Gaul, (32) and certain monasteries in Neustria, which is now called Normandy.

But because of that saying of the truthful poet that the highest things are not granted long endurance—and because it is far truer that, as the age declines amid the reins of iniquity, the love of holy life grows cold—the abundance of worldly possessions gradually deserted certain churches. Consequently, the number of those living well became small, especially when manual labor itself came to be despised.

Hence, in our own times, the most ancient monasteries, reduced in number, were content with small communities despite the abundance of possessions given in former times. In them scarcely anyone could be found who, out of disgust for sin, had rejected the world; rather, these churches were chiefly occupied by those who had been handed over to them through the devotion of their parents and raised there from early childhood.

The less they feared their own evils—since these seemed to them to have done no wrong—the more carelessly they lived within the enclosures of the monasteries.

When they received external administrations and offices according to the necessity or whim of their abbots, being eager for their own will and little accustomed to external freedoms, they began readily to squander ecclesiastical funds on easy pretexts and to distribute revenues, whether by expenditure or gratuitously [the text appears to be defective here: *coeperunt* may be missing] . . . .

And although religion was then held in less regard among them, the monks themselves became dearer because of their very scarcity.

## CHAPTER IX
## On the Remarkable Conversion of Ebrard, Count of Britoil in Picardy

When matters stood thus, and scarcely anyone of any worth came to them, a certain count of the castle of Britoil [commonly Breteuil], which lies on the boundary of the Amiens and Beauvais regions, arose to stir the minds of many. He was then in the flower of his age and possessed the most attractive elegance, especially since, just as his lineage was distinguished by nobility, so also he excelled in the remarkable beauty of his appearance; moreover, he was conspicuous through the renown of other territories and through the splendor of all his wealth. At last the man’s mind, established in the great arrogance of pride, came to its senses and, by contemplating the misery of the vices which he had begun to pursue in worldly fashion, turned back from them. Having therefore perceived the wretchedness of his soul, and recognizing that in the world he was doing nothing except condemning and being condemned, defiling and being defiled, he spent a long time discussing and considering in many ways what manner of life he should undertake, together with certain men whom he had chosen as confidants and companions of so great a desire. (39) His name was Ebrard, a man famous among the leading men of France in every respect.

At length, having brought his long reflection into the light of action, and without leaving anyone aware of his plan, he secretly departed with those whom, by covert persuasion, he had enlisted as companions for undertaking this religious life. As a fugitive he went off to some foreign provinces—I do not know which—where, since their inhabitants were entirely ignorant of his name, he gladly dwelt. He worked to earn the expenses of his living by making charcoal, and carried it here and there through the countryside and towns with his companions to sell it. Then for the first time he thought that he had attained the highest riches, and one could behold in him all the glory of the king’s daughter within. What more? I shall append the example from which he himself also took encouragement.

(40) Theobald, whom everyone today calls holy, so that many churches now established under his name honor him everywhere, had previously been a young man of noble birth. At the very beginnings of his military career, despising arms, he escaped barefoot from his own people and devoted himself to the craft mentioned above; for some time he passed his life under an unfamiliar necessity. Encouraged, I say, by this example, Ebrard had resolved to live by such a humble occupation, as we have related.

## A Specter Addresses and Terrifies Ebrard. He Changes His Purpose and His Usual Occupations, and Devotes Himself to Monastic Discipline

But since there are no good things which do not sometimes provide occasions for some evil, one day, while he was in a village to carry out some work or other, behold, someone appeared before him wearing a Tyrian cloak, with silk stockings whose feet had been cut away, and with his hair parted in a womanish fashion from his forehead and reaching to the tops of his arms—presenting himself more as a lover than as an exile. When Ebrard sincerely asked who he was, the man turned his eye slightly aside, raised his eyebrow, and, after adopting an appearance of modesty, began to speak. Ebrard, with increasingly compassionate and persistent curiosity, pressed him further. At last, scarcely overcome by what seemed almost human insistence, he burst out:

“I am,” he said—“but do not tell this to anyone”—“Ebrard, formerly count of Britoil [perhaps Britoliensis, as above], who, as you know, was once wealthy in France. By banishing myself into exile, I am paying the voluntary penalties for my sins.”

The illustrious man had spoken, and by the sudden transformation into the role he had assumed he confounded the one who had questioned him. Ebrard therefore, astonished beyond measure at the perversely shameless man, and, if I may put it so, rejecting the address of that apparition, reported the matter to his companions and said:

“Know, friends, that this way of life is useful for us, but fatal to very many others, because from what you have heard from his own mouth you can infer what follows concerning many others. If, therefore, we wish to please God completely, we must avoid whatever provides others with an occasion for scandal—or rather, for falsehood. Let us therefore settle ourselves firmly where, once the causes of the exile which we endure for God’s sake have been removed, we may deprive everyone of the pretext for this presumptuous title.”

After this declaration, having changed their plan, they went to the Greater Monastery (Marmoutier, near Tours), and there, having assumed the habit of holy religious life, they served permanently. (41)

We heard that, while he lived in the world, this same man had been so concerned with elegant clothing that he was inferior to none of the wealthiest; yet he had such a fiercely proud bearing that he could easily appear unapproachable to anyone, even by a word. Later, when we saw him living under monastic discipline, he held his body in such contempt that the cheapness of his clothing, the lowered expression of his face, and the thinness of his limbs proclaimed him not a count but a rough little peasant. And when he was sent through cities and towns at the command of the abbot, he could never be induced by his own will to enter—even once—the castles which he had abandoned.

He himself told me these things when I was still a very young man. He honored me so greatly and admitted me to his kinship that, through a particular and singular expression of his affection and regard, he bestowed this favor upon me.

He had an unusually courtly habit: whenever he encountered people whom he knew to excel in learning, he would write them down in a little book which he frequently carried with him for this very purpose and in which he compelled himself, according to his ability, to compose in prose or verse. Thus, while collecting the sayings of all those who were reputed for their zeal in that field, he also weighed the thoughts of each of them from their words. Although he could not understand these matters by himself, he would nevertheless immediately grasp, from the judgment of those to whom he displayed what he had written for reading, who had spoken most accurately either in thought or in verse.

It is enough to have lightly touched upon these matters concerning a man once noble by birth but now nobler through a good end. He, I say, among the men preserved in our memory, shone forth first with the more glorious example of conversion.

## CHAPTER X

But the one who created Paul through Stephen’s prayer propagated the same example much more successfully and more widely through another man of considerable power. (42) For a certain Simon, son of Count Ralph, enriched the religious life of our time by the splendor of an unexpected conversion. (43) How famous this Ralph was everywhere for Frankish power, what cities he invaded, and how many towns he acquired and held through remarkable shrewdness—there are many survivors who remember his deeds and can testify to it. How great he was can also be inferred from the single fact that, after the death of her husband, he took as his wife the wife of King Henry, likewise the mother of King Philip.

When the young Simon’s father died, Simon soon held the honor of his father’s counties. Some report that the following was the cause of his conversion, which came so quickly. In a certain town that had come to his father more by usurpation than by inheritance, the remains of that father had been buried. The son, fearing that this might harm his father’s soul, proposed to transfer them to what he knew belonged to him by right. When this intention was discovered before the transfer, and the body was exposed naked before the eyes of the son, Simon, having looked upon the wasted body of his once most powerful and ferocious parent, turned his thoughts toward contemplating the misery of human condition. From that time he began to despise whatever height and glory had previously pleased him.

Having conceived this very purpose, he finally brought forth the desire that had been growing within him. Fleeing from his homeland and his own people, he left the borders of France and went to Burgundy, (44) to Saint Oyend in the Jura region.

I have also heard that he had become betrothed to a young woman of extremely noble birth. When she learned that the young man she loved had renounced both her and the world, she could not bear to appear inferior to him; she joined herself as a virgin to the ranks of women serving God, intending to remain a virgin.

Some time after receiving the monastic habit, he returned to France. The purity of his speech and the humility of spirit which he displayed in his face so inspired men and women that countless throngs of both sexes gathered under him to pursue this way of life, and many from every direction were summoned to this purpose by the example of his name. His conduct particularly stirred the zeal of mounted men.

## CHAPTER XI

### The Reason for Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness; the Origin and Early Institutions of the Carthusians; the Perverse Life of Manasses, Archbishop of Reims

Since it was fitting that some learned man should also gather behind him a sacred flock of the religious order with the same devotion, there was at that time a certain Bruno in the city of Reims, a man trained in the liberal arts and a master of important studies (45). He is known to have received the beginnings of his conversion on the following occasion.

After the death of the very famous Archbishop Gervasius, a certain Manasses intruded himself into the government of the aforesaid city by simony. He was indeed a nobleman, but possessed none of that serenity which is the first ornament of a gentleman. He had conceived such great arrogance from this new position that he seemed to imitate the royal majesty—or rather the ferocity of majesty—of foreign peoples. I say “foreign,” for among the kings of the Franks there had always flourished such natural modesty that, even if they did not possess the saying of the Wise Man in knowledge, they possessed it in practice: “They have made you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1).

This man, then, since he was exceedingly fond of soldiers and neglected the clergy, is reported once to have said: “The archbishopric of Reims would be a good thing if it were not necessary to have Masses sung there.”

### Hugh of Die, Archbishop of Lyon, Strikes Manasses with Anathema

Bruno, who was horrified by this man’s utterly wicked morals and disgraceful behavior—Bruno, then the most renowned man in the churches of Gaul—left the city with certain other noble clerics of Reims, out of hatred for that infamous man.

Later, when Manasses was repeatedly struck with anathema by Hugh, called of Die, Archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See, a man most distinguished in his zeal for justice, and when Manasses attempted by military force to squander the treasures of the church, the nobles, clergy, and townsmen expelled him from the see which he had wickedly occupied. Sent into perpetual exile, he went to the excommunicated Emperor Henry, himself likewise excommunicated, and wandering here and there, eventually died without communion.

It is worth mentioning something that occurred within the city while he was acting wickedly there. Among the ecclesiastical ornaments which he had distributed to the soldiers who had served his tyranny was a golden chalice of considerable value in two respects: it was of very substantial size, and, as was reported, some portion—who knows how large—of the gold offered to the Lord by the three Magi had been poured into it.

When he was cutting the chalice apart with tongs and distributing the portions which he had allotted, no one was willing to accept so sacred an object. At last a wicked knight, no less worthy than his donor, allowed himself to receive it—or rather, boldly seized it in contempt of the majesty of the sacrament. He was immediately driven mad. He did not spend the wealth which he had presumptuously taken without right, and nevertheless he promptly paid the penalties of his reckless greed.

### Bruno Goes to Chartreuse

But Bruno, having abandoned the city, also resolved to renounce the world. Horrified by contact with his former associates, he proceeded into the territory of Grenoble. There, choosing to dwell upon a lofty and exceedingly terrifying ridge, to which access led by a most difficult and highly unusual path, while beneath it an exceedingly precipitous chasm opened into a valley, he established such a way of life, and his followers still live in this manner today.

### The Customs and Manner of Life of Bruno and His Disciples

There is also a church there, not far from the edge of the mountain, with a slightly winding slope. Thirteen monks live there. They possess a cloister sufficiently suitable for a cenobitic custom, but they do not live together in the cloistered manner of other monks.

Each has his own cell arranged around the cloister. There they work, sleep, and eat. On Sundays they receive provisions from the dispenser—namely bread and legumes—which each of them cooks for himself as his one kind of pottage. They have water both for drinking and for other uses from a conduit supplied by a spring, which runs around all the cells and flows into each little building through particular openings.

They use fish and cheese on Sundays and on very solemn feast days. By “fish,” I mean not fish which they themselves have purchased, but fish which they have received through the generosity of certain good men.

No one possesses gold, silver, or ecclesiastical ornaments; indeed, there is nothing there except a silver chalice. They assemble in the same church not at the customary hours, as we do, but at fixed times. Unless I am mistaken, they attend Mass on Sundays and on solemn feast days. They scarcely ever speak anywhere, for if anything must be requested, it is obtained by a sign.

When they drink wine, it is so diluted that it gives those who drink it no strength and scarcely any taste; it is hardly better than ordinary water. They wear hair shirts next to the body, and their other clothing is very thin. They live under a prior (46), while the bishop of Grenoble, a highly religious man, carries out the functions of abbot and administrator.

Although they humble themselves in complete poverty, (47) they nevertheless accumulate an extremely rich library. For the less their material supply of this bread is abundant, the more diligently they labor over that food which does not perish but endures forever.

### They Reject Silver Vessels Sent by the Count of Nevers

They are such guardians of their poverty, I say, that in this very year in which we are writing (48), the Count of Nevers, a thoroughly religious and powerful man, visited them out of devotion and because of the excellent reputation which proceeds from that place. He strongly warned them to beware of worldly greed.

When he had returned home and remembered the poverty which he had seen among them, but had entirely forgotten the admonitions which he had given them, he sent them certain silver objects—cups and dishes [perhaps small bowls]—of very great value. But he found that they had not forgotten what he had said. After they had immediately taken counsel together, they returned everything in full, rejecting what he had said to them.

“We have chosen,” they said, “to retain no foreign money either for our own expenses or for the ornaments of the church. And if it is not spent for one of these two purposes, why should it be accepted by us?”

The count was ashamed of this offering, which contradicted his own words. Nevertheless, concealing his displeasure, he sent back ox hides and a great quantity of parchment, which he recognized as almost unavoidably necessary for them.

### Description of Chartreuse

That place is called Chartreuse. They cultivate little of the land there for growing grain. Instead, they are accustomed to obtain whatever crops they need by means of the wool of the many sheep they keep.

Below that mountain are dwellings, more than twenty in number, occupied by very faithful laymen who live under the monks’ direction. These men are carried along by such fervor for the contemplation they have begun that they do not abandon their institution with any length of time, nor grow lukewarm through any long duration of that difficult way of life.

### Bruno Establishes a Monastery of His Order in Calabria and Avoids the Episcopate

From there, for some remarkable reason I do not know, this Bruno departed. After he had completed the beginnings mentioned above and had set them forth through many repetitions of words and deeds, he went to Apulia—or perhaps to Calabria; I do not know which—and established there a similar manner of life.

There he conducted himself with great humility and shone all around him through the complete display of pious examples. When he was sought and detained by the Apostolic See for the dignity of a bishopric, he fled. Fearing the world, lest he lose what he had tasted of God, he rejected—not divine things, but worldly ones—in the postponement of so great an office.

### Men and Women Adopt This Manner of Life, Including Children of Ten and Eleven

These, I say, were the people who at that time raised up the beginnings of conversions. Immediately throngs of men and women joined them, and every class of society hastened together.

Why should I speak of ages? Ten- and eleven-year-old children were contemplating things suitable to old age and were practicing disciplines far stricter than their tender years could bear. In those conversions there occurred what used to occur among the ancient martyrs: greater liveliness of faith was found in weak and tender bodies than in those in whom the authority of advanced age and learning flourished.

### Innumerable Monasteries Are Built

Since there had previously been monastic settlements nowhere except in the oldest monasteries, new ones began to be built everywhere, and great revenues for their sustenance began to be supplied from every direction.

Those who did not have the means to build larger houses established dwellings and provisions for as few brothers as they could support—some for two, some for four, and others for whatever number they were able to maintain. Thus it came about that in villages, towns, cities, and fortified places, and even in the forests and fields themselves, swarms of monks suddenly seemed to be teeming everywhere, spreading themselves through their activities in every direction. Those places, in which the lairs of wild beasts and the dens of robbers had existed, began to shine with the divine name and the worship of the saints.

### The Voluntary Poverty of Bruno and His Disciples; What Those Who Could Not Adopt the Institution Did

The nobility, surrounded by so many examples, therefore aspired to undergo voluntary poverty and entered monasteries, bringing with them the possessions they had despised. They also constantly pursued others in a pious hunt, seeking to draw them into the same way of life.

Women likewise, abandoning the marriages of famous husbands and freeing themselves from the claims of pious children, contributed their wealth there and devoted themselves to ecclesiastical support.

Those men and women who could not renounce all the possessions they held supported those who had renounced them through frequent gifts from their own property. They surrounded many churches and altars with offerings of the most pleasing gifts, and by prayerfully doing such things—assisting with their own resources the way of life which they could not follow by imitating such persons—they strove, as far as possible, to equal it.

Hence it happened that in those times, through the multitude both of gifts and of donors, and still more through the diligence of those who came to this purpose and assisted the inhabitants of churches through their various forms of support, monasteries advanced so greatly that, compared with the conditions of those who then flourished, they now seem to be suffering losses through the growing wickedness of modern people.

For now, alas, the children either completely withdraw what their parents, moved by such devotion, contributed to sacred places, or do not cease demanding frequent repayments, utterly degenerate from their fathers’ wishes.

## CHAPTER XII

### Guibert Again Adds Much Concerning His Mother

At last, after these reflections, I return to you, my God, concerning the conversion of that good woman, my mother.

While she was scarcely of marriageable age, she was given to my father, who was entirely a young man, by arrangement of my grandfather. She was a noblewoman with a remarkably composed face and a naturally and most becomingly serious expression. Yet from the very beginnings of childhood she produced within herself a fear of the divine name.

She had learned to dread sin not through experience but through a certain inward impulse of supernatural fear. As she herself often told me, fear of sudden death had so filled her mind that, when she had reached old age, she grieved that she no longer possessed in her mature spirit the same good impulses of fear which she had had in her inexperienced and wholly unformed youth.

It happened, therefore, that the marital union was obstructed at the very beginning of that lawful bond through the sorcery of certain people. It was said that jealousy on the part of her stepmother had not been absent from this marriage. Since that woman had several nieces of great beauty and noble birth, she sought to bring one of them into my father’s marital bed.

When this had not succeeded according to her wishes, she is said by wicked arts to have caused the consummation of the marriage to cease altogether. When the virginity of my mother had remained intact for a full three years, and this great misfortune had been concealed in profound silence, at last my father revealed the matter first, summoned by his own relatives.

Consider how many ways my relatives labored to bring about a divorce between them. They diligently stirred my father, then young and foolish, toward monasticism—although at that time there was very little discussion of such a matter—but they did this not for his salvation, rather with the intention of obtaining his possessions.

When their suggestion proved ineffective, they began to attack the girl with repeated abuse, so that, placed far from her own people and subjected to the oppression of outsiders, she might be worn down by injuries and leave without any formal repudiation.

Meanwhile she endured with equanimity the words directed against her, and, whenever disputes arose from them, pretended not to know anything and concealed the matter.

In addition, when certain very wealthy men saw that she was deprived of marital relations, they began to assail the young woman’s mind. But you, Lord, founder of inward chastity, had inspired her with a holiness which neither nature nor age could tolerate. From you, Lord, she possessed the power by which she did not burn even when placed in fire.

You caused it that, although her tender character was exposed to the dripping of evil conversations, it was not corrupted; rather, the oil poured into the furnace was the use of external enticements to natural impulses—impulses which are human and common. Yet the young woman’s spirit, always master of itself, was carried outside itself by no stimulus.

Are these not your works alone, Lord? You preserved her, placed in the heat of her earliest age and continually engaged in the very duties of marriage, for seven full years in such great continence that, in accordance with the saying of a certain wise man, even rumor would have been afraid to lie about her.

### The Dissolution of Young Women

God, you know how difficult it was—indeed, how almost impossible—for this to be preserved among the women of that age. In those days there was such modesty among them that the marriage of any woman could scarcely be attacked even by a rumor.

Alas, how miserably from that time down to our own age modesty and honor have gradually collapsed in the profession of virginity, and how the reality and appearance of matronly restraint have withered, so that in their entire bearing only buffoonery can be observed, where nothing is heard except jokes, and where everything consists of the signals of the eyes and tongue.

There is wantonness in their walk; nothing is not ridiculous in their behavior. The styles of clothing are so unlike that ancient frugality that the widening of the sleeves, the narrowness of the tunics (49), and the twisted, pointed shoes from Córdoba all seem to proclaim the universal loss of modesty.

Every woman thinks that she has reached the depths of misery if she lacks the reputation of lovers. She claims for herself so much glory of nobility and courtly status in proportion as she abounds in a more flourishing number of such suitors.

I call God to witness that at that time there was greater modesty among men who took wives—so much so that they would blush to be seen amid such things—than there is now among women who marry. These shameful affairs certainly make men more boastful and more eager for the marketplace and public display.

Why is this so, my Lord God, except that no one blushes at his own frivolity and lust because he sees everyone held under the same reproach? When he perceives that nearly everyone acts under the same impulse as himself, why, I ask, should he be ashamed of an enthusiasm toward which he sees the others likewise aspiring?

But why do I say “ashamed,” when the only thing that causes such people shame is for one of them to excel less than others in displaying his lust? No one is restrained by the number of his love affairs, or privately boastful of the particular beauty he has chosen; nor is anyone condemned before you because he has become especially swollen with pride over what he loves. Rather, he celebrates the common corruption before all people with magnificent approval.

Behold the outcry: while what ought to have been modestly concealed, what conscience accuses as weakened chastity, and what deserved altogether to be suppressed, some shameless person now proclaims here and there with the unbridled license of an unaccustomed depravity—an act deserving eternal silence.

By this and by similar means the modern age is corrupted and corrupts, scattering among others what it has conceived wickedly; what has been scattered is then carried on and, through the foulness by which it is transmitted, propagated among others without limit.

Holy God, scarcely any of these things was heard anywhere at the time when that servant of yours lived in this way. Rather, things unworthy of mention were covered with the cloak of sacred modesty, and worthy things were adorned [perhaps crowned].

During those seven years, that virginity which you miraculously preserved in her struggled under countless pressures. When her father’s marriage had been dissolved, they repeatedly threatened to transfer her to another husband or to take her away to the distant houses of my other relatives.

Although at times she resisted these importunities with the greatest bitterness, she nevertheless fought against the enticements of her own flesh and against the inducements of all outsiders with marvelous temperance—yet this was from your gift, my God.

I do not say, good God, by what virtue she did this, but that the virtue was yours alone. For how could it have been virtue when no distinction between spirit and flesh, no devout attention to God, but only concern for outward respectability or avoidance of disgrace had accomplished it?

It is plainly useful for modesty at least to resist an impending sin; just as it is useful before sin, so after sin it is blameworthy. What so disturbs the soul with pious shame that it restrains it from committing sin is useful for the time being, because the fear of God may approach and season tasteless shame with divine salt. What was useful for a time—that is, for this world—can thereby become useful not merely for a moment but eternally.

This is the shame which leads to glory; yet after guilt it is as harmful as it stubbornly obstructs the healing medicine of holy confession.

Your servant, Lord God, my mother, possessed the intention of doing nothing contrary to worldly respectability. Yet, according to your Gregory—whom she had neither read nor heard read—she did not remain in that intention, because afterward she transferred everything she intended toward you alone.

Thus, at that time, it was beneficial for her to have been attached to worldly reverence.

After seven years and more had passed, the magical practice by which the natural and lawful union was broken came to an end. It is entirely credible that, just as the power of sight is distorted by magical illusions so that magicians seem to make some things out of nothing and other things out of something else, so powers of this kind and sexual operations may be confused by much less skill. This is so commonly practiced that even the most ignorant people now know of it.

When, I say, those wicked arts had been cancelled through the agency of a certain old woman, my mother performed the duties of marriage with the same faithfulness with which she had preserved her prolonged virginity under the pressure of such great threats.

Happy indeed in other respects, in this she consigned herself to an infinity not so much of misery as of wretchedness: though then good, she gave birth to me, who afterward proved ever evil, and always worse than herself.

You know, Almighty One, how purely and holily, according to your will, she raised me; how much care she employed for me in infancy from nurses, and for me as a growing little boy from tutors and teachers; how she did not even neglect splendid clothing for my little body, so that I might seem equal to royal or comital boys in the attentions bestowed on me.

Nor, Lord, had you bestowed this affection upon my mother alone. You had also inspired other people, much richer in status, to give me clothing and nourishment, not so much because of kinship as because of the grace you had granted me through them.

God, you know how many admonitions and how many prayers she poured daily into my ears, warning me not to receive words of any corruption. Whenever solitude freed her from household cares, she taught me how and for what things I ought to pray to you.

You alone know with what anxieties she labored lest an unsound mind corrupt the beginnings of that flourishing and promising youth which you had given me. You had made her desire that I should burn continually with longing for you, so that you might grant inward virtue—or wisdom—to match my outward beauty.

And, good Lord, good God, if she had then foreseen by what mass of filth I would obscure those beautiful surfaces of your gifts with which you had adorned me at her request, what would she have said? What would she have done? What unremitting groans would she have uttered? What tearing apart of the mind would she have suffered?

Thanks be to you, sweet and moderate disposer, “who formed our hearts one by one” (Psalm 32:15). Indeed, if his most pure eye had penetrated the inner chambers of my soul, so unworthy of pure sight, I wonder whether he would not have immediately fallen lifeless.

## CHAPTER XIII

### The Pious Practices of Guibert’s Mother

Having said these things while occupied with other matters, let us return to some points omitted earlier.

We learned that while this woman was still serving the world, reverence for the name of God was always present in her, to such an extent that in her service to churches, her assistance to the poor, and her offering of sacrifices, she conducted herself in a manner that made her venerable to everyone.

But I know that this will at once introduce a great difficulty for my credibility, since the closeness of what may be considered suspicious praise will seem to block the way. If, in exalting my mother, I appear cautiously and deceptively to exalt myself, I presume to call upon you, God, as witness, since you know her soul as its inhabitant, to affirm that she excelled in every respect in what is being said.

And certainly, since it is clearer than daylight that my life has departed from the path of every good thing, and that all my pursuits are a reproach to anyone of sound judgment, what benefit will the greatness of my father’s or grandfather’s name bring me, when all its breadth will be compressed into the wretchedness of the offspring? Since I am not reborn into their ways by any conformity of will or action, it only adds to the evil of disgrace if I claim their praises for myself.

### Her Husband Is Captured in War

While she was still a young woman living under her husband, something happened to her which provided no small stimulus toward correcting her life.

In the time of King Henry, the Franks fought fiercely against the Northmen and their count William, who later conquered the English and the Scots. In an encounter between the two peoples, my father happened to be captured.

It had been that count’s custom never to compel his captives to pay ransom, but to condemn them to perpetual imprisonment for as long as they lived. When this was reported to my father’s wife—I had not yet been born, and for a long time afterward I did not exist, so I shall omit my mother’s name—she, exhausted by miserable grief, ceased eating and drinking, while desperate anxiety denied her sleep.

Her distress did not arise from the amount of the ransom; she mourned the irredeemable captivity.

### She Is Gravely Afflicted and Tormented by a Demon

When the dead of night had come and she, filled with terrible anxiety, was lying in her own bed, the enemy himself suddenly settled upon her while she was awake. This is customary for the devil: he especially plunges himself into minds worn down by sadness. He pressed upon her as she lay beneath an exceedingly heavy weight, almost to the point of extinction.

As her spirit was suffocated by this oppression, and she was deprived of the full freedom of all her limbs, unable to utter any sound whatsoever, she awaited only the help of God—entirely silent, but with a mind still free.

Then, behold, from the head of her bed a certain spirit—undoubtedly a good one—began to cry out in a voice no less full of affection than clear:

“Holy Mary, help!”

After he had said this for some time, and she fully understood what was being said, the woman who was suffering such torment felt the demon burst forth with great violence. When he burst forth, the one who had been pressing upon her rose up; the spirit who had confronted him seized him and, being violent through God’s power, overthrew him with such a crash that the impact shook the room severely and rudely awakened the attendants, who were sunk in sleep.

After the demon had thus been driven away by divine powers, the pious spirit who had called upon Mary and expelled the demon turned to the woman he had rescued and said:

“See that you are a good woman.”

Her maids, stunned by the sudden commotion, rose to see how their mistress was. They found her scarcely alive, with a bloodless face and all the strength drained from her little body. They asked about the noise and immediately heard its cause from her. They could scarcely revive her breath through their presence, conversation, and the lighting of a lamp.

Retaining the last words of her deliverer—or rather, yours, Lord God, spoken through your messenger—that woman committed them to perpetual memory and kept them for the future, to be fulfilled for God if opportunity should be granted. When her husband had died, while she still shone with much bodily and facial beauty, and I, scarcely a year and a half old, gave her alone cause for anxiety, she resolved to maintain widowhood. How vigorously she governed herself in it and what examples of modesty she displayed may be inferred from this single instance: when my father’s relatives, rivals for his benefices and possessions, sought to obtain all of them by excluding my mother, they fixed a day for the hearing of the case.

[Col. 0861C] The day arrived, and the leading men were sitting in judgment over the whole matter. My mother, having withdrawn into the church from their most eager [. . . . .] [f., certain] efforts, stood before the image of the crucified Lord, mindful of the prayer that was owed. When one of my father’s relatives, sharing the same opinion as the others and sent by them, came to her and asked her to go to those who were awaiting her, in order to hear their judgment, she replied:

“On this matter,” she said, “I will act only in the presence of my Lord.”

“And whose lord?” he asked.

Stretching out her hand toward the image of the crucified Lord, she said: “This is the Lord.”

On hearing this, he said: “Here I have an advocate before whom I shall plead my case.” He blushed at her words and, being—as he was—very crafty, went away with a forced laugh masking his wickedness, intending to report what he had heard to his associates. They too, covered with shame by such a reply, recognized that they had no just grounds against her complete integrity and ceased pressing their claim.

Without delay, one of the leading men of the place and province, my father’s nephew—a man as powerful as he was greedy—addressed the woman in these terms:

“Since you possess youth and beauty, my lady, it is fitting that you swear to marry, so that you may live more agreeably in this world, and so that my uncle’s children, whom I shall faithfully raise, may live under my care; finally, so that his possessions may, as is proper, return to my rights.”

But she replied:

“You know that your uncle was descended from a distinguished family. Since he has died, God having raised him up, he will not resume his own. Therefore, Lord Hymenaeus will perform his duties with me only if a marriage with a person of much greater rank should voluntarily offer itself to me.”

That cautious woman spoke of marrying a more noble man because she knew that it could scarcely, or not at all, happen that, once he recoiled from the name of “more noble,” she would immediately reject noble and ignoble alike and thereby deprive herself of all hope of a second marriage. When he therefore criticized her statement about a more noble man as an expression of excessive pride, she added:

“Certainly either a more noble man—or no one.”

Understanding the intention of the matron’s words, he abandoned his attempt and never again asked her anything of the kind.

Thus, under the greatest fear of God and with no less love for all her kin—and especially for the needy—this prudent woman governed us and our affairs. The fidelity that she had maintained toward her living husband she now carried over, in a twofold manner, to his soul: she did not divide, by introducing another flesh after his death, the former unity of their bodies, and she strove to assist him by offering almost daily the saving sacrifice. Although she was generally approachable to all the poor, she was, according to her means, exceedingly compassionate and generous toward some of them. The memory of her sins tormented her so greatly that she seemed to fear that, as though she had been given over to every kind of wickedness, she would incur punishment for all the evil that is done.

In frugality she could accomplish nothing, since thrift in food was entirely unsuited to her delicate constitution and accustomed comfort. In other matters, however, she behaved quite unexpectedly. For I saw with these eyes and handled with these hands something that, although she was at times covered externally with a more elegant garment, was worn next to her naked body beneath it: the roughest possible hair shirt. She wore it not only during the day, but also slept in it at night—something exceedingly strange for a body so accustomed to comfort.

[Col. 0862C] She was scarcely ever, or never, absent from the nocturnal offices, attending the common worship of God’s people at the appointed divine hours. Indeed, she arranged matters so that the unceasing devotion of the chaplains almost never ceased in her presence from celebrating God’s praise. The mention of her deceased husband was so constantly on her lips that she seemed to turn no other thought over in her mind. While praying, distributing alms, and even engaging in ordinary conversation, she continually spoke of that man, since she could not do otherwise without ceasing to think of him. When the heart overflows with love for someone, the tongue is shaped to speak of him, as though it wished—or did not wish—to do so.

## CHAPTER XIV

But let us leave aside these matters, in which she certainly advanced in goodness, though not to such an extent as to deserve our particular attention, and pursue what remains. After my father’s death, when I had almost completed twelve years, as some report, during which she had cared for the household and children in widowhood, having put aside the dress of the world, she was hastening to bring to a happy birth what long gestation had produced. While she was deliberating over this purpose and discussing the matter with my tutor, who had also been my teacher (I have spoken of him above), I heard a possessed man, who was being fed in her household, railing about some matter or other concerning her. Under the pressure of the demon, he cried out:

“The priests,” he said, “have placed a cross on her loins.”

Nothing could have been more truthful, although at the time I did not at all understand what he meant. For afterward she placed herself beneath not one cross but many.

Before long, while the matter was known to no one except the man I have mentioned, a steward of her household—who himself later followed her conversion by renouncing the world—had the following dream. He saw her taking a husband and celebrating a wedding; this event would cause the greatest wonder and astonishment among her children, friends, and relatives. The following day, when my mother was going into the countryside for a walk with my teacher and that same steward, he told her what he had seen. My mother, who was exceedingly skilled at interpreting such things, needed no interpreter. Looking at that teacher, she silently indicated that the vision signified the matters they had been discussing among themselves concerning the love of God, to whom she desired to be joined. She therefore hastened what she had begun and, unable to endure the inward heat of her desire, left the society of the town in which she was living.

### Guido, bishop of Beauvais, founds the church of Saint-Quentin. He is accused of the crime of simony, deposed, and becomes a monk at Cluny. Guibert’s native town.

During this time of withdrawal she stayed at an episcopal estate, having obtained permission from Guido, the lord bishop of Beauvais, to remain there. (50) Guido was a man accomplished in every form of courtly conduct, nobly born, and in outward appearance highly suited to the office he held. After rendering the church of Beauvais many distinguished services, among them founding from its first stone the church of the canons regular of Saint-Quentin, he was accused by those whom he had educated and promoted. They secretly charged him before Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, with simony and other crimes. Because he had not come when summoned, he was sentenced in his absence to deposition. Since he was at Cluny and feared the sentence inflicted upon him, he entered the monastery there.

When he appeared to embrace my mother and my parents, and showed me especially great affection—particularly because he had bestowed upon me every sacrament of blessing except priesthood—my mother’s relatives asked him to allow her to stay for a while in the buildings she owned near the church. He gladly consented. The estate itself is called Castanentum and lies about two miles from our town.

### Guibert’s mother withdraws to Castanentum and builds a small dwelling near the church of Saint-Geremar.

Remaining there, she had resolved to withdraw to the monastery of Flaviacum. (51) After building a small dwelling there near the church, with the help of my aforementioned teacher she finally emerged from the place where she had been staying. She knew that I was completely orphaned and had no support at all on which I could rely. Although there were many relatives and kinsmen, there was no one to care in every respect for a very tender child and attend carefully to the needs of his age. I had no lack of food or clothing, but I was often troubled by the absence of those kinds of care suited to the helplessness of that age, which cannot be administered without women.

Knowing that I was exposed to such neglect, and with your fear and love, O God, hardening her heart, she passed beneath the town in which I lived as she traveled to the aforementioned monastery. She was so torn by the anguish of her heart that merely looking at the castle seemed an intolerable torment. Bitter grief gnawed at her as she considered what she had left there. Clearly, if she had seemed to see her own limbs being torn from her body, she would have recognized—or rather heard herself called—a most impious and cruel woman for having excluded from her heart and left without support such a child, so worthy, as was said, of such affection. For I was held in high esteem not only by our own people but also by foreigners.

And you, good and merciful God, had wondrously hardened that heart, certainly most compassionate in worldly matters, through your sweetness and love, so that it would not be compassionate against itself. Against herself, indeed, she would have softened if, preferring us to her own salvation and neglecting God, she had taken care of worldly affairs for our sake. But “love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6), because the more ardently she loved you, the more securely she seemed to tear away from herself the things she had previously loved.

When she therefore came to that monastery, she found an old woman in the habit of a religious sister. Since the woman displayed a very impressive appearance of religious devotion, my mother compelled her to live with her, showing her a kind of submissive discipleship. I say “compelled,” although the older woman, having experienced her character, had gathered such a companionship most eagerly herself.

She therefore gradually began to imitate the severity of that older woman, to follow a frugal diet, to embrace the poorest dishes, to reject the soft supports of her accustomed bed, and to sleep content with a little linen cloth and straw from grain. Although she still shone with considerable beauty and showed no sign of age, she strove to appear as though she had descended into the bent years of old age, with an old woman’s wrinkles. The hair that fell down, chiefly serving women’s adornment, was repeatedly cut off with shears. Her dark garment, displeasing because of its unusual breadth, appeared patched with countless pieces, together with a little cloak of its natural color (53), and footwear pierced with uncorrectable holes, since inwardly there was One whom she desired to please beneath such an inglorious appearance.

Thus, because she had learned the confession of former sins as the beginning of good works, and because that confession was almost daily renewed, her mind was always occupied with the reckoning of her past deeds: what she had done, thought, and said as a girl entering adulthood, as a married woman, and as a widow, when her zeal had already become more capable. She constantly examined them before the tribunal of reason and brought them, once examined, to the knowledge of the priest—or rather, through the priest, to God.

From this you may understand why you saw that woman praying with such groans and wasting away in such anguish of spirit that, amid her exertions and most dreadful struggles, supplicatory words scarcely ever ceased from her sobs. Under the aforementioned old woman, she learned the seven penitential psalms, not by seeing but by hearing them; yet she meditated on them, so to speak, with relish, chewing them over day and night, so that that song, sounding most sweetly in your ears, O God, was never without sighs and groans.

Whenever gatherings of outsiders greatly disturbed the solitude she cherished—for all who had come to know her, especially noble men and women, spoke most pleasantly with her because she was remarkably witty and temperate—after they had departed, if she had allowed herself to become absorbed in conversation containing anything less than true, anything futile, or anything idle, no one can say what anxieties that produced in her mind until she reached again her customary waters of either remorse or confession.

[Col. 0865B] However great her devotion and concern in such matters, they could bring her mind no confidence or security. She nevertheless always mourned and always asked, with the most pitiful tears, whether she might obtain pardon for her offenses. And you know, O God, how many sins there were; and we are not unaware of them. How perverse, Lord, compared with hers [f., her], is the sum of certain people who neither grieve nor sigh! You know, Lord, to the extent that I was able to measure the state of her thoughts, that I never saw her spirit grow lukewarm either through fear of punishment or through love of you.

## CHAPTER XV

### Guibert indulges his natural inclinations and pleasures.

What more is there to say? As mentioned above, when she had thus renounced the world, I remained alone, without mother, tutor, or teacher. For the man who had raised and taught me so faithfully after my mother, stirred by her example, love, and admonition, had gone to Flaviacum to become a monk.

Having thus obtained a wicked freedom, I began to abuse my authority most intemperately: I laughed at churches, loathed schools, sought the companionship of my lay cousins who were being trained in knightly pursuits, detested the sign of clerical status, promised the remission of crimes, and indulged in sleep, of which formerly only a small allowance had been granted me, until I wasted away from this unaccustomed excess.

Meanwhile, the reputation of my conduct struck my mother’s ears, and, inferring my imminent ruin from what she heard, she almost collapsed, nearly lifeless. The garments I used to wear when going to church, which she herself had prepared in order to encourage me toward the clerical state, I wore for licentiousness, though my age did not even permit such behavior; I imitated older youths in their wantonness and had no regard at all for seriousness or restraint.

### He returns to a better way of life.

Since I was behaving all the more dissolutely—or rather insanely—the more strictly and chastely I had previously lived, my mother, unable to bear what she heard, went to the abbot and obtained from him and the brothers that my teacher should teach me again. The abbot, who had been my grandfather’s ward and was bound to his household by benefaction, readily agreed. Rejoicing at my arrival, he received me kindly and thereafter treated me with still greater kindness and diligence.

I call you to witness, O God who orders all things mercifully, that when I entered the basilica of that monastery and saw the monks sitting together, I conceived from their very appearance such a desire for monastic life that it could not cool. My spirit did not rest until it obtained what it desired. Living with them under the same cloister, observing their whole way of being and their habits, my mind always longing to conform itself to them, I could not help burning, just as a flame grows from wind.

Finally, the abbot of the place daily urged me with repeated prayers to become a monk there. Although I was inflamed with an infinite desire to do so, my tongue could not be loosened to make such a promise despite every kind of pressure from those who urged me. Yet, though it was already difficult for me to remain silent about such an abundance of feeling in my heart, I observed this silence without much trouble as a boy.

### He takes the monastic habit at Flaviacum.

At last I disclosed the matter to my mother. Fearing the fickleness of childhood, she rejected this plan with such reasoning that I greatly regretted having revealed what I was considering. When I told my teacher as well, he drove me away from it even more decisively.

Greatly angered by the refusal of both, I resolved to direct my mind elsewhere. I therefore began to behave as though I had never begun to desire any of this. After postponing the matter from the octave of Pentecost until the Lord’s Nativity, and longing with the most ardent wishes to carry it through, Unable, O Lord, to endure your inward prompting because of reverence for my mother and fear of my teacher, I cast those restraints aside. I went to the abbot, who was burning so greatly for me to become this, yet had been unable to draw any promise from my lips amid all his urging. I threw myself at his feet and begged him, in these very words, with abundant tears, to receive a sinner.

He gladly and favorably granted my request. As soon as possible—that is, the next day—he brought out the garments that were necessary, clothed me while my mother watched and wept from a distance, and ordered alms to be distributed that day.

Meanwhile, my former teacher, because he could no longer teach me on account of the stricter rule, at least saw to it that I was urged to examine the divine books that I was reading. He had me reconsider unfamiliar words with more learned men and compose proses and verses, and, the less care others devoted to educating me, admonished me to work all the harder.

And, O Lord, true light, I fully remember your immeasurable generosity, which you then bestowed upon me. For as soon as, at your invitation, I assumed your habit, a cloud seemed immediately to have been removed from the face of my heart, and those subjects began to enter it in which previously I had wandered blind and astray. Moreover, I was suddenly inspired with such a desire to learn that I longed for this one thing alone and considered myself to be living in vain if I passed a day without some activity of this kind.
