O how often I was thought to be asleep, warming my tender body beneath a little cloth, while my spirit was either constrained by a desire to dictate or was reading beneath a blanket, because I feared the judgment of others.

### He diligently devotes himself to letters, but in order to win human praise.

And you, merciful Jesus, knew that I did this with the intention of seeking praise, so that the honor of the present world might come to me in greater measure. I certainly had friends who, although they advised me to do good, frequently poured praise into my ears, praising my distinction in letters and promising through these things the attainment of high positions and wealth.

Thus they brought hopes, worse than any asp’s egg, to my unwary heart. Since I thought that everything they promised would be fulfilled very quickly, they deceived me with the most vain expectations. What they said would happen in old age, I thought was already approaching me as an adolescent and young man. They pointed out to me the knowledge that, with you as its author, increased day by day, as well as good birth and beauty. But they did not remember that you forbade men to ascend by these steps to your altar, where baseness is customarily revealed. “He who climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1)—that is baseness.

### With what remorse the adolescent was endowed, and how profitably he devoted himself to reading.

Yet, in these beginnings of mine, inspired by you, if I had understood anything else, my soul ought to have been prepared for temptation. In truth, at that time I understood things somewhat foolishly. Although I experienced very childish impulses of joy and anger, would that I had then feared your judgment, O Lord, and abhorred even the greatest sins as I now abhor the smallest and almost nonexistent ones!

I certainly imitated, and with the greatest eagerness, those whom I saw weeping over their own offenses; and everything that came from you was most pleasing to my sight and hearing. Whereas now in the Scriptures I seek ostentation and words—or rather I regard the infamous sayings of the pagans themselves as mere chatter—then I demanded from them tears and the causes of sorrow. Whenever, in reading itself, I encountered nothing contemplative or capable of producing remorse, I did not think I had read at all. In my conscious ignorance, I acted in this way.

### Frightful apparitions torment him greatly.

But that ancient enemy, who has learned through the long duration of his existence to adapt himself to the conditions of souls and the qualities of ages—in short, he prepared new battles for me according to the measure of my mind and little body. For by frequently bringing before the eyes of my mind in dreams images of dead men, especially those whom I had seen slain by swords or by some other form of destruction, or whom I had heard had died, he terrified my spirit, released in sleep, with such apparitions that at night, unless the vigilance of my aforementioned teacher protected me, I could neither remain confined to my bed nor refrain from shouting; indeed, I could scarcely control my senses.

Although this affliction may seem childish and ridiculous to some who have not experienced it, among those who suffer from it it is regarded as a calamity of such magnitude that the fear itself—which most people consider foolish—cannot be moderated by any method or counsel. Even when the sufferer himself makes light of what he suffers, no authority can prevent the spirit, once it has been even slightly immersed in sleep, from recoiling at terrifying visions. Indeed, a mind made restless by fear is greatly afraid to return to sleep.

For this affliction, company and solitude are equally ineffective: company does not prevent the fear, while solitary living either produces what is customary to a greater degree or produces it just as strongly.

### A terrifying vision.

At that time, O Lord God, I was very different from the state in which I now live. I was then living under profound reverence for your law and an infinite hatred of every sin, eagerly absorbing whatever could be said, heard, and known concerning you. I know, heavenly Father, that the devil was fiercely provoked by such studies in a child and that he was later to be appeased by my abandonment of all pious fervor.

One night, therefore, I awoke in such miserable anxiety that, as I think, it was winter. I remained in my little bed and, because a nearby lamp cast a very bright light, believed myself to be safer. Suddenly, and not far away above me, as I thought, a cry arose in the dead of night from many voices. It was a sound without words, [f., but] produced solely by the force of distress.

Immediately, as though the temples of my head had been shaken into sleep, I was snatched away from my senses, and I seemed to see someone dead—someone whom a certain person was proclaiming to have died in the baths. Terrified by this image, I leapt up and shouted. At the very first movement, when I looked around, I saw that the lamp had gone out. Through the darkness of the roaring shadow I plainly saw a demon standing nearby in its own form.

At the sight, so utterly terrifying, I would almost have been driven mad had the skill of my teacher, who frequently kept watch to control these terrors, not restored me when I was disturbed and out of my mind.

### The demon rages more violently against recent converts.

Nor was it hidden from me, O my God, even in the tenderness of childhood, that the zeal of good intention in which my spirit then burned greatly provoked the devil, the author of my wickedness. And, O merciful God, what victories and what crowns in exchange for those victories would I have deserved today if I had stood firm without wavering in that combat!

From many reports of events I have heard, I have also learned that demons are more violently enraged against recent converts, or against those who are constantly striving toward such a purpose. I remember that in the time of Guido, bishop of Beauvais, whom I mentioned above, there was among his household a certain young man who had been trained in knightly pursuits. The bishop favored him especially, almost more than his other companions.

When the young man was bitterly repentant of his wickedness and was attempting by every means to escape from worldly life, he was tormented most sharply by this new change in his condition. One night, while he was sleeping in the bishop’s chamber, a very religious man named Ivo, a native, I believe, of Saint-Quentin, highly distinguished in letters and almost even more distinguished in eloquence, a Cluniac monk who had long held the office of prior there under the abbot of blessed memory, Hugh, was resting in the same place with several others equally noble in holy life, while the bishop was present.

A certain man from among the leading men of a neighboring town, very courtly and prudent, remained awake while everyone else slept in the profound silence of night. As he considered whatever occupied his thoughts and looked this way and that, behold, a demon appeared to the man in the form of a nobleman, with a tiny head and swollen shoulders. It pretended to walk slowly through the chamber, looking carefully at each bed in turn.

When the false demon approached the bed of the young man whom I mentioned, and whom the bishop greatly favored, it stopped. Turning its gaze toward the sleeper, it said:

“This anxious man torments me more grievously than all these who are sleeping here.”

After saying this, it made its way toward the latrine door and withdrew into it.

The man who was observing this was so heavily oppressed while he watched that he became completely incapable of speech or movement. Once the adversary had departed, his ability to do both returned to him. In the morning he related the vision to the more sensible people and, asking them about the condition and disposition of that young man, discovered that his spirit was more eagerly inclined to undertake holier things.

If, then, there is joy in heaven over one sinner who is converted rather than over ninety-nine just persons who do not need repentance (Luke 15:7), there is surely sound faith in saying that the enemies of the human race grieve with the most bitter envy when those who are changing for the better are snatched away from them.

Indeed, just as I later had pestilential developments after good beginnings, so that man who had received testimony from the demon gradually grew lukewarm, cooled, and returned to worldly pursuits. Nevertheless, it is credible how grievously that sudden movement of our good intentions wounded the devil’s heart.

Nor is it surprising that the devil should grieve over the sudden and ineffectual feelings of some penitent, since the superficial humility of that wicked king Ahab turned even divine attention toward him before human attention did. Hence, unless I am mistaken, the Lord said to Elijah: “Have you not seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days” (1 Kings 21:29).

## CHAPTER XVI

### The author frequently turns over in his mind what he left behind in the world.

As my body gradually grew, worldly life also began to tickle my soul, which in its own measure was prurient with desires and appetites. I repeatedly turned over in my mind, almost always returning to the same thoughts, what sort and how great a person I might have become in the world, and I often imagined things much greater than truth would have allowed.

Good God, who cares for all things, you showed these matters to your servant, my mother. Whatever condition my unstable conscience turned toward, whether sound or unsound, the form of a vision followed it—not without your judgment, Lord. Yet although dreams are said to follow many cares, and although this is unquestionably true, these cares were not stirred by the fever of avarice but arose from a genuine striving for inward good.

As soon as an unwelcome vision touched her most devout mind, and since she was extremely subtle and perceptive in interpreting such matters, she immediately summoned me and anxiously asked what I was doing about my studies and what I was considering more secretly within myself. I obeyed her in such a way that I never denied her my full confidence. Whatever I had heard according to the content of her dreams, in which my spirit seemed to be growing slack, I disclosed in an open confession. When she admonished me to correct myself, I immediately promised to do so with sincere feeling.

My God, she announced to me so many times and through so many signs the condition in which I now suffer; and what she had thought had happened or would happen in my first condition, I experience and contemplate daily as being fulfilled in the innermost recesses of my heart.

Even my teacher, when the same unceasing anxiety hung upon his heart concerning me, saw, with you revealing it, the things that were happening at the time and those that would later happen, through many kinds of figures. Thus, by God’s gift, adverse and favorable things were sung by these two men—one for frightening me, the other for comforting me—so that, willingly or unwillingly, I might spare the hidden malignity which, by your miracle, was disclosed only to those who loved me, and might sometimes rejoice in the promise of better hope.

### His fellow monks envy him because of his knowledge. His intellect is sharpened still further.

Whenever I was buffeted by the spirit of listlessness—for I suffered much envy from those who were above and beside me—I desired, with the support of my relatives, to move to other monasteries. Some of our people had once seen me far beneath them in age and letters, power and knowledge. Then, because God alone had given me the desire to learn, kindling it in my senses—the desire that is the key to all knowledge—they perceived that I was becoming their equal or, if it may be said, surpassing them altogether.

Their indignant wickedness therefore blazed against me with such fury that, wearied by frequent disputes and quarrels, I often regretted both having seen and having learned letters. My studies were disturbed by them so greatly, and so many quarrels arose from the very subject of letters through continuous questioning, that they seemed to strive only to make my attention recoil from its task and to impede my intellect.

But just as oil added to a furnace, when it is thought to extinguish the fire, causes a livelier flame to spring up, so, like an oven, the more heavily my skill was pressed by that labor, the more powerfully it was restored by its own heat and driven toward improvement. The questions by which they thought to blunt me supplied my understanding with great sharpness; the difficulties of their objections, through the frequent consideration of my conjectures and the handling of various books, produced in me a multiplicity of interpretations and an effective ability to respond.

Thus, although I was grievously hated by them out of envy, you know, Lord, how little or not at all I envied them for such things. Since they could not brand me with a disgraceful mark according to their desire, they everywhere gnawed at me by asserting that I was proud of my little bit of knowledge.

### He considers changing monasteries.

Amid these vexations, which I endured with the greatest difficulty, although such pressures produced abundant benefits, my weary spirit sometimes languished under an infinite torture of thoughts. With a fearful heart and often deprived of the powers of reason, I considered what benefit adversity offered. Yet I had most willingly resolved to seek a transfer, as carnal weakness suggested.

When I had set my plan in motion, intending to leave—not so much with the willing permission of my abbot as at the urging and insistence of my relatives—my mother’s consent was also present, since she believed that this would be done with a pious intention. The place to which I wished to go was said to be highly religious. She, who had witnessed both my evils and my virtues, was then shown the following vision.

### In a vision, the Blessed Virgin shows the mother her son under her protection.

She seemed to be in the church of that monastery, namely Flaviacum [al., Flaviacensis], which is called that of Blessed Geremar. When she looked inside, she saw it utterly deserted and abandoned. The monks were not only divided and covered with excessively misshapen wrappings of faith, but all alike were diminished to the height of a cubit, like those whom the common people call dwarfs.

But since “where the treasure is, there is the heart,” and where the gaze rests, there love is also found, when she anxiously directed her eyes toward me, she saw that I was not raised above the others by any better condition, nor covered by any more honorable attire.

As she grieved over the plight of me and of such a church, behold, a woman of infinite beauty and majesty proceeded through the middle of the basilica as far as the altar. A young woman followed her, whose appearance seemed very suitable for the service of the one whom she followed.

Since my mother was extremely curious to know who the lady was, she was told that she was the Lady of Chartres. Immediately understanding what this meant, she recognized the Blessed Mother of God, whose name and relics are venerated there by almost the entire Latin world. When she reached the altar, she bent her knees in prayer; the noble attendant who seemed to enter after her did the same behind her.

Then, rising and extending her hand with something like great displeasure, she said:

“I founded this church. How could I permit it to be abandoned?”

Then, turning toward me her serene eye, the banner of her compassion, and her illustrious right hand, she said:

“I brought this man here and made him a monk. I will in no way permit him to be taken away from here.”

The aforementioned attendant confirmed these same words after her in the same manner.

That powerful woman had spoken, and, more quickly than the word itself, all the desolation and devastation was completely repaired. Everything appeared as it had at first, and, by the power of the one who commanded, that distorted shortness of stature—not only of the others but also of me—was corrected according to the rule.

When my prudent mother related the course of this vision to me, I received such words with profound remorse and tears. I restrained the freedom of my wandering thoughts under the terms of so desirable a dream so completely that I was no longer drawn by the purpose of any other monastery.

[Col. 0872A] ### The Blessed Virgin also appears to Guibert in a dream.

These and similar things, O Lord, offered by the heavenly Mother of the Sovereign, give me an occasion to return to you amid horror at my sins and amid the innumerable apostasies by which I have departed from your love and service. They give me cause to return to you while she prays for me from her heart, assuring me that the vast bosom of your mercies cannot be closed by any burden of my crimes.

I also always remember, heavenly Lady, that when, as a child, I was aspiring to assume this habit, I was one night in a vision in the church bearing your name. It seemed to me that two demons were carrying me away from her. When they had lifted me to the height of the basilica, they fled and left me untouched within the bounds of that same church.

I often recall this when I contemplate my incorrigibility. And when I repeat the same sins, or rather heap worse sins upon the worst, I return to you, most merciful Lady—not through an abuse of excessive hope or some small confidence, but solely to avoid the danger of despair.

Although I always fall through the impulse of weakness, not through obstinate pride, I nevertheless in no way abandon hope of correction. “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV, 16). If seven is solemnly used as a number signifying totality, then however a person may fall through sinning, provided he has the intention of rising again to righteousness, although he slips through carnality, if he applies the sorrow proper to one who repents, he by no means deprives himself of the name of righteous. For why is it cried out to God that he deliver us from our necessities (Ps. XXIV, 17), unless it is because, whether we wish it or not, the corruption of nature condemns us to the service of sin? “I see,” he says, “the law of sin which is in my members leading me captive; for I do not do the good that I desire, but the evil that I do not desire, that I do” (Rom. VII, 23). There is, however, a depth of certain evils into which, when the wicked has come, he despises them (Prov. XVIII, 3); yet concerning certain other depths one cries out to God, nor does the petitioner doubt that his voice will be heard. There is indeed a contempt born of the excess of sin, which can be that depth “in which there is no substance” (Ps. LXVIII, 3), a misery in which one cannot remain; finally, there is a depth from which Jeremiah is drawn by the binding of rags (Jer. XXVIII, 11), which, although [Note: [Col. 0871D] Something is missing.]. Nevertheless, it has a bottom: for although the mind may be sunk in enormous sins, it still has some such obstacle of reason that it is not carried through immeasurable gulfs without any reflection upon its entire iniquity.

## CHAPTER XVII

### Guibert takes excessive delight in poetry.

Meanwhile, when I had plunged my mind beyond all measure into the practice of composing verse, so that I set aside the serious contents of the whole divine page for such ridiculous vanity, my frivolity had already led me to the point of attempting Ovidian sayings and Bucolic verses, and of pursuing amorous trifles in patterned arrangements and interwoven letters. My mind, therefore, having forgotten the rigor it owed and having cast aside the modesty of my monastic profession, was enticed by such blandishments of this poisonous license, weighing only whether what was spoken in courtly fashion could be attributed to some poet; but it did not at all consider how greatly the purpose of the sacred order was being harmed by the industry that was being sought from it. I was indeed carried away by love or pleasure on both sides [perhaps *deest forte amore, vel voluptate*], being ensnared not only by the sweet words that I had received from poets [Col. 0873B], but also by the wantonness that I myself had poured forth; indeed, through repeatedly turning over these and similar things, I was at times held by an immoderate titillation of my flesh. Since my changeable mind, unaccustomed to every kind of severity, was being worn down by these things, no sound could proceed from my lips other than the one that thought had suggested.

### He produces obscene things in writing and speech; this is divinely revealed to his master.

It then happened that, as my inward madness boiled over, I slipped into certain obscene expressions and kept repeating some little writings that had little regard for seriousness and moderation—or rather, that knew nothing of propriety at all. When these had come to the knowledge of the aforesaid master, and he bore them very grievously, it happened that, in the aggravation [Col. 0873C] of his disgust, he fell asleep. While he slept, a vision of this kind came upon him. An elder of most beautiful gray hair—or rather, if I dare say so, he himself who at the beginning had led me to that man and had promised that his love would always be present to me—appeared to him and said with the utmost severity:

“I want you to give me an account of the writings that have been produced; but the hand that wrote those writings is not the hand of the one who wrote them.”

When this had been reported to me by my master, he and I alike formed a similar interpretation of the substance of the dream. We groaned with joy under your hope, O Lord: on the one hand, seeing your judgment in such a fatherly correction; on the other, from the meaning of the vision, expecting that some pious change would come upon my frivolities. For when the hand that had written the writings is said not to belong to the one who wrote them, it plainly and undoubtedly signifies that he will not remain in that shameful action of his. The hand had been mine, but it is no longer so, as we read: “Turn the ungodly, and they shall not be” (Prov. XII, 7), since the hand that had belonged to me in the practice of vice, once devoted to the pursuit of virtue, lost all efficacy in that most disgraceful ownership.

Yet you know, O Lord, and I confess, that at that time I did not act with greater restraint either through fear of you, through my own shame, or through reverence for this sacred vision. That irreverence was within me, and I did not at all restrain myself from the scurrilities of my foolish writings. For while I secretly composed those poems, and dared to reveal them to no one—or scarcely to anyone like myself—I nevertheless often recited them to those whom I could, under a false author’s name, and rejoiced when my companions in desire praised them. I thought it wholly inappropriate to confess that they were mine; and since they brought their author no benefit of praise, there remained only the fruit—or rather the disgrace—of rejoicing in sin.

But these things, Father, you punished when you wished. For misfortunes arose against me on account of such work; you surrounded my wandering mind with many adversities and pressed me down with bodily illness. Thus the sword reached the soul, when affliction touched the understanding.

### He reads the writings of Blessed Gregory in order to attain understanding of Holy Scripture; under Blessed Anselm he learns how to interpret them.

When the punishment of sin had consequently given understanding to my hearing, only then, with the sluggishness of useless study wasting away, although I was still impatient of leisure, did I reach more profitable exercises. As if compelled by necessity, I rejected my fantasies, received spirituality, and began—though late—to long for what many good teachers had often offered me: namely, to attend to the commentaries on Scripture, to wear down more frequently the sayings of Gregory, in which the keys of this art are chiefly found, and, according to the rules of the ancient authors, to touch upon prophetic or evangelical words in an allegorical, moral, or even anagogical sense.

In this I had as my chief inciter Anselm, abbot of Bec and later archbishop of Canterbury, from the regions beyond the Alps, born in the region of Aosta [Col. 0874C], a man incomparable in learning and most holy in life. While he was still serving as prior of the aforementioned monastery, he admitted me to his acquaintance. Although I was still quite a boy and placed at the utmost tenderness of both age and understanding, he resolved with great purpose to teach me how to conduct my inner man and how, concerning the governance of my little body, to consult the rights of reason. Both before he became abbot and while he was abbot, whenever he came to the monastery of Flavigny, where I was, out of affection for his religious life and teaching, he bestowed the benefits of instruction upon me so assiduously and labored at it with such persistence that I seemed to be the sole reason for his one and singular visit and frequent attendance among us.

[Col. 0874D] Teaching me, then, to distinguish the mind in a threefold or fourfold manner, and to treat all the relations of the inner mystery under feeling, under will, under reason, and under understanding, he showed that the first two—which many people and I myself had thought were resolved into definite divisions—were not the same, although, when the fourth or third was added, it is readily established by his assertions that they immediately became the same. When he had discussed certain Gospel chapters with me concerning this understanding, and had first explained most clearly the difference between willing and being affected—although it was evident that he had learned these matters not from himself but from certain neighboring volumes that treated them less plainly—I afterward began to imitate his meanings in similar commentaries as best I could, and to scrutinize throughout the Scriptures, with great keenness of mind, whatever pleased these moral senses [Col. 0875A].

### At the command of his abbot, Guibert delivers a sermon in an external monastery.

It therefore happened that I came with one of my abbots to a certain monastery in our region. When I suggested to him, as to a man of the highest religious character, that he should come to the chapter meeting and preach a sermon there, he transferred to me what had been requested of him and entreated and ordered me to perform his duty in this matter.

The feast day of Mary Magdalene was being celebrated there on that day. Accordingly, taking the subject of the sermon from the Book of Wisdom, I confined myself to the one saying alone that had been requested for the treatment: “Wisdom, namely, overcomes wickedness, reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII, 1). When I had explained this with whatever eloquence I could, and had pleased the hearers because of the appropriateness of the words, the prior of that church, who was very devoted to sacred letters on account of his intellectual ability, familiarly asked me to write it out for him, so that he might have material from which to draw any sermon.

Since I knew that my abbot, in whose presence I had said it, would take my writing badly, I approached the man cautiously. I begged him, on behalf of that man whom he professed to love, to grant what I requested, speaking from the side, as if from a [lacuna] of a friend, and as if I were less devoted to such matters. Suspecting that I would say something very brief, he agreed; and when I had snatched the word from his mouth, I began to work at what I had proposed.

### He publishes a treatise on how a sermon ought to be delivered and a commentary on Genesis; the abbot takes this badly.

My plan was to undertake a moral commentary on the beginnings of Genesis, namely the Hexameron. I prefixed to this commentary a fairly modest treatise on how a sermon ought to be delivered. After this preface, I poured out an exposition of the works of the six days in the tropological sense, though in language that was admittedly too forceful, setting down whatever suited my intellect. When my abbot first saw a chapter of that sacred history being annotated, he regarded it with an unhealthy gaze. After repeatedly admonishing me to bring those writings to an end, and seeing that such beginnings presented nothing but thorns to his eyes, I completed the whole work secretly, taking precautions against the presence not only of him but also of everyone who might report it to him.

For I inserted these and other little works (57) into pages by dictating and writing them, without having them impressed upon tablets, and at the same time commenting on what had to be written. Thus, during the time of that abbot, my studies remained entirely hidden in silence. When he departed, I found an opportunity while that place was without a shepherd; at last I set to work and completed the short work. Comprising it in ten books, I pursued the moral trope throughout according to the four aforesaid movements of the inner man, so that, with the order of the expressions completely changed, the beginnings were continued through to the end. I do not know whether I benefited anyone by this little work, but I do not doubt that it pleased many highly educated people greatly. This, however, is certain: it afforded me no small advantage, insofar as it freed me, a servant of vices, from idleness.

### He composes a little book on various sayings of the Gospels and the prophets; hence he devoted himself not to the allegorical but to the moral sense.

Meanwhile I wrote a little chapter-book on various sayings from the Gospels and the prophetic books, inserting some material from the Book of Numbers, Joshua, and Judges. I postpone bringing it to an end until the present, because, once I have completed what I currently possess, I intend, if life accompanies me, to exercise myself several times in similar works, with God’s prompting. In most of these I followed the tropology, and in a few the allegory, employing the same method that I had used in Genesis.

In Genesis, moreover, I devoted myself chiefly to morality—not because, if I had labored equally on the allegorical sense, there would have been no meanings to discover [Col. 0876B], but because, in my judgment, moral meanings were sufficiently more useful at this time than allegorical ones, while faith from God remained intact, the morals of nearly everyone had been overthrown by manifold vice, and because it had not been within my license or desire to extend the work to immeasurable length.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Guibert again turns his discourse to his mother’s deeds.

My mother, therefore, having admired my good successes in learning, was extremely anxious about the excesses of slippery youth that she feared. Hence she very earnestly asked me to become her imitator. Although God had bestowed such beauty upon her, she so set aside everything that was praised in herself as though she had known herself to be in no way beautiful; she so cultivated widowhood as though she had always detested and been unable to endure the obligations of a married bed.

Yet you know, O Lord, what faith and what love she showed even to her deceased husband, how she unceasingly persevered in daily sacrifices, prayers, and tears, and in no small almsgiving for the soul of one whom she knew to be hindered by sins and therefore in need of release. As a result, by the wondrous dispensation of God, it came about that through very frequent visions the sufferings he endured in his purgation were shown to her through the most patient representations.

There is no doubt that such kinds of visions come from God. For when no false security is offered through an assumed beauty of light, but incentives to prayer and almsgiving are supplied through the presentation of pain and punishments; when remedies of divine service are openly sought from the dead—or rather, from angels who care for the faithful dead—it is sufficient proof that these things occur through God, since demons never seek anything that will contribute to anyone’s salvation. Thus the anxious mind of that good woman was warmed again by these signs and constantly kindled, through the portent of inward torments, to intercede for the husband who had once been hers.

### Guibert’s father was named Evrard; she sees him in a vision.

Among other things, therefore, one night, on Sunday after matins, in summertime, when she had laid her limbs down to sleep upon a very narrow bench, she soon began to sink into sleep, and it seemed to her in a perceptible way that her own soul was leaving her body. When she was being led as if through a kind of portico, she finally emerged from it and began to approach the mouth of a certain well. When she had come close to it, behold, men sprang out of the gulf of that pit in a ghostly form. Their hair seemed eaten away by moths; they wanted to seize her with their hands and drag her inside.

And behold, a voice burst forth from behind the trembling woman, who was miserably distressed at their attack, saying to them: “Do not touch her.” Compelled by the forbidding voice, they sprang back into the well.

As she proceeded through the portico—something that had escaped me—she asked God only this: when she felt that she had left the body, that she might be allowed to return to it. Freed, therefore, from the inhabitants of the well, when she had stood opposite its rim, she suddenly saw my father standing before her in the form in which he had existed as a young man [Col. 0877B]. When she gazed at him and humbly asked whether he was called Evrard—for it had once been established that he was so called—he denied it.

Nor is it surprising if the spirit refused to be designated by the name that the man had once borne; a spirit ought to answer another spirit with nothing except what accords with spirituality. It is very ridiculous to believe that spirits possess mutual knowledge through names; otherwise, in the future age, knowledge of anyone except our own people would be rare. Spirits plainly do not need names, for their entire vision—or rather, their knowledge through vision—is from within.

When he had denied that he was called by this name, although she nevertheless perceived that he was none other than he, she afterward asked where he lived. He indicated to her, as if it were a street situated not far from that place, that he lived there. She also asked how he was. Then, baring his arm and side, he showed both of them to be so lacerated and intersected by so many wounds that great horror and a disturbance of the viscera followed in the one who looked upon him.

A child’s form was also present, making such loud cries that it caused great distress to her, who was observing it. Moved by its cries, she said to him: “How, Lord, can you endure such great wailing from this infant?”

“Whether I wish to or not,” he said, “I endure it.”

The wailing of this infant and the cutting of the arm and side [Note: [Col. 0877D] A word is missing.] expressed this meaning: when my father, because of the misconduct of certain people, had been excluded from a legitimate relationship with my mother in his first youth, some evil counselors approached his youthful mind. To test whether he could have intercourse with other women, they advised him with the most wicked persuasion. He, obeying them in youthful fashion, attempted an illicit intercourse and fathered a child by some little woman, who soon afterward died without baptism.

Thus, in the cutting of the side there was the corruption of social faith; in the cries, the destruction of the child wrongly procured [perhaps *procreati*, “begotten”]. Such, O inexhaustible Piety, were your retributions in the soul of your sinner, yet one who lived by faith. But let us return to the order of the vision.

When she had asked him whether prayer, almsgiving, or some sacrifice brought him any assistance—for she was conscious that she frequently performed these things on his behalf—and he had nodded in assent, he added: “But among you there lives a certain Leodegardis.” My mother understood that he had named her with the intention that she herself should ask Leodegardis whether she remembered him.

The aforementioned Leodegardis was a woman of the poorest spirit, who lived simply for God without the customs of the world. Meanwhile, having ended her conversation with my father, she looked toward the well, over which there was a plank. Upon the plank she saw a certain mounted man named Rainald, a man of no small standing among his own people, who on that very day—which, as I said, was Sunday—had been treacherously killed by his fellow townsmen at Balvaci after dinner.

He was therefore upon the same plank, bending both knees and lowering his neck, and, having gathered a heap of material, was kindling fire by blowing with puffing cheeks [Col. 0878B]. This was seen in the morning, and he himself died at midday, destined to come to the fires that he had kindled for himself by his merits.

She also saw upon the aforesaid plank someone who was helping him, but who afterward went far away: my brother, swearing by the dreadful sacraments of the divine Body and Blood. Nothing else can better be understood in this than that, by perjuring himself and invoking both God’s holy name and his sacred mysteries over a vain matter, he had earned these places and punishments.

In the same sequence of the vision she also saw that old woman whom we mentioned above at the beginning of her conversion, when she lived with my mother—a woman plainly always afflicted on the surface of her body by many crosses, but, as was said, less cautious in resisting the appetite for empty glory. This woman, I say, she saw being carried by two exceedingly black spirits, together with her shadowy form [Col. 0878C].

While that old woman was alive and the two lived together, they had sometimes spoken about the state of souls and the outcome of their deaths, and had mutually agreed that whichever of them died first would, by God’s grace, reveal to the survivor the condition of her state, whether good or bad, by appearing to her. They also confirmed this by prayer, earnestly beseeching God that, after the death of either, the other might be permitted to disclose the nature of her fortune or misfortune through a revelation in some vision.

The old woman herself, while dying, had seen in a vision that she was stripped of her body and, together with others like her, was approaching a certain church; as they went, she seemed to be carrying a cross upon her shoulders. But when she came to the church with that company, she was forced to remain outside because the doors were barred.

Finally, when she was already dead, she appeared to another person in a state of great stench, to whom she expressed great gratitude because through that person’s prayers she had been freed from the stench and pain. Moreover, while that same woman was dying, she saw a demon standing at the foot of the bed, of dreadful appearance and monstrous enormity, with exceedingly terrible eyes. But she, having adjured him by the divine sacraments with excessive solemnity to withdraw from her in confusion and not demand anything of hers, drove him away by a terrifying adjuration.

My mother, therefore, bringing true things together according to the correspondence of the vision, and reasoning from the immediate oracle concerning the soldier who had just been killed—whom she had foreseen already receiving places of punishment for himself in the underworld—conjectured the infant’s cries, of whose existence she had not been unaware. She was doubtful about none of these matters and devoted herself entirely to providing assistance for my father.

Accordingly, setting similar things against similar things, she took in and undertook to nourish a very young infant who had been deprived of its parents. But the devil, envying the pious intention and no less faithful action, although the child behaved most peacefully throughout the days, alternately playing and sleeping, stirred my mother and all her household at night with such senseless wailing and crying that scarcely anyone could have slept in the same cell.

I certainly heard from her about nurses who had been burdened with payment and who, through successive nights, did not cease to rock the child’s rattle—not by their own will, but at the prompting of the inner instigator. Yet no feminine cleverness could do anything to overthrow the one who was driving them [Col. 0879B].

The pious woman was tormented by immeasurable grief, since amid so many cries no effort could soothe her anxious hours at night, nor could sleep settle upon her head, utterly harassed and exhausted, when both the child’s externally provoked frenzy and the enemy, disturbing everything, were present.

And although she passed such nights sleepless, she was nevertheless never found inactive with regard to the divine offices performed at night. Because she knew that these troubles were purifying troubles for the man whose troubles she had seen in the vision, she endured them willingly. By this means, as it seemed to her—and as is true—she herself alleviated the anguish of the one who suffered by sharing his suffering.

She nevertheless never expelled the child from the house on that account, nor was she ever less attentive to him. Rather, she chose to endure with even greater equanimity whatever inconvenience arose from him, the more keenly she perceived that the devil had flared up against her in order to destroy this undertaking; for the greater the devil’s incentive had proved to be in provoking the child, the less she doubted that his evil hearings against her husband’s soul were being restrained.

## CHAPTER XIX

### Guibert’s friends attempt to draw him toward dignities.

Many other things, Lord God, you showed to your servant; and to my master, whom you had specially granted to me, you showed certain things that would be attributed to boastfulness if I wrote about them—things in which the good hope shines that I await even today under your most indulgent Mother, sweet Jesus, into whose care I was cast from the womb. Some things were shown to them while I was still almost a child, things that I wonderfully experience as I have now matured in age.

At last the heat of my desires flared up. Since you had inserted into my breast the tinder of every kind of little learning, and had granted me a person sufficiently suitable for the world, together with a moderately good birth, my own mind and certain other close associates—though not good ones in this respect—began wrongly to suggest to me that it would be fitting for me to advance in this world through promotion to some honor.

But I recognize, Lord, that in your law you had forbidden one to ascend by steps to your altar; for you had taught that in this way the disgrace of some sacred leader could be revealed. Those who have reached mystical rule through the excrement of outward excellence fall more shamefully from it because they have attempted things above themselves, not things equal to them, in their extraordinary ambitions.

While I was seeking such heights through the efforts of my parents, rumors of attaining them repeatedly disturbed my ears. Many flattered me and, wishing factionally to test the quality of my mind so that they might complete their service of informing those who wickedly rivaled me, or thinking that they would please me by my pursuit of honor, said that my advantages would be useful to their profit and therefore always sought better returns from my prospects.

### He rejects ecclesiastical dignities.

But I, as you know, my Creator, through your sole prompting and your sole inspiration, became strong enough to disdain asking any man—or giving conversation or consent to any man who was arranging it for me—for the ecclesiastical honor that belongs to you alone. And you know, Lord, that in this matter alone I neither want nor have ever wanted anything except what I may receive or may have received from you.

For I want you yourself to make me in this as in other things, not for me to make myself. Otherwise, Israel would not rightly rejoice in him who made it (Ps. CXLIX, 2).

My God, by how many adversities and by how many envies was I then oppressed! Hence my mind secretly burned toward what was being suggested to me outwardly, as though toward an escape from temptation. But although this ambition boiled within me, its heat never prevailed so far as to pass over into my tongue. Although I was troubled, I did not speak.

You know, Jesus, that once, when sin impeded me, I instructed someone who was arranging such things—but who was carrying them out without my prompting—to do more quickly what he was doing. You know, I say, how grievously I bore having said this. For although I had often been able to slip and speak impiously in other matters [perhaps *protulerim*, “had spoken”], I nevertheless always feared being a buyer—or rather, a betrayer—of the doves.

And certainly, although there is one dove, among those very people there are seats, not one seat. Whatever is divided in God and in the Church is plainly not from the one who suffers division in it: “That they may be one, as we are one” (John XVII, 12); and: “Although there are divisions of graces, it is nevertheless the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII, 4, 11); and what follows: “The throne of God,” not “thrones,” “is for ever and ever” (Heb. I, 8). And: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your seat” (Ps. CXXXI, 11; Acts II, 30). Therefore, what is one with God is made diverse through the purpose of human perversity.

Considering these things, and not being ignorant of the unity of head and body, I wanted to usurp nothing in the body, because whatever intrudes itself from elsewhere has certainly not consented to the head; and what the head does not know, what is not reckoned as being in the body, is evidently recognized by no one as such.

For those who will say, “Did we not prophesy in your name and cast out demons?” (Matt. VII, 22) are apostates, if I may put it so, not members; and therefore they hear, “I do not know you” (ibid., 23), as if he were saying: “I do not feel them to be in me, because they do not live from me.”

A hope, however frivolous, therefore relieved my weariness, and I prayed to you, God, that if ever what was being discussed concerning me should come to pass, it might happen through you alone as its author. It wearied me that I heard from others that these things were being sought for me from my parents, while others were being chosen through the pure efficacy of God, with no one arranging it carnally.

For my parents themselves, providing in such matters not so much for me as for themselves, did not discuss this business with me at all; plainly, they did not want to provoke my youthful mind concerning it. At last, while God wished me to be deceived for a longer time [perhaps “did not wish”], he inspired my agents to migrate elsewhere for the salvation of their souls, and it became necessary for the monks of certain abbeys who had relied upon them in the matter of my election to turn elsewhere.

[Col. 0881B] Thanks be to you, God, because then my childish ambition withered away completely, and I no longer desired to sigh after any earthly dignity. For at that time, Father, you scourged me, afflicted me as the corrector of my desires and frivolities, and brought me back to knowledge, so that you confined me within myself. My mind, previously wandering, no longer flew off anywhere, but deep within aspired only to humility and sincerity of thought.

Then, for the first time, I had begun, Lord, to experience and draw myself into that good solitude of the mind in which you customarily dwell, and to Mary, Mother of the heavenly kingdom, the Mother of God, my sole refuge in every necessity, I began to offer the embrace of all my inward fervor. I delighted most affectionately in being insignificant; I utterly dreaded both higher rank and the shadow of a great name in the world.

Then for the first time, through that inward savor, I learned what the unity of the will was, what its purity was, and what the undistracted purpose of perpetual poverty had been. What shall I say, Lord, of how fleeting this paradise was, how small the repose, how brief and uncertain the experience of such great sweetness?

### Against his will he is elected abbot of Nogent.

I had scarcely tasted such things for a few months, scarcely had your good Spirit, which had led me into a straight land (Ps. CXLII, 12), rested for a little while upon my enlightened reason, when suddenly it was as though you said: “When you wished, I wished; now you do not wish and it displeases you; whether you wish it or not, have it.” The election of certain distant people, utterly unknown to me, emerged.

But what kind of election? Let me truly confess myself extraordinary: among all those who were before me, I was judged, under your testimony, O God, to be the dirtier—or rather, the most foul. The electors had been made blind and bleary-eyed by the few letters I had acquired and by the outward veneer of a teacher’s persona, as it was called. Good God, what would they have said if they had then seen my interior? What would they also feel if they recognized what sort of man I now preside over them as?

You know, who foreknew hearts and kidneys, by I know not what judgment you arranged this, how indignant I am, how I dread presiding entirely out of order over men better and more honorable than myself. For you know that I had no desire at all for such a thing; nevertheless, I did not wish to be shamefully rejected. I entreated you from the depths of my heart that I might be freed from what had begun, so that I might neither undertake that burden—which was to be feared and which I dreaded beyond measure—nor, being weak, fail through my refusal.

### His mother grieves over her son’s election.

You were not unaware, my God, how harshly and painfully my mother endured the delay [election], which seemed to others a matter of honor but to her one of intolerable grief. She did not want anything of this kind to happen to me, in which she feared danger for an age still ignorant of such matters, especially since I was utterly unfamiliar with worldly affairs—things that, being once devoted solely to letters, I had taken no care to learn.

Nevertheless, she herself, and nearly everyone who knew me intimately, repeatedly foretold to me that I would not long remain without some kind of advancement. You also know, Lord, with what inward eye she spoke to me of the good and evil that would come upon me if I were promoted, things that I experience even today and that are hidden neither from me nor from others.

She also foresaw through many visions, under the appearance of myself and of others, things destined to occur long afterward. I clearly see some of them happening, and I await the fulfillment of others that have happened no less than those still to come; nevertheless, I think it right deliberately to refrain from adding them here.

God, by what admonitions she warned me to drive desires from my mind! She most certainly promised the misfortunes of adversity that I experienced: that youth would always sigh after slipperiness; that wandering minds should be restrained through the various circuits of thought. When she argued about such things, you would have judged her not to be an unlearned woman, as she was, but a most eloquent bishop.

The monastery over whose governance I was elected is called Nogent, and it lies on the boundary of the diocese of Laon, adjoining it so closely that a moderate river—though at times stagnant—called the Eagle separates the aforesaid territory from that of Soissons. Concerning its antiquities, if God gives assistance, we hope to treat in this work.

## CHAPTER XX

### Various events that occurred in the monastery of Flavigny. The prior Suggerius is seized with madness after seeing a demon.

But since we have said that in this church of Flavigny we were gathered under God the Father and under the patronage of blessed Geremarus, founder of that place, it is fitting that we commit to memory certain things that we heard and saw happening there.

After the aforesaid church had been restored from the devastation of the Danes, a certain monk named Suggerius, who held the office of prior and conducted himself with good morals, lay suffering from a mortal illness. If I am not mistaken, he was the brother of that old woman who, at the beginning of her conversion, lived with my mother.

The devil stood beside him as he lay there, holding a book in his hand and saying: “Take this and read; Jupiter sends it to you.” When he recoiled upon hearing that execrable name, the devil added: “Do you love this house?”

“I love it,” he said.

And he said: “Know that, after some time, it will be entirely disordered, with all the rigor of religious observance removed.”

When the monk had overwhelmed the speaking Satan with fitting rebukes, the enemy who had appeared departed; but the monk, after reporting what he had seen, was turned into madness, so that he had to be bound in chains. Before he expired, however, he returned to his right mind and died making a good confession.

Since we know that the devil is a liar, let us believe that this was said by his father, out of his customary envy; otherwise, may God avert its becoming true! For afterward the affairs of the church advanced well, and to this day they continue to advance well.

## CHAPTER XXI
## What happened to a monk who had hidden money without the abbot’s knowledge

I saw there, in our own time, a former soldier who had become a monk, simple in character, as was thought, and advanced in age, whom his abbot had sent to a certain cell of the church in the village of Vulcassinus, since he was a native of that place. With the permission of his prior, he proposed to restore an embankment on the public road, which had fallen into disrepair. He therefore completed the work through the gifts of the faithful; when it had been finished, he retained some of the remainder of those donations.

Meanwhile he was seized by a mortal illness, yet he did not reveal in any confession what he was wrongly concealing. He was brought to the monastery of which he was a monk. He confessed neither to the abbot nor to the prior, although the terrible torments inflicted by it—the heralds, so to speak, of death—were already being felt; but he entrusted that quantity of silver to a certain servant who ministered to the sick.

Then, when an untimely affliction of the night was growing, he was carried away from his senses, stretched out on the ground as though dead. We too (58), summoned by the rattling signal, came and fulfilled the psalms, prayers, and rites appropriate for those about to die. This done, we left the man (59), as is monastic custom, laid upon a haircloth and apparently breathing out his life only with difficulty amid his final rattles. No one promised him life; all of us promised only that, since he was already half-dead, he would soon receive the last washing. Nor was there delay: once we had gone, he began to breathe; he summoned the prior—for the abbot was away—and disclosed what he had defrauded and to whom he had entrusted the fraud. He spoke, received absolution from the prior, and shortly afterward expired, his sobs recurring.

The prior at that time was my teacher, of whom I often speak. Behold the Lord’s abundant mercies, because we have not been consumed (Lam. III, 22): he liberates whom he wills from the narrow mouth into the widest expanse. [Col. 0883D]

After the man had been removed from the company of the living, the whole matter concerning the money devolved upon the servant. He had hidden that mass of money in the straw of the cradle of a little daughter of his. But at night, when the infant was being put to bed, behold, demons in the likeness of puppies leapt upon her from the side and from behind. Beating her from every direction and pinching her repeatedly, they drove her to cries and tears. When each of her parents asked what she was crying about, she replied that puppies were eating her.

Then her mother—who had been my mother’s maidservant and at one time her attendant—ran to her own mistress, namely my mother. She reported the red purse that had been deposited with her and added that her child was in danger because of the puppies. My mother said to her: “Know that they are demons, who are amusing themselves over that devilish money and pressing upon her as though recognizing it as their own.”

When the husband learned this, although unwilling and tormented by much distress, he poured out what was being demanded of him—whether by force, secretly, or through entreaty, so to speak—and did not conceal the demonic infestation he was consequently suffering. We have heard that “God has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. VIII, 18); we shall be able to gather the meaning from what follows. And, O wondrous judgments of God! The man of whom we have spoken had spent his entire life in military exercises and in the foulness of prostitutes; whereas the man about whom I am going to speak had indeed been somewhat sluggish, but nothing otherwise dishonorable had become known about him. [Col. 0884B]

This vice of avarice is plainly so pernicious among monks—and, being less natural, so much the more so—that scarcely any crime can be found against which the devil lies in wait so persistently by means of theft.

## CHAPTER XXII

### A monk buried in the fields because of his private funds

Another monk of ours, a priest by rank, to whom no frivolity could be attributed except an eagerness for riding, had received two solidi from a certain noblewoman. Soon afterward, seized by dysentery, he fell ill at Saint-Quentin of Beauvais. When this became known at Flaviacum, he was brought back to his own church at the abbot’s command.

Although he ate a great deal and immediately discharged it indiscriminately, it happened that his abbot, about to depart for somewhere, came to speak with him, fearing that he might die in the abbot’s absence. But when the abbot arrived, the monk had gone to attend to the needs of nature. Since he could not leave, he had placed a tub before himself; when the abbot saw him seated [read: *insidentem*, “seated”] upon it in a horrifyingly disfigured state, the two looked at one another. The abbot was ashamed to address the man in such a place, and the wretched man neither could nor, indeed, wished to confess and be absolved from his crime. The abbot withdrew, and the monk went from the tub to his bed as though to rest. When he had lain down upon it, he was strangled by the devil.

You would have seen his chin and throat horribly fixed to his chest, as though forced down by violent pressure. Thus he died without confession or anointing, and without having made a will concerning that accursed private fund of his. When the corpse was stripped for washing, a purse was found hanging from his shoulder and slipping beneath his armpit.

When the woman who found it discovered it, she dashed the purse furiously to the ground, clapped her hands, and ran to the monks, bringing astonishing news to their ears. It had plainly never been heard of among them that one of their number had died in such a way.

They therefore sent for the abbot, who had already begun dining two miles beyond Beauvais, at one of his estates. Through another messenger who had arrived there, the abbot had already learned that the monk had died, but he knew nothing of the solidi and had said nothing about them. The messenger, therefore, coming on behalf of the brothers who had sent him, asked the abbot what ought to be done: whether the monk might be buried with the others, since he had so miserably separated himself from the community of the rest.

After consulting with prudent men, the abbot ordered that he be given a burial in the fields, excluded from prayers and psalms, and that the money be placed upon his chest. Nevertheless, the brothers’ private prayer for him did not cease; indeed, they persisted in it all the more because they knew how greatly he needed assistance.

As a result of this man’s sudden death, the others became more cautious concerning private funds. Let us hear further how they were scourged on other occasions and for other people.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### A great calamity by thunder and lightning in the church of Flaviacum

Scarcely a few weeks had passed when, on the vigil of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, a small peal of thunder arose and lightning flashed only intermittently, while a cloudy tempestuous sky loomed above. Thus, when we rose in the morning, the signal for Prime had sounded only a very short while before. We gathered in the church with unusual speed and, after a very brief prayer, had said, “O God, come to my assistance.” But when we wished to begin what followed, a thunderous lightning stroke descended and pierced the church in the following manner.

It scattered or burned the cock, the cross, and the dove that were upon the tower; weakened the beam on which these objects rested; and, half-burning and tearing away the shingles fastened with nails, entered through the western window of the tower. It shattered the image of the crucified Lord standing below, striking its head until it fell and piercing its right side, but it did not burn it. It burned and severed the right arm both of the cross and of the image so completely that no one found anything remaining of the whole arm except the thumb of the hand. [Col. 0885C]

### Two monks are struck

Thus, “as soon as the shepherd was struck, the sheep were scattered by wounds and deaths” (Matt. XXVI, 31). To the right, fire slid down through the arch beneath which the struck image stood, and, descending through the cement of the arch, made a forked black streak. Reaching the choir, it struck two monks standing beneath two arches, one on each side, and rendered them lifeless in an instant.

To the left, on the other side, another stroke rushed downward, scraping away the cement coating along the steps, not here and there but as though a stone were rolling through the place. It also struck a monk standing there, although no visible injury appeared either in the two or in this one, except that dust falling from the arch appeared in the overturned eyes of the latter. [Col. 0885D]

It was certainly remarkable that those who died remained sitting, while we, stunned and almost lifeless from the violence of the lightning, fell forward upon one another. Some of us who fell lost all bodily sensation below the waist; others were so badly affected that, fearing death, we immediately anointed them with holy oil. In some, the flame entered the folds of their garments and, burning all the hair and consuming the growth beneath the armpits—which they call *subhirci*, “goatish growths”—made its way out at the extremities by piercing their socks and sandals.

### The face of the image of the Mother of God appears sorrowful

It cannot be said how judicially the heavenly chastisement raged in that moment, through what winding paths it ran here and there, what it injured, what it burned, and what it broke. No one in our France, in his lifetime, had learned of a similar event.

I saw, God is my witness, an hour after these things had happened, the image of the blessed Mother of God, which stood beneath the crucifix, with a face so troubled and so changed from its customary serenity that it seemed entirely altered. Since I did not trust my own observation, I learned that the same thing had been noticed by others as well.

After we had awakened from the stupor caused by that event, and after confession, we began sorrowfully to consider beyond anything that can be expressed by human speech what we had suffered for our sins. We learned, from the expression set by God against our faces and from the examination of our consciences, how justly we had suffered. Immediately we saw the pious Mother’s face turned toward serenity.

The grief and shame that remained among us for some time surpass all belief. [Col. 0886B]

### Again concerning lightning

A few years later, when the memory of this event had almost entirely faded from everyone’s mind, God repeated a similar warning, except that it injured no one.

A peacock had settled at night beside the projecting chimney of a certain chamber, so close that, when it sank into sleep, it pressed its whole body against it. It was the feast of the holy apostle James, and also a Sunday. During the night, when a heavy crash of thunder continued, lightning struck the chimney, demolished whatever projected from the chamber, and left the peacock, which was leaning against it, standing motionless. A little monk sleeping beneath it was not even awakened from sleep; but a certain servant was severely stunned in head and limbs.

In the words of blessed Augustine, God does [not] strike mountains or insensible things without purpose, but so that we may reflect that, when he attacks things that do not sin in this way, he is holding out a great discrimination of judgment against sinners. He offers as an example a nurse who beats the ground with a stick in order to restrain an infant from being troublesome. [Col. 0886C]

### Concerning the conduct of the monks struck by lightning

While speaking of the earlier misfortune, I omitted to discuss the conduct of those three who were killed. Two of them were novices who had scarcely completed eight months in the religious life. One of them, beneath an appearance of seriousness, was less sound inwardly; the other, beneath a lighthearted manner, had nothing excessively detestable within him, so far as we knew.

On the day before they suffered, they had behaved in accordance with the difference I have described. On the morning when these things happened, when the first of them heard the thunder sounding lightly outside, he began to utter ridiculous words, and as soon as he entered the church he received the stroke at which he had laughed.

The third, named Robert, who in the world had been called Columba, was a young man just beginning to grow into manhood. Because of the sincere simplicity he possessed, he was known for complete moral integrity. In ecclesiastical and fraternal service he was so capable and diligent that he was regarded almost every day as the substitute for everyone. He had also attained a good knowledge of grammar.

That morning, at the hour that was harboring destruction there, he had preceded me, as was his custom, in sitting in the cloister while I was rising. He told me that he was oppressed by enormous pains, and by severe pains throughout the rest of his body. From time to time he looked anxiously toward the disturbed air, and from that disturbance he soon died. [Col. 0887A]

Behold: before their downfall, the hearts of those two were exalted, and, as we believe, a more severe sentence was soon to be passed upon them in God’s judgment. But humility preceded glory in the third, and no one doubts that divine exaltation would immediately follow it.

For it was soon revealed to someone that these three would all journey together to Rome, to Saint Peter; but two of them, shadowy and scarcely visible, while the third, clothed in white, alive and agile with his customary keenness, hurried onward.

After several years had passed, when these events had been forgotten and we had grown torpid in security, a third correction occurred. By then I had departed from that church. One morning, when a stormy disturbance was taking place, the monks proceeded to the high altar to sing the litanies. They did not dare remain in the choir where the first lightning strike had occurred. Suddenly a flame from above rushed down and, as those who saw it testified, descending as far as the step of the altar, filled its surrounding space with dense blackness like sulphur.

It blinded a certain priest-monk who was there. Two boys had their heads at the foot of the altar and were lying prostrate. One of them had been converted from Judaism but was faithful from the depths of his heart. The movement lifted them from the altar and carried them some distance away; without their knowing it, it turned their feet toward the altar and their heads from the apse toward the wall.

Lightning entered the chest that stood behind the altar, weakening it in places. It corrupted only the chasuble thought to be the most valuable, although the greater part of the church’s treasure was kept there. The reason for this marvel is as follows.

### The chasuble obtained through sacrilege

The chasuble had been requested by name from the king of the English, a thoroughly illegitimate man and hostile to the churches, who was called Rufus—which he also was. God killed him with an arrow from his own lover while he was hunting. [Note: [Col. 0887D] William II.]

Since he did not wish to empty his own treasuries, he sent a monk responsible for this matter to the abbot of the monastery (60) called Battle, ordering him to give the monk fifteen marks of silver. When the abbot refused, the monastery’s treasure was carried off by royal violence, and soon afterward the same abbot, willing or unwilling, redeemed it for fifteen marks.

Thus the chasuble, sacrilegious—or rather obtained by sacrilegious men—was purchased through such fraud, and composed through no lesser fraud, that its acquisition, purchase, and manufacture all consist in a curse forged together. For after this event, when it was sent in pieces and examined, it was found not to be worth even half its price. At that time much fraud on the part of the buyer was plainly detected in its very manufacture.

Thus, while all the other ornaments remained intact, this one was rightly condemned, although a like punishment appears to have spared its merchant.

Before this event, something of the following kind appeared to a certain monk who carried a biting conscience. The image of the crucified Lord seemed to descend from the cross, with blood dripping from his hands, side, and feet. As he walked through the middle of the choir, he was heard to say: “Unless you confess, you will die.” [Col. 0888A]

The monk awoke horrified at himself. Before he could confess, however, he underwent this danger with all the others. After confessing, he gave a great indication of the justice of the judgment.

Because of the calamity that had so terrified them, perpetual annual fasts and charitable alms (61) were established on the day when these events first occurred. A Mass was established for blessed Mary, and a daily Mass of her own; in addition, a Mass of the Nativity of the Lord was appointed at the altar of Saint Michael every Sunday. But let us hasten now to other matters.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Demons terrify a monk near death who perished by a bad end

That year—or rather, four months after the first event—a certain monk who was a priest, formerly my mother’s chaplain in the world, began to fall easily into illness. To outward appearance he was then religious, but at that time and afterward he was irretrievably devoted to enormous vices, from which no human vigilance could keep him away.

Unexpectedly brought to death within two days, he began to look about him terribly in every direction. When those who knew his condition asked him what he saw, he replied: “A house full of barbarous men.”

When they understood that those who appeared to him were none other than demons threatening him, they began to suggest that he make the sign of the cross and hope in the invocation of the blessed Mother of God. He replied: “I would place hope and trust in her, if these barons were not pressing upon me.”

It is remarkable that he called them “barons,” a word which, according to Greek etymology, signifies “heavy.” And, O how heavily they weighed upon him, since they could no longer be driven away by repentance or any invocation!

Finally they asked what most oppressed him. He replied that he felt as though an enormous drawn-out iron instrument, glowing with flame, were burning through his throat and vital organs.

Although the night was perfectly still, so that not even the slightest breeze could be heard, the windows of the house began to be struck against the walls and repeatedly reverberated, as though because of a crowd of people entering. Two monks watched over him while the others slept in the house. Knowing that such things did not come from anything good, they were overcome with agitation.

Amid the words we have reported, he breathed out his life. He had been devoted to many disgraces, and therefore such a life received such an end. [Col. 0888D]

A grave was being prepared in the cemetery of that church for a deceased monk. The man responsible for the task could not fail to remember that he had made a tomb in that very place. He therefore dug, and when he had gone deeper he found the slab usually placed beneath a sarcophagus. After moving it, he found the grave almost empty, except that he discovered at the feet of the sarcophagus a hood (62)—called in common speech a *chaperon* or *capuchon*—with the head placed inside, and shoes half-filled with hay. This had formerly been done at the time of burial so that the shoes might cling more firmly to the feet. In the entire middle there was nothing.

When some people saw this and reported it to us, we marveled at God’s incomprehensible judgment and at the hidden and subtle ways in which we see such things carried out. The remarkable point in this case is that the head had been left there, while the body had been removed from its place in whatever manner pleased God.

I learned of something similar from the archbishop of blessed memory, Manasses, who died with great fidelity some years ago; I learned it more certainly from the monks of Saint Remigius in the city of Reims.

A certain Artaldus, archbishop of that city, had once been buried at the feet of Saint Remigius. After a very long time, when the grave was opened because the buildings needed to be altered, nothing at all was found there of his body. Only the chasuble among his garments remained. It is clear that it had not decayed together with his body, since it appeared entirely unharmed. Certainly, if his body had rotted there, the decay would have damaged the chasuble.

In these times we see the judgments of God, reported by blessed Gregory, renewed over the corpses of guilty people who, as is established, are improperly buried in holy places.

### A nun who had lived disgracefully and had not repented is seen being tortured after death

In the monastery of virgins established at Caen, which was built by Matilda, queen of the English and wife of William, king of the Normans—formerly count of the Normans, who had conquered the English—there was a nun who had become involved in certain shameful sins. No admonition could induce her to confess.

It happened that she died in this obstinacy and said nothing useful even while dying. One of the sisters was sleeping one night in the little cell where the woman had died. In a dream she saw enormous fires being kindled in the very hearth of the house, with the dead woman placed in the middle, not merely being burned but beaten by two evil spirits, one on each side, with blows from two hammers.

As she watched the great tortures of that wretched woman, she saw a spark fly from the blow of one hammer into the eye of the observer. The nun consequently awoke when the little fire sitting upon her had burned her. Thus it happened that what she had seen in the spirit she suffered in the body, and the injury gave truthful confirmation of the truth of the vision.

## CHAPTER XXV

### The sacristan who had driven away a poor man too harshly is chastised

A certain monk of Flaviacum was named Otmundus. While still a cleric, he had given a great deal to the monastery and eventually gave himself to it as well. Once he had become a monk, he regretted the beginning of his good undertaking and bore with great difficulty what he had done.

Soon, however, chastised by God through bodily illness, he understood and afterward pursued what was closer to salvation. He no longer practiced the sacred order out of necessity but honored it willingly.

He was quick to anger. After becoming sacristan of the church [Note: [Col. 0889D] Or *aeditimus*, as though “one who guards the building”], he harshly drove from the church a poor man who persistently asked him for alms, more severely than he ought to have done.

After this had happened during the day, he went out the following night to open the doors and announce the vigils. Behold, the devil, in the form of the poor man whom he had wrongly expelled the previous day, confronted him, raising a club and rushing at the monk as though to strike him.

He had opened the doors set into the wall between the clergy and the people and was proceeding to unlock the others through which the people entered. Suddenly, with the outer doors barred, the apparition leapt forward from the middle of the basilica at the exit of the inner doors, pretending to strike him.

When the monk, terrified, withdrew, thinking that he was the man whom he had excluded the day before, he eventually came to himself. As he considered that the outer doors were closed, he finally understood that it had been the devil, who by this sign had marked his own work in the form of a man. [Col. 0890A]

### Demons cause distress to a dying man

In winter, when he rose to attend to the needs of nature, he was reluctant to put on his usual clothing and wore only a cowl. During those delays he was afflicted by deadly cold. Not long afterward, brought to death by swelling in his extremities, he bore the very name of death more painfully than was proper.

As he continually cried out to himself—alas!—amid such great anguish, he reached his final hour. He received Communion and, by God’s grace, retained it, for everything else returned by vomiting; he was now struggling to release his spirit.

Meanwhile, as these things first occurred at the beginning of the night, the church custodian, a good man, had gone to bed. Behold, he heard that an innumerable crowd of demons had assembled in the nearby cemetery.

Although he had the mental capacity to perceive these things, he was nevertheless constrained by a certain spiritual power from moving his tongue and body. The demons entered the church, passed before the dying man’s bed, rushed between the choir and the altar, and directed themselves toward the house where the sick man lay.

He felt mentally that these things were happening and prayed to God in spirit to save him from them. He knew that only the cause of death could have compelled so great an army to assemble.

As soon as they reached the cell of the dying man [read: *agonizantis*, “of the dying man”], the brothers who were around him struck the wooden board according to custom, to summon the community. While everyone was gathering, the man immediately expired.
