I have reported this not because I believe that he passed over to that evil side, but because I wish to remind everyone, with me, that “the prince of this world came” to the Son of God, “in whom he had nothing.” And if the devil’s madness came upon him with rapid assaults, how much more certainly does it come upon us [the text reads *ad nos quam potius*; corrected to *potius quam ad nos*, “rather than upon us”], in whom he possesses almost everything. [Col. 0890D]

### A woman who cursed her child to the devil is handed over to him

I saw there a woman who, in a fit of the most savage anger against her little son, cursed him with other maledictions that she hurled at the innocent child. In her wicked speech she even cursed the baptism into which he had been dipped.

Immediately seized by a demon, she began to rave with extreme madness and to speak and do detestable things. She was brought to the church and presented to the brothers. Through prayers and exorcism she was restored to her senses, and from her affliction she learned not to curse the sacraments of the Lord.

### A possessed girl desires the evil conduct of a monk

I likewise saw a little girl possessed by a demon, brought there to the shrine of the confessor Geremar. After she had stayed there for several days, her parents one day dragged her to the altar.

While she stood beside it, she turned her head toward the choir, saw young monks standing behind her, and said: “How beautiful, my God, are these young men! But among them there is one who ought by no means to live with them.”

When we heard this, we were greatly astonished and wondered what her statement referred to. Soon afterward one of them escaped by flight, and, while fleeing, his evil life was exposed by his abandoning the religious life.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Satan admits no one to learn sorcery unless he first renounces his Christian profession

Since we have begun to speak of demons, we think it appropriate to add certain matters by whose example we may be able to avoid both their oracles and the counsels of those who converse with them. They admit no one to learn their magic unless they first strip him of the honor of his entire Christianity through detestable sacrilege.

In a certain noble monastery a monk had been raised from childhood and had acquired some knowledge of grammar. His abbot sent him to an outlying cell of the church. While he was staying there, he fell ill, and, because of his illness, he found an occasion to speak with a certain Jew skilled in medicine.

From their mutual familiarity they took courage and began to reveal their secrets to each other. The monk, curious about evil arts, realized that the Jew knew magic and pressed him insistently. The Jew consented and promised to act as his intermediary before the devil.

A place and a day for the conversation were arranged. At last, through the Jew as mediator, the monk was brought before the devil. He asked to become a participant in this teaching through the devil’s authority.

That wicked master replied that this could in no way happen unless, after denying Christianity, the monk offered him a sacrifice. The monk asked what was most pleasing in a man.

“What is it?”

“You will pour out your semen,” he replied. “When you have spilled it for me, you will first taste what is owed to those who offer sacrifices.”

What a crime! What shame! And the man from whom these things were demanded was a priest. Thus your ancient enemy, Lord, brought this about to the sacrilegious dishonor of your order and your blessed sacrament. Do not be silent, and do not be restrained from vengeance, O God (Ps. LXXXII, 2).

What shall I say? How shall I say it? The unhappy man did what was demanded, you who—would that only for a time!—had abandoned him. Thus, with a horrible libation, he made a profession upon the renunciation of the faith.

Let us make known in a single example what arts he acquired through this accursed bargain.

### A woman is transformed into a dog

He had accustomed a nun of a well-known family to his conversation. She lived in a cell with only one companion, a monk who attended to external matters; this man himself remained at home occupied with foolishness.

One day, when he returned home from an errand with his companion, they were sitting there. When the woman saw them approaching, she had no side passage available, and the monk’s return blocked her way out.

Seeing his companion frightened, the new sorcerer said: “Go to meet the man who is coming. Look neither to the right nor to the left, and fear nothing.” The woman believed him and went out.

But he stood at the doorway and, reciting over her the incantation he had learned, transformed her into a monstrous dog. When she approached the returning monk, he exclaimed: “Alas! Where has such a huge dog come from?”

Terrified, she passed by. From those words alone she recognized the form in which she had escaped.

The monk himself eventually came home and asked where a dog of such extraordinary size had appeared. “It belongs to our neighbor,” she replied. “Surely you have known him for some time?” Thus he remained silent, believing what he had been told.

After living for a long time without God, he was finally struck by a serious illness, through God’s mercy, and, whether he wished it or not, confessed what he had done.

The matter was referred to the judgment of wise men, especially Anselm of Canterbury, later archbishop and at that time abbot of Bec. Under his judgment above all, the filthy profaner was expelled from every ministry of the divine mysteries.

Even while placed under this suspension, he could never erase from his mind the belief that he would yet become a bishop. He had certainly received this hope from demons—always liars, and liars in this case as well—for a few years later he died not merely without becoming a bishop but permanently an ex-priest. [Col. 0892B]

### A cleric drives away the demon he had approached for consultation by invoking the name of Mary

I shall append the beginning of a case that ended better. A certain cleric lived in the village of Beauvais by the art of writing; I too knew him, for he had been hired at Flaviacum to work on this very book.

Later, at the castle of Breteuil, while conversing with another cleric who practiced magic, he heard the following: “If you made it worth my while, I would teach you something by which, if you did it, you would receive daily gifts of money without any human administration.”

He asked what had to be done. The magician replied that he would have to offer sacrifice to a citizen of hell, namely the devil.

“With what victim?” he asked.

“With a cock,” he replied, “in such a way that the egg from which it was formed must have been laid by a hen on a Thursday in the month of March. After you have roasted it, take it with you at the very beginning of the night, with the spit still inserted in it, and come with me to the nearest fishpond.

“Whatever you see, hear, or feel there, do not presume to invoke God, the blessed Mary, or any of the saints.”

“I will do so,” he said.

A wondrous event! They came to the place by night, carrying with them an offering appropriate to such a god. When the magician invoked the demon by name, and the wicked disciple held the cock, the demon raised a whirlwind and appeared, seizing the cock for himself.

The terrified man who had been led there called upon holy Mary. When that powerful Lady’s name was heard, the demon fled with his cock, unable to carry it all the way. The following day one of the fishermen found him on an island in the fishpond.

O royal and sweet name, so dreadful to the powers of evil!

The magician was angry with the cleric because he had invoked so great a woman during such an undertaking. But the cleric, moved to repentance (63), went to Lisiard, archdeacon of Beauvais and my maternal uncle, a man learned in every respect, prudent, and renowned and experienced in such matters.

After confessing what he had done, he humbled himself in repentance through prayers and fasts, at Lisiard’s command.

Let what I have said about the things I saw or heard in the monastery suffice. But since we have spoken above of our somewhat irregular election, let us address, at the beginning of another little book, what sort of place it was, how it was established, what antiquities it possessed, and to which place, by God’s agency, we were transferred.

# BOOK TWO

## The beginnings and development of the abbey of Blessed Mary of Nogent are related

[Col. 0893]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0893B]

(64) It is indeed called Nogent (commonly Nogent-sous-Coucy). As far as monastic habitation is concerned, it is new; but as far as secular use is concerned, it was cultivated in the most ancient times.

If no literary tradition supported this opinion, there would certainly be an abundance of foreign evidence, and, as we think, not a Christian arrangement of tombs found there. For antiquity has joined together around the basilica itself and within it such a great abundance of sarcophagi, in a place so greatly sought out for its fame, that the countless bodies heaped there bear witness to it.

The tombs are not arranged according to the custom of our order. Rather, many tombs surround a single tomb in a circle like a garland. Among them certain vessels are found whose purpose the Christian age does not know. We can believe nothing other than that they belonged either to pagan peoples or to the most ancient Christians, but were made according to pagan custom.

There are also in the same church certain letters composed in meter. I would rely on no authority for them unless I saw that certain things, which greatly strengthen their credibility, still exist today.

The history is said to have occurred as follows, according to the sequence of this writing:

### A marvel concerning a king of the Britons and Saxons

(65) It is reported that before the assumption of the incarnate Word into heaven there existed among the English a certain king. He was not an Englishman—for that is the newer name, derived from a part of the Saxons who later usurped those lands—but was anciently called a Briton.

In Britain itself, that is, the island of the Ocean, this king was abundantly furnished with poetic and philosophical learning. In addition, the goodness naturally implanted in him caused him to devote himself generously to works of mercy.

When he showed himself generous toward the needy, not out of regard for God, whom he did not yet know, but moved by the exceptional humanity with which he overflowed, it was fitting that the exercise of his kindly nature should be accompanied by the gift of a clearer understanding.

He began to reason with the most eloquent conjectures available to him about what certain divinity he ought to hope for amid all the formulas of his many gods. He considered what harmony there could be among them in governing heaven and earth, when, during their lives, impurity and unmistakable conflict had existed in their marriages; and when, in their rule over their lands, cruel hostility among them had been evident, extending from sons against fathers and fathers against sons even to mutual replacement, exclusion, or death.

Since almost everything sung about them was worse than what is found among mortals, he considered it the height of madness to ascribe the rule of the earth, much less of the heavens, to such beings. And who could elevate them to arrange heavenly affairs when, in their pitiable power, they had once been unable to possess even the smallest portions of the earth without shameful collusion? [Col. 0894B]

Illuminated by heavenly light.—As this man revolved these and similar thoughts, he expelled from his heart the images of the now, as he supposed, vain divinities and turned to worship the one incomprehensible God, who ought to be worshiped without form, who alone administers all things in a single harmony, whose invisible attributes he had already perceived and understood through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20). While he was still hesitating over these useful arguments amid certain perplexities, God, who reveals better things to those of good will, summoned this man by a heavenly voice sent to him, instructing him to proceed as far as Jerusalem. There he would hear what one ought to believe about God, how the Son proceeding from God, God himself, had conducted himself among human beings and on behalf of human beings, what he had endured or what had befallen him, whom he had left behind as successors to exemplify the divine name, and whom, when he had transferred himself there, he would find as witnesses to such great mysteries—namely, his Mother together with the whole apostolate.

He renounces his kingdom. He lodges at Novigenti. Description of Novigenti.—Accordingly, that British king, having set aside his possessions and kingdom and having been told the oracle of faith, resolved to hasten to experience what he had learned. He therefore abandoned his homeland, prepared a fleet, crossed the adjacent sea, and, after passing through the extensive interval between towns and cities, reached the boundary of the province of Laon. Thus he put in at the rural place we mentioned above, Novigenti, intending to obtain lodging.

That place lies below the castle called Codiciacus (commonly Coucy), a new structure, as they say, built by the rustic inhabitants of this land—very proud and wealthy people—because of incursions by foreigners. (66) The castle itself has no antiquity at all. The place of which we are speaking was at that time surrounded by forests rich in game. (67) The river we mentioned above, the Aquila, is more useful than great: for, surpassing the waters of more celebrated rivers in the abundance of its fish, it is not confined within the course of its channel, as other rivers are, but extends in a stagnant abundance of water, like a series of fishponds. On either side, the slopes of the projecting hills are enclosed by vineyards. The soil on both sides, suited to Liber and Ceres, is praised for its earth, the mother of every good crop; and the fertility of the little river is commended by the pleasantness of the meadows extending far and wide.

There is a shrine there consecrated to the Virgin who would bear God.—It is handed down by the ancients and asserted as certain that a very ancient shrine once existed in that place, consecrated not in the name or honor of any existing god, but (68) to a woman not yet born who was destined to give birth to God and man. It was therefore devoted to the future mother of the God who was to be born. No sensible person considers this absurd, since at Athens they had worshiped the unknown God (Acts 17:23); certainly they were not wholly unaware that he would be born from a woman, just like the other common gods whose mothers they name. And if a little shrine was already being dedicated to the one who was to be born, his mother, like the mothers of the others, was by no means deprived of a similar honor. What is not to be disbelieved of her giving birth there could also have occurred here in respect of the birth.

The British king therefore happened to arrive at this place. Detained by the attraction of that very favorable countryside, he decided to restore there the bodies of himself and his companions, wearied by the journey, and refreshed the exhausted animals for eight days with the abundant pasture lying nearby.

The king puts in at Jerusalem.—Proceeding from there, after traversing the distances of land and sea, he finally entered within the walls of Jerusalem. The Savior had recently suffered, been raised from the dead, ascended to the heavens, and at last given the Spirit. He found the city divided by various disputes, some offended by what had been done and others approving it. There was no difficulty in finding those whom he sought; rather, the matter, celebrated by great rumors, readily revealed the promulgators of this new law. They were no longer confined by their customary hiding places, nor did fear of a Jewish uprising keep them from bearing witness to their Lord. It was possible to see them standing out among the crowds, so that the evident steadfastness of their position might reinforce the authority of their preaching.

Why delay? Peter, together with the Eleven, was found frequently among the people, with a very large gathering of disciples already following him, a mirror of the faith and glory of us all. Mary, meanwhile, bore witness there to her presence and to the divine flesh. That British king, soon to offer God his first fruits, addressed them and the Virgin Mother, and explained the reasons for his journey as follows:

> “You see that I have come to you, Fathers and lords, from the most distant boundaries of the earth in order to hear you. By rightful succession from my parents I have until now ruled the Britons. Although I had hitherto continued to honor the ancient rites that error of long standing had taught us to venerate, I recently withdrew from them for the following reason.
>
> “When I considered that those whom antiquity had honored as possessing divinity were the most loathsome of mortals, and reflected that, after monstrous impurities, they had paid the dues of nature, I discovered by reasonable conjectures that the beings in heaven whom antiquity had fixed there by mere opinion—beings who had lived under heaven on earth, dependent upon earthly things—could in no way have created heaven and earth and everything in them. The gentleness of the heavens and airs, and the richness of the earth, plainly show that these beings themselves came together in this world.
>
> “Having therefore dispelled the idea of their divinity, I have at last become firmly convinced that, after these beings have been deprived of divine authority forever, one can and must believe in the creation and governance of all things by the one God. Just as all things are from him alone, so he holds and harmonizes them all within himself. After my mind had been joined to God under the One, and the temples and the fabrications of temples had been cast away in eternal disgust, as though my heart had now been cleansed of the sewer of idolatry, the purity of the whole true religion immediately shone forth from heaven.
>
> “For soon I was commanded by a divine voice to come here, where I am promised that through you I shall be given the truth of the one faith concerning the dispensation of the Son of God, who recently suffered. Therefore, through the Mother of the Deity announced to me, whom I now see present, and through your offices, I adjure you to grant me the mysteries of this new regeneration.”

Instructed in the rudiments of the faith, he is baptized. The name Quilius is given to him. He asks for and receives relics.—When Peter and that blessed company heard these words, with Mary glorifying the heavenly assembly, they adored the majesty of the Son of God and man. Although he was still recent, and had brought salvation into the midst of the earth together with the preachers of grace, whose words had never yet been scattered abroad, he had already poured forth the words of this new fullness so suddenly to the regions of the West.

The rule of faith was therefore handed down to the man, and afterward he was washed in the water of baptism; there he received the name Quilius. Confirmed under the instruction of such great teachers and instructed in the sacrament he had received, as he was about to depart from them and return to his own country, he asked them with faithful heart for sacred pledges from the relics—specifically, from those things which he had learned had been in contact with the Savior’s body. He asked for and received pieces of the chains with which he knew that the Lord had been bound to the stake; of the scourges with which an impious hand had furrowed his blessed limbs; of the crown of thorns that had encircled his sacred head; of the very wood of the cross upon which he had been hung; of the tunic of the Mother of God, in which, as is said, she had given birth to the Lord; and of the garments of all the apostles themselves, through their pious devotion.

He dies at Novigenti.—He carried these things with him enclosed in a small reliquary, made preparations for his return, and, after crossing the intervening expanse of regions, reached the countryside where he had paused on his outward journey for the sake of rest. Immediately seized by an unexpected illness, he went to bed, and in a dream it was revealed to him that he would there meet the end of his present life. He was also told that nowhere else but there would his limbs have a tomb, and that beneath the same turf he should know the relics he had received from the holy apostles at Jerusalem would be buried.

Awakened, the man, with all his thoughts now constrained to a single subject by the foreknowledge of his death, considered, in hope of the glory soon to follow, how his corpse should be disposed of. He died there, and, having returned unharmed the deposit entrusted to him by the person who had entrusted it, found rest for the substance of his body in the earth of the monument; beside it, the reliquary of the relics found its place. From there, after a very long time, by God’s providence, the reliquary was removed and covered by unknown faithful hands with sheets of precious gold, fashioned in an ancient workmanship. It has come to the sight of our own age and continues to provide new testimony to ancient accounts.

Such, then, are said to have been the beginnings of that place.

## CHAPTER II

### On the church of Novigenti itself; how it was entrusted to monks; and Abbot Henry

As the support of Christian law came to life, a church of very good character had long shone there under the name of the Mother of God. Situated below the town we mentioned, Codiciacus, and surrounded also by villages of ancient renown and great wealth, it was visited by a large gathering of the neighboring population and held in veneration. It was also reported that, while it remained in that small condition, it was frequently illuminated by divine lights and often honored by miracles—not without justice, since among men it remained unduly in a lowly condition. (69)

When the castle itself, under very flourishing princes, had extended its dominion far and wide, and its nobles were endowed with great generosity and wealth, the place became renowned because of the sweetness of the reputation for holiness that everywhere arose from it. On the advice of the devout, it was therefore proposed that it be handed over to monks, so that the divine service might be celebrated there in abundance.

Since there was no hope of a greater increase from such an undertaking—for the revenues of the place seemed scarcely sufficient for the use of more than six monks—the church began to be renewed by inexperienced and poorly educated persons for the establishment or advancement of certain things. Since it had no leader or teacher of any ingenuity in building, what was constructed was indeed disjointed.

In that age, however, which was more abundant in resources than our own, the place grew through the gifts of the nobles of the castle. The generosity of its lords had preceded the first gifts, and their consent supported the donations of others. By the prudent counsel of the brothers of the place and of its patrons, adequate provision was therefore made for both. They appointed to it the magnificent man Henry, then abbot of Saint Remigius, who had long presided over the monastery of Humiliara (commonly Homblières, near Saint-Quentin). (70) He was, of course, a distinguished man, (71) who was not renowned for learning or lineage, but was so conspicuous in the administration of external affairs that, with good diligence, he was equally attentive to the order of the interior rule.

Presiding over these three monasteries, he supplied the needs of this third one, which had begun to grow, from the resources of the two wealthier houses. Among the many acts of generosity he exercised toward that church, he assembled a very great offering for its consecration. It was dedicated by Helinand, bishop of Laon, a man extremely wealthy in matters concerning the founding of churches and exceptionally careful about their adornment; he also freed it from many dues by privileges and increased it with distinguished gifts.

### Godefrid is appointed in Henry’s place

But because the aforementioned abbot was weighed down by age and was blind, he withdrew to the two wealthier abbeys, which could more easily be governed by their own resources, and proposed to abandon this third one, which could not be maintained without laborious attention. When he attempted to entrust it to a certain nephew who was a monk, after calling the brothers of the church to support the proposal, he could not obtain their agreement. Instead, the election unexpectedly fell upon a certain young man named Godefrid, who was born in that region and had been a monk of Saint-Quentin-de-la-Montagne (commonly le Mont-Saint-Quentin) near Péronne. (72) Even the old abbot was displeased by this.

When that most perceptive elder saw the electors’ votes being transferred elsewhere, he abandoned the place that he had preserved with the greatest dignity and most indulgent generosity, and made a lawful resignation in favor of the man whom they had elected.

### (73) Godefrid conducts himself wisely and prudently. The nobles generously bestow goods

After that man had been elected and promoted to the custody of the place, he conducted himself with great circumspection. Since both the townspeople and the nobles possessed both the will and the ability to increase the church’s resources, very many advantages in lands and revenues flowed to it in the period that followed.

He knew how to comport himself appropriately toward people of the external world: he made himself affable and generous to them, and had devoted no little effort to learning the conduct of secular affairs. In truth, the people of that age, about which I spoke at the beginning of this work, had generous dispositions toward establishing monasteries. They gave lands and much money, and expended their own resources on such things more gladly than their children in our own days bestow fair words upon us.

Since there was therefore less zeal for religion than there ought to have been in the monasteries situated all around, and since this man appeared to be exercising himself greatly in such matters together with his people, the opportunity arose for him to acquire a distinguished reputation. Just as a very small light has its place in the midst of darkness, so the restraint displayed by the man in charge, and the obedience of his subjects to his command, secured him an occasion for acquiring renown.

### Godefrid’s approved practices. He is made bishop of Amiens. A council is convened in the city of Troyes by the legate Richard

He therefore forbade anything simoniacal either to be done or to be possessed in that church. Excluding commercial transactions, he admitted grace alone, regarding both the deed and the name of shameful profit as equally hateful.

Since this same man was thought to be more skilled in legal affairs than several of his fellow abbots and was consequently better known in towns and cities, arrangements were first made concerning the wealthier abbeys, and afterward discussion began about obtaining a bishopric for him. The see of Amiens had then been vacant for nearly two years. He himself had also acted as agent for a certain archdeacon of that city, who was being sought with the support of factions among some of the clergy and people.

Thus, both because of his worldly cleverness and because of the regular discipline he maintained, while he was seeking the office for another, he himself was sought. Under Richard, formerly bishop of Albano and then legate of the Apostolic See in France—who had convened a council in the city of Troyes—he was appointed bishop of the aforesaid see of Amiens, and it is established that he was transferred there from his own Novigenti.

While he conducted himself there with great glory and success, and was honored by everyone to such an extent that even the bishops who presided over him feared him with particular veneration—and, not to delay, while he was regarded everywhere almost as a mirror of the whole of religion—he suddenly emerged into that which, whether he desired or feared it, God knows.

I have learned that an inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end. His beginnings were certainly full of the customary praise, and for several years a laudatory report accompanied him. But now, as can be seen, whatever glory seemed to blaze in him before people not only grew lukewarm but became cold.

On the first day of his reception within the city, when he was about to speak to the people from the higher part of the pulpit, he declared that he would pursue lofty aims, since he did not wish the following poetic line to be applied to his shortcomings:

> “The mountains are in labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.”  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 139.)

This statement, directed toward anticipating his subsequent deeds, filled everyone’s minds with expectation. For as his condition gradually and copiously slackened day by day, it began continually to make the promise itself worse than before. But for the moment let us be silent about these matters; perhaps we shall have places later in which . . . . . . (Some things are missing.)

## CHAPTER III

### Guibert, ignorant of Novigenti, is substituted as abbot in Godefrid’s place

I therefore happened to be summoned to this place, from which he had departed, which he himself had suitably and opportunely ordered, and in which, had he been willing to be content with what he possessed, he could have lived most happily and freely, subject to no one. The election having been made, as I said above, I do not know whether it occurred with God’s disapproval or his tolerance. This alone I confidently declare: that the matter was not arranged for me through such canvassing, nor with my knowledge, nor through any faction of my relatives.

In this respect, the matter proceeded reasonably well. In the other respect—namely, that I was known by none of them and knew none of them—it perhaps did not proceed advantageously or completely, as the reader who follows should attend. For when I came to them, I cannot be certain that, since I was unknown to them and they to me, we would have conceived any hostility toward one another on that account. Some people thought so. This has happened elsewhere and may happen; but here I could by no means infer that it had occurred.

No one doubts that familiarity and acquaintance ordinarily engender boldness, and that boldness very easily bursts forth into recklessness. Certainly we are accustomed to show greater reverence to those whom we know less well. Yet when I entered that place, their consciences were in no way closed to me. Rather, by such faithful confession they revealed their minds to me—and, in revealing them, united them with me—that although I thought I had seen monks somewhere else, I had known none at all comparable to them in this respect.

### Why he does not plainly disclose his sins

You know, most merciful one, that I did not begin this little work out of any arrogance, but because I wished to confess my wickednesses. I would confess them with complete clarity if I did not fear that, through my dreadful deeds, I might corrupt the minds of many who would read these things.

I confess, I say, wickednesses—but much more rightly I confess mercies that correspond not to my iniquity but to your innate grace. If it should happen that I speak about anyone, I shall set forth their character and the final outcomes of events in order to display your judgments. For you know that, in these words of mine dedicated to you and yours, I do not gladly welcome any word of spite or envy.

Since I have therefore decided to weave my fortunes and misfortunes together as a possible instrument of some sort for others, on the very day of my reception a certain monk knowledgeable in Holy Scripture, curious, as I suppose, about my future events, prepared to come out to meet me [*f.*, “he prepared”]. He deliberately opened the Gospel text upon the altar with the intention that whatever chapter first met his eyes (75) might serve as an omen for me.

### A prediction concerning Guibert. How diligently he fulfilled the duties of his prelacy

The book was handwritten, not in pages but in columns. His eye therefore settled in the middle of the third column, where the text read:

> “The lamp of your body is your eye.”  
> (Luke 11:34.)

He instructed the deacon who was to carry the Gospel text in procession that, after I had kissed the silver image affixed to its exterior, he should suddenly open the volume before my eyes with his finger inserted at the place he had marked, and carefully observe in which direction my gaze fell.

The deacon opened the book, whose edges I had pressed down on the outside according to custom after kissing it. While he watched to see where I would look, I did not look at the beginning of the page or at the end, but turned my face and eyes toward that same verse.

When the monk, who was skilled at conjecturing such things, saw that my unpremeditated action had corresponded with his intention, he came to me several days later and related both what he had done and how my action had wonderfully harmonized with his own.

God, who illuminates the lamps of all who trust in you (Ps. 17:29), you know what lamp of intention you granted me, and what favorable disposition I have toward those who have brought adversity upon me. Although my works—my heart, that is—are foul and wretched as far as I am concerned, you nevertheless know how earnestly my mind is directed toward the salvation of those whom you have subjected to me.

The more closely I consider my own evils, the more gladly I rejoice in their good works if they prosper. For I know that I am freer before the throne of your grace insofar as I make myself more pleasing through the devoted efforts of those who wish me well.

### Summary of the address he delivered before the monks

After they had received me and brought me into the chapter assembly, I preached on that prophetic oracle and said—as the Lord’s Nativity was at hand, when Isaiah is read:

> “The prophet Isaiah says what you have just heard:
>
> “‘A man will seize his brother, one of his father’s household: “You have a garment; be our prince, and let this ruin be under your hand.” And he will answer: “I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor garment; do not appoint me prince.” For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed’” (Isa. 3:6–8).
>
> “The man is one who is not effeminate against the devil [*f.*, ‘is not regarded as effeminate’]. He seizes his brother when he joins himself to someone born from God. He must also be a member of his father’s household, because one who is called to the office of shepherd ought not to be ignorant of the mysteries of God’s household.
>
> “For one who is ignorant of the Church’s sacraments is not worthy to administer them. Since the ‘scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 13:52) cannot be counted as a ‘faithful’ servant in preserving the mysteries, ‘prudent’ in distributing them, and therefore a ‘servant’ (Matt. 24:45), how can one preside over the Church who does not know the Church? Let him therefore be a member of the household.
>
> “What is meant by a garment if not the beautiful outward appearance of one’s external works? The man who has a garment is therefore asked to be prince, because it often happens that the person is sought for governance who presents himself as more disciplined in conduct, speech, and action.
>
> “The ruin is said to be under his hand because whatever loss is found among his subjects is understood to reach the reckoning of the man who presides over them. It is as though he said: ‘You appear to yourself to be well equipped outwardly, but pay attention to the virtue by which you excel inwardly.’
>
> “Knowing that he must bear everyone’s ruins, he becomes more cautious and adds: ‘I am not a physician,’ since he cannot withstand all the ruins caused by multiplying illnesses. You see an outward garment, yet there is no garment in the house, because the disposition of the mind is not the same as that of the body. Hence he admits that he is not a physician: for, by the sharpness of discernment, it is difficult to penetrate the origins and outcomes of every vice and virtue.
>
> “This could also have resulted from his need, because there is not in the house that bread which is asked of God today as daily bread (Luke 11:3)—namely, the strengthening poured in through spiritual divine nourishment, or the confirmation of charity in the inner person, without which no one can govern well anywhere.
>
> “The prince therefore rightly refuses to become prince when his mind, not imbued from above, supplies him with none of the strength required. Since ‘Jerusalem has fallen’—that is, since the inner experience of peace has perished—and ‘Judah has collapsed’—that is, since the confession of sins, which is the final stage of all evils, has failed in complete despair after the loss of inner tranquility—a just reason for rejecting the pastoral office has presented itself.
>
> “For where the mind is disturbed by emerging vices, it is assailed most shamefully; and when the mind, wickedly blinded by these things, does not detest them through confession, then, since it cannot govern itself, it is justly kept from governing others, by others and still more justly by itself.”

What I said there in explanation, I set forth more fully elsewhere in exhortation, supporting my statements with examples from Scripture.

## CHAPTER IV

### On the happy death of Guibert’s mother

Since we have long omitted speaking about my mother, whom alone, among all the temporal possessions I had, I regarded as specially good, it is fitting briefly to touch upon the better end of her good life.

Although she had passed beyond, as she herself admitted, a considerable number of years with undiminished strength of spirit, and although, as her frail body failed, the care of prayer in her spirit in no way grew slack, she was driven from sleep by an ailment of the chest and repeated the name of the Lord Jesus a hundred times each night with extraordinary wheezing. Finally, overcome by illness, she took to her bed.

At that time my brother and I were staying at Novigenti, if I am not mistaken, two years before that return to Flaviacum which we mentioned above. It was undertaken very thoughtlessly, but, through the agency of the one who makes good use of our evils, it was turned into an outcome much more prosperous than could have been believed. For God spared her tenderness, so that a heart that loved God so greatly would not be wounded by the sword of this undeserved and ignoble return.

As she lay dying, my teacher stood beside her in tears and said to her:

> “Look, your sons are far away, and perhaps you will grieve—and they even more—if you die in their absence.”

But she struck him with her eyes and replied:

> “If they were living here, as they once did, within the adjacent cloister, God knows that I would not want either them or any of my relatives to be present at my death. There is one whom I await with the powers of my inner being. Would that he alone might be present!”

She said this, and that very night, at the hour when the angel Gabriel, sent by God to the Virgin, is sung of and worshiped, she departed to that Lady whom I have mentioned, whom she had always desired with infinite love, to be received by her, as we believe, without displeasure.

Several years before her death, she had begun to desire exceedingly to receive the sacred veil. I had delayed this by invoking the authority of the statement, “Let no bishop presume to veil widows,” arguing that a life of the greatest continence without an exterior habit ought to be sufficient for her. Abbot Anselm of Bec, afterward archbishop of Canterbury (or Kent, or Cantuaria) of the English, an extraordinary man, about whom I spoke above, had also long forbidden this practice. (493)

She was thereby all the more inflamed, and no argument could turn her from her purpose. She prevailed. During the reception of the veil, in the presence of the most reverend John, abbot of that place, whom she herself had raised as a small child, she gave the following account of the divine encouragement she had received for this undertaking:

She said that in a vision she had seen a Lady of great beauty and authority, richly adorned and surrounded by attendants. The Lady offered her a most precious veil and seemed to entrust it to her for safekeeping, to be returned at the appropriate time in the manner of a deposit.

We all accepted this account without hesitation, especially since we perceived that her devotion had been stirred by divine signs. She preserved that sacred veil intact, as best she could, for nearly three years. On the day when she joyfully and blessedly received with delighted ear the announcement of salvation, she returned it to the Lady who had entrusted it to her.

I commend her to all faithful people who will read these things. It is certain that she excluded no faithful person from her frequent prayers. Before God I have said these things about her, possessing the truthful testimony of my heart and having fabricated nothing at all.

But since we made that return to the church of Flaviacum, it is fitting to remain there for a little while again before we sprinkle our backward-wandering footsteps with the sand of Laon.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0903B]

### A Jew converted to the faith puts on the monastic habit

In that monastery there is a certain monk of Hebrew origin. At the beginning of the journey to Jerusalem, when its fame was resounding through the Latin world, he was lifted out of his superstition in the following way.

One day at Rouen, those who had undertaken the expedition and accepted it under the same profession of the cross began to complain among themselves:

> “We desire to attack the East after crossing long stretches of land, as enemies of God. Since Jews are before our eyes, and no people is more hostile to God, our labor is misdirected.”

After saying this, they seized their weapons and forced their way into a certain church. Whether by force or deceit I do not know, they drove them into a certain church and indiscriminately gave persons of every sex and age over to the sword, but in such a way that those who submitted to Christian status escaped the blow of the threatening blade.

During this slaughter a certain nobleman saw a little boy, took pity on him, rescued him, and brought him to his mother.

She had once been married to the count of Eu, a woman of no ordinary distinction. Eu is a castle above which stands the abbey of Saint Michael by the sea, called Vieux-Port [commonly Tréport]. The excellent woman received the child and, with very welcoming kindness, asked him whether he wished to join the Christian law.

He did not deny it—for he thought that he was destined for slaughter such as he had seen his fellow countrymen suffer. The preparations appropriate for the baptized were quickly made, and they proceeded to the font.

After the sacrament had been conferred upon him through the mysteries of the prayers, they came to the place where, with a light burning, melted wax is dropped into the water. A single drop was seen to fall there, and by itself it impressed upon the water its own small shape, so to speak, with such exactness in the form of a cross that no human hand could have made anything comparable from so little material.

The countess herself told me this—she was so familiar with me and so uniquely well known to me that she called me only “son”—and the priest likewise related it, not without many solemn appeals to the divine name. I might have received the event rather mildly [*f.*, “lightly”] if I had not clearly observed the boy’s remarkable successes.

The countess was named Helisendis. Her son, the man who rescued him from the slaughter and received him from the sacred font, was William. Hence he gave the boy his own name when the child had been brought to him.

When he had grown somewhat older, he was transferred from the Hebrew instruction in which he had begun to be trained to Latin letters, and quickly flourished. Because William feared that the boy might be recalled by his own parents to his former state, he brought him into the monastery of Flaviacum. They had attempted this once, but had been unable to exercise any influence over him.

Once handed over to monastic life, he showed such affection for the Christian way, absorbed whatever concerned divine knowledge with such ardor of spirit, and endured with such equanimity whatever was imposed upon him for the sake of discipline, that the victory over his wicked nature and the glory of his recently transformed condition [*f.*, “glory”] won him no small reverence from everyone.

A grammar teacher, a highly religious man, had been secretly assigned to him as guardian during his childhood. Considering that this new little man needed knowledge of our law, he devoted himself diligently to educating him.

His naturally skillful intellect was sharpened each day to such a degree that, although the monastery flourished with a multitude of learned men, no one’s greater intellectual brilliance was thought possible. Although richly endowed in understanding, he is altogether without envy and disparagement. He is always cheerful, and is known for a special devotion to chastity.

To strengthen his unbroken faith, I sent him a certain little book that I had written nearly four years earlier against the count of Soissons, who was both Judaizing and heretical. I hear that he embraces it so enthusiastically that, in compiling something about the nature of faith, he devoutly attempts to emulate that little work.

The cross therefore appeared in his baptism not by chance but by divine action. It rightly revealed that an unusual faith would arise in our time in a man of Jewish origin.

### A certain old man renounces the world and vigorously guards monastic discipline against the tricks of demons

Another man, of noble origin among the Beauvaisis and wealthy also in the Noyonnais, advanced in age and already weakened in body—which is dangerous in such matters—had a wife who was still vigorous for the duties of the marriage bed. He abandoned marriage and the world and professed himself a monk there.

Persisting in almost continuous tears and unending prayers, and never ceasing to listen to the word of God, he presented himself as an example to us all. While the rigor of the rule was fervently practiced, he heard it prohibited in the chapter assembly that no one from the cloister should presume to enter the sickroom in which he lived without a definite reason. He kept this sentence carefully in mind.

And behold, one morning, while he was still half asleep and lying with his eyes closed, two demons (81), in the likeness of those religious men whom the common people call *Deonandos* [Note: [Col. 0903D] Below he identifies the *Deonandi* as laymen.], sat down on the bench beneath his bed.

The old man awoke, turned his eyes toward the head of the bed, and was astonished at such a familiar gathering of unknown people. One of them was presiding with his head uncovered, with no flowing beard, but red-haired and curly, and, as such wandering zealots customarily do, walking barefoot, with mud—so he said—thickly filling the spaces between his toes as though he had only just trodden in it.

The other had hidden behind the first in such a way that the appearance of his face could not be discerned. (82) He wore a long tunic and had his black head covered.

When he noticed these unknown persons before him, he attacked them with grave severity:

> “Since you are laymen and unknown persons, where does such boldness come from, that you have come at this hour into this place, which none of the cloister monks would dare enter without a reason?”

The first replied:

> “I had heard, lord, that there were religious men in this monastery, and I came in order to learn religion. I ask that you not take offense.”

The old man answered:

> “Religion or an order is not learned here. But if you wish to be instructed, go to those who are in the cloister. There you will find the rigor of discipline and the rudiments of holiness. Go away from here, therefore, because what is forbidden to the monks, the lords of this place, is far more and incomparably forbidden to you.”

And when he wished to repeat the same words and linger at the same time, the other, growling at them in a still more thunderous voice, compelled them to leave the building. When they had proceeded as far as the door, they stopped on the threshold. Then the one who had been the spokesman, looking back at the elder, continued:

“I would rather that you expel me from here. Certainly, if you had wished to keep me with you, one of your dependants is accused of theft; and if he should dare to deny it, I would attack him in single combat and bring you considerable profit from the affair.”

When the elder heard this, he smiled. “Now,” he said, “we have clearly perceived the danger from your conversation: you who said that you had come for the sake of religion now admit that you are a fighter. Therefore, with such a great falsehood, you deserve neither to be heard nor to be detained.”

But the elder, greatly angered that such men had been admitted into the house, rose and went as far as the portico of the building. There he found the brothers who were staying with him, infirm as they were, and vehemently reproved them for having allowed such an utterly foreign sort of men to enter. They, however, astonished and believing him to be delirious, declared that they had seen no one. He himself, recounting who they were, how they had conducted themselves, and what they had said, and indicating the time as well, learned from his own testimony and that of everyone else that he had been deceived by demons.

For some demons are intent only on mockery, while others are cruel in mind and inclined to inflict harm. As an illustration of the latter, we offer two examples beyond the present subject.

## CHAPTER VI

### A certain servant, having invoked a demon, is carried to Italy

Near the fortress of Calniacum [commonly Chauny], there was a servant from the household of Guascelin, lord of that very fortress, whose duty it was to keep watch at night over the castle’s security. One evening, when the light of day had almost completely faded and he feared that he would be late for the approaching supper, he was stationed across the river and shouted for someone on the opposite bank to bring a boat. When no one answered him, the man, driven to fury, said:

“Or you, devils, why do you not carry me across?”

Without delay, the devil appeared and said, “Climb aboard; I shall carry you.”

At once the unfortunate man, destined for a bad fall, climbed aboard. The devil took him up and, within that same hour, carried him to Italy, setting him down below the suburb of a city called Subtura [or Subura] with such kindness that he broke his thigh. That city lies about a day’s journey this side of Rome.

The man’s lord had departed for the thresholds of the apostles on the preceding day and, leaving Rome, had lodged at Subtura. When he rose before daylight—as travelers commonly do during the winter months—and, having left the city with his companions, reached the fields, he heard the voice of someone weeping not far from the public road. He searched and found the man; his master recognized him by his voice alone. Asked how he had come there, the man reported that the previous evening he had been at Calniacum and explained how he had fallen when the devil carried him away.

His lord, sufficiently and more than sufficiently astonished, carried the man into the nearest city and supplied money from his own resources for his return and medical treatment. From what he had suffered, therefore, he learned—and taught others—that God, not demons, must be invoked in one’s affairs.

### 495. Demons torment a cleric, Hugo, with severe fevers

(83) Likewise, at Saint-Medard there was a man who held an office in that abbey itself. After spending part of the night, in the manner of a watchman, keeping vigil by the gate with towers on the fishpond side, with rattles, his mouth, and horns, he finally went down to walk along the water’s edge.

As he stood there, the appearances of three women came before him. One of them said, within his hearing, “Let us enter this man.”

Another replied, “He is poor; he could not keep us properly.”

To this the third said, “There is a certain cleric here, Hugo, obese and fat, overflowing with possessions, who could nourish us well. It is good to attack him.”

As they vanished, the man withdrew into himself and understood that these were three well-known kinds of fever, which, with ridiculous curiosity, looked down on him as though he were poor and contended for possession of the man who could scarcely be drained of flesh and substance.

Without waiting for daylight, therefore, he approached the nearest monks he could find. After recounting to them what he had seen and heard, he asked that someone be sent to the aforesaid Hugo, so that they might learn how he was. A messenger was sent, and Hugo was found suffering under the greatest heat of fever.

From this it is inferred that such kinds of disease are administered by demons, with God as judge. Thus, in the Gospel, a woman who had been bent double for seventeen [another reading: eighteen] years is said to have been bound by Satan (Luke 13:11). Likewise, the one who suffered from epilepsy—that is, the falling sickness—is said to have been thrown to the ground by an unclean spirit, to have foamed, gnashed his teeth, and become rigid [or: to have withered] (Mark 9:17); and it is asserted that he could be cured only by prayer and fasting. Job, too, was struck inwardly and outwardly—that is, in body and possessions—by the infestation of demons.

### Concerning a cleric who became a regular canon and finally a monk, having led a very wicked life, and died a blessed death

Who could retain the discourse already conceived? Let us finally commit to writing the fourth matter that presents itself to memory.

A certain cleric, who gave a terrible example in our times, lived at Reims. He was moderately educated but skilled in painting. At one point, fearing the many frivolities he had committed, he became a regular canon at the Church of All Saints in Châlons. After living there for some time, as his initial fervor cooled day by day and the heat of his former passions was rekindled, he abandoned the rule to which he had entrusted himself, returned to Reims, and took a wife. After fathering several children, he was struck from heaven by an illness for his correction.

Before he fell ill, however, he had formed the intention of joining the expedition to Jerusalem, which at that time had spread remarkably widely.

When he had been ill for a long time and very severely, and his distress increased, he returned to his senses. He summoned John, then abbot of Saint-Nicaise, by letters and prayers directed to him, compelling him to come. He promised to renounce the world and asked to be clothed in the sacred habit.

That prudent abbot, suspicious because he knew the man’s fickleness from experience, delayed and refused to give him the habit he requested, although he brought the sick man into the inner parts of the monastery. When he sensed that his illness was growing worse, the man attacked the abbot and, with many lamentations, wrung the monastic habit from him, as though the abbot wished it or not.

Having obtained what he had desired, he became happier and seemed, for a very short time, to conduct himself more peacefully than usual. Then suddenly, moved by I know not what divine impulse, he had the abbot summoned and said:

“Command, Father, that your men keep careful guard over me. For know with certainty that God’s judgment is visibly approaching me within a few days. You and your men will suffer much trouble on my account; but, knowing that it will not last a day, I ask you not to be distressed.”

When he heard this, the abbot ordered guards to be assigned to him—not in fear, but in vigilance. Without delay, innumerable swarms of demons rushed upon him from every side, tore at him, and dragged him across the floors after throwing him down. When they also attempted, with rabid violence, to tear the sacred habit from him, he held the cowl in his teeth and clasped his arms so that it would not be pulled away.

As he was afflicted with this dreadful misery, amid pitiful howling, especially at night, nevertheless at intervals during the day, when the demons withdrew, he was allowed to rest for a little while. Then it was possible to ask him how he was being treated in that stormy affair. He spoke at length about the spirits of people whom he himself had known and whom they suggested to him as present, as though he could see them before his eyes.

When a certain widowed woman heard this—she feared for the danger to her husband’s soul and prayed less for him—she asked him whether she might pray for her husband and whether he knew what the man was doing.

“Why not?” he replied. “Pray for him confidently, for he was here a little while ago.”

After being subjected for several days to such torments, he was finally restored to perfect rest. For although at times he seemed to pause in the midst of his sufferings, soon afterward he saw throngs of demons emerging from the walls, from the ground, and from everywhere else, and flying at him to tear him apart.

At last, when the evil spirits had been removed and the mercy of divine judgment had been granted him, he summoned the abbot and spoke as follows:

“Behold, my lord, God is repaying me for my sins. Know, therefore, that after this examination my end will quickly follow. Grant me absolution for my errors as fully as you can, and anoint me with sacred oil to complete my remission.”

The abbot quickly and devoutly carried this out. Having received it with affection and gratitude, the man, cleansed by the punishments he had just endured from every contagion, was freed and joyful, and through the death granted to him passed into life.

# BOOK THREE

## How Bishop Galdric of Laon was butchered, and how the church and almost the whole city were burned

[Col. 0907]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0907D]

### 496. The deeds of Adalbero—from whom the destruction of the city and its calamities took their beginning—and of certain other bishops of Laon

As we promised, we shall now treat of the bishops of Laon—or rather, recount the tragedies of the men of Laon. First, it must be said that the origin of all the evil seems to have arisen from the perversities of the bishops. [Note: Something appears to be missing here; Col. 0907D.] Since the account extends over a much longer period, it is thought appropriate to attach it to this work beginning with Ascelin, who was also called Adalbero.

As we have learned, he was of Lotharingian origin, rich in wealth and well provided with possessions. After selling everything and transferring the enormous proceeds to the see over which he presided, he adorned his church with particularly splendid ornaments and increased the resources of the clergy and episcopate; but he stained all those benefits with a certain most outstanding iniquity.

For what was more wicked, what more disgraceful to him, than that he betrayed his lord, the innocent boy who was king and to whom he had sworn the oath of fidelity, and transferred the course of the royal succession to an alien line descended from Charles the Great? He committed this crime on the day of the Lord’s Supper, like Judas.

In this overthrow of those destined to reign and of the reigning king, he certainly did not secure a beneficial change for the time being, but only the fulfillment of his perverse will against the innocent. Yet prosperity continued to follow the city and its bishop in temporal matters, because God was postponing the punishment.

## CHAPTER II

### Likewise concerning Bishop Helinand

(85) Moreover, Helinand, a man from a very poor household and of obscure birth, with very limited education and a rather insignificant appearance, reached the favor of Edward, king of the English, through the acquaintance of Walter, the senior count of Ponthieu, whose county was his place of origin. His wife had somehow established a connection with the aforesaid count.

Helinand became the king’s chaplain, and because he knew elegant French, the Englishman often sent him to Henry, king of the Franks. With that king—who was very greedy and accustomed to the sale of bishoprics—he negotiated by means of lavish gifts, so that, if any bishop of France should die, Helinand himself might succeed to the episcopal insignia.

Since he held the chaplaincy of the king and queen, and since England at that time was flourishing with immeasurable wealth, he had accumulated many mountains of money. For this reason, since his lavish gifts won favor for him, his voice carried weight with King Henry.

And so it happened. Once brought into Laon, he believed that he would prevail neither through the reputation of his parents nor through learning, but through the great wealth available to him, which he had learned to distribute with the utmost caution, and through generosity, in which he had placed his hopes.

He therefore turned to embellishing and constructing churches. Although he seemed to do many things for God, he nevertheless gave the clearest indications that in his good works he was seeking only favor and the expansion of his name. By these same arts he occupied the archbishopric of Reims. After obtaining it for two years by dissipating great revenues at the court of King Philip, a man most venal in matters belonging to God, he heard from the Lord Pope [Note: Urban II] that a man who already had a wife could by no means bring another woman into the marriage.

When a certain person consulted him about why he was striving toward that position, he said that, even if it were possible for him to become pope, he would by no means conceal his ambition.

Whatever he may have been in himself, whether through ambition or through any other human quality, this honor must certainly be preserved for him: he magnificently defended the liberty of the Church and advanced both that see and its dependent churches by the most generous gifts. It was fitting that external goods should be supplied to him, to be expended on the adornment of the houses of the Lord.

## CHAPTER III

### Concerning Bishop Ingelrannus. He allowed the immunities of the Church to be ruined. He was the cause of the city’s destruction

After this had been completed, Ingelrannus succeeded him. He was as distinguished in nobility and learning, in comparison with the aforesaid bishop, as he was dreadful in his handling of the Church’s rights.

For when he had extracted from King Philip, by entreaties and gifts, certain revenues of the bishop which royal violence had once taken from that see, and when Helinand himself had confirmed their restoration to the Church by royal letters and seal, this man, at the beginning of his own ruin, returned everything to the king. The Church has now been deprived of these revenues through the succession of three bishops, and perhaps will remain deprived of them forever.

Thus, as it seems to me, he made all the bishops who followed participants in this simony: they accepted the episcopate under such a powerful fear of the king that they did not dare reclaim what he, in order to become bishop, had damnably surrendered.

Since he was entirely devoid of affection for God, and every kind of frugality and religion was a mockery to him, it was openly clear from his loquacity and wanton speech that he was worse than any buffoon or stage singer. During his days, therefore, the occasions of the destruction of that city, its churches, and the whole province began to emerge; and it came about that his end was not a wholesome one.

### Ingelrannus bestows many gifts on the churches, but is immersed in the most wicked lusts. He abuses the wife of Count Godfrey of Namur, pretending that he has married her

For there was another man of the same name—Ingelrannus of Boves [commonly Boves]—closely related to him by blood. He was indeed a very liberal, generous, and munificent man, displaying the greatest reverence and generosity toward churches wherever he had learned that religion was practiced. In other respects, however, he was so devoted to love of women that, whenever he had around him women either legitimately his or kept for his pleasure, he scarcely did anything other than what their wantonness urged upon him.

Since he was unfortunate in arranging marriages, he began to wander abroad and secretly appropriated the wife of a certain kinsman of his, the count of Namur. Having secretly solicited her, as I say, he openly joined her to himself in marriage.

They would both easily have repudiated this union, condemned by repeated anathemas and cursed by the detestation of councils, had not the bishop mentioned above been softened both by his kinship with the husband and by the cunning of the flattering woman. This softness so greatly encouraged their adulterous embraces that he secretly absolved what had been generally bound and publicly excommunicated.

Shame upon it! Those to whom he had deceitfully claimed that absolution had been granted never dared to regard themselves as absolved.

### The daughter of Count Roger of Porcien had married Count Godfrey of Namur

Meanwhile, since a little snake comes forth from the root of the serpent (Isaiah 14:29)—that is, since evils, once fostered, break out into worse things—who could describe the slaughter with which that man, after losing his wife, raged through the county of Porcien?

This woman had plainly been the daughter of Count Roger of Porcien—his final child. Setting aside the sons and daughters whom he had fathered by a much nobler wife, he gave this daughter, born of a mother of moderate rank, to that Lotharingian from Namur, namely (88) Count Godfrey, together with her county; at the stepmother’s urging, the earlier heirs were excluded.

While her husband was occupied within Lotharingia against certain enemies of his, his wife remained at his command in the fortress of Tournemelle in Porcien [commonly Porcean]. Since her husband rendered her less of the marital due than she wished, whether she had otherwise restrained herself can be known from this one fact: she would never have leapt into so manifest and monstrous a crime unless she had descended by stages of secret wrongdoing—especially since she came to the man whom she now besieges pregnant from intercourse with outsiders. Her former lusts were so notorious among all who knew her that we should be ashamed not only to conceal them but even to remember them.

Godfrey was a young man altogether handsome, whereas Ingelrannus, to whom she went, was an elderly man. Between the two, therefore, such madness of warfare began to blaze that anyone whom the Lotharingian could capture from among those belonging to Ingelrannus was either hanged from gallows, deprived of his eyes, or mutilated by having his feet cut off.

This is still plainly evident to those who visit the district of Porcien. I certainly heard from someone who had once taken part in such a slaughter that nearly twelve men caught up in such a conflict were hanged in a single day.

Certain leading men of Porcien were intermediaries and instigators of this migration, and for this reason were infamous both in life and in death. Thus Venus, not conceived in the fires of Vulcan, proceeded to Mars: the heat of lusts, foaming over, turned into cruelty.

Who could recount the raids, the fires carried out on both sides, and the other things that such a storm is accustomed to produce—things so numerous that they make even those wishing to report them speechless [possibly: make those unwilling to report them speak]?

Thus the lord bishop, in poor judgment, absolved this diabolical union. Many things could be reported about the bishop’s conduct that are wholly deserving of silence. Above all was this: he was not pierced by any awareness of sin before God.

At last, when illness touched him—though his illness did not make him any less frivolous—his senses suddenly fell asleep and he was enveloped in the cloud of death, so that he could no longer speak rationally. Confession, anointing, and communion were forcibly brought to him by the care of others, and no absolution was sought.

Yet, when his tongue and eyes were already almost swimming beneath death, that Ingelrannus whom he had wickedly absolved after binding him arrived. The clergy had excluded him from the house as though he were excommunicated, but he addressed the bishop with tears, saying:

“My lord bishop, behold Ingelrannus; I am your kinsman.”

The bishop, who had not known how to request confession, anointing, or communion, reached out his hand, drew his own man’s neck toward his mouth, and kissed him.

After this deed had scandalized everyone, he said nothing afterward except delirious utterances, until he breathed out his spirit. Certainly the very woman for whose love he had done this often recounted it publicly as an example: namely, that what he had wickedly done in life, he had, as he died, set down as the final seal of his malice.

Behold how the heavens reveal the iniquities of certain men, so that the earth rises against them and those whom they eagerly strive shamefully to please are themselves displeased with them.

## CHAPTER IV

### The see remains vacant for two years. Galdric is finally elected bishop, to the ruin of the city and province

After he had died in this way, and the Church had remained vacant for two years, we finally assembled to elect a bishop. Among us was that same Ingelrannus who, when the king had rebuked [variant reading: had repudiated] the previous bishop for his frivolities, had secured his creation through his own intervention with that same king.

His mind and speech were entirely directed toward ensuring that whoever was elected bishop would be subject to him: that the king would favor him particularly in making him bishop, and that the clergy would therefore dare oppose his marriage less strongly.

For the destruction of the city and the harm of the entire province, they elected a certain Gualdricus, a referendary of the king of the English, whom they had heard to be wealthy in gold and silver.

### A certain man who sought the bishopric is struck down by God

Before the election, two archdeacons of the Church had been raised to the cathedra amid mutual disputes among the electors: Walter, namely, and Ebalus. But they were expelled by the judgment of the Apostolic See.

Walter had always shown himself not a cleric but a military man; the other was incontinent with women. After they had been removed, a third candidate for the Church, wishing to thrust himself in, sought the court. Although he pretended that he wished to act on behalf of another, he turned the discussion of the priesthood toward himself.

What am I saying? He bargained with the king for abundant supplies of gifts, eagerly embraced swollen [variant: inflated] hopes and promises of wealth, but not the wealth itself. Having returned home, he awaited the following Sunday, when he was to be placed in the cathedra by the royal legates.

And behold, God—who places a stumbling block before such men and casts them down while they are being raised up—struck the proud man with a mortal illness. He died on the very day on which he had seemed likely to be presented in the church to receive the episcopal chair from clergy and people. When he was laid there, as I was told, he soon burst open, and an abundance of foul fluid flowed as far as the middle of the choir.

But let us return to the point from which we digressed.

### The king of the English requests that Galdric be elected bishop; all consent except Anselm

The aforesaid man, elected by the clergy in the utterly false hope of advantages, with Ingelrannus first laboring for him and the others striving for their own harm, was sought at Rouen from the court of the king of the English, contrary to the canons.

The king, who was by no means uncertain about this election, since the man held no ecclesiastical title and had received no sacred order beyond the clerical state, arranged through faction that he should immediately become a subdeacon and receive a canonry in the Church of Rouen, although up to that point he had conducted himself entirely as a military man.

When everyone had consented to receive him, only Master Anselm dissented from his election. He was a man who was the light of all France—or rather of the Latin world—in the liberal disciplines and in tranquil conduct. He knew the man’s character from reliable authorities, while we, although unwilling, were pursuing one unknown to us. We were indeed among those displeased with him, but, timidly fearing the others, who were our superiors, we followed their power.

### Galdric visits the pope with three abbots

Having been received and entering the city with the most empty pomp, he soon afterward urged us to hurry with him to Rome. He took along Adalbero, abbot of Saint Vincent, a man from Soissons and well educated, together with the abbot of Ribemont [commonly Ribemot], himself not without learning, and also me, who was younger both in knowledge and age. He provided the expenses for our journey.

As we set out and reached Langres, we learned by report that Pope Paschal, who had departed from the city some time before, was approaching the borders of that diocese. We remained in that town for eight days.

When the lord pope came to Dijon, the clerics of Laon—an enormous crowd whom the aforesaid elect had brought with him—went to meet him. While he was staying in that same castle, they spoke to him about the cause of their elect. The pope, already informed of the matter through the reports of many, promised that he would do everything according to the petitioners’ wishes.

The difficulty was that the elect was below the required orders, apart from the other charges which Master Anselm had already brought to the pope’s ears against him. But the pope’s household officials and relatives, having discovered the man’s wealth, welcomed him and carried him along with their praises. It is customary for men to become gentle when they hear the name of gold.

### The supreme pontiff examines Galdric’s election

The pope was therefore received into the city, and on the following day at Langres he held a discussion concerning our election. When I had read the document of the election before him—one in which his life and character were represented as more than sufficiently commendable—the pope summoned us abbots who were present, together with certain priests of the Church who had come with the elect, and began to address us, taking his subject from the document on the election that had just been read.

The gathering consisted of a distinguished and very eminent assembly: Italian bishops, men from our own country, cardinals, and other highly learned persons.

The pope first asked why we had elected an unknown man. When none of the priests answered—for some scarcely knew their letters—he turned to the abbots. I was seated between the two groups.

### Guibert reluctantly speaks before the pope

Since both groups remained silent in response to the question, they began pressing me from either side to speak. I was fearful because of my youth and dreaded being branded reckless in so important a place and matter; out of shame, I scarcely consented to open my mouth.

The proceedings were conducted not in the vernacular but in Latin. I therefore said, amid much embarrassment of face and heart, what suited the question being asked. In carefully composed phrases, my words were tepid, though not entirely remote from the truth: that from personal familiarity and experience we did not know the man, but that, from the goodwill of those reporting about him, we had received some favorable impressions of his character.

When the pope attempted to invalidate this by producing the Gospel testimony, “The one who saw it has testified” (John 19:35), and objected that the man had also been elected from the court—a point that he did not explicitly explain—I immediately set aside useless evasion and admitted that I could not oppose his words. This pleased him greatly, for he was less learned than his office required.

When I perceived that my defensive circumlocution carried little weight with regard to his first question, although it was very agreeable to him, I turned my words to the danger threatening the Church and briefly added that the man was not suitable for the episcopate.

Finally, he asked what orders the man possessed, and I replied that he was to become a subdeacon. Then he asked in which Church he had served. Fearing to lie, I hesitated, but my fellow abbots suggested to me that it was in the Church of Rouen. I added truthfully, however, that this had happened only recently.

At the end he asked whether the man had been lawfully born. He had plainly been told that he was illegitimate. On this point I was more steadfast than on the others, especially since I had no doubt whatever about it. The pope said:

“Do you bear witness to these matters?”

I replied, “I say nothing about the other points; but on this one I confidently affirm that he is neither a bastard (*nothus*) nor a spurious child (*spurius*).”

The lord pope did not otherwise reconsider these points when they had been raised, except as we have said. His reason for raising them one by one was not to impede the man, but that Master Anselm, who had charged him with all these matters, happened to be present. Thus, if he intended to bring them to the man’s face, he might use what he had said secretly.

The Master himself, perceiving more deeply the ambition of the pope’s household—not, I say, of the lord pope—thought it difficult to wrest Hercules’ club from his hand. Seeing the lord pope and me, if I may say so, making frivolous efforts, while the schoolmaster himself had abandoned the attempt when he saw the lords contradicting one another, he too desisted.

The entire examination was therefore immediately brought to an end, the elect was brought forward, and the lord pope granted him permission to exercise the episcopate.

When the assembly had dispersed and the pope had gone out, behold, a group of cardinals came upon me, burning with enthusiasm and saying repeatedly:

“We were very pleased with your words.”

My Lord God, you know the nature of that pleasure: it arose not so much from the elegance of my words as from the excellent expectation of the denarii from beyond [lacuna]bensium with which the man had arrived laden. For both I and my fellow abbot Adalbero of Saint Vincent carried twenty pounds each of the same coin. Perhaps that filled the great gaping expectation of those waiting, and for this reason they loved to assist him and those who assisted him.
