Finally, when they had gone away, a chamberlain of the lord pope named Peter, a Cluniac monk who had become acquainted with the man at Rouen when we sought him from the king of the English, secretly addressed me in these words:

“Since the lord pope has accepted your testimony on behalf of the man whom you wish to have, and has heard you gladly, you ought henceforth to advise your elect that he obey the lord pope’s command in everything and serve him so fully that, if need should arise, he may once again gladly hear you on his behalf and on behalf of others.”

Behold, honey smeared around the mouth of a poisonous cup. For what is better than obeying the pope’s commands? What is worse than serving men for a grace granted by God at a price? Nevertheless, I was exceedingly horrified to be the intermediary in such a matter.

### A prediction concerning Galdric

Thus, at Saint-Rufus at Anione, after he had received episcopal consecration, the text of the Gospel offered him a gloomy prediction. It read:

“Your own soul a sword has pierced” (Luke 2:35).

Certainly, when at Langres he had proceeded with the clerics to the altar of the martyr Mammes, while they sang *Te Deum laudamus* after he had received the pope’s favor, he himself opened the Gospel text for the purpose of divination. There he seized the first verse that happened to meet his eyes:

“Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26).

He immediately spread this everywhere with great boastfulness.

In word and conduct he had been remarkably unstable and remarkably frivolous. He took pleasure in speaking about military matters, dogs, and hawks, which he had learned among the English. Thus, on one occasion, when he had dedicated a certain church and I was riding with a cleric of good character to meet him, he encountered a peasant with a lance.

The bishop, who had the tiara he had worn during the sacred rites on his head, immediately removed it, spurred his horse, and charged as though intending to strike someone. To him the cleric and I replied—the cleric in ordinary speech, and I in verse:

“Not well do they agree, nor dwell in one seat:

the mitre and the lance.”

Meanwhile, the great fortune in English coin—Hanapers and Scutras—which had been badly amassed, was quickly squandered.

I certainly heard from the aforementioned Master Anselm, who had already traveled with him, now a bishop, to revisit the English, that when he arrived there, complaints about the recovery of vessels on one side and of money on the other arose wherever he turned. From this the Master understood that the wealth the man had displayed had been taken from others, not acquired by honest means.

## CHAPTER V

### The dreadful death of Gerard of Carisi, inflicted at Galdric’s command

After nearly three years of his consecration, he marked his time in the following way.

One of the city’s nobles, Gerard by name, castellan of the monastery of nuns, was a very energetic man. Although he appeared short in stature and thin in body, he had great liveliness both of tongue and spirit, and such keenness in the practice of arms that he inspired fear and the respect of many throughout the provinces of Soissons, Laon, and Noyon.

The farther his integrity extended in every direction, the more sharply he sometimes bit those around him with unrestrained speech. Yet he never directed such speech against any upright person. [Note: See chapter 3.]

For this reason, he began secretly to disparage that countess of whom we spoke above and openly to express his indignation. He acted most perversely in opposing Ingelrannus, the seducer of the aforesaid woman, who had raised him to power through her great resources.

Before he took a wife, he had been improperly intimate with the woman in question. After she had kept him for a long time in the place of a lover, once he had taken a wife he withdrew the reins from her pandering. The women themselves also began to quarrel with one another in shameful words.

For they knew each other’s former frivolities, and the more secretly they knew them, the more filthily they spoke. That countess therefore raged against Gerard, the husband of that woman, as one who had suffered repudiation rages against a spouse, from whose mouth she knew insults were frequently hurled at her. Since she herself was more harmful than any serpent, she became day by day more intent on the man’s destruction.

### Galdric departs for Rome, so that he might appear free from Gerard’s murder

But because God places a stumbling block before those who sin deliberately, a pretext for overthrowing him suddenly arose. Hostilities had broken out between Gerard and Bishop Galdric, and Gerard spoke improperly about the bishop and his associates.

The bishop bore this quietly, but not patiently. After consulting his own men and nearly all the city’s nobles about Gerard’s death, and after they had sworn to one another an oath of mutual assistance for that very purpose—in which certain exceedingly wealthy women also took part—he left the matter in the hands of the conspirators and hastened to the thresholds of the apostles, driven by a most wicked intention.

He was not seeking the apostles—God, you know—but wanted to avoid the appearance that he had merely arranged such a great crime while absent.

He departed around the feast of Saint Martin and, when he reached Rome, remained there until he learned that the death of the hated man had been carried out. The more Gerard was free from envy toward good men, the more he was hated by wicked ones.

The deed was accomplished in the following manner.

[Col. 0916C] Gerard is killed while praying in the church at Laon.—During the octave of the Epiphany, on a Friday, while dawn was still pale with twilight, he rose from his bed, intending to go to the principal church of Blessed Mary. When he had arrived there, one of the conspiring nobles reported to him a dream of that same night, saying that it had greatly terrified him. He seemed plainly to see two bears—whether they wished to tear out his liver or his lung, I do not know—from his body. But, alas, what grief! At that time he was under exclusion from communion. The cause of his exclusion was this.

A certain monk living at Barisiac of Saint-Amand had taken into his household, for the purpose of teaching them the Frankish language, two little boys who knew only German. Barisiac, together with its dependent villages, lay under his advocacy. Seeing that the boys were handsome and knowing that they were not of obscure birth, he seized them and compelled their ransom. Their mother also sent him, along with the agreed money, a tunic made of foreign-marten fur, which the boys called a *renon*.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] A type of garment, so called because it covers only the kidneys.]

Wearing this Tyrian garment over his cloak, he came on horseback to the aforesaid church with several mounted men. When he entered and stopped before the image of the crucified Lord, while his companions went here and there among the various altars of the saints and the servants of the conspirators kept watch, word was brought to the bishop’s household that Gerard of Carisiac had come to the church to pray—for he was so surnamed because that castle belonged to him.

They therefore seized swords from beneath their cloaks. Rorigo, the bishop’s brother, came through the crypt (98), which surrounds the head of the basilica, and reached the place where Gerard was praying. He was leaning against a certain column, called a pillar, with several columns standing between it and the pulpit, approximately at the middle of the church. Since it was still dark morning and scarcely anyone could be seen in the vast church, they seized the praying man from behind.

He was indeed (99) praying, with the skirts of his cloak thrown back behind him and his palms joined at his breast during prayer. One of them therefore tightened the cloak from behind and sewed him into it so that he could not easily move his hands. When the bishop’s steward had suddenly seized him in this condition, he said to him: “You are captured.” But when Gerard looked at him with his customary fierceness—he was one-eyed—he said: “Go away from here, obscene lecher!” The other then said to Rorigo: “Strike!”

Rorigo drew his sword to the left and wounded him between the very boundaries of his nose and forehead. Feeling that he had been struck, Gerard said: “Take me wherever you wish.” Then, as they attacked the man with repeated blows and began pressing him hard, despairing of his own strength, he cried out: “Holy Mary, help me!” After these words, under the extremity of his endurance, he fell.

The conspirators wound Gerard’s body with many blows and cut it into pieces.—Among the conspirators were two archdeacons of the church together with the bishop, Walter and Guido. Guido himself was also treasurer, and had a house situated beside the same church. From that house two servants soon rushed out; coming quickly, they joined the executioner. For the sacrilegious oath had been confirmed in this way: if any of the bishop’s household should dare to act, helpers would immediately emerge from that house.

When they had cut his neck and legs, among his other wounds, and he groaned in the middle of the basilica under the extremity of his anguish, the few clerics who were then in the choir, together with certain little women who were wandering here and there for the sake of prayer, murmured and stiffened with dreadful fear; they did not dare even to utter the slightest protest.

When this had been done, those two excellent soldiers returned to the episcopal palace. With them the nobles of the city, the betrayers of their own betrayal, immediately gathered, and the archdeacons likewise joined them. The royal provost, therefore, a very able man named Yvo, summoned the royal men and the burghers of the abbey of Saint John, whose advocate Gerard had been. He besieged, plundered, and burned the houses of those who had conspired, and expelled them from the city. The archdeacons, therefore, together with the nobles, pursued Gerard’s killers everywhere, while they pleaded fidelity to the absent bishop as a pretext.

## CHAPTER VI

Galdricus wins over the pope with gifts. Guibert speaks to the people about the murder.—The bishop, remaining in Rome and rejoicing as though in the presence of the apostolic lord, waited with attentive ears to hear whether any favorable report might reach him from the regions of Gaul. At last the fulfillment of his wishes was announced to him, and the pope could not remain unaware that so great a crime had been committed in so great a church.

The bishop spoke to the pope and, by gifts accompanied by flattery, drove such suspicion of this crime away from himself. Gualdricus therefore returned from the city more joyful than usual. Since the church, which had plainly been polluted by so heinous a deed, needed reconciliation, a messenger was sent to Hubert, bishop of Senlis, who had recently been deposed because of his simony; he was summoned to perform this task.

At the gathering of the people and clergy, the dean of the church, namely Master Anselm, and the canons charged me to deliver a sermon to the people concerning that misfortune which had occurred. The substance of my speech followed this meaning:

“Save me, O God, I said, for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold” (Psalm 68:1–2).

And if until now you have suffered evils of whatever kind, the sword has now reached even to my soul. You are fixed in the mire of the deep, since, by your deserving sins, you have fallen into the ultimate evils of utter despair. In the midst of these things there is no foothold, because the honor and power of those rulers and nobles to whom you ought to have run in your dangers have collapsed.

Although your bodies have at times been oppressed by mutual hostilities, the soul was at peace, because the Church—in which the concern for salvation remained—flourished inwardly and rejoiced without any evils. The waters and the sword therefore enter the soul when tribulations and dissensions from within penetrate and defile holiness.

And what dignity do you suppose this place now possesses among you, who do not understand spiritual things, when it grants no protection even to bodies engaged in prayer? Behold: “God sent upon us the anger of his indignation, indignation and anger and tribulation, through the sending of evil angels” (Psalm 77:49).

There is the anger of indignation, and anger conceived from indignation. To be indignant, as you know, is less than to be angry. Was God not indignant at the deserts of your sins when, outside your city, you repeatedly endured plunder, fires, and killings? Was he not angry when foreign wars were transferred into this city and civil hatreds began to be carried on among us? When lords were stirred against burghers and burghers against lords by mutual provocations? When the men of the abbey plundered the episcopal men, and the episcopal men the men of the abbey, with unlawful hostility?

But because indignation and anger brought you no correction, at last he inflicted tribulation upon your hardened minds. For it was not an ordinary church defiled with Christian blood, nor a movement of wars begun elsewhere, that drove fugitives into the Church and destroyed them; rather, a most wicked desire, conceived through criminal planning, slaughtered a man praying before the image of Christ Jesus hanging upon the cross.

It was not, I say, an ordinary church, but the most flourishing of the churches of Gaul, whose fame surpasses the Latin world. And what kind of man was he? Was he not one whom both distinguished birth commended and a most distinguished, though slight, body together with a magnanimous heart had made known throughout all France for his arms?

The place, therefore, the crime, and the disgrace will be proclaimed everywhere. If, then, you are not afflicted from the heart, from the depths of your inmost being, by this pitiable event; if you do not sympathize with such great holiness when it has been dishonored, know without doubt that God will make a path for the track of his anger—that is, he will expand the rage which lay hidden into the open destruction of you.

And how do you suppose God will spare you in the enclosure of beasts, that is, your bodies, when, because of your incorrigibility, he did not spare the souls to death? Since, therefore, divine vengeance advances against us by the worst progression of steps, you must know that unless you show yourselves corrected under God’s rod, you will fall, through the internal wars that are growing up among you, into some exceedingly dreadful condition.”

Guibert declares the murderers excommunicated and thereby incurs the conspirators’ anger.—Having woven these and other matters together, at the command of the clergy and with the people’s approval, I declared that the killers of that noble man, the supporters of the same crime, and his accomplice were to be excommunicated by the bishop mentioned above, who was reconciling the church; and likewise those who offered them protection or provided them companionship.

After they had been excommunicated in the hearing of all, the church was solemnly reconciled. Meanwhile, the sentence of this anathema was carried to the ears of the archdeacons and nobles who had broken away from the city’s community. The hatred of all those outcasts therefore turned against me because of the sermon I had delivered and the pronouncement of excommunication. Above all, a great madness was kindled against me in Walter the archdeacon.

It was like hearing an immense thunderclap, though, by God’s authority, no stroke of lightning followed it. Secretly against me, publicly respectful. Let us therefore return to the matter we left aside.

## CHAPTER VI bis

The bishop comes from Rome to Laon. By royal command the episcopal household is emptied.—The lord bishop returned from Rome armed with apostolic seals and letters. After Gerard had been killed, the king, since he entirely believed the bishop to be an accomplice in this crime, which he was trying to conceal by a feigned absence, had ordered the bishop’s entire household to be stripped of grain, wine, and bacon; nor did the plunder and its cause escape him, though he was in Rome.

Letters were therefore sent to the king, who had judged that he should be removed from his see and had deprived him of his possessions. Other letters were brought by him to his fellow bishops and to the abbots of his own and other dioceses. But since we have already said that the bridge of the Eagle River marked the boundary between the Laonese and Soissons territories, as he entered, his archdeacons and nobles—whom we had previously excommunicated—hastened to meet him on the first piece of his own parish land.

He received them with such expressions of kisses and embraces that he did not consider the church of Blessed Mary, in whose service we labor by God’s authority, and which he had first encountered within the boundaries of his episcopate, worthy of a visit. Instead, he spent a long time in conversation with those whom he alone considered faithful. Departing from there, he lodged with all of them at Coucy, commonly called Codiciacum.

Gualdricus gathers soldiers and threatens to enter the city by force, but in vain.—When I learned this, and had been deeply horrified by such conduct on his part, I entirely refrained from appearing before him or greeting him. After three days, if I am not mistaken, when the madness directed outwardly but breathing inwardly toward me had subsided—for his close associates had greatly incited him against me because of the matters mentioned above—he sent word that I should come to him.

When I presented myself and saw the house full of excommunicated men and murderers, I burned with indignation. Displaying the pope’s letters, he asked me not to exert myself toward his exclusion [the text appears to lack *non*]. I falsely promised whatever assistance I could, as God knows, and not from the heart.

For I saw his true evils: he was associating with those whom his Church had excommunicated and who had so greatly defiled it; that Ingelrannus mentioned above was sitting beside him; and the aforesaid countess, who, on the day before Gerard’s death, had sharpened the swords of those two authors of his death with her own tongue, was rejoicing with their sentiments [f.: *eorum affectibus*].

Because he was barred from the city by royal command, he threatened with exceedingly rash boldness that he would enter it, supported by military forces, and declared that by armed violence he would accomplish what would scarcely have been possible for Caesars and emperors. He therefore assembled a body of cavalry and, as was his custom, squandered without any profit the resources of many things which he had not properly amassed.

At last, when he had achieved nothing from all those auxiliaries except something ridiculous, through intermediaries he made terms with Louis, son of King Philip, involving himself and his accomplices in Gerard’s murder, namely the city’s nobles together with both archdeacons, by means of a great heap of gifts.

The bishop Galdricus strikes with anathema those who had risen against the conspirators.—After entering the city, and holding a small assembly at Saint Nicholas of the Grove, he announced during the Masses which he celebrated there that he would excommunicate those who, after Gerard had been killed, had deprived those conspirators of their possessions and driven them from the city.

When I heard this said, I whispered into the ear of a fellow abbot sitting beside me: “Listen, I beg you, to this perversion of order. He ought to excommunicate those who polluted his church with so dreadful a crime, yet he himself exacts vengeance upon the punishers [f.: *punitorum*] of the murderers, who exact the just penalties of the crime.”

But the bishop, fearful of every good conscience, saw me muttering and thought that I was speaking about him. “What are you saying, lord abbot?” he asked. Then Walter the archdeacon, rushing forward before I could speak, said: “Proceed, lord, with what you have begun; the lord abbot was speaking about something else.”

With wiser counsel he excommunicates Gerard’s killers.—He therefore excommunicated those who had injured the fellow-members of the sacrilegious executioners, although the clergy and people detested such an excommunication. For a long time the entire city and diocese were at odds with the bishop because he had delayed for no short time excommunicating Gerard’s killers.

At last, because he knew that everyone regarded him as suspect and almost accursed, he excommunicated the authors and accomplices. But since he had promised large sums of money to those who had helped him before the king—namely the king’s close associates and the accomplices of the aforesaid assassins—when he began to withdraw his promises, who could say how many reproaches he heard publicly? None of those who had supported his side in this matter dared enter the royal court until they had redeemed their doomed heads from the death being prepared for them with much gold and silver.

Yet even he could not be accused by the Church, since it was established that the apostolic lord had excused him.

## CHAPTER VII

The depraved customs of the citizens of Laon are described.—After some time, when the bishop had gone to England to demand money from the king of the English, whom he had once served and who had formerly been his friend, the archdeacon Walter and Guido, with the city’s nobles, devised the following scheme.

Such a deep-rooted hostility had long grown up in that city that neither God nor any human lord was feared there. Instead, according to the power and pleasure of each person, the commonwealth was thrown into disorder by robberies and killings.

To begin with the pestilential head: whenever the king happened to come there, the very man who ought, by royal severity, to have demanded reverence for himself was shamefully fined first in his own affairs. Whenever his horses were led to water, whether morning or evening, his attendants were beaten and the horses were carried away.

It was also established that the clerics themselves were subjected to such great contempt that neither their persons nor their possessions were spared, but it was as one reads: “As with the people, so with the priest” (Isaiah 24:2).

But why speak of the common people? No farmer entered the city; no one approached it except with the safest escort without either being imprisoned and compelled to pay a ransom, or being arrested on some pretext and brought to trial without cause.

Let us add one example. If such a thing were done among barbarians or Scythians, it would certainly be judged the most profane act of men who have no laws.

On Saturday, when country people from various villages came there to sell their goods, the townsmen carried around the market, as if for sale, vegetables, wheat, or some other produce in a cup, bowl, or any other container. When they had offered such things to a peasant looking to buy them, he promised that he would purchase them at the stated price.

“Follow me,” the seller would say, “into my house, so that there you may see and receive the remainder of this produce which I am selling to you.” The man followed. But when they reached the chest, the faithful seller lifted and held up its lid and said: “Bend your head and arms into the chest, so that you may see that this whole quantity does not differ from the portion I displayed to you in the market.”

When the buyer, climbing onto the rim of the chest, hung forward with his belly while his head and shoulders fell into it, the good seller, standing behind him, lifted the unsuspecting man by the feet and suddenly pushed him into the chest. Then, dropping the lid upon the falling man, he safely kept him in that prison until he paid his ransom.

Such things, and similar ones, were done in the city. The leading men and their agents openly committed thefts—or rather robberies. No security was afforded to anyone who went out at night; the only possibilities were to be dragged away, captured, or beaten.

What communion is.—Considering this, the clergy together with the archdeacons and nobles, seeking opportunities for extorting money from the people, gave them through intermediaries the option of obtaining permission to establish a communion if they paid a suitable price.

The communion, a new and exceedingly evil name, was arranged as follows (100): all the registered dependants were to pay their lords once a year the customary service owed, and if they committed any offense against the laws, they were to make amends by a lawful payment.

All other exactions of dues, which are usually imposed upon servants, were to be entirely suspended. Seizing this opportunity to buy their freedom, the people buried immense heaps of silver to block the gullets of so many avaricious men. When they had been made more peaceful by this great shower of money, the recipients confirmed by sworn oaths that they would keep faith with them concerning this matter.

The bishop returns to Gaul. Dissensions arise between him and the archdeacon.—After the clergy, nobles, and people had formed a conspiracy of mutual assistance, the bishop returned from England with a very large sum. He remained outside the city for some time, moved against the authors of this innovation.

Nevertheless, serious and highly discreditable dissensions arose between him and Walter the archdeacon, his accomplice. The archdeacon spoke very improperly about his bishop concerning Gerard’s death. I do not know what the bishop was doing with the others about this matter; I do know what he complained to me about him:

“Lord abbot,” he said, “if Walter should happen to bring some accusations against me at any council, would you bear it calmly? Is he not the one who, at the time when you left your monks and withdrew to Flavigny, was flattering you openly, secretly plotting dissension, publicly striving in favor of your side, and secretly provoking me against you?”

With such words he tried to draw me against that doomed man, being conscious of his own very serious guilt and, in the judgment of everyone, fearful and suspect in every respect.

Although he claimed that he had risen with inflexible severity against those who had conspired and against their authors, at last the grandiloquent voices were suddenly silenced by a heap of gold and silver offered to him. He therefore swore that he would uphold the rights of that communion, since written documents concerning it existed at the city of Noyon, commonly called Noviomagus, and at the town of Saint-Quentin.

The king too was compelled by the people’s gifts to confirm the same thing by oath. My God, who could say how many disputes arose after he had accepted the people’s gifts and after the oaths had been given, when they sought to reduce servants who had once been emancipated from continual exaction to their former condition?

There was indeed an implacable envy of the bishop and nobles toward the burghers. Since he could not expel French liberty according to the Norman or English custom, the shepherd, forgetful of his profession, languished in the pursuit of insatiable greed. If any commoner, having been brought to trial, had been subjected to the laws under a condition not divine but, so to speak, based on a financial settlement, his property was drained to the very end.

The debasement of the coinage.—Since the acceptance of gifts is usually followed by the overthrow of all judgment, the minters, knowing that if they offended in their office they could be saved by a monetary redemption, corrupted the coinage with such extensive fraud that many people were thereby reduced to extreme poverty.

For when they made denarii from the cheapest bronze and, within a moment, by certain wicked arts and careful work, made them shine more brightly than silver, alas! the fool was deceived. Those who parted with their precious goods for paltry value received nothing but the most impure dross.

The bishop’s patience was being purchased in this matter, and through it misery was hastened not only within the province of Laon but far and wide. Since he himself, lamentably and deservedly powerless, could neither preserve nor correct the coinage he had corrupted, he established the obols of Amiens—also a particularly corrupt currency—as legal tender in the city for some time.

When he was entirely unable to restrain these as well, he finally established a coinage struck in his own time and had a pastoral staff impressed upon it as the emblem of his person. These coins were secretly despised by everyone with such laughter that even the more impure currency was valued more highly.

Hence a cesspool of crimes.—Meanwhile, whenever edicts were issued concerning each successive increase of these new coins, no one was to mock the bishop’s abominable designs. This provided frequent opportunities for attacking the people, as though they had brought accusations against the bishop’s institution, and for extorting every kind of tax that could be extracted.

In addition, a monk of utterly disgraceful reputation named Theodoric, a native of Tournai, brought countless masses of silver from Flanders. Recasting everything at Laon into an utterly false coinage, he spread it throughout the surrounding province.

By means of his detestable gifts, with which he won over the avarice of the rich, he deprived the homeland of truth, justice, and prosperity, bringing in falsehood, perjury, and poverty. No hostility, no plunder, and no fires injured this province more severely, although the walls of that ancient city possessed a Roman coinage of great value.

The bishop tears out the eyes of Gerard, son of Ingelrannus. He is suspended from office by the pope and therefore travels to Rome.—But since:

> Artifice laid over [the face] sometimes violates modesty.
>
> Impiety, long concealed, cannot remain hidden when it becomes plain.
>
> As clear light penetrates glass, so it penetrates the face:

After some time, what he had done to one Gerard, obscurely and as though he had not done it, he made evident by what he did to another Gerard, giving a clear indication of his cruelty.

This Gerard was, I do not know whether he was the chief or dean of the peasants belonging to him. Because he was more inclined toward Thomas—said to be the son of Ingelrannus, whom we mentioned above, the most wicked man of all whom we have known in this age—the bishop was hostile to him in every way.

He therefore seized him, thrust him into custody within the episcopal palace, and during the night had his eyes torn out by the hands of one of his own Ethiopians. By doing this he openly subjected himself to disgrace and renewed what he had done to the earlier Gerard. It did not escape the clergy or the people that the Canon of Toledo, if I am not mistaken, forbade bishops, priests, and clerics to inflict death, judicial killing, or the mutilation of limbs. The report also offended the king.

I do not know whether it reached the apostolic see; I do know, however, that the pope suspended him from office, which I believe he did for no other reason. To crown the evil, while suspended he dedicated a certain church. He therefore traveled to Rome, where the lord pope was softened by his words and persuasion and sent him back to us with his authority restored.

Seeing that rulers and subjects alike were sharing in wickedness by deed and consent, God could no longer restrain his judgments. At last he permitted the malignities they had conceived to come openly into a frenzy which, driven headlong by pride, was shattered by God’s vengeance in an utterly dreadful accident.

He attempts to abolish the communion on the very day on which Ascelinus had betrayed the king.—He had therefore resolved to abolish the communion which he had sworn to uphold and had compelled the king to uphold by gifts. During the final, holy days of Lent commemorating the Lord’s Passion, he summoned the nobles and certain clerics and decided to press the matter.

He had called the king to this pious undertaking, and on the day before Good Friday, namely on Maundy Thursday, he had taught the king and his entire people to perjure themselves—he who had first plunged himself into that noose. For on that very day Bishop Ascelinus, his predecessor, had betrayed his king, as I have said.

On the day when he ought to have consecrated the most glorious chrism of the pontifical offices and absolved the people from their offenses, he did not even appear to enter the church. He was plotting with the king’s close associates so that, once the communion had been destroyed, the king would reduce the city’s laws to their former condition.

But the burghers, fearing their own overthrow, promised four hundred pounds to the king and his officials—or more, I do not know. The bishop, in opposition, urged the nobles who were with him to speak with the king, and together they promised seven hundred.

King Louis, son of Philip—. . . . [uncertain: *persona*] conspicuous, so that he seemed suited to royal majesty alone; vigorous in arms, impatient of inactivity in affairs, fearless in spirit amid adversity, and otherwise a good man—was not entirely just in this matter, because he lent too much ear and attention to persons degraded and corrupted by greed. This redounded to his great detriment and disgrace and to the destruction of many, as is known to have happened both here and elsewhere.

The king’s desire therefore turned, as I have said, toward the better promises. With the king thus ratifying, against God, the annulment of all their oaths, namely those of the bishop and nobles, they were cancelled without any regard for honesty or for the sacred days.

That night, because of the most unjust disturbance which he had inflicted upon the people, the king, who had lodging outside, was afraid to sleep anywhere except within the episcopal palace. The king departed very early in the morning, and a promise was made to the nobles by the bishop that they need not fear concerning so large a payment, since he knew that the king would pay whatever they had promised.

“If I do not do what I promise you,” he said, “hand me over to royal imprisonment for redemption.”

The communion is dissolved and everything in the city is thrown into confusion. The burghers decide to attack the bishop violently.—When the bonds of the aforesaid community had been broken, such fury and such bewilderment seized the hearts of the burghers that all officials abandoned their offices, the shops of shoemakers and cobblers were closed, and no merchandise was displayed by the tavern-keepers or innkeepers, since they expected nothing to remain for their masters who were plundering them.

For immediately the bishop and nobles assessed everyone’s property, and whatever each person was known to have given to establish the communion, he was required to spend again in order to destroy it.

These matters were discussed on Good Friday, which is interpreted as “Preparation,” and on Holy Saturday. On those days, when minds ought to have been preparing to receive the Lord’s body and blood, they were prepared on one side for murder and on the other for perjury.

What more need be said? During those days the bishop and nobles devoted all their attention to stripping the possessions of their inferiors. But the anger of the inferiors, now ferociously provoked into madness, conspired unto the death—or rather the murder—of the bishop and his accomplices, having exchanged an oath with one another.

It is said that forty men had sworn to this. Their plot could not be completely concealed. When Master Anselm learned of it, late in the day on Holy Saturday, as the bishop was going to bed, he sent him word not to go out for the nocturnal vigils, knowing that if he came he would be killed.

But the bishop, exceedingly stupid as a carved image, said: “What? Am I to perish at the hands of such men?” Although he despised them in words, he nevertheless did not dare to rise for the vigils or enter the basilica.

The next day, when he himself was following his clergy in procession, he ordered his household servants and certain soldiers to carry swords behind him beneath their clothing. During the procession, when a slight disturbance began to arise, as commonly happens amid a crowd, one of the burghers emerged from the crypt. Thinking that the sworn murder had begun, he started shouting loudly, as though giving the signal: “The communion! The communion!” repeating the words.

Because it was a feast day, the disturbance was easily suppressed, but it aroused suspicion in the opposing party. After the bishop had completed the Mass, he summoned a large crowd of peasants from the episcopal estates, fortified the church towers, and ordered his household to be guarded, even though he found those men themselves scarcely less hostile, since they knew that the heaps of coins he had promised the king would have to be drawn from their own purses.

The station at Saint Vincent. Guibert’s grain is plundered.—On the Monday after Easter it is customary for the clerics to go out to hold the station (101) at Saint Vincent. Since they realized that they had been forestalled the previous day, they decided to make their attempt on this day, and they would have done so if they had known that all the nobles were with the bishop.

They found one of the nobles in the suburb, an innocent man who had recently taken as his wife a young cousin of mine, a woman of modest character. But, lest they make the others more cautious, they did not wish to attack him.

When the third day of Easter had arrived, the bishop, having become more secure, allowed those whom he had placed in the towers and household for his protection and compelled to live there at his expense to depart.

On the fourth day, because he had plundered my grain and several sides of bacon, which are commonly called *bacones* (102), by means of his fire, I went to him. I appealed to him to rescue the city from so great a storm. He replied:

“What do you suppose they can do amid their own disorder? If my Moor John were to pull the nose off the most powerful man among them, would he dare utter even a grunt? Yesterday I compelled them, for as long as I live, to renounce by oath the thing they called their communion.”

What was I to say? When I saw that the man was thoroughly carried away by arrogance, I refrained from saying more. Before I left the city, however, we disagreed with one another in a grave mutual rebuke because of his instability. Although many warned him of the impending evil, he deigned to heed no one.

## CHAPTER VIII

The killings of the nobles and the fires of the city of Laon.—The next day, Thursday, while he was spending the afternoon in discussions with the archdeacon Walter about the collection of money, suddenly a tumult arose throughout the city, with people shouting “The communion!”

Then the burghers entered the episcopal household in a great crowd, passing through the middle of the basilica of Blessed Mary and through the doorway by which Gerard’s killers had entered and departed. They carried swords, two-edged axes, bows, axes, clubs, and spears.

When the nobles learned of this unprecedented undertaking, they hastened from every direction to the bishop, to whom they had sworn that they would bring assistance if such an attack occurred. In this rush, Guinimarus the castellan, a noble man of handsome appearance and advanced age, innocent in character, came running through the church armed only with a shield and spear.

As soon as he entered the bishop’s courtyard, a certain Rainbert, who had also been his godfather, struck him in the back of the head with a two-edged axe, and he was the first to fall.

There was no delay before that Rainerius whom I mentioned above—the man whom my cousin had married—hurried to enter the palace himself. He was struck from behind by a spear as he tried to enter, leaning against the platform of the episcopal chapel; he was thrown down there, and immediately afterward the fire of the palace burned him from the groin downward.

Ado the vicedominus, fierce in threats and still fiercer in spirit, because his isolation at that moment had made him less effective amid so many men, was attacked by the entire force as he made his way toward the bishop’s house. He resisted with spear and sword so vigorously that in an instant he felled three of those pressing against him.

Then, having climbed upon the dining table of the hall, while they had already wounded his knees, among his other bodily wounds, he leaned upon those same knees and defended himself against the besiegers, stabbing them on every side for a long time, until someone pierced his exhausted body with a weapon. Shortly afterward the fire of those houses reduced him to his final ashes.

The bishop flees into an underground place of the church.—When the insolent mob attacked the bishop and was throwing itself down before the walls of the hall, the bishop, together with some who were helping him, resisted as long as he could with stones and blows from arrows. He displayed, as he had once done, and as he did now, much of his customary vigor in arms.

But because he had wrongfully and uselessly taken up another sword, he perished by the sword. Unable to withstand the reckless assaults of the populace, he put on the clothing of one of his servants, fled into the church’s cellar, and hid himself inside a small storeroom. A faithful servant blocked the entrance with his body and shut him in, so that he thought he was concealed.

As they ran here and there shouting, “Where is he?”—not “the bishop,” but “the gallows-bird”—they seized one of his boys, but could accomplish nothing from his loyalty that pleased them. When they laid hands on another, they learned by the sign of a traitor where he was to be sought.

They therefore entered the cellar, searched all around, and at last found him in the following manner.

Teudegaldus was a most infamous man, enrolled among the dependents of the church of Blessed Vincent, and for a long time an official and provost of Ingelrannus of Coucy. Watching the temporary toll collections at the bridge called Soordi, he would sometimes lie in wait for the small number of travelers, and, after stripping them of everything they possessed, so that they might never be able to bring a complaint against him, he would throw them out into the river and drown them [Note: [Col. 0927D] He submerged them. Hence the French *plonger*]. God alone knows how often he did this. Since it is impossible to enumerate his thefts and robberies, he displayed upon his terrible face, so to speak, the immoderate wickedness of his heart. Having incurred Ingelrannus’s displeasure, he had transferred his entire allegiance to the commune of Laon. Thus the man who had once spared neither monk nor cleric nor pilgrim—indeed, no person of any sex—finally prepared himself to kill the bishop. He was the leader and instigator of this wicked undertaking, and he hunted the bishop with the greatest zeal, for he hated him more fiercely than all the others.

### The bishop is slaughtered and his body exposed to insults

As they searched through each of the containers, Teudegaldus stopped in front of the little barrel in which the man was hiding. They removed the bar and repeatedly asked who he was. Although he could scarcely move his already chilled lips after being beaten, he said: “A captive.” The bishop used to mockingly call him Isengrinus, evidently because of his wolfish appearance; for that is what some people call wolves. So the criminal said to the bishop: “So this is Lord Isengrinus, put away here?”

Renulfus, therefore—although a sinner, yet Christ’s anointed—was dragged by the hair from the vessel, pierced by repeated blows, and set out in the open air in the narrow passage of the clerical cloister, before the house of Godefridus the chaplain. When he begged them most pitifully, attempting to assure them by oath that he would never again be their bishop, that he would give them limitless sums of money, and that he would leave the country, they all stubbornly continued their assaults. One of them, Bernard by name, surnamed de Brueriis, raised a double-headed axe and savagely split open the sacred—though sinful—crown of his head. As he slipped among the hands of those holding him, before he fell, another struck him beneath the eyes, transversely across the middle of the nose, and he died. [103] There they ruined his body, hacked at his legs, and inflicted many wounds upon him.

But when Teudegaldus saw a ring on the finger of the former bishop and could not easily pull it off, he cut off the dead man’s finger with his sword and seized the ring. Thus stripped completely naked, the body was thrown into a corner before the house of his chaplain. My God, who could recount how many insulting words passers-by hurled at the man lying there, how many clods of earth, how many stones, and how much dust were thrown upon and heaped over his body?

Before proceeding to other matters, however, we must say that something recently done contributed greatly to his destruction. Two days before his death, unless I am mistaken, he was summoned into the middle of the basilica by the leading men of his clergy, because he had recently reported them to the king, who had been established in the city, saying that clerics ought not to be revered because nearly all of them had been born from royal servitude. When this was charged against him, he denied it in these words: “May the holy Communion that I received long ago from that altar”—and he had extended his right hand toward it—“come upon me for destruction; and I invoke the sword of the Holy Spirit against my soul if I ever said these words about you to the king.” On hearing this, some were greatly astonished, and affirmed under oath that they had heard him report such things to the king. The fickleness of his mind and tongue plainly gave birth to this destruction.

### CHAPTER IX

### Radulphus is killed

Meanwhile, a section of the raging populace proceeded to the house of Radulphus, who was the bishop’s dish-bearer and had been one of the closest household members of Gerard of Chérisy. He was a man of slender appearance but possessed a heroic spirit. Wearing a coat of mail and helmet, and carrying light arms, he had intended to resist; but when he saw the overwhelming force and feared that they would set fire to the house, he threw down his weapons and exposed himself naked to their mercy in the form of a cross. With God removed from his side, they cruelly slaughtered him as he lay prostrate on the ground.

Before that execution of Gerard had taken place in the church, Radulphus had seen the following vision. He seemed to himself to be in the basilica of Blessed Mary, where men of perverse appearance had gathered and were staging strange spectacles for pilgrims, providing novel entertainments for certain people seated around them. During this display, other men came out of the house of Guido the treasurer, which stood beside the church, carrying cups containing a drink of such foulness that it was intolerable to those who smelled it; the drink was passed along the row of spectators. The meaning is clearer than daylight. How terrible a manifestation of demons appeared there, how hateful the spectacle, and how an enormous stench of crime spread everywhere from that same house is now evident. For the frenzied populace first threw figs at that lord, then rushed from there into the church, and finally seized the episcopal palace.

[Col. 0929B] ### The church and all its furnishings are consumed by fire

He also saw another portent foreshadowing his future condition. In a vision he seemed to hear his own arms-bearer announce: “My lord, your horse is of extraordinary and unusual breadth in its forepart, and so exceedingly thin in its hindquarters that I have never seen its equal.” The horse had previously been of the finest wealth and greatest value; its abundance had been reduced to the meagerness of such a ruined death. For the horse signifies worldly glory.

Thus, since this happened chiefly because of someone’s crime, the most glorious church was delivered over to pitiable destruction. From the house of the treasurer, who was also a simoniacal archdeacon, fire appeared to spread into the church. Since the church had been magnificently adorned, in honor of the solemnity then being celebrated, with hangings and carpets, it is believed that only a few of the hangings were carried away by theft rather than touched by the flames. Some carpets, however, because a few people could not easily lower the ropes from the pulleys, succumbed to the heat. The golden altar panels and the reliquaries of the saints were rescued, together with the projecting apparatus of theirs called a *repa*; I think that the rest around them was seized by the fires. For one of the more distinguished clerics had shut himself beneath it and, not daring to come out lest he fall among the wandering crowds, ran toward the episcopal chair when he felt the fire laughing around him. He broke through the glass canopy placed above it by striking it with his foot, and so leapt down.

### The monastery of Saint John, the church of Blessed Mary Profunda, and Saint Peter’s are burned

The image of the crucified Lord, most beautifully overlaid with gold and adorned with gems, fell to the ground together with a sapphire vessel suspended at the feet of the image, and was recovered only after very considerable damage. When the church and palace were burning, it was a marvelous and mysterious judgment of God: a burning ember—or perhaps a coal, I do not know—flew to the monastery of the virgins [105], set fire to the church of Saint John, and reduced to ashes also Blessed Mary’s church, called Profunda, and Saint Peter’s.

### Certain noblewomen are rescued

It is not tiresome to relate how the wives of the leading men conducted themselves amid such an upheaval. When Adon’s wife, the vicedominus, saw her husband go over to the bishop’s side after the revolt had begun, and supposed death to be imminent, she began to ask his forgiveness for anything she had done against him. They embraced one another for a long time amid lamentations and exchanged their final kisses, while she said: “Why are you abandoning me among the swords of the townspeople?” He took the woman’s right hand and, holding a lance, ordered the steward to carry a shield behind him—for the steward had been among the first of the traitors. The man not only failed to carry the shield behind him but, harshly rebuking him, struck him from behind and thrust him away. He no longer recognized the man whose servant he was, although only a little earlier he had served him at table. Protecting his wife through the middle of the crowds, he finally concealed her inside the house of one of the bishop’s porters.

When she saw the assaults and the fires set beneath the buildings, she turned to flight wherever fortune led her. After encountering several townsmen’s wives, she was seized by them, beaten with fists, and stripped of the costly clothing she wore. Scarcely was she able to reach Saint Vincent’s after putting on a nun’s habit.

My cousin likewise, when her husband departed, disregarding the household goods and retaining only her cloak, climbed with manly vigor over the wall enclosing her garden and leapt down from it. Taken in by the hut of a poor woman, she soon sensed that flames were spreading behind her. She burst toward the door, which the old woman had bolted from outside, and broke the fastening with a stone. Having obtained a habit and veil from a related nun, she covered herself and, believing that she would be sheltered among the nuns, went there. But when she saw the fires raging in that place, she turned back and withdrew to a more distant house, where she remained until the following day, when her parents found her. Then the distress she had felt from fear of death turned into even more furious anger against her husband.

Others also, namely the wife and daughters of Guinimar the castellan, together with several others, sought refuge in lowly places. The archdeacon Galterius, who was with the bishop, saw that the palace was being besieged. Since he knew that he had always added oil to the hearth, he leapt through a window of the house into the bishop’s garden, and from the wall surrounding it made his way through trackless country into the vineyards. With his head covered, he hid himself in the castle of Mont-Aigu. The townsmen, unable to find him, jokingly said that the sewers were sheltering him out of fear of them.

The wife of Roger of Mont-Aigu, lord of that place, named Armengardis, happened to be in the city that same day—for her husband was castellan of the abbey after Gerard. She and the wife of Radulphus the dish-bearer, if I am not mistaken, having taken monastic veils, made their way through the valley of Bibracte to Saint Vincent’s. The son of the aforesaid Radulphus, about six years old, was being carried by someone beneath a cloak for the purpose of rescuing him. But when a certain passer-by encountered him and looked to see what he was carrying under his cloak, he immediately cut the child’s throat between his arms.

That day and night, therefore, the vineyards lying between the two arms of the mountain became a road for fugitives, clerics, and women. A man did not fear wearing women’s clothing, nor a woman men’s clothing. So great, moreover, had been the movement of the fires set on either side, with the flames twisted in these directions by the gusts of wind, that the monks feared that all their possessions would be burned. The fear of those who had taken refuge there was so great that it was as though swords were hanging over their necks.

Blessed was Guido the archdeacon and treasurer, who was absent from this affair. He had gone before Easter to pray at Sainte-Marie of Versiliac. The executioners chiefly complained of his absence.

### More are killed

After the bishop and the leading nobles had been killed in this way, the attackers turned their attention to the houses of the remaining survivors and laid siege to them. They spent the whole night attacking the house of Guillelmus, son of Haduinus, who had not joined the citizens in Gerard’s death but had gone with him to the church early that morning to pray and be killed. When they pressed against the wall, attacking it from one side with fire and from the other with axes and spears, while those inside resisted with the utmost ferocity, the defenders were finally forced to surrender. By a marvelous judgment of God, although they hated this man more than the others, they put him in fetters safe and unharmed. They did the same to the castellan’s son.

In Guillelmus’s house there was also a young man named Guillelmus, the bishop’s chamberlain, who had earned great distinction in that defense. After the house was captured, the townsmen who had besieged it confronted him and asked whether he knew if the bishop had been killed. He replied that he did not know. For some had killed the bishop, while others had stormed the house. When, while searching around, they found the bishop’s corpse, they asked the young man whether he could establish by some sign that the body lying there was indeed the bishop’s.

His head and face had been so altered by the many mutilations that he could not be recognized. But the young man said: “I remember that, while he was alive, he often spoke about military matters, in which he took an excessive interest to his own detriment. During a mock battle, when he was playfully attacking a certain soldier while riding on horseback, that horseman struck him with a spear and broke beneath his neck the object called a *canola*.” They searched and found the knot of the scar.

### Abbot Adalbero is prevented from carrying out the bishop’s body; the bodies of the saints are burned in Saint John’s church

When Adalbero, abbot of Saint Vincent’s, heard that the bishop had been killed and wished to go there, he was immediately told plainly that if he entered the mad crowd, he too would soon suffer the same slaughter. Those who took part in that affair certainly maintain that day continued into the following day without interruption, so that it showed no sign of the darkness of night’s setting. When I objected that the brightness of the fires had caused this, they affirmed under oath—and it was true—that the fires had been smothered and consumed during the day. The fire in the monastery of the virgins, however, prevailed so strongly that it burned some of the bodies of the saints.

### CHAPTER X

### At last the bishop is buried in Saint Vincent’s church outside the city

On the following day, since scarcely anyone passed the bishop’s body as it lay there without throwing something at it, insulting it, or cursing it, and since no one thought about burial, Master Anselm—who, while the revolt raged the day before, had hidden himself completely—addressed a plea to the authors of this tragedy. He asked them to allow the man to be buried, if only because he had borne the name and insignia of a bishop. They scarcely agreed.

Because he had lain naked on the ground with the vileness of a dog from the evening hour of Thursday until the third hour of the following day, he was finally ordered by the master to be lifted [110] and carried to Saint Vincent’s with a coarse woolen cloth thrown over him. It cannot be said how many threats and insults were directed at those caring for the burial, nor how many curses were hurled like stones at the dead man himself. [111]

When he was brought to the church, he received none of the rites that would have been appropriate—not, I do not say, for a bishop, but for a Christian. The earth was only half-dug as a place of burial, and the body was forced inside beneath a short plank, so tightly compressed that his chest and belly were almost crushed to the point of cracking. Since, as I have said, he had wicked men as those who prepared his body, the people present still urged them to handle the wretched corpse as brutally as possible. No divine office was performed by the monks in that church that day. But why do I say “that day”? Rather, for several days, since they were anxious about the safety of those who had fled to them and were also afraid for their own lives.

### Many noblemen are committed to burial; Radulphus, archbishop of Rheims, celebrates Masses for the dead

Without delay, the wife and daughters of Guinimar the castellan—an extremely noble family, and a painful thing to say—brought his body themselves, pushing and pulling it in a cart. Afterwards Rainerius was brought in a similarly pitiable manner by one of his own peasants and a noble young female relative. His lower body having been recovered somewhere, he was placed between two wheels upon an axle, while the upper part of his thighs still crackled from the fires.

A good report was found concerning these two, as the Book of Kings says (1 Kings 14:13), so that all who thought rightly mourned their deaths. They had done no wrong anywhere, except for their association with Gerard’s killers. Consequently, they were buried amid far greater compassion than their bishop.

The remains of Adon the vicedominus, very few of them, were found several days after the revolt and fire. Bound together in a very narrow cloth, they were preserved until the day on which Radulphus, archbishop of Rheims, came to Laon to reconcile the church. When he came to Saint Vincent’s, he celebrated solemn Masses for the bishop and his accomplices for the first time, although many days had passed since their deaths.

Radulphus the dapifer, who had died on the same day as the others, was brought by his old mother with his little son and buried as best they could; the son was placed upon his father’s breast.

### During the solemn celebration of Mass, the citizens are dissuaded from the commune

The venerable and wise archbishop, after moving certain bodies of the dead to a better place and performing the divine offices for all of them, despite the immense grief of their relatives and kin, preached during the Masses against those execrable communes in which servants violently withdraw themselves, contrary to right and law, from their lords’ authority.

“Servants,” says the Apostle, “be subject to your masters with all fear” (1 Peter 2:18). And lest servants plead the harshness or greed of their masters, let them hear further: “not only to the good and gentle, but also to the perverse” (ibid.). The authentic canons plainly condemn with anathema those who teach servants to disobey their masters for the sake of religion, or to evade them in any way, much less to resist them (Council of Gangra, canon 3).

This too is evidence of the same principle: no one is admitted to the clergy, to the sacred orders, or to monastic life unless he is regarded as free from servitude; once admitted, however, he must in no way be held against masters who demand him. On this matter he had also argued many times in the royal court and frequently elsewhere in various assemblies.

We have said this by way of anticipation; now let us return to the proper order.

### CHAPTER XI

### The depredations and frenzied cruelties of Thomas of Coucy

When the wicked citizens considered the magnitude of the crime they had committed, they wasted away in great fear, dreading the king’s judgment. Thus, instead of seeking a remedy, they added a wound to their wound. They decided to summon Thomas, son of the man of Coucy, whose castle was Marna (Marne), as protection for their defense against royal attacks.

From the beginning of adolescence he had made raids upon the poor and upon pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem, and had strengthened himself through incestuous marriages. He appeared to have attained enormous power for the destruction of countless people. His cruelty has been so unheard-of in our times that some men who are themselves considered cruel seem gentler in the killing of animals than he was in killing human beings.

For he did not merely kill people with the sword in the ordinary and straightforward manner, on account of some definite offense, as is customary; he killed them by disemboweling them through dreadful tortures. When he compelled captives to pay ransom, he would hang them by the testicles with his own hand. Often, when he had torn away the mass of their bodies, the corresponding discharge of their vital organs was not long delayed. He would suspend another by the thumbs or by the genitals themselves, place a stone upon his shoulders to weigh him down, and walk beneath him. When he could not extort from them what he wanted, he would rage with clubs over their bodies until they promised what pleased him or died in their torments.

No one can say how many perished in his prisons from hunger, wasting disease, and torture, or in his chains. Certainly, two years ago, when he had gone to the mountain of Soissons to bring aid to someone against certain peasants, three of them hid in a cave. When he reached the mouth of the cavern with his lance, he pressed the weapon against the mouth of one of them and drove it in so that, after piercing the entrails, the iron of the lance emerged through the anus. Why should I pursue the countless examples? Two others who remained there died by his hand.

One of the captives was also unable to move because of a wound. Thomas asked the man why he did not walk more quickly. He replied that he could not. “Wait,” Thomas said; “I will make you hurry with difficulty.” Leaping down from his horse, he cut off both the man’s feet with his sword, and the man died.

I shall not weave together further examples of such abominations, since another occasion no less suitable for recounting them awaits us. Let me come to the matter at hand.

### The country people, or peasants, plunder the city of Laon

Thomas had long kept Gerard’s killers under excommunication, yet had long supported them; he honored every kind of criminal, to whom that saying of Sallustius applies more than to Catiline: he was evil and cruel without cause. To him, therefore, as the culmination of their evils, they sent requests that he come to them and defend them against the king. At last he came, and they received him in the city.

After hearing their petitions, he consulted his men about what ought to be done. They unanimously replied that, after holding the city so long, their forces were not sufficient for a confrontation with the king. He had not dared to reveal this counsel to the madmen while he was still in their city. He therefore told them to go out into the open country, where he would disclose his plan.

When they had gone nearly a mile from the city, he said to them: “Since this city is the kingdom’s capital, I cannot hold it against the king. But if you fear the royal forces, follow me into my land and use me as your patron and friend.” These words left them utterly terrified.

Immediately, driven mad by fear of the crime they had committed and supposing that the king was hanging over their necks, an innumerable crowd fled with him. Teudegaldus, the bishop’s killer, was among them. He had searched through the ceiling-panels and vaults of the church of Blessed Vincent and the recesses of the cloister with his sword drawn, looking for fugitives to kill. Wearing the episcopal ring on his finger, he proclaimed himself a bishop.

He and his accomplices, not daring to return to the city, followed Thomas, who was almost empty-handed. Thomas had released in the city Guillelmus, son of Haduinus, and others whom he had captured, for Guillelmus had had no part in Gerard’s betrayal.

But the news, spreading with the speed of Pegasus, stirred up the people of the neighboring villages and towns by announcing that the city had been left empty of inhabitants. Then all the country people rushed upon the deserted city and seized houses full of goods, since no one was defending them.

The citizens, although wealthy, had presented themselves in poor clothing. They did not wish to provoke the eyes of the leading men against them.

At that time, the aforesaid unlawful and incestuous wife of Ingelrannus, although in her old age and because of her bodily bulk she was rejected by Ingelrannus under the pretense of continence, could not give up her former habit of lovers. She loved a suitable young man, but Ingelrannus completely barred him from conversation with her. She suddenly drove the man mad with such powerful seductions that she summoned him to herself, installed him in her house, and gave him her little daughter in a betrothal intended to conceal their wicked love. She also made him the defender of her land against Thomas, whom Ingelrannus—the man called her father—hated beyond reconciliation and whom he wished entirely to disinherit.

Since the young man was at that time in Coucy and had declared in every way that he would be Thomas’s enemy, he nevertheless lacked the resources from which he could undertake so much. Then the fortune of this undertaking came to him.

### Ingelrannus and Guido again ravage the city

When Ingelrannus and Guido—for that was his name—heard that Thomas had left the city and that the people had followed him, they went to Laon. They found the houses without people but filled with every abundance. There was such a quantity of goods that, if those in charge had guarded them carefully so that parasites and thieves did not wastefully carry them off, the effort to destroy the aforesaid young man would have been made in vain, and he himself would never have suffered want in his life.

Who could say, or by saying make anyone believe, how much money, clothing, and food of every kind was found there? The rustic population and the suburban inhabitants had come, as had the people of Mont-Aigu and of Pierrepont, and also those of Féran, before the men of Coucy. It is astonishing to say what the earlier arrivals found and carried away, while our more recent arrivals boasted that they had found everything clean and almost untouched.

But what restraint or moderation can be expected among gluttons and buffoons? Wine and grain, when they found them, had no value in their eyes; and since such people had no taxes to pay there, they squandered the goods in dreadful wantonness. A quarrel therefore began to arise among them over the proceeds of the plunder, and whatever had been seized by lesser men passed into the possession of the powerful. If two men encountered a third, he was robbed.

Such, then, was the wretched state of the city. Those who had fled from it had plundered and burned the houses of the clerics and nobles whom they hated. But now the remaining nobles condemned the houses of the fugitives, down to the hinges and bolts, together with all their possessions and utensils.

Not even a monk, therefore, could safely enter or leave the city without either being deprived of his horse or stripped of his own clothing. Guilty and innocent alike had gathered at Saint Vincent’s with much money. What swords were drawn there against the monks—not so much desiring their wealth as their persons!

There Guillelmus, son of Haduinus, forgetful of the deliverance God had granted him, allowed one of his godfathers to be condemned. He had shortly before promised this man immunity of limb and life and had received him into his protection in good faith; the man had been held by the servants of the nobles Guinimar and Rainerius, who had been killed. The son of the aforementioned castellan tied him by the feet to a horse’s tail. After a short distance, his brains had spilled out, and he was carried away on a fork.

His name was Robert, surnamed Manducans, a wealthy and respectable man. The vicedominus’s steward, whom we mentioned above and whose name, unless I am mistaken, was Ebrardus—the servant who had betrayed his master although he had eaten with him on that very day—was hanged aloft. Others too were put to death by these methods.

It is impossible to explain everything that happened everywhere in the punishment of those who had overturned or been overturned. It should be known, however, that Thomas came into the city on the day after the killings—that is, on Friday—and departed on Saturday; and on that very Sunday God immediately inflicted punishment for so great a crime.

[Col. 0936A] ### The vices of Galdricus are displayed [112*]

These things happened in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1112, on the Friday of Easter, the third day before the Kalends of May.

The bishop himself was a man of infinite levity, so that even if he thought of anything foolish or secular, he would very easily give it expression with his tongue. Certainly, I saw that cousin of mine whom I mentioned earlier, when she had recently married in the city and was conducting herself as modestly as she could. In my hearing he called her “filthy” and “rustic,” because she withdrew from the conversations and looks of outsiders and did not thrust herself upon him in the manner of other women.

I had also composed a book about the expedition to Jerusalem. When he wanted to see it and it was brought to him, he hated it so much, because he saw that the work’s preface was inscribed under the name of my lord Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, that thereafter he could not be induced to read it, although he valued my other little works beyond all my ability. And although he appeared energetic in acquiring wealth, he suddenly spent all of it on useless causes. But these evils had ripened prematurely in his time.

### How many evils were perpetrated at Laon in that period

It must be understood that these evils increased not only through this man’s wickedness but through that of others—indeed, through the collective wickedness of the entire people. For nowhere in all France did crimes such as those committed among the people of Laon occur.

A very short time before these events, a certain priest was killed in his own house by a boy whom he treated as one of his closest attendants. While the priest was sitting beside the fire, the boy struck him from behind. Taking the body, he concealed it in a more private room and fastened the door from outside. When, after several days without seeing their master, people asked the servant where he had gone, he lied and said that the man had gone away on business, though he did not know where.

When the body could no longer be kept inside because of the extraordinary stench, the servant gathered up his master’s possessions, placed the corpse face down upon the ashes in the household hearth, and threw over it an instrument hanging above, called a drying rack [113], so that it would be thought that the machine had fallen upon and crushed him. He then fled with the possessions.

The deans of the diocese’s priests were also conducting their affairs shortly before the Kalends. A certain Burgundian priest, excessively talkative and impulsive, had accused a neighboring priest over some trivial matter. For this offense the dean demanded only six coins from him. The man took the loss very badly. When the Burgundian returned home at night, the priest who had lost the money laid an ambush for him.

As the Burgundian climbed the steps of his house with a lamp, the other struck him on the back of the head with a club. He died from the blow without making a will.

Another priest of Exosium, while he had a priest celebrating the solemn Mass and standing at the altars, ordered one of his attendants to shoot him with an arrow. Although the man was struck but did not die, the instigator and perpetrator nevertheless acted with the intention of killing and did not escape the guilt of having ordered, among Christians, the unheard-of crimes of homicide and sacrilege. Other deeds perpetrated in the same period and district are also reported.

### Portents foretelling the aforesaid disasters: a child with twins

Visions also appeared, foreshadowing the evil we have described. Someone dreamed that a lunar sphere had fallen upon Laon, signifying a sudden calamity that would come upon the city.

One of our own people also dreamed that three enormous beams had been placed in a row before the knees of the crucified figure in the church of Blessed Mary. The place where Gerard died appeared covered with blood. The crucified figure signified the church’s highest-ranking person, whom three beams truly obstructed: a wicked entrance, the sin he had committed in Gerard, and finally that which he had committed in the populace provided an enormous obstacle to his end.

The place where he had died was covered with blood because the wickedness that had been perpetrated was erased by no repentance. Moreover, as I learned from the monks of Saint Vincent’s, something like a tumult of evil spirits and the appearance of fires in the air were heard and seen in the city during the nighttime hours.

A few days earlier, a child had also been born there with a twin upper body: that is, it had two heads and two bodies as far as the loins, each with its own arms. The upper part was therefore double, while the lower part was single. After being baptized, it lived for three days. Finally, many portents were both seen and occurred, and no one doubted that they foretold the great evil that followed.

### CHAPTER XII

### God takes vengeance for Gerard’s murder

After the storm had subsided for a time, the church gradually began to be restored through the efforts of the clerics. Since the wall beside which Gerard had been killed [the words “was killed” are to be supplied] appeared weaker than the others because of the force of the fire, they completed, at great expense, certain arches between that wall, which had been more thoroughly burned, and the outer building.

One night, when a great crash had sounded, the wall was so shaken by the force of a thunderbolt that the arches were separated from the adjoining wall, and the wall was made to lean to one side. It consequently had to be demolished from its foundations.

And, O marvelous judgment of God! What does your severity judge, Lord, concerning those whom you wished to punish—or permitted to be punished—when they punished a man standing before you and praying to you in whatever way, if you did not permit the inanimate wall beneath which these things occurred to remain unharmed? Nor was it unjust that you should have taken such an injury badly, Lord.

Certainly, if my enemy lay prostrate at my knees to ask forgiveness, and he were killed by his own enemy at my feet, all my hostility toward him would immediately be calmed because of the insult done to me. We human beings do this—and you above all, God, who are the very source of mercy.

If you crown infants entirely ignorant of you under Herod, solely because you were the cause of their destruction, can it be thought that you could harden yourself against this man, though a sinner and undeserving, who was killed to the dishonor of your name? That is not like you, infinite compassion.

[Col. 0938A] ### The reliquaries and relics of the saints are carried about, by which much money is collected for the restoration of the church

Meanwhile, according to the customary practice, whatever it may have been, the reliquaries and relics of the saints began to be carried about for the collection of funds. As a result, that merciful judge, who chastises some here and consoles others mercifully there, displayed many miracles wherever they went.

There was a magnificent phylactery, carried together with a shrine containing some memorial, in which were preserved a piece of the Virgin Mother’s tunic, a piece of the sponge applied to the Savior’s mouth, and a piece of his cross; whether it also contained hair of that same Lady, our Lady, I do not know. It was of gold and stones, with verses engraved in gold proclaiming its inner mysteries.

On their second journey they came into the district of Touraine and reached the town of a certain brigand, called Busensiacus [commonly Buzençais]. Among other things, they addressed the people concerning the calamity of their church.

When our clerics realized that the lord and his townsmen were taking the words badly and intended, once they came out of the castle, to plunder them, the man whose duty it was to preach, placed in a difficult—or perhaps elevated—position, said to the people standing there, although he himself did not believe the promise he was making:

“If there is anyone weak among you, let him come to the sacred relics. After drinking the waters touched by the relics, he will certainly be healed.”

### Miracle 1. A mute and deaf boy is healed

Then the lord and his men, rejoicing because they thought they would catch them as liars by their own words, presented to him a mute and deaf boy of about twenty years of age. No one can say how great the danger and anguish in which the clerics then stood. But while they were entreating the common Lady and her only Son, the Lord Jesus, with deep sighs, after he had drunk the sacred waters the trembling priest questioned him with—I do not know—some word. The boy immediately answered, not to the words he had been asked, but by repeating the very words spoken by the priest. For, since he had never heard what he was saying, except insofar as it was said to him, he did not understand.

Why delay? In that poor little town, hearts instantly became more generous than they had been in themselves.
