The lord of the town, who possessed only one horse, immediately offered it, while the munificence of the others almost exceeded their means. Thus they became the escorts, with great tears and praises to God their helper, of those whose betrayers they had wished to be; and they permanently bound the young man who had been healed to the companionship of the holy relics. I saw him here in our church at Novigentum: he was dull-witted and unskilled in saying or understanding anything. He, who faithfully carried news of so great a miracle, died not long afterward while carrying out this service.

### Miracle 2. A woman is cured of an affliction of her finger

In the city of Angers there was a woman who had married while still a little girl. During her childhood she had inserted a ring onto one of her little fingers and, so to speak, had kept it fixed there day and night, unable to withdraw it. As the young woman grew older and her flesh increased, flesh began to bulge around the ring on both sides and had almost covered the metal. Thus all hope of removing it from her finger had vanished.

When the sacred relics arrived, she came with the other women to offer something after the sermon had been delivered. As she stretched out her hand to place before the relics the silver she had brought, the ring split apart and collapsed beneath her hand before the holy objects. When the people saw this—especially the women, because the Virgin Mother had granted that woman so great a favor, one she herself had not even dared to request—it cannot be said how much money the people contributed, or, above all, how many necklaces and rings the women offered.

The region of Tours rejoiced, sprinkled with the fragrance of the virtues of the common Lady of all; but Angers boasted that it had the Mother of God in its hands.

### Miracle 3. A woman recovers after drinking water touched by the holy relics

On another occasion—I cannot clearly state in what town this occurred, though it was in the same diocese—the relics were carried by the clerics, at the urgent request of a respectable woman who had been held by a very long and no less desperate illness. After she had venerated them from the depths of her heart and drunk the sacred liquid with which they had been moistened, she recovered without delay, with Mary as her physician.

After she had honored the holy relics with the gifts due to God, and the bearer of the sacred objects had stepped beyond the threshold of the house, behold, a boy mounted on a horse and dragging a cart occupied the middle of the narrow street through which he was about to pass. The cleric said to him, “Stop until the holy objects have passed.” When the bearer had gone by and the boy began to urge on his horse, he could nowhere make it advance along the return route. The man carrying the relics looked back and said, “Go, in the name of the Lord.” At these words both horse and cart moved forward.

Behold what you accomplish in Mary, and what reverence she demands for herself.

### Miracle 4. A young man regains his hearing and speech

On the third journey they happened to arrive at a castle called Nigella [commonly Nelle]. Radulf, the lord of that castle, had in his household a young man who was mute and deaf. It was said that he possessed the art of divination—clearly from demons—and for that reason he was said to be especially loved by his master.

When the sacred relics were brought into the castle, the people honored them with rather meager gifts. The mute and deaf man, however, having learned through signs of the healing of the aforementioned mute and deaf boy—or rather, having apparently learned of the relics’ presence—gave his shoes to a poor man, went barefoot, and followed the sacred pledges as far as the monastery of Lehumnum [commonly Lihons-en-Santerre], with a contrite heart.

While he kept watch beneath the bier during the day, the hour of the midday meal arrived. Many of the clerics went to eat, while a small number remained to guard the sacred objects. When these too had gone out for a short walk beyond the church, they returned and found the man lying on the ground and suffering so violently that blood flowed from his mouth and ears with a terrible stench. When the clerics saw this, they hurried to summon to the scene of so great a miracle their companions who had gone to dine.

When he returned from the fit, I do not know by what words he was tested: he was asked whether he could speak. Immediately he replied with the same words he had heard from the questioner. All raised boundless praises to God on high; who could describe their songs of joy?

Finally, they were compelled to return to the town of Nigella with every possible prayer, so that what they had initially offered too little in honor of the sacred objects might be supplied in full. This was done magnificently. Here too the Lady glorified herself, whose Son is God, and she who had so far withheld nature’s gifts completed them.

## CHAPTER XIII

### The relics are carried to England

From there, intending to travel overseas, they came to this inland sea, taking with them some wealthy merchants aboard the same vessel. They were being carried forward favorably by the winds, when suddenly they saw pirate vessels of a monstrous kind, which they greatly feared, approaching them from the opposite direction.

As the pirates rowed toward them, sweeping the waters with their oars and dividing the heaps of waves with their prows, and when they were scarcely a stadium’s distance from our people, the bearers of the holy objects became extremely afraid of the pirates. Then one of our priests rose in their midst and, raising the phylactery in which the pledges of the King [or Queen] of Heaven were kept, forbade them to approach in the name of the Son and the Mother.

Immediately, as though obeying a command, the boats turned back toward the stern, and did so with no less speed than they had shown eagerness in advancing [the text is defective here; perhaps “having been driven off” is missing]. Hence praise among those who had been delivered; hence glory. The merchants, rejoicing and giving thanks to good Mary, offered her many valuable gifts.

### Rustics who refused to honor the holy relics are punished

Thus, after they had been carried safely to England, when they reached the city of Winchester, many miracles shone forth there. Similar things also occurred at Exchester and became the cause of many offerings.

Let us keep silent about the customary remedies for illnesses and touch upon what was unusual. We are not writing their itinerary (*odeporicum*); let them write it themselves. Nor do we select individual deeds, but rather those that are suitable for preaching.

They were received reverently, as was fitting, in almost every place. When they came to a certain village, however, they were admitted neither by the priest into the church nor by the rustics into habitable houses. They found there two buildings without inhabitants, and brought themselves and all their baggage into one, while they adapted the other for the sacred relics.

The wicked populace persisted in its obstinacy toward divine things. On the following day, when the clerics had departed from that countryside, behold, a terrifying crash of thunder sent a dreadful bolt of lightning from the clouds. It fell upon that village and reduced to ashes all the dwellings that were in it.

And, O wondrous discernment of God! Although those two houses stood among other houses that were burning, they remained untouched, so that God might give clear evidence that the same miserable men had suffered the fire because of the irreverence they had shown toward the Mother of God.

But the wicked priest, who had increased his cruelty toward the barbarians whom he ought to have taught, gathered up the belongings he was glad to have snatched from the heavenly fires and carried them away—whether to flee the lightning, I do not know, or to cross the sea. At that place everything he had collected, and everything he was trying to transport, was repeatedly consumed by lightning. Thus that uncivilized and disorderly people was taught, through its own punishments, to understand the mysteries of God.

### A sacrilegious man who stole money offered to the holy relics hangs himself

They had come to another town where, both because of the reputation and evident proof of miracles, and because offerings to the holy relics were pouring forth in abundance, a certain Englishman standing before the church said to his companion, “Let us go and have a drink.”

“But I have no money,” the other replied.

“I will provide it,” he said.

“Where will you find it?”

“I see these clerics drawing so much money from fools by lies and tricks. I shall certainly find a way to take enough from them to pay for our meal.”

He spoke, entered the church, and approached the shrine in which the relics had been placed. Pretending that he wished to venerate them with a kiss, he put his mouth to them and greedily swallowed with his lips the coins that had been offered.

Then he returned to his companion and said, “Come, let us drink, for we now have enough money for our drinking.”

“How did you obtain it,” the other asked, “when you did not have any?”

“I took it from what is given to those impostors inside the church.”

“You have done wrong,” the other said, “by taking what belonged to the saints.”

“Be quiet,” he replied, “and go to the nearest tavern.”

Why say more? They spent the day drinking until the sun descended into the Ocean [that is, sunset].

As evening came on, the man who had stolen the money from the holy altar mounted a mare and announced that he was returning home. When he reached a nearby wood, he made a noose, hung himself from a tree, and died a shameful death, paying the penalty for the sacrilege of his mouth.

Of the many things the powerful Virgin accomplished among the English, it is enough for us to have recorded these.

### An ox, driven by no one, swiftly offers itself to carry the relics

At Laon also, after they had returned from collecting offerings, a cleric of good character told me—for he had been assigned the task of transporting materials for repairing the church roof—that, while climbing a hill, one of the oxen had collapsed from exhaustion.

The cleric was laboring greatly with the ox and could find no animal to replace it in the exhausted team. Suddenly, behold, another ox offered itself at a run and arrived as though deliberately coming to help with the work.

With lively movement it brought the cart with the others all the way to the church. The cleric, however, was very anxious about to whom he should return the unknown ox. As soon as it was released, it waited neither for a guide nor for anyone to threaten it, but quickly went back by the way it had come.

### The fall of the gilded eagle placed atop the shrine of the saints

The same man who told me this also related the following. On the day when Bishop Gualdrius, having arranged Gerard’s murder, began to depart from Rome, this man—who was a deacon—was standing behind the priest at Mass.

Suddenly, on an exceptionally calm day when no winds were blowing, the gilded eagle that stood above the shrine containing the biers of the saints leapt from its place and fell as though violently struck.

At that time they interpreted the event as signifying that the principal person of the place—namely, the bishop—was destined to die. But we believe that this may also have signified what we now perceive: that the dignity of the city, which is especially royal among all the cities of France, had fallen, or rather was destined to fall further.

For in the crisis of the city that we have described, the king himself, whose greed had brought it about, did not revisit it even once. The royal provost, who was privy to the wickedness that was to be committed, left the city a few hours before the uprising began, sending ahead his concubine and children; and before he had traveled three or four miles, he saw the same city consumed by fire.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Hugh the dean is given the episcopate by the king without an election

After the bishop had been removed in this manner, they began appealing to the royal court to choose another. A certain dean of Orléans was given to him without any prior election. Since a royal referendary named Stephen coveted that deanery but could not become a bishop, he obtained the episcopate from the king for the dean and took possession of the deanery.

When the man was brought forward for consecration and they sought to read his prognostication, they found the page blank—as though it were saying: “I shall prophesy nothing about him, since he will scarcely have any future deeds.” For he died after a few months. He did, however, restore some of the episcopal houses. (114)

After his death, this man was lawfully and unwillingly elected. I say “lawfully” because he entered into the office without purchasing anything and intended to do nothing simoniacally. Yet the Gospel passage sounded harshly in his prognostication, since he received the same one as Galdricus: “A sword will pierce your soul also” (Luke 2:35). What misfortune awaits him, God will see.

### Teudegald, the bishop’s murderer, is brought to the gallows

Before proceeding to other matters, it must be said that Teudegald, the bishop’s betrayer and murderer, was captured by the soldiers of Ingelrannus two years after the killing and was brought to the gallows.

He was seized during Lent, after he had eaten and drunk almost to the point of vomiting and had boasted before certain people—something shameful to say—that he was full of the glory of God, extending and stroking his belly. Seized and thrown into prison, he sought repentance neither from God nor from man. Even when led out to punishment, he said nothing to anyone, and died with the same insensibility toward God with which he had lived.

But let us now return to the matters we passed over.

### Thomas is excommunicated

Thomas, who had joined in receiving those wicked men—the murderers first of Gerard and afterward of his own lord and kinsman, the bishop—was struck repeatedly by the archbishops and bishops of all France with frequent anathemas, not only in councils, synods, and royal courts, but afterward everywhere in the parishes and sees on every Sunday, as his unspeakable wickedness grew.

His stepmother, that woman who had rashly allied herself with Ingelrannus, possessed the spirit of a savage, cruel she-bear. Seeing Thomas emerging as though her rival, she compelled Ingelrannus to renounce his paternal affection for him and even the name of father. Thus, following a woman’s counsel, she began to deprive him of his rights and became his open enemy; to use the words of comedy, she turned a fool into a madman.

His mind, gradually saturated with ever-worsening evils, burst into such a frenzy that he asserted that right and justice consisted in regarding men as no different from beasts as they walked about. Because he was unjustly, as was indeed the case, disinherited by a little woman, he was thought justified in raging through slaughter, both on his own account and with his accomplices.

That most savage woman daily devised new schemes and procured enemies for him to overthrow; he, on the other hand, never ceased carrying out incessant raids, arson, and killings against him. In our time we have nowhere seen two persons come together whose administration produced so many evils under one cause. If he was the furnace, she may be called the oil.

Their conduct on both sides was plainly such that, although they indiscriminately spared no works of Venus, they nevertheless became no less—indeed more—cruel as soon as an opportunity was offered. Just as they never observed the rights of marriage, so their single spouses could not restrain them from rivalries involving prostitutes or foreign women.

What more can be said? While she goaded him daily with the contrivance of new schemes, and he could not satisfy his rage with the murder of the innocent—in fact, on one day he tore out the eyes of ten men, who soon afterward died—it happened that, exhausted on both sides, they made momentary truces. But shortly afterward, when that woman revived their old illnesses, they rose against one another in mutual slaughter.

### The disasters of Amiens, brought about by Count Ingelrannus and others

While the province of Laon was being shaken by the wickedness of both of them, by God’s judgment the calamity was transferred to Amiens.

For (116), after the disastrous destruction of Laon, the people of Amiens, having induced the king with money, formed a commune. The bishop ought to have offered it no support under any compulsion, especially since no one was forcing him and his fellow bishops’ miserable destruction and the conflict of the ill-fated citizens were no secret to him.

Count Ingelrannus, seeing that the ancient rights of his county were being cut down by the conspiracy of the townsmen, attacked the rebels with arms as best he could. Adam, as he was called, also did not fail him, nor did the assistance of the tower over which Adam presided.

Driven from the city by the townsmen, Adam withdrew from the city into the tower. When the townsmen attacked the count without respite and summoned Thomas, as though he were especially devoted to his lord, to the oaths of the commune, they stirred up a son against his own father, as is thought.

Thomas had a very shameful mother and therefore had always lacked his father’s affection. Meanwhile, Ingelrannus realized that tavernkeepers and butchers were mocking the dignity of his age. He summoned Thomas, made a pact with him, and, after giving countless pledges, also commended that stepmother to him with renewed affection.

She, certainly no fool and not a person of little weight, exacted from him a considerable treasure for this renewed peace.

Finally, after Thomas had exhausted the great heap of treasure he possessed, he also promised assistance to Ingelrannus against the townsmen, for whom the bishop was striving together with the vicedominus.

Thomas and Adam, who presided over the tower, therefore began to press the vicedominus and the townsmen with great force. As soon as the matter spread, Thomas attacked the church, since he accused the bishop and clergy of having formed a faction with the townsmen.

In one of the church’s villages he established a stronghold for himself, from which he soon destroyed the others by fire and plunder. From one of them he carried away a very large crowd of captives and much money. The remaining people, of mixed sex and various ages—a very large group that had taken refuge in the church—he burned alive when he set fire to the church.

Among the captives was a hermit who had come to the village to buy bread. He was led before Thomas. The following day, as it happened, was the feast of Saint Martin. The hermit tearfully called out to Thomas, asking what his profession was and why he had come there, and begged him at least, for the honor of Saint Martin, to have mercy on him.

Thomas drew a dagger from its sheath, pierced his breast and entrails, and said, “Receive this for Saint Martin.”

He had likewise thrust a leper into prison. When a group of lepers from the region heard of this, they surrounded the tyrant’s door, shouting that their companion should be returned to them. He threatened them that, unless they withdrew, he would burn them alive.

When they fled in terror, they gathered together in safety, opposite him, and called upon God as their avenger. With one voice and loud cries they cursed him. The leper, however, died in that penal prison.

A pregnant woman was likewise confined in the prison and died there. Some of the captives were slow in setting out. Thomas ordered the objects they call *canolae* to be pierced beneath their necks, and had ropes—six of them, unless I am mistaken, or five—inserted through them. Thus he made them travel under a cruel burden. Shortly afterward they died in custody.

Why prolong the account? In that affair alone he killed thirty men with his own sword.

When his stepmother saw the man involving himself in such dangers, she ordered the vicedominus, eager to destroy him, to watch Thomas’s movements carefully. One night, while the vicedominus had surrounded him with ambushes as he was going somewhere—I do not know where—Thomas was pierced by wounds throughout his body and received a lance thrust from an enemy on foot even in the back of his knee.

Severely wounded in several places, especially in the knee, he was forced, willingly or unwillingly, to abandon what he had begun.

### Failures during the sacred rites foretell disasters. Bishop Godefrid of Amiens resigns the episcopate; he lives for a time at Cluny and the Carthusian house, then returns at the command of the archbishop of Reims

Before his church suffered such destruction, the bishop was one day preparing to celebrate Mass on a feast day. A priest who appeared religious, however, had unknowingly prepared the sacrament before him from water alone; afterward the same thing happened to the bishop.

When the bishop took the offering and realized that it was nothing but water, he said, “Know for certain that a great evil threatens this church.” The misfortunes that had already befallen the priest confirmed this very thing.

When he saw that his presence was welcome neither to the clergy nor to the people, and that he was able to help no one, he took one of our monks and, without consulting his clergy or people, submitted what I may call a letter of repudiation. He returned his ring and sandals to the archbishop of Reims and announced on both sides that he would go into exile and would never again be a bishop.

Having thus become an ex-bishop, he reached Cluny and, once again voluntarily made a bishop, consecrated an altar there. From there he departed and went to the Carthusian house, about which we spoke at the beginning of this little work.

There he lived outside the community in a cell and retained six marks of silver from his travel allowance. After two months, he was recalled not by any of his own people but by the archbishop, and he did not delay his return; he knew that the marks would be useful to him for this purpose.

The clergy and people received him with sorrow. While he was absent, they had not failed to work toward choosing another, without greatly honoring him. He himself had stirred up a crowd that he could not calm.

Thomas having thus turned to his own affairs and already acting helplessly because of the wound mentioned above, Adam’s son, named Adelelmus, a most handsome young man, had betrothed Thomas’s daughter as his future wife. Thomas had already injured Adam, and Ingelrannus’s disgraceful concubine prepared to turn her weapons against Adam’s tower.

Thomas himself had until then stood in Ingelrannus’s allegiance against the townsmen. He therefore hired the king and surrounded the tower with a siege.

Adam had indeed rendered homage to the king, had not deserted him, and the king had received him into his allegiance. The killings committed by the men of the tower against the townsmen, both before and after the siege, cannot be adequately reported by anyone—not even by those whose side was endangered. Among the townspeople there was no action, but only suffering.

Bishop Godefrid would easily have stopped the evil when it first began, as everyone knows, had he not feared the vicedominus, who had always held him in the greatest contempt. It is plainly that man’s habit to respect no one and to show kindness to no one unless that person either speaks ill of him or does harm to him. While he fears being wounded by one man and deliberately strives to please the most treacherous, by the just judgment of God he is torn apart above all by that very man and by everyone.

### The archdeacon Walter is murdered by the deceit and command of Count Thomas

Thomas was unable to help the tower, within which he had left both his daughter and the best of his soldiers. He had committed such great evils everywhere that the archbishops and bishops, presenting a complaint to the king on behalf of the churches, declared that they would not perform God’s offices in his kingdom unless he took vengeance on Thomas.

At that time, when that pestilent man was striving against Ingelrannus with the townsmen, Walter, whom we mentioned above—the only one besides his fellow archdeacon Guido to remain among Gerard’s betrayers—had gone, around the middle of Lent, to speak with that good woman who was Ingelrannus’s close relation, namely his uterine sister, with whom he himself had arranged an adulterous union.

When Thomas learned of this, he sent an extremely swift messenger and ordered a certain Robert, the most wicked of all—for such are the servants he loves—to watch for Walter on his return from Amiens and kill him if possible.

Robert, watching from the Laon promontory, came out with his men to meet Walter along the very hollow of the road by which one descends from the mountain. Walter had sent his entourage ahead and was following, already riding a mule into the city.

Thus, taking advantage of the solitude, they cruelly cut him down with swords. After killing him, they returned cheerfully to Thomas with the mule.

### The castle of Crécy is stormed by the king

When reports of these and similar events reached the royal ears amid the greatest grief of the churches, the following Lent, after the archdeacon had been killed, the king assembled an army against Thomas and attacked the strongholds he had built in the villages of the abbey of Saint John.

Of the cavalry, scarcely any sincerely helped the king, although they were few; but there was an utterly immense army of lightly armed men. When Thomas heard that they were gathering against him, he chattered on, even while lying completely helpless in bed.

The king warned him to destroy the adulterous castles, but he rejected the command in the most shameful manner. When the assistance of many relatives was offered to him, he mocked it.

Then the archbishop and bishops ascended a high platform, summoned the multitude, addressed them concerning the undertaking, absolved them from their sins, and ordered them, under the name of penance and secure in the salvation of their souls, to attack the castle called Crécy.

They invaded it with astonishing boldness. The fortification was of extraordinary strength, so that the entire effort of the attackers seemed ridiculous to many. While those inside devoted themselves to defense, and the first rampart had nevertheless been captured, the king stood at the castle gate and urged the townsmen to surrender the castle to him.

When they said they would not do so, he stretched out his hand and swore that he would not eat until it had been captured. Yet on that day he called off the assault.

On the following day he returned and took up arms, but scarcely any of the soldiers wished to arm themselves with him. When he accused them of open treachery, he summoned the infantry and began to stand first upon the rampart and press toward the interior. Immediately they penetrated inside, found a huge supply of provisions, seized the defenders, and demolished the town.

### Thomas finally surrenders

Not far from there was another town called Novigentum. When its keys were delivered to the king, the inhabitants fled.

At Crécy, some of the captives were hanged on gallows to terrify the defenders, while others were killed in other ways. Of the attackers, I do not know whether anyone died except one soldier.

Thomas was defending himself at the Marne. After purchasing his ransom from the king and the royal officials, and making an agreement with the churches concerning the damage he had inflicted, he restored himself on one side to peace and on the other to communion.

Thus this man, the most arrogant and wicked of all, was punished by the hand of a very poor man whom he had often punished and despised.

This must not be omitted: when the king came to Laon with his army, unseasonable mildness of the weather had made everything difficult. Then the archbishop said to them, “Let us pray to God that, if he wishes what we have proposed to be accomplished, he may grant clear weather.” As soon as he said this, the sky immediately cleared.

### Bishop Godefrid returns from the Carthusian house; after laying siege to Amiens, the king tests an impregnable tower

On Palm Sunday, Bishop Godefrid returned from the Carthusian house and began to spread ideas quite different from what he had learned there. He summoned the king and, on a solemn and reverent day, delivered a speech to him and to the assembled people against the men of the tower. He intended to incite them not with the words of God but in the manner of Catiline, promising the kingdom of heaven to those who perished while storming the tower.

On the following day, enormous siege engines were extended before the wall of Castellion—for that is what it is called—and soldiers were placed upon them. The men of the tower had concealed themselves behind curtains so that their number would not be revealed.

The bishop had gone barefoot to Saint Acheolus, but was not then to be heard on this matter.

Meanwhile the men of the tower allowed the attackers to advance against the walls and bring up their engines. When the engines had been brought into position, a certain Alerannus, highly skilled in such matters, set against them two fire-projectiles that he had prepared and arranged nearly forty women to hurl the stones that had been placed there.

The soldiers inside fought hand to hand with swords against those outside. While defending their fortifications with the courage of Achilles, they were struck by the women, who proved the equal of men: the stones discharged from the engine shattered both siege machines.

As the shower of missiles grew more intense, nearly eighty men were wounded, as has been related, and even injured the king with a projectile in his armored breast. Of those pierced by spears, no one escaped except one. This was reported by Rothardus, the bishop’s nephew, a cleric.

The soldiers hanging from the engines, seeing that they were being overwhelmed, began to flee, and immediately the others followed. When the attackers had withdrawn a little, the men of the tower rushed out, cut down the engines, and carried the timber back inside. Although they saw them from a distance, the nearly three thousand who had attacked earlier did not dare to engage them.

Seeing that the place was impregnable, the king withdrew and ordered it to be besieged until hunger forced its defenders to surrender. The siege continues to this day, and it cannot be said how many of the townsmen alone die almost every day.

Adam, stationed outside in the suburbs, also harasses Ingelrannus and the vicedominus with frequent attacks. Therefore, if trouble could grant understanding to hearing, they might know that, although Thomas has fallen, not all causes are equal, nor are God’s judgments equal toward everyone, so that the bishop may have license to provoke killings.

## CHAPTER XV

### Abbess Rainsendis is killed by her servant; a certain Anselm steals sacred vessels and defeats an innocent man in single combat

Before turning to what follows, since we shall also speak of certain people from Soissons, it must be understood that the people of Laon behave more detestably than all the provinces of France.

Those who had killed priests, the bishop, and the archdeacon recently also killed the most capable of women, the abbess of Saint John, a woman of the noblest birth and a benefactress of the Church, named Rainsendis, a native of Laon. Her own servant killed her, and she endured what she suffered for the faith of the Church.

What of the fact that that very church itself did not refrain from sacrileges? Since the Queen of all did not leave them unpunished, we appropriately pursue the matter.

The vessels used in the ministry began to be stolen by those whom they call *matricularii*, who were entrusted with the more intimate safekeeping of the church’s treasures. These thefts, however, were turned back upon their clerical masters. They were plainly laymen.

At first this was done by certain men. Then a certain Anselm, a native of the city, a monstrous and uncivilized man, stole crosses, chalices, and everything made of gold before matins, on the days immediately preceding the Lord’s Nativity.

After some time he brought a lump of the stolen gold to a merchant from Soissons to sell it. In doing so he revealed the sacrilegious theft he had committed and received an oath from the merchant that he would not betray him.

Meanwhile the merchant heard that those who knew of the loss were being excommunicated throughout the parishes of Soissons. Taking note of this, he came to Laon and disclosed the matter to the clergy.

What more is there to say? That assembly denied it. (118) Anselm, after providing sureties, attacked him in combat [perhaps, in a duel] to fight him as a champion. The other did not delay.

It was a Sunday. When the clerics, in their haste, had arranged the combat, the man who had accused the thief fell defeated.

Two things are established by this: either that the man who had betrayed the thief by perjury had acted improperly, or—which is much more likely—that he had undergone an entirely illegitimate legal process. It is certain that no canon corresponded to this law.

### Another man commits bolder thefts

After his victory, Anselm, feeling safer, proceeded to a third sacrilege. By an unspeakable device he broke into the treasury and carried away a larger quantity of gold and jewels.

After these things had been taken, and after the judgment by the sacred liquid had already been conducted, he was thrown into it with the other *matricularii*. He was convicted by floating in the water, together with the others who had first discovered the loss; some of them were brought to the gallows, while others were spared.

Dragged out as well, he promised that he would tell what had happened, but once released he denied it. Raised a second time onto the gallows, he swore that he would disclose the matter. When he was released, he said, “I will do nothing without a reward.”

“You will be hanged,” they replied.

“And you will have nothing,” he said.

Meanwhile he hurled countless insults at Nicholas, the castellan and son of Guinemar, a very noble young man, by whose hands these things were being carried out.

The bishop and Master Anselm were consulted about what should be done. “It is better,” they said, “to give him money than to lose such a quantity of gold.”

They therefore agreed to pay him nearly five hundred solidi. After this promise, he returned much of the gold that he had hidden in his vineyard.

He had promised to leave the country, and the bishop had granted him a three-day safe-conduct. During this interval he wished to escape secretly and watched all the exits from the city. On one side of the city, however, the appearance of great rivers became visible to him; invisibly set before him, they completely prevented him from proceeding.

Thus those waters plainly compelled him to depart in full view, without taking any of the fruits of his theft.

When they had reached that place, he said something extremely irrational, declaring that he did not wish to leave. As the bishop pressed him more strongly, he began, as though beside himself, to mutter that he still knew certain things he had postponed revealing.

When the bishop learned this through the vicedominus, he found an opportunity. Since Anselm had sworn that he knew nothing more, the bishop withdrew the solidi he had proposed to give him and committed him to prison.

Compelled also by punishments, he confessed that he had the jewels from the broken work in his possession. Leading them to the place, he showed them hanging beneath a stone in a little linen cloth.

With all these things he had also stolen the sacred phylacteries. As long as he kept them, he could not sleep, because the saints shook his murderous spirit and the horror of so great a sacrilege had seized him.

Thus he too was raised on high and placed with his fathers—clearly, with the devils.

## CHAPTER XVI
The wicked deeds of the mother of John, count of Soissons; also of the mother of Manasses.—Meanwhile John, count of Soissons (to turn our style now toward the promised subjects), was skilled in warfare and devoted to peace, although his sole concern was his own advantage. For his paternal and ancestral wickedness always redounded to the destruction of Mother Church.

Moreover, among the other marvels of [John’s] mother’s power [Note: [Col. 0949D] Ironically.], she had the tongue of a certain deacon cut out after it had been torn from his throat [Col. 0949C], and had his eyes plucked out. Truly, parricidal boldness had dared this. For, at the instigation of a certain Jew, she had killed her own brother with poison, out of desire for the county. For this reason the fire consumed the Jew as well; and she herself, on the day before the fast of the Head [i.e. the beginning of Lent], after having dined exceptionally well, was struck by paralysis at the very beginning of that night’s sleep, lost the functions of her tongue, and suffered the debility of her whole body. Most importantly, thereafter she had no understanding of anything pertaining to God, and from then on lived like a pig. By the just judgment of God, her tongue was also almost cut out, as though for a remedy. From the beginning of Lent until the octave of Easter, when she died, this was her condition.

Between her, this John, and Bishop Manasses, her sons, there were not merely quarrels but deadly hatreds [Col. 0949D]—and these were hereditary. For that family, in turn, holds its members mutually hostile. Certainly, when she had been carried to the tomb, while she was being buried, that same count told me about her the things related above, adding: “What,” he said, “should I give on her behalf, when she herself was unwilling to give anything for her own soul?”

Guibert wrote a treatise against the Jews against that John, a follower of Jewish perfidy.—Finally, the count himself, of whom it could rightly be said, “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16:3), not only took after both parents, but perpetrated much worse things. He so honored the perfidy of Jews and heretics [Col. 0950A] that he himself uttered about the Savior what Jews would have considered too impious for the faithful even to presume. How wickedly he set his mouth against heaven (Ps. 72:9) may be understood from that little book of mine which, at the request of Bernard the dean, I wrote against him. Since these things are unspeakable to a Christian mouth and abhorrent with execrable horror to pious ears, we suppress them. While he exalted the Jews, he was regarded by the Jews as insane: in words he approved their sects, while in practice he openly followed ours.

The count utters and does unspeakable things. The noble deed of his wife.—Certainly, on the Nativity and Passion of the Lord, and on occasions of this kind, he presented himself as so humble that we would scarcely have thought him a heretic. On Easter night he had gone into the church to keep vigil and had suggested to a certain devout cleric [Col. 0950B] that he tell him something about the mystery of those days. When the cleric had explained how the Lord had suffered and how he had risen again, the count, whistling, said: “There is a fable; there is wind. If you have taken what I have said as wind and a fable, why are you keeping vigil here?” He replied: “I gladly attend to the beautiful women who are keeping vigil here.”

Indeed, although he had a young and beautiful wife, he despised her and pursued a most wrinkled old woman with such passion that, when he repeatedly had a bed prepared for himself and for her inside the house of a certain Jew, he could never be restrained by the bedclothes. Driven by the fury of lust, he would crowd with her into some shameful corner, or certainly into some storeroom. What is more, after extinguishing the lamps at night, he once ordered a certain parasite to go to bed with his wife under the appearance of being himself, so that he might pin the crime of adultery on her. When she recognized from his bodily build that he was not the count (for the count was shamefully itchy with lust), she beat the scoundrel harshly with all the strength she could muster and with the help of her maids.

What more is there to say? He had excluded neither consecrated women nor nuns from his abuse, nor had he ever spared even the rivalry of holy brothers.

That count perished by a most impious and wretched death.—When the Virgin Mother, Queen of All, could no longer endure the blasphemies of this most foul man, as he returned from a royal expedition and was already approaching the city, an enormous ball appeared to him. He came home with bristling hair and savage mind, rejected his wife that night, and slept with the old woman mentioned above; in her company [Col. 0950D] he lay dying.

When he began to suffer distress, he consulted the cleric mentioned above, with whom he had spent the vigil, about the examination of his urine. When the cleric answered him concerning his death and confronted him with his soul and the lusts he had committed, he replied: “Do you want me to hand over my wealth to gluttonous lechers—that is, priests? Not even an obol. I have learned from many wiser men than you that all women ought to be common and that this is no sin of any importance.”

He said this, and afterward said or did nothing but acts of madness. For, wishing to push away with his foot the wife standing beside him, he struck a certain soldier—[the text lacks the word, perhaps “slap” or “blow”] [Col. 0951A]—while she was sitting there, with such force that he knocked him down.

Thus the hands of the utterly insane man were restrained, lest he throw himself and his own people into ruin, until he grew exhausted, until he had wrested from the devil the spirit that was an enemy of the most virgin Mother and of God her Son.

## Chapter XVII

Summary of the heresy of Clementius, Ebrardus, and their associates.—Since we have mentioned the heretics whom this wicked man loved, a certain peasant named Clementius lived with his brother Ebrardus at Buciacum, a village near Soissons. He was said to be one of the leaders of his heresy. That most impure count used to say of him that he had found no one wiser than Clementius [Col. 0951B].

This heresy is not one that openly defends its doctrine, but one that, condemned by continual whispers, creeps about secretly. Its summary is said to be as follows:

(120) They confess that the dispensation of the Virgin’s Son is a phantom.

They invalidate the baptism of infants who do not understand, when performed under any sponsors whatsoever.

They call their own teaching the Word of God, produced, I know not by what prolonged winding course of speeches.

They so abhor the mystery performed at our altar that they call the mouths of all priests the mouth of hell.

And if, as a veil for their heresy, they sometimes receive our sacraments among others, they treat them as a dietary restriction, so that on that day they eat nothing more.

[Col. 0951C] They do not distinguish sacred cemeteries from the rest of the ground by any special separation.

They condemn marriage and the fruitfulness of sexual intercourse.

And certainly, although they are scattered throughout the Latin world, one may see men living with women without the name of husband or wife, so that a man does not remain with one woman, nor a woman with one man, according to custom; rather, men are known to lie with men and women with women. For among them it is forbidden for men to have intercourse with women.

They expel from themselves all food that comes from sexual union.

They hold meetings in hidden underground places, or in concealed chambers [penetralia, or household shrines], with the sexes mixed indiscriminately. With candles lit, they offer the backsides of a certain little woman who, as is said, has been exposed and bent forward, to one of them under the gaze of all; then, when the candles have been extinguished [Col. 0951D], they cry out “chaos” from every side, and each man has intercourse with whichever woman first comes to hand.

If a woman becomes pregnant there, after the child has been delivered they return to the same practice.

A great fire is kindled. Those sitting around throw a child from hand to hand through the flames until it is extinguished. Then it is reduced to ashes; bread is made from the ashes, and each person receives a portion as though it were the Eucharist. After consuming it, almost no one ever recovers from the heresy itself.

These people are little different from the Manichaeans.—If one rereads the heresies arranged by Augustine, one will find none that agrees more closely with the Manichaeans. That heresy, once begun by more learned people, passed down its residue to peasants, who boast that they maintain an apostolic life and embrace only the reading of their deeds [Col. 0952A].

They are summoned to judgment by the bishop of Soissons. They are questioned before Guibert.—The two men mentioned above were therefore pressed to examination by the lord of Soissons, the most distinguished bishop Lisiardus. When the bishop charged them with holding assemblies apart from the church and with being called heretics by their relatives, Clementius replied: “Have you not read, lord, in the Gospel where it says, ‘You will be blessed’?” (Luke 6:22; John 13:17.) Since he was illiterate, he thought that “you will be” signified “heretics.” He also thought that they were called *heretics* as though they were “heirs,” plainly of God.

When they were questioned about what they believed, they answered in thoroughly Christian fashion, though they did not deny the assemblies [Col. 0952B]. But since it is characteristic of such people to deny and always secretly to lead the dull-hearted astray, they were subjected to the judgment of exorcised water.

While the preparations were being made, the bishop asked me to draw secretly from them what they believed and to put to them the question of infant baptism. They said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16). Since I understood that great wickedness lay hidden under this apparently sound statement, so far as they were concerned, I asked what they thought about those baptized under another person’s faith. They replied: “For God’s sake, do not wish to scrutinize us so deeply.” Likewise, at each individual point, they added: “We believe everything that you say.”

Then, remembering that verse to which the Priscillianists once agreed, namely:

“Swear, swear falsely; do not disclose the secret.” [Col. 0952C] (Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 70)

I said to the bishop: “Since the witnesses who heard them teach such doctrines are absent, subject them to the test already begun.” For there was a certain matron whom Clementius had driven mad for a year. There was also a certain deacon who had heard other malignant propositions from the mouth of the man mentioned above.

Their faith is tested by the sacrament and water. The people consume the heretics in fire.—The bishop therefore celebrated Mass, and from his hand they received the sacred elements with these words: “May the body and blood of the Lord come to you today for your testing.” After this, the most pious bishop and Peter the archdeacon, a man of utterly unshakable faith who had rejected their promises so that they would not be subjected to the judgment, proceeded to the waters. The bishop led the litany with many tears and then performed the exorcism.

Thereafter they swore that they had never believed or taught anything contrary to our faith. Clementius was put into a barrel, and, as though by a rod, he floated on the surface. At this sight the whole church erupted in boundless joy. For the rumor had drawn there such a multitude of both sexes as no one present remembered ever having seen in that place.

The other man, having confessed his error but remaining unrepentant, was thrown into chains with his brother, who had been convicted. Two other highly esteemed heretics from the village of Durmantius had come to watch and were likewise seized.

(121) Meanwhile we proceeded to the council at Beauvais to consult the bishops about what ought to be done. But in the meantime the faithful people, fearing clerical softness [Col. 0953A], rushed to the prison, seized them, and burned them all together outside the city after placing them on a fire. So that their cancer might not spread, God’s people showed righteous zeal against them.

## Chapter XVIII

A girl who presumed to sew on the feast of Saint Nicasius pays the penalty. The Blessed Virgin comes to her aid.—At Noyon there is a parish church dedicated by Alduinus [or Harduinus], formerly bishop, in honor of blessed Nicasius. His relics themselves had also been brought there from Reims and had rested for some time, not merely in the aforementioned church but in the city.

Nearly five years ago, then, when the approaching feast of the martyr had been ordered by the priest to be honored with the proper holiday observance, a poor girl who lived alone under her mother’s care presumed on that day to undertake a little sewing [Col. 0953B]. As she prepared the thread for sewing, drawing it across her tongue and projecting her lips, as is customary, the knot of the thread—which was very thick—became so deeply embedded in the tip of her tongue that it could not be removed in any way. For if anyone tried to pull it out, the wretched girl suffered unbearable anguish.

Thus, accompanied by her mother, she went amid a crowd of people to the episcopal church, to implore in silence the mercy of the Queen of Martyrs. She could scarcely speak, since the thread pierced her tongue and hung there.

What more is there to say? The crowd of ordinary people, weeping in compassion, returned home after looking for a long time at the suffering girl. She remained there with her mother, continuing to pray throughout that day and the following night [Col. 0953C].

The next day, after they had called upon the Lady of heaven and earth with the most heartfelt prayers, and—as Ansellus, the priest and sacristan of the church, reported to me—after the mother had recited the litany and the daughter had murmured beneath her breath, weaving the words together in wondrous order as though they knew their letters, the girl approached the altar of the Virgin Mother and embraced it tearfully. Immediately the thread loosened amid repeated kisses.

The clergy and people were summoned to witness so great a grace, and the Virgin Mother was exalted with God in uncountable praises [Col. 0953D]. She proved herself Queen of Martyrs in this matter, because she avenged on her behalf the fault committed against the martyr in the manner in which, finally, it pleased her to move toward satisfaction. The martyr’s nobility was also made no less manifest: by punishing the poor and humble girl in this matter, he showed how much he opposes the proud who oppose him.

This event was reported to me in the same church where it occurred, and the thread, of extraordinary thickness, with its still bloody knot, was shown to me by the priest mentioned above. Something similar also happened in our time on the feast of the Annunciation of blessed Mary; this is recorded as having been written by Ratbodus, bishop of the city.

Soldiers who had taken away property at Novigenti are punished by the Mother of God.—In this very Church of Novigenti, which by God’s authority we serve, a certain soldier had committed robbery: he had driven away the brothers’ oxen and, coming to the castle of Calviacum, had cooked one of the oxen to be eaten by himself and his companions, as he supposed.

At the first piece of that meat that he brought to his mouth, he was struck by divine power. While he was chewing, both his eyes burst from his forehead and his tongue came out of his mouth [Col. 0954A]. Thus, whether he wished it or not, the remaining booty was returned after he had been condemned in this way.

Another man tried to claim for his own fishing a portion of the neighboring river called the Aquila, although from ancient times it belonged to the brothers of the aforementioned place. When the brothers’ fisherman was completely deterred from that part of the river by the soldier, and the Church was pressed by many lawsuits on this account, the all-powerful Lady struck the soldier’s limbs with the illness of paralysis.

But when he attributed this to Fortune rather than to divine vengeance, the most merciful Virgin appeared to him as he slept and gave him several slaps in the face, not without severity. When he awoke afterward, made more sensible by the blows, he came to me barefoot, asked forgiveness, explained what blessed Mary had intended by her anger toward him, and renounced what he had usurped. From this one thing I learned: no one has ever been hostile to this Church without coming to evident harm if he chose to persist.

Likewise at Compiègne.—At Compiègne a certain royal provost opposed the church of blessed Mary and of the blessed Cornelius and Cyprian. When the clerics confronted him in the middle of the marketplace and warned him in the name of so great a Lady and such great patrons not to do this, he showed no reverence at all for the sacred names but shamefully silenced the petitioners by reproaching them. Yet in the very midst of his words, while he was mounting his horse, he fell and immediately fouled the filthy breeches that girded him with a discharge from his belly.

He is punished for striking the relics of Saint Justus.—Since we have begun to speak [Col. 0954C] of the reverence owed to the saints, there is a town in the same district of the bishopric of Beauvais called Saint-Just. When a revolt had arisen there and worthless retainers were raging with the townsmen in monstrous insolence, the clerics brought the relics of the holy boy and martyr Justus in a reliquary to the assembled people.

A certain parasite, more opportunistic than the others, came toward the reliquary. Irreverent and wicked, he struck the most sacred reliquary with his sword. He immediately fell to the ground and, like the man mentioned above, rotted away in a foul discharge from his bowels.

A priest almost killed by poison is restored to health through the merits of Saint Marcellus.—In the same district of Beauvais, in a certain village, a priest governed a church [Col. 0954D]. A certain peasant, who persecuted him with excessive hatred, grew so powerful that he tried to bring about his destruction. Since he could not do this openly, he prepared to corrupt him by poison.

He therefore pushed a toad, cut into pieces, into the priest’s little earthen flask, in which he was accustomed to keep wine for Mass. Vessels of this kind are usually made for such a purpose, with a narrow, elongated neck and a belly projecting farther outward. The priest came to Mass and celebrated the sacred mysteries with that wine, already poisoned.

When the rites had been completed, he began to fail in a deadly collapse, to loathe food, to vomit whatever he chewed or drank, and to waste away completely. After he had lain in bed for a long time, he finally struggled with difficulty to rise. He went to the church, took the vessel from which he knew the origin of his illness had come, and, cutting through its neck with a knife, poured out across the floor whatever liquid was hidden inside.

It was also possible to see, already from the consecration, [lacuna], toad-spawn most abundantly full of tiny toads. The man learned that his very vitals had been handed over to death. While he was most despairingly awaiting his approaching end, he received this advice from someone:

“If you wish to expel the pestilence that you have conceived, ask that dust be brought to you either from the tomb of Marcellus, bishop of Paris, or from his altar. When you have swallowed it with water, trust at once in your recovery.”

When the priest hastened to do this, he swallowed the sacred dust with many devout feelings. Immediately, together with all the surrounding poison, he expelled masses of innumerable crawling creatures [Col. 0955B], and, his health entirely restored, the evil departed. It is no wonder that Marcellus, present with God, performs these things, since, while once absent from that place by the interval of his body, he performed no lesser deeds in a similar matter.

## Chapter XIX

A certain man, persuaded by the devil, killed himself, but Saint James restores him to life.—What I am about to relate, unheard of in our times, I received from the report of a religious and truly humble monk. He was called Joffredus. He had formerly been lord of the castle of Samur and of other castles in Burgundy; since his life is known to be akin to truth, we judge his words [lacuna; f., “by themselves”] worthy of comparison.

The report is as follows. There was a young man in the upper regions of the neighboring lands who had become attached to a certain woman not by legitimate, that is, due, love within marriage, but by illicit love, to speak according to Solinus [lacuna], that is, by an undue love.

At one point, beginning to recover his senses somewhat, he decided to go to Saint James in Galicia for the sake of prayer. But in the very substance of his pious intention a piece of leaven was inserted: he carried the woman’s belt with him on that pilgrimage and used it in remembrance of her, so that his proper offering was no longer rightly divided.

While he was traveling, therefore, the devil found an opportunity to attack the man. He appeared to him in the form of James and said: “Where are you going?”

“To Saint James,” he replied.

“You are not going there rightly,” said the apparition. “I am the James to whom you are hastening, but you carry with you something utterly unworthy of my dignity. Although until now you have lain in the mire of every fornication, now you wish to appear repentant and, as though presenting some fruit of a good beginning, you claim to be heading into my presence, while you are still girded with the belt of that obscene little woman of yours.”

The man blushed at these accusations and, believing that he truly was the apostle, replied: “I know, lord, that I have acted, and am still acting, most disgracefully. Tell me, I beg you, what counsel you will give me as I go to your mercy.”

“If you wish to produce fruits of repentance worthy of the disgraceful deeds you have committed,” he said, “cut off that member with which you sinned—that is, your penis—for the sake of my faithfulness and God’s; afterward, cut your throat and take from yourself the life you have lived wickedly.”

He said this, withdrew from the man’s sight, and left him in great confusion of mind.

When he reached his lodging at night, the man hastened to obey the devil, whom he thought to be the apostle. While his companions were sleeping, he first cut off his penis and then plunged a knife into his throat. When his companions heard the death rattle and the crackling of blood bursting forth, they were awakened from sleep. Bringing a light, they saw what had happened to the man.

They grieved as they contemplated the exceedingly grievous end of their companion, though they did not know what advice he had received from the demon. Since they did not know the reason why this had happened to him, they nevertheless did not deny him the care of burial; and, although the offices of Mass were improper for one who had died in such a manner, they ordered them to be celebrated for him as for their fellow pilgrim [Col. 0956B].

When these prayers had been faithfully poured out to God, it pleased God to restore life through his apostle to the man who had died, repairing the wound in his throat. The man rose, and, while all present were astonished beyond what can be said at seeing him restored to life, he began to speak.

When those present asked what state of mind he had possessed when killing himself, he confessed the devil’s apparition under the name of the apostle. Asked what judgment he had undergone in spirit after killing himself, he said:

“I was brought before the throne of God, in the presence of our common Lady, the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, where my patron, the holy apostle James, was also present. While it was being deliberated before God what should be done with me, and the blessed apostle, mindful of my intention—although sinful and still corrupt—was praying to the Blessed One on my behalf, she pronounced sentence from her most sweet mouth: the wretched man ought to be forgiven, since the devil’s malice had caused him to fall in this way under the appearance of holiness.

“Thus, by God’s command, I was returned to this world for my correction and for the warning of others.”

The old man who told me this said that he had heard it from the man who had seen the one restored to life. It was also reported that a clear and notable scar remained on his throat, bearing witness to the miracle, and that the excised penis retained, if I may put it so, a perforated remnant for urination.

A monk who had changed monasteries is brought after death to the throne of God and ordered to return to the world to perform penance.—There is also a well-known report, though I do not know whether it has been committed to writing anywhere, that a certain man, converted from lay life—unless I am mistaken—to the habit of holy conduct, had entered a monastery and bound himself there by the oath of profession.

Observing that the rule was being observed there less strictly than he wished, he obtained permission from the abbot and withdrew to another monastery, as though it were more religious, and lived there with the greatest devotion. After some time he fell ill and died of the illness.

As he departed from the present world, he immediately became involved in a dispute among different powers. For the opposing powers charged him with breach of his first profession, while the argument of the spirits of light, resting on the testimony of his good works, was strongly advanced [Col. 0957A].

The case was therefore referred to Peter, the heavenly gatekeeper; but Peter immediately referred this kind of dispute to the divine presence. When the matter had thus been brought before God, the Lord said: “Go to Richard the justiciar, and carry out whatever judgment he pronounces.”

This Richard was a man supremely powerful in earthly possessions, but much more powerful in maintaining what was equitable and just.

They went to Richard, the case was stated, and Richard pronounced sentence: “Since he is bound by his pledge, he is clearly found to have committed perjury. The demons have no just case, even though the man’s many good deeds oppose them. But my judgment, from God, declares that he must return to the world to amend this fault.”

The man therefore rose from his funeral bier and returned to the living. He summoned the abbot and explained what he had seen [Col. 0957B], openly confessing the guilt of desertion and perjury. He then returned to his former monastery.

From this let everyone who, under the name of God, professes to remain stably in any place know that he must observe what he promises to God and the saints, and that he ought not to change his place unless those who do not rule over him compel him to act wrongly.

The usurer perishes eternally.—Since it is sometimes useful to speak about the conditions of the dying, a man at Laon was devoted to lending at interest in every possible way. His end showed that his life had been worthy of such a death.

When he was at the point of death, he demanded interest from a certain poor woman even though she had already paid the principal. She implored him, beseeching him to remit it in view of the death threatening him, but he obstinately refused. In her extremity she gathered together whatever interest she had received on loan, except for one denarius, and brought it.

When she also asked that this single coin be remitted to her, he swore that he would not do so under any circumstances. What more need be delayed? She sought out the denarius, which she could scarcely find, and, while the final struggle between flesh and spirit was already making him rasp, she brought it to him. He took it as he was dying and placed it in his mouth. After swallowing it as though it were provisions for the journey, he breathed out his soul and migrated to the devil under such a guardian; for this reason he deservedly lay excluded from holy places.

The soul of another usurer is likewise handed over to demons.—I shall add what happened at Arras concerning a man of this sort. For a long time he had stuffed his moneybags with shameful profits. At last, after piling up mountains of various metals, he reached his final hours.

And behold, the devil arrived in human form, leading a black ox before him. Standing beside the dying man’s bed, he said: “My lord sends you this ox.”

The sick man replied: “I thank my lord for the gift.”

The devil said to his wife: “Go and prepare something to eat for the man who brought the ox, but bring the ox inside and take good care of it.”

He spoke, and immediately breathed his last.

Meanwhile, the man who was supposedly going to eat was sought out and fodder was brought for the ox, but neither was found. Everyone marveled and shuddered at what had happened, and they judged that such sendings of gifts could not foretell anything good.

When the funeral preparations had been made and the body placed on the bier, the customary procession of clerics, who were to perform the offices for the dead [Col. 0958A], reached the house. But the demons, celebrating the funeral rites of their servant, raised such a great disturbance of the air at their arrival that, although everything had been calm, a sudden whirlwind almost overturned the front of the house called Ymberga and lifted part of the bier placed in the middle.

This is sufficient to have said about such devourers of the poor.

Hunters capture the devil instead of a wild animal. Why the demons had such power at that time.—No one should wonder that the same evil spirits at this time can do much in deceiving or harming human beings. For what they do, they do in a bestial manner and not in the name of the Lord.

Thus, not many years ago, we learned that something happened in the district of the Vexin. Some men belonging to one of the leading men of the region were hunting somewhere in the same district [Col. 0958B]. They drove a badger that was difficult to catch into a cage—or rather, having driven in a demon, they thought they had driven in the badger—and received it into a sack.

When they pulled it out with all their strength and felt it to be heavier than that animal could be, and when they began carrying it away as night was falling, behold, a voice came rushing from the neighboring mountain through the middle of the forest:

“Listen, listen!”

When many voices cried out after them from the other side, they asked: “What is it?”

The voice replied again: “They are carrying this caduceus”—or “herald’s staff.” Perhaps it was rightly called so, and it caused many to fall.

After these words, countless hosts of demons rushed from every direction as though to rescue him, so that the whole woodland seemed to be overwhelmed by their multitude. They threw down the devil they were carrying instead of the badger and, almost driven mad, fled. When they reached home, they died soon afterward.

In the same province, a certain peasant, with his leg bare and his feet naked, had sat down beside the bank of a river at dusk on Saturday, intending to wash his extremities as he returned from work. Immediately, from the bottom of the water in which he was washing his feet, the devil fastened himself around the peasant’s feet.

When the peasant felt himself bound, he called loudly to his neighbors for help, and they carried him to his own house. The rough country people then began, by every means, to see whether they could somehow wear away the fetters. They struggled uselessly around the man and accomplished nothing; each of their efforts was mocked.

For spiritual things must be matched with spiritual things. Finally, after long circuits and attempts, a man who was a stranger to them mingled among them, sprang upon the chained man while they watched [Col. 0957D], and released him in an instant. Having done this, he withdrew freely, and they were not permitted to ask who he was.

Demonic assaults seeking the love of women, and even sexual intercourse with them, are widely reported; and, if shame did not prevent it, we could relate many such things. Some demons are also atrocious in inflicting wickedness, while others are content with mere mockery. But let us now turn our style toward more joyful matters.

## Chapter XX

An abbot, led by curiosity to inspect the body of Saint Edmund, is seized by contraction of the hands.—In England the most blessed martyr, King Edmund, exists as a wonder, both formerly [Col. 0959A] and now. I say nothing about his body, which has remained incorrupt until now through pigments not human but heavenly, in which we marvel at the growth of nails and hair as though he were alive.

But this must be said: although he is placed within so great a miracle, he allows no one to see him. A certain abbot of that place, one of our contemporaries, wished to learn for himself whether the head, once severed in the Passion, was joined to the body as was commonly reported.

After fasting with his chaplain, he uncovered the body and saw the things mentioned above: the flesh nowhere flaccid, and everything appearing and feeling as though it belonged to a sleeping man. One of them pulled at the head and the other at the feet to discover whether the body was joined; they found it solid. But immediately the hands of both withered in perpetual weakness.

I shall tell of another marvel. The monks of a monastery had raised a young roe deer from a little age. As it wandered about the buildings, and even through the church, with animal wantonness, it happened to break its leg. Though limping on three legs, it went about everywhere, moving along on foot as best it could. By chance it entered the church and tried to go to the martyr’s bier.

As soon as it submitted itself to the martyr with bestial curiosity, it recovered the health of its leg. What will the devout martyr do if he is faithfully invoked in human nature, when he displays such innate generosity—or, more properly, royal serenity—in a wild animal?

Saint Witonus heals a monk’s ulcerated hands.—Saint Witonus at the city of Winchester has likewise shown himself effective in miracles up to the present day. Not long ago, a monk whose two hands were horribly ulcerated, so that he was worse in this respect than any sufferer from elephantiasis, was entirely deprived of the use of them for every task.

Because of this, the saint was displeased when the monk was absent from the vigils of his community one night. He appeared to him and asked the general reason for his absence from the singing of psalms. The monk immediately explained to the saint that the torture and suppuration of his hands were the reason for his absence.

“Hold out your hands here,” the saint said.

When he extended them, the saint clasped both hands, drew off all that diseased skin as though it were gloves, and replaced it with the smooth flesh of a young child.

The relics of Saint Arnulf are tested by fire. They restore Guibert’s cousin to health.—The arm of blessed Arnulf the martyr was kept in the town where I was born [Col. 0959D]. Since it had been brought there by someone from those regions and had made the townspeople uncertain, it was thrown into fire for testing, but immediately sprang out and was rescued.

Not long afterward, one of my cousins, a leading man of the castle, was struck by a very serious illness. When the arm of the blessed martyr had been brought to him, the sickness was said to move from place to place at its touch. As its force fled, the touch of the sacred arm followed close behind the fleeing illness. Finally, after it had moved through his face and limbs, the whole violence of the disease wandered to the boundary between his throat and shoulders. There, after the skin had been raised slightly like a wall, it gathered into a lump [Col. 0960A] and disappeared without pain.

Because of this, every year, on the day of the martyr’s feast, he fed all the clerics who attended it most lavishly for as long as he lived; his descendants continue to do so even today. My grandfather’s wife did not cover that arm, but a certain member of the household—a woman sufficiently skilled in such matters—encased it in abundant gold and precious stones.

Another miracle of Arnulf.—Guise is a castle in this district of Laon, where the arm of blessed Arnulf is likewise said to be kept. When thieves wished to carry it away along with the treasure they had plundered from the church, and were already holding it, it tore itself from their hands and could not be carried anywhere.

The thieves themselves confessed this at the very hour when, having been caught with the other things they had carried off, they were being led to the gallows. In the gold with which the arm itself is adorned, there is a place where no gem could be held by any enclosing workmanship. Once inserted, it immediately came loose. Whenever the craftsman was changed, both craftsman and workmanship came to nothing.

Guibert is freed from a fever through the merits of St. Leodegarius.—We know Leodegarius the martyr to have been distinguished by miracles and prompt in providing aid. For while I was still a little boy, though I remember these events very well, I was living with my mother and, during the Paschal season, was burning terribly with a quotidian fever. Near the town there was a church dedicated to Saints Leodegarius and Machutus, whose perpetual oil-lamp my mother humbly and faithfully supplied. Since I loathed almost every kind of food, she summoned two clerics—the chaplain who served her and my tutor—and ordered me to be carried there under their protection. [Col. 0960C] In accordance with the perverse custom of former times, that church belonged to her jurisdiction. When the clerics arrived there, they obtained permission for a bed to be made for themselves and me before the altar that night. Behold, in the middle of the night the ground within that same church began to be shaken as though by hammers; several times the bolts of the chests were rattled with a great din, and at times a sound like rods striking the chests was heard. Awakened by the noise, the clerics began to fear greatly that terror might turn my condition for the worse. What more need be said? Although they whispered among themselves, I nevertheless overheard them, and, comforted by the lamp shining before us, I was only moderately afraid. Passing the night in this way, I returned to my mother so sound that it was as though I had suffered no discomfort; and although shortly before I had recoiled from the most sumptuous food, I was now ready for ordinary fare, and was found no less ready for play. [Col. 0960D]

The elder William, king of the English, had caused a tower to be built from his own resources in the church of the magnificent Dionysius—a tower whose size, if it had been completed and remained standing, would have been immense. [Note: [Col. 0959D] The passage is obscure.] Since the work had been put together rather poorly by the craftsmen, it seemed each day to be giving birth to its own collapse. Because Ivo, then abbot, and the monks were greatly afraid that the ruin of the new work might damage the ancient basilica—for the altar of blessed Edmund and, I believe, those of certain others were there—the anxious abbot received the following vision. He saw a woman of very dignified appearance standing in the middle of the church of Blessed Dionysius, performing the exorcism of water according to priestly custom. The abbot wondered at the woman’s authority as she did what was unusual, and watched her. After blessing the water, she scattered it here and there; after scattering it, she marked with the sign of the cross all around the places where she had sprinkled it. Without delay the tower collapsed, but, as it fell, it injured no part of the church. For that Blessed One among women, blessed is the fruit of whose womb (Luke I, 22), had protected it with her blessing, as the abbot saw. [Col. 0961A]

On another occasion, as a tower was collapsing, it covered a man walking beneath it. When everyone learned that the man was buried under the stones, they began, out of human concern, to remove the heap from him. At last, after the mountains of mortar and stone had been cleared away, they reached him and, wondrous to say, found him safe and cheerful, as though he had been sitting at home. The squared stones, fitting themselves together face to face, had formed a little chamber for him. Thus, during his long confinement there—lasting, I know not how many days—he was troubled neither by hunger, nor fear, nor the exceedingly strong smell of lime that afflicted the man shut inside. [Col. 0962A]

Let us therefore close the book, invoking the most excellent Mary, patroness of heaven and earth, together with Dionysius, lord of all France [reading: *invocantes*].

**THE END**

# APPENDIX TO BOOK III OF GUIBERT’S *LIFE OF HIMSELF*

[Col. 0961]

# THREE BOOKS OF HERMANN, A MONK, ON THE MIRACLES OF ST. MARY OF LAON, CONCERNING THE DEEDS OF THE VENERABLE BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP, AND OF ST. NORBERT

## LETTER OF HERMANN, A MONK, TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF LAON

[Col. 0961]

[Col. 0961B] 526 To his venerable father and lord, the lord Bartholomew, by the grace of God bishop of the city of Laon, Brother Hermann, the least of all monks, [wishes] to be joined with the supreme pontiffs in the heavenly court.

### The noble birth of Bartholomew.—

When some time ago you had gone to Spain to visit the glorious King Hildefons, son of your maternal aunt Felicia, and had received from him the most welcome promise that, if you returned a second time to visit him, he would give you the body of St. Vincent, deacon and martyr, as well as the most precious chasuble which the blessed Mother of God had given to St. Hildefons, archbishop of the city of Toledo, in return for the three little books he had composed concerning her virginity, you began to ask my lowliness whether I had ever seen those books anywhere, and instructed me to search for them everywhere with particular diligence. When I happened to find them in the city of Châlons and reported this to you, you immediately provided and handed me parchment, and sent me to the aforesaid city to copy them.

### Hermann copied the *Life* and books of St. Hildefons, to which he added the miracles of the Blessed Virgin.—Why the author did not prefix his name.—Through Saints Norbert and Bernard, Bartholomew caused ten monasteries to be built in the diocese of Laon.—

I therefore first wrote the *Life* of that same Hildefons; then I appended his aforementioned little books. After writing these, I added the miracles which the aforesaid holy Mother of God had performed in France and England through her relics preserved in her church at Laon.
