I composed these miracles at the command of your fatherhood; but, so that they might possess greater authority and not be despised by anyone because of the rusticity of my style, I did not wish to omit the name of my lowliness from them, but placed them under the name of the canons of that Church. After those miracles I also added how, through divine mercy, in your days nine—indeed, ten—monasteries were caused to be built through your efforts by the lord Norbert and the lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, none of which had existed in the time of your forty-three predecessors as bishops. You appointed abbots over each once it had been built, and nevertheless did not neglect to correct the older institutions that you found. If life remains with me, God willing, I have also resolved to append the other things that happened in your days, or that I shall see happen. I therefore leave this book to your fatherhood and to the Church of Laon as a memorial of my insignificance, so that I may share in the good things accomplished in it. [Col. 0962B–0964A]

# TABLE OF CONTENTS OF BOOK ONE

[Col. 0963]

[Col. 0963A] 527 **Chapter I.** On the prosperity and adversity of the Church of Laon; the killing of Bishop Gualdricus and Gerard of Cyrisiacum; and the burning of twelve churches.

**Chapter II.** On the election and nobility of the lord Bartholomew, bishop.

**Chapter III.** On the miracles of St. Mary throughout France.

**Chapter IV.** On two crippled persons healed at the castle of Issoudun.

**Chapter V.** On a deaf and mute young man healed at the castle of Beaugency.

**Chapter VI.** On peace made between two hostile castles.

**Chapter VII.** On a sick woman healed at Tours.

**Chapter VIII.** On a deaf and mute young man healed at Tours.

**Chapter IX.** On the vengeance of St. Mary at Saint-Laurent-de-Cala.

**Chapter X.** On a woman in labor healed at Angers.

**Chapter XI.** On a sterile woman made fertile at Le Mans.

**Chapter XII.** On a miracle at the castle called Mont-de-Guarda.

**Chapter XIII.** On three miracles performed by St. Mary in the city of Chartres.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0963]

## CHAPTER I.—On the prosperity and adversity of the Church of Laon, the killing of Bishop Gualdricus and Gerard of Cyrisiacum, and the burning of twelve churches

[Col. 0963B]

[Note: [Col. 0963] Here Hermann speaks under the name of the canons of Laon, as he himself indicated in the dedicatory letter.]

To all the sons of Holy Mother Church scattered throughout the entire world, the canons of the church of Blessed Mary of Laon [send greetings], that they may see the God of gods in Zion. Since, according to the blessed apostle Paul, the whole holy Church is one body of Christ (Col. I, 24), and the various Churches, or individual faithful, are members of this body—and when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, while when one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it (I Cor. XII, 26)—we make known in writing to your affection the tribulation and sorrow that our Church encountered in our days (Ps. CXIV, 3), and the consolation that, after the mourning of tribulation, it received through Our Lady, the holy Mother of God, so that you too, rejoicing with us, may give thanks to God and to his devout Mother. [Col. 0963C]

It is certain that the Church of Laon was anciently renowned among the principal Churches of the kingdom of the Franks. As is read in his *Life*, the blessed Remigius, archbishop of Reims, enriched it from his own revenues and consecrated within it the most noble and energetic man, Saint Genebaudus, as its first bishop. From his time down to our own, for nearly five hundred years and more, it had flourished in great prosperity. But behold: in the days of Louis, king of the Franks, who was the son of King Philip and the father of Louis the Younger, it experienced the harsh chastisement of the just Judge, the King of kings. For just as long ago almighty God greatly glorified the city of Jerusalem through King David and his son Solomon, but afterward, because of the sins of its inhabitants, permitted it to be utterly destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, so also in our days he allowed our Church, which—as has been said—he had exalted in distinguished glory for many years, not indeed to be wholly destroyed, but to be afflicted by excessive tribulation, so that the prophetic saying could truly be applied to it: “For she has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins” (Isa. XL, 2). [Col. 0964B]

This tribulation was preceded by a certain disturbance which appeared to have been the seedbed, root, and herald of the future calamity. A certain noble prince and castellan of Laon, named Gerard of Cyrisiacum, was piously praying on his knees in that same church of the Holy Mother when he was deceitfully surrounded by his enemies, who did not dare to attack him. As he rose from prayer, he was killed there by various sword blows. [Note: [Col. 0963] This is related at greater length in Book III of Guibert’s *Life*.] Although the church pavement, sprinkled with his blood, could not be completely washed despite water repeatedly being poured over it, and many people who came to see it marveled greatly at the sight, the most learned master Anselm—then a canon and dean of our Church, and renowned throughout almost the entire Latin world for his learning and eloquence—is said to have predicted, in confidential conversations with certain people, that this shedding of blood could be cleansed only by the burning of that same church, since so great a crime would have to be expiated not by water but rather by fire. [Col. 0964C–0965A]

The prudent man’s opinion did not deceive him. Not long afterward, with God permitting it and the devil goading them on, the lord Gualdricus, bishop of that city, was cruelly killed in his own house, together with some of his soldiers, in a sudden uprising stirred up by the citizens. The aforementioned church of St. Mary, [Note: [Col. 0965D] See Guibert at the place cited.] along with nearly ten other nearby churches, as well as the adjoining houses of the bishop and the canons and those of many citizens, was set on fire and burned. Moreover, the entire city of Laon, its citizens scattered through various places, seemed to be destroyed almost to the point of annihilation. Thus many people passing through it, when they saw its ruins and ashes, shed tears out of excessive compassion, not inappropriately repeating over it Jeremiah’s lamentation: “How solitary sits the city that was full of people! She has become like a widow, the mistress of nations” (Lam. I, 1). [Col. 0965B]

Just as in former times the Lord permitted the city of Jerusalem to be destroyed and the children of Israel to be taken captive, yet left the prophet Jeremiah there with the few who remained for their consolation, so also, when we were placed in such great calamity, he mercifully preserved for us two exceedingly wise men: the aforementioned master Anselm and his brother, master Ralph. Consoling both clergy and laity with gentleness and sustaining them with various sayings from Scripture, they exhorted them not to collapse under the burden of tribulation and adversity.

## CHAPTER II.—On the election of the lord Bartholomew as bishop and on his nobility

[Col. 0965C]

Amid these conversations of consolation, they carefully and earnestly deliberated with wise and religious men whether they could find someone through whom so miserable and dreadful a disaster might be repaired. At last, by God’s inspiration, they arrived at a salutary decision: to elect to the bishopric of that city the lord Bartholomew, canon and treasurer of the Church of Blessed Mary at Reims, a man renowned throughout the provinces of Reims and Laon both for the distinction of his lineage and for the excellence of his character. His illustrious kinsmen were celebrated not only in France but also in Spain, Burgundy, and Lorraine. For Hilduin, count of Roucy, his grandfather, married Adela, sister of the lord Manasses, archbishop of Reims. By her he fathered Ebal, count of Roucy, and Andrew, count of Ramerupt, father of Ebal, bishop of Châlons, as well as seven daughters. [Col. 0965D]

One of these daughters, named Felicia, was taken as wife in Spain by Sancho, king of Aragon. By her he fathered Hildefons, a most powerful king. Succeeding his father in the kingdom, Hildefons violently wrested from the pagans, through vigorous warfare, the strongest cities and castles and handed them over to the Christians: namely, Caesaraugusta, renowned as the archdeaconry of the blessed martyr Vincent; Tarazona, Tudela, Barbastro, and Borja, together with many others. Having brought almost the whole of Spain under his rule, he so extended the renown of his name that some called him a second Julius, others a second Charles, in memory of that illustrious Charles, king of the Franks, who once conquered Spain in victory. [Col. 0966A]

Hilduin’s second daughter was taken as wife by Rothold, count of Perche; by her he fathered Count Rothold and Juliana, mother of Margaret, queen of Navarre.

The third, named Margaret, married Hugh, count of Clermont. By her was born Count Rainald, who by Adela, countess of Vermandois, fathered Margaret, wife of that illustrious Charles, count of Flanders.

The fourth, named Ermentrude, married Theobald, count of Risnel. By her he fathered Heldiardis, mother of Count Bertrand, who died in Spain, and of her sister Beatrice. By Hugh of Montcornet, Beatrice became the mother of Bartholomew, archdeacon and treasurer of Laon. [Col. 0966B]

The fifth, named Ada, was taken as wife by Godefrid of Guise. By her he fathered Guy, father of Burchard. After Godefrid’s death, Ada married Walter of Aath. When he died, she took a third husband, Theodoric of Avesnes, and with him built the monastery called Lescy, on her own property. After Theodoric’s death, she devoted herself entirely to that monastery, where she lived religiously for many years, died, and was buried.

The sixth was taken as wife by Count Ernulf of Waren. He fathered Otho, count of Cisni; Otho fathered Aubert; and Aubert fathered Count Aubert and Ernulf, bishop of Verdun. [Col. 0966C]

A certain most noble prince in Burgundy, named Falco of Jur or of Serrata, having learned of the nobility and eminence of the aforementioned Count Hilduin, sought to have one of his daughters joined to him in marriage. But when he could not obtain this, and the father swore that he would never give his daughter to a Burgundian, it happened that King Philip of the Franks sent that same Count Hilduin, together with the lord Helinand, bishop of Laon, and several other princes, to Rome to the lord pope on a matter of common concern to the kingdom. When this was reported to the aforementioned Prince Falco, he laid ambushes for them at many places along their return route. Having captured them on the road and stripped them of everything they possessed, he refused to release them until the count promised under oath that he would give him his daughter. [Col. 0966D]

Having received this promise, Falco released them all and generously bestowed many gifts upon them, sending them back to their own lands with great honor. The count therefore returned to France and sent his daughter, named Adela, with many riches to Burgundy, where he joined her in marriage to the aforementioned prince. By her Falco fathered the aforesaid bishop, the lord Bartholomew, together with other sons and daughters. One of these was Ermentrude, whom Henry, count of Grandpré, brought from Burgundy to France and took as his wife. By her he fathered a son also named Henry, count, and her sister Adela, mother of Richard, archdeacon of Verdun and Laon. [Col. 0967A]

This Bartholomew, while still a little boy, was brought to France to his maternal uncle, Ebal, count of Roucy. Entrusted to his studies by the lord Manasses, archbishop of Reims, his mother’s uncle, he was educated there. He first became a canon of the Church of St. Mary at Reims and then its treasurer. Later, when he was already a canon of the Church of Laon, Adela, countess of Vermandois and wife of Hugh the Great—who was the brother of Philip, king of the Franks—married Count Rainald of Clermont after Hugh’s death. From Hugh she had fathered Ralph, count of Vermandois, and Simon, bishop of Noyon. Knowing that Bartholomew was her husband’s cousin, she arranged, for love of him, for Bartholomew to become treasurer of the Church of St. Quentin at Vermandois. Thus, as has been said, Bartholomew was renowned both for the nobility of his lineage and character and for the abundance of his wealth. [Col. 0967B]

Having been elected to the bishopric of the city of Laon by the unanimous assent of all the clergy and people, he was presented to the lord Ralph, archbishop of Reims, who had succeeded the aforementioned Manasses, his maternal uncle. He was solemnly consecrated by Ralph and many other bishops in the time of Pope Paschal and Louis, king of the Franks, and was sent as a new shepherd to sheep left desolate.

But when he came to Laon and found neither a church nor an episcopal residence—indeed, scarcely anything beyond embers and ashes—it cannot be said how greatly he grieved and lamented. He mourned that he had not been elevated to an honor but burdened with an honor. The saying of Scripture seemed then, not without reason, to apply to him: “Man is born to labor” (Job V, 7). And likewise the statement that the Lord makes about himself in the Gospel: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke IX, 58). Also the saying of the blessed apostle Paul: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (I Tim. III, 1)—a work, he says, not an honor. [Col. 0967C]

So this man, coming from great rest, riches, and every bodily comfort into a desolate place, did not boast that he had been promoted to the eminence of honor, but said that he had been called to the labor of work; and therefore, if he had perhaps desired the episcopate, he had desired a good work. Immediately, as though he had entered some desert, he began to renew the church and episcopal residences together and to restore them as though from their foundations. [Col. 0967D]

## CHAPTER III.—On the miracles of St. Mary throughout France

But because, as has been said, not only the principal church of St. Mary but also nearly twelve other churches, together with many houses of clergy and laity, had been burned, and because the greater part of the citizens had been scattered throughout the province, while each of those who remained was so occupied with rebuilding his own house that scarcely anyone could be found to assist the mother church, certain wise and religious men advised us to send chosen clerics—men of good reputation—with the relics of Our Lady and of the other saints through France, to seek alms from the faithful.

Following their advice, we chose seven canons from among our brothers: namely, Boso, Robert, Anselm, Herbert, Robert, Boniface, Amisard the priest, and Odo, who later became abbot of the monastery called Good Hope in the diocese of Cambrai. We also added six laymen from among the citizens: Richard, John Piot, Odo, Lambert, Boso, and Theodoric of Brueriis. We sent them with Our Lady’s bier and other reliquary chests to receive the faithful’s offerings. [Col. 0968A]

The church had been burned on the Thursday of Holy Week, while they themselves departed on the Thursday before Pentecost—that is, during the octave of the Ascension—and remained away until around the feast of Matthew the Evangelist. The Lord, to whom it is said through the Prophet, “You rejected us, O God, and destroyed us; you were angry, and you took pity on us” (Ps. LIX, 3), and elsewhere, “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. III, 4), did not delay mercifully to revive our Church, which he had permitted to be harshly scourged, once appeased by the prayers of his most compassionate Mother. For he displayed very many miracles through her relics on that journey. Passing over some of them, we commit only a few—but the best known—to writing for the knowledge of posterity. [Col. 0968B]

## CHAPTER IV.—On two crippled persons healed at the castle of Issoudun

[Col. 0968C]

In the region of Berry there is a castle called Issoudun (in the vernacular, Issoudun). The lord of this castle, a very wealthy man named Gaufred, had for a long time retained and supported in his house, for the sake of his soul, two crippled men whose heels were so attached to their buttocks that they could in no way walk or raise themselves up. When Our Lady’s bier had been received with a great procession and placed in the church, they asked to be carried there and to have their heels and legs washed with the water in which the relics had been washed.

When this had been done, in full view of all the people, the flesh attached to their buttocks immediately began to split open, and blood flowed abundantly down their legs. At once they stood upon their feet, embraced the bier, and, completely healed, followed our brothers on their return journey all the way to Laon. Every day they urged the people to assist the work of the church by carrying stones, bringing water, and preparing mortar. When the church had been completed, one of them returned to his homeland, namely to the castle of Issoudun. The other, named Benedict, remained at Laon, serving in the hospital for nearly twelve years, and died there. [Col. 0968D]

## CHAPTER V.—On a deaf and mute young man healed at the castle of Beaugency

After leaving Issoudun, they came to another castle called Beaugency (Belgentiacum, in the vernacular Beaugency). Its lord was so rapacious and savage that many inhabitants told our brothers that he took away everything they possessed. He had a son, about fifteen years old, who had been deaf and mute from birth.

Our brothers were terrified, but the Mother of Mercy quickly came to their aid. A religious monk living there, having heard of Our Lady’s miracles, received her bier in the church with great honor. Then, after vesting himself, he washed her relics in wine and water, sprinkled the head and face of the aforementioned young man with that water, gave him some of it to drink, and ordered him to lie down beneath the bier. The monk himself knelt and began earnestly to entreat Our Lady. [Col. 0969A]

Without delay the young man fell asleep. In the sight of all, sweat poured from his entire body because of his distress, the veins around his ears swelled, and blood burst abundantly from his ears. Immediately he awoke, rose, and began to utter certain sounds. [Col. 0969B]

The monk rose from prayer and ran up joyfully to him, addressing the young man. Since the young man had never before heard anything, he did not know how to answer; but whatever he heard others say, he himself repeated after them by imitating their words. At once the monk rang the bells and summoned the people, showed them the young man speaking and hearing, and, weeping for joy, began the *Te Deum laudamus*. A messenger was immediately sent to the father, who was returning from his plundering, and reported what had happened to his son. The father at once ran barefoot to the church and, prostrate before the bier, gave thanks to the Mother of Mercy. Then he offered forty solidi, since he did not have an abundance of money. [Col. 0969B]

## CHAPTER VI.—On peace made between two hostile castles

[Col. 0969C]

From there our brothers wished to go to another castle only two miles away, but because of the ferocity and plundering of that robber, none of the inhabitants dared to travel there with them. Nevertheless, that same robber, moved by the mercy of the Mother of God, together with his soldiers and the other inhabitants, placed the bier and relics upon their shoulders. All proceeded barefoot toward the castle of their enemies.

When those enemies heard this and learned of the miracle that the holy Mother of God had performed there on the robber’s son, they too immediately rushed barefoot to meet their enemies. They received the bier from them and carried it joyfully into their own castle, praising the mercy of Christ, who through his Mother had caused enemies to meet their enemies in peace. [Col. 0969D]

## CHAPTER VII.—On a sick woman healed at Tours

From there they came through Cormery (in the vernacular Cormery) to Tours, where they were received with great reverence by the archbishop of Tours. On Saturday, before Vespers, they rested in the church of St. Maurice.

The wife of a carpenter in that city had lain bedridden for eight years, so severely afflicted by illness that she could go nowhere unless she was carried. That same night, while she slept, the Mother of Mercy appeared to her and commanded her to have herself carried to her bier in the church of St. Maurice. When she awoke, the woman asked her husband to carry her there at once. Since he was not very wealthy and had no litter prepared, he had her carried in a cheap implement that we commonly call a *vannus*, in which winnowed grain is usually cleaned.

As soon as she had been placed beneath the bier, she fell asleep. After a short time she awoke and rose healed. Then, joining the bier, she followed it in the sight of the people as far as the church of St. Martin. [Col. 0970A]

## CHAPTER VIII.—On a deaf and mute young man healed at Tours

When the canons of St. Martin heard this, they went out with the abbot of St. Julian to meet them and received Our Lady’s relics with the greatest honor.

In that same city there was a young man who had been deaf and mute from his mother’s womb. One of the fullers had found him as an infant, raised and educated him, and taught him his craft. When he was brought to Our Lady’s relics, he lay down beneath the bier and fell asleep. Without delay he began to suffer distress and to sweat from his entire body. Then, when the veins around his ears had swollen, blood flowed abundantly from his ears. He immediately rose and heard, but he did not know how to speak, since he had never learned. Whatever he heard others saying, however, he repeated. Since his name was unknown, our canons called him Christian. [Col. 0970B]

He therefore accompanied our brothers and came with them to Laon, where he remained for nearly seven years in the house of Guy, archdeacon of Laon.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the vengeance of St. Mary at Saint-Laurent-de-Cala

[Col. 0970C]

After leaving the city of Tours, they came to Saint-Laurent-de-Cala on the feast of that same martyr. A monk living there refused to allow Our Lady’s bier to be placed upon the altar of St. Lawrence. Instead, fearing that he might lose the customary offering made on that feast, he had it placed upon a certain smaller altar in a part of the church.

But the people of Tours who were accompanying our relics, recounting the miracles they had witnessed, urged all the pilgrims who arrived to leave the principal altar and make their offerings at Our Lady’s bier. Struck by the venom of envy, the monk ordered the bier and all the relics to be thrown out of the church. The provost of the castle immediately reproached the monk and gave our brothers a spacious tent that he had prepared for himself. The matrons of the place also brought many curtains and endeavored to decorate the tent most beautifully; in addition, they made it splendid throughout the night with sufficient lights. [Col. 0970D]

But the just King, Jesus Christ, did not wish the injury inflicted upon his Mother to go unpunished. At Vespers the aforementioned monk was suddenly overcome by epilepsy and fell to the ground before all the people, striking great terror into those who saw it. The large bell also fell from the tower and was shattered; the tower itself split and broke apart in its upper portion with a loud crack.

When the monk saw this, he repented too late of having acted wickedly. Barefoot, he prostrated himself on the ground before the bier and humbly made satisfaction to the Queen of Heaven. He asked that the bier be carried to the principal altar, but our brothers refused to comply with his request. [Col. 0971A]

## CHAPTER X.—On a woman in labor healed at Angers

From there they came to Angers and were magnificently received by the bishop of that city. There a certain woman, the wife of a very wealthy man named Fulbert Pellicius, was tormented for several days by excessive pain in childbirth and feared that death was already close at hand.

When she heard of Our Lady’s miracles, she asked that her relics be brought to her. When they had been brought, she offered a silver spoon, drank in faith the water in which the relics had been washed, and was immediately delivered and freed from her labor. She gave thanks to God and to his devout Mother. [Col. 0971B]

## CHAPTER XI.—On a sterile woman made fertile at Le Mans

At Le Mans a certain sterile matron received our brothers as guests with her very wealthy husband. Prostrate before Our Lady’s bier, she prayed that a child might be given to her. Her faith was not frustrated. After the passage of a year, she gave birth to a son, and afterward came frequently to Laon, giving thanks to Our Lady.

## CHAPTER XII.—On a miracle at the castle called Mont-de-Guarda

Between the city of Le Mans and the castle called Mont-de-Guarda there was an exceedingly difficult passage, obstructed by the cutting down of forests by the inhabitants of the region, because of the dissension and dispute then existing between the king of the English and the count of Anjou.

Leaving the city of Le Mans late, they came to that difficult passage. Everyone they met said that they could in no way cross it or reach the castle toward which they were heading. Meanwhile day turned into night, and excessive rain arose, so that they were now almost driven to despair of their safety.

“So they cried to the Lord in their tribulation, and he delivered them from their distress” (Ps. CVI, 28). For suddenly, by God’s mercy, they crossed with such ease that they encountered absolutely no obstacle on the way. When they reached the castle, soldiers came out to meet them, greatly wondering how they had crossed, and received them most kindly, saying that the Lord’s mercy had truly been with them. [Col. 0971C–D]

The following day, when they wished to return by the same route, they could not cross it at all until the way had been cleared with great labor. Thus they gave thanks to the devout Mother of the Lord, who in the hour of their great need had shown them great mercy.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On three miracles performed by St. Mary in the city of Chartres

On the eve of the Nativity of St. Mary, before Vespers, they came to Chartres and were received with the greatest honor by the lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres. The entire procession of canons came out to meet them beyond the city, as far as the vineyards, and the bier was placed in the principal church upon the altar of St. Mary. [Col. 0972A]

Now there was in the city a certain woman who was crippled. For five years the bishop himself had supported her in the house where his bread was baked. Because of her excessive infirmity, she lay bent over so severely that she could not go even to answer the common needs of nature unless two people carried her.

At the first hour of the night Our Lady appeared to her in a dream and commanded her to rise as quickly as possible, go to the principal church, and seek her Laon bier. Immediately she awoke, rose healed, and ran through the streets toward the church, crying out joyfully: “Holy Lady Mary! Holy Lady Mary!” The bishop’s household followed her. The bishop himself, awakened from sleep, heard and rejoiced that his poor dependent had been healed. [Col. 0972B]

The woman entered the church healed, loudly asking where the bier of St. Mary of Laon was. Standing before it, she gave thanks to it and recounted to everyone how the Lady had appeared to her.

At once the bishop ordered all the bells to be rung more rapidly, and he himself began the *Te Deum laudamus*. While it was being sung, behold, another crippled woman, well known both to the bishop himself and to all the others, entered the church healed. Coming directly to the bier, she placed upon the altar the two little stools with which she had been accustomed to move about by crawling and supporting herself while begging alms. Then, standing before the people, she gave thanks to God and to his devout Mother.

Immediately the bishop again ordered all the bells to sound and began the aforementioned hymn for a second time. Before it could be finished, it pleased the divine mercy to add a third miracle.

A certain young knight—namely, the son of the viscount of Chartres—who was being held captive, chained in a certain castle, suddenly and unexpectedly entered the church. His mother, together with knights and townspeople, came to meet him; and he proceeded joyfully to the altar. Kneeling before the bier, he declared that he had been delivered through Our Lady and immediately offered her forty solidi.

When the bishop saw this, he ordered that all the bells be rung for a longer time, not only in the principal church but also in every other church throughout the entire city, even the smallest, and that praises be sung to God by messengers sent directly to them. He himself began the *Te Deum laudamus* for the third time. How great throughout the whole city was the din and pealing of the bells; what a voice of joy; how many streams of sweet tears, poured out in overwhelming exultation by both sexes and people of every age—this the devout reader can easily perceive even without our saying more. Thus our brothers, gladdened by the miracles of blessed Mary and enriched by the gifts of the faithful, returned to us joyfully around the feast of Saint Matthew the Evangelist. By such reports they greatly rejoiced the entire city of Laon and, after the mourning of tribulation, brought us a new joy. Blessed in all things be God, who lives and reigns for ever and ever.

## 534 — Book Two: Concerning Events That Took Place in England

[Col. 0973]

### Chapter I — Of a Deaf and Mute Man Cured at Nelle

[Col. 0973A]

From the offerings of the faithful collected throughout France, the church of Our Lady was largely repaired during the whole autumn and winter. But in the following Lent, while most of the work still remained to be done and the money was gradually running out, certain wise men advised us that some of the canons should once again be selected—men who would bring honor to the Church of Laon both through their knowledge of letters and through their skill in singing and musical performance—and that they should be sent to England with the bier of Our Lady and the relics of the saints. At that time England was flourishing in great abundance of wealth, because of the peace and justice maintained there by its king, Henry, son of King William.

[Note: Henry I, king of the English, son of William I.]

Accordingly, from among the canons Boso the priest and his nephew Robert, Radulf the priest, Matthew and his kinsman Boniface, Robert, English by birth, Helinandus, John, priest of the parish of Saint Martin, and Amisardus the cleric were chosen. After these men had been selected, we entrusted to them the bier of Our Lady together with many other relics of the saints. Among them one reliquary stood out both in form and in dignity; on it the following words were engraved:

> The sponge, the Lord’s cross, with the shroud and face-cloth,  
> And your hair, O Mother and Virgin, consecrate me.

Thus fortified with such great and powerful protections, we sent our companions to England, praying for their prosperity and accompanying them for a short distance in a great procession. On the Monday before Palm Sunday, we sent them away in peace from the city of Laon.

When they returned in September of that same year, around the Nativity of Saint Mary, they related to us what had happened to them as follows. “After leaving you,” they said, “we came to the castle called Nelle, in the district of Vermandois, and were honorably received by the canons and by Lord Radulf, father of Lord Ivo, the prince and possessor of that castle.

“This Radulf had in his household a certain man named John, deaf and mute from birth, whom he had raised from infancy to manhood, so that by then he had a long beard. When he saw the people hurrying to the church because of the holy relics, his master summoned him by signs; and he too ran with the others. Afterward he drank some of the water in which the holy relics had been washed, and his mouth and ears were carefully washed with it. Then he lay down beneath the bier and fell asleep.

“Before long, in the sight of everyone, he began, from extreme distress, to emit sweat over his whole body. Blood also began to flow abundantly from his ears and nostrils, and from the veins protruding around his throat and neck, as though they had burst. A short while later he awoke and rose. Standing before the bier, he began to cry out in a voice of exultation, though not with articulate speech, since he did not know how to speak—something he had never learned because he had never heard.

“Yet whatever he heard others saying, he wished to repeat in response when they urged him and spoke to him, and he said it after them. No one could adequately recount the joy of the people or the shouting that followed. Thus, completely healed, he accompanied us almost as far as the sea. He would even have crossed over with us had we not asked him to return.”

### Chapter II — Of a Blind Goldsmith Given Sight at Arras

From there, coming to the city of Arras around Good Friday, we were received with no less honor. There lived in that city an old goldsmith who had been deprived of the light of his eyes for twelve years. When he heard that the bier of Saint Mary of Laon had arrived, he asked about its form, appearance, and size.

When he had learned these things, he immediately drew deep sighs from the bottom of his heart and poured forth abundant tears. “Alas!” he said. “I, a sinner, made this bier with my own hands in my youth, at the command of Lord Helinandus, bishop of Laon. This same bishop placed precious relics in it, among them the head of Saint Walricus the abbot, as well as the head of Saint Montanus. As I heard from that bishop, when Montanus had lost his sight, he foretold the birth of Saint Remigius to his mother, the blessed Cilnia, and added that sight would be restored to him through her milk—which indeed later happened.

“But, O most compassionate Mother of God, how joyful I am that you have come here today! Will you show your mercy to me, a sinner, so that, like Saint Montanus, having received my sight, I may once again see your bier, which I made?”

Saying these things with tears, he asked that his eyes be touched with the water in which the relics had been washed. After this was done, he drank some of the same water and remained awake in prayer before the bier throughout the entire night. When morning came, he received his sight and gave thanks to God and to his devout Mother.

### Chapter III — Of a Girl Cured at Saint-Omer

From there we came to Saint-Omer, where a certain girl who had had a withered hand from birth drank some of the water of the relics, and her hand was washed with it. Thus she was healed.

### Chapter IV — Of the Deliverance of the Clerics of Saint Mary from Pirates at Sea

Afterward, hoping to cross the sea and awaiting a favorable wind, at Eastertide, on the feast of the Evangelist Mark, we were summoned by sailors early in the morning at the harbor called Wissant and entered a ship. Several merchants also came aboard with us. They wished to travel from Flanders to England to buy wool and hoped to cross more safely in our company; they were carrying more than three hundred marks of silver in their sacks and purses. The master of the ship was called Coldistannus.

When we had reached approximately the middle of the sea, one of our companions, looking far ahead, saw in the distance a ship that seemed to be lying near a corner of the shore. When he pointed it out to Coldistannus, the latter ordered a young man to climb to the top of the mast to investigate. From the young man’s report he realized that a ship belonging to pirates—men who roam the sea for the purpose of plundering—was approaching. Immediately he became extremely frightened and announced to everyone that imminent death threatened us.

At once, fear of death drained the color from all our faces. We could see the ship drawing near like a bird swooping down, with spears and shields flashing together with swords, and corselets gleaming, suffused with the sun’s brilliance. We confessed our sins to one another. Since death already seemed to be at the door, the priest was not awaited to hear confession; the priest himself, shaken by the danger of the impending events, confessed to a layman.

[Note: See our observations on book B of Lanfranc’s *On Keeping Confession Secret* in volume 150, column 625 of our *Patrologia*.]

The merchants mentioned above, now despairing of their lives and placed in such danger, offered their sacks and purses, together with all their money, to Our Lady and threw them upon her bier. With excessive weeping they implored her mercy, asking only that she rescue their bodies from the hands of the pirates and from death, while retaining all their money for the restoration of her church.

Meanwhile the pirates gradually drew closer, until they seemed scarcely more than an arrow’s shot away. But when we were in such dire necessity and had entirely despaired of life, Coldistannus urged the priest Boso—whom he saw to be senior to the others—to take the relics of Saint Mary and forbid the pirates the power to harm us.

Immediately, strengthened by the man’s faith, the priest knelt before the bier and devoutly invoked the Mother of the Lord, his face covered with tears. Then he rose quickly and confidently took up the precious reliquary containing her hair. With Coldistannus bravely supporting it with both hands, he climbed to the highest part of the stern. Raising his hand against the enemy, he firmly commanded and forbade them, by the authority of God and of the holy Mother Mary, to come any farther or to have the power to harm us.

And O wondrous power of divine might! As soon as he completed his words and made the sign of the cross with the same reliquary against the enemy, a strong contrary wind suddenly struck their ship and drove it backward. Their mast broke, and part of it fell upon one of them, crushing him and throwing him dead into the sea.

Pious Jesus, good Jesus, what joy and exultation came to us then, when you tore the sackcloth of our distress and surrounded us with the joy of your mercy! (*Psalm* 29:12.) How many praises we immediately offered to you and to your Mother, Our Lady, after being rescued from death! The wind that had been contrary to our enemies became favorable and beneficial to us, so that with joy we recalled the song of Moses and marveled that we were being carried across so swiftly.

After a short delay we reached the harbor joyfully. We planned to return to the merchants part of the money that, in fear of death, they had given to Our Lady and placed—or rather, in their agitation, thrown—upon her bier. But as soon as they reached the shore and saw that they had escaped the danger of death, they forgot their former fear. Without our permission, each one took up his own sack and purse, giving Our Lady thanks only in words and leaving her nothing.

### Chapter V — Of the Vengeance Inflicted upon Merchants at Dover

Let everyone who gives his possessions to God and then takes them back again hear what vengeance her Son, the just Judge, inflicted upon them for this offense against his Mother.

After traveling through nearly the whole of England and spending their money purchasing enormous heaps of wool, they filled a large house situated on the seashore at a place called Dover. But on the night before the day of their departure, the house suddenly burned down, together with all the wool. Thus, having lost everything and become poor, they regretted too late what they had done and grieved that they had wronged the Queen of Heaven.

### Chapter VI — Of a Woman in Labor Delivered at Canterbury

Thus delivered, as it seemed to us, not from the shadow of death but from its very jaws, we came to Canterbury, offering Our Lady hymns of thanksgiving and bringing her bier and relics with us. At that time the archbishop was Lord William, well known to us because long before, when he had sought at Laon an opportunity to hear the teaching of Master Anselm, he had remained many days in the bishop’s house and had taught there the sons of Ralph, chancellor of the king of the English.

He came to meet us with immense joy and received us with the greatest honor together with the monks of Saint Augustine. He kindly kept us there as long as we wished.

There was in that city a certain extremely wealthy matron who had been tormented for eight days by the most grievous labor pains and had been given up entirely, so that arrangements were being made only for her funeral. When she heard of our arrival, she sent her husband to us to ask whether any of us knew a remedy for childbirth.

Then the priest Boso, who had been entrusted especially with the care of preserving the relics, advised him to urge his wife to make a true confession of her sins to her priest and then faithfully to drink some of the water in which the relics had been washed.

The husband returned and reported to his wife what he had learned. But she, who because of the extremity of her pain had lost not only the power of speech but even her memory, was immediately strengthened and revived somewhat by God’s help and by the very warmth of faith. She arranged to confess her sins to the priest who came to her. Then she added that the same night, in a vision, an exceedingly beautiful Lady coming from France had appeared to her, commanded her to confess her sins truthfully, and promised that she would thereby be healed.

After the priest had heard her confession, he came to us and reported these things. Immediately, at the request of her husband, and assured by the priest’s report of her future recovery, we went with the relics to the bed of the woman lying there. We washed them before her, gave her the washing water to drink, and then departed at once.

Before we had returned to the church, a messenger ran after us and reported that she had given birth and had been healed. Therefore she and her husband, exulting, bestowed many gifts and ornaments upon Our Lady. After our return, she also sent precious priestly vestments to the Church of Laon.

It was thoroughly established among us that absolutely no one could be healed unless he belonged to the very diocese in which we were staying. As we believe, Our Lady arranged this so that no unknown sick person arriving from distant regions could be said to have been hired by us for payment in hope of profit, or to have come for the sake of receiving money, and so that we should not be made contemptible by the talk of the inexperienced populace.

Among those who did belong to that diocese, no one was healed unless he first confessed his sins to his own priest, provided that he was of suitable age. If he was a very young child, the parents were instructed to make confession in place of the child.

### Chapter VII — Of a Blind Man Given Sight at Winchester

Afterward we came to the city of Winchester and were honorably received by its bishop. We remained there for eight days, during which we saw very many miracles take place.

In that city there was an honorable knight named Radulf, surnamed Buarius, cupbearer of the king of the English, who had already been without the light of his eyes for eight years. Because of this blindness, he had obtained from the king that his office be given to his sons.

When he learned on the day of the Lord’s Ascension of the miracles that were occurring, he had himself brought to the bier. After confessing his sins to his priest, he faithfully drank the water in which the relics had been washed and had his eyes washed with it.

While the bishop was celebrating the principal Mass in the church with such solemnity, and after the sermon had ended following the Gospel, we left the church with the relics at the people’s request, so that we would not inconvenience the bishop.

When the sermon was again being delivered in the street before the church door and the bishop began the canon, Radulf suddenly received his sight beside the relics placed outside the church. He began to praise God and his holy Mother with loud cries.

This miracle was held in such great veneration that on that very day the people returned five times to hear the word, honor the relics, and renew their offerings.

[Note: Notice that in various places the sins are always said to have been confessed to one’s own priest.]

### Chapter VIII — Of Another Sick Man Cured There

In the same city there was a very wealthy man named Walter, surnamed Kiburs, who had been so afflicted by a severe illness for six years that he had never been able to rise from his bed. When he heard of Our Lady’s miracles, he asked us for help through intermediaries. In addition to his other illness, he suffered so severely from diarrhea that he could not even be carried properly in his bed.

The priest Boso therefore instructed him to make a true confession of his sins to his own priest. Since it was said that he had repeatedly taken interest from his debtors, not only before but also during his illness, he was to promise God that he would never take it again and that he would make suitable restitution to his debtors for what he had received.

He obeyed. Then he humbly asked that we come to him with the relics, since he could not be carried to us. Three of our men were sent: the priest Boso, Robert, and Boniface. They came to him, washed the relics before him and in water, gave him some of that water to drink, and sprinkled him with it.

Wonderful to relate! The man who had lain in bed for six years immediately rose healed and, leaping up, ran to the bier of Our Lady to give thanks.

He gave the three clerics who had gone to him three gold rings, and before the bier he offered three silver cups, a large sum of money, and other ornaments. When these gifts were publicly displayed in the street, some people, seeing the extent of his wealth, said that he had offered little, for it was reported that more than three thousand pounds of English currency were stored in his treasury.

He replied that for the present he did not wish to give more until he had returned the interest he had received from his debtors, as he had promised God. He therefore immediately had it proclaimed throughout the city that whoever had paid him interest should come and recover his own.

What a voice of joy and praise there was then! Everyone said that through Our Lady Saint Mary another Zacchaeus had appeared at Winchester. They praised God more for the repayment of the interest and the salvation of his soul than for his bodily healing. Even Tully himself, had he been present, could not have described it adequately.

### Chapter IX — Of Twelve Sick People Cured There

Many other sick people were also cured during the eight days we remained in the same city of Winchester. To spare our hearers the tedium, we have omitted to enumerate them individually.

We confidently assert only this: twelve were healed openly and publicly. Some had been deaf, others lame; some had been blind and some mute. All of them were either from the city itself or from the surrounding region, and therefore were known to everyone.

### Chapter X — Of a Sick Girl Cured at Christchurch

[Col. 0979D]

From the city of Winchester we came to a town called Christchurch—that is, “Christ’s Church”—where, during the octave of Pentecost, an annual festival and a very famous gathering of merchants were customarily held.

As we approached the town, we were suddenly overcome by such a great and violent deluge of rain that we do not remember ever having seen anything like it before. A certain dean held the church of that town together with twelve canons. When we asked him to receive us, he replied that the church had not yet been completely built and that for this reason he would not receive us, lest he lose the merchants’ customary offerings.

With difficulty he granted us permission to place Our Lady’s bier upon a small altar in a remote part of the church until the excessive rain should cease. But when he saw that some of the merchants who had heard of the miracles performed at Winchester were seeking Our Lady’s bier with their offerings and leaving the principal altar, he was inflamed with bitter anger and ordered the bier to be thrown out of the church.

After the bier had been expelled, it is not easy to say how great was our distress. The immense rain continued to oppress both us and our horses severely, while the entire town was filled with merchants and no place for us to lodge was available anywhere.

But in such misery the mercy of Our Lady quickly looked upon us. A certain matron, taking pity on our misfortune, begged her husband to lend that very day to the Queen of Heaven the new house he had built—which [read *eamque*] he had rented to merchants for two marks—and to allow her and her clerics to lodge there the following night, while instructing the merchants to seek another lodging in the meantime.

Her husband agreed to his wife’s request. He received us, already almost soaked through and exhausted by the violence of the rain, into his new house. He had our garments, drenched with mud, washed and dried. He placed the bier and relics of Our Lady beside a suitable hearth, decently adorned with curtains, and then took care to show us every kindness of hospitality.

One of the merchants hung three bells, which he had for sale, from the rafters of the house. By their ringing he summoned his companions, climbed to a higher place, and reported how the dean had expelled our bier from his church. He urged them not to go to that church, but all to gather at our lodging to hear the divine office.

Finally, when they had all assembled, they unanimously issued an ordinance that any merchant who entered the church should pay five solidi to his companions. It was then the Saturday before the octave of Pentecost.

Our Lady immediately showed that she had gratefully received such great kindness from our host. This same host had a house near the town where his oxen and sheep were kept. A poor peasant, assigned to guard those animals, lived there. The peasant’s little daughter had had a twisted foot from birth, so that her heel was placed at the front and the toes of her foot at the back.

At our host’s request that the girl’s weak foot be touched with the water in which the relics had been washed, we had her brought to us. She drank some of that water, and her foot was washed with it. She kept vigil before the bier that night.

When morning came, while we were solemnly singing Mass before the bier in the same house as usual—for we carried a portable altar and everything necessary for Mass with us—the little girl was healed. She showed everyone her straightened foot and brought immense joy to her masters, who had received us so kindly.

### Chapter XI — Of the Incredible Vengeance of God Carried Out There

After lunch on that Sunday, having received permission from the inhabitants and repaid them with thanks for their kindness, we left the town.

But the just Judge did not delay in avenging the injury inflicted upon his Mother. We had scarcely gone half a stadium when, behold, riders came after us at a gallop, shouting and begging us to help the town that was burning.

Looking behind us, we saw the entire town ablaze and being consumed by fire. When we asked how this had happened, they told us that a dragon had emerged from the nearby sea, flown into the town after our departure, and first set fire to the church and then to certain houses with the flame it emitted from its nostrils.

Hearing this and longing, out of human curiosity, to see so great a marvel, we entrusted the bier to suitable guardians, quickly rode back to the village, and saw a dragon of incredible length with five heads, emitting sulphurous flames through its nostrils, flying from place to place, and setting the houses on fire one by one.

When we returned as far as the church, we found it already burned—so completely that not only the wood but the walls themselves, indeed even the largest stones and the altars themselves, had been utterly reduced to sparks and ash. All who looked upon it were struck with astonishing terror.

When the dean saw that his house and church had been set on fire, he hurriedly gathered and bound together his clothing and household goods and had them carried to a ship moored on the shore of the nearby sea, hoping that they could be saved there from the fire.

But the dragon immediately flew toward the ship, as though it had come for this very purpose, and burned everything that was in it. Then—wonderful to relate and incredible to hear—it burned the ship itself as well.

We also came to the house of our host, wishing to learn how he was faring, and found him rejoicing, with his house and everything he possessed safe. He attributed his deliverance to his good hostess, the Queen of Heaven.

Not only did the house in which we had lodged remain unharmed, but also the other house, situated at a distance, where we said his animals were kept. Thus he lost absolutely nothing of all his possessions.

The merchants, too, who had shown us great kindness, were so favored by heavenly grace that they lost either nothing or very little of their property. For it was customary there for the fair to last only one day; after lunch they had already gathered all their baggage and placed it bound together before the dragon came.

Nevertheless, the sight of the dragon struck them with immense terror, so that we saw them fleeing rapidly in different directions.

But that dean, who had expelled Our Lady’s bier from his church, was moved by belated repentance. He followed it barefoot, prostrated himself before it, and, acknowledging the justice of God’s judgments, begged that what he had done wrongly might be forgiven him.

### 539 — Chapter XII — Of Seventeen Sick People Healed at Exeter

From there we came to the city called Exeter, where there was an archdeacon named Robert, who had remained for a long time at Laon to hear the teaching of Master Anselm. He received us most gladly, and we stayed there for ten days.

During that time very many miracles occurred. The most important and outstanding concerned seventeen sick people who were cured: some blind, others deaf, mute, or lame.

The citizens competed wondrously with one another over who would receive us as guests and who would provide what was necessary for those they received.

There was there a certain sick man who was said to have lain continually in bed for twenty-four years beside the temple gate, so that he could go nowhere unless two men carried him. On the seventh day after our arrival he sought advice from us, confessed his sins, drank some of the water used to wash the relics, and fell asleep after being washed with it.

Immediately—wonderful to relate!—he was completely healed. He leaped from the bed on which he had lain for so long and, while everyone looked on, ran to the bier. Standing before it, he gave thanks to God and to his devout Mother in a voice of exultation and confession.

### Chapter XIII — Of Glutinus, a Contracted Man, Cured in the Diocese of Salisbury

There was also another contracted man named Glutinus, who was rightly so called because his entire body was so tightly folded together that his heels adhered to his buttocks and his shins to his back. Thus, reduced as though into a single ball, he continually held his face upon his knees.

After he had confessed his sins and been washed with the water used to wash the relics, he was not cured during the ten days we remained there. We wondered at this and asked where he was from. He admitted that he was not from that diocese but from the diocese of Salisbury.

We immediately rebuked him severely for attempting to obtain there a healing that, as had been established and proved, was granted to no one outside his own diocese. With tears and excessive lamentation he began miserably to implore us, for the love of God and of his holy Mother, to travel to the city of Salisbury itself.

Granting the requests of both the man himself and the entire populace, who were making the same plea, we left Exeter after ten days and began to make our way back toward that city.

Behold, the man himself, familiar with the route, had already gone ahead in a vehicle and was waiting for us at the beginning of the diocese. But scarcely had we entered the first stadium of the diocese when he who had gone ahead came to meet us with his vehicle. Immediately, as though Our Lady did not wish him to be wearied any farther, he was perfectly cured, leaped from the cart, and ran along the middle of the road to the bier, giving thanks while all who saw him from every direction gathered around.

This truly proved what we said above: no one could be healed outside his own diocese. From there, as had been arranged, we reached the city of Salisbury itself, where we were honorably received by the bishop of that city because of his acquaintance with Master Anselm; his kinsmen Alexander and Nigel had remained for a long time at Laon attending Anselm’s school.

### Chapter XIV — Of a Man Suffering from Fever Cured at the Nunnery of Wilton

Afterward we came to a certain nunnery called Wilton, where they showed us the tomb of the venerable priest Bede, the distinguished teacher. Near him was buried the renowned female versifier, whose own name was Murier.

A certain man who had long been suffering from fever was lying at the tomb of the venerable priest Bede, where many people had customarily been healed. On the night of our arrival, that female versifier Murier appeared to him in a dream and said:

“You cannot now be healed here through Bede, because the blessed Mother of the Lord has descended to us.”

When he related this to us the next day and drank some of the water in which the relics had been washed, he was immediately healed.

We returned by way of Exeter, though we did not enter the city, despite being urged to do so by many people, lest we become less esteemed, since we had already stayed there for ten days.

### Chapter XV — Of a Blind Girl Given Sight at Danavexeria

From there we came into the province called Danavexeria. There they showed us the chair and oven of that famous King Arthur, according to the stories of the Britons, and said that the land itself had belonged to Arthur.

There a certain cleric named Agardus honored us greatly. He had remained for a long time at Laon and later became bishop of the city of Coutances.

[Note: In *Gallia Christiana* he is called Algarus.]

While we were there, a girl of nearly ten years of age named Kenehellis, blind from birth, came from a village called Bomine to the bier. After her eyes had been washed with the water of the relics, she received her sight.

### Chapter XVI — Of a Deaf Man Healed There

A certain young man in the same village, deaf from birth, also came to the bier. After his ears had been washed with the water of the relics, he immediately heard.

There was also a man there with a withered hand who kept vigil before the bier in order to receive healing through its holiness. But just as the Britons customarily quarrel with the Franks over King Arthur, this man began to quarrel with one of our servants named Haganellus, who belonged to the household of Lord Guido, archdeacon of Laon. He maintained that Arthur was still alive.

When a considerable disturbance arose from this, many men burst into the church with weapons. Had the aforementioned cleric Agardus not intervened, the matter would nearly have reached the shedding of blood.

We believe that Our Lady was displeased by the quarrel carried on before her bier. For the same man who had the withered hand and had caused the disturbance over Arthur did not receive his healing.

### Chapter XVII — Of a Crooked Girl Cured at the Castle of Bannistaple
After this we came to the castle called Bannistaplum, [Col. 0984A] where there lived a certain prince named Joellus of Totnes, whose wife was the sister of Guermund of Pinkeni (Pequigny). He received us most graciously, partly because of his wife's connection—for she belonged to the religious community of Amiens and thus seemed to be our fellow countrywoman—but even more because he had learned of the miracles performed through Our Lady. He kept us with him for three days and gave us a silver bowl, a precious chalice, curtains, and other ornaments, which are still preserved in the church of Laon, as well as a horse to carry them, and many other things; in addition, he gave us goods worth fifteen pounds in Laon currency.

Wishing to be an evident and prompt rewarder of this devotion, Our Lady there displayed a manifest miracle. A twelve-year-old girl [Col. 0984B] was living in his household, so bent over throughout her body that she could go nowhere, except that she dragged herself across the ground on little stools, crawling as best she could. Brought to the bier, she confessed her sins and was washed with water from the relics. She was not cured while we were there; but when we were already departing and she cried out with great weeping, “Alas, most compassionate holy Lady Mary, are you really going to leave like this and abandon me uncured?” she was immediately healed before everyone’s eyes. Throwing away the little stools, she sprang up and stood, then ran to the bier and gave thanks.

### CHAPTER XVIII — Of a lame monk healed there

A certain devout monk of Charité was also staying there, in a cell that the aforementioned prince Joellus [Col. 0984C] had built. For two years he had suffered so severely from an incurable disease, which physicians call *sciatica* [Latin: *sciam*], that he could go nowhere except by limping and supporting himself with a staff. For the entire three days that we remained in the same church, he served us most sweetly as best he could, and washed the diseased place on his thigh with water in which the relics had been washed. He was not cured while we were there; but when we had already left the castle and were asking the people for leave while giving thanks, and he was following us limping with his staff, he was suddenly healed. He threw away the staff, came running to the bier, and, while everyone looked on, gladly and cheerfully embraced and kissed it. Then he placed it upon his shoulder and carried it with us for some distance [Col. 0984D].

### CHAPTER XIX — Of another lame man healed near the castle of Totnes

After this we came to the castle of the aforementioned prince Joellus, called Totnes, with some of his men escorting us. We were honorably received there by certain monks and remained for three days. An old man lived there who had been lame from birth and was known to everyone, since he was the brother of the governor of that castle. When he heard of the miracles that were taking place, he came to the bier with faith and great devotion. He drank water from the washing of the relics, was washed with it, and immediately stood upright before the people. This miracle [Col. 0985A] was held in such great veneration that his brother, the governor of the castle, promptly offered forty shillings of English currency at the bier, and an innumerable crowd added many further gifts.

### CHAPTER XX — Of the miraculous vengeance inflicted there upon a man who hanged himself

But behold, a terrible miracle follows, such as we read rarely to have occurred since the time of Judas the betrayer. Three young men from that territory, related to one another by blood, saw so much money being brought to the bier and began to mock us, saying that we performed such miracles by magical arts for the sake of profit. One of them urged the other two to go with him to the [Col. 0985B] bier and, pretending to kiss it, fill their mouths by licking the coins placed upon the altar.

When the other two refused to commit such a crime and offend the holy Mother of the Lord, that treacherous man persisted in the evil he had begun. Leaving outside the horse on which he had been riding, he entered the church, approached the bier, and pretending to kiss it reverently, snatched as much as he could of the heap of coins with his mouth. He immediately went out, mounted his horse, returned to his companions who had been waiting for him, showed them the coins he had stolen, and invited them to go with him to the nearest tavern for a drink. They replied that they would indeed go with him, but would not drink from such a theft. The wretched man entered the tavern and, having satisfied himself as he pleased, came out.

The other two returned to the gathering of the people [Col. 0985C]; but the unhappy man mounted his horse and, as heavenly vengeance pursued him, made for the nearest forest, scarcely half a mile away. There he tied a linen cord around his neck and hanged himself from the branch of a tree. The horse on which he had been riding returned empty to the people and caused those who saw it great astonishment. At once the two young men recognized their companion’s horse and, wondering what had happened to him but not knowing the horse’s tracks, searched them and hurried after them until they quickly reached the forest. There they found him hanging by the cord and already dead.

They took him down and untied the purse hanging from his belt. In it they found the coins he had stolen, still stained with the fresh saliva of his mouth [Col. 0985D]. Immediately they carried them back with the greatest grief to the bier and placed them upon the altar. Prostrating themselves on the ground, they implored the mercy of the holy Mother of God for the soul of their dead relative, and before everyone recounted the crime that the wretch had committed. One might have seen the crowds of people, hearing of so great a wickedness, struck with amazement and, beating their breasts over the speed of the vengeance, shedding abundant tears.

### CHAPTER XXI — Of the deliverance of clerics by Saint Mary near the castle of Bristolth

From there we came to that very strong castle called Bristolth, which is surrounded by a great river. Through this river, at that time, many merchants brought maritime ships from the island of Ireland, laden with various wares [Col. 0986A]. We were gladly received by the clerics of the castle. Hearing that many ships had arrived, we rejoiced that we had found an opportunity to purchase new clothing, and we went down to the harbor. We boarded the ships and carefully and eagerly examined such a great variety of different merchandise, curious as we were to see unfamiliar things.

Seeing this, our host informed us that it was the custom of the Irish merchants to carry off unknown people who imprudently entered their ships, suddenly and without warning, once the ships had been pushed away from the shore, transporting them to foreign nations and selling them to barbarians. He warned us to beware of their traps. But we paid little attention to his warning and did not cease visiting the ships again.

Then, behold, through the kindly providence of the Mother of God, our host was warned during the following night—not while sleeping but while keeping vigil—to tell us not to enter those ships again, because if anyone entered one of them that day, he should know beyond all doubt that he would immediately be carried away and sold to barbarians [Col. 0986B]. When he informed us of this in the morning under oath, we believed that it was true—namely, that Our Lady’s mercy had forewarned us—and we did not go aboard the ships again. Instead, we bought what was necessary and departed.

### CHAPTER XXII — Of a boy healed at the city of Begea

From there we came to the city called Begea (Belga), where we were honorably received by the bishop, the clerics, and the monks [Col. 0986C]. In that city there are hot baths, which others call thermal baths. On the very day of our arrival, a twelve-year-old boy entered those baths with his companions in order to bathe. But, taking insufficient care for himself, he was overcome by the force of the hot water and submerged to the bottom of the baths.

His parents nevertheless pulled him out and carried him home mourning. Many people said that he had already completely surrendered his vital spirit. But when they heard of the miracles of Our Lady, they brought him with great devotion of faith to her bier. We saw that his body had already grown cold. We ordered two fires to be made and the body to be suspended between them so that it might receive their heat, with the head below and the feet hanging above. Then we had his mouth opened and a small piece of wood placed between his upper and lower teeth.

After this, he vomited a great quantity of water. When his body had been sufficiently warmed, it was taken down and carried to the bier; it was washed with water in which the relics had been washed, and a little of this water was also dripped into his mouth. Without delay, behold, through God’s mercy the boy recovered his spirit, and, complete health having followed as well, returned home happily with his parents.

There are many other miracles that Our Lady performed in England before our eyes, which no one’s eloquence could easily explain one by one. It is enough, however, to have related a few of the many [542] which, with God, her Son, as witness, we have reported without any falsehood in a most truthful account [Col. 0987A].

Now we ask you, as our brothers, lords, and fellow canons, at whose command we crossed the sea and endured many hardships on the journey, to commend to the Lord and to his pious Mother the souls of those who through us sent their alms to you, and to grant that they may share in all the good works performed in the church of Laon, or that may thereafter come to be performed there.

For we brought back from England one hundred and twenty marks, apart from curtains and other ecclesiastical ornaments [Col. 0988A]. We left you on the Monday before Palm Sunday, and behold, we now return to you two days before the Nativity of Our Lady, with joy, praising with you Jesus Christ our Lord, her Son, King of kings and Lord of lords, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages.

# BOOK THREE

### CHAPTER I — Of the multitude of people at the dedication of the church of Laon

[Col. 0987B]

With divine mercy assisting us, the work on our church prospered so greatly through the offerings collected from the faithful throughout France and England that, when the restoration of the building had been completed the following year, it was dedicated. In the year 1112 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the Thursday of Easter week, the aforementioned church had been burned [Note: [Col. 0987B] Guibert likewise says this, *Life*, Book III, chapter 11]. On that same day Lord Gualdric, bishop of Laon, was cruelly killed in his own house together with some of his men. Lord Hugh succeeded him in the bishopric; but when Hugh had survived for scarcely eight months and then died, Lord Bartholomew was elected to the pontificate, as has been written above.

After he had been consecrated bishop, Bartholomew was so eager to hasten the temple of Our Lady that, two and a half years after its burning, its solemn dedication was celebrated again—namely, in the year 1114 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

The bishop and the canons decided that it should be consecrated on the same day on which its solemn dedication was customarily observed each year: that is, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, specifically the third day before the Nativity of Blessed Mary. For this dedication the aforementioned Lord Bishop Bartholomew summoned with him Ralph, archbishop of Reims; William, bishop of Châlons; Lisiard, bishop of Soissons; [Col. 0989A] Godefrid, bishop of Amiens; and Hubert, bishop of Senlis.

So great a multitude of people flocked to the dedication that two hundred thousand persons of different sexes and ages are said to have attended. Great joy filled everyone’s hearts, because after so great a desolation of that church—and indeed of the entire city of Laon—they saw, within so short a time, namely within two and a half years, such a great radiance shining through the mercy of the Mother of God from so vast and profound an abyss of darkness and calamity. Thus it seemed that the saying of the prophet Haggai could appropriately be applied to our church, the saying he once prophesied concerning the restoration of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former” (Hag. II, 10). If a careful reader wishes to examine the matter more closely, he will truly be able to infer very easily that, after the mourning of its desolation, greater glory and exaltation followed in the church of Laon than it had possessed before.

Who, indeed, could adequately relate how great a splendor of religious life and new light afterward shone forth in the bishopric of Laon, and from it through almost the entire world? A few years later, Lord Norbert—this new inventor and founder of a new light and a new conversion, not only inward but also outward in its radiance—came from Lorraine to France. By divine grace going before and accompanying him, he planted in the bishopric of Laon that first vineyard which, rooted and founded in charity (Eph. III, 17), has now filled the earth. Extending its branches to the sea and its shoots to the river (Ps. LXXIX, 12), it has already abundantly intoxicated many princes and judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men together with the young (Ps. CXLVIII, 12), with the wine of its strength, which gladdens the human heart (Ps. CXLIX, 1).

Thus, being powerfully intoxicated, they seek nothing else but to praise the name of the Lord and sing a new song to him. For, stripping off the old man with his practices and putting on the new man, who has been created according to God (Eph. III, 9), they utterly reject carnal enticements. As though water at the wedding feast had been changed by the Lord into wine (John II, 9), they forget what lies behind and reach forward to what lies ahead (Phil. III, 13). Although they remain bodily upon earth, they set their minds on the things above, not on those upon earth (Col. III, 1), saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Phil. III, 20). Joined in mind to the heavenly Seraphim, they burn continually with the sole love of Christ, to whom they offer their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God (Rom. XII, 1), displaying even in their outward clothing the radiance of virtues with which they shine inwardly.

From what follows it will easily be recognized that the aforementioned Bishop Bartholomew was a companion and participant in this lofty and glorious institution.

### CHAPTER II — How Lord Bishop Bartholomew found Lord Norbert

[Col. 0990A]

After Pope Paschal had died at Rome and the cardinal John who succeeded him had been called Gelasius, and after Gelasius, wishing to come to France, had ended his life at Cluny, the cardinals who had come with him saw that they could not return to Rome to conduct an election. Compelled by necessity, they immediately elected to the headship of the apostolic see Lord Guido, archbishop of Vienne, from the neighboring city. He was a noble and able man, the uncle of the queen of the Franks, namely the wife of King Louis. Consecrating him pope in that same region, they called him Calixtus.

Before going to Rome, he wished to hold a general council in France. He ordered nearly all the bishops and archbishops of the entire West, together with abbots and other ecclesiastical persons, to assemble at the city of Reims [Col. 0990B]. King Louis of the Franks also attended this council.

For the sake of this council, the aforementioned Lord Bishop Bartholomew was traveling toward the city of Reims with his clerics and men. When he had already passed the monastery of Saint-Thierry, he saw the aforementioned Norbert sitting with two clerics not far from the road.

A short while earlier Norbert had heard two voices, as he later used to relate. The first had called from one side: “This is Norbert and his companions.” The other then called from the opposite side: “This is Norbert and his companion.” What this signified will be explained later.

After hearing these two voices from the heights of the air, Norbert, astonished, turned aside from the road and sat down on the ground with his two companions, looking around him in bewilderment. Without delay, the aforementioned bishop approached. He did not pass by them like a priest or Levite who had seen a man wounded by robbers; instead, he turned aside from the road and greeted them kindly. Then he asked who they were.

Norbert replied that he was from Lorraine and had left his parents and the vanity of the world, intending to pursue a religious life. Since this way of life was to be begun with the counsel and authority of the apostolic see, he had already spent three days at Reims. But because, amid the continual influx of the rich, no access to the pope was open to him, he had left the city sad and despairing, not knowing where to turn.

Then, moved by deep compassion, the bishop urged them to return with him to Reims, promising that he would introduce them to the pope. Since they were on foot, he ordered his men to dismount from their horses. He then had Norbert and his companions mount and ride with him. As they traveled, he questioned them more carefully and learned that Norbert had been born of noble lineage, had possessed great wealth in the church of Cologne, but had chosen poverty and abandoned all of it entirely.

When the pontiff arrived at Reims, he entered to see the pope and respectfully pointed out to him that it was not right for him, as the universal Father of the Church, to speak only with the rich while keeping the poor from his conversation. The pope immediately agreed, and the bishop introduced Norbert and his companions. They were refreshed by an apostolic conversation.

But because the pope was extremely occupied there and could not fully satisfy their wishes or converse with them at length, he promised the bishop that, once the council was finished, he would immediately go to Laon, rest there for several days, and speak with them sufficiently. He asked him to send them ahead and tell them to await him at Laon.

Therefore, for as long as they remained afterward at Reims, the bishop always kept them with him. Then, when he returned to Laon, he never allowed them to be separated from his company. When the lord pope later arrived as he had promised, the bishop received him most dutifully, as was fitting; and at last he satisfied Norbert and his companions abundantly with the pope’s conversation.

### CHAPTER III — Of the little church of Saint Martin of Laon, and how Bishop Bartholomew led Norbert through many places
