At that time, outside the walls of the city of Laon, there was a little church built in honor of Saint Martin. The same bishop had repeatedly placed religious clerics there to serve God, but since none of them had been able to make progress there, the church had returned to his possession.

Seeing that the aforementioned Norbert wished to follow a religious and poor life, the bishop began to persuade him to remain in that little church of Saint Martin. He also asked the pope to advise him to do so. But Norbert, understanding his efforts, said: “I did not leave greater riches at Cologne in order now to seek lesser ones at Laon. I do not wish to remain in cities, but rather in deserted and uncultivated places.”

The bishop replied: “I will show you many deserted and uncultivated places suitable for religious life in this bishopric, and I will grant you those I show you.”

After the lord pope’s departure, he took Norbert with him and showed him not all the kingdoms of the world and their glory (Luke IV, 5–6), but the great forest of his diocese called Terrascea. He led him to a place called Foisny, showing him the suitable advantages of its waters, pastures, forest, and lands for religious life.

Then Norbert prayed and said: “Truly, this place is entirely suitable for religious life, but it has not been appointed for me by God.”

The bishop then led him to another place in the same forest called Telonias. After it had been shown to him and he had prayed, Norbert said, as before, that it was indeed sufficiently suitable for religious life, but that this place too had not been appointed for him by God.

Then, returning to Laon, the bishop led him into the Vosges forest and showed him a certain place there called Pratum Monstratum, or Prémontré. Let anyone who reads this judge what devotion this bishop possessed: leaving aside episcopal business, he led an unknown man through so many wooded and pathless places, not without great labor. Although even today, when many people inhabit them, they appear dreadful, at that time they were much rougher and more terrifying, being far removed from every human dwelling and inhabited only by wolves and wild boars.

### CHAPTER IV — How the church of Prémontré was begun

Coming, therefore, to the aforementioned place of Prémontré, they entered, for the sake of prayer, a church built there in honor of Saint John the Baptist. It belonged by right to the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon, and a monk from that monastery was occasionally sent there to conduct the divine office. But because, once Mass had ended, no bread could be found there unless it was brought from elsewhere, the place, together with the little church, had by then become almost deserted.

When the pontiff had finished praying and, as he was leaving, urged the man of God to rise from prayer because the hour of the approaching night was pressing on [Col. 0992B], and there was no place to remain, the servant of God came out and asked him to depart with his men and allow him to keep vigil there throughout the following night.

The bishop then quickly mounted his horse and, since night was already falling, hastened to Anizy. Nevertheless, he did not forget Lord Norbert, but again sent him bread and other necessities through his messenger.

In the morning he returned to him and asked what he wished to do. Norbert, made joyful by overwhelming happiness, replied: “Here, my lord Father, I shall remain, because I know that this very place has been appointed for me by God. Here will be my rest and dwelling, and here, through God’s grace, many will be saved.

“Nevertheless, this little church will not be their principal dwelling. They will build themselves a residence on the other side of this mountain, in which they will rest. For last night I saw in a vision what seemed to be a very great multitude of men dressed in white, carrying silver crosses, candelabra, and thuribles, and circling this very place while singing.”

The pontiff was greatly rejoiced. Yet he did not wish to wrong the monastery of Saint Vincent, whose property the place was. He summoned the abbot of Saint Vincent, gave him a more useful exchange than was then available, and thus, by the authority of his privilege, confirmed that place and its church free to Lord Norbert.

The servant of God Norbert therefore remained there. The bishop returned to Laon, but he did not cease to care constantly for Norbert and his companions.

After a few days, the man of God came to Laon and entered the school of Master Ralph, who had succeeded his brother, Master Anselm, after Anselm’s death. Its schoolmaster delivered an exhortatory sermon, and immediately converted seven of its wealthiest students, who had recently come from Lorraine, leading them to his church with a great deal of money.

But the ancient enemy, who is always accustomed to envy the progress of God’s servants, sought to disturb him at the very beginning. Just as he had deceived Eve in paradise and corrupted Judas among the apostles, so he corrupted one of the two companions who had come with Norbert. Taking by stealth in the middle of the night the money brought by the scholars and entrusted to him by the master, he fled secretly from the church [Col. 0993A], leaving the aforementioned scholars in great poverty and need.

Then the man of God first remembered the voices that, as we said above, he had heard near the city of Reims. He understood them himself and explained to the bishop, who was consoling him about this matter, that the second voice, which had called, “This is Norbert and his companion,” signified that of the two companions who had come with him, only one would remain, while the other would depart with Judas. That is how he himself understood it.

But Lord Leonius, abbot of Saint Bertin, a most religious man and highly learned in both pagan and divine literature, recently [546] read this little book and immediately interpreted that voice differently. He ordered me to insert his opinion here on his behalf [Col. 0993B], saying that from consideration of the time and of the approaching person it could clearly be understood that the voice had testified that Bishop Bartholomew was Norbert’s companion.

“For,” he said, “when Norbert had spent three days at Reims without being able to speak with the pope, and had left the city sad and despairing, not knowing what he should now do or where he should turn, and when he seemed to have no consolation except God, unless it was in his two companions, in whom he trusted to remain inseparably attached to him wherever he went, a voice sounded to him from above: ‘This is Norbert and his companion.’

“It was as though it had said more openly to him: ‘Do not despair or place your confidence only in your two companions, because behold, the bishop whom God has given you as a companion is near. He will lead you back with him and make it possible for you to speak with the pope. In your troubles he will be your most gentle comforter. He will give you a dwelling and a church in which you may rest and bear fruit.’”

Lord Leonius, abbot of Saint Bertin, ordered me to write this, and because I believed that he had truly and faithfully understood the matter, I gladly obeyed him.

### CHAPTER V — How Walter became abbot of the little church of Saint Martin of Laon

Later, when the bishop saw that a considerable number of brothers living religiously had gathered at the place of Prémontré, he asked Lord Norbert to place some of them in the aforementioned little church of Saint Martin, where Norbert himself had refused to remain when asked, so that they might strive to build it up and increase it for God’s honor.

Norbert yielded to the bishop’s requests, placed a few of his brothers there, and appointed as their abbot a religious man named Lord Walter [Col. 0993D]. God, as we believe through the prayers of blessed Martin, immediately granted him such great grace that it seems possible to say of him what the angel said concerning the sacred maiden to Raguel, her father: “No one could possess her, because your daughter is destined as wife for this man who fears God” (Tob. VII, 12).

Similarly, although several men had accepted the little church of Saint Martin from the bishop to govern it, and none of them had been able to advance it, such good fortune accompanied Abbot Walter through divine grace that within twelve years a community of more than five hundred brothers serving God was found there [Col. 0994A]. Therefore I would rightly say that God had reserved it for him.

At first, however, he endured such great poverty there that, apart from one donkey called Burdinus, they had almost nothing else. Each morning they led the donkey into the nearby Vosges forest, loaded the wood they had cut onto its back, and brought it back to Laon. From the wood they sold they bought bread, often remaining hungry for a long time until the bread they had purchased was brought to them after None.

Nevertheless, comforted by Abbot Walter, they did not fail amid such poverty. They served God constantly and gradually advanced by working with their own hands. By God’s gift they have now reached such abundance that they frequently obtain three thousand measures of wine from their vineyards. In the possession of lands and mills, as well as livestock, they surpass nearly all the monasteries of the bishopric of Laon [Col. 0994B].

There is also such an abundance of charity and hospitality there that, because of the constant reception of guests and the daily relief of the poor, God seems wonderfully to multiply and increase everything there. It is now counted among the principal and most distinguished monasteries of France.

### CHAPTER VI — How Lord Hugh was placed in charge of the abbey of Prémontré

Later, in the church of Prémontré, Lord Norbert did not wish to be abbot himself. Instead, he appointed as abbot of that place one of the two companions who had remained with him, named Hugh [Col. 0994C].

Norbert also strove to convert to God not only companies of men but companies of women, so that today we see more than a thousand women converted in various places belonging to the same church. They serve God with such strictness and silence that in the most rigorous monasteries of monks one could scarcely find a similar religious life.

Norbert was not content to confine the companies of his brothers within the boundaries of the diocese of Laon. Like bees that leave the hives in which they have made honey and fly to other places to make honey there, he too began to seek out various deserted places and, sending brothers, to build new monasteries.

He established that, from all the monasteries that during his lifetime or after his death would follow the pattern and purpose of his institutions and rule, all the abbots should meet every year on the feast of Saint Dionysius at the first mother from which they had proceeded—that is, the church of Prémontré—as if to drink at a fountain. They were to hold a general chapter together and correct there whatever might need correction, whether in common or in some particular matter.

Although thirty years have not yet passed since Lord Norbert was brought there by the aforementioned bishop, so many monasteries have already sprung up from it, by divine grace, that nearly one hundred abbots are found to have gathered there from them on the aforesaid feast—not only from France and Burgundy, but also from Germany, Saxony, and Gascony [Col. 0995A]. To say nothing of the others, twelve other monasteries have already proceeded from the aforementioned church of Saint Martin, over which Lord Walter, its first abbot, still presides.

Nor are only the neighboring provinces illuminated by so great a light. The ray of this new sun has already crossed the sea and, sending several illustrious stars, has illuminated and glorified the city of Jerusalem.

I do not know what others may think; in my heart I believe, and I confidently declare aloud, that Lord Bishop Bartholomew is a companion, participant, and fellow worker in all the good works performed in all these monasteries and in those that will later be performed.

For since the Truth says in the Gospel, “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X, 41), it is entirely clear that this bishop, who not only received the aforementioned servant of God but also, as has been written above, set aside his episcopal business to lead him through so many remote and dreadful forest places, finally to plant him firmly in the solitude of Prémontré and continually water what had been planted, will certainly not lack the fruit of that work’s sweet reward.

Blessed Gregory, explaining this saying more subtly in his homily on the Gospel passage “in the fifteenth year” (Luke III, 1), says: “It should be noted that the Lord does not say, ‘He will receive a reward from a prophet,’ but ‘a prophet’s reward,’ because he should know that he himself will receive the reward which the prophet received from God for his good work—he who, by receiving the prophet, became his helper” (*Homily* 20, near the middle).

[Col. 0995C] To demonstrate the certainty of this matter more clearly, the same blessed Gregory also adds the testimony of the prophet Isaiah, who, among the cedar, olive, fir, and other more valuable trees, also mentions elms. Although an elm by itself bears no fruit, nevertheless, when it supports a vine with its cluster, it too is reckoned by the Lord among fruit-bearing trees (Isa. XLI, 19). If anyone wishes to examine this statement of blessed Gregory more carefully, I think he will not mock me for having written this, but will himself confidently declare that, although the aforesaid Bishop Bartholomew was occupied with ecclesiastical duties and seemed to be involved in secular affairs, nevertheless, since he always took such great pains to assist the servants of God who were fleeing worldly life, he also became, through God’s grace, a participant in the sweetness of their devout way of life, and therefore will not lack their reward in the future. Since this is so, I confess that the statement of Dom Leo, abbot of Saint-Bertin, mentioned above, deserves to be praised on good grounds, because he understood and declared that this same bishop had been announced by a heavenly voice as the companion of Dom Norbert.

### CHAPTER VII — The manifold commendation of Dom Norbert

But, to conclude briefly now concerning this same Norbert, many testify that, after the apostles, no one in the holy Church produced so much fruit in so short a period of time. Although some say that Dom Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, bore no less fruit at the same time, nevertheless, if anyone pays closer attention, I think he will not deny that Norbert surpassed him. For Dom Bernard was not the founder of that religious order; rather, the same order was already flourishing in the Cistercian [or Cistercian] monastery, where the aforesaid Bernard was a cleric. Having heard the reputation of that order, he assumed the monastic habit under Abbot Stephen. From that monastery, moreover, the monastery of Clairvaux arose, and Bernard, on account of his holiness, was appointed its first abbot.

Thus, although by his preaching he converted very many people and, through God’s grace, brought forth many monasteries from Clairvaux, he was indeed a great waterer and propagator of that order, but he was not its first planter. Norbert, however, was the first planter of his own foundation and, by God’s gift, its first initiator. For although his followers say that they observe the Rule of blessed Augustine, nevertheless—if we may say so with the permission of blessed Augustine—we see Norbert’s institution to be much stricter and much more severe than Augustine’s.

Moreover, in the Cistercian monastery only men are received. Dom Norbert, however, established that, together with the male sex, the female sex should also be received for conversion. Thus, in his monasteries, we see the women’s way of life to be even narrower and more rigorous than that of the men. The men, after their conversion, go out into public for necessary tasks and other affairs; they are frequently involved in ecclesiastical or even secular business, responses, or embassies; and many whom we knew in their former life to have been rustics or poor men we often see riding about in the religious habit almost ostentatiously. For the women, however, as soon as they have been converted, a perpetual rule thereafter remains: they are always to be kept enclosed within the bounds of the house, never again to go outside, and never to speak with any man—not merely an outsider, but not even a brother or relative—except at a window in the church, with two converted men seated outside with the man, and two women seated inside with the woman, hearing everything that is said.

At the very beginning of their conversion, as soon as they are received, even their hair is cut back as far as the ears, in order to cut away all pride and carnal pleasure; and, so that they may please Christ, their heavenly bridegroom, more fully, they are entirely disfigured for love of him in their frail and seductive flesh. Thereafter no one may possess any costly garment other than one of wool or sheepskin. No one may wear a silk veil, as some nuns do, but only the cheapest little black cloth upon her head. Although they are known to be enclosed in such strictness and poverty, in silence, nevertheless, by a wondrous action of Christ’s power, we see women every day—not merely rustic or poor women, but rather women of the highest nobility and wealth, both young widows and girls—hastening to the monasteries of that foundation, rejecting the pleasures of the world for the sake of conversion and running, as it were, to mortify their tender flesh. We believe that more than ten thousand women are now contained in them.

If Dom Norbert had done nothing else, but, leaving aside the conversion of men, had by his exhortation drawn so many women to divine service, would he not have been worthy of the greatest praise? But now, since so many thousands of both sexes serve Christ according to his teaching, and since so many monasteries founded according to his institution shine throughout the world, I do not know what others may think, but it seems true to me that many assert: since the time of the apostles, no one has acquired for Christ, through his own foundation, so many imitators of perfect life in so short a period. And indeed, if he had remained longer at the Premonstratensian monastery, perhaps he would have accomplished many other things. But it pleased divine predestination that he should obtain, in the religious habit, the honor which he had avoided by fleeing from secular life; and that he who before his conversion had refused to be a bishop should, after his conversion, become an archbishop.

### CHAPTER VIII — How he declined the bishopric of Cambrai

Dom Hugh, abbot of Prémontré, recently told me that, at the beginning of his conversion, after Norbert had left the church of Cologne and his parents, he came barefoot and on foot to Valenciennes. There he found Dom Burchard, bishop of Cambrai. When he heard that the aforesaid bishop was going to celebrate Mass in the morning, he came to the church and asked the same Hugh—who at that time was the bishop’s chaplain—to arrange for him to speak with the bishop. Hugh, not knowing who he was, went in and announced to the bishop that a foreign cleric was outside the door and wished to speak with him.

At the bishop’s command, Norbert was brought in. When the bishop recognized him—for he had often seen him living familiarly at the emperor’s court and enjoying great wealth—he was immediately struck with astonishment, and, overcome by abundant tears, said:

“Ah, Dom Norbert, who could have believed that you would abandon such great riches and willingly come to such poverty? Lord God, what is this that I see concerning Dom Norbert, whom I once used to see so proudly dressed and walking with such pompous arrogance?”

When the chaplain Hugh saw him weeping so wonderfully and scarcely able to speak because of his excessive weeping, he asked who this Norbert was, for whom the bishop was shedding such abundant tears. The bishop replied:

“If you knew who he had been, you would marvel that he is now such a man. When the emperor gave me the bishopric of Cambrai, he first offered it to this Norbert, but Norbert himself would neither accept nor possess it. For he was honorable and exceedingly rich among the canons of Cologne; but now, as you see, he has abandoned everything for God and strives to seek God with bare feet.”

Hugh the chaplain heard this from the bishop’s mouth and immediately became inflamed with love for Norbert. Since he too had already been considering renouncing the world, he began in his heart to give thanks to God, who had destined such a companion for him. Thus, just as Andrew once heard the Lord praised by his teacher John the Baptist and, leaving John, followed the Lord (John I, 40–42), so Hugh, hearing Norbert praised so highly by his master, Bishop Burchard, whose chaplain he had long been, left that bishop and attached himself to Norbert. Having arranged his possessions according to Norbert’s counsel, he became his inseparable companion in pilgrimage and preaching, and traveled everywhere with him barefoot, until, coming to Rheims for the council of Pope Calixtus, he was introduced, as we related above, to Dom Bartholomew, bishop of Laon.

### CHAPTER IX — How he became archbishop of Magdeburg

Since it has therefore been reported that Norbert could have become bishop of Cambrai but did not wish to be one, let us now add how he became an archbishop. After he had converted many men and women, who had abandoned the vanity of the world, to the service of God, and after many monasteries had been established far and wide so that his reputation spread everywhere, he was sent by the famous Count Theobald of Champagne, son of the brother of King Henry of England, to a certain most distinguished prince of Lorraine, whose daughter that same count married.

Meanwhile, it happened that, after the archbishop of Magdeburg had died, the clerics of that city assembled to conduct an election for another. In that same year, Dom Norbert, speaking privately with his friend Dom Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, foretold to him that he had learned through a vision that in that year he would become a bishop, but he did not know of what city or province.

When the clerics of Magdeburg had indeed elected several men but could not unanimously agree upon the election of any one of them, they were informed that two legates of the Apostolic See, religious men, had come from the city of Rome to Mainz. One was called Peter, the other Gerard, who later became pope, succeeding Celestine and preceding Eugenius. Fearing that, because of the disagreement over the election, a ruinous sedition might perhaps arise among them, the aforesaid clerics held a council, approached the legates of the Apostolic See, placed their election in their hands, and promised that they would accept whomever the legates elected.

Seeing their great devotion, the legates proposed to accept no money, which certain people were offering them through intermediaries, lest the Apostolic See, and especially the legates themselves, be defamed on this account. While they were asking for the Lord’s mercy in order to settle so great an affair properly, commendably, and without any stain of simony, and while they were carefully discussing the matter with wise men placed in the Church, behold, Norbert, coming unexpectedly and without warning from France for the sake of prayer, entered that same church, entirely unaware of the matter.

[Col. 0999A] When the legates saw him, they were astonished and amazed, and rejoiced that their prayers had been heard by God. They summoned the clerics of Magdeburg and asked whether, still remaining in their former resolve, they would accept the man chosen by the legates. When they all answered together and unanimously that they would accept without any contradiction whoever was named, the legates immediately added:

“And we, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, name and elect for you Dom Norbert, a religious and proven man, whom, as we believe, the Lord God has sent to us and to you for the completion of this present matter.”

Norbert, stunned by so incredible and sudden an event, was bewildered and amazed, not knowing whether he was awake or asleep, where he was, or from where he had come; he wondered at himself and questioned himself. At once, therefore, the clerics seized him and dragged him along. He was not led to the altar but carried there by force. In a loud voice they sang, “We praise you, O God”; then, compelled by the bond of obedience, he was consecrated bishop.

Thus, while fleeing the bishopric of Cambrai, he obtained, by God’s will, the archbishopric of Magdeburg. Living religiously there for several years, he finally rested from his labors in a blessed death.

### CHAPTER X — The transformation and improvement of the church of Prémontré

His aforesaid companion, Dom Hugh, elected abbot of the monastery of Prémontré by that same Norbert and confirmed by Dom Bartholomew, bishop, diligently strove, by exhorting and laboring alongside the brothers, to water the vineyard which Dom Norbert had planted with him; and in all things God mercifully granted it growth.

Seeing that the little church was now unable to accommodate the great multitude of brothers who had gathered and was increasing daily by God’s grace, and knowing also that Dom Norbert, as was said above, had foreseen in the spirit that a larger church would be built on the other side of the mountain, Hugh consulted with his brothers and asked Dom Bartholomew, bishop, as the founder and father of the place, to come, so that, after arranging all the buildings, he himself might lay the first stone in the foundation of the church.

When the bishop arrived, that entire army of God joyfully came to meet him in a great procession, praising God with a voice of exultation and thanksgiving. Immediately the bishop remembered the vision which Norbert had reported seeing on the first night of his arrival at that place: a multitude of men dressed in white, carrying silver crosses with candleholders and censers, and going around the place singing. He rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to God, because what Norbert had seen in a vision, the bishop now saw actually taking place in bodily reality.

Anyone who comes there may plainly inspect what sort of church, dormitory, refectory, and other buildings were constructed there by the aforesaid Hugh, and what kind of wall was built around the monastery. For even in the richest and most ancient monasteries of Gaul it would scarcely be possible to find a work like it, so that all who arrive and inspect it immediately say: “Truly, this has not been made by man, nor through man, and it is marvelous in our eyes.”

Good Jesus! With what joy is Bishop Bartholomew filled whenever he comes there for the sake of visitation and sees so splendid a monastery, constructed by the Lord in his own days, through his own counsel and initiative. It seems to me that he too could say with the Apostle Paul: “I have done more abundantly than my predecessors, the bishops of Laon”—“yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV, 10).

### CHAPTER XI — The construction of the monastery of Fuisniac

[Col. 1000B] The same bishop did not offer himself as a helper only to Dom Norbert and his followers, who serve God under the clerical order. He also wished to have monasteries of Clairvaux monks in his diocese, and gave them a place called Fuisniac in the forest of Terascia. As was written above, Dom Norbert had said that this place had been shown to him by the same bishop and was suitable for religious life, but had not been destined for him by God.

Thus the Lord, who disposes his servants and appoints them wherever and however he wishes, destined Prémontré for Norbert but Fuisniac for the men of Clairvaux. At Fuisniac the bishop would sometimes remain with the monks for an entire week, sometimes for fifteen days, bearing their labor and poverty with the greatest kindness and continually consoling them sweetly. He strove to construct and complete their church and necessary buildings, together with mills and cultivated lands.

### CHAPTER XII — The construction of Spinetum

Nor did he cease until, after Dom Goswin had been appointed abbot there and a great crowd of brothers had gathered, he saw another monastery proceed from it, in his diocese near Guise, at a place called Spinetum. There he appointed as abbot a man named Odo, who, having fled from the city of Laon in his youth, had become a monk at the monastery of Fuisniac.

### CHAPTER XIII — The construction of Valclarus

The aforesaid bishop also built a third monastery of the same order of Clairvaux monks, at a place which the inhabitants improperly call Valclarus.

### CHAPTER XIV — The construction of the church of Telonias

The bishop did not wish to leave empty the place called Telonias, which Dom Norbert had said was suitable for the region but had not been destined for him by God. He therefore placed there some of the clerics of the aforesaid church of Saint Martin of Laon, and appointed over them as abbot Dom Walfrid, a religious man. The bishop himself, as he had done at Fuisniac, remained there with them for eight or fifteen days, and began to build a stone church and other buildings.

### CHAPTER XV — The construction of Clarafontana

[Col. 1001A] He built another monastery from the aforesaid Premonstratensian order at a place called Clarafontana, and appointed there as abbot the religious man Dom Gerard.

### CHAPTER XVI — The construction of Cuissiac

He also built another monastery of clerics at a place called Cuissiac, and appointed there as abbot Dom Luke, a religious man. When he saw that the monks of Valclarus, who lived nearby, were disputing with their neighbors, the canons of Cuissiac, over a certain adjoining forest—each side saying that the forest had first been given to it by the laymen who had possessed it, and each defending its own right—so that even Dom Samson, archbishop of Rheims, and Dom Joslen, bishop of Soissons, together with the aforesaid Bishop Bartholomew and neighboring abbots, repeatedly meeting together, could not settle the dispute between them, the bishop was grieved and deeply distressed that such discord existed among the religious men of his diocese and that from it a bad example was being created for plunderers and other secular men.

He therefore decided to settle such a quarrel with his own money. Giving fifteen pounds of coin to certain knights, he bought another forest from them and granted it to the clerics of Cuissiac in exchange for the forest they were claiming. By this gift he finally calmed the long-standing conflict. As we believe, he thereby deserved to be numbered among those of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God” (Matt. V, 9).

### CHAPTER XVII — The construction of the monastery for women called Monsteriolum

Thus, by building eight monasteries in his diocese—three from the order of Clairvaux monks and five from that of the Premonstratensian clerics—and appointing a proper abbot over each, Dom Bartholomew fashioned them after the eight evangelical beatitudes. Finally, so that the number of the nine orders of angelic powers might be completed, he added a ninth monastery, for the female sex, at a place called Monsteriolum near Clarafontana, and appointed there as abbess a most religious girl named Guiburg.

On account of this one monastery, I may rightly say that the Church of Laon ought to be preferred to all others. For nowhere in the world had such an abbey of women religious previously been read of in books or heard of by human ears. These women, as executors, so to speak, of that saying of the Lord—“The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12)—striving with all their strength to ascend to that same kingdom, utterly despise earthly things. Desiring to overcome not only the world but also their own sex, they willingly and voluntarily assumed the Cistercian order, which many men and robust young people fear to undertake.

After laying aside all linen garments and furs, they use only woolen tunics. They labor continually with their own hands, not only by spinning and weaving, which are acknowledged to be women’s work, but also by digging in the fields, clearing cut forest with axe and mattock, and pulling up thorns and brambles. In silence they seek their livelihood. In every respect they imitate the life of the monks of Clairvaux and demonstrate in themselves the truth of the Lord’s saying: “All things are possible to the one who believes.”

I have therefore rightly said above that this ninth monastery of women, constructed by the aforesaid bishop, was made in the likeness of the ninth order of angels, who are called Seraphim—that is, “burning” or “kindling”—because truly, unless these women were warmed by the wondrous fire of divine love, they could certainly never endure so many and such great labors, previously unknown and unattempted by women. But while they burn mightily within, they themselves perform wondrous deeds and kindle others, by their example, to despise the world, like live coals which, when mixed with dead ones, immediately set them alight and make them burn.

These, then, are the nine monasteries which the aforesaid bishop constructed in his own time. Yet he did not cease to correct the older monasteries which he found already built.

### CHAPTER XVIII — Dom Simon, abbot of Saint Nicholas

At the monastery of Saint Nicholas, which he saw situated in the Vosges forest and somewhat lukewarm in religious observance, he appointed as abbot a very energetic monk of Saint Nicaise of Rheims, named Simon. Through him, by God’s gift, that Church was improved within a short time so greatly that it flourished both inwardly in religious observance and outwardly in possessions of many kinds.

For this reason, Count Theobald of Champagne, on the advice of Dom Norbert, placed over the very wealthy monastery of Latiniacum a certain monk of that same monastery, named Ralph, whom the aforesaid abbot had received. Dom Simon, bishop of Noyon, a very noble man and the brother of Ralph, count of Vermandois, also asked the aforesaid pontiff Bartholomew to give him two monks from that same monastery of Saint Nicholas. One of them, named Theodoric, he appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Eligius of Noyon; the other, named Absalon, he placed over the monastery of Saint Amand of Hainaut, in the diocese of Tournai.

How they corrected and ennobled the Churches entrusted to them, both inwardly and outwardly, can today be verified by sight rather than by report.

### CHAPTER XIX — Dom Gilbert, abbot of Saint Michael

The aforesaid Bishop Bartholomew also made Dom Gilbert, prior of that same monastery of Saint Nicholas, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael of Terracina. Before his conversion, he had been called Plato because of his knowledge of the arts, in which he excelled. By God’s gift, within a short time Gilbert made that monastery flourish much more abundantly than it had previously been—and more abundantly than he himself had found it—both in religious observance and in wealth.

But after several years, when the aforesaid Simon, abbot of Saint Nicholas, had died, Dom Bartholomew, bishop, with the counsel of abbots and religious men, transferred the same Gilbert from the monastery of Saint Michael, because of his reputation for probity, and placed him as abbot over the Church of Saint Nicholas, of which he had been a monk and prior. There he has endured many labors to this day, for he has often gone to Rome for the benefit of that Church.

### CHAPTER XX — Dom Anselm, abbot of Saint Vincent

In the monastery of Saint Vincent, situated outside the walls of the city of Laon and said to be the second episcopal see, the aforesaid Bishop Bartholomew appointed as abbot Dom Anselm, summoned from the monastery of Saint Medard of Soissons.

The probity of this Anselm can be clearly perceived from this single fact: from among his monks, chosen for service in different Churches, we now see nine men of proven character flourishing as abbots. In the monastery of Orbais there is Dom Baldwin; in Morimond, William; in Saint Sepulchre of Cambrai, Parvinus; at Saint Andrew of the New Castle, Adam; at Hainaut, Fulk; at Fismes, Gerard; at Virtus, Robert; at Saint Nicholas near Ribemont, William; and at Saint Michael of Terracina, John. All these are now venerable abbots, and all call the Church of Laon their mother and Bishop Bartholomew their father and shepherd.

### CHAPTER XXI — How the same Anselm was elected bishop of Tournai at Rome

[Col. 1003C] After the same Anselm had presided over the monastery of Saint Vincent for nearly seventeen years, and had gone to Rome for the benefit of that monastery with his brother Dom Walter, a monk of that place, he was found there by a wondrous event, ordained by God, and was elected bishop by the clerics of Tournai, who had been without their own bishop for four hundred years.

[Note: [Col. 1003] Because from the time of Saint Medard the bishop of Noyon governed the Church of Tournai.]

He was consecrated pontiff by Dom Pope Eugenius, unwilling and resisting, but constrained by the bond of obedience. Thus the ancient dignity of the Church of Tournai was restored through him, in the year 1145 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday.

Returning from Rome and being received at Laon with a great procession, he did not wish to leave the monks, his former sons at Saint Vincent, orphans. He therefore appointed one of them, Dom Baldwin, young in age but grave in character, as their abbot in his place, and had him ordained by Dom Bartholomew, bishop. He then set out for Tournai to govern the flock entrusted to him.

### CHAPTER XXII — The correction of the abbey of Saint John and the appointment of Abbot Drogo

After these events, the aforesaid bishop also undertook to correct the abbey of Saint John the Baptist, which is said to have been older, richer, and nobler than all the other monasteries of the diocese of Laon mentioned above.

Blessed Sallaberga built this abbey, as is read in her Life, and, placing nuns there, was herself their first abbess. She sought to exalt it with such authority that, as antiquity relates, just as it is written in the Apocalypse of John, “Write to the seven Churches that are in Asia” (Rev. I, 11), so, desiring this abbey also to be like another Asia, she built seven churches in it.

The first and most important, founded in honor of the holy Mother of God, she wished to be called Saint Mary the Deep, perhaps to distinguish it from the greater church of Saint Mary, where the episcopal see is located. The second was dedicated to Saint Michael and All the Angels; the third to Saint John the Baptist and All the Patriarchs and Prophets; the fourth to blessed Peter the Apostle and All the Apostles. After these four, at the entrance of the abbey, she built a fifth in honor of the Holy Cross, so that, through the power of that same cross, every assault of diabolical deceit might be driven back from the very entrance. The sixth was in honor of Saint Afra the martyr; the seventh in honor of Saint Mary Magdalene.

Of these seven churches, five still remain. Two—the Church of the Holy Cross and that of Saint Afra the martyr—have failed because of excessive age.

The abbey was of such dignity that whenever the king of the Franks was to be crowned at Laon on solemn days, he especially wore the golden crown there. No four-footed animal could enter within the wall or gate of the abbey without immediately becoming rabid and insane. Therefore, whenever a king, bishop, or other princes came to the abbey, all their horses had to be left outside the gate, and they themselves proceeded on foot to the church.

When blessed Sallaberga died, her daughter, the holy Austrudis, succeeded her as abbess. Thus for nearly three hundred years and more, nuns remained there, and for a long time possessed many estates received as gifts from kings and princes.

In the days of the aforesaid Dom Bartholomew, bishop, however, the ancient religious observance in that monastery had cooled considerably, and its external possessions had gradually diminished. Moreover, certain things of ill repute were being said about the virgins themselves. Greatly saddened by this, the pontiff saw that, although he frequently admonished them, they promised verbally to amend but did not fulfill their promises in deeds.

With the counsel and authority of Lord Pope Innocent, of Lord Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, and of King Louis of France, to whom the same Church was said properly to belong, he expelled all those nuns from the abbey together. He also took the religious man Dom Drogo, prior of the monastery of Saint Nicaise of Rheims, appointed him its first abbot, and placed enough monks there from various monasteries.

But when, by God’s gift, he had already made considerable progress there, and the good fragrance of his wisdom and probity had spread far and wide, the aforesaid Pope Innocent, constraining him by the bond of obedience, forced him to go to Rome and consecrated him bishop of the city of Ostia.

### CHAPTER XXIII — Baldwin, abbot of the same place

The monks of Saint John, having been made orphans without a father, unanimously elected Dom Baldwin, the son of his sister, whom he had made a monk there, as their abbot in his place. They presented him for confirmation to the aforesaid bishop. He was young in age, but in character and religious observance he displayed the maturity of old age.

When many people seeking the monastic habit came to him from different provinces, among them came a certain man from the region of Toul, named Hugh. Seeing him endowed both with the fervor of religious observance and with no ordinary knowledge of letters, the aforesaid Abbot Baldwin made him prior of his monastery, rejoicing and giving thanks to God, who had given him such a helper.

But when the aforesaid Pope Innocent, on the advice of Drogo, bishop of Ostia, summoned Dom Hugh, abbot of Humblieres, to Rome and, compelling him by the bond of obedience, consecrated him bishop of the city of Albano, the monks of Humblieres, at his recommendation by letter, elected the aforesaid Hugh, prior of Saint John, as their abbot. Thus they took him away from Dom Baldwin.

Behold, then, from the new community of the monks of Saint John, an abbot of another monastery has already arisen. This certainly redounds to the honor of Bishop Bartholomew, its founder.

But because I have heard certain less-informed people criticizing him on this matter and saying that so great a change ought not to have been made, that even the innocent should not have been expelled on account of the sins of some of the nuns, and that the whole Church should have been handed over to monks—especially since the noble matron Saint Sallaberga and her daughter Saint Austrudis had built it from the possessions of their patrimony, placed nuns there, and made it illustrious through the display of many signs—I wish, to restrain and correct their ignorance or simplicity, to recall a few examples from the divine Scriptures concerning a similar or even greater change.

Is God’s planting not greater than man’s planting? Certainly, concerning the Jews, it is said through King and prophet David:

“You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were its guide on its journey; you planted its roots, and it filled the land” (Ps. LXXIX, 9–5),

along with the other words that follow concerning its establishment.

Although the Law had been given to them through Moses, although they had received the promised land, brought forth kings and prophets who performed many miracles, and although the Lord had promised them perpetual possession of that land, nevertheless, because they cast the son of the householder out of the vineyard when he came and killed him, saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI, 38), they immediately pronounced judgment against themselves when the Lord put the matter before them. They heard him add at once:

“He will destroy those wicked men miserably and will lease his vineyard to other farmers” (ibid. 41),

and then:

“The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (ibid. 43).

In another place, too, the Lord tells the parable of a fig tree. For three successive years he came to it and, finding no fruit, ordered it to be cut down; but when the cultivator of the vineyard interceded, he granted it a postponement for a fourth year.

In like manner, Dom Bartholomew, bishop, admonished those nuns concerning correction both through himself and through religious men—first, second, and third, and also fourth, fifth, and sixth year. When he saw that he was accomplishing nothing, then, in accordance with the Lord’s command, he certainly ought to cut down the fruitless tree and entrust the Lord’s vineyard to other farmers, “who will render its fruit to him in its seasons” (ibid. 41). Since he did this not by his own judgment alone but also with the counsel of the pope and religious men, he was certainly worthy not of reproach but of praise.

Nor should one fear that on this account he incurred the anger of the holy women Sallaberga and Austrudis, who built that Church and assigned it to the order of nuns. Rather, it should be believed that, through their prayers, such a will came to him from God, and that such abbots were destined by God to devote themselves continually both to his service and to the restoration of that Church.

For in no monastery of the kingdom of the Franks that is solely of his foundation do we now see greater religious observance or more charitable hospitality flourishing than in this one. The only exception is that Abbot Baldwin himself, being greatly occupied in seeking out and recovering the possessions of the Church which the nuns had negligently allowed to be taken away, is exhausted by daily labor and complains of nothing more than that he cannot continually be present with the community of brothers or show the guests the service of hospitality as he would wish.

Therefore, when those holy women whose bodies are kept in that same Church see continually, day and night, that the divine office is performed there with such devotion; that silence and religious observance are fervently maintained; that the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood is celebrated not as before but a hundred times more devoutly and frequently; and that religious guests who arrive every day are received with the sweetness of charity—is it not to be believed that they delight in so sweet a service of God? And when they see the monks passing before the altar and humbly bowing with lowered heads before their biers, do they not often say to them:

“The blessing of the Lord be upon you” (Ps. CXXVIII, 8),

and:

“Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXIII, 24)?

I do not know what others may think; I believe it in my heart, and, believing it, confidently declare it with my mouth: that those holy women take greater delight in the divine offices of such monks than of the nuns who remained there throughout the entire time of Lord Bartholomew, and that they implore the Lord’s mercy for the salvation both of those monks and of that same bishop. And just as King David, composing the Psalms, said, “Let these things be written for the generation to come, and the people that shall be created shall praise the Lord” (Ps. 101:19), clearly showing that he composed them not for the Jews but for Christians, so I believe that those holy women rejoice that the church they built has passed to monks of this kind, and that the Lord has granted their possessions to pass to their support.

Since it was said above that nine abbeys had been built by Lord Bartholomew the bishop, though he found none of them, anyone who considers the matter carefully will declare that this is truly the tenth: it was built more than three hundred years before his time, but, having grown cold in religious fervor in his time, is known to have been rebuilt and renewed through him, by divine grace, with monks introduced. This renewal took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127.

## CHAPTER XXIV—How the Major Church of Saint Mary Was Endowed under Bishop Bartholomew

Since the aforesaid bishop had shown such zeal in constructing the other monasteries, it may readily be believed that he worked especially hard to increase the revenues of the major church of Saint Mary, in which the episcopal see was established. Although he could not introduce another religious order there—for it was not easy to compel its canons to change their ancient customs—he nevertheless worked to enlarge their former revenues in such a way that he arranged for them to eat together in the refectory for a large part of the year, and provided them daily with food abundantly and most generously, so that the canons themselves testify that he enriched their prebends by nearly twice as much as before, as can be found in his privileges preserved in that same church.

## CHAPTER XXV—Concerning Guido, Bishop of Châlons

It also belongs to the praise and honor of the Church of Laon and of Lord Bartholomew that Lord Guido, a most noble man whom that bishop had made a canon and dean of the major church of Saint Mary, while still flourishing in youthful age, was nevertheless chosen to the episcopate of the city of Châlons because, as his renown proclaimed, he was distinguished by his religious character and devotion, being both a lover of chastity and a constant attendant at the ecclesiastical office; and he was consecrated by Lord Samson, archbishop of Reims. On arriving at his see, he immediately, in the very first year of his consecration, made a certain young cleric of the Church of Laon named Haimon, who had accompanied him, archdeacon of that same see. Thus, in one and the same year, the city of Châlons received both a bishop and an archdeacon from the Church of Laon.

## CHAPTER XXVI—Concerning Theodoric of Amiens

In the following year, Lord Theodoric—who had first been a monk of the monastery of Saint Nicholas in the diocese of Laon and afterward, as stated above, had become abbot of Saint Eligius of Noyon—was consecrated bishop of Amiens by the aforesaid Archbishop Samson. Thus, within two years, two cities, Châlons and Amiens, received bishops who were sons and fosterlings of the Church of Laon.

Therefore I rightly said above that in the Church of Laon the statement of the prophet Haggai was fulfilled: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former” (Hag. 2:10). For truly, in the episcopate of Laon many monasteries that had not previously existed were added, and from it many more new foundations sprang up throughout the world, shining as though with the radiance of a new light.

Indeed, from the time of Saint Genebaud, the first bishop of Laon, when forty-three bishops had followed him and Lord Bartholomew had succeeded them as the forty-fourth, there is no record of so many miracles being performed by the holy Mother of God in the Church of Laon as occurred in the days of this Bartholomew. Yet during the time of Helinand, who was the fifth bishop of that city before Lord Bartholomew—that is, the thirty-eighth—something miraculous occurred in the same church, which we have thought worthy of committing to writing here for remembrance.

## CHAPTER XXVII—Concerning the Woman Freed from the Fire at Civiacum

In a village called Civiacum, near Laon, there lived a certain man named Guilermus, the administrator of that village [Note: Guibert relates this miracle in *On the Praise of Blessed Mary*, book 1, chapter 10.], with his wife Soiburga [Note: He calls this woman Theodeberta.]. They married their only daughter, named Guiburge, to a certain man named Albuinus; loving the couple dearly, they made them live with them in their common household.

Not long afterward, a rumor of shameful infamy began to fly from mouth to mouth and to increase day by day: the young man, it was said, had abandoned his own wife’s bed, violated his father-in-law’s marriage-bed through adulterous deceit, and illicitly abused both the mother and her daughter. When this reached the ears of that matron through the report of certain people, she was inwardly seized by immeasurable anguish and disturbed by the imputation of a false crime. She began to turn over in her mind, with profound agitation, by what means she might wipe away this stain of accusation from herself.

As she burned within, tormented by extraordinary contrivances, unable to bear her grief, and almost beside herself, she was finally infected by diabolical inspiration and, armed with that infection, resolved, though herself now guilty, to destroy the innocent man, hoping through diabolical deception that this alone would provide a remedy for her infamy.

And behold, winter’s cold had now arrived; the season of grape-gathering and autumn had passed, when many people ordinarily flock to those places from different regions to harvest the grapes for payment. From among these she selected two poor men. Offering them whatever payment they might choose, she extracted from them—faithless woman that she was—a promise that they would conceal the deed in silence and prepare their right hands to commit the cruelest and most abominable crime, as she had conceived it in her mind.

She therefore designated the place and fixed the day and hour when, rising secretly from their hiding places, they would suddenly attack and strangle the innocent man’s throat.

That fatal day was now approaching. Early in the morning, at the first hour of the day, her husband, as he was accustomed to do every day, went out to administer his estate; the household dispersed here and there, and the daughter also went outside. Adam and Eve remained alone: the innocent lamb and the savage lioness. The two poor men mentioned above also secretly entered the storeroom, with her arranging matters for them.

At last, finding the suitable hour for the intended crime, she first mingled in some pleasant conversation, and then ordered him to go down into the inner part of the storeroom and bring up wine. Suspecting no evil, he simply obeyed her as though she were his mother, took a vessel, and hurried down into the interior. As he was drawing wine into the vessel, those men suddenly rose from their hiding place, attacked the innocent man’s throat, and immediately strangled him. At their mistress’s command, they carried him between them to the bed, covered him with his own garments, and arranged him as though he were sleeping.

Meanwhile, her husband returned home, and the daughter and household came back at the hour of dinner. When everything had been prepared, the mother ordered her daughter to awaken her husband. She hastened to the bed of the one lying there and, finding him dead, cried out. All were roused by the sound of her lament and rushed in together; setting aside the meal, they turned to the funeral rites.

The report immediately filled the entire region that Albuinus, healthy only a short while before, had been found dead in his bed. At that time there was in Laon a certain vicarius named Ilbertus, a wise man and one of profound intelligence, though more cruel than was proper. When he heard this report, he first wondered and then began to be moved inwardly by a certain suspicion. He let that day pass, but at dawn of the following day, before the dead man was carried to the tomb, he came quickly with his men to the place and, pretending ignorance, deliberately began to investigate carefully how the event had occurred.

When no one’s account satisfied his mind, he could bear the inquiry no longer. He approached the bier, violently tore apart the cloths in which the body had been covered, and without delay found unmistakable signs of strangulation.

Immediately, raging like a lion in pursuit of vengeance for the crime, he dragged the man, his wife, and his daughter—bound in dreadful chains—to Laon for punishment. As they were being dragged away under cruel mistreatment, the woman said:

“Do not unjustly oppress the innocent, who know nothing of so great a crime; do not torment them with punishments and tortures. I am aware of this crime; I am the murderer of the man, and I alone am guilty. Let the whole weight of the tortures fall upon me; let the entire vengeance for the blood be turned against me. Let these people, as though blameless, be released.”

When he heard this, he released them and presented the guilty woman, who had confessed with her own mouth, to the bishop, committing her to strict custody. While clergy and people were present and different persons were putting forward different judgments, one among the clerics, called Master Quintinus, gave a sentence that she should be burned in the fire. He was indeed well educated in letters, but not well instructed to the depths in divine law, nor inwardly watered by the anointing of the Holy Spirit. When he heard this judgment, and the dead man’s friends were also urging him on, Master Quintinus hastened to carry out at once what had been decreed.

As the wretched woman was being led to execution, she obtained permission to delay and pray in the church of the Blessed Mother of God beside the bishop’s house. When she arrived there, in the presence of clergy and people, she humbly and with a pure confession recounted the whole sequence of the wickedness she had committed, moving many to compassion and to the shedding of tears.

Then, prostrating herself on the pavement, she commended her body and soul to Saint Mary amid abundant weeping. Afterward she rose, armed her face and entire body with the sign of the cross, went out, and was led to the place of execution.

There she was stripped of all her garments except for the linen garment that alone covered the nakedness of her body, and she was brought into the house in which she was to be burned. Her legs were wrapped in bonds, her hands were tightly bound behind her back, and she was fastened with strong chains to a post set in the middle, upon which the entire structure of the house rested. Wood and straw were piled around her, filling the whole interior of the house. After this, the door was closed and fire was set beneath it; immediately, balls of flame rose upward.

Meanwhile, as the cruel fire destroyed everything and the entire structure was reduced to ashes, she nevertheless appeared to stand unharmed and motionless among the embers. But her enraged enemies ran everywhere around the fences [or hedges], carrying whatever they could lay their hands on, and piled over her a heap of wood and straw even larger than the first. Again a more abundant fire was kindled; the wood and straw were quickly consumed, yet she was still seen safe and unharmed.

What increased the miracle still further was that the fire, which had no power against her, consumed the bonds with which she had been tied. When, for the third time, the enraged men again tried to set flames against her and violently threw stones at her, she cried out piteously:

“Spare me, I beg you, spare me! Do you not see that the most merciful holy Mother of God, to whom I entrusted my body today, is mercifully helping me?”

When they heard this, they were moved to pity and ceased tormenting her. The vicarius himself immediately urged her to come out of the fire. When she had emerged, everyone surrounded her and marveled that she was completely unharmed in body, hair, and clothing. With joy they returned to the church of Saint Mary, giving thanks to God and to his compassionate Mother, and led her as far as the high altar. No one could easily recount how many tears all present shed there from excessive rejoicing, or how many praises they sang to the compassionate Lady and Mother.

Afterward, the vicarius took the woman to his house, refreshed her abundantly with food and drink, and begged her to forgive him for having raged against her so cruelly. From there the woman returned to her own home at Civiacum and, after three days, as we believe, summoned by divine mercy, gave up her spirit and passed from toil into rest—perhaps so that “wickedness might not change her understanding, or deceit beguile her soul” (Wis. 4:11).

The almighty God had shown her such mercy through the prayers of his Mother that everyone who heard the story would say that, after making a true confession, one should confidently place one’s hope in the help of Saint Mary and never despair of her mercy. This miracle, which occurred at Laon during the time of Lord Helinand the bishop, was witnessed not by one, two, or three people, but by nearly the entire city of Laon.

Helinand the bishop was succeeded by Ingelrannus; Ingelrannus by Gualdricus, who was credibly murdered; Gualdricus by Hugh; Hugh by Bartholomew, in whose days Saint Mary performed throughout France and England the miracles described above. Since a miracle has been related that Saint Mary mercifully performed during the time of Lord Helinand for a woman who devoutly invoked her, let us now also relate the remarkable vengeance she exercised upon a certain thief who dared to stretch out his hand toward her treasure.

## CHAPTER XXVIII—Concerning Anselm’s Theft

Not long after his consecration, the aforesaid Lord Bartholomew the bishop dreamed that he was standing on the pulpit in the major church of Saint Mary with certain of his clerics. Turning his face toward the doors, he saw in the middle of the church what seemed to be a most splendid light proceeding from a kind of opening in the earth and wondrously illuminating the entire church, for it was night.

After the light there also followed from the same opening in the earth something like the sweetest fragrance of balsam, by which both he and those standing around him were restored in an incredible and wondrous manner. When the bishop urged his companions to approach that same opening in the earth and see what it was, none of them wished to obey him in this matter. He alone seemed to himself to descend from the pulpit and proceed toward it.

But when he was already near, just as God once said to Moses when he hastened to look at the bush: “Do not come closer; for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3:5), so the bishop heard from within a voice saying to him:

“Do not enter here, for almighty God is present here in his very flesh and bones, and no one who sees God bodily can live long. His holy mother Mary is also present here with God, and she commands you to apprehend her thief; she orders you not to permit him to depart, but to exact justice from him.”

The bishop immediately awoke and, many times wondering silently within himself what such a vision signified, turned it over in his mind.

At that time there was in the city of Laon a certain Anselm, surnamed Beessus, who, by pretending to be religious, was praised and honored by everyone to no small degree. But, as the outcome revealed, his heart was far different from what people saw in his face.

Because of his reputation for religious devotion, the church treasury was entrusted to him for safekeeping, together with other custodians. It is an ancient custom of that church that the treasury be committed to seven custodians, four of them clerics and three laymen.

Seeing that everyone trusted him greatly, Anselm secretly tore away a considerable portion of the gold and precious stones with which crosses intended to be placed upon the altar on feast days had been covered, and gave it to a certain goldsmith for sale, after first obtaining from him a pledge of faith that he would not disclose that Anselm had been responsible for the matter.

But when that goldsmith was selling the gold or the stones at Soissons, God’s will brought the canons of Laon upon the scene. They recognized the goldwork, and, immediately lodging a complaint, caused the judge to have the aforesaid goldsmith arrested. Once arrested and terrified, he confessed that Anselm had given those things to him.

He was therefore brought back to Laon and entered into a trial by combat against Anselm, who denied these charges. The goldsmith was immediately overcome and defeated, perhaps, as many thought, because of his guilt in violating the pledge of faith by which he had promised Anselm that he would not expose him [Note: Faith is not violated when an accomplice in a crime is revealed.].

Anselm, greatly elated by this victory—for he was conscious both that he had committed the theft and that he had nevertheless defeated his adversary, and had gained much praise from people who proclaimed him innocent—was emboldened to undertake still greater crimes, and was enriched with many lands and vineyards.

Lord Guido, however, who was both treasurer and archdeacon of the Church of Laon, was moved by a certain suspicion against him—or rather, was certain of his thefts—and removed him from his office, that is, from custody of the treasury. Anselm, greatly inflamed by anger and almost driven mad, sought a place and time in which to take revenge upon him.

It happened meanwhile that Countess Sibylla, wife of Ingelrannus, a most noble prince of La Fère, deposited several gold and silver vessels in the treasury of Saint Mary, where they could be kept more securely because of the strength of the place.

Anselm therefore took this as an opportunity and planned to steal those vessels, so that the countess might accuse the aforesaid Guido, under whose custody the treasury was kept, of such a theft and demand her vessels back from him.

One night, around the Epiphany of the Lord, such a violent storm of hail, rain, and wind broke out that scarcely anyone could leave his house. Anselm judged that night suitable for carrying out the wickedness he had long contemplated. Everyone was shut inside his house, and no sound could be heard except the wind. He quickly took ladders and tools that he had prepared long beforehand, climbed the tower in which the treasury was located, entered through a door cleverly breached, and stole all the countess’s gold and silver vessels.

Seeing that the sack in which he had placed them was not yet full, and unwilling to leave any part of it empty, he stretched out his hand toward the church treasury. He smashed valuable texts covered with gold and gems, leaving the books themselves, but placed the gold and gems in his sack. Then, breaking golden crosses and reliquaries, he also smashed, among other things, a golden dove. This object was especially famous and honored because, as was reported, milk and hairs of Saint Mary had been enclosed inside it, and it used to be hung above her altar on the greater feasts.

Carrying away his sack filled with such a great treasure, he descended and hid it—not in his own house, but outside the city in a place prepared and arranged beforehand.

When the dark, rainy night with its wind had passed and the signs of the broken door and plundered treasury became visible, the entire city was suddenly thrown into turmoil by such a sorrowful report. Laypeople were no less distressed than clerics, and a bitterer night seemed to have descended upon them.

People hurried to the bishop and reported the grievous event. The bishop was shaken by excessive sorrow more than anyone else, because the treasury that God had preserved from the burning of the entire city and of the church itself only a few years before had now been secretly and miserably lost.

A general assembly of the canons and citizens was therefore immediately summoned. They discussed what ought to be done, and above all consulted Master Anselm, who at that time was regarded as the lamp of the entire city.

As one most skilled in divine law, he immediately recounted the history of Joshua: how, when the theft at Jericho had been committed without anyone’s knowledge, the Lord ordered that it be investigated first by tribes, then by families and households, and finally man by man (Josh. 7:14).

Following this model of such a subtle investigation, Master Anselm was consulted about seeking the perpetrator of so great a crime by the judgment of water. One innocent child from each parish of the city was to be placed in a vessel filled with holy water; whichever parish happened to be found guilty, one child from each household of that parish was to be placed in the water; and whichever household was detected, all the men or women belonging to it would be compelled to clear themselves by the judgment of water.

When the citizens learned of this proposal by Master Anselm and his brother, Master Radulph, they were terrified. Although conscious of their innocence, they flocked to the bishop and loudly declared that the investigation should begin not with people living far away, but with the church’s custodians and those residing near the church.

The bishop agreed and summoned six men against whom there was the greatest suspicion to undergo the examination. Among them he addressed the aforesaid Anselm by name alone, saying that he had henceforth become suspicious of him.

Anselm replied that he greatly wondered how the bishop could have conceived suspicion against him concerning so great a crime, especially since the bishop knew him to be a servant of God and knew that, several years earlier, before the bishop himself had assumed the episcopate, Anselm had defeated in single combat the goldsmith who had accused him of a similar crime.

The entire people applauded his reply and proclaimed him a holy man and worshiper of God. With one voice they all added that he should not be summoned to the judgment.

Then the bishop seemed to have departed from his usual nature. For neither before nor afterward was that pontiff ever found obstinate in anything; he was always accustomed to be readily swayed from his judgment by the prayers or words of others. In this one matter alone, however, he showed such constancy that, although no one accused Anselm and nearly everyone supported him against the bishop, he could not by any means be moved, by God’s will, to release him.

When the prelate ordered Anselm to be kept in custody until the appointed day of the examination, a certain knight who strongly favored him, named Guillermus, asked the bishop to entrust Anselm to his keeping. With the bishop’s permission, he took him to his own house.

While he was being kept there, one night Anselm had a large vessel filled with water and had himself, bound, lowered into it, wishing to test whether he would sink completely in the water or float upon it. When Anselm saw that the water had received him without any delay and that he had reached the bottom of the vessel, he became cheerful and said that he no longer feared anything, but would willingly enter the water.

Why should I delay longer? The appointed day arrived, and an innumerable multitude of clerics, soldiers, and peasants of different sexes and ages gathered at the church. Young men and maidens, old men together with the young, invoked the name of the Lord and of his most glorious Mother.

The first man placed in the water came out safe and joyful; the second sank; the third emerged safely; the fourth was found guilty; the fifth was released; and the sixth, Anselm himself, was found guilty. Thus it was proved that his earlier testing of God had done him no good, and that this water was very different from the water into which he had previously caused himself to be lowered while in custody.

He was immediately bound in chains, and the bishop warned him that he would remain so until he returned the stolen treasure. He publicly invoked a curse upon himself, saying that he deserved to be hanged like Judas, who betrayed God, if he had any part of it or had stolen anything.

Seeing that exhortation accomplished nothing, the bishop handed him over to Nicholas the castellan, ordering him to force Anselm, by torture, to return the treasure. Nicholas had him stripped, thrown to the ground, stretched out, and bound, and poured hot lard over him; but he could extort nothing from him.

Then, at the bishop’s command, he had him hanged—not so as to kill him, but merely to torture him. From morning until evening he was tortured, hung ten times and lowered ten times. When Anselm saw that he was already failing, the judge also swore that, if he allowed himself to be hanged again, he would thereafter not be taken down alive.

At last Anselm asked what would be given him if he returned the treasure. When these words were heard, they immediately gave everyone hope of recovering the treasure. He demanded that one hundred pounds be given to him; but, by gradually reducing the amount, they arrived at forty pounds.

He said he would accept that sum on the condition that sureties also be provided for him, guaranteeing that he would be safely escorted with the money ten miles from Laon in whatever direction he wished.

People immediately hurried to the bishop and reported his demand. The prelate agreed and ordered that whatever he requested should be granted, on the condition, however, that he return the treasure at once, since he feared that if even a brief delay were granted, Anselm might slip away under the prompting of demons.

The daylight had already passed, and dark night had followed. Nevertheless, at the bishop’s command, torches, lamps, and other lights were kindled throughout the city, so that at that hour the Psalmist’s words might be fulfilled at Laon: “And the night shall be illuminated like the day” (Ps. 138:10). No one remained at home; everyone went out as though to a spectacle.

Anselm was led out like a bear dragged from its cave, surrounded carefully by guards and people lest he escape. He asked to be taken to the church of Saint Martin outside the city walls. As they approached a certain place near the vineyards, where a great heap of stakes used to support the vines had been piled, he descended beneath them, as though into Tartarus, down the steep slope of the mountain.

Putting his hand into the sack, he first brought out a golden panel torn from a Gospel book. Smiling at those standing around him, he said: “I have made a good bargain, returning so great a treasure for forty pounds, because this one panel alone is worth much more.”

The treasure was therefore returned and immediately brought back to the church of Saint Mary. The entire city rejoiced with shouts; the streets resounded with cries of exultation and confession, and the bells were rung for joy throughout all the churches.

A great miracle must not be left unmentioned. A certain goldsmith-monk named Sigerus, living in the monastery of Saint Vincent, was working at his craft even at night. When he opened the window of his little dwelling, from which the church of Saint Martin could be seen, he saw what appeared to be a brilliant ray of light proceeding from heaven and extending as far as the place where the treasure had been hidden.

Greatly astonished, he showed that same ray of light to some of the monks of Saint Vincent. Although they heard daily that the treasure of Saint Mary’s relics was being sought, none of them thought that it was there. The monks therefore continued to see the ray of light flashing at night for as long as the sack containing the treasure lay there.

Another miracle, which must not be silenced, also occurred. From the moment that Anselm smashed the golden dove together with the rest of the treasure—the dove mentioned above, in which it was said that milk and hairs of Saint Mary were contained—he was never able to sleep, as he later confessed to the bishop.

Whenever he closed his eyes for sleep, he immediately saw that same dove fastening its beak into his eyes and opening them. Yet, because the devil hardened his heart, he felt no remorse or penitence on account of this. After he returned the dove’s fragments with the rest of the treasure, he regained the ability to sleep.

On the following day Anselm came to the bishop and asked him to absolve him from the excommunication imposed because of the stolen treasure, to give him a cross, and to permit him to go to Jerusalem, to the Lord’s Sepulchre.

The bishop replied that he would do none of these things, because neither absolution nor the journey to Jerusalem would benefit Anselm so long as he retained the forty pounds he had received in return for restoring the treasure.

“You did not return it out of remorse,” he said, “and therefore you cannot be absolved; you are still held guilty under excommunication. But if, returning this money, you were to make a truthful confession of the theft—or rather, of the sacrilege—and then accept the penance arising from it, you could both be absolved and depart for Jerusalem.”

Anselm consented to the bishop’s words, placed the aforesaid money publicly upon the altar, and released the sureties who had promised to escort him safely ten miles from Laon from their guarantee. Thus, after being absolved by the bishop and receiving the cross, he was freely permitted to go wherever he wished, and he spent several days in familiar company with the bishop himself.

Yet, tormented inwardly by a troubled conscience, he became frightened and began to plan his escape. At last he secretly attempted to flee from the city. But when he began to descend from the mountain—strange to say!—he saw what appeared to be a great river, like the sea, surging toward him and forcing him to return to the mountain.

Astonished, he tried again to descend and flee through another gate, but immediately saw the river surging toward him as before. When this happened to him repeatedly and he could not descend from the mountain, he secretly confessed the matter to the bishop.

The bishop therefore seized the opportunity and began to urge him to return in full to Saint Mary the earlier treasure whose part, as stated above, he had handed over to a goldsmith to sell at Soissons, so that he might then go safely to Jerusalem.

Repeating his customary denial, Anselm said: “May I deserve to be hanged like Judas, who betrayed God, if I had anything from it. If you do not believe me, I am ready once again to undergo the judgment of water; and if I am found guilty, or if I refuse to undergo the judgment, have me hanged.”

The bishop then asked him at least to return the precious stones that had been set into the golden crosses, promising that he would cause him no trouble concerning the gold. But Anselm would return nothing to the bishop and completely denied that he had them.

Later, however, when he was greatly terrified by Nicholas the castellan’s threat—given on the bishop’s order—to subject him to his former tortures, he led Nicholas to the vineyards situated beneath the mountain. Placing his hand into a hollow in the earth, he drew out from a sack that had already begun to decay some extremely precious stones and handed them to the castellan.

Afterward, shaken once more by the reproach of his conscience because he had concealed them from the bishop and returned them to the castellan, he again attempted to flee.
