But when the bishop received the stones from the castellan, he remembered the dream mentioned above, in which Saint Mary had ordered him not to permit her thief to escape unpunished but to exact justice from him.

He immediately summoned his servants and ordered them to search for Anselm as quickly as possible and bring him before him. The servants ran through various places and finally found him in the valley beneath the monastery of Saint Vincent. He wished to flee but could not because of the surging river. They ordered him to come with them to the bishop.

Trembling and bloodless, Anselm begged them to allow him to speak with Lord Albero, the abbot of Saint Vincent. Unwilling to leave him, they went with him, for the bishop had ordered them to guard him carefully.

Anselm prostrated himself at the abbot’s feet and begged him to go with him to the bishop. The abbot agreed and went with him to the bishop.

Anselm fell at the prelate’s feet, begging that his life and limbs be spared. The bishop said to him:

“Who, then, is persecuting you? Return the treasure of my Lady Saint Mary, and go freely wherever you wish.”

Anselm invoked his customary curse upon himself, saying that he should be hanged like Judas, who betrayed God, if he had possessed anything of it.

Then the bishop said:

“It is clear that you are lying, because you returned the stones to the castellan and refused to return them to me. Of your own accord you promised me that, if I did not believe you concerning them, you would clear yourself by the judgment of water; or, if you refused to do so, you publicly consented to be hanged. Choose, then, whichever you wish.

“I tell you before everyone that I do not believe you when you say that you did not have Saint Mary’s treasure. Either return it, or clear yourself by the judgment of water as you offered to do, or be hanged as you consented. Of these three alternatives I grant you a choice.”

Anselm replied that he had neither possessed the treasure nor would he undergo the judgment of water on that account.

The bishop then summoned a general assembly of clerics, soldiers, and citizens and brought the case before them. By the common judgment of all, it was decided that what the wretched man had determined with his own mouth should be carried out.

He was immediately led down from the mountain into the valley and hanged from the branches of a tree, providing everyone with clear proof that God does not wish the one who has injured his Mother to be released unpunished.

These are the events that occurred at Laon during the time of Lord Bartholomew the bishop.

**The Third Book Ends Here.**

# Notes and Observations of Dom Luc d’Achery, Benedictine Monk, on Certain Works of the Venerable Guibert of Nogent

## On the Book *On the Praise of Saint Mary*

561. Fragment from Book 1 of Saint Paschasius Radbertus’s *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*—That the Virgin Mother of God did not contract the stain of original sin.

(1) **CHAP. VIII.—He abolished original sin together with actual sin.** Anyone who glanced hurriedly at these words and read them only superficially might quibble as follows: “The Holy Spirit abolished sin in the Virgin; therefore it must be admitted that this sin once existed in the Virgin.” But to anyone examining the matter more closely, this little argument is frivolous and empty. One might answer in this way: “If he abolished original sin together with actual sin, then actual sin too was abolished; but if actual sin was abolished, you must conclude that it once existed in the Virgin.” Yet to speak in this way is mere twittering and outright babbling. For in many passages our abbot [Col. 1017C] clearly reveals his view concerning the purity of the immaculate Virgin and her freedom from every stain. I therefore argue as follows: If, according to Guibert’s understanding, the Holy Spirit is said to have abolished in the holy Virgin actual sin—which was nowhere in her—why should the Holy Spirit not also have failed to abolish original sin, which, according to the mind of that same abbot, likewise never existed?

Attend, I beg you, to the words of chapter 5, col. 551:

> “Certainly, if our spirits are created before our bodies, according to the Platonic opinion, God could give some spirit the choice of the mother from whom it wished to be born. If this were done, what sort of person do you think it would devise for itself? I shall say nothing of the form and condition of the body. What honesty, what prudence would it bring with it in its soul? It would undoubtedly deprive her of nothing by which she would not be an object of envy to others. If the spirit of a human being is thus adorned, would not the Spirit of God adorn much more magnificently the city of the virginal womb which the Most High establishes for himself, in proportion to his greater power?”

If this passage is considered carefully, it will plainly be acknowledged that no one ever judged more worthily concerning the unstained conception of the Virgin.

Yet the opinion of that most vigorous champion of the Church, the blessed Paschasius Ratbertus, ancient abbot of Corbie, [Col. 1018C] will wonderfully illuminate Guibert’s meaning. His judgment is truly singular and worthy of veneration. Since the golden work of so great a man, *On the Birth of the Virgin*, has remained entirely hidden until we make it public, I think students of ancient theology will be grateful if I append a more extensive fragment:

> “But blessed Mary, although she was born and begotten from the flesh of sin, and although that flesh itself had been the flesh of sin, was no longer so at the time when, through the prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1019A] she was called by the angel blessed above all women: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’ (Luke 1:35). Otherwise, if she was not sanctified and cleansed by that same Holy Spirit, how was her flesh not the flesh of sin? And if her flesh came from the mass of the first transgression, how was Christ, the Word made flesh, without sin, when he assumed flesh from the flesh of sin? It was because the Word that became flesh first overshadowed her, upon whom the Holy Spirit came and whom the power of the Most High wholly possessed. Therefore she was truly no longer flesh of sin: God poured himself wholly into her, and the Word that became flesh came to us without sin. Rightly, therefore, he not only did not undergo at birth the law of corrupted nature; [Col. 1019B] indeed, he did not undergo even the law of the first origin, which women would have possessed had Eve, the mother of all, kept the commandment in paradise. Otherwise, when the Holy Spirit filled her, how was she not without original sin, whose glorious nativity is proclaimed happy and blessed by all, in the Catholic Church throughout the whole Church of Christ? Indeed, if it were not blessed and glorious, her feast would by no means be celebrated everywhere by everyone. But because she is honored so solemnly, it is established by the authority of the Church that she was never subject to any offenses of nature, and that, having been sanctified in the womb, she did not contract original sin. Thus, although the days of Jeremiah and Job are pronounced accursed—the days, I mean, of their births—the day on which Mary’s happy nativity began is nevertheless pronounced blessed and religiously celebrated [Col. 1019C] with fitting honor. If she had been in sin, her day would rightly have been called accursed and sorrowful rather than blessed, when her father was told that she had been born into the world. But now, because the blessed Virgin Mary illuminates the whole Church with her blessing, is she not rightly honored as venerable, having been sanctified in the Holy Spirit? No one’s nativity, therefore, is celebrated in the world except Christ’s, hers, and blessed John’s. Thus, if the blessed Virgin Mary had not been sanctified in her mother’s womb, her nativity ought not to be celebrated at all. But now, because she is venerated by the authority of the whole Church, it is clear that she was free from all original sin; through her not only was the curse of Eve, the mother, dissolved, but blessing was also granted to all. And if the illustrious Nativity of the most holy Virgin is universally honored and venerated as so holy and so glorious, [Col. 1019D] how much more is she herself so honored when she is most dutifully greeted by the angel as already full of grace? For when he says to her, ‘Hail,’ he offers the heavenly homage of veneration; when he says, ‘Full of grace,’ he shows that wrath has been wholly excluded and that grace has been restored. When he says, ‘Blessed are you,’ he demonstrates the fruit of blessing, because when the Holy Spirit [Col. 1020A] came upon her, he wholly cleansed the Virgin from stains and refined her, so that she became holier than the stars of heaven. Moreover, when the power of the Most High overshadowed her completely, it happened that the Word, eternal in the beginning with the Father, coming into her womb, became flesh in time and dwelt among us.

> “Let the new disputants and investigators of a new and unheard-of birth listen and understand first—since they are men—how they can properly dispute about the nature and sex of women. Then let them reflect, since they investigate nature and the common law of birth, on the place where everything is divine and ineffable, and where divine power performs its work. ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isa. 53:8.) Here ‘who’ is understood as impossible, because there is no saint who can fully explain—not merely his divine generation, but even the generation of his humanity—although all ought to believe both. From this it follows that the controversy of these men is superstitious and their disputation superfluous, when they say that he opened the entrances of the womb and vulva, and drew after him the discharge of blood like all others, as well as the impurities of the afterbirth. In all these things groaning and pain are multiplied, and sadness and distress increased, so that no one gives birth to a son without them. But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to suspect anything of this kind concerning the Virgin Mary, who brought blessing to the world in place of the curse of the first origin! Therefore she herself, as I have said, is proclaimed blessed among women by the angel and is most dutifully greeted as the glorious Mother of the Lord above all others; [Col. 1020C] she is also pronounced blessed by Elizabeth in the Spirit of prophecy (Luke 1:42), and the fruit of her womb is believed and venerated as blessed. Therefore, in her and through her such great blessing blossomed and grace flowed forth; it cannot be believed that her childbirth was subject to pains and groans according to the manner of women. And because the blessed Mother of God was not subject to sadness and distress, she was free from every blemish of the curse: the Holy Spirit filled her and dedicated her entirely to the Lord; the power of the Most High overshadowed her; from the sanctified flesh of the Virgin the Word assumed flesh and was joined in the unity of person.”

And after many intervening passages, addressing virgins:

> “O honor of exceptional piety and glory of virtue, proclaim the chastity of the most blessed Virgin as inviolate and undefiled, and as free from every contamination of the first origin,” etc.

Finally, near the end:

> “In her, the standards of the virtues shone forth; no sin of the first origin prevailed.”

Thus far Paschasius, who flourished during the reign of Charlemagne, that is, two centuries before Guibert.

[Col. 1021]

**ON THE BOOKS *ON THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS***

[Col. 1021A] **(2) DEDICATORY EPISTLE.—To Odo, abbot of Saint Symphorianus.** He was afterward consecrated bishop of Beauvais in the year 1135 (Antoine Loysel, *Commentary on Beauvais*, p. 98). The abbey of Saint Symphorianus still stands at Beauvais; it was founded in 1035 by Drogo, bishop of that city, and is occupied by Benedictine monks. If you wish to know more about the monastery of Saint Symphorianus, consult Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, vol. I, and Antoine Loysel, cited above, pp. 252 and 301.

In this treatise *On the Relics of the Saints*, Guibert argues with no little skill that the remains of the saints should be honored not profanely or for the sake of profit, but religiously, according to knowledge, and in the spirit. Nor should you be surprised that he attacks at such length the forgers and fabricators of relics, and those who, under the appearance of piety, display them to the people for veneration [Col. 1021B]. For in that very period so many and such varied pernicious errors had crept in, and such abominable greed for money had seized and blinded ecclesiastical and religious men—who wished to make their churches more renowned—that it is no wonder if the author appears to assail them in many passages of this treatise. He does not wish to deny piety toward relics or their veneration; rather, he openly professes that they contribute greatly to the advancement of the Christian religion and the increase of God’s glory. “For the rest,” he says in the preface, “if I have understood anything in accordance with the faith, I shall express my understanding with complete confidence in the faith; if anyone understands better, I would welcome it.”

**(3)** Augustine contradicts this more than once, and in several passages [Col. 1021C]: vol. IV, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chap. 20; and vol. VI, *Against Adimantus*, book I, chap. 17.

**(4)** A certain abbot whom that passage calls Saint Pyro. You find something similar in the chapter *We Have Heard*, *On the Relics and Veneration of the Saints*:

> “We have heard that some among you, deceived by diabolical fraud, venerate as a saint—in the manner of unbelievers—a certain man who was killed while drinking and intoxicated.”

**(5) CHAP. I.—Nor has it escaped me that Lanfrancus, etc.** I confess that I do not see what our author wishes to draw from this. It is true that blessed Lanfranc for a time did not approve the people’s excessive observance of the annual celebration of Saint Elfegus, his predecessor; but when he had conferred with his most holy disciple Anselm, he removed every scruple and ordered Saint Elfegus to be venerated with more solemn worship. “This history was not only composed by Osbern, a monk of the Church of Canterbury, of blessed memory, in a clear style for reading, but also in musical form for singing. Lanfranc himself, through his prudence and for love of that martyr [Elfegus], nobly honored it, gave it authority once honored, and instituted that the work so authorized should be read and sung in the Church of God.” Eadmer, [Col. 1022A] book II of the *Life of Saint Anselm*. See what we noted concerning the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, prefixed to his works, p. 42, E. 2, n.

**(6) CHAP. I.—What shall I say of those saints whose end is either openly evil or hidden, so that it is uncertain whether it was good or bad, etc.** On this matter, Capitularies of Aachen, chap. 42:

> “Let false names of martyrs and uncertain memories of saints not be venerated.”

A canon of the African council, canon 50, provides a remarkably apt illustration:

> “It has been decided that altars scattered through the fields and villages, at which no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, should, if possible, be demolished by the bishops who preside over those places. If popular disturbances prevent this, the people should nevertheless be warned [Col. 1022B] not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held there captive by any superstition. In general, no memorial of martyrs should be accepted as credible except where either the body or certain relics are present, or where the origin of some dwelling or possession, or of the martyr’s suffering, is handed down with the greatest reliability. Altars established anywhere through dreams and empty revelations, so-called, of various people, must be entirely rejected.”

**(7) CHAP. I.—Let it therefore be for the pontiffs to see; let it be for the guardians of God’s people to see.** Hence the capitulary of Charlemagne, chap. 28:

> “Concerning churches or saints newly discovered without authority: they are not to be venerated at all unless approved by the bishop.”

Moreover, the Fourth Lateran Council, chap. 62 [Col. 1022C]:

> “No one shall presume publicly to venerate relics newly discovered unless they have first been approved by the authority of the supreme pontiff. From now on, prelates must not permit those who come to their churches for the sake of veneration to be deceived by empty fabrications or false documents, as is accustomed to happen in many places on the pretext of profit,” etc.

Council of Trent, session 25, *On the Invocation, Veneration, and Relics of the Saints*.

**(8) CHAP. I.—Those, plainly, who have scrofulous swellings around the neck or anywhere on the body.** Scrofulous swellings, or scrofula, also called *strumae*, “which the Greeks call χοιράδες (*choirades*), are hardened glands, called *adenes* by the same people, which most frequently affect the neck, armpits, and groin.” Paul of Aegina, *On Medical Art*, book IV, chap. 33; Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, book VIII, chaps. 21 and 23; Hippocrates, *On the Glands*, section 3, beginning; and *On Affections*, section 5, after the middle. Bartholomeus Perdulcis discusses the various kinds of scrofulous swellings in book XIV, chap. 27. Writers report that the prerogative of curing the deadly disease of scrofula was divinely granted to the kings of France, and that this prerogative continues even today.

Since I know, moreover, that many have labored over this subject [Col. 1023A], and since numerous opinions are encountered, I thought it best to disengage myself from it without imprudence, although ample material for discussion is available. Those who wish may read the more recent authors: Hubert Morus, book III, *On Sacred Anointings*, chap. 5, who wrote about this subject very successfully, if I am any judge; and Guillaume Du Peyrat, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 56 and following.

Stephen de Conty, a monk of Corbie and a doctor of decrees, recorded the rites customarily observed in his own age in his manuscript *History of the Kings of France*:

> “The aforementioned individual kings, each of them, performed miracles many times during his life, namely by completely curing the poisonous, disgraceful, and troublesome skin disease called in French *écrouelles* [scrofula]. The method of healing is this: After the king has heard Mass, a vessel full of water is brought before him. At once he says his prayer before the altar; afterward he touches the sickness with his right hand and washes it in the said water. The sick, taking some of that water and drinking it for nine days while fasting and with devotion, are completely cured without any other medicine. And it is a fact that innumerable people were thus cured of that disease by several kings of France.”

Stephen was alive in the year 1400. Yet that such a rite had fallen out of use is testified by the Du Peyrat mentioned above, chap. 61. In chapter 60, near the end, he infers from Guibert’s words, “While I was supporting him and also forbidding it,” that the matter concerned alms given to King Louis the Fat. Guibert himself prevents me from accepting this conjecture: if he had been promoted to this office, would he have passed over it in his lifetime, when he reviews his actions in detail? This is not easy to believe.

It should finally be noted that, so far as I know, no one older than our author who discussed this prerogative of our kings has yet been found.

**(9) CHAP. II.—A certain woman had brought her own little child to the church to receive communion.** You see that at this time, and even later—as we shall soon demonstrate—communion of the body of Christ was administered to infants in the Church. If you wish, consult the 33rd letter of blessed Lanfranc and our note on that same letter; and Arcudius, book III, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*. That communion was given to the infants themselves, and especially to those newly baptized with water, is indicated by a letter of Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, to the abbot of Saint Florentius. Since it contributes greatly to illuminating the ancient institutions of the Church, it will be worthwhile to publish it here [Col. 1023D]:

### Letter of Gilbert Porretanus, Bishop of Poitiers

> “Gilbert, by the grace of God bishop of Poitiers, sends greetings in Christ to Matthew, likewise by that grace abbot of Saint Florentius, beloved in Christ.
>
> “You have seen fit to consult our lowliness concerning an incident of forgetfulness which is said recently to have occurred in your church: namely, that after bread had been placed upon the altar for consecration as the Eucharist, and with the chalice empty, the priest had said all the words belonging to the sacrament of bread and wine up to the breaking of the bread [Col. 1024A]. When, after uncovering the chalice, he recognized that he had erred, he put wine and water into it and repeated the sacred words of consecration not only over the chalice but also over the consecrated bread. You ask what should be done about this act, about the priest, and about that host.
>
> “We, however, do not recall something new from our own judgment, but in answer to your inquiry report what we once heard prudent men advise concerning a similar case. When a similar event came to the attention of certain prudent men, they judged that the priest should be rebuked for negligence and arranged that the community should pray for him. Following this example, we advise you confidently that your priest abstain from the host at the time of the offering, and that meanwhile, cleansed by whatever fasts or other bodily penances you prescribe, and not only by his own prayers but also by yours and those of the whole community, he should become worthy to offer. Since this incident of forgetfulness occurred not from a consciousness of error—which, when obstinate, is called heresy—but from delusions that often fill the loins of those who rightly believe, the penance may be shorter in duration, beginning, severity, and discipline [Col. 1024B].
>
> “Since, however, in either sacrament, whether of bread or of the chalice, after the customary signs made by the priest, the whole Christ is present, he ought entirely to have refrained from re-consecrating the already consecrated bread. He could have made satisfaction by pouring wine and water into the previously empty chalice, and without repeating the sacred words over the sacrament of bread, he could have received Christ in communion; for baptized children often communicate under the sacrament of the chalice alone, and the sick under the sacrament of the bread alone. Nevertheless, with regard to the reality itself and the sacrament of future incorruption, they receive as much as those who, under both the sacrament of bread and of the chalice, receive Christ in the Church from the very table of the Lord [Col. 1024C].
>
> “We answer this to your inquiry, although less fully than we might, yet faithfully, trusting in your charity, which counts what is little as much and what is mutilated as complete. We add what we ourselves customarily do, so that we may not be deceived by such forgetfulness, whether on the part of our ministers or ourselves. When our ministers have poured wine into the chalice to offer it, we do not trust them concerning the mixing of water unless, after the bread has been offered to us and the chalice is being offered, they either pour the water in before our eyes or, once a water vessel has been handed to us, we ourselves mix it into the chalice. Thus the minister-priest remains certain, and is safeguarded from any incident of forgetfulness.” [Col. 1024D]

This letter, distinguished by the gravity of its morals, its learning, and its writing, was freely given to me by Nicholas Camusat, canon of the Church of Troyes and my dearest friend; he extracted it from an old Ritual of the order of Grandmont. Hugh of Saint Victor teaches the same in *On the Sacraments*, book I, chap. 20:

> “The same sacrament under the form of blood must be administered to newly born children by the priest’s finger, because such children can naturally suck,” etc.

Concerning communion for the sick, it is worth observing what Arcudius, in the work cited above, chap. 56, reports: the Greeks customarily dip the most holy Eucharist, which they prepare for the sick on the Lord’s Supper as a viaticum, in the Lord’s blood.

That this custom was also received in certain places of the Latin Church is clear from the Council of Tours, as reported by Burchard, book V, chap. 9:

> “Let the priest have a pyx or vessel worthy of so great a sacrament, in which the Lord’s body may be carefully kept for those departing from this world as a viaticum. This sacred offering, however, ought to be dipped in the blood of Christ, so that the priest may truly say to the sick person: ‘May the body and blood of the Lord profit you.’”

Nevertheless, the Third Council of Braga, canon 1, forbade priests “to give the people the Eucharist moistened with wine as the completion of communion” [Col. 1025B]. On this subject Radulphus de Rivo, *On Canonical Observance*, book, proposition XXIII, near the end, should be read; he supplies testimonies abundantly.

I would add the statute of the Cluniac order, except that below, when discussing those near death, I shall have to give it in full. Still, I cannot refrain from appending here something of the care, diligence, veneration, and observance that the Benedictines customarily devoted to the august sacrament of the Eucharist—namely, chapter 55 of the ancient Cluniac statutes established by Abbot Saint Hugh.

### How the Hosts Are to Be Made

[Col. 1025C] Since matters pertaining to the most sacred mystery of the Eucharist ought to be carried out with the greatest reverence and diligence, it follows that the manner of carrying them out should not be passed over in silence. Although the hosts must be made whenever necessary, they are made especially before the Nativity of the Lord or the day of the holy Resurrection. Since the nights are longer in winter, the brothers may work for a longer time before dinner; after dinner, however, it is not permitted to undertake this work.

> “The grain from which the hosts are to be made, however good and naturally pure it may be, is nevertheless selected grain by grain. It is gathered by no persons other than the brothers themselves; afterward it is stored in a sack—not just any sack, but one sewn from good cloth solely for this purpose. The sack, tied up, is entrusted to a servant who is not frivolous. He carries it immediately to the mill, washes both millstones, covers them above and below with curtains, clothes himself in white, and places and ties over his head a shoulder covering, likewise called an amice, so that nothing of his face except his eyes can be seen. Thus he grinds; thus he sifts the flour, after first carefully washing the sieve as well.
>
> “If the chief custodian of the church is not a priest or deacon, he seeks a deputy to complete this work. He also seeks two others from those orders who are knowledgeable about the matter, after obtaining permission from the prior, and one lay brother. These four, when the night offices are finished, put on their shoes, wash their faces and hands, and comb their heads [Col. 1026A]. They then withdraw to the altar of Saint Benedict, where they sing the morning praises, prime also, and the seven psalms with the litany, postponing the remaining psalmody for the time being.
>
> “Then the three who belong to an order put on white garments and shoulder coverings, as was said above concerning the servant. For there are white garments and amices assigned solely to this business. One of them moistens the flour and kneads it vigorously upon a very clean board having a rim around it, its surface raised slightly all around so that the water cannot run off. They moisten it with cold water, because the hosts thereby become whiter. The other two form the hosts. The water is carried in no other vessel than the one customarily brought for Mass. The lay brother holds the iron in which they are to be baked, marked with characters, and puts on gloves. In the iron, [Col. 1026B] [lacuna] hosts may be placed together. Therefore, between the bearer of the iron and the makers of the hosts, a board is placed; two stakes are fixed into it, with a crossbar resting upon them, and the iron is placed on the crossbar for putting in the hosts. Those that have not been baked are scraped off with a knife and fall downward into a dish placed upon the board, which is continually covered with a cloth except when the hosts are being scraped.
>
> “They sing the psalmody that remains, and, if they wish, the Hours of Saint Mary; during all other Hours they maintain complete silence. They take the greatest care that not only their saliva but not even their breath should in any way reach the hosts. If anything is needed, the lay brother alone informs the servants briefly [Col. 1026C]. They make the fire only from dry wood specially prepared for this purpose. On that day the workers on the hosts eat not with the brothers but rather with the servants; and, as a relief from so great a labor, they receive from the cellarer at dinner an extra dish and spiced drink,” etc.

Let those who handle this divine matter less cautiously—in fact, no differently from the other affairs and lowest crafts of the world—read and silently consider these provisions with their whole minds.

**(10) CHAP. II.—And the little boy, still ignorant of everything, etc., cries out to his mother, etc.** “Something similar occurred in the city of Angers,” says Robert of Torigny in his *Chronicle*, etc. See under the year 1182.

**(11) CHAP. III, § I.—So that he does not even dare to say that the body of the Lord’s Mother was glorified by the resurrection.** As the ancient martyrologies of Usuard indicate under 15 August:

> “The Dormition of holy Mary, Mother of God. Although her most sacred body is not found upon the earth, nevertheless the devout mother Church celebrates her venerable memory as a feast, so that, in accordance with the condition of the flesh, she does not doubt that she departed. But where that venerable temple of the Holy Spirit has been hidden by divine will and plan, the sobriety of the Church has preferred, with piety, not to know rather than to maintain some frivolous and apocryphal teaching about it.”

This is Usuard. “Moreover, the Church of God,” adds Baronius in his note on the *Martyrology* [Col. 1027A] for this day, “appears more inclined to the view that she was assumed into heaven together with her flesh.” Among others whose opinions you may read there in Baronius is Bede, in the *Ephemeris* for 18 August:

> “On the eighteenth, the light and flower of the world, Mary,  
> Accompanied by an angelic choir, the Virgin seeks the heavens.”

And our Guibert proves this very skillfully and elegantly.

**(11*) CHAP. III, § II.—Although those of Constantinople say that they possess the head of the Lord’s Baptist, the monks of Angeriacum testify that they possess the same.** I shall not linger over these controversies concerning the head of Saint John. Nothing certain can be established except that everything is uncertain; the matter has also already been debated at length in both directions by many more learned men. I therefore gladly withdraw my pen and remain silent. Consult Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the years 391 and 1025, and his note in the Roman *Martyrology* under 29 August.

More recently, while discussing the various discoveries and translations of the head of the most holy Forerunner, Henry Spondanus, in his epitome of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year 1024, observes the following:

> “Finally, since various churches boast of possessing the same head, Robert le Viseur, a Parisian theologian and canon of Amiens, who wrote a special treatise on the subject, wished to settle the matter in this way: at Angeriacum there is a portion of the skull sent by the emperor Constantine Copronymus to King Pepin of the Franks, founder of that monastery; at Rome, in the church [Col. 1027C] of Saint Sylvester, another portion of the skull; at Augusta Praetoria, in the territory of the Alpine peoples, one jaw; another at Lyon; and at Amiens, except for the chin, everything from the upper lip to part of the forehead.”

After a few intervening remarks:

> “Since nothing at all certain seems able to be asserted concerning these matters, let us meanwhile be permitted—together with Baronius, in his letters written in reply to the same Robert—to say of them what the praetors once said by an edict to those who claimed to possess some property: ‘Possess as you possess.’ The piety of those who desire to claim for themselves the special patronage of so great a Forerunner through these sacred relics is nevertheless worthy of praise.”

Do you wish to know when those holy relics of John were translated to Amiens—for none existed there in Guibert’s time? Consult the aforesaid treatise of Robert le Viseur.

**(12) CHAP. III, § II.—Plainly, my predecessor, the bishop of Amiens, when he had the body of the martyr Firminus, etc.** Two authors of this period are found making contrary assertions about Saint Firminus: Guibert, abbot of Nogent, and Nicholas, a monk of Saint-Crépin at Soissons. The former was a serious man of mature age; the latter a young man who had scarcely passed the years of puberty when he wrote. One was a contemporary; the other nearly so. The first was distinguished by learning and dignity; the second was a simple monk, known only through his *Life of Saint Godefridus, Bishop of Amiens*, which he also composed from the reports of certain people. Whom should I believe? Abbot Guibert, who testifies that no evidence concerning the body of Saint Firminus was found when that holy bishop opened the reliquary [Col. 1028A]? Or the monk of Soissons, who confidently endeavors to prove that the body found in the same reliquary was the very body of Saint Firminus? Let us examine the matter; I hope it will not displease the reader.

This, then, is how the matter stands in Guibert:

> “Plainly, when my predecessor, the bishop of Amiens, wished—as he supposed—to transfer the body of the martyr Firminus from one reliquary to another, he found there no label, not even the testimony of a single letter, indicating who lay there. For this reason the bishop of the city soon had a leaden plate inscribed to say that Firminus, martyr and bishop of Amiens, was buried there.”

Thus he.

Nicholas, however, in book II, chap. 26 of the *Life of Saint Godefridus*, after reporting that blessed Godefridus had exhorted the people many days earlier to offer gifts for making a reliquary and to prepare themselves for the translation of the relics, adds:

> “After the casket had been carefully completed, on the day appointed for the translation of the relics, such a multitude of people came there that the whole of Europe might have seemed to have gathered. Then the bishop, with other priests, approached the place where that heavenly treasure was kept, and displayed the sacred relics for all to see, with much trembling, etc.; afterward he dismissed the people. But those who live in the suburbs of the city of Amiens were not present at this spectacle. They therefore approached Godefridus and asked him to show them also the sacred relics of blessed Firminus. But he, greatly astonished, said: ‘Where were you the day before yesterday, when I displayed them for all to behold with my own hand?’ Some brought one thing, others another, etc. At last the devout man was moved and said that on the feast of All Saints, after a fast had been undertaken, he would satisfy them by his prayers.”

Whether he did so or not, the author does not disclose.

But what will the learned reader gather from such words of Nicholas, except—at least in my judgment—that they were deliberately composed to serve as a smokescreen and obscure the truth? Yet the whole matter ultimately defeats him and brings itself into the open. What, I ask, is the coherence of his narrative? That credulous Nicholas testifies that so many peoples came together at Amiens to venerate the sacred relics of Firminus “that the whole of Europe might have seemed to have gathered.” Then he says: “But those who live in the suburbs of the city of Amiens were not present at this spectacle” [Col. 1028D]. How, I ask, can you be persuaded that the whole of Europe might have seemed to have gathered for the display of the patron of the people of Amiens, while the suburban inhabitants nevertheless kept their ears continually closed, were blind, or fell asleep in drunkenness for the entire day? The narrative is plainly tottering!

Accordingly, Guibert—if he was an eyewitness, or even if he was a contemporary—is to be heard with the greater right: a man truly devoted to justice and truth, who, whenever he found vice, falsehood, corruption of the Catholic faith, or injury to ecclesiastical liberty, knew how to spare no one and conceal nothing. This will become clearer than daylight to anyone who reads through his writings.

Finally, our abbot briefly declares where the precious relic of Firminus rests [Col. 1029A]:

> “Without delay,” he writes, “the same thing is done in the monastery of Saint-Denis in France. When a more splendid casket prepared by the abbot is being lifted from its place, and when the head is brought out together with the limbs, a little parchment is found in the martyr’s nostrils, on which it is stated that he was Firminus, martyr of Amiens.”

But lest anyone think that the author asserted this gratuitously or in the heat of anger, I would like to draw out an ancient translation, carried out at the command of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, from the castle of Piquigny to the church of Saint-Denis.

[The supplied source ends here.]

567. “In the time of the glorious and most devout king of the Franks, Dagobert, the nation of the Huns—most savage in spirit, tall in stature, accustomed to war, relying more upon its own strength than upon divine assistance—was tyrannically subjugating the neighboring provinces. Nor did this seem sufficient to it; but, hearing of the excellence of the kingdom of the Franks and the glory of its king, it resolved, with reckless audacity, to bring that kingdom under its own rule. Having taken counsel with the Flemings, it won them over to share in the crime it had planned, relying likewise upon the aid and consent of the citizens of the city of Arabianum [reading uncertain]. And behold: having prepared the necessities of war, ignorant of the fate awaiting it, it moved its camp toward France with its accomplices.

“This could not escape the vigilant foresight of King Dagobert. Calling together the Frankish army, which was entirely devoted to him, and relying wholly upon divine protection and upon the patronage of Macharius, the special protector of himself and the Franks—namely Dionysius and his companions—he swiftly went out to meet his adversaries at the place then called Leo. What more need be said? The day of battle arrived, and for a long time a fierce struggle was waged on both sides: the Huns and their allied accomplices fighting fiercely, with the ardor and desire to complete the wickedness they had undertaken, as they supposed, while the Franks fought in defense of their country’s liberty.

“Meanwhile divine mercy, which resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, mercifully regarded the faith and pious courage of the king and the Franks, as well as the treacherous pride of the Huns. It strengthened the arms of the former and humbled the adversaries so completely that scarcely one survived to carry news of the battle’s outcome back to his homeland. And the Franks inflicted such a slaughter of the Huns and such an outpouring of their blood at that spot that the place formerly called Leo was thereafter, in the language of that people, called *Lyons-en-santez* [Col. 1029D], which in Latin may be rendered ‘lion in a pool of blood.’

“Although the Huns had thus been utterly destroyed, King Dagobert’s anger nevertheless did not subside until he had exacted a fitting vengeance from the citizens of the city of Amiens, who had consented to the tyranny of the Huns against him. This did not escape those citizens; and, greatly shaken—not without reason—and tormented by their own conscience, since no guilty person is acquitted when his own conscience is judge, they took counsel together. The bishop of that city, the clergy, and the people transferred the body of the glorious martyr and bishop of that same city, Firmin, together with other relics and the treasures of the church, to a certain fortified town called Pinquigniacum [Piquigniacum; Col. 1030A]. This was done because the city seemed insufficiently fortified to withstand the king’s attack. That castle, however, both by the natural strength of its site and by human workmanship, and through the courage of its warriors, was considered extremely strong and almost impregnable. But ‘there is no wisdom, there is no understanding, there is no counsel against the Lord’ (Prov. 21:30).

“Accordingly, the king, approaching the aforesaid city with the Frankish army, entered it without great difficulty, since few opposed him. He attacked the enemies with royal indignation; he killed some, handed others over to imprisonment, while still others escaped the danger of death by means of flight. King Dagobert, having gained a glorious victory over his enemies, did not wish—God forbid—that he should return guilty of ingratitude to his glorious protectors, Macharius, namely Dionysius [Col. 1030B], and his companions. Touched by divine inspiration, he resolved within himself to bring them, in recompense for the manifest protection they had granted him, a gift more precious than every treasure.

“Therefore, after arranging royal guards in the aforementioned city, he turned his army toward Piquigniacum, where he had learned with certainty from the inhabitants that, through fear of the royal majesty, the venerable body of the most holy martyr and bishop Firmin, together with other relics, had been concealed. But what could the guards of that fortified town do except what the necessity of circumstances compelled them to do? They laid down their arms and submitted themselves and their possessions to the royal will. The king, for his part, dealt mercifully with them, as royal dignity required in such a situation.

“Having subjected the aforesaid fortified town to himself, the prudent and discerning king, in order to accomplish in action what he had previously conceived in his mind, exercised the right of a victor, to whom belongs everything that had belonged to the vanquished. He approached the place where he had learned that the precious relics of the saints had been deposited, and with all reverence lifted from their hiding place the venerable body of the most holy martyr and bishop Firmin, judging it unworthy that the bones of so great a martyr should remain hidden in darkness any longer.

“Then, summoning the nobles of the Frankish army, he commanded them by royal authority to transfer the most sacred body from that place with due and utmost honor to the church he loved above all others, while he himself humbly followed with his household.

“The venerable community of that church [Col. 1030D], hearing that the king was returning from battle in noble triumph and carrying precious relics with him, solemnly went out to meet him. With hymns and praises, as befitted the royal majesty, it ushered him into the church. The king, devoutly offering with his own hands the body of the most sacred martyr, which he had brought with him, as an inestimable treasure upon the altar of the holy Martyrs, the community received it with ineffable joy and placed it exaltedly and honorably upon the altar of the Holy Trinity, situated in the monks’ choir.”

568. Thus far the old manuscript codex of the Library of Saint-Victor in Paris. This translation had certainly not escaped Nicholas Gill, augmented by François de Belforest, when he was writing about Dagobert I. After subduing the people of Amiens and capturing the castle of Pequiniacum, he says, “he transported the body of Saint Firmin, together with other relics and treasures, and offered them to the church of Saint-Denis, where they may still be seen.”

This being so, should we not deny Nicholas of Soissons credibility in many places—although it would be impious to call all the deeds of Blessed Godefrid into question? For Nicholas appears to have added many things from mere popular rumor, or from his own imagination. He himself seems to complain in his prologue to the reader that he had been challenged on this point: “If anyone should shamelessly revile and criticize us, asking why we report not only what we have seen but also what we have heard,” and so forth.

In the dedicatory letter, since he suspected that what he was about to say about Saint Godefrid would for the most part be considered of little importance, he addresses Rohard as follows: “On the one hand, the weakness of my immature age held me back from expressing the pious praises of so great a man—for, as I remember having learned from the account of the midwife, I had not yet completed more than the span of five lustrums [twenty-five years]; on the other hand, my very limited learning held me back still more. For, to say nothing of the rest, I had not yet fully learned the joining of syllables, nor even the elements of the alphabet itself,” and so forth.

### Appendix on the Privileges of the Abbey of Saint-Valery

So that it may become clearer than daylight how disgracefully Nicholas erred, and so that our firm assertion concerning Saint Firmin may be appropriate to this place, I wish to examine thoroughly what he himself describes so elegantly in Book II, chapter 9, since I have read that many men of great reputation—whether intentionally or not, I cannot say—have been blind in this matter.

It was discovered that certain spurious privileges had been fabricated at the Council of Reims by the monks of Saint-Valery in the diocese of Amiens. I was indeed greatly astonished, when I read through the acts of Saint Godefrid as drawn up by Nicholas, that so many men of the highest learning had subscribed to so obvious an error and had even inserted such a fable into the councils. But it is useful to hear the author himself and to subject the matter to examination.

In Book II, chapter 9, he continues the narrative in his own style—or rather in the style of the Carthusian Surius:

“When the blessed man was once visiting his diocese, he came to the monastery of Blessed Valery. When Abbot Lambert and the monks learned this, they immediately hastened to the crypt where he was staying, asking why he had come there. The man of God replied: ‘These priests’—for they were standing around him—‘who are far removed from the city of Amiens, are asking me to consecrate for them the chalices and linens in which the divine mysteries are handled.’ Then, seized with great fury and scarcely able to restrain their hands, they said: ‘No bishop of Amiens has ever carried out here any ministry of consecration.’ Seeing that they were excessively agitated, the blessed man, and so forth, departed from there,” and so on.

Behold the cause of the disagreement: the consecration of chalices and linens in the church of Saint-Valery, not the wicked behavior of the monks, as the French translator of the Life of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux wrongly asserted in Book V, chapter 25.

Let us proceed further, to chapter 10:

“After the bishop returned home, he summoned the clergy and explained to them that the monks of Saint-Valery were boasting of their exemption, claiming that they were not subject to the Church of Amiens, and that they had driven him away with dishonor. Hearing this, they were greatly disturbed; and, sending letters, they summoned the abbot. He came. But what does the accursed love of gold not compel mortal hearts to do? Not a few, corrupted by gifts from the abbot, defended him most fiercely against the bishop and the mother Church. Observing this, the blessed man decided that the case should be referred to the archbishop of Reims.”

As though the abbot had been exempt from episcopal jurisdiction and synodal law—or at least had claimed to be so—and would therefore have obeyed the bishop’s and the canons’ commands so readily! Had he done so, the case would have been lost; and thus who cannot see that Nicholas’s words are fabricated?

In the following chapter he claims that “a most celebrated assembly of the nobles of Gaul was held at Reims. The venerable Godefrid, bishop of Amiens, was also present. The abbot and his monks came forward and accused Bishop Godefrid of having treated him with great injustice. He produced forged letters stating that they were subject to no one except the Roman pontiff. The letters were read at the archbishop’s command, and then those who had been corrupted by gifts insulted the bishop, and so forth. Godefrid, having little confidence in the letters they had read, asked that they be handed over to him for examination.

“Examining them carefully and lightly wiping them with his garment, he detected the fraud and exclaimed: ‘Come, I ask you all to direct your eyes here [Col. 1032C]. Behold: the parchment, ink, and writing are plainly recent, and the document is not sealed according to Roman custom.’ They understood that the matter was as Godefrid had said, and so forth. The monks, ashamed, appealed to the Roman pontiff and immediately departed for Rome.”

What color is there in this account? It certainly contains childish things painted by a child: for example, “a most celebrated assembly of the nobles of Gaul was held at Reims,” of which writers have left not even a trace to this day, nor can any record of it be found in the Reims archives.

Furthermore, if that assembly of the nobles of Gaul was so celebrated, why, I ask you, did our Guibert—who depended upon the metropolitan church of Reims, a “religious man and of great authority,” as the older martyrology of Laon calls him, and who at one time adhered to King Louis, as he himself relates in *On the Relics of the Saints*, Book I, chapter 1—why, I say, did he not sit with the other nobles of the kingdom?

Why, throughout his works, and especially in the Life in which Nicholas fabricates the synod, does he not mention it, when he shows himself more attentive to the smallest matters that occurred in his own time? Indeed, as a man of perfect integrity, he certainly would not have failed to attack the abbot of Saint-Valery in writing as a forger—if Nicholas’s account is true. That most celebrated assembly is deferred to the Greek Calends [i.e. never].

Moreover, it is hardly credible that an abbot who was subject to no authority except that of the Roman pontiff—as I previously said concerning the bishop of Amiens—would have sought a fictitious council at Reims to defend his right and bring a complaint against Saint Godefrid.

But how could the blessed bishop have demonstrated that, “lightly wiping them with his garment, the parchment, ink, and writing were plainly recent and not sealed according to Roman custom”? Recent writing on parchment cannot be removed by a light wiping; indeed, it adheres more firmly and is more difficult to erase.

If you reply that the parchments ought to have displayed wrinkles and the ravages of moths and other insects, you show yourself ignorant: they were scarcely a hundred years old. They belonged, namely, to the time of Pope Benedict VII—as I conjecture, since the monk of Soissons deliberately omitted the pope’s name—when the monastery of Saint-Valery is known to have been restored by Duke Hugh, later king of the Franks, and when privileges were granted at Hugh’s own request.

But parchments of that age—especially when documents of such importance are customarily preserved with care and reverence—cannot be recognized as having suffered the assaults and injuries of time, as we learn by daily experience.

“But,” you will say, “the bishops observed that the monks’ privileges were not sealed according to Roman custom and therefore ought rightly to be rejected.” This is the crux, at least in Nicholas’s mind, of the entire difficulty. Why so? Are you joking, or are you speaking seriously?

It would first have been necessary to establish, through continuous tradition, that the Roman Church had maintained a fixed custom in sealing or authenticating letters. But you would sooner drink the waters of the sea than demonstrate this. On the contrary, examples abound showing that the supreme pontiffs frequently changed their manner of writing. Let us select a few from the almost countless examples, reader, so as not to weary your stomach.

In *Concilia Gallica*, volume II, page 75, Pope Adrian ended the privilege addressed to Tilpin of Reims with the words: “Fare well.”

The subscription of the privilege of Saint-Denis, in the same volume, page 114, reads: “Written by the hand of Christopher, notary and archivist of our see, in the month of June, in the ninth indiction. Fare well. Given on the Kalends of July by the hand of Anastasius, chief secretary, while our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, with God the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, reigns throughout infinite ages, in the year, by God’s favor, the fifteenth year of our lord’s pontificate in the most holy apostolic see of Blessed Peter, in the ninth indiction.”

In volume III, page 217, it reads: “Written by the hand of Zacharias, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. Fare well. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May by the hand of Tiberius, chief secretary of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord Emperor Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful, reigns, in the fourteenth year of his empire, in the eleventh indiction.”

On page 481: “Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the eleventh indiction, at Troyes.”

On page 485: “Written by the hand,” and so forth, as above, but no mention is made of the emperor.

Finally, on page 521: “Written by the hand, and so forth, while our Lord God reigns forever, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Marinus, universal pope, in the first indiction.”

Let us also cite the subscription formulas of subsequent pontiffs. That of Pope Sergius IV reads: “Written by the hand of John, archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the tenth indiction. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July by the hand, and so forth, in the year, by the favor of the Lord, of the pontificate of Lord Sergius IV, pope, in the most holy see of the apostle Blessed Peter, in the tenth indiction.”

And, after other material, another reads: “Written by the hand, and so forth. Given by the hand, and so forth, in the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope VIII, in the most holy see of the apostle Blessed Peter, in the fourth year, during the reign of Lord Henry, emperor Augustus, in his third year,” and so forth.

You will find these subscriptions in volume II of Baronius’s *Annals*, under the year 1012, and in volume I of the *Bullarium*, page 50, under Gregory VII: “Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of September, the indiction beginning with XV.”

Likewise, on page 52, from a privilege granted to the congregation of Vallombrosa: “Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the year 1090 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of April.”

And on page 53: “I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.”

“I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, was present and subscribed,” and so forth.

“Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January,” and so forth.

Paschal was a contemporary of Saint Godefrid, yet this formula of subscription differs widely from the preceding ones.

From all this it is clear that the Roman pontiffs varied their formulas of sealing. Nicholas therefore wrote foolishly when he claimed that the fathers of the Council of Reims rejected the privilege of the monks of Saint-Valery because it had not been sealed according to Roman custom.

Moreover, during the time of Saint Godefrid and in earlier centuries, supreme pontiffs, as well as kings and princes, were often accustomed to send diplomas in the form of letters—whence they are called *letters* or *rescripts*. Nor was it then as common as it became in later times, especially in the age of Blessed Godefrid, to attach bulls, or leaden seals, to apostolic letters. This is evident from the examples given above.

Having dwelt long enough on matters that are already sufficiently known, let us continue to refute the remaining points.

Nicholas continues in chapter 14: “The monks came to Rome, gave gifts, and returned to their own places joyful and cheerful, having obtained from the Roman pontiff everything they desired,” and so forth.

Ridiculous! Here this author accuses the abbot of Saint-Valery of having, once, twice, and three times, corrupted with money and gifts the canons of Amiens, the prelates of the most celebrated assembly at Reims, and the supreme hierarch of the Church himself, and of having induced them to err, so that they would hold truth cheap, afflict the holy man, and deprive him of his right; thus, to speak with the Psalmist, all became corrupt and abominable.

It is as though that head of a monastery had possessed the immense wealth of Croesus, enabling him to scatter money on every occasion.

Moreover, anyone could easily persuade himself that the abbot and the monks, after their remarkable trick had been exposed at Reims—as Nicholas wishes—had so thickened their faces and hardened their tongues that they immediately went to Rome and with the greatest ease obtained from the Roman pontiff whatever they demanded; that no one from the celebrated assembly confronted those wicked men or warned the supreme shepherd of so great a crime; and that the pope himself, entirely ignorant of the cause, promptly granted the monks’ request and exempted them from episcopal obedience.

Away with such ravings!

In chapters 15, 16, 20, and 21, the biographer relates that Saint Godefrid went to Rome for this reason and suffered rejection by the supreme pontiff. But when, after going to Bari to fulfill a vow, he had returned to Rome, Pope Paschal—by then better informed about his prudence, learning, and holiness—asked his pardon for having received him badly.

“Then Pope Paschal,” says Nicholas in chapter 21, “gave him letters, which among other things stated that the abbot of Saint-Valery and his monks were obliged to obey the bishop of Amiens in everything, as their father and shepherd. He therefore,” and so forth.

Is that really so? Why, then, in the controversy concerning the privileges of the monks of Saint-Valery, so often debated and revived, have the bishops of Amiens hitherto been unable to produce the letters of the Roman pontiff which Nicholas claims existed? By this means, surely, all the disagreements would have remained entirely settled—or rather extinguished.

Therefore, in my judgment, no one who pays attention can fail to see that the letters of Paschal were nowhere given to Blessed Godefrid.

Finally, that highly reputed historian added the finishing touch to his fable in chapter 24, as follows:

“After the abbot of Saint-Valery had again been summoned, the blessed bishop produced the letters of Pope Paschal and gave them to Simon the provost to be publicly read, and so forth. The abbot and the monks threw themselves at the feet of Blessed Godefrid, asked pardon for their wrongful conduct, and obtained it without difficulty; many suitable penalties were imposed upon them. From that time the abbey of Saint-Valery obeyed the bishop of Amiens.”

But if this is how matters stood, why was a most serious dispute soon afterward stirred up between the people of Amiens and the monks of Saint-Valery? Why, then, when arbiters were delegated in the matter—as they say—by the supreme judge Alexander [Col. 1035D], and after they had heard and weighed the arguments presented by both sides, did the pontiff, following various and lengthy disputes between the parties, finally retain the abbot and monks of Saint-Valery in possession, because the arbiters had found them exempt from episcopal jurisdiction from time immemorial?

Thus, unless he is utterly incapable of judgment, no one, I think, will deny that Nicholas’s conclusion—“From that time the abbey of Saint-Valery obeyed the bishop of Amiens”—is plainly fabricated.

Although I may seem to have completed this appendix in every respect and openly dissolved the little story of that good man—a fictitious tale which he had undoubtedly received from impostors—nevertheless, since I see that this same stale dish, repeatedly reheated by those who have no taste for the immunities of monks, is being forced upon us, I wish to add the subscription of the privilege in question, which gave Nicholas the occasion to fabricate his fable.

Nothing need be added concerning the bull-bearing letters of Paschal II, since, without doubt and by the admission even of the adversaries, they were issued by the Roman see. But we shall transcribe the complete judgment of Alexander III, since it settles the entire dispute, as we noted above.

The letters of Pope Benedict have the following subscription:

“Written by the hand of Hugh, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the ninth indiction. Fare well. Given on the Kalends of April by the hand of Stephen, bishop of the Holy Roman Church, in the first year of the pontificate of Benedict VII, most holy pope, in the seventh year in the see of Blessed Peter, while Lord Otto, crowned by the Lord, great emperor, holds the empire in its thirteenth year, in the ninth indiction. Amen.”

Perhaps his rivals will scoff and shout that only the eighth year of the empire of Otto II should be counted, which corresponds to the seventh year of Pope Benedict VII.

It would hardly be worth my while to answer them in my own words. Rather, the illustrious Cardinal Baronius should be heard; since the matter does not concern him personally, his testimony is especially appropriate. In volume I of the *Annals*, under the year 974, near the end, he skillfully removes this obstacle:

“After Otto’s death,” he says, “his son, the younger Otto, began to reign alone. He had already begun his sixth year together with his father, for in his diplomas he himself reckons this as the sixth year of his empire, as will appear below,” and so forth.

Thus, under the year 981, he writes:

“In this same year there exists a diploma issued by Otto II, emperor, and so forth. At the end it reads: ‘John, chancellor, in place of Peter, bishop of Pavia and archchancellor, have examined and subscribed. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the year 981 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth indiction, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Otto, and in the eighth year of his empire, in the ninth indiction.’ His seal is attached. Other diplomas of the same kind, containing privileges, also exist there, such as that given on the sixth day before the Ides of October in this same year of our Redeemer 981, in the tenth indiction, begun from the time of his coronation, in the fourteenth year of his empire, by the hand of the same John the chancellor.”

Thus far Baronius.

From these and similar examples it is especially clear that in this century both emperors and the kings of the Franks sometimes customarily reckoned the years of their empire or kingdom from the day of their inauguration.

### Decretal Judgment of Pope Alexander III

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Asselin, abbot, and the brothers of Saint-Valery: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting and in accordance with reason that, when certain questions are brought before the apostolic see, and so forth.

For the remainder, see below, under Alexander III, for the year 1181.

To this belongs the privilege of the same supreme pontiff, issued in the same year. Among other things, it contains the following:

“Following the example of our predecessors, Popes Benedict and Paschal, of pious memory [Col. 1037A], we receive you under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, and we strengthen you by the present privilege. In the first place,” and so forth.

After many intervening matters:

“Likewise, the judgment concerning you and the Church of Amiens regarding the imposition of an abbot upon the chair at the time of election, concerning the care of souls, and also concerning every parochial right of the castle of Saint-Valery, having heard on both sides the arguments and allegations and the depositions of sworn witnesses, was issued by us with the common counsel of our brothers. By it we absolve you and impose perpetual silence upon the Church of Amiens. We confirm you and your church by apostolic authority, as is known to be contained in the document we then made concerning the matter,” and so forth.

The privileges and immunities of the monks of Saint-Valery were confirmed by the supreme pontiffs Innocent III, Gregory IX, and others. To list them would require not only a longer account but would also burden the reader and become tedious. Let this suffice, therefore, for those who are unable to refrain from disparaging the privileges of Saint-Valery and railing against them, relying solely upon Nicholas’s account. At least let them blush that, once exposed to the light, they cannot bear to see themselves, and let them henceforth close their mouths, lest they become a reproach to those who love what is right and true.

(13) CHAPTER III, § III.—So many things, similarly occurring everywhere, present themselves to my memory.

Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, laments the impious fraud of Adelbert in his letter 135 to Pope Zacharias:

“In his earliest years he was a hypocrite, saying that an angel of the Lord, in human form, had brought him relics, and that from then on he could obtain from God whatever he requested. Then, through that deception, as the apostle Paul had foretold, he entered the houses of many people and took captive little women laden with sins, and a multitude of rustics, who said that he was a man of apostolic holiness and had performed many signs and wonders.”

A little later he adds:

“He gave his fingernails and his hair to be honored and carried with the relics of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles,” and so forth.

You will find this also among the councils held under the same Zacharias.

The great Gregory, writing to the elder Boniface in Book III, letter 30, speaks of Greeks who dug up and reburied the bodies of the dead lying in the fields:

“When they were discovered,” he says, “and had been carefully questioned about why they were doing this, they confessed that they intended to carry those bones to Greece as the relics of saints!”

I pass over a certain wicked impostor whose detestable trade in the relics of the false martyr Justus was mocked in vivid description by the eyewitness Glaber Rodulfus, Book IV, chapter 3:

“That miracles sometimes occur through evil spirits because of the sins of human beings, when the Lord permits it.”

Our Menard provides abundant examples of this kind in chapter 3 of the *Concordia of the Rule*, page 125. Consult him if you wish, as well as the letter of Amulo, archbishop of Lyon, to Theobald, bishop of Langres, edited in 1633 by Camuzat, canon of Troyes.

(14) CHAPTER III, § III.—While they distribute common bones to be sold as the relics of saints.

I ask you to note the sacrilegious practice of selling sacred relics of the saints in this age. It is therefore no wonder that the author himself so fiercely attacks those who engaged in this pestilential commerce.

Accordingly, the Second Council of Poitiers, held in that period, in the year 1109, decreed in canon 12: “Those who carry the relics of saints about for the sake of money and profit are not to be admitted to preach.”

And in the chapter *Cum ex eo*, *On the Relics and Veneration of the Saints*:

“Since Christian religion has often been discredited by the fact that certain people expose the relics of saints for sale and display them indiscriminately, so that it may not be discredited in the future, we decree by the present ordinance that ancient relics henceforth be displayed in no way outside their reliquary, nor be exposed for sale,” and so forth.

(15) CHAPTER IV, § I.—I do not remember ever having read that they exchanged pure marble for golden or silver reliquaries.

I have not understood what Guibert intended in this matter. But, if it is permissible to offer conjectures, he seems to disapprove of golden or silver reliquaries for two reasons.

Either because, as soon as pious men of his time had departed from this confusion into heaven, their bodies were placed in golden and silver tombs. The author says that this was nowhere accepted in the Church, “since the Son of God is enclosed by the cheapest stone.” He indicates the same thing somewhat plainly in these words:

“What emulation of God is this, and so forth, that our age should devise what, as far as we know, has never from the beginning of the world been displayed in any worship or amid any riches?”

Or he objects to them because of the perverse custom then approved by many and because of profit. The great Bernard, inflamed by zeal for God, rebukes those involved in it with great force in his *Apology to Abbot William*, near the end:

“And, to speak plainly, is not avarice— which is the service of idols—doing all this, so that we seek not the fruit but the gift? If you ask how, I reply: in a remarkable way. Bronze is scattered by a certain art so that it may multiply; it is spent so that it may increase; and expenditure produces abundance. For by the very sight of costly but astonishing vanities, people are more greatly inflamed to offer than to adore. When relics are covered with gold, the eyes are filled and the coffers are opened. The most beautiful form of a saint or holy woman is displayed, and it is believed to be holier in proportion as it is more richly colored. People run to kiss it and are invited to adore it; they admire beautiful things more than they venerate sacred things.”

Alvarus, though far inferior to this most holy teacher, does not differ from him in Book II of *The Lament of the Church*, chapter 76:

“Many people come to church more to delight in and admire beautiful buildings and images than to correct their vices. Gold attracts gold; polished stone attracts precious stones. More is offered to gilded relics than to those covered with cloth,” and so forth.

Here it is perversity, not piety, that is condemned.

Otherwise, no one can deny that those who held the foremost places both in holiness and in dignity, impelled by divine worship, repeatedly surrounded and adorned the remains of the saints with silver, gold, and gems [Col. 1039A]. Countless examples are available, but for the sake of brevity we shall not append them. Let one example stand for all: Saint Salvius of Amiens, “who nobly adorned the tomb of Saint Firmin with gold and gems,” as stated in chapter 3 of the *Life of Saint Salvius*.

Saint Audoen, in Book I, chapter 32 of the *Life of Saint Eligius*, likewise writes:

“This same blessed man, among the other marks of his good works, made many tombs of the saints from gold, silver, and gems: those of Germanus, Severinus, Piatus, Quintinus, Lucius, Genovefa, Columba, Maximianus and Lolianus, and Julian, as well as those of many others; but especially that of Martin in the city of Tours, and so forth.

“Moreover, Eligius made a mausoleum for the holy martyr Dionysius in the city of Paris, and over it a marble canopy of wondrous workmanship in gold and gems. He also magnificently fashioned a crest and figures for the front, as well as panels around the altar,” and so forth.

Thus reads the manuscript codex of Corbie.

Furthermore, Sozomen, Book IX, chapter 2, at the end; Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 45; and Aimoins, *On the Miracles of Benedict*, Book II, chapter 19, near the end, relate that reliquaries of this kind, made of gold and silver and scattered with gems, had long been customary in the Church.

That the Franks were accustomed to place reliquaries filled with the relics of saints in the apse of a church, beneath which linen cloths and silk coverings were laid, is testified by Einhard, in the final chapter of the work *On the Translation of Saints Peter and Marcellinus*, printed by Surius under 2 June.

The reason why sacred relics of this kind are preserved in reliquaries is explained by Theofridus, abbot, in his sermon *On Relics*, near the end:

“In God’s dispensation, in so great a house as it were of a householder, the elect are believed to be and to have been vessels unto honor; therefore their relics are placed in vessels of gold and silver, adorned with gems, and in everything precious,” and so forth.

Before Theofridus, Saint Peter Damian expressed himself in similar terms at the beginning of his sermon *On the Translation of Saint Hilary*.

(16) CHAPTER IV, § I.—Certainly, if the bodies of the saints had preserved their proper places according to the requirement of nature—that is, their tombs—and so forth.

In this passage Guibert disapproves of translations and divisions of relics solely because of the impious commerce, false religion, and fraud of human beings. For this reason Blessed Augustine writes in chapter 28 of *On the Work of Monks*:

“[The devil] has scattered hypocrites everywhere under the guise of monks, wandering through the provinces, sent nowhere, settled nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere. Some sell the limbs of martyrs—if indeed they are the limbs of martyrs—and so forth.”

“For the most cunning enemy,” Baronius says, “endeavored to bring the illustrious name of monks into disrepute.”

This provided the occasion for the Emperor Theodosius to enact the following law:

“No one is to transfer a buried body to another place; no one is to dismember a martyr; no one is to trade in one,” and so forth.

Code, final law, *On the Violation of Tombs*, under Emperor Theodosius.

[Col. 1040A] Nevertheless, the custom of distributing the bones of a single saint among various churches, so that the devotion and worship of the people toward him might be increased, is shown to have remained firmly established both formerly and down to the present day by Evodius, *On the Miracles of Saint Stephen*, book I, chapter 2, in Augustine’s *Appendix*, volume X; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 36; and Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 49. Indeed, writers also testify that men distinguished for religion carried the relics of the saints with the greatest devotion, as did Saint Germanus of Auxerre, according to his biographer in Surius, 30 July; Saints Benedict and Maurus, according to Faustus in the *Life of Saint Maurus*, chapter 3; and very many others.

But, “By this practice,” writes our Guibert, lamenting, “that they are dug out of tombs, carried here and there limb by limb, and, when the opportunity for circulating them under the pretext of piety has arisen, the rectitude of the intention has begun to be twisted toward this purpose by the intervention of wickedness.” Therefore the Third Synod of Braga, chapter 6, says:

“We have learned that certain bishops, when they are about to proceed to the church on the solemn festivals of martyrs, place the relics around their necks; and, so that they may swell with the glory of greater pomp among men—as though they themselves were the ark of the relics—Levites dressed in white carry them in little litters. This detestable presumption must be abolished in every respect, lest, under the appearance of holiness, only pretended vanity prevail,” etc.

This decree, however, by no means condemns the veneration of relics by the people, or their being carried by bishops. “But if a bishop,” the same synod adds, “should choose to carry the relics himself, he should not be carried by deacons in little litters; rather, he should go on foot, with the procession of people going before him,” etc. See the note on this chapter itself.

The mind of those who, having professed the ecclesiastical life—or even the stricter life—are led by some kind of piety, or rather, I was almost going to say impiety, to tear apart bit by bit the purest and most sacred bones of the saints, so that, covered with gold, silver, and jewels, they may become ornaments, necklaces, and playthings for little women, and often the appearance and pretext of crimes for ruined and dissolute men, is as far as possible removed from the religion and zeal of that synod. Alas! What would our abbot and the Fathers of the aforesaid synod have done, and what words would they have used, to remove so wicked a practice from their midst? I spare the written record, lest I say something too severe.

Nevertheless, let those who suffer from this deadly plague hear, and take to heart, what councils and the supreme rulers of the Church teach and decree concerning the proper veneration to be shown to the pledges of the saints, and how reverently they are to be preserved.

The Council of Epaon, held in A.D. 517, chapter 25:

“Let the relics of the saints not be placed in rural oratories, unless perhaps there happen to be neighboring clergy of whatever parish who may serve the sacred ashes by frequent psalmody.”

The third capitulary of Charlemagne, *Ecclesiastical*, chapter [states]:

“Let each priest build his church with every diligence, and preserve the relics of the saints with the greatest care, through night watches and divine offices.”

Gregory the Great, book V, letter 51, writing to Brunichild, queen of the Franks, after sending relics of Saints Peter and Paul, says:

“But so that your praiseworthy and religious devotion may shine forth more and more in you, you must see to it that the gifts of the saints are deposited with reverence and honor, and that those serving there are afflicted by no burdens or vexations, lest perhaps, because of some external necessity pressing upon them, they become useless and sluggish in the service of God, and suffer—God forbid!—injury and neglect in regard to the gifts of the saints that have been deposited there,” etc.

Likewise, book VII, letter 12, concerning the relics of Saints Hermes, Hyacinth, and Maximus, to be placed in the church of Saint Mary at Spoleto:

“And therefore, most illustrious brother, if it is established that no body has been buried in that place, you shall carefully consecrate the sanctuaries of the aforesaid martyrs, received without hesitation and with reverence.”

He makes the same provision in book VII, letter 87, and book II, letter 20. Finally, book VII, letter 88, to Constantine, bishop of Milan:
