“Therefore let your Fraternity not delay to investigate with its customary diligence whether, in the places where they are to be deposited—the relics of Saints Paul, etc.—lamps or provisions for those serving God there ought to be supplied before the dedication of the place itself; and then, once the relics have been sent to those same places, let them be deposited with reverence.””

From these passages it is clear that the remains of the saints are by no means to be deposited in profane places, but only in places consecrated to God, where divine praises are accustomed to be sung day and night. I would not, however, wish to assert that it is improper for certain persons distinguished by singular moral integrity to carry relics, since I am aware that Saint Thomas, among others, approves that this is permissible, *Summa*, II–II, question 96, article 4, reply to objection 3.

(17) SAME PLACE.—“With the most illustrious Pope Gregory.” Book III, letter 30, a letter most worthy of careful reading, especially by those who sacrilegiously traffic in the relics of the saints; it will undoubtedly relieve their itch for such activity.

(18) SAME PLACE.—“That it had never been pleasing either to God or to the saints themselves.” Consult, if you please, blessed Gregory at the place cited.

(19) SAME PLACE.—“He replied that he absolutely did not dare to do so.” “For the ancient custom of the Roman Church not only shrank from allowing the bodies of the saints to be transferred from Rome, but did not even permit the slightest relics to be removed from them in any way.” Baronius reports this in his notes on the martyrology under 1 June, where he proves it at greater length, especially from the letter of Saint Germanus and his fellow legates of the Apostolic See to Pope Hormisdas in the year 520. Instead of relics, the pontiffs of the Catholic Church used to send cloths or coverings called *brandea*. What is a *brandeum*? He explains it at that place.

(20) SAME PLACE.—“A certain abbot of that place, excessively inquisitive.” His name was Letfanus. William of Malmesbury presents the story in question in *On the Bishops of England*, book II, near the end, in the section on the eastern English bishops:

“Here Letfanus, giving bad advice to certain people who wrongly doubted the incorruption of the saint [Edmund], took precautions for others at his own peril. He brought the body out and displayed it for public inspection, while he himself pulled it by the head and his monk by the feet.”

And shortly afterward:

“He had scarcely finished the prayer when, behold, the fingers of both hands—either miserably twisted backward or miserably driven into the palms—punished the man with the penalty he had requested. Later he was also afflicted with other infirmities,” etc.

Florence of Worcester agrees with this under the year 1097. Something not entirely dissimilar happened to Auxentius, bishop, in the *Life of Saint Nicetas the Martyr* in Surius, 15 September:

“For when he had undertaken to divide and take some part of his [Nicetas’] body, he received none of what he wanted; but a considerable fear seized him—not such a fear that it would fail to become evident or remain hidden, but one by which his soul too was greatly shaken. He taught others by what they saw and by the terror with which he had been affected, so that thereafter no one would stretch out a bold hand or tear away any part of his body against his will,” etc.

In this same sense Pope Saint Gregory addresses the empress Constantia, book III, letter 30:

“For in the Roman regions, or throughout the whole of the West, it is altogether intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone should attempt to touch the bodies of the saints.”

## TO THE THIRD BOOK OF GUIBERT’S *ON THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS*

In this third little book the reader may perhaps think that the author attacks the people of Saint-Médard more vehemently, inflamed by rivalry, and oversteps the bounds of brotherly love. But if his speeches are brought back to the weight of the sanctuary—if, that is, the writings of certain ecclesiastical Fathers and holy teachers, especially Jerome, Augustine, and Bernard, are carefully reviewed, and it is recalled with what mind and zeal they opposed, both in speech and in writing, the practices and wicked customs that were undermining the unity, purity, and piety of Christ’s bride, and endeavored to uproot them completely—then, together with those sacrilegious traffickings in relics (as has been amply demonstrated), which in this age were carried on under the appearance of piety but in reality for the sake of shameful profit, it must rightly be acknowledged that he published his books *On the Relics of the Saints*, and especially the third, out of a chaste love of divine worship.

Furthermore, as I understand it, there is no need or necessity to assert that the Word of God, clothed in our humanity, suffered from that seven-year illness of infants during which the milk teeth, as they are called, fall out and new ones grow again in their place. Rather, since it is the constant opinion, teaching, and faith of all the Fathers that the Son of God, although he assumed the miseries of fallen humanity—with the exception of sin—was nevertheless never subject in his own body to those diseases to which the rest of humanity was condemned through the transgression of our first parents, it follows that this replacement of the teeth is a kind of illness. The physicians acknowledge this, and daily experience proves nothing less. Paul of Aegina, *On the Art of Medicine*, book I, chapter 9; Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, book V, final chapter; Hippocrates, section, book III, *On Flesh*, before the beginning.

Relevant here also is what the authors themselves report: that certain teeth of infants do not fall out from natural necessity at all, but only because of a change or corruption in their food. What reason, then, what necessity is there for asserting that a new production of teeth took place in Christ’s body, to which such corruption did not apply? Accordingly, Guibert is by no means to be brought under accusation or charge because he contends that no tooth of the Savior ever existed in the monastery of Saint-Médard, but rather that a tooth falsely venerated under that name should be attributed to some blessed person.

(21) CHAPTER I, § II.—“He had said that not a hair from our head would perish.” He seems to adopt the opinion of blessed Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 87 and following, but especially *The City of God*, book XXII, chapters 19 and 20. That is, by those words Christ promises to restore to those who have received his ordinances not the quantity of their limbs or bodily parts, but their number. For since the bodies of the blessed will attain their final perfection in the resurrection, they must be restored in their complete substance. This was accomplished with far greater propriety in Christ when he rose again, since he is the most perfect exemplar of all. Saint Thomas, *Commentary on the Sentences*, book IV, distinction 44, question 1, article 2; and the other theologians on that same book.

Moreover, if that tooth of the Savior, left behind on earth, will eventually decay—as the author cleverly proves—or if Christ will take it back after the Last Judgment, either alternative is plainly absurd in itself.

The case of Christ’s body is certainly not equal to that of the bodies of other human beings. For Christ, having resumed not only what pertains to the integrity but also what pertains to the greater perfection and beauty of his body, raised himself from the dead by divine power. But since the others have not yet been raised from the dead, they will unquestionably receive on the day of judgment whatever belonged to their bodies; and for this reason all the parts of their bodies are preserved here for the future resurrection.

(22) CHAPTER I, § III.—“The same matter is at issue among us concerning the navel and the other things which are said to have been taken from him, no less than concerning the tooth.” I have neither anything to say about the navel, nor do I see what could be said. But, to state my own view, since Christ did not come forth from the Virgin’s womb by the same means as other infants, it seems to me discordant and repugnant both to the Virgin Mother and to the immaculate and most pure birth of the Son to declare that a navel was cut from his body. I ask you: what would this very cutting of the navel mean, if he came forth from the Virgin’s most holy womb like a ray of the sun penetrating glass, without any injury to its purity? Let us therefore withdraw our hand from such matters.

I likewise would not dare to decide anything concerning the foreskin, although some boast that they possess it and not a few writers assert that it is preserved in various places, except in accordance with the opinion of Pope Innocent III, book IV, *On the Mysteries of the Mass*:

“What shall be said about the cutting off of the foreskin in circumcision, or about the cutting of the navel? Did it likewise return to the reality of human substance in Christ’s resurrection? It is believed to be preserved in the Lateran basilica, although some say that the foreskin was carried to Jerusalem by the angel for Charlemagne, who transferred it to Aachen; but afterward it was placed by Charles the Bald in the church of the Savior at Charroux. It is nevertheless better to commit everything to God than to define anything rashly.”

Consult Titus of Bostra and Theophylact on chapter II of Luke, and Bollandus, *Acts of the Saints*, volume I, under 1 January, who brings together very many testimonies of ancient and modern writers on this matter.

[Col. 1044B] (23) CHAPTER III, § IV.—“As at Laon among us, the milk of the Blessed Virgin herself in a crystal dove.” Nor am I without reason reluctant to make some observation here; for I hear and read that throughout the world, in very many churches in France and elsewhere, drops of milk of the Mother of God are reverently venerated. Guibert, on the other hand, consistently denies that the Blessed Virgin ever expressed milk from her sacred breasts that would later become an object of veneration. To which side, then, should I incline? In both directions there is difficulty; in both directions a scruple torments my mind.

Nevertheless, some writers—and indeed very weighty ones—hold that the preserved milk was a most white liquid which the Blessed Virgin, already reigning in heaven, poured out uniquely upon those who loved her. This is recorded in an old succession of the bishops of Chartres, from which we publish the following fragment, through the kindness of Jean-Baptiste Souchet, a man learned in every branch of literature:

“Fulbertus, etc. The Blessed Virgin herself personally visited him as her chief fosterling during a certain illness, and healed his tongue, already consumed by the sacred fire, by pouring into it milk freshly drawn from her breast. It happened, therefore, that three drops of milk remained upon his face; he collected them and placed them in a precious vessel suitable for this purpose. They are venerated in the Church at appointed times down to the present.”

William of Malmesbury, book III, *Deeds of the English*, adds his authority to this account.

Something similar occurred, as recorded in a parchment book *On the Miracles of the Blessed Mary*, written down around the year 1100, chapter 76: “Of a monk whose ulcers the Blessed Virgin moistened with her milk”:

“There was a certain brother who served the Lord of heaven in a monastery. He had resolved to serve the Mother of God as diligently as her Son. When the community had finished those things which it was accustomed to sing at night, he alone remained before the altar, fulfilling what he had vowed to his mistress. Each day, at the individual hours, after completing the canonical hours, he sang the praises and thanksgivings proper to glorious Mary. He did this for a long time, not negligently but with the greatest devotion, until one day, seized by a grave illness, he was unable to render his due service. The disease, swelling excessively, had so occupied his throat, internally and externally, that there was no passage either for food or drink; indeed, within a short time all the parts of his body seemed almost lifeless, so great was the force of the illness. The man of God suffered terribly from the fever’s violence, so that some of those standing around said: ‘This man is about to give up his spirit.’ When the news was heard, the whole community immediately assembled; they wept and prayed for their brother, who was near death, anointing him with oil.

“When these things had been completed, they began to sing psalms, as is customary in such danger, marveling that he had lived so long when they could not see him draw breath. The light had failed from his eyes, his eyelids had ceased to move, his face was already discolored with pallor, and his limbs were stiff with the cold of death. Having sprinkled ashes on the floor, the brothers hastened to spread a hairshirt there, where the soul would depart from the body. Almost everyone was saying: ‘Alas! How badly we have delayed, having none of what is needed for those who are carrying out this task. Do you not see that he is dead?’

“In the meantime, while everyone was howling and uttering mournful cries for the departure of the good brother, behold the source of universal compassion: the blessed Virgin Mary, glorious mother of mercy, moved by the sighs of her chaplain, could not bear to see him afflicted by such a long illness. While the brothers were doing these things, behold, that blessed mother, unseen by anyone except him who was dying, placed herself beside his bed, exceedingly beautiful in a white garment. As he saw it, she brought her right hand near his forehead and spoke to him as follows: ‘My beloved, what are you doing? You have been worn down by excessive suffering for a long time. It is unjust that I should allow you to be tormented any longer by these pains, you whom both my Son and I have seen so devoted to us. I, the Mother of Mercy, have come here to help my chaplain. Look at me now; do not be afraid; you will recover completely.’

“A wondrous thing, unheard of in all former ages! For, as the pious mother herself seemed to him—the mother whose maternal compassion is compassion for the suffering—she drew forth, as though from her bosom, her breasts, and with sacred milk moistened the ghastly ulcers around the mouth of the sick man, namely her chaplain. When this had been done, the mother immediately departed and withdrew into the starry palaces, as though unable to endure the tumult of the brothers. Before doing so, however, she added these few words: ‘Now receive the reward for the service you have rendered me; before long you shall possess everlasting joy. For those who strive diligently to serve my Son and me may be confident of the reward for their service: they shall live a life that has no end.’

“When news of so marvelous an event was heard, the mind was struck with fear, the hearing was stunned, and the unsettled mind trembled at the thought that this was true, because I have said that the merciful Mother of the Most High had moistened the ulcers of her chaplain with sacred milk. For neither a person of such dignity nor such eloquence in philosophy or prayer is present who could deserve anything of this kind from the most excellent Mother of God. But if we recall how her Most High Son deigned to descend into the Virgin’s womb, and afterward to be born, circumcised, tempted, persecuted by the plots of the Pharisees, and finally crucified for sinners; then to be buried, to rise from the dead, and, ascending, to take his place at the right hand of the Father, assuming the form of our mortality—every doubt disappears when we remember that God did so much for sinners.

“Yet the name ‘milk’ sometimes expresses mercy, or some sweetness of heavenly contemplation. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘I gave you milk to drink, as infants in Christ, not solid food’; that is, I showed you mercy by prescribing lighter things. What wonder, then, if the glorious Virgin Mary, mother of all piety and mercy, through the likeness of milk, bestowed mercy from her sacred breast upon her devoted servant, whose tender infancy—namely, that of Jesus Christ our Lord—is nourished by the sacred milk of that same mercy, and who afterward also deigned mercifully to endure the punishments of the cross for sinners?

“It is also related in the *Acts of blessed Dionysius the Martyr*, first of Athens and afterward, by God’s gift, archbishop of Paris, with blessed Dionysius himself reporting it in his letters, that when the faith of the holy Church had been violated by certain people, the presbyter blessed Carpus prayed to the kindly Jesus Christ that he would brandish the vengeance of his power against them. The kindly Jesus appeared to him as he slept during his prayers, together with a multitude of angels. Extending the hand of his holy mercy to those wretched people, as though they had fallen into the depths of a prison, and supporting them through the ministry of the angels, he said to blessed Carpus: ‘Carpus, strike against these men with the hand that has been set against them without mercy and has not been withdrawn through mercy; strike against me. For I am prepared to suffer again in order to save human beings anew, and I take greater pleasure in this than in those who have not sinned.’

“Why, then, should the wretched human being doubt that the glorious Mother of Mercy can, in the likeness of milk, bestow mercy upon her own, when Mercy itself—namely, the kindly Jesus our Lord, who sits at the right hand of the Father, who conquered death and can no longer die—declares that he wishes to die for the faithless? But let this suffice as proof of the mighty works of our God and of his holy Mother. Let us now return to our narrative, where we said that the glorious Mother, after visiting her servant, withdrew into the heavens.

“The sick man, greatly strengthened by the Mother of the Lord, immediately raised his head; no longer sick, he sprang from his bed and, looking nowhere for medical treatment, cried out to the brothers: ‘The Queen of Glory was here to make her servant well, and you, showing her no reverence at all, certainly sinned when you saw what she was doing for me and neglected to prepare a place for her to rest.’ Thinking that they too had seen the vision as he had, he said: ‘Alas, miserable me! I was unable to prepare some beautiful seat for my Savior, who undeservedly granted me the consolation of such good health. For if your tumult had not occurred, perhaps she would not have departed so quickly.’

“When the brothers saw that the man whom each of them had thought dead had risen in this way, great terror seized them all, and they did not know what had happened. No one considered the brother’s words, for such astonishment had overcome everyone. No voice of psalmody resounded; the one who had just been weeping now resounded with fear. Meanwhile, after his strength had returned, the sick man came back to himself and recognized what had been done for him. He recounted it to the brothers in order, just as it had happened, and thus restored their minds. It is unnecessary for us to ask what praises they then endeavored to offer to so great a Virgin, since they saw their beloved brother, whom they had thought dead, living with sound limbs.

“Blessed be such a Lady,

Who brings such medicines to her own;

May she herself be favorable to us,

Granting us the remedies of life.

May she make the servants of her Son,

And her own little servants, free from sins;

And throughout the course of all our days,

Make us fit for her service.

May she prepare us as pure dwelling places for God,

Clean from every stain,

So that after the course of this life

We may rejoice with her forever.

By her aid, by her antidote,

Salvation returned to the lost world;

To her, together with her glorious Son,

Be praise, honor, power, and jubilation

Forever. Amen.”

Thus far the manuscript codex of the monastery of Corbie.

Some writers report that she also poured milk upon Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, the same Queen of Heaven. But let those who examine the deeds of that man, written by three contemporaries with whom Bernard associated very intimately, judge what foundation this claim has. For how could they, after relating more than a hundred miracles, have consigned this one—so remarkable—to oblivion? So says John Bertelius, book VIII, *On the Rule of Saint Benedict*. Chrysostomus Henríquez refutes him in the *Cistercian Menology* under 13 May, as does Angelus Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, volume II, year 1153, chapter 12.

(24) CHAPTER III, § IV.—“What those wounds, preserved after the resurrection, might signify.” Guibert’s meaning is certainly not that he denies that the scars of the wounds remained in Christ’s body, but only that he denies that they remained for the reason alleged by the people of Saint-Médard—namely, that they might be like signs and goads to the Father, refreshing his memory of what the Son endured for the sake of the human race and extorting mercy from him: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways,” God himself once said through the mouth of Isaiah, chapter LV. His infinite goodness alone, Christ’s humanity alone, is sufficient for the Father to bestow forgiveness upon sinners and pour out abundant graces upon humanity.

Nor does Guibert approve what the people of Saint-Médard argued: that the wounds endured after the resurrection because Christ’s body was destined to receive complete and final glory after the judgment. He also refutes the fantasies of certain old women who imagined that those very wounds of the Savior remained continuously open and poured out pus.

I repeat: the author does not obstinately deny that the Lord now has in heaven the stigmata of his Passion like pearls. Otherwise he would seem to rise up against the holy Fathers and set his own opinion above theirs—which God forbid!—namely, Saint Ambrose, *On Luke*, book X, chapter XXIV, near the end; Leo, sermon 1, *On the Resurrection*; and others. Why, then, the scars of the wounds? So that they may strengthen faith, console the faithful, and at some time cover the impious with shame. Thus Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII, chapters 19 and 20; Eusebius of Gaul, or Eucherius, or perhaps Faustus of Riez, homily for Tuesday after Easter; and Caesarius of Arles, homily 23. Guibert himself also states this most openly in chapter 3 of his letter *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body*, page 284, column C:

“What of the fact that, established in heaven, he did not even wish to cover his wounds or strip off the servant’s form which he will display at the future judgment?” etc.

[Col. 1047]

## TO GUIBERT’S BOOKS *ON HIS OWN LIFE*

[Col. 1047D] Anyone who has read the first book of Guibert’s life will clearly observe that he closely followed Saint Augustine, that most splendid light of the world. In the book to which Augustine gave the title *Confessions*, he reviews the actions of his life while mourning them; similarly, in his books *On His Own Life*, and especially in the first, Guibert recalls his past life with groans. Augustine offers God the greatest thanks for the infinite benefits bestowed upon him; Guibert does likewise. Saint Augustine reports that he was recalled from an immoral and heretical practice through his mother; Guibert candidly confesses in the same manner that he was led away from corrupt morals by his mother. The former praises his mother wonderfully; so does the latter praise his own. That great teacher attacked the Manichaeans and the other heretics who had arisen in his age, both in word and in writing; our abbot likewise, in order to uproot Jewish perfidy and heretical depravity, stirred up from the dregs of the Manichaeans, disputed publicly and published treatises.

Nor were there lacking other celebrated writers who committed to posterity what they had chiefly done and written, such as Jerome, Gennadius, Bede, Sigebert, and others. They judged this not inappropriate, but rather useful.

## TO THE FIRST BOOK

(25) CHAPTER I.—“Since you flow forth, you owe yourself to all.” That is, the graces and benefits which your infinite goodness and immense mercy continually send forth and pour upon human beings by decree and according to fittingness, not according to merit—as the theologians put it—are owed wholly to all. Does not nature itself proclaim, and divine Scripture affirm, that since God is the Creator of the entire world, God voluntarily owes to the things created by him not only preservation but also perfection? But if such a gratuitous debt is acknowledged in the order of nature, with how much greater reason must it be confessed in the state of grace, since it is, as the author says, “the fountain from which all good things proceed,” that whatever is suited to human salvation and perfection necessarily flows from him “whose nature is goodness, whose mercies are over all his works,” because he established this with himself from eternity?

Guibert indicates this clearly enough in book VIII, *On Genesis*, chapter XXXI, on verse 7, “But your father has deceived me,” etc. He says:

“God did not permit him to harm me; that is, since God is God essentially, and since it is proper to God to be merciful, his very natural grace does not permit him to allow the battle of the approaching temptation to be turned into my destruction.”

(26) SAME PLACE.—“Whenever I am compelled to sin by the necessity of sinning.” This is the necessity which the Doctor of the Gentiles laments in Romans VII:

“For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do. And I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin,” etc.

Accordingly, Augustine, replying to Simplicianus, book I, question 1, near the middle, explains Paul’s words:

“This whole statement is made so that it may be shown that the captive human being must not presume upon his own strength, etc. The free will that remains in this mortal life is not such that a person may fulfill righteousness whenever he wishes, but that he may turn in humble devotion to him by whose gift he can fulfill it.”

Primasius, on chapter VII of Romans:

“For I do not do what I want, etc. Overcome by habit, I do what I do not want. He therefore said that he does and practices this, not by the affection of consenting to and fulfilling it, but by the very movement of desiring. ‘Not I,’ because I am unwilling; yet ‘I,’ because through the force of habit I myself imposed this necessity upon me.”

Guibert himself explains his meaning in book III, *On Genesis*, chapter VI, verse 19:

“We often bring the feminine movements of the flesh before the mind, unwillingly or willingly, from the necessity of sinning; nevertheless, we immediately subject them to the authority of that male principle, namely reason, by whose force they are constrained to the rule,” etc.

(27) CHAPTER IV.—“Shortly before that time, and still partly during my own lifetime, there was affection for teachers of grammar,” etc. Among others, Milo Crispin records this in chapter 1 of the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, prefixed to his works:

“He was a great man born in Italy, whom the whole Latin world, restored by him to its ancient condition of learning, recognizes as its supreme master with the love and honor due to him, Lanfranc by name, etc. Passing through France with several scholars of great renown in his company, he reached Normandy, and, staying for some time in the city of Avranches, taught there.”

Likewise, chapter 4:

“Lanfranc also, with the permission of his abbot, once again conducted schools—namely, after he had become a monk in the monastery of Bec.”

From that school of Bec, as from a most limpid spring, very many men of uncommon learning and piety from Gaul, England, Italy, and elsewhere drew their knowledge; we mentioned some of them in our note on chapter 7 of the aforesaid *Life*.

Afterward, writers report, letters were restored and flourished in Gaul, especially at Laon, under the teacher Anselm, author of the Interlinear Gloss, who had been a pupil of the great Anselm, a disciple of Lanfranc. At Paris there were also Abelard and Robert Pullen, later cardinal and chancellor of the Roman Church under Innocent II. At the same time the schools of Saint Victor at Paris became especially celebrated. Abelard, letter 1; *Life of Saint Goswin*, chapter 4. We have discussed the monastic schools at length in the note on chapter 4 of the *Life of Blessed Lanfranc*, page 35.

(28) CHAPTER VII.—“Finally, my mother was trying by every means to insert me into ecclesiastical benefices.” This poison was spreading remarkably at that same time. For this reason Urban II, in the Third Roman Council held in the year 1099, decreed in chapter 5:

“Those who, while still children, obtained churches or ecclesiastical benefices through the ambition of their parents and by means of money, after they have completely relinquished them, if they wish to live canonically in those places, we permit them to remain there out of mercy,” etc.

But let us hear Bernard, that vigorous defender of ecclesiastical discipline, Guibert’s contemporary, in letter 42, or in the treatise *On the Conduct and Office of a Bishop*:

“Now, however, because glory alone is considered and not punishment, people are ashamed to be simple clerics in the Church, and regard as vile and inglorious those who have not been raised to some more eminent position. Scholarly boys and immature youths are promoted to ecclesiastical dignities because of the nobility of their blood, and are transferred from under the schoolmaster’s rod to rule over priests; meanwhile they rejoice more that they have escaped the rods than that they fear the authority,” etc.

How aptly these words apply to our own age!

(29) SAME PLACE.—“At that time there was a new apostolic-sea attack against married priests.” See chapter 2 and chapter 12 of the Council of Melfi, or chapter 9 of the Council of Clermont, held under Urban II; and also chapters 9 and 10 of the First Council of Poitiers, under Paschal II. Before this—namely, in the year 1074—Gregory VII had enacted many measures against the incontinence of the clergy. Saint Peter Damian, letter 16 to Pope Nicholas; Orderic Vitalis, book V of the *History*, and book XII, pages 866 and 888, and frequently elsewhere.

Blessed Bernard, first abbot of the monastery of Tiron, severely rebuked priests living with concubines in this same century, around the year 1108, as Goffridus Grossus attests in chapter 7 of his life:

“For it was the custom at that time throughout all Normandy that priests publicly take wives, celebrate weddings, and beget children, to whom, by hereditary right after their death, they would leave their churches, etc. Against this deadly custom the servant of God Bernard diligently argued in gatherings of priests and strove with all his might to make them abandon it, etc. One day, while he was preaching publicly to the people at Coutances, an archdeacon who had a wife and children arrived with a large company of priests and asked why he, a monk who had died to the world, was preaching to those who were alive. Bernard replied cleverly: ‘My dearest brother, have you not read in Scripture that mighty Samson killed his enemies with the jawbone of a dead ass?’” (Judges XV, 15.)

And shortly afterward:

“The dead ass signified the simple obedient people who carry Christ’s easy yoke and his light burden, follow the paths of humility, and are dead to the world—that is, mortified to sins and vices—as Scripture says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God’” (Colossians III, 3), etc.

Do you see, then, in what sense monks are dead to the world?

[Col. 1051B] (30) SAME—“Under the expectation of another’s death.” The detestable greed for benefices crept in—not only in Guibert’s age, but also through many subsequent periods—and indeed spread, to the greatest disgrace of the Church. This kind of commerce was later practiced under the name of reservations and expectative graces by those who hunted after benefices. In this matter Antonius de Raymundia, a Benedictine and a learned ascetic, in his *Treatise against Special and Nominal Reservations of Almost All Prelacies*, etc., laments the pitiable condition of the Church in these words:

“This plague was detested by our fathers. Although formerly it attempted to make little shoots emerge from the dried-up bodies of men and to cause unfruitful branches to grow together, from its very origin it was immediately torn out by the prudence of the holy Fathers from the very field of the Church, like a thorn tree—namely, the reservation of dignities, prelacies, and other benefices whose ministers and prelates are still alive—because it prepared material for scandals and gave men the desire to seek another’s death. In the sacred Lateran Council celebrated by Alexander III, it was subjected to perpetual prohibition, specifically in chapter 2, *De concessione praebendae*, etc.

“We see with our own eyes, in these tearful and ill-fated times, a strange thing: when some prelate has scarcely reached his fiftieth year, his prelacy or dignity is reserved for the benefit of another, contrary to the rule of charity, giving that person the desire to await another’s death so that he may be substituted in his place. Still more astonishing is how Christian princes do not fear to assail the ears of the supreme pontiff with importunate and—if it may be said—dishonourable petitions concerning so criminal a matter; and more astonishing still that the supreme hierarch of the Christian commonwealth, who acts as the representative of Jesus Christ, the most just judge, should wickedly grant assent to such unjust requests, contrary to every principle of right, law, and natural and positive reason,” etc.

Thus far that doctor, burning with zeal for God.

(31) CHAPTER VIII—Luxovium in Gaul. Concerning it Jonas writes in chapter 10 of the *Life of Saint Columbanus*: “The renowned monastery of Luxeuil, like a fountain of paradise, watered all Gaul with its piety, religion, and learning.” Saint Audoenus, in chapter 21 of Book I of the *Life of Saint Eligius*, writes: “Burning exceedingly with a desire for holy conduct, Saint Eligius himself was also hastening toward the monasteries, and especially toward Lussedium [Luxovium], which at that time was more eminent and stricter than all the others,” etc.

Moreover, there is a vivid description of the beginnings of the monastery of Luxeuil in the very ancient manuscript *Life of Saint Agile, Abbot of Rebais*:

“At that time a man of venerable religious character, named Columbanus, had come from Ireland into Gaul, led by Christ, desiring by divine direction to obtain from the serenity of the aforesaid king a place where he might build a monastery of monastic religion, etc. Having heard of the prince Agnoald’s intense zeal, he decided to approach him and commended to him both himself and his request. Agnoald immediately received the secret of so great a desire as though it had been entrusted to him by God, promptly brought it suitably to the king’s attention, and made Columbanus pleasing to him; he also humbly begged the king to hear his desirable petition.

“But the king, rejoicing with the moderation of magnanimity at such a speech, most willingly granted what was requested. Moreover, he magnificently promised to give more than had been asked. For there was a fortress amid the vast solitudes called the Vosges, once dedicated to the worship of idols, but by then demolished to its foundations. The inhabitants of that forest, though unaware of the omen, had called it Luxeuil.

“Most kindly considering that it could be restored more quickly, and seeing that the site was suitable for a company of monks—indeed, enlightened by the prerogative of faith and the light of wisdom, understanding that the place ought to be consecrated to God, and that where the ancients had once worshipped shrines in profane ritual, there the altars of Christ should be fixed, banners raised, and the mysteries celebrated—Agnoald obtained by his petitions from the king’s high authority that, through a written instrument, the dwelling of those serving God should be assigned perpetually. There, under the direction of Blessed Columbanus, the recruits of the heavenly King would fight against the aerial powers; and after diverse exercises of virtue, everlasting light would finally make them, as sturdy warriors, conspicuous to Christ with the palm of glory in paradise.”

(32) SAME—Some also in Neustria. Namely, Bec, Saint Stephen’s at Caen, Saint Martin’s at Sées, etc., which began in those times; and Saint Évroult, Jumièges, Saint-Wandrille, [Col. 1052D] etc., restored after an interval to their former splendour, together with very many others, which are enumerated in Robert of Torigni’s treatise *On the Transformation of the Order of Monks*, etc. See the Appendix published by us below. The Chronicle of Bec mentions these same monasteries; see Orderic Vitalis, *History*, Book III, p. 461.

(33) SAME—“The charity of holy conduct grew cold, and the abundance of possessions gradually afterward deserted certain churches.” Moral perversity therefore produces poverty, especially among ecclesiastical men; virtue, on the contrary, produces an increase of resources. Ecclesiasticus 13:30: “Good is the substance in which there is no sin in the conscience, and most wicked is poverty in the mouth of the impious.” On these words Strabo of Fulda gives the following ordinary gloss: “Wealth rightly possessed is material for the exercise of virtue through works of mercy and generosity.” Very similar is that saying of blessed Ambrose: “As riches are impediments to the wicked, so to the good they are aids to virtue,” on chapters 18 and 19 of Luke, Book VIII. Juvenal likewise, *Satire* 3:

> Unhappy poverty has nothing in itself  
> except that it makes men ridiculous.

And William, abbot of Flavigny—of whom more below in the brief history of that monastery—counselling a good and steadfast monastic life, says: “Poverty is an occasion of murmuring, impatience, and sometimes even greed.”

Thus it was not the abundance of temporal goods [Col. 1053B] that caused the ruin of the Benedictine order, as those gluttonous gulpers and devourers of things consecrated to God habitually grumble; rather, it was deviation from holy conduct. For as soon as the monks, weary of penance and deceived by pleasures, followed their desires, and, setting aside the solitary and narrow way, voluntarily plunged themselves into worldly affairs, “the charity of holy conduct grew cold.” Corrupted and made detestable, they became vain in their thoughts; and what had formerly been bestowed not only for their own food and clothing but also for glory—that, like powerful lords and earthly princes, they might lavishly distribute it to others, especially to the needy—was turned into poison and disgrace. Strangers came and consumed their strength. Therefore, rightly, with Jeremiah we should sing, Lamentations 5:2, 3, 7:

> Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers,  
> our houses to foreigners.  
> We have become orphans without a father;  
> our mothers are like widows.  
> Our fathers sinned and are no more,  
> and we have borne their iniquities.

But wherever regular observance flourishes, everything abundantly follows, as Hugh of Flavigny carefully noted in his as-yet-unpublished *Chronicle*, under the year 1078, describing the deeds of Saint William, abbot of Dijon, who afterward governed the monastery of Fécamp:

“He knew that as the zeal for religion increased inwardly, so also the supplementation of external substance would increase.”

And under the year 1088:

“In him the virtue of charity flourished, and it was so great that although that year, everywhere because of the violence of the storms, the ripe crops in the ears and the grapes on the vines had all been beaten down and utterly ruined, nevertheless there was no reduction in the refectory or in almsgiving, even though the brothers exceeded nearly one hundred in number,” etc.

Relevant here is what Suger reports of himself in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, volume IV of André Duchesne’s *History of France*, p. 311:

“He fully reformed the holy order and peacefully established the purpose of holy religion, by which one reaches the enjoyment of God, without scandal or disturbance to the brothers, although they had not been accustomed to it. The effectiveness of this divine will was followed by such an abundance of freedom, good reputation, and earthly wealth that even now, so that our faintheartedness may be aroused more strongly, we may in some manner understand that he rewards us also with a temporal recompense. For apostolic kings and princes delight in rejoicing with the prosperity of the Church, and from that source there overflows an abundance of precious gems, gold and silver, vestments, and other ecclesiastical ornaments, so that we may rightly say: ‘All good things came to me together with her’ (Wisdom 7:11).

“By this evidence of the future glory of God, we earnestly exhort our brothers and successors, by the mercy of God and his terrible judgment, not to permit holy religion—which reconciles human beings and God, repairs what is broken, restores what is lost, and enriches poverty—to grow cold. For just as those who fear the Lord lack nothing, so those who do not fear him, even if they are kings, themselves lack everything.”

[Col. 1054B] The holy Benedict supplies the grounds for my foregoing assertion. As the restorer of evangelical perfection and the founder of the monasteries of the West, he expressly decreed that before novices make profession they should reserve nothing for themselves from all that they possessed, chapter 58. Likewise, in the following chapter, speaking of the sons of nobles, he adjures their parents: “Let them promise under oath that they will never, by themselves, etc., give their sons an opportunity to possess anything.” In chapter 33 he allows a monk to possess nothing as his own, but to “hope for all necessities from the Father of the monastery.” Chapter 34 states: “Care of the sick must be provided before all things and above all things, etc.; the use of meat and baths,” and whatever is necessary for the sick, is to be granted; chapters 39, 40, and 55 provide for food and clothing. Chapters 53 and 56 state: “All guests who arrive are to be received as Christ.” Finally, chapter 66 says:

“The monastery should, if possible, be so constructed that everything necessary—namely, water, a garden, a mill, or various crafts—may be exercised within the monastery, so that the monks have no need to wander outside, because this is altogether unprofitable for their souls.”

Must it necessarily be inferred from these passages that monasteries are to be endowed with an abundance of possessions so that the Rule may be observed to the letter? That food and clothing should be provided to each person; that “the sick should be served as truly as Christ”; and that all the poor—a practice that was always customary and religious in the order so long as the monasteries’ revenues were not diverted by secular men—should be received, assisted, fed, and clothed as Christ, concerning which more will follow below.

For this reason, when Saint Junianus was asked by King Chlothar I what his profession and manner of life were, he replied with this complaint:

“He said that he was living according to the monastic order, that he had been placed over monks, that he observed the institutions of blessed Benedict and kept his regular life, except that, because of the narrowness of the place, he was unable with his companions to observe it fully.”

After a short interval he added:

“When the king heard this, he immediately said: ‘If there is anything belonging to our royal estate nearby and suitable to the location, as much as pleases your holiness and can suffice for you and yours, we grant it as necessary both for the exercise of work and for the pasture of beasts of burden and livestock, for the uses, that is, of the servants of God,’ etc.”

Thus it is written in the manuscript Life.

(34) SAME—“When the labour of those living well also became distasteful, a scarcity arose.” Saint Benedict teaches in chapter 48 of the Rule: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul; and therefore the brothers should be occupied at fixed times in manual labour.” From this some infer, and wish to maintain, that monks must be held to manual labour in order to earn the necessities of life. But Rupert the abbot and Peter the Venerable point out that such reprovers are greatly mistaken, and that Saint Benedict binds his monks to this work for only two reasons: so that they may flee sloth and relieve poverty.

[Col. 1055B] The former, in Book III, chapter 1, on that chapter of the Rule, writes:

“I mention this chapter for the following reason, since I have proposed to speak about the ministry of the altar: why did Benedict establish nothing in the Rule concerning it? Obviously because today ignorance of themselves makes certain souls negligent of that inner beauty by which they have deserved to be admitted to the service of the sacred altar. Since they are monks, and blessed Benedict prescribed manual labour for monks, they almost forget that they are priests, etc. Our silence ought to leave them to their own purpose, because, intent upon manual work, they would say that they have little or almost no concern for the daily celebration of Mass, unless they were admonished.”

Then, in chapter 2:

“Therefore, whatever you are, O soul, who are troubled by those who say: ‘You cannot be saved here, because you do not live by the labour of your hands,’ consider this saying to have been spoken by me for your sake: ‘If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and follow the tracks of the flocks, and feed your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents,’ etc.”

And below, in chapter 4:

“Regarding manual work, by which food is chiefly acquired—ploughing, sowing, reaping, and cutting down forests—it is clear that this is not a command of Benedict but merely a permission, or a consolation in patience,” etc.

Finally, in chapter 7, he proves by examples from Saints Gregory, Maurus, and others:

“Those who provided or received so many and such great estates for their monasteries did so because it was not necessary for monks to seek their food by the labour of their hands; nor can they be accused of having acted against the institution of blessed Benedict.”

In the second place, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, answers the objections of the Cistercians in Book I, letter 28:

“Let us see,” he says, “not only what the Rule commands concerning manual labour, but also why it commands it. ‘Idleness is the enemy of the soul, and therefore the brothers should be occupied at fixed times,’ etc.”

Then, after a little:

“If monks can always occupy the whole span of the day with other good works, since they are commanded to work only so that they may not be idle, do they not remain entirely free from transgression of the Rule when they perform those works? Certainly so, unquestionably so, whether the opponents wish it or not, etc. Therefore, if the mind is occupied in praying, reading, chanting psalms, fulfilling assigned duties religiously, or performing any other good works of this sort, the Rule is perfectly observed.”

And after other remarks concerning Saint Maurus and his monks, he adds:

“Since all necessities were supplied to them without their own labour, they omitted manual work and exercised themselves in spiritual matters so that they would not be idle; and thus, by always doing good works, they observed the Rule recently handed down to them by Saint Benedict in the best possible manner.”

Thus writes the Venerable, who in his statute 38, to drive away the idleness of monks—especially those called lay brothers—commands manual labour.

On this subject Saint Jerome writes to Rusticus:

“The monasteries of the Egyptians maintain this custom: they admit no one without the labour of work, not so much because of the necessity of food as for the salvation of the soul, so that it may not wander through harmful thoughts and, like fornicating Jerusalem, spread its legs before every passer-by.”

So that clerics might not overflow with excessive leisure and grow sluggish, manual labour was formerly imposed upon them as upon monks by Saint Clement of Rome, *Constitutions* I, chapter 67; the Fourth Council of Carthage, canons 51 and 52; Saint Augustine, *Retractations* II.21; and others.

(35) SAME—“When the abundance of things given in ancient times overflowed.” We showed above why Benedictine monasteries were deprived of their greatest resources. We must now briefly explain how they grew so rich. Authors commonly attribute this to various causes. Some to the gifts of kings and princes; others to the wealthier men who, upon becoming monks, acquired many estates for the monastery; some to the careful and diligent administration of the ascetics; many to those who flourished in exceptional learning and maintained public schools; and finally others to the complete renunciation of worldly possessions and the perfect observance by the monks of the holy Rule, as we have also observed above.

But it seems clear to me that the principal cause was the solemn and most religious custom, born together with the order, of continually distributing alms to the poor and receiving guests, according to the prescription of the Rule. For Saint Benedict had imbued his disciples with this teaching: “Refresh the poor, clothe the naked, bury the dead,” Rule, chapter 4; instructions 14–16: “All guests are to be received as Christ, etc. The reception of the poor and pilgrims is to be carried out with the greatest care and solicitude, because in them Christ is received,” chapter 53. For he had learned this from the Teacher and Lord of all: “Give, and it will be given to you,” etc. He also knew by experience the saying—as may be seen in his Life, in Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, Book II, chapters 21 and 29—“He lends to the Lord who has mercy on the poor, and He will repay him” (Proverbs 19:17).

Since testimonies are abundant and readily available that monasteries customarily received and comforted all kinds of poor people, we deliberately pass them over. It is a pleasure, however, to bring forth one or two testimonies from ancient parchments. The most noble abbot Saint Adalard, who governed the monastery of Corbie, established the following regulations.

[Col. 1057A]

“We have established that for the hospice of the poor there are to be given daily forty-five loaves made of mixed grain, each weighing three and a half pounds, and five loaves of wheat or spelt of the kind received by vassals, so that there are fifty altogether. These loaves are to be distributed in this manner: twelve poor people who remain there overnight are each to receive one loaf, and on the following day each is to receive half a loaf for the journey. The attendants serving there are each to receive one loaf from the number written above. The five wheat loaves are to be divided among the clerical pilgrims who are led to the refectory, for their journey, and among the sick who are maintained there.

“We entrust the distribution of the loaves to the discretion of the hospitaller, with this understanding: if a larger number of poor people should arrive, or if more or fewer needy persons come—such as those weakened by hunger or very young children—he is to judge according to what is appropriate.

“If at any time fewer poor people happen to arrive, the hospitaller, the master, and the senior porter must all carefully remember how much less than the aforesaid number was distributed because of the small number of arrivals, so that when more arrive, what remained may be distributed.

“To the other poor who arrive and depart on the same day, a quarter-measure is customarily given, or, as we have said, whatever the hospitaller determines is appropriate according to the greater or lesser number or need: bread and relish, or whatever is given according to custom.

“As for drink, half a modius is to be given daily, that is, eight sextarii, six of which are divided among the twelve mentioned above, so that each receives two cups. Of the other four, six cups are given to the clerics whose feet are washed by the brothers, one cup to each, and one cup to the servant Wilerannus. Whatever remains we leave to the discretion of the hospitaller, so that he may distribute it among the sick or other poor as he sees fit. As for wine, it is left to the discretion of the prior.

“The senior porter must provide for the needs of the sick according to his ability, whether in food or drink, and in those things that the hospitaller lacks for the use of the sick.

“If pilgrims from distant provinces should arrive and exceed the number written above, the porter is to provide them with what is necessary, so that nothing is diminished from what has been assigned for ordinary days.

“We also add thirty measures of relish for the food of the poor, distributed between cheese and bacon, and thirty modii of legumes; a fifth part of the tithe that the porter receives from the cellarer—of eels or fresh cheese, which he is appointed to provide from ten sheepfolds—as well as of that which is given as tithe from the lord’s estates.

“Likewise, a fifth of the entire tithe of livestock, namely of calves, rams, or all animals given from the flocks to the porter, including horses.

“Moreover, we have arranged that the aforesaid hospitaller receive a fifth part of all silver that comes to the gate, through the hands of the senior porter. We wish this silver to be distributed in such a way that no less than four denarii are given daily; and if the amount is smaller, the abbot, if he wishes, may supplement it from elsewhere with what is sufficient to make this daily distribution. If the amount increases beyond that, nothing is to be withheld.

“The porter is to provide wood for the poor according to custom, as well as the other things not written here, such as bedding, vessels, and everything else. All the things written above are to be given from what comes to the gate because of that supplementation in silver, as mentioned above.

“Moreover, the hospitaller is to receive from the chamberlain old clothing or footwear of the brothers, to be given to the poor according to custom.

“We therefore beseech all those who are entrusted with the office of ordering matters in this monastery to attend, in generosity and distribution, rather to God’s will than to the example of our thriftiness, since each person must render an account for himself.”

You have here Saint Adalard’s most ardent charity toward his neighbour and his piety in relieving the poor and those afflicted by sickness. This charity and piety remained for a very long time in the monastery of Corbie, surviving, indeed, until the time of the commendatory abbots. Consequently, the monastery became not only very famous but also exceedingly wealthy.

God once showed how pleasing to him were the alms of that blessed prelate. Paschasius writes in chapter 7 of his Life:

“When one day he had used up all the cheese stew in feeding the guests, and the cellarer had rebuked him for it, the saint replied: ‘The Lord will provide.’ And the other said: ‘You are always making such promises, but what you so freely pour out will not be supplied immediately.’ Meanwhile, as these things were happening, behold, two carts arrived before the doors: one carrying some kind of fish, and the other full of cheeses,” etc.

The same thing happened to Saint Judoc, Orderic, Book III of the *History*, under the year 1066. If you wish, read chapter 22 of the *Life of Saint Bernard of Tiron*, Blessed Lanfranc’s *Decrees*, chapter 8, section 3, and Statute 23 of Peter the Venerable.

I shall draw my second testimony from the ancient customs of the abbey of Cluny, arranged into an order by a certain monk named Bernard at the command of Blessed Hugh I, the abbot. It is found in chapter 14 and is as follows.

### On the office of the almoner

“As all pilgrims who travel on horseback are received by the keeper of the guesthouse, so all those who travel on foot are to be received by the almoner, except those who are of such a kind that they do not wish to go to the almonry. If the person is a legate carrying letters, the keeper of the guesthouse receives him.

[Col. 1059A]

“After each person has been received, the almoner asks the granary keeper for one pound of bread, and half a pound for those departing the following day. He gives the same measure of wine to those arriving and departing, namely half a justitia. Formerly, one denarius was also given to each person departing, provided that the almoner could turn it aside—something that never occurred in our house—or provided that the person had not returned within a year.

“Therefore, during Advent, except on the days when two meals are eaten; during Lent, except on Sundays; and throughout the year whenever, according to canonical observance, the brothers abstain from fat—as during the Rogation days, the vigils of saints, and the Ember Days—and whenever a brother is buried, whatever wine remains for the brothers in the refectory, the almoner receives in its entirety, as well as bread and, throughout the year, spiced drink. He gathers and stores this wine so that visiting pilgrims may always have some available. On the day when he receives bread from the refectory in this way, he does not merely ask the granary keeper for bread, but from that very bread he gives as much as he can to the pilgrims; whatever is lacking he asks from the granary keeper.

“Likewise, every day he receives as many complete portions of bread, wine, beans, and general provisions as there are deceased brothers whose anniversary is being observed. In addition, for each brother recently deceased who professed in our Congregation, wherever he died, he receives one complete portion for thirty days. For all the brothers whose deaths cannot be known to us because of some intervening negligence, he receives two portions daily.

“Besides these, three portions of the brothers are given daily for alms and are placed in the refectory upon the principal table: one for the most blessed Father Odilo, one for the Emperor Henry I, and one for Fredeland and his wife, the kings of Spain.

“On top of all this, twelve flat loaves are given daily, each weighing three pounds. These are to be distributed to orphans and widows, the lame and blind, old men and old women, and all who arrive.

“He also receives daily from the refectory whatever remains for the brothers, as well as half of the general provision and of the special dish; the other half is assigned to the blind among the common people. Likewise, he receives half of the beans; the other half is assigned to the oxherds of the dean who governs the estate.

“Of vegetables, fruit, and similar things, he receives everything. From the half of the general provisions and special dishes that falls to him, he customarily provides a special dish to those receiving portions, by turns, and he also customarily gives some to his servants. His senior servant receives one pound daily from the granary, because he receives the bread and wine given to those receiving portions, and half a pound from the almoner himself. The others each receive a pound and a half from the almoner, whether from the daily bread or from another bread, if he prefers.

“Besides what has been mentioned, six portions are given from the granary for alms; these are called daily portions. Five are for the servants themselves: one senior servant who serves those receiving portions, the other poor, and pilgrims; another is the doorkeeper of the alms-house; two carry wood daily with two donkeys; and one supplies the two ovens, from which some assistance comes to the alms-house. All except the senior servant go out singly whenever the almoner orders them. If the general portion for deceased brothers cannot be absent [perhaps: cannot be supplied] on the day when it is recited in chapter, he reckons it up to a certain amount; then the chamberlain pays him denarii, and sometimes the cellarer is able to provide meat in place of fish.

“He also purchases for himself with the denarii that are given to him as the tithe of the church. For he receives a tenth of all the denarii offered in the church, and thus provides so that he can give meat more frequently to pilgrims. There are eighteen poor recipients of portions. Every day the almoner’s servant receives from the cellarer as many justitiae of wine as there are recipients, and from the granary keeper as many pounds of bread and beans for four days of the week. On the remaining three days they receive only vegetables from the garden assigned to the alms-house. On the greater feasts they receive meat in place of beans; and throughout the year there are thirty-five days on which they receive meat.”

Then, after other matters:

“Even if the Mandatum is not performed by the brothers from the feast of All Saints until the beginning of the fast, the alms never cease. For in winter the almoner’s servant washes the feet of three poor people with warm water, gives each of them a pound, a justitia, and a pound of bread of the kind the brothers have in the refectory.

“It also belongs to the almoner to go through the entire village once a week, taking with him his servants, bread, and meat in baskets, and wine in other vessels. He visits those poor people who are lying sick somewhere. If the person is male, he himself enters to visit him; if female, he stands at the door and sends his servant to her. After giving them the best he can, he comforts them; and if they desire anything beyond what he has given them, he asks whether it is in any way convenient for him to provide it, and afterward sends it through his servants. It is customary that the women who are in the houses where the sick lie immediately leave as soon as they see him coming. For as long as any woman remains inside the house, he never enters.

“It must be understood that to the pilgrims of whom we spoke above, together with a pound of bread and wine, he gives on the very night of their arrival any other food, namely fish or something of that kind, and sometimes, as stated above, meat. He gives no one a justitia of wine and a pound of bread except at the gate of the courtyard; they do not enter the courtyard.

“If any pilgrim has at his lodging a weak or exhausted spouse or companion who cannot conveniently come to the alms-house, he must show mercy to them and, because of their weakness, send them through their companion who returns to them as much as he gives to the others. All the rest eat in the alms-house.

“When foot travelers or poor clerical pilgrims from a distant land come to the alms-house, the almoner tells the abbot or prior before the brothers’ meal. Having received permission, he leads them into the refectory with their bags. These people are not lent surplices; those alone receive them who travel with horses.”

William of Nangis also commends the Cistercians in this matter under the year 1176:

“There was a very great famine in Gaul. For the support of the poor, the ornaments of churches were pawned and the reliquaries of the saints were stripped; and then the generosity of the Cistercian order in supporting the poor appeared most clearly.”

It is therefore no wonder that among the monks wealth and an abundance of almost everything flourished so greatly, since they devoted themselves and all that they possessed so diligently, wholeheartedly, and abundantly to Christ, the Lord of all. For he himself testified: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40); and he promised to repay a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the next.

(36) CHAPTER VIII—“Who, having been entrusted to them through their parents’ devotion, were nourished from early childhood.” Guibert’s observation is certainly excellent. Theory and practice, instruction in virtues and their exercise, are in fact far apart. Those who have spent the years of infancy and adolescence in monasteries in solitude and innocence commonly suspect no evil at first when they mingle with the company of people accustomed to wickedness. But because human beings are naturally inclined toward sin, and because not even an infant of a single day on earth is free from defilement, having been conceived in sins, they are driven by that very evil inclination—which they call the tinder of sin—and, more readily and imprudently on every occasion, unless divine grace restrains them or a previous fall into the pleasures and delights of the flesh makes them more cautious, they become entangled in allurements and slide into evil.

Would that such things did not so often occur in practice! For this reason Saint Benedict warns those who govern souls not to allow those who have given the world a bill of divorce to go outside repeatedly: “Because this is altogether unprofitable for their souls,” he says, chapter 66 of the Rule.

We have discussed at greater length children offered to God by their parents in our treatment of Blessed Lanfranc’s letter 32. It remains for me to append here the formula by which they are placed before the altar by an elder monk.

A boy who arrives in lay or clerical clothing is led by the chamberlain into the wardrobe, to be clothed in the same manner as any novice, except that he is given a linen shirt instead of a woollen one. When it seems good to the lord abbot, he orders the cap removed from the boy’s frock and blesses a cowl to be given to him. He also orders one of the brothers to offer the boy in place of his parents. That brother, holding the written petition that he is about to present, confirms it with the sign of his own hand, then reads it publicly and places it in the hand of the lord abbot. It is as follows:

“I, Brother N., offer to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul this boy named N., in place of his parents, with the offering in his hand and the petition, with the altar cloth wrapped around his hand, in the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and in the presence of the lord abbot N. Before witnesses I hand him over, so that he may remain according to the Rule. From this day onward it shall not be permitted him to shake his neck free from the yoke of the Rule; rather, let him know that he is bound faithfully to observe the institutions of that Rule and to serve the Lord with a willing heart together with the others. And so that this petition may remain firm, I have confirmed it below with my hand and handed it over to witnesses to be strengthened.”

“The boy himself receives with the offertory a paten and chalice, with the host placed upon it and wine poured into it. The vicar then wraps the boy’s hand with the altar cloth, so that he offers both the boy himself and his sacrifice, to be received by the priest. Afterward he is clothed in the cowl. From then on his blessing is deferred until the lawful age, namely by the completion of his fifteenth year. Again, when the lord abbot wishes to bless him, he reports this to the brothers in chapter. The young man immediately asks pardon, and, released from school, comes to the feet of the abbot; nevertheless, he does not leave the other boys until the hour of the blessing. He makes profession like the other novices. The blessing of the cowl alone is not repeated; it is neither removed nor put on except as it was before,” etc.

## From chapter 29 of the Cluniac statutes, discussed above

**(37) SAME SOURCE.**—They lived within the enclosure of the monasteries with correspondingly less exacting diligence. This is illustrated by a statute of Peter the Venerable, 586: “It has been decreed,” he says, “that no one who is to become a monk, even by concession, shall be clothed in the garments of the religious order before the age of twenty. The reason for this institution was the premature and excessively hasty reception of children, who, before they could possess any measure of rational understanding, were clothed in the garments of sacred religion and, mixed in with the others, disturbed everyone with their childish foolishness. And, to pass over certain matters and gather many points briefly, they were of almost no benefit to themselves and afterward impeded the religious purpose of the others not a little, indeed sometimes very greatly.” [Col. 1062D]

**(38) SAME SOURCE.**—To squander ecclesiastical monies on difficult occasions, etc. Alas! how the property of churches and monasteries has been torn apart and divided among profane and various uses—to say nothing more serious. This property, it is said, Pope Urban I and King Edgar of the English wrote, “is the votive offering of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor”; and: “It is the patrimony of the poor and the price of Christ’s precious blood.” Almost all the foundations of monasteries report that whatever was given to God and the saints was intended so that, singing the praises of the supreme Creator of all day and night, they might have food and clothing. [Col. 1063A]

In the restoration of the monastery of Besançon, Bishop Alberic of Langres speaks as follows, after enumerating what he himself had contributed: “For the sustenance of the monks and the nourishment of the poor, and so that the servants of God may there delight in serving the Lord; and that they may continually implore the Lord’s mercy for the king, his wife, his children, and the stability of the whole empire,” etc. *Besançon Chronicle*, manuscript.

Bishop Aldric of Sens likewise addressed his suffragans in this sense in the manuscript charter of the restoration of the monastery of Saint-Remigius near Sens: “We must know that the property of the Church consists of the offerings of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor; and we must remember that we have undertaken to administer, care for, and regulate these things, and that we are their administrators; and we must apply their revenues and expenditures to those purposes for whose sake they are known to have been bound to the divine altars.” [Col. 1063B]

The unpublished *Dijon Chronicle* says: “King Guntram bestowed upon God and Saint Benignus, for the sustenance of the monks serving God in this place, so that the monks might pray for his salvation and that of the succeeding kings and for the remission of sins, that they might obtain divine mercy. Moreover, he established that, in imitation of the monastery of the Saints of Agaune, the divine office should be performed day and night,” etc.

When the Emperor Louis the Pious granted the monks of Aniane the church of Saint Martin of Arles and everything belonging to it, he used, among other words, these: “We have perpetually granted this donation of our authority to the aforesaid monastery, for the support of the brothers serving God there, for the assistance of the poor, and for providing for all the needs of that same monastery of Aniane, for the benefit of our soul,” etc. [Col. 1063C] So the most ancient parchment records.

Tertullian expresses similar thoughts about the resources of the Church in his *Apology*, chapter 39: “These are deposits of piety; for from them provision is made neither for banquets, nor for drinking, nor for gluttonous feasts, but for feeding and burying the needy, and for boys and girls deprived of property and parents,” etc.

Regarding this matter, when the Fathers of the kingdom of Portugal were recalling the extensive possessions of the order in their constitutions of Benedict, I shall note what they prefaced: “These and other things we omit, having been converted to churches.” [Col. 1063D]

> Everything which the age has worn away, ancient old age has so consumed,  
> that nothing remains except what was once ours.  
> Yet I am pleased to touch upon these matters, because although alienations are pains to our eyes and spirit, they are nevertheless signs of the most holy patriarch’s—Benedict’s—charity and merits (add also: of the piety and learning of his sons), living heralds,” etc.

**(39) CHAPTER IX.**—His name was Ebrardus. Andreas Duchesne praises him briefly in his *History of Dreux*, book I, p. 24, where he also discusses the family of the counts of Breteuil. Consult him there, if you wish.

**(40) SAME SOURCE.**—Theudebaldus, etc., or Theobaldus. His contemporary biographer records the following about him: “Theobald was born to parents who were not merely noble but also most illustrious and exceedingly wealthy,” etc. And below: “By carrying stones, cutting hay from the meadows, tending the stables, and especially, as he himself simply related, making charcoal for the work of the smiths, he provided himself with food from a small income.” Surius, vol. III, under the year 1050.

**(41) SAME SOURCE.**—They sought the Major Monastery. This famous monastery, situated near Tours on the banks of the Loire, had its beginning from Saint Martin, archbishop. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 8; Glaber, book III, chapter 4; and others discuss it.

And since I observed that the list of abbots set out by Robert in *Gallia Christiana* is defective in many respects, I judged it worthwhile to append here as many as I have been able to discover from the ancient parchments and ruins of that same abbey. [Col. 1064B]

### List of the abbots of the Major Monastery

The first abbot and founder was Saint Martin, bishop of Tours.

**II. Galbertus**, elected and blessed by Saint Martin. The regular abbots who followed him—whose names have been buried in oblivion—devoted all their efforts to ensuring that religious observance flourished in the Major Monastery.

**III.** This continued until Robert, count and brother of King Odo. He is called both count and abbot of the Major Monastery in a charter drawn up in the sixth year of that same King Odo.

After the monastery was destroyed by the Northmen and the monks were slaughtered, those who survived withdrew to Burgundy together with the most sacred relic of Saint Martin. [Col. 1064C] Some of the clergy, however, built dwellings for themselves among the ruins and occupied the place for many years. Passing over them, therefore, we must turn to the regulars.

**IV. Saint Majolus**, abbot of Cluny, at the request of Odo, count of Blois, restored the monastic order to its former state. This is stated explicitly in a charter of the donation of what Stephen, count of Blois, bestowed upon the Major Monastery:

“Where my grandfather Odo,” he says, “and his brother Hugh, archbishop of Bourges, and their mother lie buried; and which, after the devastation carried out by the Danes, they rebuilt, enlarged with its possessions after removing the canons, and restored to the monastic order which had been there from the beginning, from the time of blessed Martin; and they appointed as abbot a man named Guillebert, given to them from Cluny by Saint Majolus. Following in their footsteps, my father, both out of reverence and love for the glorious confessor of Christ, Martin, and out of regard for the religious monks dwelling there, greatly honored and enlarged that same abbey from his own resources,” etc.

Having thus thoroughly secured the monastery, he placed the abbatial dignity, jurisdiction, and every kind of authority upon the shoulders of Gislebertus.

**V. Gislebertus** was unanimously chosen by the brothers and made abbot in the monastery in the year 970.

**VI. Bernerius**, 987.

**VII. Gauzbertus**, first abbot of Saint Julian of Tours, and afterward simultaneously abbot of the Major Monastery of Baugé and of Maillezais, 1007.

[Col. 1065A]

**VIII. Sicbardus**, or Sichardus.

**IX. Ebrardus**, 1015. He labored and worked very hard to have the possessions that had been taken away restored.

**X. Albertus**, 1037. During this abbot’s tenure, Airardus, bishop of Nantes, formerly abbot and cardinal of Saint Paul in that city, bestowed many benefits upon the Major Monastery, whose monks he loved most devotedly. Isambertus, bishop of Poitiers, commends them splendidly in a document in these words:

“The monks of the Major Monastery, whose reputation among us for their distinguished holy purpose is very great, asked me to confirm the property which they possessed in the bishopric of Poitiers; and I willingly granted this,” etc.

Another Isambertus, his predecessor’s successor, appended his sign.

“Abbot Albert,” says a manuscript codex concerning the servants of the Major Monastery, chapter 32, “freed and made clerical a certain servant together with the brothers, on the condition that he should never withdraw himself from the service of Saint Martin by going over to others,” etc.

It should be observed here that the abbot then bestowed the clerical tonsure upon a secular cleric.

Moreover, that same abbot, in his own name and in that of the chapter of the Major Monastery, asked Agobertus, bishop of Chartres, for a prebend or canonry. The bishop, together with his clergy, readily agreed, on the condition that they should render one another mutual assistance through their prayers. Thus run the letters of King Henry, which are preserved in the treasury of Saint Martin of the Valley at Chartres.

Pope Alexander III, in a diploma, orders the canons of the Church of Chartres not to prevent the monks of the Major Monastery from receiving the revenues of the prebend. [Col. 1065C]

Orderic Vitalis remembers this abbot and the four immediately following him in book IV of his *History*: “In our times Albert and Bartholomew, Bernard and Hilgotus, and William of Nantes governed this monastery as abbots. By their holiness and integrity they benefited many, and, famous far and wide, they shone bravely among neighbors and strangers.”

The anonymous author of the Appendix to Gregory of Tours’ *History of the Franks*, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Tours and the Abbots of the Major Monastery*, whom we shall frequently cite, says of Albert: “He rests on the right side of the church at the altar of Saint Maurice. He carefully established and ordered good customs for the Church; whoever afterward presumed to change them committed perjury.”

[Col. 1065D]

**XI. Bartholomaeus**, 1063 or 1064. “Whoever wishes to know his life, full of signs, virtues, and miracles, may find it in our archives,” etc.

The anonymous author says: “In the time of Bartholomew, he”—King William of England—“appointed as abbot of the abbey of Battle a religious monk of the Major Monastery named Goisbertus. Under his direction, the monastic order and regular discipline flourished suitably.”

These are the words of Orderic Vitalis, *History*, book IV, at the beginning.

An old manuscript chronology of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne, under the year 1066, recounting how William the Conqueror obtained the kingdom of England by victory, says:

“The place where the battle was fought has from that time until today been called Battle. Moreover, King William built there a monastery of the Holy Trinity—of Saint Martin, as the foundation charter records—and established monks and the order of the Major Monastery, enriching it abundantly with necessary resources for those killed on both sides.” [Col. 1066A]
