From the cartulary of Vendôme, charter 28, a pact was made in the year 1070 between a knight named Gusmanus and Abbot Bartholomew:

“If anyone wishes to learn letters in the city of Tours or at the new castle of Saint Martin, we shall provide for him and his servant three loaves each day and four *justae* of wine—that is, four customary measures.”

Bartholomew died in 1084. 588 “Here he lies buried, resting on the left side at the altar of the Apostles.” Anonymous.

Tetbertus, a monk of that place and a celebrated physician, flourished at this same time.

**XII. Bernard of Saint-Venant**, 1084. In the third year of his pontificate and the thirteenth indiction, Pope Urban II granted him a privilege which declared and decreed that not only the abbot and monks but also the household members and all priories dependent upon the Major Monastery were wholly exempt from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Tours and the other bishops.

That same Urban—who had come to Tours to celebrate a council—exhorted the brothers of the Major Monastery to make daily progress toward better things and granted them absolution in chapter.

In 1093 King Philip of France entrusted to Bernard the monastery of Saint-Magloire in Paris, in order that the ancient institution of the monastic order might be restored. This is clear from his diploma, dated approximately 1095:

“Adela, countess, daughter of King William”—the charter of Saint Martin of the Valley at Chartres records—“and wife of Stephen, count of Blois, who was well disposed toward the monks of the Major Monastery and had received many benefits and gifts from her father, by whom she was especially loved; wishing to imitate her father’s love toward them, she filled them with resources as far as she could. In the year of the dedication of the basilica of the Major Monastery by Pope Urban II, while her husband had gone to Jerusalem with the army of the Christians, she gave them near the walls of Chartres a public oven called ‘Battle to See.’” [Col. 1066C]

Nor should the following event be omitted; it is taken from the original document:

“Hugh of Calvomonte, son of Sulpicius of Amboise, while he was still a boy, and his mother, who was the niece of Geoffrey of Calvomonte, consented to the sale made to the monks of the Major Monastery of two *quarters* of land at the cultivation of Rathon. Later, when he had become a young man, succeeded his father in his office, and possessed Calvomonte together with Amboise in place of his maternal uncle Geoffrey, he wished to reclaim those same quarters.

“In the meantime Pope Urban came to the Major Monastery and dedicated the basilica; Hugh himself attended the dedication. After the altar had been consecrated and anointed according to custom, the pope, seated, summoned Fulk and the crowd of nobles standing around him, warning them to provide the newly dedicated church and altar with an endowment according to the customary practice.

“Having therefore been admonished by us, he called the aforesaid Hugh to him and advised him to leave those quarters to us. Hugh gladly did so. A multitude was present at this event, having gathered from every direction for so great a celebration.” [Col. 1067A]

Among the others, the following are expressly listed: “Hugh, primate and archbishop of Lyon; Ralph, archbishop of Tours; Rangerus, cardinal and archbishop of Reggio; Bruno, bishop of Segni; Albert, cardinal priest; Tezo, cardinal priest; Gregory, cardinal deacon of Pavia. Then: Lord Bernard of Saint-Venant, our abbot, etc.

“Among the laymen: Fulk, count of Anjou; Sigebrannus, his constable; Robert of Rupes; Gausbertus, provost of Calvomonte. Finally, the sisters of the aforesaid Hugh, Adenordis and Ermensendis, had likewise consented.”

These are the ancient parchments.

In the final year of Abbot Bernard, 1099, while he was touring the obediences or priories of his monastery, two young men voluntarily presented themselves to him and became servants of Saint Martin in the following rite:

“Standing on their knees before the abbot and carrying four denarii upon their heads, as is customary, they professed themselves servants of Saint Martin.” [Col. 1067B]

“Abbot Bernard,” says the anonymous author, “rests in the right portico of the church, on the lower side. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of May.”

**XIII. Hilgotus**, or Hilgaudus, having resigned the bishopric of Soissons, put on the monastic cowl and became abbot unwillingly in 1100.

Pope Paschal II sent him letters, just as Urban II had previously done for Bernard. It is worthwhile to transcribe them here, since they may dissolve the disputes arising between the archbishop and the Major Monastery.

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hilgotus, abbot of the Major Monastery, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, forever.”

“When all the sons of the holy Church,” etc. See among the diplomas and letters of Paschal II.

589 In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1101, Alan, duke of Brittany, his wife Ermengardis, and their son Conan gave the Major Monastery the churches of the Holy Cross and Saint Saturninus in the city of Nantes: “Because he held them contrary to the sacred canons,” the charter says. In this way those distinguished princes offered their subjects an example of obedience.

“Going to England, he acquired thirty marks of silver, which we receive annually from the king and queen of the English, and many other things. Here he rests on the right side at the altar of Saint Anthony.” Anonymous.

**XIV. Guillelmus**, 1104. He received letters sealed by Pope Paschal II. In them, liberty from subjection to bishops is confirmed both for the Major Monastery and for its possessions and all its churches, which are listed one by one.

Moreover, the supreme pontiff granted the abbot the power to bless chalices and every kind of altar ornament—a power which, I think, had previously been granted to no abbot. In these letters the pope calls William his most reverend son.

Geoffrey Grisagonella, count of Vendôme, A.D. 1120. “He came into the chapter,” as the charter says, “and there humbly asked absolution for the offenses he had committed against us and our places, promising amendment and promising that he would preserve us and what belonged to us more carefully. Seeing his humility, Lord William the abbot absolved him; and, in addition, clothed him in the fellowship of our prayers and good works,” etc. [Col. 1068A]

You can understand how highly princes once valued the prayers of monks, especially those of the Major Monastery, whose reputation for holiness had spread far and wide. This is indicated by the *Cartulary of the Affairs of Le Mans*, charter 215:

“In the year of the Incarnation 1105, or the first year after Lord William was appointed abbot, when Bohemond, returning from Jerusalem, also visited this place and asked both for himself and for all his fellow Christians whom he had left in those regions in the service of God the support of our prayers, Robert of Bellême came into our chapter with his son William and received the benefit of our fellowship. He promised to be the defender of our possessions, and caused his son William to grant whatever we possessed at Ponthieu. He delivered the grant by means of a staff into the hand of William the prior, who had been archdeacon of Rennes, in the presence of William of Pois, Norman of Neafle, his brother William, William Malaherba, and Robert Oison, kinsman of Robert of Bellême,” etc. [Col. 1068B]

“This abbot,” says the anonymous author, “surrounded the whole monastery with walls and acquired many obediences, etc. He left this church free of every debt. When he died, he was buried on the right side of the chapter house, between the column and the seat.” [Col. 1068C]

**XV. Odo**, an abbot renowned for his religious life, 1124. While he governed the Major Monastery, the monastery of Saint Martin of the Valley at Chartres was restored to it. A decree of Pope Honorius and Count Theobald concerning this matter is extant.

Bishop Ulgerus shows how highly he regarded Odo and his monks in the following terms:

“I, Ulgerus, bishop of the Church of Angers, gave in the year of the Incarnation 1131 to the Major Monastery and to my brothers Odo and his monks—for I have not found others whom I know to be more fervent in divine service—the church of Bessé and the chapel of Bellifort, situated in the same parish, with everything belonging to them and with the right to present priests whenever a vacancy occurs,” etc. [Col. 1068D]

The rites by which laypeople once became participants in prayers and in the other works of piety, austerity, or discipline practiced by the monks are worthy of notice:

“Odo Canutus was invested by Abbot Odo through the handing over of the chapter book and became a participant in the benefit of the Church of the Major Monastery. Greatly rejoicing in this, Odo Canutus invested the abbot with a certain piece of land by means of a small disciplinary rod, which he carried to the high altar for confirmation,” etc.

When Sulpicius, son of Robert of Rupes—namely, of Corbon—was dying, Abbot Odo received him as a monk at the request of his father. For this reason Robert gave the tithe of the fish of the river Sextia, or Sithia. His sons Theobald and Robert consented to this donation, etc.

“Abbot Odo rests in the right portico of the church, on the upper side, near Abbot Bernard.” Anonymous.

**XVI. Garnerius**, 1137. “He was the most devout of all toward this church,” the anonymous author testifies.

Among the ancient records of the priory of Dammartin, the following words are read in a charter of donation by a certain forester named Balbinus: “Given in the year of the Incarnation 1148, which was the twelfth year of the appointment of the most devout Father Garnerius as abbot.”

In the archives of the Major Monastery are letters of Pope Eugenius III, then residing at Reims, in which, replying to Abbot Garnerius, he admonishes the bishops of Gaul:

“It is known,” he says, “that it was established in general councils that priests who serve in churches belonging to monasteries should indeed answer to the diocesan bishop for the care of souls, but should show submission to the abbot and his brothers in temporal matters. Yet we have received the complaint of our beloved son Garnerius, abbot of the Major Monastery, and of his brothers,” etc. [Col. 1069B]

The Church of Blessed Mary of the Good Tidings at Orléans, belonging to a community of canons, was handed over to the Major Monastery by Simon of Balgentiacus so that it might be restored to a better condition.

During the time of Abbot Garnerius and his monks, their strict way of life became famous once again in England. Therefore, in 1139, the foundations of the monastery of the Holy Trinity in the city of York were laid by Ralph of Paganello—Paisnel—and his wife Matilda, with the consent of their sons William and Jordan; many possessions were also assigned to it. [Col. 1069C]

An anonymous monk says of Garnerius: “He entirely repaired this house; he built the cellar, kitchen, dormitory, and also half of the infirmary cloister, etc. But when he had decided to renew the infirmary and had completed part of it, Christ calling him to the heavenly kingdoms, he departed on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, to reign there eternally with him. He rests beside Lord Gillebertus the abbot in the chapter house.”

**XVII.** “Abbot Robert the Breton of Magueri was praiseworthy in life and beloved by God and human beings,” etc. Anonymous.

He governed from 1155 to 1166. It is clear from sealed letters of Pope Alexander III sent to him in 1164 that the count of Blois caused much trouble for the abbot and the monks of the Major Monastery. In letters of the same Alexander written in 1164, I find the following:

“In the time of this abbot,” the anonymous author reports, “Pope Alexander came to Tours and spent the night in this house. After being elected abbot, he lived for ten years; in the eleventh he was gathered to the fathers and lies on the right side of the chapter house beside Abbot Garnerius.” [Col. 1069D]

**XVIII.** “Robert II, called of Blois, a very venerable and gracious man, etc. After being elected abbot, he lived for ten years, and in the eleventh departed from human affairs. He rests on the left side of the chapter house, between the column and the abbot’s seat.” Anonymous.

The supreme pontiff granted Robert the use of the mitre. The abbot himself, with the greatest submission of spirit, wished to be called the humble Steward of the Major Monastery. He held office from 1166 to 1176.

**XIX. Peter of Gascony**, 1177. “He was very simple and religious, ignorant of worldly cunning and wickedness,” says the anonymous author.

**XX. Herveus of Villa Petrosa** held the pastoral office from approximately 1178 to 1186. The anonymous author praises him extensively.

Among other things, he records his strict observance of the holy Rule. This is not at all contradicted by the bull of Pope Clement III, which praises a statute issued by Abbot Herveus and accepted by the monks: namely, that the serving of meat to guests within the monastery enclosure was prohibited.

Alexander III also confirmed all the immunities granted to the Major Monastery by his predecessors Urban, Paschal, Calixtus, Innocent II, and Eugenius III; this was in the nineteenth year of his pontificate and the eleventh indiction. [Col. 1070B]

The monastery of Saint-Magloire of Léhon was subject to Herveus. He freely granted it every right formerly possessed by Albert, bishop of Saint-Malo, in his letters issued in the presence of the king of England, in 1181.

Pope Lucius III, under penalty of excommunication, ordered Herveus not to confer any of the priories upon laypeople under any pretext, nor to allow them to possess them.

Nivello of Chérisy, bishop of Soissons, from the family of the lords of Pierrefonds, inserted the following remarks about Herveus in a charter of agreement between the rector and the monks of Saint-Sulpice of Pierrefonds:

“Herveus, then the venerable abbot of the Major Monastery, our friend and intimate, and related to us by the line of consanguinity, approved this agreement,” etc. [Col. 1070C]

**XXI. Gaufridus**, 1187. In a charter of the priory of Fréteval dated 1190, Robert of Saint-Valerian, the brother of Abbot Geoffrey, is listed.

Charters of Combourg call Geoffrey by the surname of Cursol or Curson. Matthew Paris, under the year 1196, asserts that he was given as a hostage to Richard, king of the English, on behalf of King Philip of France, together with the abbots of Cluny and Saint-Denis and the prior of La Charité.

Finally, the anonymous author says: “Geoffrey, by nationality Breton, born of noble stock, educated in clerical learning, handsome in stature and appearance. He dismissed himself, and afterward, as it pleased the Lord, rested in peace.” [Col. 1070D]

**XXII.** “Hugh,” 1210. “A native of Chartres, he was received as a monk from childhood. He was small in body and sufficiently learned.” Anonymous.

He was the brother of William of Rupes Corbon. He does not call himself abbot but minister, in the following manner:

“To all who shall see these present letters, the brothers of the chapter of the Major Monastery, and Hugh, their humble minister,” etc.

This custom, begun under Abbot Hilgotus, was continuously maintained down to the commendatory abbots. Nevertheless, when necessity required, this same Hugh used the title of abbot in public documents, for example.

At this same time sorrowful—or rather abominable—disorders and depredations arose among the counts of Blois, who boasted that they were the patrons or advocates of the Major Monastery. As a result, almost all the property of that monastery and of the priories situated in the county of Blois was alienated and plundered by them as though by public enemies. [Col. 1071A]

Robert, in *Gallia Christiana*, assigns Hugh a bishop’s seat among the bishops of Langres. Nevertheless, both the ancient records and the anonymous chronologer are silent on this matter. From the latter’s account I take the following passage concerning Hugh:

“He was in litigation against the archbishop of Tours, for the archbishop said that our abbot ought not to use the pastoral staff or the mitre. Therefore Hugh, prudent and humble, seeing that the mitre brought more burden than advantage, did not wish to quarrel fruitlessly; and so from that time onward he bore authority without the mitre, like his ancient predecessors,” etc. [Col. 1071B]

**XXIII. Gaufridus II**, 1227. This man and his successor are unknown to the anonymous author.

In this same year, Geoffrey, bishop of Saint-Malo, attempted to restrain noblemen from invading the possessions of the Major Monastery situated in his diocese. But his oil and labor were wasted, since those men had become so wickedly and obstinately devoted to retaining them that they could scarcely, if at all, be separated from them.

**XXIV. Guarinus**, 1229. Pope Gregory IX ordered the abbot of Gastines, of the Order of Saint Augustine in the diocese of Tours, to combine the smaller priories dependent upon the Major Monastery whenever two monks could not conveniently live there according to the Rule, bringing several of them together into one.

For Pope Alexander III had previously decreed in the Third Lateran Council, chapter 10: “Monks are not to be placed singly in villages and towns or in any parish churches; rather, they are to remain in a larger community or with some brothers, and are not to await alone among secular people the battle with spiritual enemies,” etc. [Col. 1071C]

**XXV. Gaufridus III of Conam**, 1235. He suffered the gravest disasters at the hands of John, count of Blois, on account of the right of advocacy. He was even confined for seven years in the castle of Guise, and the count ordered two monks to be thrown headlong from the mountain by his retainers. The anonymous author gives a fuller account of these matters.

Finally, in order to put an end to such crimes, Pope Innocent IV sent Nicholas into Gaul in the year 1254. After a judgment or sentence had been pronounced against the count as a contumacious man, Nicholas deprived him of the right of advocacy and of everything he had claimed for himself from the monastery’s property. Nevertheless, the count rejected and despised the sentence and continued to rage furiously against those same religious men.

In 1255 King Louis IX approved letters of his grandfather Philip Augustus, by which the monks of the Major Monastery were ordered to be admitted as tenants in the Norman Exchequer—since they held many possessions in that duchy—in order to pursue their rights.

The acts of the papal legates, Philip, bishop of Bourges, and Clement, bishop of Dol, as well as those of the abbot of Bourgueil in the diocese of Tours, show that regular discipline had undoubtedly been weakened by the calamity just mentioned. [Col. 1072A]

Letters of John, bishop of Rennes, however, clearly indicate that shortly afterward the monks were brought back to a better way of life. They concern the union with the Major Monastery of the priory of Sallo Gallo—Solial. They read as follows:

“We, John, bishop of Rennes, taking into consideration the fervor of charity of the monks of the Major Monastery and attending with pious affection to their needs, have granted that their house of Solial, in our diocese, where formerly a single monk was accustomed to live, and in accordance with what was established in the Lateran Council—that solitary monks should be removed—should be converted to their own uses,” etc.

[Col. 1072B]

Letters of Nantelelinus, abbot of Agaune, make it clear that in 1254 Abbot Geoffrey went to Rome to visit the thresholds of the Apostles.

**XXVI. Stephanus**, from 1263 to 1284. In approximately 1264, Vincent, archbishop of Tours, pronounced sentence against the count of Blois, who, provoked by the evil example of his ancestors, would not cease harassing the monks of the Major Monastery.

Because the Major Monastery could scarcely receive anything of what it possessed in England, Pope Gregory X, in 1274, gave Abbot Stephen permission to sell or, as they say, alienate all those possessions. He nevertheless ordered that the proceeds be invested in other, more useful things.

I think that during Stephen’s time it was established and decreed that the charters, privileges, immunities, and diplomas concerning the Major Monastery, its priories, churches, and places subject to that monastery should be brought there and preserved as in a fortress. Hence, although the fury of the Calvinists later devastated everything indiscriminately, those documents remained unharmed. [Col. 1072C]

**XXVII.** “Robert, born in Flanders,” the anonymous author reports, “was handsome and sufficiently learned; he was also prior of Celle in Brie,” etc.

Pope Martin IV granted Robert the privilege, in the fourth year of his pontificate, of wearing the mitre, ring, and other pontifical vestments everywhere except in the city of Tours, and of solemnly giving the blessing to the people and blessing altar cloths.

Since the count of Blois, following in the footsteps of his fathers, continually harassed the property of the Major Monastery, Matthew, abbot of Saint-Denis and at that time acting as the king’s representative in France, sent letters to Abbot Robert and his monks to put an end to such troubles. He ordered that if any dispute should afterward arise between them and Joan, countess of Alençon and daughter of the count of Blois, it should be heard in the royal palace.

Robert the abbot also bravely opposed and restrained Durandus, bishop of Nantes, who was attempting to extort money from the priories under his jurisdiction under the pretext of visitation. He relied upon the privileges and upon chapter 24 of the recently celebrated Council of Lyon, which prohibited this. [Col. 1072D]

**XXVIII. Odo of Braccolis**, or Braceolis, born of noble stock and learned, was appointed abbot in 1296.

He and the monks excluded the archbishops of Bordeaux from visitation of the priories and from procurations. Yet, alas, they had at that time shamefully departed from observance of the Rule: they divided the revenues of the priories among themselves and withdrew from common life.

It is therefore not surprising—as we have noted elsewhere—that secular men, God thus punishing them, and many bishops of that age coveted the monks’ wealth.

**XXIX.** “John of Montelonis, or Monteleonis, born in the territory of Poitiers and descended from a noble family, though small in stature, was distinguished by a handsome face,” etc. Anonymous.

A bull of Pope John XXII, issued at Avignon in 1320 to the abbots of Saint-Germain in Paris, Vendôme, and Rouen, indicates how many calamities and injuries the Major Monastery suffered from nobles at this very time. In it, defenders and protectors are appointed against those nobles and bishops who, by lawful and unlawful means, were occupying the possessions of the priories of the Major Monastery.

“This John resigned to Simon le Maye, chamberlain, in 1330, and died the following year, on the day after he resigned.” Anonymous.

**XXX. Simon le Maye**, 1331. “He was born in the region of Tours and was competently learned. How powerful he was in his administration, his works bear witness to the truth,” the anonymous author continues.

In 1333 King Edward of England wrote to Simon that he confirmed all the possessions of the Major Monastery situated in his kingdom and had appointed agents to protect them. [Col. 1073C]

Because he was exacting money unusually from the Major Monastery, Peter, archbishop of Bordeaux, was sentenced by Aymericus, abbot of Saint Augustine of Limoges, delegated judge of the Apostolic See.

For this matter the bishop of Troyes was also summoned by Pope Benedict XII and severely reprimanded. Simon admitted a certain cleric as a participant in the pious works performed by the monks, as is clear from the formula in which these words are especially expressed: “Masses, almsgiving, and disciplines.”

Finally, Simon himself was appointed bishop of Chartres, as the anonymous author testifies.

[Col. 1073D]

**XXXI. Peter of Puy**—Dupuy—a native of Limousin, 1357. He had previously been abbot of Saint-Florent at Saumur, as he himself indicates in a tablet written in 1357. He died in 1364 on the feast of Saint Sixtus the pope and was buried in the chapel of Saint-Florent which he had founded.

### XXXII

Gerard de Puy, Peter’s brother, 1334. Since the anonymous author records two immediately succeeding abbots of the same name, and the surname is almost always suppressed in the charters, it is no easy task to distinguish their years of rule from those of the later Gerard; consequently, reliance must often be placed on the anonymous author.

King Charles V revealed in the year of Our Lord 1370 [Col. 1074A] how favorably disposed he was toward the Greater Monastery. For although he had increased the power of his brother Louis, Duke of Anjou, with the duchy of Touraine, he nevertheless wished to reserve to himself supreme right, authority, and lordship over the affairs of the Greater Monastery.

Urban V, in the seventh year of his pontificate, and afterward Gregory XI, sent letters first to Gerard de Puy and to John, bishop of Saint-Aubin of Angers, assigning to them the investigation of the miracles of Charles, Duke of Brittany. See André Duchesne, *Historia Castilionensis*, book V, chapter 1, p. 228, and in the *Probationes*, p. 127. The anonymous author and Ciaconius, in their *Lives of the Pontiffs*, assert that Gerard was awarded the red hat and was buried at Avignon.

### XXXIII

Gerard II, Pante or Paute, formerly abbot of Saint Benedict of Fleury, a native of Limousin. [Col. 1074B] He was buried in the choir of the church. So says the anonymous author.

### XXXIV

Elias was born in an obscure place in the territory of Périgueux. First he was abbot of Saints Sergius and Bacchus of Angers; then, after an exchange had been made, he became abbot of the Greater Monastery in 1389. He not only squandered the monastery’s property but also consented to destroy monastic discipline. At this time, some of the monks of the Greater Monastery obtained the degree of Bachelor of Canon Law, publicly taught by Peter, abbot of Saint Eligius of Noyon, in 1394. Elias laid down his burden upon Guido de Luro, abbot of Saint Sergius; having renounced every prelacy and all else, he wept over the evils he had committed. He died on 29 September 1418.

### XXXV

Guido de Luro, a native of Limousin, formerly abbot of [Col. 1074C] Saint Sergius of Angers, 1413. He was quite well educated in letters. He repaired, for the most part, the losses inflicted by his predecessor both upon the household estate and upon regular observance. He was especially devoted to distributing alms to the poor and to defending the monastery’s rights and immunities. Finally, he died in peace; his body was carried to and buried in the choir of the Greater Monastery, beneath the copper tomb of Gerard Paulta, abbot [33], his uncle. Thus says our anonymous author, who carried the catalogue of the abbots of the Greater Monastery no farther.

### XXXVI

Peter Marques, from 1429 to 1453. Pope Nicholas V did not so much grant the Greater Monastery a singular privilege as approve it. I have judged it useful to insert it here, in due course, in this catalogue of abbots. [Col. 1074D]

> “Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for the future remembrance of the matter: for the adornment of sacred religion, so that its happy branches may everywhere spread more fruitfully, and so that flowers of honor and fruits of uprightness may flourish within it, for the salvation of many and in abundant growth, we more earnestly diffuse the thoughts of apostolic meditation, pursuing these matters with special aids, by which religious persons, when the losses of every disturbance have ceased, may, under the protection of apostolic liberty, more quietly and conveniently discharge their vows to the Most High in the sweetness of peace and tranquility and in the delight of holy contemplation.
>
> “Therefore, having been inclined in this matter by the petitions of our beloved son in Christ, Charles, illustrious king of the French, and of our beloved sons the abbot and convent of the monastery of the Greater Monastery near Tours, belonging without intermediary to the Roman Church, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and of the priors of the priories subject to that monastery, for greater security we wholly exempt and entirely liberate the aforesaid monastery, together with all priories, hospitals, dependencies, and places subject to it or to be subjected to it in the future, wherever they may be situated; likewise the abbots, priors, and subpriors of the monastery and of the aforesaid priories, dependencies, hospitals, and places, together with their monks, household members, servants, permanent table-companions, and persons residing in them, present and future; and all their movable and immovable goods, possessions, rights, and appurtenances, present and future, from every jurisdiction, lordship, subjection, authority, power, superiority, visitation, correction, coercion, and compulsion of the archbishops of Tours and their vicars and officials, and of any other ordinaries, prelates, or ecclesiastical persons whatsoever; likewise from the payment of any collections, tolls, charitable subsidies, levies, and burdens, and every other kind of exaction. By the fullness of apostolic power and with certain knowledge, we receive them under the right and ownership of blessed Peter and of the Apostolic See, under their special and immediate protection.
>
> “We decree that the monastery, priories, hospitals, dependencies, places, abbots, priors, monks, household members, goods, and possessions aforesaid shall be subject solely and immediately to the said See in all matters. Thus the aforesaid archbishops, vicars, officials, ordinaries, and prelates, or any others, whether generally or specifically, jointly or separately, may not, by any authority whatsoever, promulgate against them—being wholly exempt—any ecclesiastical sentences, censures, or penalties of excommunication, suspension, or interdict, or otherwise exercise any power, jurisdiction, superiority, authority, visitation, correction, coercion, compulsion, or lordship over them, whether on account of an offense, a contract, or any matter under dispute, wherever the offense may be committed, the contract entered into, or the property situated.
>
> “Furthermore, the aforesaid abbots, priors, and convents shall not be bound, on account of the goods of the monastery, priories, hospitals, dependencies, and places aforesaid, to provide any hospitality or maintenance, or to pay any contribution, charitable subsidy, customs dues, tolls, transit charges, or other exactions to any kings or other ecclesiastical or secular persons; nor may they be compelled to do so, or in this matter or any other be sued by anyone in any way, nor shall any letters of the aforesaid See, or of its legates, delegates, or nuncios, or of the local diocesan authorities or anyone else, prevent this—even if such letters expressly state that they extend to any exempt or non-exempt priories or places, and whatever indulgence may be contained in them—unless perhaps those apostolic letters should make full, express, emphatic, and specific mention, word for word, of the aforesaid order and monastery and of the present matter, and also of the monks and those residing in the monastery, priories, hospitals, dependencies, and places aforesaid.
>
> “Moreover, by the same apostolic authority we will and grant to the same abbot, convent, and priors that they shall in no way be obliged to give testimony concerning these matters and the contents of this document to any of the archbishops or other ordinaries of the places aforesaid during their lifetime, except once, if they should be summoned for that purpose; nor may they in any way be forced against their will to do so. This is notwithstanding the apostolic constitutions of our predecessor, Innocent IV, of happy memory, and other apostolic constitutions, as well as imperial laws, statutes, customs, and anything else by which the foregoing could in any way be infringed or hindered, and all enactments to the contrary.
>
> “For we declare null, void, invalid, ineffective, and empty, and of no force or significance whatsoever, all excommunications, suspensions, interdicts, and other ecclesiastical sentences, censures, and penalties, as well as all proceedings—even those containing sentences and penalties—which may be promulgated or imposed against the abbot, convent, priors, monks, resident persons, monastery, priories, hospitals, dependencies, and places aforesaid contrary to the tenor and form of this document and of this exemption; likewise everything, whatever it may be, that anyone may happen to do or attempt, knowingly or unknowingly, by any authority, contrary to these provisions.
>
> “Therefore let no human being presume to violate this document of our exemption, liberation, reception, decree, will, grant, and constitution, or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at Saint Potentiana, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1448, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the second year of our pontificate.”

595

### XXXVII

Guido Vigier, 1453. In these times the supreme pontiff Pius II—for he was preparing an expedition against the Turks—had demanded a tenth from ecclesiastics, which many refused to pay. Therefore the clergy of the province of Angers, since there were several priories of the Greater Monastery in it, admonished Guido, the abbot, to enter into partnership with them; but he considered it a sacrilege not to comply with the commands of the supreme pastor.

In 1458 he resigned the abbey in favor of his nephew, Guido Vigier. The latter, in turn, returned certain priories to his uncle. A bull of Pope Pius II was written concerning this matter in the same year; in it the pontiff notes that Guido was of noble birth, had professed monastic life in the Greater Monastery, and had also been appointed by him bishop of Biblis. I, for my part, regard both uncle and nephew as traffickers in benefices, especially the former.

### XXXVIII

Guido Vigier’s nephew, 1458 to 1499. He swore the oath of fidelity to King Louis XI in 1493, at that time at Amboise, and afterward to Charles VIII, who was staying there, as the documents testify.

### XXXIX

Louis Pot, 1499. At the same time abbot of Saint Laumer of Blois. He conferred the priory of the Seven Sleepers, which is enclosed within the monastery walls. In his letters he styles himself bishop of Tournai and of Lectoure. André Duchesne, in *Historia Montmorenci*, book V, chapter 1, p. 355, and in the *Probationes*, p. 260, discusses Louis Pot and his family. He was still living in 1504.

### XL

Francis Sforza, 1504, descended from the noble Sforza family. He swore the monastic laws in the Greater Monastery and, while still young, was elected abbot by the monks at the command of King Francis I. But while he was engaged in hunting, contrary to ecclesiastical precepts, he fell into a pit which he was attempting to leap over on a running horse. Crushed by the weight of the horse and seriously wounded, he was brought back and eventually died in 1511.

### XLI

Matthew Galter (Gaultier), 1511. A monk of the Greater Monastery and a doctor of theology of the Sorbonne community. He was deeply devoted to Saint Anne, mother of the Mother of God; therefore he obtained from the abbot of Saint Florent of Saumur a portion of her head—which, they say, is preserved in the priory of Gaya in the diocese of Troyes, dependent upon that same monastery. In a document of 1550 concerning the Priory of the Seven Sleepers, Matthew the abbot is designated bishop of Negroponte. He exchanged the abbey with Philip Hurault for the abbey of Bourgueil in the territory of Angers.

Matthew’s nephew, Adrian Galter, a priest and ascetic of the Greater Monastery and a doctor of theology, was the author of a work entitled *The Balance of the Virtues of Blessed Peter the Apostle and Saint Martin*.

### XLII

Philip Hurault, 1536. He did not hold the office of abbot for long; he was the last of the abbots, or monk-fathers, to profess the religious life. He presided over the general chapter held at the Greater Monastery on 17 April 1538. He died in 1539. He lies buried in Paris in the church of the White Mantles; his tomb inscription, on black marble, reads:

> PHILIPPE HURAULT, ABBOT OF MARMOUTIER, BOURGUEIL, AND SAINT-NICOLAS OF ANGERS, WHO DIED ON 12 NOVEMBER 1539, IS BURIED HERE BELOW.

### Commendatory Abbots

### XLIII

John, cardinal of Lorraine, the first commendatory abbot, who ruined almost all the possessions and resources of the Greater Monastery. [Col. 1078A] He conferred priories upon secular persons by fair means and foul, cut down the forests, and melted down whatever could be converted into money, turning it into coins; he committed other acts as well that ought to be erased in eternal silence. They say that he died in 1555 and was buried at Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

### XLIV

Charles, cardinal of Lorraine, titular of Saint Apollinaris, John’s nephew, 1555—or, as others prefer, 1550. At the general assembly he ordered statutes to be drawn up in 1552 for the scholars of the College of the Greater Monastery in Paris.

### XLV

John de La Rochefoucauld. He was also abbot of Cormery and Villeloup, and likewise master of the royal household musicians. He swore the oath of fidelity to Charles IX, king of France, in 1566, and from him obtained a charter of custodial protection in 1568. [Col. 1078B]

John the abbot was a man of approved life. At the Greater Monastery he habitually lived religiously among the monks, though he himself was not a monk. He bestowed many benefactions; for he devoted all his strength and purpose to repairing the losses inflicted upon the Greater Monastery by his brother, a very bad heretic. Being greatly inclined toward piety and mercy, he abundantly supplied the Church with sacred vestments and books suitable for divine worship. Whatever was necessary for the religious who served God day and night, he provided and supplied with paternal care.

Moreover, he relieved the poverty of the needy and of those afflicted by illness and other miseries, not only through lavish almsgiving and beneficence but also by refreshing them with his own presence. Finally, while engaged in exercises of this kind, he breathed his last at Verteuil in the county of Angoulême in 1583. [Col. 1078C] Would that the later commendatory abbots might follow his paths and cling to his footsteps!

### XLVI

In 1583, James d’Apurilli, a man of the lowest condition, the son of an executioner of Orléans, received the abbey as a gift from Francis of Valois, Duke of Orléans, and so forth. But after Duke Francis had died, James, deprived of his support and unable to maintain that dignity, resigned the abbey to Cardinal Francis de Joyeuse, and so forth. This account comes from the theologian James d’Huysseau, a contemporary monk of the Greater Monastery.

### XLVII

Cardinal Francis de Joyeuse, 1584.

### XLVIII

Charles of Bourbon died in 1610.

### XLIX

Sebastian Galigai, archbishop of Tours, 1610.

### L

Alexander, knight of Vendôme, 1617.

### LI

Peter, cardinal de Bérulle.

### LII

John Armand, cardinal de Richelieu, under whose auspices the perfect discipline of the Benedictine Rule was restored by the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. He died on 4 December 1642.

### LIII

Amador John Baptist de Vignerot.

### (42) CHAPTER X

#### “For a certain Simon.” Count of Crépy

We publish here the life of this man, written by a contemporary author and hitherto lying hidden in the monastery of Ourscamp near Noyon, of the Cistercian congregation of the Order of Saint Benedict; it occupies a place among the additions to the works of our Guibert. Moreover, it seemed worthwhile to excerpt from the manuscript chronicle of Bèze a passage not unworthy of reading, containing an account partly not committed to writing by the author of the Life of Blessed Simon. Thus, in Stephen, abbot of Bèze:

> “In those days Christ the Bridegroom called his bride, namely the Church, to himself, to come from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards, through the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon. For the princes who had previously been like lions because of their cruelty and terror, and like leopards because of the variety of their different iniquities, cleansed with hyssop—that is, with humble confession—were whitened through the myrrh of mortifications, brighter than snow.
>
> “The head and leader of these was a certain most noble count of the Franks, Simon by name, [Col. 1079B] son of Count Rodulf [above the line: ‘son’]. Regarding him with divine mercy, he fled the world that was fleeing and followed Christ who was calling him. He sought the monastery of Saint Eugendus of the Jura, intending there to sacrifice himself to Christ. He had sent before him two most illustrious men, Lord Rodulf and Lord Franco; with him he brought Lord Robert, Lord Arnulf, and Lord Warner. All these men, most distinguished according to worldly birth and most noble according to God, afterward offered themselves to God as a whole burnt offering.
>
> “Lord Stephen, of whom we are speaking, was still young and adorned only with military arms. But, following wiser counsel, he followed these Fathers together with them, God inspiring him, renounced the secular belt, and took up the yoke of Christ. In the aforesaid monastery he undertook the monastic life, and there under Lord Hunaud, the abbot, he sacrificed himself in God’s service for ten years. Then he went to Cluny,” and so forth.

Alberic, a Cistercian monk, briefly recounts the deeds of Blessed Simon in his as-yet unpublished chronicle, namely under the years 1074, 1076, and 1081. But since he records nothing distinctive beyond what is related in the life, I have not thought it necessary to repeat it.

Furthermore, the cartularies of Crépy and Cluny record distinguished and religious deeds performed by Simon while he was still involved in secular affairs.

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, and so forth. Everyone who understands himself to be a human being composed of two natures, namely a rational soul and a body, recognizes this, and so forth. Therefore I, Simon, Count of Crépy, and so forth, taking precautions for the salvation of my soul, indeed also for that of my father, the venerable Count Radulf, looking ahead, perceiving that the days of the present life are nothing, and fixing my mind, as far as I am able, upon the contemplation of eternity, caused the aforesaid Radulf, my father of Montdidier, who had lain there for three years after the dissolution of his body, to be carried away, and restored him to the Church of Saint Arnulf, which had been founded by him and by his predecessors in the castle of Crépy in an honorable manner, and in which he himself had also been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit. There I caused him to be placed, according to the custom of the ancients, beside the tomb of my mother, his wife, and of our predecessors, with psalms and prayers, in a double cave, so that we might have the same archbishop and martyr, namely blessed Arnulf, as an intercessor for our souls before God. To the same church, by a golden ring, I grant the whole estate of Bonœil, which I have hitherto held in my possession, together with its serfs and all its appurtenances, and so forth. Enacted at the castle of Crépy, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Incarnation 1077, indiction 15, epact 23, concurrent 6, during the reign of Philip, king of the Franks.
>
> “The sign of King Philip,” and so forth.

Thus the Cartulary of Crépy. The letter of Count Simon to Blessed Hugh that follows plainly shows that the same abbey of Saint Arnulf had been handed over to the Cluniacs.

> “To the venerable Abbot Hugh and to the entire congregation [Col. 1080B] of the monastery of Cluny, Simon, count, the little servant of your holiness, sends greetings.
>
> “Let it be known to Your Highness, most blessed Father, that I love God more than all human beings living in the flesh, and that I seek your advantage and honor as far as I am able. Therefore I grant to you and to all your successors the abbey of Saint Arnulf, which was built in the castle called Crépy, so that it may be entirely subject to you; and there you shall elect from among your monks an abbot who can govern that monastery according to God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. I wish you to know that I have done this with the counsel and consent of my men, namely the leading men; and that the king, at my request, has confirmed this charter, with Philip present and Ivo consenting. Witnesses: Simon the steward, and so forth. Done in the house of Saint Mary at Paris, on the feast of All Saints.
>
> “The sign of King Philip.”

These are the old Cluniac membranes.

The donation of the aforesaid church was also confirmed by Hugh, bishop of Senlis, as is clear from the same membranes.

### (43) SAME PLACE

#### “How illustrious that Radulf was,” and so forth

Ivo of Chartres describes his genealogy in letter 45:

> “It has been reported to our ears that the Count of Meulan wishes to take as his wife the daughter of Hugh, Count of Crépy, and so forth. Their kinship is neither unknown nor remote, as the distinguished men born from the same lineage testify and are prepared to prove. For they say that Walter the White begot the mother of Count Waleran, who begot the mother of Count Robert. Likewise, the aforesaid Walter begot Radulf, the father of another Radulf—whom Guibert mentions here—who begot the Countess of Vermandois,” and so forth.

She became the heiress of Blessed Simon, her brother; her daughter, named Adela, first married Hugh, son of Henry, king of France, and afterward Rainald, Count of Clermont, as an old charter of the monastery of Crépy reports:

> “I, Adela, countess of the Vermandois, and my sons, Count Radulf and Henry, have given to Saint Arnulf the martyr those things which the countesses of Crépy held in their private right, in my castle of Crépy and in the villages of Fère, and so forth, for the support of the Cluniac monks serving God at Crépy. We made this gift so that, together with my sons and daughters, and with my lord Hugh the Great, who died on the road to Jerusalem, and with my lord Rainald, Count of Clermont, we may share in the prayers of all the communities of the monastery of Cluny. Enacted in the year 1118, under Pope Paschal II and Louis, king of the Franks,” and so forth.

The older monuments of that place report that Radulf, Adela’s grandfather, of whom we are speaking, Count of Crépy, or of Vexin and Valois, greatly enriched the monastery of Saint Arnulf of Crépy—its founder is acknowledged to have been Walter the White, Radulf’s grandfather—with many goods, and especially adorned it with the sacred relics of blessed Arnulf. The old charters concerning Radulf have the following summary:

> “Radulf, Count of Crépy, formerly held many altars in benefice from the bishop of Soissons. But after the death of Adela, his wife, he obtained from Heddon, bishop of Soissons, that the altar of Bonœil, which he held in benefice, should be held perpetually and in its entirety by the Church of Saint Arnulf,” and so forth.

Enacted at Soissons in the year of the Incarnation 1053, in the nineteenth year of King Henry and the first of Bishop Heddon.

From this it may be observed that those who wish Radulf and his son, Blessed Simon, to have been counts of Vermandois are mistaken. See Claude Héméré, *Augusta Viromanduorum*, under the year 1046, and André Duchesne, *Historia Castilionensis*, book II, chapter 9.

### (44) SAME PLACE

#### “To Saint Eugendus in the territory of the Jura”

Jura, or the Jurassus, is the mountain in which the monastery of Saint Eugendus, now Saint-Claude, is situated. Concerning it, see Menardus, *Observations on the Benedictine Martyrology*, under 1 January. He contends that the monastery of Condat, or Condates, located there, is in no way to be distinguished from that of the Jura.

### (45) CHAPTER XI

#### “Who, having obtained the beginnings of his conversion from the following circumstance,” and so forth

Would you like to hear the reason why that most blessed founder of the Carthusians withdrew into the desert, as it was handed down to posterity by a contemporary author? Saint Bruno himself almost openly reveals it in his letter to Radulf, where he chiefly uses this argument to remind him of the pledge made to God concerning the monastic life:

> “For your affection remembers that, when I and Fulcius the One-Eyed were one day together in the little garden adjoining the house of Adam, where I was then staying, and had been discussing for some time, as I think, the false pleasures and perishable riches of this world, as well as the joys of everlasting glory, we, burning with divine fervor, promised and vowed to the Holy Spirit that shortly we would leave behind the fleeting things of this world and pursue eternal things, and also receive the monastic habit.”

Saint Bruno, already a settler at the Chartreuse, explains many other things in this vein.

The anonymous canon of Saint Martin of Tours, in an unpublished history of the Royal Library, writes:

> “In the year 1086 the Carthusian Order began in the following manner. Saint Hugh of Grenoble saw in a dream, in the solitude of the Chartreuse, the Lord Jesus Christ confirming something; he also saw seven stars providing him with guidance for the journey. Without delay seven men came to the bishop himself, inflamed by one desire: they were seeking a place for the eremitical life but had not yet found one. The first of them was Master Bruno, distinguished in religion and learning; four others were learned men, and two were laymen. Saint Hugh gladly received them and enabled them to fulfill their vow. With his counsel, assistance, and company, they entered the solitude of the Chartreuse, built structures, and there, at peace in the wilderness, served the Lord.”

So writes he, and so do almost innumerable authors, whom I am reluctant to weave into these notes, since John de Launoy, a man of profound learning and very skilled in ecclesiastical discipline, relieves me of this burden in his dissertation *On the True Reason for Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert*.

The chronographer of Maillezais briefly relates what kind of teacher Bruno had, alongside Blessed Bruno, under the year 996:

> “Gerbert taught Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and so forth. Fulbert in turn taught Berengar, a canon of Saint Martin; he likewise left Bruno of Reims and many others as heirs of philosophy. Bruno, a perfect philosopher, became a monk and hermit in Calabria, and died in Christ as the father of many monks.”

But what I observed concerning Saint Bruno—and what, I think, has escaped other writers—must by no means be omitted: namely, that he was distinguished by the office of chancellor in the Church of Reims. I learn this from the subscription of a charter written at the command of Manasses, archbishop of Reims, by which he granted the altars of Alteuil and Caprille, and so forth, to the monastery of Saint Basolus:

> “Enacted in the year 1076, in the presence of Henry of Saint-Remigius, Joscelin of Hauteville, Gibuin of Mouzon, and Raimbald, abbots of Saint-Thierry, and Bruno, chancellor of the Church of Reims.”

### (46) CHAPTER XI

#### “The bishop of Grenoble, a very religious man, carries out the duties of abbot and administrator”

You should not be surprised that Bishop Hugh, the superintendent of the new foundation, did this, since he had professed a very strict life and knew how to water, prune, dig around, and fertilize it prudently and wisely—just as in former times the most holy bishops who were monks, Athanasius, Basil the Great, Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Martin, the two Augustines—the Doctor and the apostle of England—Caesarius of Arles, Boniface of Mainz, Leodegar of Autun, Lanfranc, Anselm, and others, undertook the formation of monks. For what they had learned and practiced through long experience in monasteries, they communicated especially well to others; and, in accordance with Luke 12 concerning the faithful steward of the Lord’s household, they knew very well how to give the measure of wheat at the proper time. They also knew that it was necessary for a shepherd “to benefit more than to preside,” as Saint Benedict says in chapter 64 of the Rule; and in chapter 2, warning the abbot:

> “To show all good and holy things more by deeds than by words, so that whatever he has taught his disciples to be contrary, he may indicate by his own deeds should not be done.”

Hence, among the statutes enacted at the command of King Edgar, there was, among other provisions, a decree concerning bishops who were to preside over monks:

> “A bishop who has been ordained shall carefully and without interruption observe in all things, with his monks, the same custom of the Rule that a regular abbot observes. Nor, on the occasion of his episcopate, should he rashly neglect the precepts of the Rule, puffed up or forgetful; rather, he should show by his works how much he excels.”

Selden, in his notes on Eadmer’s *History*, p. 150.

Here, then, is the reason why so many distinguished prelates so often became heads of monasteries. But when men intruded from secular life into the episcopal throne, what could they teach by word or deed that they had never heard, read, or even practiced? It was therefore with good reason that the supreme leaders of the Church exempted those who had embraced the institutions of evangelical perfection in the monastic order from episcopal jurisdiction; indeed, many bishops themselves voluntarily renounced the governance of monks.

### (47) SAME PLACE

#### “Nevertheless, they amassed a very rich library”

This was taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, in which he repeatedly exhorts the monks to devote themselves to reading and to the study of sacred Scripture in chapter 48, and commands:

> “Let all receive individual books from the library, which they are to read in order,” and so forth.

Thus it became customary among the earliest Carthusians to furnish libraries, in order by this means to lessen the weariness of solitude. For they boast that they borrowed the greater part of their institutions from the same Rule, especially in the letters of association entered into in 1632 with the Congregation of Saint-Maur, using these words:

> “Indeed, in this matter it is just that we share with you, as with brothers or fellow soldiers, a common joy, since we serve under the banner of that same most holy Father, Benedict; and since from his wise and religious instruction we receive the principal rights and laws of our Carthusian service,” and so forth.

Furthermore, the surviving traces of ancient monuments in the Benedictine Order testify that, while regular observance flourished, it was customary to construct extremely well-stocked libraries, from which ascetics received the bread “that does not perish” and “that strengthens the human heart.” See Cassiodorus, *Divine Institutions*, chapter 32; Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 838.

How great a concern it was for those same Benedictine monks to accumulate books is proclaimed by a sealed bull of Pope Alexander—if I am not mistaken, Alexander III—to the abbot and monks of ancient Corbie:

> “Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and chapter of Corbie, greetings and apostolic blessing. Since you wish to promote the usefulness of your monastery,” and so forth.

See Alexander III, under the year 1181.

599

Similarly, the abbot of Saint Benedict of Fleury decreed in a general chapter:

> “I, Macharius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Fleury, seeing that the books of our library, worn out by excessive age and damaged by the gnawing moth, need to be restored, and that new books or parchment must be acquired,” and so forth.

And below:

> “Therefore I, and the man who succeeds me, shall give twenty sous annually, and our prior ten sous, and the prior of the Rule ten sous,” and so forth.

This constitution appears among the ancient customs of the library of Fleury, p. 409.

Following the example of their predecessors, the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur likewise decreed in their declarations on chapter 48 of the Rule:

> “And lest books be lacking in the libraries to be given to the brothers according to their capacity, the superiors shall take care that they be furnished with useful books according to the resources of the monastery,” and so forth.

### (48) SAME PLACE

#### “The Count of Nevers”

William III, if I am not mistaken, after administering the county for some time, abandoned the splendor of his birth and, from the sea of worldly affairs, reached the secure station of monastic life. In the Carthusian Order he piously professed the humble status of a lay brother—or, as they call them, a servant. William of Nangis is a witness in his manuscript *History*, under the year 1138:

> “William, the distinguished Count of Nevers, also flourished; his remarkable devotion shone forth when, from being a powerful prince of the world, he became in the Chartreuse a humble poor man of Christ.”

Guido Coquille, *History of Nevers*, p. 145.

Many other examples of men distinguished by birth who, setting aside the vanity of the world, withdrew into cloisters at this same time to profess the regular life come to mind. I say nothing about them here, since they can all be read elsewhere; I shall give only two examples, from a parchment codex of the Greater Monastery written about the year 1116, chapter 45.

> “A certain illustrious viscount of the Chartrains, named Ebrard, heard the Lord’s saying: ‘Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14:33), and so forth. Fearing that, if he made himself alien to this most gracious admonition of the Lord, he might in the future also be alienated from the kingdom of heaven, he began to consider how he might draw nearer to the Lord himself and devote himself more familiarly to his service. And because both the present world and everything he seemed to possess in it presented great obstacles to this, and because it was not easy for him to fulfill what he wished, he preferred to abandon everything altogether rather than suffer eternal torments in hell on account of these things. Therefore he left his honor and possessions to his brothers, while everything else he could possess in gold and silver he distributed to the poor, so that, no longer concerned about transitory things, he might pursue divine matters more securely and freely, and so forth. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1073.”

A little later it continues:

> “But to return to our subject: Lord Ebrard, having become naked and poor, left his homeland and his relatives and went abroad. When he returned from that pilgrimage, during which he had stayed for a long time, he came to the Greater Monastery to receive the monastic habit there. While he remained for some time in secular clothing because of certain obstacles connected with his wife, Hugh, his brother, came to him. Hugh had succeeded him in the honor of viscount; and when he had heard many admonitions concerning his salvation,” and so forth.

And chapter 42, where cited above:

“You ought to know, whoever you may be among our successors—namely, inhabitants of the greater monastery of Saint Martin—that a certain knight named Bernard, surnamed Flagellum, when he came to receive the monastic habit among us, gave us half of the land called Ostrulvilla, with the consent also of the lords from whom he held it, namely Hugh of Putatiol, viscount of Chartres, and Ebrard of Levaisvilla, with the approval also of his uncle Stephen,” etc.

(49) CHAPTER XII.—The shoes of Córdoba. Nothing elucidates this passage as does Orderic Vital, who was composing his History at almost the same time. In Book V, toward the end [Col. 1085B], he writes: “They gave Simon five solidi, and Robert Cordovan slippers (shoes).” Likewise, in Book VIII, page 682, he vividly depicts the shoes of his own period, and this does not differ from the custom of our age:

“This man—Fulk of Anjou—was reprehensible and infamous in many respects. Since he had deformed feet, he ordered long shoes to be made, exceedingly sharp at the tip, called *subtolares*, so that they covered his feet, etc. This unusual fashion spread into the western world and greatly pleased frivolous people and lovers of novelty. Hence shoemakers make on footwear what are virtually scorpion tails, which they commonly call *pigaciae*. Almost all rich and poor alike eagerly seek this kind of footwear; for previously, at all times, rounded *subtolares*, shaped according to the feet, were worn,” etc.

And William of Malmesbury, his contemporary, in *De Gestis Anglorum*, Book IV, chapter 1, concerning William II, says: “Then appeared the flowing of the hair, then the luxury of clothing, then the use of shoes with pointed spikes,” etc.

(50) CHAPTER XIV.—“With these Guido,” etc., among whom he had founded the church of Saint Quentin from its first stone for regular canons. The *Life of Saint Romana, illustrious virgin and martyr*, contains an excellent testimony concerning this matter:

“When Baldwin, count of Flanders, was advancing the boy Philip, son of King Henry, to the throne, and was arranging the kingdom on his behalf, the city of Beauvais was left without its bishop. Therefore, with the equity of heavenly mercy consenting, Guido, dean and custodian of the church of Saint Quentin of Vermandois, and archdeacon of Laon, was appointed bishop of Beauvais by the aforementioned prince. He was ordained by the illustrious Gervasius, metropolitan of Reims, together with the other bishops of that province.

“For this nobleman, ascending prudently through the higher degrees of the Church, attained the episcopal dignity. Since he could not easily endure being deprived of the presence of the martyr, from whose breasts he had sucked the milk of spiritual teaching in the Church, he built, in his honor and memory, a church not far from the walls of the city of Beauvais, etc. Although it is admirable in the beauty of its design, it may be considered even more admirable for the extraordinary speed of its construction. No human power could have accomplished so great a work in so short a time unless divine power, through the intervention of the martyr, had come to its aid. For the same venerable Bishop Guido began and completed it within two years, having whitened it throughout and adorned it with painted ceilings, etc.

“Then, inspired by God and making use of wise counsel, with great honor and accompanied by throngs of chanting clergy and laity, he transferred the body of the aforementioned virgin and martyr Romana from the shrine of Saint Peter to the church that he had built,” etc.

Thus far extends the fragment from the *Deeds of Saint Romana*, written in manuscript, which a certain regular canon of the Gallican congregation lent me, together with the following privilege of Pope Gregory VII, later granted to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and with the other material concerning Bishop Guido that is to be transcribed below.

“GREGORY to his beloved son in Christ, Ivo, provost of the church of Saint Quentin, situated in the diocese of Beauvais, and to his successors who are regularly to be appointed:

“‘In consideration of heavenly mercy,’” etc.

See under Gregory VII.

The verses inscribed in an ancient manuscript indicate at what time the aforementioned basilica of Saint Quentin was founded and dedicated:

> In the year one thousand and sixty-nine,  
> This place was made in honor of blessed Quentin of the Incarnate Word,  
> And was dedicated to God.

The day of Bishop Guido’s death is recorded in the necrology of the same church as follows:

“On the ninth day before the Kalends of May, Lord Guido, bishop of Beauvais, died. He was the founder and builder of this church, which he endowed with many possessions and adorned with many ornaments. For in our church he made a silver crown, silver panels, a silver bier, etc.; two Gospel books—one of which bears a likeness of Guido—a silver cross, nine better-quality copes with one chasuble, and ten large and small bells. He also made all the old buildings and gave us this village,” etc.

Read the letters of Ivo, 151, 181, and 193. Robert of Torigni’s additions to Sigebert, under the years 1066 and 1069, state: “Guido, bishop of Beauvais, dedicated the church, completed in two years, in honor of his patron, the martyr Quentin, on the fourth day before the Nones of October.” From this statement and the verses quoted above, one may observe that the author of Ivo’s *Life*, prefixed to his works as a kind of prologue, must be reproached, among other errors, for assigning the foundation of Saint Quentin of Beauvais to the year 1078.

(51) SAME PLACE.—The monastery of Flaviacum. Commonly called Saint Geremar, it is situated in the diocese of Beauvais, four leagues from that city.

Moreover, whatever concerns the church of Flaviacum has been fully reconstructed from its earliest monuments, ancient records, papal letters, and royal and princely charters—rescued from secular hands after immense labor and toil—by the Reverend Father Dom Jean-Baptiste de Boulogne, then prior of that monastery of the Congregation of Saint Maur, a man of great learning. From this source we present in advance a summary of the same history, arranged by us.

[Col. 1087A] Summary of the History of the Monastery of Flaviacum

You will learn from a letter of John V, bishop of Beauvais, that the monastery of Flaviacum, situated in the countryside of the diocese of Beauvais near the river Epte, was founded and endowed by Saint Geremar—after whom it was later named—during the time of Dagobert, about the year 650, or, as others maintain, 660. The letter reads as follows:

“John, by divine mercy bishop of Beauvais, sends greetings to all who shall see this present letter.

“Our beloved sons, the venerable and devout religious men—the abbot, convent, and priors subject to him—of the most devout monastery of Saint Geremar of Flaviacum in our diocese, have sorrowfully reported to us that contemptuous, or rather scornful, despisers of holy religion reproach them by asserting that their monastery, formerly dedicated to God in honor of the most holy Trinity by their most devout patron Geremar, with the assistance of the most blessed Audoen, archbishop of Rouen, was never founded from the revenues of Geremar himself, but from partial goods coming from elsewhere. Without the support of truth, they allege that the most blessed Geremar endowed his monastery and many other religious establishments subject to it from his own patrimonial and paraphernal goods. Therefore they asked us to testify to whatever we might find concerning its foundation in our sacred histories, charters, registers, books, and ancient writings, or in those of our church and bride.

“We make it known that, wishing to silence the mouths of those who bark maliciously and rejoicing to bear witness to the truth, we certify that the ancient books, readings, charters, and writings, whose testimony is free from suspicion and untainted by any reproachable mark, contain the following.

“Namely, in the time of the most serene King Dagobert, the glorious Geremar, born of royal stock, was a man of the greatest holiness. By his sacred counsel that King Dagobert governed the kingdom in beloved peace. But although that glorious Geremar had formerly served among men as a soldier, he desired, after setting aside worldly warfare, to become a participant in the heavenly warfare, like a new recruit under the veteran and approved commander of the heavenly army and the vicar of the heavenly prince, Saint Audoen, archbishop of Rouen and chancellor of the aforementioned king. He resolved to wage war against the flesh, the world, and demons.

“Following the counsel of this Audoen, who was already enjoying great holiness, Geremar entered religious life with the consent of the aforementioned King Dagobert, in the place called Flaviacum. Not long afterward, when his own children had departed to the Lord, and with the consent and approval of King Clovis, the aforementioned Dagobert’s son, and preceded by an angelic revelation, he built, at his own expense, the monastery now called that of Saint Geremar, together with many other religious establishments, for the worship and veneration of the most holy and blessed Trinity. He endowed it with his own estates, villages, castles, and revenues, desiring and striving to worship the Lord God in many places from the earthly goods given to him by God.

[Col. 1088A] “The aforementioned monastery continued in existence and in its established condition for two hundred and fifty years, or approximately that long. But the wicked disturber of peace and destroyer of the human race, who fell from heaven into hell, disturbed by the service being celebrated in that monastery, entered the heart of the impious Rollo and caused the monastery of Flaviacum to be utterly destroyed down to its foundations. After the religious had soon died or fled, it remained deserted, empty of inhabitants, barren of produce, and uninhabitable for one hundred and thirty years. Nor have we found anyone who acted as helper or comforter during the aforementioned devastation, or who wished to preserve the charters, papyri, registers, or books of that monastery. This is not surprising, since among plunderers and enemies of the Christian faith it was customary, and remains so even today, to consume by voracious fire whatever bore the mark of Christian religion.

“But because the omnipotent Creator wished to have mercy on the people, and wished them once again to venerate his most blessed confessor Geremar in the place of his holiness, he inspired the mind of our predecessor, Drogo of blessed memory, bishop of Beauvais, with the grace of the Holy Spirit and moved him to rebuild that monastery. Following the prior will of the aforementioned Geremar, and ordering—as was his right—that the monastery be named after the most holy Trinity, he decreed that, to the praise of God and of its founder Geremar, it should be called the Monastery of Saint Geremar. In testimony of this matter, we have deemed it proper to affix our seal to this present letter.

[Col. 1088C] “Given in the year of the Lord 1478, on Wednesday, the third day of June.

“By order of the lord, thus signed: R. Champdesus.”

Furthermore, the ancient monuments of that place record that twenty abbots presided over the monastery from its beginnings until the destruction inflicted by the Northmen. From them, and also from the chronicle of Fontenelle, or Saint-Wandrille, we shall derive their names, except for the few whom the injury of time has erased.

The first abbot was Saint Geremar, the founder of the monastery of Flaviacum, initially dedicated to the most holy Trinity. We have placed among the additions the deeds of Saint Geremar, written by an ancient author and copied by our care from an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Conques.

III. Saint Gennard—the second having been consigned to oblivion—was greatly beloved by Saint Ansbert. Hence it was decided that he should be given burial beside the body of the latter in the monastery of Fontenelle, over which Ansbert had also presided.

IV. Saint Benignus had previously presided over the monastery of Fontenelle; but after being expelled by Regenfred, mayor of the palace, he was chosen by the monks as abbot of Flaviacum.

V. Adebrardus, renowned for the glory of his integrity, prudence, and intellect, “was so acceptable to the Emperor Louis the Pious, on account of his deserved prudence”—as a handwritten codex concerning Adebrardus says—“that among his leading men he was always first in settling affairs of peace, both in the Church and in the kingdom, even among distant peoples.”

VI. Hincmarus, formerly a monk of Saint-Denis in France, as Flodoard reports in Book III, chapter 1:

“Having been summoned to the king’s service, he undertook the administration of the monastery of Saint Mary, Holy Mother of God, and of Saint Germain, by royal and episcopal command and by the order of his abbot Louis.”

Here, however, one should read “Saint Geremar,” as Flodoard himself indicates in the same book, chapter 18, in these words:

“Likewise”—Hincmarus writes—“concerning the cell or monastery of Flaviacum, which that same king had given him while he was serving him before his episcopate, and which he had confirmed by a precept so that he might hold it during his lifetime; and which, after it had been destroyed by a certain invader, he rebuilt and restored religious life in it as far as he could,” etc.

We shall refrain from writing more about Hincmarus, archbishop of Reims, since his deeds and writings—contained in two volumes—are more familiar and celebrated than to require us to set them out here.

VII. Odo, formerly abbot of Corbie in Picardy and bishop of Beauvais, obtained first from the king of the Franks and then from Pope Nicholas I that the monastery of Flaviacum and another monastery of nuns—both almost leveled to the ground—be placed under episcopal jurisdiction, so that they might be rescued from lay hands and their poverty relieved.

The papal diploma states:

“Let it be done in such a way that from the goods of that monastery, whether already bestowed or yet to be bestowed, assistance may be given to the needs of the church of Beauvais, according to the will and judgment of the bishop who presides over that church; and let the monasteries themselves not be deprived of support, whether for the buildings of their houses, the restoration of their churches, or the needs of those serving God there. Rather, let the bishop of the church of Beauvais so arrange their goods that the monasteries themselves may be restored and maintained according to the measure of the resources bestowed upon them, and that those serving God there may be helped by appropriate support. Thus, let places dedicated to God and the goods bestowed upon those churches serve chiefly where the offerings of the faithful to God are known to have been given.

“For it is neither pious nor just that the said churches should be stripped of their goods and made to serve the needs of another church in such a way that no care at all appears to be given to them. Therefore let the bishop of Beauvais take care to assume responsibility both for the women serving God there, and for men of whatever order, and for the restoration and preservation of the monasteries, so that he may rejoice that he has provided worthy care for the house of God, and that the rector who presides over it may not incur the judgment of heavenly censure on account of negligence.

“Moreover, let these monasteries never again come into the hands or power of secular persons for any reason or under any pretext. For it is no small danger in the sight of the supreme Judge to place secular authority over religious places and monasteries dedicated to God, and to entrust the care of shepherding to one who neither knows nor seeks what a shepherd is, seeking not the profit of souls but a financial census—not service for divine worship, but service for his own uses and according to his desire for domination,” etc.

“This privilege was granted in the fifth year of the reign of Louis II, and in the year of Christ 860.”

VIII. Ansigisus, a man distinguished in religion, learning, and practical affairs, laid aside his human life in the year 882.

[603] Many years later, namely around the year 900, the monastery was overturned and utterly destroyed by the Northmen. The sacred bones of blessed Geremar were transferred and placed in the church of Beauvais, where they are still seen today.

But in the year 1030 Drogo, bishop of Beauvais, a man equally devout and prudent, earnestly applied himself to its restoration—or rather, to rebuilding it from the ground up—and did so with such success and magnificence that within a short time he completed the church and all the buildings necessary for monastic life. In both size and elegance, these surpassed not only the old buildings but also the principal structures then existing in Gaul.

After the monastery had been built and furnished with monastic goods and sacred vessels, and after the estates formerly possessed by the monks had been restored, he summoned monks from the monastery of Saint-Maur of Fosses, placing Guntherius over them. Finally, he strove with all his strength to restore the sacred bones of Saint Geremar, but in vain, since the people resisted and obstructed him.

IX. Gunterius, formerly a monk of Fosses, restored the discipline of ascetic life in the monastery of Saint Geremar and there earned great renown for virtue and learning. His reputation for outstanding discipline moved even outsiders to renounce the world and place themselves under his instruction. Indeed, several women, later attracted by the same reputation, lived in small buildings adjoining the church: among them Leodegardis, the sister of Prior Suger, and the mother of Guibert, abbot of Nogent. Guibert himself speaks of them in Book I of his *Life*. In later centuries there were likewise Albreda of Saint-Ouen, a converse, wife of William of Henouville; the wife of Girard of Hanuoiles; and very many others. After giving over their possessions there to the monastery’s support—or, as the codicils call them, their prebends—they lived there under the name of converse and sisters, wearing the habit of nuns. Traces of their small buildings still exist to this day.

Gunterius died on the Ides of March in the year of Christ 1058, in the twenty-second year of his administration.

X. Garnerius succeeded Gunterius. He was distinguished for probity, learning, and prudence in administration. He greatly enhanced regular discipline and increased the monastery’s possessions. During his administration, several churches or priories were transferred to Flaviacum, and Abbot Garnerius assigned them colonies of monks who would protect and instruct the people by their prayers, preaching, and example.

This is shown especially by the account of the foundation of the priory of the Holy Sepulchre at Villers, founded by Lanscelinus, the most noble count of Beauvais. We are pleased to insert that same charter, since it breathes the profound piety of this count.

[Col. 1091A] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Our charity has decided that it will be pleasing to all who have been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit if we record in written letters how our church was founded, with the Lord’s assistance, by certain persons.

“Lanscelinus the elder, son of Fulk of Beauvais, was a man of vigorous nobility and, according to the pride of this age, of great power.
