As the outcome of the matter proved, by the will and command of God he went to Jerusalem and to the holy places where our Lord Jesus Christ was born, where he was crucified, and where the tomb was in which he was laid. He was accompanied by many people from this province. This was at a time when no confessor of the Christian name dared to go there, except secretly, or, so to speak, by stealth, because of fear of the hostile pagans.

“After suffering many dangers both by land and by sea, he finally attained his desire. Having worshiped there with sufficient humility, he returned to Gaul with all his companions. After not much time had passed, the piety of our Creator, who ‘wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of his name’ (1 Tim. 2:4), put it into his heart to build, from his own resources, a church in honor of the Holy Sepulchre and to establish monks there to perform God’s service day and night.

“After revealing his plan and will in this matter to his wife, his sons, and his own men, they all praised it with one voice and affirmed together that it would be pleasing to God.

“After this he sought Lord Garnerius, abbot of the monastery of Flaviacum, and begged him with the humblest prayers to deign to send with him monks worthy to undertake such a task. His request was made on the condition that the church he wished to build should remain subject to the church of Flaviacum for all time, and that the abbot and his successors should send whichever monks they wished and recall whichever they wished.

“The abbot most willingly granted what so great a man requested. He not only consented, but also exhorted him with holy encouragement to complete so holy a work. Then, when they had set a date for beginning the work, Abbot Garnerius arrived with his monks. Lanscelinus also came, accompanied by a troop of noblemen, bringing with him from the city of Beauvais men skilled in masonry, together with his sons.

“For all who had gathered agreed that the place was suitable for the monks’ habitation, considering the proximity of the waters, the breadth of the meadows, the abundance of the woods, the fertility of the vineyards, and the multitude of trees bearing fruit of various kinds.

“When everything necessary had finally been prepared, and the lines had been laid out by the masons according to the intended dimensions, Lord Lanscelinus, with great devotion in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, was the first to open with a ditch the ground where the foundations of the basilica were to be laid.

“This work was begun in the month of March, in the year 1060, while Philip was reigning as king in Gaul and the most noble King William was governing the duchy of Normandy and the kingdom of England.”

The illustrious Lanscelinus’ generosity did not fail the monks serving God there. To provide them with sufficient daily nourishment, he gave them the mill of Crevecœur, situated on the bank of the Tara, and the entire watercourse from Cailot to Pont Harmis for fishing. He also gave them his guests residing there, together with the entire holding of Hildefred and the meadows belonging to that holding; the oak grove of Burgerius, the adjoining alder-and-oak grove, the wood of Hes, and Faiolum. He granted all the brushwood for burning and lodging.

He gave them the beehives found in his woods; two parts of the tithe of Harmis; and two parts of the tithes of Serency and Medianavilla. Likewise, he gave two parts of the tithe and the cultivation-land of Crene, as well as the enclosure of the little monastery, which he bought from a certain man named Gildinus for seven pounds of Beauvais currency and one modius of grain. The monks supported Gildinus himself until the end of his life with the monastic habit and daily food.

He also gave a certain holding, which he had purchased for one hundred solidi of Beauvais currency from Hemelin of Saint-Lucian, with the consent of Peter, abbot of Saint-Lucian, and the consent of all the other monks of Consenfiscus. In this matter Lord Lanscelinus rendered homage to the abbot of Saint-Lucian. The abbot, however, gave him one tooth of Saint Lucian to augment his treasury.

After this he made the following confirmation: if any of the monks’ men were ever seized by his dependents, whether while cutting their woods, as is customary among peasants, or on account of any other offense, his dependents were to refer their complaint against that man to the monks, and the monks were to administer justice in their own court.

He further confirmed, and had his sons reinforce by their hands, that if any of his knights wished to give something from his treasury to the church, he might do so freely without his command or that of his sons, provided that he did not thereby lose the military service owed from it.

He also confirmed, with the consent of his men, that whenever he wished to go to that church or village, he should have nothing there except the provision due for one monk. He retained nothing at all for himself in the village: neither jurisdiction, nor blood-right, nor thief, neither tallage, nor harsh exaction, nor forfeited property.

“Let those now present and those who shall come in the future know that I, Renaud, lord of Bul, deeply repentant of my sins, have renounced certain unjust customary payments—namely, tallage and all other exactions and provisions—which for several years I had unjustly received in the village called Villers of the Holy Sepulchre. I asked to be released from them by the monks of Flaviacum residing in that village, and I obtained this release.

“And so that this settlement might not thereafter be violated by any of my successors, I have entirely forbidden it and confirmed it with the impression of my seal.”

King Philip of the Franks granted privileges and estates to the monastery of Flaviacum as a favor to Garnerius, whom he loved greatly. In particular, he sent letters to the bishop of Beauvais and the clergy, ordering them to restore the most sacred relics of their blessed patron Geremar. But these letters produced no result.

Finally, out of love for a more tranquil life, so that he might offer and devote his entire self to God, Garnerius renounced both burden and honor. He lived privately for eleven years and, in the year of the Lord 1095, on the Nones of June, happily ended his last day.

XI. Hugo I was, as Guibert testifies, a man of manifold religion and learning. He presided after Garnerius’ voluntary resignation. During this period, while Hugo administered the monastery with distinction, monks of great virtue, learning, and steadfast discipline flourished there; among them Guibert himself shone like a star.

William of Besencourt and Gamelinus of Boweresces renounced the world and bound themselves by monastic vows in the monastery of Flaviacum.

The venerable Hugo was called to heaven on the Nones of December in the year of Christ 1100, in the fifteenth year of his administration.

XII. John, an abbot of approved moral integrity—Guibert’s mother had raised him from childhood—was born in the region of Clermont. He brought William, a boy of excellent character, from Jewish error to Christian truth. On his account Guibert composed his *Treatise against the Jews*, in Book II, chapter 5, of *On His Own Life*.

In the fourth year of John’s administration, that same Guibert was elevated to the abbacy of the monastery of Nogent near Coucy. Toward the end of John’s life, Guibert’s venerable mother, having cast off mortality, breathed out her soul and left her body to be buried at Flaviacum.

John died on the third day before the Ides of March in the year 1106.

XIII. Hildegarius succeeded John on account of his outstanding natural gifts and religious character. The wealth of the monastery of Flaviacum increased so greatly that it not only sufficed to support a very large community of monks, but also abundantly supplied what was necessary for guests arriving from every direction and relieved the want of the poor, both healthy and sick. For this reason many men of noble birth devoted themselves to divine worship at Flaviacum.

The strict discipline of the monks of Flaviacum also caused the illustrious Ansellus to transfer to them the monastery of Maurigny near Étampes.

This is reported in the prologue to Book II of the *Chronicle of Maurigny*, toward the end, in volume IV of André Duchesne’s *Histories of France*:

“A certain Ansellus, vigorous in years and judgment, moved by the religion and friendship of the monks of Flaviacum, first offered to the monks of Flaviacum the church of Stripiniacum and whatever he possessed in that village. Then, with the grace of Christ going before him, he transferred the estate of Maurigny, in which this church had been founded in honor of the holy Trinity.”

Odo, a monk of Flaviacum, was chosen as father by the monks of Saint Symphorian of Beauvais, although he resisted greatly. Guibert recalls that he flourished in holiness, wisdom, and learning in the dedicatory letter prefixed to his books *On the Relics of the Saints*. But because he greatly preferred to be subject rather than to preside, he laid down his dignity and chose to live again in his Flaviacum monastery under the discipline of obedience.

The perfect observance of the Rule also attracted noblemen to increase the revenues of Flaviacum. Among them was especially Matthew of Maurigny, as is shown by this document:

“In the name of Christ, I, Matthew, lord of Mont-Maurigny, wish it to come to the knowledge of those present and those to come that my father Burchard, of blessed memory, out of zeal for charity and for the remedy of his soul, granted as alms to the monks of blessed Geremar of Flaviacum that the servants of Saint Geremar might bring from anywhere goods for the use of those monks, and might pass freely and peacefully through his land without any customary payment.

“I and my brothers have likewise granted this with a simple and devout intention. But because I frequently hear of the good and honorable conduct of those monks, I not only grant that same alms of my father but also fully approve it. And so that it may remain valid forever, with the consent also of my sons Burchard, Matthew, and Hervaeus, I confirm it by the impression of my seal and wish it to be confirmed there by the testimony of the men present.”

Many young men of illustrious lineage devoted themselves to the service of Christ in this monastery, namely Hugo—called “Oat-Bread”—Drogo of Calvomonte, the sons and grandsons of Hugo surnamed Borgnus, Walter of Rebez, Roger of Constantin, Aszo of Ferrières, and others.

Hildegarius died on the fourth day before the Kalends of May in 1123.

XIV. Odo, of renowned virtue and wisdom, was appointed in succession to Hildegarius.

After expending all his own efforts and those of his associates in vain to restore the sacred relics of Geremar to the church of Flaviacum, he finally obtained the bone of the arm called the radius, and arranged for it to be brought to Flaviacum with solemn rites on the eighth day before the Kalends of August in the year 1132.

Toward the end of that same year, the abbot himself was elevated, by the unanimous vote of all the clergy, to the administration of the church of Beauvais. He bore that burden with great distinction from the year 1133 until approximately 1145.

XV. Leodegarius succeeded him. He worked hard, using many exhortations, to persuade Odo to accept the episcopate. King Henry I of the English granted Leodegarius permission to transport selected oak trees from the Forest of Lyons for the customary restoration of buildings.

After serving for ten years as abbot, he laid aside mortality in the year 1145, on the fifth day before the Ides of December.

XVI. Fulbertus, a man of utterly blameless life and morals, obtained extensive letters of privileges and immunities from Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, in the year 1151; from the supreme pontiff Eugenius, in that same year; and from Odo, bishop of Beauvais, in 1146.

Radulf of Mavoison, brother of Samson, archbishop of Reims, also conferred many benefits in the year 1148, with the consent of his wife Bertha, his sons Radulf, William, and Manasseh, and his daughters Agnes and Queen Joanna.

Louis VII likewise gave the monks of Saint Geremar a sign of Christian piety, favorable disposition, and benevolence by granting various immunities. For the sake of brevity, I pass over their charters.

Hugh of Gournay approves all that he had granted to the monastery of Flaviacum in these words:

“Let it be known to all present and future that I, Hugh of Gournay, confirm by the impression of my seal all the alms from my own demesne, both in England and in Normandy and France, which I have given forever to the church of blessed Geremar of Flaviacum. In addition, I confirm all the other alms that lie within my fief and protection, which my men have given or shall give to that church. I likewise grant the freedom of the servants of that church who have not made a denial. So that this may remain valid, I strengthen it with my seal and the subscription of witnesses. The witnesses are John of Hodane,” etc.

Fulbertus the abbot settled, as far as possible, the disputes that had arisen between the monks of different monasteries; a charter was drawn up for this purpose. “Let peace,” he said, “which is better than anything else, not be disturbed by a dispute arising at some time among the sons of peace.” The following men strengthened such a charter with their names: Theoldus the prior, Lambertus the subprior, Landricus the cantor, Odo the cellarer, Walnerius the second cellarer, Petrus the plowman [also called *Carrucarius*], Godzo the provost, Herbertus the treasurer, Drogo of Calvomonte, and many other monks.

He attended the assembly at Beauvais of the bishops, abbots, and nobles of Gaul, summoned by King Louis, who had asked that the question be debated whether Alexander or Victor should be admitted as supreme pontiff.

After administering the monastery with great distinction for nineteen years, Fulbertus was taken from human affairs on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

XVII. Gerardus. He obtained a brief from Henry II, king of the English, by which what Henry I had granted was confirmed. Saint Thomas, then chancellor of England, appended his mark to it.

Gerardus presided for only three years and ended his mortal life on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, 1167.

XVIII. Hildegarius II. “Having little regard for the salvation of the souls entrusted to him and showing greater concern for transitory and perishable things” (contrary to the prescription of chapter 2 of the Benedictine Rule), he loosened the reins of religious discipline. In particular, he assigned fixed annual revenues to the monastery’s officials, whom they call claustrals.

He died in the year 1172, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March.

XIX. Hugo II—whom some claim was the son of the count of Clermont—was abbot of Flaviacum, then of Saint-Lucian of Beauvais, and finally of Cluny. In the year of Christ 1178, Pope Alexander III confirmed by bull all the rights of the monastery of Flaviacum.

He died on the sixth day before the Ides of April 1188, as the manuscript chronicle of Fontenelle and the codices of Saint-Lucian and Saint Geremar report; or, if the Cluniac chronicler is to be trusted, in 1199. He lies in the church of Cluny, as the same author testifies, in the Cluniac Library, page 1663.

XX. Lambertus, formerly cellarer of the same monastery, around 1180. Count Radulf of Clermont granted him a protective charter. He died on the day before the Ides of June 1190.

[Col. 1096B] XXI. Hugo III, surnamed the Poor, was born of an equally wealthy and noble family. In the first year of his administration, he arranged for the possessions located in the diocese of Rouen to be confirmed by Walter, archbishop. He also obtained from Richard, king of the English, a protective charter, which reads as follows:

“Richard, by the grace of God king of the English, duke of Normandy, Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, justiciars and viscounts, ministers, and all his bailiffs and faithful men throughout his entire land, greetings. Know that the abbey, abbot, and monks of Saint-Germer-de-Fly, together with their men and all their goods and possessions, are in our hand, custody, and protection. Therefore we wish and firmly command [Col. 1096C] that you guard, protect, and uphold the abbey itself, the monks, their men, goods, and possessions—both ecclesiastical and secular—throughout our land, whether there is peace or war; so that you do not inflict, or permit anyone else to inflict, any injury, insult, or burden upon them. And if anything should happen to be wrongfully taken or done against them in any matter, render them full justice concerning it, as you would to me myself. At Vallena Rudolii, 15 June.”

That the priory of Saint Arnulf the Martyr, near Clermont, was granted by Philip, bishop of Beauvais, to the church of Saint-Germer is established by the following document:

“Let it be known to those present and to those to come that I, Philip, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, [Col. 1096D] grant in perpetual possession to the church of Flaviacum the chapel founded in honor of the most blessed martyr Arnulf, saving the rights of the surrounding parishes. For I am bound to preserve each person’s rights in such a way that grants made to others do not perish. I also confirm, by this present instrument and by the authority of our seal, those grants which were made to the aforesaid church or to its minister.”

Philip II, king of the Franks, declares the monastery of Flaviacum to be under his protection—or rather, he confirms by his letters the diploma of Louis VII.

After laying aside the burden of the flesh, Hugo was translated to eternal rest on 26 September 1200.

**XXII. Eustachius**, distinguished among the other abbots of the Flaviacum monastery by singular learning, holiness, [Col. 1097A] and illustrious achievements, was appointed through the common vote of the brothers and the assent of the bishop of Beauvais, whose secretary Eustachius had been, as is made clear by the following formula requesting the bishop’s consent:

607 “We give thanks to your immense kindness, which not only assents but also rejoices with our election, because it was made unanimously and according to the rule of justice. Having invoked the mercy of the Holy Spirit—for without him all prayers are fruitless—we have elected Eustachius, namely your secretary, an honorable, approved, simple, and upright man, possessing a good testimony both within and without. We present such a man to you, most reverend Father, and humbly ask that you lay upon him, when presented, the hand of blessing.” [Col. 1097B]

After the duchy of Normandy had passed into the possession of the Franks, King Philip II fortified the men of Flaviacum with letters of protection in July 1202.

While Eustachius was serving once and again in England and Scotland as a legate empowered by Innocent III, “he preached the word of the Lord,” as Roger of Hoveden records, “and for transgression against the Lord’s Day and the other festivals he gave the people penance and absolution, on the condition that thereafter they would show due reverence to the Lord’s Day and the other festivals of the saints, doing no servile work on them and conducting no market in goods on Sundays, but [Col. 1097C] devoting themselves diligently to good works and prayer. He decreed that these observances should be kept from the ninth hour of Saturday until sunrise on Monday.

“But the people, devoted to God in response to his preaching, vowed to God that thereafter on Sundays they would neither buy nor sell anything, except perhaps food and drink for travelers. They also vowed that from every five shillings’ worth of any goods they sold, they would give one quarter for the purchase of a light for the church and for the burial of the needy. For collecting this, the aforesaid abbot ordered a hollow chest to be made in each parish church, under the custody of two or three trustworthy men, into which the people would cast the aforesaid money.

“The same abbot also ordered that a charitable dish should be kept every day on the tables of the wealthy, into which they would place part of their food for the benefit of the needy who had not prepared food for themselves. The aforesaid abbot further prohibited anyone from buying, selling, or conducting legal business in the churches or their courtyards.” [Col. 1097D]

Finally, after he had trained his brothers in approved and religious conduct, increased the monastery’s goods, and caused the fame of his supreme piety to spread far and wide, he migrated to the heavenly homeland on 8 September 1211, marked by a reputation for holiness that is still widely proclaimed. He lies buried in the middle of the church, with this inscription carved on his stone tomb:

> Here lies a true cultivator of honor and piety,  
> [Col. 1098A] A treasury and bearer of the law, a pattern made for the flock.  
> Given as food to worms, he has gone where we all are bound:  
> Abbot Eustachius—God, be gracious to him.

**XXIII. Girardus II**, called d’Eraigny, either from his family or from his birthplace, which lies near Gisors. In the first year of his rule he surrendered the office, more unwillingly than voluntarily.

**XXIV. Girardus III**, from Fraxino. He entered into a fellowship with the monks of Fosses in 1214. It will not be out of place to reproduce their charter:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Radulphus, by the grace of God abbot of the church of Fosses, and the entire convent of that place, make known to all who see this document that between us and the venerable Girardus, abbot of Flaviacum, and the brothers of that [Col. 1098B] church, the following fellowship has been established and granted:

“If the abbot of one church comes to another church, he shall be honorably received by the abbot and monks of that church, as is fitting; he shall occupy the abbot’s place in the choir, hold chapter as abbot of that place, absolve at his pleasure the brothers placed under sentence, and punish those who must be punished as he judges appropriate.

“When the day of the other abbot’s death is known, whatever the one monastery is bound to pay for its deceased abbot shall likewise be paid for the other. When his death is heard, his office shall be solemnly celebrated with the bells rung, and a complete thirty-day commemoration, with the due provision, shall be paid for him.

[Col. 1098C] “But since the deaths of deceased brothers often fail to come to the knowledge of the other congregation through negligence or forgetfulness, it has been established that each year, on the day after Saint Paul’s feast—that is, on the Kalends of July—we shall perform a thirty-day commemoration for the deceased brothers. During each of these thirty days, the full provision shall be distributed to the poor both among us and among them.

“Whenever the death of a brother of either church is heard, we shall solemnly celebrate the office and Mass in the convent; each priest shall celebrate one Mass for each deceased person. The others who are not priests shall recite one Psalter each, and the lay brothers thirty Paternosters. On the day of his office they shall have the full provision in the refectory.

[Col. 1098D] “Furthermore, if any monk of either congregation should incur the anger or indignation of his abbot—which God avert!—and withdraw to the other monastery, he shall be treated as one of that place, sharing both in chapter and in food and clothing, until peace is restored between him and his abbot; unless—which God forbid!—he is such a person that, according to the Rule, he ought not to be reconciled because satisfaction is impossible.

“The names both of the abbot and of the 608 deceased brothers shall be written in the martyrology.

“To make this fellowship between us and them firm and stable forever, we have granted them this charter, strengthened by the protection of our seals, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1214.” [Col. 1099A]

To the parish church which the men of Flaviacum had recently built at Coriletum, Philip, bishop of Beauvais, granted the right of presentation, as it is called, in the following form:

“Philip, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, to all the faithful in Christ, eternal greetings. Let all of you know that when Girardus, abbot, and the convent of Saint-Germer of Flaviacum had leased to cultivators the arable lands which they possessed in our diocese, and had newly built there a village called Coriletum, they founded a church there by common consent and at their own expense, enriching it with revenues.

“We likewise, at their request, grant the right of presentation of the said parish to the church of Saint-Germer, to possess perpetually. As testimony to this matter, we have delivered this document to the aforesaid monks, strengthened by the protection of our seal.

“Given at Flaviacum in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1215.” [Col. 1099B]

Girardus completed the course of his life on 11 March 1215.

**XXV. Girardus de Haraigny**, or Eraigny, whom we mentioned above, was again appointed to govern the abbey by the common vote of the monks.

As he lay dying, Philip, bishop of Beauvais, bequeathed to the men of Flaviacum a golden cross and ecclesiastical ornaments, together with part of the village of Spalburgum, commonly called Espaubourg. His successor Milo, having first obtained from the canons the right which they held in the same village, approved this donation [Col. 1099C] in the following words:

“Milo, by the grace of God humble minister of the church of Beauvais, to all Christ’s faithful to whom these present letters shall come, eternal salvation in the Lord. We make known to all that when a certain part of the village of Espaubourg, with its men, fiefs, champart, lands, meadows, woods, and other appurtenances belonging to that part of the village, had devolved from Harmericus Ruffus, formerly a knight of Beauvais, upon Philip, of pious memory, formerly bishop of Beauvais, our predecessor, and when that same Philip had granted it perpetually to the canons of Saint Mary of Beauvais, the same canons, with the consent of the chapter of Saint Peter of Beauvais and having received sufficient exchange for it, released it to us forever to hold or to transfer to whomever we wished.

[Col. 1099D] “Therefore, embracing the church of Flaviacum with paternal affection, we have granted all these things to it and to the monks dwelling there, to hold forever freely and peacefully, with full jurisdiction, together with the other things which, from ancient times and in the days of our predecessors, the said monks freely and peacefully possessed there—namely, their messuage, men, fiefs, lands, meadows, woods, tithes, mills, waters, champart, and complete jurisdiction. Thus, among the appurtenances of the said village, we retain nothing, but the named monks shall enjoy full freedom in all the matters mentioned above. And we, [Col. 1100A] by episcopal authority and in good faith, are bound to warrant the foregoing. In testimony of which, etc.

“Milo, bishop.”

Abbot Girardus prescribed statutes concerning the principal festivals and their solemn observance, following the ancient customs of the same monastery.

With the consent of the chapter, he founded an anniversary observance of the day of his death in the year 1235.

He died on 1 September 1236. He lies in the chapter house, where this epitaph may be seen carved on his tomb:

> What are we doing when we neglect to beware of sins?  
> He who lies here always strove to foster every good.  
> When Gerardus dies, he is not abandoned below;  
> He is carried to heaven, richly endowed by the gift of God.

[Col. 1100B] **XXVI. Guillelmus de Vilaincs**, renowned for the integrity of his conduct. He sat with the other abbots of the province of Reims in the chapter, or congregation, convened at Saint-Vincent of Laon.

With Guillelmus, formerly a monk of Flaviacum and then abbot of Cluny, and Guillelmus de Vilaines standing by, Guillelmus, bishop, imparted his blessing to a silver reliquary adorned with gold and precious stones in a solemn ceremony, and the sacred arm of Saint-Germer was placed within it.

In 1255, Guillelmus, displaying a father’s loving concern, selected and assigned certain estates so that nothing would be lacking to his monks, whether healthy or ill. He wished this statute to be approved by Guillelmus, bishop of Beauvais, and by Alexander IV, of pious memory. This was done. He gives the following reason for the [Col. 1100C] decree: “Poverty is often an occasion of murmuring, impatience, and even greed.” Excellent foresight on Guillelmus’s part! He ended his last day on 16 May 1259.

**XXVII. Petrus de Vesencourt.** At the very beginning of his 609 rule he acquired immortal glory through a work of outstanding excellence. For he built and consecrated, with marvelous workmanship, a chapel for God’s supreme Mother and Virgin. It still stands and surpasses nearly all the chapels of France both in beauty and in size. He established in it sacred offices to be performed daily and hourly prayers to be recited through the efforts of his own community.

He entered into a pact or fellowship with the monks of the monastery of Saint-[Col. 1100D] Ouen of Rouen in 1261.

The annual commemoration of Petrus’s deposition, instituted in May 1269, indicates the great increase in Saint-Germer’s possessions through Petrus’s most generous gifts.

In July 1275 the men of Saint-Germer and the monks of Saint-Lucien of Beauvais entered into a fellowship together.

Petrus completed the course of his life on 29 April 1272, and was buried in the courtyard of the chapel he had built, with this rhythmic epitaph:

> A stone covers Petrus the abbot, who ruled well  
> The monastery of Germer; may Christ preserve him from the sword.  
> He was always devoted to a life of piety and without dispute.  
> He chose the cell which he himself founded, the chapel  
> Of the Virgin, in praise of heaven, so that he might rest in the church.  
> May the Virgin Mary, the road to heaven, be gracious to him.

[Col. 1101A] **XXVIII. Michael of Castaneto**, commonly Catenay, born near Clermont in Beauvaisis. Formerly cellarer of the Flaviacum monastery, he carefully observed monastic discipline. He obtained confirmation of the privileges from Philip III, king of the Franks, in 1275. In August 1276 he granted certain possessions: “For the solemnity of the office to be performed on the anniversary of our death, and for repairing the books of our church,” he said.

Guillelmus and Reginaldus, castellans of Beauvais, lie buried in the church of the Mother of God the Virgin; their annual day of deposition is recorded from the year 1271. Other sacred tombs may also be seen in this same church.

[Col. 1101B] Michael paid nature’s debt on 4 August 1284 and was buried before the altar of that same church.

**XXIX. Petrus II.** King Philip IV of the Franks, at Petrus’s urging, granted the men of Flaviacum a diploma by which he declared all their immunities and possessions to be under royal protection, just as his predecessors had provided, in the year 1287. Petrus died on 23 September 1299.

**XXX. Fulco.** The monastery’s documents show that Fulco was dear to those within and outside the monastery and that he promoted the brothers’ concord and upright conduct. He acquired for the monastery the village of Reilly in the district of Vexin, where he arranged for an elegant chapel to be built, along with many other [Col. 1101C] properties. He was deprived of life on 17 January 1317; the inscription on his tomb is as follows:

> Under this stone Fulco lay hidden in the year one thousand three times,  
> And seven as well, with ten joined to it.  
> Happy the Church, fosterling of so great a shepherd.  
> Now she mourns, because such a pillar has been taken from her.  
> No one seemed better: whatever bitter  
> Or fortunate event occurred, he met it with an unchanging mind.  
> This abbot was humble, learned, and chaste,  
> A holy and prudent man, always a friend of peace.  
> This man knew no deceit, because he served you alone:  
> Do not let him perish, Christ, but grant him blessedness in heaven.

**XXXI. Robertus.** He died on 20 September 1333. He was buried in the church of the Virgin Mother of God and distinguished by this epitaph:

[Col. 1101D] “Here lies Brother Robertus de Marcellis, formerly abbot of this monastery. He migrated to the Lord in the year 1333, on the vigil of Saint Matthew. May his soul rest in peace.”

**XXXII. Joannes II.** A man of no insignificant reputation: feeling the burden of the office too heavily, he preferred to be subject rather than to preside. Therefore he laid it upon the shoulders of Arnulphus, a monk of distinguished life; and, having completed three years of religious living, he fell asleep in the Lord on 11 July 1353.

**XXXIII. Arnulphus.** In the year of the Christian era 1364, Charles, king of the Franks, vindicated the freedom of the men of Flaviacum by this rescript:

“Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to all who see these present letters, greetings. We make known [Col. 1102A] that when the religious men, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Saint-Germer of Flaviacum, in the diocese of Beauvais, because of a certain house with certain rents which they possess in the town of Beauvais, were compelled by the burgesses dwelling in that town to contribute and pay with them the tallages and impositions imposed in the said town for the repairs and fortifications necessary for it, they were thereby compelled to contribute and pay with them the tallages. The same religious men paid a certain share or portion during the wars, which could nevertheless cause them harm in the future.

“Therefore, since we desire with all our strength to preserve the liberties and franchises of ecclesiastical persons, we have granted and hereby grant to the same religious men, also by special grace, through these presents, that they and their said 610 house and the aforesaid rents shall henceforth remain entirely free and exempt from such contributions as aforesaid, or from other similar ones to be imposed in the future by the burgesses and inhabitants of the said town of Beauvais, just as they were before.

“And so that no prejudice may thereafter arise against the same religious men or their church because of such a contribution made while the wars were raging, notwithstanding any letters obtained or to be obtained to the contrary.

“Given at Paris on 1 March, in the year of the Lord 1364, in the first year of our reign. By the king, upon the report of the council. Signed at Reims.” [Col. 1102C]

Arnulphus ended his life in 1371, on 22 May.

**XXXIV. Joannes III.** After completing seven years of administration, he ended his life on 24 November 1378.

**XXXV. Joannes IV, Remon.** In accordance with ancestral custom, Charles, king of the Franks, issued letters confirming everything belonging by right to the Flaviacum monastery, in the seventeenth year of his reign, and in the year of Christ 1380.

Joannes de Rochers, doctor of canon law, formerly a monk of Flaviacum and administrator of the alms of the monastery of Fécamp, was summoned to govern the monastery of Fontenelle, or Saint-Wandrille, and finally met his last day on 4 May 1412.

[Col. 1102D] Joannes, bishop of Flaviacum, was buried on 31 August 1391 in the chapel of Saint-Germer, where his likeness is displayed.

**XXXVI. Eustachius II.** During the abbacy of this man, Queen Blanche of France, formerly wife of Philip VI, established annual divine offices to be performed with greater solemnity, as follows:

“Blanche, by the grace of God queen of France, makes known to all present and future who see this document that, because of the special devotion which we bear toward the church of Saint-Germer of Flaviacum, and in order to increase the worship of God there, we have granted and given, and by these presents grant and give, [Col. 1103A] the entire tithe of the village of Hardencourt in the parish of Ferrières, diocese of Beauvais, in our castellany of Gournay, with its rights and appurtenances, to be possessed perpetually.

“We recently acquired it from Joannes le Feure, called Fraillon, parish priest of Bellière, as is more fully contained in the letters drawn up concerning this matter. It is nevertheless stipulated that this tithe shall always be used entirely by the convent, and that no part of it shall ever be assigned to the abbot’s use.

“We have also today delivered to them, together with the aforesaid tithe, the sum of fifty gold francs, to be spent on repairs to the church and the other places subject to it, on this condition: each year, on our birthday, which is 2 April, for as long as we live, a solemn Mass of the Holy Spirit shall be celebrated in the aforesaid church, with deacon [Col. 1103B] and subdeacon clothed in dalmatic and tunicle, and with one collect, for the salvation of the souls of Philip, king of the Franks, our lord and beloved husband, and of Joanna, our daughter.

“After our departure from this life, each year on the day of our death, the solemn vigils and Mass for the dead shall be sung for the souls of the aforesaid lord King Philip, Joanna, and ourselves, with deacon and subdeacon clothed as above. We wish their names to be entered there in the Greater Missal and in the martyrology, so that this our ordinance may not be forgotten.

“In testimony and for the stability of this grant and of the acquisition of the aforesaid tithe, we have delivered these letters to the aforesaid religious men and ordered our seal to be affixed to them.

“Given in our castle of Neaufle, in the year of the Lord 1398, on 26 June.” [Col. 1103C]

John XXII, or XXIII, Supreme Pontiff, honored Abbot Eustachius with a privilege granting him the right to use pontifical ornaments during solemn sacred ceremonies. The letters read as follows:

“John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Eustachius, abbot, and the convent of the monastery of Saint-Germer of Flaviacum, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Beauvais, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“The sincerity of devotion and the excellence of religious conduct require me to raise to worthy honors both you, whom we cherish with special affection, [Col. 1103D] and your monastery. Therefore, yielding to your supplications, we grant you and your successors, the abbots of the said monastery, by apostolic authority and special grace, through these presents, the privilege of freely using the mitre, ring, and other pontifical ornaments whenever you hold office.

“We further grant that in the said monastery, and in the priories subject to it, and in the parish and other churches belonging to you jointly or separately, even though they are not fully subject to you by right, you may impart a solemn blessing after the celebration of Mass, Vespers, and Matins, provided that no bishop or legate of the Apostolic See is present for such blessing. The constitution of Pope Alexander IV, our predecessor of happy memory, beginning ‘Abbates,’ and all other apostolic constitutions to the contrary, shall in no way stand in the way.

“Let no one, therefore, be permitted to violate this document of our grant or rashly oppose it. Whoever should presume to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

611 “Given at Saint Anthony outside the Florentine walls, on the Kalends of November, in the fourth year of our pontificate.” [Col. 1104A]

[Col. 1104B] The English, together with the Burgundians who supported their side, captured the castle of Gondray, where the abbot and monks had taken refuge, through the treachery of Peter de Villequain, to whom it had been entrusted; they plundered everything, both sacred and secular vestments, books, charters, and other things of that kind.

Eustachius fulfilled his office and died on 28 August 1415.

**XXXVI. Joannes V.** After suffering many calamities for three years because of the depredations of soldiers, he departed this life in the year of the Lord 1418.

**XXXVII. Joannes VI, le Veneur**, illustrious for his reputation for integrity and learning. In the year of salvation 1456, the thirty-eighth of his rule, preferring quieter circumstances, he voluntarily resigned his office and entrusted it to [Col. 1104C] Petrus, a monk of Saint-Wandrille; after seven years, he departed from among men on 29 January 1462.

**XXXVIII. Petrus III**, surnamed Aubert, assumed control of the monastery after his predecessor’s resignation, with the approval of the entire congregation. Throughout almost the whole period of his administration he endured many labors to restore possessions that had been taken by force.

In the forty-sixth year of his rule, he received from Joannes, bishop of Beauvais, the lengthy document which we placed at the beginning of this Compendium. He ended his bodily life on 4 December 1500, in the Christian era.

[Col. 1104D] **XXXIX. Guido de Villiers de l’Isle-Adam**, born of noble stock. He was chosen by divine providence to bear the burden during those very storms of war and to restore to their former integrity all things that had been thrown into confusion. He recalled the scattered monks and supplied what was necessary for their sustenance. He restored the church and furnished it with sacred equipment. Finally, this excellent shepherd accomplished so many and such great things that he deserved, not without reason, to acquire the name of restorer.

At last, after enduring continual labors in repairing the monastery, the venerable Guido was summoned to heaven and buried on the right side of the choir. On his tombstone one may see his carved likeness together with the following epitaph:

“Here lies the Reverend Father in Christ, Dom Guido de Villers de l’Isle-Adam, monk and abbot of this monastery, who died in the year of the Lord 1536, on 23 June. May he rest in peace.”

[Col. 1105A] On the nearby wall this encomium is inscribed on a bronze plate:

“Here lies the Reverend Father in God, Guy de Villers, during his lifetime religious and abbot of this place, descended from and related to the noble and ancient houses of l’Isle-Adam and Aubremont; son of the high, noble, and powerful lord Messire Antoine de Villers, during his lifetime knight and lord of l’Isle-Adam, provost of Paris, etc., and of the noble lady Madame Jeanne de Nelle; brother of the late, good-memory Reverend Father Philippe de Villers, knight and Grand Master of Rhodes.

“Likewise brother of the late Reverend Father in God Louis de Villers, during his lifetime bishop-count of Beauvais, vidame of Gerberoy, and peer of France; uncle of the late Reverend Father in God Charles de Villers, likewise bishop-count of Beauvais. Also uncle of the noble and powerful lord and knight of the Order of the King our lord, Messire [Col. 1105B] Anne de Montmorency, lord and baron of Montmorency, count of Beaumont-sur-Oise, Grand Master, marshal of France, governor of Languedoc, and later constable of France; and of Messire François de Montmorency, lord of La Rochepot and Merlou, governor and lieutenant for the king in Picardy. The Most Reverend Odet de Coligny, commonly called de Châtillon, cardinal of the Holy See, archbishop of Toulouse, bishop-count of Beauvais, peer of France, etc., is nephew of these lords of Montmorency.

“This Guy de Villers, during his lifetime, after restoring the church of this place and doing many other good works, and, moreover, acquiring the land and lordship of Boisville, founded an obit to be celebrated thirteen times each year: namely, on the first Saturdays of each month and on the day on which he departed this world, which was the [Col. 1105C] twenty-third day of June in the year of grace 1536. Pray to God for his soul.”

**Commendatory abbots.**

**XLI. Joannes of Lorraine**, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, titular of Saint Onuphrius, retains the abbey in commendam, despite the opposition of the monks.

612 **XLI. Georgius of Narbonne**, through Joannes’s voluntary resignation.

**XLII. Franciscus de Tournon**, cardinal bishop.

**XLIII. Odettus de Coligny**, commonly called de Châtillon, infected with the Calvinist heresy; therefore, after he was expelled,

**XLIV. Carolus de Bourbon de Vendôme** obtained the administration in the year of Christ 1569.

[Col. 1105D] **XLV. Carolus de Bourbon de Vendôme**, nephew of the aforesaid Carolus.

**XLVI. Franciscus d’Espinay**, lord of Saint-Luc, claimed the revenues for himself, with Stephanus Auxdents as steward.

**XLVII. Franciscus de Monceaux de Villers-Hodanc**, after Franciscus d’Espinay’s resignation, took possession of the affairs of Flaviacum. Whenever he subscribed documents, he used the title “knight abbot.”

**XLVIII. Carolus de Monceaux**, to whom his brother Franciscus transferred the abbey, reserving for himself a pension of six thousand pounds.

**XLIX. Franciscus de Tiercelin de Brosse**, great-grandson through a niece of Carolus de Monceaux.

[Col. 1106A] In the year of the Lord 1644, Augustinus Potier, bishop of Beauvais, most distinguished for seriousness of character, piety, and learning, restored observance of the Benedictine Rule, partly by entreaties, partly by threats, and partly by authority, summoning for this purpose monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. By God’s favor, that observance still flourishes today. Thus that prelate acquired an immortal memory.

**(52) CHAP. XIV.**—Thus, after chapels had been built there near the church. Many authors report that this was often done, not only in the time of Guibert’s mother but also many centuries earlier. The extensive Chronicle of Bèze provides a notable memorial of this matter, namely a letter of Adalsinda, abbess, by which she surrendered both herself and everything she possessed to the monastery of Bèze and lived beside their church. We publish it here for the first time.

“To the holy lord and beloved brother in Christ, Waldalenus, Adalsinda, abbess.

“Since, harassed by the injuries of evil men and by various adversities, I could not remain there, I and my brother Adalricus asked you and your brothers that, in God’s name, we might live at the monastery of Saint Peter under its Rule and discipline; and you granted this out of your zeal for charity.

[Col. 1106B] “Therefore, in God’s name, you are to receive the monastery of Dornatiacum, situated in honor of Saint Martin, which my father Amalgarius and my mother Aquilina built and to which they assigned the greater part of their possessions, together with the villages belonging to that place and all its appurtenances in general—namely, the village of Assona, the village of Parniacum, Potentiacum, and the half which our parents held at Balatonna.

[Col. 1106C] “The remainder which our parents assigned to the monastery of Dornatiacum you shall from this day receive in God’s name. And from the estate of Montaniacum, which our father Amalgarius and Amoloaldus jointly obtained from the fisc, accept our share from this day under your authority, so that neither I nor anyone from our side, through any person appointed for the purpose, may presume to bring against you any claim or trouble concerning the matters mentioned above.

“If anyone should do so, let him pay, together with the sacred fisc, twenty pounds of gold and fifty weights of silver.

[Col. 1106D] “Publicly enacted at the monastery of Fonte-Bèze, in the name of God. I, Adalsinda, have subscribed this conveyance of ours. Aga, nun, at the command of my lady Adalsinda, have subscribed this donation. S. Dagnius. S. Munulfus, priest. S. Victor. S. Proculus. S. Walibertus. S. Landebertus. S. Trasgarius. S. Rogitus.

“I, Allo, wrote and dictated this conveyance, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1152, indiction 10, epact 6, while Clotharius was reigning in Francia, in the first year of his reign; when the venerable Donatus occupied the see of Besançon, on the Wednesday immediately before the middle of February.”

[Col. 1107A] The biographer of Saint Godefridus of Amiens, book I, chapter 27: “Adelheidis, viscountess of Cocy, displayed many distinguished examples of generosity and chastity. Having distributed a large part of her possessions among the poor, orphans, and churches, and having despised the pomp of the world, she came to Nogent and there led her life in great purity and holiness.” This occurred while Saint Godefridus was serving as abbot.

The Chronicle of Bec, at the end of the Works of Blessed Lanfranc, under the year 1089: “In the time of Saint Anselm, abbot of Bec, three noble matrons placed themselves under the authority of Bec: namely, Basilia, wife of Hugh of Gournay; Amfrida, niece of that same Basilia; and Eva, wife of William Crispin,” etc.

But what Gilbert Crispin reports in the Life of Blessed Herluin, page 35, after the Chronicle of Bec, cannot fail to amaze you: “In the same place,” he says, “his noble mother likewise devoted herself to servitude for God’s sake, and, having granted to God the estates she [Col. 1107B] possessed, she performed the work of a handmaid, washing the clothing of those serving God and carrying out with the greatest care whatever menial task was assigned to her.”

I shall add here, for the benefit of lovers of antiquity, a similar event that occurred a century later in the case of Jauseranna, born of the noblest lineage:

### 613

“Let those now living know, and let posterity learn, that in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1223, in the month of May, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, I, Janseranna, formerly the daughter of Lord Guillelmus of Medullio and formerly the wife of Bernard of Saint-Saturninus, dedicate myself to God, to the monastery of Saint Andrew, and to the church of Saint Lawrence of Barreto. For the salvation of my soul and of my parents, I give and offer to that monastery and to that church of Saint Lawrence certain portions of my paternal property, situated in the lower castle of Barreto, within and outside it, leaving the rest to my sons B., W., and B. I do this freely, under no compulsion, induced by no persuasion of anyone or of any persons, purely and without any agreement or condition, as an irrevocable gift made in perpetuity. I give, I say, seven homesteads of men, together with those men and their successors.”

After other clauses had been inserted:

“All the matters stated and named above, the aforesaid brothers, sons of the aforesaid Jauseranna, promised to Lord Bermundus, abbot of Saint Andrew, and to the prior of the aforesaid church of Saint Lawrence, that they would observe and preserve them accordingly and would never at any time act against them; and, touching the sacred Gospels, they swore this oath. Moreover, I, the aforesaid Jauseranna, make my profession, and subject myself to the authority and command of Lord Bermundus, the abbot, and of his successors; and, by command of that lord abbot, I promise, in the hands of Calverius, to live without personal property. I also promise to observe obedience and continence insofar as divine grace permits; I receive the monastic habit, and for as long as I live I promise to live according to the rule of blessed Benedict, and I renounce the period of probation.”

“And I, Bermundus, the aforesaid abbot, receive from you, Jauseranna, the profession you have made, and grant you the monastic habit.”

“And I, Raymbaudus of Kalma, chief lord of the lower castle of Barreto, approve and perpetually commend the aforesaid gift or offering, made by you, the aforesaid lady Jauseranna, with my consent and will, to the monastery of Saint Andrew and to the aforesaid church of Saint Lawrence; and I confirm it in the presence of your sons. For the greater remembrance of this matter and for its future validity, I have caused this charter to be strengthened by the protection of my seal. And all of us, the aforesaid brothers, sons of the aforesaid lady Jauseranna, by her command, strengthen this charter of the aforesaid gift or offering with the protection of our seals. This was enacted below the church of blessed Lawrence, in the meadow belonging to that church, in the presence of Lord Raymbaudus of Kalma, John of Andusia, official of the monastery of Saint Andrew, B. Laurgerius, prior of Saltus, Rainardus, and John Bertrandus, monks, Hugh of Pino, Raymond and William of Pino, brothers, and Bertrand of Pennis, knight,” and so forth.

This document from the archives of the abbey of Saint Andrew near Avignon was excerpted by my associate Dom Claude Chantelou, an experienced investigator of antiquity, while he was in those regions, and he kindly brought it to my attention.

### (53) CHAPTER XIV

“And with shoes pierced by incurable perforations.”

That is, he wore a shoe, or shoes, completely worn through. I conjecture that *partusura*, or *pertusura*, derives from the verb *pertundo*, “to pierce.”

Saint Roger, abbot of Ellant, conducted himself in this way: “He frequently wore perforated shoes for so long that straw came out through the soles.” His *Acts*, chapter 7, under 4 January in Bollandus.

Regarding the word *sutularis*, writers differ: some write *subtalaris*, others *sutalaris*, and some *sotularis*. In the *Life of Saint Gudila the Virgin*, chapter 2: “She used half-shoes, so that the upper part of her feet could be seen.” The author of the *Life of Saint Eguinus, Bishop of Worcester*, chapter 4, has *sotulares*. John, biographer of Saint Odo, book II, after the middle: *subtalares*. Ordericus Vitalis, *History*, book V, page 591, has *subtolares*; on page 596, *sotulares*. It is therefore clear that *sotulares* or *sutulares* was used for shoes or coverings of the feet.

### (54) CHAPTER XV

“To compose prose pieces and little verses.”

Only the prose, or, as it is called, the Sequence of Saint Geremar, remains; it is still sung on his feast day and bears this heading:

“Sequence for the feast of Saint Geremar, which Dom Guibertus, a monk of this church, composed by his own ingenuity. It begins:

> The chief subject is present,  
> Brothers,  
> In harmony with the day;  
> Give forth praises,

and so forth.

What prose and antiphons are is explained by Saint Isidore, *Etymologies*, book I, chapter 37, and book VI, chapter 19.

### (55) CHAPTER XVI

“For I suffered many envious attacks,” and so forth.

Hence he cannot refrain from repeatedly recalling in his writings the troubles inflicted upon him—especially at the beginning of each book of his *Commentaries on Genesis*, and also in the letter addressed to Odo, abbot of Sansymphorianum, prefixed to the book *On the Relics of the Saints*.

### (56) SAME PLACE

“Whose name and relics.”

I believe that by these words he means the undergarment or shirt of that glorious Virgin, on whose account the celebrated shrine at Chartres is famous.

### (57) CHAPTER XVII

“Impressed on no tablets.”

In former times it was customary for writers to inscribe the offspring of their minds with a stylus on wax tablets or writing tablets; afterwards, when they had revised them with file and anvil, they copied them onto parchment. An example survives at the end of the *Life of Saint Boniface of Mainz*, by Saint Willibald, published by Serrarius:

“I, Wilibald, bishop, and so forth, composed the life and passion of Boniface, first on wax tablets for the examination of Lullus and Megengaudus. After their review I recopied it on parchment,” and so forth.

### 614

That the place where monks formerly devoted themselves to writing was customarily called a *scriptorium* is attested, among countless testimonies of the ancients, by the very old *Sacramentary* of our monastery of Corbie, under the title “Prayer in the Scriptorium,” which reads as follows:

“Deign to bless, O Lord, this scriptorium of your servants and all who dwell in it, so that whatever of the divine Scriptures is read or written by them, they may understand with their minds and grasp in their works. Through the Lord,” and so forth.

### (58) CHAPTER XXI

“With a rattling signal.”

The author himself explains more clearly what he intends to suggest in that passage in chapter 23 or 24, page 486, column C:

“To summon the rest of the community, they strike a board according to custom.”

This practice continued in monasteries down to our own times, alongside bells and small bells: boards or wooden mallets were used to summon the monks to certain private exercises or to rouse them from sleep.

*Lives of the Fathers*, book V, little book 17, no. 20: “Strike the signal in the brothers’ cell, so that they may all gather here.”

Cassian, *Institutes of the Renunciatory Life*, book IV, chapter 12: “When they hear the sound of someone knocking at the door and striking the various cells—inviting them, of course, to prayer or to some work—each one rushes eagerly from his chamber.”

Adolius of Tarsus, *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 14: “At the appointed time he struck the cells of all with the rousing mallet,” and so forth.

Lanfranc, *Decrees for the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 9: “Let the infirmarian take care of administering the board, which the prior strikes according to custom,” and so forth.

And chapter 23, concerning those near death: “When he sees that the man is already struggling as he departs, carrying a board in his hand, let him run to the cloister door and strike it sharply and repeatedly until he knows that the sound has been heard in the community.”

The *Declarations of the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 8: “All the brothers were awakened from door to door by the noise of the little mallets.”

### (59) SAME PLACE

“As is monastic custom, laid upon a hair shirt.”

In former times nothing was more customary than to place those professed in the ascetic life, when they were at the point of death, upon a hair shirt and ashes, so that they might more closely imitate the example of the Son of God passing from the cross to glory.

In the passage of blessed Lanfranc’s *Decrees* cited immediately above:

“When a sick man lies in agony, the brother appointed for this purpose shall spread out a hair shirt, and upon it, within the length of the hair shirt itself, shall make the sign of the cross from ashes; then he shall place the dying brother upon it,” and so forth.

What the custom was in the Cluniac congregation in the time of blessed Hugh is expressed in statute 26. Although the passage is lengthy, it will not be unwelcome to insert it, since it contains many things deserving of notice:

#### Concerning the death and burial of a brother

“A brother who, as his illness grows worse, feels that he is soon to depart from this world shall confess his entire conscience to the lord abbot or the prior. If he wishes to go to the chapter, he shall inform the prior either personally or through the infirmarian. Afterwards, if he is so weak, two brothers shall lead him between them; he asks pardon and confesses himself guilty of many negligences against God and against them. The prior absolves him, with all responding, ‘Amen.’ He himself absolves all if they have offended against him, and all bow more deeply from their seats.

“Afterwards he is led back. Once returned, he asks to be anointed with the oil of the sick. He is then placed in a bed of a certain kind—that is, one lowered to the ground—where the brothers can stand around him on every side. The prior who is in charge informs the sacristan, and the sacristan prepares everything necessary for this purpose: namely, a priest, whom he has clothed in an alb and stole; lay brothers to carry holy water, the cross, and candlesticks; and he himself carries the oil.

“When everything has been prepared, the procession goes first, and the priest follows; then, according to ancient custom, the entire community follows, the fiftieth Psalm having been begun, and afterwards, if necessary, other things are added,” and so forth.

A little later comes the following:

“Meanwhile the priest performs the anointing in this manner. He coats his thumb with oil and, with his thumb, impresses the sign of the cross over each eye, saying: ‘Through this anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord forgive you whatever you have sinned through sight.’ Over each ear: ‘through hearing.’ Over both lips: ‘through taste.’ Over the nose: ‘through smell.’ Over the hands: ‘through touch.’ (And the brother turns toward the inside, if the priest is on the outside.) Over the feet: ‘through walking.’ Over the loins: ‘through the burning of lust.’

“When this has been done, he washes his hands, first rubbing them in ashes. Formerly this was done on crusts of wheat bread. This washing is customarily poured out only into a fire or in a clean and hidden place. Then, if the sick man does not receive Communion, the priest alone says all these collects, after the following petitions have been recited: ‘Save your servant,’ and so forth.

“After they have come into the church, either the priest himself or the sacristan takes from the sacristy one of the ordinary chalices—having first washed his hands—and pours in wine and water as though Mass were about to be sung. The priest then approaches the high altar, upon which the Lord’s body is kept, and before receiving it he censes it. Afterwards, having taken it, he breaks it over the chalice; he holds over the chalice the portion he is going to bring, and puts the other portion into a pyx. Then both the priest’s hands and the chalice are covered by the sacristan with a very clean cloth.

“If the community is in choir at that time, when he departs from the altar the entire community asks pardon out of reverence for the Lord’s body. The brothers do the same wherever they see him passing. Meanwhile care is taken to wash the sick man’s mouth, since he is to receive the Lord’s body.

“Before he receives it, the *Confiteor* is said, and when the brothers respond together, ‘May he have mercy upon you,’ the priest alone continues: ‘Pardon and remission of all your sins,’ and so forth. The Lord’s body is dipped into wine mixed with water. After drinking it, he also drinks the ablution of the chalice; and, if he can, the ablution from the priest’s fingers as well. If he cannot, another drinks it.

“The priest also brings the cross to him, so that he may adore and kiss it. He also kisses the priest, as though about to bid a final farewell; then all the brothers, and, according to ancient custom, the boys as well. The community returns.

“After a brother has come to such an illness, a servant is assigned to him who has nothing else to do except attend the sick man. At night all the servants in the infirmary keep careful watch, lest his death occur unexpectedly. A cross is fixed opposite his face, and the light of a candle does not fail until broad daylight.

“If there is a brother so religious that, out of singular devotion, he wishes to remain and keep watch with the sick man himself, the prior willingly permits it. The servants who are greatly practiced and experienced in such matters, when they see that the hour of his departure is already approaching, spread a hair shirt on the ground, scatter ashes in the form of a cross, and, lifting the sick man from his bed, place him upon the hair shirt.

“Then the infirmarian must notify the prior that the brother is so near his end. If the sick man still has his memory, the prior orders one of the brothers to read the Passion narratives before him. If he no longer has it, he orders two or four brothers to sing psalms there without interruption until it is known and evident that the soul is about to leave the body without lengthy delay.

“When the servant, who is well trained and accustomed to this office, sees this, only then is he to seize the board and strike it forcefully and with great haste in the cloister before the dormitory steps—first, if it is night, lighting the lamps in the infirmary cloister, and through the passage by which one goes into the infirmary,” and so forth.

Thus far the manuscript book.

Peter the Venerable describes the place where the body of the dying was customarily laid down, *On Miracles*, chapter 19:

“There is, moreover, at Cluny, in the central house of the infirmary, a place capable of holding one body, prepared for this purpose, so that the brothers, placed there upon ashes and a hair shirt, may give their final breath to God,” and so forth.

He also adds, in the same book, chapter 4, that this is the custom of Christians and “especially of monks,” who sought, not merely in writing and speech but above all when they had risen to higher positions and presided over churches, to draw people promptly toward the stricter and more rigorous practices of the ancient Christians—as the very learned John de Launoy rightly observed—“so that they might be conformed to the image of the Son of God” (Romans 8:29), and so forth.

The Apostle says, “that they might be conformed to the image of the Son of God” (Romans 8:29). Indeed, Saint Benedict says in chapter 58 and in the prologue to his Rule that “hard and rough are the ways by which one goes to God, for the correction of vices and the preservation of charity,” and that they wholly befit those who have given their name to Christ. Gregory the Great calls Saint Benedict “the best teacher of the strictest life” in book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 9.

Hence, in the schools of monks, who were instructed both in piety and in learning, they retained so deeply in their minds what they had learned through sight and practice that afterwards, throughout their lives, they expressed it in their conduct.

Let Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, stand as an example for all. His father, Philip, had offered him as a boy to be educated under the discipline of the monks of Saint-Denis. As a result, he became both most Christian and most prudent and wise, as the eyewitness Suger testifies in his life.

The same author indicates what example of religion that pious king left when he was near death:

“He, being prudent in counsel and caring for himself, and so forth, desired above all things, with the whole affection of his soul, that he be carried in whatever manner to the holy martyrs, his protectors, Denis and his companions, and before their most sacred bodies, laying down his kingdom and crown, profess the monastic order of blessed Benedict upon the ground—crown for crown, and monastic poverty for royal and imperial ornaments. Let those who disparage monastic poverty observe how not only archbishops but kings themselves, preferring eternal life to the transitory, flee with complete security to the singular protection of the monastic order.”

And below, near the end:

“Accordingly, having ordered a carpet to be placed on the ground and ashes to be laid upon the carpet in the middle of the cross, he was placed there by the hands of his own people; strengthening his presence with the sign of the holy cross, and so forth, he gave up his spirit.”

Thus it is found in volume IV of the *History of France* by André Duchesne.

### (60) CHAPTER XXIII

“To the abbot of the monastery called ‘of the Battle.’”

It was so called because of the battle in which William the Conqueror defeated Harold on the coast of Sussex. Selden reports the charter of its foundation in his notes on Eadmer’s *History of Recent Events*, page 165:

“William, by the grace of God king of England, and so forth. Let it be known to you that I have granted and confirmed, with the assent of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and so forth, that the church of Saint Martin of the Battle, which I founded by vow for the victory that God granted me in that place, shall be free and undisturbed from every form of servitude,” and so forth.

He wished to exempt it entirely from both lay and episcopal jurisdiction.

### (61) SAME PLACE

“Mass for blessed Mary, and daily Mass of her.”

This is certainly a most praiseworthy custom, received from ancient times in monasteries of the Benedictine order: namely, to sing Mass every day at the sixth hour of the morning in honor of the Virgin Mother of God. *Chronicle of Bec*, page 17.

### (62) CHAPTER XXIV

“The cowl.”

That is, *cuculla* and *cucullio*. It is a kind of covering for the head, called by the author, through a corrupt form of the word, *capero*, in French *chaperon*. On this subject see our Menardus on chapter 62 of the *Harmony of the Rules*. The reason why cenobites use this kind of garment is explained there, page 887. Benedict Haeften also treats the cowl, and its various uses, at great length and not without learning, *Monastic Investigations*, treatise 3, investigation 1.

### (63) CHAPTER XXVI

“To Lisiardus, archdeacon of Beauvais, my uncle.”

Ivo of Chartres addressed letter 92 to him. But whether this same Lisiardus was later endowed with the bishopric of Soissons is uncertain. Rather, it seems necessary to conclude that at this same period there were two persons of the same name: one the archdeacon of Beauvais, who is mentioned here, and the other raised from the provostship of Soissons to that see. For our author, in that passage, and below in book III, chapter 11, as well as in the preface to the *History of the Deeds of God through the Franks*, gives no indication at all that Lisiardus of Soissons was related to him; rather, he presents him as not particularly well known or familiar.

## TO THE SECOND BOOK

### (64) CHAPTER I

“For it is called Novientum.”

What, indeed, could I say about that monastery, worthy of lamentation? Calvinist fury shook, plundered, and devastated it more than once. Indeed, the commendatory abbots themselves, infected with this unspeakable heresy and, as secular men, joined in marriage, squandered whatever resources remained and handed over the charters either to the fire or to friends and relatives, so that they might more easily add the revenues sacred to God to their own possessions, lawfully or unlawfully.

The remaining documents and instruments, however, were left in the monastery with such supine negligence that they now lie rotted under the rainwater or gnawed through by cockroaches and moths. Nevertheless, with the greatest care and through immense labor and zeal, the Reverend Father Dom Simeon Maubaillard, of our congregation and formerly prior in that monastery, a man of no ordinary learning, rescued the remnants of the charters that had survived so great a destruction. We shall insert some of them into our observations below.

Furthermore, the learned Souchet has reviewed much concerning Novientum in his notes on the life of blessed Bernard of Tiron, page 246.

### (65) SAME PLACE

“Among the English, before the Incarnation of the Word,” and so forth.

If the things which the author relates throughout this chapter seem astonishing to you, nevertheless take care, I ask, not to brand him with ignorance, fraud, or calumny. For although there was profound silence about these matters among both sacred writers—especially Luke the Apostle—and secular authors, particularly those who wrote about British affairs, and although the mind may in some way shrink from believing certain things in this narrative, what crime or fault, I ask, did he commit when he openly disclosed what he found recorded in writing by his ancestors? None at all.

For he does not present these things as matters to be believed with unquestionable certainty. They are historical accounts; they contain nothing absurd and do not openly display anything false. That is sufficient.

Indeed, Guibertus, an eyewitness, testifies that everything corresponds to the tomb and to the other more ancient monuments that remained:

“There are, however,” he says, “in that same church certain writings composed in verse, which I would rely upon with no authority at all, unless I saw that certain things which greatly strengthen their credibility still exist today. The history is handed down as having occurred in this way, according to the sequence of the writing,” and so forth.

Do you see how, although these things are handed down in those verses, he does not commit them to writing as though they were more certain than certainty itself?

At the end of the chapter, when he has discussed the sacred relics brought to Novientum by King Quilius, he adds:

“After a very long time, by God’s providence, the casket was brought out and, covered by certain faithful persons—whether I know who—with plates of precious gold made by ancient craftsmanship, it came before the sight of our age and continues to offer new testimony to the ancient accounts. Thus the beginnings of that place are said to have been as follows.”

It is therefore enough, learned reader, to place as much faith in Guibertus’s account as other good authors deserve for the things they have transmitted to posterity. Have not many, and even the most weighty authors, inserted into their writings histories which they had received from others or learned by reading? Witness Saint Gregory the Great in his *Dialogues*; Gregory of Tours in *On the Glory of the Confessors* and elsewhere; and, in Guibertus’s age, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, in his book *On Miracles*.

Moreover, no one is unaware that in the regions of Britain there were almost as many petty kings as there were strongly fortified cities. It is therefore not surprising if British writers make no mention of Quilius.

I wish, therefore, to warn you in advance, learned reader, not to detract from the authority of so great a man when you encounter something that may perhaps give your mind occasion to hesitate, and thus make little of matters deserving the greatest confidence. Rather, may you be able to regard as carefully selected those things that preceded the author in past ages, those that lay before his own eyes, and those that occurred in his own time.

### (66) SAME PLACE

“Therefore the castle has no antiquity.”

Papirius Masso vividly describes Codiciacum according to the author’s conception in *Description of France by Its Rivers*:

“Codiciacus is a place situated high and prominently, naturally fortified, and overlooking on every side the plain lying beneath it, an exceedingly fertile plain that may be called the marrow of the earth. No one, so far as I know, who lived before Flodoard has called it Codiciacum. It lies within the boundaries of the city and bishopric of Laon and is included within the territory of the Viromandui.”

### (67) SAME PLACE

“By the river which we mentioned above, the Aquila,” and so forth.

The common people now call it the Elette or Ailette; antiquity called it the Aiglette.

### (68) SAME PLACE

“If the woman not yet born who was to give birth to God and man.”

There is a similar tradition concerning that distinguished church at Chartres: namely, that before the coming of the Incarnate Word it was dedicated by the Druids to the Virgin who was to give birth. On this matter I believe that no conclusion should be made.

### (69) CHAPTER II

“But under the most flourishing princes of the castle itself,” and so forth.

André Duchesne has composed the history of the lords of Codiciacum. If you are especially eager to know anything about them, consult him; he will satisfy you.

### (70) SAME PLACE

“He presided over the monastery of Humolarium.”

It would seem that I were merely repeating what had already been done if I inserted into our observations a history or list of the abbots of this monastery, since our Claude Hemeraeus, doctor of the Sorbonne, worked extensively and with great learning on this subject during his lifetime in his *History: Augusta Viromanduorum Illuminated*, page 65 and pages 94–99.

Nevertheless, so that I may not leave the reader’s mind entirely empty, I thought it useful to append a very small portion from page 65:

“Almost up to the very walls of Augusta [Saint-Quentin], the monastery of Humolarium became famous, while Eligius occupied the episcopal see of Noyon, for the remarkable holiness of its nuns, but especially when its administration was entrusted to the virgin Hunegundis. She was born among the household retainers of Lambaidus, two miles from Augusta, and so forth. Bernerus, abbot and chronicler of the reform of that place, wrote her life under Albert the Pious, count of the Viromandui, in the year 948, after the nuns who had departed from the rule had been expelled.”

You will find the *Life of Saint Hunegundis* among the lives of the saints edited by Surius, under 25 August. You will also find the command of Louis from overseas concerning the introduction of monks into the monastery of Humolarium after the nuns had been expelled, together with various charters relating to the matter, in the register at the end of the aforesaid history, page 29 and following.

### (71) SAME PLACE

“And they also placed Henry in charge of a small monastery.”

When you hear that Henry was placed in charge of three asceteries, you must not suppose that he appropriated their revenues and possessions for private use, as though he had been afflicted by the stain and plague of sacrilege and by that obstinate wickedness which infected later ages to such an extent that it seems to have resisted and overcome every remedy up to the present: namely, that infamous separation, by royal or princely grant, of the revenues of abbeys and churches into lay or secular benefices.

On the contrary, he allowed these burdens to be laid upon him and willingly undertook them, following the examples of those distinguished archimandrites renowned for religion and holiness: Benedict of Aniane and William of Dijon, or of Fécamp, who restored the monastic canons, disfigured by the corruption of the age, to their former purity.

Concerning the former, see the diploma of the emperor Louis the Pious in volume II of the *Gallican Councils*, and the letter of the fathers of the monastery of Inda to the monks of Aniane at the end of the *Life*, which precedes the works of Saint Benedict himself.

Concerning Saint William, the manuscript chronicle of the monastery of Bèze (*Besuensis*), of which he was also abbot, says:

“But because he watched over the flock entrusted to him with diligent care, by divine grace he deserved to rejoice in this life in the fruit of his works. For he restored by correction to its original state the regular discipline that had already fallen through the negligence of former times, as Saint Benedict had established it; and throughout various parts of the world, in many monasteries that had strayed from the regular path, he subjected them to the monastic order, both personally and through those whom he had appointed abbots.”

It relates below that, at the request of Richard, duke of the Normans, he undertook the governance of the abbey of Fécamp.

After other intervening material:

“King Robert also asked the aforesaid Father [William] to take over the abbey of Saint-Germain in Paris and regulate it according to the regular institution, which he did. Count Odo likewise, with equal devotion, entrusted to the same venerable Father the monastery of Saint-Faron in the city of Meaux; and the honorable bishop of the church of Metz, Theodoric, commended the abbey of Gorze to him with the same zeal for God,” and so forth.

Finally, the handwritten *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*, under Bruno, bishop of Langres, says:
