“Now Lord Bruno, observing that Father William was so fervent in religion and monastic discipline, and that the places entrusted to him were progressing from day to day toward improvement, delegated all the monasteries in his bishopric to his care,” and so forth.

### (72) SAME PLACE

“And Saint-Quentin of the Mount,” and so forth.

The abbey of Saint-Quentin is situated on a hill, a mile from the city of Péronne, at a distance from it. There is another abbey dedicated to Saint Quentin at Augusta Viromanduorum, commonly called l’Abbaye d’Ille or de l’Ile—the abbey of Saint Quentin in the Island—so called because, before that city was captured by Philip II, king of Spain, it stood beside the Somme River. It is now in the middle of the city of Augusta Viromanduorum. Sigebert mentions it under the year 964.

For the monastery of Saint-Quentin of the Mount, which was levelled to the ground by the Normans, no records of its original foundation have survived to us except the charter of Adalbert, count of the Viromandui. From it we can learn both about its restoration and something about the origin of that monastery:

“I, Adalbert, count, wish it to be known to those present and to those who will come after that, from ancient times, there existed in my county of Vermandois a church dedicated in honor of Saint Quentin the martyr, situated on a mountain near the town of Péronne. Once, by the authority of King Dagobert, through the donation of the prefect Erchenaldus and the blessing of Saint Eligius the bishop, a certain Ultanus, a Scot by birth and a monk by profession, established it according to ecclesiastical sanctions and monastic institutions and held the office of abbot. After his death, through neglect and the attacks of barbarians, the church itself fell into such desolation that scarcely any traces of its former habitation were visible.

“I therefore, moved by divine inspiration, ordered it to be rebuilt from its foundations for the remedy of my soul and the salvation of my predecessors and heirs; and, having appointed an abbot, I endeavored, with the counsel of my faithful men, to endow the abbey, so that this might remain forever confirmed and undisturbed.

“These are the properties of this endowment: in the district of Vermandois, one small estate called Aisilcourt; and in the same district, in a place called Curticulus, seven homesteads, together with half the church of Duriacum; at Black Castle on the river Ingon, a bridge with the land belonging to it; in Tegeri, two homesteads; and in the place called Saint Radegundis, three homesteads.

“In the village, half the chapel of Saint Quentin, with fourteen tenants. In the estate of Alania, on the river Halle, twelve tenants, with arable land and one meadow. The estate called Vivarius, with its dependencies, on the river Grinsio, belongs to the church of that mountain. In the estate called Douin, one mill, with a third part of the meadow belonging to it. In the district of Soissons, in the estate called Allemans, three homesteads with a demesne court.

“Therefore, with respect to these properties given to the holy lord martyr Quentin, none of my heirs or relatives, neither count nor viscount nor any freeborn man of his, shall henceforth receive anything by way of customary due or advocacy—neither ban, justice, nor jurisdiction—unless at the faithful request of the abbot of that abbey. Whoever presumes to violate this shall, for the audacity of his presumption, be subject to threefold curses and shall be compelled by public laws to repent. The witnesses and approvers of this act have confirmed it:

“I, Adalbert, count, who ordered this to be done, have confirmed it.

“Seal of Heribert, count; seal of Vidon, count; seal of Philbert; seal of Luntbertus; seal of Walchisius; seal of Odo; seal of Ivo; seal of Boslevus; seal of Walcelinus; seal of Amalricus; seal of Walnerus; seal of Odo; seal of Macharius.

“I, Leudulfus, bishop of the church of Vermandois and Noyon, have subscribed and confirmed.

“Enacted at the court of Saint Quentin, on the day of his passion.”

A brief chronology of the abbots must also be added, drawn from the ancient charters and ruins of that monastery by the learned and eloquent Reverend Father Dom Stephen le Gris, now the most deserving prior of our congregation. In order not to exceed the limits of our undertaking, we shall condense it in as brief a style as possible.

#### Summary Chronology of the Abbots of the Monastery of Saint-Quentin of the Mount

The proto-abbot, Saint Ultanus, born of royal blood in Ireland and distinguished both for outstanding holiness and for exceptional knowledge of monastic discipline, was appointed abbot of Saint-Quentin of the Mount in the year 643 of the restored salvation, by Erchenaldus, count of the Viromandui, as is evident from the aforesaid charter of Adalbert.

He departed to heaven in the year of Christ 686.

**II. Evraldus.** The same charter records that, after the monastery had been restored, he was appointed abbot in the year 943 of the Christian era. Yet shortly thereafter—for all earthly things are subject to change and decline—the buildings again fell so far from their former restoration that they scarcely deserved the name of a cell, much less the title of an abbey.

But Robert, prefect of the city of Péronne, a man distinguished for his religion, who possessed the place by right of benefice, obtained letters from Robert, king of the Franks, compelling the unjust possessors of the monastery’s resources to restore what they had taken away. Afterwards, in the year 1028, he repaired the monastery at his own expense, and did not wish the monks to lack estates and resources.

**III. Baldwin.** Distinguished by the noble lineage of the counts of Flanders and Namur, 1028.

**IV. Walteranus.** He died in 1040.

**V. Walteranus II.** In the year 1040. The obituary records of him: “The wisest organizer and builder of this church from its foundations.” When he came to Rome on a devout pilgrimage, however, he there ended his life and left his body to be buried.

**VI. Gaudefridus.** 1058.

Nicholas the monk, author of the *Life of Saint Gaudefridus*, who had that abbot as his teacher, commends him in this way in book I, chapter 2:

“There is a famous monastery in the territory of the Viromandui, founded in honor of blessed Quentin the martyr and situated near the town of Péronne. At that time a pious man, Godefridus, presided over it, distinguished both by integrity of conduct and by nobility of birth. For he was the paternal uncle of Ida, daughter of Albert, the most noble count of Namur, who was married to the distinguished consul Eustace of the province of Boulogne, and so forth.

“These things have been recalled by me so that the illustrious lineage of so great a father may be understood. It is also established that he watched over his flock with great care; he was exceedingly famous for his religion and especially well instructed in literary knowledge and in the understanding of external and political affairs.”

The same book contains much more about Godefridus in chapters 3, 4, and following.

Having breathed out his soul, he entered his heavenly homeland in 1098.

**VII. Henry.** 1098. A man of the highest piety and learning; he died in 1133.

**VIII. Hugh.** 1133. He died in 1148.

Pope Eugenius III approves his rights and possessions in these words:

“Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Quentin of the Mount, situated in the district of Vermandois, and to his brothers, both present and future, and so forth. It is fitting for the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious men, and so forth. See under Eugenius III, at the year 1153.”

620 **IX. Roger**, formerly a monk of Aquicinctum, was made abbot of Mont-Saint-Quentin in 1148. Concerning him, see the *Biographer of Blessed Goswin*, Book II, chapter 12, where, mentioning the disciples of that venerable man, he says: “Roger diligently watched over Mont-Saint-Quentin.” He departed this life in 1150.

**X. Hugh II**, in 1150. “Hugh, abbot of Corbie [Col. 1118D] and of this congregation.” *Obituary*.

A letter of Lucius III, supreme pontiff, to Hugh, in which the authority of the monastery’s immunities and exemption is confirmed, was handed down in the following form:

“Lucius, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Mont-Saint-Quentin and his brothers, both present and future, etc. To grant the effect to those who make just petitions, etc. See under Lucius III, for the year 1185.”

621 Hugh died in 1182, or 1185.

**XI. Baldwin II.** He gave up his spirit in 1188.

**XII. Robert.** The year of his death is given in the Martyrology as 1192.

**XIII. Walter**, 1192. At the compulsion of the monks, he relinquished the office in 1198.

[Col. 1119A] **XIII. Walter II.** In the flower of his age, distinguished by lineage and character, he was unanimously elected. He governed the monastery so vigorously that he surpassed both expectation and his years. He was exceedingly devoted to regular discipline and to the other virtues. He increased its resources and built a chapel of the Blessed Virgin. He amassed a vast sum of money in order to construct the sacred basilica from its foundations; but, overtaken by death in 1241, he left the completion of the work to his successor. Some assert that Walter sprang from the illustrious family of Hardecourt.

**XIV. Simon de Valencourt**, 1241. Following in the footsteps and obeying the final wishes of his predecessor, he built the church in the magnificent structure visible today. He exchanged life for death in 1257, in the year of the Virgin’s birth.

[Col. 1119B] **XV. Gerard of Péronne**, 1257. A vigorous defender of rights, privileges, and immunities, he completed his mortal course in 1267.

**XVI. Robert**, 1267. He likewise opposed himself with a courageous spirit lest the monastery’s privileges be violated. Persuaded by advanced age, he voluntarily resigned the office in 1275 and departed this life a few days later.

**XVII. Baldwin III.** He did not conduct the office religiously. He died in 1280.

**XVIII. Matthew.** He was gentle and mild, and was also the author of many buildings. He departed this life in 1293.

**XIX. John de Villaribus**, a man of no ignoble birth, originating from Saint-Quentin. At this very time, when the ancient grandeur of the church of Mont-Saint-Quentin [Col. 1119C] had fallen into decay, and its possessions—transferred to outsiders and mortgaged because of debts contracted by his predecessors—had left the monks in utter poverty, he was finally overwhelmed by misfortunes and withdrew to Péronne. There, having spent his life in ashes and sackcloth, he breathed his last in 1313.

**XX. John II.** Born of the distinguished family of Hinchin. He is noted as an energetic administrator of domestic affairs. For by singular foresight he freed the monastery, burdened with debt, from its obligations. He repaired most of the buildings disfigured by ruins. Ecclesiastical affairs, and the more decent and attentive performance of the divine office, lay especially close to his heart. Finally, he showed a father’s compassion toward the monks and the poor. [Col. 1119D] He was translated to heaven in 1337.

**XXI. John III**, called “the Horseman” because of his skill at riding. Having laid aside his canonical habit, he put on the monastic cowl in the monastery of Mont-Saint-Quentin and was made abbot in 1337. He died in 1361.

**XXII. John IV**, of Hercourt de Combles, 1361. He walked with more magnificent display than was suitable for a humble servant of Christ; nevertheless, he was exceedingly dear and familiar to his own people. He closed his final day in 1370.

**XXIII. Hugh III**, of Augusta Viromanduorum, that is, a citizen of Saint-Quentin. Whether willingly or because of his insufficiently provident administration, he squandered the monastery’s goods. He died in 1379.

[Col. 1120A] **XXIV. Peter de Barville**, 1379. He consumed what remained of the resources and pledged them away. He died in 1398.

622 **XXV. Matthew de Dury**, 1398. He is marked by extraordinary thrift. For when he saw that ruin had been brought upon the possessions, decay upon the buildings, and a cloud upon the ancient splendor of discipline, he repaired and restored everything through prolonged labor and the greatest diligence. He surrendered to nature in 1413.

**XXVI. John V de Hennon**, 1413. He died in 1438.

**XXVII. James Rausson.** First in sacred service to the duke of Burgundy, then professing the monastic life, he was endowed with the priory of Lehuno in Santerre (Lihon-en-Santerre); then he was elected abbot of Mont-Saint-Quentin in 1461, and finally abbot of Old Corbie. He died at the age of eighty in 1480.

“He was everywhere a most gentle man [Col. 1120B] (as the manuscript *Chronicle of Corbie* relates), and exceedingly humane; he was highly learned in grammatical science, an excellent writer, and magnificent and splendid. Although born in a humble station, he nevertheless proved himself outstanding in every respect. At communal gatherings and banquets he was very witty, and in jesting he was an exceedingly amusing mocker.”

This is entirely at odds with the gravity of the holy rule of monks and of ecclesiastical institutions.

**XXVIII. John VI Dansquenet.** He laid down his life together with the abbacy in 1481.

**XXIX. John VII Karquendlan**, canon of Poitiers and apostolic protonotary. He was the first to seize the abbacy as a commendatory benefice, in 1481. But the monks caused him much trouble; consequently, worn down by vexation [Col. 1120C] and consumed by grief, he ended his day in 1487.

**XXX. John VIII d’Estrée**, descended from an ancient noble family and bound by monastic vows. The brothers adopted him as their father; he was also confirmed by the supreme pontiff in 1487 and adorned with pontifical insignia in 1505. He departed this world the following year, 1506.

### Commendatory Abbots

**XXXI. Louis de Constin** obtained the abbacy, together with that of Souillac, as a commendatory benefice in 1506.

**XXXII. Anthony Ragault**, Louis’s nephew, took possession in 1527.

**XXXIII. John IX de Genouillac**, 1532.

**XXXIV. Verdun du Mas**, 1544. He died in 1563.

**XXXV. James d’Aplincourt**, 1563. He was removed from the world [Col. 1120D] in 1575.

**XXXVI. Francis Pascanet.** He was the king’s almoner and a canon of the Church of Bourges in 1575. But, with the consent of Marshal de La Châtre, whom he had chosen as his procurator, he resigned the abbacy in 1596.

**XXXVII. Sebastian Robelin**, chief officer of the supreme senate of Paris. Nicholas Damerval, lord of Liencourt, acted as his representative. He departed this life in 1613.

**XXXVIII. Claude d’Argouges**, than whom no one of this age was more distinguished in conduct and manner of life. Having taken possession in 1613, he raised the monastery, whose buildings were dilapidated and indeed nearly collapsing into utter ruin. He rebuilt from the foundations the dormitory, cloister, chapter house, and refectory—in short, all the buildings commonly called the regular buildings—at his own enormous expense and caused them to be constructed. He supported the basilica with new works, adorned it with sacred furnishings of various kinds, enriched it with silver vessels, and, most importantly, desiring to bring the light of regular discipline to Mont-Saint-Quentin, handed the same monastery over to monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, who were thoroughly instructed in that discipline, to possess.

**XXXIX. Francis d’Argouges**, Claude’s nephew and his immediate imitator in virtue, a doctor of the Sorbonne. Concerning him, if I may rise to the level of sacred prophecy—“Praise him after death; magnify him after the end”—I think silence is preferable.

[Col. 1121B] **(73) CHAPTER II.**—“Therefore, when that man had been elected,” etc. Since the author passes over in silence the manner in which the election and blessing were to be carried out, I am pleased to publish what came into my hands while I was making these notes.

First, it must be observed that kings or princes were formerly accustomed to confirm the elections of abbots—and likewise of bishops—after the power of electing had been granted both to clerics and to monks. Hence certain modern writers, entirely ignorant of ecclesiastical affairs, have dared to conclude that these same kings possess supreme power and supreme right over all churches and abbeys, and can use them according to their pleasure and inclination.

The reason for such approval or concession, however, is readily apparent: churches and monasteries possessed not only extensive estates [Col. 1121C], but also extremely wealthy lordships and rights of patronage—for example, lordships, duchies, counties, and other things of that kind. Accordingly, since bishops and abbots were governors over all these matters, and since a very great multitude of people, both nobles and commoners, depended upon their will, and even towns, castles, cities, and provinces were subject to their jurisdiction, was it not therefore reasonable that the supreme rulers of kingdoms and principalities should be assured of the fidelity of those who held the office of governor?

The ancient grants and confirmations of elections plainly support this view. The decree of immunity granted by Charlemagne to Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, contains, among other provisions, the following:

“And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid venerable Benedict [Col. 1121D] 623 the abbot, or his successors, shall have departed from this light to the Lord, the holy congregation itself shall have permission, by this our authority, to elect as abbot whichever better man, and one faithful to us in all things, it wishes to choose from the aforesaid monastery or from any place whatsoever, provided that he is able to govern that holy congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict,” etc.

From the ancient documents of that same monastery.

And from the cartulary of Saint-Aubin of Angers:

“Count Goffridus, at the request of Bishop Nefingus, for the remedy of the soul of his mother Gerberga, etc., grants the monks the power henceforth to elect an abbot and exempts them from secular authority,” etc.

[Col. 1122A] I shall also add the ancient formula of an election that was carried out, which is found in this same cartulary:

“To all those in the Lord for whom Christ is life and death gain (Philippians 1:21), and especially to those who willingly submit their necks beneath the yoke of the rule of Saint Benedict—which commands that monks living in a monastery should desire an abbot to preside over them—we wish it to be known that, in the year 988 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when Gunterius, abbot of Saint-Aubin, was departing from the place—which the most noble Count Goffridus among his people had appointed over that place, for the sake of God’s fidelity and the remedy of his own soul—and was seeking Rome, or, what is greater, Jerusalem, the mother of cities, for the sake of prayer, he had, with prophetic spirit, provided for himself a successor to whom he would entrust the care of souls as well as bodies: [lacuna] distinguished by the integrity of his life [Col. 1122B] and conduct, whom he himself had nurtured in Christ’s name, yet with the consent of the brothers of the aforesaid place and of the most distinguished [lacuna] son of the aforesaid Count Gaufridus, who happily succeeded his father in that place, by the name of Fulk.

“To this election, by the providence of God’s grace, as we believe, the agreement of the wisest pontiffs, as well as of clerics and noble laymen, and above all the election and acclamation of the aforesaid congregation, appears to concur for the better, namely on the condition that, according to the rule of Saint Benedict—who, after God, is the father, leader, and advocate of all faithful monks, both in this age and in the future—he should strive to conduct himself in all things according to his ability and knowledge, and should take greater pains to be useful than to preside, and should arrange everything prudently and justly with the counsel of the brothers who fear God [Col. 1122C]; so that, when the Shepherd of shepherds comes (1 Peter 5:4), to whom he must render an account of the souls entrusted to him, and of his own soul as well, he may joyfully deserve to hear what was said to the good servant who expended the talent entrusted to him upon his fellow servants in due season: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Luke 19:17).

“Sign of Bishop Wido.

“Sign of the illustrious Count Fulk.”

The outstanding example of Christian piety shown by Louis, truly the Pious emperor, must by no means be omitted. It had until now lain hidden in the archives of the monastery of Aniane, from which our Claude Chantelou brought it forth.

[Col. 1122D] **Letter of the Emperor Louis to the monks of Aniane, or Gellone, concerning the elected abbot Trutesindus.**

“In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s appointment Augustus emperor, to the venerable brothers established in the monastery of Aniane or Gellone. Recently it happened that Archbishop Agobardus, etc. See among the letters and diplomas of Louis the Pious, *Patrologia*, vol. CIV.”

624 Let no one therefore dare to infer from this that the elections of bishops belong by right to kings or princes.

“It is the priests’ election, and the consent of the faithful people must be added, because the people must be taught, not followed,” says Pope Stephen to the archbishop of Ravenna. See also canon 25, distinction 63, [Col. 1123A] and the Gloss.

The Second Council of Nicaea likewise decreed, canon 3:

“Every election of a bishop, priest, or deacon made by princes shall remain invalid.”

The approval of elections by the king is discussed by James Bruellius in Book III, chapter 2, of Aimoinus’s *De gestis Francorum*, and by Juretus in his note on Ivo, letter 104.

The ancient rite for conferring the blessing upon an abbot should now be appended. It was arranged and observed by Blessed Theodore of Canterbury and is taken from the oldest collection of canons in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

### Concerning the Ordination of Abbots

“In the ordination of an abbot, the bishop must celebrate Mass and bless him with bowed head, in the presence of two or three witnesses from among his brothers; and he shall give him a staff and sandals.

[Col. 1123B] “For the sake of humility, an abbot may, with the bishop’s permission, leave his place; nevertheless, the brothers shall choose an abbot for themselves from among them, if they have one; otherwise from among outsiders. Nor should the bishop act forcibly in his place [reading uncertain].

“The congregation must choose an abbot for itself after his death, or while he is alive if he has departed or sinned. He cannot appoint anyone from among his relatives or outsiders, nor give him to another abbot, if the brothers do not wish it.”

625 “But if the abbot has sinned, the bishop may not take possession of the monastery; rather, he shall send him to another monastery, under the authority of another abbot.

[Col. 1123C] “Neither an abbot nor bishops may transfer the land of a church to another church, even if both are under his authority. If he wishes to send a witness, he shall do so with the consent of both.

“If anyone wishes to establish his monastery in another place, he shall do so with the consent of the bishop and his brothers, and shall leave a priest in the former place for the service of the church.

“An abbot and a bishop may retain a wicked man as a slave if he does not have the price with which to redeem himself.

“If an abbot has a monk who is worthy, he must give him to the bishop if necessary.”

**(74) CHAPTER II.**—“He had convened a council in the city of Troyes.” Nicholas, in the *Life of the same Blessed Godefridus*, Book I, chapter 30, and Ivo of Chartres, letter 208 to Pope Paschal, describe more explicitly the election of Blessed Godefridus [Col. 1123D] and the reason for the council. Likewise William of Nangis, in his manuscript *History* under the year 1109:

“Pope Paschal,” he says, “came to France, etc. The pope, honorably received by the king of the Franks, traveled through various parts of France and solemnly celebrated a universal council at Troyes, both because of the affection of the Franks, who had served him greatly, and because of fear and hatred of the Germans,” etc.

**(75) CHAPTER III.**—“He would have it as an omen for me.” Such prognostic signs may frequently be read, especially in the time of Guibert, in the *Acts of the Bishops*. From them they used to conjecture the future character of the elected man, whether bishop or abbot. William of Malmesbury, Book I, *On the Bishops of England*, folios 121–122, concerning Blessed Lanfranc, says:

“They say that his prognostic was: ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’ (Luke 10:41).” To this he, with joyful face, directed himself from those acclaiming him toward the Lord: “Let us therefore contend in mutual exchange—you by giving, I by distributing,” etc. “Nor was he sluggish in giving out,” etc.

**(76) Ibid.**—“Let his mind be intent upon the salvation of my people, whom you have subjected to me.” How conspicuous in moral integrity and religion our abbot and his monks were is proclaimed by Manasses, bishop of Soissons, in a donation of a certain church. It is worth describing it in full, lest it perish together with other documents.

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1124B] Amen.

“I, Manasses, by the grace of God bishop of Soissons. Although we are debtors to all the faithful entrusted to us by [lacuna], we are nevertheless required to devote greater diligence to these people and greater devotion toward those whom we see voluntarily withdrawing from worldly affairs and choosing quiet and seclusion in order to devote themselves to God and persist in prayer.

“Among these, therefore, are those brothers who live a monastic and religious life in the monastery of Saint Mary at Nogent. By their devotion and sincerity they have been so dear to us and to our predecessors that, although they do not reside within our bishopric, we have honored them no less than our own people and have increased them with benefits and gifts [Col. 1124C]. What our beneficence has therefore bestowed upon them for the love of God, we have thought it pleasing to commit to writing for remembrance, lest posterity be able to alter anything through either ignorance or malice.

“Now the lord Wibertus was presiding over that monastery. By his wisdom and innocence he bound us very closely to himself, and at his request I was asked to confer upon the same monastery the altar of the village called Crécy, which a certain powerful man, Wido, son of Wido of Coucy, held from us and from our Church by the benefit of his ancestors.

“That abbot, relying on the religious counsel in which he excelled, had negotiated with the aforesaid Wido so that the layman would consider it dangerous to possess that altar, and had brought matters to the point that he should return it to the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1124D] for the sake of his salvation. Since it was mine by whose benefit he held it, if I consented and carried this out, I willingly and truly did so. For I did not regard this as a diminution of our benefice, but as a useful exchange, as though transferring something from the left hand to the right.

“I therefore granted the altar of Crécy to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, mother of God, with the consent of our archdeacon Ausculfus and the will of our clerics. Thus, its administration was to be handled through the dean of our principal church, and five solidi were to be paid from it each year to our canons on the feast of Saint Gervasius, and after my death on my anniversary. So that this concession, with its definition, might remain unshaken [Col. 1125A], we confirm it by the imposition of an anathema, strengthen it by the impression of our seal, and corroborate it with the appropriate signs.

“Sign of Manasses, bishop. Sign of Ausculfus, archdeacon. Sign of Lisiardus, provost. Sign of Bernard, dean. Sign of Peter, archdeacon. Sign of Fulk, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh, precentor. Sign of Odo, priest. Sign of Walter, priest. Sign of Robert, dean. Sign of Odo, deacon. Sign of Fulk, deacon. Sign of Ausoldus, subdeacon. Sign of Laurence, subdeacon. Sign of Hebertus, subdeacon. Sign of Adam, subdeacon. Sign of Ausculfus, acolyte. Sign of Augenulfus, acolyte. 626 Sign of Durandus, acolyte. Sign of Leo, acolyte.

“Done in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation.”

Moreover, it will not be inappropriate to record here the succession of abbots of the monastery of Nogent [Col. 1125B], since the author describes its ancient records in this Book II, so that curious investigators of such material may in some manner draw from it a complete history.

### Abbots of the Monastery of Blessed Mary of Nogent

**I. Henry**, at the same time abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims, concerning whom our Guibert speaks in Book II of his *Life*, chapter 2.

**II. Saint Godefridus** governed the monastery until 1104, when he was raised to the bishopric of Amiens. The same is reported by Guibert in the same place and in Book III, chapter 13.

Nicholas, a monk of Saint-Crépin the Greater of Soissons, wrote the deeds of Blessed Godefridus; Surius reports them, polished in his own style, under 8 November.

To relieve the monastery’s poverty, Hugh, bishop of Soissons, generously bestowed three altars, or churches, upon Blessed Godefridus [Col. 1125C]. He left a written record of this in the following manner:

“I, Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Soissons, recognizing the account of the order and place in which God has unworthily set me, an account by which I am debtor to all the faithful to the extent that lies within me, so that I must be prepared, if necessary, to lay down my life not only for those entrusted to me but also for all who believe in Christ, rather than merely provide earthly and external substance, have decided to benefit in the following way the beloved brothers, the monks humbly serving God and the holy mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, in the monastery at Nogent in the county of Laon.

[Col. 1125D] “For I had frequently, though with sufficient humility, been asked by the lord Godefridus, abbot of the aforesaid place, a religious man and most dear to us, to look mercifully upon the poverty of his monastery and the needs of the brothers serving God there, and to become a helper and supporter of their labor and devotion toward the worship of God. Deeming it right to yield to just petitions, I devotedly granted, for the support of that monastic community, three altars—for the love of God, for the welfare of our church, and for the hope of eternal life—namely, the altar of Jouaigny, the altar of Valsalion, and the altar of the village called Pont-Saint-Médard.

“And because sacred authority commands that what a bishop wishes to establish he should do with the counsel of his clerics, [Col. 1126A] we make this concession with the consent and will of our clerics and decree that six solidi shall be paid each year for these same altars to the holy Church of Soissons, over which I preside unworthily, on the day of my anniversary. The dean of this church shall always be the representative of these altars, and their care and administration shall belong to him.

“Desiring, therefore, that this grant of ours remain inviolate for all time, and that no one ever become its violator, we have prohibited this by the imposition of excommunication and have strengthened it by a document secured with the impression of our seal. We have also ordered that the signs of lawful witnesses be added.

“Sign of Hugh, bishop of Soissons.

“Sign of Lisiardus, provost. Sign of Hugh, dean. Sign of [lacuna], archdeacon. Sign of Fulk, archdeacon. Sign of Ebalus, archdeacon. Sign of Robert, precentor. Sign of Guarnerius, priest. Sign of Hugh, priest. Sign of Odo, priest. Sign of Peter, Robert, and Bernard, deacons. Sign of Theobald, Ivo, Giroldus, Odo, Bartholomew, Alexis, and Rainaldus, subdeacons. Sign of Ansoldus, Laurence, Ivo, Herbertus, Arnulfus, Walter, and Ingelrannus, acolytes.

“Hugh, chancellor of the holy Church of Soissons, subscribed and reread this charter.

“Done in the year 1100 of the Incarnate Word, in the eighth year of Bishop Hugh, with epact XVIII, current year VII, indiction VIII.”

**III. Guibertus or Wibertus**, 1104, formerly a monk of Saint-Geremar of Flaviacum, distinguished by birth, religion, and every kind of learning [Col. 1126C], as his works—which we now publish for the first time—also testify.

I shall add here Guibertus’s disposition concerning the day of his death, made three years before he departed from human life. It reads as follows:

“I, Guitbertus, by the grace of God servant of the holy mother of God, Mary, at Nogent. Since every ruler ought to care for the increase of his church, I purchased, on the feast of Saint Martin, the eight solidi that were received from our guests at Landicourt in the churchyard, in the following manner.

“A certain woman’s husband had held a fief from us; his name was Paganus. After he died, his widow, Hildeburgis by name, who had received in her dowry the property given her by her husband, having a son and daughter and being in great need, and since she was not permitted to sell our fief to anyone other than us, finally sold it to us and received one hundred solidi from us. This was done so that, in the presence of the nobles of the castle of Coucy, both she and her son and daughter would divest themselves of the authority of the fief, return it to me and to the church, and likewise place her gift upon the altar. Those present were Robert the Castellan, Rainaldus Belehere, Ado and Iterius with their father Guido, Robert Anguilla, and Gerard Dolle.

[Col. 1126D] “Moreover, from a certain soldier named Guermundus we received as alms a certain manse at Remeias, which he possessed as an allod. A certain Fortmundus, whose entire family belonged by right to our church, also held it, together with its appurtenant land, from Guermundus. Nevertheless, I was not ungrateful for his generosity, but gave him thirty-five solidi, since I knew him to be poor. That manse pays three solidi of Laon currency each year on the feast of Saint Remigius. His wife Furmelina willingly consented to this gift. The witnesses to this matter are Guido de Guni, Ado his son, Elias de Fera, Guido, son of [lacuna], Gerelmus [lacuna], and Albericus de Traveci.

“With the counsel of our brothers, I assigned these eight solidi together with the three which are paid from the manse for the day of my anniversary, to be given to those same brothers for the provision of a feast, insofar as they might suffice. On that day, all the priests of the churches are to sing Masses, each one individually, as they customarily do on the day of my ordination.

“During my lifetime, even if I should depart from the abbacy [Col. 1127A] or migrate elsewhere for any reason, we have established that the same money is to be given on the feast of Saint Lucy for the refreshment of the brothers. Therefore, by the authority of God and of all of us, we excommunicate and consign to God’s judgment all who divert the aforesaid expenditure of eleven solidi from the purpose for which it has been assigned.

“Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1121. Sign of Alardus. Sign of Radulfus. Sign of Rainaldus. Sign of Alardus, refectorer. Sign of Godfrey, cantor. Sign of Odo. Sign of William. Sign of Addelmus [lacuna]. Sign of Adam. Sign of Fulk. Sign of Leodegarius, and of all the others.”

**IV. Andrew**, 1124. Formerly prior of the monastery of Nogent. With benevolent intent he granted several possessions to the Premonstratensians, especially at Bonouil.

[Col. 1127C] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

“Let all present and future know that I, Andrew, abbot of Saint Mary of Nogent, with the consent of our chapter, have granted to the church of Premontré all the land of our allod that we possessed at Bonouil, for an annual rent of thirteen solidi in Vermandois currency, to be paid each year on the Purification of Saint Mary, mother of God. We confirm this as settled and firm by the attestation of our seal and decree that it remain unshaken.

“The witnesses to this concession are: Godfrey, monk and cantor of Nogent; Bernard, almoner; Adelard, monk; Adelelmus, secretary; Albericus, provost; Herberius, cellarer; Fulk, boy; Iterius, boy; and others.

“And from the same church of Premontré: Hugh, then abbot; Gerard, prior; Hardwinus, cantor; Peter, deacon; Almoricus, deacon; Adam and Theobald, subdeacons; Rainaldus, John, and the boys.

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1129, indiction VII, epact XXVIII, concurrent I.”

Radulfus the castellan and Ivo of Noyon, with the approval of Simon, bishop of Noyon, transferred to Abbot Andrew and the monks of Blessed Mary of Nogent the church which they had unjustly usurped. Here is the deed of donation:

[Col. 1127D] “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

“I, Simon, by the grace of God bishop of Noyon [Col. 1128A], to all the faithful in Christ forever. Since the Apostle commands, ‘While you have time, work what is good toward all, but especially toward those who belong to the household of faith’ (Galatians 6:10), we, as pastoral prudence requires, while we have time, must pursue together the things that belong to piety and mercy.

“We wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Radulfus, castellan of Noyon, held from Ivo, lord of Noyon, by hereditary succession, a half-share in the altar of Courcy, both in the small tithes and in the guests of the churchyard, as well as in the offerings of the priest, and that both of them came humbly before us, acknowledging their fault in this matter. Radulfus returned this fief into Ivo’s hand, and Ivo freely and absolutely remitted it into our hand. Together they earnestly begged us that, for the souls of their predecessors, and especially for the soul of William, Radulfus’s brother, who had become a monk and been buried in the monastery of Blessed Mary of Nogent, we should transfer this ecclesiastical benefice to that monastery and establish it canonically.

“Therefore, rejoicing in their devotion, we grant to you, brother Andrew, venerable abbot of the aforesaid church, and to your successors and the brothers serving God there, whatever Radulfus held in secular possession in the altar of Courcy, so that it may henceforth be possessed ecclesiastically for the souls of our predecessors and of my mother. Thus, what a lay hand [Col. 1128B] has until now wrongly held in God’s sanctuary, may your church henceforth possess rightly and freely.

“Let a priest be placed in the parish with your consent, through the hand of the bishop. Whatever you and your successors may be able, with God’s help, to acquire in the same parish, we confirm by the sanction of this charter.

“So that all these things may remain settled and unshaken, we command it and strengthen it by the impression of our seal and the addition of witnesses. And lest any presumptuous person ever dare to violate this gift, we prohibit it by the ban of anathema and by the authority of the Holy Spirit. The witnesses to this matter are as follows:

“Sign of Simon, bishop. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Baldwin, dean. Sign of Peter, cantor. Sign of Master Peter. Sign of Theoderic, abbot of Saint-Eloi of Noyon.

[Col. 1128D] “Done at Noyon in the presence of Bishop Simon, in the year 1132 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Hugh the chancellor, subscribed.”

**V. Bruno**, 1140. Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, by the following charter declares valid the church of the canons of Coucy and certain other pious donations of Ingelrannus:

[Col. 1128D] “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I, Bartholomew, by the grace of God bishop of Laon. Since the Apostle commands, ‘While you have time, work what is good toward all, but especially toward those who belong to the household of faith’ (Galatians 6:10), we, as pastoral prudence requires, while we have time, must pursue together the things that belong to piety and mercy.

“We wish it to be known to all, future and present, that Ingelrannus, son of Thomas, finally, moved by divine inspiration, freely returned into our hand the church situated in the castle of Coucy, which he had until then held contrary to ecclesiastical right. He had been repeatedly admonished concerning this by me and by our venerable brother Goislenus, bishop of Soissons. He earnestly and devoutly requested that we transfer the same church to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Nogent and establish it canonically.

“Therefore, gladly granting his request, we concede to you, brother Bruno, venerable abbot of the aforesaid monastery, and to your successors and the brothers serving God there, the aforesaid church to be possessed in perpetuity, namely on the condition that, when the canons die, you shall have their prebends and, according to the resources of the place, shall consequently substitute monks in their number.

“The aforesaid Ingelrannus also had a chapel built beneath the church tower. In it, so that a daily Mass for the dead might be celebrated for the soul of his father Thomas and for the souls of all the faithful departed, at the exhortation of religious men and also at the request of his mother Milesendis, his brother Robert, and his sister Milesendis, and with the consent of his nobles, he transferred a vineyard free from every customary due; two modii of grain from the terrage of the village of Coucy; thirty at the toll of Blarencourt; and ten solidi at Casnels, to be paid each year on the feast of Blessed Remigius.

“He gave twenty solidi at the Coucy crossing for preparing the church lights, and confirmed the gift of two solidi which his father and mother had previously made, to be paid every week for the refreshment of the brothers.

“The peers of the aforesaid castle also bestowed upon the same monastery, for their own souls and those of their predecessors: Robert de Cais, five solidi of good currency each year at the Coucy crossing; Rainaldus Belehere, eleven solidi of rent currency to be received from his rent at Morlencourt; Ado de Luni, eleven solidi of current currency; Iterius, his brother, eleven solidi; Robert Vitulus, twelve denarii; [Col. 1129D] Simon Crassus, twelve denarii; Peter de Fresnencourt, twelve denarii; Guido, son of Albericus, twelve denarii; Boniface, twelve denarii; Rainaldus Rufus, three sextarii of wine; Lambert Gruellus, three sextarii of wine, which he held in the aforesaid vineyard; Robert de Curval remitted the customary dues he held in that same vineyard.

“Let the posterity of the faithful also know that at the crossing of the bridge of Cuiaperit—which Drogo, nephew of Matilda the Fat, had bestowed upon Blessed Mary of Nogent when he came to conversion—the same Ingelrannus granted to the abbot and monks in perpetuity one denarius of good currency from each cart, two denarii from the wagon, one denarius from Trussell, situated at Sella, five solidi at Puisler, and one obol of good currency from each house of the neighboring villages, for repairing the bridge.

“So that all these things may remain unshaken in the future, we confirm them by the imposition of an anathema and strengthen them by the impression of our seal and the addition of witnesses.”

“Sign of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon. Sign of Ernaldus, archdeacon. Sign of Bartholomew, archdeacon and treasurer. Sign of Guido, dean. Sign of Milo, precentor. Sign of Anselm, abbot of Saint Vincent. Sign of Baldwin, abbot of Saint John. Sign of Leo, abbot of Saint Michael. Sign of Walter, abbot of Saint Martin. Sign of Gislebert, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Saltus.

[Col. 1130B] “Done at Laon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138.

“Given through the hand of Ernaldus, chancellor.”

Bruno confirms what his predecessor had granted to the members of the Norbertine family.

But the controversy between Bruno and Hugh, abbot of Prémontré, was finally settled by this definitive judgment of Bartholomew of Laon.

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Bartholomew, by the grace of God humble minister of the holy Church of Laon, to his beloved son Bruno, abbot of Saint Mary of Nogent, and to his successors forever. What has been justly arranged and canonically established by Catholic bishops for the peace of Churches, especially between religious persons, ought to be secured by firm and perpetual peace.

[Col. 1130C] “Therefore, beloved son, we have taken care to settle fully, with the grace of God cooperating through our fellow bishop, our venerable brother Goislenus, bishop of Soissons, the dispute that has arisen in our time between you and our beloved son Hugh, abbot of Prémontré, and to make it known to those present and to those in the future by this present document.

“It is indeed established that the church of Cocciacovilla and its parochial revenues belong to the church of Blessed Mary of Nogent. Moreover, within the boundaries of the same parish, in the place called Roserias, Milesendis, the mother of Ingelrannus, built a monastery and granted it to the aforesaid abbot of Prémontré for the religious life. Concerning the dedication of this monastery, although you and your Church opposed it, the matter was finally settled in the following way, in the presence and with the cooperation of the aforesaid fellow bishop of ours, Goislenus:

[Col. 1130D] “Namely, that your church shall suffer no diminution whatsoever of its possessions, but shall possess in perpetual peace, in full, the tithes, due offerings, the care of the living and the dead, and whatever else derives from parochial right. The Premonstratensians themselves shall be able to usurp nothing of all these things that belong to your jurisdiction. So that this may remain ratified and unshaken in the future, I and the bishop of Soissons confirm it by the peace of this present charter and seal it with our seals.

“Done at Laon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1141.

[Col. 1131A] “Sign of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon. Sign of Goislenus, bishop of Soissons. Sign of Wido, dean. Sign of Richard, archdeacon. Sign of Bartholomew, archdeacon. Sign of …, abbot of Saint John. Sign of Ansellus, abbot of Saint Vincent. Sign of Gillebertus, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Saltus. Sign of William, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Prato. Sign of Milo, cantor.”

VI. Ingelrannus, 1157.

VII. John, from 1164 to 1185. During his rule the monastery’s possessions increased, and the supreme pontiffs fortified them with privileges.

VIII. Elias, 1185. He entered into several agreements with various persons, especially with Hugh, abbot of Prémontré.

[Col. 1131B] IX. Robert, from 1190 to 1201.

X. Peter Claudy, commonly called “the Lame,” was elected in 1201 as abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims, where he had earlier professed the monastic institution.

XI. Robert II, 1213. He undertook, at great expense, to have the church itself rebuilt from its foundations, together with two dormitories, one for the priests and the other for the novices; scarcely even ruins of all these now remain. During the abbacy of this man, the body of Thomas of Marle was translated, as is clear from the following charter of Ingelrannus.

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Ingelrannus, by the grace of God lord of Coucy, to all the sons of holy Mother Church who shall see this present document. I make known that, when the noble man Lord Thomas of Marle, of good memory, [Col. 1131C] my predecessor and formerly lord of Coucy, had long lain buried in a certain chapel [630] which the illustrious and piously remembered Lord Ingelrannus, my grandfather and son of the same Thomas, had caused to be built beneath the old tower of the church of Blessed Mary of Nogent—for a daily Mass to be celebrated there by the monks of that church for the soul of that same Thomas, his father, and for the souls of all the faithful departed—then, in my time, when the church of Nogent had begun to be rebuilt anew, and it became necessary to remove the same chapel on account of the new construction, which had to be enlarged and extended through the space occupied by that chapel and by the burial place of the aforesaid Thomas, Lord Robert, then abbot of Nogent, and the monks [Col. 1131D] of the same place, with my consent and approval, and in my presence, together with several of my knights and servants, honorably transferred the body of that same Thomas from the place where it had previously been buried; and after the solemn celebration of Masses, they solemnly buried it in the middle of the choir of their new church. By my will they also arranged that the Mass which had previously been celebrated in the old chapel for the soul of the often-mentioned Thomas and for the souls of all the faithful departed should henceforth be celebrated daily and perpetually in the new building.

“And so that in succeeding ages this translation of the body of the aforesaid Thomas might not be consigned to oblivion, the abbot and monks of the same Church asked me to commend to posterity in letters confirmed by my seal both the translation and the day on which it was made.

“I, therefore, gladly consenting to their request, ordered this present letter to be drawn up and confirmed by the protection of my seal; and, as a memorial of this event, I entrusted it to the aforesaid abbot and monks of Nogent to be preserved forever.

“Done in the year of the Word Incarnate 1218, in April, on the third day before the Nones of that month, the Wednesday before the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

It is clear from this charter of Ingelrannus that all the monuments of antiquity were utterly thrown into ruin; it is therefore unsurprising that nothing survives of what Guibert touched upon concerning the tomb of King Quilius and the other traces of antiquity in that monastery, in Book II of his Life. [Col. 1132B]

XII. Walter, or Galterus, 1231. He had assumed the monastic cowl at the monastery of Saint Vincent in Laon.

XIII. John III, 1240.

XIV. Iterius, 1248.

XV. Matthew, 1281.

XVI. John IV of Palye, 1300.

XVII. Robert III, 1332.

XVIII. John V Despagnyes, from the Despagnyes marquises of Picardy, 1347.

XIX. Laurence du Rasse, 1415.

XX. John Roussel. Because he had squandered the monastery’s goods, the bishop of Laon deprived him of his office and appointed Nicholas de Lestoc as administrator.

[Col. 1132C] XXI. Nicholas de Lestoc, elected in 1464 after John’s death.

XXII. John IV Mareschal, from 1475 to 1489.

Commendatory abbots.

XXIII. Arthur Donnoy, canon of the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, disregarding every right and rejecting the monks’ election, harassed Nicholas Mavart, whom the monks had placed in charge of the abbey; finally, in 1489, he obtained the abbey in commendam.

XXIV. John VII of Beaumont, archdeacon of Langres, from 1512 to 1529.

XXV. Charles de Vignacourt, archdeacon of Rouen and canon of Paris, 1529.

XXVI. John de Longueval, through the cession of Charles, [Col. 1132D] from 1544 to 1557, when, in July, he resigned the abbey in favor of his brother Charles.

XXVII. Charles II de Longueval, John’s brother, administered the monastery’s affairs most wickedly in 1564, indeed dissipating them. After taking a wife, he shamefully went over to the Calvinist party.

XXVIII. Gabriel le Seneux, to whom that Charles nominally ceded the abbey—for by a nefarious bargain he immediately retained its possessions—but before le Seneux could take possession, death overtook him in 1571.

XXIX. Gaspard de Brenier, a Dauphinois, obtained the abbey from the king in September 1572. After acquiring possession, he brought a lawsuit against the aforementioned Longueval, who had added the monastery’s goods to his own possessions, plundered the sacred shrines adorned with gold and silver, the sacred chalices, gems, and whatever valuable objects could be found, and cut down the forests. He demanded that Longueval not only restore everything, but also rebuild the tower and choir of the church, which had collapsed on the very day of his wedding. But all Gaspard’s efforts remained fruitless. For, after receiving money, he made an agreement with Charles, who thereafter peacefully possessed the Church’s property by right and by wrong.

XXX. John VIII de la Grange, a Parisian, pursued Charles de Longueval with both litigation and arms, but in vain. Harassed by many calamities, he was therefore compelled to resign the abbey and cede it to James du Val, as they call him, the confidant [631] of Charles de Longueval.

[Col. 1133B] XXXI. James du Val became abbot in name only, namely on the condition that, as soon as Philip de Longueval, the son of the often-mentioned Charles, came of age, he would resign the abbey in his favor. This was done in 1586.

XXXII. Philip de Longueval, Charles’s firstborn son, held the abbey until 1624, when, retaining a pension, he handed it over to Anthony de Longueval, his nephew through his brother.

XXXIII. Anthony de Longueval, still only twelve years old on 15 November, devoted himself, as far as his age and circumstances allowed, to restoring the abbey and regular discipline. For this purpose he summoned monks both from the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris and from the monastery of Casalis Benedicti, and finally from the Congregation of Saint Maur. To the latter he affiliated the monastery of Nogent, by an agreement concluded for this purpose, on 21 October 1646. He died on 7 July 1649 and was buried in the church of Saint-Germain of Auxerre in Paris; his heart was carried to the monastery of Nogent and given burial there.

XXXIV. John de Grasse, a provincial, obtained the abbey in 1649.

(77) CHAP. V.—The castle of Eu: a county whose principal town is Eu, adjoining Lower Picardy and the territory of Calais. You will find the family of the counts of Eu, or Aucy, at the end of the History of the Normans written by André Duchesne, p. [Col. 1133D] 1086.

(78) Ibid.—The abbey of Saint Michael by the sea, called Ulterior-Portus. If you wish to know about its founder and origin, as well as its resources, what older, nobler, or more trustworthy document could I produce than its foundation charter? I therefore bring this to light from ancient documents:

Charter of the abbey of Ulterior-Portus concerning the donation and confirmation of Robert, count of Eu, founder of the church of Port-en-Bessin.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1036. I, Robert, count of Eu, with the counsel of Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, and William, duke of the Normans, as well as with the approval of the other bishops and nobles of Normandy and of my men, and especially at the urging of my wife Beatrice, the countess, establish an abbey at Ulterior-Portus in honor of God and Saint Michael the archangel. I establish it from my possessions, with the consent and approval of my wife Beatrice and my sons, namely Ralph, William, and Robert, so that monks may live there and continually pray to God for my salvation and that of my own people.

[Col. 1134A] “Therefore I give them at Ulterior-Portus the church where that abbey has been built, with the entire tithe and with everything belonging to the same church; and twenty houses in the same village, six of them in the cambis [term uncertain], and two free vavassor men, and the rent of timber from the same village; and the marshland, the adjoining land and meadows, and all the arable land that I possess in my demesne in the same village, that is, at Port-en-Bessin, and every customary due from those men who belong to Saint Michael, whatever it may be.

[Col. 1134B] “Likewise, at Ulterior-Portus and in the town of Eu, and the tithe of pennies from the viscounties, and in both villages whatever the abbot and monks may acquire. If the abbot’s men catch the fish called the turium, it shall all belong to Saint Michael; if a large fish is caught, one fin and half its tail shall belong to the monks.

[Col. 1134C] “I, Robert, count, also give to the same Church at Eu the dwelling of a certain man who is called [lacuna] with its garden; and three other dwellings; and the tithe of the pannage of the forests of Eu, together with all the clearings made in those forests, wherever they may be made; also free timber for the work of the monastery and the monks’ service.

“I also give the land of Maisnil-Val, with the port and whatever I possess in that place; and the oak forest of Criol; and Maisnil-Soreth, free and exempt from every customary due, together with whatever proceeds from it. I also give Maisnil-Alard; and the village called Ramicheon-Maisnil; and another called Grimonth-Maisnil. I grant half of Boiteal-Maisnil at Mount Fucard. From my demesne I give two gardens, five dwellings for guests, and [Col. 1134D] one mill. At Fontaines, however, excepting the toll and the parish, I give what I possess in my demesne in lands, meadows, alder groves, and marshes, together with one free house and one mill, to which all the grain from Grimonth-Maisnil must come if the lord of the village has no mill.

“I also give the tithe of the mill of Blangecy, and the Seven Mills. At the Seven Mills I give the church of the same village and whatever belongs to it, together with land for one plough and the entire tithe from my demesne. At Criole I give one mill with all its milling rights, [632] and the floscis [reading uncertain], and Estaelonde-Vinliothuil, and two free dwellings.

“I also give the church of Anedinace and the fisc of Roger of that same village, who became a monk, [Col. 1135A] and all the land of Gozondimare. At Verle I give one mill for the soul of Roger, son of Turlod, and the land that Romeldis, Roger’s grandmother, had held at Verle, and which Roger himself, in my presence, gave to the church of Saint Michael; namely, I, Robert the count, give half the village free.

“From Boeville, Penley, and Brunville I give churches, the entire tithe, and land for four oxen. I also give the church of Guillemercourt with a third of the sheaf; and the church of Saint Peter in the Valley with the entire tithe; and the church of Saint Valery of Mount Aquosus with land and the other things belonging to it; and the church of the Burgh of Turlod with the entire tithe and thirty-five acres of land; at Basilics, land for one plough, together with the church, [Col. 1135B] the entire tithe, whatever belongs to it, and twelve dwellings for guests. I also give Roscelin of Matun-Maisnil, a mason, with his fisc; and Saint Martin of the Forest, free and exempt, with lands, guests, and whatever belongs to that place, where formerly Lord Gervinus, abbot of Saint Richarius, led the eremitical life; likewise the place called Flamengueville, land for one plough, and a portion of my Warance; and the tithe of the toll of the Seven Mills; and at Grandinciae, all the fish for my kitchen; and salt and all the meat that comes to me or to my heirs from England.

“Likewise I give the tithe and the water of Criol eight days before the feast of Saint Michael and on the very night of that feast; I give that water to the same abbey. Likewise, before the feast of the Translation of Saint Benedict, I grant the water of Criol to the same church for four days and on the very night of the feast.

“In England I give Bonitone and whatever belongs to it, in lands, guests, and other things.

“All these things I give to the same abbey as a free and exempt alms-gift; and by this charter I attest the gifts which my son William, in my presence and with my consent, granted to the same church as an alms-gift, namely the church of Haymies with its entire tithe and land belonging to three guests of the same church.

“I also attest all the gifts which, in my presence, with my will and at my request, the barons, knights, and inhabitants of my land granted to the same church as a free [Col. 1135D] and exempt alms-gift: namely, thirty acres of land at Ulterior-Portus, given by Hugh the viscount, father of Guibert of Dimey; given by William Caucheis, two dwellings in the village of Ulterior-Portus, all the land of Mount Goisbert, two acres of meadow at Flamengueville, two other acres of meadow at Criol, the land he held in the town of Eu, one garden, and whatever he possessed at the Seven Mills; given by Richard Boistel, Hilduin of Blangey, Gustin of Grimonth-Maisnil, and Henry Jaillard, two sheaves of the tithe from their fiefs at Blangey; given by Henry Mostellenc, at Fontaines, twenty acres of land and two sheaves of the tithe; given by Ancher of Riu-Senes, his tithe from Riu; [Col. 1136A] given by Imbert of Basinval and by Helduin the Forester, two sheaves of the tithe from their lands at Basinval; given by Walter “ad Barbam” of Daiville, two sheaves of the tithe from his fisc at Monchey; given by Gosselin of Bernoumaisnil and Osmeldis, his wife, the land of Sifridi’s village; given by Roger, son of Terold, at Guillemercourt, the fisc of two men, namely Geoffrey, son of Romoldis, and Roger, son of Henry; given by Ralph “who does not see,” father of Ralph of Grantcourt, a certain tithe at Grantcourt; given by William Tallebot the service owed from the land of Sansogolin at Guillemercourt; given by Alund of Grantcourt, father of Robert, two sheaves of the tithe from his land at Grantcourt; given by Ralph, son of Alvered, all [Col. 1136B] the tithe from his land at Penley; given by Geoffrey, son of Rainold of Saint Martin Jaillard, the tithe from the lands of his men that he held in his demesne, at Saint Martin, at Letot, and at Merlimchamp; given by Claremboud, father of Richard of Tokeville, two sheaves of the tithe from Tokeville; given by Roger of Salchey, brother of Richard of Freaville, the church of Salchey with the entire tithe, whatever belongs to that church, and one acre of meadow; given by Richard, son of Robert of Freaville, the entire tithe from …; given by Picard of Lonrey, father of Bartholomew, the tithe from Richard’s Wood; given by Milo of Ayssigny, two gardens and two sheaves of the tithe from Ayssigny, [Col. 1136C] so freely that the men of the village now bring them to the monks’ house, just as they had formerly been bound to bring them to his own house; given by Robert of Petrepont and his brother Geoffrey, the tithe from Cuverville, which they held from Oylard, lord of that village, and they did this [633] with the consent of that lord; given by Oystelland, my knight, who raised my son William, the village called Maisnil-Oystelland. I granted this at the request of my son William, so that the same village might forever be free and exempt as an alms-gift for the poor.

“And I wish that whatever the monks of Ulterior-Portus hold or possess from my gift or from the gifts of my successors, they may hold it so freely and peacefully that neither my heirs nor their men may demand from them or their men any services, aids, tallages or collections, or any exactions whatsoever. To our successors who assent to this and increase the goods of this church to the best of their ability, I grant a blessing; but those who bring accusations against them and withdraw the goods of this church I condemn to eternal malediction, and I bind them with the bond of dreadful excommunication. The witnesses of these gifts, both mine and those of the other benefactors of this church whom I have mentioned, are:

“I, Robert, count of Eu; Ralph, William, and Robert, my sons; Hugh the viscount; Geoffrey of Bailiol; and Walter ‘ad Barbam’ of Davitusville.” And many others, whom it would take too long to name.

[Col. 1137A] John, likewise count of Eu, confirms this instrument of donation in the following manner:

“In the year of the Incarnation 1149, while Pope Eugenius governed the Roman Church, while Hugh the archbishop sat in the see of Rouen, and while Geoffrey, count of Anjou, ruled in Normandy: I, John, count of Eu, by granting, gave and confirmed to this church of Saint Michael the archangel of Ulterior-Portus, and with my own hand placed upon the altar all those gifts which my predecessors—namely Count Robert and his son William, my father Henry, and their men—granted, gave, and confirmed, and whatever the church had held for one day by any arrangement while the aforesaid counts were alive. I wish especially that the things which the monks ought to have be held by them firmly and fully and possessed forever,” etc.

Yet a few years later, after the treasure of the church of Saint Michael had been seized by that same count or by his knights in monstrous sacrilege, the prince, moved to repentance, endeavored to compensate for everything that had hitherto been taken, so that he piously granted the additional things contained in the following charter. It will be useful to transcribe it, so that from it the commanders of the armies of our own age—alas, how many unspeakable acts have been committed!—may take a noble example of Christian religion and indeed of justice.

“Let it be known to all the sons of God’s Church that I, John, count of Eu, for the pay of the knights and servants whom I maintained during the king’s war, pledged a very large and excellent portion of the treasure of the church [Col. 1137C] of Saint Michael of Ulterior-Portus: namely, two precious books, two precious censers, one silver chalice, finely gilded, twenty-four costly copes, and an embroidered and good-quality chasuble. Moreover, I burdened the aforesaid church so often with such numerous and great exactions that I could not count the occasions of those burdens. Therefore, repaying a little for much and small things for great, I grant and give forever to the aforesaid church the oats and grain of Verle that belong to the forest dues. I earnestly beseech my heirs not to burden the Churches of their land, but to honor and protect them. If I have given anything to them for the salvation of my soul and of my parents, or have restored anything taken away, let them cause it to be held securely and peacefully, remembering that they themselves will die, just as our predecessors have died. The witnesses of this donation are: Henry and Robert, the count’s sons; N., countess of Eu; H., abbot of Fécamp; Stephen, abbot of Foulcardmont; Thomas of Brienchon; Alvered of Saint Martin; Master Richard; and William Billuar”—and many others.

To this is added the list of the abbots of the same monastery.

From the necrology of the abbey of Saint Michael of Ulterior-Portus.

“On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, Lord Abbot Rainerus, of pious memory, the first shepherd of this church, died.

“On the third day before the Nones of March, Lord Abbot Drogo, of pious memory, the second rector of this church, died.

[Col. 1138A] “On the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the most reverend man Lord Abbot Alfred, the third governor of this place, died.”

There is nothing concerning the fourth and fifth.

“On the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, Lord Abbot William, the sixth shepherd of this Church, died.

“On the Kalends of June, Lord Richard, abbot, the seventh shepherd of this Church, died.”

There is no mention at all of the eighth.

“On the sixth day before the Kalends of March, Lord Abbot William, of pious memory, the ninth shepherd of this Church, died.

“On the Kalends of March, Lord Abbot Arthur, the tenth shepherd of this Church, died.”

The necrology is silent about the eleventh.

“On the fifth day before the Nones of March, Lord Abbot Hugh, the twelfth rector of this [Col. 1138B] Church, died.

“On the sixth day before the Kalends of May, Lord Abbot Henry, rector, most noble rebuilder and thirteenth abbot of this place, died; on his anniversary we receive [634] forty shillings.”

There is nothing concerning the next four.

“On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, Lord Robert, abbot, the twenty-first of this Church, died.

“On the third day before the Ides of July, John, abbot of this Church, its most noble rebuilder and restorer and its twenty-second shepherd, died.”

There is no mention of the twenty-third.

“On the sixth day before the Nones of May, Richard de Longuemor, abbot, rector, most noble rebuilder, the twenty-fourth, of pious memory, died.

[Col. 1138C] “On the fifth day before the Kalends of April, Andrew, abbot, rector, most noble restorer of the chapel of Blessed Mary, the twenty-fifth, of pious memory, died.

“On the sixth day before the Kalends of October, Lord Abbot Richard de Longuemor, of pious memory, most noble rebuilder and twenty-sixth rector of this Church, died.”

There seems to be an error here, or the twenty-fourth and twenty-sixth were namesakes.

Nothing survives concerning the twenty-seventh.

“On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord 1521, the illustrious Lord Charles de Cleves, count of Eu, eldest son of Lord Gilbert, count of the same place, full brother of Lord Francis de Cleves, the current commendatory abbot of this Church, the first of that kind and twenty-eighth in order, died.

[Col. 1138D] “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, Lord Abbot Alberic, most temperate rector of the Church of Saint Leufredus and the first builder of our place, died.”

I do not present this series of abbots as entirely sound and certain. Robert of Mont, in his treatise On the Change of the Monastic Order, below among the Additions, contradicts it:

“Count Robert of Eu,” he says, “built the monastery of Saint Michael of Ulterior-Portus. Its first abbot was Herbert, a monk of Holy Trinity of Mont-Rouen; the second was Alvered; the third Osbern, a monk of the same place; and the fourth Fulcher, a Cluniac monk.”

(79) CHAP. V.—Countess Helisendis. Married to Robert, count of Eu, she bore William, his second son (the one discussed in that place), as may be seen in the subscriptions to the foundation of Saint Michael cited above. William of Jumièges, History, Book V, chapter 3, concerning Richard II:

“To him, William, not long afterward he handed over the county of Eu, and gave him a certain girl, Lescelina. By her he fathered three sons, namely Robert, who after his death inherited the county,” etc. But this note has the force only of a conjecture.

(80) Ibid.—“Where a multitude of learned men flourishes.” Among the ancients was Ralph of Flavigny, commonly so called, a writer of no low distinction, who published a commentary on Leviticus, printed many times.

(81) Ibid.—“Like those religious men whom they commonly call Deonands.” I think they were Deonands, that is, Donates or Oblates, whom in the vernacular we call Donnés or Oblats. They serve monasteries in a lay habit, especially in those duties outside the monastery which monks, whose task is to devote themselves to sacred matters, cannot easily perform. They are not bound by every observance, especially the stricter ones. Blessed Lanfranc calls them lay monks, Decrees, chapter 1, section 4, after the beginning; and in section 5, near the middle, lay brothers. Read Menard, Observations on chapter 70 of the Concordance of the Rules, p. 1028.

Furthermore, I think that Deonands, or lay brothers, appear under the name of monks ad succurrendum—“for assistance”—from time to time in ancient charters and in martyrologies or necrologies. Not only men but also women devoted themselves to this service, so that the monks might more easily apply themselves to the studies of theory, as was shown above, p. 12D and following. The Chronicle of Bèze supplies testimony to this effect as follows:

“Let the faithful in succeeding ages know that a certain free man named Lambert, while living at Setas with his wife named Ereburgis and with his children Framverus and Dominicus, all of the same condition, freely gave himself to Saint Peter for service at the place called Fons-Besua and to the monks living there and serving God, so that liberty might come to their souls. But he did this on this understanding, condition, and agreement: that he and his successors should faithfully guard the alms-gift which Rainaldus, count of the region, together with his wife, gave to the aforesaid Saint Peter. For whatever they might gain from it through profit or business, they were to return it for the clothing of the brothers in the chamber of the aforesaid place. And so that this writing might remain firm, in the present they gave to this community, in memory of it, a man two asses, and the man’s wife ten shillings, for repairing the boiler; likewise they gave one boat. Let the monks of that place know that he has no other advocate except them, and therefore that at all times they are to provide him with clothing, footwear, and food. And so that they might remain free from suspicion, the elders of the place anathematized anyone who should do anything against him or cause him any harm, or harm his children, with perpetual anathema, by the authority of God [Col. 1140A] and Saint Peter, for whose love Lambert himself gave himself to service, unless satisfaction should earn forgiveness. The witnesses to this subscription are all the inhabitants of the holy place, namely Ado the provost, Humbertus, Wido the dean, Orbertus, Necteus, and Ramerius. These things were done in the time of William, abbot, and of the provost of the place, Benedict by name.”

[635] And a charter copied from the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Maxentius:

“In the name of the Lord. I, Gauterius the priest, son of Adhemar of Guarda, gave my soul and my body to Lord Goffredus, abbot, seated in the chapter with his monks, on a certain Sunday of Advent, into the fellowship and benefit of the entire monastery. And whenever I wish to become a monk, let them receive me with whatever possessions I may have, whether I am well or ill. I gave them one small holding of land and one quarter-acre of meadow, for the benefit and salvation of the souls of my parents, as an alms-gift, without any claim by my descendants. They, for their part, clothed me and my brother Lucius in this benefit according to the Rule, and kissed us. There we agreed that we would preserve this gift from our lay lords. We made this gift with this parchment upon the altar, in the sight of the witnesses written below.

“Martin Espernus; Hugh Porcheus, etc.

“And I, Gauterius, confirmed it with the sign +.

“This charter was made in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, while Louis was reigning as king in France, William as count in Aquitaine, and Peter as bishop of Poitiers.”

A document records that a man and his wife gave themselves to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Val-Bonne; not long ago our Claudius Chantelou copied it from the charters of that priory, formerly an abbey, in the diocese of Grasse, and reduced it to summary form:

“In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1232, in the fifth indiction, on 18 December, Blacacius of Sartols and his wife Jordana give themselves and all their goods generally to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Val-Bonne and to Lord P., abbot of the said monastery. More specifically, Blacacius gives all his movable and immovable goods and the rights that he has in the castle of Sartols and throughout its territory, whether they consist of houses, men, services, lordships, vineyards, trees, meadows, fields, woods, waters, pastures, etc. Jordana specifically gives all the goods and rights that she has in the castle of Torrenco and its territory, and in the castle of Upper Grauleriis and its territory, whether they consist of houses, etc. The said Jordana also gives thirty-five pounds, one denarius, and one hundred Raimundian shillings in goods, retaining for the spouses the usufruct during their lifetime. The spouses promise the aforesaid abbot that whichever of them should first fail or die, the survivor will remain chaste and continent for as long as he or she lives, and they immediately promise obedience to the same lord abbot, in the name of the said monastery, with joined hands. Thereupon the abbot receives Blacacius and Jordana, with joined hands, as brothers, associates, and Donates of the said monastery of Val-Bonne, promising that whenever they wish to come, he and the monastery will kindly receive and treat them like the other brothers of the said monastery, and will provide them with food, clothing, and footwear according to the monastery’s means. Written by B. of Sclannola, notary of Lord Raymond Berengar, count of Provence.”

The necrology of Saint-Denis also expressly states: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of February, Girard, a monk ad succurrendum, died; and on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, Vincent, [Col. 1141B] a monk ad succurrendum, died.” The martyrology of Corbie states: “On the day before the Ides of January, Walter, a monk ad succurrendum of our congregation, died.” Likewise: “On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, Odoard, a monk ad succurrendum of our congregation, died.” The mortuary register of Saint Andrew near Avignon states: “On the fourth day before the Ides of January, Lord Isuard, Lord of Bareto, a monk ad succurrendum, died.” Finally: “On the third day before the Nones of November, Rostagnus of Podium Altum, a knight and our monk ad succurrendum, died.” So too elsewhere.

It has also occurred to me that I once read in ancient parchments of monks being called ad succurrendum in another sense, namely for laypeople suffering from some illness, who were received into monasteries either at their own request or by the monks for the love of God. The monks assisted and served them and provided whatever goods they could for their comfort; hence those monks acquired the name ad succurrendum. Among very many examples, two occur. In the charter of the priory of Saint Giles of Meulan: “Odo, son of Ruffinus, afflicted by a very serious illness, assumed the monastic habit, etc., and became a monk ad succurrendum.” The Chronicle of Bèze states: “Wido, a knight from the village called Eretas, having fallen ill, became a monk,” etc.

(82) **CHAP. V.—In a long and black garment, with the head covered.** It seems clear to me that *birrus* or *biretum* is meant here for a cap. The words relevant to this are found in Book XIV, title 10, of the *Codex Theodosianus*, “On the clothing that ought to be worn within the city”:

> “We permit the slaves of everyone—except those whose masters are known not to be constrained by military service—to wear either *birri* or *cuculli*.” [Col. 1141D]

The Cluniac Statutes, issued about the year 1290, chapter 53, state:

> “Each religious is permitted to have two tunics, etc., two cowls with two caps, one black and the other white.”

I am nevertheless aware that *birrus* has another meaning among highly authoritative writers, namely a short cloak or little mantle. Consult Henry Spelman in his *Glossary* and Gerard Vossius, *On the Errors of Speech*, etc. A canon of Laon, in his manuscript *Chronicle*, explains *birrus* as follows:

> “And behold, a certain man dressed in the guise of a pilgrim, in a *birrus*, that is, wearing a Jerusalem garment,” etc.
