(83) **CHAP. VI.—At Saint-Médard.** Dom Ildefonsus Vrayet, a priest and by no means unfamiliar with our congregation, is devoting his efforts and industry to composing a history of the Abbey of Saint-Médard of Soissons; therefore we shall say no more about it. [Col. 1142A]

(84) **IBID.—[Those] sent to John, at that time abbot of Saint-Nicaise.** Who this John was will become clear from the following epitome of the history of the monastery of Saint-Nicaise and from its succession of abbots. Both were willingly supplied to me from his manuscript history of the diocese of Reims—a work which he prepared over many years with tireless zeal and care—by my very dear friend Dom Guillaume Marlot, formerly prior of that same monastery, a doctor of theology and a man distinguished both for the gravity of his character and for his singular learning.

### Beginnings and development of the Monastery of Saint-Nicaise at Reims, of the Order of Saint Benedict

The Monastery of Saint-Nicaise, of the Benedictine Order, situated in the city of Reims, is regarded as illustrious in origin and celebrated for its development. It was formerly an ancient basilica dedicated to Saint Agricola, to whom it was first consecrated, and was distinguished as the burial place of the archbishops of Reims. It later became famous under the name of the most blessed Nicaise, who received the crown of martyrdom during the Vandal persecution; it was Jovinus, prefect of the Roman military forces, who made it illustrious in the year 330. In the year 407 it happily received the most sacred relics of Nicaise and of his sister Eutropia, as Flodoard records in Book I, chapter 6.

In this same basilica rests that same Jovinus, its munificent founder. This is confirmed by the testament of Saint Remigius, which likewise lists the archbishops buried there, in these words:

> “To the Jovinian Church, bearing the title of Saint Agricola—where that most Christian man Jovinus and Saint Nicaise, together with many martyrs of Christ who belonged to his fellowship, rest; and where also five confessors, the immediate predecessors of Dom Nicaise, together with the most holy virgin and martyr Eutropia, have been laid to rest—three solidi.” [Col. 1142C]

Today the marble tomb of Jovinus, renowned throughout all Gaul, may be seen in the nave of the church, erected beside the wall and projecting outward on three columns. On its front is magnificently carved the notable image of a certain mounted knight striking a lion with a weapon, surrounded by numerous attendants or servants. A curious and learned explanation of it was provided by Nicholas Bergier of Reims in his most scholarly work *On the Roads of the Empire*, as well as by Monsieur Tristan. [Col. 1142D]

A manuscript indicates how elegantly Jovinus constructed the aforesaid basilica:

> “There is a certain church situated in the suburb of Reims—now enclosed within the city walls, since the city’s built-up area was enlarged three hundred years ago—adorned with an extraordinary arrangement of columns, arches, gold, and shining glass stones set among them. It was founded by Jovinus, formerly the glorious prefect of the city of Rome, etc.; and he gave it the following inscription in golden splendor.”

From Flodoard:

> “Jovinus, blessed, assumed the devoted  
> Belts of military service, advanced to the summit  
> Of virtues and raised to the heights, etc.”

Ammianus Marcellinus speaks very highly of this Jovinus in Book XV; so does Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*; and he is also mentioned in the Nicasian Necrology under 7 September, the anniversary of his death being solemnly celebrated on that day. [Col. 1143A]

How greatly the ancient Jovinian basilica surpassed other churches in dignity, after it had been enriched with the relics of the holy martyrs, is sufficiently and abundantly shown by Flodoard in Book I, chapter 17. Indeed, during those earliest centuries it was commonly venerated under both the titles of Agricola and Nicaise, and it enjoyed the name of an abbey, although divine offices there were performed not by monks but by clerical brothers, as can be gathered fully from a diploma of Philip I, king of the Franks, and from chapter 8 of Flodoard.

Although it gradually declined—as is perhaps the fate of human affairs—possibly through the negligence of the clerics, it nevertheless survived for seven hundred years, down to the time of Flodoard. But under Henry I, when the most reverend bishop Gervasius was transferred from the bishopric of Le Mans to the see of Reims by the special providence of God, the basilica had been so worn down by age and disfigured by rain that its roofs and walls were collapsing everywhere, and its ancient majesty had been utterly extinguished. Thus the venerable Gervasius, seeing the fabric of so magnificent a work everywhere crumbling into ruins, resolved to restore it from its foundations. He carried this out splendidly with the assent of the most powerful King Henry I, while Philip I, king of the Franks, advanced his undertaking with royal magnificence. The principal words of his diploma should be set forth here.

637

> “In the name of the supreme God and of the Savior of the world, Jesus Christ, Philip, by the clemency of divine dispensation king of the Franks. [Col. 1143C]
>
> “Since it belongs to royal excellence to devote oneself to fostering, exalting, and protecting the churches of God, and since divine clemency has deigned to raise us to this dignity, if we endure any burdens for their safety, then, as circumstances require, these ought to be supplied to them by our royal liberality. Let all our faithful, both those living now and their posterity in the future, know that Gervasius, venerable archbishop of Reims, has built a certain abbey within his archbishopric and earnestly requested our royal serenity to confirm by this document of our confirmation the acquisitions obtained through his labor and industry.
>
> “There is a church situated in the suburb of Reims, formerly built with marvelous workmanship by the prefect Jovinus. At the beginning of his archbishopric he found it largely consumed by age and neglect. Although it was called by the name of the holy martyr, its first founder having established it under the title of Saint Agricola, nevertheless, out of love for God and for his holy predecessor, he undertook to restore from their foundations all that had completely collapsed within it, to restore by some artifice what hung half-ruined, and to reform the ruined church most becomingly into the appearance of a new work.
>
> “In addition, he added, in distinguished workmanship, a refectory, dormitory, and other dwellings necessary for the use of the servants of God, which had never previously existed there. He gathered there brothers serving the Lord under an abbot and the Rule of Saint Benedict, and assigned sufficient revenues from which they might live, etc.” [Col. 1143D]

> “The sign of Philip, king of the Franks. The sign of Gervasius, archbishop. The sign of Adelard, bishop of Soissons. The sign of Ermengard, bishop of Laon. The sign of Roger, bishop of Châlons. The sign of Baldwin, bishop of Noyon. The sign of Guy, bishop of Beauvais. The sign of Leibert, bishop of Cambrai. The sign of Walter, bishop of Meaux.
>
> “Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnation 1066, the seventh year of King Philip, the ninth year of Archbishop Gervasius, in the church of Saints Agricola and Nicaise, martyrs, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October.
>
> “Baldwin, chancellor, subscribed in place of Gervasius, archbishop.”

We also learn from an ancient manuscript that the illustrious Archbishop Gervasius consecrated the church he had newly built, which he had recently enriched with the relics of blessed Nicaise brought back from the city of Tournai after their return, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October. In it he established a new abbey of Benedictine monks, which, as long as he lived, he took care to adorn with extensive possessions and immeasurable wealth. But, since it had no monks of its own, he was compelled to entrust it to foreign administrators, monks of either condition, etc.

These words make it clear that Gervasius appointed no abbot—although the royal diploma reports what he would have done had he remained alive for a longer period—but reserved the title of abbot to himself as founder, placing foreign administrators under him so that he might exercise paternal care over that tender and scarcely yet united flock. After his death, however, since they had no legitimate leader, they returned to their own places; the possessions left by Gervasius were dissipated by wicked men; and the newly founded abbey was reduced to so wretched a condition that the solemn masses themselves were celebrated by outside priests, since no one was present in the church to perform them. The canonical hours were also recited rather than sung by a certain young man named Jorannus, who had been raised in that place. We shall presently see this man adorned with the dignity of abbot and with the Roman purple. [Col. 1144C]

After Manasses, who had trampled upon sacred and profane alike, Rainaldus first attained the archiepiscopal dignity, and a new light seemed to rise over the region of Reims. For, gathering together what had been dispersed and exterminated, and restoring what had been scattered, he followed the example of the venerable Gervasius and, among other undertakings, attempted to restore the aforementioned Jovinian church to its former condition.

While traveling to the Auvergne region in the king’s company, he visited the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu, recently founded by Saint Robert and at that time distinguished for its observance under the venerable Seguinus, a disciple of the blessed founder Robert. Seizing the opportunity, he earnestly begged the aforesaid Abbot Seguinus to grant him selected monks, together with an experienced superior, in order to restore regular discipline in the monastery of Saint-Nicaise. He obtained this request, as can be gathered from a charter of Rainaldus himself:

> “It seemed good to us—and, as we believe, was divinely inspired—to appeal to the venerable Seguinus, abbot of the monastery called La Chaise-Dieu, and to beg him to undertake with us, for God’s sake, the labor of restoring that abbey, and to send from his congregation a brother suitable to preside over it, together with others as his collaborators in this work,” etc. [Col. 1145A]

This excellent beginning made by Rainaldus was confirmed by the supreme pontiffs Paschal II and Calixtus, who also granted the monks permission to elect an abbot in chapter, to be consecrated by the archbishop of Reims.

Thus, when regular observance had been renewed, Seguinus himself, the venerable man, assumed the government of souls and imposed upon some of his disciples certain observances borrowed from La Chaise-Dieu, so that they could be distinguished from others professing monastic life by these marks. They retained them for many years, until, as discipline grew slack, the abbeys of the provinces of Reims and Sens were reformed by the constitutions of Gregory IX, Nicholas IV, and Benedict XII, drawn partly from the Cluniac Order and partly newly composed.

The habit of the Nicasian monks, although in many respects it resembled that of others, had this peculiarity: they used black-fur *almutia* in place of cowls—concerning which see the *Clementina*—and, as they say, lined boots when they rose at night for matins; they were buried in these same boots after death.

While regular observance continued and the monks cultivated virtue, the Nicasian monastery gradually began to grow wealthy. It became the mother of eight cells and supported a fairly large number of monks. A canonically elected abbot, assisted by four deans or claustral priors, governed it commendably down to modern times, when, after elections had been abolished, the monastic Order declined throughout France and regular observance was neglected, especially in rural places.

Nevertheless, for the past sixteen years the senior monks, moved by the affection they bear toward the holy Rule, have attempted with the greatest zeal to renew it. They summoned the reverend Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, to whom, not under compulsion but out of frank and simple charity, they ceded the church, richly furnished with sacred vessels, all the cloister revenues, and the rights which they had preserved intact until then, retaining almost nothing for themselves, so that the buildings might be maintained permanently.

Hence it came about that the Nicasian abbey, which from its foundation had remained independent, having been renewed in every respect after the example of the royal abbeys of the kingdom of France, was united with this congregation, established by authority of the supreme pontiff. We pray that it may have a prosperous and happy outcome. But enough of this.

### The abbots presided in the following order

**I. Gervasius**, illustrious founder and first abbot, governed the monastery through foreign administrators as long as he lived, according to the custom of that age. An uncertain succession of abbots attempts to thrust upon us a certain Remigius, and after him Albericus and Henricus, borrowed from the cloister of Saint-Remi; but the series is fabricated and legendary. For when Gervasius died, the appearance of the monastery was not so much changed as the congregation was dispersed, and, through the negligence or departure of the administrators, no one remained who could govern or be governed. (From a manuscript chronicle written by a contemporary author.)

The monastery, moreover, which had been enriched by its founder with extensive possessions, was stripped and despoiled like Horace’s crow, by the tyranny of Manasses, who, as I believe, intruded himself into the see of Reims after Gervasius and laid waste everything far and wide. We learn from letters of Gregory VII that under him the monastery of Saint-Remi was likewise oppressed by the same persecution and could not obtain a legitimate abbot, much less provide for others.

Add to this that Guibert of Nogent, speaking of the later Henricus, calls him shepherd of three abbeys—namely Saint-Remi, Humilières, and Nogent—but nowhere mentions Saint-Nicaise, which he would not have omitted. The date of the death of Gervasius, archbishop, is recorded in the Nicasian Necrology under 4 July, on which day the monks solemnly celebrate his anniversary, 1068. [Col. 1146B]

**II. Blessed Seguinus**, formerly abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, became the first regular abbot of Saint-Nicaise in 1086. He was a disciple of Saint Robert, whom Rainaldus I, archbishop of Reims, summoned with twelve religious men in order to restore the Benedictine Order, as recorded in Rainaldus’s charter. He is mentioned in the chartulary of Saint-Thierry in 1093. After resigning, he returned to La Chaise-Dieu after seven years of government, and was succeeded by the following abbot.

**III. Nicholas I**, also from the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu and a disciple of blessed Robert, is likewise recorded in the chartulary of the monastery of Saint-Thierry near Reims in 1093.

**IV. John I**, selected from the same cloister, is mentioned by Guibert of Nogent. As soon as he had obtained the government, he departed for the Holy Land with other abbots, hermits, and recluses who, having unwisely abandoned their homes, set out to travel there, as Orderic Vitalis says in *On the Journey to Jerusalem*. [Col. 1146C]

**V. Guy I** made peace with Nicholas, lord of Rumigny, concerning the tithes of that place in 1100. Manasses II, archbishop of Reims, granted him the tithes of Mont-Valesii in an instrument drawn up in the sixth year of his pontificate, which begins as follows:

> “Both episcopal holiness requires us to care for the poor, and the usefulness of the soul invites us to do so, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s word, our abundance may supply their want, and their abundance may in the future supply our want (2 Corinthians 8:14).” [Col. 1146D]

He presided for four years.

**VI. Jorannus**, educated from childhood in the monastery of Saint-Nicaise and steadfastly attached to regular observance, deserved, because of his outstanding intellectual gifts and exceptional merits, to be promoted first to the dignity of provost and then to that of abbot, which he administered so commendably that he was a mirror of upright life and an example of salutary conduct to others.

Rainaldus, archbishop, calls him “a man worthy of imitation by all good people because of his holiness.” During his rule, distinguished men emerged from the monastery of Saint-Nicaise to spread regular discipline far and wide. Among them are mentioned:

- **Drogo**, claustral prior, who, after expelling the nuns from the monastery of Saint John of Laon in the time of Bishop Bartholomew, brought in a colony of monks in their place. He himself was their leader and first abbot, and later became cardinal-bishop of Ostia. His letter *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion* survives in volume II of the *Library of the Fathers*.

- **Simon**, restorer of fallen regularity in the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Bosco, whom Dom Bernard mentions in Letter 83.

- **Blessed Arnulf**, later a Cistercian monk at Signy.

- **Godefridus**, likewise prior of Saint-Nicaise, who, through the efforts of Calixtus II and Louis VI, king of the Franks, was transferred to Saint-Médard of Soissons to restore the condition of the Rule. Saint Bernard speaks of him in Letter 66, as do several others. [Col. 1147B]

Jorannus also increased the monastery’s possessions with many good acquisitions, including numerous altars, cells, or priories, both in this kingdom and in Flanders. At last, however, touched inwardly by a greater devotion, he resigned and entered the Carthusian Order in 1138, according to the manuscript of Mont-Dieu. There he conducted himself so excellently that Innocent II enrolled him among the cardinals.

**VII. Nicholas II** is recorded in the chartulary in 1139. With the support of blessed Bernard, he obtained the priory of Blessed Mary of Château-Porcien in 1143. He died on 28 September 1144, after fifteen years of rule. He lies in the priory of Fignies near the islands.

**VIII. William** attended the translation of the relics of Saint Gibrian at Saint-Remi under Archbishop Samson in April 1145. He ruled for three years “in all learning and goodness,” as recorded in the Necrology under 21 July. [Col. 1147C]

**IX. John II** received a bull of Eugenius III concerning the union of the priory of Château-Porcien. He died on 1 October 1158. He lies near the altar of the beautiful chapel called La Verde, beneath a stone tomb.

**X. Guy II**, formerly a monk of Saint-Remi. See Sirmond in his notes on Book V of Peter of Celle. He entered into an association with the monks of Saint-Remi and went the way of all flesh on 5 October 1179.

**XI. Pontius** is mentioned in the Necrology under 11 June and presided for two years. So far I find only his name. [Col. 1147D]

**XII. Reginald** was duly and solemnly elected by his religious confrères in 1181. Clement III confirmed his privileges, and he obtained the union of the priory of Berbais. He resigned in 1193 and lies in the chapter house.

**XIII. Walter**, elected after the resignation of his predecessor, was venerable for his life and learning. His reputation spread throughout the entire province, and his works speak for him among us. The brothers of Saint-Amand-en-Pévèle immediately requested him as abbot. He therefore presided for only a few years.

**XIV. Hardericus** is named in the association entered into with the reverend brothers of Saint-Amand in 1193. He too resigned voluntarily after three years in office.

**XV. Drogo**, most ardent in the love of God and exceptionally well educated in the liberal arts, arranged for the anniversaries of benefactors and former abbots to be entered in the Necrology, so that the monks might earnestly apply themselves to satisfying them. But while consulting justice by introducing longer chants and increasing the daily divine office, he provided an occasion for relaxing observance of the Rule.

He renewed the association with the monks of Saint-Remi and died on 18 November 1221. He lies in the chapter house. [Col. 1148A]

**XVI. Simon of Lyons** restored the church according to the design in which it is now seen, not without admiration: in the form of a cross, 305 feet long, 130 feet wide, and 95 feet high from the pavement to the vault; supported by 28 columns or piers; adorned with incomparable glass windows, gifts of kings and nobles; and with a choir paved in varied marble, containing 76 seats on either side.

Simon presided for eight years. He lies in the cloister beside the chapter house. [Col. 1148B]

**XVII. Simon II of Dampierre**, born of very noble parents, ruled for twelve years. He obtained from Innocent IV permission to increase the number of monks to sixty. He lies in the cloister chapel.

When the first fervor of religious life had declined, however, the Rule was enclosed within new constitutions by Gregory IX in 1233, and afterward by Nicholas IV and Benedict XII. These additions to the earlier regulations produced another manner of life. Indeed, I think they also produced a different habit; for, in addition to the use of the cap, they covered their heads with black *almutia*. Clement V confirms this in the following words:

> “Let the monks be content with *almutia* in place of cowls.”

**XVIII. Simon III of Marmoutier** was blessed by the bishop of Soissons while the archiepiscopal see was vacant in 1242. In 1249 he obtained confirmation of immunity from levies and requisitions from the most reverend Thomas de Beaumets, archbishop. After fourteen years of rule, he died on the fifth day before the Nones of July 1254. [Col. 1148C]

**XIX. Gerard of Cernay, or Cerny.** Alexander IV confirmed his privileges. Innocent permitted the feast of blessed Nicaise to be solemnly celebrated by both clergy and people throughout the province of Reims; he also permitted religious men to succeed to their paternal goods and decreed that they could neither be excommunicated nor prohibited from celebrating the divine offices during an interdict, with the doors closed.

In Gerard’s time a dispute arose concerning the preservation of the keys of the city gate called Saint-Nicaise. He died on 17 May 1263.

**XX. Milo Croissart** was elected by John of Courtenay, archbishop of Reims, without prejudice to the rights and liberty of the monastery, as the archbishop himself declares in a charter authenticated by his own seal. He presided for five years and died on 26 October 1269.

**XXI. John III**, called of Saint-Ferreol, presided for only one year. He is noted in the Necrology under 21 August.

**XXII. Guibertus** assumed the administration in 1270. He received Philip and Queen Mary in his monastery; they were very fond of him. In 1284 he acknowledged that the abbey was under the guardianship or protection of the archbishop. He died after eighteen years of rule and lies in the cloister chapel. [Col. 1149A]

**XXIII. Odo le Plat**, canonically and solemnly elected at Reims, was blessed by Archbishop Peter, who had consented to his election. Theobald, duke of Lorraine, rendered him homage in the church of Saint-Sulpice at Rumigny for the fiefs dependent upon the monastery.

He began in 1289 and ended in 1297. He lies in the chapel of Saint-Quentin.

**XXIV. Giles I of Landre** ruled for two and a half months. He was buried in the chapel called La Verde in 1298.

**XXV. Roger** was alive in 1299. He is mentioned in the Nicasian proceedings concerning the right to defend the choir in the procession to Saint Maurice. He lies in the chapel of Saint Mary called of Coucy. When he had been taken from the living—

**XXVI. Giles II of Montcornet**, of the Castilone family, was elected in 1303. He entered into an association with the monastery of Saint Peter of Châlons in 1310. Lord Castilone, count of Château-Porcien and constable of France, rendered him homage for the fief of Rumigny on behalf of his wife Mary in 1313.

In his time Robert of Courtenay authenticated the relics of Saint Nicaise by opening the reliquary, in the presence of Roger, abbot of Saint-Remi. Giles lies in the chapel of Saint-Quentin, decorated with the insignia of the Castilone and Bar families in the stained-glass windows. [Col. 1149B]

**XXVII. Philip la Coque** was elected in 1316. He was a man of great courage and the highest prudence. Ferric, duke of Lorraine, rendered him homage for the fiefs of Rumigny in the Reims district, at a place called Le Barbastre, in 1318, after Philip had declared that the homage ought to be rendered in the town of Rumigny.

Philip entered into an association with the chapter of Reims, in which the manner of proceeding in public processions was prescribed. He is mentioned in the *History of Liège*, folio 384. He united the priories of Ham and Betencourt to the abbatial table. In 1346, worn out by old age, he resigned. He was buried in the chapel of Saint Eutropia in 1348. [Col. 1149C]

**XXVIII. Guy Morel.** After his election, on 8 December 1349, he swore an oath to the church of Reims and generously defended the rights of the monastery and its possession of the relics of Saint Nicaise against the chapter of Reims.

He died on 5 January 1363 and was buried in the chapel of Coucy, or of Blessed Mary of Gladness.

**XXIX. Peter Cocquelet**, having obtained the abbey by resignation, rendered obedience to the archbishop on 6 May 1364. Urban V confirmed the privileges of the monastery. He lies in the chapel of Coucy after seventeen years of rule. When he had laid aside his human life—

**XXX. William of Illiniis**, formerly abbot of Saint-Basle, was promoted through an expectative provision in 1381. After eight years in office he became bishop of Viviers; he is omitted by Claude Robert. He is named in the king’s council in 1398, in the *History of Montmorency* by André Duchesne.

**XXXI. Josserand of Illiniis**, through the resignation of his predecessor, presided for three years. He died on 28 December 1392.

**XXXII. Simon Maubert of Troyes** swore obedience to the archbishop in January 1392 and received the office of blessing from him in the same month. Florentia of Ribemont, lady of Chiny and Germigny, rendered him homage in 1398 for the fiefs dependent upon the monastery, in the presence of Guillaume Fillastre, vicar general.

He died on 19 January 1405. He lies in the chapel of Blessed Mary, called La Verde, behind the high altar. [Col. 1150A]

**XXXIII. Giles III Jennart** rendered obedience to the church of Reims on 24 March 1406, according to French custom. He died in Paris on 18 March 1408.

**XXXIV. Nicholas Duchet**, formerly provost of Saint-Remi and abbot of Saint-Basle, obtained the union of the priory of Fignies for the benefit of the abbatial table and the convent. He died on 22 December 1430. According to the Necrology, he lies near the sacristy in the nave of the church.

**XXXV. James I Gueulart**, canonically elected in chapter, made the customary oath of obedience to the church of Reims on 28 June 1430. He was delegated by the supreme pontiff as judge to settle disputes between the parish priests of the city of Reims and the mendicant religious.

He ruled for twenty-one years and was buried on 19 April 1451. After his death, a conflict arose between the royal officers and the archbishop’s bailiff concerning the guardianship or protection of the monastery’s temporal goods. [Col. 1150B]

**XXXVI. James II Champion** ruled for eleven years and four months. He died on 15 September 1462.

After his death, Guillaume Bouille, canon of Noyon, obtained the abbey in commendam through apostolic letters. The city aldermen, together with the monks, had interceded on his behalf, as is clear from the acts of the chapter of the cathedral church dated 14 February 1465.

After him, Richard de Longueil, cardinal of Coutances, took possession by virtue of letters obtained through an expectative provision, but resigned in favor of the following abbot. [Col. 1150C]

**XXXVII. John IV Jacquier**, through the resignation or voluntary relinquishment of the cardinal, took possession. Nicholas Bouille, protonotary and dean of Noyon, disturbed him in his peaceful possession, but he was confirmed by Paul II in 1467.

He entered into an association with the monks of Saint-Corneille of Compiègne in 1471. He died on 14 July 1483 and was buried beneath the tomb of Giles of Montcornet. [Col. 1150D]

**XXXVIII. John V Fransquin**, treasurer and doctor of canon law, was canonically elected in August 1483; but Robert Lescot, vidame of the church of Reims, disturbed him for a year. He died on 2 July 1500, after seventeen years of rule. He lies in the chapel of Blessed Mary, called La Verde and now the chapel of the Good Tidings. The abbey remained vacant for three months.

**XXXIX. John VI Willemet of Rethel**, distinguished for his virtue and learning, adorned the church with many ornaments, erected a pulpit, and left sufficient revenues for the celebration of the anniversary of his death on 10 October 1521. He was buried in the middle of the choir beside the bronze eagle. [Col. 1151A]

**XL. James III Joffrin**, the last of the regular abbots, was disturbed by many in his peaceful possession of the abbatial dignity. He retained it for only ten years, but can never be praised enough for what he accomplished so excellently for the enlargement of the monastery. The anniversary of his death is perpetually celebrated on 13 January 1530.

### Commendatory abbots

**XLI. Charles des Ursins**, protonotary and archdeacon of Champagne in the church of Reims, was nominated by the king according to the Concordats. He ruled for thirty-eight years and finally resigned, exchanging the abbey for the priories of Saint Peter of Coucy and Saint Theobald.

**XLII. Claude of Guise**, a monk of Saint-Denis in France, swore an oath to the church of Reims in December 1568. He enlarged the abbey, enriched the sacristy with many ornaments, and later became abbot general of Cluny. He died on 23 March 1612. [Col. 1151B]

**XLIII. Francis of Paris of Lorraine** was nominated by the king as royal administrator in 1612, but never obtained canonical possession. He was carried off by premature death on 1 June 1614.

**XLIV. Daniel de Hottemant**, venerable for the merit of his life and his prudence, took possession in April 1616. He resigned in favor of Henry of Lorraine in 1626 and devoted himself to the society of the Fathers of the Oratory, as one who loved a more peaceful and tranquil life. He died there in 1634. [Col. 1151C]

**XLV. Henry of Lorraine** took personal possession in chapter in May 1626.

With his approval, twelve Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur were received with the greatest kindness and generosity within the monastery precincts. They had been sent from the royal monasteries of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Vendôme by the very reverend Father Superior General Dom Gregory Tarrisse, through Dom Columbanus Regnier, visitor of the Province of France. The senior monks, wishing to renew the ancient discipline, which had declined somewhat, welcomed them.

The Fathers were earnestly engaged in this work throughout France, as well as in restoring buildings that in many places lay disfigured by rain and frost, or even by age and the negligence of the commendatory abbots. [Col. 1151D]

After Henry of Lorraine’s resignation in 1643, Louis XIII, king of France, united the Abbey of Saint-Nicaise with the chapter of the holy and royal chapel of the city of Paris, in place of the regalia which were customarily received after the death of the bishops of the realm. Thus far extends the end of the catalogue of abbots.

But what benefit is there in burdening the catalogues of monasteries with the names of so many illustrious men, when it is better that the monastery should flourish through the zeal of a vigilant pastor’s excellent way of life than through their useless and ostentatious lineage?

Thus far Guillaume Marlot, the same author mentioned above.

## TO THE THIRD BOOK

(85) **CHAP. II.—Furthermore, Helinandus, etc.** The canon of Laon, in his handwritten *Chronicle*, writes:

> “In the year of the Lord 1095, Bishop Elinandus endowed with twelve prebends the church of Saint John in the Borough, formerly an abbey of nuns but reduced to the administration of a single priest.” [Col. 1152A]

A little later he adds:

> “Ingelrannus succeeded Elinandus in the bishopric.”

He lies buried in the church of Saint Vincent of Laon.

(86) **CHAP. III.—Ingelrannus, namely of Botheu.** Consult André Duchesne, *History of Coucy*, Book VI, chapter 2, and the proofs, pages 317 and following, where he borrowed a great deal from our Guibertus. 642

(87) **IBID.—Of Roger, count of Porcien.** Concerning him, see the *History of Luxembourg* by the author already cited, Duchesne, page 34, and the proofs, pages 36 and 38.

(88) **IBID.—To Count Godefridus.** The same Duchesne, in the places cited.

(89) **CHAP. IV.—They elect a certain Gualdericus**, referendary of the king of the English. Thus the canon of Laon writes in the passage cited above, under the year 1112:

> “Waldericus,” he says, “had been chancellor of Henry, king of the English. He was an insolent man, entirely without competence in literature, holding learned men in contempt and loving soldiers above all others. He was equally arrogant and presumptuous.” [Col. 1152B]

(90) **IBID.—He is sought from the court contrary to the canons.** See canons 1 and 2 of Distinction 51, especially canon 3. It will also be useful to hear Pope Hadrian, writing to Leo, Constantine, and Irene much later:

> “We have again been exceedingly troubled and disturbed because one appointed from the order of the laity and assigned to imperial service was suddenly elected to the height of the patriarchate, and, contrary to the judgment of the holy canons, was made patriarch as an *apocalligus* [term uncertain]. And—what it shames one to say and is grievous to keep silent—those who still ought to be governed and taught do not blush to appear as teachers, nor do they fear shamelessly to assume the leadership of souls, although the way of a teacher is entirely unknown to them.
>
> “How wicked and rash this is is demonstrated by secular order and discipline. For a military commander is chosen only after labor and careful consideration. What kind of leaders of souls can those be who, with immature haste, desire to ascend to the summit of the episcopate?” etc. [Col. 1152C]

(91) **IBID.—Master Anselm alone, etc.** That often-mentioned canon praises Anselm and assigns the year of his death as 1117:

> “The renowned Master Anselm, dean of Laon, second to none in literary learning in his own time, venerable for the uprightness of his character and the maturity of his counsel, died. Among his other works, with a useful style and diligent industry, he also arranged the marginal and interlinear glosses on the Psalter, derived from authoritative expositions, with polished brevity.” [Col. 1152D]

Commentaries on the Song of Songs and on the Apocalypse are likewise attributed to him, although some inscribe them to Blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

I have also found a letter to the abbot of Saint-Laurent of Liège which escaped the ruin of that enormous manuscript library at Bec. Since it had been weakened by decay, we now publish it lest it perish together with the others.

### Letter of Master Anselm

> “To the venerable abbot H. of Saint-Laurent, Anselm, humble son of the Church of Laon, sends greetings. It must be considered, my lord,” etc.

See it among the works of Anselm of Laon under the year 1117.

643–6 Thus far the exceedingly learned letter of Anselm, which, being most worthy of reading, ought not to have endured darkness any longer.

How shamefully those who wish to make this Anselm a monk are deluded is left with no room for doubt by the foregoing material and by what Guibert writes. The opportunity for error, however, was supplied by several men distinguished by this name in the same period—namely, Anselm of Canterbury, whose pupil he was, and Anselm, formerly abbot of Saint-Vincent at Laon and later bishop of Tournai.

Master Anselm was buried in the church of Saint-Vincent. Andrew Duchesne reports the epitaph carved on his tomb in his notes on Abelard, p. [Col. 1153B] 1163; he also praises this same Anselm at greater length in the same place and on p. 1147. He must, however, be corrected in his citation of the history of a certain canon: in fact, the genuine author is the monk Hermannus, whom we are publishing. See the Appendix to Book III of Guibert’s *Life*.

## Catalogue of the Deans of the Church of Laon

Since we have mentioned certain matters concerning Anselm, dean of Laon, and since Guibert himself and Hermannus praise him extraordinarily in many passages and append much concerning the Church of Laon, it will not be out of place to add a catalogue of the deans of that same church. Most of it was collected from ancient papers by the learned Antoine Bellotte, who now conducts the office of the deanery with distinction, chiefly from the cartulary which James of Trecis, canon and archdeacon of Laon, later elevated to the supreme governance of the Church under the name of Urban IV, had arranged to have compiled; we have fashioned it according to our customary method of annotation.

But since the citizens left absolutely no traces of the Church of Laon’s more ancient monuments when, in the manner of duelists, they almost entirely destroyed and devastated the city by slaughter, bloodshed, and fire—as Guibert records for posterity in Book III of *On His Life*, and Hermannus in Book VI of *On the Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon*, cited above—we shall not delay over the more ancient material. In weaving together the catalogue of the deans of the aforesaid church, we shall investigate only the writings of the Middle Ages, beginning with that celebrated master Anselm.

[Col. 1153D] **I. Anselm**, dean and archdeacon, whom Abbot Guibert commends in these words, addressing Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, in the prologue to the *Moral Interpretations of Genesis*:

“God placed two eyes brighter than the stars upon so great a head, while on your right you have Anselm, proclaimed as a master throughout the whole Latin world. His severity in asserting Scripture and the faith is so sincere that by his teaching he has proved more people to have been true Catholics than any mistaken person of this age could have established as heretics; on the other side, Ralph …”

And in Book III of *On His Life*, p. 498:

“Master Anselm, a man who was the light of all France, indeed of the Latin world, in the liberal disciplines, and of tranquil character.”

The same author says more in this vein in the cited place, p. [Col. 1154A] 505, and elsewhere. Hermannus likewise heaps many praises upon Anselm in Book I, p. 528, and Book III, p. 558.

Rupert of Deutz magnifies Anselm’s learning in his book *On the Omnipotence of God*, chapter 1, speaking of Anselm in these words:

“Anselm of Laon, the Lucifer …”

And in chapter 26:

“He whose faith and knowledge, beyond those of others, have until now borne fruit in the Church of Christ with a good and fragrant reputation—Anselm of Laon—strengthens them by his authority, as we have truly discovered …”

Finally, in Book I of his *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, before the middle of the work, Rupert indicates that he came to Gaul so that he and William, bishop of Châlons, might confer about the free will of God. But when Anselm—“more famous than any bishop, although he himself was not a bishop,” as Rupert says—had set foot in the city of Laon, Rupert implies that he found him “drawing his last breath.”

Finally, it is reported that Anselm firmly refused the bishopric of Laon with the greatest humility of spirit.

He subscribed a charter of Bartholomew of Laon dated 1113, in Hemeraeus, *Augusta Viromanduorum Illustrata*, p. 140:

“I, Anselm, chancellor of Saint Mary of Laon, have reread and subscribed.”

From the schools of Laon, under Anselm as their head, emerged many men of outstanding learning and wisdom who shed glory upon Gaul. Among them were Peter Abelard; William of Champeaux, archdeacon of Paris and later bishop of Châlons; Alberic, archbishop of Bourges; William, archbishop of Canterbury; Gilbert Porretanus, bishop of Poitiers; and Algarus, or Algardus, bishop of Coutances.

Ralph, Anselm’s brother, succeeded him as head of the schools, as Hermannus testifies in Book III, chapter 4:

“After a few days, the man of God Norbert, coming to Laon, entered the school of Master Ralph, who had succeeded his brother Anselm after the latter’s death …”

**II. Guido, or Wido of Anco**, was appointed in Anselm’s place. “Young in age, but old in character,” says the manuscript history. It also states: “While he was dean, he was a lover of chastity and a constant attendant at the church’s divine office.” He was likewise dean and archdeacon.

He himself, according to the charters of the Church of Laon, “caused a certain office of provost to be suppressed, since it was a great burden to that church.”

He granted certain possessions to the abbey of Saint-Vincent at Laon in the following terms:

“I, Wido, dean of the holy Church of Laon, and the entire community … make known that, since in the territory of our village called Brisseium, toward Mechannia, in the place called Report, we possessed uncultivated land, we have granted in perpetuity by right to Abbot Anselm and the monks of Saint-Vincent, who have a farmstead in Mechannia itself, two ploughlands of that land, with all their furrows, subject to the rent of a ninth sheaf, as freely as we ourselves possessed them.

“And since the aforesaid church of the Blessed Martyr is recognized as being especially a daughter of our church, and since we ourselves are bound to be buried in it, we have granted to the brothers of that church, to possess freely, whatever they have acquired up to now or may hereafter acquire in our churches, and whatever the bishops of Laon have granted or may in future grant to them. Done in our chapter in the year of the Lord 1139.”

So the cartulary records it.

But when the fame of his holiness and learning resounded everywhere, he was appointed to the bishopric of Châlons in 1140 or 1142. Hermannus, cited above, Book III, chapter 352.

**III. Gualterus of Mauritania**, in 1152. Following the example of Louis VII, king of the Franks, who had given to the Premonstratensian Church every right he possessed in the mill of Argentré, Gualterus, together with his chapter, also transferred its right in the aforesaid mill, chiefly for this reason: “because the said Premonstratensian church had been begotten by the dean and chapter themselves and remained in the midst of their household as a daughter.” These are the words of the donation made in 1149.

He himself and the chapter also granted the property which the Premonstratensian abbey possessed at Valiscurt, as is clear from these letters of 1153:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Since, by reason of the defect inherent in mutable nature, one generation passes away and another comes, and since old age produces forgetfulness, and forgetfulness confusion and contention, the custom has necessarily arisen that the benefits or possessions of churches should be committed to writing and transmitted to the knowledge of posterity.

“Therefore I, Gualterus, by the grace of God dean of the Church of Saint Mary of Laon, and the entire community of our chapter, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that we have granted to the Premonstratensian church, subject to an annual census, the allodial lands of Valescurt with their appurtenances—namely, the wood of Mesloi, the cultivated land situated on the boundary of Landerfai, and all other dependencies—as well as the altars with their endowments and tithes, both in the territory of Moncels and in that of Murci and Valescurt.

“We also grant them the appointment in those places of suitable priests, whom they shall present in our presence and who shall render us fealty, undertaking to uphold, as far as they are able, our jurisdictions, both individual and common. This on the condition that the same Premonstratensian church shall pay us each year, at the synods of Murci and Valescurt, circatas, seven modii and four galetae of grain, and one modius of peas, measured according to the measure current in the city of Laon at the time these acts were drawn up. Both payments shall be maintained without reduction or increase.

“This grain shall be paid in the form in which, in two, three, or more markets, it is found to be worth one denarius less than the more expensive grain. The peas likewise shall be paid at the price of one denarius less than the more expensive peas.

“The time for payment shall extend from the feast of Saint Remigius to the middle of Lent. Within that period, on whatever day or at whatever time they wish or are able, they shall make payment and convey it to our granary at Laon in their own vehicles. On that day, the two carriers assigned to the cart and the one assigned to the wagon shall receive food from us if we dine in the refectory.

“The aforesaid Premonstratensian church shall also pay us annually five solidi in good coin for a certain portion of the land described above, concerning which there had for some time been a dispute between us and the monks of Saint-Vincent and which had been settled under a record of the same census.

“It should further be known that we have agreed that, if the monks of Saint-Nicolas-des-Prés renounce the land of Tuscis, which they hold from us subject to a census, the Premonstratensians shall receive it under the same census as they did—namely, twenty galetae of grain measured according to the measure of Laon.

“If anyone therefore disturbs them in these matters and evades justice, we shall labor for their liberation, even to the court of Reims, at their expense; and if it should be necessary to go farther, we shall offer counsel and assistance without expense to ourselves. But if anyone evades the hearing of malefactors, we shall pursue the same justice with them which we customarily pursue from our own revenues.

“So that this may remain confirmed and unshaken, we first delimited the aforesaid allodial lands in our presence and with the testimony of the surrounding inhabitants and assigned them to the Premonstratensian church. Their names are these: Bernard, the steward of Moncelles; Wibert, son of Constantius Siuvart; Paganus of Derci; Odo Aldent; Herbert of Boisnero and of Parem; Odo the knight; Robert the steward; Richard and his son; Terricus; Wascelinus.

“Afterward we caused this page to be secured by the drafting of a charter, by the attestation of the lawful witnesses of both chapters, and also by the impression of both seals. The sign of Walter, bishop of Laon. The sign of Richard, and so forth. And it was done at Laon, in the year 1153 of the Incarnation of the Word, in the first indiction, with the twenty-third epact and the third concurrent.”

The ancient membranes, written in the years of the Lord 1151, 1155, 1156, 1157, and 1159, also record that the chapter of Laon, while he was dean, granted certain other possessions to the monastery of Saint-Nicolas-de-la-Selve.

After Gualterus’s death, the elected bishop of Laon went to Rome and was inaugurated there as bishop in 1155; John of Guise, Book XXIV, chapter 3; Sigebert; and the Martyrology of the Church of Laon.

To prevent the royal power from later usurping, according to its wicked custom, the many goods he had acquired for the bishopric, he obtained the following royal order from Louis VII, king of the Franks:

“I, Louis, king of the Franks, to Gualterus, bishop of Laon, and to his successors forever. We wish the concern which we visibly bear for the churches of the kingdom to appear to posterity after the course of the present life has run its way.

“In the Church of Laon, Master Gualterus had been bishop, and for a long time had been its dean. He had seen very many things taken away from the bishops of his time. Terrified by the example of his predecessors and taking precautions for himself, once seated upon the pontifical throne he devoted himself to agriculture, and so forth.”

Publicly enacted at Paris in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1158, in the twenty-second year of our reign.

He took part, together with his metropolitan Henry, in the council held at Tours in 1163 by Pope Alexander III—not, however, together with William, as Robert asserts in *Gallia Christiana*. William was transferred from the see of Sens to that of Reims only in 1177; but that council was convened in 1163.

Gualterus died in 1173.

**IV. Liziardus** was appointed in 1153, as I gather from various charters which he himself subscribed as dean up to the year 1168.

Among other regulations, one finds the following:

“It was also decreed that no one who had not held an ecclesiastical benefice (personatus), or who was not twenty-five years old, should be admitted to the seat of the subdeacons before becoming a subdeacon. To prevent this institution from being altered or violated by anyone, we caused it to be secured by the impression of our seal and by the subscriptions of those approving it. The sign of Lord Gualterus, bishop, and of Liziardus, dean, and so forth. Done at Laon, in the chapter, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1159.”

His work is the book chained to the stalls in the lower part of the choir, commonly called the *Ordinary Book*, in which the matters belonging from ancient times to the ceremonies and divine office of that church are properly arranged.

The Synod of Angers in 1261 states:

“We decree that in every church there shall be a book called the *Ordinary*, which the priests shall consult each day before the beginning of vespers, so that they may perform and carry out vespers, matins, and the office of the following day according to the ordinary instruction.”

So it is found in the book of decrees of the Gallican Church, collected by Laurence Bochellus, Book I, title 19, chapter 1.

The material arranged by this Liziardus in the *Ordinary* concerns only the offices of ferial days and Sundays. The material concerning feast days, discussed below, was arranged by another dean.

A certain exchange was made with Dean Liziardus in the following form:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. It is our duty to bear witness to what is done in our presence and, lest it be consigned to forgetfulness, to entrust it to writing.

“Therefore I, Liziardus, by the grace of God dean of Laon, make known to those present and to those to come that, with the common consent of our chapter, we have given to the Church of Saint Martin, to be possessed freely, the parcel of land contiguous to the land of the church of Saint Martin in the suburb of Laon, enclosed within the wall of that church, which belonged to the endowment of the altar of Saint Quiricus and paid us two denarii annually in census, together with the jurisdiction, enforcement rights, and sale-rights of that land.

“We gave it in exchange for half of the field situated below the clerics’ hill, which pays six denarii annually in census. Garinus, abbot of the aforesaid church, with the consent of his chapter, in turn gave us that half-field, together with its jurisdiction, enforcement rights, and sale-rights, in exchange.

“So that this exchange may henceforth remain valid, we caused it to be secured by the impression of our seal and that of Saint Martin, by a charter, and by the subscription of witnesses. The sign of Gualterus, treasurer of Laon. The sign of Robert, and so forth. Done at Laon, in our chapter, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1165.”

“Agotus, chancellor, reread, wrote, and subscribed.”

**V. Anselm** added his sign to a charter of Gualterus, bishop of Laon, confirming a donation made to the monastery of Saint-Vincent in 1168.

**VI. Robert** held office from 1172 to 1173. The cartulary of the Church of Laon.

**VII. Raynerus**, dean; his name is written in ancient papers, where it is found under the year 1178.

**VIII. Robert II.** Up to that time, the monastery of Saint-Vincent had preserved its right firm and secure, so that the church of Saint-Vincent was called “the inviolable burial place of the bishops, canons, and dependants (casati) of the Church of Laon.” The same privilege had not long before been enjoyed by the church of Saint John of Laon.

Nevertheless, while Robert was performing the office of dean, the canons attempted to establish a cemetery for themselves. Hence arose many lawsuits and disputes. For this reason, arbitrators were chosen by the common consent of both parties. Hugh, abbot of Saint-Vincent, explains their arbitration in his letters as follows:

“To the venerable brothers and most beloved friends Robert, dean, and the chapter of Laon, Hugh, humble abbot of Blessed Vincent of Laon, and the entire community of that church, greeting in the Lord.

“Let everyone know that, when a disagreement arose between us and you concerning our cemetery, which you appeared to have newly constructed contrary to our right and ancient custom, we finally compromised, having pledged our faith on both sides, in the hands of Lord William, archbishop of Reims and cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See; Simon, abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims; and Master Melior, vice-dominus of the Church of Reims.

“They, having deliberated among themselves with due maturity of counsel, arranged the matter between us and you for the sake of peace as follows. Your cemetery shall remain free to you forever, so that bishops, canons, and dependants (casati) of your church, as well as all other persons, clerical and lay, may freely choose burial there.

“If any of those dependants (casati) should be buried elsewhere than with you or with us, we shall pursue our right and yours at common expense and through common labor, and shall share the income in good faith. Your canons, however, shall be free to be buried either with you or with us, and wherever they wish.

“Therefore, in recognition of our ancient custom, you shall pay us annually twelve denarii of Laon currency on the feast of Saint Vincent. So that this may remain confirmed, we caused this charter to be secured by the impression of our seal. Done in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1183.”

[Col. 1159A] The privilege granted to the dean of Laon by Innocent II is repeated in these words by that archbishop, acting as the pope’s representative:

“Furthermore, we grant you what Pope Innocent, of blessed memory, granted you: that whether your bishop is present or absent, you may excommunicate or absolve your wrongdoers; and when anyone has been excommunicated by you, no one may absolve him unless satisfaction has first been made, and so forth. Done in the year of the Incarnation 1179.”

Ancient membranes record that Robert remained dean until 1190.

**IX. Gislebertus**, in 1199, held the office of dean for scarcely a year.

**X. Michael of Corbeil**, brother of Reginald of Corbeil, the seventy-seventh archbishop of Paris; first a canon of Paris, then dean of Meaux, and finally dean of Laon in 1191.

When the Parisians afterward elected Michael as their dean, the people of Laon opposed them. To induce them to yield, Stephen of Tournai wrote them a letter. Finally, when the fame of his learning and piety had spread far and wide, he was elected patriarch while still dean of Paris. But while he was on his journey, he was unwillingly taken to the see of Sens. James of Guise and Demochares count Michael among the archbishops of Sens.

**XI. L. . . . . . . .**, dean, is found in the year 1193.

**XII. G. . . . . . . .** entered into an agreement with the monks of Saint John of Laon in 1193.

**XIII. Adam of Cortlandon**, a nobleman born in a village of the county of Roucy adjoining the town of Fismes.

He founded seven prebends on the condition that, if the canons should ever be unable to continue in them, their revenues would belong to the Church of Laon.

At this time that church had as its most bitter enemy Enguerrand of Coucy, who, like the most savage tyrant, plundered and stripped all the goods of the church’s domain—fields, villages, and so forth—committed the dean to prison, and reduced the canons to the utmost misery.

For this reason all the bishops of the provinces of Laon and Reims ceased from the divine praises and struck the aforesaid Enguerrand with anathema, while all offered help and consolation to the people of Laon.

Among other testimonies, the canons of the Church of Reims provide abundant evidence of this matter. Their letter reads as follows:

“To the venerable men and most reverend friends, Adam, dean, and the entire chapter of the Church of Laon: M., provost; H., cantor; and the other brothers of the Church of Reims, greeting and the sincere affection of true and steadfast love.

“God, the examiner and knower of thoughts and deeds, knows that the injury inflicted upon you … We know that this affair affects all churches in common, and that through the impunity of so great a crime a common danger threatens ecclesiastical liberty.

“But lest what we have done thus far appear insufficient to you, in order to offer you some remedy of consolation and to remove suspicion from your hearts, we have decreed that the bodies of the saints resting in our church shall be brought down with their biers onto the pavement and surrounded with thorns. Before the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, we shall humbly make public supplication each day against the persecutors mentioned above, lying prostrate.

“And if we should learn that the said Enguerrand is present in the church or city of Reims, we shall cease from the divine offices.”

To these may be added the letters of the bishop and canons of the Church of Soissons, which are not unworthy of being reported:

“Hugh, by the grace of God bishop; S., provost; G., dean; and the entire chapter of the mother Church of Soissons, to the venerable men and most beloved in Christ, the dean and chapter of Laon: greeting, and courageously standing for the liberty of the Church, without failing in adversity.

“Since in such a mire we have had no secure dwelling, nor do we yet have one … We are troubled and grieve that a church of such renown and dignity, which was accustomed to assist other churches with counsel and aid and to extend the breasts of consolation to the desolate, now in our time already feels the forerunners of Antichrist.

“Therefore, to bear your burden and your desolation—or rather, ours—with fervent spirit and ardent desire, we offer our hearts and bodies to all of you and to each of you. We ask you with all the affection of which we are capable, and under the bond of love and steadfastness to be preserved between us and you in the future, most earnestly to accept confidently and securely, out of regard for our mutual affection and because we are debtors to one another, the possessions that we place before you as your own, and to use them in every way as your own.

“And if it pleases you to come to us, we are ready to meet you and to receive you honorably and generously in our houses, with every due and devoted honor.”

Ivo of Chartres indicates in Letter 121 that ecclesiastics were accustomed to abstain from the canonical prayers and from the divine sacrifice until the seized goods had been restored.

At last, when Enguerrand had regained his senses and repented of his crimes, Stephen, bishop of Noyon, and Anselm, bishop of Laon, delegated by the supreme pontiff, absolved him from his offenses.

Adam entered into an association with the monks of Saint-Vincent in 1196. He wrote the book entitled *The Ordinary of the Church*, or *Order of the Divine Office*, in which the observances for feast days are prescribed.

It is certain from the cartulary of the same church that he remained dean until 1223.

**XIV. Gualterus of Chambly**, whose family is still highly distinguished in the bishopric of Laon, went to Rome to request what is called an inquiry rescript against the bishop of Laon, which his successor obtained. He died in 1229.

**XV. Stephen of Bria** obtained from the Roman pontiff the aforesaid inquiry rescript, by which he compelled the bishop to revoke the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the dean and chapter.

The Laon cartulary mentions Stephen from 1230 through 1232. It adds that James of Trecis—called Pantaleon, or of Gnatopalace, a canon of Laon and later supreme pontiff under the name Urban IV—was executor of Stephen’s will.

**XVI. Guido of Castro Portuensis.** “He,” says the cartulary, “was unwilling to act as dean for nearly a year and more; therefore the chapter sat with the title of dean suppressed.” But after resigning the deanery, he was elevated to the bishopric of Soissons.

**XVII. Guido of Triangulum**, from archdeacon of this church, became dean in May 1234.

“For at that time the aforesaid Guido of Porto-Castro resigned the deanery, and Lord Guido of Triangulum was elected dean.”

So says the frequently cited cartulary. Following his predecessor’s example, however, after sitting as dean for a year he resigned the dignity in the middle of the chapter, namely in 1235. The same cartulary records this.

**XVIII. Iterus of Malonido**, brother of Anselm, bishop of Laon and archdeacon, was elected dean by the common vote of the canons. He held office from 1236 to 1238.

The cartulary reports that, while Iterus was performing the duties of dean, James of Trecis—mentioned above, a canon and archdeacon of Laon, highly learned especially in canon law and theology—built and founded a chaplaincy in his cloistered house. The right of conferring it belonged to the dean, or to the person who celebrated the divine offices, commonly called the weekly celebrant.

The foundation charter reads:

“To all who shall see these present letters, Iterus, dean, and the chapter of Laon, greeting in the Author of salvation.

“Let your whole community know that, when our beloved canon Lord James of Trecis had newly built, at considerable expense, a house of his own in the Laon cloister, which he had purchased from us for his lifetime, we, considering … Done in the year of the Lord 1237, in July, on the Tuesday after Pentecost.”

**XIX. Garnerus**, dean from being archdeacon of Laon, and afterward bishop of that same church, was appointed in place of Anselm.

Upon his death in 1249, he was the first of all to receive burial in the middle of the choir of the cathedral church. Before this, as noted above, the bishops had been buried in the church of Saint-Vincent.

**XX. William**, archdeacon of Reims, was designated dean when Garnerus was chosen bishop. He subscribed letters in 1244. Finally, Pope Urban IV granted him the red hat in 1263.

**XXI. Elias of Cahors**, a man distinguished both by uprightness of character and by learning, first a canon of Paris, was appointed dean of Laon by the supreme head of the Church in 1261 or 1262.

Not long afterward, however, he returned that office to the pope for conferment upon another person, as is clear from the following bull-letters of that pontiff:

“You, gratefully receiving the favor of this kind graciously bestowed upon you by us, and recognizing more fully through it the paternal goodwill which we bear toward you, accepted this provision. Finally, in your letters, having set forth certain reasonable excuses of yours, you humbly petitioned us to admit those excuses, to release you from the provision mentioned above, and to arrange that the same deanery be conferred upon another suitable person. We, therefore …”

**XXII. John**, formerly provost of Torlatum, was appointed in 1263 by the pope. He was a professor of theology at the University of Paris, distinguished for learning and piety, as that pontiff indicates:

“Seeking with great care an eminent person, adorned with the insignia of virtue, who might, through the application of great diligence, multiply the ornaments of dignity in that same Church of Laon, we turned our apostolic attention toward our beloved son Master John, provost of Torlatum in the diocese of Thérouanne, our chaplain, as toward a man renowned by reputation and, as we learn from trustworthy persons, a man of approved virtue and tested integrity, teaching in Paris in the Faculty of Theology …”

When John was taken from mortal life in 1268 or 1269,

**XXIII. William of Matiscone** took his place until approximately 1271.

He was then summoned to the episcopal see of Amiens. In 1279 he issued a judgment in favor of the people of Laon, which among other things states:

“We, William, bishop of Amiens, and so forth, also considering how, during the time when we held the office of dean, we peacefully exercised authority in the matters aforesaid …”

**XXIV. John Raynaldus**, canon of Laon, whom Pope Gregory X declares dean in these terms:

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Master John Raynaldus, our chaplain, and so forth.

“Since we, favoring your person with the special grace of our goodwill because of the excellence of your merits, grant you the deanery of the Church of Laon with its rights, liberties, and dependencies, through the free resignation made into our hands by our beloved son Master William of Matiscone, then dean of that church, we, by special grace, make provision for you, a canon of that church, confer it upon you, and invest you with our ring, and so forth.

“Given at Orvieto, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the first year of our pontificate.”

This fell in the year 1271.

**XXV. Stephen of Villa Mauri** subscribed certain papers in 1290.

**XXVI. Milo.** His letters state:

“To all who shall inspect these present letters, Milo, dean, and the chapter of Laon, greeting in the Lord.

“Know that, in the year 1295, on the Thursday before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, at the hour of the chapter, when the bell had been rung according to custom, we were assembled in our general chapter concerning the reform of the condition of our Church of Laon …”

[Col. 1163A] **XXVII. Hugh of Châtillon.** While residing at Poitiers, Pope Clement V granted him, in the second year of his pontificate, the privilege of being absent from the Church of Laon for certain private affairs. He held the deanery from 1298 until 1310.

**XXVIII. Garnerius**, from the family of Thoulis, as is clear from the words of this document:

“In the year of the Lord 1312, on the fourth day of December, the discreet man Lord Garnerius of Thoulis, dean of the Church of Laon …”

From Garnerius, Robert of Martigny obtained permission to take possession and be admitted to the chapter on Good Friday itself in 1313, something previously unusual. He died in 1322.

**XXIX. John**, dean until 1326.

**XXX. Adam of Bugnivilla** held the office until approximately 1329.

**XXXI. Guido.** While he was performing the office of dean, many lawsuits arose because Albert of Roya, bishop, claimed jurisdiction over the canons and the other clerics of the Church of Laon and over their ministers. It availed him nothing, however; for the canons preserved their right perpetually in such a way that they have remained entirely exempt from the bishop’s authority up to the present.

**XXXII. Dionysius of Quadrollis**, in 1350. He led Robert, bishop of Laon, after his inauguration, to take possession of the see; this is recorded in an old book of ceremonies called the *White Book*.

**XXXIII. Adam Decola.** He likewise conducted Geoffrey le Maingre, formerly dean of Tours, into the choir as bishop of Laon. The cartulary indicates that the deanery was vacant in 1370.

**XXXIV. Stephen Lescaillart.** From letters written by Pope Clement VII at Avignon in 1389, it appears that he held the office. The supreme pontiff granted the revenues of the parish of Marche to the Church of Laon for the restoration of its sacred basilica, which had been damaged by winds and rain. He lived until approximately 1396.

**XXXV. Baldwin of Mepa**, in 1397. The church register.

**XXXVI. John of Choisy**, not yet initiated into holy orders, was appointed by Pope Benedict XIII.

“As a result, the chapter,” as written in the same register, “decided on the third day before the Ides of June and on the day preceding them, in the year of the Lord 1398, that he should be invested on the condition that, when he was installed and had sworn his oath of fidelity, he should not himself possess the almutium or armilansa, but should deposit it in the hands of the butler or syndic of the said church. After this, he obtained from the chapter the favor of being permitted to use such an armilansa, provided that he carried it on his arm and did not wear it on his head, as was then customary.

“The chapter was moved to grant this because he would not be present in person: the pontiff had released him from the attendance owed to the Church because he was attached to the court of the duke of Burgundy.”

After eighteen months, he returned the deanery to the chapter.

**XXXVII. Peter of Bieura**, on 21 June 1400. He was still performing that office in 1412.

[Col. 1164A] **XXXIX. John Marteguin**, in the years 1421–1426. He is recorded as dean.

**XL. Peter Goudeman.** A final judgment of the supreme court of Paris, issued on 19 November 1442 in favor of the chapter, was rendered for Dean Peter in the dispute between the bishop of Laon and his vicar, the bishop of Pamiers.

**XLI. Peter of Longueil**, in the years 1451–1455.

**XLII. John Dixme** exchanged the archdeaconry of Thiérache with Peter of Longueil in 1456. By order of the king, he attended, together with Antoine de Crespin, or Crespy, bishop of Laon, the general assembly of France at the town of Montargis.

**XLIII. Thomas of Poissy**, in 1460. He died in 1463, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 1164B] **XLIV. Charles of Luxembourg**, canon of Laon, was received as dean by the unanimous consent of the canons on 17 January 1463. His father was Charles of Luxembourg, count of Saint-Pol, and his mother Joan of Bar, daughter of Mary of Coucy.

Charles of Luxembourg was the last person whom the chapter elected and appointed bishop of Laon, in 1472.

XLV. Guillelmus de Armire, formerly archdeacon of Évreux, obtained the deanery from the Apostolic See in 1472, but because of various disputes between him and the chapter, he was compelled to remain absent and resign the dignity.

XLVI. Stephanus Marque, when Guillelmus resigned, was made dean with the consent of the chapter in 1479. He died on 5 June 1480.

[Col. 1164C] XLVII. Polyenus, or Pollius Claudet, the king’s almoner, was appointed dean on 30 October 1480 by three arbiters constituted by the chapter, as appears in the following letter:

“We, after various discussions involving many persons, finally, by the favor of divine grace, etc., recalling the letters of recommendation of our lord the king of France concerning the person of the learned master Poly Claudet, unanimously directed our votes toward that same master Poly Claudet—a prudent and discerning man, commendable in every respect for his learning, life, and morals; established in sacred orders and of legitimate age; born of a lawful marriage; our lord the king of France’s almoner; and highly circumspect in spiritual and temporal matters.”

[Col. 1164D] Since Pollius was not yet a canon, however, the bishop conferred a prebend upon him, and only then was he accepted as a canon.

XLVIII. Joannes Godefridi, although the king had another candidate whom he recommended, the canons chose with resolute spirit, as their letter to the king in 1483 declares in these terms:

“Because the benefice of the deanery is of the greatest importance, carrying responsibility for the souls of all those dwelling in the said Church, and also for directing and supporting all and each of the burdens of the said Church, both spiritual and temporal, the said capitular lords intend, on the appointed day, with the favor of the Most High, to proceed in such a way and to complete such an election according to their conscience [Col. 1165A] that the aforesaid king will rightly have cause to be satisfied.”

Joannes departed this life in April 1494.

XLIX. Joannes de l’Or obtained the deanery by secret ballot on 19 July 1495 and held it until 12 May 1516, when he died.

L. Gaufridus de Bonavalle. Frequent letters were sent to the chapter in his favor, both by the king, by the duke of Vendôme, and also by Cardinal Ludovicus Borbonius, at that time bishop of Laon. The cardinal was finally appointed arbiter and declared Gaufridus dean in 1517, on 12 August. He held the office more in name than in reality.

LI. Valeranus de la Haye is known as dean from 1522 to 1530, but from the records [Col. 1165B] of the abbey of Saint John of Laon it appears that he resigned. For Cardinal Joannes of Lorraine, archbishop of Reims, when appointing Vallerannus vicar general of the said monastery—which he held as commendatory abbot—calls him only a canon and treasurer of the Church of Laon. Add also the Register of the same Church, which records him under these very titles from 1537 to 1542.

LII. Claudius Carpentier, 1537.

LIII. Philippus Esmery, from 1548 to 1554, when he resigned.

LIV. Anthonius de Herbes, a medical doctor, was admitted to the chapter on 24 December 1554 and died in 1556.

LV. Christophorus de Hericourt took possession on 24 June 1556. [Col. 1165C] He was a man born of noble family in the diocese of Laon and endowed with learning. He composed a Brief History of the triumph of Jesus Christ, enacted at Laon against the demon possessing the body of a little woman, Nicola Obrie of Vervins. He dedicated the same History to Charles IX, king of France. This miracle occurred in 1565.

He exchanged the deanery first for an archdeaconry. He gave the Church of Laon a very rich library, and finally departed this life in 1570 and was buried at the very entrance of the choir.

LVI. Firminus le Normand, also called de Trouville, a doctor of theology; after an exchange had been made between the archdeaconry and the deanery, he was installed in possession in 1549. He was an outstanding canon and preacher of the Church. [Col. 1165D] He died on 19 October 1578.

LVII. Petrus Emotte of Laon, distinguished by the title of doctor of theology, gave up his soul on 1 August 1580.

LVIII. Joannes Bertrand, elected on 20 November 1580, held the office for about twenty years.

LIX. Nicolaus Triplot, easily the foremost among the doctors of this century and an indefatigable vanquisher of heretics. From archdeacon, he was elected dean by the unanimous vote of all the canons on 31 August 1600, and shortly afterward resigned this dignity.

LX. Dionysius Hangart, a canon of Laon and doctor of theology, obtained the deanery by royal diploma while the episcopal see was vacant, on 26 October 1601.

[Col. 1166A] LXI. Joannes Bellotte was elected by the common vote and acclamation of the entire chapter on 31 August 1605; he strove more to be useful than to win praise for himself. Among his other virtues, his blameless religious devotion, his open-handed generosity toward the poor, and his prudence in administering the deanery are especially praised, as are his inviolable observance of ecclesiastical laws and his exact observance of the rites in divine services. Hence such a brightness of discipline shone forth in the Church of Laon that scarcely anywhere in the whole of France could one find a college of canons that seemed worthy to be compared with the Laon institution. He saw to the restoration of the city hospital and its renewed return to Christian piety. Nearing his eightieth year, he worked nobly to ensure that the immunities and privileges of the clergy remained unimpaired [Col. 1166B], and endured many hardships for that cause. While he was engaged in these and other works, God called him to Himself on 8 September 1650, in order to reward him.

LXII. Antonius Bellotte, Joannes’s nephew, doctor of canon law, canon of Laon, formerly vicar general of the most illustrious and most reverend lord Philibert de Brichanteau. Before his uncle departed this life, he laid the burden of the deanery upon Antonius’s shoulders—the resignation being subsequently confirmed by the supreme pontiff—and afterward he was elected by the chapter on 16 September 1550. He was a man endowed with integrity and gravity of character, closely following his uncle’s virtues and also highly learned in ecclesiastical affairs.

(92) CHAPTER IV.—With the abbot of Ribodimont. Ribemont, Riburgis mons, Ribodium: “Of all these, Ripemontium is best, situated on a mountain, on the banks of the Isara as it flows past, two leagues from Augusta,” says Nemeraeus in *Augusta Illustrata*, under the year 1095. Nevertheless, in the old records it is consistently written Ribodimons. The monastery of Saint Nicholas in the Meadows, which that abbot governed, recognizes as its founder Anselm, lord of Ribemont; I judged it useful to publish the charter of its foundation.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

“I, Anselm, count of Ribodimont, because the world is already inclining toward old age, human nature is frail, life is brief, and memory unstable,” etc. See under Anselm for the years 1099–1101.

646 Both documents were transcribed and kindly communicated by Dom Furseus Beaurain, a priest and theologian of our Congregation.

The soldiers allow us to say no more at present. At the very time when I am writing these words, after first surrounding the city of Guisia with a siege—though they certainly did not capture it—they have plundered by armed force everything in the monastery and destroyed its buildings.

Robert, in *Gallia Christiana*, in the catalogue of abbeys, under the entry Ribodimonte, inserted the confirmation of the foundation made by Philip I, king of the Franks, in 1084.

(93) SAME PLACE.—At Saint Rufus of Anione. At Avignon, a monastery of canons regular. Consult the same Robert at that place, under “Saint Rufus.”

[Col. 1167A] (94) SAME PLACE.—“I, poetically,” etc. This is touched upon by the canon of Laon in his chronicle:

“When he [Gualdricus] had once returned from the dedication of a certain church, and had ridden out with stole and mitre, in order to administer confirmation if necessary, being light-minded he seized a lance from the hand of one of his attendants and carried it about with lively gestures; whereupon they began to mock him, saying in the vernacular what Abbot Wibertus expressed poetically in this way:

> The tiara and the spear do not well agree,  
> Nor dwell together in one seat.

Here, in the Church of Laon, he took a silk cloth woven with gold, which the queen of England had sent through him to the queen of France, and ordered it to be made into a chasuble in honor of the same Mother of God. [Col. 1167B] As time passed, however, when the aforementioned queens met and had conversed with one another for a long while, the queen of England wondered that the other made no mention of the aforesaid cloth. She said to her:

> ‘You did not like my little gift; yet it was among the finest things that our hands were able to obtain.’

The queen of France replied:

> ‘What are you saying, my queen?’

The other answered:
