> ‘The cloth which I sent to you through the bishop of Laon is what I mean.’

She denied knowing anything about it. The bishop, who was present at that royal gathering, was summoned, and they asked him why he had not presented the cloth sent to the queen. He replied that no one had given him any cloth to deliver to her; but, he said:

> ‘You sent a cloth to the queen of France, and when I came I presented it to her without delay.’

Both queens were amazed, but the queen of England most of all, thinking herself deceived and that she had been conversing with another woman in place of the queen. She said to the bishop:

> ‘Where, then, is the queen of France?’

The other said likewise:

> ‘What is this, my lord bishop? Do you not recognize me?’

He replied:

> ‘Indeed I do.’

The queen said:

> ‘Certainly, you did not present it to me.’

He answered:

> ‘I presented to the queen of France the cloth sent to her by this lady, who is the pious Mother of God, the immortal Queen, whose kingdom is established without end.’

Both queens praised what had occurred and approved the gift.”

647 “Waldericus was succeeded by Hugo, dean of the Church of Orléans. When he died after six months, Bartholomaeus became bishop of Laon. Through his diligence the cathedral church was soon repaired and consecrated again; and in many places where the fervor of religion had been lacking, it was spread through him.”

And Guillelmus de Nangis, in his unpublished *History*, under the year 1113, does not differ from this:

“After Valdricus, bishop of Laon, had been wickedly killed by his fellow citizens, Hugo, dean of the Church of Orléans, was substituted. When he died after seven months,” etc.

(95) CHAPTER IV.—“The tiara and the spear do not well agree,” etc. This alludes to Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.5.14.

(96) SAME PLACE.—“Of goblets and scutrae.” A *hanap* is a drinking bowl or cup, French *hanap*, *tasse*. A *scutra* is a type of vessel, like a shallow dish. Plautus, *Persa*, Act I, scene III:

> Mix the honeyed wine; prepare the struthia and coluthia,  
> So that they may grow thoroughly warm in the scutrae, and add the reed.

[Col. 1168A] (97) CHAPTER V.—“The castellan of the convent of nuns.” I know well that *castellanus* is commonly used for the governor of a fortress, in Book II, *On Border Estates*, Book II, Code, Title 59. But here, as I believe, it is used differently, namely for an advocate whose principal duty was to protect churches or monasteries. Nothing is more common among ancient writers. *Capitulary*, Book VII, chapter 308:

“For the causes and needs of churches and of their servants of God, executors, or advocates, or defenders, whenever necessity presses, are to be requested from the prince; and by him they are to be appointed faithfully and willingly, most faithfully in accordance with the canonical sanctions.”

Advocates were of two kinds: hereditary and appointed. See Pithaeus’s *Glossary* on the capitularies of Charlemagne, and the highly learned observations of Franciscus Bosquet on letters 122, 134, and 191 of Innocent III, [Col. 1168B] pages 143, 149, and 188.

Louis the Pious granted an advocate to the monastery of Aniane in letters composed for this purpose. They contain these words:

“In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the gracious mercy of God, Augustus emperor.

“If, for love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of the servants of God,” etc. See among the diplomas of Louis the Pious, in volume 104 of *Patrologia*.

648 (98) CHAPTER V.—“Which was the head of the basilica.” The more prominent part of a church, so called because it was like a pillow; in the vernacular, the *chevet*. Such heads can still be seen in the basilicas of Saint Denis in France, Saint Genevieve in Paris, Saint Benedict of Fleury, and elsewhere [Col. 1168C].

(99) SAME PLACE.—“The *mastigia* of the cloak thrown back behind.” It is extremely difficult to determine the etymology of *mastigia*. But if conjecture may be admitted, I think *mastigia* was a kind of fastening of the cloak, by which the two front parts were joined together like a thong. Our conjecture seems to be supported by Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 4:

“They all rise together to the blows; the punishment of the Gallic mules wears out the whips.”

From that passage you see that *mastigia* was a kind of whip or leather strap.

(100) CHAPTER VII.—“As head-counted persons.” In a single word, that is, bondservants who were required to pay tribute each year. A charter of the monastery of Flavigny, cited by André Duchesne in the proofs of the *History of Vergy*, page 21:

“Archivisa and her sons under such a census that the males should pay four denarii per head each year.”

(101) SAME PLACE.—“At Saint Vincent.” Since I have at hand a History of the monastery of Saint Vincent, drawn from old records by the learned priest and theologian Emilien de la Bigne, our scholar, from which we shall extract what we are about to report and add a few things through our own study, I am pleased to dwell here somewhat longer, both to survey the ancient monuments of that monastery and to review the succession of its superiors and the noteworthy deeds of certain of them.

### Summary of the history of the monastery and succession of the abbots of Saint Vincent of Laon

The monastery of Saint Vincent almost adjoins *Laudunum Clavatum*. It is situated about one stone’s throw from that city, on a mountain, with a valley lying between it and the city itself, which is likewise placed on a mountain.

It was founded, as is conjectured, by Bruna, daughter of Clovis I, king of the Franks. Her brother Childebert, who then held the kingdom of France, had brought her back to Gaul after rescuing her from the tyranny of the king of the Goths. The beginnings of that monastery are so enveloped in darkness, historians are so silent, and the lack of ancient monuments is so great that it can scarcely rest on anything but conjecture. Yet, lest it appear that I have put these things forward without evidence, Dom Emilien supplies the following testimony from an ancient manuscript codex of the official archive of Laon:

“In the year of the Lord 506, Queen Bruna of Spain founded several monasteries of saints [Col. 1169B] and buildings of wondrous workmanship, among them the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon, in the time of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, and Saint Genebald, bishop of Laon.”

It is more probable, however, that Bruna was Brunichildis—not the wife, but the daughter of the king of the Goths—who was married to Sigibert, king of Gaul. The origin of the name Bruna is indicated by the Chronicle of Besançon:

“Now when Sigibert saw his brothers taking wives of low condition, he sent Gogo, master of the household, on an embassy to Anagildus, asking him to give his daughter, named Bruna, in marriage, etc.; and, to embellish her name, it was enlarged so that she was called Brunechildis,” etc.

This is also the opinion of Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book IV:

“So many evils and bloodshed were brought about in France by the counsel of Brunichildis [Col. 1169C] that the prophecy of the Sibyl might be fulfilled, which said: ‘Bruna will come from the regions of Spain, before whose sight nations will perish; but she will herself be torn apart by the hooves of horses.’”

After its foundation and the establishment of monks, the abbey of Saint Vincent was weakened by various disasters. Clerics occupied it at different times; and finally, in the year of salvation 948, Roricius, or Rorico, son of Charles the Simple, a bishop of Laon distinguished for piety and learning, was ordained. Observing that his predecessors, Dido and Adelletus, had been unable to restore the abbey of Saint Vincent of Laon to its former splendor through the ministry of canons [Col. 1169D], he judged it worthwhile to employ monks. For this reason he summoned twelve monks from the monastery of Saint Benedict above the Loire and installed them in the same sanctuary, placing Mecalmus over them as abbot and drawing up a diploma for this purpose.

These are Dom Emilien’s words. To make the truth still clearer, that diploma should be added.

649 Charter of the restoration of the monks.

“With the merciful aid of heavenly favor, I, Rorico, although unworthy, having obtained the episcopate of the holy Church of Laon, considering that the fate of our final summons awaits me also, as it awaits others, and reflecting upon how greatly I am weighed down by the burden of my sins, began silently to deliberate within myself about something that might benefit this see over which, by God’s authority, I preside, but which would also, as I think, be absolutely necessary for the remedy of my offenses. For on the side of the mountain over which the city rises, plainly in view of it, stands the church of Saint Vincent, a distinguished martyr, venerable in worship and honor. It was reported that in ancient times it had been renowned for monastic observance, but in our own time it had collapsed under every kind of destitution and poverty, until our predecessor Adelmus, at great expense and from every direction, established there a permanent community of twelve canons, with a religious manner of life. After his death, as the evils of various calamities increased, it nearly fell back into the ruin of its former desolation. I could not bear this with equanimity [Col. 1170B], especially since not only bishops of this see but also canons, clerics, nobles, and laypeople were buried there. Having summoned a general assembly, I deliberated with its counsel to restore it to the state of monastic observance that, as was reported, had existed in ancient times, and, as the opportunity of the time permitted, to gather there whatever number of monks might be possible.

“Accordingly, having summoned twelve monks from the monastery of Saint Benedict situated above the Loire, I placed the venerable Melcalanus over them as abbot. Among the other benefits that I conferred upon them, I approved and confirmed the dignity of the second see of the episcopate, granted to that Church by our predecessors from ancient times. I also granted the burial place of bishops, canons, householders, custodians of the mother Church, chaplains and servants, together with their households. I likewise granted the district surrounding the mountain and valley; and, so that they might hold it without any dispute, I defined it as I had granted it, with the counsel and consent of the aforesaid community. We also determined to send this to the venerable synod held at the mountain of Saint Mary in the district of Tardenois, in the month of May, where this was read, with Lord Adelbero the archbishop presiding, together with his fellow bishops, and confirmed by their unanimous consent.

“I, S., archbishop of the Church of Reims, have subscribed and confirmed.

“Done at Laon in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord [Col. 1170D] Jesus Christ 961, indiction 4, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the seventh year of King Lothair.”

From the Greater Cartulary, folio 1.

From this diploma two uncommon privileges of the Church of Saint Vincent can be discerned: first, that it was the burial place of bishops, canons, and others; and second, that it was a second see—that is, it was endowed with the prerogative by which the abbots of Saint Vincent should sit immediately after the bishop in the Church of Laon and at synods, and, in the bishop’s absence, should solemnly celebrate the sacred rites; carry the holy Body of Christ in procession; and bless the people with solemn ceremony. For this reason bishops customarily called that Church not merely the second see but also the first daughter of the Church of Laon. The cartularies, folios 1, 4, 352, etc., bear witness to this [Col. 1171A], as do the more ancient ritual books both of Saint Vincent and of the Church of Laon. This privilege continues to the present day.

There is also another prerogative of the abbot of Saint Vincent, one that should not be considered insignificant. He receives the bishop in his own church, when the bishop is taking possession of the episcopate, and afterward conducts him into the city and presents him to the chapter of the Church of Laon. Thus the Laon Cartulary and the Greater Cartulary of Saint Vincent, folio 122.

King Lothair praised the institution of the monks completed by Rorico in a diploma issued at Compiègne in these terms:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Lothair [Col. 1171B], by the gracious mercy of God, king of the Franks. If we favor the well-considered petitions of our faithful, etc. Therefore we wish it to be clearly known to all the sons of that holy Church and to our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Rorico, bishop of the city of Laon, humbly petitioned our clemency that we might deign to renew, by our royal authority, the precept concerning the basilica of Christ’s most precious martyr Vincent, built upon a mountain in the suburb of the said city and so honored that it has from ancient times been called the second see, and has been the burial place of the bishops, canons, and noble laypeople of the whole city, on account of certain possessions newly gathered there through the generosity of the faithful. For, at the request of the aforesaid bishop, we had previously granted that place the protection of our precept, when he established there, for the protection of himself, his people, and the city, a monastic [Col. 1171C] rule. Since we have found his petition suitable and beneficial, for the love of God and of His most excellent martyr Vincent, for our salvation, that of our wife and offspring, and that of all our posterity, we establish by this precept of our authority and renewal that the monastic order shall, with God’s help, continue in the aforesaid basilica. We also establish that the abbot and monks serving or destined to serve the Lord there shall quietly and freely hold whatever has from ancient times been possessed by that place, etc.

“Done at the royal palace of Compiègne, in the year of the Lord’s [Col. 1171D] Incarnation 975, in the twenty-second year of the reign of King Lothair,” etc.

From the Greater Cartulary, folio 3.

The supreme pontiffs also wished to confirm this privilege many years later, especially Honorius II. “Among these things,” he says in a bull issued at the Lateran in 1135, “we judged it necessary to note by name the burial of bishops, canons, casati, etc., burial having been prohibited within the walls of the city of Laon, since the city itself, from the time of blessed Remigius, had deserved an episcopal see and had been honored with a pontifical cathedral,” etc. Thus wrote Pope Honorius, when Bartholomaeus, bishop of Laon, was acting at Rome.

It remains for us to append a list of the abbots—not indeed the earliest ones, but only those who governed that monastery after the restoration of regular discipline [Col. 1172A].

### List of the abbots of Saint Vincent of Laon

Melchalmus, formerly a monk of Fleury, the first after the institution of the monks, in 948.

II. Bellandus, or Beilandus. On his account Adalbero, bishop of Laon, granted the Church of Petrapons to Saint Vincent, together with its revenues and appurtenances. He died in 989.

III. Lampertus, or Lambertus.

IV. Seigerus.

V. Cadros.

VI. Rogierus.

VII. Hercanneus, or Hervaeus. In 1031, Henry I, king of the Franks, granted him the toll in the suburb of Semilly, at the foot of the mountain of Laon [Col. 1172B].

VIII. Reginerius, born at Corbie. Elinandus, bishop of Laon, gave him the altar of Saint Gobinus, which he also erected into a priory.

IX. Saint Gerard, likewise born at Corbie, was substituted in the place of his brother Reginerius. He was a man distinguished for piety and holiness, as his Acts testify; Hugo Menard continued them in his own style. See the Benedictine *Martyrology*, *Observations*, Book II, under 5 April. We too shall publish them complete, with Christ’s favor, together with other works. He laid the first foundations of the monastery of the Greater Forest in 1079.

X. Rogerius.

XI. Adalbero, equally learned and upright, and also not moderately experienced in legal affairs [Col. 1172C]. He greatly ennobled monastic life and increased the resources of the monastery. In 1088, Rabbodus, bishop of Noyon, granted Adalbero the priory of Saint John the Baptist of Vendolio, above the Fère on the bank of the Isara. The Church of Saint Gobert of Hautmont in the Ardennes, formerly belonging to canons, was subjected to that abbot and his monks. *Lesser Cartulary*, pages 16 and following.

How inclined the minds of nobles were toward piety in those times, in the words of Emilien de la Bigne, may be recognized from a single Anselm, or Ansellus, count of Ribemont. Not content merely to endow the renowned abbey of Anchin in the district of Cambrai, or to build from its foundations another, namely Saint Nicholas, at the foot of his castle, he repented of the wrongs [Col. 1172D] that he had inflicted upon the brothers of Saint Vincent of Laon and their dependents. He appeared in their chapter with his shoulders bared and had himself scourged by the monks; and, as compensation for the loss suffered by the church, he granted its religious and dependents free passage through his lands, namely Mauchery and Ribemont, etc. So it is recorded in the same Cartulary.

Bishop Elinandus, when near death, confirmed this donation. Finally, Adalbero laid aside the burden of the flesh and was buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary Magdalene, which he himself had built. On the tomb were these words:

> Abbot Adalbero

[Col. 1173A] XII. Sifridus, equal to Adalbero in religion and learning, was most steadfast in regular observance. He was, I believe, formerly prior of Saint Nicholas—Guibert, our author, addressed to him the letter *On the Morsel Given to Judas*—and became abbot of Saint Vincent. At the request of the venerable Bartholomaeus, bishop, he granted the place of Prémontré to Blessed Norbert. Letters concerning this matter are preserved in the Premonstratensian library.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, etc.

“I, Bartholomaeus, by the grace of God bishop of Laon. Since the Church of Saint Vincent possessed the place called Prémontré, which belonged to the bishop’s personal table, through the gift of our predecessor, Bishop Elinandus, as is contained in the privilege of that same church, the monks occupied the place for a long time [Col. 1173B] and, after many labors, obtained little or no fruit from it; considering this, I asked Abbot Adalbero and the monks to grant me the aforesaid place freely, so that I might dispose of it according to my will. The abbot and monks, agreeing to my request, freely and without contradiction granted me whatever they possessed in that place. I, for my part, not ungrateful for their willingness, granted to the Church of Saint Vincent the altar of Bariacum to be held in perpetuity, saving the right of the synod. I also gave them half a measure of grain at the mill situated near the village called Broncourt. Seeing that the aforesaid place called Prémontré was extremely useful to religious men, I freely and without contradiction granted it in perpetuity to Brother Norbert, his subjects, and his successors. But Brother Norbert, being in no way desirous of what belonged to another, initially refused to accept it, until Seifridus, abbot of Saint Vincent, and his monks had confirmed the gift in chapter by common consent. So that this grant might not thereafter be altered in any way, we took care to confirm it by the impression of our image, by the seal of the Church of Saint Mary of Laon, and by the seal of Seifridus, abbot of Saint Vincent.

“Sign of Bartholomaeus, bishop of Laon. Sign of Seifridus, abbot of Saint Vincent. Sign of Simon, abbot of Saint Nicholas of the Forest, etc.

“Done at Laon, in the chapter of the Church of Saint Mary of Laon [Col. 1173D], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121.”

Seifridus also freely offered half of the place in which the Church of Saint Martin, the first daughter of Prémontré, is situated, since it was subject to the jurisdiction of Saint Vincent.

Pope Honorius II sent a letter to Seifridus in which he confirmed all the possessions of the monastery of Saint Vincent. He died around 1131 and was buried in the lower part of the choir.

XIII. Anselmus, from the monastery of Saint Médard of Soissons, was elected abbot by the monks in 1131. He governed the monastery religiously, learnedly, and prudently for approximately seventeen years. He restrained the audacity of soldiers and knights who were violently and tyrannically seizing estates [Col. 1174A]; relying on the authority of Pope Innocent II, who was then at Laon, he compelled them to return everything. In 1133, the Church of the canons of the castle of Lescheries in the territory of Guisia, and another in the castle of Montaigu, near the chapel of La Fère, were granted to Saint Vincent.

Having gone to Rome, he was elected bishop by the canons of Tournai, who at that very time were in the city arranging for the appointment of a pastor. Since he resisted, however, he was compelled by the supreme pontiff to consent under threat of anathema. How excellently he conducted himself in these offices, both as abbot and as bishop, Hermannus indicates in the Appendix, Book III, chapters 20 and 21. See *Gallia Christiana* under the bishops of Tournai.

XIV. Balduinus governed for only five years [Col. 1174B]. The aforementioned Hermannus discusses him in that place.

XV. Guillelmus. In 1153, Bishop Galterus of Laon gave him the Church of Saint Julian in the suburb of Laon; the same bishop also confirmed the Church of the castle of Nonavilla, which had been granted by Helluinus of Tyre and was erected as a priory.

XVI. Galterus.

XVII. Hugo laid the foundations of the basilica of Saint Vincent, which still exists, and completed it. A dispute between Hugo and Joannes, abbot of Nogent, was settled in 1177 by Rodulphus of Coucy acting as arbiter. He built a sacred church for Saint Genebald, the first bishop of Laon, with twelve canons, and enriched it with estates belonging to the monastery of Saint Vincent. He died in 1200; his tomb in the middle of the choir [Col. 1174C] is adorned with this epitaph:

> Here lies Hugo, the beauty of goodness, the cloister’s discipline, cautious in action,  
> With a royal brow, a clear and abundant fountain of learning.  
> Behold the flower of abbots lies here; may He who reigns everywhere  
> Grant him, according to his merits, the joys of eternal life.  
> The third light after the middle of August closed his life.

XVIII. Ingelrannus, in 1208, received with solemn ceremony a sacred bone of the throat of Saint Vincent the martyr from the bishop of Carcassonne and Simon de Montfort, in the year of our Lord 1215. At nearly the same time, the abbot and monks of the Church of Castres, now a bishopric, sent Ingelrannus part of the arm of the same martyr. They also relate that, in 1234, the chapel of Blessed Mary of La Fère was begun by the lords of Apia, who are buried in the church of Saint Vincent.

[Col. 1174D] XIX. Balduinus II.

XX. Joannes.

XXI. Balduinus III.

XXII. Thomas.

XXIII. Gosbertus. While traveling by order of Pope Gregory X to the Council of Lyons, he was overtaken by death around 1273 or 1274.

XXIV. Guido de Boveriis. Under this abbot, the boundaries of the abbey’s jurisdiction were surveyed in 1280.

XXV. Joannes II, in 1300.

XXVI. Joannes III, surnamed de Saint-Quentin. He died in 1345.

XXVII. Petrus de Suisi, or of Namur, became abbot while Joannes of Saint-Quentin was still alive, in 1333.

652 XXVIII. Petrus II of Villiers is mentioned [Col. 1175A] in an agreement made with the count of Roucy in 1349, concerning a certain right of Saint Vincent at the mill of Petrapont.

XXIX. Joannes IV of Nouëlles, commonly called of Guisia, in 1370. He was highly cultivated in letters. He composed a *Compendium of Universal History* in eight books, divided into four volumes. Under Abbot Joannes, the library of Saint Vincent was exceedingly rich; it contained eleven thousand volumes. He sat in the council held at Compiègne, presided over by Petrus, abbot of Lesnes, together with other abbots of the archbishoprics of Reims and Sens. At that council the letters of Urban IV and Gregory X to the bishops of those metropolitan sees were read; by these letters abbots were exempted from episcopal synods. Joannes died in 1396, and his disciples placed the following epitaph on his tomb:

> Born at Guisia, here beneath the stone lies Joannes,  
> A historian and skilled in law.  
> He was the first of the abbots to be adorned with the mitre.  
> His fame, though unburied, remains, and will sing a wondrous song:  
> A pious mind, a humble mind, a light to his homeland, a Martha in labor.  
> May God illumine the departed man with blessed life.  
> In the year one thousand four hundred, less four,  
> On the eighth day before the Ides of April he departed.

XXX. Joannes V de Sylva, 1396. He died in 1419.

XXXI. Simon a Porta.

XXXII. Thomas Vastel.

XXXIII. Joannes VI, Corbeau.

XXXIV. Helias d’Arson, an apostolic protonotary, seized the abbey under the title of commendatory abbot. He died [Col. 1175C] in 1502.

XXXV. Franciscus de Frechencour, formerly a monk, became abbot. In the Necrology he is noted as born of a noble family. He died in 1506 and was buried in the choir.

XXXVI. Carolus Morel, formerly prior of Saint John of Vendolio, in 1510.

XXXVII. Joannes VII Charpentier, the last abbot from the monastic order. He completely restored the church of Saint Vincent and bestowed many benefactions. He lies in the middle of the choir, honored by this eulogy:

> Here lies Dom Joannes Charpentier of Reims, while he lived the most devout pastor of this Church; he died happily on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the year of our salvation 1538.

### COMMENDATORY ABBOTS

[Col. 1175D] XXXVIII. Carolus Borbonius, cardinal of Vendôme.

XXXIX. Crispinus de Brichanteau, formerly a monk of Saint Denis in France, became abbot of Saint Vincent and bishop of Senlis. He died in 1590.

XL. Godefridus de Billi, first a monk of Saint Denis, then of Saint Vincent, obtained the abbey and the bishopric of Laon. He inflicted various calamities upon the monks. He harassed and expelled from the monastery the prior, Antonius Danis, who complained of the imminent ruin of the buildings; nevertheless, that abbot was compelled by a decree of the Paris court to recall him and receive him amid the sounding of the organs and bells.

[Col. 1176A] XLI. Philibertus de Brichanteau took possession in 1612 and was afterward endowed with the bishopric of Laon. Robert, in his account of the bishops of Laon, says of him: “A man of great piety and prudence:

“Who saw the customs of many men and cities.”

He devoted every effort to repairing regular discipline; therefore, in 1643, he affiliated the monastery of Saint Vincent with the Congregation of Saint Maur.

## Catalogue of certain abbesses of Saint John of Laon

The first abbess and foundress was Saint Salaberga, whose Life we are now publishing for the first time; you will find it below among the Additions.

This monastery, dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God, [Col. 1176B] and subsequently distinguished by the name of Saint John, was founded approximately in the year 640 of the Christian era.

Saint Anstrude, blessed Salaberga’s daughter, consecrated to God by her most holy mother from infancy, was scarcely twelve years old when she saw herself sought in marriage by a young man both most illustrious and most wealthy. Renouncing marriage, indeed the world itself, and leaving her homeland, she came to Laon. Received amid a great concourse of clergy and people and led to the monastery, she assumed the monastic habit under the religious discipline of her holy mother. Eight years later, after her mother’s death, she was elected abbess in the twentieth year of her age; with the consent of Clovis II, king of the Franks, and the acclaim of all the region’s nobles, she was installed by Peregrine, bishop of Laon, after receiving the blessing. [Col. 1176C] She died about the year 707 of Christ, on 15 October; she was renowned for her virtues and miracles during her life and after her death. From her Life, in manuscript.

Adalsinda succeeded blessed Anstrude; she is mentioned in the same Life of Saint Anstrude.

Adelis: her death is recorded in the old manuscript necrology of Saint Vincent on 27 July.

A second Adelis is named in a very ancient codex written in Gothic letters, called the Psalter of Saint Salaberga. In it, though in a more recent script, one can see a catalogue of the church’s ornaments, inventoried before the aforementioned abbess after Walburgis, the treasurer, had died.

Queen Ogina, wife of Charles III, surnamed the Simple. This too was the sacrilegious custom of that age, [Col. 1176D] which had crept into Gaul from the year 845 onward: namely, that kings, as they pleased, very often bestowed possession of abbeys upon their courtiers, indeed even upon their wives. See Lupus of Ferrières, Letters 22 and 42; and Chopin, book III, chapter 8, *On the Domain of France*, where, concerning Ogina, wife of Charles III, and Gerberga, wife of Louis IV, he says:

“We read that, through the corruption of that depraved age, monasteries were handed over to profane persons by King Charles the Simple, so that scarcely ever did Caesar Commodus undermine the condition of the state more harmfully than this Simpleton, who was simpler still. And who was this Louis, Charles’s son? He took from the Empress Ogina the monastery of Laon, dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God, which she had bestowed upon Herbert of Vermandois, the parricide of her husband Charles after his death. Later Louis gave the same monastery to Gerberga, his wife and empress.”

Ogina, however, remained in the monastery of Laon until the year 951.

Queen Gerberga, wife of Louis IV, surnamed Transmarinus, usurped the monastery in the same manner as Queen Ogina.

Pope Alexander II mentions an unnamed abbess of Saint John of Laon, Letter 12, in these words:

“A complaint has been brought that the abbess of the monastery of Saint John of Laon is being expelled from her administration without canonical hearing and the judgment of her bishop, etc. We instructed our brother Elinandus, bishop of Laon, to investigate this case carefully and settle it canonically, [Col. 1177B] but in such a way that the same abbess, before the investigation takes place, be restored to her administration, as the sacred canons prescribe,” etc.

Rainsendis was abbess in the time of Guadricus, bishop of Laon, that is, in the year 1112. Guibert writes of her in Book III, chapter 14, of *On His Life*:

“The most diligent abbess of women of Saint John, of most distinguished birth, the benefactress of the church, named Rainsendis and a native of Laon, was killed by her own servant; and what she suffered, she endured for the faith of the Church.”

Adelis, about the year 1113. The cartulary of the monastery of Saint-Thierry near Reims mentions her, specifically in a grant of a certain piece of land made to that monastery in her own name and that of her chapter.

[Col. 1177C] Queen Adelais, wife of Louis VI, possessed the abbey not under the title of abbess, but by right of her marriage-dowry. This kind of wicked transaction had become customary in that very age: kings placed their wives’ dowries in monasteries. This is especially clear from the famous council of Arras mentioned below.

So much for the abbesses of the monastery of Saint John of Laon; for all the monuments of antiquity perished in that fire of the city, which Guibert presents at greater length in Book III of *On His Life*.

Nevertheless, what an anonymous author—though a canon of Laon—in his as yet unpublished *Chronicle* recorded must by no means be omitted. He says:

“In the year of the Lord 1095, Elinandus, bishop of Laon, [Col. 1177D] endowed the church of Saint John in the suburb, formerly an abbey of nuns but reduced to the administration of a single priest, with twelve prebends.”

We reported this above, column 1151.

The nuns having been removed from the monastery of Saint John, monks were substituted in their place.

What induced Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, to expel the nuns and substitute monks may be observed both from Hermann the monk, Book III, chapters 22 and 23, and from the documents of the archive of Saint John of Laon set out below. For at the provincial council of Reims held at Arras on 10 May 1128, all the prelates, with the king’s approval, decreed that monks should occupy the monastery of Saint John after the nuns had first been expelled. Once this decree had been confirmed by Cardinal Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul—then, that is, in the same year at the council of Reims—and shortly afterward by Innocent II, supreme hierarch of the Church, the nuns were sent away in 1128 to spend the remainder of their lives at Grandelainville.

## Diploma of Louis VI, king of the Franks

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. I, Louis, raised by the mercy of God to be king of the Franks, wish it to be known to all the faithful, both those present and those to come, that at the council which our faithful man Rainaldus II, venerable archbishop of Reims, held at Arras on 10 May with all his suffragan bishops and abbots, where we too were present, he and Bartholomew, venerable bishop of Laon, humbly approached us, earnestly entreating us to permit the church of Laon of blessed Mary and blessed John, which is a royal abbey, to be brought to a better state of religion and monks to be substituted there, because the nuns who had long been there were behaving most disgracefully and outrageously. Recognizing their petition as reasonable and useful, we assented to their wishes and counsel; and we graciously granted that an abbot and monks be installed and maintained there in perpetuity, with every royal right and the dower of Adelais, our wife and queen, preserved, provided that this abbey should owe and render to the same bishop the subjection which our other abbeys in the diocese of Laon owe and render to the bishop of Laon, without any impairment of royal right. We have committed this matter to writing so that it may not be erased by forgetfulness, and, so that it may not be weakened by posterity, we have confirmed it below by the authority of our seal and the mark of our name. Enacted publicly at Arras in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1128, the twentieth of our reign, in the presence at our palace of those whose names and signatures are set below.

“Sign of Louis, the butler. Sign of Hugh, the constable. Sign of Alberic, the chamberlain; no seneschal being present; issued through the hand of Simon, the chancellor. Sign of Rainaldus, archbishop of Reims. Sign of Joscelin, bishop of Soissons. Sign of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon. Sign of Simon, bishop of Noyon and Tournai. Sign of John, bishop of Thérouanne. Sign of Garinus, bishop of Amiens. Sign of Robert, bishop of Arras. Sign of Clarembald, bishop of Senlis. Sign of Peter, bishop of Beauvais.”

## Decree of Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See

“Matthew, by the grace of God bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, to all the faithful, greeting. What at the council of Arras, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was established by our venerable brothers Rainaldus, archbishop of Reims; Bartholomew, bishop of Laon; Goslenus, bishop of Soissons; and the other bishops and abbots of that diocese, together with other religious persons, concerning the expulsion of the nuns living less honorably in the church of Saint Mary and Saint John of Laon and the substitution of an abbot and monks, who would serve God there religiously, in the presence and with the consent of Louis, king of the Franks, who confirmed it by his command—we approved at the council of Reims, on the advice and petition of our venerable brothers, the archbishops of Reims and Sens, the bishops of Laon, Soissons, Paris, Meaux, and Troyes, and many abbots and other religious persons, and we confirmed it in perpetuity by the authority and protection of the Apostolic See.”

## The sealed letters of Pope Innocent II

[Col. 1179B] “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Drogo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint John the Baptist in the city of Laon, and to his brothers, greeting and apostolic blessing. For this purpose the care of the pastoral office has been entrusted to us by the Lord,” etc. See under Innocent II, at the year 1143.

In the following year, the venerable Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, could not fail to record in writing the joy he had felt at the substitution of monks in the monastery of Saint John. He wished to confirm the possessions of that monastery to those very monks in the following form:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Bartholomew, by God’s grace unworthy minister of the holy Church of Laon. Since, by the Lord’s generosity, although unworthy, we labor in the care of the Lord’s fold, and since, because of the duties entrusted to us, we are drawn into the affairs of secular people, if we are unable fully to steady and cleanse our feet, touched by the dust of earthly activity and stumbling on the slippery ground of the world, let us strive to earn the support of those who are counted among the blessed portion of his bride, who, with their feet washed and their tunic laid aside, enjoy ineffable delight with the heavenly bridegroom in the bed of inward rest. For the more they have rejected care of the body through contempt for unstable affairs, and, lamenting the enormity of their former sins and silencing the tumult of invading thoughts, rise with a purified and clean conscience to heavenly things alone, the more gratefully we believe service is offered to the divine majesty through them, if those who have not yet been able to attain Rachel’s desirable companionship endure the laborious service of Leah for the needs of this fleeting life, and their advancement is increased so that, tested by lack of earthly support, they are not compelled to interrupt the leisure of holy contemplation.

“We therefore wish it to be known, both to those now living and to those to come, that when the regard of divine mercy visited the abbey of Laon of blessed Mary and Saint John the Baptist—so that, after the removal of the troop of irreligious women who, by the incorrigible disorder of their lives, had both disgraced the place and become causes of dangerous offense or ruin to many, a religious order of monks might be established there—we rejoiced with divine providence over the correction of that place, offered our willing assent with all the favor we could, and, seeking through the intervention of religious men to obtain some protection for our imperfection during life and, after death, desiring to secure there an everlasting memorial of our soul, we gladly granted what they asked of us. Whatever that place had long possessed from ancient times by the gift of our predecessors, we likewise confirmed to them by our own hand, lest anyone should attempt to bring any charge against their possessions on the pretext that a change of order had been made in that monastery. We ordered this charter of our decree to be strengthened by the subscriptions of witnesses and the impression of our seal, and we forbade under anathema that anyone should thereafter presume either to weaken it in any way or to bring any charge against it.

“Sign of Bartholomew, the bishop who ordered this privilege to be made. Sign of Wido, the dean. Sign of Letoudus, the archdeacon. Sign of Blihardus, the cantor. Sign of Hubert, the priest. Sign of Alberic, the priest. Sign of Benedict, the priest. Sign of Robert, the priest. Sign of John, the deacon. Sign of Peter, the deacon. Sign of Joscelin, the deacon. Sign of Roger, the deacon. Sign of Arnulf, the subdeacon. Sign of Milo, the subdeacon. Sign of Ebalus, the subdeacon. Sign of Robert, the subdeacon.

“Enacted at Laon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1129, indiction 8, epact 9, concurrent 1; in the twenty-first year of the reign of our lord Louis, and the first year of his son Philip; in the seventeenth year of the episcopate of lord Bartholomew.

“I, Radulphus, chancellor of Saint Mary, have reread this.”

## Chronological table of the abbots of the monastery of Saint John of Laon

I. Drogo, formerly prior of the monastery of Saint-Nicaise of Reims, was appointed the first abbot of Saint John by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, in the year of the Lord 1128, on 16 May. He governed the abbey until 1136, when he was summoned to Rome by Pope Innocent II and created cardinal-bishop of Ostia. Chacon and Ferdinand Ughelli in *Italia Sacra* are therefore clearly mistaken: the former places Drogo’s elevation to that dignity at Rome in the year 1133, the latter in 1134. For it is evident from the archive of Saint John that Drogo signed documents with the title of abbot in 1136.

Hermann recounts Drogo’s deeds in the passage cited above, chapter 22. The author of the Appendix to Sigebert, under the years 1128 and 1138, writes: “Drogo, bishop of Ostia, a man distinguished for religion and wisdom, died in good memory.”

He wrote a sermon on the Passion of the Lord; it is extant in the *Library of the Fathers*.

He is also recorded in the manuscript *Bibliotheca Belgica* as having published *Soliloquies*.

II. Baldwin was elected abbot from the office of provost. Hermann discusses him in the passage cited, chapter 23. Ancient parchments indicate that he sealed documents in 1147.

III. Roger, formerly prior of Saint-Medard of Soissons, 1153.

IV. Bruno, until about 1160.

V. Ingelrannus, formerly abbot of Blessed Mary of Nogent, 1160–1164.

VI. Simon died scarcely a year after taking office.

VII. Radulphus, 1164–1165.

VIII. Ingelrannus II, 1165–1182.

IX. Baldwin II, first of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai, then of Saint John of Laon in 1189 and 1193, and finally abbot of Blessed Mary of Signy, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Reims.

X. Nicholas, 1188–1186. [The dates appear inconsistent in the source.]

XI. Ebalus, formerly an ascetic of Saint-Thierry, 1200–1201.

XII. Hugo, a monk of Saint-Remigius of Reims; the monks of Saint John took him as their father.

XIII. Renerus, formerly provost of Saint John, was appointed in 1210–1214.

XIV. Robert, formerly provost of Saint-Thierry near Reims, 1215–1235.

XV. Peter, 1240. During this abbot’s tenure, on the eve of Saint John the Baptist in 1247, the body of blessed Anstrude, virgin and second abbess of this monastery, was transferred by Garnerus, bishop of Laon, from a wooden chest into a more elegant one, in which it is preserved to this day.

XVI. Hugo II, 1240–1277.

XVII. Stephen, 1286.

XVIII. Peter II, 1299.

XIX. Garnerus.

XX. Aegidius of Dizy.

XXI. Peter III of Courpalais, formerly a monk of Saint-Martin of Paris, abbot of Saint John of Laon, and subsequently of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, 1303. He died in 1334. Our Jacobus du Breuil praises Peter in the as yet unpublished *Chronicle of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*:

“Peter of Courpalais,” he says, “abbot of this monastery, obtained a place of burial in the choir of the church near Abbot Morard. Covered with multicolored stone, it records many praises of him: that he was firm in counsel, filled with every goodness, generous to the poor, watchful like Argus; that the clergy held him dear, as did the king and the people; and that, clear in countenance like a monarch, he was sober and chaste in body. The rest, erased by age and the trampling of feet, cannot be read. At the end, however, the dating inscription is clearly visible, as follows:

“‘April drew him away on the third day before the Nones, one thousand three hundred and thirty-four.’

“His tombstone can now be seen before the high altar, beneath the choir screen.”

XXII. Peter IV of Moy. In his time, Stephen of Suisy, a village in the territory of Laon—which is subject to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Saint John—was archdeacon of Burgus, or, as others have it, Bruges, not Bourges, as Chacon says; afterward he became chancellor of France and finally cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Cyriacus in the Baths. Around the year 1310, after providing certain revenues, he built a chapel of the Blessed Virgin and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. He also founded there an anniversary observance of the day of his death. Chacon says that he died at Vienne, whereas he died at Avignon in 1311; in December he was buried in the church of Saint John beneath a marble tomb, on which this epitaph was carved:

“Stephen, born of Suisy, lies buried here:

“Who so conducted himself in life that he was first archdeacon

“Of Burgus, then likewise chancellor

“Of the royal court; thereafter cardinal,

“Once M, thrice C, twice V, once I, by a foul death

“Made to depart in December; may he have rest.”

XXIII. Aegidius de Platea, 1333–1353. In 1342 he assigned certain revenues toward the celebration, on 17 September, of the feast of Saint Flocellus, a child and martyr of Autun.

XXIV. Gerardus, following Aegidius’s resignation, 1353.

XXV. John. In a charter, Hugo, the immediately succeeding abbot, mentions John and Gerard, his predecessors; he expressly calls upon the faithful to send prayers to God for their souls.

XXVI. Hugo III of Châtillon, 1385–1403; he was adopted as abbot of Bellilocus. André du Chesne, *History of the Same Family*, p. 559.

XXVII. Chatardus, 1407.

XXVIII. John Jacquinot, commonly called La Codasse, 1436–1456.

XXIX. James Botin, 1461–1463. After he resigned the abbacy, Pope Pius II inaugurated him as bishop of Hierapolis.

XXX. Anthony Crespin, first bishop of Laon and then archbishop of Narbonne in 1460, obtained the abbey in commendam in 1464 upon James’s transfer of it, from the same supreme pontiff.

XXXI. John Aubinet was elected abbot from among the monks. He was the first of the abbots of Saint John to receive pontifical insignia from Pope Sixtus IV, in 1482. He ceased to hold office in September 1491.

XXXII. Charles of Luxembourg. The chapter, having drawn him last from among the bishops of Laon, received him in 1472; after John Aubinet’s death he became commendatory abbot. He died in 1509.

XXXIII. John Moynet, 1510. The last abbot to profess the monastic life, he died in 1520.

## Commendatory abbots

XXXIV. Matthew l’Evesque, called de Marconnay, [Col. 1182D] a native of Poitiers and bishop of Troyes; he took possession in 1120. He was simultaneously abbot of Saint-Nicolas of Ribemont and Saint-Michel-en-Thiérache.

XXXV. John of Lorraine, son of René, duke of Lorraine, and Philippa of Guelders, took possession through Valeran de la Haye, canon and treasurer of Laon, who acted as his procurator in this matter, from 1533 to 1535.

XXXVI. Peter Cauchon, or de Maupas, 1535; in 1566 he transferred the abbey to Claudius, his kinsman.

XXXVII. Claudius Cauchon, Peter’s brother, simultaneously abbot of Saint-Denis of Reims, 1566. After Claudius’s death, Matthew Brice, the steward, was appointed.

XXXVIII. Stephen Penet, a religious priest, [Col. 1183A] 1601; Matthew, however, did not cease managing the monastery.

XXXIX. John Aubert, doctor of theology, 1608; he died in Paris in 1626 and was buried in the church of Saint-Landeric.

XL. Gabriel Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, who raised the distinction of his family through the episcopal insignia, adorned the dignity of the mitre through the study and writings of the sacred canons and ancient theology, and illuminated it. He obtained the abbey of Saint John about 1627 and died in 1629.

XLI. Charles Albaspinaeus, Gabriel’s brother, marquis of Châteauneuf and keeper of the royal seals, etc. He was likewise abbot of Saint-Eloi of Noyon, Pratelles, and the Black Lake; a man distinguished by the praises of a blameless and vigorous life and of actions nobly performed. He devoted outstanding effort to restoring and propagating in the aforesaid monasteries of Saint-Eloi, Prémontré, and the Black Lake the observance of the Benedictine Rule, as it is known to flourish in the Congregation of Saint Maur. For this reason, when Benedictine fathers of that congregation had been summoned by him to the monastery of Saint John of Laon, the most illustrious Philibert de Brichanteau, bishop of Laon, received them, celebrating the solemnities of Mass according to the pontifical rite, on 1 January 1648.

## On the monastery of Saint Martin of Laon, of the Premonstratensian order

The documents of the donation of the church of Saint Martin of Laon to the Premonstratensian order, made by Bishop Bartholomew, must by no means be passed over by me. For Hermann published three books *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary of Laon*, composed in order to preserve for posterity the illustrious life of that prelate in virtue and holiness. I, likewise moved by the same considerations, thought it would not be unwelcome if I inserted into my observations whatever might bring distinction to that aforementioned bishop.

## Privilege of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, concerning the establishment of the house of Saint Martin

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Bartholomew, by the grace of God unworthy minister of the holy Church of Laon. Since, by the necessity of the office entrusted to us, which by God’s authority we serve, we are bound by the duty of pastoral care to the Church whose governance we have undertaken, we must watch diligently over every part of its members, advance good beginnings toward improvement, and, with the Lord’s help, correct whatever may have been done somewhat imprudently, according to the measure of our ability and competence. We therefore wish it to be known, both to those now living and to those to come, that when, in the church of Saint Martin in the suburb of Laon—which had previously belonged to secular clerics—certain brothers in our time had turned themselves toward regular life, and, remaining there for some time, day by day, had increasingly abandoned their external possessions because of their sins, ignorance, and negligence, while making no interior progress either in number or in religion, we at last, anxious and concerned about the decline of that place, resolved by our counsel that we should entrust that church to the care and direction of Brother Norbert, who in the forest of the Vosges, at the place called Prémontré, had established an eremitical life under canonical profession with a great company of servants of God. When he had agreed to our requests, it was decreed that, just as that place had formerly existed in the hands of our predecessors, so it should now remain in ours and those of our successors; and that the brothers who should come to him through pious devotion for the salvation of souls should, after appointing an abbot for themselves according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, live canonically according to the discipline of the place of Prémontré. But if the abbot of Saint Martin should, at the devil’s instigation, deviate from the path of his rule, and if, having been summoned by the bishop of Laon and the abbot of Prémontré in the presence of the Church of Laon, he should persist in his obstinacy and defiance, then, with the co-abbots of the same religious order summoned to Prémontré, his observance of the rule should be investigated and corrected on their testimony. If, however, he remained obstinate in his wickedness and, after being refuted, proved incorrigible, he should without any retraction be deposed by those same abbots according to the institution of their order; and another suitable man should immediately be substituted in his place by their common counsel and election and ordained by the bishop of Laon.

“Sign of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon. Sign of Wido, dean and archdeacon. Sign of Radulphus, archdeacon. Sign of Seifridus, abbot of Saint Vincent. Sign of Simon, abbot of Saint-Nicolas in the Wood. Sign of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Sign of Rainaldus, abbot of Foigny. Sign of Blehardus, cantor. Sign of Drogo, priest. Sign of Ebalus, subdeacon. Sign of Wido, subdeacon. Sign of Robert, acolyte. Sign of Robert, dean of Saint John. Sign of Geoffrey, cantor. Sign of Haimo, treasurer. Sign of Henry. Sign of Guntrannus. Sign of Hugh. Sign of Clarembald of the market. Sign of Nicholas, castellan.

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124; indiction 12, epact 20.”

## A short catalogue of certain distinguished canons of Saint Martin of Laon

The necrology of that church seems to imply that Walter of Mauritania, who became bishop of Laon from dean, had previously been a canon of Saint Martin:

“On 14 July died lord Walter of Mauritania, formerly bishop of Laon and canon of this church,” etc.

In the same church of Saint Martin he is honored with this epitaph:

“Here I cover Walter, whom I uncover, and beneath mute stone

“I speak of the deeds of a bishop; verses serve me for a tongue.

“By counsel, admonitions, and virtues, in this manner of life,

“He ruled, corrected, and raised up the sheep and the fold.

“Piety was present in him, but seasoned with the salt of severity,

“Lest virtue become sluggish and lacking in flavor.

“The separation of his disciples took him away from the world.

“May he live forever, aided by their merits.”

Godescalcus, canon of Saint Martin of Laon, then abbot of Mont-Saint-Martin, and finally bishop of Arras. The necrology says:

“On 7 August: Godescalcus, bishop of Arras and canon of this church, who among other episcopal benefactions gave us vestments, a golden chalice, silver basins, little ewers, and candelabra, forbidding under anathema that anyone should alienate them from the church.”

Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XII, under the year 1148, gives a substantial testimony concerning Godescalcus.

Concordatus became bishop of Autun. *Necrology*, under 22 March.

[Col. 1186A] Arnold, bishop of Cauria in the Philippines. *Necrology*, 6 February.

Pope Gregory VIII, formerly a canon of Saint Martin. Thus the necrology reads:

“Commemoration of the venerable memory of Pope Gregory, a canon of this church.”

John Comnenus, emperor of Constantinople. The necrology mentions him in this manner:

“On 17 April, commemoration of John, emperor and brother of this church, [a brother] for succor.”

Tradition says that he donated the sacred wood of the Lord’s cross, which can still be seen today, distinguished by images of the Greek emperors formed upon its cover.

Guido, abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon. “He was a brother for succor of this church.” *Necrology*, under 30 August.

We discussed the brothers “for succor” above in the observations, column 1139.

Robert, who professed the Premonstratensian rule in the cloister of Saint Martin, was elected the first abbot of the island of Blessed Mary in Guelders. They say that Robert was a kinsman of Henry, king of the English.

## Notes

(102) CHAPTER VII.—Commonly they call them *bacons*. We French now call them *jambons*, hams. Matthew Paris mentions *bacones* in his *Henry III*, p. 404 of the latest edition:

“Ten thousand loads of grain and ten thousand of oats were sent, together with the same number of bacons.”

In Lorraine and elsewhere, *bacons* is the vernacular term commonly used for *bacones*, namely, the sides and backs of salted pigs. See the glossary at the end of Matthew’s *History*.

(103) CHAPTER VIII.—“Struck down, he died.” The day of the death of Galdricus, bishop of Laon, is commemorated in the Laon necrology:

“On the sixth day before the Kalends of May, the death of Waldricus, bishop, etc. This man was great-hearted and vigorous in secular matters; when the arrogance of the citizens demanded it, because of certain private laws of their rulers, through the illustrious king of France and others . . . he arranged for the commune of Laon to be annulled,” etc.

After recounting what Guibert relates, the necrology adds:

“These and very many other matters pertaining to so enormous a crime, the aforementioned abbot Guibert, who was present in those days, recorded with complete fidelity and truth. Therefore, in mournful memory of so great and so pitiable a crime, it was decreed in our chapter that an anniversary of the aforesaid bishop should be celebrated every year.”

(104) CHAPTER IX.—“Their projecting ornament, which they call *repa*.” A *repa* was a certain ornament made of gold or silver, like a small crown, placed upon the tombs or burial niches of saints; Saint Audoin seems to indicate this in Book I, chapter 32, of the *Life of Saint Eligius*:

“He also made a *repa* at the front of the tomb and built an altar beside the martyr’s feet.”

Yet I am somewhat doubtful whether *repa* and *crepa* are synonyms, since that same Audoin, at the end of Book II, chapter 39, says this about Saint Balthild:

“She also ordered a *crepa* to be magnificently made of gold and silver, which was to be placed above the remains of the confessor Eligius.”

Again, at the beginning of the following chapter:

“When Lent arrived, they girded such a *crepa* with a linen cloth, so that, covered during the days of penance, it might conceal the mass of shining metal,” etc.

From these words everyone can see that *crepa* signifies a burial niche or funerary urn. Could *freda* also be related to the words *repa* and *crepa*? Concerning it, Herricus of Auxerre writes in Book I, chapter 27, of the *Miracles of Saint Germanus*:

“Chlothar, son of Chlothildis, in the time of Saint Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre, had a *freda* made at royal expense, beautiful with gold and silver, in which the names of the founders were inscribed.”

Nothing certain can be established.

(105) CHAPTER IX.—“And, setting fire to the church of Saint John.” From its foundation, this had been a monastery of nuns; many centuries later, by order of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, monks of Saint Vincent of that city began to inhabit it. Hermann the monk, Book III, chapter 22, *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary*. Also William of Nangis, under the year 1128:

“At Laon, in the church of Saint John, by the counsel of the king and nobles of France, the infamous nuns were expelled and monks were substituted in their place; there Drogo, venerable for religion and eloquence, was appointed the first abbot by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon; afterward, by Pope Innocent II, he was made cardinal-bishop of Ostia at Rome.”

At present, nothing concerning the monastery of Saint John is available to us except the Life of Saint Salaberga [Col. 1187C]—which we are bringing to light. It will appear in the Additions.

(106) SAME PASSAGE.—“Radulphus, the nuns’ *discophorus*.” I am persuaded that by the name *discophorus* an administrator is meant, or, as they call him, a procurator, to whom responsibility for conducting affairs and administering resources is entrusted. Guibert likewise called Radulphus the bishop’s *discophorus* at the beginning of chapter 10.

(107) SAME PLACE.—“He would carry [something] under a *birrus* for the sake of release.” Above, we explained *birrus* as a hat; here, however, that a cloak or cape is meant is made quite clear by the words that follow: “But a certain parasite, meeting him, saw what he was carrying under his cloak.” Evidently, the obsolete word *cappa* is to be understood here as a broad cloak [Col. 1187D], a garment which in ecclesiastical usage is still often called a *pluviale*—in the vernacular, *chappe*. Although learned writers of the Latin language derive *cappa* from *caput*. Consult Spelmann’s *Archaeologus* and Vossius, *On the Faults of Speech*.

Concerning the *birrus*, the canon of Laon writes in his manuscript *Chronicle*: “Peter the Hermit, from the territory of Amiens, first a monk at Saint-Rigaud in Forez, and later becoming a preacher, began to be surrounded by so great a multitude of peoples, to be presented with so many gifts, and to be acclaimed with such praises of holiness that many generations do not remember anyone being held in similar honor. The hairs of his mule were snatched away as relics. He wore a thin tunic down to the feet, a cuculla over both ankle-length garments, and a *birrus* [Col. 1188A] over it; he was scarcely nourished by bread, and never by wine or fish,” and so forth.

(108) SAME PLACE.—“To the monastery of Saint Mary at Versiliacum or Vessellicum” (Vézelay), formerly of the Benedictine order in Burgundy, and from its very origin assigned to nuns, as is attested by the testament of Count Gerard of Roussillon and his wife Bertha. The learned Vignerius, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, inserted a substantial part of this testament, in various places, among his proofs concerning the origin of the Alsatian family. We have judged that it would be not burdensome, but indeed most welcome to learned men, to present it here in full rather than piecemeal, together with the letters of Pope Nicholas I and Charles the Bald approving it. The testament reads as follows:

[Col. 1188B] Testament, or foundation charter, of the monasteries of Pultherium and Vézelay.

“To all the faithful of Christ who, with piety, love, and fervent desire, await the blessed life, and who everywhere remain in the unity of Christianity under obedience to God’s commandments; both to those who are present and to those who shall come, who will live in the structure and bond of charity and, until the consummation of the age, shall succeed one another in the Church of the saints.

“I, Gerard, raised by the gift of divine mercy to the dignity of count under the glorious royal clemency, by the common will and desire of my most beloved wife and dearest Bertha—since, by the Lord’s inspiration, it has pleased both of us, unanimously and in agreement, to establish from our possessions and the titles to our property an everlasting memorial to our Lord God, a place where his praise might continually be offered.

“And since, through the pious gifts of our lords and seniors, who have most generously increased us in honors and dignities—that is, our most clement emperor and lord Louis, and the glorious lady and queen Judith, and their son, likewise our senior and lord, King Charles—our possessions have greatly increased, it has seemed most just to us, moved by love for them, to found the very site of a church where, in return for their gracious gifts, solemn and perpetual supplication might be offered to God in prayer, and continual intercession for their salvation.

[Col. 1188D] “Nor are we forgetful of their benevolence toward us: namely, that of our lord and senior Louis Augustus, of Lady Judith and queen, and of their son Charles, likewise our lord and senior, who now survives and reigns. We also render worthy honor to their fathers and parents, namely Leuthard and Gymuld [elsewhere, Grimild], and to the most gracious Hugh and Dava, and to their beloved sons and daughters—whether they have already fallen asleep in the Lord or still live—and to those joined to us by blood, marriage, and kinship, namely the most renowned counts Leufred and Adalard—so that intercession and continual prayer might be made for them, and atonement for their sins obtained.

“And in the place which, with Christ’s help, we shall found, their perpetual remembrance shall endure in succeeding ages. Thus, too, the everlasting memory of all their other relatives, through whom we have succeeded to these same possessions by hereditary right, as well as of all the rest, and of all our friends and all the faithful generally, shall endure; and there, throughout the ages, common prayer shall be offered for everyone.

“I, therefore, Gerard, together with my most beloved wife, have established and built, with pious and faithful devotion, a monastery and dwelling-place for the servants of God in a suitable and fitting location. From the gifts and offerings of our means and possessions, we have, with pious and diligent care, according to the strength God has granted us, provided whatever is necessary for the support of those serving God and whatever is required for the observance of religion; and with the readiest mind, we have offered the very things which we received from his hand, returning thanks for his benefits.

[Col. 1189B] “The place of our devotion, therefore, was founded and established in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, beside the flowing river Seine, in the territory facing the village which from ancient times is called Pultarias, in the district of Laticum, in the kingdom of Burgundy. There a venerable dwelling of prayer might be frequented by the vows and supplications of the faithful, and the heavenly way of life of those living under the regular discipline and institution of blessed Benedict might be sought and desired with all inward longing and ardor.

“There we have bestowed these estates: Pultarias itself, the very place near which the monastery is situated; whatever shall be there from the inheritance [variant: *ibi*, “there”]; whatever our senior, King Charles, has granted us there by the authority of his charter; whatever has accrued to our possessions by any other lawful agreement, with all their appurtenances and whatever belongs anywhere to them.

“In the district of Sens, moreover, we have given Sexta, with everything belonging to it and all its appurtenances; likewise Mannista, with everything belonging to it and all its appurtenances; and also a demesne in the aforesaid district, with everything belonging to it and its appurtenances. Likewise, in the same district, in the village called Piscatoria, situated on the river Yonne, we have given wholly and entirely whatever [Col. 1189D] we acquired from the [lacuna] royal vassal, and whatever pertains to Piscatoria, in every respect in which our lordship there appears or our authority is known to exist, together with whatever belongs by right to us in the district of Troyes.

“We likewise founded another monastery, with the same care and devotion, so that it might become a dwelling-place for the handmaids of God, living under the regular discipline and institution of Saint Benedict, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the place or territory called Virziliacus, in the district of Avalois, in the kingdom of Burgundy. There we also bestowed these estates.

“Virziliacum itself, where the holy and venerable monastery is situated, which we exchanged with the lady and glorious Queen Judith, who acted and petitioned on our behalf before our lord and senior, the most piously remembered Emperor Louis; whatever that most clement emperor, under the confirmation of his charter, granted and bestowed upon us relating to the same estate; and whatever things belonging to that estate pertain to it anywhere, we have assigned to the aforesaid monastery.

“Finally, the estate of Dorviciacum, the estate of Cisternas Fontanas, and Molintium, or whatever we have acquired in the named district of Avalois or in the district of Tornodorum, with all the appurtenances of the aforesaid estates, wherever or in whatever district they may be.

[Col. 1190B] “We have therefore joined in their entirety to these sacred places and monasteries everything whatsoever that we have acquired, or have been able to acquire, in the estates and territories named above, and have permanently attached it to the unity and welfare of those who shall serve God there, reserving for ourselves only the usufruct of them while we remain alive.

“We also retain under our care the protection and defense of the aforesaid monasteries. Therefore, whatever has been bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery by our religious offering, whatever through God’s inspiration shall at any time be contributed or added in property or in services of any kind, or offered by any of the faithful at any time, shall remain inviolate by the perpetual force of this present testament, free from all external services and demands for services, except for the stipends and necessary expenses of those who serve the Lord there.

[Col. 1190C] “Except that, each year, two pounds of silver are to be offered, as a blessing, to the venerable see of the blessed apostles to which we have subjected these places, to the blessed pontiff of the City at Rome.

“And since the daily exercise of benefits is taught by spontaneous charity and the duty of humaneness, nevertheless, free from other payments, let the monks live under regular discipline in quiet service, solemnly offering the service of prayer to God for our most glorious lords and seniors Louis Augustus and his son Charles, and for the ladies of exalted memory Judith and Ermengarde; and likewise for the fathers, mothers, sons, and daughters of the highest remembrance, whether they live or have already fallen asleep in the Lord; for us also, and for our living or deceased sons and daughters, and for all our friends and the entire multitude of the faithful.

[Col. 1190D] “We have subjected this monastery, and the other named above, with all the property bestowed upon them, to the blessed apostles at Rome. By a testamentary document delivered forever to the pontiffs of that City who in succeeding years shall occupy the apostolic see, we have entrusted them with governing and ordering the monasteries—not, however, with beneficiary authority.

“And since the power of giving or of advancing [to office] is to be arranged, we have permanently entrusted them with ensuring, through their careful efforts and watchful provision, that, in accordance with our devotion, the religion of piety and uprightness may always increase there for the glory of God, and that richer fruit may be produced before God.

“We wish this to remain perpetually firm: whenever an abbot or abbess of the aforesaid monasteries, established by our devotion and entrusted to the holy apostles, shall, by divine judgment, depart from this life, the communities themselves, which God wills to exist in those venerable places, shall have the granted power—after consultation and with the advice of holy men—to appoint over themselves, from their own fellowship and association, a man or woman of good life and good reputation, with the Lord’s assistance; and the pontiff who at that time shall merit to hold the apostolic see shall confirm the appointment.

[Col. 1191B] “The amount of property must also always be considered when brothers or sisters are received, lest those communities, God forbid, collapse under an excessive number. We also strongly admonish and, under solemn protest, prohibit anyone ever to alter the vow of our piety or to disturb it by breaking in with a perverse order.

“But if anyone—something we do not believe will happen—should presume to do so, let him be condemned by the command of our lord and senior, King Charles the Pious; and, with the Lord our God rendering him the due recompense for his deed, let him, by the judgment of the holy pontiff, incur, unless he repents, eternal punishment as both a sacrilegious person and a defrauder of sacred things, excluded from the assembly of God’s people.

[Col. 1191C] “We also beseech all of you, most holy Fathers and bishops, by our Lord the Redeemer, that you may always deign to be guardians and helpers in every respect of this work of our devotion.

“This, finally, must be urged upon our pious and dearest servants of God who dwell in the monasteries founded by us with such care: that, with pious and watchful concern, they attend to devotion and religion, ‘and in all things show themselves as servants of God, giving no one any occasion for reproach’ (2 Cor. 6:3), preserving the most religious and sacred order of their monastery. Let the pontiff of the apostolic see be for them a constant ruler, consoler, and protector, so that, joined to the body and members of the Church by most faithful charity and most religious obedience, they may also deserve to be united in fellowship to the head of the whole body, which is Christ.

[Col. 1191D] “This testament, therefore, composed by us with complete piety and devotion, so that it may possess irrefragable force for all time, we have also decreed should be strengthened by the subscription of our own hand and those of illustrious men.

“[The seal] of Gerard the count, and [the seal] of Bertha his wife, who offered this gift to God for the salvation of their souls, established it by testament, and ordered it to be confirmed.

“[The seal] of Eva, their daughter, who, by hearing and confirming, consented to the will of her parents and the offering made to God, and by consenting confirmed it.

“[The seals] of Sanvarius; Simon; Fanvel; Baunarus; Wideric; Gerard; Rotard; Abo; Auzgarius; Optad; Galfar; Atho; Ardulf; Bercharius; Raganaud; Leuderic; Alvert; Fredebert; Radulf; Gerard; Sigibert; Gislemar; Ganzelin; Ayrbald.

[Col. 1192A] “[The seals] of Zeno; Odolard; Odebert; Austoric; Amalbert.”

Confirmation by Pope Nicholas I of the foundation of the monastery of Vézelay.

“Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the religious woman, dedicated to God, who by divine will and divine providence shall have been established in the monastery,” and so forth. See among the letters and diplomas of Nicholas I, in volume 119 of Migne’s *Patrologia*.

657 Diploma of Charles the Bald approving the foundation of the monastery of Vézelay.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, king by the grace of God. If noble and illustrious …” and so forth. See among the diplomas of Charles the Bald in volume 124 of the *Patrologia*.

658 Some years later, after the nuns had been sent away, monks succeeded them in the monastery of Vézelay. Finally, after several centuries had passed, namely in 1537, having deceitfully obtained sealed letters from Pope Paul III, they abandoned the cowl and adopted the customs and garments of secular canons.

(109) CHAPTER IX.—“But Adalbero, abbot of Saint Vincent.” He is the man whom we counted above in the succession of the abbots of Saint Vincent of Laon; he was the eleventh.

(110) CHAPTER X.—“And with a *salban* thrown over him.” Read *saban*. Our author uses this word in his book *On Virginity*, chapter 10: “And to be covered with a *saban* and garments as though asleep.” It is used for linen, as ancient writers explain.

Victor of Utica, in the third book, near the middle, has the deacon Muritta address Elpidophorus, a deserter from the Christian religion and a cruel persecutor whom he had received from the sacred font: “Secretly, unknown to everyone, he carried those things with which, when receiving him from the font, he had formerly covered him—the *sabana* [linen cloths].” Below he explains what a *saban* is: “These are the linen cloths, Elpidophorus, which will accuse you when the majesty of the Judge comes.”

See Saint Gregory the Pope, *Dialogues* IV, chapter 55, concerning the priest of Centumcellae; Saint Boniface of Mainz, letters 10 and 145 at the end; Pope Paul I, in his letter to King Pepin, volume III of the *History of the Franks* by André Duchesne, p. 746.

(111) SAME PLACE.—“Carried to the church, etc.”—We gave the reason why Galdricus, bishop, was buried in the church of Saint Vincent in the summary of the history of that monastery: namely, that this church had been the cemetery of the bishops of Laon. Galdricus’s epitaph, almost obliterated, stands before the altar of Saint Benedict in these words:

The fruit and love of his flock, and the moderation of either law:

While it was permitted him to live, this man was Waldricus.

A bishop of prudent mind over exalted affairs,

May God therefore be his church’s shield.

[lacuna] Scarcely did the earth receive [him];

[lacuna] The sheep slaughtered the shepherd.

(112) CHAPTER XI.—“For Thomas, the son, as he is called, of Codiciacum.” Sugerius also depicts Thomas’s abominable character in vivid colors in his *Life of Louis the Fat*, p. 97 of the *History of the Franks*, volume IV, edited by André Duchesne. Nevertheless, the following charter shows that this same Thomas was at some point a religious man and practiced acts of piety:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I, Thomas, by the grace of God lord of Codiciacum, considering how great is the reverence owed to holy Church, which under God the Father is called our Mother, in which we are reborn through the sacrament of baptism, and from which we are gathered principally toward our mother, the Jerusalem above; observing that the church of Saint Mary of Novigent, established under our patronage after God and from our benefactions, was greatly failing in the freedom due to it and was miserably subject to the usurpations of our servants, I have decided, by God’s inspiration, to distinguish it with the following privilege.

“For I have determined to confirm in writing, by our authority and by the testimony of our nobles, the reverence which I have found was shown to this church by my predecessors.

“We have therefore judged that, within the established boundaries of the estate itself, there should be such freedom that none of our dependents or officials should dare, within those boundaries, to seize either a person or anything else, nor should anyone among men presume to exact anything forcibly from anyone, except the abbot and monks. Rather, the place itself shall be immune from every invasion, as though it were consecrated.

“The people of this place, except for the five whom I have retained for myself, I have left to serve God and the Church. I do not wish them henceforth to be compelled into my service except with the permission and consent of the abbot and brothers. If one of those whom I have retained for myself should refuse to come to me when I have summoned him through my servant, the matter shall be reported to the abbot, or to the prior or provost, so that he may make him come to me.

“If he refuses to come because of the abbot, he shall never be seized within the jurisdiction of the church’s territory by any of my men. But he shall be allowed to be seized within the jurisdiction of my castle.

“And if, from this day forward, some outsider wishes to live there, if he is demonstrably free, he may devote himself to the service of the Church. The same applies to a newcomer. But if it is established that he belongs to some saint, he shall be mine.”

(112*) SAME PLACE.—“These things were done, etc.” A similar account is given by the canon of Laon:

“In the year of the Lord 1112, when Walderic, bishop of Laon, had attempted to recall the citizens of that city from the oath of the sworn commune, and the citizens had turned to rebellion, he was wickedly pierced with their weapons on the Thursday of Easter week, the eighth day before the Kalends of May [April 24], during the greater litany, while certain of his loyal nobles wished to come to his aid. As a result, amid the confusion and tumult of the crowd, the cathedral church and the episcopal residence were set on fire. The church of Blessed John the Baptist in the nuns’ abbey was also burned, together with nine other nearby churches belonging to it.

“King Louis of the Franks avenged this grave crime upon the authors of the sedition so severely that his punishment should terrify both those who were then living and those yet to come from a similar crime.”

(113) SAME PLACE.—“What they call *siccatoria*.” I think it is derived from *sicca* (“dry”). But what kind of instrument or machine a *siccatoria* was, I have not yet found in reading.
