(114) CHAPTER XIV.—“When he died, this man lawfully …” It is self-evident that by the demonstrative *iste* the author means Bartholomew, who succeeded Hugh. Concerning him, William of Nangis writes in his manuscript history under the year 1113:

“When Hugh had died after seven months, the illustrious man Bartholomew was raised to the bishopric of the city of Laon. Through his industry the episcopal church, which had been burned, was restored within a short time,” and so forth.

Hermann relates Bartholomew’s deeds in the Appendix. Since, among other things, he states that this bishop founded the abbey of Foigny for the Cistercian congregation, I have thought it worthwhile to reproduce a few details of its foundation, drawn from the Foigny archive itself:

Concerning the abbey which Bishop Bartholomew built in the place called Foigny.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Bartholomew, by the grace of God bishop of Laon, wish it to be known to those present and to those who shall come that Foigny was an allod of Saint Michael. Since that place was not very useful to the same church, we asked Abbot Elbert and the monks of that place to return it to us free and unrestricted, so that we might do with it whatever we wished.

“We, however, with the consent of the aforesaid abbot and his chapter, returned that same place, free and unrestricted, to Bernard and the monks of Clairvaux, so that they might establish an abbey there and serve God freely and peacefully.

“Done in the year of the Lord 1121.”

The same venerable bishop also bestowed many other benefactions upon the monastery of Foigny. He lies buried in the church of that monastery, where the following two epitaphs may be seen:

Epitaph of the most reverend prelate Bartholomew, bishop of Laon

Born from the stock of kings and the blood of dukes, among illustrious

Ancestors Bartholomew bears an illustrious name.

Ready for arms, while still young he went against the enemy;

He won many trophies and scarcely has an equal.

But God, in pity, draws back the man who is rushing headlong;

Without delay he flees the camp and casts aside the commander’s arms.

From there, as a cleric at Reims, he follows Manasses in virtue—

Indeed, he carries and serves in place of the weary old man.

Meanwhile, at Laon, struck down in the sacred church,

The bishop suddenly dies; and, as the see lies vacant,

Clergy and people seek this man as their shepherd;

They bring him from Reims and set him over themselves.

Thus, having rightly attained the merit and name of a bishop,

He performs and fulfills the office he bears.

By example and word he governs the flock, becoming all things

To all, so that he may gain interest from Christ’s sheep.

At once he hastens to restore the church of Mary,

Which had been burned; he repairs the episcopal buildings.

Then, giving the cloister of the Baptist to monks, he causes

Crimes to perish and scandals themselves to flee.

Afterward he founds a monastery under Mary’s name,

Consecrates it to God, and calls it Foigny.

So that, poured from heaven into chaste hearts, the fire

May burn and grow warm in pious breasts.

And so that, with three vows as though with triple cords,

He may entangle the enemy and direct his line to battle.

[Col. 1195A] Thus it is fitting also to … untie the cords,

To cast down pride, to strike the worldly goads of the flesh.

By founding Bohéries, he tears out the thickets of sin,

And the land bears fruit which he himself first cultivates.

He drives darkness from minds, and, pouring back light,

He gives the Clairvaux, bearing the weapons of light.

Lest the virgin carry an empty lamp, he increases the olive;

Planting Monstreuil, he causes the olive tree to sprout from it.

By giving Prémontré, suitable for those who travel by deserted ways,

He shows the path, which the new order of the Fathers follows.

Establishing by the laws of Norbert the Martinian townsmen,

He corrects their evil customs by these means.

By casting Quissiacum, he shakes the bow and turns back

The demon’s arrows, removing all that harms souls.

Taking the forceps and the coal of Thenalia, he cleanses

The lips and gives pure speech like that of the Cherubim.

He supplies the makers of clear springs with water, and from them

Removes the turbid streams of worldly water.

Like a trumpet he proclaims war against the vices of Buccilici,

And makes mouths fit for divine praises.

[Col. 1195B] At last, weary beneath the burden of the episcopate, he abandons

Honors, the clergy, all prosperity, and wealth.

He seeks Foigny; there he fulfills what he had come to do;

Of his own will the bishop becomes a monk and hides there.

That he might be free for God, wholly intent upon his salvation,

He rejoices to endure bitter things.

Oppressed by old age, he dies, and his body possesses

A worthy marble tomb; his mind seeks the heights of heaven.

660 Thus he enjoys the crowns of his share in virtue,

And his brow is encircled with three little laurels.

Another inscription around the tomb:

The prelate who lies here founded Mary’s church

At Laon, and likewise the burned houses of the bishop.

He built ten churches; one he gave to Benedict,

Four to Bernard; five he cleansed for Norbert.

William of Nangis adds in his manuscript history: “In the thirty-eighth year of his episcopate, Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, scorning the appearance of the world, put on the monastic habit at Foigny.”

He is numbered among the blessed in the Cistercian *Menology* on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, by Chrysostom Henriquez. Many authors discuss Bartholomew; Henriquez cites them for that day, as do Angelus Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, year 1120, chapter 2, no. 1, and year 1142, chapter 1, no. 3.

(115) CHAPTER XIV.—“He was struck with anathema by the archbishop of all France and the bishops.” Abbot Sugerius gives a fuller account in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, cited above:

“Wearied by his [Thomas’s] intolerable harassment, when the Gallican Church was sitting in a general assembly at Beauvais, etc. The venerable Cono, legate of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Praeneste, burdened by innumerable complaints, etc., cutting him down with a general anathema, strips him of his military belt, although absent, and, in the judgment of everyone, deposes him from every honor as a criminal, a man of ill repute, and an enemy of the Christian name,” and so forth.

The author of the Appendix to Sigibert briefly indicates Thomas’s disastrous end: “In the year 1130, Thomas de Marle, deceitfully capturing merchants under his own safe-conduct, was attacked by King Louis with an army; wounded and captured by Ralph, count of Vermandois, in vengeance for his brother Henry, he died at Laon.”

(116) SAME PLACE.—“After the disastrous destruction of Laon.” The people of Laon did not, in fact, put an end to their crimes at this point; they advanced still further. After several years they again disturbed the city, and the festering wound broke open once more. The frequently cited canon of Laon is witness:

“In the year 1177, the men of the Laon region, to the prejudice of the bishop and church of Laon, having agreed with King Louis upon a payment of money, organized a commune. Thus, wrongly imagining that they could shake the yoke of servitude from their own necks and those of their heirs, they believed themselves free.

“But Roger, the distinguished bishop of Laon, went in person and through his friends into the king’s presence, and pleaded in every possible way that he should have mercy on his church and take pity on the commune of his serfs. The king, however, as is said, clinging to the promised payment, did not listen to the bishop or his people.

“The bishop, being magnanimous, saw that his repeated appeals to the king were accomplishing nothing. He therefore summoned his own kin, so that through them he might take vengeance upon the serfs who were ungrateful to him and wished to rebel. Princes of his family came to him from every direction, together with other friends and kinsmen, namely James, lord of Avesnes, and the count of Roucy.

[Col. 1196B] “The opposing party, not unaware of this, waited under arms for their arrival with their own supporters. Many came to their assistance from other communes, under the leadership of Geoffrey of Senlis, then provost of Laon. By order of the king, however, the men of Saint-Médard of Soissons gathered to help them. The commune of Crépy and the commune of Velly assembled to their aid.

“When armed forces had thus been prepared on both sides, the entire rustic multitude, terrified merely by the name of the soldiers who had gathered, chose flight. A considerable number were killed there, but the number of those who perished in the waters is unknown.

“These events took place on the Monday after *Invocavit me*, at the mill of Saint Martin of Laon, called Comporte, which place they had plundered. In the following summer of the same year, King Louis prepared to avenge the slaughter of the men of the Laon region upon the bishop’s brother, Reynald, lord of Rosoy.

“He reached the castle of the count of Roucy, called Nizy. When the friends of the said lord of Rosoy satisfied the king, they obtained a reconciliation on his behalf, though on the condition that he would thereafter acknowledge that his castle was held from the king.

“The venerable bishop, avoiding the king’s anger, concealed himself in Burgundy with Walter, then bishop of Langres.”

(117) CHAPTER XV.—“They call them *matricularii*.” These were the men in each church who cared for the poor registered in the *matricula* and distributed their stipends; today they are called *marguilliers* [churchwardens]. See more in the notes of the most distinguished and learned Bignon on the ancient *Formulas of Marculf*, p. 615, II, and in Vossius, *On the Faults of Speech*, p. 496.

(118) SAME PLACE.—“He attacked him, having given pledges, intending to fight a judicial duel.” Nothing is more common among ancient writers, and nothing occurs more frequently in old documents—especially those of the Middle Ages—than settling disputed matters by a duel, or single combat. But since many have dealt with this subject, I have thought it best to refrain from it, although I have much material at hand, lest by repeatedly inflicting the same matter upon the stomach of the learned reader I should provoke nausea. Consult Pithou’s *Glossary to the Capitularies*; Sirmond’s notes on book III, letter 28; Geoffrey of Vendôme; Bosquet on book II, letter 136; Innocent III; and Spelmann in his *Glossary*, under the words *campus*, *duellum*, and *judicium*.

661 I choose one example among many, a remarkable duel drawn from the parchment documents of this archive of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It shows that the practice of single combat continued for a very long time in Gaul. The document reads:

“In the name of Christ, I, Geoffrey, by the grace of God abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and the convent of that monastery, wish it to be known to all present and future that Stephen of Mathiaco seized one of our men, Ingelrannus of Antogniacum, because he was digging a certain ditch beside the public road, where that same Stephen and Eustace of Bivera, his kinsman, claimed to possess half of the *vicaria*.

“We, however, brought before the lord king this injury inflicted upon us through the unjust seizure of our man. He came to the royal court after being summoned, and claimed that all the lands—except the arpents outside the village of Antogniacum and outside the villages belonging to it—belonged to the *vicaria* which he claimed. For this reason he had seized our aforesaid man, who was digging beside the road without his consent.

“He further said that his father, and he himself after his father, had by custom at Mathiaco and at Colliacum brought forward battle sureties whenever five cases arose in the village of Antogniacum. To prove this he produced two men.

[Col. 1197C] “We, for our part, denying all these claims on behalf of our church, showed, through Landric of Antogniacum, one of his proof-witnesses, that he was defective in making the proof which he had promised, after Lambert of Mathiaco. After several intervening intervals, therefore, that same Stephen came on the day appointed by the lord, with his champion, to the court of the lord king at Paris. Our brothers Rainard and Philip, whom we had sent in our place, appeared there, well equipped for the duel.

“After the case had been examined in the presence of the provosts of Paris—William of Gournay, Reynold of Beaumont, and Baldwin of Flanders, who held the lord king’s place—and since peace could not be established between us and the aforesaid Stephen, each champion was brought into the middle and set for combat.

“After the two had fought long and hard and had grievously injured one another, at last, with God’s help, our champion, attacking his adversary manfully and boldly, tore out his eye and overpowered him with such force that, when the latter admitted himself defeated, the victory fell to our man.

[Col. 1198A] “Moreover, on that same day the aforesaid Stephen had brought two men forward, through whose testimony he wished to prove that he or his servants, without our consent and that of our officials, had the legal right to provide measures of grain from the estate of Pyrodium.

“But Ingelbert of Antogniacum contradicted one of these men, named Odo, and publicly declared that he would prove the man’s testimony on this matter false. Thus, after battle sureties had been exchanged between them, the same day was appointed for the duel.

“When victory had fallen to our first champion, as stated above, our brothers Rainard and Philip brought our champion, namely Ingelbert, into the middle with proper hostages and presented him to the judges, ready to prove what he had promised.

“But the aforementioned Stephen was not present there, nor did he present his champion to the judges with the stipulated hostages, as is customary. Therefore, the same judges gave our brothers Rainard and Philip, together with our champions and hostages, permission to withdraw from the court.

“And as those judges were leaving the court and returning home, they encountered the aforesaid Stephen. Because of his failure to appear for both duels, they seized him and placed him, together with his champions and hostages, in the castle.”

(119) SAME PLACE.—“By the judgment of the sacred waters.” Concerning such ordeals, by hot water and red-hot iron, consult the authors just cited, as well as Juretus on Ivo’s letters 73 and 168. Nevertheless, duels and ordeals were prohibited by Pope Stephen V, *Decretum* II, question 5, “Consuluisti”; by Celestine III, chapter *Cura suscepti*, *On the Vulgar Ordeal*; by Innocent III, chapter *Ex litteris*, *On the Excesses of Prelates*; by Honorius III, chapter *Dilecti*; and elsewhere.

It is not a common judgment that was pronounced—one confirmed by a remarkable miracle—by Saint Pontius, abbot of Saint-André of Villeneuve-lès-Avignon; for that reason it should be recorded here. Specifically, the tenth chapter of his Life, not yet published in print and written by a contemporary, should be transcribed:

“We judge that it would be unworthy to pass over in silence or conceal what we heard from the report of those who were present. One day, then, the man of God, Pontius, had decided to cross the Rhône on certain business connected with his office. After he had humbly celebrated the sacred mysteries at the customary morning hour, he went down to the bank with several companions. At once a cultivator of the land and keeper of his oxen came before him, holding a ploughshare in his hand and quarrelling with his companion, loudly calling him a thief. For three days earlier, this same ploughshare had been covered by the same ploughman beneath the soil, not far from the plough, with no one present or watching except his companion, who was nearby. Sought on the following day, it was not found for three days. Because of this, one complained against the other, accusing him of theft and calling him a thief of the ploughshare.

“The man who had hidden it said: ‘With no one present or nearby except you alone, it was placed beneath the earth; therefore we say that you took it.’ The aforementioned man of God, hearing this complaint made before him, smiled at both and pronounced this judgment: ‘Let the ploughshare be placed near the bank, so that it may be seen in the water of the Rhône, and we shall mark it in the name of the Lord.’ What the man of God had said was promptly carried out.

“Then, sanctifying the water with the sign of the holy cross, the man of God said: ‘With his arms bared, let the one about whom there is greater doubt first lift the ploughshare from the water; and if he is guilty of the theft, may God, just and true, reveal this by his goodness.’ Thus, boldly conscious of his theft, he thrust his hand into the water to draw out the ploughshare, but withdrew it burned as though he had put it into a cauldron of boiling water, and without the ploughshare.

“A wondrous event, such as our age had never before heard. For water naturally cold, in order to reveal the conscience polluted by theft, made manifest its vengeance by burning the thief’s arm. While the people marvelled at this deed and attributed the present miracle to the holiness of the man of God, he himself said with prayers: ‘Let us praise the Lord in his holy works’ (Ps. XXXIX, 19), since ‘he alone works wonders’ (Ps. LXXI, 18), as the truthful Prophet says. Certainly no mortal has ever worked wonders except God, made man in the Virgin Mary. Let him, therefore, be praised, honoured, and glorified; for by his mercy he has made known to us what had remained hidden from our eyes. To him be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

(120) CHAPTER XVII.—They confess that the dispensation of the Son of the Virgin is a phantom, etc. This is the delirium of the Manichaeans. One should consult Blessed Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 46, after the middle; Saint Leo, Sermon 5, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*, toward the middle; Sermon 4, *On Lent*, near the end; and his letter 93 against the Priscillianists, chapter 7; and *Praedestinatus*, heresies 46, 60, and 70.

Indeed, in Gaul, not only after the Berengarian heresy had been subdued was the territory of Soissons infected by this pestilential corruption of Clementius, whom Count John protected, but the archbishop Hugh of Rouen also teaches that various heresies spread into the province of Armorica during that same period, in his treatise *On Heresies*. For this reason we now publish it for the first time. You will find it among the additions.

(121) SAME PLACE.—Meanwhile we proceeded to the council of Beauvais. Cono, the legate of Paschal II, presided over it in the year 1114, as was shown above. See the Appendix to Sigebert, and Nicholas, *Life of Saint Godefrid*, book III, chapter 9.

(122) CHAPTER XVIII.—“Very filthy trousers.” Ovid, *Tristia*, book III, elegy 10, mentions *braccae*, concerning whose ancient use Vossius may be consulted, *On the Faults of Speech*, p. 10. What they mean among our people is indicated by the monks of Molesme in Orderic Vitalis, *History*, book VIII, p. 712:

“Among all the peoples of the western climate, trousers are worn; nor do they know how to do without them so much because of the cold as because of shame. For these reasons, the same custom exists in our order.”

They evidently understand *braccae* as garments covering the thighs; hence *braccile*, a diminutive, which some interpret as *subligaculum*—an undergarment. Consult Menard, *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 42, p. 894, and Haeften, *Monastic Investigations*, p. 495.

[Col. 1200A] (123) CHAPTER XIX.—“For the habit of holy conduct.” The author himself, book I of his Life, chapter 8: “Having assumed the habit of holy conduct, to serve the Lord perpetually.” Thus Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 1, near the middle: “And he bestowed upon him the habit of holy conduct.” The very ancient author of the *Life of Saint Geremarus*, chapter 3, below among the additions: “He established a congregation of monks living under holy conduct.” Hence in former times our predecessors, whenever monastic institution was discussed, habitually spoke of it with the highest veneration. The Fathers of the council at the palace of Verny call it “the holy order,” those of Soissons in 744, chapter 3, “the holy rule,” and those of Mainz under Pope Leo III, chapter 11, “the holy rule.”

[Col. 1200B] Likewise Charles the Great, in a parchment decree to Benedict, abbot of Aniane, concerning the donation of Cella-Nova and elsewhere:

“It is recognized that Benedict has the aforementioned places anew by a decree of our authority, and that, with fullest deliberation, we ought to cede and confirm them to him and his monks dwelling there under the holy rule, for the reward of our soul,” etc.

Pious Louis, son of Charles, in the confirmation of the same monastery’s abbot, which we cited above:

“Masters and teachers not only of holy regular life but also of every spiritual norm,” etc.

Pope Nicholas II grants Pontius, the archimandrite of this monastery, a privilege, approving everything that the kings and the other Christians had conferred:

“We grant, by apostolic authority, that he have permission to impose penance upon those humbly hastening to him from every quarter, and power to excommunicate the wicked and to absolve those who make satisfaction, etc. And lest the congregation of the aforesaid place find even the smallest occasion for carrying out what is holy and just and conforms to the holy rule,” etc.

From the records of the same monastery. When Neufingus, bishop of Angers, established monks—after expelling the canons—in the monastery of Saint-Albin, he expressed himself thus in ancient documents:

“We should also confirm by our authority the privileges that had formerly been obtained for the canons of the same church, now for the brothers who serve God there according to the rule; and we did this because we desire to exalt the holy order,” etc.

[Col. 1200D] But if we proceed farther and consider earlier centuries, we shall observe that the Fathers of the Church heaped extraordinary praise upon the coenobitic life. Saint Athanasius, as Cedrenus reports, in number or chapter 91 of his *History*:

“Since there are two kinds of life, one ordinary and suited to human life, the other angelic, apostolic, incomparable, namely virginity and the monastic life,” etc.

And a little later:

“And hence that apostolic Dionysius: ‘Of all the sacred orders, the order of monks is the highest and most exalted,’” etc.

For this reason the Emperor Theodosius, addressing the monks there below, chapter 130, says:

“Blessed and most fortunate indeed are you, monks,” etc.

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus delivered a discourse in praise of Saint Athanasius; it is discourse 21, where, near the middle, he says:

“He withdrew to those sacred and divine monasteries of Egypt, in which men, drawing themselves away from the world, live for God more than the other men who dwell in the body.”

For this reason Saint Chrysostom, homily 70 on Matthew 22, says:

“The retreats of the monks are not to be considered lesser than heaven. Angels—and indeed the Lord of the angels himself—very often visit them.”

Again Gregory of Nazianzus, in his discourse to Julian the Tribune, calls monks:

“Servants and disciples of God, observers of heavenly realities, the first fruits of our race, these pillars, these crowns of our faith, these stones of the temple,” etc.

And Salvianus, book VIII of *On the Government of God*, near the middle, calls them “the holy ones of God.”

[Col. 1201B] The Fourth Council of Toledo under Pope Honorius I, chapter 50:

“Clerics who aspire to the monastic purpose because they desire to follow the better life ought to be granted by the bishops free entry into monasteries.”

Pope Boniface IV, replying to English clerics who, with every effort and all their strength, tried to exclude monks—because they were dead to the world—from the duties of clerics, writes among other things:

“Therefore monk-priests and canons, who daily proclaim the commandments of God, are not improperly called angels. But each angelic order is affirmed to be more exalted in dignity the more closely it contemplates the glory of God; for just as the Cherubim are veiled with six wings, so are monks,” etc.

Ivo has this in his *Decretum*, part VII, chapter 22. An anonymous poet agrees on this point in Sirmond’s notes to book IV of Godfrey of Vendôme, letter 1, at the end:

“Thus the Cherubim remain in heaven, the monks on earth;

Both render one service to the one Lord.”

Finally, let us look briefly at later times. At the council of Limoges in 1034, the presiding bishop addressed those assembled as follows:

“For the monks should not be bound by our laws, since they enter life by a gate narrower and more constricted than ours.”

Then, shortly afterward:

“I do not compel regular abbots to come to the synod of this see so that they may be accused, but so that they may provide me with counsel concerning the governance of ecclesiastical affairs, so that they, spiritual men, may share with me in the reward of the crown.”

Hence Pope Leo IX, concerning the monks of Saint-Remigius at the council of Rheims:

“He devoutly sought their fellowship” (an old charter records) “and received it, and humbly granted himself to them when they asked,” etc.

In the year 1049, Ivo of Chartres declares in his letter to Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval, the esteem in which he held those bound by monastic vows. With this we shall soon bring our observations to an end.

Saint Bernard, in his sermon *On the Words of the Lord*:

“Truly, my brothers, the cloister, truly religion, is paradise.”

Peter of Blois, letter 13, near the end:

“According to the judgment of my heart, if paradise exists in this present life, it is either in the cloister or in the school.”

And the devout John Gerson, book III of *On the Imitation of Christ*, chapter 56:

“Truly, the life of a good monk is a cross, but the guide to paradise.”

For the rest, believe that I have set forth these opinions of the holy Fathers not out of vanity or self-love, nor because, having embraced the monastic institution, I wish to place it before the other orders:

“Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

Rather, my chief purpose was to place before those who, despising earthly things, have willingly taken Christ’s gentle yoke upon their shoulders what I had gathered in the course of reading, as though in a mirror, so that they might repeat inwardly what Gerson, in the chapter cited above, chapter 10, values so highly:

“For it is not given to everyone,” he exclaims, “that, having renounced everything, they should renounce the world and assume the monastic life.”

Likewise, it was my purpose that they should recognize what the powers of soul and body ought to direct themselves toward, and what summit of virtue and holiness they ought to aim at. Moreover, let those be struck with shame who have no desire for this kind of life—for abstinence, fasts, vigils, sleeping on the ground [*chameuniis*, reading uncertain], silence, solitude, and the other exercises that truly seem burdensome and troublesome to the flesh—and who disapprove of binding themselves by vows to accomplish them, both in speech and in writing. They strive to instill distaste for the practices mentioned above, wrongly teaching that the use of things offers no hindrance whatsoever to Christian perfection, provided that charity is present—as though charity itself could be preserved, that charity, I say, “which does not seek its own” but the things of Jesus Christ (I Cor. XIII, 5), unless the body is disciplined and brought into subjection (I Cor. IX, 27), as the Apostle and all those whom we venerate in the Church under the name of holiness have practiced.

664 Letters of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, to Bernerius, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval.

[Col. 1202D] “Since the pages of decrees and canons grant that the arrangements of ecclesiastical affairs are to be made under episcopal care,” etc. See among Ivo’s letters, in the volume that we shall publish shortly.

[Col. 1201] THE END.

HONOUR AND GLORY TO GOD ALONE.

ADDITIONS ILLUSTRATING THE WORKS OF GUIBERT.

[Col. 1203]

THE LIFE OF SAINT GEREMARUS, ABBOT OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT, BY AN ANONYMOUS BUT VERY ANCIENT AUTHOR.

665–667 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 1203A] In the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, when the faithful of Christ incurred hatred for the sake of the truth and suffered many things throughout Gaul at the hands of the members of the devil for the name of Christ, blessed Geremarus was born, by God’s merciful will, at the villa called Giviarandra, situated on the border of the Beauvaisis, beside the river Itta, to crush the fury of the faithless and strengthen the faith of Christians.

His father was named Rigobert, and his mother Aga, descended from a noble Frankish family. Born, then, of distinguished parents, he was baptized at the sacred font and marked with the holy faith; for he was handed over to be instructed in the sacred mysteries. His parents, loving him tenderly as their only son, entrusted him to the schools to be educated and instructed in the teaching of Christ.

After their death, blessed Geremarus, burning more and more with love for Christ, did not cease distributing his substance among the poor; for he knew that what he gave to the poor he bestowed upon the Lord Jesus Christ himself, as the same Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

He prepared eternal things for himself from transitory goods, and rewards that would endure without end from things that perish. Strengthened by these and many other examples, he continually spent his substance on captives, orphans, widows, and the poor.

But when it had already pleased the Lord to reveal the merit of blessed Geremarus to many—for, as he himself says in the Gospel, “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke XI, 33)—many Franks began to flock to him and enjoy his most holy instruction. Feeding them daily with the bread of the heavenly word, he admonished them to retain inviolate faith, charity, love of God, and love of neighbour, along with the many other heavenly weapons by which they could ascend to heaven and overcome the enemy of the human race.

While he was acting thus, King Dagobert heard of his reputation for holiness and wisdom. He sent messengers and summoned him to his palace. Seeing him refined and learned in speech and wise in counsel, he placed him over his councils. As long as he followed his advice, he held the kingdom of the Franks vigorously.

CHAPTER II.

After spending not many years of his youth in the palace of King Dagobert, he began to consider with himself whom he might associate with himself as heir to his inheritance. While he was thinking about this, with the consent of the king and the other Franks he joined himself in marriage to a young woman named Domana.

He did this chiefly so that he might have an heir who would come after him, lest after his death serious disputes should arise among his relatives over his inheritance. For he possessed very many estates, and many of his relatives were at the palace of King Dagobert.

After taking his wife, the Lord fulfilled his mercy toward him: he fathered two daughters by her. When the elder reached a mature age, she was betrothed; but, death intervening in the flesh, she remained a virgin. The younger was handed over to monastic discipline and remained in virginity. Thus both, remaining virgins in body, deserved to be counted among the wise virgins. Blessed Geremarus buried them in the church of Saint Remigius in the aforesaid village, where he gave much from his own property.

After many days had passed, God gave them a son. Rejoicing and exulting over him, blessed Geremarus sent him to blessed Audoenus, who in those days was staying at the king’s palace, acting according to whose counsel he did everything and doing nothing outside his command. He was his most intimate friend and privy to all his secrets. Geremarus told him everything that had happened and that a son had been born to him.

When Audoenus heard all this, he rejoiced, took the child, and catechized him. Having prepared the baptismal font, he baptized him in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, naming him Amalbert. After initiating him into the mysteries appropriate to the holy faith, he sent him back to blessed Geremarus. As he grew and advanced daily, he became honoured among the princes of the Franks.

CHAPTER III.

Blessed Geremarus, filled with the Spirit of God, considering all the things of the world as nothing and desiring a celibate life, gave much of his substance to the monasteries of monks. On the advice of blessed Audoenus, he founded from his own resources a monastery called Insula, and built there all the structures suitable to the holy rule.

There he built churches in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul, placed there the relics of many saints, and established a congregation of monks living under holy conduct. He appointed Archarius over it as abbot, a man of great merit, through whose teaching and wisdom Christ’s flock might daily strive toward heavenly things. Archarius himself governed the flock entrusted to him properly and vigorously until the end of his life.

But when it pleased the Lord that the life of blessed Geremarus should become an example to others, he put into his heart that he should abandon everything and give himself solely to the service of the Lord. After this desire had entered his mind, before confessing it to any mortal, he approached the king and asked him to transfer to his son Amalbert, before all the princes of the Franks, everything that belonged to Geremarus’s jurisdiction, and to grant it to him freely in the presence of all the Franks.

When the king heard this, he began greatly to wonder. At length, willingly agreeing to his request, he granted the young man not only what Geremarus had asked but also added much more.

After acquiring everything within his authority for his son, he approached Saint Audoenus, who was then at the palace itself, in order to open to him all the secrets of his heart. Calling him aside, he addressed him in these words:

“I ask you, holy Father, not to refuse to show me the way of God by which I may reach eternal joys and escape the shipwreck of this world; for I see that everything passes away and returns to nothing.”

When blessed Audoenus heard this, he rejoiced greatly and, drawing sighs from his heart, answered him:

“The way of God that you ask me about, brother, is shown to you in the words of the Gospel. For the Lord says to Peter, who was asking about recompense and the future reward:

‘Everyone who has left house, or brothers or sisters, or father or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life’ (Matt. XIX, 29).”

When blessed Geremarus heard this, he replied to Saint Audoenus:

“I know, holy Father, that everything I hear from your mouth is true. I shall abandon all the transitory, vain, and perishable things of the world, which, when they seem most firmly established, pass away and lead the wretched to destruction. And, to use the Lord’s words: ‘What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?’” (Matt. XVI, 26.)

When these holy conversations between them were completed, blessed Geremarus returned home and instructed his son and his household concerning faith, hope, charity, and all the other virtues pertaining to the care of souls.

CHAPTER IV.

At that time, after Dagobert had died, in the eleventh year of the reign of King Clovis, blessed Geremarus was redirected into the way of eternal salvation. Seeing that he was acquiring nothing in the world that would bring an everlasting reward to his soul, but rather preparing perpetual loss for it, he approached King Clovis at the urging of blessed Audoenus.

He asked him to grant his son what his father had granted, to permit his hair to be cut, and to allow Geremarus to give himself to God in a monastery for service. By the king’s command, although the Franks opposed it, blessed Audoenus tonsured him, gave him the monastic habit, and instructed him in heavenly disciplines. He then sent him to the monastery called Pentallium, so that he might there be abbot and shepherd of Christ’s sheep in obedience, and an illuminator of souls.

Blessed Geremarus recalled the Psalmist’s words:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXXIII, 8).

And again:

“The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. XXVI, 1.)

Placing all his hope in the Lord God, he did not delay obeying the command of the holy [page 669]. With great groaning, tears, and sighs of heart, he accepted the governance of the monastery.

After abandoning his wife and son and all the cares of this world, according to the evangelical command, he followed the footsteps of Christ Jesus and went to the monastery mentioned above, Pentallium, in the district of Rouen, beside the river Lirizinus. What kind of life he led there, and how holy it was, shining before all, are attested by the healings and many miracles performed for the inhabitants.

By day and by night he mortified himself in prayer, vigils, and fasts, and in all things fitting for the contemplative life. He fasted daily, spending the entire day in hymns and praises of God, and taking nourishment in the evening. His food was dry bread with a few vegetables, and his drink the saltiest water, so that his belly might not be filled to satiety. He was dead to the world and alive to Christ. He never ceased showing all who flocked to him the way of salvation, and he warned each one to meditate on the law of God.

There was a very large multitude of monks in the same monastery, and Father Geremarus had been appointed to govern it. In this congregation many who loved what was good and feared the Lord willingly listened to him and accepted his correction. But since the life of the good is always hateful to the wicked, there were certain malicious and impious men there, some of whom belonged to Belial.

Unwilling to accept his preaching, they began plotting his death, seeking a suitable opportunity to kill him through some kind of treachery. It was his custom to rise at the first cockcrow for the praise of God and to spend the night awake in God’s praises until the dawn. After completing his office, he customarily returned to the dormitory and placed himself upon his bed.

Knowing this, the envious and insolent men agreed among themselves to place a knife beneath the bedding, so that when the holy man returned from the church he would throw himself with the force of his body upon the knife and thus kill himself. And so they did. They fixed the handle of the knife in the ground and raised the naked blade into the air.

O unspeakable wickedness, horrifying to all at every time! When blessed Geremarus returned from the church to his bed as usual, the Holy Spirit prompting him, he did something he had not been accustomed to do. He normally did not touch the bed but threw his whole body into the middle of it. This time he touched the bed with his hand and, moving his hand around, found what had been hidden.

As soon as he realized that a plot had been prepared, he left the bed and returned clothed to the church. He spent what remained of the night pouring out tears in hymns and praises of God, and at first light told no one what had happened to him.

At the third hour of the day, after the discussion of the reading, he prostrated himself before everyone’s feet in the chapter house and asked them to release him from pastoral care and choose any better Father over themselves. There was a certain crypt in a vast solitude beside the Seine, from which Saint Samson had driven out a serpent; Geremarus asked that it be granted to him as a dwelling.

What a cry! What grief there was among all who feared the Lord, lamenting over Father Geremarus and saying:

“Why do you abandon us, Father? To whom do you leave us desolate? What have we done? What have we committed against you? How have we opposed you?”

He answered them:

“None of you has ever opposed me in anything; none has been alien, none evil, none harsh. You have all been to me as fathers, as brothers, as lovers of truth.”

He did not wish to reveal publicly what he had found hidden in the bed, lest that very place become an example of evil.

Again and again he prostrated himself before everyone’s feet and asked them to release him from the pastoral seat. They refused, however, and instead begged him not to abandon them. At last, overcome by his requests, they granted him the crypt he had asked for.

Leaving the monastery, blessed Geremarus went to the place mentioned above. There he devoted himself to prayers by day and by night, practicing very great abstinence, greater than he had been accustomed to practice. The Lord bestowed such grace upon him, as upon his chosen servant, that he transcended all worldly things in mind and was often present at heavenly mysteries.

CHAPTER V.

When blessed Audoenus heard of his reputation for holiness and knew his merit, he ordained him to the priesthood. Geremarus tried very hard to resist his will, but when the Holy Spirit compelled him, he obeyed the commands of the holy bishop.

Having become a priest, he strove to please the Lord. Every day he offered sacrifice to him with tears and contrition of heart. There, set before all as an example, he remained for five years and three months sincere and devoted in all the commandments.

While he was staying there, a messenger came to him concerning his son Amalbert, whom he had left at the palace. Returning from Gascony with the king, Amalbert had been struck by a serious illness and began to grow sick. As the disease worsened, he was unable to escape it; when the moment of death stole upon him, he lost his bodily life. For he was still a virgin and ignorant of worldly corruption.

Because he was dear to the king and the Franks, he was carried as far as the place of his own inheritance. When this was announced to Geremarus, he assumed the patience of blessed Job and said:

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

Leaving that crypt, with all the clergy accompanying him, he sang praise to God in David’s hymns:

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me” (Ps. XV, 5).

Proceeding with a great choir of singers, he reached the district of the Vexin. Crossing it, he entered the Beauvaisis, where his dead son’s body lay. Coming to the place where it lay, he was not at all shaken by his son’s death; rather, he praised the Lord God because he had deigned to receive his only son in virginity.

They lifted him onto a bier and carried him to the monastery that blessed Geremarus had built in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul. A multitude of people followed, weeping and mourning over him.

When they came to a place called Baujacus-Pons, they stopped briefly on the ground. I must not keep silent about what the Lord deigned to accomplish there. Around the dead body, on account of the merit of blessed Geremarus—so that all might recognize that he was a man of great merit, and that his son likewise possessed it—the body of blessed Amalbert suddenly became so heavy that those carrying him could not move it. Nor could it be moved in any way.

All the men and women cried out, and such bewilderment seized those walking both behind and ahead that they could scarcely continue.

Then blessed Geremarus, perceiving that this was the will of God, ordered the body to be set down. After it had been placed on the ground, he knelt and poured out a prayer to the Lord, praying for a very long time before everyone.

When the prayer was completed, he said to those who were looking at the body:

“Remove the covering with which he is covered, so that we may see what has happened.”

When they had removed the sword [probably *pallium*, “covering”] and looked more closely, they found his face wet with blood, as though he had been killed in battle that very day. Blood was flowing from his nostrils and wetting his entire face.

This is exceedingly astonishing and marvellous, and should be preserved in memory with devout praise. A considerable time had already passed since he had departed this life while returning from Gascony with the king and the Franks. What could have made this clearer by that deed than the power of him by whose power the four-days-dead Lazarus is raised, through the merits and virtues of blessed Geremarus? This judgment shows that blessed Amalbert was living with Christ through the merits of Saint Geremarus.

[Col. 1209A] Then blessed Geremarus ordered a church to be built at that place in honour of Saint John. He established twelve monks there, whose life would be salvation for himself and for his son’s soul. So that they might live without want and serve the Lord without murmuring, he left them many villas, namely his own estates, by written charters.

After these arrangements had been made, the body was immediately found to be so light that one man could carry it. They moved on and reached the aforesaid monastery, which blessed Geremarus had built while still in the world, and there they buried him honourably.

Then blessed Geremarus received back his inheritance and made the Lord Jesus Christ heir to it. For he was hastening to reach the heavenly homeland and to touch the robe of immortality. He desired to have as heir the one from whom, in whom, and through whom the highest good exists, beyond which nothing should be desired.

CHAPTER VI.

After all these things had been divinely completed, he returned to himself and began to consider how the cunning of the ancient serpent, by a thousand arts of harming, strives to overthrow the hearts of God’s servants, leading them to the destruction and condemnation of everlasting death.

For, when some have been made perfect through the virtue of prayers, others devoted to fasts, and others renowned for the excellence of a solitary life, he often thrusts upon them a certain torch of vainglory and, with the foolish virgins, makes their lamps empty. Such people, when the Bridegroom comes, will not enter with him into the wedding feast (Matt. XV, 2).

Foreseeing this, blessed Geremarus, lest praise of the solitary life should touch his heart, began to address his companions with the greatest familiarity:

“O brothers, who have endured many labours for Christ’s name, run continually along the path toward the highest and incomprehensible good, and remain in the work of God that you have begun. We must use this counsel: let us hasten to Saint Audoenus and ask him to show us by his prayer a place where we may dwell and persevere in good works until the end of our lives.”

The counsel of blessed Geremarus pleased them all. Going to Saint Audoenus, he addressed him thus:

“I beg you, holy Father, to pray to the Lord for me and by your prayers show me a place in which I may dwell. For I trust that God will hear you and that you will obtain whatever you ask.”

When blessed Audoenus heard this, he answered him:

“Do not, do not say such things, brother. Who am I to do this? It will be accomplished not by my merits but by your faith. If you have faith, whatever you ask, you will obtain. By faith Abraham became the friend of God; by faith Peter was saved. Let us await the mercy of God for three days with fasts and prayers, to see whether he will perhaps look upon our humility.”

After these intimate words between them, a three-day fast was proclaimed for everyone. On the third night, while they were occupied with fasting and prayers, an angel of the Lord appeared in a vision to both of them and said:

“The Lord has heard your prayers. Go to the place now called Flaviacus, and there you will find what you desire.”

[Col. 1210A] When morning came, each reported what he had seen. Giving thanks to the Lord, they made their way to the place indicated by the angel.

When they were not far from the village, by God’s prompting and will they turned away from the straight path. Wandering around the wilderness of a vast solitude, they reached the appointed place. When they arrived there and were greatly uncertain, not knowing what they should do, behold, a cloud descended from heaven and surrounded the entire place where the monastery was to be built.

From within the cloud a voice from above said:

“Chosen ones of God, behold, this place is fearful. Forty years have passed since the Lord blessed and sanctified this place and destined it for his faithful servant Geremarus. It will be habitable by a multitude of monks as long as they persevere in the commandments of the Lord. But no access to it will ever be open to women.”

When the two holy men heard this, they rejoiced greatly. As they fixed their eyes upon the cloud, it was immediately withdrawn from their sight.

From the same cloud, around the circuit of the place, there remained something like a geometrical rod encircling the whole site, so that it might be understood that what the heavenly voice had proclaimed was true. Then, as they went around the place, they discovered the mark of heavenly dew impressed upon it.

Blessed Audoenus, certain of the angelic vision and the heavenly voice, took a rod in his hand and measured by the traces of the cloud the area around which the church was to be built, where the workshops were to be constructed, and the other things useful to monastic life. After marking out the place for blessed Geremarus, he departed from him.

[Col. 1210C] Then blessed Geremar came, together with all those entrusted to him, to build the site. There he built a church in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, of holy Mary the Virgin, of Saint John, and of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles; and there he handed over his entire inheritance. He constructed there everything suitable and necessary for monastic life, as well as the various crafts that it is useful to practice within the monastery, so that the monks would have no need to wander outside: “For, as blessed Benedict says, it is altogether not beneficial for their souls” (*Rule*, chapter 66). When the monks round about heard of this, they flocked to him as to a garden of every virtue. He refreshed them with the grace of the word of God and admonished them to persevere in their chosen way of life [Col. 1210D] and to keep themselves strangers to the pleasures of the world.

When he had completed all his work, he devoted himself to prayer and remained occupied in God’s service for three years and six months. Thus he gave up his spirit in the Lord and passed over to the joys of the angels. His body was buried with great honor and reverence in the same church, where many benefits are bestowed through his merits. The sick come to his tomb and are healed; the blind are given sight; the lame are restored to walking; hearing is restored to the deaf; demons are driven from possessed bodies; and many are healed of various illnesses, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory, praise and power, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

Here ends the Life of Saint Geremar, abbot.

[Col. 1211]

# The Life of Blessed Simon, Count of Crespy, by a Contemporary Author

His feast is on the second day before the Kalends of October [September 30].

## Prologue to the Life of Blessed Simon, Count of Crespy and Monk of the Order of Saint Benedict

[Col. 1211A] Since the entreaty and need of certain men of God urge us to say something about the deeds of the blessed man Simon, for the benefit of those who hear, we have undertaken to gather his individual deeds, to recognize what is certain, and to set them forth both in speech and in writing. For it is fitting that what he accomplished in action should be displayed in letters, since no one in this age could be compared with him in life. Rightly is the Lord praised, as it is written, as wondrous in his saints (Psalm 67:36). “For his Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8); [Col. 1212A] turning away from perversity those whom he finds perverse, he makes them simple in action, innocent in mind, gentle in speech, and at the same time partners and helpers of the holy Church of God. But in whom is the Lord proclaimed wondrous more than in Simon? For he saw a wolf and made him a most gentle lamb; he saw a robber and appointed him a sheep of innocence (Augustine, Sermon 14, *On the Saints*). And since the Lord is proclaimed wondrous in Simon, it is necessary that his wondrous deeds—which he deigned to display in Simon—not be suppressed by silence.

## Chapter I

[Col. 1211B]

There was, then, a certain man named Simon, wondrous in life, outstanding in character, and distinguished by birth. First a consul and chief officer of the king of the Franks, he afterward became a most exemplary monk. His father was Rodolphus, exceedingly powerful in wealth and strength; his mother was called Adela. How, therefore, he brought his purpose of faith to the completion of action, the lucid order of the narrative will reveal.

When he was still in the first flower of youth, excelling many in the art of war and almost wholly intent upon the things of the world, he happened one day to go out into the countryside for a walk, holding a hawk in his hand in order to deceive a bird and catch it. But, catching nothing, he himself was deceived. As he himself related, this event was followed by such a terrible and perverse thought that he resolved not to love anything good, but in no way to hate what was evil, just as it is found written about blessed Benedict (Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 2); for, when the bird had departed, he was bitterly bitten by the sharp tooth of an unclean suggestion. But by the grace of the Holy Spirit that perversity vanished so suddenly, and the devil’s suggestion was so utterly destroyed, that what he had previously loved became altogether displeasing to him. There he made a beginning of holy conduct and continually held the good in his will, although, being involved in worldly affairs, he was unable to fulfill it in action.

When he had been deprived of both parents, Philip, king of the Franks, moved by a spirit of wickedness and eager to seize the inheritance that had come to Simon by right—for he thought that he could easily overcome a young man alone, without counsel and without the aid of his parents—first plotted to attack him by ambush; then he stirred up the tempest of open war. For the king himself began, with fire, plunder, and sword, to destroy villages and to scatter entirely, as far as he could, the estates, fortified towns, and everything that appeared to belong to Simon. Simon, however, confidently trusting in the Lord and rising up against him—for he was being unwillingly dragged into doing evil—girded himself and prepared to resist bravely. He roused his people and, like a roaring lion, though grieving in his heart, disturbed and devastated whatever he found under the king’s control, declaring that he would in no way turn back until he possessed what was his own.

Who would not marvel at the fullness of the Lord’s goodness in him? Behold, placed amid so many scourges and hindered by the affairs of war, he nevertheless grieved for his father, already dead. For he knew that, while still alive, his father had been excessively devoted to worldly affairs and grievously entangled in the desires of the world; and he remembered that his father had violently taken from its possessor a certain castle, which he had prepared as a place of burial for himself, and had retained it as though it were his own. Simon therefore sent a messenger to consult the Roman pontiff about what should be done concerning this and how he might assist his father, who had died in such a state.

## Chapter II

Pope Gregory, who was called Hildebrand, piously took care to command that the body be removed entirely from the place from which it had been unjustly taken, and that solemn Masses and abundant almsgiving be offered to God in supplication for the father’s soul. Simon kindly received the command and obeyed in everything that had been prescribed for him; [Col. 1213A] he removed the body and, at the castle of Crespi, endowed most generously from his own resources the church called that of blessed Arnulf, to which it was transferred. He distributed an abundant supply of food to widows, orphans, and all those in need.

This is true faith, and this is the firmest love: not the fleshly life but everlasting life is taken into consideration; it is not the flesh that dies, but the soul, which is destined to live forever. In this deed the man of God had been struck with fear, judging that the world which he had formerly regarded as contemptible was now dreadful; and if he had loved anything in it, he taught that it must be fled like a poisonous serpent. Although outwardly he was held by worldly struggle and the affairs of war, inwardly, by entering the service of the Lord, he bore the Lord’s weapons.

For when, for nearly three years, he was occupied with the labor of war, so that his flesh had no rest, yet at night he was not at all detained by the fatigue of arms. Content with only one companion, he entered the thresholds of churches and rejoiced always to attend Matins. If he found anywhere a monk, cleric, or pilgrim distinguished for religious devotion, he supplied him with what was bodily necessary and commended himself to that person’s prayers. He was also strong in fasting and generosity in almsgiving. For the meat, seasoned dishes, spices, and other things of this kind that were placed on the table—while others believed that he was being satisfied—he gave to the poor, remaining hungry despite never lacking those foods. Although outwardly clothed in a variety of garments, he tormented his body with a harsh hair shirt.

## Chapter III

[Col. 1213C]

Meanwhile, while the king’s and Simon’s territory was being consumed by fortification and war, people were driven from their own homes, and Simon embraced fear because of his misdeeds. Soon postponing the struggles of war for a time, he resolved to visit the dwellings of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and to approach Pope Gregory so that he might impose penance upon him. Without delay, after preparing everything necessary for a traveler, he reached Rome under the Lord’s guidance. There, finding the bishop of the holy apostolic see, he explained what he was seeking. But the pope did not immediately grant his request unless he first laid down his arms, saying: “Absolution of one who resists would be empty.”

673 Then the man of the Lord Simon hesitated for a little while in doubt, but, remembering the evangelical command, [Col. 1213D] “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33), immediately promised that he would do whatever the pope commanded. The bishop therefore imposed penance upon him on the condition that he surrender his arms, and retained part of the prescribed penance for himself, distributing another part to two most devout men who were then present. Thus, having absolved him from his offenses, he sent him back to his own country, re-equipped with arms those whom he had despoiled, and again entrusted him with governing the land until he should restore peace with the king. He also appointed as guardians men of good reputation and the highest authority: namely, Hugh, bishop of Die, who was then serving as papal legate in Gaul, and the abbot of Cluny, so that, subject to their instruction [Col. 1214A] and obedience, Simon might be trained according to divine law.

Returning filled with holy joy, he again confronted the king and embraced the struggle like an excellent soldier. Although unwilling, he was not released from the business of war until he became victorious. At last, when the region had been devastated and both sides were weighed down by the heavy burden of their labor [al., “and by the burden of their losses and labor”], a plan for peace was formed, and a meeting was arranged by both parties. What more need be said? The nobles assembled; judgment was given by the wise; the inheritance that had come to Simon by right was adjudged and restored to him; peace and concord were confirmed.

## Chapter IV

When peace had been restored and, with everything put in order, the matters that had been disarranged by the prolonged war had been settled, a wife was chosen for him: elegant in form, exceedingly beautiful in face, noble in birth, and apparently second to no woman in the whole region of Auvergne. He himself, as though rejoicing in such an arrangement, announced that he would go there, intending to conceal completely the good that lay hidden within him. He immediately set out and departed. When, by God’s arrangement, he arrived, he was honorably received by the bride’s father, Hildebert, the count, and stayed there for some time. After words appropriate to such an arrangement had been exchanged, and a pledge had been given and received, he affirmed that he would take her, unless something otherwise occurred; and when the wedding day had been fixed, he returned joyfully to his own home.

Behold, the appointed day approaches; a multitude of nobles is summoned, and a variety of adornments is sought. When everything had been arranged in due order, he returned to the region of Auvergne and, as was proper, went back to the promised marriage agreement. As they drew near, they were met by the shouting of a clamoring crowd. The bride, offering kisses to Simon as he came, embraced him.

Who would not be astonished on hearing this? Who, moved by such sweetness, would not grieve? Kisses were exchanged, seasoned with holiness; embraces were joined, with lust removed. While others believed that their words were filled with playful delight, the man of God was implanting in her heart the word of preaching and sweet conversations about life, so that both might renounce the world. Without delay, she obeyed his admonitions and vowed to receive the religious habit and become a nun.

On the following night, without her father or the others knowing, the blessed man sent her, together with two companions united to her by conversion and kinship, to the monastery called Casa Dei, intending that they should live there. Immediately changing their secular clothing, all three together assumed the monastic habit. One of them, distinguished for religious devotion, was afterward ordained bishop of the city of Bourges; the other, remaining in humility, stayed for a long time in the monastery, devoting himself to religion. The devout lady, living a most holy life, survived for many years afterward.

When the father awoke from sleep, believing that his daughter had been carried away by a harlot’s love and had followed some pimp, he thought that he had been deceived. Then, grieving and lamenting, he summoned Simon and addressed him as though guilty of the deed:

“O dearest young man, I utterly do not know what I should do or what I should say. I betrayed you, after you had entrusted yourself to my faith, and, having called you to us from so great a distance, I laid snares for you. I have been defrauded of the price that I promised; the promise has been taken away, but I did not know it. Therefore forgive me, forgive me, for I do not know that I have sinned.”

But Simon, restoring joy to his heart and outwardly offering comfort, replied: “Do not, my lord, do not grieve. Whomever she has loved more, she follows more devotedly; and if I have become dearer to you, perhaps she is of little value to him.” With these words, having obtained his permission, he hastened back to Gaul.

He took care to send Hildebert a message explaining what his daughter had done and how she had vowed herself to become a nun. O man worthy of praise in every respect! Whom could we say was more like the holy Alexius? [Col. 1215B] For when he and his bride had already entered the bedchamber to rest together, just as Simon did, he introduced a word of preaching, warning her to shun lust and preserve chastity. She, obeying the words of her admonisher, vowed herself a virgin and consecrated the purity of her flesh to the Lord.

Thus the blessed man wiped away the deadly contagion of unclean depravity by the hand of holy conversation. Then, disregarding the father’s pleasures—whose greatness seemed infinite—he secretly departed at that very hour of the night. But let us return to what must be said about Simon.

674 ## Chapter V

When Simon had scarcely rested for a short time in his own home, behold, the most powerful king of the English, named William, who had raised him, sent an urgent command that he come to him. The message also stipulated that he should not marry the wife destined for him under any circumstances, nor remain in a castle or village except for a single night’s rest, until he should hasten to Normandy for an audience with the king. Fearing the king’s decree, Simon immediately resolved to depart from the place where he had intended to remain.

When the king saw him coming to him, he was pleased. Calling him privately, he said:

“Since I have long experienced your loyalty and affection, and wish to increase in you the nurture I have given you, disregarding the envoys of Anfursus [read: Alphonsus], king of Spain, and of Robert, prince of Apulia, who had long been with me to ask for my daughter, I have chosen you as my son-in-law and selected you to marry her. I adopt you as heir to my inheritance. My pleasures shall be reckoned yours; my friends shall be your friends, and likewise my enemies.”

At this the blessed man, believing that this prosperity came from the devil, who surrounds the hearts of the elect with many snares, regarded it in his heart as worthless and empty. Nevertheless, he gave thanks in the humblest voice, saying:

“Great and manifest is the benefit that you bestowed upon me in my youth; but I give you thanks for promising me something far better. Your dignity, as it is written, descends in humility so that it may be exalted. My humility, unless it continually submits itself to you in thanksgiving, deserves to fall more disastrously. But an obstacle is set before us, one that is very doubtful [Col. 1216A] and serious and seems to trouble my thoughts. For my lady the queen, namely your wife, and I are said to be related by blood and connected by kinship of lineage. Therefore the wise must inquire whether this can somehow be managed and by what means.”

The king replied: “If our people’s ancient men and elders establish that the kinship is genuine, it will be necessary to assemble and investigate bishops, abbots, and prudent clerics who know the law and understand profound matters, to determine whether the matter can be settled by generosity in almsgiving, by the construction of monasteries, or by some other suitable means.”

Simon, however, always placing his hope in the Lord, said:

“There remains one other possibility, if only you are willing, and it is necessary and salutary. I wish to go to Rome and ask the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the apostolic lord for counsel and assistance in this matter, so that, once spiritual permission has been received, whatever must be done in this affair may be undertaken with confidence.”

The king assented and replied: “Whatever seems good to you in this matter, with God’s favor and my consent, arrange it.” With these words they departed from one another.

## Chapter VI

Then, after everything that seemed necessary had been prepared and arranged in due order, he left his home and abandoned his pleasures, whose abundance flowed to him so plentifully that scarcely anyone in the whole region, after the king, seemed richer or more prosperous in possessions. When he was to go to Rome, he vowed to become a monk and resolved to visit Saint Eugendus. [Col. 1216C] When he arrived there, he gathered to himself several noblemen from his household, and all together joyfully received the habit of the religion of the Holy Trinity.

For when he had formerly still been living in the world and was suffering from a fever, blessed Arnulf, Saint Eugendus himself, and another man whose name and face he did not know appeared to him as he slept in a garden. They admonished him to go there, to remain there serving God, and, remaining there under an abbot, to be ordained and live as a monk. He immediately rose from his bed and recovered from his illness, and cried out in a loud voice: “I am well! And these three lords who were here—where are they, and where have they gone?” Those of his household who were present, not knowing what he meant, professed that they did not know.

Thus, when news of so great a man had been received throughout Flanders, Normandy, and the other parts of Gaul as far as the borders of Germany, all were filled with amazement and wonder. He was known in those regions, beloved by God, and so dear to everyone that Hugh, duke of Burgundy, the count of Mâcon, and many others of the same rank, inflamed by devotion and by the sweetness of love for him, laid down their arms and abandoned the world. Who, indeed, would not entirely desire a change of conduct after his example and alter his manner of life for the better? Nobles and commoners alike were changed when they heard his name. Let us now return to what the monk accomplished.

## Chapter VII

[Col. 1217A]

This is Simon the obedient—but not the first Simon. To prove himself the heir of his name, he is said never to have resisted obedience. When he assumed the monastic clothing, he placed his bed in the church sacristy; at night, rising from his silent bed, he alone remained in the oratory devoted to prayer. He was so powerful in fasting that, at a time when, because of the poverty that severely afflicted that region, even wheat for making bread was lacking for his use, he received dry oat bread at his meal, giving thanks.

When the bending of his knees and the affliction of his fasts had made his legs swollen with the illness that had violently attacked him, so that, as though benumbed, he scarcely felt it even though he seemed to endure the burning of fire, his abbot humbly asked him to remove his leggings so that they might be eased. But he, gentle in speech as he was, humbly refused and replied that he could bear it for a little while and endure it lightly. On the following night, with the Lord’s favor and without his knowledge or that of the others, the leggings were removed. When he rose in the morning as usual to go to Matins, he felt his legs and found that the leggings were no longer on them. Astonished at what had happened, he found them folded before him on his bed; taking them again, he put them back on as he had been accustomed to do.

## Chapter VIII

There is another event worthy of remembrance that the Lord deigned to show his servant. One night, before the brothers had proceeded to the duty of their appointed service, he went ahead of the others and entered the monastery to pray before the Lord’s altar. While he remained at prayer, he raised his head and observed the church windows flashing with the brilliance of light. He also saw three men of exceedingly radiant appearance enter the monastery and hurry toward the presbytery. One resembled a priest, another bore the appearance of a deacon, and the third the appearance of a subdeacon. There, upon the holy altar, while the man of God watched, they celebrated the solemnities of Mass with the greatest devotion. When the final prayer had been completed, the one who appeared to be the priest blessed Simon and vanished from his sight together with his companions.

[Col. 1217D] As is customary, he did not conceal this from his abbot when making his confession, but required him not to reveal it to anyone at all as long as he lived. The abbot, seeing that the man of God was advancing in virtue and gradually embracing many of the things that belong to God, ordered him to ascend and sit in a place in the chapter higher than the one he had entered. Simon took this exceedingly hard and, by repeatedly asking pardon, sought mercy. This continued until he merited being recalled to his former seat.

## Chapter IX

Considering the honor shown him by the brothers and fearing that the hardship of his fasts or any other necessity of the soul might appear burdensome or troublesome to someone in the community, he desired the solitude of the desert. He therefore approached the father of the monastery and asked with no small insistence that permission be granted him to go there, and he obtained it. Having received permission, he took with him a few of the brothers whose lives were distinguished by religious devotion and departed humbly.

What he did in his work when he arrived there, and how much he endured for the name of Christ, must be made known as an example to those who hear. He began to live from the labor of his own hands, cutting down uncultivated ground with an axe wherever new land was to be cleared. His food was meager: bread with water, legumes, and wild apples, with severe labor, and this only once a day except on Sunday and feast days. Carrying water on his neck, he himself cooked the apples with broth. Whenever he went outside to perform some task, if a poor person met him there and asked for alms, he had instructed his steward never to let him go away empty-handed.

## Chapter X

It happened one day that a hungry traveler asked there for a charitable meal. The servant offered him the pound of bread that alone remained. Then the man of God, returning from the forest with the brothers, asked whether they could be refreshed. The servant replied: “There is no bread; there are wild apples. The bread that remained yesterday I gave to a person in need.”

At once Simon rejoiced, gave thanks to God, blessed the brother who had done this, and entered the church to devote himself to prayer. He had not yet finished the words of his prayer when, behold, a certain man arrived carrying loaves of bread. He handed them to the steward in Simon’s name. The steward summoned the man of God and his companions and explained what had happened and how the Lord had not forgotten his servants. Astonished at such an event and attributing it to the faith of the man of God, they praised God together and ate the food at their meal.

Again, in the forest, where almost no time was ever free from labor, while he was cutting wood, a tool dislodged from a tree struck and wounded his foot, leaving him severely afflicted, so that he had to return home supported on another man’s shoulders. The brothers were deeply saddened and suggested that he should be sent to a physician. He refused them, replying that, except for God’s medicine, he did not wish to be healed in any way. Nevertheless, through God’s providence, he was soon restored to his former health.

At about the same time, a certain religious man, having heard the fame of so great a man, came from a distant place to see him, dressed in an iron garment over his naked body. He came devoutly and was received by Simon even more devoutly. After Simon had spoken with him privately and, without knowing who had instructed him, discovered that he was dressed in this manner, he earnestly begged the man to give him that penitential garment. The man yielded to his pleas, though unwillingly, and departed.

Simon, having scarcely obtained permission from his abbot, discarded the hair shirt he had been wearing and put on that harsher garment over his tender body. He wore it for many days, tormenting his half-dead corpse. Stained with rust and worn by the pounding of nails, it made him so bruised and lacerated [Col. 1219A] that whoever saw him declared that even a heart of stone seemed capable of being softened by pious tears.

## Chapter XI

At that time, the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, asked that the blessed man himself go to Gaul to address and rebuke on his behalf Philip, king of the Franks, who was taking certain possessions from him. In obedience to his abbot, Simon set out for Gaul.

As he was traveling, it happened at Compiègne, a town of the king, that the Lord’s sudarium was to be raised and the golden reliquary set down more fittingly. When the man of God heard this, he turned aside somewhat from the more direct road in order to go there, and in a short time, with the Lord’s guidance, he arrived. He entered the church of blessed Cornelius, as though to pray in secret, but was immediately recognized by some of those attending the feast. Soon the news spread, and the report reached the ears of the people. The voice of the people and the shout of the rejoicing crowd rose up: “Simon!” he was being called by almost everyone. Simon was eagerly sought out, and thus, pressed by the crowd, he was scarcely able to withdraw all the way to the king’s palace.

The king, who had recently arrived, gazed at him most attentively and received him with the honor he deserved. Speaking graciously to him, he readily promised that, if Simon requested anything of him, he would gladly be prepared to comply. Simon, not forgetting his request, made known what he was seeking and obtained what he had asked.

The following day, after the solemnity had been completed and he had viewed the Lord’s relics, he hastened as far as Normandy to visit the king and queen of the English, who had raised him. When he arrived there, he found the king fighting against his son, Robert. Taking pity on both sides, he restored peace and drove the evil of the plague from the region.

When those who had been called his friends in the world heard of his fame, others and many more—nearly a thousand knights—joyfully came out to meet him. Each one most devoutly begged him to accept gold or silver from his own possessions, a mule, or a palfrey. He, giving thanks outwardly but regarding all this as nothing in his heart, accepted nothing at all and viewed all these things with indifference.

At last he went privately to the king and queen and made them at once sorrowful and joyful through affection, to such an extent that the queen, as is characteristic of women of good character, could not speak because her words were interrupted by weeping. After their sweet conversations, they offered him relics, gold, silver, and other small gifts of this kind, earnestly begging him to accept them graciously. But, except for the relics, he despised all these things and gave no indication of accepting them. Nevertheless, without his knowledge, some of his companions secretly took certain excellent gifts and carried them away. Thus, after this wrong had been done and the gifts accepted, he began to plan his return to the monastery.

O wondrous dispensation of God! Who is said in these times to have merited so great a gift of love bestowed by human beings? Both the known and the unknown loved Simon and rejoiced to see him. This must be believed to have happened not by chance but by God’s providence.

Behold, there comes to mind a remarkable example of his patience, which he endured under compulsion on that same journey.
