When he was staying at the castle of La Ferté, formerly called his own inheritance, a certain friend came to him from a village, eager for the desire to see him. One of those called raiders suddenly sprang out, seized the man, carried him off, and departed. The soldiers and noblemen there noticed this and, greatly distressed, searched for him and found him. They threatened to tear out the raider’s eyes or otherwise execute justice.

But the man of God, keeping his innocence in mind and retaining in his heart what is written—“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19)—strictly forbade this. Then one of his companions summoned him and spoke with him privately, wishing to know how and with what spirit he endured the injury inflicted upon him. Simon replied that, if he himself experienced such an insult from anyone in his own land, he would be even more joyful and would give thanks to God, because “by patience we shall save our souls.”

## Chapter XII

When he had completed on the journey whatever had to be done, he returned to the desert, began again what he had previously undertaken, and there, as far as he was able, devoted himself to bodily labor and rested in humility. But, lest a city set upon a mountain and a light remain hidden in darkness, the bishop of the holy Roman see, having heard the name of so great a man, notified Simon’s abbot by letter that he should be sent to him.

The abbot, moved to grief by the report of so great an evil, is said to have hidden and not revealed the seal, lest the others be disturbed, until the lord pope sent another letter, one that carried harsher demands. For in a second letter he declared that, unless the abbot hastened to send for Simon as quickly as possible, the abbot and the entire community would be deprived of spiritual office. What more need be said? The abbot was troubled, and the brothers were likewise saddened. What else could they do? The Church was losing its consolation.

After arranging the journey and everything that seemed necessary for preparation, Simon set out for the City together with his companions. When the apostolic lord learned that he was coming and saw him approaching, he rejoiced and received him with the honor he deserved. After speaking graciously to him, he gave him the kiss of peace. A suitable house for him to live in was chosen near the church of the virgin Thecla. While Simon lived there in the greatest holiness and devoted himself to prayer, all his companions were taken from him by death because of the unhealthiness of the place. Only two monks were left: one returned to the monastery, while the other served him until the end of his life and endured the unhealthiness of the City together with him.

## Chapter XIII

At that time it happened that the lord pope and a certain Robert, prince of Apulia, were in disagreement with one another. [Col. 1221A] Fearing that the city might in some way be disturbed by the conflict of war, the bishop summoned Simon and earnestly begged him to go there to make peace. Simon immediately obeyed, promising that he would depart, and, taking with him a most devout man, set out with the blessing of the one who had ordered him to go.

When he arrived there, he sought and found the prince. Once he had found him, he refreshed him as though with a feast in his presence. Thus he restored peace and accomplished in action what he had intended. When peace had been established everywhere there, he returned, admonishing the people along the way to turn to the Lord. They accepted his exhortation, and nearly sixty knights, abandoning worldly affairs, took up the Lord’s weapons. Thus, through the preaching of the man of God, they received the monastic habit in various places throughout the province, with a blessing.

After returning to the City, Simon approached the pontiff and reported everything he had done concerning peace. The pontiff was pleased with what he heard and approved what Simon had accomplished. Not long afterward, wishing to return to the monastery, Simon humbly asked him for permission. The pontiff did not listen to his request either the first or the second time, but is said to have given him this reply:

“Just as, dearest son, you came here when summoned neither by my merits nor by my authority, but by the pastoral rule of the lord Peter, so it is not within my power to promise your return. Go, therefore, enter the oratory of blessed Peter, and discover through prayer what he wills.”

On the following night, as the pontiff had instructed him, Simon entered the church to pray. He spent the entire night in vigil and devotion to prayer, and before he could leave, he was seized by the illness of death—the illness by which he was taken from this life. He then went to his dwelling, collapsed onto his bed, and invited the pontiff to hear his confession and visit him. The pontiff complied with his wish, absolved him after he had been cleansed from his faults, blessed him, and departed.

Not long afterward, strengthened by the protection of the precious body and blood of Christ, Simon returned his spirit to God on the day before the Kalends of October [September 30]. The holiness of his final passing at his assumption revealed how steadfastly he had persevered in religious devotion throughout his life.

## Chapter XIV

[Col. 1221D] Behold, the whole city is shaken by the report. People of every sex and age hasten to the funeral; and the service that they had given him less abundantly while he lived is now rendered to his funeral. Then, at the bishop’s command, a place of burial is prepared among the apostolic tombs. Because he had striven to imitate the apostolic life, he rightly attained the dignity of this summit.

The bishop himself was not present, being detained by illness. But he summoned the entire clergy and sent there bishops, abbots, clerics, and nuns with candles and lamps, so that thirty-five communities, together with crowds of people, might render service at his funeral. Thus, with solemn Masses and exceptional ceremony, the princes of Rome carried his body [Col. 1222A] to the grave and laid it there. A considerable sum of money contributed by the bishop was distributed to the poor. Behold, the servant of God, without money or any family connection, poor shortly before, becomes rich at the end; but he becomes richer still when he is placed in the heavenly seat.

The queen of the English, named Matilda, rich and exceedingly powerful, because she had raised him and was said to be closely related to him by blood, sent a monk to Rome bearing a great quantity of gold and silver to prepare his burial, in memory of the man of God. The tomb, carefully inlaid with squared and polished stones of marble of various colors, still offers examples of goodness to those who travel by.

## Chapter XV

[Col. 1222B]

The monk who, having long lived with Simon, had endured many bodily hardships out of love for him, after his assumption, and after arranging his burial, 678 left Rome and returned to the monastery. There, devoting many days to abstinence and labor, he displayed examples of the greatest humility. Before he had drawn near to death, which is the departure from life, Simon, mindful of the benefit and service he had received, appeared one night to him as he lay resting with the others. He called him and said: “Robert—for that was his name.” But he replied: “Who are you?” Then Simon answered: “I am Simon,” and added: “Why did you once wish to do this to me? For when you transferred my body at Rome [Col. 1222C] to the new place of burial, you gave nothing to the poor for my soul.” Robert replied: “I was poor, and I had no money.” He answered: “It is certain that you had something which you ought to have given.” And, as Robert himself later reported, he had two gold coins.

Robert asked him again: “My dearest friend, if it pleases you, reveal to me what glory and what rest await you.” “My rest and glory,” he replied, “are great. For my Lord has granted me rest and a glorious seat among the apostles.” Robert then said: “And what is the joy, and what singing before the Lord? I ask you, if you can, to tell me.” “The joy,” he said, “is great and incomprehensible; it can neither be related in words nor conceived by the mind. Yet if you had parchment, a pen, and [Col. 1222D] ink nearby, I would certainly have made some return to you by writing.” And he added: “I wish you to announce on our behalf to Anselm, abbot of Saint Mary of Bec, a prudent and most reverend man, that he rendered me a small measure of assistance in God. For I judged that he had no little faith and love concerning the salvation of my soul.” After saying this, and encouraging him toward salutary service and obedience, he disappeared.

The brother related to the holy man what he had heard, just as he had been commanded. The abbot replied to him with tears: “Believe me, brother, believe me: the servant of God spoke truly. For, because my sins demanded it, I postponed through sloth what I ought to have done; but if by praying, giving alms, or presenting through action anything else pleasing to God I can accomplish it, I earnestly desire by every means to share in these things.” Having said this, they departed together.

This is that most religious man Anselm, who, having been an abbot, became archbishop of Canterbury and attained the dignity of apostolic legate in England.

Those who had received the spiritual habit with Simon—men of the greatest religious devotion in the world, members of his own household—testified that these and the other things written about Simon were indeed so, as we have written them, for they had seen them with their eyes and heard them with their ears.

## Epitaph of Count Simon, written on his pyramid by Pope Urban, surnamed Odo

[Col. 1223B]

I, Simon by name, of illustrious ancestral blood,  
was a great part of the nobility of the Franks.

Loving poverty, I left my homeland and the world,  
setting the spirit before all riches.

Afterward, to the heavenly court of the apostolic Prince,  
the exceptional love of so great a Father led me.

Under his guidance, may I at last deserve to be raised above the stars.  
Here I lodge, buried before the sacred gates.

### Other verses

Once renewing the deeds of the Father at a brother’s dictation,  
I wrote the rule for the disciples in poor form;

but because God neither rejects these things nor those poorer still,  
Moses showed that lesser things suffice for undertaking the work.

Therefore, desiring the reader to be my helper,  
I ask him to read me, absent and lacking strength.

[Col. 1223]

# Life of Saint Salaberga, Abbess of Saint John of Laon, by an author of comparable standing

## Author’s Prologue

[Col. 1223C] 679 To the pope Omotarius, adorned with the honor of priestly vestments and religious devotion, and also to the priest, the most chaste virgin of Christ, Anstrudis the abbess, and to Salaberga:

I did not delay obeying your commands, O venerable glory of parents and nourishing vigor, by which especially I ought to have fashioned with my pen the life and sequence of deeds of the gracious mother—and of a woman to be preferred to our own times—insofar as circumstances permitted and divine piety favored me. Yet in this matter I consider myself very unequal to the task, since I have scarcely been instructed in the first elements of letters and was raised in Christian simplicity.

But I remember the proclamation of that Lord and Savior who says: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew [Col. 1223D] 7:7). And the oracle of the Psalmist: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11). Therefore I beseech the reader: if anyone should decide to read these deeds, which I have undertaken to weave, though rashly, out of love for the holy mother, let him not seek in them Ciceronian eloquence, the fluency of orators, the flowers of philosophers, or the various assertions of the Stoics, but the truth and simplicity of history.

For the eagle does not always fly toward the ether with outspread wings, but sometimes it is accustomed, with wings relaxed, to descend to the earth; and among royal banquets, even humble apples and rustic lettuces are often judged the best things.

God the Father must be entreated to uncover the clouds of a very dense breast and dull understanding. Our Savior Jesus Christ must also be entreated to deem us worthy to breathe the breeze of the Holy Spirit, so that, when the darkness of the mind has been removed, he may grant us the ability to speak, enabling us to explain the deeds of the venerable mother—who always burned with love for monasteries and churches—and to publish them briefly and concisely for posterity. May he grant what I ask, with your prayers assisting, he who “made the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wisdom 10:21).

# The Life Begins

[Col. 1223]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1223D]

Thus the holy Salaberga began her life among human beings in the suburban town of the Leuci, on the border of the territory of Langres, born of illustrious lineage [alternative: “in the territory bordering Langres, she was born to parents most distinguished according to the dignity of the world, not of low station, and wholly devoted to the service of God”]. They call it the district of Uternus because of the river flowing through those same places. [Col. 1225A] But the more illustrious or noble she was by birth, the more solicitous her parents were in raising her.

For at that time the people of the Bavarians—whom Orosius, a most learned man and knowledgeable in history, calls the Boji by their ancient name, situated in the farthest part of Germany—were infected with the error of Bonosus. The defenders of the holy Church marked out the Bonosian heresy: caught in the reins of the ancient and crafty enemy, it perversely judged our Lord Jesus Christ to be a mere human being, without the divinity of the Father.

To refute, indeed to cut away, this wicked and insane doctrine, the venerable man Eustasius, abbot, prompted—as was fitting—by the divine Spirit, soon came from the monastery of Luxeuil in the Vosges forest. This monastery had been built with great devotion and labor, through the generosity of King Childebert, by Columbanus, a man of admirable appearance and outstanding holiness, a pilgrim [Col. 1225B] who had come from Ireland.

## Chapter Two

But since we have mentioned so great a man as Columbanus, it is not necessary for us to unfold his deeds in our work, since they have been diligently published by the most eloquent man Jonas: how, amid the storms of the world and during the reign of King Theodoric, through the cunning instigation of Queen Brunechildis, he endured the plots of the wicked enemy; how, through tyrannical boldness, he was expelled by the brothers and entered the borders of Italy; and how, with the permission and authority of Aigulf, king of the Lombards, he built the monastery of Bobbio in marvelous order [alternative: “with marvelous workmanship”] and established the rule of the monks. The aforementioned Jonas recounts all this in his book, which he published in his own style [Col. 1225C] under the title *On His Life and Miracles*.

There survive writings of that same Father Columbanus addressed to the blessed and eloquent man Gregory, Roman pontiff, in the book which [alternative: “what he”] he drew from his vigilant care for shepherds. Gregory was held in such renown at that time and was so endowed with holiness that, with the Holy Spirit favoring him, even the secrets of heaven were opened to him; and, after the Apostle Paul, he alone or almost alone spoke in such a remarkable manner about the nine orders of angels. Through his teaching of the beauty of eloquence and the remedies of repentance, the whole of the West is illuminated to this day. That same venerable man also sent honey-sweet writings in reply to the aforementioned Father. But now let us return to our subject.

## Chapter Three

[Col. 1225D]

The man of God Eustasius approached the aforementioned people through the regions of Germany so that the lamp of the Creator might by no means be placed under a bushel, but on a lampstand and made visible to all, and so that the talent given from above might not be buried but rather become evident to everyone with doubled interest (Matthew 5; 25). Having erased the path of their spreading error, he cut it down with the sword of the evangelical word, insofar as the Lord granted him power. He preached that our Lord Jesus Christ, just as he possessed equality with God the almighty Father in divinity, also took on the humanity of a mother’s body and our nature, which he himself had created, without sin; and that no diminution affected his divine nature through the union [Col. 1226A] [alternative: “with no alteration diminishing the divinity”]. Since that divinity had always been with the Father and had suffered no reduction in its dignity, Christ was therefore called true God and true man.

At last, returning from the Bavarians, the distinguished man, after the arduous road through Germany and Belgica, finally reached a certain man illustrious for his wealth and riches, renowned according to the dignity of the world, and suited to courtly affairs. His name was Gunduinus [alternative: Gundomus]. At that time he was staying at a certain estate called Mosa, so named because of the river flowing through that place. The river rises in the territory of Langres, and after many windings and frequent circuits through the land, receiving into itself part of the waters of the swiftest Rhine, enters the Barbarian Ocean.

Gunduinus received the venerable man as a most welcome gift. Moreover, as commonly happens and as circumstances require, amid words of wholesome exhortation, the spirit of pious men grew during the conversation of faithful men [alternative: “the minds of the shepherds were favorably disposed”]. The man of God began to inquire whether the illustrious man, born of Frankish lineage, had any offspring. For, as I suppose, the man of God perceived that the child whom subsequent events proved to have been foreknown by God was destined for this purpose.

Then the illustrious Gunduinus, with his wife Saretrudis, an elegant-looking and noble woman, presented two boys of good character in order to receive a blessing: the elder was Leudinus [alternative: Leudeinus], surnamed Bodo; the younger was Fulculphus, [Col. 1226C] who was also called Bodo by another name.

The man of God asked again whether any offspring still remained. They confessed that they had a Germanic girl, older in age but long blind. The man full of God said to them: “Let her come, I ask, and let her be presented to your [alternative: “our”] sight.” For, as I believe, he had perceived in the spirit that the Lord would grant her health.

After the man of God had imposed a three-day fast upon himself, he poured blessed oil over the girl’s eyes. Wonderful to relate! Immediately, with the grace of Christ assisting, the girl recovered her former health. Nor is it without reason that almighty God promptly obeys the prayers of his servants, who have crucified their own wills for his sake.

[Col. 1226D] Another splendid miracle follows. When the same girl had long been suffering from a flow of blood and was held weakened and afflicted by the gravest bodily distress because of it, the distinguished Eustasius, as soon as he clearly learned of this, sought divine and customary assistance with abundant prayers. The eternal Creator of all things heard the prayers of his faithful servant, he who is accustomed to be present to his saints when they piously obey his commands. Why say more? Once the girl had received health, she was restored whole.

## Chapter Four

Meanwhile, when she had reached the years of full maturity, her parents saw that the girl was growing in grace and adorned with good conduct—for she was lovely and beautiful [Col. 1227A] in face. Yet, as often happens, after the uncertainties of life many people’s spirits grow lukewarm amid prosperous success. Thinking about the continuation of their offspring, they gave her, against her will, in marriage to a man distinguished by his nobility, named Richramnus. This man, having her in lawful marriage for two months [alternative: “scarcely two months”], was removed from human affairs and deprived of life.

When these things had taken place, Eustasius returned to Luxeuil. Then he proceeded to the Warasci, who inhabit part of the province of the Sequani and the banks of the river Duni [alternative: Duvii] on both sides. They too, overturned and stained by the same error of Bonosus and Fontinus, were wasting away in old age [alternative: “already aged and wasting away”].

Coming to them, the man of God recalled them to the bosom of the holy Church with the evangelical plow and the cautery of the sacred Scriptures, exercising these tools not without labor, lest the Lord’s crop, as the soil hardened and weeds choked it, should grow into oats and darnel. By the grace of divine inspiration, they have continued to this day in the same rule that they received from him.

Thus blessed Eustasius, after many dangers, immense labors, the dreadful storms of heretics, and the deceptions of rustic schismatics—matters contained more fully in his deeds—departed to God after completing a blessed life like a good athlete, distinguished by the greatest miracles. After the departure of his master, he had governed the brothers for almost three lustrums [Note: [Col. 1227D] Here the author appears to be a contemporary of blessed Salaberga.].

In his place, Walbert, of blessed memory, had already been elevated to govern the brothers [Col. 1227C]. He was a man praised by everyone’s report, of exceptional holiness, and not moderately learned in ecclesiastical disciplines; conspicuous for goodness, piety, and charity, and overflowing with doctrine. In his time, throughout the provinces of Gaul, companies of monks and communities of sacred maidens multiplied according to the rule of the blessed Fathers Benedict and Columbanus—not only through fields, estates, villages, and fortresses, but also through the vastness of the wilderness—whereas before that time monasteries were scarcely found in those few places. But now let us return to the point of the history.

## Chapter Five

The most prudent woman Salaberga, having now lived as a widow for two years, although dwelling in secular dress [Col. 1227D], devoted herself, as far as her strength allowed, to vigils, fasts, and almsgiving, eagerly returning to God the things that belong to God [alternative: “being intent upon vigils, fasts, and almsgiving, as far as her strength sufficed”]. She ruminated upon the teaching she had received from blessed Eustasius like a clean animal.

While matters stood thus, she resolved in her mind to seek refuge by flight in the monastery of sacred virgins that the venerable man Romaricus, magnificently converted from the palace, had built in the Vosges forest through the exhortation and consolation of blessed Eustasius. She would have fulfilled her vows if her sex had not created an impediment and royal obstacles had not intervened.

[Col. 1228A] At that time Dagobert held the scepter of the Franks and the governance of the kingdom. He was especially keen-minded, held the principate [alternative: “renowned in his principate”], and was feared for his reputation not only by those subject to him by the law of faith but also by foreign and neighboring peoples. The aforementioned Gunduinus [alternative: Bundoinus], fearing that he would incur the king’s anger and cruelty because of his daughter, gradually drew her back from the road along which she had freely decided to go. For her intention had already reached the king’s ears.

At that time there lived in the court of the aforementioned ruler a certain vigorous man, welcome for his counsel to the king and most famous among his own people, named Blandinus [alternative: Blaudinus]. He had received the surname Baso. Since he too was born from the distinguished lineage of the Sicambri, he took the aforementioned Salaberga into his marriage—not with her consent, because she had long known herself bound to the divine commandments [alternative: “had vowed herself to them”], but nevertheless by royal command and for the purpose of producing children.

Thus joined to the aforementioned man, although under the law of marriage, they both practiced Christian works and most devoutly preserved the baptismal purity. They were hospitable and devoted to almsgiving, especially toward members of the household of faith, in accordance with the eminent preacher Paul (Galatians 6:10), and toward strangers; they obeyed the servants of Christ with the greatest reverence, remembering the Savior’s command: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40); and that of the blessed Apostle Peter: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” [Col. 1228C] (1 Peter 4:9).

But although, with the Lord’s favor, they excelled in these good ways and lived according to Christian custom [alternative: “lived a life of Christian vigor”], and were unable to have any offspring, the most Christian woman, anxious and deprived of so many privileges, placed before herself the faith of the holy women Anna and Elizabeth. These women, keeping watch in the temple of the Lord with vigils and prayers (Luke 2:37; 1:6), after prolonged barrenness were deemed worthy of holy births and brought forth children.

Salaberga went to the basilica of the blessed bishop Remigius, who illuminated the city of Reims and the land of Champagne with sacred powers and miracles. There she kept watch in vigils and prayers and made a vow that, if offspring were granted to her by divine favor, she would dedicate the child to the Lord.

[Col. 1228D] She returned home without delay, and what she had faithfully and anxiously requested was granted to her by the Lord. She conceived and gave birth to a daughter, whom she named Saretrudis after her grandmother. Again she bore another daughter, whom she called Ebana. Thereafter she bore a third daughter, whom, having been regenerated by the grace of baptism, she named Austrudis [alternative: Astrudis]. In the course of time, with the entire company consenting, Austrudis succeeded to the care and governance of the sisters.

She gave birth to a fourth child, a boy whom the priests likewise consecrated through the grace of baptism and named Eustasius; he too died in childhood. [“She has survived to the present under Christ’s auspices through divine privileges. She bore only one child, whom the priests likewise, through the grace of baptism, . . . gave the name Eustasius; he too died in childhood, etc.”] She then bore a fifth child of good character, named Balduinus [alternative: Baldonus], whom she likewise dedicated to almighty God, like the earlier children. Thus the servant of Christ acted and strove with all her effort to make her entire household—not for herself alone, but also for her husband and children—a Church of Christ.

## Chapter Six

Meanwhile, the reputation of Walbert, whose memory we have mentioned, was flourishing exceptionally throughout nearly all the boundaries of the Franks, and his skill in preaching, from Christ the Lord, without whom nothing good is done, was burning abundantly. He was welcome to all who worshiped the Lord, and monasteries of men and women were being founded abundantly according to his rule.

The blessed Salaberga, seeing the servant and distinguished soldier of Christ flourishing with so many examples and burning with heavenly virtues, and seeing the flocks of Christ constantly gathered everywhere as though snatched from the jaws of wolves, frequently summoned him to her own house. She joyfully received him as a divine gift granted to her by the Lord, and desired to draw from his honey-sweet mouth salutary words suited to the healing of souls. Her spirit burned most intensely with the desire that, having scorned the trappings of the world and set aside worldly pomp, she might ascend to the summit and pinnacle of virtue.

The Lord and Savior also speaks in the Gospel about this summit of virtue, saying: “Everyone who has left father, or mother, or houses, or fields for my name will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29); and: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).

What more need be said? With God as author, she placed all her hope after God in the blessed man. Her husband converted, her children were consecrated to God, and she received the garment of religion. After taking counsel with blessed Walbert, with her husband’s agreement [alternative: “with his acquiescence”], she undertook to build a monastery of girls in the suburb of the city of Langres, on her paternal inheritance or succession.

She nobly enriched it with the revenues of her estates, from her paternal inheritance, making Christ the heir. To carry out this work, the venerable Walbert provided and assigned assistance, craftsmen, and capable men. Although the site lay near the borders of the Austrasians, it was nevertheless close to Burgundy, somewhat less than forty miles from the monastery of Luxeuil. There she dedicated to Christ the Lord a group of one hundred or more girls, both from noble families [alternative: “of noble birth”] and from her own household.

But when the greater part of the monastery’s construction had already been completed, the servant of Christ, prescient because she was filled with the Spirit of God, began carefully to weigh with the man whether a monastery of girls was safe in that place and whether it possessed any stability or fortification. [Col. 1230A] For although barbarism was far away, the fact that the boundaries of kings were intermingled on every side was a sign of danger for the future—a danger that we later witnessed.

Recently, indeed, a civil war had been waged between the Frankish kings Theodoric and Dagobert around those regions, and the entire neighborhood had been ravaged: fields, estates, houses, and—what was more grievous—the bodies of the saints themselves had been burned by fire. Hence it is plainly evident that she had been imbued with the divine Spirit, since she anticipated the danger long beforehand.

## Chapter Seven

Having therefore taken counsel with the aforementioned abbot Walbert, who possessed intelligence, discerning strength, and a good nature suited to such matters, and whom she later had as her companion on the journey and partner in the labor, she chose [Col. 1230B] a journey under Christ’s leadership, like the most holy patriarch Abraham, who departed from Mesopotamia of Syria, became a settler among the Philistines, and, by God’s promise, received that land as his portion for his descendants.

Imitating him, the servant of God left her native soil, preferring to be poor with Christ rather than possess the profits of mammon. Though she had to endure so many hardships, she set out, with the provisions of life, for the city of Laon, called Clavatum, with the greatest retinue and with the souls entrusted to her by God.

Although that city can be surrounded by enemy siegeworks, it possesses a strong fortification by nature, being situated on the summit of a rock, so that it cannot be broken by barbarians and is free from danger. For in ancient times, when the Vandals, Alans, Huns, and the other peoples of Germany [Col. 1230C] and Scythia had besieged it in vain, they could not capture it by any engineering of earthworks, by the missiles of slings, by the darts of weapons hurled against it, or by the assaults of battering rams. Frustrated by their futile labor, they withdrew in defeat.

Apart from the circuit of the walls, which extends outward along the height of the hill, the inner circuit of the wall is level with the ground. Consequently, the town cannot be harassed by any art of siege engines; natural rocks also surround it on both sides. Within, the city is well supplied with wells, and at the very exits of the gates perennial springs flow forth, providing drinking water for human beings, sheep, and beasts of burden.

Thus, when the venerable woman with her holy followers had drawn near to illuminate the city like a ray of the sun, the bishop of that town, Attilo [alternative: Attila, Attola], went to meet her with the greatest enthusiasm. He rejoiced as though a divine gift and an angelic crowd had arrived [alternative: “as though a divine gift and an angelic crowd had arrived”]. With a choir of psalm-singers, with psalmody and hymn-singing, and with the highest praises, he escorted the holy servants of Christ into the city.

But that magnificent miracle which took place in the city on that same night must not be left unmentioned.

## Chapter Eight

The aforementioned bishop therefore ordered the boys and servants entrusted to him to be present in order to prepare food for the household of Christ on the following day. The ministers, astonished, entered the town through the gate quickly during the night, and saw various kinds of wild animals and beasts coming toward them. One saw an ox, another a deer; one a bear, another a boar; some saw wolves, and many likewise foxes; another meanwhile saw a playful ass and a savage lion. They were all going out and fleeing from the city at the same time, along with other monstrous beasts whose inclusion here would make the account too long and cause the reader to grow weary.

All the ministers, struck with fear by this miracle, marveled, since those beasts had never before appeared in that place. What else can be understood except that the ancient enemy, unable to endure the holiness and strength of the handmaids of God, fled and departed with his satellites?

Nor is it without reason that he assumes the distorted and monstrous forms of wild beasts and animals and brings forth various [Col. 1231B] fabrications. Although he had been created a good angel by the good Creator, he later became swollen with pride and had once said in his heart: “I will ascend above the stars of heaven; I will set my throne toward the North; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). Now, cast out from heavenly splendor and the paradise of delights, he works the mystery of iniquity with his followers, driven into the form of ants, worms, mice, or any other deformed shape.

Indeed, in former times—as many still remember, and as those who witnessed the crime are known to have survived—the cunning of the ancient serpent cruelly prevailed in that same town, as is believed. By his crafty art he deceived commoners, peasants, and foolish people. Of him it is written: “His arts of doing harm are a thousand.” Under the guise of [Col. 1231C] idolatry [alternative: baptism], he claimed them as his own. After a short time had passed [alternative: “after time had passed”], they even called it an idol; as though beginning with a game, while the devil raged among them, murders were frequently committed.

That most wicked demon had brought this about through cunning trickery: if anyone there weakened another person in any way, he would remain free from the shedding of blood at the hands of relatives or those connected by affinity. Thus the wicked custom might increase its malignity over time, and the unjust robber might claim the wretched city, ensnared in his reins, as his own.

But the Lord, almighty and merciful toward all things, “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), mercifully looking upon the creature subject to his authority, long ago completely expelled this sacrilegious and wicked crime from that city.

## Chapter Nine

But now let us return again to the narrative we began. After examining the condition of the place, and seeing that it was suitable and most agreeable, and that it was a fortified site without danger, they began to lay the foundations of churches and houses.

When these works had been properly completed and successfully carried out, the children of the nobility and servants began to flock together for the service of praise to God almighty, our Lord Jesus Christ. For what powerful man, or noble woman, living in those regions, would not love the blessed Salaberga from the heart? [Col. 1232A] She was always cheerful and had a peaceful countenance; she was conspicuous for charity and humility, most ready in almsgiving, and deeply devoted to the things that concern the worship of God.

What more need be said? Within a short time, more or less three hundred servants of Christ had been gathered in that place and united in the monastery.

Having arranged them in groups like the monks of Agaunum, she established a rule for maintaining chastity [alternative: “a rule for maintaining it”]. By day and night she commanded the sound of psalmody to resound to almighty God and, in accordance with the eminent preacher Paul, to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). This institution is still observed in that monastery, with Christ’s favor.

For an intense love of singing hymns burned strongly in that place. As we said above, she gathered many women of noble birth, thirsting to collect them for the service of Christ.

Among the other noble women of the Sicambri was Odila, distinguished by nobility, intelligence, and a good natural disposition [alternative: “by a good nature of intellect”]. She too had earlier received from the venerable Walbert the insignia of Christian strength and a salutary antidote. After taking counsel with the illustrious lawful [alternative: “royal”] husband Bodo, whom we mentioned above [add: “Leudinus”], who at that time was capable, powerful, and flourishing according to the dignity of the world, they turned to the Lord, setting aside the trappings of the world. Having contributed their possessions to the monasteries, they followed the same road as blessed Salaberga and hurried to Laon.

Bodo, having his hair cut, performed the office of a monk insofar as circumstances permitted. Not long afterward, having obtained the bishopric of the town of Toul, he paid the debt of nature. The venerable Odila too, having received the mark of Christ and joining the choir of sacred virgins, lived a blessed life under the rule of obedience and gave back her spirit to him to whom all things are owed.

### Miracle I

When the blessed Salaberga, advanced in holiness [alternative: “steadfast in holiness”] and with a comely [alternative: “beautifully adorned”] countenance, was leading a devout life with the sisters, a certain religious girl in the same monastery was seized by the disease of epilepsy [alternative: “the madness of falling sickness”]. When she began to sing the appointed course in the church, she collapsed to the ground before everyone with an unrestrained mind.

The blessed and venerable mother immediately took her familiarly into her care and, diligently praying to God for her, cleansed her of that affliction with the help of divine grace. She ordered her, restored to health, to depart freely into the service of Christ. For very many and highly celebrated deeds are inserted by the pen into the praises and memory of the venerable mother; they will later be assigned to their proper places.

## Chapter Ten

### Miracle II

At a certain time, while she was awaiting the arrival of the blessed man Walbert, there was no supply of Falernian wine, nor of the drink made from wheat or barley that they call beer and prepare by human craft, which most Eastern [alternative: “Western”] nations use. She ordered it to be made.

[Col. 1233A] When it had been poured into a vessel which in the vernacular they call a *tonna*, and the vessel was not yet completely full of the liquid drink, the servant of Christ who, that year, in accordance with the rule, had been assigned the duty of guarding the cellar and serving the sisters for the sake of obedience, came to the venerable mother with the greatest humility and said:

“Lady mother, what shall we do? The vessel is not full of the beer, and the air is hot. If the holy abbot delays in arriving, I fear that the liquid will turn sour into the bitterness of vinegar [alternative: “will increase”].”

She said to her: “Go, and pour into the vessel whatever has subsequently been prepared from the liquid.”

Without hesitation, she went quickly to fulfill her mother’s command and found the vessel full, although a little earlier she had left it half-empty [Col. 1233B]. Thus, by the mercy of almighty God, it came about that, while the mother’s faith was armed, the force of obedience was strengthened in the disciple [alternative: “obedience was loved, and strength was in the disciple, etc.”]. Divine power was immediately revealed, and the drink, which had been scant, was increased to a greater quantity.

The servant of God returned and, with joy and humility, told the holy mother of the miracle. She gave thanks to the Lord, our Creator, almighty Jesus Christ, who is accustomed to be quickly present to those who serve him in truth.

## Chapter Eleven

### Miracle III

Another miracle was subsequently performed. A certain sister, coming—as was customary—to the workshop cell where the washing of soiled clothing was usually carried out, took a small vessel such as necessity required for those tasks and arrived carrying it together with a small amount of wood.

But because the chain from which the vessel hung was thin and too short, so that it did not approach the fire, the servant of God deliberately found another chain and joined the two together. Then another companion arrived with another vessel made of bronze and, desiring to perform a similar task, humbly said to her companion:

“Lend me one chain, sister, so that we may both work more quickly.”

Her companion replied: “For the sake of charity I will lend it to you, but you go and bring as much wood as you wish, because the vessels are suspended with difficulty, so that we may complete what necessity compels us to do.”

When she had gone away, she did not find what she had requested. Then both servants of Christ began to be anxious, not knowing what they should do. Suddenly, with a great crash, the workshop cell, as though it were about to collapse, bent once and was brought close to the fire.

The servants of Christ and all the sisters then came at a run to see what had happened and asked what the crash and noise might be. But when they saw the miracle, they were astonished at the event.

The venerable mother then ordered the man of God Italus, a priest and provost of the same monastery, to come and contemplate this kind of miracle. When the man of God arrived and saw that the cell, despite the crashes, had not been destroyed but remained unharmed, he rendered abundant thanks to God, considering the merit of the mother, [Col. 1234A] who had disciples so well instructed and devoted that even the elements served their fervent charity.

## Chapter Twelve
Finally, one day, while walking outside the wall of the town but still within the precincts of the monastery during the summer, she saw her monk Landefrid, the gardener, searching around the garden enclosure for some kind of vegetable and cutting harmless grasses. In a low, whispering voice—so quietly that none of the sisters could possibly have heard—she said to him: “Bring us some lettuce, 685 Brother Landefrid.” She addressed him more by gesture than by speech. The aforesaid brother, who is still living, was accustomed to relate this. Wonderful to say! The voice, uttered with a slight breath and with no one else hearing it, [Col. 1234B] reached the brother’s ears as fully as though it had been spoken in his very presence. There was a distance between them of about four stades, or more.

## CHAPTER XIII

Another kind of miracle also occurred. Once, while she was serving the sisters for her appointed week in the kitchen, as was customary, and there was no small fish or anything else suitable for monastic use available, Basinus, archdeacon of that city, was reclining at home. Suddenly a voice sounded in his ears, saying: “You know that the abbess is burdening the sisters with the work of the kitchen. You ought to hurry as quickly as possible to visit her.” But he, treating the matter lightly, [Col. 1234C] neglected it. When he had been warned as many as three times, the voice additionally threatened to beat him. He had nothing suitable for such a task: what could he do, and what small gift could he bring to so great a mother? At last, having gone out of the house, he found at the doorway a man carrying a fish of extraordinary size. Believing that it had been brought by divine prompting, he paid only the price demanded and carried the fish to the blessed mother. From it she prepared a dish for the sisters and refreshed them all to satiety. This should not be thought to have been done intentionally by anyone, but rather to have been prepared by divine will so that her nourishment might be secured. Since, moreover, it must not be passed over in silence with how great a love almighty God loved her in this life—or rather, with what love he purified her like refined gold—

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1234D]

At a certain time, when the fever’s fire [alternative: “vein”] had been kindled, she endured severe bodily distress, to such a degree that she lost the power of speech. But when, with Christ presiding, she had recovered somewhat, the sisters questioned, indeed earnestly asked, what that illness had been. With her spirit aflame, she replied:

“O sweetest sisters, why do you wish to investigate the cause of this matter? I was being oppressed by exceedingly savage and dreadful demons [alternative: spirits]. But when I was recovering, two wings came around me, coming toward my back [alternative: ‘coming from my back and encircling me’]. Their appearance was more beautiful than the purest gold. Their tips, moreover, seemed sharper than a two-edged sword. When I was surrounded by them, the most dreadful spirits fled. What else is this [Col. 1235A] to be understood as meaning except that almighty God was purifying his own creature in this present life alone and, having strengthened it by the protection of his right hand [alternative: ‘by the protection of his right hand’], was joining it to the saints? For in Holy Scripture wings signify the powers above.”

Having recovered in body but become stronger in mind, she lived barely nine full months after the trial had ended. Who could recount in worthy praises the sagacity and prudence of her holiness, whose charity and humility surpassed those of all her subjects through an affection of extraordinary sweetness and goodness? She was cheerful in countenance and pleasing in appearance, lively in conversation, restrained in speech, prudent in counsel, outstanding in arranging the affairs of the monastery, shrewd in understanding, devoted to the love of almsgiving, and not [Col. 1235B] negligent in hospitality; she was discerning in the regular discipline and imitated the life of holy women—namely Melania and Paula.

Melania, as Blessed Jerome says, was the noblest of Roman women and the daughter of Marcellinus, once consul. She sailed to Jerusalem, where she became so distinguished for humility and charity that she received the name of Thecla. Paula, on the other hand, leaving behind her urban patrimony and born of Greek ancestry, sought the countryside of Bethlehem. Living there with the greatest goodness and humility, she breathed forth her holy spirit to the Lord.

And, to return to still earlier examples, Blessed Salaberga imitated Helena Augusta, the mother of Constantine Augustus. As ecclesiastical history relates, after mortifying the members of her flesh and setting aside the world’s display, she served God daily. Whatever was lowly in the monastery and whatever acts of cleanliness had to be performed, she assigned to herself. She also took turns, during her appointed weeks, serving in the kitchen and handling the other tasks ordinarily carried out for monastic needs.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 1235C]

Although she shone, with Christ presiding, in these and other similar virtues, at a certain time she saw, in the dwelling where she was accustomed to stay, a tabernacle descend from the sky, of extraordinary brightness and splendor. It appeared spacious below and steep above. A bird of marvelous radiance received her, seized her while she was in ecstasy—or rather, transported her—and carried her across a certain immense river. It set her down in exceedingly pleasant meadows, where various kinds of flowers and immeasurable sorts of fragrances gave off their scent.

Among shining lilies and blossoms of red roses [Col. 1235D] she saw immense companies of infants of both sexes, rejoicing in snow-white cloaks and with laurel-crowned heads. Among them was the little boy Magobert. When she saw him, he said:

“Do you recognize me, mother?”

She replied: “I do not know.”

The boy answered: “I am Magobert, the son of Amiliana, whom you sent before you; I am now in this radiance that you see.”

Immediately she saw the blessed and venerable bishop Ansericus coming to meet her. He said to her: “Do you recognize me?” And she confessed that she did not know him.

“I am,” he said, “Ansericus, bishop of Soissons, whom you often saw summoned to your house. I have come to show you the gates of paradise.”

And he showed her [Col. 1236A] the city of the Most High God and the twelve seats of the apostles, gleaming with gold and jewels. He also said to her: “Behold, a place has been prepared for you.”

“But because the eyes of Blessed Mary are set with jewels, and her eyes are filled with tears, and she cannot endure the prayers of the sisters, since you are still necessary to them, she has entreated her Son that you return more quickly from the realms above, so that you may possess the rewards conferred upon you by the Lord.”

Meanwhile, that bird once again seized her in its beak and, after she had recovered her breath [alternative: “after breath had been given”], sent her back from the realms above.

## CHAPTER XVI

Therefore, while she was resting one night [alternative: “while she was falling asleep”], an angel of the Lord appeared to her a third time in the likeness of the venerable man Waldebert. He saw her belt [Col. 1236B] and carried it away with him after removing it from her waist; the belt never appeared again. In my opinion, this signified that honor would increase through successive generations among her descendants.

As she herself used to relate, his garments shone with extraordinary whiteness, and he addressed the woman in an astonishing voice:

“O sweetest daughter, prepare yourself to receive the prize, and await your departure, because I too desire to receive a prize from your victory. For the hundredth day from this day will be the day of your calling, so that you may store in the granary of your Lord the fruit of your labor, which you sought with great sweat, together with multiplied interest.”

When she heard this, she summoned one of the sisters who was close to her and disclosed to her the force of the dream and the substance of the matter, but she delayed revealing it to the others.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 1236C]

The angel of the Lord ordered her to complete the Psalter during each day and night within that hundred-day period. From that day, therefore, she began to offer the Lord more than usual through vigils, fasts, psalms, and prayers—becoming all the more cheerful in her service the more firmly she trusted the promise.

Before the twentieth day of her calling, afflicted by pain in her feet, she lay down on her bed [alternative: “died”]. Thus it is also said of the perfect man:

“‘The almond tree shall blossom, the locust shall be fattened, and the caper shall be scattered, because a man shall go to the house of his eternity’ (Ecclesiastes XII, 5).”

At last, when she had completed the office, she summoned the companies of sisters and addressed them in these words:

“Remain in the service of almighty God, O servants of Christ, because, according to the divine oracle, it is not the one who has begun who will be saved (Matthew X, 22), but the one who has persevered to [Col. 1236D] the end.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

Meanwhile, just as discord is accustomed to arise even among relatives amid an abundance of possessions, her brother Bodo was retaining by unlawful seizure certain estates that the monastery had been granted to him through a series of charters. But when he learned of his sister’s illness, and she anxiously prayed to the Lord concerning this matter, he came to her with the greatest haste. Soon the mutually confirmed sanction of the documents was strengthened, and it remains valid to this day [alternative: “and, having mutually confirmed the charters, he brought the whole matter to validity to this day”].

When she realized that she was about to depart from the body, she bade farewell to the sisters and asked for the Italian priest to perform [Col. 1237A] the funeral office for her, as is customary. While making this request, she breathed forth her holy spirit, joined to the company of the saints, destined to receive double rewards in eternal glory, through him who possesses honor, glory, power, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1238A]

The aforesaid servant of Christ died on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, the day on which the sacred martyrdom of the Thebans under the leadership of Mauritius is celebrated at Agaunum. Her relics also lie buried in the same place. At her tomb, brilliant miracles became manifest after her death.

[Col. 1237]

The heresies of the Greeks, 371 and following. Because of their sins, various provinces were handed over to other peoples, ibid. The unspeakable crimes of the Greeks, 372. Brothels, ibid. The benefit of expectative grace, 579. The necessity of grace, 578. God does not compel the will, 642. The will cannot by itself be directed toward what is greater, or remain in the good, ibid. Divine grace is ready to help, but not to compel, ibid. If the forewarned will hears and consents, it is directed by grace, ibid. If it refuses, it is abandoned, and when left to itself it collapses, ibid. What it means for God to abandon, ibid.
